en: Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa and Nara, the most excellent of men,
and also to the goddess Sarasvatī, one should then utter the word "Victory.
He who attained whiteness in the Kṛta age and redness in the Tretā age...
He who was Kapila in the *yuga* has, in the Kali age, attained the state of Lord Kṛṣṇa;
he whom the sages who know the Vedānta declare, and who is praised by the yogis—
whether he be Brahmā, or Hara, or Hari— may he protect the world from misfortune.
Know that Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana Vyāsa is Nārāyaṇa himself;
for who else but the Lotus-Eyed One could be the author of the Mahābhārata?
I am the best of the twice-born, named Gopāla, whose abode is the temple of Lakṣmī.
Having paid homage to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, I write this with the desire for liberation. O Bhārata, having reached Hastināpura from Śibira, the highly wise Sañjaya entered the residence of Dhṛtarāṣṭra.

Overwhelmed by grief, the charioteer was distraught and deeply afflicted; reflecting upon the terrible slaughter of the Sūta’s son by the Pāṇḍavas, Vaiśampāyana said: *13,001.000*0004_03 Overcome by sorrow, the charioteer was distraught and deeply afflicted; *13,001.000*0004_04 reflecting upon the terrible slaughter of the Sūta’s son by the Pāṇḍavas. *13,001.000*0005_00 Vaiśampāyana said:
Approaching the high-souled and unconquered one as he lay upon the bed of arrows,
Yudhiṣṭhira prostrated himself and spoke these words.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you have described tranquility (*śama*) in many forms and as something subtle;
yet, having done such a thing as this, there is no peace in my heart.
O Sinless One, you have spoken of various kinds of tranquility regarding this very matter."

"O hero, what peace could there possibly be for one who has acted thus, even through manifold tranquility? For, beholding your body covered with arrows and your grievous wounds, I find no peace as I contemplate my own evil deeds."

O tiger among men, seeing you with your limbs drenched in blood, flowing like a mountain, I am despondent as a lotus in the rains. What indeed could be more painful than this on my account, that the Grandfather—
"Reduced to this state by enemies on the field of battle—
likewise other kings, along with their sons and kinsmen,
have met their death for my sake; what indeed could be more grievous than that?"
"For we and the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, having followed the sway of time and wrath,
and having committed this censurable deed, O King, what destiny shall we attain? Yet,
O lord of men, I consider this [course] to be for the welfare of Dhṛtarāṣṭra's son."
That he does not see you, who have reached such a state, causes me great pain;
for I am the one who brought about your end and the slayer of your friend. Seeing you thus afflicted upon the earth, I find no peace.
For Duryodhana— accompanied by his army and his younger brothers,
that evil-souled defiler of his lineage— has been slain in battle according to this duty of the Kṣatriyas;
that wicked-minded one does not see you today fallen upon the earth.
Therefore, I consider death better than life for myself here; for,
O hero, I would have been brought to destruction by the enemies in battle,
had I not previously perished along with my brothers, O Acyuta.
"I have never before seen you so afflicted by suffering and pierced by arrows.
Surely, O King, we were created as doers of evil deeds by the Creator;
for even in another world, we must surely be freed from this sin."
"O King, if you wish to do what is pleasing to me, then govern me accordingly.
Bhīṣma said:
"How can you regard yourself as the cause when you are dependent on another?"
O highly fortunate one, in this matter, this is indeed subtle and beyond the reach of the senses.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between Mṛtyu and Gautamī, and [the account of] Time, the hunter, and the serpents.
O son of Kuntī, there was an elderly woman named Gautamī who was endowed with tranquility.
She saw her own son bitten by a snake and deprived of consciousness.
Then, filled with indignation, she bound that snake with a cord of sinew.
A hunter named Arjuna brought him to Gautamī and said to her:
"O highly fortunate lady, here is that lowest of serpents who killed your son;
tell me quickly, for what reason should he be slain?"
"Let him be thrown into the fire, or let him be cut into pieces;
for this wicked killer of a child does not deserve to live long.
Gautamī said:
"Release him; you are lacking in discernment, Arjunaka, for he is not to be slain by you.
For who, when faced with what must be done, would make himself his own burden? Those whose virtue makes them light float in this world like rafts upon the water."
Those heavy with sin sink down like a weapon dropped into water.
Or, if this serpent is slain by you, O Arjunaka,
and this child of mine lives, even that would not be pleasing to me, O Arjunaka.
If he is slain, immortality will certainly not come to pass; what harm would there be for people if he were not slain? And even by slaying him, this [immortality] would not become mine.
If he lives, what harm could there be for you?
If he is slain, immortality will certainly not be yours.
If he lives, who would be dead while this Infinite One lives?
"Upon the release of this living being endowed with breath,
who indeed would go to the infinite world of Death?
The hunter said:
I know this well: those who do not discern virtue and vice are not appointed here as teachers;
for these instructions are intended only for one who is established in well-being.
Therefore, I shall kill this petty serpent.
Those who desire the proper timing wait for it;
however, those who understand the true purpose abandon grief immediately.
"For those who constantly grieve, dwelling in their misery is indeed better;
therefore, you must abandon it—cast off this grief once he has been slain.
Gautamī said:
No affliction exists for those such as us,
for the virtuous person always delights in the Dharma;
there is no such thing as a fool who is eternally tormented.
For this is the nature of things; I have no power over it.
Brahmins harbor no anger, so how could there be torment born of anger? Be gentle and forgive, O virtuous one; let this serpent be released.
The hunter said: "Killing brings a gain that is truly beneficial and inexhaustible;
immediate gain is praised by the powerful."
"If a gain were to occur immediately from time,
it would be better to kill such a contemptible person as this.
Gautamī said:
What peace can there be after seizing one's enemy and slaying him? Or what peace after capturing an enemy and releasing him?
O gentle one, why should I not endure [the bite] of a serpent?
"Or for what reason should I not grant him liberation?
The hunter said:
"Many must be protected from this single individual."
O Gautamī, one person should not be protected from many;
those who know the Dharma abandon even a wrongdoer—
slay this wicked serpent!
Gautamī said:
"O hunter, if this serpent is killed, my little son will surely not regain his life."
"I see no other merit in killing him;
therefore, O hunter, release the serpent alive.
The hunter said:
Having slain Vṛtra, the king of the gods indeed obtained the most excellent portion;
and having slain the sacrifice, he likewise obtained his share.
O god who wields the trident, you too must follow the conduct of the gods.
"Kill the serpent quickly; let there be no hesitation.
Bhīṣma said:
Although Gautamī was told this repeatedly regarding the snake, she remained hesitant.
The highly fortunate one did not set her mind on evil toward the hunter.
Sighing slightly, the serpent, having steadied himself with difficulty while tormented by the noose, uttered these faint words in a human voice.
"O Arjunaka, what fault of mine is there here, you fool? For it was Death who, having rendered me powerless and helpless, urged me on.
It was at his command that I bit him, not out of anger nor out of desire."
"O hunter, if there is any sin, that sin belongs to him.
The hunter said:
"If this evil deed was committed by you while under the control of another, O serpent,"
"You too are indeed a cause in this matter; therefore, you also are guilty.
For just as the staff, the wheel, and other tools are designated as causes in the making of a clay vessel, so too are you, O serpent."
"O serpent, you are a sinner and deserve to be slain, for you yourself have declared the cause of this matter, O snake. The serpent said:

"Just as all these things—the horse, the reins, the whip, the wheels, and so forth—are not independent, so too am I; therefore, this reason of yours is not accepted by me. Or rather, if it is your view that even those [factors] act as mutual instigators,"
A doubt regarding cause and effect arises from mutual instigation;
this being so, there is no fault in me, nor am I one to be slain, nor am I a sinner.
If you consider it a sin, that sin would reside in the collective assembly.
"For you consider this a sin, and thus you speak as if it were something that ought to be killed.
The hunter said:
"If there were indeed no underlying cause, then even you would not be its doer."
"You are the cause of his destruction; therefore, in my view, you deserve to be slain.
O serpent, even when an action has not been performed, one is not stained by it here in this world.
Thus, there is no reason for you to remain here; you deserve to be killed—why do you speak so much?"
The serpent said:
"In the absence of a purpose, there can be no action, regardless of whether a cause exists or not.
Therefore, you must specifically state to me the reason for this."
"If I am truly considered the cause [of this death], O hunter,
then another must be the one guilty of the act here, the destruction of the living being.
The hunter said:
"O evil-minded one, you deserve to be killed by me, for you are a slayer of children and a doer of cruel deeds.
O lowest of serpents, why do you speak so much more when you are already deserving of death?
The serpent said:
"Just as greedy officiating priests who offer oblations at a sacrifice do not obtain any fruit here or in the next world, so it is with me. Bhīṣma said:
While that serpent, impelled by Death, was speaking thus, Death himself arrived; and having arrived, he spoke these words to the serpent:
"O serpent, I have been sent to you by Time."
Neither you nor I am the cause of the destruction of this living infant; rather,
O serpent, I am subject to the power of Time, just as the wind drags clouds hither and thither, and just as I myself am like a cloud driven by that same force.
I am of that same nature and under its control; for a long time I have been subject to Time.
Whether they be of the nature of *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*, all states of being, which are essentially Time itself, indeed proceed within living creatures.

Whether moving or stationary, whether in heaven or on earth, O serpent, all things have Time as their essence; this entire world has Time as its essence. So too do the activities that proceed in the world, as well as their cessations.
Whatever modifications there are of these, all are remembered as being of the nature of Time (Kāla). The Sun, the Moon, Viṣṇu, Water, Wind, Indra,
Fire, Space, Earth, Mitra, the medicinal herbs, and likewise the Vasus— [all these are Time].
"O serpent, rivers and oceans, as well as existence and non-existence—
all these are created by Time and are likewise withdrawn again.
Knowing this, how can you consider me to be at fault, O snake?"
"Moreover, since this is the case, if there is fault in me, you too are at fault.
The serpent said:
"O Death, I do not call you either faultless or faulty."
"I say only this much: 'I have been urged by you.
Whether there is a fault in the timing, or even if it is not desired there, no fault at all should be examined by me, for we are not authorized in this matter."
"However, I must effect the liberation from this fault by whatever means possible;
my purpose is such that I shall remain free from blame even at the hands of Death.
Bhīṣma said:
Then the serpent said to Arjunaka: "You have heard what Death has spoken.
You ought not to torment me, who am innocent, with this snare.
The hunter replied:
"O serpent, I have heard the words of Death and yours as well.
For the time being, O snake, you are not entirely without fault;
for both Death and you are the causes of this creature's destruction."
I consider both to be causes; there is no cause that is not a cause.
Fie upon Death, the evil-souled one, cruel and a bringer of suffering to the virtuous! And I shall slay you as well, O sinner, the very cause of this sin.
Death said:
"We two are powerless, subject to Time, and merely carrying out what is ordained. If you see things correctly, we two should not be held guilty of any fault."
The hunter said:
"If you two are indeed subject to time like serpents of death, how could joy and anger exist? This I wish to know."
Death said:
"O hunter, whatever activities there may be here, they are all impelled by Time;
indeed, this was previously stated by me as being due to Time."
"Therefore, both of us are subject to the power of time; we are merely the executors of that destiny. O hunter, you must never consider us to be at fault.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, at that time of uncertainty regarding dharma and artha, Kāla approached and spoke to the serpent Mṛtyu, to the hunter Arjunaka,
and to him [the king]. Kāla said:
Neither am I, nor is this Death, nor is this sinful serpent the cause of the creature's death; for we are not the instigators.
Whatever action this one has performed, O Arjunaka, that alone is our impeller.
There is no other cause for his destruction; he is slain by his own karma. Because of the deed he committed, he has met his end.
Karma is the cause of his ruin; we are all subject to the power of karma.
The world is an heir to its own actions, characterized by the bonds of karma; just as actions impel one another here, so do we [impel one another].
Just as a maker fashions whatever he desires from a lump of clay, so does the agent create his various destinies.
In this way, a human being experiences the karma created by oneself;
just as shadow and light are always closely and inseparably bound together,
so too are the action and the agent bound together by their own karmas.

"Thus, it is neither I, nor death, nor the serpent, nor you, O King, nor this aged Brāhmaṇa woman; rather, the child alone is the cause here. While he was speaking thus, O King, the Brāhmaṇa woman Gautamī—
Reflecting that the worlds are conditioned by one's own karma, he said to Arjuna:
"Neither time, nor the serpent, nor death is the cause here;
through his own actions, this boy has met his end at the hand of Time."
"By me was that deed performed by which this son of mine has died. Let Time and Death depart; release the serpent, O Arjunaka!
Bhīṣma said:
Then Mṛtyu, Kāla, and the serpent departed as they had come; Arjunaka became free from anger, and Gautamī was likewise freed from grief.
Having heard this, O King, attain tranquility and do not be consumed by anxiety.
"Know, O bull among men, that these three worlds are conditioned by one's own karma.
It was not done by you, O Pārtha, nor indeed by Duryodhana;
know that it was done by Time, by which the kings were destroyed."
13,001.076 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard these words, the highly effulgent Yudhiṣṭhira, who knows the dharma, became free from his feverish distress and asked this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, O expert in all the scriptures—
O best among the intelligent— I have heard this great narrative."
"O King, I desire to hear further from you something consistent with dharma and artha; you should explain some such matter to me. By what householder was death conquered by resorting to dharma?"
"O King, explain all of this to me in its true essence.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
Just as Death was conquered by a householder through recourse to dharma— O King, the Prajāpati Manu had a son named Ikṣvāku;
to that king, who possessed the splendor of the sun, a hundred sons were born.
His tenth son, O Bhārata, was named Daśāśva;
he became the king in Māhiṣmatī, a righteous soul whose prowess was truth. The son of Daśāśva, however, was a most virtuous king.
He whose mind was always devoted to truth, austerity, and charity,
that lord of the earth renowned on the world as Madirāśva,
was ever intent upon both the science of archery and the Vedas.
The son of Madirāśva was the king named Dyutimat,
who was highly fortunate, possessed of great splendor, great being, and great strength.
The son of Dyutimat, however, was the king named Suvīra.
The king was supremely righteous,
renowned throughout all the worlds;
virtuous in soul and possessed of great wealth, he was like another King of the Gods.
Suvīra’s son was one who was invincible in all battles;
he was renowned as Durjaya, an expert in all the śāstras. He was also known as Sudurjaya, the best among all wielders of weapons.
The son of Durjaya, who possessed the form of Indra and a splendor like fire,
was the great king named Duryodhana, O best of kings. Ikṣvāku had a hundred sons, of whom Daśāśva is remembered as the tenth.
In Māhiṣmatī there was a king named Madirāśva; from him was born Dyutimat, and his son was Suvīra. Durjaya was the son of that one, and his son is remembered as Duryodhana.
For him, whose prowess was equal to Indra’s and who never retreated in battles, both his dominion and his power increased in equal measure; within his realm,
Vāsava poured down rain in perfect abundance.
With jewels, wealth, livestock, and various kinds of grain,
his city and kingdom were then completely filled. Within his realm, there was neither a miser nor anyone who was destitute.
In that [realm], there was nowhere any man who was diseased or even emaciated;
no person was seen who was afflicted by illness or in a state of misery. Sudakṣiṇa was sweet-spoken, free from malice, and had his senses fully subdued.
He was righteous in soul, compassionate, valiant, and free from boastfulness;
he was a performer of sacrifices, generous, wise, devoted to Brahmanas, and true to his word.
He never treated others with contempt, was a giver of gifts, and had mastered both the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
O Bhārata, the auspicious and holy celestial river Narmadā, with her cool waters, desired that best of men out of her own affection; then,
a lotus-eyed maiden was born to him by that river.
"O King, she was named Sudarśanā and was beautiful to behold;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, no woman of such form had ever existed before among women as that fair-complexioned daughter of Duryodhana."
Agni himself desired that princess Sudarśanā; she,
for her part, having resolved to serve the king in his fire-sanctuary,
was appointed there by her father’s command, desiring to propitiate the flame-haired god.
Seeing her enchanting form, the god Hutāśana,
Agni,
was possessed by the god of love and strove to win her as his wife.
"O lady of faultless limbs, O lotus-eyed one, love me out of desire! O lady with thighs like plantain stalks, O fawn-eyed one, O you whose face resembles the full moon—
having beheld this enchanting face of yours, with eyes like lotus petals."
The god of love indeed torments me with that lovely, creeper-like brow;
seeing your forehead, which resembles a crescent moon and is adorned with hair marked by decorative leaf-patterns, the god of love torments me most intensely.
Her face, with its bimba-fruit-like lower lip, is agitated by the morning sun, covered in perspiration and bristling with horripilation; like a fully blossomed lotus,
it is exceedingly beautiful in its radiant movement and brings me great joy.
Your speech is well-guarded, restrained by the rampart of your teeth;
this tongue of yours is captivating, resembling copper-colored sprouts.
Your teeth are even, glossy, well-formed, and closely set.
O beloved of the twice-born, be gracious; favor me, for you are truly fortunate. Your face is charming and captivating, with its well-formed, sidelong glances.
O timid one, your breasts are firm and adorned with necklaces and ornaments.
"Resembling ripe *bilva* fruits, firm and capable of union—
O Bhīṣmā,
O woman of excellent complexion, resort to me, who am blessed with a deep navel."
Thus addressed by the high-souled Pāvaka in that secluded place,
she, her heart slightly trembling and filled with shame, spoke these words:
"Is it not indeed the case that for daughters of noble birth, especially— "
The mother and father have authority over the giving away [of the daughter], as do her kinsmen;
but once the marriage mantras have been recited and the fire has been offered into,
for the maiden seated among the virtuous, the husband is her refuge.
"O Lord, I am not my own mistress; choose a father for me.
Then, after a short time, King Duryodhana, it is said, summoned his ministers who were experts in the preparations for sacrifices and spoke to them.
"I shall perform a sacrifice; let the necessary materials be gathered for me. Then, with a concentrated mind, his sacrifice was prepared by the best of Brahmins.
And having become a Brahmin in person, he chose that king as his officiant.
In the form of a brahmin, the consumer of oblations (Agni) requested the maiden from the king;
however, the king did not set his mind upon giving her to him,
thinking, "He is poor and of a different caste than mine."
13,002.022 “He does not wish to give that daughter Sudarśanā to that brahmin.
Thus the lord of men did not intend to give the maiden to him.
13,002.023 Then, while his sacrifice was being performed, the carrier of oblations (Agni) disappeared.
Then King Duryodhana addressed these words to the officiating priests:
"O bulls among the twice-born, what evil deed could have been committed by me or by you,
such that the fire has gone out as if it were offered to wicked men?"

"Indeed, there is not even a slight misdeed belonging to us, by which fire has met its destruction—whether it belongs to you or to me; let this be investigated according to the truth. Having heard these words of the king, O bull of the Bharatas, those Brahmins...
Restrained and with speech controlled, they sought refuge in the Purifier.
Then the Blessed One, the carrier of oblations, revealed himself to them at that time during the initiation of that high-souled one for the sacrifice.
The fire, which had been placed upon the altar for the purpose of sacrifice, was extinguished.
Thereupon, the king, terrified and with his senses deeply distressed, questioned his ministers and the brahmins: "What could this be?"

"The Blessed One was kindled at the sacrifice, yet my bearer of oblations has vanished. Thus he was enlightened by those very brahmins, who were skilled in counsel and masters of the Vedas, [who told him], "This is a superhuman transformation."
"O Hero, it is not fitting for you to create an obstacle to the Dharma.
Let the Blessed One, the Fire-god, be praised by Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas;
let the Consumer of Oblations be extolled by officiating priests skilled in the mantras."
Then, by those who had mastered the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus Vedas— those who had reached the further shore of the Vedas,
skilled in the true meaning of the Vedic principles— the Purifier (Agni) was praised with hymns preceded by chants,
as his secret names were being proclaimed.
Assuming his own radiant form, possessing a brilliance equal to the autumnal sun,
the high-souled Fire-god then spoke to those bull-like Brahmins:
"I choose the daughter of Duryodhana for my own sake."

Then, having risen at dawn, all those Brahmins, filled with wonder, reported to the king what had been spoken by the Fire-god. Then that king, having heard those words of the speakers of the Veda, [acted accordingly].
Attaining supreme joy, the wise king said, "So be it. Then the monarch requested a boon from the blessed Vibhāvasu: "O Citrabhānu, may you be ever-present here."

The Blessed One Agni said to him, "So be it," regarding that earthly [kingdom]. Consequently, even today, the presence of Vibhāvasu is seen in Māhiṣmatī by Sahadeva while he was conquering the quarters at that time.
Then, having adorned that maiden with unwashed garments,
King Duryodhana gave her to the high-souled Pāvaka;
and Agni accepted that princess, Sudarśanā.
According to the ritual prescribed in the Vedas, like the stream of clarified butter (*vasordhārā*) poured at a sacrifice,
Agni was filled with joy by her beauty, character, lineage, form, and splendor; he then deposited his seed within her.
From her was born a son named Agneya Sudarśana. Sudarśana, in appearance like the full moon, mastered all of the eternal Brahman even while still a child.
Now, there was a king named Oghavān, who was the grandfather of Nṛga. He also had a daughter named Oghavatī and a son named Ogharatha.
Oghavān himself gave that daughter, Oghavatī, to him.

To the wise Sudarśana, for the sake of a wife, [the gods] gave one of divine form. O King, devoted to the householder stage of life, Sudarśana dwelt at Kurukṣetra together with her, accompanied by the Oghavatī river.
"O Lord, O ruler of the people, that wise son of Agni, blazing with splendor, made this vow: 'As a householder, I shall conquer Death.
Then, O King, that son of the Fire-god spoke to her, Oghavatī."
"You must never, under any circumstances, act in opposition to your guest.
Whatever may please your guest, you should always provide that—even if it requires the giving away of yourself; you need have no hesitation in this."
"O fair-hipped one, this vow always revolves within my heart:
for householders, O beautiful woman, there is nothing higher than the guest.
If you consider my word authoritative, O lovely lady with shapely thighs,"
"O auspicious one, you should always hold these words in your heart without distraction— whether I have departed or am present here, O sinless one—
if I am an authority to you, no guest must be disregarded by you."
To him, Oghavatī spoke, her head bowed with palms joined in reverence:
"There is nothing whatsoever that I would not do at your command.
However, while he was still desirous of victory within his own home, Mṛtyu [Death] then [attacked] Sudarśana."
O King, he followed behind him at all times, constantly seeking for a vulnerability. When Sudarśana, the son of Agni, had gone out for the sake of firewood,
a glorious Brāhmaṇa guest then spoke to that Oghavatī.
"O lady of excellent complexion, I desire that hospitality be offered by you today,
if the dharma esteemed for the householder's stage of life is your authority.
Thus addressed by that brahmin, the illustrious princess—
O lord of the people, he received him according to the rites prescribed in the Vedas;
having offered a seat and water for his feet to that twice-born one, Oghavatī said to the brāhmaṇa: "What is your purpose? What may I give to you?"
Then the brahmin spoke to the princess Sudarśanā:
"O auspicious lady, my purpose depends on you; therefore, perform it without hesitation, provided that dharma, as approved for the householder stage of life, is your authority."

"O Queen, you ought to do what is pleasing to me by giving yourself to me. Though he was thus entreated by the princess with other desired things, that twice-born man chose no boon from her other than the gift of herself.
But that princess, remembering her husband’s words from the beginning,
said "So be it" to that bull among brahmins, feeling abashed.
Then that brahmin-sage and she sat down together in private.
Remembering the words of her husband, who desired the householder stage of life,
the daughter of the Fire-god then returned, having gathered sacrificial fuel;
she was constantly accompanied by Death in his fierce form, as if by a kinsman.
Then, having returned to the hermitage, that son of Agni repeatedly called out to Oghavatī, "Where have you gone? Where are you?
But she gave no reply to her husband at that time.
Touched by that brahmin with his two hands, she who was devoted to her husband felt that she had become defiled; thinking thus and feeling ashamed before her husband,
the virtuous woman became silent and said nothing at all.
Then Sudarśana spoke to her once again:
"Where is that virtuous woman? Where has she gone? What is more important to me than this?
She was devoted to her husband, truthful in character, and always delighted in uprightness."
"Why does she not come forward today with a smile as she did before?
To him, while staying in the hut, the brahmin replied to Sudarśana:
"Know that I have arrived as a guest; O Fire, know me to be a brahmin."
"O best of beings, being entreated by this wife of yours with various honors due to a guest, her mind is firmly fixed on uprightness;
by this method, this lady of beautiful countenance pays me honor."
"Whatever is appropriate in this matter today, you ought to say it.
For Death himself, with a spiked mallet in hand, will surely pursue him, thinking:
'I shall slay him here for breaking his vow.'"
But Sudarśana, having abandoned envy and anger through his mind, actions, eyes, and speech, spoke these words with a smile:
"O foremost of brahmins, may you be well; for my pleasure is indeed supreme."

For the foremost duty of a householder is the honoring of a guest who has arrived. When a guest departs from a householder's home having been honored, he leaves that one man with his vow fulfilled; but when he departs from one who has arrived, he leaves him with his promise unfulfilled.

"13,002.069c The wise have said that there is no dharma higher than this. 13,002.070a For my life, my wife, and whatever other wealth I possess must be given to guests; this is the vow I have undertaken."
"Without doubt, these words have been uttered by me to you.
By that truth, O Brahmin, I swear this very oath:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth."
Intellect, the self, mind, time, and the directions— these are the ten qualities,
O best of the upholders of dharma; for these, residing within the bodies of embodied beings, constantly behold both their good and evil deeds.
"Since these words uttered by me today are not false,
by that truth, O gods, protect me or consume me!
Then, O Bhārata, a roar arose in all directions.
"This is indeed the truth; it is not false in any way," he said repeatedly.
Then that twice-born man emerged from that hut, pervading both the sky and the earth with his body like the wind rising up.
Making the three worlds resound with his voice trained in the science of phonetics (*śikṣā*), the Brahmin addressed that knower of dharma by name and said:
"I am Dharma; blessings be upon you, O sinless one, for the sake of testing you."
Having realized that you have attained the Truth, my joy toward you is supreme;
for you have conquered Death, who now follows you, ever seeking your vulnerabilities, yet has been brought under control by your fortitude.
"O Supreme among Men, there is no one in the three worlds who has the power even to look upon this virtuous woman devoted to her husband;
she is protected both by your virtues and by the qualities of her own devotion."
Whatever this unassailable woman may say shall be so and not otherwise;
for she is endowed with her own ascetic power and is a speaker of Brahman.
Indeed, she shall become the best of rivers for the sake of purifying the world.
"With half [of her body], she who is named Oghavatī shall follow you, while with the other half, the highly fortunate one shall remain; for yoga is under her control.
Together with her, you shall go to the worlds won through ascetic penance."

13,002.084c Therein one does not return, reaching those eternal and everlasting realms. 13,002.085a With this very body, you shall attain those worlds; death has been conquered by you, and your sovereignty is supreme.
Having transcended the five elements through his own prowess, he has become the mind-born;
by this dharma of a householder, you have conquered both desire and anger.
Affection, passion, sloth, delusion, and pure malice—[all these have been overcome].
"O King, by your service, they were conquered by the princess.
Bhīṣma said:
"With a thousand white horses, [he yoked] an excellent chariot."
Taking up his resolve, the Blessed One departed;
he had conquered death, the self, the worlds, and the five elements,
as well as intellect, time, mind, space, desire, and anger.
Therefore, O tiger among men, reflect in your mind that for one established in the householder stage of life, there is indeed no other deity than the guest;
for when a guest is honored, he meditates upon what is auspicious in his mind.
The wise say that even a hundred sacrifices are not equal to this: he who, having encountered a guest— a worthy recipient rich in virtue— does not honor him,
wastes the merit of his own good deeds by failing to offer them due respect.
13,002.093 This unsurpassed narrative has been told to you by me, my son,
concerning how death was indeed conquered in the past by a householder. 13,002.094 This supreme narrative bestows wealth, fame, and long life.

This should be contemplated by one desiring prosperity, for it removes all evil conduct. O Bhārata, the wise man who recites this account of Sudarśana’s deeds day after day shall attain the meritorious worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lord of men, if the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain by the other three castes,
how was it attained, O great king, by that high-souled Kṣatriya?"

"O righteous-souled one, O bull among men, I wish to hear in truth how Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa; tell that to me, O Grandfather. For by him of immeasurable prowess, [the lineage] of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha..."
O Great-Grandfather, by means of his ascetic power, he instantly slew a hundred sons;
and many Yātudhānas and Rākṣasas of fierce energy, resembling Time and the Destroyer, were created by him when his body was possessed by wrath.

The great lineage of Kuśika, crowded with hundreds of brahmarṣis, has been established here in the world of men— learned and praised by the brahmins. And likewise, Śunaḥśepa, the son of Ṛcīka, is a man of great asceticism.
Released from the great sacrifice, he entered the state of a sacrificial animal;
then, having gratified the gods by his own splendor at the sacrifice of Hariścandra,
he attained the status of a son to the wise Viśvāmitra.
O lord of men, he did not pay homage to his elder brother Devarāta;
furthermore, five hundred sons were cursed and reduced to the state of outcaste dog-cookers (śvapacas).
Triśaṅku, the descendant of Ikṣvāku, was abandoned by his kinsmen, yet [the king] treated him with affection.
With his head hanging downwards, he was led to heaven and took refuge in the southern quarter.
There flows the vast river of Viśvāmitra, frequented by royal sages;
known as the Kauśikī, it is auspicious, holy, and served by hosts of Brahman-sages.
Furthermore, the highly esteemed Apsaras named Rambhā, who had five topknots and was a creator of obstacles to his asceticism, was turned into a mountain by his curse;
likewise, in former times, Vasiṣṭha bound him in the water out of fear of him.
He submerged himself in the Vipāśā and rose up again;
from that time forward, the great river became holy as the Vipāśā,
renowned for that deed of the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
And when the Lord, the sovereign leader of the divine army,
was praised with these words, he became pleased in mind and released him from the curse.
This occurred in the presence of Dhruva, the son of Uttānapāda, as well as the brahmin-sages.
"That which always blazes in the middle, relying upon the northern direction—
O Kaurava, these and other deeds belong to it as belonging to a Kṣatriya; for this reason, this curiosity has arisen in me."
"O bull among the Bharatas, tell me truly what this was.
How did that Brahmin become such [a being] without having attained another body?
O King, you ought to explain all of this to me according to the truth."
"Tell me this exactly as it is, according to the truth of Mataṅga's case.
It was only right, O bull of the Bharatas, that Mataṅga did not obtain Brahminhood;
for how could one born from a Caṇḍāla womb attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa?"
Bhīṣma said:
Listen, O Pārtha, to the truth of how in ancient times Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa,
my dear, as well as that of a Brahmarṣi.

In the lineage of Bharata, O best of the Bharatas, there was a king named Ajamīḍha, a performer of sacrifices and the foremost among the upholders of dharma. His son was the great lord of men named Jahnu.

To that great-souled one, Gaṅgā became a daughter; his son was the highly illustrious Sindhudvīpa, who possessed equal virtues. And from Sindhudvīpa was born the royal sage Balākāśva, who was endowed with great strength.
His son was Vallabha, who was like another Dharma incarnate;
his son was Kuśika, whose splendor was equal to that of the thousand-eyed Indra. The illustrious son of Kuśika was the lord of men named Gādhi.
Childless, that mighty-armed one retired to dwell in the forest. While he was living there in the woods, a daughter was born to him;
she was named Satyavatī, and she was peerless on earth in her beauty.
The illustrious lord, the descendant of Bhṛgu and son of Cyavana, renowned as Ṛcīka, who was established in vast asceticism, chose her as his wife. He,
however, did not give her to that high-souled Ṛcīka.
Thinking, "He is indeed poor," Gādhi, the destroyer of enemies and best of kings, rejected him as he was departing and said:
"Let the bride-price be paid to me; then you shall have my daughter."
Ṛcīka said:
"O Indra among kings, O monarch, what dowry shall I give to you for my daughter? Speak without hesitation; let there be no further deliberation on your part."
Gādhi said:
"O Bhārgava, give me a thousand horses, brilliant as moonbeams, swift as the wind, and each with one black ear."
Bhīṣma said:
Then that powerful son of Cyavana, a tiger among the Bhṛgus,
spoke to the god Varuṇa, the Āditya and lord of the waters.
"O best of gods, I beg of you a thousand horses with the luster of the moon, swift as the wind, each having one black ear. "So be it," said the god Varuṇa, the Āditya, to the best of the Bhṛgus.

"13,004.015c 'Wherever you desire, there the horses shall rise up. 13,004.016a As soon as Ṛcīka had thought this, a thousand horses, radiant as the moon and possessed of immense vigor, emerged from the waters of the Gaṅgā."
Not far from Kanyakubja, on the excellent bank of the Gaṅgā,
is that Aśvatīrtha which even today men still point out.
At that time, O dear one, Gādhi gave him a thousand auspicious horses.
13,004.018c Ricīka, the best among those who recite prayers, joyfully gave [the wealth] as the bride-price.
13,004.019a Thereupon, King Gādhi, both amazed and fearing a curse,
13,004.019c gave that daughter, having adorned her well, to the son of Bhṛgu.
The best of Brahman-sages took her hand according to the prescribed rite;
and she, having obtained him as her husband, attained supreme joy.
And that Brahman-sage was gratified by her conduct, O Bhārata.
And he invited that woman of excellent complexion to choose a boon;
she chose as her boon from him a son who would be the best among the Brahman-sages. That maiden then related all of this to her mother, who [in turn] told it to the best of kings.
Then her mother spoke to that daughter, who stood with her face slightly cast down:
"O daughter, my husband too ought to show you favor by granting you offspring; he is capable of it, being one of great ascetic power."
Then, having gone quickly, she reported all of her mother's intentions, O King; thereupon Ṛcīka said to her:
"Both you and she shall give birth to virtuous offspring."
"O auspicious lady, let not the affection of your mother toward you be otherwise.
O beautiful one, a son shall be born to you who will praise your virtues;
he will be glorious and the perpetuator of our lineage, and your brother shall likewise be the founder of his own line."

"O auspicious one, when you have bathed after your menses, you and he should embrace an *aśvattha* tree and an *udumbara* tree respectively; then you shall obtain your desire. And here are two portions of sacrificial porridge (*caru*), purified by mantras, O lady of pure smiles."
"You and she should both consume it; then you will obtain two sons.
Thereupon, Satyavatī, filled with joy, replied to her mother and told her everything that Ṛcīka had said regarding the two portions of sacrificial rice (*caru*).

Then, O Great King, the mother and the daughter ate the two portions of sacrificial porridge (caru) by mistake; consequently, they both conceived a fetus. Once, seeing his own wife, Ṛcīka spoke these words:
Then her mother spoke to her daughter Satyavatī at that time:
"Daughter, grant my request, for I have come to you with my head bowed low.
This sacrificial porridge (caru), consecrated with mantras, which was given to you by your husband—"
"Give this to me, and you take mine; O lady of pure smiles, let us also exchange these two trees.
O woman of excellent complexion, we shall indeed perform an exchange of the two trees."
"O blameless one, if the word of my mother is authoritative,
then it is clear that the Blessed One has acted in such a way here, for everyone desires their own offspring to be distinguished and untainted."
"O slender-waisted one, my affection was then fixed upon your rice-porridge and the tree;
I thought only of how your brother might become superior.
And so, both your mother and Satyavatī acted accordingly."
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, when both of them had conceived,
that great ṛṣi, the best of the Bhrigus, seeing his wife Satyavatī pregnant, spoke to her with a troubled mind.

"O auspicious lady, it is evident that you have used the sacrificial porridge (caru) in reverse; indeed, a reversal has clearly been made by you even regarding the tree. For I have placed the entire Brahman within your porridge."
The entire essence of Kṣatriya valor has been placed within her sacrificial oblation;
you shall give birth to a Brahmin whose virtues are renowned throughout the three worlds, while she shall indeed give birth to an eminent Kṣatriya. Therefore, this was ordained by me.
"Because this exchange was made by you and likewise by your mother,
therefore, O blessed lady, your mother shall give birth to the best of Brahmins,
while you shall give birth to a Kshatriya of fierce deeds."
"O beautiful lady, you have not done what was right out of affection for your mother.
Hearing this, O King, the fair-complexioned Satyavatī, tormented by grief, fell to the ground like a lovely creeper that has been severed.
Having regained consciousness and prostrated with her head at his feet,
the daughter of Gādhi, his wife, spoke to her husband, that bull among Brahmins:
"O best of those who know the Veda, [be gracious] toward me, your wife, as I seek to propitiate you."

"O Brahmin-sage, show me favor; let there not be a Kṣatriya son for me. While it is true that my grandson may indeed be one of fierce deeds according to my wish, let there not be a [Kṣatriya] son for me, O Brahmin—let this boon be granted to me."
"So be it," said the one of great asceticism to his wife.
Thereupon, she gave birth to the auspicious son Jamadagni;
and Gādhi’s illustrious wife gave birth to Viśvāmitra.
O Indra among kings, by the power of the sage, Viśvāmitra of great asceticism— though he was a Kṣatriya— thereupon attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa, becoming a Brahmarṣi who speaks of Brahman,
and thus became the founder of a lineage of Brahmins.
His sons were high-souled, increasers of the lineage of Brahmā;
they were practitioners of austerity, knowers of Brahman, and founders of lineages— namely,
the blessed Madhucchandas and the heroic Devarāta.
Akṣīṇa, Śakunta, Babhru, Kālapatha, the renowned Yājñavalkya, Sthūṇa of great vows,
Ulūka, Yamadūta, and the ṛṣi Saindhavāyana.
The venerable Karṇajaṅgha, the great Ṛṣi Gālava,
the Ṛṣi known as Vajra, and Śālaṅkāyana;
Lālāṭya, Nārada, and likewise the one remembered as Kūrcamukha.
Vādulī and Musala, as well as Rakṣogrīva;
Aṅghrika, Naikabhṛt, Śilāyūpa, Sita, and Śuci;
Cakraka, Mārutantavya, Vātaghna, and then Āśvalāyana.
Śyāmāyana, Gārgya, Jābāli, and Suśruta; likewise Kārīṣi, Saṃśrutya, and Parapauravatantava;
as well as the great seer Kapila and the seer Tārakāyana.
Likewise Upagahana, the Ṛṣi Ārjunāyana,
Mārgamitri, Hiraṇyākṣa, Jaṅghāri, Babhruvāhana, Sūti, Vibhūti, Sūta, and likewise Suraṅga.
Ārāddhī, Nāmaya, Cāmpeya, Ujjayana, Navatantu, Bakana-kha, Śayonarati, Śayoruha, Cārumatsya, Śirīṣī, and Gārdabhi.
Ujjayani, Adapekṣin, and the great ṛṣi Nārada—
these and many other high-souled ones who had conquered their senses were all sons of Viśvāmitra, sages who discoursed on Brahman.
"O King, this is not a Kṣatriya; he is Viśvāmitra of great ascetic power.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this supreme Brahmanic power was bestowed upon him by Ṛcīka.
All this has been told to you in truth, O bull of the Bharatas."
The birth of Viśvāmitra, who possessed the splendor of the moon, the sun, and fire, has been told.
O best of kings, whenever you have further doubt regarding anything, speak to me there; I shall sever your uncertainties.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, I wish to hear in its entirety the virtues of compassion, of dharma, and of devoted people; tell that to me."
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Vāsava and the high-souled Śuka.
In the territory of the King of Kāśī, a hunter, having departed from his village and taking up a poisoned arrow,
was indeed hunting for deer in that great forest, being greedy for meat.
Seeing a deer not far away, he fixed an arrow; with that irresistible shaft, which was as swift as fate, he—
desiring to kill the deer— pierced a great forest tree instead.
Overpowered by that arrow smeared with potent poison,
the tree shed its fruits and leaves and fell into a state of withering.
While the tree was in such a condition, [the bird] had long dwelt within its hollows.
Out of devotion to that lord of the forest, Śuka did not leave his dwelling;
though he ceased all movement, went without food, grew weak, and even his speech faltered,
that righteous-souled one, grateful for the tree's hospitality, withered away along with it.
Having recognized that noble Great Being, whose conduct transcended that of ordinary men and who shared equally in both sorrow and joy, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, was struck with wonder.
Thereupon, Śakra fell into reflection: "How is it that this twice-born man..."
"Having established such compassion as is inconceivable even among those born as animals—
'Or rather, there is nothing wonderful here,' thought Vāsava,
'for among all living beings here, everything is seen everywhere.'"
Then Śakra, assuming a human form in the guise of a brahmin and descending to the earth, spoke to that bird:
"O Śuka, best of birds, Dakṣa’s daughter has indeed borne you as a noble son."
"13,005.012c I ask you: why indeed do you not abandon this withered tree?
13,005.013a Thus questioned, Śuka, having saluted him with his head bowed, said: 13,005.013c 'Welcome to the King of the Gods; I have recognized you through my ascetic power.'"

Then the Thousand-Eyed One (Indra) exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! and said, "Oh, what wisdom! Thereupon, he honored Śuka with the fruits of his asceticism—Śuka, who was thus a performer of auspicious deeds and supremely righteous.
Although he already knew of that attainment, the slayer of Bala questioned him;
though Indra, the subduer of Pāka, was aware of its acquisition, he asked nonetheless:
"It is leafless, fruitless, withered, and no longer a refuge for birds."
"For what purpose do you serve this tree when this forest is so vast?
There are many other trees here as well— covered with leaves, containing hollows, auspicious, and providing ample space for movement— in this great forest."
"O wise one, having reflected with your wisdom upon this tree that has reached the end of its life, lacks strength, has its essence exhausted, and its splendor destroyed— abandon this unstable tree.
Having heard what was spoken by Śakra, the righteous-minded Śuka [responded].
Sighing very deeply, he spoke these words in distress:
"The divine powers, O Lord of Śacī, are not to be transgressed. Listen, O Lord of the Gods, to what has become of you and where you now abide."
Born from this tree and endowed with virtuous qualities, I was well protected during my childhood and never overcome by enemies. O sinless one, why do you cause the fruitlessness of my compassion?
One should not touch fire for one who is devoted and faithful;
for one who is devoted to compassion, faithful,
and submissive, compassion is indeed the great characteristic of dharma for the virtuous.
Compassion always bestows joy upon the virtuous.
You alone are questioned by all the deities regarding doubts concerning dharma;
therefore, O God, you are established in the sovereignty over the gods.
"O Thousand-eyed One, you ought not to cause me to abandon my devotion here;
O Best of Beings, you ought not to make me forsake that devotion.
How indeed could I abandon this capable one today, upon whom I depend for my livelihood?"
"How could one who subsists on that which is level abandon that which is uneven?
Delighted by his gentle words and gratified by his benevolence, Indra, the subduer of Pāka, spoke to Śuka, the knower of dharma.

"Choose a boon," he said; and then that parrot chose a boon: "If there is to be favor shown toward me, let this tree live again, for I am always devoted to compassion. Thus he requested the restoration of that tree.

And having recognized that firm perfection of virtue in the parrot, Śakra was delighted; he then quickly sprinkled the tree with nectar. Consequently, its fruits, leaves, and branches became beautiful to behold.
Because of Śuka’s firm devotion, that tree attained splendor;
and by virtue of that act of benevolence,
O great king, at the end of his life, Śuka attained the same world as Śakra.
"O lord of men, in this very way, one who has taken refuge in a devoted person attains the fulfillment of all goals, just as a tree does upon reaching the parrot.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, you who are learned in all the scriptures:
between destiny (*daiva*) and human effort (*puruṣakāra*), which indeed is the more excellent?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Vasiṣṭha and Brahmā,
concerning which of the two— divine or human— actions is superior.
Long ago, the venerable Vasiṣṭha questioned the Grandfather;
then, O King, the lotus-born Grandfather, the god of gods,
spoke these sweet words, which were meaningful and adorned with reason.
For from a seed arises a sprout, from the sprout the production of leaves,
from the leaves stalks are produced, and from the stalk the trunk is produced.
From the aggregates arises the flower; from the flower arises the fruit. From the fruit arises the seed; from the seed there is further production.
Nothing whatsoever is born without a seed, nor is there a fruit without a seed.
From seed comes seed; it is taught that from seed alone the fruit arises.
Whatever kind of seed a farmer sows after reaching a field, whether it be well-done or ill-done, he reaps a fruit of that same kind.
Just as a field sown without seed becomes fruitless,
so too destiny does not succeed without human effort.
Human effort is said to be the field, while destiny is the seed.
From the union of the field and the seed, the crop then flourishes.
The agent himself experiences the production of the fruit of his action;
this is seen directly in the world, both for what has been done and for what has not been done.
Through auspicious action one obtains happiness, and through sinful action one obtains suffering.
One reaps everywhere what has been done; what has not been done is never experienced anywhere.
A doer, even if his fortune is impaired, finds a firm footing everywhere.
The unskilled man, having fallen from his state, receives the sprinkling of caustic on a wound.
Through austerity one obtains beauty, good fortune, and various jewels;
everything is attained through action, not by fate for one of undisciplined soul.
In this world, heaven, enjoyment, and whatever goal is desired—
all these are brought about through human effort once it has been performed.
The celestial luminaries, the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the moon, the sun, and the winds [all depend upon it].
13,006.014c Through human effort alone, all have gone from the human state to the state of a deity.

13,006.015a Whether it be wealth, a circle of friends, sovereignty accompanied by noble lineage, 13,006.015c or even prosperity— these are difficult to enjoy for those who have not performed their duties.
A Brahmin obtains prosperity through purity, a Kṣatriya through valor,
a Vaiśya through manly effort, and a Śūdra through service. Wealth does not attend one who does not give, nor one who is impotent, nor one who is inactive.

He who created the three worlds, the Daityas, and all the deities— he is this very Lord Viṣṇu, who performs austerities in the ocean; he is neither one of unrighteous character, nor a coward, nor likewise one devoid of asceticism.
If one's own fruit of action did not exist, everything would indeed be fruitless; the world would not remain indifferent by relying solely on fate,
for he who follows fate without performing human effort [is lost].
Having obtained a husband who is impotent, a woman exerts herself in vain;
in the world of men there is no such fear regarding good or evil as the fear that arises from even a slight cause in the world of the thirty gods.
Human effort, once exerted, follows destiny alone; destiny cannot bestow anything upon anyone if no effort has been made. For even among the gods, positions are seen to be impermanent.
How can action exist without destiny, or how will it establish anything? In this world, the deities do not engage in the affairs of anyone;
they create intense obstacles out of fear of being surpassed by their own selves.

13,006.025a There is always conflict between the sages and the deities; by whose word, then, could there be that which is non-divine, since it is from the divine that everything proceeds? 13,006.026a And how does its origin come about, and in what manner does the divine proceed?
Thus, even in the world of the thirty-three gods, many such deceptions are encountered.
For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self;
the self alone is the witness of one's own deeds, both those performed and those left undone.
Whether it be something done or something slightly modified, when an action is performed, it succeeds.
A wicked deed does not attain its intended result when a virtuous one has been performed. Merit is the refuge of the gods; everything is obtained through meritorious deeds.
Having encountered a man of virtuous character, what can destiny do?
In ancient times, Yayāti, though fallen, cast down, and dropped to the earth,
was raised once more to heaven by his grandsons through their meritorious deeds.
In ancient times, the royal sage Purūravas, renowned as Aila, was addressed by the twice-born; that lord of the earth attained heaven,
having been honored by the performance of horse sacrifices and other rites, O Lord of Kosala.
Due to the curse of a great seer, Saudāsa became a man-eater;
and both Aśvatthāman and Rāma, though sons of sages and wielders of the bow,
do not go to the heavenly world by virtue of their meritorious deeds here.
Having worshipped with hundreds of sacrifices like a second Vāsava, Bali,
the son of Virocana, went to the depths of the netherworld due to a single false statement and was bound by the gods with the noose of dharma.

By the personal exertion of Viṣṇu, he was made to lie upon the netherworld (Pātāla). Why was Janamejaya, who set out after uprooting the foot of Śakra and committed the slaughter of Brahmin women, not prevented by destiny?
Having killed a Brahmin out of ignorance and having touched [the corpse] of a child,
why was the brahmin-sage Vaiśampāyana restrained by fate during that great sacrifice when he falsely offered cows to the Brahmins?
In the past, the royal sage Nṛga was transformed into a lizard,
and the royal sage Dhundhumāra reached old age while engaged in sacrificial sessions;
having renounced his gift of affection, he fell asleep at Girivraja.
The kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas, which had been seized by the mighty sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
was recovered once again— not through destiny, but by relying on the strength of their own arms.
Even sages, endowed with asceticism and self-restraint and firm in their vows, [attain their goals through such means].
Do they release a curse through the power of fate, or not through their own action? In this world, having encountered everything that is very difficult to obtain,
a man who has fallen into greed and delusion is not protected by fate.
Just as a fire, though subtle, becomes great when fanned by the wind,
so too does destiny, when joined with action, increase effectively.
Just as a lamp meets with extinction through the exhaustion of its oil, [so does destiny wane].
Likewise, through the exhaustion of karma, destiny withers away.
Even after obtaining a vast flood of wealth, enjoyments, or women,
a man in this world is unable to enjoy them if he is devoid of karma.
Even wealth that is well-hidden and guarded by the gods,
and even a virtuous person who possesses the quality of expenditure,
a high-souled man here, being ever-diligent, attains through his action.
The world of the gods is superior to the world of men;
by reason of its far greater prosperity, the houses of humans appear like dwellings in a cemetery to the immortals.
Fate does not bear fruit for one who performs improper actions; fate removes one from the wrong path, yet there is no power over fate.
Just as toward a teacher, so too does fate follow the preeminent action that has been performed.
"Destiny, though unimpaired and not diminished, is led by human effort according to one's own will; that effort, accumulated here and there, brings it about.
All this has indeed been told to you by me, O best of sages."
Constantly perceiving in truth the fruit of human effort, through the favor of destiny and through well-commenced action,
as well as by following the prescribed rule and performing one's duty, one shall attain the path to heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, O best of men, tell me, who am asking you, about the fruits of all great and auspicious deeds."
Bhīṣma said:
"Alas, O Bhārata, I shall tell you that which you ask of me.
Listen, Yudhiṣṭhira, to that secret which belongs to the ṛṣis."
Whatever destiny is attained by one after death, which is long-desired,
and whatever specific action a person performs with whatever specific body,
he experiences that very fruit with that very same body.

In whatever state one performs a virtuous or non-virtuous deed, in that very same state one experiences its result, birth after birth. An action performed here never perishes, for it is always present through the five sense faculties.
For these are his eternal witnesses, and the self is likewise the sixth.
One should give sight, one should give mind, and one should give pleasant speech;
one should follow [the teacher] and attend upon him—that is a sacrifice with five sacrificial fees.
He who gives unblemished food to one traveling on a road,
who is weary and has never been seen before, gains a great fruit of merit. For those who sleep on the bare ground, he provides houses and beds.
To one clothed in rags and bark, garments and ornaments;
to one whose soul is absorbed in yoga and rich in asceticism, vehicles, seats, and conveyances;
and to one who lies near the sacred fires—his royal prowess is thus described.
By abstaining from savory tastes, one attains good fortune;
by abstaining from meat, one obtains cattle and sons. Furthermore, he who hangs with his head downward or dwells in water as a penance [attains these rewards].
He who always sleeps alone shall attain his desired goal. Furthermore,
one who provides water for the feet, a seat, a lamp, food,
and shelter for the sake of honoring a guest performs a sacrifice that possesses five sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).

For one who practices the hero’s posture, the hero’s bed, and the hero’s station, his worlds are indeed imperishable and grant the fulfillment of all desires. O lord of the people, one obtains wealth through giving and authority through silence.
Through austerity and celibacy, one enjoys enjoyments and a long life;
one partakes of beauty, sovereignty, and health—the fruit of non-violence.
For those who subsist on fruits and roots, there is sovereignty; likewise, for those who subsist on leaves, there is heaven.
It is said that by fasting unto death one gains a kingdom, and happiness everywhere;

through truth one attains heaven, and through initiation (dīkṣā), an exalted lineage. One who is rich in cattle attains heaven by the "vegetable-initiation" (śākadīkṣā), while one who subsists on grass likewise goes to heaven.

By bathing at the three periods of the day and subsisting only on air, a woman obtains the merit of a sacrifice (kratu). A twice-born man who subsists on water alone and maintains the sacred fire becomes consecrated;
for one who practices the Maru-vow, there is sovereignty, and for one who fasts until death (anāśaka), there is the vault of heaven.
O King, by performing fasting, initiation,
and consecration for twelve years, one excels even the station of a hero;
indeed, by studying all the Vedas, one is immediately liberated from suffering.

Through the recitation and retention of that [Veda], one attains heaven; through the knowledge of its meaning, the supreme goal. For those free from craving, the fruit of Vedic chanting is declared to be both heaven and liberation.
Indeed, by practicing dharma with the mind, one shall attain the heavenly world.
Those twice-born ones in the world who are devoted to that [truth] possess eternal worlds. That thirst which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays,
and which is a disease that ends only with life— for him who abandons that thirst, there is happiness.

Just as a calf finds its mother among a thousand cows, so does the karma performed in the past follow the doer. Just as flowers and fruits ripen without being prompted, [so does one's own action follow].
Just as one's own time does not pass by, so too does the karma performed in the past [not fail to bear fruit]. As one grows old, the hair withers; as one grows old, the teeth decay;
the eyes and ears also grow old, but craving alone does not grow old.
By that which pleases one's father, Prajāpati is pleased;
by that which pleases one's mother, the Earth is honored;
by that which pleases one's preceptor, the Brahman is thereby honored.
All duties are honored by him by whom these three are honored;
but for him by whom these are not honored, all ritual actions are fruitless.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard those words of Bhīṣma, the bulls among the Kurus were struck with wonder;
their minds became gladdened and they were filled with joy at that time, for when counsel is employed in vain...
Whatever occurs when Soma is pressed in vain, and whatever occurs when an oblation is offered in vain into the fire—
all that becomes fruitless when [the Veda] is recited in vain.
"O Lord, I have related to you that which was proclaimed by the Seer.
What do you wish to hear from me next regarding the attainment of the fruits of good and evil?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who are worthy of worship? Who are to be saluted? To whom do you pay homage, O Bhārata?
Tell me all this, O King—those for whom you have longing.
Just as those who are to be saluted by you were described by Śakra, O giver of honor," [he asked].
In the same way, O King, tell me of those for whom you have longing; tell me of that in which your mind dwells even when you are beset by the greatest calamity—
whether it be in the entire world of men, or in the hereafter, or even in this life.
Bhīṣma said:
I envy those twice-born ones for whom the Veda is the supreme wealth,
and for whom heaven is their own conviction, achieved through the means of austerity and the study of sacred texts.
I truly envy those whose elders and children alike uphold the ancestral burden of their fathers and grandfathers and do not falter—
those who are well-trained in the sciences, self-controlled, and gentle in speech.
Of those virtuous ones, endowed with learning and good conduct, who always know the eternal syllable (akṣara) and speak in assemblies like flocks of swans—
their voices are auspicious in form, beautiful, and possess the resonance of divine clouds.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, the words properly uttered by those endowed with knowledge and realization are indeed heard;
they bring happiness both in this world and after death to a king who is intent on listening,
and I hold them in high esteem."
And those who are their listeners, always honored in the assembly, endowed with wisdom and virtue— of them too I am envious. [They speak words] well-refined, disciplined, pure, and full of merit.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who give food to Brāhmaṇas for the sake of their satisfaction—
I, O King, always envy them. For it is indeed possible to fight in battle, but not to give while free from malice."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, there are hundreds of heroes and warriors in this world;
yet among them, when they are all being counted, the hero in generosity stands preeminent.
O gentle one, may I become fortunate once more, even if it be as a mere Brāhmaṇa."
Born into a noble family, devoted to the path of Dharma and dedicated to austerity and knowledge,
having attained an auspicious birth, he may yet become a mere Brāhmaṇa;
though born into a lineage among his kin, he may obtain that which is very difficult to attain.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, there is no one in this world dearer to me than you;
yet, O bull among the Bharatas, the Brahmins are even dearer to me than you.
O perpetuator of the Kuru race, just as the Brahmins are dearer to me than you," so it was said.
By that truth, may I go to those worlds where Śantanu dwells;
for neither my father was dearer to me than the Brahmins,
nor was my grandfather, nor even my other kinsmen and friends.
Indeed, O scorcher of foes, no transgression whatsoever— whether minute or gross— is known by me here among the brahmins, whether committed through action,
mind, or speech, as observed by those of virtuous deeds.
Because of what I have done for the Brahmins, I do not suffer today.
They call me "devoted to the Brahmins" (brahmaṇya); I am satisfied by that very word. This alone is considered the highest of all purifying acts.
"I see worlds that are stainless and pure, accessible to those who follow the path of Brahman;
to them, my dear, I must go, both swiftly and after a long time. Just as in this world, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the duty of women is to have their support in a husband."
O twice-born ones, for a Kṣatriya, that deity is his goal and there is no other.
A Kṣatriya who is a hundred years old and a Brāhmaṇa who is ten years old are to be understood as father and son; indeed, between the two, the Brāhmaṇa is the father.
When a husband is no more, a woman indeed takes her brother-in-law as her husband;
when a Brāhmaṇa is not available, the earth takes a Kṣatriya as her lord.
And the kingdom, along with the royal chaplains, should be accepted with the permission of the Brāhmaṇas.

By protecting them, heaven is his; by provoking their anger, there is inexhaustible hell. Therefore, O best of the Kurus, Brahmins are to be protected like sons, served like gurus, and indeed honored like fire.
One should always serve the twice-born who are upright, virtuous, devoted to truth, and intent on the welfare of all beings, as if they were enraged venomous serpents;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should constantly stand in awe of their spiritual power and ascetic fervor.
From afar, the wives of Brahmins should be honored like mothers with diligent protection;
yet both of these— vital energy (*tejas*) and asceticism (*tapas*)— must be abandoned,
for the impulse toward both exists swiftly in each of them.
O Great King, those ascetic Brahmins, when enraged, could slay [even the gods];
yet by the offense of provoking one who is free from anger, one suffers further in hell.
Furthermore, both worlds are bestowed upon that Brahmin who remains unprovoked.
He should leave a remainder on both sides, but he must not leave a remainder of what has been given.
Just as a cowherd with staff in hand remains ever vigilant among his cattle,
so should the Kṣatriya protect the Brāhmaṇas and the Veda.
"O Bhīṣma, you should protect the Brāhmaṇas of spiritual luster like a father protects his sons; and you should look after their households to ensure that they have the means for their livelihood."
In this regard, they cite this ancient history;
O son, listen to this dialogue of the four Vedas from the Ṛgveda.
The Yajurveda says: "If an unexpected guest is turned away at evening from one who has taken refuge in his home and is offering the Agnihotra sacrifice, that guest takes away all of his merit."
It does not overflow, it does not suffer distress, and its passion (rajas) does not rise upward;
this is the Sāmaveda.
It is superior to the Agnihotra sacrifice when offered into the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa.
If he does not kill his father or mother,
nor a Brahmin, nor does he utter slander,
whatever other sin he may commit—
A guest who is pleased destroys that evil which one incurs when one sacrifices or gives while being angry.
Whatever austerity one performs or whatever oblation one offers, Vaivasvata takes it all away from him—
so said Bhīṣma.
The exertions of one who is prone to anger become fruitless.
Furthermore, O Indra among kings, best of those who uphold dharma, listen again to these duties;
in this regard, they cite this ancient history.
Listen as I speak of Indra, Indra and Agni, and Sūrya and Śacī. In the kingdom, I behold Brahmins who are free from desire and anger.
"O Agni,
by this truthful word, let the foot of the jar be filled,
so that I may not eat there where the twice-born do not eat."
O Sūrya,
by this word of truth, let the foot of the water-jar be filled,
since I do not perform penance according to my strength for the sake of cows or Brahmins.
"O Śacī,
by this word of truth, let the foot of the jar be filled!
In deed, thought, and speech, I do not disregard Purandara."
Bhīṣma said:
"By this word of truth, let one foot of the water-jar be filled.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
The dialogue between the King of Madra and the high-souled Vyāsa,
concerning the performance of the Vaitāna sacrifice as it was conducted in the past by the sons of Kuntī.
[Then] the King of Madra...

The Blessed One was asked regarding the purpose of sacrifice, and you have heard what he said there: "O Blessed One, which are the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), and what are the stages of life (*āśrama*) here that lead to fruit?
Who is worshipped, what is the sacrifice, what is the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), and who is it that performs the rite?"
Who is praised at the sacrifice with the sounds of song?
Who is sung of at the sacrifice with charming speech?
And who is lauded with hymns of praise using the word *brahman*?
Whose oblation do the Adhvaryu priests prepare here?
What is the Gophala in the system of castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama*)? What is in the Soma sacrifice? What is the syllable *Oṃ*? And what is the path of the meaning of the Vedas?
"O Great Seer, being thus questioned by me, tell me all of that—
[the teaching] of Dvaipāyana, whom they call the eldest in the world in terms of wisdom."
13,008.028d@001_0040 They call him the eldest in the world, whose wisdom is supreme;
13,008.028d@001_0041 they say his birth is the eldest of all origins; 13,008.028d@001_0042 the Brāhmaṇas, pure-souled and foremost in the Veda, [proclaim him].
O Brāhmaṇa,
let this question be given to Keśava;
he is a youth by birth, yet his character is devoted to the duty and purpose of a Kṣatriya.
O hero, born of Devakī by the son of Śūra,
Vāsudeva is indeed a Kṣatriya worthy of knowing the Vedas.
The lotus-eyed one, the best among the Dāśārhas,
spoke with a joyful soul, being like Brahmā himself and possessed of great wisdom, O son of Parāśara; tell us what he said to the Brāhmaṇas.
Questioned regarding the purpose of the sacrifice for the son of Pāṇḍu, the exceedingly radiant Vyāsa declared:
"This is for his own welfare and indeed for that of the world."
Regarding the speech you have spoken to me—
this wonderful question— I am not able to resolve it clearly today; for such a task rests indeed with one like you.
O Vāsudeva,
O you who are the eldest in the world, whose form is the universe, and who possess the beautiful navel—
O Great Seer, speak those words which you [have for me].
In which Kṛṣṇa is indeed described exactly as he is,
I am pleased with you for your knowledge and power, exactly as they are. —
Vaiśampāyana.
"Therefore, speak of the accomplishment of deeds in this instruction,
O best of speakers among the Yādavas. Thus addressed,
Kṛṣṇa Vyāsa, with palms joined in reverence, [spoke] to Vāsudeva.
While worshipping Kṛṣṇa Viṣṇu Vāsudeva, the God of gods, together with the Brahmins,
Vyāsa spoke.
O Viśvakarman, yours is infinity; such is your form—ancient, eternal, and constant. Who could comprehend this among the declarations of the Vedas?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this world, you are indeed the ruler, just like a father;
as this best of sages previously declared regarding Dvārakā."
Now hear how Vāsudeva consists of the Vedas and the Brahmins: one who knows Viṣṇu Vāsudeva to be the sacrificial post (yūpa) perceives all Brahmins as the vision of reality.
Knowing Viṣṇu, the pervading Vāsudeva, the Brahmin who perceives reality attains the state of a true Brahmin;
Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, and Viṣṇu is also worshipped as the sacrifice.
Kṛṣṇa is Viṣṇu, who is the whole and the Lord; Kṛṣṇa is the Vedāṅgas and the declarations of the Vedas. Knowing this, a Brahmin attains Brahman.
The entire station in the path of sacrifice belongs to Viṣṇu;
there, Kṛṣṇa, who is of the nature of Viṣṇu, is worshipped with all dispositions and for the fulfillment of all desires through the Cāturhotra rite.
The Brahmins attain the meritorious worlds who drink the Soma born of true being, and who, possessing knowledge,
perform radiant deeds.
Those who dwell in heaven, contemplating their desired goal in solitude,
indeed attain that station, for they are knowers of the vow;
meditating on this "Om," one should not depart.
Even a brahmin who has committed evil deeds crosses the difficult path;
for by performing meditation upon Vāsudeva as the all-encompassing darkness, brahmins do not go to a state of misery.
Clarified butter is the sacrifice; the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles are the giver of the sacrifice. Desire is the wife; the wife’s chamber is the sacrificial offerings.
The fuel-sticks are the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); the performer of the *hotṛ* priestly function is ever-present.
He who fully knows Viṣṇu attains Him. In every application of ritual actions, and in the performance of the *vaitāna* rites prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa—
Dvaipāyana said: For matters concerning nourishment, one shall attain success in action;
for matters concerning peace, one shall attain all-encompassing peace.
He who maintains faith, renunciation, and peace, as well as reverence;
who adheres to truth, righteousness, and what has been done;
and who, having abandoned desire and hatred, is equal toward all—[he is a true ascetic].
Purified by faith, one is fit for all sacrifices;
in that sacrifice, all beings rejoice,
and all undertakings proceed according to the vision of the scriptures.
Those who worship with rites that are righteous and purposeful are certainly purified in soul; they devote themselves solely to the one Dharma,
which is both the single syllable and the two syllables.
Always sacrificing, self-restrained and confident, the Brahmins, having seen [the truth] and paid their respects even slightly,
firmly devote themselves to that path of the virtuous.
Even those of evil nature, overcome by anger and passion,
who chant the names of the devotees of Kṛṣṇa,
become purified in soul, devoted to sacrifice, and highly wise.
At the conclusion of the sacrifice, they enjoy the worlds of glory. There was once a single Veda for the Brāhmaṇas;
it had four quarters, consisted of the three qualities, and had Brahman as its head.
The Brahmins say that the Veda consists of foot by foot; know that Dvaipāyana taught it as such in the Tretā age, and that each [portion] is a head.
All the Vedas, all that is to be known through the Vedas, along with the Shastras; all sacrifices and all acts of worship are Krishna. Those Brahmins who know Krishna in truth [know Him as such].
O King, for them all sacrifices have been completed. This Kṛṣṇa is to be known as a yogi by the Brāhmaṇas who know the truth of the Vedas and the Āraṇyakas, because of his sovereign power.
Pervading all sacrifices, the Brahmins, and even the Veda itself,
that God of gods remained present throughout the three worlds;
he is this very deity who was sacrificing to Śakra, the Lord.
Out of affection, he spoke to the foremost performer of sacrifices:
"Śakra does not know me, for he lacks the true essence of the meaning of the Vedas;
whereas I am his devotee, devoted with devotion, preeminent in pure disposition."
They know me as Brahma-śiras, the most excellent; the All-knowing One, the source of the universe, yet unborn. I am everywhere—the eternal Lord of the eternal.
The entire Veda is devoid of qualities and possesses infinite splendor;
all the gods worship Vāsudeva,
seeking through their intellect the path for their own bodies.
They obtain all vast desires within these three worlds by invoking the name of Kṛṣṇa;
Kṛṣṇa is worshipped with sacrifices by those who perform repeated rites.
Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by heroes who display their prowess;
Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by those reflecting through his words;
Kṛṣṇa is worshipped by those liberated from delusion.
Those who possess knowledge, who drink the Soma, and who are free from sin—
the Blessed Ones— having sacrificed with rituals, pray for the sphere of the senses.
They traverse the entire vast realm of the gods;
having gone to its end, they resort to the world of mortals.
Thus it is with all those who abide in the stages of life and are firm in their vows.
Knowing me, they go to worlds that are not miserable; whatever initiation they undertake, being free from sin,
they become light and partake of the world of the gods.
Worshipping me while worshipping [others], they rejoice; knowing me as Vāsudeva with faith,
I am pleased by their devotion and bestow upon them true being (sattva).
Touched by the quality of goodness (sattva) and free from delusion, this Dvaipāyana proceeds toward those luminous bodies which are white in the world.
The three worlds, the guardians of the world, and the triple Veda;
the three fires and the five oblations—
thus spoke Bhīṣma.
"All the gods are indeed the son of Devakī.
Having heard these words of Vyāsa, the King of Madra, together with the sages, [spoke].
Vaiśampāyana.
With a joyful heart, he honored Vyāsa and Kṛṣṇa according to the prescribed rites. Then Dvaipāyana, the son of the great seer and the foremost among poets, having heard those words—
The high-souled Bhīṣma went to the earth with his head and offered salutation to Kṛṣṇa;
Yudhiṣṭhira [did likewise].
