"O Grandfather, O mighty-armed one, it was previously stated by you while praising Śvetavāhana that Garuḍa is the best among birds.
Regarding this, I have a curiosity; my mind is set upon hearing more."
O scorcher of foes, how did Garuḍa attain preeminence among birds?
Why is he called Suparṇa and Vainateya, and why is he the enemy of the serpents? What is his prowess and what is his strength? You ought to tell me this, O Bhārata.
Bhīṣma said:
O Vāsudeva, O mighty-armed one, Devakī has indeed given birth to a noble son through you.
You have heard, O enhancer of the joy of the Yadus, what was said by Dharmarāja.
"O descendant of Kuru, he said to me, 'Recite the Suparṇa.
Commanded by you, O one of great splendor, I wish to recite this.
For you, O Śauri of mighty arms, were called Suparṇa in ancient times."
O Keśava, you were Garuḍa in time without beginning or end;
therefore, having first propitiated you for the sake of the wise son of Dharma,
Vāsudeva—
"O Mādhava, I wish to speak of Garuḍa, the best of winged creatures;
just as you know him, so too does Yudhiṣṭhira know him."—
Bhīṣma.
And so, O King, speak to Garuḍa according to the truth;
O mighty-armed Yudhiṣṭhira, listen, O King, to the matter exactly as it is:
[to] Garuḍa, the best of birds, the son of Vinatā, who possesses great strength.
And so, O King, hear from me as I describe how Garuḍa became Suparṇa and how he slays the serpents. Long ago, my dear son, I was [challenged] by the wise Rāma, the son of Jamadagni.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, while he was slaying deer by the thousands,
O dear one, as soon as I saw him, I cast aside all my weapons and,
having first offered my salutations, stood before Rāma with humility.
At the conclusion of our conversation, O Yudhiṣṭhira, I asked that granter of boons about the strength and vigor of Suparṇa; and he, being pleased with me, replied:
"Kadrū and Vinatā were both daughters of Prajāpati."

Then the lord Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci, married her according to the sacred law; the great ascetic, being pleased with his two wives, granted them a boon. Thereupon, Kadrū chose as her boon a hundred sons, each possessing the strength of ten elephants.
O best of the Bharatas, Vinatā chose two heroic sons who were equal in splendor and power, equal in birth to all others,
and possessed of speed and prowess equal to a thousand sons of Kadrū.
Having said "So be it," that great ascetic granted them the boon;
he begot those sons through them, and they became as they were before. Kadrū, however, gave birth to one hundred eggs.
Two eggs, most beautiful and auspicious, were laid by Vinatā. Then, attendants placed those two eggs of both Kadrū and Vinatā in vessels that were kept warm with steam.
Then, from those eggs, the sons of Kadrū, the serpents, emerged;
at the time of five hundred years, they were seen possessing strength and vigor equal to that of a breath.
When those high-souled *pannagas* had been born, Vinatā [beheld them].
Afflicted by the grief of having no son, she broke open one of her testicles.
She spoke these words: "What shall I do with this?
For in former times, when five hundred [sons] had passed away, she had never seen two sons at once.
She saw the high-minded one departing with his staff, without his garment;
endowed with the upper half of his body, yet indeed deprived of the other.
Having seen him in such a state, with his body incomplete, she—

Overcome with grief for his son, he lamented, and the bird likewise fell into that state. Then, filled with joy yet with eyes brimming with tears, he spoke repeatedly to his mother: "You were fickle! I am slain!"
"You did not wait for the time that had previously passed;
rather, we two shall become your sons, more powerful than Vāsava himself. Because you were overcome by envy and anger, you have been treated in this manner by me."
"Therefore, O my mother, you too shall enter into the state of a slave.
For five hundred years, you indeed vied with her;
you shall become her slave," she said, shedding tears.
And this very Bhīṣma, O highly fortunate mother, the powerful one who is the best among the strong, your younger brother, shall liberate you from the state of slavery to me.
O Bhārata, Vinatā, afflicted by grief for her son and fearing the curse,
awaited that time which had been specified for her son. Then,
when five hundred years had passed in the course of time, she waited further.
Then the mighty Garuḍa was born, powerful and a devourer of serpents;
he had a broad face, a crest, and a sheath-like covering for his wings;
he was great with claws like tortoise-shells, red eyes, a thick neck, short feet, and a massive head.
O bull of the Bharatas, that son who was first born from the egg and emerged from it is seen in the sky as Aruṇa, the elder brother of Vinatā,
facing the eastern direction toward the rising of the sun.
Ruddy, resembling the dawn in appearance, he was known by the name Aruṇa. As soon as he was born, the bird Garuḍa, the devourer of serpents,
quickly left his mother and went in every direction.

Thus he grew exceedingly great, honored with all objects of desire through the food bestowed by his grandfather, O lord of the people; and while that bird flourished there according to his wish, [the king] likewise prospered.
Kadrū and Vinatā both went toward the ocean;
there they saw Uccaiḥśravas approaching nearby,
the horse who had just bathed, emerged, and quickly drunk [the water].
Then Kadrū, laughing, said this to Vinatā:
"Vinatā, O auspicious one, tell me now: what is the color of the horse according to your opinion?"
"O Queen, in my opinion, the horse should be of a single color, entirely white. Kadrū asked: 'O wise lady, what kind of color do you think it should be?'"
"This most excellent of horses, who is considered by you to be entirely white—
O Vinatā,
speak, O auspicious and beautiful lady, let us play by wagering on his color."
"If you play against me, O Noble Lady, what shall be our stake?
Kadrū, having understood that, said: "Once I have known the stake, I shall indeed play; but once it has been staked by you, [I shall not withdraw]."
"O dark-eyed one, you shall become my conquered slave, and I too [shall be yours], O Vinatā;
whether it be a matter of many colors or a single color, this pleases you. This wager, O Queen, that I am to be your slave, pleases me; of this there is no doubt."
Bhīṣma said:
"Abide in truth—blessings be upon you—and I too shall abide in truth. Vinatā, having thus agreed to the wager, spoke with her mind resolved.
Kadru also, having said "So be it," spoke thus to her sons:
"O sons, O serpents, listen to this: a wager has been made by me with Vinata concerning Uccaiḥśravas, the celestial steed."
I spoke to him who was of many colors, and then he, being of a single color, replied:
"O sons, there is no doubt that she or I shall become a slave,
once this horse of a single color, shining with the luster of the moon and the red lotus, has been won."
"I shall become a slave, O sons; you have been defeated, there is no doubt. Therefore, you must enter this preeminent horse without weariness, O serpents."
"Even if all [the horses] were white, with their manes appearing like the luster of collyrium;
victory gained through deceit is not superior, O Mother—listen to these words of truth. Neither for the future nor for the present is there any righteousness in this."
Therefore, O Mother, you must never seek victory through deceit— a path that deviates from righteousness and brings harm to your own family.
If we were ever to desire victory through unrighteousness, [it would be for naught].
"Surely you must have forbidden us, saying, 'Do not do this.
Yet, deluded by greed, you now desire to charge even us— who are virtuous, sinless, and upright in mind— with a stain."
"Abandoning you, we shall flee in the ten directions,
O Mother, where we shall never again hear such words from you—
even from a teacher who is arrogant and ignorant of what ought and ought not to be done."
Kadrū said:
"The abandonment of one who has set out upon a wrong path is ordained. I hear various reasoned arguments being advanced."
"Because it is crooked and intended for my own withdrawal, I do not approve of that for you.
Nor, O dull-witted ones, can that wager be won otherwise.
Having heard that victory through deceit is improper, O dear sons, do what is right."
"O sons, tomorrow at dawn, I shall be defeated by Dharma;
there is no doubt that I will become a servant to Vinatā.
Mothers desire sons for the sake of benefit both in this world and the next."
This hope of mine has been frustrated by encountering you all together.
A son might rescue his father here in this world, or he might rescue his ancestors after death;
that he purifies them through the very fact of being a son—therein there would be nothing surprising.
"O my sons, swift as thought, you must enter this best of horses for the sake of our deliverance; becoming hairs with the luster of collyrium, take possession of it.
I know all that is unrighteous, and Vinatā shall be conquered."
Through deceit, even the state of servitude might oppress you;
whether victory comes through deceit or servitude follows defeat,
having resolved upon both possibilities, a righteous victory is indeed better.
"Even if unrighteous victory should again touch you alone,
by adhering to the word of your elder, that will become righteousness for you."—
Bhīṣma.

Having heard the words of their enraged mother, those serpents—with great difficulty—consented; some, however, abandoned her and fled in all directions. As they departed for the various quarters, she, being furious, cursed them severely.
Then Kadrū, the mother of the serpents and a source of enmity,
spoke: "Indeed, a royal Pāṇḍava named Janamejaya shall be born."
From Dhananjaya, the son of Kuntī, the best of archers, there shall come that descendant of the Kuru lineage who,
when enraged, will perform a snake-sacrifice. At that sacrifice, he will, by means of fire, bring you all to the state of the five elements.
Thus the mother, filled with rage, cursed the serpents who practiced righteousness:
"This act of abandoning your preceptor shall have no other consequence.
Having been thus cursed, the serpents who practiced righteousness fled in all directions.
Then, having abandoned her mother, she departed in anger toward Vairakarī.
Those serpents there who had not committed any offense against her became his dark-complexioned horse-tails.
Seeing her sons standing at the tail, Kadrū then spoke to Vinatā, who was filled with joy: "O blessed one, let this horse be examined;
our wager was well-established as being whether it is of a single color or not."
O Bhārata, as that horse was emerging from the water, the beautiful lady Vinatā, whose mind was set on overtaking him, spoke somewhat mockingly to her sister Jihmagābhinī.
"Come, let us go and see; our wager shall be well-earned, O beautiful one!
Either I shall become your slave, or you shall become my slave.
Having thus made this firm wager, they both beheld the horse.
"O best of the Kurus, having made herself her own witness,
Vinatā, upon seeing that dull horse— white as the rays of the moon, with a black tail and the speed of thought— was emaciated by grief."
There, modest and bowed, with tears falling from her eyes, she spoke these words:
"This horse Kālavāla has been won by you;
O noble lady, O auspicious one, send me as a slave, subject to your will as you desire."
"Servants must indeed act according to the will of their masters; there is no doubt in this matter," said Bhīṣma.
Then Kadrū, as if laughing, addressed Vinatā, who was walking in accordance with righteousness.
She sent her like a maidservant, and she performed all of that;
neither pale, nor agitated, nor angry, nor distressed,
Vinatā, whose eyes were like lotuses, carried out her task as a servant.
These four directions have been placed at her service;
then, indeed, the pride of strength approached Vainateya.
As he, overcome by that pride, was running close by—
O King, the celestial seer Nārada beheld him filled with pride;
and the celestial seer Nārada, as if laughing, said to him:
"Why have you fallen under the sway of pride? Do you not indeed see your mother?"

Always arrogant because of his strength and constantly filled with self-conceit, he [spoke] to that female servant of the king of serpents who was staying within her mother’s inner apartments. To him, Vainateya said: "What is that deed, O great sage?"
"My mother, that poor woman, became a slave when I was born as her son.
Then the sage Garuḍa spoke these words: "O bird, she is playing and has been won."

"In former times, how was that mother of mine defeated by deceit along with her sons, the lords of serpents? O Blessed One, tell me that exactly as it happened; having heard it, I shall understand what follows."
Then, O best of the Bharatas, Nārada related to him everything that had occurred regarding the bird exactly as it had happened;
upon hearing this from the son of Vinatā, anger took possession of his heart.
O scorcher of enemies, he rebuked all the serpents along with their mother.
Then, rising up swiftly out of anger and grief, the king of birds went to where his mother was enduring great hardship.
There he then beheld his mother, dejected, with matted hair, soiled, and emaciated; she was like the radiance of the sun obscured by a water-bearing cloud.
And from both her eyes, tears flowed due to his sorrow and her indignation.
To her who stood firm in human resolve regarding both worldly engagement and renunciation,
that virtuous soul, the preeminent among the best of birds, addressed these words not to his mother Vinatā,
but to Kadrū alone.
"Whether my mother won by right or even by unrighteousness, you are my eldest mother; all that is considered righteous in my view.
But this poor woman, O Mother, must be suffering for my sake as a son."
"Please grant her leave for my sake, O seer of Dharma.
Having heard these words of the wise son of Vinatā, Kadrū—
foolish, overwhelmed by grief, and fainting with sorrow— spoke these words.

"O Vainateya, I shall by no means do what is pleasing to you or to your mother; you speak to me, O twice-born bird, with an unkind heart. To her, who was then speaking such unpleasant and cruel words, [he replied:]
Garuda proceeded to conciliate her with harsh yet truthful words:
"O blessed one, you are my mother’s eldest daughter, O beautiful lady."
"Kadru, you are my uterine sister and my elder mother; of this there is no doubt.
O bird, O twice-born one who can go wherever you wish, depart as you desire."
"O bird, it is not possible for you to deceive your mother with pleasant words if you do not bring back the nectar for her, O winged one."—
Bhīṣma.
"Behold this handmaid of mine, O Vainateya; of this there is no doubt.
Having said "So be it," the bird of great splendor made his promise and then spoke these words to his father regarding the recovery of the nectar.
Indeed, she repeatedly uttered many words of pleasant truth,
yet she did not grant me permission, for she would not consent; she indeed discharged various kinds of speech against me that were like thunderbolts.
"O Lord of great splendor, Vinatā is my slave;
Kadrū has sent her here, saying, 'This woman is a slave. Vinatā will be released from slavery only when she brings back the nectar."
Saying, "I shall bring [the nectar] for the sake of my mother's liberation," Kaśyapa,
having been requested for the nectar, indeed rejoiced to bring it quickly.
"O dear one, the nectar is difficult to obtain even for the gods; how then could it have been obtained by you?
Listen to me, my son, for it is guarded most strictly by protectors:
it is well-concealed by waters and completely surrounded on all sides."
Immediately thereafter, guarded by the blazing Jātavedas (Fire),
hundreds of thousands, millions,
and tens of millions of Rākṣasas named Kiṃkaras protect the nectar most vigilantly.
Their spears, swords, tridents, *śataghnīs*, and *paṭṭiśas*—
O dear one, those weapons of the guards were like thunderbolts, as were their stones;
then, it was bound all around with a great net.
"O dear one, by the command of the slayer of Vṛtra,
it was indeed made of iron; O son of Vinatā, O bird, how can you thus desire that nectar which is so well-guarded by the wielder of the thunderbolt?"
By Indra, by the gods, by the *nāgas*, by the sword-beings, and by those born of the mountains and waters—
Garuda,
out of longing for his son, speaks these words; listen, O father, to this certain conclusion.
"I am powerful and possessed of skillful means; what more may I do for you?
His father, delighted, spoke to him again and again with a smile:
"If, my son, you would devour those two cruel creatures, the tortoise and the elephant..."
Thus, your strength shall be immeasurable; of this there is no doubt. O Garuḍa, you will indeed be the bringer of the nectar of immortality; of this there is no doubt.
"O illustrious one, where do those two cruel ones, the elephant and the tortoise, dwell?
Father, I shall eat them for the sake of strengthening my strength. Kaśyapa [replied].
At the edge of the ocean stands a mountain that reaches up to support the sky;
it is named Uraga, difficult even for the hosts of gods to reach in ancient times,
vast as the stride of a bull, with its peaks covered in flowering trees.
"O dear one, a path has been made there by a powerful elephant;
O son, its height is nine and seven cow-hides.
That great mountain was worn away by his coming and going."
O dear one, a path as vast as the earth has arisen;
having traveled along it, that elephant, thirsting for battle, desires combat.
But beyond that lord of mountains lies a lake filled with red lotuses.
There, a very powerful tortoise known as Kanaka lived;
that tortoise was as broad as a cow’s hide, and he was also like an elephant in stature—
both were equal in height and endowed with splendor and strength.
These two, Madhu and Kaiṭabha, having returned to this world,
were utterly deluded in another birth and sought to slay one another.
When that serpent went to that reservoir of water, being thirsty, [he encountered them].
Then that mighty turtle, out of anger, rushed toward him;
repeatedly diving in and emerging, that water-dweller gored that elephant with his claws and tusks and struck it with his trunk.
Even the king of elephants, though thirsty and seeking water, wards off the lotus with his trunk, tusks, and even his feet;
yet that elephant leader does not rise from the water to seize the lotus.
With his claws and his tusks, he repels the elephant;
once restrained, that best of elephants returns again to its own forest,
thirsty and with its trunk-tip soaked, drenched in blood.
"Go together with them, my son, and eat them if you are able;
those two, established in their strength and vigilant, cannot be overcome by you individually."—
Garuḍa.
"O Blessed One, how may I be able to seize both that elephant and that tortoise simultaneously? Kaśyapa, you should tell me the means for that."
When that elephant desired to fight,

the aquatic creature would quickly emerge from the water for a moment, desiring to fight again and again; O dear one, [it attacked] the water-born [elephant] when it was out of water and even when it was heedless.
"O Lord of Birds, you shall grasp it; no other means exists here," said Bhīṣma.
Having been addressed thus, the bird went to that excellent forest.
He beheld that lordly elephant, whose splendor was like a mountain of clouds.
O Bhārata, that elephant was like one who had reached the path of a mountain.
Seeing him, the illustrious one’s hair stood on end with joy.
O King, as that fierce and great-souled one desired to devour the elephant and the tortoise, he was filled with immense joy. Then, that mighty sky-ranger, with great speed—
Contracting all his limbs, he proceeded with great difficulty;
having thus traveled that distance, the powerful and preeminent elephant,
out of exhaustion, let out a great sigh to rest himself.
By the wind of his breath and by the scent of his rut,
a great tortoise that restrains elephants rose up;
the Lord of Birds beheld a most tumultuous battle between those two.
O Bhārata, as if between the lord of tortoises and the king of elephants, or like Indra and Prahlāda,
the aquatic creature warded off the leader of the elephant herd with its tusks and claws as he touched the water with his trunk.
In this manner, the elephant likewise repelled the aquatic creature with its feet and its trunk,
as it was repeatedly submerging and emerging;
for a moment, their battle was a terrifying sight to behold.
Then, O King, the tortoise emerged from that water and stood upon dry land;
yet that nāga, though defeated, did not turn back, for he was parched with thirst. Greedy for water, he slowly retreated behind him out of thirst.
Seeing that lotus quickly retreating from the battle,
he rushed forward with speed like Vajrapāṇi against an asura.
He pursued that excellent elephant as it had emerged onto dry land but had not yet reached its destination, out of rage.
The son of Vinatā seized both together;
with his left foot he grasped the best of elephants,
and with his powerful right foot he seized the quivering tortoise.
Then the invincible slayer of the lord of serpents swiftly flew up,
covering both heaven and sky with his two wings;
as he rose rapidly, he seized [the enemy] firmly with his talons.
With their well-sharpened vajra-like hearts, they quickly released their lives. Seizing those two, whose feet and necks were limp, the powerful one,
leaping as if playing in the sky, departed like a sky-goer.

Desiring a place to rest, O Lord of the Earth, that hero then surveyed the earth, but he did not see a tree sufficient for him to sit upon. Then, having reached Naimiṣa, the forest of the gods, he of great splendor—
He saw a certain tree, its branches and trunk completely covered,
resembling a peak of the Himalayas, rising two yojanas high,
and measuring a nalva in circumference on all sides, O king of kings.
One of its branches extended for five yojanas;
it was firmly rooted, possessed a sturdy trunk, and was covered with leaves like adamant.
Seated there, Vainateya suddenly seized them both.
Desiring to eat, he then rushed with speed toward a branch of that tree.
Seeing it falling,
O Lord of the World, he looked upon the hosts of sages seated there together with the Vasus during their sacrificial session.
O Bhārata, fear entered that lord of birds there upon seeing those ascetics named Vaikhānasas and the hosts of Vālakhilyas, who were seated there together with the gods.
Having beheld those ascetics sitting there along with the deities, he was struck with awe.
Seizing that branch with his beak, the Lord of Birds soared upward;
and those two birds, devourers of serpents, proceeded as if sporting in the sky.
Seeing that bird who had flown up, having seized that heavy burden, [the people watched].
All those sages said, "This is Garuḍa indeed;
no other being can endure like this powerful bird. There goes that righteous-souled one, burdened with a heavy weight."
"Because he moves as if playing in the sky, he is indeed Garuḍa. Thus all the Vasus and the inhabitants of heaven made this agreement regarding the king of birds, giving him the name "Garuḍa."
Running here and there across the entire earth, that bird, seeking to escape, could find no branch of any tree nor any place of refuge. Then he heard a divine voice speaking from above.
Having clearly addressed the divine messenger as "Garuḍa," [he said]:
"O Vainateya, O one of great strength, among the weavers at the edge of the ocean, let the branch of the tree be cast down; for you have no certainty in the Dharma."
Having heard that, Garuḍa went swiftly to the region of the salt waters where those dull-witted, evil-doing weavers were;
having gone there, the best of birds released his branch.
O King, O tiger among kings, at that time those thirty-six provinces were destroyed by her; that region became renowned as extremely terrible and fearsome. 13,008.028d@001A_0336–0338 Bhīṣma.
"O you wicked weavers, he is but a bird on a branch!"— having slain that multitude of weavers,
that tiger among birds sat down upon the mountain peak and devoured them both.
The king of birds, filled with joy, [seized] both the elephant and the tortoise;
having drunk their blood and consumed their fat, O scorcher of foes,
that best of winged creatures was delighted, having regained his unsurpassed strength.
The eater of serpents went to the palace of the king of the gods;
having bowed down to that high-souled Pāvaka,
who was emitting sparks and blazing day and night for the protection of the nectar.
Upon seeing him, a sharp fear then took possession of the lord of birds;
yet he felt no such fear from the waters nor from the *rākṣasas*,
for he perceived his own state as a bird and beheld the blazing fire.
Then, having gone to his grandfather, the eater of serpents beheld him;
having bowed to that high-souled one with palms joined in reverence, Garuḍa,
the lord of birds, spoke these words without hesitation.
"O Blessed One, I am intent upon this weighty task and am resolved upon the Dharma; indeed,
for the sake of liberating my mother from her state of servitude,
O Lord, I must fetch the nectar from Kadrū."
Then, O God, my mother shall be liberated from her state of servitude;
there, the Lord Hiraṇyaretas, ever blazing, protects the nectar by the command of Pākaśāsana.
Then, O Lord of the gods, a sharp fear entered me upon seeing the blazing fire and my own state as a bird, O Lord:
"How might this fire be crossed by me?"
"O Giver of Boons, O Lord, you are capable of telling me the means for that.
To the bird who was thus performing penance, the illustrious one,
smiling again and again, spoke regarding the means for the pacification of the fire.
O child, fire is extinguished by milk and by clarified butter;
though it dwells within the bodies of living beings, how much more so when it blazes upon the earth?
You should therefore apply fresh butter or even milk to the fire.
"Bhīṣma said:
'Therefore, go as you please; the fire shall not burn you.
Having heard the words of the Grandfather, Garuḍa, the best of winged creatures,"
Desiring to take some fresh butter, he went to Gokula; there he saw the churned butter situated in a jar. Taking that—which was like nectar—he then departed for the place where it was guarded.
Having gone there, that mighty bird, moving horizontally through the water,
avoided the fire and caused the butter to fall away. Satiated by that clarified butter, the flaming fire became slow in its movement.
The comet did not blaze; it emitted only smoke.
Having quickly passed over that fire, Garuḍa, with a joyful soul, bypassed the Rākṣasas, felling them with the wind from his wings.
They fell with their heads, knees, and likewise their feet;
having cast aside their weapons and armor, they were struck by the wings of the birds. Having leaped up and slain the obstructing *nāgas*, the discus passed beyond them.
Breaking through the net with his head between the spokes, he rushed forward;
having pierced the net with his head, that powerful one, possessing the speed of a thunderbolt,
swiftly extracted the nectar from there, O eater of serpents.
Taking that [chariot], Garuḍa rushed swiftly like the wind.
Then the slayer of Vṛtra made his preparations together with the gods.
Thereupon, [he mounted] the chariot joined by Mātali and drawn by bay horses adorned with golden garlands.

He swiftly ascended a chariot possessing a splendor equal to the sun and fire. Raising his sharpened thunderbolt, the mighty wielder of the thunderbolt, the slayer of Vṛtra and subduer of Pāka, rushed toward the king of birds.
In that very manner, O King, Garuḍa rushed toward the wielder of the thunderbolt.
Then he said to Mātali, "Drive the horses swiftly!
Thereupon, he discharged a divine and most terrible weapon at Garuḍa.
Knowing that the Lord of the Thirty-three was about to hurl his thunderbolt, the thousand-eyed one of fierce speed and prowess—
the best of those who fly— quickly became even swifter and departed.
Having learned of the boon obtained through the creation of the Grandfather, the bird, having received the boon,
spoke then to Śakra, the best of weapon-bearers:
"O slayer of Vṛtra, this thunderbolt has been obtained by you as a boon from the Grandfather."
Therefore, desiring honor, I relinquish this single hair. O slayer of Vṛtra, if you are able with this king of weapons, strike him with your supreme power; I shall depart unharmed.
Then, O Bhārata, that thunderbolt, by its own momentum, struck him with supreme force; yet it did not burn him severely. Thereupon, O King, the celestial sages traveling through the sky—
Seeing that vajra stuck in the bird's feather, they spoke these words:
"The great weapon of the King of the Gods, the eternal slayer of Vṛtra, is stuck in the feather of this Suparṇa, the Garuḍa among birds."
Thus the powerful Vainateya, the bird Suparṇa,
is known by the sages as belonging both to Agni and to Viṣṇu;
he is highly praised in the Vedas and bestows the fruit of the path to heaven.
They seized the slender feathers of the *suparṇa* and likewise those of the peacock;
all the peacocks, filled with wonder, rushed toward the wielder of the thunderbolt (*vajrin*).
Then, seeing his excellent weapon, the thunderbolt, stuck fast, and seeing the sages, the thousand-eyed Indra suddenly said this to Suparṇa:
"I do not see your power, O Suparṇa; therefore, I shall not fight with you."

When this was said, I replied: "Protection cannot be afforded by me in any other way. This thunderbolt shall return with me, just as it came. Then, once the thousand-eyed one had departed, Garuḍa likewise withdrew.
O descendant of Bharata, Garuḍa quickly approached Kadrū, having seized the nectar of immortality;
"I have swiftly brought this nectar for the sake of my mother."
"Let Kadrū become a slave today, and let Vinatā be the one who practices righteousness.
Welcome, O son of Vinatā; this nectar has been well-offered."
"O son, today your auspicious mother has become a slave, overcome by desire.
When this was said, Vinatā then arrived at the house;
having brought her there according to custom, the bird, the best among the strong, [addressed her].

Remembering the victory achieved through deceit, he now seeks to exact vengeance upon his mother; and as for the slaughter of the serpent lords, those who were the hairs of that horse have become like black clouds— indeed, you have been conquered by deceit.
Then the bird, the best among the strong, spoke to her with justice;
he quickly seized the nectar and flew up with great speed. Having taken that nectar, the unconquered one departed swiftly.
Kadrū, the mother of the serpents, spoke thus to Suparṇa:

O Suparṇa,
today for the sake of my mother, you have performed the bringing of the nectar;
by your word, I too shall bring this nectar.
"This has been quickly brought here, and my mother has been released.
Now I shall take it back again to that place from which it was brought by me.
If you would say to me, 'Give me the nectar,'" he said.
"Whether I should do so or not, you are certainly not capable of immortality.
Bhīṣma said:

Then, having gone there, Garuḍa said to Purandara:

And Vāsava, filled with joy, exclaimed, "By good fortune! By good fortune!

Then all the sages and the gods, O bull of the Bharata race, spoke joyfully to Purandara: "Let Garuḍa receive a boon.
Thereupon, the Lord of Śacī, as if smiling, spoke these words.

having divided himself for the sake of protecting Dharma, the eater of serpents [will take birth].
O best of the Pāṇḍavas, this Garuḍa, the king of birds, is celebrated as Suparṇa and Vainateya; may it be well with you. Thus has this narrative been proclaimed by me, O best of givers.
"O mighty-armed one, what more shall I tell you concerning Suparṇa?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, regarding those in the world who, having made a promise to Brahmins..."
"O Mahāmati, who are those that do not give out of delusion?
O Bhīṣma, my conviction regarding the duty of giving has always been this.
Tell me this truthfully, O best among the upholders of dharma."
"Those evil-minded men who, having given their word,
do not deliver [what was promised]," Bhīṣma said: "He who, having promised, does not give— whether it be little or much— "

All his hopes are destroyed, like the fruit of offspring for a eunuch. O Bhārata, whatever merit he may have earned during the interval between the night that the sinner is born and the night that he perishes— [all that is lost].
O bull among the Bharatas, whatever he has offered in sacrifice, whatever he has given as a gift, or whatever austerity he has practiced— all of that is destroyed.
"O best of the Bharatas, having heard this with a highly disciplined intellect, those who know the treatises on dharma have declared these words; moreover,
those who know the treatises on dharma cite this as well."
He is liberated by means of a thousand horses with black ears. In this very context, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between a jackal and a monkey.
O scorcher of foes, those two were indeed friends in their former human state;
having entered other wombs— namely those of a jackal and a monkey—
they then conversed there with one another regarding their friendship.
Then, seeing the jackal devouring corpses in the middle of the cremation ground, the monkey, recollecting his former birth,
said: "What terrible and evil deed did you commit in the past?"
"You who eat corpses, putrid and loathsome, in the cremation ground!"—
thus addressed, the jackal then replied to the monkey:
"Having promised it to a brahmin, I have not yet brought it to him."
"O monkey, because of that [deed], I have fallen into this sinful womb;
therefore, being hungry, I eat such food as this. This is how I have told you how I became a jackal."
The monkey said:
"Tell me, by what action did you attain this state of being a monkey?
In the past, out of greed, you stole fruits belonging to others."
Bhīṣma said:
"Because of that defect in my past actions, I attained the state of a monkey.
Having thus conversed with one another regarding their respective defects of karma, they [departed].
The jackal and the monkey also returned the way they had come.
Bhīṣma said:
O best of kings, the jackal spoke once again to the monkey.
“What sinful deed did you commit that you have become a monkey?
He replied: “I was a monkey who subsisted on the fruit of brahmins;
therefore, a wise person should never seize the property of a brahmin.”

"In a dispute over boundaries, what has been promised must be released and given. O King, I heard this being spoken by a Brāhmaṇa who was recounting an ancient and meritorious tale concerning the knowledge of Dharma.

Furthermore, O lord of the people, O Pāṇḍava, I have also heard this story told by Kṛṣṇa himself in the past concerning a Brāhmaṇa: "The wealth of a Brāhmaṇa must not be seized; one must always forgive them."
"Even children, the poor, and the wretched should not be despised;
in this very way, the brahmins always instruct me:
'Once a promise has been made, it must be fulfilled; one should never cause the hopes of brahmins to be frustrated.'"
O Lord of the Earth, a Brahmin who has previously formed an expectation is considered to be like a well-kindled, blazing fire; such is he when,
filled with anger, he looks upon someone because of that prior expectation.
For it would consume him, O King, just as an insatiable fire consumes dry grass;
yet when that very same person, being pleased, welcomes one with his words,
he becomes like a healing medicine within his domain, O Bhārata.
Sons, grandsons, cattle, kinsmen, as well as ministers,
the city, and the countryside— all these flourish through peace, as if by a desired sacrifice. For this indeed is seen here to be the supreme power of a Brāhmaṇa.
Like the thousand-rayed sun upon the surface of the earth,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one must therefore certainly give what has been promised here,
if one desires to attain a noble birth, O best of the Bharatas.
For by giving to a Brāhmaṇa, the unsurpassed heaven is certainly attained;
indeed, it is possible to reach it, for giving is a great act.
By what is given from here, the deities as well as the ancestors are sustained.
Therefore, gifts should be given to the Brāhmaṇas by one who possesses discernment;
for, O best of the Bharatas, the Brāhmaṇa is said to be a great sacred ford (*tīrtha*). Indeed, a Brāhmaṇa should never go [to a house] unhonored, even at any time whatsoever.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O royal sage, does a fault accrue to one who offers instruction out of a spirit of friendship and affection to a person of inferior birth, or not?"
"O Grandfather, I desire this to be explained by you in its true essence,
for the course of dharma is subtle, and in it men are indeed bewildered.
Bhīṣma said:

13,010.003a Here, O King, I shall relate to you; listen according to the tradition. 13,010.003b O King, as it was rightly and duly received, so was that ill-spoken word heard by me previously from the sages as they were speaking.
Instruction must not be given to anyone who is devoid of caste;
it is said that a great fault accrues to the teacher if he provides instruction. One should not teach a Śūdra in this world, nor likewise should one officiate at his sacrifices.
"O King, O bull of the Bharatas, hear from me this illustrative example regarding the consequences of harsh speech, O Yudhiṣṭhira,
as it occurred in the past on the auspicious slopes of the Himavat at a hermitage of Brahmins."
There was a holy hermitage, filled with various groves of trees,
thick with many shrubs and creepers, frequented by deer and birds, resounded by throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and beautiful with its blossoming forests.
It was crowded with many observers of vows and graced by ascetics;
it was filled with highly fortunate Brahmins who resembled the blazing sun and were perfected in their restraints and observances.
O best of the Bharatas, it resounded with the chanting of the Vedas by those who were consecrated, self-restrained in diet, and perfected in soul; O bull of the Bharatas,
it was frequented by many Vālakhilyas and ascetics.
There, a certain Śūdra, filled with compassion, having summoned his resolve,
came to the hermitage and was honored by the ascetics. Upon seeing those hosts of sages, who were like gods and possessed of great majesty, he [was moved].
"O Bhārata, let various initiations be performed; rejoice!
(13,010.011c). Then, O bull of the Bharatas, the thought occurred to him regarding asceticism:
"O Bhārata, he then spoke to the head of the community, grasping his feet. (13,010.012a-c)
"O bull among the twice-born, through your grace I wish to practice dharma.
Therefore, O Blessed One, you ought to instruct me and initiate me into the wandering life.
O Blessed One, O best of beings, I am inferior in caste; by birth I am a Śūdra."
"I wish to perform service; be gracious to me who have sought refuge.
The Kulapati said:
"It is not possible for a Śūdra here to live while assuming the outward marks [of an ascetic]."
13,010.015c "If it is your intention, then sit down; be intent upon service.
13,010.015d Through service you shall attain the highest worlds, of this there is no doubt.
13,010.016 Bhīṣma said:
O King, having been addressed thus by the sage, that Śūdra reflected:
"What should be done by me in this matter? For my faith in dharma is supreme.
Let it be understood thus: I shall do what is pleasing to myself."
Having gone a considerable distance from the hermitage, he constructed a hut there; and having established an altar, a sacred ground, and shrines for the deities,
O best of the Bharatas, he dwelt there happily, remaining steadfast in his vows.
Having performed consecrations and observances in the temples of the deities,
and having offered oblations and made burnt offerings, he worshipped the gods as well;
endowed with resolve and self-restraint, subsisting on fruit, he had his senses fully conquered.
With medicinal herbs and fruits always kept at hand,
he honored guests who arrived according to the prescribed rites;
in this manner, indeed, a very long time passed for him.

Then, by chance, a sage came to that hermitage. Having honored the ṛṣi with a welcome, he satisfied him according to the prescribed rites. After engaging in agreeable conversation, he questioned him properly.
O bull of the Bharata race, that rishi, possessed of supreme splendor, righteous in soul, and with senses fully restrained,
went thus many times to the hermitage to see that śūdra, O best of men.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, that Śūdra said to the ascetic:
"I shall perform the ancestral rites; grant me your favor in this matter.
"So be it," the Brahmin replied to him, O bull of the Bharatas.
Then, in order to provide for the Brahmin, the Śūdra, having purified himself, brought wild rice grains; that Śūdra,
having become pure and having paid his respects, then brought water for the sage's feet.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, he brought darbha grass and wild herbs,
as well as a purifying seat and a cushion. Then,
turning to the south, [he placed] the cushion with its head-end toward the north.
Seeing that it had been made improperly, the seer then said to him:
"Make this with its head facing east; be pure and face the north.
And that Śūdra did everything exactly as the seer had instructed.

The wise man [performed] those rites with *darbha* grass and other materials exactly as instructed; the entire procedure for offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*) had been taught by that ascetic seer, and he remained steadfast on the path of dharma in the performance of ancestral rites.
When the rites for the ancestors had been performed, he was dismissed and departed.
Then, after a long time, that Śūdra ascetic,
performing austerities in the forest, met his death through that very merit.
13,010.031e He was born into the lineage of great kings, possessed of great splendor.
13,010.032a Likewise, O dear one, that rishi, having met the law of time, was born as a brahmin in the family of the domestic priest, O bull of the Bharatas.
Thus, those two Śūdra sages were born there at that time;
they both grew up in due course and became proficient in the sciences. The Ṛṣi became firmly established in both the Atharvaveda and the Veda.
When the application of the *kalpa* had been completed and he had attained supreme mastery in astrology,
their friendship also grew to the highest degree of affection. And when his father had passed away, O Bhārata, he performed the rites of purification.
That prince was consecrated as king by the subjects;
and that seer, having been consecrated, became the consecrated domestic priest.
Having placed him at the head [of the priesthood], O bull of the Bharatas, he dwelt there in happiness.
He ruled the kingdom with righteousness, protecting his subjects; he was constantly engaged in the recitation of auspicious prayers and repeatedly occupied with religious duties.
Yet, upon seeing the domestic priest, the king would smile and even laugh at him.

13,010.037 Thus, O King, he mocked the family priest on many occasions. 13,010.038 But the priest, having observed that lord of men repeatedly and seeing him constantly smiling with derision, became filled with resentment.
Then, in that empty place, the priest met with the king and delighted him with agreeable conversation. Thereupon,
O bull of the Bharatas, that priest spoke to the lord of men.
"O you of great splendor, I desire one boon granted by you.
The King said:
"I would grant you a hundred boons, O best of the twice-born; how much more so a single one?"
"Out of affection and great respect, there is indeed nothing that I would not give to you.
The family priest said:
"If you are pleased, O King, I desire one boon."
"O Great King, speak the truth; do not speak what is false.
Bhīṣma said:
"The king, Yudhiṣṭhira, replied to him, 'So be it.'"
"If I know it, I shall speak; if I do not know it, I will not speak falsely.
The family priest said:
"In the proclamation of an auspicious day (*puṇyāha-vācana*) and constantly in various religious duties (*dharma-kṛtya*)."

"O King, why do you always laugh at me when looking upon me during the peace-offerings (*śānti-homa*)? Indeed, my mind becomes filled with shame because of your laughing; I adjure you by my love, O King, you ought not to speak otherwise."
"For there must be a cause for this; you should not laugh without reason. My curiosity is very great; tell it to me in truth.
The king said:

"O Brahmin, when you have spoken thus, even that which ought not to be said must certainly be told; listen with a focused mind, O twice-born one. Understand, O best of the twice-born, how it happened in your previous body."
"O Brahmin, I remember my former birth; listen to me with attention. Formerly, I was a Śūdra who was intensely devoted to asceticism.
And you, O best of the twice-born, were at that time a seer of fierce penance."
"O Brahmin, may you indeed be pleased, for with a mind intent on showing me favor,
you previously gave instruction regarding the ancestral rites, O sinless one,
O best of sages, concerning the seat of grass, the darbha blades, and the offerings to the gods and the ancestors."
"O best of Brahmins, it was due to this fault in my past action that you were born as my domestic priest; I too have become a king. Behold the reversal of time!
Indeed, because of my instruction, you have obtained this fruit for my sake."
"For this reason, O Brahmin, best of the twice-born, I laugh at you.
It is not out of contempt for you, O Brahmin, that I laugh; you are my superior.
My anger arises from the contrary situation, and because of it, my mind is tormented."
"I remember my birth with yours; therefore, I am indeed laughing at you.
For thus has your fierce asceticism been destroyed by my instruction. Abandoning the office of domestic priest, strive for rebirth."
"O twice-born one, may you not obtain another womb inferior to this. Accept this wealth, O Brahmin; become purified in soul, O best of men.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, dismissed by the king, the brahmin gave away wealth, land, and villages in their entirety as numerous gifts to other brahmins; thereafter,
that best of the twice-born performed the penances as prescribed.
Having visited sacred fords and bestowed various gifts,
including cows upon the brahmins, that twice-born man became purified in soul;
returning to that very hermitage, he practiced intense austerity.
Then, O best of kings, that brahmin attained supreme perfection and became highly esteemed among those residents of the hermitage. Thus, O best of monarchs, did that ṛṣi undergo great hardship.
A Brāhmaṇa must not speak [of such matters] to people of a lower caste;
therefore, O King, a Brāhmaṇa should always avoid giving instruction [to them].
For a twice-born man who gives instruction [in this manner] shall incur great hardship.
A king should always seek counsel from the best of the twice-born;
indeed, he should not speak here to people of lower castes.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas—these three castes are the twice-born.
O King, a Brāhmaṇa does not incur fault by speaking of these matters;
therefore, the virtuous should not speak of anything before anyone,
for the course of Dharma is subtle and difficult to comprehend for those who have not disciplined their souls.

Therefore, O King, sages respectfully undertake vows of silence and initiation; out of fear of ill-spoken words, they do not utter anything at all. They are righteous, endowed with virtues, and devoted to truth and uprightness.
Those struck by harsh speech incur misfortune in this world.
Instruction should never be given to anyone at any time;
for through such instruction, a Brahmin would incur that very sin.
Therefore, having reflected, a wise person who desires righteousness should speak;
for instruction given through a mixture of truth and falsehood indeed causes harm. One who is questioned here should speak only after having determined the opposite [of what might be false].
And that instruction should be given by which one may attain the Dharma.
All this has been told to you once the instruction has been performed;
for great affliction arises [from it], therefore one should not instruct [it] anywhere.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, O bull of the Bharatas, in what kind of man or in what kind of woman does the lotus-seated Śrī always dwell? Tell me that, O Grandfather."
13,011.002 Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, I shall relate to you what was seen and heard. Rukmiṇī questioned [the sage] in the presence of the son of Devakī.
Having seen Śrī, whose face was like a lotus, blazing as she sat upon the lap of Nārāyaṇa,
her beautiful eyes were wide with wonder and curiosity.
The mother of Makaradhvaja asked:
"Which beings do you serve here?
Which ones remain present that you do not serve?"
"O beloved of the one who has become the Lord of the Three Worlds,
tell me the truth of these things, O daughter of a great seer.
Thus was Śrī addressed at that time.
In the presence of the goddess and the one whose banner is Garuḍa,
the moon-faced woman, being gracious, spoke these sweet and captivating words.
I dwell with a man who is truthful, fortunate, and bold; one who is skillful, engaged in his work, free from anger, devoted to the gods, and grateful.

I do not dwell in a man who has conquered his senses, who is always resolute in spirit, and whose nature is not prone to unrighteous action; nor do I dwell in one who is an atheist, a mixer of castes, or ungrateful.
Not with one of broken conduct, nor with one of cruel conduct;
nor with a thief, nor with one who harbors malice toward gurus;
nor with those who are deficient in splendor, strength, courage, and essence.
O Goddess, I do not dwell among such men who rejoice and grow angry here and there,
whose desires are merely dormant.
He who desires nothing for himself,
and whose inner self is impaired by his own nature— he [is superior] to those who always delight in meager contentment.
"O Goddess, I do not dwell among men;
I dwell among those of virtuous character, who know the Dharma,
who are high-souled, who serve their elders, who are self-controlled, and who possess knowledge of the true nature of beings."
In those whose time is never spent in vain, who are always devoted to ritual bathing and purification, who cherish celibacy, austerity, knowledge,
cows, and the twice-born; and in women who are patient, self-controlled, and devoted to the gods and the twice-born.
I dwell among those whose conduct is truth, who delight in their own nature, whose household utensils are pure, who take pleasure in grain, and who,
knowing the Dharma, are devoted to their own duty.
To one who is devoted to serving the elders, self-controlled, disciplined in soul, intent on patience,
and capable; and likewise to women who are patient and self-restrained.
I dwell among those women who are endowed with truthfulness, essential nature, and uprightness,
and who are honored by gods and the twice-born—
women who scatter their household utensils and act without foresight.
I avoid such a woman as she who always speaks contrary to her husband, who delights in the house of another, and who is shameless.
Fickle, unclean, and licking [her lips],
devoid of fortitude and fond of quarreling,
she was constantly overcome by sleep and remained lying down.
I avoid such a woman as this,
though she be always truthful, pleasant to behold,
endowed with good fortune, and possessed of virtuous qualities.
I dwell among women who are devoted to their husbands, who are of virtuous character and well-adorned; I dwell in vehicles, in maidens, and in ornaments.
I dwell in sacrifices and in rain-bearing clouds, in blossoming lotus ponds,
and in the autumnal paths of the stars.
Upon the mountains, in cow-pens, and likewise in forests;
at lakes filled with blooming blue and white lotuses;
and at rivers resounding with the cries of swans;
Adorned with the beautiful sounds of the cries of curlews,
graced by expansive banks and lakes,
and frequented by ascetics, perfected beings, and brahmins;
I dwell eternally in waters that are very abundant,
yet whose currents are agitated by lions and elephants— waters that are like those of a rutting elephant, a bull, or a lord of men.
In that house where the sacrificial fire is perpetually offered, and where cows, Brahmins, and the deities are honored, [there dwell] the lion-throne and the virtuous man. (13.011.017a)
In that sacrifice where people offer oblations into the fire,
where they honor cows, Brahmins, and the deities,
and wherein the carrier of oblations is invoked—
In that house where offerings of flowers are made at the proper time to cows, Brahmins, honored deities, and other divinities, I always take up my residence.

I dwell constantly among the twice-born who are ever devoted to the study of their own scriptures; always among the Kṣatriya who is ever intent upon his duty; and among the Vaiśya who is devoted to agriculture.
And in the Śūdra who is constantly devoted to service,
I dwell with a single-minded focus upon Nārāyaṇa; through his entire being, he has become my very body.
For in him is established the greatest dharma,
as well as devotion to Brahman and kindness;
O Goddess, I do not dwell within his body.
It is not possible for me to describe it here in this way; rather,
that man in whom I dwell with my very being increases in virtue, fame, wealth, and desire.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me the expiation for those who are ungrateful,
and for those who, deluded by ignorance, show contempt toward their mothers, fathers, and teachers."
"O dear one, I also wish to hear in truth, O mighty-armed Bhīṣma, about the destination of those others who are ungrateful and shameless."
O dear one, the destiny of the ungrateful is an eternal residence in hell for many years;
those who do not abide by the teachings of their mother, father,
and teacher are born among worms, insects, and ants, or among stationary plants.
For indeed, their rebirth in the human state is difficult to obtain again.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history:
the great seer Vatsanābha, possessed of great wisdom and firm in his vows.
The Brahman-sage, having become an anthill, performs most intense ascetic penance.
While he was performing that penance, O bull of the Bharatas,
Vāsava sent down a very great rain accompanied by lightning and thunder.
There, the subduer of Pāka (Indra) released rain for seven days;
with eyes closed, the twice-born one indeed received that downpour while cold winds blew.
With its peak shattered and ruined, the anthill was struck by a thunderbolt.
While that great-souled Vatsanābha was being beaten,
Dharma, out of compassion for him, then manifested as kindness.
As he was reflecting upon the most virtuous Brahmarṣi performing his austerities,
a thought born of his own nature quickly arose within him, appropriate to the situation:
"Having assumed my own form as a buffalo, vast and captivating..."
Standing upon four legs for the sake of protecting Vatsanābha,
when the rain accompanied by wind had ceased,
then Dharma, the best among the upholders of dharma, appeared in the form of a buffalo.
Slowly leaving the anthill, O bull of the Bharatas, he fled away. While that downpour of rain continued, the great ascetic gazed upon the vast quarters of the sky and the peaks of the mountains.
Seeing the entire earth submerged by water,
and beholding those reservoirs of water, the brahmin became overjoyed;
filled with wonder, he thought, "By whom have I been protected from the rain?"

13,011.020d@002_0032 He saw a buffalo standing there not far away. 13,011.020d@002_0033 How is it that one who is a lover of Dharma is seen even in an animal womb? 13,011.020d@002_0034 Therefore, this auspicious buffalo is stationed upon a stone slab.
"He shall become stout, strong, and full of flesh;
this thought has arisen in that sage, born from his attachment to the Dharma.
Those who are ungrateful and those who betray the trusting go to hell."
"I see no way whatsoever for those who are ungrateful to find atonement in this world,
except by the renunciation of life— according to the words of those who know the Dharma. Without having provided maintenance for my parents and without having given the teacher’s fee,"

Having incurred ungratefulness, the atonement ends only with death; if one neglects a request for help, it is a supreme minor offense (*upapātaka*). Therefore, I shall renounce my life for the sake of expiation.
Having gone to the peak of Mount Meru with a detached inner self,
Dharma was intent on casting off his body, desiring to perform an act of expiation.
And that righteous soul, the knower of dharma, was seized by the hand according to the law,
O highly wise Vatsanābha who lives for many hundreds of years; I am well-pleased with your selfless renunciation of yourself.
Thus all those upholders of the Dharma reflected upon what had been done and what remained to be done;
there was no one whose mind was not struck with grief for Vatsanābha,
except for him who, being blameless and capable, practiced the Dharma in every way.
"Turn back, O one of great wisdom, for you are a pure-souled and eternal being.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In the union of a woman and a man, whose touch would be superior?"
"O King, you ought to explain this doubt of mine to me exactly as it is.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
Just as in ancient times there was enmity between Śakra and Bhaṅgāśvana—
formerly there was a royal seer named Bhaṅgāśvana who was exceedingly righteous;
being childless, O tiger among men, he performed a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son.
The royal sage named Agniṣṭuṃ was possessed of great strength and was hated by Indra. This sacrifice is prescribed for mortals seeking atonement and for one desiring a son.
But when the highly fortunate Indra, the lord of the gods, learned of that sacrifice, [he took action].
Seeking a lapse in that royal seer of restrained soul,
O King, he could find no such lapse in that high-souled one. Then, after some time had passed, as the king was wandering on a hunt—
Thinking, "This is the opportunity," Śakra deluded the king;
and the royal seer, wandering with a single horse, was bewildered by Indra. At that time, the king, afflicted by hunger and thirst, could not discern the directions.
Running here and there, O King, afflicted by fatigue and thirst,
he saw a most beautiful lake filled with excellent water. Having plunged into the lake, my dear son, he caused his horse to drink.
Then that best of kings, having tied his horse, which had drunk its fill, to a tree, entered the water;
having bathed there, the king indeed attained womanhood. Seeing himself transformed into a woman, that most excellent of monarchs was filled with shame.
With his entire being consumed by anxiety, his senses and mind agitated, he thought:
"How shall I mount the horse? How indeed shall I go to the city?
I have performed the Agniṣṭut sacrifice and begotten a hundred legitimate sons."
I shall indeed declare those [omens] born of great powers; however,
among our own wives and among the people of the city and the countryside,
there has appeared softness, thinness, and likewise a state of dejection.
Whether it be curiosity arising from the grace of gestures, expressions, and other feminine charms,
or the qualities of women as described by the seers who perceive the true meaning of the principles of Dharma—
exertion, toughness, and vigor are the qualities of a man.

"My manliness has utterly perished; somehow womanhood has come upon me. How can I, being in this female state, venture to mount the horse again? Then, with great distress, the lord of men mounted the horse.
"O dear one, O best of kings, having become a woman, he returned again to the city.
Your sons, wives, servants, and the people of both the city and the countryside,
perceiving this and wondering 'What indeed is this?', were struck with the utmost amazement."
Then that royal sage, who had become a woman and was the best among speakers, said:
"Surrounded by my forces, I set out on a hunt with great determination;
bewildered and deluded by fate, I entered a formidable forest."

In a most terrible forest, afflicted by thirst and deprived of my senses, I saw a lake of exquisite beauty surrounded by birds. Having plunged into it, I clearly became a woman; this was surely due to fate, there is no doubt.
As if never satiated with his sons, his wives, and his wealth,
that best of kings, having become a woman, addressed his wives and ministers by their names and lineages, and then spoke to his sons.
"Enjoy the kingdom with mutual affection; I shall go to the forest, my sons.
Having thus consecrated his hundred sons, the king departed for the forest.
Having spoken thus to his hundred sons, he indeed went to the forest.
Having consecrated his hundred sons as kings, that monarch retired to the forest. O dear one, an ascetic took up with that woman in the hermitage;
through that ascetic, he too had a hundred sons born in the hermitage.
Then, taking those sons born of her former birth, she spoke to them:
"O sons, you were born as sons when I was a man, and these hundred sons were born when I was a woman;
O dear children, let us enjoy the kingdom together in brotherly affection."
Then those brothers together enjoyed that kingdom. Seeing them enjoying that supreme sovereignty with brotherly affection,
the lord of the gods, overwhelmed by resentment, began to reflect.

"I have done a service for this royal seer; I have not done him any harm. Then Śatakratu, the king of the gods, assuming the form of a brahmin, went to the city and sowed dissension among those sons of the king.
There is no brotherly affection among brothers, even those who are sons of the same father; the gods and asuras, though both born of Kaśyapa, quarreled for the sake of the kingdom.
You are the offspring of Bhaṅgāśvana, while they are the sons of the other ascetic.
The gods and the asuras alike were the sons of Kaśyapa;
yet your ancestral kingdom is being enjoyed by the sons of ascetics.
Having been sown with dissension by Indra, they have caused one another to fall in battle.
13,012.028c Having heard that, the female ascetic was also deeply distressed and wept aloud.
13,012.029a Then Indra, having approached her in the guise of a Brahmin, questioned her:
13,012.029c "O lovely-faced one, by what sorrow are you so tormented that you weep?"
Then, seeing the Brahmin, that woman spoke piteously:
"O Brahmin, two hundred sons have been struck down by Time;
O learned one, I was the king there, and by me [were raised] a hundred sons."
O best of the twice-born,
once, while wandering lost in the dense forest during a hunt,
that man of handsome form and great prowess plunged into a lake and was transformed into a woman, O most excellent of brahmins.

Having established my sons in the kingdom, I then departed for the forest. O Brahmin, a hundred sons were begotten by me upon my wife in the hermitage by a high-souled ascetic; they have been brought back to the city by me.
"O twice-born one, through the course of time, enmity indeed arose among them. O best of Brahmins, overwhelmed by fate, I grieve over this.
Seeing her thus distressed, Indra spoke these harsh words:
"O blessed one, in the past you caused me unbearable suffering by performing a sacrifice against Indra while disregarding me, O evil-minded woman.
I am Indra, O foolish one; I have exacted my vengeance upon you."
But upon seeing Indra, the royal sage fell at his feet with his head bowed, saying:
"Be gracious, O best of the thirty gods! This sacrifice was performed out of a desire for a son, O tiger among the thirty gods; you ought to forgive me for that."
Indra, the lord of the gods, wielder of the thunderbolt, possessed of great strength,
mounted upon the elephant Airāvata— O thousand-eyed one, homage be unto you!
By his prostration, Indra was well-pleased and granted him a boon.
"O King, tell me which of your sons shall live—
those who were born while you were a woman, or those who were born when you became a man?
Then the female ascetic, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to Śakra.
"O Vāsava, may those who were born while I was a woman live for me!
Indra, both amazed and delighted, questioned that woman again:
"How is it that those sons produced by you as a man are so hateful to you?"
"How is it that the affection felt for those born [as my children] when I was a woman is greater than this?
I wish to hear the reason; you ought to tell it to me here.
The woman said:
"A woman's affection is indeed greater, and not so that of a man.
Therefore, O Śakra, let those who were born from what was done by a woman live.
Bhīṣma said:
When this had been said, Indra was pleased and spoke these words:
"O speaker of truth, let all your sons here live!
And choose a boon, O king of kings, whatever you desire, O observer of noble vows."
"Whether it be manhood or womanhood that you desire from me," [Indra said].
The woman replied:
"O Śakra, O Vāsava, since you are pleased with me, I choose womanhood alone."
Thus addressed, the lord of the gods replied to that woman:
"O powerful one, why do you desire womanhood after having abandoned manhood?
Thus addressed, that best of kings, who had become a woman, replied:
"In union with a man, a woman’s pleasure is always greater;
for this reason, O Śakra, I choose womanhood alone. And I truly find greater delight in being a woman, O best of gods."
"Indeed, I am pleased by your state as a woman; you may go, O Lord of the Thirty-three.
Having said, "So be it," and having taken leave of her, he departed for heaven.
Thus, O Great King, it is said that a woman possesses superior affection.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What should be done by a man who seeks the welfare of his journey through this world?
How indeed should he conduct his worldly course, and what character should he cultivate?
Bhīṣma said:
Devotion to the divine Nārāyaṇa and to Śaṅkara should be cultivated through the worship of the virtuous,
through meditation, through recitations, and by means of one's own duties performed with pure luster.
One should abandon the ten paths of action: threefold action by way of the body, fourfold by way of speech, and likewise threefold by way of the mind;
specifically, the taking of life, theft, and also adultery with another's wife.
One should completely avoid the three evils of the body in every respect:
idle chatter, harsh speech, slander, and likewise falsehood.
O Indra among kings, one should neither utter nor even contemplate these four [evils] of speech.

Absence of covetousness regarding the property of others, friendliness toward all sentient beings, and the conviction that there is a fruit for actions— one should practice these three kinds [of conduct] with the mind.
Therefore, a person should not perform unwholesome deeds through speech, body, or mind.

For by performing good and evil deeds, one indeed experiences their respective fruits. Indeed, one who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa and performs only auspicious deeds in this world shall, through his grace, attain that very supreme and subtle state.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, my heart is pained because I do not find the ultimate [truth] in this world;
all this universe, both stationary and moving, is impermanent."
"O Grandfather, nothing appears more meritorious than Nārāyaṇa.
For Nārāyaṇa is the Soul of the Universe, the Supreme Person, the lotus-eyed one."—
Bhīṣma.
"O sinless Yudhiṣṭhira, you have heard all this concerning the son of Devakī;
O highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira, it was also witnessed by me in the battle.
—Yudhiṣṭhira.
O Indra among kings, from you alone have I heard the abundant duties of kingship;
and I have heard the entire Purāṇa as it was related by Nārada—
the secret narrative of Nārāyaṇa, which destroys the threefold afflictions.
O highly fortunate one, by your grace, you have indeed explained the exclusive regulations of dharma, formulated both in brief and in detail;
for the protection of the world is the very office of that Lord of honeyed intellect.
The rules of hospitality, the ascetic practices, and the various observances;
the sacrifices such as the Vājapeya, which are renowned through Vedic declarations;
and the rituals accomplished with material wealth, protected by the Agnihotra.

The various *japayajñas* (sacrifices of recitation) of the ascetic Brahmins are declared to be of eleven kinds; likewise, the *haviryajñas* (oblation sacrifices) of the twice-born are proclaimed to be of eleven kinds, as well as their specific fruits and the rules for gathering grain (*uñchadharmas*).
The great sacrifices prescribed for the twice-born to be performed day after day,
the duties regarding the hearing of the Vedas, the fruit of the Brahmayajña,
the rules for Vedic vows, and the Vedic observances as well.

Svāhā and Svadhā, as well as the fruit of sacrifices and charitable works performed; the fruit of serving each successive stage of life (āśrama), and the fruit of reaching the final perfection of each stage of life, O Great-minded One.
The fruit of fasting for months and fortnights has been correctly described; as have the worlds of those who do not eat, of men who perform the "five-fire" penance,
of those who have set out on the path of heroes, and the destiny of those who maintain the sacred fire.
Whatever fruit is proclaimed for those who practice the "five fires" in summer, for those who dwell in water during the winter, and for those who sleep on the bare ground during the rains;
and whatever fruit is remembered in the world for the twice-born who wander with a wheel— [all that is attained by this].

Whatever fruit has been proclaimed for gifts such as food, and whatever arising of merit belongs to men who have bathed in all the sacred fords, and whatever are the duties of kings who properly protect their subjects in this world— [all these are attained by him].

Those in the world who are devoted to the vow of truth, those who have exerted themselves at sacred fords, those who are dedicated to their mothers and fathers, and those who rely upon the conduct due to teachers; likewise, those who protect cows and Brahmins, and those who transcend the boundaries of the kingdom.
Those who, fearless and relying on their inner strength (*sattva*), abandon their lives while facing the enemy;
those who give gifts accompanied by a thousand-fold sacrificial fees, O best of givers;
and those who properly perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*) according to the great vows—[all these attain that same goal].
O best of the Kurus, I have also heard the prescriptions for yoga as proclaimed in the scriptures, as well as the Vedas and other sacred revelations (śrutis),
and the definitive conclusions of the established doctrines (siddhānta-nirṇaya) issued from the mouth of Dvaipāyana.
I have heard the five great sacrifices in which everything is established;
I have also heard in their entirety all the dharmas that exist within their various divisions.
For they were spoken thus by the virtuous, and cannot be refuted.
Among these religious duties, it is said that the Vaiṣṇava rite is indeed supreme;
the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu protects his devotee like his own body.
For whatever action is performed here according to desire by the best of the twice-born, [it is fulfilled].
"The seer Dvaipāyana has declared that the fruit [of one's actions] must necessarily be experienced;
and at the end of enjoyment, a fall is the destiny previously proclaimed.
These things do not bring me joy, for I consider them to have sorrow as their ultimate result."

O one of great splendor, I consider dwelling in the womb to be more painful than death. O Lord, those sufferings which a person encounters at the end of his allotted lifespan are far more grievous than those he experiences here while dwelling in the womb.
Then, O dear one, at the time of emerging from the womb and as the karmas draw near, a man experiences an even more intense and piercing pain;
therefore, O Bhārata, this conviction has arisen in me regarding these matters of dharma.
O best of the Kurus, O high-minded one, through your grace I desire to know that Dharma which destroys old age, birth,
and death, and by which one may overcome the scorching Vaitaraṇī river and the forest of sword-leaves.
There are cauldrons heated by fire, as well as the path of razor edges;
and the most terrible Śālmalī tree, made of iron and possessing fearsome thorns—
for the sake of one's mother and father, and for the sake of friends and companions.
The seer Dvaipāyana has declared that for those men who have committed sins here for their own sake, the arising of the fruit is painful—
[the suffering] of those boiling in the Kumbhīpāka hell and of those crying out while tormented by spikes.
For those being cast into the Raurava hell, their souls crushed by blows,
groaning as they are mangled and drinking their own blood—
there is no compassion for them as they cry out from the machinery of that place.
With throats and palates parched by thirst, agitated and deprived of their senses,
tormented by every kind of suffering and crying out in the pain of affliction,
they indeed wail, filling the ten directions.
One person commits sins, yet the kinsmen share in them;
alone he reaps the fruit in the painful abode of Vaivasvata.
By what means may one not go to this state, slippery with excrement, urine, and bones?
In the midst of excrement, urine, and worms, inhabited by many creatures—
what other hell is ordained beyond dwelling in the womb? For it is there that the experience of dwelling is ordained as dwelling within the belly.
One born [into this world] experiences vast suffering, yet you remain free from fever. This desire is not attained once a human being has been born;
for here, sufferings of mind, speech, and body enter him.
By these [karmas], one becomes dependent and is tormented by terrifying things;
through them, one enters the womb and is born thus against one's will.
Helpless, the living being yearns for existence, and indeed, it proceeds only in a state of helplessness.

Indeed, one inevitably undergoes the destruction of one's form through old age; one inevitably reaches the dissolution of the body and decays while utterly powerless. For in this way, death is always occurring among men in an uncertain manner.
Some die in the womb, and likewise others while being born;
many die after being born, and others while still in their youth; they perish in the prime of life, while the elderly are already dead.

Who would not tremble at birth, even if he were the Self-Existent One himself? How much less so one like me, O dear one, who is subject to death? O best of the Kurus, my mind is perpetually possessed by fear.
O high-minded one, I do not find peace even for a moment; though eternally devoid of those qualities, I have become concealed within Time as its very self.
Though nourished by various kinds of food and clothed in diverse garments, [I remain thus].
His limbs were anointed with sandalwood and aloe-wood, and he was adorned with jewels and pearls;
he traveled in various kinds of vehicles, cherished exclusively,
and [attended] by women whose forms were exalted by youth and whose gait was unsteady with intoxication.
Others, having enjoyed for a very long time their bodies of immeasurable radiance— unrestrained by beautiful and delightful women of excellent form—
will depart without being satiated, even as they cast off their lives.
Even in heaven, prosperity is uncertain, just as it is for those who dwell in the sky; even the gods are subject to their underlying conditions. Therefore, I do not desire divinity.
There is no foundation for desires, but one who is free from desire turns away from them.

Without a doubt, O knower of dharma, all these dharmas for the welfare of the world have the same nature as a swing; the seer Dvaipāyana has declared this. Why, therefore, would a wise man ascend to such uneven suffering?
When an even path exists that is free from the nature of oscillation,
who indeed in this world would subject their own beloved self to the state of being like a swing?
All beings, both moving and unmoving, should proceed without hesitation.
From this world to the next world, one must enter a terrible darkness— without provisions for the journey, without a guide, without a protector, and without kin— for those who,
though supposedly knowers of dharma, [reject] that dharma proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa.

With undistracted minds, self-controlled and firm in their vows, they remember [the Lord]; therefore, they do not see [anything else] and attain the supreme state. The Blessed Viṣṇu protects his devotees like his own body.
O Teacher, while living beings revolve like a potter’s wheel,
I have encountered thousands of mothers and fathers; driven by affection, I have drunk from the various breasts of many mothers.

Thousands of sons and wives, and hundreds of beloved and unloved ones, have been obtained through the power of the physical basis (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and likewise have passed away; nowhere has happiness been attained, nor anywhere has an eternal state been reached.
There is repeated downfall from high positions attained with great difficulty,
and the loss of wealth after having acquired it with hardship;
such is the meeting of beings, like travelers resting in the shade along a road.

Thus, by the power of karma, the world meets with its kin; having rested there, it departs again toward the destination shown by its own actions. Having seen and understood this very nature of such encounters, [one should remain detached].
"O best of the Kurus, who would not be afraid, like one about to eat excrement?
And an understanding has arisen in me regarding the extensive dharma of Viṣṇu;
therefore, O Blessed One, I have come before you with my head at your feet."
I have taken refuge in that which is the firm refuge when one must go;
exhausted by birth, death, and old age, and oppressed by the three kinds of suffering,
O Great Sage, I desire to be protected by you from these.
O bull among the Kurus, by hearing of this dharma of the first age, one understands that which arose in the first age but was concealed during the Tretā age. Bhīṣma.
That very sage Dvaipāyana proclaimed the entire dharma,
O tiger among kings, which is consistent with both conduct and lineage.
Who, having taken possession of a vast kingdom, a great city of flourishing appearance, [would act otherwise]?

O lord of men, O Indra among kings, having cast aside the sovereignty of a kingdom— which is like the bliss of the realm of the gods and wherein all the qualities of royalty have been conquered by you— you perceive only defect in this body composed of the five elements.
"O King, by your conduct you have surpassed your great-grandfathers— Dharma incarnate, the steadfast Vidura of great fame,
the highly energetic Sañjaya, and those others who possess divine vision."
O King, those who possess active knowledge and are knowers of the truth have transcended even Brahmā and the others, including the gods and asuras;
there is no doubt that this world is impermanent and tormented by suffering.

Thus, O mighty-armed one, constantly behold these beings, from Brahmā down to the gods and asuras, as impermanent; what then can be said of humans and the like? But they say that Nature (prakṛti) is eternal, which is characterized by productivity.
