Formless, indefinable, uncreated, and transcending the person— that which is known as Nirvana, the ultimate bliss and supreme happiness—
is indeed called the primordial state by the ancient Brahman-sages and the great seers on earth.
O sinless one, through that woman who possesses the form of a man, he whose nature is dharma indeed attains that which is known as *prakṛti*,
namely Nirvāṇa. O King, this very dharma of *prakṛti* shines forth in the first age.
O bull among the Bharatas, O hero, in the remaining ages, those subject to the nature of transformation shine forth even more intensely as they range along the path of saṃsāra; yet,
among all these primordial natures (prakṛtis), that which is uncreated is remembered as the true Prakṛti.
Thus, those whose nature is characterized by *prakṛti*, relying upon the supreme *prakṛti*, perceive that which is the highest in the world— perceiving both the seen and the unseen—
during the emergence of the Tretā Yuga, from the age of *sattva* up to the end of *yuga*.
O Kaurava, while the Brahmins were desiring their own desires, [the Dharma] remained hidden; but when unrighteous paths appeared,
O King, Dharma became slow in its movement in the Kali age.
The eternal Puruṣa should be known as omniform and stainless; he whom even the gods, beginning with Brahmā, always worship— know him to be Nārāyaṇa, the supreme, eternal Brahman.
Perform that action with your body, meditate upon him with your mind,
and proclaim his name everywhere with your speech, O Lord of the Earth;
thus attain that eternal state which is to be reached and from which there is no rebirth.
"O mighty-armed one, this liberation from the grasp of saṃsāra by taking refuge in Viṣṇu has thus been told to you. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira [said].
While living beings are being afflicted in the ocean of birth and death,
O Bhīṣma,
tell me that which, having attained, one does not experience further suffering, O Grandfather.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Nārada.
The venerable Sanatkumāra, the son of Brahmā, was of great renown.
Three who were born before him are declared by those who discourse on Brahman:
Sanaka, Sanandana, and the third, Sanātana.
According to the sacred tradition, they were all enlightened as soon as they were born.
And the fourth among them was that Blessed One, the supreme knower of yoga; the great seers indeed call him Sanatkumāra. That sage, the son of Hiranyagarbha, is remembered as the fifth, Vasiṣṭha.
That Blessed One, the immeasurable-souled wielder of the trident, was the sixth Sthāṇu. Then,
from that terrible sacrifice,
others were produced by the mind of the Self-Existent One— namely, these [sages] headed by Marīci.
Bhṛgu was the younger brother of Marīci; likewise, Aṅgiras was the younger brother of Bhṛgu.
Then Atri was the younger brother of Aṅgiras, and Pulastya was the younger brother of Atri. The learned Pulaha, of great splendor, was the younger brother of Pulastya.
These [beings] of immeasurable splendor are indeed recited by the learned as born of Brahmā.
O Great King, performing all this, the Great Primordial Teacher,
the Lord, the All-pervading One, of infinite glory, Brahmā, the Grandfather of the worlds— [is he].
Embodied yet having become immortal, endowed with splendor and supreme ascetic power— Sanaka and the others who have reached that highest state there,
having attained complete dissolution, are liberated from the bondage of form.
But the powerful Sanatkumāra, a knower of yoga, having resorted to yoga,
constantly traversed the three worlds by means of supreme sovereignty; and the highly illustrious Rudra also attained yoga multiplied eightfold.
O King, O best of monarchs, Sūkṣma was eightfold;
O dear one, O tiger among kings, Marīci and all the others were appointed for the sake of creation. Listen to me as I describe their creation.
"These seven are determined in the Purāṇas as the Brahmās; they are all mentioned in the Vedas and in the Khilas, without a doubt. This is the eternal Śruti in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."
Those Brahmins who have reached the further shore of the Vedanta declare these to be the bestowers of boons. O dear one, they say that their fathers are [in fact] their sons.
O great king, there are seven groups, both those with form and those without form.
O king of kings, the sacred tradition (śruti) declares that the sons of the ancestors are indeed the gods;
we have heard this repeatedly that these worlds are pervaded by the gods.
This was likewise learned from Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and from Devasthāna.
O best of men, I have heard this from Devala and from Kāśyapa;
likewise from Gautama, Kauṇḍinya, and Bhāradvāja;
and similarly from the seer Mārkaṇḍeya and from Devamata.
O Indra among kings, at the time of the *śrāddha* ceremony, my father spoke to me this supreme secret of Vedānta, which is indeed dear to the Supreme Self.
Beyond this, O Bhārata, I shall declare that which you ask of me.
Therefore, O King, listen here with a focused mind and attentive intellect to this dialogue between Svāyambhuva and the wise Nārada.
The blessed Sanatkumāra blazed with divine splendor.

Having become the size of a thumb, he of great splendor indeed wandered about. Once, O best of men, that illustrious one arrived upon the summit of Mount Meru together with the sage Nārada, who was a teacher of the Brahman.
Then, O dear one, desiring to know each other in the presence of Brahmā, those two— who were intent upon the meaning of the supreme truth— became absorbed in the nature of Brahman;
the wise one [approached] the best of the wise, and the intelligent one [approached] the most intelligent.

O subduer of enemies, [he approached] the venerable Sanatkumāra, the knower of the field (*kṣetravid*), the best among those who know the field, the knower of knowledge (*jñānavid*), the most excellent among those who know knowledge, the knower of reality (*tattvavid*), the knower of the worlds (*lokavid*),
the best among those who know the worlds, and the knower of the self (*ātmavid*), the most excellent among those who know the self.
Nārada, who is skilled in the meaning of all the Vedas, proficient in all the scriptures, and who knows Sāṃkhya and Yoga as clearly as an *āmalaka* fruit in the palm of his hand.
Then, O best of men, the highly effulgent Nārada questioned him:
"O great sage, I wish to hear in truth about the origin of the twenty-three principles and of the Unmanifest."
The internal self, the elemental, and likewise the divine; the calculation of time, creation, and the Lord Puruṣa,
the creator upon whom the universe depends and by whom all this is pervaded.
Sanatkumāra said:
"You ought to tell me that which, having attained, they do not return;
that upon which the universe depends, and which they call the Supreme Person."
Listen, O one of great intelligence, to that Nārāyaṇa who is free from all affliction.
He who is named Nārāyaṇa is the one upon whom the entire universe depends;
he is the creator, the ordainer, the destroyer, the protector, and the Lord.
Having reached this, the ascetics who contemplate the supreme self do not return.
O Nārada, as much as you have asked me, this alone is what must be said; I know nothing beyond this—neither the extent of that creation nor how it dissolves.
Listen, O best of sages, as I carefully describe the nine creations in their proper sequence, according to the duration of time, and the principles (tattvas),
including the internal self (adhyātma), the objective world (adhibhūta), and likewise the divine realm (adhidaiva).

O Great Sage, the calculation of time and the entire process of creation— when one creates a world of darkness (*tamas*), he is indeed called *Tāmasa* by the twice-born who know Brahman and who are constant contemplators of the supreme self.
The wise declare these to be its synonymous names;
I shall proclaim them to you—listen here with a focused mind. They are Mahārṇava, Arṇava, Salila, and likewise Guṇas.
The Vedas, austerity, sacrifices, and the various duties are the Lord, the all-pervading one;
he is the vital breath, the fire of universal destruction, the ether, and likewise time— these,
O Brahman-sage, are indeed the names of the body of the Supreme Lord.
O best of the twice-born, these have been recounted by me according to the authority of the scriptures. O subduer of enemies, a thousand cycles of four yugas—
what the Brahmins who perceive the truth call a thousand kalpas— is [the duration of] one day of Brahmā.
Ten thousand kalpas constitute the great night of the Imperishable One;
likewise, the practitioners of Yoga and the followers of Sāṃkhya declare his day to be of equal duration according to the truth.
Then the Blessed One, having slept during the night, awoke at the end of the night.
Afterwards, having become conscious, he created the waters and cast his seed into them. That became a golden egg, radiant as the thousand-rayed sun.
Then the Lord, the Sovereign, having performed the act of self-consciousness (*ahaṃkāra*), emitted [the elements] within it.
Hiraṇyagarbha, the soul of the universe, Brahmā, the sage who dwells in the waters,
the sinless and all-pervading creator of the past, present, and future— the embodied Great Soul, the source of bliss for the world, the Self-born.

The Lord of great renown, having performed this and manifested *aṇimā*, *laghimā*, *prāpti*, and supreme mastery over the luminaries, made himself invisible. Those who have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas say that even for him, this [period] constitutes a night.
Five thousand kalpas constitute a single day for him, and his night is of exactly the same duration. During that period, Brahmā effects the creation of the tamasic realm in due order;
indeed, he brings forth the imperishable Ahaṃkāra, the Supreme Lord.
The worlds are indeed pervaded by egoism, along with all that possesses self-conceit; possessed by which, all beings sink into the ocean of the unmanifest.
[So it is with] gods, sages, dānavas, men, yakṣas, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
They emerge, they submerge, upwards, downwards, and even transversely;
they say that this [day] is the third night for him as he performs [this],
and his day is likewise three thousand kalpas.
The ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), indeed, creates the five great elements:
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth.
The twice-born say that these have five qualities as their true nature.
Delighting in these qualities— sound, touch, form, taste, and likewise smell— they do not emerge, being as helpless as elephants stuck in the mud,
attached to the ocean of the unmanifest.
For him who performs this fourth creation here,
a thousand cycles of four yugas constitute a single day and night;
this fifth creation is known as Ananta.
There are eleven sense-faculties, according to the teaching and the traditional exposition.
O dear one, the mind is this entire universe; the mind is this whole world. No other elements are as powerful as the mind.
The twice-born indeed call this the sixth creation;
a day consists of a thousand kalpas, and the night is of equal duration. They know the seventh creation of Brahmā to be that of the *ūrdhvasrotas*.
The eighth is the downward flow, and the ninth is known as the horizontal;
these, O great sage, are the nine creations and the principles (tattvas). Thus, O sinless one, the enumeration of the principles consists of twenty-four principles.

O great sage, it has been stated previously that the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the source of all; he is both the inexhaustible and the source of the Unmanifest. I shall now declare another truth: who is the lord of whom.
"Understand from me, exactly as it is, according to what has been heard and seen, the internal, the elemental, and likewise the divine—
Sanatkumāra."
In the downward-flowing creation and likewise in the transverse-flowing creation—
one should know the Lord through these two, as well as through the upward-flowing.
He is the Lord of the five organs of action and is the object of the intellect.
Now, the mind is said to be the lord of the sense organs;
they say the five elements, together with their qualities, are the lords of the mind. One should know Brahmā Parameṣṭhin to be the lord of the elements.
For you are indeed skilled in these supreme dharmas;
like the fire of time at the end of a kalpa, you consume the world with your rays. Then all beings, both stationary and moving, [are destroyed].
The great elements were indeed consumed and returned to their own source;
the earth, resembling the back of a tortoise, with its *kuśa* grass and thorns burnt away,
was then devoid of trees and grass, scorched by the fire of time.
The world dissolves into the world, and the world dissolves into water.
Then, with its subtle fragrance lost, it becomes water alone. Thereafter, the sun is swallowed by the mass of its rays, and the water [is consumed].
O best of Brahmins, when the essence of taste dissolves into the sun,
fire then consumes the beings situated in the intermediate space; at that time,
they declare that the sky becomes fire.
Indeed, the great wind causes that which is thus quivering to decay;
with great force and speed, the sun indeed seizes it. And when space swallows even the quality of touch belonging to the wind, [it is consumed].

Then the wind becomes still, and the ether remains resounding; the mind then indeed takes up that sound, its resonance. Then he, whose self is devoid of the quality of sound, remains truly possessed of form.
And then, O dear one, he experiences the sky, which consists of the quarters and is of the nature of the mind.
When that which is of the nature of the sky has perished, that which is of the nature of volition (saṃkalpa) increases;
indeed, by its own power, it takes up the mind which is of the nature of volition.
O best of sages, at that time, ego (ahaṃkāra) indeed devours the mind;
and when the mind has perished, the great ego comes into being.
Then the Great Brahmā, the Lord of Creatures (prajāpati), takes up that ego.
But when conceit has perished, the Great Brahmā shines forth;
him who was born from the primordial form, by whom this entire universe was indeed fashioned through the pursuit of the qualities, [one then perceives] in those three worlds within the very forms.

The Lord Brahmā, the consumer, undoubtedly devours even the embodied form of Varuṇa, which consists of the quality of resolve, as well as the manifest and the unmanifest. This dissolution of the Imperishable has been described by me to you.
Let the internal, the elemental, and the divine be heard:
taste is the elemental; Varuṇa is the presiding deity. (4)
Earth is the fifth;
thus, this group of four has been described as consisting of the five elements.
The nose is the elemental principle within; odor is the elemental principle without; and Vāyu shall be the presiding deity. //5//
The sun is the *adhibhūta* (with respect to the elemental sphere), and it is the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity). //3//
Water is the fourth element; the internal organ is the tongue.
Space is the first element; the internal organ is the ear, sound is the external element, and the quarters are the presiding deity. //1//
Air is the second element; the skin is its internal correlate (*adhyātma*), touch is its elemental correlate (*adhibhūta*), and lightning is its divine correlate (*adhidaivata*). // 2 //
The third element is light; the eye is its internal organ, form is its object, and the moon is its presiding deity. //7//
Egoity (ahaṃkāra) is the internal [aspect], self-conceit (abhimāna) is that with respect to beings (adhibhūta), and Viriñca is the presiding deity (adhidaivata). // 8 //
The intellect is the internal self; resolve is the fire with respect to the deities.
The mind is the internal; that which is to be thought of is the elemental;
Brahmā is the presiding deity. //9//
13,013.006d@003_0345 Hereafter, we shall describe the faculties (indriya). // 1 //
The feet are the internal;
Prajāpati is the presiding deity with respect to the external world. // 5 //
Speech is the internal correlate; that which is to be spoken is the external correlate. Indra is the presiding deity. (3)
The anus is the internal;
its external correlate is the act of evacuation, and Viṣṇu is the presiding deity. (2)
The two hands are the internal;
Mitra is the external element and the presiding deity.
The lap is the internal bliss;
likewise, it is there that [the sound] perishes when mixed with thundering and roaring.
Thus is the unmanifest.
It creates and withdraws the qualities. //4//
13,013.006d@003_0346 It rises upward and withdraws. // 3 //
And just as a mass of clouds arises from the atmosphere, it emits and withdraws its qualities. // 2 //
Just as a multitude of garlands of waves arises from the ocean for the sake of sport. //1//
Just as the sun casts forth and withdraws its web of rays, so too does the unmanifest Lord [the Unmanifest] simultaneously create and withdraw the entire universe. Why?
Because the nature of the unmanifest Lord consists of both activity and non-activity.
Pure, that primordial nature (prakṛti), presided over by Him, is always conscious along with its attributes (dharmas).
Just as a tortoise extends its limbs at will and withdraws them again, so does the Unmanifest manifest the worlds and withdraws them. //1//
Thus, the Blessed One is the conscious one, the twenty-fifth; he is the possessor of action, ageless and immortal, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), Nārāyaṇa, the Puruṣa. //3//
Bhīṣma said:
"This was told to Nārada by the wise Kumāra.
Having heard this, O King, a twice-born man shall obtain the fruit of all sacrifices."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O descendant of Kuru, those twice-born ones who, having established these fires within themselves, are observant of vows and devoted to the sacrifice of silent recitation (japa-yajña)."

13,013.006d@003A_0003 Those who perform sacrifices of undertaking (*ārambhayajña*) are established in mental sacrifice (*mānasayajña*). 13,013.006d@003A_0004 For those for whom there is nothing higher than the sacrificial fires, such is their established rule. 13,013.006d@003A_0005 O one of great wisdom, what is the destiny of those people, and what is their ultimate state?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Grandfather, I desire to hear this from you in its true essence.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."
O Bhārata, [this is] the dialogue between Vaikuṇṭha and Suparṇa regarding the production of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*),
during which a war between the gods and the *asuras* lasted for sixty thousand years.
There, the gods were being slaughtered by the Daityas in a most cruel manner;
being struck down by the great Asuras, they found no protector. Afflicted and seeking refuge, they approached the Lord of the Gods of gods.
While they were being slaughtered by the non-gods, those deities beheld the highly wise Grandfather (Brahmā). Seeing them, Brahmā, his senses and mind agitated,
sought refuge with the god Vaikuṇṭha along with them.
Then, O lord of men, the lotus-born Brahmā, accompanied by the gods,
joined his palms in reverence and praised the healthy Nārāyaṇa,
saying: "By meditating upon Your form, by remembering Your names, and even by worshipping You..."
Through asceticism, yoga, and other means, the wise attain the highest good.
O Lord who is affectionate toward His devotees, lotus-eyed Supreme Ruler, destroyer of sin,
O Nārāyaṇa, the unchanging Supreme Self— salutations be unto You!
Homage to you, the foremost of all worlds, the soul of all, whose prowess is immeasurable;
Lord of all beings and of the future, Great Sovereign of all beings;
you are the God even of the gods, the ultimate refuge of all knowledge.
O aggregate of the seeds of the world, you are indeed the supreme one of the universe. O Hero, O God, protect us who are severely oppressed by the Dānavas and other foes;
protect the worlds, the guardians of the quarters, and the sages, O best among victors!
The Vedas, along with their auxiliary limbs, the Upaniṣads, the secret doctrines, and the compendiums—
accompanied by the syllable *oṃ* and the exclamation *vaṣaṭ*— proclaim you as the supreme sacrifice;
you are the purifier of all purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
"The ascetic power of the ascetics, and even the divinity among the deities"—
with such introductory verses and hosts of *Ṛk*, *Sāman*, and *Yajus* hymns,
all the gods, together with the celestial sages (*brahmarṣis*), praised Vaikuṇṭha.
Then, from the sky, a voice arose with a resonance as deep as a thundercloud:
"In battle, you shall conquer the Dānavas along with me.
Then, while the hosts of gods and the Dānavas were fighting, [the voice spoke].
The one of great splendor, bearing the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the mace, appeared; mounting the back of Suparṇa and as if burning with his radiance,
he scattered all the Dānavas by the power and majesty of his arms.
Having encountered him in battle, O great king, those foremost among the Daityas and Dānavas perished like moths in a fire. Having thus conquered all the Asuras and Dānavas, that high-minded one—
Even as the gods were looking on, he vanished right there. Seeing that god Viṣṇu of immeasurable splendor thus disappeared, the gods,
their eyes wide with wonder, spoke this to Brahmā:
O Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, Grandfather of all worlds!
You ought to explain to us this most wonderful event,
by which we were saved, O Lord, in this battle between the gods and the asuras.
We wish to know this: who was he, and from where did he truly come?
Who was this divine being who, having rescued us, returned silently just as he had arrived? You ought to tell us that.
Thus addressed by all the gods, Brahmā, who understands the meaning of speech,
spoke regarding the former form of the Lord Padmanābha.
Indeed, the world does not know him in his true essence, the Lord of the World;
nor can one enumerate himself, being devoid of qualities yet the foremost among those possessing qualities.
In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history.

O deities, in ancient times, on the slopes of the Himalayas, Suparṇa held a conversation with the ṛṣis; likewise, the Brahmanical seers and the Siddhas, having taken refuge there, engaged in various discourses with the Lord of the World.
While they were speaking there, at the conclusion of their discourse,
the preeminent steed of the wielder of the discus and mace appeared, endowed with great splendor;
approaching those sages, his face bowed in humility.
Having descended, the one of great heroism approached those sages;
honored by the sages with words of welcome,
that mighty and radiant one, the best among the swift, sat down upon the ground.
To that high-souled Vainateya of great splendor as he sat there,
the great-souled ascetic seers inquired:
"O Vainateya, a supreme curiosity dwells within our hearts."
"O eater of serpents, there is no one else here who can speak of this except for you. Therefore, we wish to have this most excellent question explained by you.
Thus addressed, the son of Vinatā replied with palms joined in reverence.

"I am blessed and I am graced, since these most excellent Brahman-sages, full of affection and free from envy, desire to ask me what ought to be asked. Tell me, O best of speakers, what should I say and what task must I perform?"
"For you all ought to ask me everything according to what is appropriate. Having paid homage to the Infinite One, those best of sages then proceeded to question the mighty Vainateya there.

You worship the god of gods, the high-souled Nārāyaṇa, who is free from ailment and the bestower of boons; who is he in reality, and from where does he come? What is his nature or his transformation, and what is his mode of existence?
"O venerable one, we ask you this: where has this god established his abode?
This god is fond of devotion, and likewise, he is devoted to devotion;
and you, Kāśyapa, are dear to him and devoted to him—no other such person exists."
Stealing, as it were, the mind and the eyes, the all-pervading Lord has an unperceivable form;
having no beginning, middle, or end, we do not know from where he comes,
for even though the Soul of the Universe is sung of in the Vedas, we do not truly know him.
In reality, the Self is the essence of reality, all-pervading, eternal, and ancient.
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth— these elements,
their qualities in due order, as well as existence and non-existence, [are likewise established].
Tamas, sattva, and rajas, as well as the states of being composed of these,
the mind, the intellect, and the fiery energy— all these are, in truth, objects of the intellect.
From what, O dear one, are they born, and why does that all-pervading Lord abide within them?
Having reflected in many ways with our intellects, we do not arrive at a certain conclusion regarding that supreme deity.
Tell us, exactly as it is, the truth concerning that god;
for we are filled with curiosity regarding this very supreme question.
O Suparṇa, we ask you this; you ought to explain it to us. For the Blessed One, by his own very nature, is indeed vast.

For the sake of protecting the three worlds, he is seen assuming this form. But formerly, a great marvel was witnessed by me in the eternal Lord who dwells in the Śrīvṛkṣa; listen to that in its entirety.
It was not possible for me to know it, nor for you in any way;
therefore, listen to me as the Blessed One has told it to me. O best of sages, while the gods looked on, I [obtained] the nectar of immortality.
Having torn open that machine and routed the guardians of the nectar,
and having turned away the gods— including Indra and the Maruts— from the battle,
he swiftly crushed the mountains and agitated the great ocean.
Seeing my prowess, an incorporeal voice spoke to me:
"O Vainateya of noble vows, I am pleased with this deed of yours. Let my word not be in vain; tell me, what shall I do for you?"
To her who spoke these words, I then replied:
"I wish to know who you are, for only then will you grant me a boon. Are you Prakṛti or Vikṛti, or are you a god or even a Dānava?"
Then, laughing with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud, that best of speakers, the granter of boons, spoke joyfully: "O virtuous one, at the proper time you shall recognize me;
become my vehicle, and I shall grant you an excellent boon."
In this world, there shall be no one equal to you in valor; O best of winged beings, neither a god nor a *dānava* shall be your peer. Having attained friendship with me, you shall become invincible.
To that supreme God of gods, who was speaking thus to me, I, having become disciplined with palms joined in reverence, bowed my head to the Lord and said:
"O mighty-armed one, it shall be exactly so; all this will come to pass."
"I shall become your vehicle, just as you have spoken to me. O one of great intelligence, hear now my resolve as well:
I shall become your banner upon the chariot; of this there is no doubt."
Having said to me, "So be it," that high-minded one spoke further:
"Today there shall be no obstruction to your progress, except for the attainment of the deathless (amṛta). Having thus established this agreement, the eternal God of gods [departed].
Having said to me, "Accomplish [this]," he departed according to his intention. Then, O best of beings, having conversed with that certain being,
I was filled with curiosity and went to my father, Kāśyapa.
Having approached my father, prostrated, and paid him homage,
I related all of this exactly as it was to my father.
But having heard me, the Blessed One entered into meditative absorption.
Having meditated for a moment, that best among speakers said to me:
"O dear one, you are blessed and favored, since you have held a conversation with that Great-Souled One, the Supreme Self, who is hidden from view."
By that very same cause, that Blessed One,

who exists in an unmanifest form as the Pradhāna— the source and dissolution of all— is perceived as a gross object; for he, possessed of great splendor, cannot be seen by me through any other yoga or meditative absorption.
By means of fierce austerity, that radiant storehouse of asceticism was propitiated by me. Then, as if to please me, O son, he revealed himself—
appearing white, yellow, and reddish-brown, and dark, tawny, and reddish-brown.
Resembling red, blue, and black, possessing a thousand bellies and hands,
with two thousand great mouths, one eye, and a hundred eyes;
motionless, abstaining from food, they were equal in brilliance to the sun.
They worship that supreme, secret, imperishable, and immutable one.
Having approached that All-pervading One and bowed my head in reverence,
I have sought refuge in that protector, praising him with the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāman hymns.
With a voice as deep and steady as a great mass of clouds, the Best of Victors addressed him,
saying "Son, son," and spoke these firm words:
"O great sage, you have practiced asceticism out of a desire for spiritual advancement."
"You are not liberated; you do not see me today because you are not free from attachments.
O Brahmin, when you become liberated from attachments, free from delusion, and devoid of longing, then, O twice-born one, you shall truly contemplate me."
"Having formed a resolute conviction, my devotee who is intent upon me shall,
O Brahmin, then know me truly and be freed from delusion. Therefore, you have entered into conversation with him, who naturally desires the welfare of all."
"By the god of universal form, the Great-Souled Puruṣa—propitiate him quickly; by propitiating him, you shall not perish. O best of Brahman-sages, having been thus addressed by my lordly father, I—
Having been praised according to the proper rite, Suparṇa returned to his own abode.
Then I, with my mind fixed upon his state, took leave of my father.
Having returned to my own abode, I reflected upon that very same object;
with my being absorbed in his state of being and my mind fixed upon him,
I remained contemplating Govinda— the eternal, supreme, and imperishable.
My heart was held fast by the desire to behold Nārāyaṇa. Therefore, assuming great speed with the velocity of mind and wind,
I went to the beautiful and vast Badarī, the hermitage of Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having seen there Hari, the all-pervading source of the universe,
Govinda, the lotus-eyed one, he bowed his head to Hari and praised him with the utmost joy through the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas.

Then I beheld a vast *aśvattha* tree, a refuge for the gods; there appeared a person, the eternal one, clad in yellow garments, with shoulders broad and thick fourfold, bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Resembling the midday sun, illuminating the quarters with his splendor,
praised and having established consciousness, he who is devoted to the highest good said,
"Go," and the divine Puruṣottama set out toward the northeastern direction.
Illuminating the cardinal and intermediate directions with his own splendor,
that divine person of immeasurable power was proceeding; as he moved slowly, I followed him with speed, though he remained immutable.
Sixty-eight thousand and one hundred yojanas,
as well as a hundred thousand and twice a hundred—
having traveled that long distance, I beheld a marvel.
That great yogin, possessing a fiery luster, entered a vast, blazing, and radiant fire that required no fuel—
a fire one hundred yojanas wide and twice that in length.
There, Śambhu, the Great God, performed austerities together with Umā.
Having entered into an agreement with him, he passed beyond the fire.
Overcome by exhaustion, I followed after him with great difficulty.
Having traveled a long distance illuminated by the sun, he entered a vast darkness that was devoid of light and without boundaries; then,
my vision was indeed obstructed there.
That being of great splendor entered the self of all beings according to their own natures.
Thereupon, I became bewildered, like one who is dull, blind, and deaf;
enveloped in darkness, I could not distinguish the cardinal directions nor the intermediate points.
Knowing nothing at all in that enveloped darkness, with a deeply bewildered mind, I fell into the utmost distress; therefore,
I have sought refuge in the eternal God of gods.
With palms joined in reverence and with a focused mind, he then spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the past and the future, creator of all beings, imperishable one,
O subduer of enemies, it behooves you to protect me, who have come to you for refuge."
"But I am desirous of knowing the truth: who are you, to whom do you belong, or from where have you come?
O Lord, you have reached my path; you ought to save me.
Thus spoke the eternal, ancient Self, manifesting himself, saying, "Come to me!"
Then, from the far limit, the self-possessed Lord, the refuge of the universe,
whose form is difficult to discern, bewildered me there; the omnipresent one, manifesting his own nature there by himself through himself.
The Lord, the giver of fearlessness, caused me fatigue and fear;
thinking that I was exhausted, the imperishable and infallible Blessed One comforted me with his voice and plunged into the great darkness.
But I, overcome by exhaustion and walking with faltering steps due to fatigue,
began to meditate in my mind upon the Lord of the Gods.
Knowing that I had reached such a state, the Blessed One of immeasurable splendor—
Out of a desire to show me favor, he dispelled the darkness. Then, when the darkness had vanished, I beheld him of blazing splendor,
pervaded by light like the sun at midday.
In that region, I calmly beheld thousands of most wonderful men and women who were self-luminous; there,
neither the sun nor the stars shone.
There the moon does not shine, nor does the dusty wind blow;
there many musical instruments and sweet songs are heard from every direction— unseen yet delightful to the mind.
There flow beryl-crested streams, teeming with lotuses, water-lilies, and fish; there are rivers of pure water with banks of pearl-sand.
Therein, neither gods nor asuras have access.
There, humans of wondrous appearance are seen who are self-luminous, as well as gandharvas, nāgas, yakṣas, and likewise rākṣasas;
for those of purified selves, there are no deities equal to them in radiance.
Having transcended even those, and being honored by the deities as well,
he entered the blazing fire— flameless, incomparable,
and radiant in every direction— even as it blazed with tongues of flame. And me, having entered, it blazed on all sides.

Having approached that imperishable fire, garlanded with flames, which was unbearable even for the Daityas, Dānavas, Rākṣasas, and the gods, I reflected thus in my mind, considering it to be utterly insupportable.
For in many battles, the fire of great splendor has entered me and been cast away by me, yet it has never burned me anywhere;
and this [fire] is ever difficult to endure, being a truly great consumer by its brilliance.
A great fire blazes with flames more brilliant than the sun;
though he is being consumed by that fire of blazing radiance,
he has sought refuge in the God who bears the conch, the discus, and the mace.
"O Lord, you ought to protect me, for I am both your devotee and your follower.
O God, act in such a way that the fire may not consume me instantly. Having understood these words of mine as I was thus lamenting, the Lord—
"Do not fear," he said, his voice deep as a thundercloud.
Having comforted me with these words, the all-pervading Blessed One spoke this further:
"O gentle one, you are known to me exactly as you truly are in the vision of reality."
And that which was made known by my father is also known as something great, O Vainateya;
likewise, I am to be known by you in this same way.
This true nature of mine is great; it is not to be known by you in any other manner whatsoever.
For the wise who are firmly established in knowledge find Me— those who are free from "mine-ness," free from egoism, and released from the bonds of desire;
but you, O best of birds, have been My devotee constantly, with your mind fixed on Me.
"Suparṇa will recognize me as something substantial, established as the cause of the world.
O best of sages, having been granted this assurance by him, I then [departed].
At that moment, I was suddenly freed from all weariness, fatigue, and fear;
yet the Blessed One, moving with light-footed prowess, proceeded slowly,
while I followed him, exerting great speed.

Having traveled a long distance through the sky, he of immeasurable splendor reached the god who is inaccessible even to the mind; for he was a knower of the true nature of the self. Then the god, having approached him with a speed equal to that of thought—
Having deluded me there, he vanished in an instant.
Then, with a voice as deep as a rain-cloud and resonant with the sound "Bho!", he who was skilled in speech uttered these words: "O, it is I!"
Following the sound, I then proceeded toward that place;
there I beheld a lake graced by majestic swans. Having reached that lake, the Blessed One, the supreme knower of the Self, [remained there].
With a voice that did not respond, yet was addressed by the word "Bhoḥ!", the god entered his own womb and spoke this to me:
"Enter the water, O gentle one; we shall dwell here in comfort."
Then I entered there together with that great-souled one;
and in that lake, I beheld a most wonderful sight:
blazing fires, unprepared and without fuel.
In places where [fires] were always blazing, sprinkled with clarified butter, and radiant with flames,
the splendor of those [trees], though not sprinkled with butter, became like that of fires already receiving the offering.
They were like virtuous men who, though unkindled, appear as if kindled and shining brightly.

Then I did not see the boon-granting god gathered there; consequently, I fell into a state of confusion and experienced supreme despondency. And I beheld hundreds and thousands of *agnihotra* sacrifices.
Then, according to the prescribed rites, oblations accompanied by clarified butter were offered upon the sacrificial hearths;
the altars, though their surfaces had not yet been swept, were strewn with flowers,
along with golden jars containing clusters of *kuśa* grass and *padma* and *utpala* lotuses.
I have seen here, on many occasions, hundreds and thousands of various *agnihotra* sacrifices, as well as whatever materials are required for the *agnihotra*.

And there, most pleasing to the mind, fragrant, and marked by merit, was the scent of clarified butter— captivating to the heart and bringing delight to both the sense of smell and the eyes. Of those thousands of Agnihotra sacrifices performed there, which were worthy of praise, [the fragrance arose].
In its vicinity, however, I beheld something most wondrous and imperishable:
thousands of sacrificial altars, as bright as moonbeams and the sky, possessing the luster of breaking forth frost and the radiance of the stainless sun.
He beheld great and radiant [beings] near the fires;
and near those fires, he heard voices speaking with distinct syllables,
though their forms were concealed by their supernatural power.
And the sweet, melodious voices of those chanting the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas [resounded].
By means of those large, brightly shining, and blazing hearths with their well-swept surfaces,
my soul was purified and my stride became light.
Then, while those sacrificial altars of the sacrificers were blazing, I bowed down to that region and began to search for it;
having traversed those many thousands [of places] with great speed.
Not seeing that god, I then became distressed. Then, while those *agnihotra* fires were blazing with pure flames and radiant light,
I did not see the eternal God of gods.

Then, having circled those blazing [fires] with my senses distressed, I could not see their end, and suddenly exhaustion came upon me. Having cast my gaze in every direction, I was possessed by fear and delusion.
Having fallen into the utmost exhaustion, I think, deprived of my senses:
"Do I indeed exist in this world, or what is this that is like this?
The resonance of the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma* Vedas is heard, yet it is not seen."
"And yet I do not see that god by whom I have been impelled here.
Having fallen into such reflection, he began to brood deeply. Then, as I was thinking thus, my mind was possessed by delusion.
A great sound arose, causing me extreme distress;
then I suddenly heard a vast clamor there,
and I beheld thousands and tens of thousands of *suparṇas*.
They rushed toward me alone with immense splendor and speed;
by their power, I became utterly inferior in every respect. Thus, I was surrounded on all sides by all those Suparṇas of exceeding brilliance.
Seeing himself surrounded, he was overcome with supreme agitation; bowing low with humility, he paid homage to the Great Soul,
the Supreme Self who is without beginning or end, by means of these names.
To Nārāyaṇa, the pure, the eternal, and the constant;
to the Lord of the past, the future, and the present; to Śiva, whose form is auspiciousness;
to the source of auspiciousness, who is the beginning of auspiciousness, and who is most worthy of auspicious worship.
To the one of terrible form, the great one who brings about the end of the age; to the Universal One, the God of all, the Lord of the universe, the Great Soul;
to the one with a thousand bellies and feet, and with a thousand eyes.
Salutations to the thousand-armed and the thousand-faced,
to the one of pure renown, to the great one, to the year of the seasons,
and to the one whose mouth is the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, and whose head is the Atharva Veda.
To Hṛṣīkeśa, to Kṛṣṇa, and to Druhiṇa-Urukrama; to Brahmodreka, to Tārkṣya, to Varāha, and to Ekaśṛṅgin;
to Śipiviṣṭa, to Satya, to Hari, and then to Śikhaṇḍin.
Salutations to the one who has offered oblations, to the upward-striving, to the crooked, to the one with a fierce army, to the virtuous,
to the ocean, to the destroyer of the ocean-rain, and to the ocean of the gods. Salutations to the one with eagle-wings,
to the three-eyed, to the possessor of nectar, and to the bull among bulls.
To Samrāṭ, to Ugra, to Saṃkṛti, to Viraja, to Sambhava, and to Bhava; to Vṛṣa, to Vṛṣarūpa, to Vibhava, and to Bhūrbhuva; to the one who has emitted light, to Yajña, to Sthira, and to Sthavira.
To Acyuta, Tuṣāra, Vīra, and Sama;
to Jiṣṇu, Puruhūta, Vasiṣṭha, and Vara;
to Satyeśa, Sureśa, Hari, and Śikhaṇḍin.
To the one worthy of the sacrificial grass, the excellent, the Vasu, the knower of all;
to the one wearing a crown, the one with beautiful hair, Vāsudeva, the powerful;
to the one praised with great hymns, the one with a noble army, the twin, and likewise to Dundubhi.
To Bhava, to Sakhāya, to Vibhava, and to Bharadvāja for the sake of fearlessness;
to Bhāskara, to Candra, to Padmanābha, and to Bhūrī; to Punarvasu, to Bhṛtatva, and to Jīvaprabhaviṣa.
Salutations to the *vaṣaṭkāra*, to the *svāhā*, to the *svadhā*, and to the *nidhana*;
salutations to the *ṛc*, the *yajus*, and the *sāman*, and to the Lord of the three worlds. Salutations to the one who resembles the lotus of Śrī, the supreme upholder and supporter of the earth.
Homage to the gentle one, to him of gentle form, and to the gentle-minded one;
homage to the All-pervading, to the Well-all-pervading, and to the bearer of universal forms;
homage to Keśava, to the one with beautiful hair, to the one whose hair is rays of light, and to the Abundant One.
Salutations to Hiraṇyagarbha, to the gentle one in the form of a bull;
to Nārāyaṇa of foremost form, to Puruhūta, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
to the righteous one, to Vṛṣasena, to Dharmasena, and to Rodhas.
Homage to the sage who is free from fever, the lord of fevers;
homage to the eyeless one, the three-eyed one, the tawny-hued, and the one who transcends the dharma;
homage to the treasury of austerity and sacred knowledge, who moves through the succession of the ages.

Homage to the refuge, the one worthy of refuge, and the beloved refuge of those who are capable; homage to the Lord of all existence, the source of the past, the future, and the present. Protect me, O Lord of the gods of gods; you are some eternal, unborn being.

Thus have I gone for refuge to the one worthy of refuge, the source of Brahman. May that darkness of mine perish as I offer this hymn of praise to the one worthy of praise; and may my fear depart, and the birds vanish from sight.
And I hear a divine, auspicious voice, coming from within the air:
"Do not fear, O Garuḍa; you have been tamed. Once again, the dwellers of heaven, including Indra, shall behold you when you have returned to your own abode and seen your sons and kinsmen."
Then, at that very moment, suddenly, that radiant and glorious one appeared before me in my presence; thereafter,
he was joined by Śiva, the Supreme Self.
And I saw him approaching at the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa— that eternal deity, whose form is arranged with four times two [eight] limbs—
as he was sacrificing to those sages and gods, and speaking to and meditating upon the munis.

[He saw] the hermitage of Nara and Nārāyaṇa, frequented by the disciplined, the perfected, and those established in the ultimate vow; where they were chanting and performing sacrifices in their dwellings; strewn with heaps of flowers, perfumed, illuminated, and offered oblations; honored, sprinkled, and swept clean.
Having seen that wonder, O sinless ones, I was then struck with amazement;
with my head bowed and my inner self restrained, I approached the God,
wondering, "What is this that appears so utterly marvelous?"
I did not find anything superior or divine belonging to him, the soul of all existence.
Having prostrated before that one who is so difficult to overcome, and having gazed upon him again and again with eyes wide open in wonder, I placed my joined palms upon my head.
I spoke thus to him, whose purpose is undiminished, the most excellent among the excellent, the supreme one:
"Homage to you, Blessed One, O God, Lord of the past, the future, and the present!
O God, this wonder which I have seen, centered upon you—"
What is that which has no beginning, middle, or end? You should deign to describe it.
If you know me to be a devotee, or if you have favor toward me, then tell me everything without omission, if it is something I may hear.
Your intrinsic nature and the manifestation of existence are difficult to comprehend;
O Lord of the past, present, and future, you are in every way profound. Tell us all of that wonder in its entirety, O Great Sage.
What was that most wonderful event occurring all around those fires?
What were those *agnihotra* sacrifices, and whose voice was heard by me as I listened to the constant recitation of the Veda by those invisible great-souled ones?
O Blessed One, O Kṛṣṇa, tell me all of this in its entirety:
who are those masses of Brahman that chant in the presence of the fires?
O Blessed One.

Neither the gods, nor the gandharvas, nor the piśācas, nor the rākṣasas know me in truth as I abide established in reality, the subtle self. Having divided my own self fourfold, I exist out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
The past, the present, and the future, beginningless, the supreme creator of the universe;
earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth;
mind, intellect, consciousness, as well as darkness, goodness, and passion.
Nature and its transformation, knowledge and ignorance, the auspicious and the inauspicious—all these are born from me; I am not born from them in any way whatsoever.
Endowed with a certain degree of excellence, he determines the state of superiority.

I am that which is endowed with Dharma and merit, and I am free from all affliction. I am that eternal inner self, without beginning, middle, or end, who is perceived through causes known by those who understand the reality of the nature of the self.
That supreme secret form of mine which is perceived by those who see subtle truths and who know the nature of the subtle— that eternal one am I, who cannot be conceptualized;
that supreme secret of mine by which this entire world is pervaded.
I am that one who has become all beings, the source of all, the imperishable. From me all beings are born; by me they are sustained day and night.
They go to dissolution in me alone at the time of universal destruction, O eater of serpents.
"O Kāśyapa, O bird, for whomever knows me as I am, I enter their mind and intellect and bestow what is most beneficial.
But you, O best of birds, have set your mind upon knowing me."
Listen to who I am, from whence I come, and for what purpose I have exerted myself. There are those of disciplined soul who hold the three sacred fires as their highest object of worship,
who are constantly devoted to fire-rites, and dedicated to the practice of silent recitation and burnt offerings.
Having established the sacred fires within themselves, self-restrained and with senses controlled,
they all worship me alone with undistracted minds;
performing sacrifices through the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) and mental offerings, they remain perfectly disciplined.
They constantly rise toward the fires, remaining ever established within the fires; free from other duties, pure, and eternally devoted to the fire—
those wise ones who possess such an understanding go to Me.
With their intentions free from desire, they are eternally composed in knowledge;
having established the sacred fires within the self, they are without food and without hope. Free from engagement with sense objects, they are liberated, possessing the eye of wisdom.
With undistracted minds, steadfast and endowed with the discipline of their own nature,
they saw that lake in the sky filled with lotuses and water-lilies;
there, fires blazed forth without any fuel.
O bird, there are those whose intentions are pure through wisdom, who are as stainless as the rays of the moon;
they attend upon the fire, chanting with clearly articulated syllables,
pure and longing [for liberation] within those fires.
Those whose selves have been cultivated by me and who always take delight in me alone, who worship me as the light, free from all affliction— they,
whose natures are free from passion and who are imperishable, must dwell in that very place.

For those devotees of mine who are without food, motionless, with a radiance like the rays of the moon, stainless, free from egoism, without support, and without desire— they are indeed my constant devotees, and I too am devoted to them.
Dividing myself fourfold, I move about for the welfare of the world;
for the sake of sustaining the worlds, I ordain the cosmic order.
You ought to hear that from me in its entirety and exactly as it is.
One form is called "without qualities" (nirguṇa) and is established in supreme yoga;
the second, O dear one, creates the multitude of beings, both moving and unmoving;
and the third withdraws the created world, both stationary and moving.
Established in the Self, as if destroying and deluding [beings] through her *māyā*,
casting down and bewildering them by means of her own *māyā*—
that fourth great form of mine bestows prosperity upon the world.
I am that one who, being self-restrained, protects [the world] and moves through the sky;
by me all this is pervaded, and in me everything is established. I am the seed of the entire world, the omnipresent, the imperishable.

O bird, those who have performed the *agnihotra* sacrifices and those who are like masses of moonbeams, who constantly recite the Veda— into those fires they come to me in due order, happy and endowed with knowledge.
Their blazing austerity and perfectly concentrated energy are always directed toward me; and I, unwearied, abide in them,
through a one-pointed concentration fixed on me alone, with all attachments relinquished.
I can indeed be reached by means of the eye of knowledge;
know me to be the coarse-seer, the cause and effect of the world.
Know that the worlds, together with the gods, have truly issued forth from me.
And by me also, the Self has been divided fourfold and established among living beings:
Vāsudeva, who is the Self itself, is indeed situated in the intellect; Aniruddha is situated in the mind; Saṃkarṣaṇa is in the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra); and Pradyumna is situated in the mind (manas).
Furthermore, you ought to hear correctly about the fourfold [manifestation] otherwise:
Hiraṇyagarbha, known as Padma, wherein Brahmā was born;
and from Brahmā, Śiva was also produced—let this be understood.
From Śiva, Skanda was born; this is the fourfold creation.
Know me always as the destroyer of the pride of the Daityas and Dānavas. Whenever dharma is oppressed by Daityas, Dānavas, and Rākṣasas, [I manifest].
Then, for the sake of the increase of Dharma, I shall become manifest in embodied form. But those who are steadfast, whose intellects are certain, who are devoted to Vedic vows,
and who are yogis engaged in yoga— they alone behold me, and no others.
I am conjoined with five [aggregates] and disjoined from five;
thus I exist within them and have likewise ceased from them.
Those who possess the conceptualization of birth perceive me in such a manner.
Space, wind, water, light, and earth as the fifth—
know me to be composed of these, and be certain that I am not anything else;
I remain unmoving within the five aggregates, both present and past.

Those whose intellect is undiscerning, being possessed by passion and darkness, do not perceive my true nature— even with regard to sounds, touches, forms, tastes, and smells— even through great austerity.
Neither by fasts, nor by observances, nor even by various vows,
can the supreme goal be seen or known;
for those submerged in the mire arising from great delusion, Hari is the refuge.
Those who are single-mindedly devoted to meditation, having abandoned the state of asceticism, go to me;
those whose intellect is endowed with the quality of goodness (*sattva*) and is solely certain of the Self—
they behold their own Self as the imperishable Supreme Self.
Non-violence toward all beings, and uprightness established within them— by fixing his mind upon these very things, he rightly attains me, the Unborn.
This supreme secret narrative is most wonderful.

You ought to hear that in its entirety and exactly as it is, with diligence. Those who are devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice and dedicated to the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) constantly worship me— those very ones whom you have seen.

Those who know the methods prescribed by the scriptures and are unattached in any other way— by them I can be known in my supreme, immutable state. But those who, even after knowing both Sāṃkhya and Yoga, remain without firm resolve...
Those who are unskilled do not reach that supreme, unsurpassed goal.
Therefore, one who knows the self, whose mind is purified by pure knowledge and who is stainless,
attains that Brahman, having gone to which one does not grieve.

O best of the twice-born, those endowed with pure lineage and a mind possessed of faith, through devotion to me, attain the supreme goal— that which is the supreme secret of the intellect and that which is the ungraspable by any mark.
That subtle [reality] is grasped by the wise, by ascetics who perceive the truth.
There the wind does not blow, nor does the movement of the luminaries exist there;
neither are there waters, nor earth, nor even space, nor the movement of the mind.
From him all these are born, O bird;
and from them all, he—the stainless and omnipresent one—comes forth. This which has been seen by you, O sinless one, is my gross perception.
This is the gateway to the subtle; I am indeed the cause of all effects.
O you of immeasurable prowess, you have truly seen this in the lake.
That which is reckoned as a day and night of Brahmā by those who understand calculation—[this is it].
This very time has arrived for you there, along with the secret doctrine.
Those who know sacrifice call me the sacrifice; people learned in the Vedas call me the Veda; and the sages also declare me alone to be the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*).
I am the speaker, the thinker, the taster, the smeller, the seer, and the demonstrator; I am the knower, the awakener, the goer, the hearer, and the one whose nature is consciousness.
By worshipping me, people come to heaven and likewise attain the Great.
Knowing me alone, they prosper with a heart free from attachment.
I am the splendor of the twice-born; the twice-born are my splendor. Let it be understood that the body which exists by my splendor is indeed Agni.
"I am the protector of life within the body; I am the Lord of yogins.
For the followers of Sāṃkhya, this very world exists first within me.
[I am] dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, as well as uprightness and the recitation of mantras."
Darkness (*tamas*), goodness (*sattva*), and passion (*rajas*)— which arise from action and constitute the origin and dissolution of existence—
I am that eternal one who appeared in such a form and was seen by you at that time; yet,
as the Supreme beyond that, I can only be known through time.

That which is my supreme secret—eternal, constant, and imperishable—is likewise the supreme secret: the Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari. That cannot be understood by those who are merely endowed with worldly prosperity, O serpent.
Free from ritual undertakings and salutations, and likewise free from the bonds of desire,
those great-souled ones go to that eternal Supreme Brahman.
O sinless bird, you have seen me in this way as one who is gross.
And no one other than you, O eater of serpents, knows this;
let not your intelligence perish, for this is the unsurpassed goal.
Be my devotee eternally, and then you shall know my state.
13,013.006d@003A_0540 All this secret, pertaining to both the divine and the human, has been told to you.
13,013.006d@003A_0541 Know this to be the supreme good and the path for those seeking liberation.
13,013.006d@003A_0542 Having spoken thus, the Blessed One vanished right there.
While I was looking on, the great yogin departed by means of his own power of movement. Such was the majesty of that high-souled one,
the infallible and immeasurable, which I beheld in the past.
All this activity of that wise one has been told to you;
O sages,
having witnessed with my own eyes the marvelous deeds performed by him.
Oh, what a most wonderful and great narrative you have recited!
It is meritorious, conducive to fame and long life, leading to heaven, and a source of great well-being.
This is the purifier of the gods; this is the supreme secret, O scorcher of foes.
This is what should be known by those possessed of wisdom; this is the unsurpassed goal.
The learned man who causes this narrative to be heard on each of the sacred festival days shall attain the meritorious worlds praised by the celestial sages.
And at the time of a *śrāddha* ceremony, if one who is pure should cause this [text] to be heard by the Brahmins,
there shall be no portion for *rakṣasas* nor for *asuras* therein. [He who does so should be] free from malice, having conquered anger, and devoted to the welfare of all beings.
He who, being constantly disciplined, recites this, shall go to that same world. A Brahmin masters the Vedas; a king becomes victorious.
Bhīṣma.

The Vaiśya shall become rich in wealth and grain, and the Śūdra shall attain happiness. Then all those sages, having honored the son of Vinatā, returned to their own hermitages and became devoted to tranquility.

"O Great King, best among the upholders of dharma, this sacred revelation concerning dharma was proclaimed by Brahmā to the gods who were filled with wonder, O scorcher of foes; it is difficult to be understood by those of unrefined soul who perceive only the superficial."

O father, I too have related this story in the presence of my mother; and by you, who are endowed with the wealth of spiritual essence (*sattva*), this has also been told by me. Therefore, those who are devoted to the *agnihotra* sacrifice and dedicated to the sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*)—
Being free from the bonds of desire, they attain identity with the Imperishable. Abandoning sacrifices involving material undertakings, devoted to recitation and burnt offerings,
and meditating on Viṣṇu with their minds, they go to the supreme goal.
"That alone, O Bhārata, is the supreme liberation and the gateway to liberation,
by which those who have ascertained the Self go to the highest goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O son of the River (Apagāputra), you have heard here the names of the Lord of the World;
O All-pervading One, tell me the names of the Grandfather, the Lord, Śambhu,
the Tawny-hued One, the Master of Universal Illusion, and his great majesty according to its true nature."
Bhīṣma said:
"I am unable to describe the qualities of the wise Mahādeva, the god Śaṅkara, whose origin is unmanifest, and who is the preceptor of both the gods and the asuras."
For he is the all-pervading God who is not seen everywhere;
he is the Lord and the creator of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Sureśāna,
whom the gods— from Brahmā down to the Piśācas— indeed worship.
He who is higher than the primordial natures (*prakṛti*) and higher even than the person (*puruṣa*),
whom the seers who know yoga and perceive reality contemplate;
whom they call the supreme imperishable (*akṣara*), who is both the non-existent and the existent.
Having agitated both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* by his own splendor,
the God of gods, Prajāpati, created Brahmā from that;
for who indeed is able to describe the qualities of the wise God of gods?
Bound by the cycle of conception, birth, and old age, and accompanied by death— what mortal like me, O son, is capable of knowing Bhava, the Supreme Lord,
except for Nārāyaṇa, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace?
This wise one, the best of the Yadus, Viṣṇu, who is supremely invincible, possessed of divine vision and great splendor, beholds [all] with his eye of yoga. Indeed,
by Kṛṣṇa, the high-souled devotee of Rudra, the entire world is pervaded.
O descendant of Bharata, having then propitiated that god at Badarī, he indeed attained, O king of kings,
the state of being most beloved in all the worlds,
as well as golden eyes from Maheśvara.
For a full thousand years, this Mādhava performed austerities,
having propitiated the boon-granting god Śiva, the teacher of all that moves and is stationary;
indeed, Maheśvara was gratified by Kṛṣṇa in age after age.

O King, through supreme devotion, Hari Acyuta was pleased with that high-souled one; he directly beheld such sovereignty as belongs to that high-souled source of the universe for the sake of obtaining a son.
O Bhārata, because I see nothing else whatsoever that is superior to this,
no one is capable of explaining the names of the God of gods in their entirety;
only this mighty-armed one is capable of speaking of the attributes of the Blessed Lord.
13,014.001d*0073_30 Vaiśampāyana said:
13,014.001d*0073_30 "O King, [having described] the true majesty of Maheśvara in its entirety," 13,014.001d*0073_31 having thus spoken to Vāsudeva at that time, the highly illustrious Bhīṣma—
The Grandfather (Brahmā) spoke this, which is endowed with the greatness of worldly existence:
"One should always perform one's own duty as is appropriate through meditation and recitations;
being devoted to the god Nārāyaṇa, worship Śaṅkara well."
He spoke these words to the high-souled Vāsudeva.
Bhīṣma said:
"O God, O Viṣṇu, preceptor of the gods and asuras, you ought to speak."

That which Yudhiṣṭhira asked me concerning Śiva, who possesses all forms— that thousand names of the God formerly revealed in the world of Brahmā by Tandi, who was born from Brahman— [I shall now declare].
"Let Dvaipāyana and these other ascetics,
sages of firm vows, self-controlled, and devoted to penance, listen as you speak.
[Salutations] to Dhruva, Nandin, Hotṛ, Goptṛ, Viśvasṛj, and Agni."
"O Lord, tell me of the great majesty of the shaven-headed one and of him who wears matted locks.
Vāsudeva said:
"The course of the actions of the Lord cannot be known in its true essence."
Even the gods headed by Hiraṇyagarbha, along with Indra and the great seers who possess subtle vision, do not know his end or his beginning;
how, then, can he— the goal of the virtuous— be known by a mere mortal?
"I shall proclaim to you the various qualities of that Blessed One, the slayer of Asuras, who is the Lord of Vows, exactly as they are.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having thus spoken of the virtues of that great-souled one, the Blessed One, having touched water and become pure, related [the story] of the wise man. Vāsudeva said:
"Listen, O best of Brahmins, and you too, my son Yudhiṣṭhira;
and you, O son of the River (Apageya), hear the names of the Lord of the Universe.
Listen also to that which was formerly accomplished by me, a most difficult task, for the sake of Sāmba."
Just as the Blessed One was previously seen by me through meditative concentration,
when Śambara had been slain in the past by the wise son of Rukmiṇī;
for after twelve years had passed, Jāmbavatī indeed spoke to me.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, having seen Pradyumna, Cārudeṣṇa, and her other sons, Rukmiṇī,
desiring a son, approached me and spoke these words:
"A hero, the best among the strong, of lovely form and stainless."
"O Acyuta, grant me a son equal to yourself without delay;
for there is nothing whatsoever in these three worlds that is unattainable for you.
O upholder of the Yadu lineage, if you so desired, you could create other worlds."
Having propitiated Paśupati for twelve years while you remained as wind and withered away, sons were begotten by you upon Rukmiṇī:
Cārudeṣṇa, Sucāru, Cāruveṣa, and Yaśodhara.
Cāruśravas, Cāruyaśas, Pradyumna, and Śambhu—
just as these sons of beautiful prowess were born to Rukmiṇī,
so too grant me a son who is endowed with great strength.
Thus urged by the queen, I spoke to that slender-waisted lady:
"Give me your leave, O Queen; I shall do as you say.
And she said to me, "Go for victory and for prosperity."
Brahmā, Śiva, Kāśyapa, the rivers, the gods who follow the mind, the fields, the medicinal herbs, the carriers of sacrifice, the meters, the hosts of seers, the earth,
the oceans, the sacrificial fees, the musical chants, the constellations, the ancestors, and the planets.
The wives of the gods, the daughters of the gods, and the mothers of the gods;
the Manvantaras, cows, the moon, the sun, and Hari; Sāvitrī, the knowledge of Brahman, the seasons, the years, and the nights.
May the moments, the lava-measures, the muhūrtas, the nimeṣas, and the cycles of the yugas protect you everywhere as you travel, O Yādava, bringing you happiness.
Go upon a path free from misfortune; remain vigilant, O sinless one.
Having thus had the rites for my well-being performed by her,
and having received leave from that daughter of the lord of monkeys,
I went into the presence of my father, the best of men.
Having informed him of that matter which my mother, King Aṣṭaka, and myself had told me,
the daughter of the Vidyādhara lord spoke, being deeply distressed.
Having then granted them leave out of extreme sorrow,
they likewise spoke at that time with affection to Gada and the exceedingly powerful Rāma.
"May your perfection in asceticism be free from obstacles.
Having obtained permission from my elders, I thought of Tārkṣya;
he carried me to the Himavat mountains, and upon reaching it, I dismissed him.
Having received permission from the mouth of his guru, O descendant of Ajamīḍha,
he then meditated upon Tārkṣya with his mind and offered obeisance with his head to Bhava.
Then I went toward the delightful north-eastern direction;
thereupon, dispatched by me, the king of birds spread his wings and soared into the sky.
When Vainateya had departed for the sky,
he then went to that mountain endowed with all desires,
which was properly filled with flowers and fruits in full abundance.
Standing there, joyful and permeated by the nature of existence,
I then had the rites for my well-being performed by her and presented myself before my mother and father.
Having thus obtained the permission of all my elders,
I indeed thought of the mighty Tārkṣya;
having reached the side of the Himavat, I dispatched Tārkṣya.
There, on that best of mountains, I beheld wondrous sights;
I saw a field of supreme austerities, an excellent hermitage belonging to the high-souled Upamanyu, the descendant of Vyāghrapad, which was truly divine.
It was honored by gods and gandharvas and endowed with divine splendor; it was filled with dhava, kakubha, kadamba, and coconut trees,
as well as kurabaka, ketakī, jambu, and pāṭala trees.
With *vaṭa*, *varuṇaka*, *vatsanābha*, and *bilva*;
with *sarala*, *kapittha*, *priyāla*, *sāla*, and *tāla*;
with *badarī*, *kunda*, *punnāga*, *aśoka*, *āmra*, and *atimuktaka*.
It was filled with *bhallātaka*, *madhūka*, *campaka*, and *panasa* trees,
as well as various other wild trees that yield fruit and flowers; it was thick with flowering shrubs and creepers, and graced by groves of plantain trees.
It was adorned with trees bearing fruits that serve as food for various birds,
beautified by rows of forests arranged in their proper places,
and surrounded by dense trees perpetually endowed with flowers and fruit.
It was filled with beautiful flowers, creepers, and shrubs, and inhabited by fearless deer;
it contained spacious fire-sanctuaries where the sacred fires were maintained in their proper places,
and it teemed with ruru deer, elephants, tigers, lions, and leopards.
It was strewn with deer and peacocks, covered with cats and snakes,
frequented by herds of various species of wild animals and inhabited by buffaloes and bears, and adorned with elephants that had recently burst into rut.
Frequented by various kinds of joyful birds, and adorned with diverse forests of trees that shine like clouds and are covered in beautiful blossoms.
There, a pleasant breeze blew, mingled with the pollen of various flowers, scented by the ichor of elephants, and filled with the songs of celestial women;
it was accompanied by the sound of falling rain and the warbling of birds.
O hero, with the auspicious and amplified trumpeting of elephants, the sublime songs of the kinnaras,
and the beautiful chants of the Sāma-singers;
Inconceivable even by others through the mind, it was adorned with lakes and graced by spacious fire-sanctuaries strewn with *kuśa* grass;
it was further embellished by a river of holy and purifying waters.
And it was always frequented by the daughter of Jahnu, O King,
and adorned by great-souled sages, the best among the upholders of dharma, who were like fires themselves.
By ascetics who subsist on air, who drink only water, who are constant in recitation, who are thoroughly cleansed, and who are constant in meditation;
by those who consume smoke, who drink vapors, and who subsist on milk;
It was adorned on all sides by the foremost of brahmins—
by groups of sages in various numbers who had mastered the Vedas and their six auxiliary sciences, who delighted in the Dharma, and who were composed in meditation.

Those who wander the pastures, those who grind with stones, and likewise those who use their teeth as a mortar; those who drink the rays of the sun, those who drink foam, and likewise those who follow the manner of deer; those who subsist on the fruit of the *aśvattha* tree, and likewise those who sleep in water.
Seeing those wearing rags, skins, and garments of bark, observing them as they endured various extremely painful observances while devoted to great austerity,
he entered with eyes wide open in wonder.
O Bhārata, that circle of hermitages, always well-honored by the hosts of high-souled gods beginning with Śiva who perform meritorious deeds, shone brilliantly.
O King, like the solar orb in the sky,
mongooses play with serpents and tigers with deer as if they were friends,
endowed with the qualities of proximity due to the power of his blazing asceticism.
In that most excellent hermitage, delightful to all beings, frequented by tigers among the twice-born who had mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences,
and by high-souled sages renowned for their various religious observances.
As soon as I entered, I beheld the Lord wearing matted hair and bark garments,
blazing with splendor and ascetic power like a fire;
he was a young bull among Brahmins, peaceful and seated in the midst of his disciples.
As I was bowing my head in salutation, Upamanyu addressed me:
"Welcome, O lotus-eyed one! Our austerities have become fruitful, since you, who are worthy of worship, honor us; and you, who are worthy of being seen, desire to see us."
"Recognizing you as the omnipresent one through your conformity to the human state, we remain [in our places]. Then,
with palms joined in reverence, I inquired after his well-being regarding the beasts and birds, the sacrificial fires, the Dharma, and the circle of disciples.
Then the Blessed One spoke to me with words that were exceedingly beautiful and gentle:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you shall undoubtedly obtain a son equal to yourself. Having undertaken very great asceticism, propitiate Īśāna, the Lord."
"Here, O Adhokṣaja, the God sports together with his consort.
It was right here that, in ancient times, the gods along with the hosts of ṛṣis [attained the highest state] through austerity, celibacy, truthfulness, and self-restraint— [the best of deities]."
Having gratified him, O Janārdana, those people obtained auspicious desires. That Blessed One is here the treasury of splendors and ascetic powers;
he both emits and withdraws all states of being, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
O slayer of enemies, he whom you seek is that inconceivable one who dwells together with the Goddess; he was the Dānava Hiraṇyakaśipu, who made even Mount Meru tremble,
and by him, through Śarva, the sovereignty over all the immortals was obtained for the duration of ten million years.
His eldest son was the renowned Mandara, who,
by virtue of a boon from Mahādeva, fought against Śakra for ten million years.
Both the terrible discus of Viṣṇu and the thunderbolt of Ākhaṇḍala [were rendered powerless against him].

"O dear Keśava, in former times that discus which was previously given to you by the Blessed One— O sinless one, which moves within the waters and slew the Daitya who was arrogant in his strength— became shattered upon the limbs of the planet."
Produced by the Bull-bannered One, it resembles a blazing fire;
bestowed upon you by the Blessed One, it is wondrous in its splendor and difficult to behold.
It cannot be seen by anyone else, with the exception of the wielder of the Pināka bow.
"May you be Sudarśana," Bhava then said to him;
thus, the name Sudarśana became established for him in the world,
O Keśava, as that [discus] became worn upon the limbs of the planet, my dear.
On the body of the wise Graha Atibala, who had been granted a boon,
even hundreds of discuses and thunderbolts could not take effect;
for when it was said, "May it be as you wish," it was so by that very sight.
Being oppressed by that exceedingly powerful planet,
the gods struck the lords of the asuras— who had received boons from Śiva— violently;
and being pleased, [the planet] also granted Vidyutprabha sovereignty over the three worlds.
For one hundred thousand years, he became the lord of all the worlds;
and [the Lord] said, "You shall be my constant attendant.
Likewise, the Lord granted him ten million sons.
The Lord Aja gave Kuśadvīpa as a kingdom to him;
likewise, there was a great Asura named Śatamukha, created by the Creator,
who for more than a hundred years offered his own flesh into the fire.
The Lord Śaṅkara, being pleased, said to him, "What shall I do? To him,
the hundred-faced one replied, "Let there be for me a wonderful yoga,
and grant me eternal power, O best of deities."
"So be it," the Blessed One, the all-pervading Lord, said in response to those words.
In ancient times, Svāyambhuva Kratu also performed a sacrifice for the sake of obtaining a son;
having entered his own self through yoga, he remained thus for three hundred years.
To him the god granted a thousand sons equal in merit to sacrifices;
O Kṛṣṇa, you undoubtedly know the Lord of Yoga who is praised by the gods,
the most righteous ṛṣi renowned as Yājñavalkya.

Having propitiated Mahādeva, he attained supreme knowledge; and the sage Vedavyāsa, the son of Parāśara, whose soul was devoted to yoga, having likewise propitiated Śaṅkara, attained incomparable fame.
Long ago, it is said, the Vālakhilyas were treated with contempt by Maghavan.
Enraged by this, they gratified the blessed Lord Rudra through their ascetic penance. Then the Lord of the World, the foremost of deities, being pleased, spoke to them.
Through ascetic penance, you shall bring forth Suparṇa, the stealer of Soma. O Lord, the waters had formerly vanished due to the wrath of Mahādeva toward Durvāsas, the son given by Atri’s wife.
And those others were set in motion by the gods with the seven potsherds;
thereafter, when Tryambaka was pleased, water appeared upon the earth.
Even the wife of Atri, a speaker of sacred truth, abandoned her husband.
"I shall never again, under any circumstances, be subject to the will of that sage. Having spoken thus, she indeed sought refuge with Mahādeva,
remaining without food for three hundred years out of fear of Atri.
For the sake of propitiating Bhava, she lay down upon the pestles.
Laughing, the god said to her, "A son shall indeed be born to you;
he will be born without a husband and from a *caru* offering—of this there is no doubt."
And Vikarṇa, having propitiated Mahādeva, who brings happiness to his devotees,
attained perfection, O Madhusūdana;
and he shall attain the desired renown under your very name within your own lineage.

Śākalya, whose self was indeed disciplined, propitiated Bhava for nine hundred years with a sacrifice of the mind alone, O Keśava. And the Blessed One, being pleased, said to him: "You shall become an author of books."
"Your fame shall indeed be imperishable throughout the three worlds;
may your lineage be eternal, adorned by great seers.
O best of the twice-born, your son shall become an author of Sūtras."
In the Kṛta age, there was a renowned sage named Sāvarṇi;
he performed austerities here for sixty hundred years. The blessed Lord Rudra appeared to him in person and said, "O sinless one, I am pleased with you."
The author of this work shall become world-renowned and free from old age and death.
Long ago in Vārāṇasī, O Janārdana, the naked god smeared with ashes was worshipped by Śakra as a devotee.
Having propitiated Mahādeva, he obtained the sovereignty of the gods. In former times, Bhava was worshipped with devotion by Nārada;
pleased with him, Mahādeva, the preceptor of the gods and the supreme teacher, spoke.

In splendor, ascetic power, and fame, there shall be none equal to you; through divine song alone, you shall follow me eternally. Śākalya was the author of the treatises, and Sāvarṇi likewise became so.

Bāṇa attained equality with Skanda, Kāma the shedding of his pride, Lavaṇa immunity from death by others, and Daśāsya (Rāvaṇa) further strength; even Antaka (Yama) met his end [at his hands]. Therefore, who else is more powerful?

And furthermore, O Mādhava, listen to how I myself formerly beheld the omnipresent Lord of Gods, Paśupati, in person, my dear; and hear also for what purpose Mahādeva was previously propitiated by me with great effort.
The Lord Mahādeva, possessed of great splendor, was propitiated by me with great effort; hear now the details of that in full.
