"O sinless one, whatever was previously obtained by me from Maheśvara, the God of gods, all that I shall today relate to you in its entirety.
Long ago, O dear one, in the Kṛta age, there was a highly illustrious ṛṣi."
Known as Vyāghrapāda, he was a master of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences. I was his son, and Dhaumya was my younger brother.
Then, after some time had passed, O Mādhava, together with Dhaumya—
While wandering through the hermitage of sages of purified souls, I arrived there;
and there too, I saw a milch cow being milked,
and I observed that the milk was sweet, like nectar itself.
From that time forth, O Madhusūdana, I did not weep;
I cried out, "Mother, give me milk! Give me milk!
Then, O Mādhava, having stirred flour together with water, [she gave it to me].
"13,014.078c 'Our milk'—with these very words, it was brought to us for the purpose of drinking.
13,014.079a But then, my dear, cow's milk was once tasted by me. 13,014.079b For at the time of a sacrifice, I was led by my father to a great kinsman's house."
There that divine cow, the celestial one who delights the gods,
flows [with milk]. Having drunk her milk, which is like nectar in its flavor, and having understood the qualities of that milk and realized its origin, I [attained this state].
13,014.079c Then, dear one, the taste of flour did not bring me pleasure.
13,014.080a Thereupon, out of childishness, I then said to my mother: 13,014.080c "Give me food consisting of rice cooked with milk."
"O mother, this rice-milk that you have given me is not [ordinary] rice-milk;
for at that time, my mother was distressed due to the very lack of milk. Then my mother, filled with pain and grief, spoke to me."
13,014.081c Embracing him out of affection for his son and smelling the crown of his head, Mādhava said:
13,014.082a "Whence, my child, could there be milk-rice for sages of purified soul, 13,014.082c who dwell eternally in the forest, subsisting on roots, tubers, and fruits?"
[They saw] those who had settled by the divine river frequented by the Vālakhilyas—
those sages dwelling in the forest, living on the mountains, pure, subsisting on forest produce, and residing in forest hermitages; from where did they obtain milk?
"For those who have desisted from village food and subsist on wild fruits,
there is no milk in the forest, O son, for it is devoid of the lineage of Surabhi.
[It is found] in rivers, caves, mountains, and various sacred bathing places."
For those who are constant in austerity and recitation, Śiva is our supreme refuge. Without propitiating Virūpākṣa— the boon-granting, immutable Sthāṇu—
whence, my child, could there be milk-rice, comforts, and garments?
This creator Rudra, the three-eyed one, is the cause of all;
he has eight arms, matted hair, and is adorned with serpents, with the moon as his crest-jewel;
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread, accompanied by his attendants, he is the blue-throated lord of Umā.
With beautiful tusks, a lovely smile, and snake-earrings, he is radiant with ashes.
Bestowing all desires when worshipped with devotion using flowers and roots— O child, always take refuge in that Śaṅkara with your whole being.
"Through devotion, Hara, the granter of all desires, has been brought before your very eyes. By his grace, my son, you shall obtain the fruit of your desires.
O slayer of enemies, having heard those words of your mother, from that time forward..."
With palms joined in reverence, I bowed down and questioned my mother thus:
"Mother, who is this Great God? How may he be propitiated? Where does the Lord dwell, and how is he to be beheld?"
"How can Śarva be pleased, or what is his form like? How is he to be known when he is propitiated, or how might he show himself to my mother?
When she had spoken thus, O Kṛṣṇa, my mother, who is deeply affectionate toward her son, [replied].
O Govinda, smelling my head with eyes clouded by tears,
my mother, O Madhusūdana, was indeed wiping my limbs.
Summoning her fortitude, O best of gods, the mother said this:
"Mahādeva is difficult to understand, difficult to propitiate, and difficult to bring to an end;
he is indeed unassailable, difficult to grasp, and difficult to behold by those who have not disciplined themselves."
The wise proclaim that his forms are manifold,
his abodes are diverse, and his manifestations are likewise many;
for who indeed knows in truth the auspicious conduct of the Lord?
Indeed, those forms which the God of gods assumed in ancient times—
how Śarva plays and how he truly becomes gracious— the Maheśvara of universal form who dwells in the hearts of all beings.

Out of compassion for his devotees, he granted them visions according to what they had heard from the sages as they recounted the divine narrative of Īśāna’s deeds; he manifested those very forms that had been described by the celestial dwellers.
For the sake of favoring the Brahmins, listen, my child, in brief;
I shall proclaim to you those things about which you ask me—
concerning Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the lords of the gods, as well as the Rudras, Ādityas, and Aśvins.
Bhava assumes the form of all the gods,
as well as that of men, divine women, and likewise of pretas and piśācas;
he also assumes the forms of Kirātas, Śabaras, and various aquatic creatures in manifold ways.
The Blessed One assumes even the forms of forest-dwelling Śabaras;
he becomes a tortoise, a fish, and likewise a conch adorned with sprouts of coral;
and [he takes the forms] of Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents, as well as Daityas and Dānavas.
The god assumes once again the forms of those dwelling in caves—
tigers, lions, deer, hyenas, bears, birds, owls, dogs,
and jackals.
He creates the forms of swans, crows, peacocks, lizards, and cranes; he also creates the forms of herons, vultures, and ruddy geese, or even assumes the form of a mountain.
And Mahādeva assumes the form of a cow, as well as the shapes of elephants, horses, camels, and donkeys;
he takes on the forms of goats and tigers, and bears the bodies of many kinds of wild beasts;
furthermore, Bhava assumes the bodies of divine egg-born creatures.
He carries a staff, an umbrella, and a water-pot; he is likewise the sustainer of the twice-born.
He has six faces and indeed many faces, three eyes, and many heads;
he possesses many hips and feet, and bears many bellies and mouths.
With many hands at his sides and surrounded by many hosts,
he assumes the forms of ṛṣis and gandharvas, and takes on the appearance of siddhas and cāraṇas;
his body is pale with ashes, and he is adorned with the crescent moon.
Resounding with many cries and extolled by manifold hymns of praise,
he is the ender of all beings, the All, established in all worlds;
he is the inner self within all worlds, the omnipresent, and the speaker of everything.

The Blessed One is to be known as dwelling in the hearts of all embodied beings everywhere. Whatever desire one may wish for, and whatever purpose for which he is worshipped again—that the Lord of Gods knows it all; therefore, take refuge in him if you so desire.
He rejoices and becomes angry, and likewise utters the sound "huṃ.
He holds a discus, a trident, a mace in his hand, a club, a sword, and a battle-axe;
he is the upholder of the earth, wears a girdle of serpents, and has earrings made of snakes.
Wearing a serpent as his sacred thread and having a serpent’s skin as his upper garment,
he laughs, sings, and dances most enchantingly;
surrounded by his hosts, he also plays various musical instruments.
He leaps and yawns, weeps and even causes others to weep; he speaks with the appearance of one who is mad or intoxicated, yet with a beautiful voice;
and being exceedingly fierce, he laughs loudly, terrifying people with his eyes.
He keeps watch and sleeps, yawns as he pleases;
he mutters prayers and is muttered at, performs austerities and is again subjected to them;
he gives and receives, exerts himself and meditates as well.
In the middle of the altar, likewise at the sacrificial post, in the midst of the cow-pen, and before the fire,
he is seen and indeed seen again— whether as a child, an old man, or a youth—
and he plays with the daughters of the sages as well as with the wives of the sages.
With hair standing erect and a massive phallus, naked and with distorted eyes;
fair, dark, black, pale, and smoke-red;
with deformed eyes and wide-open eyes, unclothed and yet the wearer of all garments.

Who can truly know the end of this one who is formless, whose primordial form is formless, who transcends all forms yet possesses the primordial formlessness, who is without beginning or end, and unborn? Within the heart reside the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), the individual soul (*jīva*), the self of yoga, and that which is designated as yoga.
He is meditation, he is the Supreme Self, the Great Lord (Maheśvara) who is perceivable through contemplation; he is the speaker and the singer, possessing hundreds of thousands of eyes;
he has one face, two faces, three faces, and many faces.
"Devoted to Him, always intent on Him, established in Him, and having Him as your supreme goal— worship Mahādeva, my son, and you shall thereby obtain what you desire.
Having heard those words of his mother, O slayer of enemies, from that time forward...

13,014.085c My steadfast devotion to Mahādeva was fully established. 13,014.086a Thereupon, having undertaken ascetic penance, I gratified Śaṅkara for a thousand divine years, standing poised on the tip of my big toe.
For one hundred years I subsisted on fruit;
for a second hundred, I ate withered leaves; for a third, I lived on water;
and for seven hundred years, I subsisted on air alone.
Thus, for a thousand divine years, I propitiated him.
Then Mahādeva, the Lord and Master of all the worlds, being pleased,
recognized me as one devoted to him alone and then put me to the test.
Having assumed the form of Śakra, surrounded by all the hosts of gods,
the highly illustrious one then became the thousand-eyed wielder of the thunderbolt;
[he appeared] white as nectar, with red eyes, stiff ears, and intoxicated with pride.
Mounted upon a fierce great elephant with four tusks and its trunk curled,
the Blessed One, blazing with his own splendor,
arrived wearing a diadem and adorned with necklaces and armlets.
With a white parasol being held over his head,
served by *apsarases*, and accompanied by the music of divine *gandharvas*,
the Lord of the Gods then said to me: "O best of the twice-born, I am pleased with you."
"Choose from me whatever boon is in your heart.
But upon hearing the words of Śakra, O Kṛṣṇa, my mind was not pleased; and then I spoke these words to the king of the gods.
"O Madhusūdana, I said to that Lord of the Gods,
'O dear one, I do not desire a boon from you, nor from any other deity,
except for Mahādeva; O gentle one, I tell you this truly.'"
"Truly, truly, O Śakra, this word of ours is well-ascertained:
no other discourse pleases me except that which concerns Maheśvara.
Truly, O Kauśika, may there be for me no cessation from the cycle of existence."
Today, by the word of Paśupati, I shall immediately become someone else to listen to this other story composed by Maheśvara—
be it a worm or even a tree with many branches.

Even the sovereign splendor of the three worlds, born from the grace of Śiva’s boon, would be undesirable to me; let my birth be even among the outcaste dog-cookers, provided I am devoted to worshipping the feet of Hara.
Even if one were to subsist on air and water, how could there be an end to suffering for that man who is not devoted even to the abode of Śakra?
For he indeed lacks devotion toward the Lord of the Universe, the teacher of gods and asuras.
Enough with those other discourses of theirs, however exceedingly endowed with dharma,
for those who do not find it pleasing even for a moment to interrupt the remembrance of Hara’s feet; having reached this crooked age, one must have a mind devoted to the feet of Hara.
Having drunk the elixir of devotion to Hara, the fear of saṃsāra does not exist—
whether for a day, half a day, a muhūrta, a kṣaṇa, or a lava. Indeed,
devotion to Śaṃkara does not arise in one who has not obtained his grace.
"By the command of Śaṅkara, I would even become a worm or a moth;
but, O Śakra, I do not desire even the three worlds given by you.
Even as a dog, by the word of Maheśvara, I shall exist—for that indeed is our supreme desire."
Indeed, I do not desire even the sovereignty over the host of the thirty-three gods if it is not commanded by Maheśvara; nor the vault of heaven, nor the kingdom of the gods,
nor the world of Brahmā, nor even the state of being partless.
I do not choose all desires in their entirety; I choose the state of servitude to Hara,
as long as he bears upon his crown the pure crescent of the moon.
The blessed Lord Paśupati, my master,
does not take pleasure [in me] as long as I continue to endure the sufferings ordained for the body through hundreds of blows from birth, old age, and death.

Having failed to propitiate Rudra— the one who blazes like the sun, the moon, and fire; the essence of the three worlds, boundless, primordial, singular, undecaying, and immortal— [one cannot attain this].
Who in this world could find peace here,
if birth were to occur again through my own faults? In each and every such birth, may I possess inexhaustible devotion.
"Fie upon them! Fie upon them again! And fie upon them—fie upon those in whose hearts Rudra, the liberator from the path of evil ways, does not dwell!
Śakra said:
Upamanyu said: "What indeed is your reason for [seeking grace] from the Lord, the cause of all causes, such that you do not desire favor from any other deity?"
That which the exponents of Brahman call both existent and non-existent, manifest and unmanifest,
eternal, one, and yet manifold— that supreme boon I choose from him,
which is without beginning, middle, or end, and possesses inconceivable knowledge and sovereignty.
Since he is the supreme self, we choose him as our boon;
since his sovereignty is complete, unproduced, and imperishable—
arising from the seedless as the source of all seeds— we choose him as our boon.
The supreme light beyond darkness, the highest state for those devoted to austerity—
knowing which they do not grieve, we choose that as our boon; the knower of the existence of the creator of beings, who transcends all beings.
I worship the all-pervading, all-bestowing God, O Purandara,
who is free from the discourse of causal reasoning, who grants the supreme goal of Sāṃkhya and Yoga,
and whom the knowers of reality worship; from him we choose the boon.
O Maghavan, we choose that boon from him whom they call Maghavat, the Lord of the Gods, the divine teacher of all beings;
he who formerly created the god Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
Having filled the cosmic egg and space, we choose that as our boon.
Fire, water, wind, earth, ether, intellect, mind, and the Great Principle—
even if there were another creator of these, tell me, who could he be other than the Supreme Lord?
"O Śakra, tell me: among mind (*manas*), intellect (*mati*), ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), and the sense organs (*indriya*), who else could be more supreme than Śiva?
Here in this world, they call the Grandfather (*pitāmaha*) the creator."
Having propitiated the Lord of Gods, he enjoys great prosperity;
for the supreme sovereignty over Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others indeed exists within Mahādeva— tell me, who is there superior to the Supreme Lord?
Who other than the Lord of Gods is able to grant sons— who crush the enemies of the sovereign Daityas and Dānavas—
except for him whose splendor is like that of the quarters, time, and the sun, and who is the planets, wind, moon, and stars?

Know that these [powers] come from Mahādeva; tell me, who else is there besides the Supreme Lord? Whether it be the origin or the destruction of the sacrifice, or of Tripura, or the subjugation of the lords of the Daityas and Dānavas, he is the crusher of enemies.
Furthermore, O Purandara, what is the use of many well-spoken words or arguments of logic here?
O best of gods, having seen you yourself— the thousand-eyed one—
honored by Siddhas, Gandharvas, deities, and likewise by the Ṛṣis.
O best of the Kuśikas, all that [is obtained] through the grace of the God of gods.
This entire self-nature belongs to the omnipresent one whose hair is unmanifest and disheveled;
O Śakra, know that [it exists] within the conscious and unconscious beings from Maheśvara.
In the great realms beginning with Bhūḥ, in the intervals between the worlds and the Lokāloka mountain,
in the locations of the continents, and amidst the splendors and spaces of Mount Meru—
O Blessed One, those who perceive reality call the god Maghavan by this name.
O Śakra, if the gods and *suras* see another form of yours,
why do those gods not seek refuge when they are crushed by the *asuras* during the assaults upon the gods,
including the *yakṣas*, *uragas*, and *rākṣasas*?
Existence, which bestows sovereignty over one's own station amidst mutual destruction,
[was experienced] by Andhaka, Śumbha, Dundubhi, and Mahiṣa,
as well as among the lords of the Yakṣas, Bala, the Rākṣasas, and the Nivātakavacas.
Who else but Maheśvara could grant such a boon?
Tell me, into whose mouth was the seed of the preceptor of gods and asuras offered as an oblation in ancient times?
Or into whose other seed was it cast, by which the golden mountain was formed?
Who else in the world is celebrated as being "clothed in space" (*digvāsas*), and who is one whose vital energy flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*)?
With whom does the beloved consort dwell, and by whom was the bodiless god (*anaṅga*) conquered?
O Indra, tell me: whose supreme station is praised by the gods?
In the cremation ground, for whose sake is there dancing as a sport, or who is being addressed?
Whose sovereignty is equal [to theirs], or who plays with the *bhūtas*? With whom are the hosts of gods, arrogant in their power, of equal strength?
For whose sake is this immovable station, honored by the three worlds, proclaimed?
Who else rains down, who else shines with heat, and who else blazes with splendor?
From whom does the abundance of medicinal herbs arise, or who sustains the wealth of the world?
Who indeed in the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, sports with such delight? Being served by yogins through the application of knowledge, supernatural powers,
and ritual action, he is the supreme cause ordained by the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and siddhas.
Served by gods and asuras through the performance of ritual sacrifices and the yoga of action,
I shall declare that Cause which is eternally devoid of the fruits of action—
vast, subtle, incomparable, ungraspable, yet the sphere of the qualities.
The supreme state of Maheśvara, devoid of qualities yet the presiding lord of all qualities;
the Lord of the Universe, the primordial teacher, the cause of the light and darkness of the worlds;
the progenitor of the past, present, and future, and the cause of all things.
The manifest and the unmanifest, the imperishable and the perishable, knowledge and ignorance,
the performed and the unperformed, merit and demerit— from which these arise, O Śakra, that I declare to be the cause.
O Lord of the Gods, behold here with your own eyes the mark characterized by the female organ.

By Rudra, the god of gods and the cause of creation and destruction, this cause of the world was previously told to me as its measure. O Śakra, there is nothing higher than the Lord; resort to him if you so desire.

O Lord of the Gods, surely this is known to you through direct perception: that the three worlds, arising from the mark of conjunction, together with their qualities and modifications, are produced from the seed of Brahmā and the others;
and that the gods, including Brahmā, Indra, Mahendra, and Viṣṇu, as well as the Daityas and Asuras [are likewise so born].

Those whose minds are fashioned by a thousand desires praise no one other than the Lord; therefore, seeking desire and wealth, yet with a restrained mind, I choose that god Śarva, the auspicious Śiva, who is the supreme object of knowledge declared for the entire world of moving and unmoving beings, for the sake of liberation.
Upamanyu said:
"O Lord, what need have you for other reasons? We have never heard of the emblem of any other being being worshipped by the gods as the cause of all causes."

"Except for Maheśvara, tell me if you have heard of any other whose linga is worshipped— or has ever been worshipped— by all the gods together? For it is his linga that Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and even you, along with the deities, revere."
13,014.102c Worship the *liṅga* always; therefore, it is indeed the most excellent.

13,014.102d*0113_01 Since creatures are neither marked with the lotus, nor marked with the discus, nor marked with the thunderbolt, 13,014.102d*0113_02 but are marked with the *liṅga* and marked with the vulva (*bhaga*), therefore the progeny belongs to Maheśvara.

All women are marked with the sign of the vulva (*bhaga*), produced by the nature of the Goddess as their cause; likewise, all men are visibly marked by the phallus (*liṅga*) of Hara. Whoever asserts that there is another cause for this than the Lord, or that anything is not marked by the Goddess—

In the three worlds, including all that is mobile and immobile, he who considers that man to be external is a person of evil intellect. Know that everything characterized by the masculine gender is Īśāna, and that which is characterized by the feminine gender is Umā.
Indeed, this entire world of mobile and immobile beings is pervaded by these two bodies.
Therefore, O Kauśika, I desire either this boon or even death;
go or stay as you please, O Śakra, slayer of Bala! Let this be my boon, or else let it be a curse from Maheśvara.
"I do not desire any other deity, even for the sake of all the fruits of my desires.
Having spoken thus to the Lord of the Gods, his senses agitated by grief, he thought, "Rudra is not pleased with me; what could this mean?"
Then, in an instant, I saw that very same Airāvata once again—
resembling a swan, jasmine, or the moon, with the luster of a lotus stalk or a white water-lily,
bearing the form of a bull like the Ocean of Milk itself in person.
With a black tail, a massive body, and eyes tawny like honey,
he had horns made of the essence of diamond, glowing with the luster of refined gold;
with those sharp, hard, and crimson-tipped horns, he seemed to be tearing up the earth.
It was adorned all over with a girth-band of Jāmbūnada gold;
it had red eyes, a very large nose, beautiful ears, and well-formed hips; it had shapely flanks, broad shoulders, a handsome form, and was lovely to behold.
His hump shines forth, standing filling out his shoulder,
resembling the peak of a mountain of snow and like the summit of a white cloud.
And seated upon it is the Blessed One, the God of gods, together with Umā.
Mahādeva shone like the lord of stars on a full-moon night;
his crown, mass of matted hair, ornaments such as serpents, his thunderbolt and other weapons, his trident, his elephant, and his deep smile all appeared together.
The fire born of his splendor stands enveloping everything like a thousand suns, accompanied by clouds and thunder;
that lord of immense majesty is like the Saṃvartaka fire at the end of an eon.
Like one intent on burning all beings at the end of the eon,
he then stood with his splendor pervading everything, making him difficult to behold from any side;
with a heart again filled with agitation, [Rāma] wondered, "What is this?"
Having pervaded all ten directions for a mere moment,
that splendor was pacified in an instant by the illusory power (*māyā*) of the God of gods.
Then I beheld the Blessed Maheśvara, Sthāṇu, standing there.
The gentle one, seated upon the bull, like a smokeless fire—
the three-eyed, unconquered Lord whose mind is tranquil—
was accompanied by Pārvatī, whose every limb was beautiful.
The high-souled Nīlakaṇṭha, unattached, a treasury of splendors,
eighteen-armed Sthāṇu, adorned with all ornaments—
the god wearing white garments, white garlands, and white unguents.
He bore a white banner, was invincible, and wore a white sacred thread;
he was surrounded by divine attendants whose prowess equaled his own, who were singing, dancing, and leaping here and there.
He who bears the crescent moon as his crest-jewel, pale-white like the risen autumnal moon;
who is illuminated by three eyes like three risen suns;
the God who is the sovereign of all sciences, possessing a radiance equal to the autumnal moon.
I beheld the Supreme Lord, gentle and pleasing to the eyes;
and upon the body of the God, which possessed a white radiance,
shone a garland woven with golden lotuses and adorned with jewels.

O Govinda, I beheld the personified weapons of Bhava, who possesses immeasurable splendor, all composed of every kind of radiance. The bow of that high-souled one shone with the brilliance of a thousand rainbows.
Known as Pināka, it was indeed a great serpent with seven heads, massive in body, possessing sharp fangs and virulent poison;
its great neck was encircled by the bowstring, and it stood there in human form.
And Śara, resembling the sun and possessing a brilliance like the fire of time,
with a thousand arms, tongues, and mouths, terrifying and having the form of a serpent,
stood there embodied, equipped with conchs, tridents, swords, and spears.

By him Tripura was consumed with an arrow composed of all the gods; and the trident, endowed with youth, stood in the hand of Lavaṇa. By the command of Śaṅkara, Rāma became the wielder of the axe that exterminated the Kṣatriyas.
That great and most terrible divine weapon, the Pāśupata,
which is peerless, indescribable, and brings fear to all beings— emitting sparks and appearing like a vast body of fire— is being discharged.
He had one foot, great tusks, a thousand heads and bellies,
and a thousand arms, tongues, and eyes, as if vomiting forth fire;
he was more powerful than Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, Indra, Agni, or Varuṇa.

O mighty-armed Govinda, that which is distinguished as the destroyer of all weapons— by means of which, in the past, Mahādeva effortlessly burnt the triple city (Tripura) and reduced it to ashes in an instant with a single arrow.
And the trident that slew Yauvanāśva was held in the hand of Lavaṇa.
Having thus beheld Mahādeva, he fell to the earth upon his knees;
[the god] then consumed the entire world, the three realms with all things moving and unmoving.
Released from the arm of Maheśvara in less than half a blink of an eye— of this there is no doubt—
it could not be slain by anyone in this world, even by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or the gods. O dear one, I beheld that supreme, wondrous, and marvelous sight.

It is a supreme and secret weapon, equal to or even superior to that [other weapon]; it is known throughout all the worlds as the *śūla* (spear) of the Wielder of the Spear (*Śūlin*). It could tear asunder the entire earth or dry up the great ocean.
He could withdraw the entire universe created by the wielder of the trident;
he by whom Yauvanāśva was slain in the past, along with Māndhātṛ and his army—
that king who was a universal monarch of great splendor and the conqueror of the three worlds.

Possessing great strength and great heroism, with prowess equal to Śakra, O Govinda, that extremely sharp-pointed, most terrifying, and hair-raising spear of the Rākṣasa Lavaṇa was already in his hand.
With his three-pronged brow furrowed, he stood as if threatening;
smokeless yet flaming, dark as the sun risen at the end of time,
with a serpent in his hand, he was indescribable, like Death himself with a noose in his hand.
O Govinda, I have seen that weapon in the presence of Rudra;
it is the sharp-edged axe which was given to Rāma in the past,
and that weapon of his which was formerly possessed of supreme, keen power.
By Mahādeva, being pleased, he was made the destroyer of the Kṣatriyas;
by him, the universal monarch Kārtavīrya was slain in a great battle,
and by him the earth was cleared of Kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
O Govinda, by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, whose deeds are effortless, [the bow]—
with its blazing edge, its most fierce face, and its neck encircled by a serpent— became like a crest of blazing fire in the presence of the wielder of the trident (Śiva).
The divine weapons of that wise one are indeed innumerable;
O sinless one, I have recounted these to you according to their principal ones. On the left side of the god, however, is Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds.
Mounted upon a divine celestial chariot yoked with swans and swift as thought,
Nārāyaṇa likewise stood at his left side,
mounted upon Vainateya and bearing the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Skanda, mounted upon a peacock, stood near the Goddess,
holding a spear at his throat like a second Fire-god;
and before the God, I saw Nandin stationed.
Standing there, propping up the trident like a second Śaṅkara,
all the Manus beginning with Svāyambhuva, the sages beginning with Bhṛgu,
and the deities beginning with Śakra, all approached him together.
All the hosts of spirits and various classes of Mothers were present there;
having saluted the Great-Souled One and surrounded him on all sides,
the gods then praised Mahādeva with diverse hymns of praise.
In the midst of that, [Brahmā] beheld the Great Liṅga, the form of the universe, possessing a vast manifestation.
Then Brahmā, praising Bhava while chanting the Rathantara,
and Nārāyaṇa likewise sang to the Lord of Gods with the Jyeṣṭhasāman.
Chanting the Śatarudrīya, the supreme and highest Brahman, Śakra shone resplendent;
Brahmā, Nārāyaṇa, and Kauśika, the king of the gods—
these three great-souled ones were as beautiful as the three sacred fires.
In their midst, the blessed Lord Śiva shone like the sun surrounded by [clouds] when released from the autumnal clouds;
and in the sky, O Keśava, I beheld tens of thousands of moons and suns.
Then, O god of excellent vows, I praised the deity with this hymn: "Salutations to the God of gods, salutations indeed to Mahādeva;
salutations to Śakra, to him who has the form of Śakra, and to him who wears the guise of Śakra."
Salutations to you who hold the thunderbolt in hand, who are tawny and ruddy;
salutations eternally to you who carry the Pināka bow in your hand, and who bear the sword and the trident. Salutations to you who are clothed in black and whose hair is dark and curled.
To him who has a black antelope skin as his upper garment, who delights in the eighth day of the dark fortnight;
to him who is white in color, who is pure, who wears white garments;
to him who is smeared with white ashes, and who delights in white (pure) deeds.

Homage be to the one of red complexion and wearer of red garments; to the one with red banners and flags, and to the one adorned with red garlands and unguents. Homage be to the one of yellow complexion and wearer of yellow garments.
Homage be to him who has yellow banners and flags, who is adorned with yellow garlands and unguents; homage to him who bears a raised parasol and wears an excellent crown,
whose ears are graced by half-necklaces, half-armlets, and half-earrings.
Homage to you who possess the speed of the wind; homage indeed to the god, homage to the lord of the gods, to the lord of sages, and to Mahendra—homage be to you!
Homage to him who wears a garland of half-lotuses interspersed with blue lotuses.
Salutations to him who is smeared with half-anointing of sandalwood and adorned with half-a garland;
salutations to him whose face is the sun and whose eyes are the sun;
salutations to him whose color is the sun and who is the likeness of the sun.
Homage to Soma, to the gentle one, and to him who bears a gentle face;
homage to him of gentle form, the foremost one, adorned with gentle tusks. Homage to the dark one, to the fair one, and to him who is half-yellow and half-pale.
Homage be to you, whose body consists of both woman and man, O Strīpuṃsa! Homage be to you who ride upon a bull and who possess the gait of a lordly elephant!
Homage to you, the difficult to traverse, and to you who go where it is forbidden to go!
Homage be to him who is praised by the hosts, and to him who delights in the multitude of hosts;

homage to him whose path is followed by the hosts, and to him whose vow is eternal among the hosts; homage to him who has the color of white clouds, and to him who possesses the radiance of the twilight glow.
Homage be to you, whose nature is unnameable and beyond designation! Homage to him who wears red garments on his head and carries a red thread;
to him who is variegated with red garlands and who wears red robes!
Homage to him whose head is adorned with jewels, who is decorated with the crescent moon; homage to him whose head is crowned with variegated gems and who bears eight flowers;
homage to him whose mouth and eyes are fire, and who possesses eyes like a thousand moons.
Homage be to the one whose form is fire, to the beloved, and to the profound;
homage to you who move through the sky and who delight in the sensory realm; homage to the one who moves upon the earth, to the world itself, to the infinite, and to Śiva.
Salutations always to the sky-clad one, who is beautifully perfumed even without clothing;
salutations to the abode of the world and to the bliss of realization;
salutations to the one whose crown is eternally bound and who wears great armlets.

Salutations to the one who is the offering for the serpent’s throat and who wears variegated ornaments; salutations to the one with the eye of the three-eyed god, the one with hundreds and thousands of eyes;
salutations to the female, the male, and the neuter; salutations to the follower of Sāṃkhya and the practitioner of Yoga.
Homage, homage to Atharvan, who flows with auspiciousness;
homage to the destroyer of all afflictions, and homage to the remover of sorrow;
homage to him whose voice is like the roar of clouds, and who possesses manifold powers of illusion.
Salutations again and again to the protector of the seed and the field, to the Creator; salutations again and again to the Lord of gods and asuras, to the Lord of the universe;
salutations to him who possesses the speed of the wind, salutations to him whose form is the wind.
Salutations to Kāñcanamāla and indeed to Girimāla; salutations to Surārimāla and indeed to Caṇḍavega;
salutations to the one who severed the head of Brahmā and indeed to the slayer of Mahiṣa.
Salutations to the one who assumes the form of a woman and to the one who bears all forms;
salutations to the destroyer of Tripura and to the destroyer of the sacrifice;
salutations to the annihilator of the body of Kāma and to the bearer of the staff of Time.
Homage to Skanda and Viśākha, and indeed homage to Brahmadaṇḍa; homage to Bhava and Śarva, and indeed homage to Viśvarūpa;
let there be homage to Īśāna, the slayer of Bhaga, the destroyer of Andhaka.

Salutations to the one who is all-pervading, the master of illusion; salutations indeed to the one who is both conceivable and inconceivable. You are Brahmā among all the gods, and Nīlalohita among the Rudras;
you are the Self of all beings, and in the Sāṃkhya system, you are called Puruṣa.
Among purifiers you are the Bull; among yogis, you are the partless Śiva. Among stages of life you are the householder; among lords, you are Maheśvara.
Among all yakṣas you are Kubera; among sacrifices, you are said to be Viṣṇu.
Among mountains you are Mahāmeru; among the stars, the moon; you are said to be Vasiṣṭha among the sages and the sun among the planets. Among wild animals, O Supreme Lord, you are the lion.
Among domestic animals, you are the bull, O Blessed One, worshipped by the world;
among the Ādityas you are Viṣṇu, and among the Vasus you are Pāvaka; among birds you are Vainateya, and among serpents you are Ananta.
Among the Vedas you are the Sāmaveda; among the Yajus formulas, you are the Śatarudriya. Among yogins you are Sanatkumāra, and indeed, among the Sāṃkhyas, you are Kapila.
O God, among the Maruts you are Śakra, and among the ancestors, you are Dharmarāja.
Among the worlds, you are said to be the world of Brahmā; among destinies, you are liberation.
Among oceans, you are the Ocean of Milk; among mountains, you are the Himavat peak. Among the social orders, you are the Brāhmaṇa; and among the twice-born, you are the consecrated priest.
"You are the origin of the worlds and indeed their destroyer, Time itself.
Whatever other being in the worlds is known for its superior splendor—all that is the Blessed One alone; such is my firm conviction."
Homage to you, O Blessed Lord, O God; homage to you, O you who are affectionate toward your devotees.
Homage be to you, O Lord of Yoga; homage to you, O source of the universe.
Be gracious to me, your devotee, who am wretched and miserable.
O Eternal One, grant me a refuge for one who is deprived of sovereignty.
O Lord of Gods, whatever offense I have committed out of ignorance, you ought to forgive all of that, remembering that I am your devotee.
"O Lord of Gods, I was bewildered by the transformation of your form;
therefore, O Lord of Suras, I did not offer you the *arghya* or even the *pādya*.
Having thus praised Īśāna with devotion, I offered the *pādya* and the *arghya*."
With my palms joined in reverence, I reported everything to him.
Then, O dear one, a beautiful shower of flowers— mixed with cool water and endowed with divine fragrance— fell upon my head.
Then a divine drum was struck by the servants of the gods,
and a holy wind blew, pure-scented and bringing comfort.
Thereupon Mahādeva, the bull-bannered god, together with his consort, was filled with joy.
Then, as if gladdening the gods there, he said to them:
"Behold, all you thirty-three gods, the supreme and divine devotion of the high-souled Upamanyu toward me, which remains steadfast through single-mindedness."
Thus addressed by the wielder of the trident,
all those gods, having bowed to the bull-bannered one, spoke with palms joined in reverence: "O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Protector of the worlds, Master of the universe!"
"O best of the twice-born, may he obtain from you the fruit of all his desires.
When he had been addressed thus by the gods, beginning with Brahmā, the blessed Lord Śarva,
Śaṅkara, spoke to me as if smiling.
"O child Upamanyu, I am pleased; behold me, O bull among sages!
You are firm in devotion, O brahmin-seer, for you have been tested by me. Because of this very devotion of yours, I am exceedingly pleased."
"Therefore, today I grant you all desires exactly as you wish.
When I had been addressed thus by Mahādeva, O Lord,
tears flowed from my joy and my hair stood on end.
Then, having knelt upon the earth and bowed down again and again, I spoke to the God with a voice faltering with joy:
"O Lord, today I am truly born; today my ascetic penance has borne fruit."
Since Mahādeva himself stands before me, gracious and manifest,
my birth has today become fruitful;
for the God, the teacher of gods and asuras, stands before me.
"I have seen that god of immeasurable prowess whom even the gods do not behold despite their worship; who else is more fortunate than I?
Thus do the wise meditate upon the supreme, eternal reality."
That which is known as the twenty-sixth, the imperishable syllable beyond the supreme,
is this very Blessed Lord, the God who is the source of all principles (tattvas) and is immutable; he is the knower of the arrangement of all principles, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
The Lord, from whose right limb he created Brahmā, the source of the worlds,
and likewise from his left side Viṣṇu for the sake of protecting the worlds; and when the end of the age has arrived, the Master creates Rudra from his own body.
That Rudra,

possessing great splendor, becoming Time itself like the fire of universal destruction at the end of an eon, stood as if swallowing all beings— both mobile and immobile— as he withdrew the entire world.
This god, Mahādeva, having created the world with all its moving and unmoving beings,
remains at the end of the kalpa after withdrawing the memory of all. He is omnipresent, the self of all beings, and the source of the existence of all beings.
He remains eternally omnipresent, invisible to all the gods.
Having bowed my head to him once more, I spoke to Bhava:
"If a boon is to be granted to me, and if the Lord is pleased with me,"
Then, having been granted permission, I spoke to Śaṅkara:
"O Lord, having bowed my head to you and propitiated you, I pray:
O Śaṅkara, may I possess eternal and constant devotion toward you."
"O Lord, O Supreme among the Gods, by your grace may my intellect be such that I may know the past, the future, and the present;
and may I eat inexhaustible milk-rice together with my kinsmen."
"And may you always have your supreme presence in my hermitage.
Thus addressed by me, the Blessed One, worshipped by the world— the great Maheśvara of immense splendor, the Lord and teacher of all that moves and is stationary— spoke to me.
By my grace, you shall become undecaying and immortal, free from suffering,
renowned, endowed with splendor, possessed of divine knowledge,
and worthy of being approached by the sages.
"May you be virtuous, endowed with excellent qualities, omniscient, and pleasing to behold; may your youth be inexhaustible and your splendor like that of fire,
O Sage, wherever you desire, even in the Ocean of Milk."
There, you shall have your heart’s desire; the treasure-house of milk will be present in every place there, without a doubt. And you yourself shall eat rice-milk mixed with nectar.

Together with your kinsmen, you shall remain for an eon; thereafter, you will come to me. O best of the twice-born, your relatives, family, and lineage shall forever be imperishable, and your devotion to me shall be eternal.
"O best of the twice-born, I shall always maintain my presence in this hermitage.
Stay here, my child, as you desire; you should not feel any anxiety.
O Brahmin, whenever you remember me, I will always grant you my vision."
"O Brahmin, I have remembered you; I shall grant you my vision once again.
Having spoken thus, the Blessed One, whose radiance is equal to ten million suns, the Lord, having granted me this boon, vanished right there.
"O Kṛṣṇa, thus was the God of gods beheld by me through meditative absorption (samādhi).
And all that was spoken by that wise one has been attained by me.
Moreover, O Kṛṣṇa, behold for yourself these Siddhas standing here before your very eyes."
Behold the sages, *vidyādharas*, *yakṣas*, *gandharvas*, and *apsarases*; behold the delightful trees, always endowed with flowers and fruit;
behold the trees, creepers, and shrubs that yield every kind of flower and fruit.
13,014.199c Adorned with flowers of every season, possessing glossy leaves and beautiful branches;
13,014.199e All this, O mighty-armed one, is endowed with a divine nature. 13,014.199f Thus, O Keśava, have I obtained all this from Mahādeva.
13,014.199f*0137_01 Through the grace of the God of gods, the Great-Souled Īśvara.
13,015.000*0138_01 Having heard these words of his, as if seeing him face to face.
Having attained a state of supreme wonder, I said to that great sage:
"O best of Brahmins, you are blessed; what other doer of merit is there like you, for whom the God of gods manifests his presence in your hermitage?"
"O tiger among sages, may that Blessed One, Śiva, likewise grant me his vision and his grace, O Śaṅkara. Upamanyu said:
"O lotus-eyed one, you will behold Mahādeva without a doubt;
in a very short time, O sinless one, just as he was seen by me,
I shall see him with my divine eye, O you of immeasurable prowess."
"In the sixth month, O Puruṣottama, you shall behold Mahādeva;
and from Maheśvara, together with his consort, O best of the Yadus, you shall obtain sixteen boons. I tell you this as the truth."
"O mighty-armed one, by the grace of that wise one, the past, the future, and the present are constantly known to me. Hara has likewise meditated upon these and thousands of others."

O Mādhava, why would the Blessed One not show favor to you? For an encounter with one such as you— who is devoted to Brahman, compassionate, and full of faith— is indeed praiseworthy even for the gods.
"I shall give you a mantra to be recited (*japya*), by which you will behold Śaṅkara.
Kṛṣṇa said:
"O Brahmin, O great sage, I then said to him: 'By your grace...'"
"I shall behold the Lord of the Thirty, the crusher of the hosts of the sons of Diti. O Bhārata,
as he was thus recounting this story concerning Mahādeva,
eight days passed by like a single moment.

On the eighth day, I was initiated by the Brahmin according to the prescribed rite; I was equipped with a staff, my head was shaven, I held *kuśa* grass, wore rags, was anointed with clarified butter, and likewise wore a girdle.
For one month I subsisted on fruit, and for the second month I lived on water.
O Bhārata, subsisting on air alone, standing on one foot with arms upraised and unwearied, I beheld the splendor of a thousand suns in the sky during the third, fourth, and fifth [periods].
And in its center, O son of Pāṇḍu, was a mass of energy resembling a dark mountain range, its body encircled by a rainbow, with lattices of lightning-garlands,
and adorned with rows of cranes like clouds.
And seated upon that [throne], the Lord of great splendor, together with the Goddess—
blazing with ascetic power, brilliance, and beauty along with his radiant wife—
the Blessed Maheśvara shone forth there.
Like the sun accompanied by the moon situated within a cloud,
O son of Kuntī, with my hair standing on end and my eyes wide with wonder,
I beheld Hara, the remover of affliction, who is the refuge of the hosts of gods.
Wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a trident in his hand;
clad in a tiger skin, with matted hair, and carrying a staff in his hand;
wielding the Pināka bow and the thunderbolt, and possessing sharp fangs.
Wearing beautiful armlets and a serpent as a sacred thread,
he bore upon his chest a divine garland of many colors that hung down as far as his ankles.
Just as the moon surrounded by a halo at twilight,
so did I behold him at the end of the rainy season—
Maheśvara, accompanied by Nandin, Vināyaka, and the others.
He was surrounded on all sides by hosts of Pramathas,
like the sun enveloped in autumn and difficult to behold;
likewise, the eleven Rudras stood around him, whose mount is the bull.
The eleven Rudras, who bring him happiness, having arrived, praised him with self-restraint as one whose deeds are virtuous;
likewise the Ādityas, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the two Aśvins.
With all hymns of praise, they together extolled the god who is the lord of all gods;
and the illustrious Śatakratu and Viṣṇu, the two sons of Aditi,
as well as Brahmā, chanted the Rathantara Sāman in the presence of Bhava.
Many lords of yogins, as well as the Brahman-sages with their sons and the celestial sages, [worshipped] the father and guru who bestows yoga; likewise,
the earth, the intermediate space, the constellations, and the planets [were present].
O King, the months, half-months, seasons, nights, years, moments (kṣaṇas),
instants (muhūrtas), eye-winks (nimeṣas), as well as the cycles of the yugas, and all divine sciences and the quarters of the sky likewise pay homage.
Sanatkumāra, the Vedas, and likewise the Itihāsas;
Marīci, Aṅgiras, Atri, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu;
the seven Manus, Soma, Atharvan, and Bṛhaspati.
Bhṛgu, Dakṣa, Kaśyapa, Vasiṣṭha, and Kāśya; the Vedic meters, the initiations, the sacrifices, the sacrificial fees, the fire, and the oblation;
and all the materials required for sacrifice, O Yudhiṣṭhira, were present there in embodied form.
All the lords of creatures, the rivers, the serpents, and the mountains; all the mothers of the gods, the wives of the gods, and their daughters;
and thousands, tens of thousands, and hundreds of millions of sages.

O King of kings, the mountains, the oceans, and the quarters of space pay homage to the peaceful Lord; so too do the trees, the medicinal herbs, and various minerals. Furthermore, the Gandharvas and Apsaras, who are skilled in song and instrumental music, [also offer their praise].
Singing with divine voices, the Vidyādharas, Dānavas, Guhyakas, and Rākṣasas likewise praise the wonderful Bhava; indeed,
all beings, both stationary and moving, do so as well.
"O Great King, they pay homage with speech, mind, and action to the All-pervading Lord. O Bhārata, Śarva, the lord of the thirty gods, stood before me; and seeing Īśāna standing before me,"
The entire world, ending with Prajāpati and Śakra, gazed up at me;
yet at that time, I had no power to look upon Mahādeva.
Then the God said to me, "Behold, O Kṛṣṇa, and speak!"
Indeed, I have been propitiated by you hundreds and thousands of times;
there is no one else in the three worlds as dear to me as you.
When the god was saluted with her head, the goddess Umā became pleased.
Then I praised Sthāṇu, who is praised by the gods beginning with Brahmā;
then I praised the God of gods and the Goddess endowed with auspicious marks.
Many masters of yoga praised Maheśa in manifold ways.
The great elements, the Vedic meters, the lords of creatures, and the sacrifices; the rivers, the oceans, the nāgas, the gandharvas, and the apsarases;
and the vidyādharas likewise worshipped him with song, instrumental music, dance, and other such offerings.

At that time, I did not have the power to behold Mahādeva, the Lord of the World, who was a mass of splendor situated in the midst of those radiant beings; then the God addressed me, saying, "Look! and "Speak!"
Having seen the God and likewise the Goddess being praised by the deities, he offered this hymn of praise:
"Salutations be unto you, O Eternal One, the source of all!
The seers declare you to be the sovereign of Brahmā."
The virtuous declare that you alone are austerity, goodness, passion, and darkness, as well as truth itself.
You indeed are Brahmā, Rudra, Varuṇa, Agni, Manu, and Bhava.
You are Dhātṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, and Vidhātṛ; you are the Lord whose face is turned in every direction.
From you all beings have been born, both the stationary and the moving.
You are the beginning of all beings, and indeed, you alone are their dissolution.
By you this entire triple world, with all that is moving and unmoving, was created;
as were the objects of the senses, the mind, the whole [universe],
the seven winds, and likewise fire.
Or whatever deities dwell in heaven for men;
therefore the seers declare you to be beyond them.
The Vedas, the sacrifices, Soma, the sacrificial fee, the purifier, and the oblation—[all these are you].
Whatever is required for sacrifice, O Blessed One, all that is undoubtedly yours;
whatever has been offered, given, studied, and whatever vows and observances have been performed— all these,
as well as modesty, fame, fortune, splendor, contentment, and success, are dedicated to you alone.
"O Blessed One, desire, anger, fear, greed, pride, arrogance, and envy; mental agonies and physical ailments—these indeed are your sons.
You are action, transformation, dissolution, primordial matter, the source, and the imperishable."
The supreme source of the mind and eternal nature itself,
you are the unmanifest, the purifier, the all-pervading Lord, the golden thousand-rayed one;
you are indeed the origin of all qualities and the refuge of all living beings.
The Great Self (Mahān Ātmā), Intellect (Mati), Brahmā, the All-pervading (Viśva), Śambhu, and the Self-existent (Svayaṃbhū);
Intellect (Buddhi), Wisdom (Prajñā), Perception (Upalabdhi), Consciousness (Saṃvit), Renown (Khyāti), Fortitude (Dhṛti), and Memory (Smṛti)—
by these synonymous terms the Great Self is manifested.
Having realized you, the learned Brāhmaṇa does not fall into delusion;
the wise Brāhmaṇa who knows reality likewise possesses an immeasurable state of being. You are the heart of all beings, the Knower of the Field (Kṣetrajña) praised by the seers.
You have hands and feet everywhere; you have eyes, heads, and faces on all sides; you possess ears everywhere in the world, and you abide pervading all things.
O you of piercing rays, you are the fruit in actions such as the blinking of an eye.

You indeed are the radiant light, the Puruṣa dwelling within the heart of all; you are the powers of atomization, levitation, and attainment, the sovereign lord, the imperishable light. In you are established the intellect and the mind, as well as the worlds and those who have sought refuge and taken shelter in you.
They are meditators, ever-devoted to yoga, true to their word, and masters of their senses—
those who know you as the eternal one dwelling in the cave of the heart,
the ancient Lord, the Puruṣa of universal form.

13,015.044c This golden [state] is the supreme goal of the wise; having transcended even that wisdom, the wise one abides [there]. 13,015.045a Having understood the seven subtle elements and you, who possess six limbs, in your embodied form, [he attains this].
"O wise one, established in the application of the primary injunction, you shall enter into me alone.
When I had spoken thus, O Pārtha, regarding Bhava, the destroyer of affliction,
the entire world of moving and unmoving beings let out a lion’s roar.
The gods and asuras together with the assembly of Brahmins,
the nāgas, piśācas, ancestors,
and birds, all the hosts of rākṣasas and the hosts of bhūtas;
The great seers likewise bowed down;
heaps of fragrant, divine flowers fell upon my head, and a most pleasant breeze blew.
Having gazed upon the goddess Umā, upon me, and upon Śatakratu for the welfare of the world,
Lord Śaṅkara himself spoke to me:
"O Kṛṣṇa, slayer of enemies, we know your supreme devotion toward us."
"Let that which is for your own welfare be done, for my affection for you is supreme.
Choose eight boons, O Kṛṣṇa; I shall grant them to you, O best of beings. Speak, O tiger among the Yādavas, of those things you desire, however difficult they may be to obtain."
13,016.001 Kṛṣṇa said: Then, with self-restraint, having prostrated his head before that mass of splendor,
he bowed his head to the god Bhava, the imperishable Lord Īśāna.
Attaining supreme joy, I then spoke to the Blessed One:
"Grant me steadfastness in dharma, the slaying of enemies in battle,
as well as foremost fame and supreme strength."
"Your fondness for yoga and your proximity to me— I choose [these], as well as hundreds upon hundreds of sons.
"So be it," Śaṅkara said in reply to those words spoken by me.
Then the Mother of the World, Dharaṇī, who purifies all,
Umā Śarvāṇī— the storehouse of ascetic powers— addressed me with focused intent:
"O sinless one, a son named Sāmba has been granted to you by the Blessed Lord."
"O son of Pāṇḍu, bowing her head, she said to me as I spoke: 'Grant me eight desired boons from you as well; I shall give them to you. [I replied:
'Absence of anger toward Brahmins and favor from your father.'"
I choose a hundred sons, supreme enjoyment, joy within the lineage, grace from my mother,
the attainment of tranquility, and also skillfulness.
13,016.007 The Goddess said:
"O you of immortal power, it shall be so;
I never speak a falsehood at any time."
And there were exactly sixteen thousand wives; among them, he possessed such belovedness, inexhaustibility,
and the highest affection from his kinsmen.
I grant you the loveliness of your form;
indeed, seven thousand guests shall always be entertained in your house.
"May there always be many hundreds of joyful guests in your home. Vāsudeva said:

O descendant of Bharata, O elder brother of Bhīma, having thus granted these boons to me and my queen, the god, together with his attendants, vanished in that very moment. All this was most wonderful, [told] to the Brahmin of exceeding splendor.
O best of the Kauravas, I have related this entire account to Upamanyu.
Having offered salutations to the God of gods, he, firm in his vows, said:
"There is no one equal to Śarva in generosity; there is no one equal to Śarva in battle."
There is no god equal to Śarva; there is no goal of existence equal to Śarva.
O dear one, in the Kṛta age there was a seer renowned as Taṇḍi, by whom the God [was worshipped] through meditative absorption for ten thousand years.
He was propitiated by that devotee; hear now the result of that.
He beheld Mahādeva and praised the Lord with hymns. Thus, through the power of his austerity and yoga, Taṇḍi [beheld] the imperishable Supreme Self.
Having reflected upon that Great-Souled One, he, filled with wonder, said this:
"That which the followers of Sāṃkhya always recite and the practitioners of Yoga contemplate—
the Supreme, the Primal Matter (pradhāna), the Person (puruṣa), the Overlord, and the Sovereign."

I bow to that unborn Lord Īśāna, who is without beginning or end, whom the wise know to be the cause of both the origin and the destruction of the gods, asuras, and sages, and beyond whom nothing else exists.
"Go for refuge to that sinless god who is possessed of ultimate bliss.
While he was speaking thus, he then beheld that treasure-house of asceticism—
imperishable, incomparable, inconceivable, eternal, and constant.
Brahman is both partless and possessed of parts, devoid of qualities yet the sphere of qualities;
it is the supreme bliss of yogis, the imperishable known as liberation,
and the goal of the mind, Indra, Agni, the Maruts, and of the entire universe.
Ungraspable, immovable, pure, graspable by the intellect, and consisting of mind;
difficult to discern, incalculable, and unattainable by those of unrefined self;
the source of the entire world, beyond darkness and supreme.
The supreme, ancient Puruṣa, higher than the high and beyond the beyond—
he who desires to behold that God, the seer [waited] for many groups of years, [seeking] the self endowed with breath, the light, the mind abiding as the individual soul (jīva).
Having established himself in fierce austerity and beheld [the Lord], he praised the Lord:
"You are the purifier of purifiers, the goal of those who have a goal, O best of beings;
you are the most intense splendor of splendors, the supreme austerity of austerities."
O Viśvāvasu, Hiraṇyākṣa, you who are saluted by Puruhūta; O All-pervading One, bestower of abundant auspiciousness, True Person, let there be homage to you!
O All-pervading One, for the ascetics striving with effort who are fearful of birth and death—
O giver of Nirvāṇa, thousand-rayed one, homage be to you, the refuge of happiness!
Brahmā, Śatakratu, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the great ṛṣis do not know you in truth; how then shall we know you?
From you time proceeds, and into you time dissolves;
for you alone are indeed designated as Time, as Puruṣa, and as Brahmā. Your three bodies have been described by the celestial sages who are knowers of the Purāṇas.

You alone are indeed the presiding principle over the person, the internal self, the elements, and the deities; you are the presiding principle over the worlds, over consciousness, and over the sacrifice.
For having known you, who abide within the body of the self, you are difficult to be perceived even by the gods.
The wise, being liberated, go to the supreme state that is free from affliction.
O Lord, though you do not desire it, birth and death recur for you in manifold ways;
you are the gateway to heaven and liberation, both the one who withdraws and the one who bestows them.
You alone are liberation and heaven; you indeed are desire and anger. You alone are goodness, passion, and darkness; you alone are below and above.
You are Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra; Skanda, Indra, Savitṛ, and Yama.
You are Varuṇa and the Moon; you are Manu, Dhātṛ, and Vidhātṛ; you are the Lord of Wealth.
You are earth, wind, light, and water; you are speech, intellect, thought, and mind.
You are both action and truth and falsehood; you alone are "it exists" and "it does not exist."
The senses and the objects of the senses, that which is beyond them, and the eternal nature (prakṛti);
the state that is both the universe and beyond the universe, the conceivable and the inconceivable—you alone are indeed all these.
That which is this supreme Brahman, and that which is the supreme goal; [you are that].
"That which is the goal of the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga, that you are—of this there is no doubt.
Surely today we have achieved our purpose; surely we have attained the goal of the virtuous, that goal which those whose intellects are purified by knowledge reach in this world."
"Alas! For this long time we have been fools, devoid of sense, since we did not know the Supreme, Eternal God whom the wise know. He has now been encountered by me in person after many births."
The Lord, who bestows grace upon his devotees— knowing whom one partakes of immortality—
is the eternal secret of gods, asuras, and humans;
that Brahman is deposited in the cave of the heart, difficult to be known even by the gods.
This very Lord, the Divine One, is the creator of all, facing in every direction;
he is the self of all, the seer of all, omnipresent, and the knower of all.
He is the maker of life, the sustainer of life, the living being, the giver of life, and the final resort of all living creatures.

The creator of the body, the sustainer of the body, the embodied one, the enjoyer of the body, and the goal of all embodied beings— he who is the goal of those meditators who know the Self, who are established in the path of the supreme self, and who desire never to return to death— he is this very Lord.
He is the bestower of auspicious and inauspicious destinies for all beings; he ordains birth and death among all creatures;
and he is the Lord who grants success to the sages desiring spiritual accomplishment.

And this Lord is the bestower of liberation upon the twice-born who desire release. Having produced all the worlds, beginning with the earth, along with the celestial dwellers, that God sustains them and grants [their desires] through his eight forms.
From this everything proceeds; in this everything is established; and into this everything goes to its dissolution. This is the one eternal [Brahman].
This is that supreme world of truth for the virtuous who desire the truth.
This is the liberation of the emancipated and the absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) of those who proclaim the Self; this Lord has been hidden in the cave by Brahmā and the perfected ones (*siddhas*),
so that He might not be revealed to gods, asuras, and humans.

The gods, asuras, and humans do not know you, Bhava, in your true essence; indeed, they are deluded, for they have been entered by this very desire dwelling in the heart. And those who take refuge in him through the yoga of devotion, O Bhārata—
This one dwelling in the heart reveals his own self to those very selves;
having known him, there is no further birth nor even death. Having known him, the supreme object of knowledge, there remains nothing else to be known.
Having obtained which, he considers no further gain to be superior;
he attains that supreme, subtle state of life which brings about imperishability—
[that state] which the followers of Sāṃkhya, who know the principles of the qualities (guṇatattva) and are experts in the Sāṃkhya scriptures, [seek].

Those who formerly delighted in subtle knowledge, having understood it, are liberated from their bonds. They who know the Vedas, who are established in the Upanishads (Vedāntas), and who are devoted to the regulation of breath (prāṇāyāma), constantly enter into and chant that which is to be known.
Having ascended the chariot of the syllable *oṃ*, they enter Maheśvara. This Āditya is said to be the gate of the paths of the gods (*devayāna*),
and this Candramas is said to be the gate of the paths of the ancestors (*pitṛyāna*).
This course of time is manifold throughout the years, yugas, and so forth;
it consists of existence and non-existence in the present, as well as the southern and northern solstices.
Thus, in former times, Prajāpati was propitiated with many hymns of praise.
He chose him, known by the name Nīlalohita, to be his son—
he whom the Bahvṛcas praise with Ṛg-verses during the ritual performance,
and whom the Adhvaryus, knowing him through the threefold Veda, offer as oblations with Yajus-formulas at the sacrifice.
He whom the chanters of the Sāmans, pure in intellect, sing with *sāman* hymns;
whom the twice-born masters of the Atharvans praise as the Right, the Truth, and the Supreme Brahman; he is remembered as the supreme source and the Lord of sacrifice.
Night and day are his ears and eyes; the fortnights and months are his head and arms; the seasons are his vigor, austerity, and fortitude; and the year is his secret organ, thighs, and feet.
He is Death, Yama, and the sacrificial fire—Time, possessing the impetus of destruction.
He is the supreme source of time, and he is this eternal time. Along with the moon and the sun, together with the constellations, the planets, and the wind;
along with Dhruva, the seven ṛṣis, and the seven worlds themselves.
Pradhāna, Mahat, the Unmanifest, and the specific elements along with their transformations; that which begins with Brahmā and ends with a blade of grass; all beings, both existent and non-existent;
the eight primary natures (prakṛtis), and that which is beyond the primary natures.
That which revolves entirely as the portion of this god is the supreme bliss, and it is indeed eternal. This is the goal of those free from passion; this is the highest state of the virtuous.
This state is free from agitation; this is the eternal Brahman. For those who know the scriptures and the Vedāṅgas, this meditation is the supreme goal.
This is that ultimate limit; this is that supreme attainment.
This is that supreme accomplishment; this is that supreme goal;
this is that supreme peace; this is that highest liberation—attaining which, the creators thought, "We have accomplished all that was to be done."
This is contentment, this is perfection, this is sacred revelation, and this is tradition;

it is the imperishable attainment of the wise who are established in the course of the inner self. It is [the goal] for those performing sacrifices and desiring sacrifice through rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
O Eternal One, that divine goal which belongs to the gods, that goal you are. O God,
that goal which belongs to those who perform austerities through recitations, oblations, vows, hardships, observances, and the emaciation of the body—
that goal is you in the realm of Vairāja.

O Eternal One, you are the destination of those who have renounced all actions performed repeatedly and who are detached from this world and that; you are the destination of those who desire no further rebirth and abide in supreme dispassion within the abode of Brahman.

O Eternal One, you are the goal of all transformations and dissolutions; you are the ineffable and stainless state for those established in knowledge and realization. O God, that supreme goal which is absolute liberation—that goal is you.
"These five destinies are declared in the Vedas, the Shastras, and the Puranas;
for they are attained through your grace, O Lord, and not otherwise.
Thus did Tandi, through the power of his asceticism, praise the imperishable Ishana.
And he sang the supreme Brahman, which the Creator of the World sang in ancient times. Upamanyu said:
"Thus was Mahādeva praised by Taṇḍi, the expounder of Brahman."
The blessed Lord, the Master, together with Umā, spoke:
"Brahmā, Śatakratu, Viṣṇu, the Viśvedevas, and the great ṛṣis do not know you. Thereupon, Śiva, being pleased, said to him:
He shall be inexhaustible and immutable, free from suffering,
illustrious, endowed with splendor, and possessed of divine knowledge. He will be worthy of being approached by the seers, the author of Sūtras, and your son.
"O best of the twice-born, by my grace this shall come to pass; of this there is no doubt.
What desire shall I grant you today? Tell me, my child, what you long for.
With palms joined in reverence, he replied: "May my devotion to you be firm."
Having thus granted the boon, the Lord, being saluted by the celestial sages and praised by the gods, vanished right there;
and when the Blessed One had disappeared along with his followers, O Lord of the Yādavas.
"O best of men, listen for the sake of your success to those names which the seer Taṇḍi first proclaimed to me here when he came to my hermitage."
The Grandfather declared ten thousand names of Śarva in the Vedas,
and likewise one hundred names in the Śāstras;
these secret names of the Lord Acyuta were [revealed] by Taṇḍi.
13,016.075c By the grace of the God, O Lord of Gods, he spoke in the past to the high-souled one.
13,017.001 Vāsudeva said:
13,017.001a Then, O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, having become purified, he [spoke] to me.
With palms joined in reverence, the brahmin-sage Upamanyu spoke from the beginning the compendium of names.
Upamanyu said:
[I shall speak] with those words proclaimed by Brahmā, proclaimed by the sages, and originating from the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas.
I shall praise Sthāṇu with names renowned throughout all the worlds— names that are great, established, true, perfected, and accomplishers of all goals,
composed with devotion by the seer Taṇḍi, whose soul was dedicated to the gods.
As taught by the world-renowned sages who perceive reality— taught which is preeminent, foremost, conducive to heaven, beneficial to all beings, auspicious,
and heard throughout the entire world as it descended from the realm of Brahmā.
O best of the Yadu clan, listen attentively to me as I declare that supreme, eternal secret which has been proclaimed by Brahmā. You are a devotee of the divine Parameśvara as the Supreme Being.

Therefore, I shall cause you to hear that which is the eternal Brahman. It is not possible for anyone to describe the entirety of Śarva’s manifestations in detail, even by one who is disciplined, even in hundreds of years.
O Mādhava, who could possibly describe in their entirety the virtues of Him whose beginning, middle, and end are not even perceived by the gods? Nevertheless,
[I shall speak] of that Great God using words and syllables of concise meaning.
I shall describe his conduct according to my ability, indeed through his very grace;
for without having obtained his permission here, it is not possible to praise the Lord. Only when authorized by him may one ever praise Bhava.
I shall indeed declare a certain enumeration of the names of that Great Soul, who is without beginning or end, the source of all, whose origin is unmanifest,
the giver of boons, the most excellent, the universal-formed, and the wise.
Listen to this summary of names as it was spoken by the Lotus-born One— those ten thousand names which the Great-Grandfather spoke,
extracted by him with his mind like clarified butter from curd.
Just as gold is the essence of the mountain, as honey is the essence of the flower,
and as the scum is the essence of clarified butter, so too has this essence been extracted. This [work], which destroys all sins, is endowed with the four Vedas.
It must be acquired with effort and retained by one whose self is disciplined;
it is pacifying, nourishing, a destroyer of demons, purifying, and great. This should be given to a devotee who possesses faith and is a believer.
O Kṛṣṇa, he who lacks faith, who is an atheist, who has not conquered his self,
and who harbors malice toward the God who is the soul of all beings, the wielder of the Pināka bow—
he goes to hell together with his ancestors and his followers.
This is meditation; this is yoga; this is the unsurpassed object of meditation.
This is the mantra to be recited; this is knowledge; this is the supreme secret.
Having known this, even at the time of death, one shall indeed attain the highest goal.

O mighty-armed one, I shall recite this supreme hymn, the best among all hymns— purifying, auspicious, meritorious, and most excellent. In ancient times, Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds, composed this.
He appointed [him] as the sovereign over all divine hymns of praise;
from that time forth, this [hymn] became renowned in the world as the "King of Hymns" (Stavarāja) of the high-souled Īśvara, worshipped by the immortals.

This king of hymns was brought down from the world of Brahmā; because Taṇḍi recited it in ancient times, it became known as the work of Taṇḍi. Indeed, it was brought down by Taṇḍi here from heaven to the world of mortals.
O mighty-armed one, I shall proclaim this supreme hymn among all hymns— the most auspicious of all auspicious things and the destroyer of all sins—
which is the Brahman even of the Brahmanas and the highest of the high.
That which is the radiance even of radiances, that which is the austerity even of austerities,
that which is the peace even of peace, that which is the splendor even of splendors,
that which is the self-control even of the self-controlled, and that which is the wisdom even of the wise.
He who is the god even among gods, the sage even among sages,
the sacrifice even among sacrifices, and the auspicious one even among auspicious things;
he who is Rudra even among the Rudras, and the Lord even among those who possess power.
The yogi who is the yogi even among yogis, and the cause of causes;
from whom the worlds arise and into whom they cease to be—
of that Hara, whose splendor is immeasurable and who has become the self of all beings.

Listen to these one thousand and eight names of Śarva from me, O best of men; having heard them, you shall obtain all your desires. He is the Steadfast, the Motionless, the Lord, the Radiant, the Most Excellent, the Giver of Boons, and the Supreme.
He is the soul of all, renowned as all, the All, the creator of all, and the source of existence;
he has matted hair, wears skins, and bears a crest-lock; he is the embodiment of all limbs and the progenitor of all beings; he is the tawny one, the deer-eyed one, the lord who withdraws all beings.
Mahāroṣa, Mahārūpa, Makha, the Lord of the Three Worlds;
Satya, the Refuge of Truth, Siddha, Caṇḍāṃśu, and Sarpakuṇḍala;
Vṛṣa, Vṛṣarūpa, Vṛṣastha, and Vṛṣabhākṣaga.
Bhīma, Śitikaṇṭha, Śiva, Śveta, Śivottama,
Niṣaṅgin, Śitikeśa, Ditipa, Nīlalohita,
Śarabha, Śaṅkukarṇa, Vilāsa, and Viśvakartṛka.
Para, Pāśupata, Bhadra, Nīlagrīva, Vibhīṣaṇa, Gaṅgādhara, Pṛthu, Janaiśvara, Kuleśvara,
Uttamastrīsahāya, Madhuvinda, and Mahāgraha.
Divya, Sūkṣma, Parāga, Vīrabhadra, Vibhinnaga; Śiva, Śambhu, Bhuvobhartṛ, Śrīkaṇṭha, Tridaśārcita;
Kravyāda, Kīrtimān, Krīḍī, Kālāgni, and Kāryakāraṇa.
The Egg, the external Egg, and Virāṭ who has become the creator of distinctions;
the cause of Hiraṇyagarbha, and that which has become external as the impeller; the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and the fourth (turīya) state, which is free from agitation.
Mind, intellect, and ego—constituting the manifest internal organ;
the Pure One, the Valiant, the All-pervading, and the Gatherer of the Universe; the Formless, the Fierce-formed, the Thunderbolt-handed, and the Destroyer of Cities.
Jātavedas, Jāgarti, Viśvāvāsa, Vināyaka, Ājānu, Vainateya, Viśvakarman, Vicakṣaṇa,
Hiraṇyākṣa, Sukeśa, Ṛkṣa, Kakṣatara, and Tamas.
The bull, rich in bulls, the slayer of Vṛṣa, whose limbs are like bulls, the destroyer of progeny; he who is active and withdrawn, the restrained, the eternal, the firm;
the lord who wanders the cremation ground, who moves through the sky, who moves within the senses, and the tormentor.

He of great deeds, the ascetic who brings all beings into existence, is worthy of salutation; he is the Lord of Progeny for all the worlds, disguised in the garb of a madman. He possesses a magnificent form and a vast body; he is the embodiment of all forms and is of great renown.
Mahātman, Sarvabhūta, Virūpa, Vāmana, Manu,
Lokapāla, Antarhitātman, Prasāda, Hayagardabhi,
Pavitra, Mahat, Niyama, and Niyamāśraya.
He is the performer of all actions, the self-existent, the beginning, the first creator, and the treasure-store.
He is the thousand-eyed, the diverse-eyed, the moon, and the accomplisher of the constellations.
He is the course of the moon and sun, the comet, the planet, the lord of planets, and the most excellent one.
The mountain-dweller whose abode is the mountain, the creator, the one who delivers arrows at the deer, the sinless one;
he of great asceticism, of terrible penance, the undepressed, the achiever for the distressed; the maker of the year, the sacred mantra, the supreme authority, and the highest austerity.
The Yogi, the one to be united, the great seed, the one of great semen, the one of great austerity; the one of golden semen, the omniscient, the excellent seed, the one whose vehicle is the bull;
the ten-armed, the unblinking, the blue-throated, the Lord of Umā.
Viśvarūpa, Svayaṃśreṣṭha, Balavīra, Bala-gaṇa; Gaṇakartā, Gaṇapati, Digvāsas, and Kāmya;
the Purifier, the Supreme Mantra, the Creator of all states of being, Hara.
Carrying a water-pot, armed with a bow, with arrows in hand and bearing a skull-cup;
great in weaponry, possessing the thunderbolt, the *śataghnī*, the sword, and the *paṭṭiśa*;
holding a sacrificial ladle, handsome in form, splendor itself, the creator of splendor, and a treasure-trove.
Uṣṇīṣin, Suvaktra, Udagra, and likewise Vinata; Dīrgha, Harikeśa, Sutīrtha, and Kṛṣṇa;
Sṛgālarūpa, Sarvārtha, Muṇḍa, Kuṇḍī, and Kamaṇḍalu.
Aja, Mṛgarūpa, Gandhadhārī, Kapardin,
Ūrdhvaretas, Ūrdhvaliṅga, Ūrdhvaśāyin, Nabhastala,
Trijaṭa, Cīravāsas, Rudra, Senāpati, and Vibhu.
Moving by day and by night, possessing fierce wrath and great splendor;
slayer of elephants and slayer of Daityas; the world, the sustainer of the world, and a mine of virtues;
having the form of a lion and a tiger, and clothed in garments of wet hide.
The one joined with time, the great roar, the dweller in all, the crossroads; the night-walker, the wanderer among the departed, the wanderer among spirits, the Great Lord;
the one who has become manifold, the possessor of great wealth, the support of all, the immeasurable goal.
He who loves dance, the eternal dancer, the performer, the one who causes all to dance; he who holds a bow, the long-armed one, the greatly terrible, the one of great asceticism;
the formidable, the one of great asceticism, the noose, the eternal, the mountain-roamer, the sky.
Thousand-armed, Victorious, Resolute, and indeed Irreproachable; Indignant yet Forgiving in nature, Destroyer of Sacrifice, and Annihilator of Desire;
Seizer of Dakṣa’s Sacrifice, Enduring, and likewise the Middle One.
13,017.052a Stealer of splendor, destroyer of strength, joyful, purposeful, victorious, excellent;
13,017.052b Deep-voiced, whose self is yoga, destroyer of sacrifice, destroyer of desire;
13,017.052c Deep-voiced, profound, possessing profound power and movement.
Nyagrodharūpa, Nyagrodha, the pervasive Lord whose ears rest upon the trees; he who has exceedingly sharp teeth, the great-bodied one with the vast mouth;
Viṣvaksena, Hari, the Sacrifice, whose vehicle is the Saṃyugāpīḍa.
Tīkṣṇatāpa, Haryaśva, and Sahāya, who knows the proper time for action;
the sacrifice propitiated by Viṣṇu, the ocean, and Vaḍavāmukha;
and Hutāśana, whose nature is tranquil, accompanied by the fire-god.
He of fierce splendor, of great majesty, victory, the knower of the time of triumph, the course of the luminaries, success, peace,
and indeed war; he who bears the crest-lock, the staff, and matted hair, the flaming one, born of the primordial form, dwelling upon the head, the powerful one.
The flute-player, the drum-player, the cymbalist; Time, the one who is dark and formidable;
