the ordainer of the forms of the constellations, the increase of qualities, the dissolution, and the pathless one; the Lord of Creatures, whose arms are the quarters of space, the division, and the one facing in all directions.
Vimocana, Suragaṇa, Hiraṇyakavacodbhava, Meḍhrāja, Balacārī, Mahācārī, and likewise Stuta; Vīṇī, Paṇavī, Tālī, Nālī, and Kaṭikaṭu.
He who resounds with all musical instruments and embraces all types of musical performance;
he who has the form of a serpent, dwells in a cave, wears a golden garland, and is skilled in the waves;
he who belongs to the thirty [gods], who sustains the three times, and who effects liberation from all bonds of karma.
Bandhana, the destroyer of enemies in battle among the lords of the Asuras; Sāṃkhyaprasāda, Durvāsas, who is served by all the virtuous;
Praskandana, Vibhāga, Atulya, and Yajñabhāgavit.
Praskanda and Avibhāva, equal [in power], who know the distribution of sacrifice;

He who is the grace of all times, the one possessed of great strength, and the bearer of power and form; he who grants the boon of all desires, who is present at all times and faces in every direction;
he whose form is the treasury of space, the one who descends, the serpent, and the bird.

The sage, the lord of himself, he who is to be honored by the world and the giver of thousands; the bird and the one in the form of a bird, the exceedingly radiant lord of the people; the intoxicated one, the embodiment of passion, the hairy one who effects the purpose of all aims.

The stealer of perfected yoga, the perfected one who accomplishes all aims, the mendicant, the one in the form of a mendicant, the horned one, the gentle, the imperishable,

Vajrahasta, Viṣkambhin, and Camūstambhana;
Ṛtu, Ṛtukara, Kāla, Madhu, Madhukara, and Acala;
Vānaspatya, Vājasena, and he who is eternally honored in the hermitages.
The student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*), the wanderer of the world (*lokacārī*), the all-wanderer (*sarvacārī*), the one who causes good wandering (*sucāravit*);

Nandīśvara, Nandi, Nandana, and Nandivardhana; the destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, Kāla, the best among the knowers of Brahman;
Caturmukha, Mahāliṅga, and likewise Cāruliṅga.
The overseer of signs, the overseer of gods, the overseer of worlds, the bringer of the ages;

The giver of well-being, the embodiment of well-being, the possessor of portions, the maker of portions, the light; the lap, the large-limbed, the great-wombed, the supreme, the youth;
the dark-colored, the golden-hued, and the sense-organ of all embodied beings.
He has great feet, great hands, a great body, and great fame; he has a great head, great proportions, and great eyes, with the quarters of the sky as his abode;
he has great teeth, great ears, a great penis, and great jaws.
He has a great nose, a great conch-shell [throat], and a great neck; he dwells in the cremation ground. He has a broad chest and a wide breast; he is the inner self and the abode of wild beasts.
He has great hips, a great neck, great arms, and great hands.
Hanging down, with hanging lips, the great illusionist, an ocean of milk;
hanging down, with hanging lips, moving with a swaying gait, a treasury of glory;
possessing great teeth, great fangs, a great tongue, and a great mouth.
Mahānakhah (Great Nail), Mahāromā (Great Hair), Mahākeśaḥ (Great Hair), Mahājaṭaḥ (Great Matted Locks);

Asapatnaḥ (Without Rival), Prasādaḥ (Grace), Pratyayaḥ (Trust), Girisādhanaḥ (Accomplisher of Mountains); Snehanaḥ (The Moistener) and Asnehanaḥ (The Non-moistener), and Ajitaḥ (Unconquered), the Great Sage.
He has the form of a tree, the tree as his banner; he is fire, whose vehicle is the wind.
He is the one who possesses the mystic circle (*maṇḍala*), whose abode is Mount Meru, and who destroys the pride of gods and *dānavas*.
He has the *Atharvaveda* for his head, the *Sāmaveda* for his mouth, and eyes as numerous as a thousand *ṛg* verses.
Yajurpādabhuja, Guhya, Prakāśa, Jaṅgama,

Upahārapriya, Śarva, Kanaka, Kāñcana, and Sthira.
Nābhi, Nandikara, Bhāvya, Puṣkara, Sthapati, Sthira;
the twelfth is Trāsana, the first sacrifice, and he who is absorbed in sacrifice; Nakta, Kali, Kāla, Makara, and he who is worshipped by Time.
He who is with his host, the creator of the hosts, the charioteer of the source of all beings;

Śaṅku became Triśaṅku, who was pure and frequented by beings;
established in the hermitage, he was the excellent lord Viśvakarman, abiding as a pigeon,

Kapila, Akapila, Śūra, Āyu, Para, and Apara;

The binder and the creator of bonds, the liberator from strong fetters; he is the enemy of sacrifice, the enemy of desire, possessing great tusks and great weapons;
he is the master of illusion who fulfills all desires.
He should be considered the Great Compassionate One;
Śarva is the blameless-armed, the bringer of welfare, the benefactor, and the one who is without worldly wealth.
He is the Lord of the Immortals, Mahādeva, the God of All, and the slayer of the enemies of the gods.
Ahirbudhnya and Nirṛti, Cekitāna and Haris, Ajaikapād and Kāpālī, Triśaṅku, Ajita, Śiva,

The creator of the Kurus, the embodiment of Time, Maheśvara who has become the Kuru;
whose intention is all things, who lies upon *darbha* grass, the Lord of all living beings;
the mouth of the God of gods, unattached, both existent and non-existent, the knower of all jewels.
Dwelling on the peak of Kailāsa, taking refuge on the Himavat mountain;

Sāragrīva, Mahājatru, Alola, and Mahauṣadha; Prāṇeśa, Bandhakī, Vṛkṣa, Nakula, and likewise Ādrika; Hrasvagrīva, Mahājānu, Alola, and Mahauṣadhi.
The achiever of goals, the one whose goals are accomplished, the master of prosody and grammar; the lion’s roar, the lion’s fangs, the lion-gone, and the one whose vehicle is a lion;

He is lifeless yet living, the mantra, auspicious-eyed, and very harsh; he is the source of jewels, red-limbed, and the knower of the great ocean and the water-drain;
he is the root, vast, immortal, manifest and unmanifest, and a treasury of asceticism.
Ārohaṇa, Niroha, Śailahārī, and Mahātapas;

The foot that extinguishes through logic, for he is wise and like a mountain;
he who possesses many garlands, the great garlanded one, the beautiful garlanded one, and the many-eyed one; he who is vast, the salt, the well, the flower, and the source of fruitful results.
Vṛṣabha, Vṛṣabhāṅkāṅga, Maṇibilva, Jaṭādhara;

and the Blessed Gandhamālin, the source of all actions.
Manthāna, Bahula, Bāhu, Sakala, Sarvalocana;

Shaven-headed, deformed, and distorted, with a staff and a shorn head, he is a performer of transformations;
he has tawny eyes, is the Kakubha, the wielder of the thunderbolt, with a flaming tongue and a thousand feet;
he is the thousand-headed lord of gods, the teacher who embodies all the deities.
He who has a thousand arms, whose every limb is perfect, the refuge of all, the creator of all worlds;
he who is the purifier, the triple-sweetness, the sacred mantra, the youngest, the dark-brown; the wielder of the staff of Brahmā, the bearer of the *śataghnī* weapon and the hundred nooses.
The one whose womb is the lotus, the great-wombed, the womb of Brahman, the water-born; the rayed one, the creator of Brahman, Brahman, the knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa, the goal;
the one of infinite forms, the manifold-souled, the fiercely radiant, the self-existent.

The upward-moving soul, the Lord of Creatures (Paśupati), possessing the speed of the wind and the swiftness of thought; he who is anointed with sandalwood, adorned with a preeminent garland of lotuses, the man who is fragrant and leads others across;
he who wears a great wreath of *karṇikāra* flowers, who has a dark-blue crest, and who bears the Pināka bow.
Lord of Umā, beloved of Umā, bearer of the Ganges, consort of Umā; the Excellent One, the Boar, the Giver of Boons, Lord of Boons, of great and mighty roar;
possessed of great grace, the Subduer, the Slayer of Foes, white and tawny.
He whose soul is joyful, whose soul is disciplined, whose soul is restrained, and who upholds the primary essence;
he who is the son of all sides, Tārkṣya, the excellent one common to all dharma; he who is the soul of the moving and the unmoving, the subtle soul, the excellent bull, and the lord of bulls.
He is the seer to be realized, the Vasu, the Āditya, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Mṛḍa;
he is Vyāsa, the summary of all things, the expansion, the transition, and the method.
He is the season, the year, the month, the fortnight, and the completion of calculation.
The *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, *lava*, *mātrā*, *muhūrta*, day, night, and moments;
the field of the universe, the seed of creatures, the primordial mark, the blameless one; the existent and non-existent, the manifest and unmanifest, the father, the mother, and the grandfather.
The gateway to heaven, the gateway to progeny, the gateway to liberation, the triple-heaven, Nirvana, and indeed delight; the world of Brahmā, the supreme goal;
the creator of gods and asuras, and the ultimate refuge of gods and asuras.
The god who is the teacher of the gods and asuras, honored by gods and asuras;
the great minister of the gods and asuras, the refuge of the hosts of gods and asuras; the presiding lord of the hosts of gods and asuras, the leader of the hosts of gods and asuras.
The god beyond gods, the divine seer, the bestower of boons upon gods and asuras; the lord of gods and asuras, the god, the great sovereign of gods and asuras;
composed of all the gods, the inconceivable, the self-born soul of the deities.
The breaker-through, the one who takes three strides, the physician, the stainless one, the one whose garment is stainless;
he who is worthy of praise, the elephant, the tiger among gods, the lion among deities, the bull among men;
the foremost of the preeminent wise ones, the best, the most excellent of all the gods.
The one who employs the excellent thunderbolt, the Sovereign, the immutable Lord;
the Guru, the beloved, the innate creation, the purifier, the one who carries all as his vehicle;
the one with horns, the lover of horns, the tawny-hued, the king of kings, the one free from disease.
Delightful to the hosts of gods, the cessation of all things, the means of all accomplishment;
he whose eye is on his forehead, whose body is the universe, the deer-marked one, possessing the splendor of Brahman;
the lord of all immobile beings and the increaser of the senses through self-restraint.
Siddhārtha, the purpose of all beings, inconceivable, true to his vows, and pure;
the lord of vows, the supreme Brahman, the ultimate goal of those who are liberated;
the one who is freed, whose splendor is liberation, the glorious one, the increaser of prosperity for the world.
Thus have I praised the Blessed One with devotion according to his preeminent qualities—
he whom neither the gods, beginning with Brahmā, nor the great seers know;
he who is this nectar, infinite and immeasurable.
It removes the suffering of all people, encompasses everything that is to be known,
is recited by many, and is proclaimed as the preeminent [mantra],
intense through its union with the mantra of the state of Śiva.

Who could praise that Lord of the World, who is worthy of praise, worship, and salutation? O bulls among the gods, you know the truth of that which was offered by me with devotion as "Salutation to Śiva" and as "The Blessed One."
Placing devotion alone at the forefront, I then obtained his permission and praised Vasu, the Lord of Sacrifice, that best among the wise;
I lauded the auspicious God with these names that increase prosperity.
Being ever-disciplined and pure, one attains the Self by means of the self;
for this is the supreme Brahman, sung by the Self-existent One himself,
which the seers and the gods praise as that which is highest.
Being praised with his own names, Mahādeva is pleased;
the Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, establishes them within himself.
And likewise among men, those who are preeminent among men [attain this].
Those who possess faith and are devoted, through praises offered over many births,
worship with devotion the peerless Īśāna, the supreme,
eternal God of immeasurable splendor, by means of action, mind, speech, and inner feeling.
Whether sleeping or waking, walking or sitting, whether opening or closing their eyes, they thought of it again and again—
waking and sleeping, walking along the path, or standing still.
Hearing [it], causing others to hear it, and speaking of it, they honor existence;
being praised themselves, they are satisfied and take delight,
throughout thousands of millions of births in various wombs of saṃsāra.

For a living being whose sins have been purified, devotion toward Bhava arises; and once devotion toward Bhava has arisen, it becomes exclusive and total in every respect. This is the cause cultivated by one who is liberated in every way from all things.
This [state] is difficult to attain among the gods and is not found among men:
unwavering, unimpeded devotion to Rudra that is never-failing.
And it is only through his grace that such devotion arises in human beings.
Those whose minds are absorbed in that state by which they attain supreme perfection—
those men who have reached all states of being and have become the Supreme— may the God who is compassionate toward those who seek refuge deliver them from the cycle of worldly existence.

"Other gods do not effect liberation from *saṃsāra* for human beings in this way, except through the power of asceticism (*tapas*) from Mahādeva. Thus was the Blessed One, the Lord of the existent and non-existent, addressed by him who was like Indra.
O Kṛṣṇa, the wearer of the animal skin was praised by Tāṇḍin of pure intellect.
Brahmā himself preserved this hymn to the Blessed One;
having attained this hymn, Brahmā himself propitiated all creatures.
And when it is sung, he shall awaken Brahmā in the presence of Śaṅkara;
this [work] is meritorious, purifying, and always a destroyer of sins,
bestowing yoga, liberation, heaven, and likewise satisfaction.

Those who recite this with single-minded devotion to Śaṅkara attain that same goal which belongs to the followers of Sāṃkhya and Yoga; they go to that state by always reciting this hymn with effort in the presence of Rudra.
For one year, the devoted practitioner should perform this; he shall obtain his desired fruit.
This supreme secret resides within the heart of Brahmā.
Brahmā proclaimed it to Śakra, and Śakra proclaimed it to Mṛtyu.
Mṛtyu spoke it to the Rudras; from the Rudras it came to Tāṇḍi. Attained by Tāṇḍi through great austerity in the abode of Brahmā, Tāṇḍi spoke it to Śukra, and Bhārgava spoke it to Gautama.
O Mādhava, Gautama spoke it to Vaivasvata Manu; the wise and beloved Manu spoke it to Sādhya Nārāyaṇa;
and the blessed, infallible Sādhya Nārāyaṇa spoke it to Yama.
The blessed Yama, son of Vivasvat, spoke it to Nāciketa;
O Vārṣṇeya, Nāciketa recited it to Mārkaṇḍeya;
and from Mārkaṇḍeya, O Janārdana, it was obtained by me through disciplined observance.
O slayer of enemies, I too shall today offer you a celebrated hymn of praise that leads to heaven, promotes health, bestows long life, brings wealth, and likewise grants strength;
neither Dānavas, Yakṣas, nor Rākṣasas can cause obstacles for one who recites it.
Piśācas, Yātudhānas, Guhyakas, and even Bhujangas [flee].
Whoever, having become pure, observing celibacy, and with senses conquered,
should recite this with unbroken yoga for a year, shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice.
13,018.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then the great yogi, the sage Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, spoke: "Recite, my son; may it be well with you; may Maheśvara be pleased with you."

"O son, O great king, formerly while I was performing supreme austerities on Mount Meru for the sake of a son, this hymn was recited by me. Indeed, O joy of the Pāṇḍus, I obtained those very desires."
"In that same way, you too shall indeed obtain all your desires from Śarva.
Then Kapila, the sage of Sāṃkhya honored by the gods, said:
"Through my power, Bhava has been propitiated by me throughout many births."
And the Blessed One, being pleased, bestowed upon me the knowledge that brings an end to existence. Then the four-headed one, the beloved friend of Śakra,
known as Ālambāyana, who is compassionate by nature, spoke.
Having reached Gokarṇa and performed austerities for a hundred years, I beheld those born not from a womb, who were self-controlled, knowers of dharma, and possessed of great luster;
who were free from old age and suffering, and lived for a hundred thousand years.
"O son of King Pāṇḍu, in former times you obtained a hundred sons from Śarva.
Then the venerable Vālmīki also addressed Yudhiṣṭhira:
"In a dispute with the sages regarding conciliation, you were indeed called a slayer of a Brahmin."

O Bhārata, in that moment I was possessed by that unrighteousness; then, having sought refuge, I praised the sinless Īśāna. And I, though powerless, was liberated from that sin by him who destroys all suffering.
The destroyer of Tripura said to me, "Your fame shall indeed be preeminent.
And the son of Jamadagni, the best among the upholders of dharma, standing in the midst of the rishis like the scorching sun, O dear one, spoke to the son of Kuntī.
"O eldest of the Pāṇḍavas, afflicted as I was by the slaughter of my father and a Brahmin, O King,
I became pure and sought refuge with Mahādeva.
I praised the god with his names, and thereupon Bhava became pleased."
The god gave me an axe and divine weapons as well. "No evil shall befall you today; you shall be invincible.
Death shall have no power over you, and you shall be illustrious."
"The Lord Śikhaṇḍin, whose form is auspicious, said this to me:
'Everything that has been attained by me was through the grace of that wise one.
Viśvāmitra then said: 'In former times, I was a Kṣatriya.'"
"I am a Brāhmaṇa, O Bhavānī," [he said], and thus I propitiated Bhava.
By his grace, I attained that great and difficult-to-attain status of a Brāhmaṇa.
Asita and Devala likewise spoke thus to the king, the son of Pāṇḍu.
"O son of Kuntī, by the curse of Śakra, my accumulated merit (*dharma*) was destroyed.
Therefore, Bhava took from me that merit, as well as preeminent fame and long life.
[He was] the seer named Gṛtsamada, the beloved friend of Śakra."
The blessed Vasiṣṭha, whose splendor was equal to that of Bṛhaspati and who was the son of Cākṣuṣa Manu,
spoke to Ajamīḍha during the thousand-year sacrificial session of the inconceivable Śatakratu.
While the *sāman* was being chanted by me, he spoke these words:
"O best of the twice-born, the *rathantara* is not being performed correctly.
O foremost of the twice-born, cast aside your joy and examine it again with your intellect."
"O evil-minded one, you have committed a sin that cannot be expiated by sacrifice.
Having spoken thus, filled with great wrath, he spoke these words again in anger:
"Deprived of wisdom, miserable, and perpetually afraid, you shall wander the forest."
For ten thousand years and eighteen hundred more,
he dwelt in a region devoid of water and fodder, abandoned by other animals,
lacking trees fit for sacrifice, and frequented by ruru deer and lions.
"You shall become a cruel deer, beset by great suffering. At the conclusion of those words, O Pārtha, I was indeed born as a deer;
then the yogi Maheśvara spoke to me as I had come to him for refuge.
"You shall be ageless, immortal, and indeed free from suffering;
may there be equality and equal happiness for you both, and may your sacrifice prosper.
Thus does the Lord, the All-pervading One, bestow these boons.
The Ordainer and the Disposer [of all things], as well as pleasure and pain at all times—
this Blessed One is inconceivable through action, mind, or speech.
O dear one, best of warriors, there is no scholar equal to me in learning.
Then Vāsudeva, the best among the wise, spoke again:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, the great god Suvarṇākṣa was gratified by me through my ascetic penance;
thereupon the Blessed One, being pleased, indeed said this to me."
"O Kṛ�ṣṇa, by my grace you shall become dearer than food;
you shall be unconquered in battles and possess a splendor like that of fire. Thus Mahādeva granted him boons thousands of times over.
Formerly, on the mountain Maṇimantha,
I propitiated him for a hundred thousand times ten thousand years.
Then the Blessed One, being pleased, spoke these words to me:
"Choose a boon, may it be well with you; let that which dwells in your mind be granted.
Then, bowing my head, I spoke these words:
"If Mahādeva, the Lord, is pleased with my supreme devotion..."
"O Īśāna, may my devotion to you remain steadfast at all times.
"So be it," said the Blessed One there, and having spoken thus, he vanished.
Jaigīṣavya then declared that Maheśvara, the sustainer of the world, was indeed so.
Jaigīṣavya said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, in the past, the Blessed One granted me eightfold sovereignty with little effort in Vārāṇasī by means of his power."
The sage Parāśara, who was formerly gratified by me, spoke thus.
Gārgya said:
"He bestowed upon me the wonderful knowledge of time (*kālajñāna*) consisting of sixty-four branches."
O Pāṇḍava, on the bank of the Sarasvatī, I was gratified by a mental sacrifice;
my thousand sons, all of whom were expounders of the Veda, were equal to that,
and the lifespan of my son was ten million years.
13,018.027 Parāśara said: O King, having previously propitiated Śarva, I reflected in my mind [upon him who is] of great austerity, great splendor, a great yogi, and of great fame.

13,018.027e Vedavyāsa, the abode of Śrī, devoted to Brahman, and compassionate by nature, [thought: "May I indeed have a desired son from Maheśvara. 13,018.028a Having understood that thought of mine, Śaṅkara, the destroyer of Tripura, said to me:
"The daughter of Vasiṣṭha’s father, the daughter of Vasu, born in the house of a fisherman due to a curse—
Viṣṇukṛtā by name, she is the purifier of the virtuous through her knowledge. Thinking this in his heart, that best of gods spoke thus to me.
"Because he shall be born from me as a result [of his penance], he will become Kṛṣṇa;
in the creation of Sāvarṇa Manu, he will also become one of the seven Ṛṣis. He shall indeed be the divider of the Vedas and likewise the restorer of the Kuru lineage."
Your son, a benefactor of the world, shall be the author of the Itihāsa;
that great sage, the beloved of Mahendra,
shall be your son Parāśara, free from old age and immortal.
Having spoken thus, that Blessed One—the great yogin, the heroic, the inexhaustible, and the immutable—vanished right there, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
And Māṇḍavya said: "O Lord of Gods, may I be devoted to the welfare of the world."
13,018.033 Māṇḍavya said:
"When I, though not a thief, was impaled upon a stake due to the suspicion that I was a thief,
the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the God, being praised by me while I remained there, spoke to me."
"You shall attain liberation from the stake and you shall live for ten billion years;
moreover, O Brahmin, there shall be no pain caused by the stake for you,
and you shall be free from both mental afflictions and physical diseases."
"Capable of making your indignation fruitful and partaking in dharma free from obstacles—
since you, O Sage, have arisen from my fourth foot,
you shall be peerless; indeed, make this birth fruitful."
"O Brahmin, you shall obtain the fruit of bathing at the sacred fords without obstacle, and I grant you exalted, imperishable heaven.
Having spoken thus, the venerable and most excellent Lord whose vehicle is the bull—
"O great king, Maheśvara, the wearer of the animal skin, possessed of great splendor, the best of deities, vanished right there along with his attendants. Gālava said:
"Permitted by Viśvāmitra, I have indeed come to my father.
Then my mother, distressed and weeping bitterly, said to me:
"My son, who is adorned with the Vedas and permitted by Kauśika..."
"O sinless one, your father does not see you, though you are young and self-controlled. Having heard these words of his mother, I became despondent regarding the sight of my elder;
yet, with a restrained soul, I beheld Mahādeva, and he spoke to me.
"O son, your father, your mother, and you shall all be freed from death. Enter quickly; you shall see your father in his abode. Having been thus permitted by the Blessed One, Yudhiṣṭhira went home.
"O dear one, I saw my father after he had emerged from having performed a sacrifice. Having sipped water and taken up sacrificial fuel and *kuśa* grass from the sanctuary for his elders,
my father released them and spoke to me with eyes clouded by tears."
Embracing the one who was bowing down and smelling his head, the Pāṇḍava said:
"By good fortune, my son, you are seen by me here, having returned after completing your studies.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"13.018.045 These most wonderful deeds of the Great-Souled One have been recounted by the sages; having heard them, the Pāṇḍava was filled with amazement.
13.018.046 Then Kṛṣṇa, the best among the wise, spoke these words once again."
Vāsudeva said: "Upamanyu spoke to me, O Yudhiṣṭhira, who are ever devoted to dharma, like the Lord [Indra] to Puruhūta, as if he were the scorching sun."

Those men who have been defiled by impure and evil deeds do not take refuge in Īśāna, for their conduct is characterized by *tamas* and *rajas*. But the twice-born, whose inner dispositions have been purified, take full refuge in the Lord.
In every way, even while living in the world, he who is devoted to the Supreme Lord is equal to the forest-dwelling sages of purified soul;
[he attains] the state of Brahmā, or the state of Keśava, or the state of Śakra along with the gods.
Rudra, being pleased, bestows even the sovereignty of the three worlds; O dear one, those men who take refuge in Śiva even with their minds,
having shaken off all sins, dwell together with the gods.
Having broken through and torn apart the riverbanks, and having destroyed this entire world,
one who worships the god Virūpākṣa is not smeared by sin—
even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks or joined with every kind of transgression.
That evil is entirely destroyed by one who meditates upon Śiva within oneself.
O Keśava, even for worms, birds, insects, and other animals,
there is no fear anywhere once they have taken refuge in Mahādeva.

"In the very same way, those men on earth who are devoted to Mahādeva do not fall under the sway of *saṃsāra*; this is my firm conviction. Then Kṛṣṇa spoke these words to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma.
The sun and the moon, wind and fire; heaven, earth, water, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas; Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Śukra, and Bṛhaspati.
The Rudras together with the Sādhyas, Varuṇa the guardian of wealth,
Brahmā, Śakra, the Maruts, Brahman, Truth,
the Vedas, the sacrifices, the sacrificial fees, and those who carry the Vedas.
Soma is the sacrificer, as are the oblation and the offering;
the protection, the initiation, and whatever restraints there may be—
svāhā and vaṣaṭ are the Brāhmaṇas, the sons of Surabhī.
Dharma, the wheel, time, the cycle, and movement;
fame, self-restraint, intelligence, stability,
the auspicious and inauspicious, and the seven sages.
Supreme intelligence in thought and vision, perfection in touch, and that perfection which comes from ritual actions; the hosts of gods who drink the warm libations and those who drink the soma;
The Lekhas, Suyāmas, Tuṣitas, Brahmakāyas,
Ābhāsvaras, Gandhapās, and Dṛṣṭipās;
those with discordant speech and those with discordant minds.
The pure gods who delight in Nirvana, those who feed on touch, those who drink from sight, those who drink clarified butter,
and those who have attained the state of thought— these are the foremost among the gods.
And those other deities as well, O Ajamīḍha—
suparṇas, gandharvas, piśācas, dānavas,
yakṣas, as well as pannagas and cāraṇas;
The subtle and the gross, that which is soft and that which is not subtle;
pleasure, pain, and that which lies between pleasure and pain;
Sāṃkhya and Yoga, and that which is higher than the highest.
Know that which I have proclaimed as born from Śarva;
from him were produced the most excellent creators of beings,
all the gods who are the guardians of this world.
I praise with a mind full of devotion him who, having entered this earth, protected it— the ancient creation of that God— searching for it with his intellect.
I bow down for the sake of my life to whatever reality [there may be];
may that Lord grant us the desired boons here,
for the immutable Master is forever praised by us.
That man who, having restrained his senses and become pure, should recite this hymn for one year with unbroken yoga and self-restraint;
He shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice,
as well as the entirety of the Vedas— a Brāhmaṇa would obtain—
and a king would conquer the entire earth as well.
A Vaiśya would obtain profit and skill;
likewise, a Śūdra would attain a good state after death as well as happiness.
Having composed this King of Hymns, they fixed their minds upon Rudra.
It removes all defects, is meritorious, purifying, and glorious.
O Bhārata, for as many thousands of years as there are hair-pores on his body, a man dwells in heaven.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, regarding this which is called 'common dharma' (*sahadharma*) at the time of taking the hand of women— how was this ordained in the traditional law (*smṛti*)?"

"Is this dharma that of the Ṛṣis, or that of Prajāpati, or perhaps that of the Asuras? Since the great seers previously declared that 'dharma is performed together,' this is a very great doubt; it seems to me to be contradictory."
"Where indeed does this shared dharma (sahadharma) ordained for us exist after death? O Grandfather, does that shared dharma persist in heaven for those who have died?
Furthermore, tell me: when one dies first, where does the other remain?"
When there are many humans endowed with various fruits of karma, dwelling in various karmic states, and reaching various ends in hell,
the author of the Sūtra determines that "women are untruthful."
"O dear one, when women are untruthful, how can a shared dharma be prescribed?
Indeed, it is stated even in the Vedas that 'women are untruthful. This dharma is an ancient designation; it is a conventional usage and a rule of action."
"As I reflect upon this incessantly, it appears to me as a profound abyss.
O Grandfather, all this is undoubtedly just as the sacred tradition (śruti) declares—
whatever this is, of what nature it is, and how it has been set in motion."
"O one of great wisdom, please explain this to me in its entirety.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O Bhārata, [this is] the dialogue between Aṣṭāvakra and Diśā.
Formerly, the great ascetic Aṣṭāvakra, desiring to marry,
chose the daughter of the high-souled and generous seer Vadānya.
She was known by the name Suprabhā, peerless on earth in beauty; she excelled in virtues, was virtuous in character, and radiant in her conduct.
As soon as he saw that woman of auspicious eyes, she captivated his heart.

Like a variegated row of forest trees covered in blossoms in the springtime, the sage said to him: "Listen to me; my daughter must be given to you—provided that you are not devoted to other women, are wise, do not travel abroad, and are pleasant of speech."
Handsome, esteemed, heroic, virtuous, an enjoyer of wealth, and pure; one who performs sacrifices with the consent of his wife should then marry under an auspicious constellation.
Together with his servants and kinsmen, he rejoices both in this world and after death.
"Go first to that auspicious northern direction; from there you shall see [it].
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"What is it that I must see there? Your Honor ought to tell me."
"Therefore, I shall now act exactly as you shall tell me.
Vadānya said:
"Beyond the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) and likewise beyond the Himavat mountains,"
Having beheld the abode of Rudra, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
graced by joyful attendants with various countenances who were dancing,
and likewise by Piśācas of diverse kinds from the forest with celestial unguents;
With the rhythmic clapping of hands, the beating of cymbals, and the regular striking of hand-drums, Śarva is worshipped there by those who are exceedingly joyful and dancing;
indeed, we have heard that this divine place on the mountain is highly cherished.
The god is always present there, as are his auspicious attendants.
There, the goddess performed most difficult penance for the sake of Śaṅkara;
therefore, it is heard that this place is beloved by the god as well as by Umā.
There, by the side of the god to the north, is a great well. Indeed,
it is said that all the seasons, Kālarātri, and those who are divine as well as those who are human,
attend upon the god there in embodied form.
Having passed beyond that abode, you must indeed proceed;
then you will see a dark woodland region resembling a cloud.
There, you will surely behold a woman who is delightful and captivating to the mind.
"You must see that illustrious ascetic woman there, who is aged and engaged in her consecration; she should be honored by you with great effort.
Having seen her, you may then turn back and take my hand."
"If this agreement is true, let it be fulfilled;
go there. Aṣṭāvakra said, "So be it; I shall fulfill it and will go there without doubt."
"O virtuous one, may you be true to your word regarding what you have said.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then that Blessed One departed toward the northern, most excellent direction."
13,020.002c To Himavat, the best of mountains, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas;
13,020.003a Having gone to the great mountain Himavat, that tiger among the twice-born approached the holy river Bāhudā, the bestower of dharma.
Having bathed at the pure and sorrowless holy ford (Aśokavimala-tīrtha) and having offered libations to the deities,
he dwelt there comfortably upon a bed of kusha grass for the night.
Then, when the night had passed, that twice-born man rose in the morning.

Having bathed and kindled the fire according to the prescribed rites, and having offered oblations, he approached the well of Rudrāṇī and rested there by the lake. Once rested, he rose up and proceeded toward Kailāsa.
He beheld a golden gate, as if blazing with splendor,
and the lotus-lake Mandākinī belonging to the high-souled Dhanada.
Then all those Rākṣasas who were guarding the lotus-lake [approached].
Led by Maṇibhadra, they rose up before the Blessed One. He, in turn, honored those Rākṣasas of terrifying prowess and said,
"Announce me quickly to the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada)."
Then, O King, those Rākṣasas spoke to the Blessed One:
"That King Vaiśravaṇa himself is coming into your presence;
the Blessed One knows both his purpose and the reason for his arrival."
"Behold this highly fortunate one, blazing as if with splendor.
Then Vaiśravaṇa, having approached the blameless Aṣṭāvakra and having duly inquired after his welfare, spoke to that Brahmarṣi.
"Have you attained happiness? Or what do you wish to have done by me? Speak, O twice-born one; I shall do everything that you tell me.
Enter my palace as you desire, O best of the twice-born."
"Having been honored and having accomplished your task, you shall depart without obstacle.
Having taken that best of the twice-born with him, he indeed entered his own palace;
he then offered him his own seat, as well as water for his feet and the respectful offering (arghya).
Then, as the two of them sat there, the followers of Kubera— the Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Rākṣasas— led by Maṇibhadra, took their seats. When they were seated, Dhanada spoke these words to them:
"Perceiving your desire for existence, the hosts of Apsarases shall dance;
likewise, supreme hospitality and service to you must be performed. "Let it be so," the sage said in a sweet voice.
Then Urvarā, Miśrakeśī, Rambhā, and likewise Urvaśī; Alambuṣā, Ghṛtācī, Citrā, Citrāṅgadā, and Ruci;
Manoharā, Sukeśī, Sumukhī, Hāsinī, and Prabhā.
Vidyutā, Praśamā, Dāntā, Vidyotā, and Rati—
these and many other beautiful Apsarases danced;
and the Gandharvas played various kinds of musical instruments.
Then, while the divine Gandharva music was proceeding, the Ṛṣi of great asceticism dwelt there, taking his pleasure for a divine year. Thereupon,
King Vaiśravaṇa spoke to the Blessed One.
"More than a full year has passed while you have been observing here, O Brahmin.
This realm, O Brahmin, is known by the name Gāndharva; let it proceed according to your will, O sage, or as you may direct."
"You are a guest worthy of worship, and this is your home; let everything be commanded quickly, for we are entirely subject to you. Then the Blessed One, being pleased, replied to Vaiśravaṇa.
"I have been honored by you according to what is right; I shall now depart, O Lord of Wealth.
I am pleased, O Sovereign of Riches, for everything you have done is worthy of you.
This is through your grace, O Blessed One, and that of the high-souled great seer."
"By my command, you shall go today; may you be prosperous and successful.
Then, having departed, the Blessed One set out facing north, and beholding and bowing before Śaṅkara’s abode on Kailāsa.

He wandered across Kailāsa, Mandara, and all the golden mountains, [beholding] Gaurīśa, Śaṅkara, the self-controlled one who is affectionate toward those who seek refuge, the bearer of the Gaṅgā, the lord of rays (the Sun), and the stainless one surrounded by his hosts.
Having passed beyond those great mountains, he reached the supreme abode of Kairāta;
then, bowing his head with devotion, he performed a circumambulation. Having descended to the earth, he then became purified in soul.
Having circumambulated that mountain three times while facing north,
he proceeded with a joyful heart along level ground.
Then, he beheld another delightful forest region.
Provided with roots, fruits, and birds of all seasons,
and adorned here and there with delightful forest regions,
the Blessed One then beheld a divine hermitage there.
He then beheld mountains of various forms, made of gold and adorned with jewels,
as well as lotus ponds situated upon grounds of precious gems; moreover,
he saw many other exceedingly beautiful sights.
The mind of that great seer of purified soul rejoiced exceedingly.
There he beheld a divine golden house, composed of every kind of jewel, appearing wonderful and superior even to the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera).
There are various great palaces resembling mountains,
as well as delightful celestial chariots and diverse jewels; likewise,
the river Mandākinī is strewn with mandāra flowers.
The ground was adorned with self-luminous jewels and diamonds,
and with various mansions featuring wonderful jeweled archways,
draped with nets of pearls and embellished with precious gems.
Surrounded on all sides by beautiful and auspicious things that captivate the mind, the sage beheld delightful sights everywhere;
then, the thought arose in him: "Where might my dwelling be?"
Then, having gone to the vicinity of the gate and standing there, he spoke:
"May those who are here indeed grant permission to me, a guest who has arrived.
Then, surrounded by maidens, [the king's daughter] emerged from that house.
"O Lord, there were seven maidens of various forms, all of them captivating.
Whichever maiden he beheld, she captivated his mind;
he was unable to restrain his mind, and thus it became despondent."
Then, firm resolve arose in that wise brahmin.
Thereupon, the women said to him, "May the Blessed One enter.
And he [beheld] those beautiful women and that very palace.
Overcome with curiosity, the twice-born man entered the house. There he saw an old woman, advanced in years, seated upon a couch, adorned with all ornaments, and wearing garments free from dust.
Then, having been addressed with "Svasti" by him, that woman replied;
rising up, she said to the Brahmin, "Please be seated.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"Let all of them go to their own abodes; let one remain with me—she who is well-known and perfectly tranquil. Let the others depart as they please.
Then those maidens circumambulated that seer.
Stepping out from that house, the old woman then stood there. Honored by her there upon that exceedingly pure bed,
he then spoke to her as he lay down upon that radiant couch.
"O blessed lady, you too should sleep, for the night is passing away.
Thus addressed by that brahmin through their conversation,
she lay down there upon a second celestial bed of great splendor.
Then, with her limbs trembling, she made the cold the pretext for that moment and ascended the bed of the great seer.
"Welcome! Welcome! the Blessed One said to her.

13,020.051c Then, O bull among men, she affectionately embraced the seer with both her arms. 13,020.052a Seeing the seer then to be unchanging, like a piece of wood or a wall, she, being distressed, engaged in conversation with the seer.
"O Brahmin, women have no power of their own; their stability depends on men. Deluded by passion, I am devoted to you—accept me!
Be joyful, O brahmin-sage, and unite with me."
"O Brahmin, embrace me, for I am deeply afflicted by desire for you.
O righteous-souled one, this indeed is the fruit of your asceticism that is being honored;
since I have sought it from the very moment I beheld you, please accept me as I devote myself to you."

This palace, this forest, and whatever else you see—all these are yours to command everywhere, including myself; of this there is no doubt. I shall provide for all your desires; rejoice together with me.
"O Brahmin, in this delightful forest that yields the fruits of all desires,
I shall come under your control; you shall take your pleasure with me,
enjoying every desire, both divine and human."
Indeed, there is no task for women greater than this: that they should seek union with a man; for this is our supreme fruit. Impelled by the god of love, women act according to their own desire.
And they do not burn as they walk, even upon the most scorching sands.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O blessed lady, I would never, under any circumstances, go to another man's wife."
In the treatises on Dharma, the violation of another's wife is declared a defilement.
Now, the expiation for killing a Brahmin in a "pure field" is being described; furthermore, a heinous sin is seen to be especially grave when committed in the field of a Brahmin.

"O blessed lady, know that I desire to marry you; I swear this truly by the truth. However, there is a great expiation required for taking a wife in this case, for the seed of the one who has not performed atonement is not purified."

A son should be known as truly pure by virtue of his mother and father; I am indeed unacquainted with worldly objects, for offspring are intended for the sake of dharma. Thus, through my sons, I shall go to the higher worlds—of this there is no doubt.
"O blessed lady, understand the Dharma, and having understood it, desist from this.
The woman said:
"Neither Anila, nor Agni, nor Varuṇa, nor any other of the thirty gods [can stop me], O twice-born one."

Out of ten thousand women, one may perhaps be dear to her husband; for women are by nature devoted to pleasure according to their desire. Yet, among hundreds of thousands, it is only rarely that one finds a woman who is truly devoted to her husband.

They know neither father nor family nor mother; they know neither brothers nor husbands nor sons nor brothers-in-law. Sporting wantonly, they destroy their families just as great rivers erode their banks.
And Prajāpati declared that the defects in those who are dull-witted are themselves dull.
Bhīṣma said:
Then that sage, with one-pointed mind, addressed that woman.
"Sit down; what beautiful meter shall we compose, or what task shall I perform for you? Tell me.
That woman replied, "O Blessed One, you shall see it in due time and place. Dwell here for now, O man of great wisdom; once your purpose is accomplished, you shall depart."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, that Brahmarṣi then said to her, 'So be it;
I shall dwell here as long as you have the strength, of this there is no doubt.
Then the Ṛṣi, having gazed upon that woman who was overcome by old age..."
13,020.071c He fell into the deepest anxiety and became as if consumed by distress.
13,020.072a For whichever limb of hers that bull among brahmins beheld at that time, 13,020.072c his gaze did not find satisfaction there, being utterly captivated by her beauty.
"This deity of this house has surely been disfigured by a curse;
it is not proper for me to hastily discover the cause of this. Thus he reflected, intent on his thought and desiring to know that matter.
He passed the remainder of that day with a troubled mind.
Then that woman said to him: "O Blessed One, behold indeed the form of the Sun joined with the twilight clouds; what [offering] should be presented to you?"
He said to that woman, "Bring water for bathing here;
then, with speech restrained and senses controlled, I shall perform my twilight devotions.
Bhīṣma said:
Then that woman, having said "So be it" to the brahmin,
took divine oil and brought a bathing garment. Permitted by that high-souled sage, the woman [prepared for the bath].
Then he rubbed all his limbs with oil;
having been gently massaged there, he approached the bathing hall.
Then the Ṛṣi sat down upon a new and variegated auspicious seat.
Then, when he had sat down upon that auspicious seat,
he gently bathed the seer with comforting hands;
and he then performed for the sage the divine rites according to the prescribed rules and with all attendant services.
Because of that very warm [water] and the comfort of her hand,
that man of great vows did not realize that the entire night had passed.
Then, having risen, the sage was filled with supreme wonder.
In the eastern direction, he beheld the sun risen in the sky;
"This is the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), which destroys all sins"— so he thought, "Is this delusion, or could this be the truth?"
Then, having worshipped the thousand-rayed sun, he said to her, "What shall I do?
She then brought forth food for the sage that resembled the essence of nectar; because of the deliciousness of that food, he did not eat much of it.
The remainder of the day passed away, and then evening arrived once more.
While he was eating, the day ended, and then evening came, O Lord.
Then that woman urged the Blessed One, saying, "Please sleep."
There, upon two celestial beds prepared for him and her, that woman and the sage then lay down to sleep separately. Then,
at midnight, that woman approached that bed.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"O blessed lady, my mind does not become attached to the wives of others. Arise, O blessed one; may it be well with you; sleep indeed, and desist."

13,021.011 Bhīṣma said: At that time, having been thus turned back by that brahmin through his steadfastness, she said to him, "I am my own mistress; there is no deception regarding dharma on your part."
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"Women possess no independence, for women are indeed dependent;
this is the doctrine of Prajāpati, that a woman does not deserve autonomy."
The woman said:
"O Brahmin, sexual desire afflicts me; behold my devotion! O Brahmin, you will incur demerit if you do not accept me."
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"The various defects carry away a man who acts according to his whims.
O blessed lady, I am always able to remain steadfast through fortitude; go now to your own bed."
The woman said:
"O Brahmin, I bow my head to you; you ought to show me favor. O sinless one, become the refuge for me as I fall upon the ground."
"Or if you perceive any fault in my approaching another's wife, I shall touch myself today; take my hand, O twice-born one.
By this truth, I declare that no fault shall arise."
"Know me to be independent; let whatever unrighteousness there may be rest upon me. My heart is fixed on you, and I am my own mistress; accept me.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
"Action belongs to one, yet another lacks autonomy; that is not tenable. O blessed lady, tell me truly: how can you be independent? For there is no woman in this world who deserves independence."
In childhood, the father protects her; in youth, the husband protects her; and in old age, the sons protect her. A woman does not deserve independence.
O sinless one, I do not consider you aged or incapable, nor do I have any desire for you.
The woman said:
"I have observed celibacy since my youth; I am still a maiden, there is no doubt. O Brahmin, do not harbor ill-will toward me, and do not destroy my faith."
13,021.021 Aṣṭāvakra said:
"As it is for me, so it is for you; as it is for you, so it is for me.
13,021.021 Then that sage Aṣṭāvakra, filled with wonder, reflected.
"Is this the desire for knowledge of that seer, or could it truly be an obstacle?
This is indeed a supreme marvel; what would truly be for my highest good? For this maiden, adorned with divine ornaments and garments, has presented herself before me."
"But how was her supreme form aged, and how did it become the form of a maiden again right here today? What might be the answer to this,
so that I shall never at any time deviate from the maintenance of my supreme power?"
"I do not desire to depart; rather, by my steadfastness alone, I shall accomplish this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How is it that she does not fear the curse of one of such supreme splendor?"
"How did the Blessed One turn back? May you explain that to me.
Bhīṣma said:
"Aṣṭāvakra asked her: 'How do you transform your form?'"
"And you must not speak an untruth; speak out of a desire for the welfare of the Brahmin.
The woman said:
"O best of Brahmins, she is as desirable as heaven and earth themselves."
Listen attentively to all this, O you of true prowess:
know me to be the northern direction, and you have witnessed my feminine fickleness. By your steadfastness, O you of true valor, the worlds have been won by you.
"O sinless one, this inquiry has been undertaken by me to make you firm in resolve.

Even for elderly women, the fever of sexual desire causes affliction. One who does not trust [others], who is not addicted, who is not excessively attached, and who does not live abroad—[such a person is secure]."
A wise man of good character, together with his wife, enjoys happiness.
Today your grandfather is pleased, as are the gods along with Indra.
For what purpose have you, O Blessed One, arrived here?
Sent by that brahmin, the father of the maiden, O bull among the twice-born,
deceitful women— who are devoted to sensual pleasure and speak sweet words— are restrained from wandering abroad by means of coarse clothing and the like, and by following a life of non-attachment.
One may approach one's wife even on nights that are not the prescribed seasons, provided they are not forbidden days;
nor should there be excessive restriction regarding the night, yet it should certainly not be entirely unrestricted. Indeed, I have carried out everything that you requested me to teach.
"You shall go home in safety and shall not suffer fatigue;
O Brahmin, you will obtain that maiden, and she shall bear you sons.
Since you questioned me out of desire, this answer has been spoken."
"This is always impossible for all the three worlds to transgress.
Go forth after performing meritorious deeds; what else do you wish to hear? O brahmin-sage Aṣṭāvakra, I shall speak to you exactly as it is."
"O bull among the twice-born, I have been propitiated by the Ṛṣi for your sake;
it was for the purpose of honoring him that these words were spoken by me to you.
Having heard her words, that Brahmin stood with his palms joined in reverence.
Permitted by her, he returned once more to his own home.
Having arrived at his house, rested, and honored his kinsmen,
O joy of the Kurus, he approached that brahmin in accordance with the prescribed rules.
Questioned by that brahmin regarding this vision he had seen,
the brahmin then spoke to the other brahmin with a deeply pleased heart:
"Permitted by you, I have set out for Gandhamādana."
And in the region to the north of that place, I beheld that great deity;
having been permitted by her, you were also announced to me, and I have come home, O Lord, having been made to hear her words.
Then the Brahmin said to him, "Accept my daughter;
for at the conjunction of the lunar mansion and the lunar day, you are indeed a supreme recipient.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Lord, having said 'So be it' and having accepted that maiden, the supremely righteous Aṣṭāvakra then became filled with joy. Having indeed accepted that most beautiful maiden as his wife,"
Yudhiṣṭhira dwelt there in his own hermitage, joyful and free from all anxiety.
[There were those] born from the womb of Vaiśyas, and likewise from the womb of Śūdras.
"O best of the twice-born, those ancient ones were called *brahmarṣis* in the past.
O great king, you ought to explain how this is so; [tell us] the truth.
Bhīṣma:
"I see a contradiction here: how could a Brāhmaṇa be born from a non-noble womb?
Enough with this curiosity; understand this, O Yudhiṣṭhira. You ought not to dwell upon whether it is auspicious or inauspicious."
"They are masters of themselves"—this is their state, and their course does not cling [to worldly things]. "They have become Brahman"—thus are the sages impelled by the Vedas.
They are not to be censured, O King of kings, for they are the authorities among those who possess authority.

The world approves of these, for in this matter austerity is indeed the authority. Thus, O dear one, the duties set forth by those great-souled ones endowed with austerity and knowledge are themselves the authorities, O best of beings.
O Indra among kings, according to his own dharma, a Brāhmaṇa may have four wives:
a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā, O bull of the Bharatas.
But for kings (Kṣatriyas), O bull of the Bharatas, [there are] a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā.
O bull among the Bharatas, for a Vaiśya, a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman are prescribed as wives;
for a Śūdra, one wife is ordained, but in the reverse order there is a mixture of castes (saṃkara). O best of men, for a Śūdra woman, four husbands are ordained.
But for a woman of the highest caste, there is only one husband of her own caste;
for a Kṣatriya woman, two are ordained—a Brāhmaṇa and a Kṣatriya;
and for a Vaiśya woman, O best of men, three husbands are ordained.
O lord of the people, the Kṣatriyas and Brāhmaṇas were of the same caste;
thus, having remembered this rule, those high-souled sons, the Brahmarṣis, were produced by the sages in the past.
By the two ancient seers Mitra and Varuṇa, as well as Vasiṣṭha, Agastya, the Barhiṣads,
Kakṣīvat, Ārṣṭiṣeṇa, and the man Kakṣa.
The sons of Māmateya are remembered as the offspring of Gautama:
the venerable Vatsapriya, Sthūlaraśmi, and Akṣiṇi;
these were indeed the sons of Gautama born of a maidservant.
The Brahmanical seer Kapiñjalāda was born from a Caṇḍālī woman; likewise, the bird Vainateya was born from Vasiṣṭha through a fourth-order woman,
by virtue of Vasiṣṭha’s grace and his acceptance of a bride-price.
In former times, the father of Adṛśyantī was a Vaiśya named Citramukha;
however, O Kaurava, he attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa and became a Brahmarṣi. That Vaiśya Citramukha [married] the daughter of Vasiṣṭha’s son.
Because he was born from Śubhā,
the Brahman-sage Parāśara likewise begot the great seer Vyāsa, the sage composed of yoga, upon Satyavatī, the daughter of the fisherman.

From Vibhaṇḍaka and a deer was born the highly illustrious ascetic Ṛśyaśṛṅga, a sage whose essence was the power of penance and a lifelong celibate student. Furthermore, from Śāṅgarī and Mandapāla were born four sons who were exponents of the Veda.
From them were born the meritorious Brahman-sages by whom the bearer of oblations was praised:
Droṇa, Stambamitra, the wise Śārisṛkva,
and Jaritāri— these four renowned ones who were like the sun.
The venerable great seer Hiraṇyahasta, who possessed a golden radiance, was born from the great seer Kālavṛkṣa upon Śakuntī;
O dear one, he was produced from fire and by means of the mind, as were the great seers.
O Indra among kings, the Grandfather’s [sons] were Pulastya, Pulaha, and others;
and the royal sage Savarṇa was also born of Savarṇā,
O best of the Bharatas, by Vivasvat, the son of Aditi, from that earthen vessel.

And Śāṇḍilya was born from fire; the lord Kāśyapa was his son. And from a clump of reeds, Kṛpa was born along with Kṛpī to Śaradvat. And from a lotus, O king of kings, was born the high-souled Somapa.
Reṇu and Reṇukā, the illustrious mother of Rāma,
were born on the Yamunā by the high-souled Somaka;
and from them was born the great Ṛṣi Arkadatta, renowned throughout the earth.
From the Āhavanīya fire and from Drupada, who possessed the splendor of Indra,
Dhṛṣṭadyumna was born, O Bhārata, as well as Kṛṣṇā on the sacrificial altar;
they were then born from the womb of a tigress by the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
There were nineteen sons renowned as Vyāghrapada and the others:
Mandha, Bādalomaśa, the great seer Jābāli,
Manyu, Upamanyu, and likewise Setukarṇa.
These and others were renowned on earth as having attained the status of lineages. Of the high-souled royal seer Viśvakāśa of the Ikṣvāku race,
there was a son named Bālāśva, who emerged after piercing through the crown of his head.

The royal sage Māndhātṛ was also personally sustained in the womb by the wise Yuvanāśva; furthermore, the royal sage Gaurika was a highly illustrious universal monarch (*cakravartin*) endowed with the power of divine weapons.
From King Subāhu, a son was born on the river Bāhudā;
and from Bhūmi were born Naraka, Saṃvarta, and Puṣkala. Furthermore, the highly effulgent seer Gārgya was born from Adbhi.
These and many other kṣatriyas and brahmins were likewise produced through the power of the great-souled maharṣis;
for nothing was impossible for them by means of their asceticism, their knowledge, and their supreme personal qualities.
On this matter, O lord of men, a verse was sung by Manu while he was establishing the law, O King;
listen to it, Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Among the sages, the rivers, and the high-souled virtuous men..."

The source of women’s misconduct must not be pursued; therefore, no anxiety should be felt regarding the birth of great seers. For just as fire is omnipresent, so too is splendor found within the high-souled.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Great King, how may a man be rescued by his sons?
For as long as a man has not obtained a son, O King, he remains fruitless."
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
which was formerly sung by Nārada to Mārkaṇḍeya when he questioned him.
Parvata, Nārada, Asita, and Devala,
as well as Āraṇeya and Raibhya— these had previously come there to the confluence of the Bhogavatī, between the Gaṅgā and Yamunā.
Having previously seen them seated together, Mārkaṇḍeya approached them.
Upon seeing the sage, the ṛṣis rose and stood facing him;
having honored the worthy brahmin, they said, "What shall we do?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"This meeting with the virtuous, which I have attained through great effort,
is here where I shall obtain certainty regarding both dharma and right conduct."
In the Kṛta age, dharma is straightforward; when that has declined, one becomes deluded.
Age after age, I desire to know dharma from the great seers. Nārada was addressed by the seers: "Speak regarding that in which he has doubt."
"O knower of the truth regarding dharma and adharma, you shall indeed sever our doubts.
At the command [of the sages], Nārada spoke these words approved by the ṛṣis;
he then addressed Mārkaṇḍeya, who knows the true essence of the purpose of all dharmas.
O long-lived one, radiant with asceticism, knower of the truth of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences! O Brahmin, let that matter concerning which doubt has arisen in you be stated—
whether it be regarding Dharma, what benefits the world, or whatever else you wish to hear.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"I shall tell you that; speak, O you of great asceticism! As each age passes away, this bridge of dharma perishes."
Nārada said:
"O Brahmin, it was my thought: 'How might I obtain [this] through a pretext of dharma? O sage, in former times, during the Kṛta Yuga, Dharma had four feet."
Then, in the course of time, Adharma was born and rose slightly;
thereupon the age known as Tretā-yuga began, which brought about the corruption of Dharma. When that had passed, the third age, Dvāpara-yuga, arrived.
Then, when the Dvāpara age has completely declined and the Kali age has arrived, unrighteousness will destroy two of the four feet of Dharma;
listen to me as I describe the conduct of the world and the nature of Dharma.
The fourth, named Nandika, [contains] the verses on Dharma in their entirety.
From that time onward, men were born with diminished wisdom and lifespan.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
In this world, those whose vitality and wealth are exhausted are cast out from the practice of Dharma.
Thus, when the Dharma is thrown into confusion and the world is joined with unrighteousness,
Nārada—
He ensures that the *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors) of the four castes are duly administered.
When the *havya* and *kavya* are always purified by mantras, they do not perish;
the gods accept those offerings when they are bestowed by a donor who gives according to the law.
Endowed with virtue and being a donor, one shall obtain all desires.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having attained his desires, he shall be honored in heaven according to his wish.
If those belonging to the four castes offer oblations to the gods and ancestors with mantras that are deficient or through improper methods, where does what has been given to them go? — Nārada.
What is given by Brahmins goes to the Asuras; what is given by Kshatriyas goes to the Rakshasas;
what is given by Vaishyas goes to the Pretas; and what is given by Shudras goes to the Bhutas—thus said Markandeya.

Then those born of inferior castes, who merely claim the designation of the fourfold order (*cāturvarṇya*), will offer the sacrificial oblations to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*). To whom does what is given to them go? —Nārada.
Neither the gods nor the ancestors themselves accept the offerings of *havya* and *kavya* from those beings who are inferior in caste;
rather, it is the *yātudhānas*, *piśācas*, and those beings belonging to the *nairṛtas* [who take them].
Their livelihood was ordained as being derived from offerings to the ancestors and the gods;
for those who give all things, they, being composed in mind, [partake] of the *havya* and *kavya*.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
Whatever they offer according to the prescribed rules, that indeed the deities consume.
O Nārada, it has been heard that when given to one of lower caste, the *havya* and *kavya* offerings [fail].
Nārada.
Tell me also about the union with sons and daughters;
[tell me] about the giving away of daughters and the marriage of sons and women. Listen to me as I explain these matters to you properly and in their correct sequence.
As soon as she is born, a maiden should be given to a suitable bridegroom;
when a maiden is given at the proper time, the father is joined with righteousness. But he who, being a kinsman, does not give away a maiden who has reached puberty [is at fault].
Every month that passes, the kinsman of a maiden who is kept confined at home, deprived of the pleasures of village life, incurs the guilt of killing an embryo;
for such a kinsman of the maiden is as one who has slain an embryo.
A girl who has been defiled by the mere touch of a hand receives the funeral rites upon the death of her husband;

that woman, however, receives them when her second husband dies. She is called a *punarbhū* (a remarried woman), and such a maiden, having borne sons, is entitled to offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Among the offspring born in the marriage rites of people, she is irreproachable who gives birth to a daughter or who is found to be pregnant [at the time of marriage].
"Then, O best of sages, she might again enter into the act of marriage.
Nārada said:
"The maiden offers a word determined by the true meaning to the Fire."

Therefore, those girls indeed possess a state of being; they are not mere children. [They are] purified by the rite of conception (*garbhādhāna*) through a third part of the sin of killing a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*).
— Mārkaṇḍeya.

One should take a fourth part of that [wealth] once it has been purified again from its source. O Great Sage, how is it that those born of women who are always defiled by their kinsmen— who will they offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations to?
Nārada:
But the sons of a maiden born to her father are the *kānīna* sons; they are the ones who offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations.
Mārkaṇḍeya.
But he who takes the hand of a woman already pregnant is known as a *sahoḍhaja* (born with the bride). Now, O Nārada, regarding that case where a fetus has been placed within a maiden by someone...
Nārada said:
"How can he obtain the fruit of a son? Explain this to me.
Those who are constantly defilers of righteous conduct, though they have performed purifications, their seed perishes and their efforts become futile."
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Now, suppose there might be a certain maiden who has been purchased, given away, or even abducted.
Nārada [said]:
O best of sages, how could that [offspring] of hers be considered "son-made"?

A maiden who has been purchased, given away, or even abducted, but whose hand has not been taken in marriage—that wife is called *kaumārī* (belonging to a youth); she may give birth to sons born of her own body (*aurasa*).
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"A virtuous woman is not said to be intended for the sake of a husband in that [act] which is unconquered;
by whom, then, are maidens employed in auspicious rites?"
Nārada said:
"O great sage, I wish to understand this in its true essence here:
why does Lakṣmī always dwell, firmly established, among young maidens?"
She is beautiful, worthy of auspicious rites, and to be honored in ceremonies for prosperity;
just as a jewel within its mine yields the fruits of all desires,
so too is the maiden Mahālakṣmī the auspiciousness of the entire world.

In this way, a maiden is the supreme fortune, the delight, and the satisfaction of embodied beings; she is the touchstone for the character and conduct of noble families. That man who, having brought a maiden from his own caste, should cherish her—
She gives birth to a son who is a giver of offerings to the gods and ancestors;
such a virtuous woman increases the lineage, for she is the supreme prosperity in the home.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.

O high-minded one, you have related the virtuous conduct, fortune, passion, splendor, lineage, and the various kinds of learning and behavior of maidens. Now I wish to hear about the dharma and adharma regarding the acceptance of women as wives.
Nārada said:
Eight types of women are lawful for men to take as wives in marriage;
those who are accompanied by sons and who offer oblations to the gods and ancestors are beneficial both in this world and after death.
A virtuous woman who was married in her youth but deprived of her husband’s hand may,
as the wife of her brother, give birth to a legitimate son of her own body;
thus spoke Mārkaṇḍeya.
Three ways of taking a wife are known, in which dharma is not destroyed.
Nārada said:
"Tell me of the other five later wives and their sons."

A wife from one's own clan, one purchased, one who is the wife of another, one who has come and gone, and one brought from a hermitage— these are the five ways of obtaining a wife; furthermore, these are those who become wives again.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"These are the wives whom men may approach, and their sons are the offerers of *havya* and *kavya*.
O great sage, you have heard in detail about these wives and sons."
Nārada said:
"Tell me, how is it that women dwelling in the hermitages do not become corrupted?
Among women residing in hermitages, their kinship ties are lost."
These women, having lost their lineage from both their kinsmen and their husbands,
become wives of others, freed from blame, established in their respective stages of life,
masters of their own bodies, desirable, and with minds fixed upon them.
In this way, women do not incur blame for the offspring born of men;
these wives, together with their sons, become the givers of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
Regarding another's wife who, after her husband has previously died, again resorts to another husband—whether she has sons or is sonless—how is this so? Nārada: [How is it so?]
Whether they have borne children or not, the wives of others among householders— having been touched by another—
are to be avoided, for they are defiled in their religious practices;
nor do the deities accept the offerings to the gods or the ancestors from them.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: A man who,
out of fickleness, sows his seed in the fields of others may produce sons through those women, yet he shall not obtain the fruit of a son through them.
Nārada said:
"O best of sages, how can he obtain the fruit of a son? For what man would sow his seed in another's field that belongs to no owner?"

If one has sown seed in a field that belongs to oneself, that seed does not perish. But if a man, out of pride, should sow seed in the fields of others, that seed belongs only to the owner of the field; the sower of the seed does not receive the fruit.
There is nothing more unrighteous or more disgraceful than this.
Furthermore, among those [wives], even if they are equal [in status], she who has given birth to many children from the womb and so forth should be abandoned.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.

Now, O Nārada, regarding those sons who are born from the wives of others—O you of supreme luster, whose kinsmen and heirs do they become? Nārada replied: [They belong to him] from whose seed they were produced.
Two kinds of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, are born from the wives of others. If the husband is alive, the son is a *kuṇḍa*; if the husband is dead, he is a *golaka*.
These two, born in the field of another, bring suffering to embodied beings both in this world and after death.
They destroy the sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral offerings (kavya) given by the donors;
indeed, these lead the father to hell, and Golaka especially so.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
Those born of such [actions] are like outcasts; indeed, they perish both in this world and in the next.
Whose reproachable sons are these, who offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations to the ancestors?
Nārada.
He in whose field they are born, or he who begets those sons—
both the owner of the field and the sower of the seed go to hell,
for he does not protect his own wife and yet goes to another's wife.
Those men are always to be censured, for they are excluded from the practice of dharma.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
A man who eats from a *kuṇḍa* (a vessel or a specific caste), whether he is the one being fed or the one feeding, is despised by the ancestors and the gods.
O Nārada, to whom do these censured sons perpetually offer the *havya* and *kavya* offerings? Or what is the fruit of dharma in them? —Nārada.
The Yātudhānas and Piśācas receive that which is offered by them;
they, along with those beings who roam at night, partake of the *havya* and *kavya* given by them.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
"Then those Rākṣasas, being pleased, what do they bestow upon their donors? Or what might be the fruit of dharma for them, O best of sages? Nārada asked.
Nothing given by givers among all living beings ever perishes.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Those who give enjoy that prosperity both in this world and after death.
Now, as for whatever lineage shall arise from Golaka and Kuṇḍa,
how indeed will their various kinsmen provide for them?
Nārada said:
The virtuous sons born of those who follow that way of life please the ancestors and the gods, being intent upon the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*).
In this same manner, there are those known as *golaka* and *kuṇḍa*, who merely bear the designation of caste.
The deities accept the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) from those who are pure.
Mārkaṇḍeya:
I have heard of the fickleness that arises in men toward the wives of others.
Nārada said:
"I wish to understand the fault in the fickleness of women;
for even within a single caste, there is the fault of having previously engaged with another."
Authorized by Viṣṇu, Dhātṛ did exactly that. O highly wise one, having previously created the female and male organs, Prajāpati, being authorized, brought about their union.
Then, it is said that Bhaga received a boon through the grace of Viṣṇu;
by that very grace, he enjoys all the worlds.
Therefore, there is indeed a greater fault in the man himself; of this there is no doubt.
Among those of the same caste, women should not be abandoned for having sexual intercourse, except when pregnancy is involved;
a wise man should impose penance according to the rule and administer punishment accordingly.
Or, [if bitten] by dogs, one should bathe and perform the three daily ablutions at night.
Sleeping on the ground and on ashes, giving gifts while devoid of enjoyments,
the gravity of the fault, the time, and the gravity of the substance—
these were the boundaries established previously when he had gone to another sacred ford.

O long-lived one, there is no fault in women’s transgression; Bhaga was purified at another sacred ford, but here [he was cleansed] by the word of Viṣṇu. And they are to be protected from conversations with others and from being led away to the houses of others.
One who especially purifies these [senses] reaps the fruit of their actions.
One who desires well-being should not revile, nor kill, nor afflict them.
Thinking, "By the grace of Viṣṇu," Bhaga went to another sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).
Month after month, their menstrual flow carries away their misdeeds.
Women are the bringers of satisfaction to men; women always bestow contentment.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
O you of great splendor, women in this world establish sons and set up sacred foundations;
O best of sages, the learning, strength, and power of women have been heard by me.
Nārada.
I wish to know the dharma of a man who has many wives—
of that embodied being attached to many wives and to the enjoyment of women— who, failing to approach his wife during her fertile season, is considered by tradition to be a slayer of an embryo.
By avoiding an old woman, a barren woman, one who is strictly observant of vows, one whose children have died, one who has not yet reached puberty,
a maiden, and a woman with many sons, one is released from fear. This applies when one is afflicted by disease, imprisoned, traveling abroad, or on sacred festival days.
At the proper times for women, one releases them from the sin of destroying an embryo.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Sons born of women who are prostitutes or those who serve others [are likewise freed].
Nārada said:
"O Great Sage, whose kinsmen and heirs are those sons born of courtesans? Whose children are they? [The Buddha replied: "They belong to him whose wife they are; those sons are his."
Sons are acquired through purchase, and those who are given away become sons by adoption. In the case of courtesans, a man’s interest is certainly not restricted.
"In this case, whose son do they say belongs to a woman who has not yet conceived?
Nārada replied:
'Among women who are like sacred fords (*tīrtha*), he is known as the one who approaches her.'"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"In the fertile season, a woman who has no misgivings may conceive a child from him; [so too for] men who, out of lust or anger, abandon a virtuous wife."
Nārada said:
"I ask you for the atonement regarding those who abandon a woman— whether she has borne children or not—
thinking from the very beginning that she was virtuous and sinless."
For one who abandons his own lineage or his own duty, there is indeed atonement;
but for that man who abandons a wife who is menstruating yet childless,
his lineage is destroyed, and he, being joined with his ancestors, shall be cast out by the gods.
A wife who has given birth to offspring and produced sons and grandsons— by abandoning such a wife and family, one does not attain purification. Indeed,
for men who thus forsake their wives, there is no means of atonement.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Women who are established in the care of their sons and grandsons do not deserve to be abandoned. By abandoning what kind of wife does a man not become tainted by faults?
Nārada said:
"O best of sages, I desire to know this in its true essence:
[the conduct] of those established in the dharma of liberation who recognize one another."

For husband and wife who have been released from their bonds, no unrighteousness is prescribed. For men who, having investigated a woman who has attached herself to another, whose children have gone elsewhere, who has gone to a Śūdra, or who has gone to a stranger, abandon her, there is no sin.
Even if they have fallen into sin, both mother and father must nevertheless be supported.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
When a man, out of anger, abandons a wife who has been unfaithful...
Nārada said:
"O Great-minded One, how can even dharma become adharma in this world? For he who abandons a woman—whether she be unchaste or chaste—is likewise [guilty]."

A man who fails to protect his own wife becomes a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*). A woman who, for the sake of offspring, should transgress against her husband must be guarded as one whose senses are fickle; she must not be abandoned under any circumstances.
Rivers and women are of a similar nature;
they do not become corrupted when entered by men. The currents of a river carry away whatever falls into them.
Just as a woman returns to purity through her menses,
so too women are not defiled even by infidelity toward their husbands;
for month after month, there is a shedding [of blood], and through that they become pure once again.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"O Blessed One, which sacred sites (tīrthas) indeed reside within the bodies of men? Pray, tell them to me as they truly are, for I ask you."
"O Knower of Holy Places, among all holy places, what is the supreme place for men,
by bathing in which a person becomes eternally pure in soul?
Nārada.
The holy fords (tīrthas) of the gods, sages, and ancestors, as well as those of Brahmā and Viṣṇu— these five holy fords of men are said to be present within the hand. Indeed,
among all holy fords, the Vaiṣṇava portion is called the foremost of holy fords.
By performing ablutions there, the lineage of the four castes prospers.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Rituals for the ancestors and the gods flourish both in this world and after death.
"O Nārada, tell me about those women who are unrestrained among men driven by desire— those women for whom there is no restraint. Nārada:
The hunter’s wife, the courtesan, the actress, the cowherd woman, the weaver woman, and the tailor woman;
Mārkaṇḍeya;
the Nārī, the Kirātī, the Śabarī, and the dancer who is free from worldly attachments.
Among these women born of all the social orders (varṇas),
O Nārada,
best of sages, which among those sons become the heirs to their paternal kin?
For those who take these [women] as their wives, they alone are the fathers of their sons.
But when [sexual intercourse] occurs with all women indiscriminately, the seed of embodied beings is lost.
— Mārkaṇḍeya.
Men who have set their hearts upon all women, who are devoid of virtuous Vedic knowledge,
who are mere archers (Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas), and who are excluded from the Vedic mantras—
how can that which is given to those who are appointed to the offerings for gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) bear fruit?
Twice-born men who are excluded from the Sāvitrī do not deserve offerings to the gods or the ancestors.
