The giving of food to those who have fallen from their caste (vrātyas) is exactly the same as it is for Śūdras. But the minds of men who are authorized in the duties [of higher castes] become deluded.
— Nārada.
"How indeed does an obstacle arise? This I wish to know.
Both wealth and women are alike in this regard;
they delude the better qualities of men in this world."
Women captivate through the joy of passion;
wealth destroys enjoyments and even dharma.
A righteous śrotriya is worthy of all that is offered to the gods and the ancestors.
For a gift given to a virtuous *śrotriya* is like an oblation cast into a blazing fire.
[She was] born into a family of *śrotriyas*, who had realized the self through knowledge of the meaning of the Vedas.
Nārada said:
"Why have they abandoned the triple Vedic knowledge and resorted to the livelihood of the *vārtā*?
In former times, the system of the four castes was established among the highly learned twice-born."

Therefore, one's livelihood should be divided according to the castes, free from any intermixture. And those others who were born from Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*)—refined [sons] desired by those greedy for offspring—[are the *mārkaṇḍeyas*].
Mārkaṇḍeya.
Relying on a mode of existence that has arisen and been extinguished since the beginning,
how is it that those born of the Vedic tradition are unrefined, while the wise are refined? — Nārada.

One who lacks Vedic refinement and is not a son of a *śrotriya* is not to be honored; however, one of pure lineage who is a *śrotriya* is equal to the learned otherwise. Furthermore, those whose sons do not study and who are devoid of Vedic refinement [are likewise disregarded].

Therefore, those Brahmins who possess Vedic knowledge and are skilled in the Vedas were created in the past from the mass of Brahmā, consecrated by the purificatory rites of the Vedas— Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Therefore, those virtuous men who uphold their lineage are born from them alone.
But as for those men who procreate upon female slaves purchased by themselves—
whose wives and sons do they truly become, O best of sages?
Nārada said:
That man who, out of delusion, procreates upon his own female slave is a doer of evil;
he is censured both in this world and after death, and he leads his offspring to servitude.
His wife, those sons of his who offer the *havya* and *kavya* oblations, and whatever relatives of his are attached to him or have fallen into servitude—
all these, through their connection with her, are released from their duties as servants.
All this that was spoken by you has been related to you.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Or rather, if you have any further doubt, you should ask again.
Nārada, who possesses unerring vision in this world and is skilled in all things,
is Bhīṣma;
he is a direct witness of the worlds, like the Self-Existent One, O best of beings.
Having thus conversed with the sages, Mārkaṇḍeya of great asceticism honored Nārada, and being likewise honored by him,
the sage took his leave of the sages and departed for his hermitage.

The sages also undertook the service of sacred fords (tīrtha). Through the purification of the seed in a fertile field and through celibacy, one is purified; by bathing regularly and on specific occasions, and through the purity of the mind, one becomes pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O best of the Bharatas, what do the Brahmins say is the eternal worthy recipient (pātra)— one who possesses the marks of a Brahmin and follows the outward signs, or a Brahmin who is without such signs?"
13,023.002 Bhīṣma said:

13,023.002a "O Great King, they say that alms should be given to one who has adopted his own proper mode of life, whether he bears the outward marks of an ascetic or not; for both of these are practitioners of austerity."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, what fault would there be for one who, purified by supreme faith, offers oblations to the gods (*havya*), oblations to the ancestors (*kavya*), or likewise gifts to a twice-born man?"
"Bhīṣma said:
'Brahmins who are worthy recipients and pure are not so [regarded] toward their own fathers in this world.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, a man purified by faith, even if he is difficult to subdue, becomes purified in every respect; of this there is no doubt. How much more so, O lord of the earth, in your case?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
A man should never examine a Brāhmaṇa when it concerns offerings to the gods;
however, the wise know that a Brāhmaṇa must be examined when it concerns the offering of *kavya* (ancestral oblations).
Bhīṣma said:
A Brahmin does not accomplish the oblation; it succeeds through the divine. By the grace of the gods, the sacrificers perform their sacrifices; of this there is no doubt.
O best of the Bharatas, the Brahmins are constant exponents of the Veda.
In ancient times, the wise Mārkaṇḍeya spoke thus regarding these worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Whether he be a stranger, or a learned man, or even one who is a kinsman—"
"How can one who is an ascetic or devoted to sacrifice become a worthy recipient?
Bhīṣma said:
"One who is of noble birth, a performer of ritual acts, learned in the Vedas, and likewise compassionate."
"Modest, upright, and truthful—these three are worthy vessels, O Pārtha;
now hear from me this teaching regarding the splendor of these four:
of the Earth, of Kāśyapa, of Agni, and indeed of Mārkaṇḍeya."
The Earth said:
Just as a clod of earth thrown into the great ocean quickly perishes,
so too does all evil conduct perish through the threefold repetition [of the Veda].
Kāśyapa said:
"All the Vedas together with their six auxiliary limbs, as well as Sāṃkhya, the Purāṇas, and birth in a noble family."
"O King, none of these states of existence become the destiny for a man who is devoid of moral conduct.
Agni said:
O Brahmin, he who, while studying, considers himself a scholar and destroys the reputation of others by means of his learning,
commits through that act the murder of a Brahmin.
"For his worlds indeed become finite.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale."
"I do not know if I might obtain even half of this truth;
for truth indeed excels a thousand horse-sacrifices.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, those four of immeasurable splendor— Pṛthivī, Kāśyapa, Agni, and Prakṛṣṭāyus the Bhārgava— departed quickly.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"When the Brahmins in this world who observe vows eat the sacrificial offering (havis),
how can that which has been eaten for the sake of a Brahmin become a meritorious deed?
Bhīṣma said:
"O Indra among kings, those Brahmins who have received an invitation and are masters of the Vedas,
yet eat for the sake of [mere] worldly power (*brahmakāma*), become violators of their vows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The wise say that the Dharma has many ends and many doors. What, then, can be considered certain therein? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, compassion, self-restraint, and likewise straightforwardness— O King of kings, these are definitively the characteristics of dharma.
Those who, praising dharma, wander this earth, [are the ones who truly practice it].
O Lord, those who do not practice that dharma and are instead devoted to social confusion—
whosoever gives them jewels, gold, a cow, or horses,
dwells in hell for ten years, subsisting on excrement.
The deeds performed or left undone by Medas, Pulkasas, and likewise Antyavasayins, who prattle under the influence of passion and delusion;
and those fools who offer the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice to a Brahmin who is a mere student (brahmacārin).
"O Indra among kings, those who give gifts here do not experience inauspicious worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is superior to celibacy? What is the supreme characteristic of dharma?"
"Furthermore, O Grandfather, tell me what is the most excellent form of purity.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, celibacy and the avoidance of honey and meat are supreme."
Dharma stands within its bounds; tranquility is the characteristic of purity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
At what time should one practice dharma? At what time should one pursue artha?
"At what time would one be happy? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"One should practice material prosperity at the proper time, and immediately thereafter, dharma."
Afterwards, he may indulge his desires, yet he should not become addicted to them;
he should hold Brahmins in high esteem and honor his teachers;
he should be well-disposed toward all beings, gentle in character, and sweet-spoken.
Falsehood uttered in a legal proceeding, slander directed toward the king,
and deceiving one's teacher— these are equal to the murder of a Brahmin. One should not strike at sovereigns, nor likewise should one kill a cow.
Both of these, whoever practices them, are equal to the killing of an embryo.
One should never abandon the sacred fire, nor should one abandon the Vedas;
nor should one revile a Brāhmaṇa, for that is equal to the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me: what kind of brahmins are virtuous; to whom does a gift given yield great fruit; and from what kind of people should one eat? Tell me that."
13,023.033 Bhīṣma said:

13,023.033a Those who are free from anger, devoted to dharma, constant in truth, and delighting in self-restraint— 13,023.033c such are the virtuous Brahmins; what is given to them yields great fruit.

To those who are free from pride, patient with all, who have seen the truth, have conquered their senses, are devoted to the welfare of all beings, and are friendly— gifts given to them yield great fruit.
They are free from greed, pure, learned, modest, and speakers of truth.
Whatever is given to those who are devoted to their own duties yields great fruit.
O bull among the twice-born, the sages know that he who studies the four Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs, having desisted from the six worldly occupations, is a worthy recipient.

But for those who possess such qualities as these, a gift given to them yields great fruit; the giver obtains a thousandfold reward by bestowing upon one who is worthy of such qualities. One who is endowed with wisdom, sacred learning, conduct, and virtuous character—
Even a single bull among the twice-born can deliver his entire lineage here;
one should bestow a cow, a horse, wealth, or food upon such a person,
as well as other articles, for then one does not grieve in the state after death.
Even a single best of the twice-born in this world can deliver his entire lineage; how much more so, then, one individual? Therefore, one should carefully attend to a worthy recipient.
When he is satisfied, all the gods, the ancestors, and even the sages are satisfied.
Having heard of a Brāhmaṇa endowed with virtues and esteemed by the virtuous,
one should have him brought from afar for the sake of a task and honor him in every way.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, regarding the time for ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), rites for the gods (*daiva*), and also matters of dharma—
whatever has been ordained by the celestial sages, I desire that it be explained here by you.
Bhīṣma said:
One should perform rites for the gods in the forenoon, but those for the ancestors in the afternoon;
endowed with auspicious conduct, having performed purification, and being diligent,
one should offer gifts to human beings at midday according to one's means.

They know that gift which is given at the wrong time to be the portion of the Rākṣasas. They know that gift which is stepped over, licked by animals, offered with strife, or seen by women in their menses, to be the portion of the Rākṣasas.

O Bhārata, they know that food which has been publicly proclaimed, that which is eaten by one who has not observed his vows, and that which has been touched by a dog, to be the portion of the Rākṣasas. Likewise,
food into which hair or insects have fallen, or that which has been sneezed upon, or looked upon by dogs [is likewise unfit].

They know that which is eaten while weeping or with contempt to be the portion of the Rākṣasas. O Bhārata, they know that which is eaten without the utterance of *oṃ*, by one who bears weapons, or by one who is evil-minded, to be the portion of the Rākṣasas.

Whatever is eaten as the leavings of another, or whatever has been enjoyed by another, they know that portion to always belong to the *rākṣasas* in rites for the gods and the ancestors. Likewise, food that is contemptible, censured, or served with anger [is theirs].
Whether it be an offering to the gods or one to the ancestors, they know that portion to belong to the Rākṣasas.
O best of men, that Śrāddha which is served by the three castes while being devoid of mantras and devoid of ritual action, they know that portion to belong to the Rākṣasas.
Whatever is served without an oblation of clarified butter,
and whatever is eaten by those of wicked conduct— know that portion to belong to the Rākṣasas.
O bull of the Bharatas, those portions which have been declared for the Rākṣasas have thus been described.
13,024.012c Now hear from me, O Brāhmaṇa, the examination of those who have renounced their status (visarga).
13,024.013a As many fallen Brāhmaṇas as there are, as well as those who are mentally deficient or insane, O King, they do not deserve an invitation to rites for the gods or the ancestors.

O King, one who has white leprosy, one with skin disease, one who is impotent, one afflicted by consumption, one who suffers from epilepsy, and one who is blind do not deserve hospitality. Nor do physicians,
temple-priests, or those who observe vows in vain.
Furthermore, those who sell Soma do not deserve an invitation to a Śrāddha. O King,
singers, dancers, acrobats, musicians, storytellers,
and warriors likewise do not deserve an invitation.
O King, those who act as priests for Śūdras, as well as Śūdra teachers and Śūdra pupils, do not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast. Furthermore,
O Bhārata, that Brahmin who is a questioner and he who is questioned [in such a manner] likewise do not deserve it.

Even those two are not worthy of the *śrāddha*, for they are sellers of the Veda. O King, even a Brahmin who was formerly made a leader but has taken a wife from a lower caste, though he be learned in all branches of knowledge, is not worthy of an invitation.
O King, those Brahmins who maintain no sacred fires, those who carry out the dead, thieves, and those who have fallen from their caste do not deserve an invitation to a funeral feast. Nor,
O Bhārata, do those whose ancestry is unknown or those who previously belonged to a social group (gaṇa).
Those who have only daughters as their first-born sons do not deserve an invitation to a *śrāddha*.
O King, he who is a debtor, the twice-born man who is a usurer,
and he whose livelihood consists of the sale of living beings— O King, these do not deserve an invitation.
O bull of the Bharatas, as many as there may be who were formerly women, those who carry arrows on their backs (Kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas),
and Brahmins who do not recite the Vedas, are unworthy of an invitation to a Śrāddha.
O bull of the Bharatas, these are the Brahmins specified for both the Śrāddha and the Daiva rites.
Listen further to the benefit for both the giver and the recipient: O King,
even those who are farmers, provided they have observed their vows, are endowed with virtues,
know the Sāvitrī, and are observant of ritual duties, are worthy of being invited.
One should designate a twice-born man of noble birth who follows the dharma of a warrior in battle,
but one should never, my dear, appoint a merchant at the *śrāddha* rites. Furthermore, that brahmin who maintains the sacred fire and is a resident of the village—
O King, he who is free from theft, who knows how to honor guests, and who is worthy of being invited,
and who, O bull of the Bharatas, recites the Sāvitrī mantra at the three times of day—
even if he is a servant of the king— reciting the Sāvitrī constantly with a concentrated mind, [attains the highest state].
O King, one who subsists on alms, who is active in religious duties, and who is worthy of being invited [for a feast], is such a person.

One’s mother is a worthy recipient (*pātra*), one’s father is a worthy recipient, and those kinsmen whose wealth is exhausted are worthy recipients. A distressed person is a worthy recipient, one observing vows is a worthy recipient, and one adorned with virtuous conduct is a worthy recipient.
O King, he who has risen after sunset, as well as he who has set after sunrise, who is non-violent and possesses few faults— he is worthy of being invited [to a sacrifice],
O bull of the Bharatas, for such a Brāhmaṇa is free from guile and free from contentious thought.

O King, one who has regained his senses, one who subsists on alms, and one who is capable of accepting an invitation— even if he was previously vowless, a gambler, a thief, a seller of living beings, or a merchant,
provided he has subsequently drunk the *soma*— is worthy of an invitation, O King.
Having first acquired wealth through harsh agricultural labors,

O King, one may later become a host to all guests and worthy of being invited. Wealth designated for the sale of the Veda, as well as that which is earned by a woman, [is not to be used for such purposes].

That which is unfit to be given to the ancestors or the gods, and that which is acquired through impotence— O bull of the Bharatas, when the ritual conclusion is being performed, if a twice-born man does not utter what is appropriate, his sin is equal to the falsehood of denying a cow.

O Yudhiṣṭhira, the proper time for a *śrāddha* is when a Brāhmaṇa has arrived, when curds and ghee are available, during the waning of the moon, and when there is forest meat. It is traditionally taught that the first three *muhūrtas* of the day are known as "morning."
In that [time], the Brahmins should perform auspicious vows such as recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*).
The period called *saṃgava* consists of three parts, while midday (*madhyāhna*) lasts for three *muhūrtas*.
During *saṃgava*, half of the worldly activities take place, whereas bathing and other rites occur during the midday period.
The fourth [period], the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*), consists of three *muhūrtas* and is for the ancestors (*pitryaka*);
the evening (*sāyāhna*) also consists of three *muhūrtas*. This is remembered by the wise as the intermediate [time].
O King, one should always perform the *śrāddha* during the fourth period known as the afternoon.

The Brahmins face the northeast, and the Viśvedevas face the south. When they have been made to hear [the mantras] and are well-satisfied, one should offer the *piṇḍa* along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
At the conclusion of the *śrāddha*, for the Brahmin, the *svadhā* indeed becomes well-savored.
Then one should say for the Kṣatriya as well: "May the ancestors be pleased.
But at the conclusion of the Śrāddha rite for a Vaiśya, O Bhārata, the word "inexhaustible" (akṣayyam) should be uttered; for a Śūdra, O Bhārata, the word "well-being" (svasti) should be used.
The recitation for the declaration of an auspicious day (*puṇyāhavācana*) is prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa in rites for the gods;
this very same rite, performed without the syllable *oṃ*, is prescribed for a Kṣatriya.
Regarding the injury of a cow, one who has previously established himself as a Brāhmaṇa or similar [status] must pay a fourth part [of the fine].
If a Brahmin eats at the houses of those of lower castes, the penalty increases fourfold for each successive Śūdra.
A Brahmin who has been previously invited by another Brahmin must not eat elsewhere; otherwise, he incurs sin, and he should avoid the invitation of a Śūdra.
A twice-born man whose body is nourished by the food of a Śūdra shall not attain a higher state. He must not eat while impure, nor should he be an atheist devoid of human virtue.
O King, even one of the same caste must not, out of greed, step over another who is seated before him.
The Brahmins are known as the gods of the earth, excluding those who are still students (*upakurvāṇa*).
For a Vaiśya, it should be said: "May the deities be pleased.
Now hear the sequence of the rites performed according to the rule.

O Bhārata, O Yudhiṣṭhira, all the rites beginning with the birth-ceremony (*jātakarman*) for the three castes are indeed prescribed with mantras for the Brāhmaṇa and the Kṣatriya; for the Vaiśya as well, O Yudhiṣṭhira. The girdle of a Brāhmaṇa is made of muñja grass, while that of a Kṣatriya is made of *maurvī* (bowstring) fiber.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the duty for a Vaiśya: [his staff] should be made of *bālvaja* grass. O Yudhiṣṭhira, the staff of a twice-born man should be made of *pālāśa* wood, that of a Kṣatriya of *aśvattha*, and that of a Vaiśya of *audumbara*—this is the law."
Listen to these two matters regarding the merit and demerit of both the giver and the receiver:
for a Brāhmaṇa, speaking untruth is declared to be an unrighteous act termed a sin;
for a Kṣatriya it is fourfold, and for a Vaiśya it is recorded as eightfold.

A Brāhmaṇa should not eat elsewhere if he has been previously invited by another Brāhmaṇa; for if he does, being younger [in merit], he would share in the same guilt as the injury caused to the sacrificial animal. However, if he eats when invited by a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, he incurs no such fault.

A younger brother who participates in the injury of cattle shall incur half the guilt. O King, if a Brāhmaṇa eats at a rite for the gods or for the ancestors while among other Brāhmaṇas without having bathed, his unrighteousness is equal to that of a lie regarding a cow.

O King, if a Brāhmaṇa who is in a state of ritual impurity should eat among Brāhmaṇas and others, whether out of prior knowledge or through greed, his sin is equal to that of a false oath regarding a cow. And he who,
O Bhārata, seeks food with food for the sake of performing rituals [is likewise at fault].

O Indra among kings, it is declared that untruth is unrighteousness; O Yudhiṣṭhira, those of the three castes who do not observe the Vedic vows and conduct yet serve food with mantras— among them lies the unrighteousness of the "cow-lie."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, regarding that which is given as an ancestral offering (*paitrya*) or a divine offering (*daiva*),
I wish to hear about those to whom gifts are given that yield great fruit."
13,024.049 Bhīṣma said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, feed those whose wives wait for them as farmers await a good rain— those who have only the remnants and leftovers remaining.
O King, that which is given to those who are restrained in conduct, who are emaciated and of meager means,
and who approach as supplicants, yields great fruit.
O King, they have devotion to him, their home is his, their wealth is his, and they take refuge in him.
To those who are seekers of wealth, a gift given for the sake of their purpose yields great fruit. O Yudhiṣṭhira, for those who are afflicted by fear— whether from thieves or from others— and who,
as seekers, desire to enjoy [safety], a gift given to them yields great fruit.
For that Brahmin who is free from guile and has dedicated himself to a heap of alms-food, and whose young students beg for their own sustenance— the gift given to them yields great fruit.
Likewise, for those Brahmins whose property and wives have been seized during a calamity of the land...
Those who approach for the sake of wealth—the gift given to them yields great fruit.

Likewise, those Brahmins who observe vows, abide by their restraints, and are esteemed for their learning, desire [gifts] for the sake of completing their observances; a gift given to them yields great fruit.
Those who have not deviated from the true Dharma nor from the traditions of the heretics,
whose vital strength is diminished and whose wealth is meager— in giving to them, the fruit is great;
as is the case for the purpose of breaking a fast during vows, for the sake of a teacher, or as a sacrificial fee.
For the sake of providing a dwelling, what is given to those wise ones yields great fruit;
for the sake of protecting one’s parents, for the sake of one’s children and wife,
and for the sake of liberation from great diseases— what is given to them yields great fruit.
Fools and women desire excellent food even when they lack the means;
by giving to them, one goes to heaven and does not enter the hells. Even when their entire property has been seized by powerful men, these innocent people remain blameless.
They long for food that has already been eaten; a gift given to them yields great fruit.
Those who are ascetics devoted to austerity, and those who wander for alms—when they, being seekers, desire even a little, a gift given to them yields great fruit.
O bull among the Bharatas, you have heard the rules regarding gifts that yield great fruit;
now hear those by which people indeed go to hell or to heaven,
with the exception, O Yudhiṣṭhira, of [giving] for the sake of a guru or for the sake of providing safety.
13,024.060c Those who speak untruths are indeed destined for hell;
13,024.061a those who carry off another's wife, those who violate another's wife, and those who incite others toward another's wife— they too are indeed destined for hell.
13,024.062 Those who steal the property of others, those who cause the destruction of others' possessions, and those who are informers against others— these indeed go to hell.
13,024.063 O Bhārata, [those who destroy] water-stations, assembly halls, and bridges...
Those men who break into houses go to hell;
and those men who deceive a woman who is unprotected— whether she be young, old, frightened, or an ascetic— they indeed go to hell.
O Bhārata, those who destroy a livelihood, destroy a household, or destroy a wife, as well as those who destroy friendships and hope— they indeed go to hell.
So too do informers, those who break treaties, and those who subsist on the livelihoods of others.

Those who are ungrateful toward their friends, indeed, go to hell; likewise, heretics, those who revile others, those who violate established agreements, and those who have fallen away from their vows—
these indeed go to hell.
Those who engage in dishonest dealings and practice usury with unjust interest rates,
and those who are likewise unjust in their profits— they indeed go to hell.
So too do those men who engage in gambling transactions and act without due examination.

Those who are intent on harming living beings are indeed destined for hell. Those who, through divisive means, alienate one who has fulfilled his expectations, fulfilled his obligations, fulfilled his duties, and fulfilled his labors— they too are indeed destined for hell.
Those who eat while neglecting their wives, the sacred fires, their servants, and guests— those who have abandoned the worship of the ancestors and the gods— truly go to hell.
So too do those who sell the Vedas and those who defile the Vedas.
Those who are scribes of the Vedas indeed go to hell; likewise,
those men who stand outside the four stages of life (āśramas), those who are outside the revealed scriptures (śruti),
and those who live by improper occupations, they indeed go to hell.
O King, those who sell hair, those who sell poison,
and those who sell milk— these indeed go to hell. O Yudhiṣṭhira, [this applies] to Brahmins, cows, and maidens as well.
Those who find fault with others in their affairs,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, go indeed to hell; likewise, those who sell weapons and those who manufacture arrows and bows go indeed to hell.
O bull of the Bharatas, those who obstruct the path with thorns, stakes, or pits are indeed destined for hell.
O bull of the Bharatas, [those who neglect] their teachers, their dependents, and their devoted followers...
Those who abandon those who are incapable are indeed destined for hell. Likewise, those who break in horses before they are ready, those who pierce their noses,
and those who bind animals, are indeed destined for hell.
Those who do not protect [their subjects], who embezzle wealth, who are solely intent on collecting the sixth part as tax, and who, though capable, do not give— these indeed go to hell;
likewise those who, having made a promise, fail to give, and those who revile the poor.
Those who revile Vedic scholars who are disciplined yet poor,
and those who revile even the patient, are indeed destined for hell.
Likewise, [those who revile] the forbearing, the self-controlled, the wise, and those with whom they have lived for a long time— [they too go to hell].
Those who, having fulfilled their own purposes, abandon others, are indeed destined for hell.
Furthermore, those men who eat first without giving to children, the elderly, or servants, are indeed destined for hell.
"These have been observed by the ancient seers and declared to be those who go to hell.
O bull of the Bharatas, I shall now describe those who are partakers of the heavenly world.
Indeed, in all undertakings, O Bhārata, one should begin with the divine."
The transgression committed against a Brahmin destroys all one's sons and cattle.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who follow righteousness through charity, austerity, and truth are destined for heaven.
O Bhārata, those men who, having acquired sacred learning through service and austerities, remain free from attachment to receiving gifts, go to heaven; likewise,
those who [act] out of fear, sin, affliction, poverty, or the assault of disease [attain the same].
Those men for whose sake [these gifts] are bestowed go to heaven;
those who are patient, steadfast, and diligent in performing righteous deeds, and those who are endowed with auspicious conduct— those men go to heaven.
Those men who have abstained from honey and meat, as well as from the wives of others,
and who have likewise desisted from intoxicating drinks, go to heaven,
O Bhārata; they are the founders of hermitages and of noble lineages.

Those men who give garments and ornaments, as well as food, drink, and sustenance, and those who provide for families, go to heaven. (13,024.088c–089) Those men who [give] countries and cities go to heaven. Those men who have desisted from all violence, who are patient with everything, and who have become a refuge for all— those men go to heaven.
Those who serve their mother and father, having conquered their senses, [go to heaven].
Those men who are affectionate toward their brothers go to heaven,
O Bhārata; likewise, those who are wealthy, powerful, and in the prime of youth—
provided they are wise and have conquered their senses— those men go to heaven.
Those men who are affectionate toward those who have offended them, who are gentle and devoted to their friends, and who find joy in serving others, go to heaven; likewise,
those who provide for a thousand people and those who give away a thousand [gifts] go to heaven.
Those men who are protectors of thousands,
O bull of the Bharatas, and givers of gold and cows,
as well as givers of vehicles and mounts— they are the ones who go to heaven.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those men who give garments to brides being married, to female servants, and to slaves, go to heaven. Likewise,
those who provide pleasure-pavilions, dwellings, gardens, wells, groves, and assembly halls [attain the same].
Those men who construct embankments for ponds go to heaven;
likewise, those men who give food, drink, and clothing, as well as sandals,
according to their ability, are indeed the enemies of hell.
O Bhārata, those men who are givers of dwellings, fields, and habitations as requested, go to heaven; likewise,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who give juices, seeds, and grains.
Men who give gifts after producing them themselves go to heaven; born into whatever family they may be, those men who have many sons, live for a hundred years,
are compassionate, and have conquered their anger go to heaven.
Those who are devoted to sacred fords such as the Gaṅgā, those who perform ancestral rites at holy sites, and those who are intent on sacrifices and charitable works— those men go to heaven.
O Bhārata, this which has been told concerns the rites for the gods and the ancestors for the sake of the next world.
And the merit and demerit of giving as established by the ancient seers.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O King, descendant of Bharata, you ought to tell me this according to the truth.
"By not having killed anyone here, how is the slaying of a Brahmin ordained?
Bhīṣma said:
"O king of kings, this is what I asked Vyāsa in the past."
I shall explain that to you; listen to it here with a one-pointed mind. "O Sage, you are the fourth [disciple] of Vasiṣṭha; tell me the truth:
by what act here, without actually killing, is the sin of Brahman-slaughter incurred?"
13,025.004 Thus questioned, O Great King, the son of Parāśara,
who was expert in dharma, spoke these unsurpassed words free from doubt. 13,025.005 Having himself summoned a Brāhmaṇa of meager means for the sake of alms—

One who later says "it does not exist" regarding what was previously stated, one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin. O Bhārata, that evil-minded man who seizes the livelihood of a neutral Brahmin who is well-versed in the Vedas, one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
O lord of the earth, one who creates an obstacle for the sake of water for the thirsty Gokula should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin. Likewise,
one who [rejects] the Veda that has come forth correctly, or the scripture composed by the sages—
Indeed, by insulting Brahmins because of their birth,
by cutting off their livelihood, and by violating their wives— know that one who commits such acts out of ignorance is a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmaghātī*).
One who does not bestow his daughter, endowed with beauty and of marriageable age, upon a suitable bridegroom, should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin.
So too is the fool who, devoted to unrighteousness, behaves falsely toward the twice-born.
If one should cause a Brahmin to do that [evil], one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin (*brahmaghātaka*). One who is envious, deceitful, and fraudulent toward Brahmins of virtuous conduct,
and who inflicts grief that pierces the vitals— know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
One who seizes all the property of a man who is deprived of sight, or who is lame, or who is mute, should be known as a slayer of a Brahmin.
Whether in a hermitage, in the forest, in a village, or in a city—
13,025.012c He who, out of delusion, should abandon the sacred fire, one should know him to be a slayer of a Brahmin.
13,026.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
13,026.001a O bull of the Bharata race, visiting sacred fords and bathing therein is conducive to welfare.

"O one of great wisdom, I wish to hear in truth about Śravaṇa. O bull of the Bharatas, you ought to tell me of those holy pilgrimage sites (*tīrtha*) on earth; I shall listen with self-restraint, O Lord."
Bhīṣma said:
"O you of great splendor, you ought to hear this lineage of sacred fords (tīrtha) proclaimed by Aṅgiras; may it be well with you, and you shall attain the highest dharma."
O hero, Gautama, firm in his vows, having approached the great sage Aṅgiras, a brahmin dwelling in the forest of asceticism, questioned him:
"O Blessed One, I have a certain doubt regarding dharma concerning sacred fords."
"I wish to hear all of that; tell it to me, O great sage.
What indeed would be the fruit of touching for water at those sacred fords, O sage? Tell me exactly as it is, O man of great wisdom, regarding the state after death."
Aṅgiras said:
Having plunged into the Candrabhāgā and the wave-garlanded Vitastā for seven days,
one should remain without food, free from the sense of "mine," like a sage.
Whatever rivers flow into the great river within the region of Kaśmīra,
by reaching those rivers and the Sindhu, one possessed of virtuous conduct shall attain heaven;
having reached the Sindhu and plunged into its pure waters, one shall attain heaven.
Having bathed at Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and the waters of the ocean,
as well as at Devikā, Indramārga, and Svarṇabindu,
he is awakened while seated in his celestial chariot, being praised by Apsarases.
Having disturbed the Hiraṇyabindu and having respectfully saluted it,
as well as the Kuśeśaya, his sin is purified;
and having reached the Indratoyā in the vicinity of Gandhamādana.
A man who fasts for three nights at Kuraṅga on the Karatoyā river,
having plunged into the water, self-controlled and pure, obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
[Likewise, one obtains it] at Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, and Mount Nemi.
Likewise, having bathed at Kanakhala, one whose sins are washed away shall go to heaven;
by touching the waters at Apāṃhrada, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice—
provided one is a celibate student, has conquered anger, is true to one's word, and is non-violent.
Where the Bhāgīrathī Gaṅgā flows toward the northern direction,
at the dwelling-place of Maheśvara,
the man who bathes there and remains without food for one month beholds the deities themselves.
At Saptagaṅgā, Trigaṅgā, and Indramārga, while offering libations,
a man who is reborn obtains nectar indeed to consume;
and having touched the waters at Mahāśrama, he who is pure and devoted to the agnihotra sacrifice [attains the same].

Remaining without food for one month, he shall attain perfection within that month. Having bathed at Mahāhrada on the Bhṛgutuṅga mountain, being free from greed and having fasted for three nights, he is liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin.
Having touched the waters at Kanyākūpa and performed the water-libations at Balākā,
one gains renown among the gods and shines with glory.
Likewise, having touched the waters at Deśakāla and at the Sundarikā lake, [one attains the same].
By [worshipping] the two Aśvins, a man indeed obtains beauty and luster after death.
Likewise, by touching the waters of the Mahāgaṅgā during the Kṛttikās and on a Tuesday,
one who remains without food for a fortnight attains the stainless heaven.

Having touched the waters at Kiṅkiṇīkāśrama, one who moves at will is honored in the divine abode of the Apsarases. Having reached Kālikāśrama and performed the water-libations at the Vipāśā river, [one attains the same].
A celibate student who has conquered anger is liberated from worldly existence after three nights. Having bathed at the hermitage of the Kṛttikās and offered libations to the ancestors,
one who gratifies Mahādeva shall attain the stainless heaven.
Having performed ablutions at Mahāpura and fasted for three nights,
a man shall cast off fear of both moving and stationary beings, as well as of bipeds;
he encounters no fear anywhere and obtains auspiciousness everywhere.
Having bathed in the Devadāru forest, purified of sin and performed the water-libations, one who remains there for seven nights, pure and self-controlled, attains the world of the gods;
likewise at Kauśānta, at Kuśastamba, and at Droṇaśarmapada.

Having bathed at Āpaḥprapatanam, he is served by hosts of Apsarases. Having plunged into Citrakūṭa, Janasthāna, and likewise the waters of the Mandākinī while fasting, he indeed attains royal splendor.
Having gone to the hermitage of Śyāmā, having stayed there and performed the consecration,
and having observed three periods of three nights, he shall dwell in a city of the Gandharvas. Furthermore,
by touching the waters at Ramaṇyā and likewise at Gandhatārikā, [he attains the same].
By remaining without food for one month, one obtains the fruit of invisibility.
Having reached Kauśikīdvāra, a man who subsists on air alone and is free from greed ascends to heaven within twenty-one nights.
He who bathes in the Mataṅga-pool attains perfection in a single night;
indeed, he plunges into the eternal, supportless Andhaka.
Having performed ablutions at Naimiṣa and Svargatīrtha, one whose senses are conquered [attains the same].
By performing the water-libation rites for one month at Gaṅgāhrada and likewise at Utpalāvana, one obtains the fruit of a human sacrifice (puruṣamedha);
by performing the water-libation rites there for one month, one attains the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
At the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, as well as on Mount Kālañjara,
and having performed ablutions at the Ṣaṣṭihrada, no other gift is superior. Ten thousand holy sites (tīrthas), as well as thirty million others, [are present there].
O bull of the Bharatas, on the full moon day of Māgha, they all gather at Prayāga.
O best of the Bharatas, one who is self-controlled and firm in his vows, having bathed at Prayāga during the month of Māgha, shall become stainless and attain heaven.
Having touched the waters at Marudgaṇa in the hermitage of the Pitṛs, a man becomes pure; and by touching the waters at the Tīrtha of Vaivasvata, he himself becomes a sacred ford.
Likewise, having gone to Brahmaśiras and performed the water-libations in the Bhāgīrathī, [he attains the same].
By fasting for one month, one shall attain the world of Soma.
Having bathed at Kapotaka and offered water libations at Aṣṭāvakra,
a man who fasts for twelve days shall obtain the fruit of a human sacrifice (naramedha).
By visiting Muñjapṛṣṭha, Gayā, Nirṛti, Devaparvata,
and the third mountain, Krauñcapāda, one is purified of the sin of killing a Brahmin;
on the third mountain, Krauñca, one is cleansed of the murder of a Brahmin.
Having sipped water at Kalaśī and at Vedyā, which abounds in water,
and having remained without food for one month, a man shall obtain the fruit of a horse-sacrifice (vājimedha).
Having bathed in Agneḥpura and performed the water-libations at Viśālā, a man [attains the same].
He shall dwell in the city of the Fire-maidens;
having bathed in the city of Karavīra and performed ablutions at Devahrada, he becomes one with Brahman and shines forth resplendent.
Having indeed frequented Purāpavartana, Nandā, and Mahānandā,
the self-controlled and non-violent man is served by Apsarases in the Nandana grove;
he who, being well-composed, goes [to bathe] during the conjunction of Urvaśī and Kṛttikā—
Having bathed according to the prescribed rites at Lauhitya, one obtains the fruit of the *puṇḍarīka* sacrifice.
Having touched the waters at Rāmahrada and performed the water-libations at Viśālā,
one who remains without food for twelve days is liberated from sin.
Having touched the waters at Mahāhrada with a pure mind,

a man who remains without food for one month shall attain the state of Jamadagni. Having disciplined himself on the Vindhya mountains, remaining truthful to his vows and non-violent, he likewise attains that goal.
Having remained at Padam for six months, one is purified in a single month;
likewise, by touching the waters of the Narmadā and the waters of Sūrpāraka,
a prince is ordained to be purified after fasting for one fortnight.
On the Jambū-mārga, self-restrained and well-concentrated for three months,
one attains perfection in a single day and night;
having plunged into the waters at Kokāmukha and gone to the Caṇḍālikā hermitage.
Subsisting on vegetables and wearing rags, he obtains ten young maidens;
he shall never go to the abode of Vaivasvata. He whose dwelling is at Kanyāhrada goes to the world of the gods.
O mighty-armed one, at Prabhāsa, a man who remains concentrated for a single night on the new moon day attains perfection here;
he shall go to heaven and be liberated from all sins.
Having touched the waters at Ujjānaka and at the hermitage of Ārṣṭiṣeṇa,
and having bathed at the hermitage of Piṅgā, one is liberated from all sins; likewise,
by touching the waters at Kulyā and reciting the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, one is purified.
Having fasted for three nights and remained pure, one obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice;
having touched the waters at Piṇḍāraka and remained there for one night,
a man who is pure obtains the merit of an Agniṣṭoma when the night has dawned.
Likewise, having gone to the Brahma-lake adorned by Dharmāraṇya,

one who is pure obtains the merit of the Puṇḍarīka sacrifice when the night has dawned. And likewise, having bathed on Mount Maināka and performed the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), [one attains the same].
Having conquered desire for a month, one indeed obtains the fruit of the Sarvamedha sacrifice. By approaching Kālodaka, Nandikuṇḍa, and likewise Uttaramānasa,
even from a distance of a hundred yojanas, a killer of an embryo is liberated.
By beholding the image of Nandīśvara, one is indeed liberated from all sins.
Having bathed at Svargamārga, a man goes to the heavenly world.
Renowned is the holy Himavat, the mountain that is the father-in-law of Śaṅkara.
The source of all jewels, frequented by *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, one becomes purified by merely seeing it or going there, even through fasting;
one should cast off the body there according to the prescribed rite of fasting unto death (*anāśaka*).
Knowing that life is unstable, the twice-born who has mastered the Vedanta,
having worshipped the deities there and likewise paid homage to the sages,
shall then, as a perfected one, go to heaven, to the eternal world of Brahmā.
He who, having conquered desire, anger, and greed, dwells at a sacred ford (tīrtha),
has attained nothing that could not have been gained by visiting such fords.
As for those fords that are inaccessible, difficult to reach, and treacherous—
13,026.061c These [sites] are to be understood by the mind as a summary of all sacred fords (tīrtha).
13,026.062a This is pure; this is auspicious; this leads to heaven; this is blissful.
13,026.062c This is the secret of the gods and the purifier of those who bathe therein.
One should give this to the twice-born, to the virtuous, or to one's own son;
one should whisper it into the ear of friends or of a devoted disciple.
Indeed, the great ascetic Aṅgiras gave this to Gautama.
Permitted by his gurus and by the wise Kāśyapa,
one who constantly recites this supreme purifying prayer of the great seers while remaining upright shall attain the stainless heaven.
"And whoever shall hear this secret doctrine approved by Aṅgiras will obtain birth in a noble family and remember his former life. Vaiśampāyana said:
Equal to Bṛhaspati in intelligence, equal to Brahmā in forbearance,
equal to Śakra in prowess, and possessing splendor like the sun—
he of great luster, the son of Gaṅgā, was slain by Arjuna in battle.
Accompanied by his brothers and others, Yudhiṣṭhira sat waiting upon the infallible one as he lay upon the hero’s bed, awaiting his time. Then,
O best of the Bharatas, great ṛṣis arrived, desiring to see that foremost of men.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bhṛgu, Pulastya, Pulaha, Kratu, Aṅgiras, Gautama, Agastya, Sumati, the self-possessed Svāyu,
Viśvāmitra, Sthūlaśiras, Saṃvarta, Pramati, and Dama.
Uśanas, Bṛhaspati, Vyāsa, Cyavana, Kāśyapa, Dhruva, Durvāsas, Jamadagni, Mārkaṇḍeya, Gālava,
Bharadvāja, Raibhya, Yavakrīta, and likewise Trita.
Sthūlākṣa, Śakalākṣa, Kaṇva, Medhātithi, Kṛśa, Nārada, Parvata, Sudhanvan, Ekata, Dvita,
Nitaṃbhu, Bhuvana, Dhaumya, Śatānanda, and Akṛtavraṇa.
Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, Kāmya, and other such high-souled great seers assembled there to see Bhīṣma. Yudhiṣṭhira offered worship to those great-souled ones who had arrived.

Together with his brothers, he performed [the rites] duly and in proper sequence. Those great seers, being honored and seated comfortably, engaged in very sweet conversations concerning Bhīṣma, which were captivating to all the senses.
Having heard those stories of the sages of purified souls, Bhīṣma,
filled with supreme satisfaction, considered himself as dwelling in heaven.
Then those great seers, having taken leave of Bhīṣma and the Pāṇḍavas...
All of them vanished while everyone was looking on. Even as those highly blessed rishis had disappeared, all the Pāṇḍavas praised them and bowed down to them again and again.
With serene minds, all those best of the Kurus approached the son of Gaṅgā,
just as those skilled in mantras approach the rising sun;
and the Pāṇḍavas, beholding the power of the asceticism of those sages, [were filled with wonder].
Illuminating all directions, they were filled with the utmost wonder;
reflecting upon the supreme good fortune of those sages,
the Pāṇḍavas, together with Bhīṣma, then engaged in conversations concerning them.
At the conclusion of the discourse, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and son of Dharma, touched Bhīṣma’s feet with his head and asked him a question concerning righteousness:
"Which regions, which provinces, which hermitages, and which mountains [are most excellent]?"
"Which rivers, O Grandfather, are to be known as preeminent in merit?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, [I shall relate] the conversation between one who subsists by the practice of *śiloñcha* and a perfected being (*siddha*). Having traversed this earth adorned with mountains many times,
that best of bipeds [arrived at] the home of an excellent householder.
Having arrived at the house of Śilavṛtti, he was honored by him according to the prescribed rite;
there the fortunate seer dwelt that night in great happiness. Then Śilavṛtti, being pure, performed whatever duties were to be done in the morning.

Having accomplished his purpose, he then approached that perfected guest. Having met, those two high-souled ones sat comfortably and engaged in auspicious conversation concerning the Vedas and the characteristics established by their supplementary branches.
At the conclusion of the discourse, Śilavṛtti, having carefully addressed Siddha, that wise man asked the very question which you are asking me. Śilavṛtti said:
Which countries, which provinces, which hermitages, and which mountains are preeminent in merit? Which rivers should be known as such? Let that be told.
The Siddha said:
Puṣkara, Prabhāsa, Naimiṣa, and the Himavat mountain;
the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, as well as Vedī, Mathurā, and Gayā;
the Sarasvatī and the Aruṇā, Kurukṣetra, and Pṛthūdaka.
Śilavṛtti said:
"O best of Brahmins, which of these shall I describe to you in terms of their greatness? From my very childhood, O lord of sages, there has been both devotion and curiosity."
"O best of Brahmins, [I have told you] the greatness of the Gaṅgā according to its true nature.
The Siddha said:
"Those regions, those districts, those hermitages, and those mountains..."
That goal which a living being cannot attain through austerity, celibacy, sacrifices, or renunciation, one attains by serving the Gaṅgā— the best of rivers— through whose midst the Bhāgīrathī flows.
For those embodied beings whose limbs have been touched by the waters of the Gaṅgā, their bodies are laid down such that they are never again ordained to fall from heaven. Indeed,
for those whose [bodies] are cast off, through that very casting off, heaven is ordained.
O Brahmin, those embodied beings for whom all rites are performed with the waters of the Gaṅgā,
or those who have bathed in the Gaṅgā according to the rules while reciting the *Aghamarṣaṇa* hymn— having left the earth, O twice-born one, those men remain immovable in heaven.
Those men who, having committed sinful deeds in their youth,
later devote themselves to the Gaṅgā, they too attain the supreme goal;
even those joined with great sins become pure after casting off the body.
Those who cast off their bodies at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā are liberated; for those of purified soul who have bathed in the pure waters of the Gaṅgā,
the spiritual reward that accrues cannot be attained even by hundreds of sacrifices.
As long as a human's bone remains in the waters of the Gaṅgā,
for that many thousands of years he is honored after reaching heaven;
having dispelled the intense darkness, he shines like the sun at its rising.
Having thus destroyed their evil, one shines when sprinkled with the waters of the Gaṅgā; just as nights are without the moon or trees are without flowers,
so too are countries and directions when deprived of the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā.
Just as all the castes and stages of life are [devoid] when deprived of their own dharma and knowledge, and just as sacrifices are [ineffective] without the Soma, so is the world without the Gaṅgā;
just as the sky is [empty] without the sun, the earth without its mountains, and the atmosphere without the wind.
Likewise, there is no doubt that countries and directions devoid of the Gaṅgā are likewise [devoid].
Whatever living beings exist within the three worlds,
they all attain supreme satisfaction when satiated with the auspicious waters of the Gaṅgā.
Other gods, sages, and departed spirits, together with the ancestors,
attain complete satisfaction throughout the three worlds in every respect. But he who drinks the water of the Gaṅgā, heated by the sun—
It excels barley-gruel obtained without the slaughter of cows; yet,
he who would perform a thousand moon-vows for the purification of the body and he who would drink the waters of the Gaṅgā— would these two be equal, or not?
Suppose a man were to stand on one foot for a thousand *yugas*,
and another were to stay for one month at the Ganges— would these two be equal, or would they not? Suppose a man were to hang with his head downward for ten thousand *yugas*.
He who remains as he pleases even for a moment on the Gaṅgā is superior;
dwelling in the waters of the Gaṅgā for a year is considered equal to that.
Just as cotton, O best of the twice-born, is consumed when cast into a fire, [so too are sins destroyed].
In the same way, for one who has plunged into the Gaṅgā, all evil is utterly consumed.
For all beings here whose minds are afflicted by suffering and who are searching for a refuge, there is no refuge equal to the Gaṅgā.
Even if one should utter "Gaṅgā, Gaṅgā" from across hundreds of *yojanas*,
one is liberated from all sins and goes to the world of Viṣṇu;
for those places where the Gaṅgā is not present, expiations are prescribed.
Wherever the Gaṅgā is found, how can there be atonement? Purity arises from the mere sight of her; through bathing, one attains the supreme goal.
Blessed is the Gaṅgā at Kanakhala, and the Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra.
Whether in a village or in a forest, the Narmadā is meritorious everywhere.
Just as serpents become devoid of venom at the sight of Tārkṣya,
so too one is liberated from all sins by the sight of the Gaṅgā.
Those who are without support and those who take refuge in unrighteousness—
for them, O Gaṅgā, you are here the support, the refuge, the peace, and the armor.
[You save] those lowest of men who are seized by many preeminent evils.
The Gaṅgā delivers those who have taken refuge in her from falling into hell after death.
Surely they are shared out among the sages and the gods, including Indra,
who constantly resort to the Gaṅgā frequented by the deities.
Even those who are devoid of discipline and conduct, inauspicious, and the lowest of men,
become auspicious, O Brahmin, if they have taken refuge in the Gaṅgā. Indeed, even those who have resorted to the Gaṅgā become auspicious.
Just as the nectar is for the gods and the *svadhā* offering is for the ancestors,
and just as the *sudhā* is for the *nāgas*, so too is the water of the Gaṅgā for human beings.
Just as children afflicted by hunger wait upon their mother, [so do they wait upon her].
Likewise, embodied beings here who desire their own welfare worship the Gaṅgā;
she is the sustainer of the worlds like a cow, or like the Veda itself,
and just as Soma is the inexhaustible essence among oblations, so is she in crossings.
Just as the realm of Svayambhū is said to be the most excellent of all abodes,

so too is the Gaṅgā declared here to be the best among rivers for those who have bathed. Just as the cow is traditionally held to be the source of sustenance for living beings, the earth is remembered as such for the gods and others.

Just as the gods subsist upon the nectars residing in the moon and the sun through sacrifices such as the *satra*, so do men here subsist upon the water of the Gaṅgā for the sake of all living beings.
Sprinkled with the sands rising from the banks of the Jāhnavī,
a man considers himself as radiant as if he were dwelling in heaven;
for he who bears upon his head the clay produced on the banks of the Jāhnavī.
He bears the form of the sun, utterly stainless due to the destruction of darkness. Furthermore,
when the wind, drenched by the waves of the Gaṅgā, touches a person,
it instantly wipes away even that man's sin.
In that way, touching him, it draws away all his evil.
For a man tormented by calamities and on the verge of perishing,
the joy born from the sight of the Gaṅgā sweeps away those misfortunes.
With the cries of swans, the calls of ruddy geese, and the sounds of other birds,
the Gaṅgā indeed generates a joy that bestows eternal happiness;
the Gaṅgā vies with the Gandharvas by means of her banks and with the mountains by means of her sandbanks.
Seeing the Gaṅgā, crowded with herds of cows and surrounded by very many various birds such as swans, even heaven was forgotten;
that delight which belongs to one dwelling in heaven and enjoying all desires is not equal to this.
Whatever supreme joy there was for men on the banks of the Gaṅgā,
even a man here who is seized by sins born of speech, mind,
and action becomes purified upon beholding the Gaṅgā; of this I have no doubt.

By beholding, touching, immersing oneself in, hearing of, longing for, seeing, touching, drinking, and bathing in the Gaṅgā, a man delivers seven generations of ancestors below him, seven generations above him,
and those who are even beyond them.
The Gaṅgā especially delivers both lineages of men;

for those dwelling on her banks, there is nothing superior for humans than [attainment] through austerity, ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), the recitation of scriptures (*pārāyaṇa*), and other such sacred sites beginning with Gaṅgādvāra.

One should remember the Gaṅgā every evening and morning; one should always recite her name during bathing. One should remember her during the libations for the ancestors (tarpaṇa), in ancestral rites (pitṛpūjā), and even at the time of death.
[This is because] through seeing, touching, drinking [her water], and likewise through reciting "Gaṅgā," [one attains purification].
He purifies men who lack merit by the hundreds and by the thousands.
He who desires that his birth, his life, and even his sacred learning be fruitful,
should approach the Gaṅgā and likewise satisfy the ancestors and the gods.
Neither by sons, nor by wealth, nor by ritual action, nor by its fruit,
can a person obtain that which one obtains upon reaching the Gaṅgā in its ultimate sense;
such people here are equal to those born blind, to the dead, and to the lame.

Who among men would not serve the Gaṅgā— she who possesses auspicious and meritorious waters, whom the great ṛṣis, knowers of the past, present, and future, have attended upon, and whom the gods together with Indra honor? (13,027.066c–067)
What man indeed would not take refuge in the Gaṅgā, resorted to by forest-dwellers, householders, ascetics, and students, and by those possessed of learning? And he who,
with his vital breaths departing, remains self-restrained and honored by the virtuous— [he too attains the highest goal].

He who mentally contemplates the Gaṅgā shall attain the supreme goal. For that man who worships the Gaṅgā here until the fall of his body, there is no fear from dangers, nor from sins, nor from kings.
Maheśvara bore upon his head that goddess of great merit as she fell from the sky; he still honors her in heaven. The three worlds have been adorned by these three stainless paths.
But the man who partakes of her water becomes one who has accomplished all his purposes;
just as the sun is the light in heaven and the moon is for the ancestors,
so is Gaṅgā here among rivers, like the Lord of Gods among men.
The sorrow experienced by one separated from mother, father, sons, wife, or wealth is not as great as the sorrow born of separation from the Gaṅgā.
Neither forests, nor desired objects, nor sons, nor the acquisition of riches can provide such [consolation].

Just as the vision of men becomes serene upon seeing the full moon, so too does their vision become serene upon beholding the Gaṅgā, the river that flows through the three paths. Just as the sight of men is cleared when they see the full moon, even so is their vision clarified by seeing the Gaṅgā.
One whose mind is fixed on her, who is devoted to her, who makes her his ultimate goal, and who follows the Gaṅgā with devotion— he shall become dear to her,
even by all beings, whether they dwell on earth, in the atmosphere, or in heaven, high or low.
The Gaṅgā must be entered constantly; this is the highest duty for the virtuous.
Because of the holiness of the Gaṅgā, her fame is celebrated throughout the three worlds. She has led even those who died a miserable death and those who were childless to heaven after their passing.
By means of these [waves]— driven by the wind, possessing a great roar, swift, and exceedingly high— this [river] led the sons of Sagara, known as ashes, to heaven.
Enkindled by the radiant waves of the Gaṅgā,
he shines like the thousand-rayed sun;
[he who possesses] the milk-yielding, ghee-providing, and most noble [speech].
Those wise ones who, having gone to the Ganges— abundant, swift, and difficult to fathom— have cast off their bodies,
have attained equality with the gods.
Gangā— the illustrious, vast, and universal-formed— is for the blind, the dull-witted, and those destitute of wealth;
she is [honored] by the gods including Indra, by sages, and by human beings.

Those who have resorted to the Gaṅgā— who is served by all desires, who is full of vigor, sweet as honey, of great merit, flowing through the three paths, and the protectress of the three worlds— have gone to heaven.
To whatever mortal shall dwell [there] or even behold it,
the gods bestow happiness;
for those who are purified by that, [it grants bliss] through touch and sight.
To him the gods grant the desired goal:
the skillful, vast, far-reaching, auspicious, true, sweet-tasting, and most gracious earth.
Those who have gone to the Gaṅgā— the night of all beings, the foundation of all creatures— have gone to the third heaven;
she whose fame eternally pervades the sky, the heavens, and the earth.
In ancient times, she stood pervading the cardinal and intermediate directions;
by partaking of the water of that best of rivers,
all mortals become fulfilled in their purpose.
This is the Gaṅgā, established as certain—
the womb-woman of Guha and Rukma;
in the morning she is the three-pathed one, carrying clarified butter, free from sin.
Descending from the sky as the Viśvatoyā, she has entered the Gaṅgā;
having performed her ablutions at the three paths at dawn,
she is spread forth as the protector of all who are free from sin.
Born previously from the imperishable Nārāyaṇa,
from the foot of Viṣṇu, from Śiṃśumāra, and from Dhruva;
from Soma, from Sūrya, and from Viṣṇu in the form of Meru.
Having come from the summit of Śiva to the Himālaya—
the daughter of the Mountain and the wife of Hara—
she was worthy of both heaven and earth according to her excellence.

O King, the auspicious Gaṅgā, destined to be the earth's glory, shines forth, bestowing merit upon the three worlds; she flows with streams of honey, her waters drawn up by the color of clarified butter.
Adorned with great waves and served by Brahmins,
that meritorious goddess is to be worshipped with one's whole being—
she who was [honored] by Śaṅkara, the benefactor of the three worlds.
Falling from heaven and held upon his head by Bhava,
Gaṅgā is the garland of the mountains of the triple heaven;
she is the daughter of Jahnu who washes the feet of Viṣṇu.
The most excellent womb, stainless and expansive; the vital strength, the refreshing food, the bearer of waters, the giver of glory;
all-encompassing, the form, the sacrifice, and the kindled flame.
The paths of the world are sprinkled by the Gaṅgā;
through her forbearance, she protects and sustains the earth,
and through her brilliance, she is like fire and the sun.
To the Brahmins, the Gaṅgā was always considered equal to Guha because of his constant devotion to the sacred word (brahmaṇyatā);
[she is] the ancient river praised by the ṛṣis, who flows from the foot of Viṣṇu.
Those who have sought refuge in the Jāhnavī, whose waters are exceedingly meritorious, with their whole being and even with their minds,
have gone to the abode of Brahmā.
She who, like a mother her sons, leads these worlds—

thirteen thousand, two hundred and seven point nine three— who is endowed with every quality through her entire being, by those desiring the beloved station of Brahmā here in this world; [she should be worshipped].

The Gaṅgā is always to be worshipped by those who have self-mastery— she who is cherished as the dawn, who blinks, whose waters flow everywhere, who is nourishment, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the wealthy one, and the supporter of the mountains.
One who possesses self-control and desires perfection should take refuge in Gaṅgā— the refuge of the learned, the immortal, and beloved by Brahmā—
after having propitiated all the gods together with their lords.
Bhagīratha, having approached her constantly through fierce austerity, brought Gaṅgā to the earth; by resorting to her,
a man shall know no fear here or in the hereafter.
13,027.096a Thus, having examined them with my intellect, I have described to you in every way but a single portion of your virtues;
13,027.096c I possess no power whatsoever here to speak further.
In the same way, it would be possible to measure all the virtues [of the Buddha],
as well as all the jewels of Mount Meru and the ocean, or even the number of pebbles or the volume of water.
It is not possible here to describe the qualities of the waters of the Gaṅgā, nor likewise to measure them;
therefore, [listen to] these [qualities] spoken with supreme faith.
One should cultivate all the virtues born of the Ganges through speech, mind, and action,
endowed with supreme devotion and full of faith.
Having spread his fame throughout these three worlds,
and having attained that great perfection so difficult to achieve, he will,
before long, reach the worlds created by the Gaṅgā.
You shall wander among your beloved ones as you desire;
may that high-minded lady always delight in her devotion to her own duty through the virtues of both you and me.
For the Gaṅgā is affectionate toward those who approach her;
she favors and unites the devoted one with happiness.
Bhīṣma said:

Thus, having instructed Śīlarati in many ways on the manifold virtues that take the form of the practice of the three paths— virtues which are of a truly authentic nature— the one of supreme intelligence [spoke].
The radiant Siddha entered the expanse of the sky. But Śilavṛtti, having been awakened at that time by the words of the Siddha,
worshipped the Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rites and attained a success that is very difficult to achieve.
"Therefore, O son of Kuntī, endowed with supreme devotion, go constantly to the Gaṅgā; you shall attain the highest perfection.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard this history spoken by Bhīṣma, which was joined with the hymn of praise to Gaṅgā,
Yudhiṣṭhira, together with his brothers, attained supreme joy.
Whoever should hear or recite this meritorious history, [shall likewise attain great merit].
One who recites this hymn dedicated to the Gaṅgā shall be liberated from all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"In wisdom, learning, conduct, and character, you are as you are."
Endowed with all virtues and possessed of [advanced] age,
you are distinguished above all born beings by your intellect, wisdom, and likewise by your asceticism;
of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, O best among the upholders of dharma, I ask you about dharma;
for there is no one else in the worlds besides you, O lord of men, who should be questioned—
whether he be a kṣatriya, a vaiśya, or a śūdra, O most excellent of kings.
"By what means may one attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa? You ought to explain that to me:
is it by great asceticism, or by ritual action, or by sacred learning? If one should desire the status of a Brāhmaṇa, tell me that, O Grandfather."
13,028.004 Bhīṣma said:
"O dear Yudhiṣṭhira, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain for the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas; for this is the supreme station among all living beings."
Wandering through many wombs and being born again and again, O dear one, in a certain turn of events one is born as a Brāhmaṇa. In this regard, they cite this ancient history.
And [he heard] the dialogue between Mataṅga and the she-ass, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
My dear son, a certain twice-born man had a powerful son who was his equal in appearance;
he was named Mataṅga and was endowed with all excellent qualities.
O Kaunteya, that performer of sacrifices, created by his father, O scorcher of foes,
departed on a swiftly moving chariot yoked with donkeys;
mounting that chariot drawn by asses, he approached with great haste.

O King, he repeatedly pierced the young donkey on the nose with a goad while it was pulling [the cart] near its mother. Seeing him with those severe wounds, the she-donkey, out of affection for her son, [cried out].
He said, "Do not grieve, my son; a Caṇḍāla stands over you.
There is no cruelty in a Brāhmaṇa; a Brāhmaṇa is said to be friendly. He is the teacher of all beings and their instructor; how could he strike you?"
"But this one, evil by nature, O child, shows no compassion;
he honors his own kind, for such is the way of existence following existence.
Having heard these harsh words of the female donkey, Mataṅga—
Quickly descending from his chariot, he addressed the female donkey:
"Speak, O auspicious donkey! By whom has my mother been defiled?
How do you know me to be a *caṇḍāla*? Tell me quickly, O donkey!"
"By what was I born as a Caṇḍāla, by which my status as a Brāhmaṇī perished?
O lady of great wisdom, tell me all this in truth and without omission.
The she-ass said:
"You were born of a Brāhmaṇī woman by a barber who was intoxicated;
you are a Caṇḍāla, and therefore your Brāhmaṇahood has perished.
Having been addressed thus, Mataṅga returned toward his home.
Seeing that he had arrived, his father then spoke these words:
"I appointed you to a weighty task for the successful completion of the sacrifice;
why have you returned? Is all not well with you?"
13,028.019 Mataṅga said:
Whether one be born without a womb or from a superior womb, he may indeed be well-off;
but from what source could there be well-being for one whose mother, O Father, is this [cow]?

"O Father, this non-human she-donkey informs me here that I was born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra; therefore, I shall perform great ascetic penance. Having spoken thus to his father, he set forth, firm in his resolve.

Then, having gone to the great forest, he performed intense austerity. Endowed with that ascetic power, Mataṅga then caused the gods to burn with heat, desiring to obtain through his virtuous conduct a state of supreme bliss.
To him who was thus engaged in asceticism, Indra, whose vehicle is green horses, said:
"O Mataṅga, why do you perform penance, having renounced human pleasures?
Lo, I shall grant you a boon; choose whatever you desire."
"And whatever else is to be attained by you, tell me all of it without delay.
Mataṅga said:
"Desiring the status of a Brāhmaṇa, I have undertaken this ascetic penance."
"May I attain that [state] here; this is the boon chosen by me.
Having heard these words, Purandara said to him:
"O Mataṅga, this state of being a Brahmin which you seek is difficult to obtain."
"O evil-minded one, seeking the status of a Brahmin—which is unattainable by those who have not disciplined their souls—you shall perish; therefore, desist from this without delay.
That which is the highest among all beings is austerity (*tapas*), which nothing can surpass."
"Seeking that which is supreme, you will soon perish. That which is remembered as the highest purity among gods, asuras, and mortals cannot be attained in any way by one born from a *caṇḍāla* womb."
13,029.001 Bhīṣma said: Thus addressed, Mataṅga, whose soul was refined and who was firm in his vows,
stood on one foot for a hundred years, O Acyuta.
Then Śakra, of great renown, spoke again to him:
"O dear Mataṅga, you shall not obtain the Brahminhood you seek, for it is difficult to attain;
you are seeking a supreme state that is exceedingly hard to reach."
"Do not commit this rash act, my son; this is not the path of dharma for you.
For it is impossible for you to attain the status of a Brahmin here, O evil-minded one;
by seeking that which cannot be attained, you will surely perish before long."
"O Mataṅga, though I have forbidden you once, you still desire to perform supreme asceticism; by all means, you shall cease to exist. If anyone born of an animal womb should attain human birth,"
He is born as a Pulkasa or a Caṇḍāla at some time, or as a libertine, or one of sinful birth— whosoever is observed here;
O Mataṅga, he wanders in that very state for a very long time.
Then, after a period ten times as long, he attains even the state of a Śūdra;
thereafter, he transmigrates many times within the womb of a Śūdra.
Then, after a period thirty times as long, he indeed attains the state of a Vaiśya.
For a long time he remains in the state of a Vaiśya, revolving right there;
then, after a period sixty times as long, he is born as one named a Rājanya;
and for a long time he remains in the state of a Rājanya, revolving right there.
Then, after sixty times that period of time, one attains the status of a *brahmabandhu*.
As a *brahmabandhu*, one revolves in that very state for a long time.
Thereafter, after twice that period of time, one attains the status of a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*.
Those who are engaged with all women and those who have been cast outside the Veda—
these should be known as *kāṇḍapṛṣṭhas*, excluded from all ritual acts.
A *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha* wanders about in that very state for a long time.
Then, after a period of three hundred [births], he attains the status of the twice-born;
having attained that, he continues to revolve in that very state for a long time.
Then, after a period of four hundred [births], he is born as one known as a *śrotriya*.
For a long time, he remains in that very state of being a Vedic scholar (śrotriya).
At that time, O son, anger and joy, desire and hatred,
as well as excessive pride and harsh speech, enter that lowest of the twice-born.
If he conquers those enemies, he then attains a happy state;
but if they indeed conquer him, he is cast down as if from the top of a palm tree.
O Mataṅga, having reflected upon this, I have urged you [to act].
"Choose some other desire, for the status of a Brahmin is very difficult to attain.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, Mataṅga, whose soul was disciplined and who was firm in his vows, [replied].
For a thousand years, he remained standing on one foot;
after that period of a thousand years had passed, Śakra came to see him.
Mataṅga said:
Then the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra spoke those very words again:
"Śakra, for this thousand years you have indeed remained a celibate student (*brahmacārī*), fully concentrated.
Śakra said:
"I have stood on one foot [for so long] thinking, 'How might I attain the status of a Brahmin?
Having been born from the womb of a Caṇḍāla, it cannot be attained by me in any way whatsoever.
Choose another desire; let this exertion of yours not be in vain."

Thus addressed, Mataṅga, overcome with intense grief, went to Gayā and remained there for a hundred years, standing on his big toe. Carrying out that most difficult yoga, he became emaciated, his body covered with a network of veins.
Reduced to skin and bone, that righteous-souled one fell, so we have heard;
Vāsava, the lord and giver of boons who delights in the welfare of all beings, ran toward him as he was falling and caught him.
Śakra said:
"O Mataṅga, your attainment of Brahminhood has been obstructed by impediments;
it is seen here to be contrary [to the rules]."
Brahminhood is even more difficult to attain.
By honoring it, one obtains happiness; by failing to honor it, one obtains suffering.
In the Brahmin, the security and well-being of all beings are established.
Through the Brāhmaṇas, the ancestors and likewise the deities are satisfied.
O Mataṅga, the Brāhmaṇa is said to be the highest among all beings; for he accomplishes whatever he intends and whatever he desires.
Wandering through many wombs and being born again and again, my dear, one finds the status of a Brahmin here in this world only at some point in the course of time. Therefore,
do not abandon that status of a Brahmin, which is difficult to attain even for those who have not disciplined their souls.
"Choose another boon, for this boon is indeed difficult for you to obtain.
Mataṅga said:
"Why do you pierce me, who am already afflicted by grief? You are killing me while I am as good as dead!"
But I grieve for him who, having attained the status of a brahmin, does not strive to maintain it.
O Śatakratu, if the status of a brahmin is so difficult to attain by the other three castes, then those men who,
having obtained that which is so hard to find, do not practice its duties, are truly to be pitied.
He who is more sinful than the sinners among them is indeed the lowest of all—

he who disregards his status as a Brahmin, having obtained that which is so difficult to attain. For the state of being a Brahmin is indeed hard to reach, and once attained, it is difficult to maintain.
"13,030.011c Having attained this which is so difficult to attain, men do not practice it.
13,030.012a For I, O Śakra, delight in solitude alone, free from dualities and without possessions;
13,030.012c established in non-violence, self-restraint, and charity, how am I not worthy of the status of a Brahmin?"
"O Purandara, it must surely be destiny that I, though a knower of dharma, have fallen into this state due to the fault of my mother. Indeed,
destiny cannot be overcome by human effort."
"O Lord, since I have exerted such effort yet do not attain freedom from rebirth,
O Knower of Dharma, this being the case, you ought to grant me a boon,
if I am worthy of your favor or if I have performed any merit whatsoever."
Bhīṣma said:
"Choose [a boon]," the slayer of Bala and Vṛtra then said to him;
thus urged by Mahendra, Mataṅga spoke this.
"O God, O Vāsava, I choose this boon: may it be granted to me! May I be able to travel wherever I desire, assume any form at will, and move through the air as a bird;
and may I receive honor without causing conflict with the Brahmins or the Kṣatriyas."
"O Purandara, you ought to act so that my fame may become inexhaustible;
O Lord, I propitiate you with my head bowed low.
Indra said:
"O Mataṅga, go quickly; it shall be exactly so.
And all women in the world will worship you for the sake of rites for prosperity.
Thus, O one whose wealth is asceticism, your fame shall be imperishable."
"Known as Chandodeva, you shall be honored by women;
and your fame, my child, shall spread throughout the three worlds.
Bhīṣma said:
Having thus granted him the boon, Vāsava vanished;
and Mataṅga, having cast off his life-breaths, attained that supreme station. Such, O Bhārata, is this highest state known as Brāhmaṇya.
And that state, O bull of the Bharatas, is indeed difficult for mortals to attain in this world, just as were the words of Mahendra;
the high-souled Indra declared that what is called Brahminhood is difficult to attain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of speakers, O perpetuator of the Kuru lineage, I have heard this great narrative; you speak of brahminhood, which is so difficult to attain."
