"It is heard that in ancient times Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa; you speak of this, O best of beings, as something difficult to attain. Furthermore, I have heard that the royal sage Vītahavya reached the state of a Brāhmaṇa."
"O Gāṅgeya, O Lord, I wish first to hear that very thing:
how, O Great King, Viśvāmitra attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa. You have related everything in detail, O Grandfather."
"O King, best among the wise, all of that was heard by me;
for our supreme authority, O delighter of the Kurus, is you.
And the royal sage Vītahavya, O Grandfather, is indeed renowned."
"O King, that one of great fame attained the status of a Brahmin.
By what action, O best of kings, did he attain this Brahminhood—was it by a boon or by asceticism? You ought to explain that to me."
13,031.005 Bhīṣma said: Listen, O King, how the highly illustrious king Vītahavya,
though being a Kṣatriya, attained once again the status of a Brāhmaṇa, which is honored by the world.
O dear one, while the high-souled Manu was ruling according to the law of subjects,
there was born to him a righteous son renowned as Śaryāti. O King, in his lineage two kings were born.
O best among victors, Hehaya and Tālajaṅgha were born among the Vatsas.
O Bhārata, from the ten wives of Hehaya,
there arose a famous hundred of heroes who never retreated in battle.

O King, there was also a king among the Kāśis, the grandfather of Divodāsa, who was equal in form and power to those learned men skilled in battle; he had exerted himself in every respect in both the science of archery and the Vedas.
13,031.010c There was one renowned as Haryaśva, the best among victors.
13,031.011a O bull among men, having been approached by the heirs of Vītahavya,
he was struck down in battle between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā.
O King, having been utterly defeated in battle along the banks of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā,
those great car-warriors of the Haihayas slew that best of men and returned,
free from fear, to the beautiful city of the Vatsas.
The heir of Haryaśva was consecrated as the King of Kāśī;
he was Sudeva, who resembled a god, like another Dharma incarnate.
While that righteous son of Kāśi was thus protecting the earth, he remained steadfast in his duty.
Having arrived with all those Vītahavyas, he was completely defeated in battle;
but having also conquered him in the fray, they returned the way they had come. Then Divodāsa, the son of Sudeva, was consecrated as the lord of Kāśī.
But Divodāsa, of great splendor, having recognized the prowess of those high-souled ones,
established Vārāṇasī by the command of Śakra;
it was crowded with Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas, and filled with Vaiśyas and Śūdras.

O best of kings, on the northern bank of the Gaṅgā, at the edge of the embankment, and on the southern bank of the Gomatī, [he saw] a city filled with many heaps of goods and prosperous marketplaces and shops,
like Amarāvatī belonging to Śakra.
O Bhārata, while that tiger among kings, the lord of the earth, was dwelling there, the Haihayas arrived once more and surrounded him. That king of great strength went out and gave battle to them.
The immensely radiant Divodāsa fought a terrible battle equal to that between the gods and the asuras. O great king, having fought for ten times ten days in that conflict,
he, whose mounts were mostly slain, then fell into a state of dejection.
Then, O King, with his warriors slain and his treasury exhausted,
King Divodāsa abandoned the city and became intent on flight.
Having reached the hermitage of the wise Bharadvāja, he approached him.
The king, the subduer of enemies, went for refuge with palms joined;
having sought his protection, he prostrated himself with his head at his feet.
He spoke to that blessed one, the son of Bṛhaspati who was worthy of honor.
The King said:
"O Blessed One, my lineage has been destroyed by the Vaitahavyas in battle;
I alone, desolate, have come to you for refuge."
To him, Bharadvāja— the eldest son of Bṛhaspati, a family priest endowed with virtuous character— spoke to King Divodāsa:
"O sinless one, tell me everything regarding the purpose of your arrival."

"I shall do whatever is pleasing to you; I have no hesitation in this matter. O Blessed One, out of affection for your disciple, you ought to protect me, for my lineage has been utterly destroyed by those evildoers."
To him spoke the illustrious and powerful Bharadvāja, the family priest of that wise King Divodāsa, O Indra among kings:
"Do not fear, do not fear! O son of Sudeva, let your fear depart."
"O lord of the people, today I shall perform a sacrifice for the sake of a son for you,
so that you may overcome thousands of the Vaitahavyas. Thereupon, the ṛṣi performed that sacrifice intended to grant him a son.
Then a son was born to him, renowned as Pratardana. As soon as he was born, O Bhārata, he grew for thirteen years in a single day and mastered the entire Veda as well as the science of archery.
Possessed by the wise Bharadvāja through yoga,
he withdrew his worldly energy and entered that place.
Thereupon, clad in armor, armed with a bow and arrows, he appeared like a blazing fire.
Being praised by the celestial seers and lauded by the bards, he shone like the risen sun;
that charioteer, with his sword girded, [shone forth].
Shaking his bow like a rain-cloud pouring forth water, he advanced.
Seeing him, the son of Sudeva experienced supreme joy; that king considered in his mind the descendants of Vitahavya as already consumed by fire.
Then, having installed Pratardana in the position of heir apparent,
the king rejoiced, considering himself to have fulfilled his duty.
Thereafter, that lord of the earth set out for the destruction of the Vaitahavyas.
He dispatched his son Pratardana, the subduer of enemies. Then that valiant conqueror of hostile cities, having quickly crossed the Gaṅgā with his chariot, set out for the city of the Vītahavyas.
Hearing the loud roar of the chariots,
the sons of Vitahavya set out with chariots as large as cities, capable of crushing the chariots of enemies.
Having emerged, those tigers among men, clad in armor and skilled in diverse modes of combat, advanced.
Raising their weapons, they struck Pratardana with showers of arrows,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, and with various kinds of missiles and multitudes of chariots;
they rained upon the king as clouds rain upon the Himavat.
Having warded off their weapons with his own missiles, King Pratardana,
endowed with great splendor, struck them down with arrows equal to the fire of the thunderbolt.
O King, their heads were severed by the hundreds of thousands of broad-headed shafts (bhalla).

With their limbs drenched in blood, they fell like *kiṃśuka* trees that had been cut down. When all those sons had been slain, Vītahavya then fled, abandoning his city and even the hermitage of Bhṛgu.
King Vitahavya went to Bhṛgu for refuge; and O King, Bhṛgu likewise granted that king freedom from fear. Then his disciple offered him a seat.
Bhṛgu then assigned another seat for him in the midst of the disciples.
Immediately thereafter, Pratardana arrived there with great speed;
having reached the hermitage, the son of Divodāsa spoke.
"O sirs, who among the disciples of the high-souled Bhṛgu are present here in this hermitage?
I wish to see the sage; point me out to him.
Having recognized him, Bhṛgu then emerged from the hermitage.
Then he worshipped him with the highest rites.
And he said to that king of kings, "O Indra among monarchs, what is your purpose? And the king told him the reason for his arrival.
The Blessed Lord Bhṛgu himself greeted him with honor;
and having been thus honored, the Blessed One said to him, "What is your business?
Thereupon, King Pratardana, the son of Divodāsa, spoke to him.

"O Brahmin, let this King Vitahavya be released from here. For by his sons, O Brahmin, my entire lineage has been destroyed and the kingdom of the Kāśīs, with its accumulation of jewels, has been laid waste."

"O Brahmin, the hundred sons of this man, who was arrogant because of his prowess, have been slain by me; now, by killing him, I shall be free from my debt to my father. To him, Bhṛgu, the best among the upholders of dharma, spoke, filled with compassion:
"There is no Kṣatriya here at all; indeed, all these are twice-born.
Having heard these truthful words of Bhṛgu, Pratardana slowly touched his feet and, smiling, spoke these words:
"Even so, Blessed One, I am undoubtedly one who has accomplished his task, since by my valor this king has been made to abandon his own caste;
for the word of the seer is true: 'All shall become brahmins.'"
"O Brahmin, grant me leave; meditate upon me with auspicious intent. For this king has been made to renounce his birth by me, O descendant of Bhṛgu.
Then, permitted by him, King Pratardana departed.
"O Great King, having cast off [the state] as he had come, like a snake casting off its venom,
Vītahavya attained the status of a Brahmarṣi and the rank of a teacher of the Veda by the mere word of Bhṛgu, O Great King."
His son was Gṛtsamada, who in appearance was like another Indra;
he was indeed once seized by the Daityas with the words, "You are Śakra!
O lord of the people, a preeminent Vedic revelation concerning him exists here in the Ṛgveda.
O Brahmin, where Gṛtsamada is honored by the Brahmins,
that illustrious Gṛtsamada became a celibate student and a brahmin-sage. The son of Gṛtsamada was also a twice-born named Sucetas.
Varcas was the son of Sutejas, and Vihavya was his son. The son of Vihavya was Vitatya, and Satya was his son. Santa was the son of Satya.
Śravas was his son, a seer; and from Śravas, Tamas was born. From Tamas, O best of the twice-born, was born Prakāśa as his son;
and from Prakāśa was born Vāgindra, the foremost among victors.
His son was Pramati, who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas;
from him, through Ghṛtācī, a son named Ruru was born.
And from Ruru, through Pramadvarā, a son was born.

O king of kings, O bull among Kṣatriyas, the royal sage Vītahavya, who was a Kṣatriya, thus attained the status of a Brahmin through the grace of Bhṛgu; he was the Brahmin-seer named Śunaka, whose son was Śaunaka.
"In this very manner, O Great King, the lineage of Gārtsamada has been recounted by me to you in detail; what else do you wish to ask? Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who are to be honored and who are to be saluted by human beings, O bull of the Bharatas?
Tell me that in detail; for I am not yet satiated with what is being told. Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between both Nārada and Vāsudeva.
Seeing Nārada with palms joined in reverence, honoring the foremost of the twice-born—

13,032.003c Keśava asked: "O Blessed One, to whom do you pay homage? 13,032.004a Toward whom is your supreme respect, that you pay them homage? If it may be heard, I wish to know; tell me this, O best of those who know dharma."
13,032.005 Nārada said:
Listen, O Govinda, O crusher of enemies, to those whom I worship;
for what other man in this world besides you is worthy to hear this?
Varuṇa, Vāyu, Āditya, Parjanya, Jātavedas,
Sthāṇu, Skanda, as well as Lakṣmī, Viṣṇu, and Brahmā;
Vācaspati, Candramas, the Waters, the Earth, and Sarasvatī.
O Lord,

O tiger among the Vṛṣṇis, I always pay homage to those who constantly offer salutations to the ascetics who possess the wealth of austerity, who are knowers of the Vedas, ever devoted to the Vedas, and most worthy of honor; to them, I too offer my salutations.
O Lord, I bow down to those who perform their duties for the gods without seeking reward, who are free from boastfulness, contented, and endowed with forgiveness;
and to those who give what is desired in the proper manner, being patient, self-controlled, and masters of their senses.
O Yādava, I bow down to those who subsist on grain, wealth, land, and cattle;
O Yādava, I bow down to those who abide in austerity within the forest, subsisting on roots and fruits, free from accumulation, and devoted to their sacred rites.
O Yādava, I bow down to those who are intent on supporting their dependents, who are always fond of guests, and who eat only what remains after the gods; and to those who,
having mastered the Veda, are invincible, eloquent, and exponents of Brahman.
I constantly honor those who are engaged in officiating at sacrifices and teaching;
I always honor those whose hearts are ever gracious toward all living beings, and those who are devoted to the private recitation of the Vedas until their backs are heated by the sun.
O Yādava, I bow down to those who strive in the grace of their guru and in the study of the Vedas, who are firm in their vows, desirous of serving, and free from malice;
and to those sages of excellent conduct who are devoted to Brahman and true to their promises.
O Yādava, I bow to those who carry the offerings to the gods and the ancestors;
O Yādava, I bow to those who are devoted to the practice of begging for alms, who are emaciated, who dwell in the houses of their gurus, and who are without pleasure or wealth.

O Keśava, I bow to those men who are free from possessiveness, free from rivalry, devoid of shame, and without worldly purpose; to those who are devoted to non-violence, who are committed to the vow of truth, and who are self-controlled and intent on tranquility.
O Yādava, I bow to those householders who are devoted to the worship of the deities and guests, who always live like pigeons,
and who do not let time pass in vain as they strive for the three goals of life without greed.
And those who are endowed with distinguished conduct, O Nārāyaṇa— to them I bow.
Those for whom the three aims of life (trivarga) prevail in their actions and are never diminished, and who are engaged in the practice of the conduct of the virtuous— I always pay homage to them.
O Keśava, I bow to those brāhmaṇas in the three worlds who are devoted to the three goals of life, who are free from greed, and whose conduct is virtuous—
those who always subsist on water, subsist on air, and subsist on nectar.

O Mādhava, I bow down to those twice-born ones who are engaged in various vows— those not born from a womb, those born from fire, those likewise born from Brahman, and those whose source is the self of all beings. I pay homage to those brahmins.
I constantly pay homage to these sages who create the worlds, O Kṛṣṇa—
the eldest in the world, established in knowledge, destroyers of darkness, and suns of the world.
Therefore, you too, O scion of the Vṛṣṇis, should always honor the twice-born.
"O sinless Yudhiṣṭhira, those who are worthy of worship, when they are indeed honored, will grant you happiness. O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, you are learned in all the scriptures."
"O best of the Bharatas, I wish to hear from you about dharma:
O foremost of the Bharatas, what is the fruit in truth for one who protects the fourfold assembly of beings that have come to him for refuge?"
Bhīṣma said:
O great king, son of Dharma, you of great fame, listen to this ancient history concerning the purpose of seeking refuge, which yields great fruit.
Being pursued by a hawk, a dove of lovely appearance sought refuge with the highly fortunate king Vṛṣadarbha. Seeing that the bird had come to his lap out of fear, he, whose soul was pure, [acted].
"Take heart, take heart," he said; "there is no fear for you, O bird.
From what does this great fear of yours arise? Where is it from, or what have you done, that you have arrived here unconscious and with a bewildered mind?"
O you who wear a crown of fresh blue lotuses, O one of beautiful complexion, O handsome one!
O you with eyes like pomegranate flowers and *aśoka* blossoms, do not fear; there is no cause for fear for you. No one shall dare to harm you once you have come into my presence.
To take possession of it mentally, the kingdom of Kāśī, placed before you by its protector, is yours today, as is your very life for your sake—
thus [spoke] Śyena.
"O pigeon, be confident; I shall release you. You have no cause for fear.
O King, this food has been ordained for me; it is not right for you to protect it. It has come to me by chance and has been prepared with great effort."

"His flesh and blood, as well as his marrow and fat, are beneficial to me; for he brings me complete satisfaction. Do not stand before me! A most violent thirst afflicts me, and hunger seems to consume me."
"Release him, O King, for I am not able to appease my hunger. For he was pursued by me and wounded by the claws of my wings;
O King, you ought not to protect one whose inhalations and exhalations are so faint."
"O King, if you are the master in protecting men within your own domain,
then you are not the master over me, a sky-dweller afflicted by thirst. [This applies] whether it concerns enemies, servants, or the conduct of one's own kin."

Do not exert your prowess against the objects of the senses and the senses themselves within the void, O Bhīṣma; for by exerting your power over those who truly destroy your wings, you will be overcome.
"If you are a seeker of dharma here, you ought to see me as well.
Having heard those words of the hawk, the royal seer was filled with wonder;
honoring his speech and desiring its fulfillment, he replied.
Whether it be a bull, a boar, a deer, or even a buffalo—
let one be prepared today for your sake to appease your hunger.
"I shall not abandon one who has come for refuge"— this is the vow I have undertaken.
"Behold, O twice-born one, this hawk does not release my limbs;
it is not a boar, nor a bull, nor various other birds."
"O Great King, what use have I for that food? For the eternal food ordained for me by the gods themselves is this:
hawks devour pigeons; such is the eternal law."
O sinless King Uśīnara, if you have such affection for the dove,
then give me today your own flesh, weighed against it on a scale.
"What a great favor you have bestowed upon me today, that you have spoken thus to me here!
Having said, "Certainly, I shall do so," that best of kings cut off pieces of his flesh again and again and weighed them on a scale.
Then, in his inner apartments, the women adorned with jewels,
hearing [the news], emerged in a state of utter distress, crying out "Alas! Alas!"—
and by the sound of their weeping, as well as that of the ministers and the servants, [the palace was filled].
A truly great roar arose, sounding as deep as the thundering of clouds;
the entire bright sky was obstructed on all sides by clouds,
and the earth trembled because of his truthful deed.
That king, cutting away flesh from his sides, from his arms, and from his thighs, gradually filled the scale;
yet even so, it did not equal that pigeon.
When the king had become mere bone, fleshless and streaming with blood,
he then ascended the scale, relinquishing his own wasting flesh.
Thereupon, the three worlds, together with Indra, approached that lord of men.
There, celestial drums and divine kettledrums were sounded by those moving through the sky;
and King Vṛṣadarbha was sprinkled with nectar and showered again and again with divine, most delightful garlands.
Surrounded on all sides by hosts of gods and gandharvas and by apsarases,
he was attended by dance and song like the Lord Grandfather himself;
[he entered] that palace crowded with golden mansions and adorned with jeweled and golden archways.
That royal seer, presiding over a celestial palace supported by pillars of lapis lazuli,
went to the eternal heaven by virtue of that deed.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, act in this same manner toward all who come to you for refuge.

A protector of devotees, the affectionate, and those who have sought refuge, compassionate toward all beings, prospers in happiness in the next world. For that king who is of virtuous conduct indeed follows the path of the righteous.
What could not have been attained by him through this deed performed under his own pretext?
That royal sage, pure in soul, steadfast, and of true prowess,
was renowned throughout the three worlds for his actions as the lord of the Kāśīs.
O best of the Bharatas, whoever else should likewise provide protection to one who has come for refuge would also go to that very same destination.
For by proclaiming this account of the royal seer Vṛṣadarbha, [one attains such merit].
He who listens to this constantly shall indeed become a purified soul in this world;
for these [verses] always bestow happiness both in this world and in the next. Indeed, when these are held in honor, they will grant you happiness.
Those who are always hospitable to all guests, who are ever devoted to cows and Brahmins,
and who are constantly intent upon truth— they cross over all difficulties. Likewise, those who are always dedicated to tranquility and who are free from malice [cross over all difficulties].
Those who constantly engage in the private recitation of the Vedas cross over all difficulties;
those who bow to all the gods, yet take refuge in the One God,
and those who are full of faith and self-controlled— they too cross over all difficulties.
Likewise, having paid homage to the most eminent Brahmins who are firm in their vows—
those who are devoted to giving cross over all difficulties—
and those who are constant ascetics, lifelong celibates from their youth.
Those whose souls are purified by austerity cross over all difficulties;
those who are devoted to the worship of the gods, guests, servants, and ancestors,
and who eat only the food left over [from their dependents], they too cross over all difficulties.
Those who, being self-restrained, duly establish the sacred fires and maintain them according to the rules,
and who likewise offer the oblation of Soma, overcome all difficulties.
Those who always behave properly toward their mother, father, and teachers, [attain the highest state].
"O tiger among the Vṛṣṇis," having spoken thus, he fell silent.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you too should properly honor the ancestors, the gods, the twice-born, and guests, by which you shall attain your desired goal.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, among all the duties of a king, which would be the most important?
By performing what action does a monarch enjoy both worlds?"
Bhīṣma said:
"O Bhārata, for a consecrated king who desires ultimate happiness, this— namely, the service of the Brāhmaṇas— is his most important duty."

O bull of the Bharatas, know this: a king who desires his own happiness must here protect the brahmins and honor them. He should always pay homage to those brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and advanced in age.
He should honor the citizens and the country folk, as well as the highly learned Brahmins, with conciliatory words, the granting of enjoyments, and salutations;
he should recognize that this is indeed the king’s most essential duty at all times.

One should protect these [brahmins] just as one protects oneself or one's own sons; and those among them who are most worthy of honor, one should honor with firm devotion. When they are at peace, that entire kingdom shines resplendently.
They are to be honored, they are to be saluted, and they are to be protected like fathers;
upon them alone depends the course of the world, as all beings depend upon Vāsava.
Even by means of sorcery and stratagems, they might consume [their enemies] with their splendor.
When enraged, these fierce ones of true prowess would leave nothing remaining;
I see no end to them, nor even the directions that remain unobstructed when they look upon us in anger, like crests of fire in a forest conflagration.
Among them, some possess qualities that are truly heroic;
others are like wells hidden by grass, while still others are as pure as the sky.
Some act with impetuosity, while others are as soft as cotton.

Among them, some are virtuous and not to be censured, while others are wicked; some are exceedingly deceitful, and likewise others are great ascetics. Some are engaged in agriculture and cattle-rearing, while others are devoted to the life of mendicancy.
There were others who were thieves, others who were liars, and likewise others who were actors and dancers; they were seen engaged in all kinds of occupations, both peaceful and otherwise,
as well as Brahmins, O bull of the Bharatas, who were endowed with various modes of conduct.
One should constantly recite [the names] of those virtuous ones who are engaged in various tasks, who subsist by many occupations, and who possess knowledge of the Dharma—
[namely] the ancestors, the gods, humans, serpents, and *rakṣas*es.

O lord of men, these highly fortunate brahmins who serve as domestic priests— these twice-born ones cannot be conquered by the gods, nor by the ancestors, nor by the gandharvas, nor by the rākṣasas, nor by the asuras, nor by the piśācas.
They could make a non-god into a god, and even a god into a non-god;
whoever they wished to be king would become king, and whoever they hated would be defeated.
And those mindless ones who would utter slander against the Brahmins—
"I tell you the truth, O King:
those twice-born ones who are skilled in censure and praise, and who are intent on fame and infamy, will undoubtedly perish; for they are constantly provoked to anger by your enemies, O King."
The man whom the Brahmins praise prospers;
he who is reviled by the Brahmins is surely defeated in an instant. The Śakas, Yavanas, and Kambojas—these various classes were once Kṣatriyas.
Due to their failure to see Brāhmaṇas, they fell into the state of being Śūdras.
The Dramiḷas, the Kaliṅgas, the Pulindas, the Uśīnaras,
the Kaulas, the Sarpas, and the Māhiṣakas— these were all originally Kṣatriya lineages.
"By failing to see the Brahmins, they have fallen into the state of outcasts (vṛṣalatva). O best among victors, defeat at their hands is better than victory over them;
for even one who might destroy this entire world is not equal to a Brahmin."
"The supreme ṛṣis have said that the killing of a Brahmin is a great evil.
One must never listen to the slander of the twice-born;
one should either remain silent with head bowed down, or rise and depart."
Neither one born nor one yet to be born here on earth will ever venture to live happily by opposing the Brāhmaṇas. Wind cannot be grasped with the fist, nor can the moon be touched with the hand.
"The earth is difficult to support with the head; the Brahmins on earth are difficult to conquer.
Bhīṣma said:
"One should always and most earnestly honor the Brahmins alone."
For these, with Soma as their king, are the lords of pleasure and pain;
they are always to be honored, saluted, and protected by kings with enjoyments, ornaments, and whatever else they may desire, just like one's own ancestors.

13,034.002e Therefore, let there indeed be peace for the kingdom, as for all beings from Vāsava; 13,034.003a let there arise in the kingdom a pure Brāhmaṇa endowed with spiritual luster (brahmavarcas),
and a Kṣatriya who is a great chariot-warrior (mahāratha) and a scorcher of his enemies.
"Thus Nārada has always told me for the welfare of all beings:
'O King, one should maintain in one's home a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with noble birth, knows the Dharma, and is firm in his vows; indeed, there is nothing superior to him.'"
The deities accept the sacrificial oblation given to the Brahmins;
they are the ancestors of all beings, and there is nothing superior to them. The sun, the moon, the wind, the earth, the waters, the sky, and the directions—
All [the ancestors], having entered the Brāhmaṇa, always enjoy his food.
The ancestors do not eat the food of that man whose Brāhmaṇas do not eat;
nor do the gods eat the food of that sinner who hates the Brāhmaṇas.
When the Brahmins are satisfied, the ancestors are always pleased;
likewise, O King, are the deities—there is no need for hesitation in this matter.
In the same way, those for whom that oblation is intended are also gratified.

They do not perish after death; they go to the supreme goal. With whatever very oblation a man satisfies the Brāhmaṇas, by that very same [oblation] the ancestors and likewise the deities are gratified.
That being arises from the Brāhmaṇa alone, from whom all creatures originate;
from whom this world proceeds after death, and where it goes. Through the Vedas, he knows the path to heaven as well as that to hell.
The brahmin, the best among bipeds, knows both the past and the future;
O best of the Bharatas, through his wisdom, the brahmin knows his own dharma.
And those who follow him do not meet with defeat.
Those who receive the words obtained from the mouth of a Brāhmaṇa do not perish after death, nor do they suffer defeat;
for those self-realized and high-souled ones do not go to ruin.
The splendor and the strength of Kṣatriyas,
though they blaze with brilliance and power, are extinguished only by Brāhmaṇas.
The Bhṛgus conquered the Tālajaṅghas, and the Aṅgirasas conquered the Nīpas.
O bull of the Bharatas,
those whose banners were black antelope skins conquered the Vaitahavyas and the Ailas, as well as the Citrāyudhas; having cast away their water-pots, they then set out to reach the further shore.
Whatever is spoken in the world, whatever is heard, or even whatever is seen—
all that resides within the Brahmins alone, like fire hidden within wood. In this regard,
they also cite this ancient history.
13,034.019c The dialogue between Vāsudeva and the Earth, O bull among the Bharatas.
13,034.020 Vāsudeva said: 13,034.020a O auspicious one, I ask you, the mother of all beings, about a doubt.
"By what action indeed does a householder man cast off his sin?
The Earth said:
"One should serve the Brāhmaṇas alone, for this is the supreme means of purification."

For one who serves the Brāhmaṇas, all impurity (*rajas*) perishes. From this, prosperity arises; from this, fame arises; and from this, wisdom is born—for others, for those beyond them, and even for those further beyond.
The man whom the Brahmins praise prospers; but he who is reviled by the Brahmins soon meets with ruin,
just as a clod of raw clay thrown into the great ocean perishes.
In the same way, evil conduct leads to one's downfall.
Behold the mark placed upon the moon, the salt water in the ocean,
and likewise Mahendra marked with a thousand female organs.
By their very power,
O Mādhava, behold how he became the thousand-eyed Śatakratu;
for one who desires prosperity, fame, and the worlds, O Madhusūdana, [this is the means].
"A man who is pure and self-possessed may abide with the consent of the Brāhmaṇas.
Having heard these words from the Earth, Madhusūdana said, "Excellent! Excellent! and then honored the Earth in return.
O Pārtha, having heard this parable, being self-restrained, [approach] the bulls among Brahmins— being self-restrained, O bull of the Bharatas—
the Brahmins who are perfected in sacred learning.
"You should worship him constantly; from that, you will attain the highest good.
Bhīṣma said:
"By his very birth, one becomes a highly blessed person known as a Brāhmaṇa."
Worthy of homage by all beings, the guest who eats first from what is set forth—
O dear one, all these Brāhmaṇas, our well-wishers with faces brightened by goodwill,
will slay us all when their anger is aroused.
When honored,
O dear one, the Brahmins— whose wrath has been aroused— meditate upon all our enemies with auspicious words; but when unhonored, they strike them down with words joined with cruelty.
In this regard, those who know the past recite these verses sung by Brahmā:
"Having created the twice-born, the Creator indeed established them as they were before;
nothing further is to be done by you here beyond what is prescribed according to the rules."

"Guarded, protect the Brahman; by that, prosperity will be beautiful for you. As you perform your own duty, the glory of the Brahman will be yours, and you shall become the standard for all beings and attain a position of leadership."
A wise Brāhmaṇa must not perform the work of a Śūdra;
for by performing the work of a Śūdra, his dharma is obstructed.
Prosperity, intelligence, splendor, and powerful majesty [are lost].

By means of Vedic study alone, you shall attain stainless greatness; and by offering oblations into the *āhavanīya* fire, you will be established in great fortune— becoming the first to be fed among all progeny, and endowed with the splendor of Brahman.
Endowed with supreme faith acquired through non-malice,
and devoted to self-restraint and sacred study, you shall obtain all desires—
whatever exists in the world of men and whatever exists among the gods.

All that is to be accomplished through austerity, wisdom, and discipline; likewise, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others attain here and in the hereafter the honor, joy, and purification found in the stage of life of a Kṣatriya by honoring you.
"Unprotected by you, they fall into ruin when they oppose [the world].
Since the worlds are sustained by your splendor, protect the three realms.
Thus, O sinless one, these songs of Brahmā have been recounted to you by me.
This was indeed spoken by that wise one for the sake of compassion toward the brahmins:
"I consider the power of those ascetic kings to be even greater;
they are difficult to approach, fierce, impetuous, and swift in action."
Among them, some possess the nature of lions, and others likewise the nature of tigers; some possess the nature of boars or deer, and others the nature of elephants.
Some are as soft as cotton, while others are as fierce as crocodiles.
Some are slayers of those who explain the scriptures, while others are destroyers of the eyes;
some resemble venomous serpents, and others are dull-witted.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, the conducts of Brāhmaṇas here in this world are of various kinds.
The Mekalas, Dramiḍas, Kāśas, Pauṇḍras, and likewise the Kollagiras;
the Śauṇḍikas, Daradas, Darvas, Cauras, Śabaras, Barbaras,
Kirātas, and Yavanas— these were all various lineages of Kṣatriyas.
By failing to see Brahmins, they fell into the state of being outcasts (vṛṣalatva);
by their contempt for Brahmins, the Asuras became dwellers in the waters;
and by the grace of Brahmins, the gods became inhabitants of heaven.
The sky cannot be touched, and the Himalayan mountain is immovable;
the Gaṅgā cannot be dammed by a bridge, and Brahmins are invincible on earth. The earth cannot be ruled by one who stands in opposition to Brahmins.
For the high-souled Brahmins are indeed the deities even of the gods; therefore,
if you wish to enjoy this earth girt by the oceans, constantly honor them with gifts and service.
"O sinless one, for the spiritual power (*tejas*) of Brahmins is indeed extinguished by the acceptance of gifts. O sinless one, you must also protect those who do not desire to accept gifts.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history, the dialogue between Śakra and Śambara; listen to that, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
For Śakra, having assumed an unknown form, became one with matted hair, reddened by dust.
Assuming a deformed appearance, he questioned Śambara:
"By what conduct, O Śambara, do you preside over those of your own kind?
By what do they consider you the best? Tell that to me as I ask."
Śambara said:
"I never harbor ill-will toward the Brahmins or toward Brahmā, the Grandfather; I honor the Brahmins as they speak the scriptures, according to my pleasure."

Having heard [their words], I do not disregard them, nor do I ever commit an offense against them; I inquire after those worthy of honor and I clasp the feet of the wise. They speak with confidence toward me and always restrain me.

While they are heedless, I am vigilant; while they sleep, I remain awake. Teachers sprinkle me—who am devoted to the path of the scriptures, dedicated to Brahman, and free from envy—with [wisdom] just as bees collect honey.
Whatever they spoke while satisfied, I grasped each word with my intelligence;
constantly contemplating a concentration that was in harmony with myself,
I became a taster of the essences produced by the foremost of speech.
I preside over my own kin as the moon over the stars.
This is the nectar on earth; this is the unsurpassed eye:
that the teaching which proceeds from the mouth of a brahmin is heard and put into practice here.
Having understood this cause and having witnessed the battle between the gods and the asuras in the past, my father, with a joyful heart, was filled with wonder;
and he beheld the greatness of the high-souled brahmins.
He questioned Niśākara, "How have these become perfected (siddha)? Being thus asked, Niśākara spoke this to those perfected ones there.
Soma said:
All Brahmins achieve perfection through austerity, for they are always masters of the power of speech;
indeed, kings possess the strength of their arms, while the twice-born have speech as their weapon. Even when traveling abroad or dwelling in many difficult lodgings, one should continue to study.
Free from anger and free from pride, the ascetic should be one who perceives all things with equanimity.
Even if he were born of noble lineage and should study all the Vedas in his father's house as if boasting of them, they know him to be merely a village-dweller.
The earth swallows these two, just as a snake swallows creatures dwelling in holes:
a king who does not fight and a Brahmin who does not travel abroad.
Excessive pride destroys the prosperity of a man of little intelligence.
A maiden is defiled by pregnancy, and a twice-born man by residing in a household. Those who know the Vedas, who know the world, and who are endowed with austerity and self-restraint—
such twice-born men are always to be honored and saluted by those who desire welfare in both worlds.
"Having heard this from Soma of wondrous appearance, my father honored the Brahmins who observe great vows; and in the same way, I have honored them. Bhīṣma said:
Having heard these words falling from the mouth of the lord of the Dānavas,
Śakra honored the twice-born and attained the status of Mahendra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Is a worthy recipient one who has never been seen before, or perhaps one who has resided there for a long time?
Or is it one who has arrived from afar? What constitutes a worthy recipient, O Grandfather?
Bhīṣma said:
For some, the highest vow is the practice of action:
"Whatever anyone may ask for, we shall give it all," provided that one does not cause distress to the circle of dependents; thus indeed have we heard.
For by oppressing one's circle of dependents, one indeed brings about one's own downfall.
The wise know that a worthy recipient is one who is unprecedented, or one who has resided [in the community] for a long time, or even one who has arrived from afar.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Without causing distress to our dependents and without violating dharma through non-violence,
may we truly recognize the worthy recipient to whom a gift given would cause no regret."
Bhīṣma said:
"The officiating priests, family priests, teachers, disciples, kinsmen, and relatives—
all those endowed with learning and virtuous conduct— are worthy of worship and honor."
All those who act otherwise than this do not deserve honor.
Therefore, one should always examine men with focused attention. Freedom from anger, truthful speech, non-violence, self-restraint, and straightforwardness—
O Bhārata, he in whom are seen freedom from malice, absence of arrogance, modesty, patience, austerity, and tranquility— and in whom no improper acts are found—
being established in these through his true disposition, such a person is a worthy recipient and deserves honor.

Whether one has resided [with him] for a long time or has only just returned, whether he is a stranger or an old acquaintance— that worthy recipient deserves honor. Furthermore, there is the invalidation of the Vedas and the transgression of the scriptures.
This lack of stability in all matters is the destruction of the self for that brahmin who considers himself wise yet reviles the Vedas,
being devoted to the useless science of logic (*ānvīkṣikī-tarkavidyā*).
One who speaks with reasoned arguments among the virtuous is a conqueror of those who speak without reason.
One should not accept gifts from one who is deficient in learning and austerity; for by accepting such a gift, one leads oneself to ruin.
Even though he is capable of receiving gifts, he does not accept them;
he attains those abundant worlds that belong to those whose nature is generosity.
For he has always been one who reviles and speaks excessively against the Brahmins.
O dear one, a man who is suspicious of everyone, foolish, childish, and harsh in speech— such a person should be recognized as a "man-dog," for they know him to be such.
Just as a dog is let loose both to bark and to bite, so too is he.
Thus, for the sake of mere conversation and for the destruction of all the scriptures,
those of little learning and fallacious reasoning have been seen and encountered as false scholars;
whereas others truly know the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, Purāṇas, Araṇyakas, and Vedas.
One should attend upon those who are deeply learned, those who know the essence of things, and the wise;
one must observe the conduct of the world, the sacred law, and what is beneficial for oneself. A man living in this manner prospers for eternal years.
Having discharged his debt to the gods and likewise to the sages,
as well as to the ancestors, the brahmins, and fifthly, to guests—
by means of a succession of pure and thoroughly refined deeds.
Thus, a householder performing his duties does not fall away from dharma.
Those who contemplate dharma say that among all vessels, this is the most excellent vessel.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Bharatas, I wish to hear about the nature of women;
for women, O Grandfather, are the root of all evils and are fickle-minded.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Nārada and the unchaste woman Pañcacūḍā.
Long ago, the wise celestial sage Nārada, while wandering through the worlds, [encountered her].
He beheld the irreproachable Apsaras Pañcacūḍā, born of Brahmā.
Seeing her, whose every limb was beautiful, the sage questioned the Apsaras:
"O slender-waisted one, there is a certain doubt in my heart; tell me that."
Thus addressed, she replied then to the brahmin Nārada:
"If there is a subject at hand, I shall speak; you consider me capable.
Nārada said:
"I will not, under any circumstances, O blessed lady, employ you in a matter outside your domain.
O fair-faced one, I wish to hear from you concerning the nature of women.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard these words of that celestial sage, the most excellent of Apsarases replied: "Being a woman myself, I am not able to speak ill of women;
you already know who women are and what they are like by their very nature."
"O divine sage, you ought not to command me regarding such a question.
To her, that divine sage said: "Speak the truth, O slender-waisted one;
there is fault in falsehood, but no fault is found in truth."
Having been addressed thus, she of the lovely smile became resolved in her mind and proceeded to speak the eternal and true faults of women. Pañcacūḍā said:
"O Nārada, women who are of noble birth, beautiful, and have protectors do not abide by the bounds of propriety; that is the fault in women.
Indeed, there is nothing else more wicked than women."

For women are indeed the root of all faults, as you yourself well know. Even when their husbands are renowned, prosperous, handsome, and submissive, women are unable to remain faithful once they have found an opportunity for intimacy.
"O Lord, this is indeed an ignoble custom for us women,
that we abandon our modesty and consort with men who are even more wicked than ourselves. For he who desires a woman and seeks her company [is truly base]."
Women desire only that man who pays them even slight attention; because men do not solicit them and out of fear of their attendants,
women who are otherwise unrestrained remain within the bounds of fidelity toward their husbands.

There is no one inaccessible to them, nor do they abide by any fixed age; whether he be ugly or handsome, they enjoy him simply because he is a man. It is never out of fear, nor out of compassion, nor for the sake of wealth that they act in this way.
Women do not remain faithful to their husbands merely because of ties of kinship;
noble women envy those independent women who, in their youth, wear polished ornaments and fine garments.

O divine sage, even those beloved women who are constantly cherished and guarded well may become attached to hunchbacks, the blind, the mentally dull, and the dwarfed; indeed, O celestial rishi, they may even consort with the lame and other men who are held in contempt.
"O great sage, there is no one in this world who is inaccessible to women. O Brahman, if men's access to them cannot be achieved by any means,
they even engage with one another, for they do not remain faithful to their husbands."
It should be understood that they are generally of wicked conduct, devoted to evil, untruthful, and shrouded in deceit;
they abound in unenlightened intellects because of their failure to obtain men [as husbands] and out of fear of their kinsmen.
Out of fear of death or imprisonment, they protect themselves;

yet, being fickle by nature, they are difficult to serve and hard to grasp in their true disposition. Though seemingly pleasing and charming to a friend, they are actually the abodes of enmity and anger.
In this world, women are like the speech of a wise man.
Fire is never satiated with wood, nor is the great ocean with rivers; Death is never satiated with all living beings, nor are beautiful-eyed women ever satiated with men.
13,038.026a Furthermore, O celestial sage, this is another secret concerning all women:
13,038.026c Upon merely seeing a man who is pleasing to the heart, a woman’s womb becomes moistened.
13,038.026d Seeing a man who is well-bathed and sprinkled with fine sandalwood paste, [she is moved].
The womb of women flows like water from the foot of a leather bag;
even toward a husband who is the giver of their desires, the provider of mental comfort, and their protector, women show no gratitude. They do not tolerate such a supreme lord.
They do not value abundant sensual enjoyments, nor ornaments, nor the accumulation of wealth,
as much as they value the favor found in sexual union.
Antaka, Śamana, Mṛtyu, Pātāla, and Vaḍavāmukha—
A razor's edge, poison, a serpent, and fire—these are on one side; women are on the other. For from them come the five great elements, and from them the worlds were fashioned by the Creator.
"O Nārada, from the very moment that men and women were created, faults were likewise created in women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, these men in this world are constantly attached to women, being possessed by supreme delusion ordained by fate;
and women likewise [are attached] to men, as is evident before the eyes of the world."
13,039.002a Here, a sharp doubt revolves intensely within my heart:
13,039.002c O descendant of Kuru, how do men form attachments to these women, 13,039.002e or how do those women take pleasure in them, or perhaps become detached from them again?
"O tiger among men, how can these women be guarded by a man here? You ought to explain this to me,
for they deceive men in this world with the illusions of Māyā."
No man who has once fallen into their grasp is ever released;
like cows seeking fresh grass, they seize ever-new prey.
Such was the magic of Śambara, and such was the magic of Namuci as well.
They know all those women of Bali and Kumbhīnasa to be such:
they laugh when he laughs and weep when he weeps;
and according to the requirements of the moment, they win him over with endearing words even when he is unkind.
Even if one were to have a thousand tongues and live for a hundred autumns,
if one speaks of the faults of women with undivided attention, one would meet one's end without having finished.
Whatever treatise Uśanas knows, and whatever Bṛhaspati knows—
They are not distinguished by the intellect of women; how then are they to be guarded by men?
They say that falsehood is truth, and likewise that truth is falsehood. Alas, men are attached to these women, who are a locus of faults and impurity!

"How, O hero, are those women to be guarded by men here? O slayer of enemies, I believe that the treatises on statecraft (*arthaśāstra*) were indeed composed by the virtuous, beginning with Bṛhaspati, for the purpose of extracting the intelligence of women."
When being honored by men, women disturb the minds of those men; likewise, O King, when rejected, they likewise disturb the minds of men.
O mighty-armed one, we have heard that these subjects are righteous.
Whether treated with honor or dishonor, they always cause the mind to waver.
Who would be capable of protecting them? This is my great doubt.
Tell me that, O mighty-armed one, you who increase the lineage of the Kurus!
"O best of the Kurus, if it is possible to protect them in any way whatsoever—
whether by doing so now or as has been done before— you ought to explain that to me.
Bhīṣma said:
"O mighty-armed one, it is even so; there is nothing false in this at all, O Kauravya, ruler of men, regarding the woman as you describe. In this regard, I shall relate to you an ancient history."

O bull of the Bharatas, O lord of the earth, I shall tell you, my son, how protection was previously provided by the high-souled Vipula, how women were created by Brahmā, and for what purpose this was done.
"O son, there is indeed nothing more wicked than women. For women are like a blazing fire, O Lord, and like the illusions born of Māyā;
they are, all at once, the edge of a razor, poison, a serpent, and death."
"O mighty-armed one, we have heard that these subjects are righteous;
they will go to the state of gods themselves, and from that, fear will come upon the gods.
Then, O subduer of enemies, those gods approached the Grandfather.

Having offered their mental oblations, they sat in silence with downcast faces. Knowing the thoughts within those gods, the Lord Grandfather (Brahmā) created women as a *kṛtyā* for the purpose of deluding human beings.

"O son of Kuntī, in the previous creation, women here were virtuous; however, unvirtuous women arose from the creation of Prajāpati by means of a *kṛtyā*. To them, that Grandfather indeed granted all desires according to their wish."
Then those women, greedy with desire, began to crush the men.
The Lord, the Master of the Gods, created Wrath as an ally to Desire;
all creatures became attached, having fallen under the sway of desire and wrath.
For the twice-born, for gurus, and for great gurus such as kings and others,
there is indeed incessant torment arising from the desire for union with women even for a moment— [a torment] for those whose minds are not attached and who are always pure-souled through celibacy.
For those engaged in austerity, self-restraint, worship, and meditation, purification is supreme;
yet it is established as the law that for women there is no ritual action whatsoever. For the Veda declares: "Women are devoid of sensory power, they lack the sacred mantras, and they are falsehood."
Prajāpati gave women beds, seats, ornaments, food, drink, ignoble conduct, harsh speech, and pleasure;
it is not possible for a man to guard them in any way whatsoever.
"Even by the Creator himself, O dear one, how much less so by men here?
Women cannot be protected by words, or by imprisonment and execution, or likewise by various kinds of hardships; for they are eternally unrestrained."
"O tiger among men, I have previously heard this account of how protection was formerly provided for the preceptor’s wife by Vipula. Listen to that, O Great King; I shall relate it to you in brief."
There was a highly fortunate ṛṣi renowned as Devaśarman.
His wife, named Ruci, was peerless on earth in her beauty;
intoxicated by her beauty were the gods, gandharvas, and dānavas.
But especially, O Indra among kings, Vṛtrahaṇ Pākaśāsana and the great sage Devaśarman, who knew the conduct of women,
protected that wife according to their power and according to their zeal.
He knew Purandara to be one who wanders about lusting after the wives of others;
therefore, he took great care to protect his wife. Once, O dear one, that rishi then set his mind upon performing a sacrifice.
"How might the protection of my wife be ensured? he thought.
Having reflected in his mind upon the means of protection, that great ascetic summoned his beloved disciple Vipula, the descendant of Bhṛgu, and spoke to him.
"O performer of sacrifice, I shall depart; this Ruci, O lord of the gods, is constantly sought after by my son. Protect her to the best of your power.
You must always remain vigilant against Purandara."
"For he, O descendant of Bhṛgu, creates various forms," so was the ascetic Vipula addressed by him— one who had restrained his senses,
O King, who was always engaged in fierce austerities, and whose splendor was like that of fire or the sun.
The knower of dharma and speaker of truth replied, "So be it.
Then, O Great King, he questioned his renowned preceptor once more:
"O Sage, what are the forms that Śakra assumes when he approaches?"
"What indeed is the nature of his form and splendor? You ought to explain that to me.
Then, O Bhārata, the Blessed One related to that high-souled Vipula the truth concerning the illusion of Śakra.
O brahmin-sage, that Indra, the subduer of Pāka and slayer of Bala, possesses great illusory power;
he repeatedly assumes various and manifold forms.
Wearing a diadem, bearing the thunderbolt, armed with a bow, crowned, and adorned with earrings—so does he appear.
In a mere moment, O son, he becomes like a *caṇḍāla* in appearance; again he becomes one with a topknot, matted hair, and garments of bark;
and again his body becomes large, then stout, and then emaciated.
He further transforms his complexion into fair, swarthy, and dark; he becomes deformed and handsome, as well as young and likewise old;
he becomes wise, dull-witted, mute, short, and likewise tall.
The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, the Vaiśya, and likewise the Śūdra,
as well as those born in the inverse and natural orders— all these become Śatakratu (Indra).
He assumes the form of a parrot and a crow, and takes on the appearance of a swan and a cuckoo.
Furthermore, he assumes the forms of lions, tigers, and elephants;
he also takes on the bodies of gods, Daityas, and kings.
At times he is emaciated, with limbs broken by the wind, or likewise a deformed bird.
He becomes a four-footed creature of many forms, yet again he becomes a fool;
he even assumes the bodies of flies, mosquitoes, and the like.
It is impossible for anyone, however great, to capture him.
O dear one, even though Śakra, by whom this world was created through his role as the maker of all,
has again become invisible, he is perceived by the eye of knowledge;
moreover, that king of the gods becomes once more like the wind.
"The subduer of Pāka constantly performs such deeds as these;
therefore, O Vipula, protect this slender-waisted woman with great effort.
Having said, "She must be protected by you at all times," the sage departed.
"O best of the Bhrigus, just as the Lord of the Gods would not lick the sacrificial oblation placed and set out for the sacrifice, like a wicked dog, so did Indra act toward Ruci.
Having spoken thus, that sage, the performer of the sacrifice, then departed.
O best of the Bharatas, after the illustrious Devaśarman had spoken thus,
Vipula became lost in thought upon hearing his preceptor’s words;
he then established an extraordinary protection against the mighty King of the Gods.
"What indeed can I do to protect the wife of my guru?
For that lord of the gods is a master of illusion, difficult to overcome, and full of prowess;
the subduer of Pāka cannot be kept out even by concealing the hermitage."

Or perhaps Indra, assuming the form of the wind, might violate the preceptor’s wife; for such is his capacity to take on various forms. Therefore, having entered this hut, I shall indeed remain here today within Ruci.
"Alternatively, she cannot be protected by me through human effort alone,
for the Lord whose vehicle is the green horse (Indra) is heard to possess manifold forms.
Therefore, by the power of yoga, I shall protect her from the subduer of Pāka (Indra)."
With my own limbs, I shall enter her limbs— 13,040.046c— in order to protect her.
13,040.047a If my preceptor should see this wife of mine, Ruci, while she is impure, 13,040.047c that man of great asceticism and divine knowledge will undoubtedly curse her out of anger.
"And she cannot be guarded by men as other women can;
for this lord of the gods is a master of illusion—alas, I have fallen into peril! Yet, the command of my preceptor must certainly be carried out here."
"If I were to do this, it would be a marvelous deed accomplished by me:
having entered the body of my preceptor's wife here through yoga, I would be free from the form of passion, and thus no offense would be mine."
The mind alone is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings. In one way a beloved wife is embraced; in another way a daughter is embraced.
Just as a son residing in the womb is not defiled when he is being born.
13,040.050 Thus, the man of knowledge is not defiled by worldly actions at all.
13,040.051 Just as a traveler might occupy an empty hall on the road, so shall I today occupy the body of my preceptor’s wife.
"Just as a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf is unattached and fickle,
even so shall I dwell within her body with a concentrated mind.
Having thus perceived the Dharma and all the Vedas and Vedāṅgas in their entirety, [he spoke].
Having observed the vast ascetic power of both his preceptor and himself,
that descendant of Bhṛgu resolved thus in his mind regarding the protection [of the sacrifice];
hear now, O King, the supreme effort he undertook accordingly.
Seated near his preceptor’s wife, that Vipula of great asceticism delighted her— she of faultless limbs who was likewise seated there— with various stories.
Then, through the power of yoga, Vipula entered into Ruci.
To protect the preceptor’s wife from Indra, who possesses many forms,
Vipula joined the rays of his own eyes with those of her eyes,
and entered her body like the wind enters the sky.
With his body against her body and his face against her face,
the sage remained motionless, as if merged within her like a shadow;
then Vipula held the body of his preceptor’s wife firmly in place.

For thirteen thousand, forty, and five hundred and eight years, he dwelt there, intent on protection, and she did not perceive him. O King, for as long as it took his high-souled preceptor to complete his sacrifice and return to his own home, he guarded that time.
13,041.001 Bhīṣma said: Then, on one occasion, the lord of the gods, assuming a body of divine form,
thinking "this is the opportunity," approached the hermitage.
Having assumed an incomparable and alluring form, O lord of men,
and becoming most beautiful to behold, he entered that hermitage. There he saw the massive body of Vipula seated.
Motionless with fixed eyes, as if depicted in a painting—
she who possessed lovely outer corners of the eyes, full hips and breasts,
large eyes like lotus petals, and a face resembling the full moon.
Upon seeing him, she suddenly desired to rise to meet him;
struck with wonder by his beauty, she then wished to ask, "Who are you?
Yet, though she longed to stand up, she remained rooted there by Vipula’s power.
O lord of men, being thus restrained, she was unable to move.
To her, the lord of the gods spoke with words that were exceedingly beautiful and gentle:
"Know me, O lady of pure smiles, to be the lord of the gods who has come here for your sake."
"O fair-browed one, I am indeed being tormented by the god of love born from my thoughts of you; take me up, for before long the time will pass us by.
The sage Vipula heard Śakra speaking in this manner.
Remaining within the body of the preceptor’s wife, he beheld the lord of the gods.
O King, that blameless woman was unable to rise up,
nor, O King, could she speak, for she was paralyzed by Vipula.
Having perceived the disposition of his preceptor’s wife, that descendant of Bhṛgu,
endowed with great splendor, O Lord, forcibly restrained her through yoga;
he bound all her senses with the bonds of yoga.
But seeing her thus free from any change of emotion, O King, the Lord of Śacī was again filled with shame and spoke to her, who was bewildered by the power of yoga:
"Come, come! And then she desired to reply to him.
Vipula repeated those words of the preceptor’s wife:
"Sir, what is the purpose of your coming? From her moon-like face, these words issued forth, adorned with grammatical refinement.
Having spoken those words while under the power of another, she was then filled with shame;
and Purandara, for his part, became terrified and despondent.
O lord of the people, the king of the gods, having observed that transformation, [was struck with fear].
Then the thousand-eyed one gazed with his divine vision and beheld the sage within her body,
like a reflection appearing upon the surface of a mirror.
Seeing him engaged in such terrible asceticism, O Lord, Purandara then trembled,
greatly terrified and fearing a curse.
But Vipula, of great ascetic power, having released his preceptor’s wife, [departed].
Entering his own body, he then spoke to the terrified Śakra:
"O Purandara, you whose senses are unsubdued, you evil-souled one, you who are possessed by desire! Neither the gods nor human beings shall honor you for much longer."
"O Śakra, have you forgotten that? Does it not remain in your mind—that you were released by Gautama while marked with the sign of Bhaga's organ?
I know you to be of childish intellect, undisciplined, and fickle."
"O fool, this [city] is protected by me; go, O wicked one, back the way you came!
O deluded soul, I would not burn you today with my own splendor;
however, out of compassion, O Vāsava, I do not wish to consume you."
That wise teacher of mine, possessed of terrible ascetic power, will today consume you—a man of sinful mind—with his eyes blazing with anger upon seeing you.
O Śakra, you must never act in this way again; the twice-born are to be honored by you.
Do not go to your destruction along with your sons and ministers, afflicted as you are by the power of a Brahmin. Do not persist in the belief that "I am immortal";
do not hold me in contempt, for there is nothing indeed that cannot be accomplished through ascetic power.
Having heard those words of the high-souled Vipula, Śakra, feeling ashamed, said nothing and vanished right there. When a moment had passed, the great ascetic Devaśarman [saw] Śakra.
Having performed the sacrifice according to his desire, he returned to his own hermitage.
O King, when the preceptor had arrived, Vipula, who was ever intent on doing what was pleasing to him,
presented his blameless wife, protected by him, to the preceptor.

Having saluted his preceptor, the tranquil-souled Vipula, who was devoted to his teacher, attended upon him as before without any apprehension. Then, for him who had rested and was seated together with his wife, [Vipula...]
Then Vipula reported that deed of Śakra.
Having heard it, the powerful sage was pleased with Vipula because of his character, conduct, asceticism, and self-restraint.

Seeing Vipula’s conduct toward his guru, his devotion toward himself, and his steadfastness in dharma, the lord said, "Excellent! Excellent! And the righteous-souled one, having congratulated his disciple who was devoted to dharma, [spoke further].
The high-minded Devaśarman, who was devoted to his guru, invited him to choose a boon; he then accepted the steadfastness in the Dharma.
Having been permitted by his guru, he practiced unsurpassed austerity. Likewise, the great ascetic Devaśarman, together with his wife,
wandered fearlessly through the lonely forest, free from the threat of Bala and Vṛtra-slayer Indra.
13,042.001 Bhīṣma said:
13,042.001a Having carried out the words of his preceptor, Vipula performed intense austerities;
13,042.001c and the heroic one then considered himself to be endowed with the power of asceticism.
O lord of the earth, through that deed,
he wandered the world with joy and free from fear, having attained fame as the best among men;
and the powerful one likewise considered both worlds already conquered.
O descendant of Kuru, by virtue of that deed and through his vast asceticism,
after some time had passed, O joy of the Kurus,
a gift consisting of wealth and grain was indeed given by his sister Ruci.
At that very time, a certain divine and excellent woman, possessing supreme beauty, traveled through the sky. Then,
flowers fell from her body onto the surface of the earth.
Not far from that hermitage, O Bhārata, were flowers of divine fragrance;
then, O King, that lotus-eyed woman gathered them.
At that moment, her attendant quickly approached her side.
For her elder sister, O dear one, was named Prabhāvatī;
she became the wife of Citraratha, the lord of Aṅga. Having fastened those flowers in her hair, that woman of excellent complexion—
Then, having been invited, Ruci went to the palace of the lord of Aṅga.
Upon seeing those flowers,
the beautiful-eyed and excellent wife of the king of Aṅga then urged her sister to go for the sake of the flowers.
Ruci, her face most radiant, related everything to her husband;
the sage approved all that his sister had said. Then Devaśarman, of great asceticism, summoned Vipula.
"Go, go," O Bhārata, he urged him for the sake of flowers.
"Go, go for the sake of flowers to my hermitage," he said, O Bhārata. But Vipula, a man of great asceticism, did not hesitate at his teacher's word.
"So be it," he replied, O King, and he went to that place where those flowers had fallen from the sky;
there they remained unfaded, and other flowers were found as well.
Then, O Bhārata, he took those divine and beautiful flowers, which had been obtained through his own ascetic power and possessed a celestial fragrance; having received them,
his heart was filled with joy as he acted according to the command of his preceptor.
Then he went quickly to Campā, which was garlanded with campaka flowers. There, O dear one, in a lonely forest, he saw a pair of men moving about like a wheel, holding each other’s hands.
There, one went quickly, shifting his footstep;
but the other did not do so, O King, and thus they then began a quarrel.
One said, "You are walking too fast," while the other replied, "No."
"Neither this, nor that," they both said to one another, my dear;
as they thus contended with each other, this oath then ensued. Then, referring to Vipula in their minds, they both spoke these words.
"Whoever speaks a falsehood concerning us two— may he receive in the next world the same destination as that twice-born Vipula.
Upon hearing this, Vipula’s face became dejected.
"Though my asceticism is thus intense, this burden of maintaining a family is painful. What sin must I have committed that I should now face such a destiny—
one so loathsome to all living beings as has been proclaimed by him today?"
While reflecting thus, O best of kings, Vipula,
with his face cast down and his head bowed, brooded over his own misdeed.
Then, [he saw] six other men with dice made of gold and silver.
He saw them indeed playing at dice, filled with greed and excitement; they were then making that very oath which had been made by the couple,
and addressing themselves to Vipula, they spoke these words.
"Whoever, resorting to greed, should venture to act unjustly toward us,
shall attain that destiny which awaits Vipula in the next world.
Having heard this, however, Vipula saw no violation of dharma.
O descendant of Kuru, having heard such a curse, he then brooded over everything he had done since birth, like fire placed within fire, O King,
his mind burning with grief.
O dear one, as he was reflecting thus, many days and nights passed. And this thought arose in his mind regarding the protection provided by Ruci:
"The auspicious mark [on her breast] has been matched by the auspicious mark [on my own], and her face by my face."

"O Kauravya, having performed that act, I did not say 'this is the truth' to my guru at that time. O highly fortunate one, Vipula then considered this evil deed to be within himself; of this there is no doubt."
Having arrived at the city of Campā, he gave the flowers to his preceptor;
and being dear to his preceptor, he worshipped the preceptor according to the prescribed rites.
Bhīṣma said:
Seeing that his disciple had arrived, the highly effulgent Devaśarman then spoke these words; hear them, O lord of men. Devaśarman said:
"Vipula, what indeed have you seen today in that great forest?
Your teacher, Nipuṇa, as well as Ātman and Ruci, know of this.
Vipula replied:
"O Brahmarṣi, what is that couple? And who, O Lord, are those men who know me in truth? You ought to tell me about them as well.
Devaśarman said:
"O Brahmin, know that this couple is indeed day and night;
it revolves like a wheel, and it knows your misdeed.
And those men, O sage, who play with dice as if they were joyful,"
"Recognize those seasons; they know your evil deed. A man of sinful soul, O twice-born one, should not think 'no one knows me' and thus place his trust in committing a wicked act in secret."
For even as a man always performs a sinful deed in secret,
the seasons behold it, as do day and night;
indeed, those worlds shall become exactly like those who commit evil.
"Having performed that deed for me, you did not announce it; yet they,
seeing you with a smile of joy while failing to report your master's work,
spoke to you in such a way as to remind you of what you have heard."
He constantly perceives day and night, as well as the seasons,
and the evil deeds of a man or the auspicious deeds of one who performs good works within that person.
Therefore, that deed of yours toward me— which was born of transgression and fear— [is known].

"O twice-born one, those people said to you thus because they knew that you had not disclosed that which consisted of the fear of malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). Indeed, they would have become like those who commit sinful deeds."
"O twice-born one, you did not report my deed when it was performed by you; furthermore, O brahmin, it is possible for a woman of evil conduct to be guarded,
yet you have committed no offense at all, and for that I am pleased with you."
For those who are free from defects of mind, no fault shall arise for you in that way;
otherwise, a beloved wife is embraced with one kind of affection, while a daughter is embraced with another.
Likewise, the perception regarding the form of a woman differs between an ascetic and those possessed by lust.

The world is generally deceived by its own lack of training in the mind: it recoils from what is called "fickleness," yet craves what is called "the wine of the mouth. Thus, for those whose minds are unfit for liberation, this is the mantra that serves as their deity.
That great fruit of those who perform action is not for one blinded by passion, affection, or greed;
you are free from impurity and pure, untainted by the onset of desire. O best of the twice-born, had I seen you acting wickedly, [I would have acted differently].
"I would curse you out of anger; of this I have no doubt.
Women are attached to men, and that is a great advantage for them.
Had you guarded her otherwise, there would have been a curse upon you and that would have been your fate."
"O son, she has been protected by you and reported to me as well. I am pleased with you, my dear; may it be well with you, and you shall go to heaven.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, the great rishi Devaśarman, filled with joy,
rejoiced as he ascended to heaven together with his wife and his disciples. And this narrative the great sage related to me.
O King, in ancient times on the bank of the Gaṅgā, during the course of a conversation, Mārkaṇḍeya said:
"Therefore, O Pārtha, I tell you that among all women,
both the virtuous and the non-virtuous are constantly seen."
Virtuous women, highly fortunate, esteemed as the mothers of the world,
sustain this earth, O King, with its groves and forests;
yet there are also those who are unvirtuous, ill-behaved, destroyers of their families, and fixed in evil intent.
"O King, these [women] are to be recognized by their own innate bodily marks as being corrupt.
In this way, O high-souled ones, protection can indeed be afforded to them;
otherwise, O tiger among kings, women cannot be protected."
For these, O tiger among men, are fierce and possess fierce prowess;
they have no such thing as "dear" when it comes to sexual union with men. They are sorceresses, those who cause action, and those who have already acted, O bull of the Bharatas.
"O son of Pāṇḍu, these women do not find delight in a single man;
O lord of men, men should neither feel affection for them nor harbor envy toward them. Rather, one should enjoy them with a sense of detachment, while remaining firmly established in dharma."

O lord of men, in this world, one who avoids the faults of the forbidden days (*parva*) and so forth may engage in untruth; yet, O joy of the Kurus, a man who commits such acts while avoiding those specific faults remains free from affliction. Otherwise, by acting contrary to this, he would be destroyed.
"In every way, O tiger among kings, skillful means (*yukti*) is honored everywhere. By that one [means] alone, indeed, has extensive protection been provided for the woman;
no other in this world of men, O King, is capable of protecting a woman."
Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Grandfather, tell me that which is the root of all duties, of procreation, of the household,
and of the ancestors, the gods, and guests."
13,044.002 Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of the earth, this is indeed considered the most worthy of reflection among all duties:
for what kind of man should a maiden be given?"

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, having ascertained his character, conduct, learning, lineage, and deeds, a daughter should be given with water alone to a bridegroom of merit; this is the eternal dharma for virtuous Brāhmaṇas."
One who, acting with favor, should thus bring about a marriage by inviting [the bridegroom],
this is the eternal dharma for cultured Kṣatriyas:
that which sets aside one's own preference and follows instead the preference of the maiden.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, that woman who is desired by a man should be given to him;
those who know the Dharma call this the Gāndharva rite.
Having purchased her with much wealth and having enticed her kinsmen, [she is taken].
"O King, the wise have declared this to be the law of the Asuras:

the forcible abduction from the home of a weeping woman by one who, having slain and severed the heads of those who weep, carries her away— this, my dear, is the defining characteristic of the Rākṣasa rite."
When one approaches a woman in secret while she is asleep, intoxicated, or mentally deranged, that is known as the Paiśāca form of marriage; it is the most sinful and the lowest among marriages.
Of these five, O Yudhiṣṭhira, three are righteous and two are unrighteous.
The *paiśāca* and the *āsura* forms must never be performed under any circumstances.
O bull among men, the *brāhma*, the *kṣātra*, and the *gāndharva* are righteous;
they may be performed either separately or combined, of this there is no doubt.
A Brāhmaṇa may have three wives, while a Kṣatriya may have two wives. A Vaiśya should take a wife from his own caste; among these, the offspring shall be equal.
However, for a Brāhmaṇa, the Brāhmaṇī wife is the senior, and for a Kṣatriya, the Kṣatriyā wife is the senior.
Some say that even for the sake of pleasure, a Śūdra woman may be taken as a wife; however, other people say this is not so.
The virtuous do not praise the procreation of offspring upon a Śūdra woman;
a Brāhmaṇa who begets children on a Śūdra woman is ordained to undergo penance.
Others, seeking offspring, marry women who are not too young because of the impermanence [of youth].
Those engaged in ritual action marry her with regard for internal purity—
[a woman] born of another lineage and free from defects such as those seen in dreams.
In that [state], desire is forbidden, though some maintain it is permissible in times of distress.
A man of thirty years should take as his wife a maiden of ten years who is still naked;
or a man of twenty-one years may obtain one of seven years.
But if she has neither brother nor father, O bull of the Bharatas,
one should never marry her, for she is subject to the status of an appointed daughter (*putrikā*). A maiden who has reached puberty should wait for three years.
But when the fourth [period] arrives, she should seek a husband for herself;
for her offspring and sexual pleasure are diminished, O bull among the Bharatas. Acting otherwise than this, she would be censurable by the Lord of Creatures.

"She who is not a *sapiṇḍa* of the mother and not of the same *gotra* as the father—one should marry such a woman; this is the law that Manu has declared. She is recommended for the twice-born in the rite of marriage for sexual union."
13,044.018 Yudhiṣṭhira said: One man may have paid the bride-price; another says, "I shall give it";
another might speak with force, while yet another displays his wealth.
"O Grandfather, if there should be another who has taken her hand in marriage, to whom does the maiden belong?
May you be the eye for us who desire to know the truth.
Bhīṣma said:
Whatever human rite is undertaken for the sake of a formal establishment,

if it is performed with mantras yet consecrated by a false statement, that falsehood is a sin. [Likewise, one must not speak falsely regarding] a wife, children, officiating priests, teachers, students, or sub-teachers.
"Those who speak falsely deserve punishment," say some people; others, however, say "no. For Manu does not thus praise a conversation with one who is unwilling;
for that which is false brings ill repute, is contrary to dharma, and subverts righteousness.
O Bhārata, that gift which they bestow according to the Dharma and that which they purchase does not incur the fault of being one-sided;
having obtained the consent of his kinsmen, he should perform the recitation of mantras and the fire-oblation.

In that way, those mantras are accomplished; they are never accomplished for one who has not been given [in marriage]. However, the mantra-pledge (*mantra-samaya*) made here between husband and wife is said to be weightier than that which is made by their kinsmen.
"By the decree of Dharma, a husband knows his wife as one given by the gods;
she, therefore, sets aside both divine and human speech that is false.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

If a bridegroom who is endowed with virtue, desire, and wealth should arrive when the bride's dowry has already been received, should falsehood be spoken in this matter or not? Since there is fault on both sides [in either case], one should act in such a way as to achieve the better outcome.

This Dharma of all dharmas is considered by us to be the most worthy of reflection. May you become the eye for us who desire to know the truth. Tell us all this, for I am not yet satiated with what is being said.
13,044.030 Bhīṣma said:
"Knowing that a bride-price does not bring about the ultimate fulfillment [of dharma], he did not take one;
for virtuous men never give a daughter away with a bride-price as their primary motive."
But when kinsmen demand a bride-price (*śulka*) for a girl endowed with other excellent qualities, saying,
"Adorn her and take her away," and he gives both that price and the girl out of compliance, that is not a sale; it is not a bride-price.
Having accepted [the gift], it should be given back; this is the eternal law.
