It was not previously stated by me, "I shall give my daughter to you.
Whether they say so, or do not say so, or even those who speak with certainty—[this remains the rule].
"Therefore, until the grasping of the hand, they solicit one another;
we have heard that in ancient times the bridegroom was bestowed by the Maruts.
A maiden must not be given to one who is undesired—this is the injunction of the seers."
That is the root of desire and of procreation; such is my opinion.

Having considered the many faults arising from the cohabitation of two who are hostile to one another, listen now to how the nuptial fee (śulka) was established so that it never resulted in a final settlement.
I brought two maidens as wives for Vicitravīrya after conquering all the Magadhas, the Kāśīs, and the Kosalas;
one had her hand taken in marriage, while the other received the bride-price.
"Once she has been taken by the hand, she must be released right there," my father said regarding another maiden; yet that Kaurava took her away.
Suspecting his father's words, he questioned even others.

"For my father’s desire for righteousness was exceedingly great. Therefore, O King, desiring to observe proper conduct, I spoke these words again and again: 'I wish to know the truth regarding right conduct.'"

13,044.041 Then, when these words had been spoken by me, O great king, my father Bāhlīka, the best among the upholders of dharma, spoke these words: 13,044.042 "If your finality depends on the bride-price and not likewise on the taking of the hand in marriage,"
One who has received the bride-price (śulka) should wait for her chosen husband until the ceremony with parched grain (lāja).
For those who know the Dharma have not declared that the mere word [of the groom] is considered authoritative;
rather, for them, the finality of marriage lies in the taking of the hand, not in the bride-price.
It is well known that speech regarding the giving [of a maiden] is established;
however, for those who consider it a purchase or a fee, they are people who do not know the Dharma.
Such a woman should not be given to them, nor should she be wedded by them.
A wife must never be bought, nor must she ever be sold under any circumstances. Those people who buy her like a slave-girl, and those who sell her—
such shall be the end for those greedy and evil-minded ones.
Regarding this matter, people indeed questioned those possessed of truth:
"When the bride-price for a maiden has been received, but the giver of the price has passed away,
and there is another who has taken her hand— regarding this, we have a doubt concerning the law."
"O one of great wisdom, sever that for us, for you are indeed esteemed as wise.
May you become the eye for us who desire to know the truth.
To all those speaking thus, Satyavān spoke these words:
Wherever she desires, there she should be given; no deliberation should be made in this matter.
They perform [this] even for one who is living; when he is dead, there is no doubt at all.
A maiden may enter [the household of] her brother-in-law, or she may perform great ascetic penance.
Having become devoted solely to him, she would write the name of her husband;
yet for some others, she would write it very slowly. Those who speak thus in this matter know this to be the settled conclusion.
That which follows prior to the taking of the hand, wherein the subsequent [ceremony] takes place, consists indeed of mantras that are all-auspicious; however, false speech therein is a sin.
The completion of the mantras for the taking of the hand occurs at the seventh step.
She who is given by the waters becomes the wife of the one who takes her hand.
A twice-born man of the highest rank should take a wife according to the rule— one who is well-disposed, of a compatible lineage, given by her brother, and led around the fire.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me this: if a maiden has received the bride-price but no husband has been found for her, what should be done in that case?"
13,045.002 Bhīṣma said:
That [woman] would then be the acquisition of one who has no son and no inheritance.
13,045.003 But if she should take a bride-price, she belongs to the giver of that price, being purchased for it.
For her sake, one should seek offspring by whatever means possible;
no one should perform any rite for her accompanied by sacred mantras.
Indeed, Sāvitrī herself chose him as her husband when she was given away by her father.
Those others who know the Dharma praise that [conduct] of his, and not other people. But this is what others have never done, nor have other virtuous men ever done it;
for the conduct of the virtuous is the weightiest characteristic of Dharma.
In this very context, Sukratu,
the grandson of the high-souled Janaka, King of Videha,
spoke these words: "How can there be any praise for a path practiced by the wicked?"
This further question or doubt may be censured by the virtuous;
for negligence regarding dharma is indeed unrighteousness, the way of the Asuras.
We have never heard of such a thing occurring among those of former births.
"For the relationship between husband and wife—that of man and woman—is indeed equal;
pleasure is a common duty," so said that king.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"By what authority, then, is wealth taken from men? For a daughter ought to be like a son to her father.
Bhīṣma said:

Just as one's self, so is a son; a daughter is equal to a son. While she remains as one's own self, how could another take the wealth? Whatever may be the mother’s separate property (yautaka), that indeed is the portion of the unmarried daughter.
Or rather, the daughter’s son alone shall take the inheritance of a father who has no son;
for he indeed offers the funeral cake (piṇḍa) to both his father and his maternal grandfather.
In this world, no distinction is recorded by the law between a son and a daughter’s son.
For a son strives through offspring born of another [woman],
yet a daughter excels even by means of a son born of another;
I see no reason for this in terms of the dharma pertaining to a grandson.

And those sons who are born of women sold belong to the father alone. But those born of the Asura rite are envious, most unrighteous, misappropriators of others' property, deceitful, and their conduct is contrary to dharma.
13,045.018 In this regard, those who know the past recite the verses sung by Yama, which are established in the treatises on dharma as bridges of righteousness.
13,045.019 "That man who, desiring wealth, sells his own son..."
He who, for the sake of his own livelihood, gives away a daughter for a bride-price,
shall dwell for seven kalpas in the most terrible hell called Kālasūtra;
there, as a ghost (preta), he must consume sweat, urine, and excrement.

"Regarding the *ārṣa* form of marriage, some say that a pair of cattle is the bride-price (*śulka*), but that is surely false. Whether it be small or large, O King, it remains nothing other than a sale. Even if it has been practiced by some, this is by no means the Dharma."
The activities of others as well are seen to proceed from greed—
those who enjoy a maiden who has been rendered submissive by ritual means;
these are the doers of evil, and they lie in blinding darkness.
"Furthermore, even another human being is not to be sold, much less one's own offspring;
for there is no purpose whatsoever in wealth that has its root in unrighteousness.
Bhīṣma said:
Those who know the past recite the words of Pracetas:
"When the kinsmen do not take anything at all from a girl, that is not a sale;
it is an honoring of the maidens and the highest form of compassion."
And all that [was given] must be returned to the maiden in its entirety by her fathers,
brothers, fathers-in-law, and brothers-in-law,
who desire her great welfare; she is to be honored and cherished by them.
If a woman is not pleasing, she will not delight her husband; and because of his lack of delight, procreation does not increase. Therefore, O lord of men, women must always be honored and cherished.
Where women are honored, there the gods rejoice;
where they are not honored, all ritual actions there become fruitless.
That family does not exist at all when the female relatives (jāmayaḥ) grieve.

"O King, houses cursed by a kinsman appear as if they have been struck down by a malevolent spell; deprived of prosperity, they neither shine nor flourish. When Manu was about to depart for heaven, he entrusted women to the care of men."
Weak, with but scanty loincloths, they are friends who seek to conquer through truth;
yet they are envious, desirous of honor, fierce, unfriendly, and ignorant. Women deserve to be honored; therefore, O men, honor them.
For women, indeed, your duty consists solely of sexual pleasure and enjoyment;
let the service of household tasks and the preparation of food be dependent upon you. The procreation of offspring and the nurturing of those already born [are likewise your concern].
"Behold how the course of worldly life is bound up with women for the sake of pleasure;
being honored by them, you shall accomplish all your tasks.
And here, the daughter of the King of Videha sang this verse:
For women, there is no sacrifice whatsoever, nor a *śrāddha*, nor a fast;
rather, service to her husband is their dharma, and by it she conquers heaven.
The father protects her in childhood, and the husband protects her in youth.
In old age, sons [should protect her], for a woman does not deserve independence.
These women are indeed named "Prosperity" (Śrī); they should be honored by one who desires well-being.
O Bhārata, a woman who is both cherished and restrained becomes true Prosperity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O knower of the ordinances of all the śāstras, O best among those who understand the purpose of the duties of kings—
you are indeed renowned upon the earth as the supreme dispeller of doubts."
"But I have a certain doubt; tell me that, O Grandfather.
In this painful calamity, whom else should we ask? What ought a man to do, and what is the eternal dharma?"
"O mighty-armed one, you ought to explain all of this:
O Grandfather, four wives are ordained for a Brāhmaṇa who desires pleasure— a Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, a Vaiśyā, and a Śūdrā."
O best of the Kurus, when sons have been born to all of them there,
who among them deserves, according to seniority, the paternal inheritance? And by whom should what portion be taken from that ancestral wealth of the father, O grandfather?
"I desire this to be told: what division among them is prescribed in the tradition? Bhīṣma said:
"The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya—these three castes are the twice-born."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the dharma ordained for a Brāhmaṇa among these [classes]. However, O scorcher of foes, if through partiality, greed, or even desire, a Brāhmaṇa should take a Śūdra woman as his wife, it is not sanctioned by traditional precedent.

If a Brāhmaṇa causes a Śūdra woman to ascend his bed, he becomes afflicted; he must also perform penance according to the methods prescribed by rule. O Yudhiṣṭhira, if offspring are born from that union, the penalty shall be doubled.
Therefore, O Bhārata, I shall now fully declare to you the rule regarding wealth:
the son of the Brāhmaṇī wife shall take one share from the father’s estate, consisting of a marked bull, a vehicle, and whatever may be the most excellent possession.
But the remainder, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the property of a Brāhmaṇa, should be divided into ten parts;
from that paternal wealth, four shares must be taken by him alone.
Furthermore, a son born of a Kṣatriya wife who is a Brāhmaṇa is likewise [entitled], without a doubt.
But by virtue of his mother’s excellence, he is entitled to take three shares.
However, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one born from a Brāhmaṇa to a Vaiśya woman— who belongs to the third caste—
must take two shares from the Brāhmaṇa’s property.
A son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is traditionally held to be one whose wealth must never be taken away;
yet, O Bhārata, even a small amount should be given to the son of a Śūdra woman.
This is the rule regarding wealth divided into ten parts.
One should assign equal shares to those born of wives of the same caste (savarṇā).
However, out of ignorance, people consider the son of a Śūdra woman by a non-Brāhmaṇa to be a non-Brāhmaṇa;
for one born from a Brāhmaṇa father among the [other] three castes becomes a Brāhmaṇa.
The four castes are traditionally recognized, and no fifth is found;
however, the son of a Śūdra may take a tenth part of the father’s wealth.
But he may take only what has been given by the father; he is not entitled to take what was not given.

"O Bhārata, wealth must certainly be given to the son of a Śūdra woman; it is given to him because compassion is the highest dharma. Wherever he may have been born, he is fit only for the cultivation of virtue."
Whether he has but one son or whether he be sonless,
O Bhārata, one should not give more than a tenth part to the son of a Śūdra woman;
by law, it is ordained that his share is one-fourth of a [Brahmin] share, while the daughter’s share is likewise determined by dharma.

Others, however, know that she who has no brother and is fully entitled [to inherit] is worthy of the wealth. When a twice-born man possesses more than three years' worth of provisions, he should perform a sacrifice with that wealth; he should not acquire riches in vain.
A woman’s share of wealth is indeed limited to three thousand [kārṣāpaṇas] from the inheritance of the three-thousandfold world-system;
and she is not entitled to enjoy that wealth given by her husband if it was not formally bestowed upon her.
For it is recorded that the inheritance of a wife has enjoyment as its sole fruit.

Women must never, under any circumstances, make an appropriation from the husband’s property. But whatever wealth may belong to a woman, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having been given by her father—a Brāhmaṇa woman’s—her daughter shall take it; for she is just like a son.
"For she was ordained as one equal to a son, O King, O delighter of the Kurus.
Thus has this been declared regarding duties, O bull of the Bharatas;
remembering this dharma, one should not acquire wealth in vain."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If it is traditionally held that a son born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman is not entitled to inherit wealth,
by what specific distinction is even a tenth part given to him?"
One born of a Brāhmaṇa woman by a Brāhmaṇa is undoubtedly a Brāhmaṇa;
the same would apply to one born of a Kṣatriya woman, and indeed even of a Vaiśya woman. O best of kings, why then should they receive unequal shares?
"13,047.029c When all three castes were called 'Brāhmaṇas' by you,
13,047.030 Bhīṣma said:
13,047.030a O scorcher of foes, in this world they are called 'wives' (dārāḥ) by a single name."
By this single name thus declared, there would be a very great distinction:
if a man has taken three wives previously and subsequently marries a Brāhmaṇī woman, she is the eldest;
she is to be honored, and she is more venerable than the others.
Bathing, adorning, the husband’s cleaning of his teeth, the application of collyrium,
the offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*), and whatever else in the home may be consistent with dharma—
no other woman is ever entitled to perform these while she is present.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, a Brāhmaṇī alone should perform that [duty] for her Brāhmaṇa husband;
food, drink, garlands, garments, and ornaments—
these should be given to the Brāhmaṇī, for she is indeed weightier than her husband.
O descendant of Kuru, O great king, this eternal dharma is also seen in that scripture which was proclaimed by Manu; yet,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, if one should act otherwise out of desire, [it is not dharma].
Just as a *brāhmaṇa-caṇḍāla* was seen before, so too is he;
the son who belongs to a *brāhmaṇī* is equal to one who belongs to a *kṣatriyā*. O King, there is no distinction here between these two castes.
But in this world, a Kṣatriya woman cannot be equal by birth to a Brāhmaṇī woman.
O best of kings, Yudhiṣṭhira, the first-born son of the Brāhmaṇī woman shall be superior; moreover, he may take even more from the paternal wealth than the others.
Just as a Kṣatriya woman can never be the equal of a Brāhmaṇa woman,
so too a Vaiśya woman can never be the equal of a Kṣatriya woman. Prosperity, sovereignty, and the treasury belong to the Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
O King, the earth as far as the edge of the ocean is seen to be governed [by you]. For a Kṣatriya attains abundant prosperity through his own duty;
O King, the king is the wielder of the rod of punishment, and protection exists nowhere else but in the Kṣatriya.
For the highly fortunate Brāhmaṇas are the deities even of the gods;
toward them, the king should proceed with worship according to the prescribed rule,
recognizing that this is the eternal and imperishable Dharma proclaimed by the sages.
When [the people] are being deprived of their own duty, the Kṣatriya protects the subjects;
when wealth and wives are being carried off on all sides by bandits,
the king becomes the protector of all the social classes.
The son of a Kṣatriya woman is superior to the son of a Vaiśya woman; of this there is no doubt.
For that reason also, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he is entitled to take a larger share from the paternal estate.
Furthermore, the son of a Vaiśya woman is also superior to the son of a Śūdra woman; of this there is no doubt.
It certainly produces fear; therefore, that wealth should be given away.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, O Grandfather, you have duly explained to me regarding the property of Brāhmaṇas."
"But how can there be a regulation for the other castes?
Bhīṣma said:
"O descendant of Kuru, even for a Kṣatriya, two wives are ordained."
And the third [wife] may be a Śūdra woman, though she is not mentioned as a precedent;
this indeed should be the order for Kṣatriyas, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Furthermore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the property of a Kṣatriya should be divided into eight parts.

The son of a Kṣatriya woman shall take four shares from the father's wealth; he shall also take whatever was acquired by the father through warfare. But the son of a Vaiśya woman shall take three shares, and the son of a Śūdra woman likewise an eighth.
He may take what has been given by his father, but he is not entitled to take what has not been given.
For a Vaiśya, O descendant of Kuru, there should be only one wife;
or a second may be a Śūdra woman, though this is not recorded as a precedent in the traditional law.
O bull among the Bharatas, for a Vaiśya living with a Vaiśya wife,
O son of Kuntī, and likewise with a Śūdra wife, the rule regarding their property is ordained as follows:
the wealth of a Vaiśya, O bull among the Bharatas, shall be divided into five parts.
13,047.053c O lord of men, I shall now describe the offspring of those two and their division [of the inheritance].
13,047.054a Four shares of the father’s wealth are to be taken by the son of the Vaiśya wife;
13,047.054c but the fifth share, O Bhārata, shall belong to the son of the Śūdra wife.
He may take what has been given by his father, but he does not deserve to take what has not been given. A Śūdra born of the [three] castes in this manner shall have wealth that is to be given away.
For a Śūdra, there may be only a wife of his own caste, and never any other.

If a Śūdra has a hundred sons born of wives of the same caste, they shall share the inheritance equally; for among all castes, it is ordained that sons born of wives of equal status shall have equal shares in the wealth without distinction.
The share of the eldest shall be the preeminent one; that which is the primary portion constitutes the extra share for the eldest.
This rule of inheritance, O Pārtha, was declared of old by the Self-existent One himself.
O King, there is another distinction regarding those born of wives of equal caste.

Among those distinguished by their specific marriages, each preceding one is superior to the next. Even among sons born of wives of equal status, the eldest shall take one principal share; the middle son likewise takes a middle share, and the youngest a smallest share.
"Thus, among all castes, those of the same varṇa attain preeminence;
even the great seer Kāśyapa, the son of Marīci, has declared this.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Whether through wealth, or through lust, or from uncertainty regarding castes,
or even through ignorance of castes, the intermixture of castes arises.
For those born from such an intermixture of castes according to this rule—
"What is dharma? What are the duties? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"The duties of the four social orders and the four social orders themselves—these alone [constitute dharma]."
In the beginning, Prajāpati created those four wives for the sake of sacrifice for the Brahmin; from two of them his own self is born,
while from the other two, in due order, inferior sons are procreated who belong to the caste of their mothers.
This son of a Brāhmaṇa born from a Śūdra woman is called Pāraśava; they say he is "beyond" (para) the corpse (śava).
He should be a servant to his own family.
Having carefully considered all possible means, one should never abandon one's own conduct,
for it is by this that one sustains the lineage of one's family.
Even the youngest son of a twice-born man who is devoted to service and intent on giving gifts [attains merit];
through his connection with a Kṣatriya woman, he produces offspring from two wombs.
A man of inferior caste who marries a third wife of the Śūdra class is known as an *ugra* according to the tradition.
A Vaiśya may have two wives, and from these two, his own offspring is born. A Śūdra has only one wife, a Śūdra woman, and from her he procreates only Śūdra children.
But one who violates the wife of his guru is even more base;
he procreates an outcaste caste despised by the four social orders.
A Kṣatriya who fails to perform sacrifices begets a Vrātya and a Sūta, who is devoted to the performance of panegyrics.
From a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka and a Maudgalya are born;
from a Śūdra, a Caṇḍāla, an Atyugra, a Vadhyaghna, and a Bāhyavāsina are born. These are said to be born of a Brāhmaṇī woman, and they are the defilers of their lineage.
13,048.011 These, O Lord, are the offspring born of the mixture of castes, O best among the wise.

13,048.012 A Bandī is born from a Vaiśya woman, while a Māgadha, who lives by his speech, is born from a Śūdra woman; and a Niṣāda, a fisherman, is born from a Kṣatriya woman through such transgression.
From a Śūdra father and a Vaiśya mother is born an Āyogava, who follows the customs of a village;
he is a carpenter whose work is not to be accepted by Brāhmaṇas, and he lives by the forest.
These [mixed castes] also produce offspring of similar caste when they procreate within their own wombs.
Those of superior birth procreate offspring within the mother’s own caste, even when born from inferior wombs;
just as among the four castes, one's own self is born from two [of them],
so too are those outside [the fold] born primarily through immediate succession.
And they also produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs;
however, by engaging with one another, they produce those who are censured.
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcast being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so it is here.
In this way, from those further outside the fourfold caste system, one who is even more outside is born.
But those who proceed in the reverse order (pratiloma) produce yet another who is further outside than the outside;
these inferior castes are born from the inferior, and they number fifteen.
And from approaching those who should not be approached, the confusion of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) proceeds.
Among the *vrātyas* here, there are born *sairandhrīs* among the *māgadhas*—
women skilled in personal adornment and service, who are not slaves yet live as slaves.

From this [Vaiśya], the Vaideha begets the Āyogava, who lives by means of snares and the forest; and he also begets the Maireyaka and the Mādhuka. The Niṣāda begets the Mudgara, a fisherman who subsists by means of boats.
The Caṇḍālī also gives birth to the Mṛtapa, the Śvapāka, and the most despicable [outcaste].
The Māgadhī bears four cruel sons who live by means of deceit:
the Sūda, who prepares meat for flavoring, and the one known as the Saugandha.
From a Vaidehaka is born the most wicked Niṣāda, who is cruel, lives off his wife, and travels in a donkey-cart; from a Madranābha is born one who likewise travels in a donkey-cart;
and from a Caṇḍāla is born a Pulkasa, who eats the flesh of donkeys, horses, and elephants.
Those three are born from *āyogava* women of low caste: one who is clothed in the garments of the dead, one who eats from broken vessels,
and the *kṣudra*, the *vaidehaka*, and the *andhra*, whose dwelling is outside the village.
From a Niṣāda woman, a Kārāvara is born from a Carmakāra; from a Caṇḍāla, a Pāṇḍusaupāka is born, who deals in bamboo;
and an Āhiṇḍika is born from a Niṣāda by a Vaidehī woman.
A Caṇḍāla woman, however, gives birth to a Sūpāka who follows the same conduct as Maudgalya;
and a Niṣādī woman also bears to a Caṇḍāla a son called an Antāvasāyin,
who frequents cremation grounds and is excluded even by those already outside the pale.
Thus, these castes arising from intermixture through the transgression of fathers and mothers—
whether concealed or manifest— are to be known by their respective actions;
for dharma belongs only to the four [principal] castes, and not to any other.
Among those of the four castes who have fallen from their dharma, no one here possesses a true designation [of caste].
Those excluded from sacrifices and from the virtuous, having come together by mere chance,
are born as outsiders through their outward conduct and their associations.
At crossroads, cremation grounds, mountains, and other great trees,
as well as at sacred trees, cemeteries, mountains, and groves—
always taking hold of ornaments made of black iron.
They should dwell there, subsisting by means of their ancestral occupations; they employ ornaments as well as utensils,
and they undoubtedly provide assistance for the sake of cows and Brahmins.
Compassion, pity, truthful speech, and likewise forbearance—
protecting others with one's own body brings about success for outsiders;
O tiger among men, there is no doubt in this for me.
When the [women] have been proclaimed according to the instruction,
a wise man, having reflected, should procreate a son;
for a son born of inferior lineage would bring ruin.
Just as a stone in the water sinks to the bottom,
so do women lead astray in this world— whether it be an ignorant man or even one who is wise— a man who has fallen under the sway of desire and anger.
"The very nature of women is the corruption of men in this world;
for this reason, the wise do not become attached to women.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, how may we recognize a man who is devoid of his proper caste, unrecognizable, born of a defiled womb, and who, though appearing noble, is actually ignoble? Bhīṣma said:
Born from a womb defiled by impurity and characterized by various improper conducts,
the purity of one's birth is to be recognized through deeds practiced by the virtuous.
Unnoble character, lack of proper conduct, cruelty, and a disposition toward inaction [are the marks of the contrary].
In this world, it reveals the person born from a defiled womb;
he inherits either the character of his father, or that of his mother, or both. In no way does one born of mixed parentage suppress his own innate nature.

Just as one is born with a form resembling that of one's mother and father, so too does a man, like a tiger with its stripes, enter his own womb. When the stream of the lineage is obscured, there occurs a confusion of wombs for him.
Whether it be small or great, a person inevitably adopts that very character;
for one who practices the conduct and appearance of a noble person, even while on a path of pretense,
his own character— whether of his own caste or another— will certainly reveal him.
Among beings of diverse conduct and engaged in various actions,
nothing in this world is so perfectly integrated with one’s birth and conduct as the body;
here, a man's body is drawn along by his inner essence (*sattva*).
Whether it be superior, middling, or inferior, one rejoices in a being of equal character. One should not honor even a superior person if they are devoid of good conduct;
however, one should indeed honor even a Śūdra who is well-behaved and knows the Dharma.
A person proclaims themselves by their own actions—
by deeds performed through their own conduct and behavior, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
For a man reveals himself through his actions—
through the auspicious and inauspicious deeds performed according to his own character and conduct— even if his own lineage has been utterly lost.
Furthermore, he manifests through his own karmas within all these wombs— whether they be mixed or otherwise—
and a wise man should avoid those wombs in which he would not cause himself to be born.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Kurus, tell me separately about the sons of the various castes;
of what kind are they, and which sons belong to which [father]?"
"O King, very many conflicting reports regarding the son are heard; you ought to sever the doubt of us who are bewildered in this matter."—
Bhīṣma.

The son is to be known as one's own self; he is the first among the many kinds recognized by others. That son whom a man himself begets in his own consecrated field (womb) should be understood as the *aurasa* (legitimate) son, the foremost of all.
Having worshipped Agni and Prajāpati,
she is bestowed upon a husband; she may be a *putrikā* (appointed daughter) even by mere intention,
or a son born on the bed of one who is deceased, impotent, or fallen from his caste.

He who is appointed by his own duty [as a son] is known as the *kṣetraja* (field-born) son. He whom the mother and father, being pleased and acting in times of distress, give away with a libation of water, should be understood as the *dattaka* (given) son, provided he is of equal status.
But he whom one may make similar [to oneself], who is discerning of virtues and faults,

and who is endowed with the qualities of a son— he should be known as the *kṛtrima* (adopted) son. Furthermore, he who is born in secret and whose parentage is not known by anyone— [he is the *gūḍhaja*].

He who is born from another's wife [but] belongs to him whose wife he is born from is called *gūḍhaja* (secret-born). One whom a man receives as a son after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either one of them is called *apaviddha* (cast-off).

If a maiden, while in her father's house, should secretly give birth to a son, he is called by the name *kānīna*; he is born of the maiden, yet belongs to the one who marries her. If a woman who is already pregnant is married—whether her condition be known or unknown—[the child belongs to the husband].
That embryo belongs to the one who carries it, and he is called "the son of a woman remarried" (sahoḍha). If a woman, whether abandoned by her husband or even by her own will,
gives birth to a child while still a virgin, he is called "the son of a remarried woman" (paunarbhava).
One who is bereft of parents, or who, out of no cause, remains attached [to his parents], and who offers himself up— such a person is called *svayaṃdatta* (self-given). Furthermore,
one whom [a man] purchases from the presence of his parents for the sake of obtaining offspring [is also considered a son].
That son of his who is similar [to him] is known by the wise as "the purchased" (*krīta*). These others, twelve in number, are thus declared by the reciters of the Dharma.
If she should be one whose womb is unviolated, even if she has gone away and returned;

She deserves to undergo the sacramental rite again with a husband who takes her as a second wife. But the son whom a Brāhmaṇa may father out of lust upon a Śūdra woman is a corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.

Whether born of a Śūdra’s slave-woman or of his slave-woman’s slave-woman, whatever son he may have, that son, being permitted, shall take a share; such is the established law. These eleven types of sons, beginning with the *kṣetraja*, have been declared as they were described.
The wise declare that these are substitutes for a son, intended to prevent the omission of religious rites.
Manu has declared that if among brothers born of the same father one should have a son, they all become possessed of sons through that son.
"If among all those women who have but one husband, even one should have a son, Manu has declared that they are all possessed of sons by virtue of that son. Bhīṣma said:

The son born of one's own self (*ātman*) is to be known as the first; so too is the son born immediately thereafter, the son born of an appointed woman (*niyuktaja*), and likewise the son born of a woman who has gone astray (*prasṛtaja*). Furthermore, [the son] born of the wife of an outcaste by a husband who is fully united with her [is also to be recognized].
Likewise, the son given (datta), the son made (kṛta), and another, the son of a pregnant bride (adhyūḍha);
furthermore, there are those born of a violation (apadhvaṃsaja), as well as the son of an unmarried girl (kānīna) and the outcasts (apasada).
These have been fully described; know them thus, O Bhārata.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who are those born of the six types of degradation, and who likewise are the base-born (apasada)?
You ought to explain all of this to me according to the truth."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, those sons of a Brāhmaṇa who belong to the three [lower] castes,
and those two who belong to the two [lower] castes of a Rājanya, O Bhārata."
Furthermore, one who possesses two castes is likewise observed right here;
for those six are born of degradation, so now hear of the outcasts (apasada):
the Caṇḍāla, the Vrātya, and the Vena, born respectively from a Brāhmaṇī and Kṣatriyā woman.
Three *apasadās* (low-born offspring) are observed for a Śūdra from a Vaiśya woman:
the Māgadha and the Vāmaka are recognized as the two born of a Vaiśya woman,
while there is only one such offspring for a Kṣatriya from both a Brāhmaṇī and a Kṣatriyā woman.
"In a Brāhmaṇa woman, a Sūta is produced; these are known as the base-born (apasada).
For the seed of a son, O lord of men, cannot be made otherwise.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Some say the son born of the field (*kṣetraja*) is the true son, while others say it is the one born of the seed (*śukraja*). To whom do these two sons belong equally? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:

"A son may be born of the seed [of another], or one who is abandoned may become a *kṣetraja* (field-born) son; likewise, an *adhyūḍha* (one who has married while his elder brother remains unmarried) violates the agreement—learn from me this very point.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"We know the son born of seed; how can there be the acquisition of one born of the field?
We know the son of a remarried woman; and how can there be one who abandons the agreement?
Bhīṣma said:

If one, having begotten a son who is his own offspring, should abandon him for some other reason, the seed is not the cause in that case; he belongs to the owner of the field. For, O lord of the people, she whom a man desiring a son chooses for the sake of a son—
In that case, the field (the womb) would be the measure [of paternity], for the son born of one's own self is certainly not [the only son] there;
rather, O bull of the Bharatas, a son born of the field is observed elsewhere,
for it is impossible to kill the self, as it is established by scriptural precedent.
"And an adopted son is recognized solely by the act of being taken in;
in that case, O Yudhiṣṭhira, neither seed nor field constitutes the authority.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What kind of son is one who is 'made' (kṛtaka), who is recognized solely through being taken in? Is he defined by the seed, the field, or both? Wherein is he to be recognized, O Bhārata?
Bhīṣma said:
If one should discover on the road a child abandoned by its mother and father,
and neither its mother nor its father is known, that child is indeed "artificial" (kṛtrima). For in such a case, one may recognize ownership over a child who has no owner.
A man of the same caste shall nourish him, and a son of the same caste is born to him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
How should his sacramental rites be performed, by whom, and in what manner?
"O Grandfather, tell me how a daughter should be given away.
Bhīṣma said:
"One should perform her consecration (saṃskāra) as one does for oneself, and likewise as one does for one's own master."

O Acyuta, if one who has been abandoned by his mother and father enters into the caste of those of his own class, one should perform the sacramental rites for him according to that lineage and caste; once he has been consecrated,
his caste and lineage become established accordingly.

13,049.025a Now, O Yudhiṣṭhira, if a maiden is to be given in marriage, she should be given by one of her own caste; 13,049.025c [this applies] for the sake of consecrating the maternal lineage when the caste of the mother is certain.

13,049.026a Furthermore, the son born of an unmarried girl (kānīna) and the son of a woman remarried after widowhood (adhyūḍhaja) should be known as sons who bring blemish upon their father's lineage.

It is the settled rule that even those two [the son of the appointed daughter and the son of a pregnant bride] are to be consecrated like one's own sons; likewise, for the *kṣetraja* son, the *apasada* sons, and those born of a woman married after her elder sister (*adhyūḍha*),
Brāhmaṇas and others should perform the sacraments for them just as they would for themselves.
"In the treatises on Dharma, this definitive conclusion regarding the social orders (varṇas) is observed.
All of this has been explained to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, what kind of affection exists toward cows in sight and in their company? Tell me that, O Grandfather, as well as the great fortune of cows.
Bhīṣma said:
"Come, O you of great splendor, I shall relate to you an ancient account—
the dialogue between Nahuṣa and the great seer Cyavana.
Long ago, O bull of the Bharatas, there was the great seer Cyavana Bhārgava."
Having undertaken the vow of dwelling in the water, the sage of great asceticism,
firm in his observance, remained for twelve years living in the water, having subdued pride, anger, joy, and even sorrow.
Inspiring the highest and most auspicious confidence among all beings,
like the cool-rayed moon over creatures that dwell in the water,
he became motionless as a pillar, purified himself, and bowed down to the deities.
He entered the waters between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā;
he received upon his head the most terrible current of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, which roared with a fearsome sound and was equal to the force of the wind in its speed.
The Gaṅgā, the Yamunā, and the rivers that follow them circumambulated the ṛṣi, yet they did not distress him;
within the water, that great muni slept as motionless as a piece of wood.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, that wise one stood upright;
he became a pleasing sight to the creatures dwelling in the water,
and the fish, with joyful hearts, then began to smell him.
13,050.010 There, a great length of time passed for him while he remained there.
13,050.011 Then, at a certain time, O one of great luster, some fishermen arrived at that place with nets in their hands.
There were many Niṣādas there, intent on catching fish— tall, strong, and brave, who never turned back from the waters;
they approached that place, determined in their work with the nets.
And they set up nets specifically, O lord of men;
then, having reached the fish-filled waters, O best of the Bharatas,
those fishermen, desiring fish, employed many methods.
Then they sprinkled the waters of the Gaṅgā and Yamunā with nets;
those nets were well-stretched, made of new thread, and possessed of such length and breadth as was suitable for that water.
Then, having spread that very great, powerful,
and well-fashioned net on all sides, they all pulled it together;
fearless in appearance and greatly rejoicing, they acted in mutual subordination to one another.

There they caught fish and other aquatic creatures; and so, O great king, they happened by chance to drag along with their net Cyavana, the descendant of Bhrigu, who was surrounded by those very fish.

Seeing him, who had mastered the Vedas, then caught in the net— his limbs smeared with river-moss, his beard and matted hair tawny, and his body covered with clusters of shells that made it appear as if variegated with scales— [they were amazed].

13,050.020c All the fishermen, with palms joined in reverence, prostrated themselves on the ground with their heads. 13,050.021a Due to exhaustion and terror, and from the dragging of the net, 13,050.021c the fish became distressed by being dragged onto the dry land.
13,050.022a Seeing that slaughter of the fish then, the sage was overcome with compassion and sighed again and again. 13,050.023 The Niṣādas said:
"Whatever sin has been committed by us out of ignorance, grant us grace in that regard. What pleasing service may we perform for you? Tell us that, O great sage.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, Cyavana, standing in the midst of the fish, spoke these words:
"Listen with focused minds to that which is my supreme desire today:
I shall undergo either the abandonment of life or sale together with the fish."

"I cannot bear to abandon these fellow-dwellers who have lived together with me in the water. When they were addressed thus, all those Niṣādas, trembling violently with fear and with dejected faces, reported this to Nahuṣa.
13,051.001 Bhīṣma said: Then, having heard that Cyavana had come to such a state, Nahuṣa went there in haste, accompanied by his ministers and family priest.
Having performed his purification according to the rules, the king, self-restrained and with palms joined in reverence, announced himself to the high-souled Cyavana;
and the king’s domestic priest also honored him.
"O lord of the people, [he was] Satyavrata, highly fortunate, like unto a god.
Nahuṣa said:
"What dear thing may I do for you? You ought to explain that to me."
"O Blessed One, I shall do all of it, even if it should be extremely difficult.
Cyavana said:
"The fishermen who live by catching fish are occupied with great toil."
"Give them my price along with the proceeds from the sale of these fish.
Nahuṣa said,
"O priest, let a thousand [pieces] be given as the price to the Niṣādas."
"For the purpose of redeeming the Blessed One, as the descendant of Bhrigu has said.
Cyavana said:
"I do not deserve even a thousand; what, O King, do you think?"
"Let a price be given that is appropriate; make your decision by your own judgment.
Nahuṣa said:
"Let one hundred thousand [coins] be given quickly to the Niṣādas."
"13,051.008c This may be its price; or what else do you think?
13,051.009 Cyavana said:
13,051.009a "O bull among kings, I am not to be bartered for even a hundred thousand."
"Let a fitting price be given; deliberate on this with your ministers.
Nahuṣa said:
"O Purohita, let ten million be given as the price to the Niṣādas."
"Even this is not a worthy comparison; therefore, let more be given.
Cyavana said:
"O King, O you of great splendor, I do not deserve ten million, nor even more."
"Let a suitable price be given; deliberate on this together with the brahmins.
Nahuṣa said:
"Let half the kingdom, or even the whole of it, be bestowed upon the Niṣādas."
"I consider this to be the price; or what else do you think, O twice-born one?
Let it be given to you, O priest, without delay, so that the sage may be released from his suffering."
13,051.013 Cyavana said:
"O King, I do not deserve half the kingdom or even the whole of it;
let a fitting price be given, and let it be deliberated upon together with the sages."
13,051.014 Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of the great seer, Nahuṣa, emaciated by grief,
then began to reflect along with his ministers and domestic priest.
There, however, a certain other forest-dweller, a sage born from a cow who subsisted on roots and fruits,
was staying near Nahuṣa.
That best of the twice-born, having addressed the king, spoke to him.
"I shall satisfy the brahmin so that he will be pleased. I would not speak a false word even in jest, much less otherwise;
whatever I tell you, that must be done without hesitation."
Nahuṣa said:
"Let the Blessed One state a price worthy of the great seer Bhṛgu;
protect me from this, as well as my kingdom and my lineage."
For if the Blessed One were enraged, he could destroy even the entire triple world;
how much more so me, who am devoid of ascetic power and rely solely on the strength of my arms? He would sink me, along with my ministers and my sacrificial priests, into fathomless waters.
"O great seer, become a boat for me; determine the price.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard the words of Nahuṣa, the powerful one born from the earth (the bull) [replied].
13,051.021c He spoke, gladdening all the ministers and that king: 13,051.021d "The lineage of the Brahmins and of cows is one and the same; it has simply been divided into two."

In one place the mantras reside, and in another the sacrificial oblation resides. O Great King, the twice-born are beyond price, being the highest among the social orders; and so too are cows, O Protector of the Earth—let a price for a cow be determined.
O King, having heard those words of the great seer, Nahuṣa was filled with great joy; accompanied by his ministers and family priest,
he approached Cyavana, the son of Bhṛgu, who was firm in his vows.
O King, he spoke these words as if to satisfy him with his speech:
"Arise, arise, O brahmin-sage! You have been purchased with a cow, O Bhārgava.
I consider this to be your price, O best among the upholders of dharma."
13,051.026 Cyavana said:
"I am rising, O Indra among kings; I have been properly purchased by you, O sinless one. I do not see any wealth here, O Acyuta, that is equal to cattle."

O King, O Hero, the chanting of their names, listening to them, giving them away, and even seeing them is praised as auspicious and the remover of all sins. Cows are always the root of prosperity; no evil exists within cows.
Cows are indeed always food; they are the supreme oblation for the gods.
The utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are eternally established in cows. Cows are indeed the leaders of the sacrifice, and likewise, they are the mouth of the sacrifice.
For these cows flow with and carry divine, imperishable nectar;
they are the abode of immortality and are honored by all the worlds. In their brilliance and physical form, cows on earth are equal to fire.
For cows are indeed a very great splendor and bestowers of happiness upon living beings. Wherever a herd of cows settles and breathes fearlessly,
they illuminate that region and drive away all evil.
Cows are the ladder to heaven; cows are honored even in heaven. Cows are divine wish-fulfilling cows; nothing else is considered superior.
Thus, O bull among kings, has this majesty of cows been declared to you by me.
"It is possible to recite even a single portion of its qualities, but not the entire Pārāyaṇa.
The Niṣādas said:
"O Sage, we have already performed both the sight of you and our conversation with you."
"Friendship with the virtuous is formed by walking seven steps together; O Lord, show us your favor!
Just as the consumer of oblations (Agni) partakes of all sacrificial offerings, so too do you, O righteous-souled one, a man who is like fire and possessed of great majesty."
"O learned one, we bow down before you and seek to propitiate you. For the sake of showing us favor, please accept this cow.
Indeed, for those capable of acting, providing protection during an extreme calamity is their duty."
"The destination that has been known by you today is hell; you are our refuge.
Cyavana said:
"The eye of a pitiable man, the eye of a sage, and the eye of a venomous serpent—"
Like a blazing fire that consumes a thicket along with its roots, [this sin] burns a man to the very core.
O fishermen, I accept your cow; may your sins be released. Go quickly to heaven together with the fish drawn up from the net.
13,051.040 Bhīṣma said:
13,051.040a Then, by the grace of that great seer of purified soul,
those Niṣādas, along with the fish, went to heaven because of his words.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, King Nahuṣa was struck with wonder upon seeing the fishermen ascending to the third heaven,
as well as the fish; O Bhārata, he beheld the ascent of both the Niṣādas and the fish.
Then both the one born from the cow (Bṛhaspati) and Cyavana, the scion of Bhrigu,
invited the king with two suitable boons.
Thereupon, the immensely powerful King Nahuṣa, the lord of the earth—
"Excellent! he said then, being pleased, O best of the Bharatas.
Thereupon, that king, who resembled Indra, took his stand in righteousness;
and being thus urged with "So be it," he joyfully honored those two sages.
Having completed his initiation, Cyavana then departed for his own hermitage;
and the immensely radiant one born from a cow also went to his own hermitage grounds.
O lord of men, the Niṣādas and those fish also ascended to heaven.
Having obtained the boon, Nahuṣa also entered his own city.
This, O dear one, which you asked me, has been told to you:
such is the affection felt at the sight [of a kinsman], O Yudhiṣṭhira, and such as it is during their dwelling together.
The great fortune of cows and likewise the definitive determination of dharma have been told.
O hero, what more shall be said? What is it that you desire to speak in your heart?
O King, you too must give a cow, and she should be adorned with ornaments.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O one of great wisdom, I have a very great doubt, vast as the ocean. Listen to it from me, O mighty-armed one; having heard it, you ought to explain it."

"O Lord, I have a very great curiosity regarding the son of Jamadagni, Rāma, the best among the upholders of dharma; you ought to explain that to me. [Tell me] about these men, beginning with Cyavana, who were fully endowed with the power of Brahmā."
"How was this Rāma, whose valor is truth, born?
And how did one possessing the dharma of a Kṣatriya arise in the lineage of a Brahmanical seer?
O King, recount his birth in its entirety."
"How did a Brāhmaṇa arise from the Kṣatriya lineage of Kauśika? Oh, how great was the power of those two high-souled ones—
of Rāma and Viśvāmitra, O tiger among men!"
"How is it that, bypassing his sons, this [lineage] came to be among their grandsons?
This is a flaw; having set aside the sons, you ought to explain this to me.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Cyavana and Kuśika. Having previously observed this defect, the descendant of Bhṛgu, Cyavana, at that time—
The bull among sages, possessed of great intelligence, reflected in his mind upon all the merits, defects, strengths, and weaknesses of the future [lineage] within his own family;
that one whose wealth is asceticism then desired to consume the entire clan of the Kuśikas.
13,052.010a Having approached Kuśika, Cyavana spoke these words:
"O sinless one, a desire has arisen in me to dwell with you.
13,052.011 Kuśika said:
"O Blessed One, this is the dharma that is upheld here by the wise;
it is always declared by the learned at the time of giving away daughters. But as for that gateway to dharma which has already passed, O you whose wealth is asceticism—"
"I shall perform that task; you ought to grant me permission.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, having taken a seat for the great sage Cyavana,"
Kuśika, together with his wife, arrived where the sage was;
taking up a water-pot, the king offered him water for washing his feet and caused all the rites to be performed for that high-souled one.

Then that high-souled king, steadfast in his vows and composed, caused Cyavana to accept the madhuparka offering according to the prescribed rites. Having thus honored the brahmin, he spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, we two are at your service; tell us what we should do.
O you of firm vows, whether it be a kingdom, wealth, or cattle, or likewise sacrifices and gifts—tell us, and I shall give you everything."
"This house, this kingdom, and this seat of dharma are yours.
You are the king; rule the earth. I am your servant, dependent upon you.
When these words had been spoken, Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage then [responded].
Filled with supreme joy, he replied this to Kuśika:
"O King, I do not desire a kingdom, nor wealth, nor women;
nor cows, nor your lands, nor sacrifices—listen to this."
"If it pleases you both, I shall undertake a certain vow: that I may serve those two [parents] with you both, free from any hesitation. When he had spoken thus, the couple rejoiced.
"O Bhārata, they replied to that ṛṣi, 'So be it.
Then Kuśika, delighted, led him into an unsurpassed part of the house and showed him there a beautiful sight."
"This is the bed of the Blessed One; please stay here as you desire.
O one whose wealth is asceticism, we two shall strive to bring you joy. Then, while they were thus conversing, the sun passed away.
Then the Ṛṣi urged him for food and drink as well.
Thereupon King Kuśika, bowing down, asked him:
"What kind of food is desired by you? What shall I provide?"
Then, with supreme joy, he replied to the lord of men: "O Bhārata, provide me with food that is appropriate for the occasion. Having honored those words, the king said, "So be it."
The lord of men gave him whatever food was available.
Then, having eaten, that Blessed One, the knower of dharma, said to the couple:
"O Lord, I wish to sleep; sleep overcomes me."
Then, having reached the bedchamber, the Blessed One, the best of sages, lay down;
the king, however, remained standing together with his wife.
Then Bhārgava said, "I am not to be awakened while I am fast asleep."
"Your feet must massage mine, and you two must remain awake through the night.
"Without hesitation, we shall do so," said Kuśika, who knew the dharma.
And at the end of the night, the two of them did not wake him.
O great king, at that time the husband and wife became intent on serving the great seer according to his instructions, remaining disciplined and self-controlled.
Then that venerable brahmin, having given instructions to the lord of men, [departed].
He slept on one side for twenty-one days;
on the twenty-second day, the ascetic arose and went forth.
But that king, O descendant of Kuru, remained without food together with his wife.
Delighted and intent on propitiating Cyavana, they waited upon him. But the descendant of Bhṛgu, whose wealth was his asceticism, rose up of his own accord;
without saying anything at all, that man of great austerity departed from the house.

Hungering and emaciated by fatigue, the husband and wife followed after him; yet that best of sages did not look back at them. Even as they were watching, the upholder of the Bhṛgu lineage [proceeded on].
O Indra among kings, having vanished, the king then fell to the earth. Having recovered for a moment with the queen, that one of great splendor then made a supreme effort once more to search for him.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When that brahmin had vanished, what did the king do then?
And what of his highly fortunate wife? Tell me that, O Grandfather.
13,053.002 Bhīṣma said: 13,053.002a Not seeing that Ṛṣi, the protector of the earth, together with his wife,
13,053.002c turned back, exhausted, ashamed, and deprived of his composure.
Having entered the city, he was dejected and did not say anything at all; he thought only of that very deed of Cyavana. Then, with a vacant mind, the king entered his palace.
On that bed, they beheld the descendant of Bhṛgu lying down. Having seen him and reflected upon that marvel, they were filled with wonder;
and from the mere sight of that sage, they both became fully refreshed.
Remaining in their respective places, the two of them massaged him once more;
then that great sage lay down on his other side,
and at that very same time, the valiant one awoke.
Frightened by fear, the two of them did not cause him any disturbance;
but when the sage awoke, O lord of the people, he said to them,
"O Bhārata, let an oil massage be given to me, for I shall bathe."
Then, O lord of the people, the Blessed One, having awakened, said to those two:
"O King, provide an oil massage; I wish to bathe. Having promised him, saying "So be it," the two of them, though hungry and emaciated by fatigue, [prepared for his service].
They attended upon him with highly precious oil that had been processed a hundred times.
Then, while the seer sat comfortably, they both massaged him in silence;
yet the descendant of Bhṛgu, a man of great ascetic power, said, "It is not enough."
When Bhārgava perceived that those two were indeed free from any change of state,
he rose up suddenly and entered the bathing hall. There, everything necessary for a bath suitable for a king had already been prepared.
Having treated all that with disrespect, it vanished right there. Then, O bull of the Bharata race, while the king was looking on, that sage [reappeared], and the couple felt no resentment.
Then, having bathed, that blessed Lord, the descendant of Bhṛgu, seated upon his lion-throne, revealed himself to Kuśika and his wife.
With a joyful countenance, King Kuśika, together with his wife, [beheld] the sage.
"Success! The food is ready," he announced, bowing low and remaining composed.
"Let it be brought in," the sage said to that lord of men;
and the king, together with his wife, brought forth that food.
Various kinds of meats and diverse vegetables, preparations of *vesavāra*, light drinks, various *rasālā* and cakes, as well as *modakas* and *ṣāḍavas*.
Various kinds of juices, forest fare fit for sages,
diverse fruits, and abundant edibles,
as well as jujubes, iṅguda, kāśmarya, bhallātaka, and vaṭa fruits.
Whatever food belonged to householders and whatever belonged to forest-dwellers,
the king had all of it brought forth out of fear of the sage’s curse. Then, all of that was placed before Cyavana.
Then, having gathered all of that— including the beds and seats— the sage Cyavana,
the joy of the Bhṛgus, covered everything with beautiful cloths along with the utensils for the meal and set it all ablaze.
And that couple, firm in their great vows, did not give way to anger; even as they were looking on him, he vanished once more. And there, at that very spot, the royal seer remained for that night.
Accompanied by his wife, the illustrious king remained restrained in speech, and no anger entered him. In the royal palace, there was always various kinds of refined food,
excellent beds, and abundant bathing facilities.
Various kinds of garments had been gathered there;
because of this, Cyavana was unable to see any opening at that time.
Then the brahmin-seer spoke once more to King Kuśika.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, take me with my wife quickly by chariot wherever I tell you.
"So be it," the king replied without hesitation to the one rich in penance.
"Is this a pleasure-chariot, O Blessed One, or is it a war-chariot?"
Having been addressed with these words by that joyful king, the sage Cyavana,
likewise delighted, replied thus to the conqueror of enemy cities:
"Quickly prepare the chariot which you consider fit for battle."
Equipped with weapons, banners, spears, and iron staffs;
resounding with the tinkling of hundreds of small bells; fitted with javelins and other implements; bound with maces and swords; and provided with hundreds of excellent arrows.
Then, having said "So be it" to him and having prepared the great chariot,
he placed his wife at the left yoke and himself at the right;
and there he took up a goad with three prongs and a point like a diamond needle.
Having given all of this, the king then spoke these words:
"O Blessed One, where shall the chariot go? Let the descendant of Bhṛgu say.
"O Brahmin-sage, wherever you shall direct it, there your chariot will go."
Thus addressed, the Blessed One then replied to that king:
"From this point onward, you must proceed slowly, step by step, so that I do not become weary; likewise, let my two attendants move according to their own will."
"I must be carried comfortably, and let all people behold me;
no traveler at all is to be turned away from them, for I shall bestow wealth upon them,
as well as upon the Brahmins who shall request their desires from me on the road."
"I shall give you everything without exception—both wealth and jewels. Let this be done in its entirety; do not hesitate, O King.
Having heard those words of his, the king then spoke to his attendants.
Whatever the sage may say, all that must be given without hesitation.
Then there were many jewels, women, draft animals, goats and sheep, gold both wrought and unwrought, and lordly elephants resembling mountains.
The king’s ministers and all others followed that ṛṣi from every side; the entire city became filled with cries of "Alas! and was overcome with distress.
Suddenly, the two of them were urged on by a sharp-pointed goad.
With their backs and hips pierced and remaining motionless,
trembling and without food, emaciated by fifty nights of fasting,
the two heroic husband and wife somehow managed to pull that excellent chariot.

Deeply pierced many times and shedding the blood born of their wounds, O great king, those two appeared like two *kiṃśuka* trees in full bloom. Seeing them, the multitude of citizens was utterly overcome with grief.
Terrified by the fear of a curse, he said nothing at all.
Then they all spoke together in pairs: "Behold the power of asceticism!
Even though we are angry, we are not able even to look upon this best of sages."
"Only Brahmins would be born, and never anyone of another caste;
who else but such a person would venture to live after mounting such a chariot? Oh, the power of the Blessed One, the Great Seer of cultivated soul!"
Behold also the fortitude of the king together with his wife;
though exhausted and having drawn this chariot with great difficulty,
the descendant of Bhṛgu did not perceive any sign of agitation in them.
13,053.048 Bhīṣma said: Then, seeing those two free from any change of emotion, that scion of Bhrigu’s lineage bestowed wealth upon them just as Vaiśravaṇa does.
Thereupon, the king, with a joyful heart, carried out exactly as he had been commanded.
Then the Blessed One, the best of sages, became pleased with him;
descending from his excellent chariot, he released the royal couple.
Having released them both according to the prescribed rites, Bhārgava then spoke these words in a voice that was affectionate, deep, and very gracious:
"O Bhārata, I shall grant you both an excellent boon; therefore, speak it."
O best of the Bharatas, that wise and most excellent of sages, out of affection, touched those two delicate youths with his hands which were like nectar.
Then the king spoke these words: "We have no fatigue here."
"O Bhārgava, by your own power, you two shall find rest through meditation alone.
Then the blessed Cyavana, being greatly delighted, said to them:
"That which was previously spoken by me shall not be in vain; it shall come to pass."

"O King, this auspicious region on the bank of the Gaṅgā is delightful. Devoted to my vows, I shall dwell here for some time. Go back to your own city, my son; once you have rested, you shall come again."
"O lord of men, tomorrow you shall see me here with my wife;
you must not harbor any resentment, for a great good fortune has arrived for you. Whatever desire resides in your heart, all of that shall come to pass."
Thus addressed, Kuśika, with a delighted inner self, spoke these meaningful words to that tiger among sages:
"O highly blessed one, I have no resentment; O Lord, I am purified by you."

Having returned to our natural state, we stand in the prime of youth, handsome and endowed with strength. Those wounds which you inflicted upon me and my wife with your goad—I no longer see them upon our bodies; I am well, together with my wife.
"And I see this lady, O Sage, resembling a divine *apsaras*,
endowed with supreme splendor just as she was seen by me before.
All of this has come to pass through your grace, O Great Sage."
"O Blessed One, this is not surprising in you, whose prowess is truth.
Having been addressed thus, Cyavana then replied to Kuśika:
"O lord of men, you should come here together with your wife."
Having been addressed thus and granted permission, the royal sage, saluting him,
departed endowed with a magnificent form like the king of the gods toward his city.
Then the ministers, together with the family priests, approached him.
Accompanied by his army, courtesans, and all his subjects, King Kuśika— blazing with supreme splendor and surrounded by them—
entered the city joyfully, being honored by bards.
Then, having entered the city and performed all his daily duties,
that lord of the earth ate with his wife and spent the night there. Then, beholding their fresh youth;
Free from old age like two immortals,
they rejoiced as they lay upon their bed,
possessing embodied forms and endowed with that splendor bestowed by the best of the twice-born.
And that sage, who increased the fame of the Bhrigu lineage and whose wealth was his asceticism,
by his mental power created a delightful and prosperous forest adorned with many kinds of jewels.
He created that which even Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices, does not possess.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, at the end of the night, that high-minded king awoke.
Having performed his morning rites, he set out with his wife toward that forest.
Then the king beheld a palace made entirely of gold,
enriched with a thousand pillars of jewels, resembling a city of the Gandharvas.
Then, O Bhārata, Kuśika beheld there divine visions:
mountains with beautiful peaks, lotus ponds filled with blossoms,
various picture galleries, and ornamental gateways.
[He saw] ground covered with lush grass as well as golden pavements; and *sahakāra* trees in full bloom, along with *ketaka*, *uddālaka*,
and *dhava* trees, as well as *aśoka*, *mucukunda*, and blossoming *atimuktaka* trees.
He beheld here and there *campaka*, *tilaka*, *bhavya*, *panasa*, and *vañjula* trees, as well as flowering *karṇikāra* trees; he also saw the *śyāmā*,
the *vāraṇapuṣpī*, and the *aṣṭāpadikā* creeper.

In various places, the lord of the earth beheld trees laden with lotuses and water-lilies, as well as flowers of every season; he also saw palaces resembling lotuses, fashioned in the shape of celestial chariots.
In some places there were cool waters, O Bhārata, and in others warm ones;
there were various seats and excellent couches,
as well as beds made entirely of gold, spread with the most costly coverlets.
Infinite varieties of food and drink were prepared here and there; as well as parrots that spoke like human speech, śārikās, bhṛṅgarājas,
cuckoos, woodpeckers, koyaṣṭikas, and wild cocks.
He beheld on all sides, most enchanting, peacocks and cocks, putrakas and jīvajīvaka birds, cakoras, monkeys, swans, cranes, and ruddy geese, all uttering their cries.
In some places, O King, he beheld hosts of Apsarases and Gandharvas; there he saw others embraced by their beloveds. And the king did not see them again, yet he saw them once more.
The king heard the very sweet sound of singing as well as the sound of Vedic recitation,
and he also heard the most melodious cries of swans there. Having seen that great wonder, the king then reflected upon it in his mind.
"Is this a dream, a derangement of the mind, or is it indeed reality?
Ah! Have I, together with my physical body, attained the supreme goal—the holy Northern Kuru region or even Amarāvatī?"
"What is this great marvel that I behold? he thought.
While reflecting thus, he saw the bull among sages within that golden celestial chariot, which was crowded with pillars of jewels.
As the descendant of Bhṛgu lay upon a divine and highly precious couch,
the lord of men, together with his wife, approached him with great joy;
then Cyavana and that couch vanished once more.
Then, in another part of the forest, he saw that man of great vows once again,
seated upon a cushion of kusha grass and muttering prayers;
thus, by the power of yoga, the brahmin deluded the king.
In an instant, O King, that forest, those hosts of Apsarases,
the Gandharvas, and even the trees— all vanished;
and the bank of the Gaṅgā became silent once again.
It became abounding in *kuśa* grass and anthills, just as it was before. Then King Kuśika, together with his wife, attained the highest wonder upon seeing that great marvel resulting from that deed.
Then Kuśika, filled with joy, said to his wife:
"Behold, O blessed lady, how these various states of being have been seen, so difficult to obtain—
what else could this be but through the grace of the foremost of the Bhṛgus and the power of asceticism?"

13,054.025c For that which cannot be attained by mere desires is indeed attainable through austerity (tapas). 13,054.026a Indeed, austerity alone is superior even to sovereignty over the three worlds.
13,054.026c For by means of well-performed austerity, this one whose wealth is austerity sports at will.
"Oh, how great is the power of the high-souled Brahman-sage Cyavana!
If he so desired, by the force of his asceticism,
he could even create other worlds where only Brāhmaṇas would be born, possessing merit in speech, intellect, and action."
Indeed, who else but Cyavana would have dared to do this in this world?
For the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain in the world; having attained that, asceticism is difficult to achieve;
even within that, spiritual perfection is hard to reach; and beyond perfection lies the supreme goal.
"Brahminhood is difficult to attain in this world, whereas kingship is easily obtained by men;
indeed, it is through the power of brahminhood that we two are yoked to the chariot like draft animals. While he was reflecting thus, he was indeed recognized by Cyavana.
Having observed him, he said to the king, "Please come quickly. Thus addressed, the king went with his wife to that great sage and bowed his head in salutation to him who was worthy of worship.
Having offered those blessings, the wise sage, O bull among men, spoke soothingly to that lord of men, saying, "Be seated. Then,
O King, Bhārgava returned to his natural state toward the monarch.
O Bhārata, as if gratifying him, he spoke in gentle words:
"O King, because you have properly conquered here the five senses with the mind as the sixth among the five objects, you are indeed liberated from hardships."
"O son, best among speakers, I have been properly propitiated by you;
indeed, not even the slightest trace of sin is found in you.
Grant me leave, O King, for I shall depart as I came."
"I am pleased with you, O Indra among kings; let a boon be accepted.
Kuśika said:
"O Blessed One, while standing in the midst of the fire and in your presence, this [was done] by me."
"O tiger among the Bhṛgus, that I have not been consumed by this [fire] is a great deal;
O descendant of Bhṛgu, this indeed is the primary boon obtained by me,
that you are pleased with my conduct, O sinless one, and that my lineage has been purified."
"O Brahmin, this is my favor, and this is the purpose of my life;
this is the very fruit of my kingdom and my supreme asceticism.
O descendant of Bhṛgu, if you, O Brahmin, are pleased with me,"
"I have a certain doubt; you ought to explain it to me.
Cyavana said:
"Choose a boon from me, and whatever doubt is in your heart, let that also be addressed."
"And tell him that, O best of men: 'I shall accomplish everything for you.
Kuśika said:
"If you are pleased with me, O Blessed One, then speak to me, O Bhārgava."
"O bull among sages, I wish to hear the reason for staying in my house,
for lying on one side alone for twenty-one days,
and for departing outside without saying anything."
O Brahmin, there was a sudden disappearance and then a reappearance;
furthermore, for twenty-one days, you remained lying down,
and then you went out anointed with oil and ate in my house.
The various things you brought together that were consumed by the fire,
your swift and sudden departure on the chariot,
the distribution of the wealth, and the sight of the forest— [all these have been witnessed].
O Great Sage, I wish to hear the reason why there was the sight— and then the subsequent disappearance— of those many golden palaces with legs of jewels and coral, as well as the couches.
For I am utterly bewildered here, reflecting day and night;
yet I do not attain any certain conclusion regarding all of this. O one rich in asceticism, I wish to hear the truth of this in its entirety.
Cyavana said:
"Listen, O King, to all of this in its entirety and for what reason it occurred; for it is not possible to leave it unexplained when one is thus questioned."
"O King, listen as I relate that which I heard long ago from my grandfather as he spoke in an assembly of the gods:
'Through the conflict between the Brahmins and the Kshatriyas, there shall be a confusion of the lineages.'"
"O King, a grandson shall be born to you, endowed with splendor and heroism. Therefore, for the sake of protecting your own lineage, I have come to you,
desiring to bring about the destruction of Kuśika’s line and wishing to consume your family."
"Then, O lord of the earth, having come to you in the past, I said:
'I shall undertake a certain vow; let service be rendered to me. Yet, I did not find any misdeed whatsoever in your house."
"O royal sage, it is by this that you live; otherwise, you would not exist.
Having adopted this resolve for twenty-one days, O King, I lay asleep thinking, 'If anyone should awaken me.'"
"O best of kings, when you did not wake me while I was fast asleep along with your wife, at that very moment I was pleased with you in my mind.
And if you had risen and departed, O lord of the earth, I would have left."
"O Lord, I would say to you, 'Where are you going? and thus curse you.
Yet, having resorted to yoga, I have remained hidden within your house again and again for twenty-one days."
"O lord of men, you might have thought, 'He is hungry,' or 'He is weary.
Relying on this understanding, I caused both of you to be emaciated by hunger;
yet not even the slightest resentment arose in your mind, O King."

"O best of men, because you did this together with your wife, I am pleased with you. As for that food which I had brought and then set on fire, I forgave you because I thought you might have become angry out of resentment."
Furthermore, O lord of men, when you had been driven by the chariot and were overcome with anger born of exhaustion,
I mounted the chariot and said to you,
"Carry me along with your wife," and you did exactly as I requested.

"O lord of men, I am free from suspicion and I am pleased with you; even though this great expenditure of wealth was made, anger did not overcome you. Therefore, O King, being pleased with you, I have performed this for you once again."
"O lord of men, know that this forest belongs once more to you and your wife. This vision of heaven was created by me for your pleasure;
it was a divine manifestation, O King, which you beheld here in this forest."

"O King, O best of monarchs, for the sake of illustrating the power of asceticism and righteousness, you have experienced heaven for a moment in your own physical body along with your wife, O lord of men."
O King, that longing you had there is also known to me. For you, O lord of the earth, desire the status of a Brahmin and the power of asceticism, O monarch,
while disregarding both the sovereignty of a king and the lordship of the gods.
"13,055.029a It is exactly as you have said; dear one, the status of a Brahmin is difficult to attain.
13,055.029c Once Brahminhood is achieved, there is the state of a seer, and within that state of a seer, the power of asceticism.
13,055.030a This desire of yours shall be fulfilled: from Kuśika, a Kauśika shall be born as a twice-born."

"Upon reaching the third generation, he will attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa. O best of kings, your lineage shall indeed possess the splendor of the Bhṛgus; your grandson, O sage, will be an ascetic with the brilliance of fire."
He who shall instill fear among gods and men— O highly fortunate one, he will be born in the lineage of Jamadagni, whose self is purified by austerity—
and that tiger among the Bhṛgus shall also uphold that Veda.
"I tell you this truth regarding all three worlds:
choose a boon, O royal sage, whatever dwells in your mind. I shall set out on a pilgrimage to sacred fords before time passes me by."
Kuśika said:
"O great sage, O sinless one, this alone is the boon I seek today—that you are pleased with me; let it be as you have said regarding my grandson’s asceticism."
"O Blessed One, let there be Brahminhood for my lineage; this is my boon.
Furthermore, O Blessed One, I wish to hear explained in detail, O descendant of Bhṛgu, how my lineage shall attain the status of Brahmins."
"Who will be my kinsman, and who will be esteemed by me?
Cyavana said:
"O bull among men, I must certainly tell you this."
"O lord of men, for this purpose have I come to exterminate you:
O ruler of people, the Kṣatriyas have always been the patrons of the Bhṛgus;
yet they shall fall into dissension due to a cause ordained by fate."

O lord of men, oppressed by the rod of destiny, the Kṣatriyas will slaughter all the Bhṛgus, cutting them down even from the womb. Then, there shall be born in our lineage one who increases the glory of the clan.
The one named Aurva, possessed of great splendor and a radiance equal to the blazing sun,
will generate a fire of wrath for the destruction of the three worlds—
he who shall reduce the earth, along with its mountains and forests, to ashes.
For some time, that best of sages will himself extinguish that fire by casting it into the mare’s mouth (vaḍavāmukha) in the ocean;
[he shall do so] through his illustrious son Ṛcīka, the joy of the Bhṛgus.

O sinless one, the entire science of archery (*dhanurveda*) will manifest directly before him due to a cause ordained by fate, for the destruction of the Kṣatriyas. Having received it, he in turn shall transmit it to his son.
When the highly fortunate Jamadagni has purified his soul through austerity,
that tiger among the Bhṛgus will uphold that Veda; and he,
O righteous-souled one, will obtain a maiden from your lineage.

Thinking, "May there be a slayer of the Kṣatriyas who is fierce," he worshipped the eternal god Nārāyaṇa and, by his grace, desired a son for the sake of the manifestation of your lineage, O best of kings.
Having obtained the daughter of Gādhi— your granddaughter— that man of great asceticism will procreate a son named Rāma, who is a Brāhmaṇa by birth but possesses the duties of a Kṣatriya;
he will be a Kṣatriya in conduct yet performs the works of a Brāhmaṇa, equal in splendor to Bṛhaspati.
"O one of great splendor, Viśvāmitra, the most righteous son of Gādhi in your lineage and endowed with great ascetic power, will grant you [the boon] there; however,
two women will be the cause for that exchange."

"By the command of the Grandfather (Brahmā), this shall indeed not be otherwise; in the third generation from you, the status of a Brāhmaṇa will be attained. And you shall become a kinsman of the Bhṛgus, whose souls are purified."
13,056.015 Bhīṣma said: Having heard the words of the high-souled sage Cyavana, King Kuśika became delighted and spoke these words.
