"So be it," said the righteous one, O best of the Bharatas. Then Cyavana, of great splendor, urged the lord of men once more for the sake of a boon, and that king spoke to him.
"Very well, O great sage, I shall certainly accept this from you with pleasure. May my lineage become one established in Brahman, and may its mind be fixed upon dharma.
Having been addressed thus, the sage Cyavana replied, "So be it."

Having taken leave of the king, he then departed on a pilgrimage to the sacred fords. O King, I have now related to you in its entirety this entire account of the cause of the alliance between the Bhṛgus and the Kuśikas.
"O King, it happened exactly as the Sage had spoken:
the birth of Rāma and of the sage Viśvāmitra.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
13,057.001a As I hear this and reflect upon it again and again today, I feel as if I am fainting.
13,057.001c This earth, once crowded with assemblies of glorious kings, is now bereft of them.
13,057.002a O Bhārata, even after conquering the earth and attaining kingdoms by the hundreds, [I find no peace].
"O Grandfather, having slain ten million men, I am consumed by remorse. What indeed will now be the condition of those excellent women,
who have been deprived of their husbands, sons, maternal uncles, and brothers?"
"Having slain those elders, as well as our kinsmen and friends, we shall fall headlong into hell; of this there is no doubt.
O Bhārata, I wish to yoke my body to fierce asceticism."
"O lord of the people, I desire to hear this taught here according to its true essence.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, the high-minded Bhīṣma—"
Having examined him thoroughly with his intellect, he spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira:
"Listen to a secret and marvelous thing that I shall tell you,
O Bhārata— namely, the destination that is attained by one through which [the soul] proceeds after death."
"O Lord, heaven is attained through austerity; fame is attained through austerity.
Longevity, enjoyments, knowledge, specialized wisdom, health, beauty, and likewise prosperity are all obtained through austerity."
O bull of the Bharatas, good fortune is attained through austerity;
one acquires wealth through austerity, silence bestows knowledge,
enjoyment is gained through giving, and life through celibacy.
The fruit of non-violence is beauty; the fruit of initiation is indeed birth in a noble family.
For those who subsist on fruits and roots, there is sovereignty; for those who subsist on leaves, there is heaven.
One who subsists on milk goes to the celestial realm, and through ritual bathing, one becomes enriched with wealth.

Knowledge is attained through service to the teacher; progeny through constant performance of the *śrāddha* rites. They say that one becomes rich in cattle through vows of eating only herbs, and attains heaven by subsisting on grass.
By bathing at the three periods of the day, one gains mastery over women; and by subsisting on air alone, one obtains the merit of a sacrifice.

A diligent twice-born man who bathes daily and recites prayers at the two twilights attains sovereignty; by fasting unto death, he attains the vault of heaven. For those who sleep upon the bare ground, houses and beds [are the reward].
For one rich in asceticism who is devoted to yoga, garments of rags and bark, clothes, ornaments, beds, seats, and vehicles [are the rewards];
for one who enters the fire with self-restraint, the world of Brahmā is ordained.
By abstaining from savory tastes, one finds good fortune in this world; by abstaining from meat, one's progeny shall be long-lived. He who dwells in the water shall become a lord of men.
O best of men, one who speaks the truth rejoices together with the gods.
Fame comes through giving, and likewise health through non-violence;
through service to the twice-born, one attains either sovereignty or even abundant status as a brahmin.

By the gift of water, eternal fame is attained; by the gift of food and drink, one is satisfied through the enjoyment of desires. By bestowing consolation upon all beings, one is liberated from all sorrows.
By serving the gods, one obtains a kingdom and a divine form;
by the gift of the light of a lamp, a man becomes possessed of sight;
and by the gift of beautiful objects to behold, one acquires memory and intelligence.
By abstaining from perfumes and garlands, one’s fame becomes abundant;
for those who maintain their hair and beard, their progeny becomes preeminent. O King, [one should likewise observe] fasting, initiation, and ritual ablution.
Having performed [this] for twelve years, one excels even the station of a hero.
By giving away female and male slaves, ornaments, fields, houses,
and a daughter as a *brahmadeya* gift, O bull among men, one attains [great merit].
O Bhārata, by means of sacrifices and fasts, a man goes to the third heaven;
and the man who offers oblations and flowers attains a long-lasting station.
[He who gives cows] adorned with golden horns...
"A man who gives a thousand cows attains the merit of the divine world in heaven";
thus say the hosts of sages and gods.
He who gives away a tawny cow (kapilā) together with a cloth,
accompanied by a bronze milking vessel, and possessing horns tipped with gold—
becoming his wish-fulfilling cow through those various qualities— she provides for him.
That cow approaches the man who gives her away;
for as many hairs as there are on the cow, so much fruit does the giver of the cow obtain.
It delivers one's sons, grandsons, and the entire lineage up to the seventh generation in the hereafter.
[One should give] a cow with beautiful golden horns and accompanied by a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
For one who gives to a twice-born man a cow made of bell-metal with a milking vessel, accompanied by wealth and a garment, along with sesame seeds,
the worlds of the Vasus become easily attainable.
A human being bound by his own actions,
falling into a hell of intense darkness,
is like a ship driven by the wind upon the great ocean.
The gift of cows delivers one to the next world;
likewise, he who gives a maiden in marriage as a Brahma-gift and bestows land upon a Brahmin [attains the same].
And he who gives food according to the prescribed rule attains the world of Purandara,
as well as a residence endowed with every excellence.
Indeed, that man who gives to a twice-born one endowed with the virtues of Vedic study and good conduct,
his worlds shall be among the Uttarakurus.
By the gift of draft-oxen, as well as by horses,
a man attains the worlds of the Vasus;
indeed, they say that the gift of gold leads to heaven.
The gift of gold is superior to that;
by the gift of an umbrella, one obtains an excellent house;
likewise, by the gift of sandals, one obtains a vehicle.
By the gift of clothing, the fruit is a beautiful form;
by the gift of fragrance, a man shall become fragrant. [He should give] that which is laden with flowers or that which is laden with fruit.
He who gives a tree to a twice-born man obtains a house that is effortlessly attained, abounding in women and filled with many jewels.
He shall obtain his desires and be free from disease,
as well as possess a beautiful form in the world of men—
he who is a giver of food, drink, and flavorful delicacies.
One who bestows shelter and clothing obtains all flavors to their heart's content;
there is no doubt in this matter.
The man who gives garlands, incense, perfumes, ointments, bathing powders, and wreaths to the twice-born shall be free from disease.
Likewise, that man who gives a house to a twice-born— one which is beautiful in the world of men, not lacking in seeds, and provided with beds— [attains great merit].
O King, he obtains an excellent capital city, delightful with merit, filled with many jewels,
and provided with fragrant and variegated carpets.
The man who gives a bed to a twice-born man shall obtain, without effort, a wife endowed with beauty, possessed of wings, and delightful to the mind.
A man who lies down as a hero becomes an attendant of the Grandfather (Brahmā);
the supreme sages say that there is nothing superior to this.
Likewise, the gift of a book, cows, and a maiden is likewise [meritorious].
"Those men who will not give, what happiness can they have from another?
Vaiśampāyana said:
"Having heard those words of his, the joy of the Kurus was pleased in heart."
He did not find pleasure in dwelling in the hermitage, desiring instead the path of heroes.
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord, spoke to the Pāṇḍavas, O bull of the Bharatas:
"May that which was the word of our grandfather be pleasing to you."
Then all the Pāṇḍavas and the illustrious Draupadī honored those words of Yudhiṣṭhira, saying, "So be it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull among the Kurus, regarding those gifts which are proclaimed as being outside the sacrificial altar— what gift do you consider superior to them?
O Lord, a great curiosity indeed dwells within me concerning this."
"Tell me, what is that gift which follows the giver after it has been given?
Bhīṣma said:
"The granting of fearlessness to all beings, and providing assistance in times of distress."
Whatever one might give to a thirsty person who asks for it,
and having given it, considers that very thing as truly given— that gift is called the best,
O bull of the Bharatas, for such a gift follows after the giver.
The gift of gold, the gift of a cow, and likewise the gift of the earth—
these indeed are purifiers that rescue one even from evil deeds.
O tiger among men, give these constantly to the virtuous.
For gifts indeed liberate a person from evil, there is no doubt.
Whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is dear to one in the home— that very thing should be given to a virtuous person by one who desires that it become inexhaustible.
One who gives what is dear and acts for the benefit of others obtains dear things in this world;
likewise, such a person becomes beloved by all beings both in this life and in the next.
[This applies even] to one who, out of pride, refuses a petitioner who is full of hope and destitute.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he who does not worship according to his ability is a cruel man. Even if it be an enemy, one who is distressed and has come seeking refuge—
he who shows favor to such a person in their calamity is indeed the best of men.
O dear one, there is no man equal to him who dispels the hunger of those who are emaciated, modest, deprived of their livelihood,
and sinking in distress; for he relieves the virtuous who are restrained by shame and impoverished along with their sons and wives.
O Kaunteya, invite with every means those who do not ask;
those who offer no benediction to either gods or mortals, who are worthy, eternally established in goodness, and subsist on whatever they happen to obtain.
"O Bhārata, protect yourself from them, for they are like venomous serpents.
Having tested those best of the foremost twice-born by means of the words spoken [to them],
you should always provide them with dwellings complete with servants and furnishings."
"O Kauravya, you should invite them with offerings that bring all desires and happiness;
O Yudhiṣṭhira, if those righteous ones of meritorious deeds accept what is purified by faith, they will do so thinking, 'This must indeed be done.'"
Those Brāhmaṇas who have bathed in knowledge and bathed in their vows, who live by depending on nothing else, who keep their Vedic study and austerities secret, and whose vows are strictly observed;
in them— who are pure, self-controlled, and devoted to their own wives— [one should offer].

Whatever auspicious deed you shall perform will sustain you in the worlds. Just as the Agnihotra sacrifice is well-offered by a twice-born man morning and evening, so indeed does a gift given to the twice-born by one of purified soul become [efficacious].

"O dear one, this sacrifice of yours is extensive, purified by faith, and accompanied by sacrificial fees; it is superior to all other sacrifices. Let it proceed for you who are giving, O Yudhiṣṭhira; for such as these, a distribution of gifts is equal to the act of giving itself."
By scattering [offerings] and honoring them, one attains freedom from debt toward them—
those who do not become angry with us and do not covet even a blade of grass;
they are most worthy of our worship, as are others who speak kindly.
Those who do not hold us in high regard, and others who do not even engage with us—these should be protected like sons; homage to them, and likewise, let there be safety for them.
For the officiating priests, domestic chaplains, and teachers are indeed the gentle upholders of the Veda.
For even when combined with the power of the *kṣatra*, energy indeed subsides within a *dvija*.
"I possess strength, I am powerful, I am a king," O Yudhiṣṭhira—
do not thus disregard the *brāhmaṇas* by withholding from them clothing and food.
O sinless one, whatever wealth you possess for the sake of splendor or strength,
with that you should honor the brahmins while abiding by your own duty; the learned ones, conducting themselves according to their true nature, are to be saluted by you.

"O best of the Kurus, let them sport upon you as they please and according to their enthusiasm, like sons; for who else besides you, O most excellent of the Kurus, is worthy of providing the livelihood for friends who are so gracious and easily satisfied?"
Just as in this world the eternal duty of women is to rely upon their husbands— as he is their god and their only refuge, and none other— so too are the twice-born for us,
O dear one; if the Brahmins were to abandon us, being left unhonored.
Beholding this cruel deed constantly committed by those established in the Kṣatriya order— deeds that lead to the lack of the Vedas, infamy, loss of heaven, and the absence of sacrifice—
what purpose is there for us in living? For that [life] of ours depends entirely upon the Brāhmaṇas.

In this regard, O King, I shall describe to you how the eternal dharma was practiced in ancient times: that a Kṣatriya served a Brāhmaṇa, a Vaiśya served a Kṣatriya, and a Śūdra served a Vaiśya; such is the sacred tradition.
A Brāhmaṇa, blazing like fire, should be attended to from a distance by a Śūdra; however,
he may be served by close contact by a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya—
those who are gentle-natured, truthful in character, and observers of the duty of truth.
Attend upon those twice-born ones who are like enraged venomous serpents—
those who are superior to others, superior even to the superior, and indeed superior to those who are superior to them,
all Kṣatriyas blazing with splendor and strength.
13,058.035 Only among Brāhmaṇas do fiery splendors and ascetic powers find their rest.
13,058.036 Neither my father was dearer to me, nor were you, O dear one, so dear;
neither my grandfather, O King, nor my own self, nor even my life itself.
"O bull of the Bharatas, there is no one on earth dearer to me than you; yet even more dear to me than you are the Brahmins.
O son of Pāṇḍu, I tell you this truth."
By that truth, may I go to those worlds where Śantanu dwells;
may I behold the pure worlds of the virtuous, which have Brahman at their head.
There, O father, I must go—both swiftly and for eternity.
"O best of the Bharatas, O King, having seen such worlds as these,
I do not regret what I have done for the sake of the brahmins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
But between two who are equally endowed with conduct,
and who are alike in learning and birth— to which of these two is a gift more distinguished?
"To one who does not ask, and to one who asks"—
Bhīṣma said:
"O Pārtha, they say that what is given to one who asks is indeed better than what is given to one who does not ask."
Indeed, the most worthy of honor is the steadfast one, for he is superior to the wretched man who lacks self-control.
A Kṣatriya has steadfastness in protection, while a Brāhmaṇa has steadfastness in the absence of desire.
A learned Brāhmaṇa who possesses steadfastness and contentment truly delights the gods.
"O Bhārata, they say that begging is for one who lacks power, and it is a form of theft;
for he who begs always causes distress to living beings like a bandit. Indeed, the beggar dies, and the giver dies after him."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, by giving, one revives both this person and oneself.
Compassion is the supreme dharma; that which is given to one who asks is compassion, while one should invite with every means those who do not ask but are suffering.
If such supreme twice-born ones should dwell in your kingdom,
you must vigilantly recognize them as fires covered by ashes;
blazing with ascetic power, they could consume even the entire earth.
O Kauravya, those who are worthy of worship yet remain unworshipped— even such as they—

must indeed be honored, for they are endowed with sacred knowledge (*jñāna*), realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), austerity (*tapas*), and yoga. O scorcher of foes, you should offer worship to those Brāhmaṇas.

Bestowing various kinds of gifts and inducements upon those who did not beg for them, the fruit that would result from a well-performed Agnihotra sacrifice performed morning and evening is said to be the fruit of such a gift to one possessed of knowledge, the Vedas, and vows.

To those Brāhmaṇas who were purified by their knowledge of the Vedas and the observance of vows, who lived without dependence on others, who were devoted to secret Vedic study and asceticism, and who were firm in their vows—
he provided them with delightful dwellings, complete with servants and all necessary furnishings.
"O Kaunteya, you should invite the best of the twice-born with various desirable things. O Yudhiṣṭhira, they may accept what is purified by faith,
for those who know dharma and possess subtle insight consider that it must simply be done."
"Have those Brahmins, having eaten, departed for their homes with their offerings—
those whose wives wait for them as farmers wait for the rain? The disciplined students have received food at the morning libation."
"O dear one, let the Brahmins, while eating, gratify your three sacred fires;
O dear one, let the midday libation proceed for you as you bestow cows,
gold, and garments— through this, may Indra be pleased with you."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, that third libation of yours, which you offer to the gods, the ancestors, and the Brahmins, is the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice. Non-violence toward all beings and the practice of universal distribution in every way [constitute its essence].
"May self-restraint, renunciation, fortitude, and truth serve as your final purificatory bath (avabhṛtha).
This sacrifice of yours, expanded, purified by faith, and accompanied by sacrificial fees—
may it always proceed, O dear one, as the most distinguished of all sacrifices."
"Whatever white flower there may be, and whatever unguent there may be,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, these should always be offered for the removal of misfortune.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Between the act of giving and the performance of sacrifice here on earth, which indeed yields greater fruit after death?
Of which is the fruit said to be superior, and to what kind of persons, in what manner, and at what time?
[If] virtuous men, devoted to constant practice, accept [the gifts].
"O Bhārata, I wish to know this according to its true nature. O learned one, please explain the duties of giving to me, who am desirous of knowledge—
specifically regarding that which is given within the sacrificial altar with faith and compassion."
13,060.003c "What indeed, O dear one, is the highest good? Tell that to me, O grandfather.
13,060.004 Bhīṣma said:
13,060.004a "O dear one, the duty of a Kṣatriya always consists of fierce deeds."
For him, the performance of Vedic sacrifices and the giving of gifts are indeed means of purification in this world;
however, virtuous men and the best of the twice-born priests do not accept gifts from kings who have committed evil deeds.
"Because [the merit] of those who give truth in the presence of wealth [is so great],
for this reason a king should perform sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). Furthermore, if they should accept [the offerings], the king should give [them] day after day."
Relying upon supreme faith— for this is indeed the highest purifier—
one who is firm in their vows should then gratify the Brahmins with gifts at the sacrifice;
those who are friendly, virtuous, knowers of the Vedas, and endowed with good character, conduct, and austerity.

Whatever they shall do for you with that [wealth], by that it will be as if already accomplished. Accomplish sacrifices for the virtuous, consisting of sweet food and accompanied by ritual fees; consider yourself as one who has sacrificed and given through the act of charity.

One should honor those who frequently perform sacrifices so that one may have a share in their merit; by bestowing gifts upon the learned, one gains a share through that act of worship. Furthermore, having given to both the performers of sacrifice and the learned, one causes the world to be bestowed [as a reward].
One should give to those who bestow knowledge; thus one becomes a sharer in the merit of the gift of knowledge. One should support Brahmins who have offspring and who bear many burdens;
by that, one becomes possessed of offspring, just like the progenitor himself.
"Indeed, O Yudhiṣṭhira, as many virtuous dharmas as the righteous practice,
all those men who bear great burdens must also be supported; being prosperous,
bestow gifts upon the Brāhmaṇas."
O Bhārata, [he gave] cows, oxen, food, umbrellas, garments, sandals, clarified butter, various kinds of eatables for the sacrificers,
as well as vehicles drawn by horses, houses, and beds.
O Bhārata, these [gifts] should be given as they bring prosperity and are easy means; having recognized that the Brāhmaṇas are free from reproach yet emaciated by lack of livelihood,
provide for them with sustenance, whether secretly or openly.
That [gift] is more meritorious for Kṣatriyas than the Rājasūya or Aśvamedha sacrifices.
Thus, liberated from sins and purified, you shall attain heaven;
for you will protect the kingdom after having replenished the treasury once again.
And from that, O Bhārata, you shall attain the state of Brahman and wealth; protect the livelihood of both yourself and others,
and cherish your own servants and subjects as if they were your own sons.
O Bhārata, may you always possess security and well-being (*yogakṣema*) toward the Brahmins;
let your life be for their sake, and never fail to protect them. For a Brahmin, the accumulation of great wealth is a source of misfortune.
For constant association with prosperity would surely cause pride and lead to delusion.
When the Brahmins are deluded, Dharma will certainly perish. Upon the destruction of Dharma, there will be the non-existence of all beings; of this there is no doubt.
When a king, having entrusted his kingdom to his guards, plunders the realm himself,
saying, "I shall perform a sacrifice; bring me wealth from that kingdom," and when that [wealth] is taken—
given out of fear at his command— it is most terrible.

A king should perform sacrifice, yet the virtuous do not praise that sacrifice [of one who oppresses]; rather, those who give favorably when they are neither oppressed nor impoverished— by such means should one sacrifice, and not with what is acquired through exertion.
When he has been duly consecrated according to the prescribed rites, the king should then perform great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*).
He must protect the wealth of the elderly, children, the blind, and the miserable.
One should not engage in digging up what has been previously buried, nor should one take the wealth of a weeping woman.
For the seizure of a miser’s property destroys the kingdom and the king’s prosperity. Furthermore, one should bestow great enjoyments upon others and dispel the fear of hunger for the virtuous.
If children, upon seeing delicious foods before them,
do not eat them according to the prescribed rules, what indeed could be more sinful than that,
if such a learned twice-born man should perish from hunger within their kingdom?
"You would incur the sin of killing an embryo, as if having committed the ultimate evil. Fie on the life of that king in whose kingdom a person perishes—
whether he be a twice-born, another, or even a common man," so spoke Śibi.
In whose kingdom a *snātaka* (a learned householder) suffers from hunger, that kingdom, along with its king, meets with decline. Indeed,
in whose kingdom women are forcibly carried away while crying out, [that kingdom likewise perishes].

While husbands and sons wailed, he died— he did not live [as a king]. The subjects, having gathered together, should slay that merciless king who is a mere calamity, who fails to protect, who plunders, who destroys, and who does not give.
That ruler of the earth who, having declared "I am your protector," does not protect you,
should be destroyed by the people acting together, like a mad dog afflicted with disease.
For whatever evil the subjects commit when they are unprotected by the king, [the king incurs a share of that sin].
"O Bhārata, the king incurs a fourth part of that sin.
Some say he incurs the whole of it; however, the settled conclusion is that he incurs half.
Having heard the instruction of Manu, our own opinion is that he incurs a fourth part."

O Bhārata, whatever merit the subjects perform when well-protected by the king, the king obtains a fourth part of that merit. O Yudhiṣṭhira, may all the subjects live depending upon you while you live.

O scorcher of foes, let your kinsmen and friends depend upon you for their livelihood, as all beings depend on the rain-cloud, as birds depend on a great tree, as the Rakshasas depend on Kubera, and as the immortals depend on Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Vedic injunction declares, 'This is to be given; this is to be given.
Kings have many things to give; what, indeed, is the unsurpassed gift?"
Bhīṣma said:
"The gift of the earth is said to surpass all other gifts;
for the earth is immovable, inexhaustible, a milch-cow yielding unsurpassed desires."

The giver of cows obtains clothing, jewels, cattle, as well as rice and barley; the giver of land prospers eternally among all beings for many years. As long as the life-span of the earth endures here, so long does the giver of land prosper.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, there is nothing here superior to the gift of land.
We have heard that in former times people gave even a small portion of the earth; all those people who now enjoy the earth were once givers of land."
In this world and the next, men subsist solely upon their own karma.
The earth, the great goddess Bhūti, makes the donor dear to her.
That lord of the earth who gives this imperishable sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) [attains such results].
Having attained human status once again, he shall become a lord of the earth. It is the certainty regarding the laws of righteousness that enjoyment corresponds to the nature of one's giving;
thus, one should either cast off the body in battle or bestow this earth as a gift.
"This, they say, is the supreme blessing for those of the kṣatriya lineage:
'The earth, when given, purifies the giver'—so have we heard.
Even one of sinful conduct, even a slayer of a Brahmin, or even a liar [is purified]."
She alone purifies sin; she alone may liberate one from evil.
Even toward kings who have committed wicked deeds, the virtuous accept gifts;
they desire nothing else as a purifier as much as their own mother.
"Her secret and eternal name is *Priyadattā*.
Whether it be a gift or knowledge, this name is most dear to her. A lord of the earth who gives this [name] to a learned man [gains great merit]."
This is desired on earth; he should go from one kingdom to another kingdom. Having undergone birth once more, he will undoubtedly become a king again.
Therefore, having obtained the earth, the ruler should give it to a Brahmin.
The earth must never, under any circumstances, be occupied by one who is not a lord of the earth;
nor should he conceal it with a vessel, or move about by means of invisibility.
And others who might desire the earth should act in this manner without doubt.

He who seizes the land of a virtuous person finds no land for himself; but by giving land to the virtuous, he indeed finds land. That righteous-souled man attains great fame both in this world and after death.
Having given a single meal, one ascends sixty thousand [yojanas];
having stolen that same amount of food, one falls into hell, doubling upward [in depth] for each [act].
Indeed, the land always belongs to that virtuous man whom the Brahmins instruct.
O King, his enemies do not rule over the earth. Whatever sin a man commits when distressed by the lack of livelihood,
he is purified by the gift of land even as small as a cow-hide.
With a bamboo pole ten cubits long, one should measure out ten such poles on all sides, adding five more cubits; this is called a *gocarma*.
Even those kings who perform mixed deeds or engage in fierce actions [are purified by this].

To them, the gift of land— the supreme purifier— should be proclaimed. Ancient people have always considered this to be virtually indistinguishable from one who performs the horse sacrifice or bestows land upon a virtuous man.
Even if the wise, having performed a virtuous deed, should feel apprehensive,
[they should know that] this single gift of land is unsurpassed and impossible to equal—
whether it be gold, silver, clothing, jewels, pearls, or wealth.
O one of great wisdom, he who bestows the earth bestows all of this:
austerity, sacrifice, sacred learning, virtuous conduct, freedom from greed, and fidelity to truth;
as well as the worship of gurus and deities—none of these surpass the giver of land.

Those who, intent on their master’s ultimate welfare, have sacrificed themselves and been slain in battle, attain the world of Brahmā as perfected beings; they do not surpass the merit of one who gives land.
Just as a mother always nourishes her own son with her milk, so does the earth sustain him who bestows it.
Just as the earth favors the donor with all its flavors,
so too do the servant of Death, the staff of punishment, the most dreadful heat of fire,
and the terrible nooses of Varuṇa not approach the giver of land.

He who, with a tranquil soul, bestows the earth, satisfies the ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers and the deities in the world of the gods. [He who gives it] to one who is emaciated, dying, deprived of livelihood, or sinking in distress—
By giving land that provides a livelihood, a man becomes a performer of a perpetual sacrifice (*satrin*).
Just as a cow runs toward her calf while discharging milk, even so, O highly fortunate one, does the earth run toward the giver of land.
By giving land that has been ploughed, provided with seed, and even yielding fruit,
or likewise by providing a lofty shelter, one becomes a granter of all desires;
[as does giving] a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with good conduct, who maintains the sacred fires, and who is pure in his vows.
A man who has received a gift of land does not go to the abode of Yama.
Just as the growth of the moon occurs day after day,
so too a gift of land increases with every harvest.
Regarding this, those conversant with the past recite verses sung by the Earth herself:
"Having heard these words, the son of Jamadagni indeed gave the earth to Kāśyapa:
'Give me alone; give me; by giving me, you shall obtain me.'"
In this world, in the next world, and thereafter in the state beyond rebirth,
that Brahmin who is devoted to the Veda and knows this utterance attains union with Brahman when the *śrāddha* oblation is being offered.

This great expiation pacifies the ill effects of malevolent spells and curses resulting from ill-performed rites; by performing it, I purify ten generations on both sides. Whoever knows this, and I likewise, purifies [themselves].
The earth is indeed considered the eternal source of all beings. Having consecrated the king, one should cause him to hear this sacred tradition,
so that upon hearing it, he may bestow the land [in times of need] and not seize it from the virtuous.
This entire purpose of the Brahmins and the purpose of the king is undoubtedly this:
for a king skilled in dharma is the primary sign of prosperity.
Now, those whose king is ignorant of dharma and an atheist—
They do not wake in happiness, nor do they sleep in happiness; people are always anxious because of his misconduct,
for many forms of security and prosperity no longer enter that kingdom.
But those for whom there is a wise and righteous king awaken in happiness and sleep in great peace;
for the subjects of that king are brought to fulfillment by his auspicious and noble deeds.
Through security and rain, they prosper by their own deeds.
He is of noble birth, he is a true man, he is a kinsman, and he is a performer of merit; he is a donor and he is valiant—he who bestows the earth.
Like the Ādityas, those men shine upon the earth with splendor who bestow fertile land upon a twice-born man learned in the Vedas;
just as seeds, when scattered upon the surface of the earth, sprout forth.
In this way, desires flourish when acquired through the gift of land.
Āditya, Varuṇa, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, Soma, Hutāśana,
and the Lord who wields the trident— all rejoice in the giver of land.

Men are born upon the earth and they reach their end upon the earth; for this fourfold world is composed of the qualities of the earth. O Lord of the Earth, she is indeed both the mother and the father of the universe.
"O lord of men, there is no being whatsoever equal to this [gift of land]:
where there are golden palaces and showers of wealth that grant all desires; where Gandharvas and Apsarases go—there do those who give land go."
In this regard, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they cite this ancient history, a dialogue between Bṛhaspati and Indra,
following [Indra’s] performance of a hundred great sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Maghavat asked this of Bṛhaspati, the best among those who know speech:
"O Blessed One, by what gift does one who has gone to heaven prosper in happiness?
Tell me that which is inexhaustible and of great value, O foremost of speakers."
Thus addressed by the lord of the gods, the priest of the deities,
Bṛhaspati of great splendor, then replied to Śatakratu:
"O slayer of Vṛtra, the gift of gold, the gift of cows, and the gift of land— [these are the foremost]."
The gift of knowledge and the gift of maidens are supreme destroyers of sin;
by giving these, O one of great wisdom, one is liberated from all evils. O Lord Indra, there is nothing superior to the gift of land.
I consider this to be superior, as the wise have declared:
those who die for the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, during the destruction of a kingdom, or for the sake of their master,
when noble women are being insulted, shall dwell together with the givers of land.
O best of the gods, those heroes who were slain in battle and have gone to heaven, being devoted to charity— none of them surpass the giver of land; nor do those who,
intent on their master’s welfare, were killed in battle having sacrificed their own lives.

Even heroes who have reached the world of Brahmā do not surpass the giver of land. Eleven ancestors— the five preceding men and the six who followed— along with himself, the man who gives land rescues them all here.
O Purandara, he who gives the earth strewn with jewels is liberated from all impurities and is glorified in the heavenly world; likewise,
a king who gives away the flourishing earth endowed with all desirable qualities [attains the same].
He becomes a king of kings; for that gift is indeed unsurpassed— he who bestows the earth, endowed with all objects of desire,
O Vāsava, all beings think, "He is giving me."
O Thousand-eyed One, that man who gives a cow that milks all desires and precedes the fulfillment of every wish goes to heaven;
likewise, [he who gives] rivers flowing with honey and clarified butter, as well as milk and curds.
O Lord of the Gods, by satisfying the rivers here, one bestows the earth;
by the gift of land, a king is liberated from royal sin.
Indeed, no other gift excels the gift of land.
O Purandara, people here speak of him who gives away the earth, bounded by the ocean and conquered by the sword, for as long as this earth endures—
provided he bestows that holy land whose essence is abundant.

The worlds acquired through the merit of the gift of land are never exhausted for him. O Śakra, a king who desires prosperity and seeks happiness in every way must always give land according to the prescribed rites to a worthy recipient.

A king should bestow land that he has conquered by his own power, purchased by himself, or acquired through service; or even land that has been well-prepared, well-sold, or well-maintained. Even if a man has committed a sin, O King, by giving land to a twice-born man, he is purified.
He casts off that evil like a snake sheds its worn-out skin.
O Śakra, by giving the earth, a man gives all of this: the oceans, the rivers, the mountains, and the forests in their entirety.
By giving land, one gives tanks, wells, streams, and lakes; one gives all kinds of oils and juices.
One gives medicinal herbs rich in milk and trees endowed with flowers and fruit.
By giving land, one gives forests, stones, and mountains;
and even by performing sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees,
one does not obtain that fruit which one enjoys from the gift of land.
The giver benefits ten generations; likewise, he who seizes it destroys ten.
By seizing land previously given, one goes to hell. He who does not give after having promised, or who takes back what has been given, [falls into hell].
Bound by the nooses of Varuṇa, he suffers under the command of Death.

O best of the twice-born, those who support a preeminent brahmin— one who maintains the sacred fires, performs sacrifices constantly, sustains his servants, and is kind to guests— do not approach Yama.
O Purandara, for a king, [the land] should exist as a debt toward the Brahmins;
however, among the other castes, he should rescue those who are emaciated and weak.
O Lord of the Thirty-three, he must not confiscate land that has been granted by another.
O best of gods, if anyone [should seize] the field of a Brahmin who has but a few servants,
then the tears shed by those wretched and despairing Brahmins, once fallen,
would destroy the lineage for three generations.

O Thousand-eyed One, he who re-establishes a protector of the earth who has fallen from his kingdom shall dwell and be honored in the vault of heaven. When the land of the poor is seized, the shedding of tears is most terrible.
[The sin] would destroy the merit of sacrifices and charitable works for three generations of this man’s family.
One should cause [the recipient] to touch land covered with sugarcane, thick with barley and wheat, and fully filled with plantain groves, mango trees, and the like.
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the heavenly world, having given land filled with cattle, horses, and vehicles, acquired through the strength of his own arms,
containing hidden treasures, and furnished with all kinds of jewels.
He obtains inexhaustible worlds, for that is his "earth-sacrifice" (bhūmisattra). Having shaken off all impurity, free from passion and esteemed by the virtuous,
he who gives away the earth is glorified among the righteous in this world.
Just as a drop of oil fallen upon water spreads abroad, O Śakra,
so does a gift bestowed upon the earth spread through every harvest.
Those kings who are heroes at the forefront of battle, the ornaments of the assembly—
O Śakra, those who face death [in battle] go to the world of Brahmā.
O Lord of the Gods, women devoted to dance and song, adorned with divine garlands,
always attend upon the giver of land in heaven.
He who duly bestows land here upon a twice-born according to the prescribed rite rejoices happily in heaven, honored by gods and gandharvas;
and a hundred apsaras, adorned with celestial garlands, [attend him].
O Lord of the Gods, spirits always attend upon that man who bestows land;
they attend upon the giver of earth in the world of Brahmā.
The conch shell, the auspicious throne, the parasol, excellent horses, and noble elephants;
likewise, flowers and heaps of gold result from the gift of land. Furthermore, his command becomes forever unimpeded, and the cry of "Victory! arises.
O Purandara, the flowers of the gift of land are its fruits, which are heaven itself.
A man who gives land obtains a ground whose flowers are gold, whose herbs are kusha grass and golden shoots, and which yields the nectar of immortality.
There is no gift equal to land; there is no teacher equal to a mother. There is no dharma equal to truth; there is no treasure equal to charity.
Having heard this from the descendant of Aṅgiras, Vāsava [ruled] over this earth.
He then gave to the descendant of Aṅgiras that land strewn with wealth and jewels.
Whoever causes this praise of the gift of land to be heard at a *śrāddha* ceremony—
for him there shall be no share for the *rakṣasas*, nor indeed for the *asuras*.
"What is given to the ancestors shall become inexhaustible; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, at the *śrāddha* ceremonies, a Brahmin should cause the twice-born who are eating to hear this.
Thus, O sinless one, this has been declared to you as the best of all gifts."
"13,061.093c O tiger among the Bharatas, what more do you wish to hear from me?
13,062.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
13,062.001a What gifts should a lord of the earth, desiring to give, bestow in this world?"
"O best of the Bharatas, one should give to Brahmins who are superior in their qualities.
By what means are they immediately satisfied, and once satisfied, what do they bestow?
Tell me that, O mighty-armed one—the great fruit produced by such meritorious deeds."
"O King, what gift is fruitful both in this world and in the next?
I wish to hear that from you; tell it to me in detail.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Bhārata, listen as I relate what Nārada, the seer of the gods, said when he was previously questioned about this very matter. Nārada said:"
In ancient times, the gods together with the hosts of sages praised food alone;
for the governance of the world and all sacrifices are established upon food. There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift equal to that of food.
Therefore, human beings especially desire to give food;
for food provides vigor in this world, and the vital breaths are established in food.
By food, O Lord, all this entire universe is sustained.
In this world, householders depend on food, and from that very food do the mendicants likewise depend.
From food, vital breath arises; this is perceptible, there is no doubt about it.
Even by causing distress to one's family, [one may give] to a high-souled Brahmin.
Food should be given to a monk by one who desires his own prosperity. Whoever gives food to a worthy Brahmin who asks for it lays up for himself the most excellent treasure for the world beyond.
A householder seeking prosperity should honor an elderly person worthy of respect who has arrived at his home, exhausted from traveling on the road;
having abandoned rising anger, he should be well-behaved and free from envy.
O King, the giver of food attains whatever happiness exists both in heaven and here on earth. One should not despise a guest who has arrived, nor should one ever turn him away;
even if it be a dog-cooker or a dog, a gift never goes to waste.
He who gives unblemished food to one traveling on the road— exhausted and previously unknown— shall attain great merit,
O lord of men, [honoring] the ancestors, the gods, the seers, the brahmins, and guests.
The man who gratifies others with food gains a great fruit of merit. Even if one has committed a sinful deed, if he gives food to a seeker—
especially to a Brāhmaṇa— he is not joined with that sin.
A gift given to Brahmins is inexhaustible, while food given to a Śūdra yields great fruit;
indeed, the gift of food to both a Śūdra and a Brahmin is distinguished as superior.
One should not inquire about [the recipient's] lineage, conduct, Vedic study, or even his native land.
In this birth, he was begged for food by a brahmin who had approached him with hope for a meal;
and for that giver of food, there arose trees of grain endowed with the fruits of all desires.
O King, there is no doubt that [the merit] will accrue here or in the hereafter;
for the ancestors hope [for it], just as farmers hope for a good rain, thinking,
"Our son or grandson will offer us food."

For a Brahmin is a great being; whether he asks "Give me yourself" out of desire or without desire, one who gives him shall obtain merit. A Brahmin is the guest of all beings, entitled to eat the first portion of what is offered.
O Bhārata, that house into which learned brāhmaṇas always go seeking alms,
and from which they return well-honored, increases exceedingly;
and after death, one attains birth in a family of great wealth.
By giving food in this world, a man attains an unsurpassed station;
indeed, he who gives the finest, most delicious food dwells honored in heaven.
For food is the life-breath of men; everything is established upon food.

O King, the giver of food becomes possessed of cattle, sons, wealth, and enjoyments; he also becomes endowed with vital strength and beauty. Indeed, in this world, the giver of food is said to be a giver of life and a giver of everything.
For by giving food to a guest who is a Brāhmaṇa according to the prescribed rule,
the donor attains happiness and is honored even by the gods. Indeed,
the Brāhmaṇa is a great being who moves about like a footed field.
Whatever seed is sown there indeed yields great fruit of merit; it produces manifest joy for both the recipient and the donor,
whereas all other gifts possess fruits that are beyond direct perception.

"Know, O Bhārata, that from food comes progeny; from food indeed comes pleasure. Know that from food come both dharma and artha, and likewise the destruction of disease. For in a former age, Prajāpati declared that food is indeed the nectar of immortality."
Food is the earth, the heavens, and the sky; everything is established upon food. When food is destroyed, the five constituent elements (dhātus) in the body fall apart;
even the strength of the strongest perishes here through the loss of food.
O best of men, without food, marriages, unions, and sacrifices do not proceed; even the Veda perishes therein. For all this—whatever is stationary or moving—indeed arises from food.
Therefore, O King, food should be given for the sake of dharma by the wise throughout the three worlds.
For the man who gives food, strength, vigor, fame, happiness,
and renown increase eternally throughout the three worlds.
The auspicious wind gathers the waters within the clouds for the sake of living beings;
and Śakra, O Bhārata, causes that water residing in the clouds to rain down. Furthermore, the sun draws up the terrestrial moisture with its own rays.
The divine Lord Prajāpati, through the wind, draws those juices from the sun;
O Bhārata, when that water falls upon the earth from the clouds, then the goddess Earth becomes moist.
From that, the crops grow by which the world subsists;
from that, furthermore, the manifestation of flesh, fat, bone, and semen occurs;
and from that semen, O lord of the earth, living beings come into existence.
For Agni and Soma nourish that seed and cause it to procreate.
Thus, food, the sun,
and the wind are considered a single mass of pure essence from which all beings were born.
"O bull of the Bharatas, he who quickly gives food to a seeker who has come to his house bestows life-breaths and splendor upon all beings. Bhīṣma said:
"O King, having been addressed thus by Nārada, I always gave food.
You too, being free from malice and devoid of anxiety, should therefore give food.
O Lord, O King, you too should give food to the Brahmins according to the prescribed rites."
By giving appropriately to those who are worthy, you shall then attain heaven. O lord of men, hear now of those worlds belonging to givers of food;
the palaces of those great-souled ones shine resplendently in the sky.
They possess various forms and structures, and are endowed with diverse pillars; they are as bright as the lunar orb and adorned with networks of tinkling bells;
some have the hue of the rising sun, and they are both stationary and moving.
There are palaces with many hundreds of stories, containing internal waters and groves;
they possess the brilliance of lapis lazuli and the sun, and are made of silver and gold.
Furthermore, trees that yield every desired fruit are situated within those dwellings.
Everywhere there were ponds, walkways, assembly halls, wells, and oblong lakes;
there were thousands of resonant vehicles already yoked,
as well as mountains consisting of various kinds of food and drink, and garments and ornaments.
Rivers flowing with milk, as well as mountains of food,
palaces with the luster of white clouds, and couches radiant with gold—
those who give food attain these; therefore, become a giver of food.
"These worlds belong to the high-souled doers of merit who give gifts of food;
therefore, food in particular should be given by men on earth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard from you the rule regarding the gift of food.
Now, please tell me the ritual for giving gifts in conjunction with the lunar mansions.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Devakī and the celestial seer Nārada,
concerning Nārada, who possesses divine vision, when he arrived at Dvārakā.
Then Devakī, who perceives the dharma, asked him this question.
O lord of the people, listen as the celestial sage Nārada duly explained everything to her as she was thus inquiring.
13,063.005 Nārada said: O highly fortunate lady, by satisfying virtuous Brahmins with milk-rice mixed with ghee under the constellation Kṛttikā, one attains unsurpassed worlds.
On the Rohiṇī asterism, for the sake of discharging one's debt, one should give to a twice-born man well-known meats, mung beans, food, and clarified butter, with milk as a drink;
and having given a milch cow together with her calf on the asterism presided over by Soma (Mṛgaśiras).
Having fasted and offered *kṛsara* mixed with oil under the constellation Ārdrā, a man goes from the world of mortals to the unsurpassed heavenly realm;
he crosses over difficult passages and mountains with edges as sharp as razors.
By giving cakes and likewise various foods under the asterism Punarvasu, O auspicious one,
one is born into a family endowed with fame and beauty and possessing abundant food.
By giving gold, whether wrought or unwrought, under the asterism Puṣya, [one attains similar rewards].
In worlds devoid of light, he shines like the moon. Furthermore,
he who gives silver or a bull under the asterism Āśleṣā becomes liberated from all fear and overcomes his enemies.
Under the asterism Maghā, a person who gives copper vessels filled with sesame seeds— measuring thirty palas and shaped like *vardhamāna*—
becomes possessed of sons and cattle in this world and rejoices after death.
During the period of Pūrvaphalgunī, one who has fasted and given to Brahmins food mixed with molasses attains good fortune;
likewise, by offering sixty-day rice (ṣaṣṭika) combined with ghee and milk according to the rules, one gains prosperity.

Having given gifts in the region of Uttarā, one is glorified in the heavenly world. Whatever gift is bestowed by men in the region of Uttarā, it becomes of great fruit and infinite; this is the settled conclusion.
Having fasted and given an elephant-chariot yoked with four animals in the month of Hasta,
one attains the supreme worlds filled with merit and desire. O Bhārata, by giving a bull and sacred perfumes under the asterism Citrā, one likewise attains such rewards.
He wanders in the world of the Apsarases and likewise rejoices in the Nandana grove. Furthermore, by giving wealth at the Svāti constellation— whatever is most dear to oneself—
he attains auspicious worlds and great fame in this very life.
By giving a bull, a milch-cow, a cart with its yoke-pole, along with grain and cloth, under the constellation Viśākhā,
one gratifies the ancestors and the gods, and after death, attains infinity.
He does not encounter difficulties and goes to the heavenly world;
having given to the Brahmins as prescribed, he finds his desired livelihood.
It is certain that he shall not suffer the afflictions of hell and other such realms.
Having fasted and given a cloak or another garment under the constellation Anurādhā,
a man is honored in heaven for a hundred yugas. Furthermore,
by giving black potherbs together with their roots to the Brahmins, a mortal [attains great merit].
In Jyeṣṭhā, one indeed attains prosperity and the desired goal. By giving roots and fruits to the Brahmins with a concentrated mind in Mūla,
one pleases the ancestors and goes to a desirable destination.
Then, under the *pūrvā-aṣāḍhā* nakṣatra, one who has fasted, having given vessels of curd to a Brāhmaṇa who is perfected in family and conduct and is a master of the Vedas,
is born after death into a family possessing very many herds of cows.
By giving *udamantha* mixed with ghee and abundant honey and molasses under the *uttarā-aṣāḍhā* asterisms, one shall obtain all desires.
Having given milk saturated with honey and ghee under the *abhijit* conjunction, [one obtains the same].
Constantly devoted to dharma, he is honored among the wise in the heavenly world.
By giving a woolen blanket covered with another cloth to one who recites [the scriptures],
he travels by means of a white vehicle through all the unobstructed worlds.
Having given a vehicle yoked with oxen under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā while remaining composed,
one who wears garments and holds reins immediately attains a kingdom after death.
Having given perfumes along with aguru and sandalwood during the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj, [one likewise attains great merit].
After death, he attains the worlds of the Apsarases and eternal fragrances. By giving king-beans (*rājamāṣa*) under the conjunction of Pūrvabhādrapadā,
he indeed becomes happy after death, endowed with all kinds of food and fruits.
He who offers the meat of a ram under the constellation Uttarāphalgunī truly gratifies the ancestors and attains infinity after death.
He who gives away a cow with a bronze milking vessel under the constellation Revatī—
Taking those desires with her after death, she attends upon the giver.
By giving a chariot yoked with horses under the asterism Aśvinī, O best of men,
one is born into a family endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, and becomes possessed of splendor.
"By giving a cow made of sesame seeds to the twice-born under the asterism Bharaṇī,
a man indeed obtains abundant cattle and likewise fame after death.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus has this enumeration of characteristics been declared according to the conjunctions of the lunar mansions (nakṣatras).
Here, Nārada spoke this to Devakī, and she, in turn, told it to her daughters-in-law.
Bhīṣma said:
"Those who bestow gold grant all desires"—
thus spoke the Blessed Atri, the son of the Grandfather (Brahmā). It is purifying, pure, conducive to longevity, and for the ancestors, it is inexhaustible.
This was proclaimed by Hariścandra, the lord of men, as being worth 13,064 gold pieces.
Manu has declared that the gift of water is the supreme among all gifts;
therefore, one should cause step-wells, wells, and tanks to be dug.
A well that has water flowing from it and is constantly well-maintained removes half of a man's sinful karma in this world;
he for whom such a reservoir was dug carries his entire lineage across.
Cows, Brahmins, and virtuous men always drink from him whose water remains available without restriction during the heat of the summer season;
he never encounters difficult, treacherous, or painful circumstances.
Through clarified butter, there arises satisfaction for the venerable Bṛhaspati, as well as for Pūṣan, Bhaga,
the two Aśvins, and Agni;
for this is the supreme medicine and the highest of all sacrifices.
This is the best of liquids and this is the best of fruits. A man who desires fruit, who desires fame, and who always desires prosperity,
being pure and self-controlled, should give ghee to the twice-born.
To him who bestows clarified butter upon Brahmins in the month of Āśvayuja,
the two Aśvins, the gods, being pleased, grant their own form here in this world.
He who bestows milk-rice mixed with ghee upon the twice-born—
The Rākṣasas never dare to assault the house of one who gives water-jars; he does not die of thirst and appears well-favored;
and he shall never encounter misfortune, he who bestows water-jars.

A man who, being self-restrained and endowed with supreme faith, offers wood to the foremost of Brahmins, always obtains a sixth part of the merit of their ritual ablutions. This applies to one who gives wood to the Brahmins for the purpose of fuel.
O Indra among kings, for the sake of majesty, a man who always gives to those of virtuous conduct finds that his various objectives and undertakings are always successful; moreover,
he shines with physical splendor above all his enemies.
The Blessed One, the Fire-god, is always well-pleased with him;
cattle do not forsake him, and he is victorious even in battle. He who bestows an umbrella obtains sons and prosperity.
One does not suffer from eye disease and partakes in a share of the sacrifice.
He who provides an umbrella during the summer heat or the rainy season never experiences any burning affliction of the mind.
O Brahmin, through this [gift], one attains liberation from hardship and indeed from adversity.
The gift of a cart is distinguished above all other gifts;
thus spoke the illustrious and highly blessed seer Śāṇḍilya.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what fruit accrues to him who gives a pair of sandals to a Brahmin who is being burned."
13,065.002 Bhīṣma said: 13,065.002a He who, with a concentrated mind, bestows sandals upon Brāhmaṇas,
13,065.002c tramples all thorns underfoot and crosses over even the most treacherous difficulties.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, he stands above his enemies in battle;
O lord of the people, O son of Kuntī, a bright chariot yoked with mules and adorned with silver and gold attends upon him.
Indeed, a cart yoked with draft animals is given as well.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What fruit is proclaimed for the gift of sesame seeds and for the gift of land?"
"Tell me further, O Kaurava, regarding the gift of cows and the gift of food.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen to me, O son of Kuntī, concerning the fruit that results from the gift of sesame seeds."
"Having heard this, O best of the Kurus, grant [the gift] according to the rule.
Sesame seeds were created by the Self-Existent One as the first food for the ancestors;
therefore, indeed, the host of ancestors rejoices through the gift of sesame."

He who offers sesame seeds to Brahmins in the month of Māgha does not behold the hell crowded with all manner of beings. He who worships the ancestors with sesame seeds performs a sacrifice with all objects of desire.
A sesame *śrāddha* must never be given by one who is unwilling in any way.
These sesame seeds issued from the limbs of the great seer Kaśyapa;
therefore, O Lord, sesame seeds have attained a divine nature in the context of gifts.
They bestow nourishment, grant beauty, and likewise destroy evil;
therefore, the gift of sesame seeds is distinguished above all other gifts.
So too say Āpastamba, the wise Medhāvī, Śaṅkha, and Likhita.
The great seer Gautama also went to heaven by means of gifts of sesame seeds. Brahmins devoted to the oblation of sesame seeds, all of them restrained in sexual conduct,
became equal to those who offer oblations of cow's ghee and were established in the path of worldly activity.
Among all gifts, the gift of sesame seeds is remembered as supreme;
among all gifts, the gift of sesame seeds is said here to be inexhaustible.
And in ancient times, when the sacrificial oblation had been prepared, the seer Kuśika, O scorcher of foes, [proceeded].
Having offered three fires with 13,065.014c sesame seeds, he attained the highest state.
13,065.015a Thus has been declared, O best of the Kurus, the unsurpassed gift of sesame seeds,
13,065.015c according to the rule by which the ritual for sesame seeds is praised here.
13,065.016a Thereafter, O great king, learn of this meeting of the gods who desired to perform a sacrifice, with the self-existent Brahmā himself.
13,065.017a Having assembled before Brahmā, the gods, desiring to sacrifice, sought a portion of the earth.
"O King, they requested a beautiful place, saying, 'Let us sacrifice.
The gods said:
'O Blessed One, you are the lord of the earth and of all the triple heaven.'"
"O highly fortunate one, let us perform a sacrifice with your permission;
for one who has not obtained the land's consent does not enjoy the fruit of the sacrifice.
For you are the master of the entire world, both the stationary and the moving."
"Therefore, you are the master; you ought to grant me permission.
Brahmā said:
"O bulls among the gods, I shall give a portion of the earth to you."
"In whatever region you shall perform the sacrifice, O delighters of Kaśyapa," [they said].
The gods replied:
"O Blessed One, our desires are fulfilled; we shall perform the sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees."
"13,065.021c But the sages always attend upon this region.
Bhīṣma said:
"13,065.022a Then Agastya, Kaṇva, Bhṛgu, Atri, and Vṛṣākapi..."
Asita and Devala likewise approached the sacrifice of the gods. Then, O Acyuta, the high-souled gods, those bulls among the Suras, performed the sacrifice and completed it at the proper time.
Those gods, who had performed their sacrifices, were on Himavat, the best of mountains;
they determined that the gift of land should constitute one-sixth of that sacrifice.
For he who gives even a span's measure of land, provided it is not defiled, [attains great merit].

He does not falter in times of distress, nor does he encounter difficulties. By bestowing a well-prepared site for a house that can withstand cold, wind, and heat, one dwells in the world of the gods and is not displaced even at the exhaustion of merit.
The wise man dwells in joy together with Śakra, O King; even the giver of shelter is honored in heaven. Born into a family of teachers, he is a learned Vedic scholar with his senses restrained.

He in whose house [a guest] dwells contented attains the foremost world; likewise, O best of the Bharatas, he who provides for the sake of cows a large shelter capable of withstanding cold and rain saves his lineage up to the seventh generation.
By giving a field of arable land in this world, O son, one obtains prosperity;
by giving a land of jewels, however, one causes the lineage of the family to flourish. One should never, under any circumstances, give land that is barren or scorched.
Nor [should one perform it] in a place surrounded by a cremation ground, nor in a place frequented by evildoers. If one should offer the ancestral oblation (nirvapet) on land belonging to another,
that *śrāddha* rite is obstructed by the ancestors of the owner of that land.
Therefore, a wise person, having purchased land, should give it away, even if it be very small;
for the funeral cake (piṇḍa) offered to the ancestors upon it becomes eternal.
This applies to forests, mountains, riverbanks, and whatever sacred bathing places (tīrthas) there may be.
"13,065.034c All things are said to be ownerless, for there is no possession therein.
13,065.035a Thus has the fruit of the gift of land been declared, O lord of the people.
13,065.035c Hereafter, however, I shall proclaim to you, O sinless one, the gift of cows."
"Since cows are superior to all ascetics whatsoever,
therefore the god Maheśvara has resorted to austerity by means of them.
O Bhārata, these dwell in the world of Brahmā together with Soma."
The perfected Brahman-sages seek the supreme goal through these [gifts];
by giving such a cow, they attain that state, liberated from all sins—
whether by means of its milk, sacrificial oblation, curds, dung, or even its hide.
O Bhārata, they assist with their bones, horns, and hair;
for them, cold and heat are ever present as they perform their labor. Neither rain nor uneven terrain causes them any suffering.

Accompanied by Brāhmaṇas, they proceed to that supreme state beyond; therefore, the wise declare that a single cow and a Brāhmaṇa are one and the same. At the sacrifice of Rantideva, they were prepared to serve as sacrificial animals.
Then, O King, the Carmaṇvatī river was set in motion from the cow-hides;
and those [hides], released from their state as cattle, were prepared for distribution. He who gives these to the foremost of Brahmins, O lord of the earth—
O King, even when situated in a precarious position, one who bestows ten thousand cows overcomes a difficult and dire calamity; such a giver of a thousand cows does not behold hell after death,
O lord of men, and attains victory everywhere.
"The milk of cows is indeed nectar," so said the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.
Therefore, he who gives a cow bestows nectar. For those who know the Vedas understand that this is the imperishable sacrificial fuel for the fires.
Therefore, he who gives a cow offers the sacrificial oblation itself;
for this bull, the lord of cattle, is heaven incarnate. He who gives him to a virtuous Brahmin is indeed glorified in heaven.
"O bull among the Bharatas, these cows are said to be the very life-breaths of living beings. Therefore, he who gives a cow truly bestows life-breaths.
Those who know the Vedas understand that cows are the refuge of all creatures."
Therefore, he who gives a cow provides a refuge;
she should not be given for the purpose of slaughter, nor to a farmer, nor to an atheist,
O bull among men, nor should a cow be given to one who lives by the breeding of cattle.
The wise have said that a man who gives cows to such evil-doers— those who sell dairy products and those who do not perform the five sacrifices— goes to an inexhaustible hell.

One should not give to a Brāhmaṇa a cow that is emaciated, one whose calf has died, one that is barren, nor likewise one afflicted by disease; nor should one give a cow that is mutilated or exhausted. One who properly gives ten thousand cows rejoices together with Śakra.
A man who gives a hundred thousand [cows] obtains inexhaustible worlds. Thus has the gift of cows and the gift of sesame seeds been proclaimed;
likewise, O Bhārata, hear now concerning the gift of land and the gift of food.
"O Kaunteya, they declare that the gift of food is indeed preeminent;
for by the gift of food, Rantideva ascended to heaven. O lord of the earth, he who bestows food upon one who is weary and hungry [attains great merit]."

O lord of men, he beholds the highly fortunate Svāyambhuva Manu; O Bhārata, O Lord, men do not attain such supreme welfare through gifts of gold, nor through garments, nor through the gift of horses, as they do here by givers of food.
Food is indeed the supreme substance; food is considered the highest prosperity.
From food, vital breath arises, as do energy, vigor, and strength.
That man who always gives food to the virtuous with a one-pointed mind, [attains these rewards].
"He does not encounter difficulties," thus said Parāśara.
Having honored [the guests] according to the rule, one should offer food to the gods; for whatever food a man eats, O King, his deities eat that same food.
Furthermore, he who bestows food during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika crosses over all difficulties and,
after death, enjoys infinity.
He who, with a concentrated mind, offers food to a guest before eating himself, [attains the same].

O bull of the Bharatas, he shall indeed attain the worlds of those who know Brahman; even when fallen into a most difficult calamity, the man who gives food shall cross over it. He crosses over sin in this world and casts off his evil deeds.
Thus, indeed, has been proclaimed the fruit of the gift of food, the gift of sesame seeds, the gift of land, and the gift of cows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O dear one, I have heard the fruit of giving that has been proclaimed by you. But among these, O Bhārata, the gift of food is especially praised here.
How is it that the gift of water is supreme and of such great fruit in this world?"
"O Grandfather, I wish to hear this in detail.
Bhīṣma said:
"Behold, O bull of the Bharatas, I shall relate it to you exactly as it is."
"O you of true prowess, listen now as I speak here;
O sinless one, I shall tell you everything from the time of that gift of water. Whatever food and whatever drink a man enjoys after having first bestowed them [upon others],"
It is my conviction that there is no gift superior to that;
for, dear one, all living beings subsist entirely upon food.
Therefore, among all gifts in this world, food is said to be the supreme.
From food, strength and energy always increase for living beings;
therefore, Prajāpati has declared that the gift of food is the most excellent.
Indeed, O son of Kuntī, you have heard these auspicious words even from Sāvitrī.
For this reason and in this manner, O Mahāmati, at the sacrifice to the gods,
when food is given by a man here on earth, life itself is indeed bestowed;
for there is no gift in this world superior to the gift of life.
"O mighty-armed one, you have indeed heard those words of Lomaśa as well—
how Śibi attained his goal in the past by giving up his own life for the sake of a pigeon.
O lord of the people, one attains that same state by giving food to a twice-born man."
"We have heard that those who give life go to an exalted state.
Furthermore, O best of the Kurus, even food originates from water;
indeed, nothing at all proceeds without that which is born from water."
The Blessed One, Soma, the lord of the hosts of planets, is free from passion;
likewise are nectar, ambrosia, *svāhā*, and *vaṣaṭ*;
as well as food, medicinal herbs, O great king, and creepers born of water.
O Lord of the People, from this [soma] the life-breaths of all living beings arise;
it is the nectar (*amṛta*) of the gods, the ambrosia (*sudhā*) of the serpents,
the *svadhā* of the ancestors, and likewise the herbs for animals.
The wise say that food alone is the life-breath of human beings;
and all of that, O tiger among men, originates from water.
Therefore, there is indeed nothing superior to the gift of water anywhere.
A man who desires his own prosperity should always give that [gift], O Lord of the People; for the gift of water brings wealth, fame, and long life.
Furthermore, O Son of Kuntī, the giver of water always stands above his enemies.
He obtains all his desires and eternal fame in this world;
after death, he attains infinity and is liberated from all sins. O tiger among men, O one of great luster, the giver of water goes to heaven.
"Manu declared that one attains imperishable worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What kind of gift is there for sesame seeds, and likewise for a lamp?"
"Tell me further about food and clothing.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."

And [herein is] the dialogue between a Brahmin and Yama, O Yudhiṣṭhira. In the Middle Country, there was once a great village of Brahmins situated between the Gaṅgā and the Yamunā, at the foot of the Yamunā mountain.
"O lord of men, there is a delightful place known as Parṇaśālā;
at that time, many learned Brāhmaṇas resided there.
Then Yama spoke to a certain man dressed in black garments:"

"Go to the village of the Brahmins; having gone there, bring that Agastya, who is known by his lineage and by the name Śarmin— [he who has] red eyes, hair standing on end, and whose shins, eyes, and nose resemble those of a crow."
Do not bring another teacher who is established in tranquility, wise, and respected; nor one who belongs to the same lineage as he,
for such a person would be equal to him in both learning and birth.
"Regarding offspring and likewise conduct, he was entirely wise;
bring him here as instructed, for I must pay him honor. Having gone, he acted in opposition to that command of Yama.
Having seized him—who had been forbidden by Yama—he brought him back.
Rising up and offering him honor, the powerful Yama said to him:
"Let this one be led away; let that other one be brought here."
When these words had been spoken by the King of Dharma, that twice-born man,
despondent with his Vedic studies, replied to the King of Dharma:
"O Acyuta, I would dwell here for whatever time remains to me."
Yama said:
"I do not, by any means, encounter here that which is ordained for Time;
indeed, I know only him who practices righteousness."
"Go now this very day, O Brahmin of great splendor, to your own abode.
Or rather, tell me as you wish: what may I do for you?
The Brahmin said:
"Tell me that by performing which there would be very great merit;
for you, O best of beings, are the authority for all, even for the three worlds.
Yama said:
"Listen, O brahmin-sage, to the supreme procedure for giving in its true essence:
sesame seeds are the highest gift, meritorious and eternal in this world.
O bull among the twice-born, sesame seeds should be bestowed according to one's capacity."
Through constant giving, sesame seeds indeed fulfill all desires;
they praise the gift of sesame at a *śrāddha*, for this is an unsurpassed offering.
Bestow them upon the Brahmins according to the rites prescribed by rule.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, one should give sesame seeds to the twice-born;
by giving them on the full moon day of Māgha, one shall obtain all desires. Sesame seeds should always be eaten, and one should also perform anointing with them.

Those who desire their own welfare should always strive with all their soul for what ought to be done within the home; likewise, water should always be given and offered for drinking— of this there is no doubt—
and one should have lotus-pools, ponds, and wells dug there.
"O best of the twice-born, this is exceedingly difficult to attain in this world.
You should constantly give water, for this is indeed the unsurpassed merit. Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, you should always establish water-stations for the purpose of providing drink."

"Even when you have finished eating, water must especially be offered to you. When he had been told this by that messenger of Yama, he was led back to his home and carried out everything according to Yama’s command.
Having led him away and seized Śarmiṇ, the messenger of Yama then went to the King of Dharma and presented him before him.
The powerful King of Dharma, having honored that knower of dharma, [spoke].
Having made an agreement with him, he sent him back as he had come;
and Yama gave him all instruction, which he, upon returning, carried out exactly as Yama had told him.
In this way, Yama praises those who offer lamps out of a desire for the welfare of their ancestors.
Seeing one who requests water, one should give it with joy and haste; by giving even as much oil as the thickness of a thread in a lamp, one obtains a year’s worth of merit for every moment.
One enjoys the pleasures of heaven in proportion to the number of hairs on a cow;
[one gains it] in proportion to the number of drops of water [offered]. Therefore, you should offer these. Consequently, one who constantly gives lamps truly delivers his ancestors.
Therefore, O best of the Bharatas, lamps should always be offered;
for they are considered, O Lord, to be the eyes of both the gods and the ancestors.
And the gift of jewels, O ruler of men, is said to be a source of very great merit.

Having sold those [goods], a Brāhmaṇa performs sacrifice, for he is the granter of fearlessness. Whatever a Brāhmaṇa gives to other learned men after having himself received it, that becomes inexhaustible for both the giver and the receiver.

Manu, the knower of dharma, has declared that when one who is established in his own station gives a gift to another likewise established, the merit of both is inexhaustible. Furthermore, by the gift of garments, a man remains devoted to his own wife.
"He becomes well-clothed and well-attired; so we have heard.
Cows, gold, and likewise sesame seeds have been described at great length, O tiger among men, based on the authority of the Vedas."
One should indeed perform marriages and procreate sons;
for the acquisition of a son, O Kauravya, excels all other acquisitions.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
13,068.001a Furthermore, O best of the Kurus, tell us once more the supreme rule regarding gifts, 13,068.001c especially concerning the gift of land, O man of great wisdom.
A Kṣatriya should give the earth, and a Brāhmaṇa [should receive] it through his own duty.

One should accept [it] according to the prescribed rule, but no one else is entitled to give it. You ought to explain to me that which can be given by members of all castes who desire the fruit, or that which is recited in the Veda.
Bhīṣma said:
Three things have identical names and yield identical fruits;
they grant all desired rewards in this world: cows, the earth, and Sarasvatī.
He who imparts to a disciple the righteous, divine Sarasvatī [the Veda] enjoys a fruit equal to that of giving land and cows;
likewise, they praise cows, and there is nothing superior to them as a gift.
For they yield immediate fruits and provide easy benefits, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
cows are the mothers of all beings, bestowing every happiness. One who constantly desires prosperity should always circumambulate cows with reverence.
One should not strike them with the foot, nor should one walk through the midst of cows.
O Goddess, since they are the abode of auspiciousness, they must always be honored. The impelling of cows toward their tasks is ordained by the gods.
The syllable [Om] alone is the primary [object], and nothing else whatsoever is to be expressed.
Whether they are grazing or at a watering place, a wise man should not cause alarm to the cows; for thirsty cows, looking up [at him], might destroy a man along with his kinsmen.

The abodes of the ancestors and the temples of the gods are constantly purified by the dung of those [cows]; what, then, could be more pure than them? He who gives a handful of fodder to another's cow for the duration of a year—
By not taking food oneself, one performs that vow which fulfills all desires.
Indeed, such a person attains sons, fame, and prosperity;
it destroys inauspiciousness and dispels evil dreams.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

What are the characteristics of the cows that should be given as gifts, and which ones should be avoided? To what kind of person should they be given, and to what kind of person should they not be given?

13,068.014 Bhīṣma said: A cow should never, under any circumstances, be given to one of evil conduct, to a sinner, to a greedy man, to a liar, or to one who has abandoned the offerings to the gods and ancestors.
By giving ten cows to a learned Brahmin who has many sons and maintains the sacred fires, a donor attains unsurpassed worlds;
and whatever righteous deed he performs, as well as the fruit of that merit— [he gains all of these].

When one offers oblations, feeds others, or gives gifts with the products of cows, the giver becomes a sharer in every part thereof; all activities are undertaken for that purpose. Furthermore, the giver of wealth receives a tenth part of it for the sake of turning away from [unwholesome] activity.
