He who procreates him, he who protects him from fear, and he who provides his livelihood—all three of these are fathers. Service to the guru destroys sin; pride destroys great fame.
Three sons [remedy] childlessness, and ten cows [remedy] lack of livelihood—
for one who is established in the Vedānta, who is deeply learned,
who is satisfied with wisdom, and whose senses are conquered.

For one who is disciplined, self-controlled, and restrained, who always speaks kindly toward all beings, and who indeed does not perform improper acts out of fear of hunger— (13,068.020a) [he shall attain the highest state].
Gentle, self-controlled, and always hospitable,
he should provide a livelihood to that brahmin who is of similar character and who has a wife and sons.
Whatever merits there are in the gift of a cow when placed in a worthy recipient,
such is the fault incurred in the theft of a Brahmin’s property; indeed, the theft of a Brahmin’s property is a transgression under all circumstances.
And their wives must be avoided from afar.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Furthermore, how great is the fault incurred by the theft of a Brāhmaṇa’s property?"

"What is said to be the property of a Brahmin? Tell me that, O Grandfather. When the wife of a Brahmin, his wealth, or his collection of property is seized by another, those who are capable of rescuing them—whether they do so or die in the attempt—to them I offer my salutations."
Yama, the son of Vivasvat, does not release those who do not protect [the cows] once they have been slain; constantly punishing and rebuking them, he casts them into the hells.
Likewise, regarding the protection or the mistreatment of cows, there is merit or demerit.
Whether among Brahmins, cattle, or especially in protected houses,
one who has died does not attain heaven while accompanied by sons and grandsons.
Bhīṣma said:
In this very context, O bull of the Kurus, the virtuous proclaim the great hardship that was endured by Nṛga for violating the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
so it is heard, O Pārtha, that in ancient times, when Dvāravatī was being established as a city.
A great well, covered over with grass and creepers, was seen there.
Those seeking water from that well made an effort,
yet they were joined by great exhaustion because that water was so completely concealed.
They beheld a giant lizard standing there;
they made thousands of efforts to pull it out,
having bound that mountain-like creature with reins and leather straps.
They were unable to lift it out; therefore, they went to Janārdana.
"A great lizard remains covering the opening of the well;
there is no one who can lift it out," they then reported to Kṛṣṇa.
He was rescued by Vāsudeva,
and when questioned regarding his desires,
King Nṛga then revealed himself.
To him who was speaking thus, describing himself as an ancient performer of a thousand sacrifices, Mādhava said:
"An auspicious deed has been performed by you, not an evil one."
"O Lord of Men, tell me how you have come to such a miserable state; what is the cause of this?
[I would give] a hundred thousand, indeed a hundred cows."
Furthermore, we have heard here that you previously gave eight hundred and thirteen thousand and nine (13,069,009) [coins] to the twice-born; O King, where indeed has that of yours gone?
Then Nṛga said to Kṛṣṇa: "A certain cow belonging to a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires and was away from home strayed into my herd of cattle;
she was counted among my thousand cows by my herdsmen at that time."
"She was given by me to a brahmin who desired her for the sake of the afterlife. And searching for her, that twice-born man saw her in another's house;
the brahmin to whom she belonged said, 'She is mine.'"
Both of them arrived together, disputing and burning with intense fever;
then they both said to me, "You are the giver! You are the taker!"—and indeed, by means of an exchange of a hundred cows, numbering exactly one hundred.
I entreated the recipient, but he said this to me:
"This cow, endowed with the right place and time, yielding milk, patient, and exceedingly affectionate, provides sweet milk; she is a blessing who has always resided in my home."
"The cow that sustains my emaciated, infantless son—she cannot be abandoned by me. Having said this, he departed.
Then, I indeed entreated that other brahmin for an exchange.
"Let a hundred thousand cows indeed be accepted for his sake.
The Brahmin said:
"I do not accept gifts from kings; I am capable of seeking my own livelihood."
"O Madhusūdana, let that very cow be given to me quickly!
Though he was being offered gold, horses, silver, and chariots,
that bull among brahmins did not accept them and departed.
At that very time, however, impelled by the law of time,
I reached the world of the ancestors and approached Dharmarāja. Yama, having honored me, then spoke these words:
"O King, there is no end to the counting of your meritorious deeds;
yet you have also committed some sin through ignorance. You may undergo the consequences of that sin either later or earlier, as you wish."
"You said, 'I am protected,' yet your promise has proven false;

furthermore, you have seized the property of a Brāhmaṇa—thus, O Lord, you have committed a threefold transgression. First I shall undergo penance, and afterwards [I shall perform] what is auspicious."
"O Dharmarāja, as I was speaking thus, I fell to the surface of the earth. Having fallen, I heard Yama speaking loudly:
'Vāsudeva, Janārdana, shall be your deliverer.'"
When a full thousand years have passed and your evil karma is exhausted, you shall attain the eternal worlds won by your own deeds. Indeed,
I saw myself fallen headlong into a well.
"Though I have entered the womb of an animal, my mindfulness has not abandoned me.
I have been delivered by you today; what could this be other than the power of asceticism?
Grant me leave, O Kṛṣṇa, for I shall indeed go to heaven this very day."
Permitted by Kṛṣṇa and having paid homage to Janārdana,
that subduer of enemies ascended a divine celestial chariot and departed for heaven.
Then, O best of the Bharatas, when Nṛga had reached heaven, [the people were filled with wonder].
O descendant of Kuru, Vāsudeva recited this verse:
"A wise man must not seize the property of a Brāhmaṇa;
for the property of a Brāhmaṇa, once seized, destroys the taker, just as the Brāhmaṇa’s cow destroyed Nṛga."
"O Pārtha, an assembly with the virtuous never exists without fruit for the virtuous.
Behold Nṛga, who was liberated from hell through association with the righteous. In such a gathering, a gift bears fruit, and likewise, an act of malice is fruitless."
"Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should avoid any neglect toward cows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sinless one, tell me of the attainment of the fruits for those cows that have been given as gifts."
"O mighty-armed one, tell me in detail; indeed, I am not satiated.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The words of both the seer Uddālaka and Naciketas: Having undertaken the consecration for sacrifice, the seer Uddālaka then addressed his son Naciketas, saying, "You must attend upon me."
When that observance was completed, the great seer spoke to his son:
"For one who is devoted to ritual ablutions and intent upon the private recitation of the Vedas,
there should be fuel-sticks, *darbha* grass, flowers, and a water-pot placed near the water."

"I forgot it; having taken it from the riverbank, come here. Having gone there and not found any of it, as it had been swept away by the force of the river, the sage said to his father, "I do not see it."
Then the sage Uddālaka, overcome by hunger, thirst, and fatigue— that man of great asceticism— cursed his son, saying, "Behold Yama!
Thus struck by his father with that thunderbolt of a word, he stood with palms joined in reverence.
Even as he was saying, "Be gracious," his life departed and he fell to the ground.
Seeing Naciketas fallen, his father fainted from grief;
crying out, "What have I done? he collapsed upon the surface of the earth.
As he embraced his own son, overwhelmed by grief,
that remainder of the day passed away, as did that fierce night,
O best of the Kurus; and through the falling of those paternal tears, Nāciketa [was restored].
He stirred upon his silken bed like a crop drenched by rain.
He questioned that praiseworthy son who had returned once more—
himself now anointed with divine fragrances, like one risen from the exhaustion of sleep.
"O son, by your own deeds you have surely won auspicious worlds;
by good fortune you have returned again, for your body is no longer human.
Having been questioned by my high-souled father, I am one who has seen everything with my own eyes."
In the midst of his father and the great seers, he announced that [name] which was true to its meaning:
"Carrying out your command, I have indeed gone quickly to Viśālā, which possesses beautiful splendor."
Having reached the assembly hall of Vaivasvata, I beheld it,
extending for thousands of yojanas with a ground of gold;
as soon as he saw me approaching toward him, [he spoke].
Having offered him a seat in his home,
Vaivasvata honored me with guest-offerings and other rites of hospitality, and he worshipped me for your sake.
Then I spoke softly to him,
who was surrounded by the members of the assembly and being honored:
"O Dharmarāja, I have arrived within your domain."
"Grant me those worlds which I deserve.
Yama replied to me, "O gentle one, you are not dead;
however, that ascetic told you, 'Behold Yama.'"
"O Brahmin, my father possesses a splendor like a blazing fire; it is not possible for me to speak a falsehood to him.
You have seen me; now go back, dear father."
That creator of your body grieves;
O dear guest, I shall grant whatever is desired by your mind— choose your wishes.
Being addressed by him in this way, I replied to him:
"I have reached your domain, from which it is difficult to turn back;
I desire to see the prosperous abodes of those who have performed meritorious deeds."
"If I am worthy of a boon, [then] that god, having placed me upon a vehicle yoked with horses— resplendent and radiant— to see the worlds," (13.70.20a)
Then, O best of the twice-born, he showed me all the worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds;
there I beheld the luminous abodes of those who had purified their souls.
They possess various forms and shapes and are composed entirely of jewels; they are as bright as the lunar orb, adorned with networks of tinkling bells,
and consist of many hundreds of stories containing internal groves and forests.
Shining like lapis lazuli and the sun, made of silver and gold,
with the hue of the rising sun— both stationary and moving,
mountains consisting of various kinds of food, as well as garments and beds.
And there were trees situated within the dwellings that bore the fruit of every desire;
everywhere there were rivers, streets, assembly halls, ponds, and oblong lakes;
and there were thousands of resonant vehicles already yoked and ready.
The rivers flow with milk and the mountains likewise with pure ghee and water. Indeed,
the rivers flow with milk and the mountains likewise with ghee.
The water was pure and indeed sweet in every way;
I beheld many regions, never seen before, approved by Vaivasvata.
Having seen all that, I spoke to the ancient and powerful Dharmarāja:
"These are rivers of milk and clarified butter."
"Whose food, O Śaśvat-srotas, are these said to be?
Yama replied, "Know that these are to be eaten by you—
those who are virtuous givers of dairy products."
Other worlds, eternal and free from sorrow,
are crowded with those who delight in the gift of cows;
yet, the mere act of giving these [other gifts] is not praised in the same way.
Having understood the recipient, the time, the specific qualities of the cow, and the ritual procedure, one should indeed give a gift of cattle to a Brahmin;
for it is difficult to discern the difference between them when they have become like fire and the sun.
A Brāhmaṇa who is rich in Vedic study, who practices excessive austerity, and who is established in the performance of the Vedic sacrifices, is a worthy recipient for these [gifts].
So too are those released from hardship and those who have come seeking nourishment.
Through these gateways, specific types of cows are praised:
13,070.031a. Having fasted for three nights on water while sleeping on the ground, satisfied cows should be given to those who have been gratified.
Delighted by their calves, possessing good offspring, and provided with attendants,
they should subsist on dairy products for three days after giving [the gift].
Having given a cow of excellent character, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel;
One who possesses a cow that has healthy calves and does not flee shall enjoy the heavenly world for as many years as there are hairs upon her body.
Likewise, having given to a Brahmin a bull that is well-trained, capable of bearing the yoke, strong, young,
capable of supporting his family, vigorous, and large in stature;
He enjoys worlds equal in number to ten thousand cows given as a gift.
They say that one who is patient toward cows, a refuge for cows, grateful, and destitute of a livelihood— such a person is a worthy recipient.
In cases of distress regarding one's livelihood, or in times of emergency, or for a great purpose;
for the sake of agriculture, or for the purpose of a fire-oblation, or upon childbirth;
or for the sake of a preceptor, or for the nourishment of children, or due to an affliction; [one may take what is not given].
The time and place for giving cows are not restricted:
those born in one's own household, those acquired through fair purchase or knowledge,
those bought with one's life, those won in battle, and those obtained from water.
He who desires to go to the world of the gods should give cows that are righteous in nature to the twice-born.
Nāciketa said:
Having heard the words of Vaivasvata, I spoke to him again:
"How does one who possesses no cows attain the worlds of those who give cows?
Thereupon, the wise Yama described the supreme goal attained through the gift of cows.

In the alternative procedure for the gift of a cow, there are those who give cows even in the absence of a cow. He who, being restrained in his vows, gives a cow made of clarified butter when cows are unavailable—
these [streams of clarified butter] flow for him like affectionate mother-cows.
And he who, firm in his vows, should give a sesame-cow when ghee is unavailable,
is delivered from misfortune by that cow and rejoices in a river of milk.
And he who, firm in his vows, should give a water-cow when sesame seeds are unavailable, [attains the same reward].
"He enjoys this cool river named Kāmapravahā.
O Acyuta, the King of Dharma showed me these and other such things there,
and upon seeing them, I experienced supreme joy.
I also wish to announce something pleasing to you:
O father, a great sacrifice requiring little expenditure has been obtained by me; it shall be performed by me.
Engaged in the performance of Vedic injunctions, he shall attain [his goal];
for this curse of yours was obtained by me as a favor,
wherein Yama was seen by me.
Having seen there the great fruit of giving,
I shall undoubtedly practice the dharma of charity.
And the King of Dharma said this to me:
O best of the twice-born, being repeatedly delighted,
you have always been diligent in giving, my dear;
indeed, you should especially practice the gift of cows.
For a pure person should not be disregarded regarding his own duty;
a gift should be given to a worthy recipient when the proper place and time have arrived.
Therefore, cows must always be given by you.
And let there be no doubt in you regarding this:
in former times, those whose minds were tranquil and who were established on the path of giving constantly bestowed these [gifts].
Performing fierce austerities without hesitation,
they indeed gave gifts according to their capacity; at the proper time and according to their means, having abandoned all stinginess.
Those of pure self, endowed with faith and virtuous conduct,
having given gifts and performed austerities, have attained that world;
and those of virtuous conduct shine brilliantly in the celestial realm.
This gift, acquired through righteous means, should be bestowed upon the twice-born after examining whether they are worthy recipients; one should observe the vow for ten days on the Kāmyāṣṭamī.
One who gives a bull becomes a keeper of Vedic vows, subsisting on the milk, dung, or urine of cows;
by the gift of a pair of cows, one attains the acquisition of the Vedas.
By the gift of a cow yoked to a plow, one attains the merit of visiting sacred fords (*tīrtha*);
by the gift of a *kapilā* cow, there is the casting off of sins. Having bestowed even a single *kapilā* cow, [one obtains this reward].
One who acts with justice shall be liberated from sin.
There is nothing superior to the essence of cows;
they say that the gift of cows is exceedingly great.
Cows sustain the worlds by flowing with milk;
cows produce food in the world. He who, knowing this, does not attain the heart of the cows—
That evil-minded man will surely go to hell,
even though you intended to give him a thousand cows, or a hundred,
or fifty, or ten, along with their excellent calves.
Or even a single one to a virtuous Brāhmaṇa; by that, she becomes for him in the next world a river of sacred bathing-places (puṇyatīrtha),
through its attainment, nourishment, and protection of the world.
Cows are equal to the rays of the sun upon the earth (13,070.053); their sound is one, as is their lineage and their utility;
therefore, the giver of cows shines like the sun.
A disciple should choose a preceptor for the gift of a cow;
he indeed is the speaker who invariably bestows heaven.
This is the most excellent dharma among those who know the ritual injunctions.
For all ordinances depend upon the primordial ordinance. Therefore, having examined it, you should bestow this gift— righteously acquired— upon the twice-born who are worthy recipients.
"O Great Seer, when I was thus addressed by the King of Dharma: 'The immortals and human beings place their hopes in you, and we too, being of virtuous character, do so as you spread abroad.'"
Having bowed my head to that righteous-souled one and being permitted by Vaivasvata,
I have returned to the presence of the Blessed One's feet.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, you have indeed described the gift of cows to the sage Nāciketa,
and you have also spoken of the greatness of cows in brief."
O Grandfather, O high-minded one, you know how the great-souled Nṛga experienced suffering due to a single offense committed through ignorance;
and how he was delivered when Dvāravatī was being established.

"Kṛṣṇa became the cause of my liberation; that too has been understood by me. However, O Lord, I have a doubt regarding the world of the cows, which I wish to hear in its true nature—where those who give cows enter."
13,071.005 Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
just as Śatakratu once asked this very same thing of the Lotus-born One.
Śakra said:
"I see the inhabitants of Goloka surpassing the splendor of the dwellers of the heavenly world with their own radiance as they travel; herein lies my doubt."
"O Blessed One, O sinless one, tell me what kind of worlds those are for cows, which the givers inhabit; I wish to know this.
What are they like? What are their fruits? And what indeed is the supreme quality therein?"
And how do men go there, freed from all feverish distress?
For how long a time does the giver enjoy the fruit of his gift?
And how may a gift be of many kinds, or how may it be even though small?
13,071.010a What kind of gift is given by many, or what kind by few? 13,071.010c How can there be givers of cows without having given [anything else]? Tell me that.
13,071.011a And how, O Lord, can one who gives much be equal to one who gives little?
"O Lord, how can one who gives little become a giver of much in this world?
What kind of sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is especially distinguished in the gift of a cow?
O Blessed One, you ought to explain this to me truthfully."
Brahmā said:
"O Śatakratu, as for this question concerning the eligibility for the gift of cows that you have asked,
there is indeed no one else in this world besides you who could ask it."
"O Śakra, there exist various worlds that you do not see;
yet I see those worlds, as well as women who have been devoted to a single husband and sages of excellent vows through their most auspicious deeds."
For those Brāhmaṇas of auspicious conduct go to those worlds with their very bodies;
through the liberation of laying down the body and by means of a pure mind,
those of firm vows behold those worlds even here as if they were in a dream.
O Thousand-eyed One, hear now what qualities those worlds possess:
there time does not pass, nor does old age, nor does evil;
likewise, there is nothing else inauspicious, nor is there disease or fatigue there.
O Vāsava, whatever those cows desired in their minds,
they brought all that to pass before my very eyes; moving at will and acting according to their desire, they enjoyed every object of their longing.
Ponds, lakes, rivers, various forests,
houses, mountains, and whatever material objects there may be—
all that is pleasing to all beings is seen there.
Know that such are those worlds; there is no world superior to them.
There, O Śakra, the best of men—those who endure all things, who are patient, compassionate, devoted to their teachers, and free from egoism—go to dwell.
That man who does not eat any kind of meat at all,
who is ever intent upon reaching the end [of suffering], who honors his mother and father, and who is joined with truth;
He was irreproachable in his service to the brahmins,
free from anger toward cows as well as toward the twice-born,
devoted to dharma, and a servant of his gurus.
Devoted to truthful conduct for as long as he lives,
intent on giving, and patient toward offenses; gentle, self-controlled, and devoted to the gods.
Likewise, a man who is hospitable to all guests and compassionate—
one possessing such qualities— proceeds to the eternal and imperishable world of cows.
The adulterer does not see this world,
nor indeed the killer of a guru, nor the speaker of falsehoods,
nor the Brahmin who is constantly slanderous and has abandoned the Vedas.
Furthermore, that evil-souled man who is possessed of other faults—
one who betrays friends, is deceitful, ungrateful, treacherous, crooked, and a hater of dharma— [is also excluded].
"Even in thought, a slayer of a Brahmin shall not behold the world of cows, the abode of those who perform meritorious deeds.
All this has been explained to you with precision, O Lord of the Gods."
O Śatakratu, hear now the fruit for those who delight in the gift of cows:
he who, having purchased cows with wealth obtained through inheritance, bestows them upon others,
enjoys imperishable worlds acquired by means of wealth earned through righteous conduct.
O Śakra, he who, having won wealth at dice, purchases cows and bestows them [upon others], enjoys the fruit of ten thousand celestial years. Indeed,
his cows are an inheritance, acquired through righteous means.
Those cows, when given away, become imperishable and eternal for their donors. And he who, having received them, should give them away with a perfectly pure heart—
for him too, O Lord of Śacī, know that there are eternal worlds here that are imperishable.
He who has restrained his senses since birth, who speaks the truth,
who endures his teacher and the twice-born, and who is patient— his destination is equal to that of the cows.
O Lord of Śacī, one must never address anything improper to a Brāhmaṇa.

One should not bear malice toward cows even in thought; one whose conduct is that of a cow-protector, who is compassionate toward cows, and who is devoted to truth and righteousness—listen, O Śakra, to the fruit thereof:
for him, even a single cow becomes equal to a thousand cows.
Listen to the fruit for a Kṣatriya endowed with these qualities:
it is certain that even for him, the cow becomes equal to a hundred.
If these qualities belong to a Vaiśya, his [reward] shall be fifty.

For a humble Śūdra as well, a one-fourth share of the fruit is ordained. And he who, being disciplined, practices this very way— endowed with truthfulness and service to his teacher— [attains the full reward].
Self-controlled, patient, worshipping the deities, tranquil, pure, awakened, virtuous in dharma,
and free from the notion of "I," he attains a great fruit for the sake of the twice-born.
Having given a milch cow according to this rite,
one should always eat but a single meal daily and remain ever established in truth, devoted to the service of the guru.
One who studies the Vedas, one who possesses devotion toward cows,
one who always rejoices upon seeing cows,
and one who bows to cows from birth;
O Śakra, understand this fruit of that [merit]:
it is the very fruit one would obtain by performing the Rājasūya sacrifice,
or by sacrificing with vast amounts of gold.
All the virtuous ones, the ṛṣis, and those who have attained perfection say that the fruit of this is equal to the highest; he who,
having first partaken of something himself, should give it to his devotees.
One who constantly observes the cow-vow toward cows, speaks the truth,
is peaceful, and awakened— such a person of virtuous conduct shall, within a year, obtain the merit of a thousand cows.
He who eats but a single meal and gives one [cow] to others, observing the cow-vow and showing compassion for cattle for ten endless years;
and he who, having purchased a cow with the proceeds of that very single meal, bestows it [as a gift].
For as many days as are proclaimed for him, O Śatakratu,
for that many hundreds of cows he obtains eternal fruit;
such a person attains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
This fruit which has been declared for a *kṣatriya* is indeed [half] that of a *brāhmaṇa*; listen. This fruit of a *kṣatriya* is traditionally held to last for five years;
half of that belongs to a *vaiśya*, and a *śūdra* is traditionally held to receive half of the *vaiśya*'s portion.
And he who, having sold himself and purchased cows, bestows them as a gift— indeed,
for as many cows as he may touch, for that many years he enjoys the fruit; O highly fortunate one, it is taught that for every single hair on those cows, his worlds shall be inexhaustible.

"O Kauśika, know that those cows which one bestows after acquiring them in battles are equal to the sale of one's own self; they yield eternal fruit. If, however, one is unable to obtain cows, he who, firm in his vows, gives a cow made of sesame seeds,"
Rescued from distress by the cow, he rejoices in a river of milk.
However, it is not merely the act of giving these cows that is praised;
rather, the recipient, the time, the specific type of cow, and the ritual procedure are all essential.
O Brahmin, the knowledge of time regarding the interval between cows is indeed difficult to comprehend, for it is like fire or the sun;
yet you are rich in Vedic study, of pure birth, and tranquil.

One who is established in the sacrificial fires, who fears sin, who is grateful, patient toward cows, not overly harsh, a refuge for others, and whose livelihood is failing— such a person they call a worthy recipient.
When one is distressed for a livelihood or suffering excessively,
or for the sake of agriculture, or for the purpose of a fire-oblation, or at the time of childbirth,
or for the sake of a preceptor, or for the nourishment of a child;
One should give a cow at a distinguished place and time.
Those born within [the household], those obtained through fair purchase or knowledge,
those bought with one's life, those conquered in battle, and those born of the fire-pit (aukaja).
Those rescued from hardship and those acquired through nourishment— by these means,
such specific types of cattle are praised;
they are endowed with strength and possessed of good character and age.
All who possess fragrance are praised;
for just as the Gaṅgā is the best among rivers,
so is the Kapilā the best among those that are white.
Having fasted for three nights on water while sleeping upon the ground,
one should give cows that are well-satisfied to those who have been gratified—
cows that are well-behaved, nourished by their calves, and drinking milk.
Having given [the gift], one should subsist on cow-products for three days.
Having given a cow that is well-behaved, with a good calf,
of auspicious conduct, and not prone to running away;
As many hairs as there are on that [cow],
for so many years does one dwell in the hereafter.
Likewise, [one who gives] a draft-ox capable of bearing the yoke to a Brāhmaṇa...
By giving away a young, strong,
and well-trained ox of infinite vigor as a bearer of the plough,
one attains the worlds of the giver of ten cows.
O Kauśika, listen to the fruit of the merit of one who rescues brahmins and cows in the wilderness and is safely released from it. He who,
having entered the wilderness, gives a cow to a twice-born man—
He will safely reach that destination without a doubt; likewise,
one who boards a ship and one who bestows a cow shall cross the ocean in safety and return home as a householder.

O Thousand-eyed One, he who bestows a cow at the time of death attains happiness at the moment of passing and reaches unsurpassed worlds. And whatever Kṣatriya bestows [a gift] at the time of a journey, [he likewise attains these rewards].
Contemplated by the *gobhiḥ* (the rays of light/the cows), he who has conquered his enemies is glorified.
Whatever action any person among men begins to perform,
by giving cows, he accomplishes all of that through easy means.
Whatever desire one has in mind when bestowing a cow upon a twice-born man,
that desire shall be fulfilled, and he shall attain an auspicious state in the hereafter;
his reward shall be eternal and equal to that of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha).
O Thousand-eyed One, at the time of death, whatever state of being a man desires, or whatever various divine worlds dwell within his heart,
he attains all of that through that very action.
He who is authorized by cows is honored everywhere.
But he who follows the cows in the forests according to this very rule— eating grass, cow-dung, and leaves, free from desire, self-restrained, and pure— is likewise exalted.
"O Śatakratu, he must dwell joyfully in my world together with the gods, even in whatever other world he may desire.
Indra said:
"If one who knows [the truth] should steal or sell a cow for the sake of wealth, I wish to know this: what indeed would be his fate?
Brahmā said:
"Listen now to the fruit of that [act] for those who indeed commit theft for the sake of eating, for the sake of selling, or for the sake of giving to a Brāhmaṇa.
For he who, unrestrained, would destroy or eat [it] for the sake of selling— "
For those seekers of wealth who would consent to a man being caused to be killed—
the killer, the eater, and likewise he who consents—
sink for as many years as there are hairs upon his body.

"O Lord, whatever faults and of whatever kind exist in the case of obstructing a sacrifice performed by a twice-born man, those very same faults are recorded as applying to its sale and its theft. Furthermore,
he who, having stolen a cow, bestows it upon a Brāhmaṇa [incurs such sin]."
As great as is the fruit of her gift, so great does she fall into hell.
O one of great splendor, they say gold is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the gift of a cow;
indeed, gold is declared to be the supreme object for a sacrificial fee, without a doubt.
The gift of a cow delivers seven ancestors as well as seven descendants;
by giving gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), it is said to be twice that merit.
Gold is the supreme gift, and gold is the highest sacrificial fee.
"O Śakra, gold is purifying; it is remembered as the supreme among all purifiers.
O Śatakratu, they say that *jātarūpa* (gold) purifies entire lineages.
This, O one of great splendor, has been declared by me to you in brief as my sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
13,073.011 Bhīṣma said: O bull of the Bharata race, this was told by the Grandfather (Brahmā) to Indra;
Indra told it to Daśaratha, and likewise his father told it to Rāma.
Rāghava also [related it] to his illustrious and beloved brother Lakṣmaṇa;
and by Lakṣmaṇa, while dwelling in the forest, O Lord,
this was told to the sages who are firm in their vows, having been handed down through traditional succession.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, even righteous kings were unable to uphold that which was difficult to maintain;
this was told to me by my preceptor, and he said:
"The Brāhmaṇa who should constantly recite this in an assembly of Brāhmaṇas..."
"In sacrifices and in the gifts of cows, when both [types of merit] come together,
his worlds are indeed eternal and imperishable, along with the gods forever.
Thus spoke the blessed Brahmā, the Supreme Lord.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, I have been inspired with confidence by you as you discourse upon the duties;
yet I have a doubt—I shall speak of it—so explain it to me, O Grandfather."
"O one of great splendor, what fruit is declared for vows, and of what nature is it?
What is the fruit of observances, and what is the fruit of that which has been well-studied? What is the fruit here of self-restraint, and what is the fruit of retaining the Vedas?"
"What is the fruit of teaching, and I wish to know all of it?
O Grandfather, what is the fruit in this world for one who does not accept gifts?
And what fruit is seen for him who bestows what he has heard?"

What is the fruit for those devoted to their own duties and for heroes as well? What fruit is declared for truthfulness, and what fruit for celibacy? And likewise, what is the fruit for service to the father and for service to the mother?
"O Grandfather, knower of dharma, I wish to understand all this in its entirety and exactly as it is— service to teachers and gurus, compassion, and sympathy; for my curiosity is great."
Bhīṣma said:
"He who undertakes the vow exactly as it has been prescribed—
unbroken and properly commenced— for him there are eternal worlds."
O King, the fruit of observances is seen here in this world directly;
this very fruit has been obtained by you through your observances and sacrifices.
Furthermore, the fruit of well-studied [scriptures] is seen both in the next world and in this one.
He is always possessed of wealth in this world and rejoices in the world of Brahmā.
O King, listen now to me as I describe in detail the fruit of self-restraint (*dama*):
those who are self-restrained are happy everywhere; those who are self-restrained find peace everywhere.
Wherever they wish to go, the self-controlled conquer all their enemies; and whatever the self-controlled desire, they obtain it without a doubt.
For the self-controlled, O Pāṇḍava, are joined with all objects of desire everywhere.
In heaven, those who are self-controlled and endowed with forbearance rejoice through their asceticism, their valor, and their various acts of charity and sacrifice; indeed,
self-restraint is superior to giving, for even a small gift bestowed upon a twice-born man [yields great fruit].
The giver who is not self-controlled becomes angry; therefore, self-restraint is superior to giving. For he who gives without becoming angry attains eternal worlds.
Since anger destroys the merit of a gift, self-restraint is superior to giving.

There is nothing superior to the gift of knowledge; the knowledge of the Vedas yields great fruit. O Great King, there are tens of thousands of invisible abodes in heaven belonging to the ṛṣis throughout all the worlds, to which the deities go from here.

O King, those supreme sages who, desiring the great state, attain it through self-restraint— therefore, self-restraint is superior to giving. A teacher, despite his hardships, enjoys imperishable fruit.
O lord of men, having offered oblations into the fire according to the rules, he dwells in the world of Brahmā;
for even he who, after studying the Vedas, imparts them to those who know the proper method,
and who praises the duties toward his teacher, is likewise honored in heaven.
A Kṣatriya who is devoted to study, to performing sacrifices, to the act of giving,
and who is a protector in battle— he too is glorified in heaven.
A Vaiśya who is intent on his own duty obtains great merit through the act of giving.

A Śūdra who is devoted to his own duty attains heaven through service. Various kinds of heroes have been described; hear from me their purposes and the fruit ordained for heroes and those born of heroic lineages.
Listen now to the certain fruit ordained for heroes:
there are men who are heroes in sacrifice, heroes in self-restraint, and others who are heroes in truth;
likewise, there are those declared to be heroes in battle and heroes in generosity.
Some are heroes of intellect, and others likewise are heroes of forbearance;
some men are heroes in uprightness and abide in tranquility. There are many other heroes as well, distinguished by various such disciplines.
Some were heroes in the study of the Vedas, and others were heroes devoted to teaching them;

some were heroes through service to their gurus, while others were heroes through service to their fathers; some were heroes through service to their mothers, and likewise others were heroes in the practice of begging for alms.
Many are heroes in Sāṃkhya, and others likewise are heroes in Yoga;
there are heroes in the forest and in the life of a householder, as well as heroes in honoring guests—
all go to the supreme worlds won by the fruits of their own actions.
The retention of all the Vedas and bathing in all the sacred fords may or may not be equal to one who always speaks the truth;
indeed, a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were once held together on a scale.
Truth indeed excels even a thousand horse-sacrifices.
By truth the sun shines; by truth the fire blazes;
by truth the wind blows; everything is established upon truth.
By truth one pleases the gods, the ancestors, and likewise the brahmins;
they say truth is the supreme dharma, therefore one should not transgress truth. The sages are devoted to truth; the sages have truth as their prowess.
The sages have oaths of truth; therefore, truth is superior.
O bull of the Bharatas, those possessed of truth rejoice in the heavenly world.
Self-restraint is said by me to be the attainment of the fruit of truth, with my whole soul.
Without doubt, everyone who has disciplined their self is honored in heaven.
But hear from me, O lord of the earth, the virtues of celibacy (*brahmacarya*):
he who remains a celibate here in this world from birth until death.
"Know this, O lord of men: for him there is nothing unattainable.
Furthermore, many millions of ṛṣis dwell in the world of Brahmā—those who are constantly devoted to truth, self-controlled, and whose vital energy is drawn upward."
"O King, the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), when observed, burns away all sins;
this is especially true for a Brāhmaṇa, for a Brāhmaṇa is said to be fire itself.
And this is evident even to you regarding these ascetic Brāhmaṇas."
For just as Śakra fears when he is assailed by one practicing celibacy,
so too is the fruit of that celibacy seen here among the sages.
Now hear from me also about that dharma which consists in the honoring of one’s mother and father.

O King, know that for him who serves his father and never finds fault with him in any way, and likewise serves his mother, his humble elder, and his preceptor without egoism, the fruit is an exalted station in the heavenly world.
13,074.039c And one who serves his elders and possesses self-control shall not behold hell.
13,075.001 Yudhiṣṭhira said:
13,075.001a I desire to hear, according to the truth, the supreme ordinance concerning cows.
"By which we may attain all those eternal worlds.
Bhīṣma said:
"O lord of the earth, there is nothing superior to the gift of cows."

For a cow acquired by righteous means, when given away, immediately delivers one's entire lineage. He who has properly produced wealth for the sake of the virtuous has indeed performed a perfect sacrifice for the benefit of all creatures.
Therefore, O King, listen to me regarding the procedure for the gift of cows that was practiced in ancient times at the beginning of the age. Long ago,
when cows had been brought forward, [a man] whose vision was clouded by doubt regarding them—
Bṛhaspati spoke regarding the question posed by Māndhātṛ:
"Having honored a twice-born man and announced the time for the following day,
one who is firm in his vows should engage him for the purpose of giving away Rohiṇī."
One should employ the invocation "samaṅge bahule" and,
having entered into the midst of the cows, one should recite this sacred tradition:
"The cow is my mother, the bull is my father."
Heaven is my refuge and the earth is my support.
Having thus entered [the cowshed] and stayed through the night among the cows, the sage should utter this speech at the gift of cows: 13.075.007c.
Having shared the same companionship and the same vows with those cows for that single night,
he is instantly liberated from his impurity through the attainment of oneness with them. Indeed,
the cows should be released along with their bulls and calves at the sight of the sun.
The threefold [mantras] are to be understood as explanatory praises (arthavāda), benedictions (āśis), and hymns of praise (stava).
They are full of vigor, possessing the essence of strength; they are the sacrifice, the womb of immortality, and the foundation of the world.
On earth, the source of prosperity is always the progeny of Prajāpati; thus is the explanatory praise (*arthavāda*).
May the sun-like cows drive away my sin.
Likewise, may the auspicious Vedic recitations that grant me refuge lead me to heaven;
and likewise, may all blessings, even those not explicitly mentioned, be mine.
When the body is released through the exhaustion of karma at the time of death,
you Sarasvatīs are ever engaged in the highest good, borne along by meritorious deeds.
"Grant me the desired goal, for you have sought refuge [in me].
Indeed, that which you are, that am I today, being of one essence; having given yourselves, I am the giver of myself."
"Fallen from the mind, they have entered the mind itself;
kindle yourselves, O you of gentle and fierce forms!
Thus one should first speak the former half in her presence."

The giver of cows, according to the prescribed rule, should first recite the traditional formula (13,075.014c), while the twice-born recipient, being knowledgeable in the ritual for the gift of cows, should respond with the remaining half.
The giver of the arghya, the garment, and the wealth should say, "I give a cow.
He should urge her on, saying, "She is full of milk," "She is to be nourished," and "She belongs to Viṣṇu.
Then he should indeed proclaim her name according to the sequence.
The fruit is twenty-eight thousand, six hundred and twenty-five;
thus the giver of a cow obtains all these increased virtues in their proper order at the eighth stage.

O Bhārata, he who gives a cow, who is virtuous, fearless, and a giver of honor, shall not suffer; nor shall he who gives land and fulfills desires. And he who is learned and supports his dependents, O Bhārata, shall likewise not suffer.
The Vaishnava worlds of the moon have been explained to you.
Having given cows, one should observe the cow-vow for three nights;
he should dwell here for one night together with them.
On the eighth day of the lunar fortnight when it falls on a Friday, one should observe a three-night fast, subsisting on the products of the cow—
either its milk, its dung, or its urine;
such a person, a giver of a bull, shall be one who has fulfilled the Vedic vow.
The attainment of the Vedas results from the gift of a pair of cows (13,075.020c);
likewise, by following the prescribed rite for cows, the sacrificer attains the highest worlds, whereas one ignorant of the rite does not.
One who might bestow all earthly desires gathered together in one place,
and one who might give a cow that milks all desires—
these two would be equal, provided those [desires] were fully capable of providing floods of offerings to the gods and ancestors.
The gift of those superior bulls is 13,075.022a; one should not bestow them upon one who is not a disciple, nor upon one who does not observe vows,
nor upon one who lacks faith, nor upon one of crooked intellect.
For this Dharma is secret to all the world;
one should not discourse upon this Dharma here and there.
There are, however, people in the world who possess faith.
There are base Rākṣasas among human beings who find it undesirable that gifts be given,
and these meritless ones resort even to atheism.
Having heard these words of Bṛhaspati,
those kings who were virtuous in conduct and of good character attained the celestial worlds by making gifts of cows.
O King, learn from me as I recount them:
Uśīnara, Viṣvagaśva, Nṛga,
Bhagīratha, and the renowned Yauvanāśva.
Māndhātṛ and King Mucukunda; Bhūridyumna, the Niṣadhan king Somaka, Purūravas, and the universal monarch Bharata.
In whose lineage were all the Bhāratas,
as well as the heroic Rāma, son of Daśaratha, and those others who are renowned and illustrious.
Likewise, King Dilīpa,
a performer of vast deeds who was knowledgeable in the ritual for the gift of cows, attained heaven through sacrifices, gifts, asceticism, and the duties of kingship.
Māndhātṛ was also endowed with the merit of giving gifts of cows.
Therefore, O Pārtha, you too should retain this speech of Bṛhaspati as spoken by me.
"Having obtained the kingdom of the Kurus, bestow with a joyful heart these sacred cows upon the foremost of the twice-born.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus did the King of Dharma perform everything exactly as Bhīṣma had instructed regarding the ritual gift of cows,
according to the method taught by the God of Gods to Māndhātṛ.
Thus, O King, the monarch constantly upheld the true Dharma by giving away cows,
even while drinking water mixed with barley-grains and cow-dung.
Sleeping on the surface of the earth, with matted hair and self-restrained,
that king then became like a bull among bulls; he was always devoted to them.
With a focused mind, he indeed praised the cows,
yet he did not yoke a cow again to the burden of the chariot;
instead, he traveled here and there by means of excellent horses.
13,076.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, O King, the wise King Yudhiṣṭhira, filled with humility, again questioned the son of Śantanu regarding the details of the gift of cows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhārata, tell me once again in full of the merits of the gift of cows;
for I am not yet satiated, O hero, as I listen to such nectar."
13,076.003a Thus addressed by Dharmarāja, O King, the son of Śantanu then 13,076.003c fully described to him the exclusive merits of the gift of cows.
13,076.004 Bhīṣma said:

By giving such a cow— one that is affectionate, endowed with good qualities, young, and covered with cloth— to a Brahmin, one is liberated from all sins. Those worlds named Asurya go to by one who has given a cow there.
Having given a cow that has drunk its water, eaten its grass, lost its milk, and is devoid of strength—
a worn-out beast like an old well whose water has been used up— one enters darkness; one should not join a twice-born man with such hardship.
One who, through hardships, unites a Brahmin with fruitless labors— such as one that is defective, angry, diseased, or weak, or one whose price has not been paid— should not give it.
For him, the worlds are devoid of vigor and indeed fruitless;
yet all those endowed with strength, possessed of virtue and age,
and fragrant, praise them.
"Just as the Gaṅgā is the most excellent among rivers,
so is the Kapilā the most excellent among reddish-brown cows.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O high-souled one, since the giving of many [cows] is equal, why is the gift of a *kapilā* cow praised by the virtuous? I wish to know this distinction."
"For you are indeed capable of both hearing and speaking.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, I have heard from the elders as they spoke that which you are now declaring."
I shall describe that in its entirety, how Rohiṇī was created.
Long ago, Dakṣa was commanded by the Self-born One, "Create progeny. Out of a desire for the welfare of living beings, he first created their means of subsistence.

"Just as the dwellers of heaven subsist by relying upon the nectar of immortality, so do all creatures subsist by relying upon their means of livelihood, O Lord. Among immobile beings, mobile beings are superior; among these, human beings are the best."
The Brāhmaṇas are therefore the most excellent, for in them the sacrifices are established. Through sacrifices Soma is nourished, and he is established in the cows.
All the gods rejoice because of this, as do the subjects who have acted according to ancient custom.
Then, after the creatures had been created by Dakṣa and the others, those creatures, being hungry,
approached the Lord of Creatures, the four-faced one, having reached a decision;
these very beings cried out in their desire for a means of subsistence.
Thirsting for sustenance, they approached him like children do their father or mother. Having thus resolved in his mind for the sake of the creation of progeny,
Prajāpati then drank the nectar that bestows strength.

Having attained satisfaction, he emitted a fragrant scent; from his mouth, the Creator brought forth Surabhi, the mother of the world. He beheld Surabhi, his daughter born from his mouth, who had emerged through that emission.
Surabhi, the mother of the worlds, created the Saurabheyīs—
tawny cows of golden hue who provide the means of subsistence for all creatures. As they flowed with milk from every side, their color was like that of nectar.
13,076.019c A foam born of nectar arose, like the foam produced by the waves of rivers.
13,076.020a Released from the mouth of the calf, it fell upon the head of Bhava as he stood upon the earth. 13,076.020c Enraged, the Lord then cast his gaze upon it.
With the eye produced from his forehead, as if burning up the Rohiṇīs,
O lord of the people, that fierce energy of his then rendered the tawny cows multicolored,
just as the sun does to the clouds.
"But those who, departing from him, took refuge in Soma alone—
remaining in their own respective castes as they were originally born— they were not reduced to other castes.
Then Prajāpati spoke to the enraged Mahādeva.
"You have been sprinkled with nectar; there is no such thing as impurity in cows.
Just as Soma, having taken up the nectar, flows forth again, so do these Rohiṇīs, born of nectar, pour out milk."
The wind is not defiled, nor is fire, nor gold, nor the ocean; nectar does not lose its nature when drunk as nectar, nor is a cow that has suckled her calf any less affectionate.
These worlds shall be sustained by oblations and by the flow of milk.
"Enjoy the auspicious sovereignty over these [goddesses], which consists entirely of nectar.
And Prajāpati gave him a bull along with them;
by that act, O Bhārata, he propitiated the mind of Rudra.
And being pleased, Mahādeva then made the bull his banner and his vehicle; therefore, he is known as Vṛṣabhadhvaja.
Thereafter, Mahādeva was established by the gods as Paśupati.
He is the Lord among cows and is called the Bull-bannered One (Vṛṣāṅka).
Thus, for all Kapila cows of unblemished color and great luster,
the gift of such a cow is proclaimed as the primary rule.
They are the eldest in the world, engaged in the conduct of the world;
accompanied by Rudra, they are the outflow of the Soma;
gentle, meritorious, bestowers of desires, and givers of life.
By giving cows, one becomes the granter of all desires.
Always reciting this supreme ordinance concerning the origin of cows, one remains pure and becomes beloved by the most auspicious deities.
A person is liberated from the impurities of the Kali age;
likewise, they shall obtain beloved sons, cattle, and wealth.
[They shall perform] offerings to the gods, offerings to the ancestors, libations, and rites for peace.
O King, a giver always obtains all these benefits through the gift of a cow: vehicles, clothing, and the nourishment of the elderly and children.
13,076.034 Vaiśampāyana said: Then, having heard the words of his grandfather,
King Ajamīḍha, together with his brothers, [acted].
Then Pārtha gave cows that yielded milk into vessels of gold and bronze to the best of the Brahmins;
in the same manner, he bestowed them upon those twice-born ones.
He gave hundreds and thousands of cows for the sake of sacrificial fees directed toward the rituals,
in order to conquer the worlds and attain supreme fame.
13,077.001 Bhīṣma said: At that very time, regarding Vasiṣṭha, the best of sages,
they cite this ancient history as well.
And [he heard] the conversation between Vasiṣṭha and the high-souled Saudāsa.
King Saudāsa, born of the Ikṣvāku lineage and the best among givers,
[beheld] the eternal treasury of Brahman, perfected and wandering through all the worlds.
Having saluted his family priest, he began to ask him this:
Saudāsa said,
"O Blessed One, O sinless one, what is said in the three worlds to be the most purifying?"
"O Best of Sages, O Blessed One, O Creator of the World, what supreme merit would a mortal obtain by constantly reciting [your names] throughout the three worlds? Bhīṣma said:
Then, having paid homage to the cows and being purified, the learned sage spoke these beneficial words to him who was bowing before him: "The secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) concerning cows is this:
cows possess a fragrant scent, as well as the fragrance of *guggulu* resin."
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are the great means of securing well-being.
Cows are the past and the future; cows are eternal nourishment. Cows are likewise the root of prosperity; what is given to cows is never lost.
For cows are indeed the constant food and the supreme oblation for the gods.
The utterances *svāhā* and *vaṣaṭ* are eternally established in cows. Cows are indeed the fruit of sacrifice; sacrifices are established in cows.

Cows are the future and the past; sacrifices are established in cows. O high-minded one, at the time of the fire-oblation, morning and evening, cows indeed provide the sacrificial offering for the sages, O bull among men.
O Lord, those who give a cow cross over whatever difficult obstacles they have created through their evil deeds and transcend all sin;
one who possesses ten cows should give one, and he who possesses a hundred cows should give ten.
One who possesses a hundred cows and one who possesses a thousand cows should both give [the guest] a hundred; for they all yield equal fruit.

One who maintains no sacred fires despite possessing a hundred cows, one who does not perform sacrifices despite possessing a thousand cows, and one who is wealthy yet miserly—these three do not deserve the guest-offering (*arghya*).
Those who bestow a tawny cow, together with her calf, accompanied by a bronze milking vessel,
well-behaved and covered with cloth, conquer both worlds—
[as does one who gives] a young bull, endowed with vigor, along with a herd of a hundred.
O scorcher of enemies, those who bestow upon a preeminent Brāhmaṇa a lordly bull, adorned with massive horns,
are born again and again endowed with sovereign power.

One should not go to sleep without having recited [the names] of cows, nor should one rise again without being mindful of them; by bowing to cows in the evening and in the morning, one shall thereby obtain prosperity. One should never feel aversion toward the urine or dung of cows.

One should not eat their flesh; in that way, one attains prosperity through cows. One should always praise cows and likewise never treat them with contempt. Upon perceiving an inauspicious dream, a man should recite the praises of cows.
He should always bathe with cow dung and lie down upon dried cow dung;
he should avoid spitting, urinating, defecating, and striking others;
and he should eat on a moist hide while gazing toward the western direction.
Restraining his speech, with clarified butter, he should eat upon the ground; thus he attains the prosperity of cows.

One should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter, cause blessings to be recited with clarified butter, give clarified butter as a gift, and consume clarified butter; thus one attains the prosperity of cows.

Whoever, having consecrated a cow made of the essence of jewels with sesame seeds by means of the Gomatī-vidyā, should give it away, would not grieve over what has been done or left undone. "May cows with golden horns and yielding milk attend upon me."

May cows and the offspring of Surabhi always look upon me, as rivers flow toward the ocean; may I likewise always look upon the cows. "The cows are ours, and we belong to them; where the cows are, there we are."
Thus, by reciting this at night and by day, in times of both even and uneven circumstances,
and during great terrors, a man is liberated from fear.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"For one hundred thousand years, we have performed austerities most difficult to practice,
thinking: 'May we attain preeminence through the cows previously released,
so that in this world we may be the best among all sacrificial gifts.'"

"O scorcher of foes, [if one thinks], 'May we not be defiled by fault,' yet that very person, being struck by that [thought] in his mind, would always be tainted. Even gods and men would use excrement for the sake of purification."
"O giver of honor, [he said: 'In this way, may all beings, both stationary and moving, as well as those who bestow gifts, go to the world of cows (Goloka).
At the conclusion of their ascetic penance, the Lord Brahmā himself granted this boon to them."
"So be it," said the All-pervading Lord, "and may you deliver the worlds.
Desiring spiritual perfection, those Mothers of the past and the future rose up.
By bowing to them in the morning, one shall thereafter attain prosperity.
At the end of their ascetic penance, O Great King, cows became the ultimate refuge of the world.
Therefore, cows are highly blessed and are said to be the supreme purifier;
likewise, cows stand at the very head of all living beings.
By giving away a tawny cow that has a calf of the same color, one that yields milk,
is well-behaved, and is covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Likewise, by giving away a red cow that has a calf of the same color and yields milk...

By giving a well-behaved, milk-yielding cow, covered with cloth and accompanied by a calf of similar appearance, one who is virtuous in conduct is honored in the world of Soma.
