Having given away a white, milch cow with a calf of the same color,
one who observes good vows and has covered her with cloth is glorified in the world of Indra.
Likewise, having given away a black, milch cow with a calf of the same color—

By giving a well-behaved, smoke-colored cow that yields milk, along with a calf of the same color, covered with cloth, one is honored in the world of Agni. By giving a well-behaved, smoke-colored cow that yields milk, along with a calf of the same color, covered with cloth, one is honored in the world of Yama.
By giving away a cow with the color of water-foam, accompanied by its calf and a bell-metal milking vessel,
and covered with a cloth, one attains the world of Varuṇa. Likewise, by giving away a cow with the color of wind-blown dust, accompanied by its calf and a bell-metal milking vessel...
Having given [a cow] covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu. Having given a golden-colored, tawny-eyed cow, accompanied by its calf and a bronze milking vessel,
and covered with cloth, one attains the world of Kubera.
By giving away a cow of the color of smoky straw-ash, together with her calf, a bronze milking vessel,
and covered with cloth, one is glorified in the world of the ancestors. Likewise,
by giving a fat, white-throated cow, adorned and accompanied by her calf, [one attains the same].
One attains the Vaiśvadeva realm, an unobstructed and most excellent station.
By giving away a milch cow of the Gaurī breed that has a calf of the same color,
is well-behaved, and is covered with a cloth, one enjoys the world of the Vasus.
By giving away a cow with the color of a pale woolen blanket, accompanied by her calf and a bronze milking vessel,
and covered with cloth, one attains the world of the Sādhyas. Likewise, by giving a bull with a variegated back, adorned with all kinds of jewels, [one attains the same].
By giving [this], one attains the undecaying worlds of the Maruts. By giving a dark-limbed cow accompanied by her calf and endowed with all kinds of jewels,
a man reaches the worlds of the Gandharvas and Apsarases.
Having given a white-throated bull adorned with all kinds of jewels,
one becomes free from sorrow and attains the worlds of Prajāpati. One who is devoted to the gift of cows proceeds forth, having pierced through the masses of clouds.
O King, he shines in the sky in a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun;
and a thousand beautiful women of lovely hips and exquisite attire delight that best of men who is devoted to the gift of cows.
He is awakened from sleep by the tinkling of lutes, harps, and anklets, and by the laughter of deer-eyed women; as many hairs as there are on a cow...
For that many years he is honored in heaven;
and when he falls from that heavenly realm, he will be born in the world of men into a family of cattle-owners.
Vasiṣṭha said:
May cows that yield ghee and milk, whose source is ghee, from whom ghee originates,
who are rivers of ghee, and who have whirlpools of ghee, always be in my home.
Ghee is ever in my heart; ghee is established in my navel. Ghee is in all my limbs; ghee resides in my mind.
Cows are always before me, and cows are likewise behind me.
"O cows, [you belong] to me everywhere; I dwell in the midst of cows.
Having sipped water (ācamana), a person should always recite this at evening and at dawn;
whatever sin he commits during the day, from that he is completely liberated.
Where there are palaces made of gold and where that stream of wealth flows,
there the givers of thousands go— to places where Gandharvas and Apsarases dwell,
where the mud is fresh butter, the waters are milk, and the water-weeds are curd.
Wherever rivers flow, there indeed go those who bestow thousands. He who bestows a hundred thousand cows according to the prescribed rite attains supreme prosperity and is glorified in Goloka.
And such a man, after death, establishes ten ancestors on both sides— his parents and his grandfathers—
in the worlds of the righteous and purifies his lineage,
provided the cow given is equal in measure to the standard measurement of a milch-cow.
By giving a cow made of sesame seeds,
and by being a giver of water, one does not undergo any torment whatsoever in the world of Yama.
Having attained infinite worlds, the wise and virtuous man rejoices in the heavenly realm;
it is the supreme purity and the foundation of the universe.
The immeasurable mothers of the gods should touch him from the right and follow him as he walks;
and one should give to a worthy recipient, having carefully considered the proper time.
Having given away a tawny cow with her calf, possessing large horns,
accompanied by a bronze milking vessel and an upper garment,
he crosses that which is difficult to cross.
A fearless man should always recite: "May the Mothers—Surūpās, Bahurūpās, and Viśvarūpās—approach me in the southern assembly hall. (13.079.012)
There is no gift more meritorious than this, nor any fruit more meritorious than this;
there is no being in the worlds that can possibly be superior to it.
[It provides benefit] through its skin, its hair, its horns, its tail-hair, its milk, and its fat.
When they come together, they carry out the sacrifice; what is there that is superior to this?
I bow my head to that Cow, the mother of the past and the future, by whom this entire world—both moving and unmoving—is pervaded.
O best of men, this is but a partial collection of the qualities of cows that has been proclaimed by me to you;
for there is no gift in this world superior to that of cows.
"Nor do they become a final refuge, nor anything else.
Bhīṣma said: "Reflecting that 'this is supreme,' the lord of the earth—"
Then the high-souled one, self-restrained, bestowed the excellent words of the seer upon the twice-born; he gave them very many cattle and attained the worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that which is the purifier among purifiers, that which is the most excellent in the world, and that which is the supreme means of purification."
13,080.002 Bhīṣma said: Cows are of great significance and are meritorious; they deliver human beings.
Furthermore, they sustain these creatures with their milk as well as with sacrificial oblations.
O best of the Bharatas, there is nothing more meritorious than cows;
they are pure, holy, and unsurpassed in the three worlds. Indeed, cows dwell even above the gods.
O King, having given these, wise men go to heaven;
Māndhātṛ, Yauvanāśva, Yayāti, and likewise Nahuṣa,
constantly gave away cows numbering hundreds of thousands.
13,080.005e They have gone to the supreme station, which is very difficult even for the gods to attain.
13,080.006a Moreover, O sinless one, I shall relate to you here an ancient account concerning the Saurabhyas— those of meritorious deeds, pure, and of auspicious appearance.
"O best of gods,

O slayer of enemies, listen to me in its entirety as I tell you the purpose for which those hundred gentle cows were given away in the past, during the age of the gods, among the high-souled lords of the Daityas."
Having saluted Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the wisest among sages, and having performed his daily rites with a pure and restrained mind, the intelligent Śuka,
who had seen the higher and lower worlds, questioned his father.
13,080.008a Which sacrifice among all sacrifices is observed as the most excellent?
13,080.008c And by performing what do the wise attain the highest heaven? 13,080.009a By what means of purification, O Lord, do the gods enjoy the heavenly realm?
Furthermore, what constitutes the sacrificial nature of a sacrifice, and upon what is a sacrifice established? What is the highest among gifts, and what is the supreme among sacrificial sessions?
And tell me, O sinless one, that which is the purifier among all purifiers.
Having heard these words, Vyāsa, the knower of the supreme dharma,
related everything in its true essence to his son, O bull of the Bharatas.
Vyāsa said:
Cows are the foundation of all beings, and cows are their ultimate refuge.
Cows are meritorious and pure; they are both sanctification and righteousness itself.
We have heard that in former times, cows indeed possessed no horns.
They say that they desired horns to ward off rain and heat,
and heavy human skin to withstand cold, wind, and sun;
thus there was no mutual conflict between the cowhide for clothing and the human skin.
Then Brahmā gave them the supreme [mantra] held in his mind;
indeed, they attended upon the imperishable Lord for the sake of obtaining horns.
Then Brahmā, seeing that the cows were seated in the vow of fasting (prāya), [spoke].
The Lord bestowed upon each of those cows whatever they desired.
Having summoned a human being, he said to him: "Place your own body among the cows;
O men, you must take up clothing and shelter."
"By means of this, those who seek the welfare of their subjects endure cold, wind, and heat;
you shall clothe them in garments so that their skin may remain delicate.
Saying "So be it," they gave him their own skin and hide.
Horns grew upon them, each according to her own inner desire;
O son, those various-colored horned creatures shone brightly.
By Brahmā, they were granted boons and made auspicious as the providers of offerings to the gods and the ancestors.

Meritorious, purifying, auspicious, and characterized by divine forms, cows possess great and divine splendor; therefore, the gift of cows is highly praised. And those virtuous men, free from envy, who bestow these [cows] upon others—
13,080.017c They are indeed called doers of good deeds, and they are givers of all gifts. 13,080.017e And they, O sinless one, attain the meritorious world of cows,
13,080.018a where the trees bear honeyed fruit and are laden with divine flowers and fruits.
O best of the twice-born, there are divine flowers of sweet fragrance,
and fruits rich in flavor, soft and beautiful;
the entire ground is made of jewels, with fine golden sand.
Everywhere it is pleasant to the touch, free from mud, stainless, and auspicious. There,
the reservoirs of water shine with groves of red lotuses and golden stalks of jewels, resembling the rising sun.
With lotus ponds possessing petals of highly precious gems and filaments with the luster of gold,
interspersed with blue water-lilies and abounding in many lotuses;
and with groves of blossoming *karavīra* trees surrounded by thousands of whirlpools.
Adorned with blossoming *saṃtānaka* groves and flowering trees,
the rivers there have their sandy banks strewn with spotless pearls, precious gems, and gold.
It is covered with various excellent mountains composed of all kinds of jewels,
and others made of gold, possessing a brilliance equal to fire;
there are golden mountains there, which are great peaks of precious gems and stones.
They shine with lofty, beautiful peaks composed of every kind of jewel.
There, O bull of the Bharatas, the trees are always laden with flowers and fruit and are crowded with birds; their flowers and fruits possess divine fragrances and tastes.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those of meritorious deeds always delight there, their every desire fulfilled, free from sorrow and devoid of anger,
upon various and delightful celestial chariots, O Bhārata.
O King Yudhiṣṭhira, those of meritorious deeds, illustrious and sporting about, rejoice; and beautiful throngs of Apsarases play with them. Indeed, by giving a cow, one attains these worlds.
The man who gives a cow shines indeed together with the Apsarases.
May those Yugandharā mountains protect me— those for whom Pūṣan is the lord, the powerful and mighty Māruta is the ruler, and King Varuṇa holds sovereignty.
"O Brahmin, one who is restrained in his vows should daily recite: 'The Mothers—Surūpā, Bahurūpā, and Viśvarūpā—are the daughters of Prajāpati.
Furthermore, he who serves cows and follows after them in every way [attains these rewards]."
To him, being pleased, they grant even boons that are very difficult to obtain.
One should not bear malice toward cows even in one's mind, for they are the bestowers of happiness;
one should always honor them and worship them with prostrations.
13,080.033e One who is self-controlled and always joyful in mind likewise enjoys the prosperity of cows.
13,080.034a By means of that purifier by which the gods enjoy the highest world,
13,080.034c that ghee, which is the purifier of purifiers— one should carry it upon one's head.
One should offer oblations into the fire with clarified butter and cause blessings to be recited with clarified butter.

One should consume clarified butter and give clarified butter as a gift; thus one attains the prosperity of cattle. For three days one should drink warm urine, and for three days one should drink warm milk.
Having drunk the warm milk of ten thousand cows for three days, one should drink warm ghee for three days;
having drunk warm ghee for three days, one should subsist on air for three days. For one month, one should consume a handful of barley-gruel made from barley that has been carried away by cows.
All sin equal to the killing of a Brahmin is purified by this.
For the sake of overcoming the Daityas, this purification was performed by the gods;
and they attained godhood, being perfected and endowed with great strength.
Cows are purifiers, meritorious, and the greatest, supreme means of purification;
by giving them to the twice-born, a man attains heaven. Having become pure in the midst of cows, one should mentally recite the *Gomatī* mantra.
Having sipped pure water, one becomes pure and stainless.
In the midst of the fire, in the midst of cows, and in the assembly of Brahmins—
there are Brahmins who have bathed in knowledge, the Vedas, and vows, and who perform meritorious deeds.
One should indeed cause the disciples to study the Gomatī, which is equal to a sacrifice. Having fasted for three nights and heard the Gomatī, one obtains a boon;
and one who desires a son obtains a son, as well as wealth.
A woman desiring a husband and a man desiring all objects of desire obtain them; cows, when served with devotion, grant these things without a doubt.
Thus, these highly blessed ones are worthy of sacrifice and bestow all desires.

"Know that they are called Rohiṇīs; there is nothing superior to them. Thus addressed by his high-souled father, the immensely radiant Śuka constantly honored the cows; therefore, you too should honor them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
“O Grandfather of the gods, the asuras, and all beings,
the Lord, the Creator, the Blessed One, the All-pervading One, is praised by the sages.”
13,080.045d@009_0003 How indeed did this Goloka come to occupy that position above it?
13,080.045d@009_0004 This is my great doubt; you ought to explain it to me.
O best of the Kurus, mind, speech, and intellect are first established as one;
thereafter, listen from me in its entirety to the supreme and great majesty of the cow,
which is meritorious, conducive to fame and long life, and a source of great well-being.
May Kīrti, who is devoted to the yoga of cows, dwell in the world;
for it is heard in the Purāṇas regarding the great-souled maharṣis at the time of the dissolution of all worlds and the manifestation of the gods.

O Bhārata, for the sake of the deities, for the sake of the nectar of immortality, and indeed for the sake of sacrifice, there was a cow renowned by the name Surabhi— she was Rohiṇī, capable of assuming any form at will,
who had previously conceived in her mind and possessed a face like that of the nectar of immortality.
Having undertaken terrible ascetic penance, Viśvakarman created [her];
and furthermore, through his splendor and austerity, he created a Puruṣa who was radiant with body like a kindled fire.
Then he beheld that Surabhi, Rohiṇī, of divine form;
and upon seeing her, he became deeply distressed, deluded by passion. Then, perceiving him to be afflicted by desire, the Self-Existent One, the creator of the world, [acted].
"Be Mārta," thus spoke the Blessed One.
Then the Blessed One, seeing his supreme state of distress, gave him the name by which he is renowned there as Mārtaṇḍa.
The Blessed One gave to that high-souled Mārtāṇḍa a beautiful,
fragrant maiden, auspicious and composed of the essence of ascetic power;
just as I was produced by him, so too were you and this Rohiṇī.

And having engaged in sexual union, offspring shall thus be born; that progeny will be meritorious, and it shall be the supreme purifier for you both. Furthermore, you shall never incur any fault from approaching one who is forbidden.
The milk produced from your offspring shall become a supreme oblation;
in sacrifices, the ritual rule for the portions of clarified butter (*ājya*) shall originate from your progeny. And those who shall be devoted to the service of their offspring, O Rohiṇī—
By that very merit of yours, may human beings go to Goloka.
This supreme purifier named Ṛṣabha is indeed such that,
by knowing it, the twice-born in this world shall be liberated from the confusion of rebirth.
13,080.045d@009_0035 These rites, consecrated by the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas, shall be undertaken;
13,080.045d@009_0036 preceded by offerings to the gods (havya) and the ancestors (kavya).
13,080.045d@009_0037 Then, O Rohiṇī, by this merit, your offspring [shall flourish].
"Even above my world, they shall dwell free from affliction.
May there be welfare for them, and may there be welfare for those who indeed exist among the subjects. And let your sons be Yugaṃdharas in the upholding of the world."
Whatever worlds you desire, those worlds you shall follow;
indeed, all the hosts of gods shall become your sons,
drinking the supreme nectar produced from your breast.
Thus, at that time, Surabhi accepted all these boons from the lords of all the worlds as they spoke,
and she attained supreme bliss;
for she had indeed created abundant progeny for the sustenance of the world.

Permitted by Brahmā, Surabhi entered the world. Thus, O Bhārata, by the granting of this boon by the Self-Existent One himself, the entire world of cows situated above has been described to you from the beginning.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Bhīṣma, who were the offspring of Surabhi that existed previously, before Mārtaṇḍa?
Bhīṣma replied:
"Tell me this in its true essence; my mind is deeply attached to cows.
Listen specifically to the divine names of the mothers of the cows, by which auspicious ones the three worlds are pervaded, O lord of men."

Listen to those who were first born from Surabhī and who shall be the first progeny as described by me; you shall attain great fame. Having performed austerities, the fiercely ascetic Surabhī, blazing with splendor, [gave birth].
He produced eleven sons, the Rudras who are praised in the Veda:
Aja-Ekapād, Ahirbudhnya, the highly illustrious Tryambaka,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Kapālī, and likewise Raivata.
Hara, Bahurūpa, Ugra, and the fierce Vīryavān;
and his illustrious son, the highly renowned Viśvarūpa—
these eleven Rudras have been declared by their names.
These high-souled ones, great yogis, endowed with splendor and great strength,
are of most excellent birth among the gods who discourse on Brahman;
for they alone are renowned in this world as the very nature of the Brahmins.
These eleven Rudras, the lords of the three worlds, have been declared;
this collection of one hundred [verses] concerning those great-souled ones is known as the Śatarudra.
Then Surabhi gave birth to her first daughter, the Earth.
The cow who milks all desires and sustains embodied beings is called "Suta" (the Son), O King; she alone is designated as such. Surabhi is celebrated as the mother of cows and Brahmins.
Having first created the Rudras, the givers of boons who were born from Brahmā,
he afterwards brought forth the Lord, the master of the planets, honored by the world—
the immortal King Soma, the supreme essence of all sacrifice.
From the essences of medicinal herbs, from the [essences] of the gods, and from the life-force itself,
she then gave birth to four daughters— Śrī, Medhā, Kīrti, and the goddess Sarasvatī— who remained steadfastly engaged in their respective yogic practices.
Having created these offspring, this Surabhi, who can assume any form at will,
further gave birth to the divine and auspicious mothers of cattle— those holy ones who flow with honey, who are auspicious, swift, and the best of rivers.
The golden-hued, auspicious one, rich in cattle, speckled, covered with a rug; the one possessed of limbs, full of clarity, abounding in curds, milk, and water;
the unerring, sweet-scented, truthful, wealthy, belonging to the Maruts, and full of essence.
[She gave] Ajā, Sikatā, Śuddhadhūmā, Adhāriṇī,
Jīvā, Prāṇavatī, Dhanyā, Śuddhā, Dhenudhanāvahā,
Indrā, Ṛddhi, Śānti, Śāntapāpā, and Saridvarā.
Forty-one fortunate ones were honored there in heaven.
Furthermore, from Surabhi was born a glorious bull, radiant as the rays of the moon,
known as Dakṣa, with a neck possessing the luster of a jeweled ornament.
Wearing a garland, hump-backed, radiant, and possessing a luster like that of a lotus stalk—
this is the banner of Maheśvara, granted with the approval of Surabhi. These cows, capable of assuming any form at will, are the most excellent for the sake of merit.
They bestowed boons upon the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the Viśvedevas.
Then Surabhi, having performed austerities, gave birth once more to cows,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, those which were given to the world-protectors, Indra and the others.
Suṣṭutā, Kapilā, the illustrious Rohiṇī, and Sarvakāmadughā— the cow of the Maruts who assumes any form at will—
these four cows yield pure milk and are consecrated with nectar.
Those who were formerly my calves used to drink the most excellent nectar;
[I offer] a well-praised Kapila cow to the high-souled Vāsava, king of the gods, a Rohiṇī cow to Dharmarāja, and one to Varuṇa.
To King Vaiśravaṇa, he gave a cow that milks all desires. Thus, O bull among sages, these world-famous offspring of Surabhi have filled the earth with their progeny.
"Everything beautiful whatsoever that exists here originates from cows;
this is the sequence of names for you, beginning with Surabhyapatya (Offspring of Surabhi).
Yudhiṣṭhira.

"O Indra among kings, you have been glorified; tell me, what more shall I relate to you? At that time, from the goddess Surabhi, there arose the four renowned and preeminent goddesses: Kīrti, Lakṣmī, Sarasvatī, and Medhā."
"Are these [qualities] distinct from the cows, or are they dependent upon the cows?
Bhīṣma said:
O Grandfather, tell me which deities are established within the cows."
The cow that has taken refuge in that god—know that god to be designated as "divine" (daiva).
Whatever is dependent on a deity, O twice-born ones, the wise know that to be divine.
Indeed, at the original creation of all the gods...

13,080.045d@009_0115 Indra, the lord of the gods, approached Surabhi for the sake of the nectar of immortality. 13,080.045d@009_0116 "O Goddess, I desire the nectar granted by you, which is superior in flavor."
"By your grace, may there be auspiciousness for me and immortality," said Surabhi.
"O Lord of the Gods, becoming my calf, drink from my udder."
"Then you shall attain immortality and that station of Indra;
nor shall you suffer any distress from enemies in battle, O slayer of Vṛtra.
For the sake of your own strength, O powerful Śakra, drink my distillation, O Lord."
Then Bhīṣma,
the best of gods, suckled at the breast of that Surabhī;
[he obtained] immortality, a beautiful form, strength, and the highest station.
Having drunk the nectar, Purandara approached, greatly delighted:
"I am your son; may prosperity be yours! Tell me, what shall I do for you?"—thus spoke Surabhi.
"O son, you have accomplished everything; go now to the celestial realm. Protect all the gods and slay those who are the enemies of the gods.
Furthermore, one who desires peace must never show contempt for cows or Brahmins."

The breath of a cow or a Brahmin could even wither the gods. Always fond of cows and Brahmins, uttering the word "svasti," one may stride across the earth, the intermediate space, and the vault of heaven.
And whatever other task you may have, tell it to me in brief;
I shall perform all of that for you—I tell you this in truth. —Indra.
"O Goddess, I wish to dwell constantly among the cows; I tell you this, O Surabhi!
Grant me your favor along with these hosts of gods."
O Kauśika, I perceive this body of cows directly before me.
That deity who is capable of dwelling wherever he may choose shall dwell there;
every limb of the cow is supremely pure and highly honored.
"O Śakra, do as you think best; may prosperity be yours.
Having heard those words of Surabhi, the best of the gods [replied].
Together with all the hosts of gods, he entered the offspring of Surabhi.
The King of the Gods (Indra) entered her horns, her mouth, and her tongue;
the Wind-god (Vāyu) entered all her apertures, and the hosts of Maruts entered her feet.
Rudra, the omnipresent, is his hump; the consumer of oblations (Agni) is in his belly.
Sarasvatī is foremost in his udders; Śrī, beloved by the world, is in his dung.
Great fame is in his urine; eternal wisdom is in his milk.
The god Soma is indeed in his mouth; the blessed Yama is in his heart;
Dharma is in his tail; Action is in his hair; the Sun is stationed in his two eyes;
the Siddhas and Success are in his joints; and austerity and splendor reside in his movement.
Thus all the hosts of gods are fixed within the pathways of their bodies;
cows are the great deities consecrated by the Brahmins,
for the powerful gods indeed take refuge together in the cow.
13,080.045d@009_0153 What else could you not provide as a favor for one who desires all things?
13,080.045d@009_0154 O Lord of Men, worship [them] with sincerity and supreme devotion.
13,080.045d@009_0155 For cows are the supreme purifier in the world, the sanctifying oblation.
Having been cast down from heaven, the descendant of Bhṛgu, who subsisted on foam, was indeed devoured;
yet he regained his life-breaths and thereafter took refuge in Goloka.
Yudhiṣṭhira.
Who was this one named Phenapa, and how was he devoured in the past?
Why was he restored to life after death, and how did he take refuge in Goloka?
How did he do so in this world of humans, which is full of contradictions, as well as within the paths of conventional conduct?
"Indeed, without destiny, it is difficult to attain among human beings, especially so.
Bhīṣma said:
I have a great doubt in this matter; you ought to explain it to me."
O Bhārata, it is heard that in the lineage of Bhṛgu there was one named Sumitra,
who was accomplished in the study of the Vedas, established in vast asceticism,
devoted to the stage of the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and always intent upon his own duty.

13,080.045d@009A_0009 One who knows the true nature of the conduct of the Vinaya, who is skilled in the meaning of all dharmas, 13,080.045d@009A_0010 who is diligent, bathing at the three sessions of the day and devoted to the worship of the twilights (saṃdhyopāsana),
13,080.045d@009A_0011 who delights in the fire-sacrifice (agnihotra), and who is patient, constantly muttering prayers and offering oblations.
Constantly honoring the ancestors, the gods, and guests,
and offering whatever was necessary for the maintenance of life,
[he dwelt] where the river named Triśikhara originates from the mountain.
In the Purāṇas, it is renowned as Kulaheti, fashioned by Rudra. On its bank, in a level region adorned with garlands of flowers,
abounding in wild medicinal herbs and trees, and filled with various birds and deer—
In that place free from gadflies and mosquitoes, unvisited by crows and vultures, abounding in black *darbha* grass, most delightful, and radiant with the light of stars;
it was surrounded by sacrificial trees, all of them lofty, uniform, and dark-hued.
In ancient times, there was a sacred hermitage belonging to the Bhṛgus. There lived a self-restrained descendant of Bhṛgu named Sumitra,
following the virtuous path as prescribed by his ancestors, the Bhṛgus.
To him, a certain descendant of Aṅgiras gave a beautiful, auspicious cow during the last month of the rainy season, on the full-moon day; he, being pure in his vows, received her.
Having obtained her, that man of virtuous character, intent upon his purpose, reflected:

With supreme devotion, Sumitra treated her like his own mother; being thus nurtured by him, that excellent Rohiṇī, who moved according to her will, attained great growth and became beautiful even in her very life-breath.
With the sides of its flanks free from veins, it bore a vast splendor;
with dark-colored flanks, sides, and back, it was fragrant, honey-tawny,
large, with fine hair on its limbs, preeminent in form, and possessed of thin skin.
With a black tail and a white face, her udders were perfectly rounded;
her back was elevated while her forequarters were lowered, and she had spike-like ears and beautiful eyes.
She possessed a long tongue and short horns, with the spaces between her teeth fully complete.
Her throat was thick with flesh, she was serene and of auspicious appearance;
she was always endowed with tranquility, gentle, and possessed a full, noble voice.
She was constantly characterized by the excellent marks of cattle belonging to Prajāpati.
Like a woman established in her youth, she shone with the beauty of her form;
having approached the bull, that auspicious lady of sweet appearance gave birth to a pair of twins who seemed as if they were her own likeness.
The Bhārgava ṛṣi reared that cow along with her calf; through the union of their offspring, a thousand cows were produced, and from those cows,
thousands of breeds were mutually born.
O Indra among kings, no end to those bulls could be seen;
by them, the delightful hermitage and the entire forest were completely filled,
just as the vault of heaven is covered by clouds.
Some were the color of lotuses, some had the luster of *kiṃśuka* flowers;
others were the color of gold, resembling the rays of the moon,
while some were silver-colored and indeed some were red.
Blue, crimson, copper-colored, black, and tawny; variegated with many hues and numerous in their herds—
yet they do not subsist on milk or ghee out of affection for their calves.

Bhārgava alone was devoted solely to the maintenance of the cows' vital breaths. As he thus served them and looked after their welfare, subsisting on the remnants of the calves' food, a very great length of time passed away.

Exhausted by hunger and thirst, he constantly drank the abundant milk that flowed from cows, which was offered as remnants by their calves; because of this, he became widely known by the name Phenapa (the Foam-drinker).
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, it happened thus for Gautama. Once, cows capable of assuming any form at will took on the appearance of women."
13,080.045d@009A_0062 Endowed with auspicious marks, they played joyfully in the lake, singing songs.
13,080.045d@009A_0063 Indeed, his cows beheld them with eyes wide open in wonder. 13,080.045d@009A_0064 [So too did] the women.
And they said, "Who are you? in human voices as women. "We are all cows, endowed with auspicious deeds;
we all assume the form of women and wander according to our will."
Cows are [the source];
cows are the supreme divinity; cows are the supreme goal. Women... [are likewise].
"Tell us here, by what means have you attained this state of merit?

By our sacrificial offerings, the gods and the brahmins have been gratified; likewise, the ancestors have been gratified by the *kavya* offerings, and Agni has been gratified by the *havya* offerings."
And likewise, our agriculture was always uplifted by our offspring;
it was indeed joined with carts drawn by a thousand ten-horsed teams.
By these abundant merits and by those very children of ours, we [prosper].
13,080.045d@009A_0074 You have all attained Goloka, which is beyond the sphere of desire. 13,080.045d@009A_0075 But you are all Rohiṇīs, together with your offspring and your bulls— cows indeed.

With our divine eye, we see that they are indeed destined for the lower realms; thus, cows are the supreme deity and cows alone are the ultimate refuge. You must deliver those who belong to your own side, for we have come to you for protection.
"What must we do, and how indeed should we conduct ourselves,
so that we women may attain Goloka and not be held in contempt?"
The sacrificial session of Rantideva continues for a thousand years.
Therein, that king quickly attains the state of being a sacrificial animal;
then, through his utilization while in that state of being an animal, [the rites] are consecrated as sacrifices.
"Endowed with that merit, you shall attain the auspicious worlds of the cows (Goloka)," said Bhīṣma. Having heard these words of theirs, their minds were filled with joy.
They set their minds on departing and felt a great longing to go;
for Bhārgava would not grant us the use of him as a sacrificial animal,
since that king’s sacrifice was proceeding according to the Dharma.
"We are not able to depart by any means without being permitted.
Then those people there said, "Let this descendant of Bhṛgu be killed;
all of you agree to this, for it cannot be otherwise."
"Let this resolution be made by us together to reach the worlds;
yet among those gathered here, not one, even if she were honored with due respect, would be able to look upon the descendant of Bhṛgu with her terrible gaze."
Then those women, who had the luster of lotuses and a radiance equal to the rays of the sun,
with eyes as red as hibiscus flowers and copper-colored, and with fleshless, hard faces—
those tawny Rohiṇīs spoke in the presence of them all.

13,080.045d@009A_0098 With voices like the thundering of clouds and radiant with splendor, 13,080.045d@009A_0099 we shall indeed slay that Sumitra; of this there is no doubt. 13,080.045d@009A_0100 [The cows...]
"Having cast our good deeds behind us, what supreme good will you ordain for us?
O tawny ones, among all the social orders (*varṇa*), you shall attain preeminence.
Bhīṣma said:
By giving a single cow that yields the fruit of a hundred cows, one shall obtain that fruit.
Having heard these words of the cows, the Kapila cows were delighted in their minds.
Bhīṣma.
All of them resolved to slay Sumitra, the descendant of Bhṛgu. Those who were his cow-mothers, moving at will,
had come into the presence of Sumitra and stood there, full of gratitude.
Having praised him, those of auspicious appearance said to that seer:
"O seer, we are the mothers of the cows who have come from Goloka.
We are well-pleased; choose a boon, O great sage, whatever you desire."
since you have always maintained the highest regard for cows, 13,080.045d@009A_0111 I am pleased and I am graced by the fact that the auspicious cow-mothers [have come] to me.
With hearts full of joy, all of them remain there as bestowers of boons:
"May my devotion toward cows always be exactly as it is today;
O Mother Cows!"
"May those who kill cows and those men who hate the Brahmins perish.
O best of sages, what you have spoken thus for our benefit is pleasing to us.
Sumitra said this.
"Come, O best of sages, go with us to Goloka.
May you all attain your desired destination; indeed, I am not able to go.
— Bhīṣma.
"Release these cows, who are ascetic and dear to me. Having heard those most cruel words of his regarding the Kapila cows,
they lifted up that seer Bhārgava and carried him away, bearing him through the sky.
Having cast off his body right there, his mothers extracted the subtle instrument (*karaṇa*) from him through yoga and brought it to Bhārgava;
they then related to him all of Kapila’s activities.
For the sake of which the cows, the mothers of the world, had carried him to Goloka; then,
seeing his body there,
those tawny cows crushed it with their horns and hooves in accordance with their vow.
Then, O best of kings, having cut the descendant of Bhṛgu into many pieces,
they went to where the other cows were and reported all of that to them.
Then those cows, wandering upon the earth, were cursed by their mother-cows.
"O slayers of Brahmins, may you quickly become as foul-mouthed as excrement!
For thus, O King, are cows grateful, like mother-cows;
the sage attained the celestial realm, and the cows were fully liberated."

13,080.045d@009A_0133 Having gone to the sacrifice of the wise Rantideva, those cows made themselves known in the presence of the great seers. 13,080.045d@009A_0134 They announced their identity before the assembly of the maharṣis.
Then King Rantideva, purified, with palms joined in reverence and being clean, bowed down and spoke to the cows: "What is the purpose of your coming? Thus he addressed the cows.
"O Indra among kings, we desire your employment in this sacrifice.
O Rantideva,
you ought to show us favor by allowing yourself to be turned into the state of a sacrificial animal."
"I am not capable of slaughtering cows by the hundreds of thousands.
Having caused you to be slaughtered, how could I save myself? For he who, having joined you to the state of being cattle, would lead you here to heaven [is truly a benefactor]."
"O cows,
come together with yourselves through ascetic power;
you who are righteous-souled and established in austerity are engaged in our deliverance."
"O King, we have heard of you as Rantideva; therefore, we have come here of our own accord.
If this is indeed your intention, then let us become animals for my sacrifice."
"By this agreement, I shall offer you into the sacrificial fire.
If at any time any of you cows should be employed against your will,"
"Then the conclusion of the sacrificial session shall be with cows; this is the final decision.
"So be it, O Great King, just as you tell us. "When the cows become unwilling, then let the sacrificial session be concluded."
13,080.045d@009A_0151 Then, when the *gosatra* sacrifice of the wise Rantideva had commenced,
13,080.045d@009A_0152 thousands of cows were slaughtered day after day by the immolators.
O lord of men, in this manner many years passed away; yet no end was seen to the cows being slaughtered. Indeed, there were heaps of thousands of cow-hides resembling mountains.
O tiger among the Kurus, they became manifold like clouds;
and a great river, carrying fat and moisture, began to flow.
Even today, that auspicious river is renowned on earth as the Carmaṇvatī.
Then once, a cow, distressed, addressed her own calf:
"Come, my child, drink from my udder; do not later be afflicted by hunger.
You will surely suffer in dejection when I have been killed."
"Indeed, these Caṇḍālas are approaching with weapons, desiring to kill me. Then, O Great King Rantideva, he heard that human voice uttered, and thereupon he restrained her.
Then that bull among kings established a cow-sacrifice (*gosattra*). Other cows, which had been released and abandoned during that sacrifice, took refuge [with him]—
those very cows of that high-souled king which had been slaughtered in the sacrifice.
13,080.045d@009A_0168 Sprinkled by those who discourse on Brahman, they went to Goloka.
13,080.045d@009A_0169 The royal seer Rantideva, having performed the sacrifice according to the prescribed rites,
13,080.045d@009A_0170 then attained friendship with the Lord of the Gods and the imperishable third heaven.
13,080.045d@009A_0171 The calves born from foam rejoiced in Goloka for eternal years.
13,080.045d@009A_0172 And those cows that remained became forest-dwellers.
13,080.045d@009A_0173 This is the narrative of the foam-born ones, as well as the majesty of the cows.

This purifying and meritorious account, uttered by Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, has been told. O bull of the Bharatas, even the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, having beheld the supreme glory residing in cows, performed the highest service and devotion toward them.
Therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should worship cows, O Bhārata;
and always bestow them upon the twice-born, O best of the Kurus—
Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O Bhīṣma, O highly fortunate one, tell me that which is the most excellent among purifiers, the supreme purifier honored throughout the worlds— O Grandfather, speak of that great vow."
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between father and son, Vyāsa and Śuka,
concerning Kṛṣṇa, the best of sages, whose self is purified and who is infallible.
One who knows the distinctions of the lineage and is skilled in the meaning of all scriptures—
there, Śuka, having performed his purification, having completed his recitations, and having finished his daily rites,
remained established in the supreme discipline and took refuge in the highest dharma.
Having bowed his head to Vyāsa, the seer who perceives the subtle meaning of reality,
Śuka, filled with curiosity regarding the dharma of giving, indeed asked this question:
"O Sage, you have repeatedly praised many diverse kinds of gifts."
What gift is of great purpose, purifying, meritorious, and of great fruit? By what does one cross over difficulties, and by what does one attain the worlds?
Or by what does one obtain greatness in this world and in the next?
Who are the carriers of the sacrifice? Upon what is the sacrifice established?
What constitutes the sacrificial nature of the sacrifice, and what is the remedy for the sacrifice?
And what is the highest among sacrifices? May your lordship explain these to me.
To him who was devoted and filled with curiosity,
Vyāsa, the treasury of vows, spoke this unsurpassed discourse concerning cows—
discourse that is auspicious, conducive to fame and longevity, and brings delight to the ears in this world.
That which is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things,
which pacifies all sins— listen to it from me in brief. It is that by which this world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, exists.
Having reached Goloka, those cows of auspicious appearance remain there;
they are indeed the mothers of all beings and of the entire universe,
and they alone are the mothers of the Rudras and the Sādhyas.
These are indeed the mothers of the Rudras and are remembered as the sisters of the Ādityas;
they are the daughters of the Vasus, born from the root of the lineage of Brahmā. Pūṣan is their sovereign, and the Maruts are those who bind their hair.
King Varuṇa possesses sovereignty, and the Viśvedevas are dependent upon them;
he who knows this— those cows are mothers honored by the gods—
and that Brahmin is certain for the world of Brahmā or the world of cows.
One should not treat cows with contempt in deed, thought, or speech.
He who desires the supreme goal should seek the highest station in the world that belongs to cows. One should not strike cows with the feet, nor with a staff, nor with the fist.
Having relied upon this purifying knowledge created by Brahmā,
a man should not discharge urine or feces while following behind his mothers, nor in the midst of cows, nor in a cow-pen. Upon seeing [these], he should perform the ritual purification.
Pure, with limbs cool as sandalwood and radiance equal to the rays of the moon—
gentle, fragrant, auspicious, and smelling of guggulu incense—
all the gods entered the cows, just as rivers flow into the ocean.
He attains the splendor of cattle in both heaven and the intermediate space.
One should offer oblations into the fire with curds and cause [the priest] to pronounce a blessing with curds. One should give curds and consume them; thus one attains the splendor of cattle.

One should offer oblations to the fire with clarified butter; one should cause blessings to be recited with clarified butter. Having touched clarified butter, one should consume it; one attains the prosperity of cattle. Cows are indeed the source of life; cows are the unsurpassed gift.
May those merit-guardians, yielding excellent fruit, attend to me as I worship. By that purifier through which the gods have gone from here to the heavenly world—
that purifier among purifiers is established upon my head.
The lute, the drum, and the small kettle-drum are established upon the bodies of cows;
for the sake of play, delight, and recreation, they exist throughout the three worlds. Therein the gods do not dwell, nor do they offer the *agnihotra* oblations.
No sacrifice is truly performed here where a cow is not milked;
for milk, curds, and clarified butter are the supreme among all flavors. Cows are the source of nectar, by which the three worlds are sustained.
Having summoned *iḍā* and the cow with her calf, the mother of sacrifice—
whom the Brahmins call upon as the cows that prepare the sacrificial oblation—
she who is pure and the first act [of ritual], this cow is Sarasvatī.

Endowed with all the qualities of desire, she fulfills every wish through her calf, the Paurṇamāsa sacrifice. That cow, in whom this entire moving world is woven, is indeed the first and most meritorious, devoted to the welfare of all beings.

May the *dhāraṇās*, which are purifying, meritorious, and the source of all beings, protect me in this world and in the next. This is the sacrifice together with its ancillaries; this is the eternal sacrifice.
The Vedas, together with the Upaniṣads, are established in the form of cows.
My dear son, this which I have proclaimed is considered here to be the supreme view regarding cows.
One who is self-restrained should constantly cause this to be heard everywhere in an assembly of Brahmins.
Having heard this, one shall obtain those worlds which have been proclaimed by me;
even by causing others to hear it with a joyful heart, one attains those same worlds.
One should always give a single purifying cow day after day.
A Brahmin who constantly recites the Gomatī shall indeed attain that same merit.
Now, if a cow is not available, one should give an unsurpassed sesame-cow according to the ritual procedure for the Gomatī; that cow is purifying in every way.
The man who always recites the *Gomatī* daily shall be liberated from all sins, provided he practices it with a self-restrained mind.
Or, having constantly touched clarified butter or consumed it, one should mutter the *Gomatī*.
Having bathed with cow-dung, one who recites [the *Gomatī*] is liberated from sin. One should mentally mutter the *Gomatī*; one’s daily ritual (*āhnika*) should always be performed with the *Gomatī*.
A reciter of the *Gomatī* must never spend a day in vain.
Indeed, by chanting the *gomatī*, the gods attained godhood;
the sages also attained the state of sages through the *gomatī*—they obtained everything.
One who is bound shall be released from bondage; one shall be liberated from hardship and from distress.
Whoever serves the Gomatī attains union with the beloved. This is pure in its entirety; this is the unsurpassed vow.
O protector of the earth, this is always purifying for those who hear it.
Whatever men desire sons, and whatever men desire wealth—
by reciting the *Gomatī*, one is liberated from thieves and enemies on the road,
as well as from those intent on violence in battle and from the persistence of former enmities.
One who constantly recites the *Gomatī* attains victory swiftly;
this applies even to Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, and those twice-born ones who are devoid of mantras.
Vyāsa said:
"O Father, how could it be that those who subsist on the Kapilā cow—
whether they be Kṣatriyas, Śūdras, or even twice-born men devoid of mantras— [attain such merit]?"
I shall declare the definitive conclusion regarding those who subsist upon the *kapilā* cow.
The *kapilā* is indeed supreme in the world and is considered the most excellent among cows. The giver of such cows attains heaven, as does he who serves them according to the prescribed rule.
Whoever should touch a *kapilā* cow with a staff or with his foot, by that mere touch he is reborn in hell. One should employ the *kapilā* with a mantra; by the mantra alone she is released.
But he who employs [a mantra] devoid of its mantra-syllables is born from a womb of worms.
With his vital organs and limbs struck down by blows, rendered insensible by suffering,
for as many steps as he walks, for that long shall he remain a worm in the worlds.

For as many drops of her blood as fall upon the earth, for that many thousands of years shall he fall into hell. One should employ a tawny cow with mantras; one should apply her [to the task] with mantras.
O Lord, those devoid of mantras who engage in [such acts] shall be immersed in darkness. O King,
even those men who, possessed by delusion of intellect, live off the milk of a *kapilā* cow,
fall into hell for thousands of years.
13,080.045d@009B_0109 Now, those Brahmins who, according to the rule, make use of a Kapilā cow,
13,080.045d@009B_0110 rejoice in that world, and the people there are free from disease.
13,080.045d@009B_0111 Understand that those who do not perform [the rite] according to the injunction are Śūdras.
Śuka:
O best of sages, what is the significance of cows endowed with various colors?

13,080.045d@009B_0113 Among all colors, the Kapilas attained the state of being the most excellent.

13,080.045d@009B_0114 Listen, my son, how the Kapilas are remembered as the most excellent among cows; 13,080.045d@009B_0115 and how they attained their status as Kapilas and became objects of constant worship among men.

We have heard that in ancient times Agni departed from the gods. He said, "O you who provide refuge, protect me who has come to you for shelter. Thereupon, they all spoke together: "Welcome to you, O Purifier!"
"Protected here by us, you shall not be found by the gods.
Then the gods, desiring to find Pāvaka, wandered about;
and having discovered him hidden among the cows, they quickly approached them.
"Fire dwells within you," they urged the cows.
"Let the bearer of oblations be made manifest; you ought not to obstruct the worlds.
Having consented, saying "So be it," they revealed the fire.
Having obtained the fire, those gods were immediately satisfied; they then urged Agni, "Let favor be bestowed upon the cows. For the fire was established within the bodies of those cows.

The Fire-god granted them the state of being tawny (kapila), as well as the state of being most excellent, and great fruitfulness in this world; therefore, one should cause a tawny cow to be given among all social classes.
To a learned Vedic scholar who is tranquil, self-restrained, and maintains the sacred fire—
such a gift purifies the donors for as many eons as there are hairs on the cow.
When given, it purifies the recipients;
a parrot [purifies] through being taught; but a cow purifies through the act of bestowal upon one who is learned.
By what distinction of color is she to be known as *kapilā*?
Vyāsa:
How many characteristics of her were seen by the sages in the past?
Listen, dear one, to how a Kapilā cow is to be recognized among cows:
by her eyes, her horns, her hooves, and her testicles;
and also by her ears and her nose—these are known as the six types of Kapilās.
If even one of these characteristics is observed, one should recognize her as Kapilā; thus say the wise. A cow with tawny eyes is of Agni, while she with [tawny] hooves belongs to Maheśvara.
In the neck, Vaiṣṇavī is to be known; from Pūṣan’s nose she was born.
From the ear, however, through Vasantas, she is born from her own source.
And the birth of Gāyatrī from the two testicles is recorded as having six qualities.
Thus the cows, the Brahmins, the Gāyatrī, and Truth itself;
the spring and Suparṇa—these were born together as one.
He who would drive or milk a tawny cow (kapilā) from her two eyes [would incur great sin].
That evildoer finds his place established in hell;
once released from hell, he resorts to the womb of an animal. When he eventually attains human birth, that man is born blind from birth.
He who would drive or milk a tawny cow (kapilā) by its two horns shall,
upon being born again and again, enter an animal womb.
He who would drive or milk a tawny cow by its hooves...
A base man devoid of wealth may sink into shoreless darkness; he who drives a tawny cow by her tail or milks her,
if he is without support, will always be born as a worm.
He who, even though knowing them to be tawny-colored, makes a living by them,
shall become a worm for thousands of lifetimes and then perhaps attain human birth;
or that lowest of men is born as a Caṇḍāla or one of evil deeds.
But he who, out of negligence, subsists on a Kapilā cow by smelling her [excrement],
shall also be born among the animal womb for thousands of years;
and when he returns to human form, he shall be afflicted by disease, dull-witted, and diseased.
Those who, according to the scriptures, subsist upon the honey, ghee, and fragrant products of tawny cows (kapilā),
are also reborn among the animals;
even if they subsequently attain the state of a stationary being and then reach human form, [they remain afflicted].

He will be born short-lived and originating from a low-caste family. But those wicked ones who, out of envy, cause a *kapilā* cow to be driven [for labor] shall remain established in the hells until the dissolution of all beings.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard that the dung of cows is indeed endowed with prosperity (*śrī*);
I wish to hear about this, for I have a great doubt regarding it."
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O best of the Bharatas, they cite this ancient history concerning a conversation between cows and Śrī regarding a king here on earth.
13,081.003a Having assumed a lovely form here on earth, Śrī entered into the midst of the cows. 13,081.003c Then the cows were struck with wonder upon seeing the perfection of her beauty.
13,081.004 The cows said:
"Who are you, O goddess, and from where have you come? You are peerless in beauty upon this earth.
We are filled with wonder, O highly fortunate one, at the perfection of your form.
We wish to know you: who are you, and where will you go?"
"O you who shine like gold, tell us all this in its true essence. Śrī said:
"I am the beloved of the world; may it be well with you. I am renowned here by the name Śrī."
By me the Daityas were abandoned and destroyed for eternal years;
and by me the gods were favored and they rejoice for eternal years.
Indra, Vivasvat, Soma, Viṣṇu, the Waters, and Agni [are likewise].
"Those sages and deities who are protected by me prosper;
however, those cows whom I hate perish entirely,
becoming bereft of virtue, wealth, and pleasure, and filled with misery."
"O cows, know me to be of such power, the bestower of happiness.
I desire to dwell among you all forever;
O sinless ones, I have come seeking you, endowed with glory."
The eleven thousand and eight cows said:
"You are unstable and fickle, common to many;
I do not desire you—blessings be upon you—go wherever you please."
"We are all possessed of beautiful forms; what need have we of you today? Go wherever you please; we have had our purpose fulfilled by you.
Śrī said:
"O cows of excellent vows, is this appropriate for you, that you do not welcome me here? Why indeed do you no longer accept me, even though I am so difficult to obtain?
And this worldly proverb circulates in the world as true, O you of firm vows:"
It is a settled conclusion that when one approaches [the goal] on one's own, one encounters humiliation;
yet, having performed great and fierce austerities, human beings, as well as gods, dānavas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and rākṣasas, attend upon me.
"O cows, it is indeed fitting for you; accept me here.
For I am not to be disregarded, O gentle ones, within the three worlds with all that is mobile and immobile.
The cows said:
"O Goddess, we do not despise you, nor do we treat you with contempt;
rather, because you are unstable and fickle-minded, we therefore avoid you.
What is the use of saying more on this matter? Go wherever you desire."
"O sinless one, we are all possessed of beautiful forms; what need have we of you?
Śrī replied:
"O givers of honor, I shall be held in contempt by all the worlds."

"By refusing me, you should instead show me favor. O highly fortunate ladies, you who are worthy of being a refuge, please protect me, who have come to you for shelter, who am ever devoted to you, and who am blameless."
"O auspicious ladies, I desire that you always honor me;
I wish to dwell even in a single limb of yours, however loathsome it may be. For in none of your limbs, O sinless ones, is anything loathsome to be perceived."
"O meritorious, pure, and auspicious ones, grant me a place where I may dwell;
you ought to explain to me which limb that may be.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, O lord of men, those auspicious cows, who are compassionate and affectionate,
consulted together and all spoke to Śrī:
"O illustrious lady, you must certainly be honored by us."
"O auspicious one, dwell in our excrement and urine; for this is indeed meritorious for us.
Śrī said:
"By good fortune, you have shown me favor in the form of this grace."
"So be it; may prosperity be yours! I have been honored by you, O givers of happiness.
Bhīṣma said:
"Having thus made this agreement with the cows, O Bhārata, Śrī—"
While they were looking on, he then vanished right there.
O son of Gośakṛt, this majesty of yours has been described;
now hear further from me as I speak of the majesty of cows.
Bhīṣma said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for those who bestow cows and those who eat only the remnants of what has been offered in sacrifice, there are always sacrificial sessions and sacrifices.
Without curd and ghee, the sacrifice does not proceed here;
therefore, the very nature of the sacrifice is established by them, and they are seen to be its root.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of cows is praised as supreme.

Cows are the most excellent and pure; indeed, they are the supreme purifier. One should attend to them for the sake of nourishment and also for the sake of peace, for their milk, curd, and clarified butter liberate one from all sins.
Cows are declared to be the supreme splendor both in this world and in the next;
there is nothing more purifying than cows, O bull among men.
In this regard, they also cite this ancient history.
13,082.006 O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the dialogue between the Grandfather and Indra. 13,082.007 When the Daityas had been defeated and Śakra had become the lord of the three worlds,
all creatures flourished, being devoted to truth and righteousness.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, the ṛṣis along with the gandharvas, kinnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas,
as well as the gods, asuras, suparṇas, and the lords of creatures,
were once seated in attendance around the Grandfather.
Nārada, Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā, and Hūhū were singing upon divine instruments and waited upon that Lord. There,
the wind likewise blew celestial flowers.
And the seasons also brought forth their respective fragrances. In that assembly of gods, where all beings had gathered,
it resounded with celestial musical instruments and was filled with divine women and celestial singers.

13,082.011 Indra, having saluted and bowed down to the Lord of the Gods, asked: 13,082.012 "O Blessed One, O Grandfather of the gods and lords of the world, why is the world of cows situated above [all others]? This I wish to know."
"O Lord, what austerity or celibate practice have the cows performed here,
that they dwell happily above the gods, free from passion?
Then Brahmā spoke to Śakra, the slayer of Bala.
"O slayer of Bala, cows have been constantly disregarded by you;
therefore, O Lord, you do not know their majesty— listen to that,
O bull among the gods, regarding the supreme power and majesty of cows."
"O Vāsava, cows have been declared as a constituent part of the sacrifice, and the sacrifice itself depends upon them;
for without them, the sacrifice could not proceed in any way whatsoever.
Furthermore, they sustain all creatures with their milk and likewise with the sacrificial oblation."
Their sons, moreover, devote themselves to the practice of agriculture;
they produce grains and various kinds of seeds. From these, sacrifices proceed in every way, including both *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors).
O Lord of the Gods, these cows carry milk, curd, and ghee;
they bear various burdens while being tormented by hunger and thirst. By their very nature, they sustain the sages and all living beings here on earth.
"O Śakra, these rivers that carry the waters of Vāsavākūṭa, by virtue of their well-performed deeds,
always dwell above us;
this indeed is the reason for our dwelling here today."
"O Śatakratu, it has indeed been declared that cows are superior even to the gods.
For these Saurabhyas, O Vāsava, have been granted boons and are themselves givers of boons; they perform meritorious deeds, they are purifying, and they possess auspicious marks."

O best of gods, O slayer of Bala, listen from me in its entirety as I tell you the purpose for which these cows of Surabhi have come. Long ago, O dear one, during the age of the gods, among the high-souled lords of the Daityas—
While Viṣṇu was governing the three worlds, he entered the state of being an embryo within Aditi, who,
O best of immortals, was constantly performing severe and most difficult penance on one leg for the sake of a son.
But seeing that great goddess performing such intense austerity,
the daughter of Dakṣa, the goddess named Surabhi,
being joyful and devoted to righteousness, herself performed formidable penance.
On the delightful peak of Kailāsa, frequented by gods and gandharvas,
she stood on one foot, established in supreme yoga for ten thousand years and ten hundred years.
Scorched by her asceticism, the gods, along with the ṛṣis and great serpents,
went there and sat in attendance upon that auspicious lady together with me. Then, I spoke there to that goddess who was endowed with ascetic power.
"O blameless goddess, for what purpose do you perform such terrible asceticism?
O illustrious and beautiful one, I am pleased with this penance of yours. Choose a boon, O goddess; I shall grant it," said Purandara.
Surabhi said:
"O Blessed One, O Grandfather of the worlds, my wish has been fulfilled by this boon.
This alone is my boon today, O Sinless One: that you are pleased with me."
13,082.033 Brahmā said: O Lord of the Thirty-three, O Indra, O Lord of Śacī, listen to what I said in reply to that goddess Surabhī as she was speaking thus.

"O Goddess, because of your desire for non-attachment and because of your auspicious asceticism, I am pleased; therefore, I grant you the boon of immortality. You shall dwell above even the three worlds."
By my grace, that Goloka shall become renowned. And among human beings, your sons who perform their duties as subjects, O highly fortunate lady, along with all your daughters, shall dwell there.
"O Goddess, whatever divine or human enjoyments have been conceived by you in your mind,
and whatever happiness of heaven exists— that shall be yours, O auspicious one. O Thousand-eyed One, her worlds shall be endowed with all objects of desire."
There, neither death nor old age nor fire prevails;
there is no wretchedness nor anything inauspicious there, O Vāsava. There are divine forests and divine palaces.
O Vāsava, there are also thirteen thousand eight hundred and twenty-three celestial chariots that travel at will,
obtained through celibacy, austerity, truthfulness, self-restraint,
various meritorious vows, and likewise by frequenting sacred fords.
"O lotus-eyed one, Goloka can be reached through great austerity and through well-performed deeds.
All this has been told to you by me, O Śakra, in response to your inquiry."
"O destroyer of enemies, you must not treat cows with contempt.
Bhīṣma said:
"Having heard this, the thousand-eyed one honored him constantly."

O Yudhiṣṭhira, he showed great honor toward the cows and always maintained a constant devotion to them. All this has been told to you, O one of great splendor; it is purifying, supreme, and the most excellent majesty of the cows.

O tiger among men, this [account], which destroys all sins, has been proclaimed. He who, with a concentrated mind, would constantly recite this to Brahmins during offerings to the gods and ancestors, in sacrifices, and indeed in rites for the manes— [he attains great merit].
That which is all-fulfilling and inexhaustible attends upon his ancestors;
and a man who is devoted to cows obtains whatever he desires. Even women who are devoted to cows shall attain their wishes.
One desiring a son obtains a son; a maiden shall obtain a husband. One desiring wealth obtains riches; one desiring merit attains merit.
One desiring knowledge shall attain knowledge; one desiring happiness shall attain happiness.

O Bhārata, for one who is devoted to cows, nothing whatsoever is difficult to obtain. Having uttered, "Salutations to those who endure all things," he who pays homage to the cows day after day travels that path with ease.
13,083.000*0386_01 Vaiśampāyana said:
13,083.000*0386_02 Having thus heard of this supremely meritorious and unsurpassed gift of cows,
Dharmarāja, his soul filled with joy, spoke again to the Kaurava.
Yudhiṣ�ṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, you have described this unsurpassed gift of cows as being especially for kings who regard righteousness."
For sovereignty is constant suffering, and the stages of life are difficult to master; indeed, living with a retinue is a hardship that cannot be borne by those who have not disciplined their minds,
and for kings, for the most part, no auspicious destiny exists.
"Those who bestow the earth here are surely purified;
and previously, O joy of the Kurus, you described to me the duties [regarding this],
as well as the gift of cows that was indeed spoken of by Nṛga."
This was demonstrated long ago by the seer Nāciketa;
it was indeed shown previously by the seer Nāciketa.
Furthermore, in the Vedas and Upaniṣads, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is prescribed for all ritual acts.
"In all sacrifices, it is prescribed that land, cows, and gold [are gifts];
however, the supreme scriptural authority in that regard is indeed that gold is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
O Grandfather, I wish to hear this exactly as it is."
What is gold? How was it born? At what time did it arise? What is its essential nature? What is the gift of gold, and what is its fruit? Why is it said to be supreme?
For what reason do the wise revere the gift of gold?
And why is that gold praised for the purpose of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in sacrificial rites?
And why is gold the most excellent purifier among things on earth and among cows? O Grandfather, tell me that which is supreme for the purpose of sacrificial fees.
13,083.010 Bhīṣma said: Listen attentively, O King, to the detailed account of the origins of gold and that which was experienced by me.
"My father, the highly effulgent Śantanu, has passed away.
Desiring to offer him the śrāddha rites, I have come to Gaṅgādvāra. Having arrived there, O son, I have begun the śrāddha ceremony for my father."
At that time, my mother Jāhnavī herself rendered me assistance.
Then, having seated many sages who were perfected in austerity before me,
I began the rites starting from the offering of water.
Having completed that preliminary rite as prescribed with a concentrated mind,
I began to properly offer the funeral oblation according to the rules.
Then, Surucira-aṅgada broke through that arrangement of darbha grass.
O lord of the people, an arm adorned with long pendants rose up;
seeing it raised, O bull of the Bharatas, I was struck with great wonder, thinking, "My father himself is here to receive me."
Then, reflecting upon the scriptures, this thought occurred to me once again:
"O Lord, this rite of offering a hand is not ordained in the Vedas;
rather, a ball of rice (piṇḍa) should be given here by a man. Thereupon, such was my conviction.
"13,083.018a The ancestors of a human being are never directly present here in visible form.
13,083.018c They accept only what is prescribed; thus, the funeral cake (piṇḍa) should be offered upon kuśa grass.
13,083.019a Therefore, disregarding that demonstration of my father's hand,"
"O King, recollecting the subtle injunctions from the authority of the scriptures,
I then placed all of that upon the darbha grass, O bull of the Bharatas;
know that, O best of men, it was performed according to the path of the scriptures."
Then that arm of my father vanished, O lord of men. Thereupon,
at the end of a dream, my ancestors appeared to me and,
being well-pleased, said to me, "O bull of the Bharatas, we are gratified."
"13,083.022c Because of this wisdom of yours, you do not become deluded regarding the nature of reality (dharmatā).
13,083.023a For by you, O King, the treatises have been made the authority here;
[so too have] the self, dharma, sacred learning, the Vedas, and the ancestors been established by the great seers."
Brahmā, the Grandfather himself, as well as the preceptors and Prajāpati,
have indeed established the authority [of this law], and that established order has not been shaken.
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, you have today rightly undertaken this task.
"But let gold be given for the sake of the earth and the cattle;
in this way, we, Dharma, and all our ancestors will indeed be purified, for that is the supreme purifier."
"Those who bestow gold deliver ten ancestors and ten descendants; thus my ancestors spoke to me. Then, O King, lord of the people, I awoke filled with wonder.
"O best of the Bharatas, I have set my mind upon the gift of gold.
O King, O Lord, listen also to this ancient history concerning Jamadagnya, which is both auspicious and conducive to long life."
In former times, Rāma, the son of Jamadagni, filled with intense wrath, thrice seven times rid the earth of the kṣatriya caste. Then,
having conquered the entire earth, the lotus-eyed Rāma—
The hero performed the Vājimedha sacrifice, O great king— a rite honored by the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas, endowed with all desirable objects,
purifying for all beings, and increasing one’s splendor and radiance.
Though he was free from sin and possessed of splendor, that son of Jamadagni did not at all fall into a state of insignificance because of the fruit of that sacrifice.
Having performed that excellent sacrifice accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees, the high-souled one—
Filled with compassion, the descendant of Bhṛgu asked the ṛṣis and the gods, who were perfected in the sacred scriptures:
"O highly fortunate ones, tell me that which is the supreme purifier for men engaged in fierce deeds. Thus he spoke.
Then the venerable sage Vasiṣṭha replied to them:
"O Rāma, let the brahmins be honored, for the authority of the Vedas is evident;
furthermore, the hosts of brahmin-sages should be consulted regarding the means of purification."
Whatever those of great wisdom might say, that you should practice accordingly.
Then the descendant of Bhṛgu, possessed of great luster, questioned the celestial sage Vasiṣṭha, as well as Agastya and Kaśyapa, regarding that very same matter.
"O best of Brahmins, this thought has arisen in me: how might I be purified?
By what application of action, or by what gift in this world?
O most virtuous ones, if your minds are inclined toward showing me favor,"
The sages said:
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, tell us what may become a purifier for me hereafter—
whether by giving cows, wealth, or land, O descendant of Bhṛgu."
"O Bhārgava, we have heard that even a mortal who has committed evil is liberated [from it].
But listen, O brahmin-sage, to another great purifying gift:
the divine offspring of Jātavedas (Fire), which possesses a most wonderful form."

"Having formerly consumed the worlds through his prowess, we have heard that he was born here as one renowned as Suvarṇa; by giving him away, you shall attain perfection. Then the venerable Vasiṣṭha, firm in his vows, spoke to him.
Listen, O Rāma, to how gold of the brilliance of fire came into being,
what fruit is ordained for its gift, and the supreme excellence that is proclaimed here regarding it—
by whom, from what source, and in what manner it became possessed of such superior qualities.
O mighty-armed one, understand all this as I declare it to you:
know for certain that this gold has the nature of Agni and Soma;
the goat is Agni, the ram is Varuṇa, and the horse is the Sun—such is the traditional teaching.
Elephants are known as *nāgas*, and buffaloes as *asuras*. O descendant of Bhṛgu, chickens and boars are *rākṣasas*.
The sacred revelation (*śruti*) declares that cows are *iḍā*, milk is *soma*, and the earth is likewise [the sacrificial vessel].
Having churned the entire world, a mass of splendor arose.
O brahmin-sage, gold is the supreme and most excellent jewel among these.
For this reason, the gods, gandharvas, uragas, and rākṣasas [revere it].

O best of the Bhṛgus, both humans and Piśācas, purified and adorned with various ornaments such as crowns and armlets shining with gems, as well as those fashioned from gold, shine resplendently there.
Therefore, it is remembered as the supreme purifier among all purifiers;
know that, O bull of the Bharatas, it surpasses land, cows, and even jewels.
Whatever else there may be, such as giving land and cows here in this world—
O Lord, the gift of gold is distinguished as the supreme;
O you of immortal splendor, gold is indeed inexhaustible and purifying.
Bestow it upon the foremost of the twice-born, for this is the highest purifier.
Gold alone is prescribed for all sacrificial gifts;
those who bestow gold indeed become eternal givers.
Vasiṣṭha said:
The deities grant gold to those who give it;
for Agni is all the deities, and gold is of his very essence.
Therefore, by one who gives gold, all the deities are given.
"O tiger among men, they do not know anything superior to this. Furthermore,
O best of all wielders of weapons, O brahmin-sage, listen as I describe to you further the majesty of gold."
O descendant of Bhṛgu, I previously heard this in the Purāṇa as Prajāpati Svāyambhuva Manu was recounting it to the high-souled, blessed Rudra, the wielder of the trident.
13,083.040c O descendant of Bhṛgu’s lineage, at that time on the excellent Himavat mountain,
13,083.041a when the marriage of the goddess Rudrāṇī had been concluded, O joy of the Bhṛgus,
there occurred the union of the Blessed One with the high-souled goddess.

13,083.041 Then, all of them, filled with anxiety, approached the Blessed One. 13,083.042 Having propitiated Mahādeva, who was seated there, along with the boon-granting goddess Umā, they all spoke to Rudra with their heads bowed, O descendant of Bhrigu.

"O sinless Lord, this meeting of yours with the Goddess is that of an ascetic with an ascetic, of one of great splendor with one of exceeding splendor. O Lord, you possess unfailing power, and so too does this Goddess Umā."
"O Lord, O God, the offspring of you two shall be powerful;
it will surely leave nothing remaining in the three worlds.
Therefore, O large-eyed one, [grant this] to these gods who bow before you."
"O Lord of the World, out of a desire for the welfare of the three worlds, grant this boon:
restrain your supreme, blazing, and most excellent energy for the sake of offspring,
O All-pervading One."
"You two are indeed the essence of the three worlds; you will cause the world to burn with grief. For that offspring of yours will surely overcome the gods.
Neither the goddess Earth, nor the sky, nor heaven itself can contain him, O Lord."
"It is our opinion that all of us together are capable of sustaining this vigor;
by the power of our splendor, this entire world would not be consumed.
Therefore, O Blessed One, O Lord, you ought to show us favor."
"O best of gods, a son shall not be born to you from the Goddess;
therefore, restrain yourself through fortitude alone.
While they were speaking thus, the Blessed One, whose banner is the bull, [appeared].
"So be it," he replied to those gods, O brahmin-sage. Having said this, the one whose vehicle is the bull drew that seed upward;
from that time forth, he became known as Ūrdhvaretas (the one with upraised seed).
But then Rudrāṇī, enraged because the destruction of her offspring had been thus accomplished,
spoke these harsh words to the gods there out of her feminine nature:
"Since my husband, who truly desired offspring, has been turned away..."
"Therefore, all of you gods shall remain childless. Since you have indeed brought about the destruction of my progeny today, therefore,
O sky-goers, there shall be no offspring for any of you."

But at the time of the curse, O descendant of Bhrigu, Pāvaka was not present there; likewise, due to the curse on the goddess, the gods then became childless. However, Rudra then held that incomparable splendor.
Then, a small portion of it spilled from that [vessel] and fell upon the earth;
it then fell into the fire and grew in a manner like a miracle.
That splendor, having merged with the splendor [of the fire], attained a state of common origin.
At that very time, however, the gods led by Śakra were being severely tormented by an Asura named Tāraka—
the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, Maruts, and even the two Aśvins.
All the Sādhyas were terrified by the prowess of the Daitya; indeed,
the abodes of the deities, their celestial chariots,
their cities, and even the hermitages of the ṛṣis were seized by the Asuras.
With dejected minds, all those gods and sages went for refuge to the god Brahmā, the undecaying Lord;
they began to praise that supreme Lord, the boon-granting deity worthy of choice.
The gods said:
"O Lord, the Asura named Tāraka has been granted boons by you;
he torments both the gods and the sages—let his destruction be ordained."
"From this, O Grandfather, fear has indeed arisen for us.
Protect us, O God, for there is no other refuge for us.
Brahmā said:
"I am equal toward all beings; I do not approve of unrighteousness here.
Let Tāraka, the oppressor of the hosts of gods and sages, be slain quickly, O best of gods, so that the Vedas and the laws of dharma do not come to ruin."
"13,084.004c This has indeed been ordained by me here from the very beginning; let your fever depart.
13,084.005 The gods said:
13,084.005a 'O Blessed One, because of the granting of a boon, the son of Diti has become arrogant with power.'"
"He cannot be slain even by the gods; how then could he come to his end?
For he obtained from you, O Grandfather, this boon: 'May I not be subject to death by the gods, nor by the asuras, nor by the rākṣasas.'"
"In former times, when the destruction of progeny was brought about by Rudrāṇī, the gods were cursed:
'Your offspring shall not exist,' O Lord of the entire world.
Brahmā said:
O best of gods, at the time of the curse, Hutāśana was not present there;
he was to beget a son for the purpose of slaying the enemies of the thirty [gods].
Indeed, that [son] shall surpass all the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas.

With a spear by which his missiles fall unfailingly, he will slay him— [the one] from whom fear has arisen for you, as well as the other enemies of the gods, including humans, Gandharvas, Nāgas, and birds.
For that eternal resolve is designated as "desire" (kāma). That seed of Rudra’s vital energy, having been emitted, fell into the fire.
That energy became the great being Agni, like a second purifier.
"He shall procreate [the son] in the Gaṅgā for the sake of slaying the enemies of the gods.
But he did not receive that curse; having vanished at that time, the consumer of oblations (Agni) escaped it.
Therefore, O gods, the son of Pāvaka (Kārttikeya) shall arise as the remover of your fear.
"O sinless ones, let Agni be sought out and likewise commissioned today;
for the means to slay Tāraka has indeed been told by me.
For the curses of those possessing spiritual power have no effect upon other powers."
Upon encountering the exceedingly powerful, even the strong indeed become weak;
