he can slay those who are unslayable, even boon-granting ascetics. Kāma, whose delight is in resolve, is the most ancient fire.
The Lord of the World, indefinable, all-pervading, and the creator of all beings— he who dwells in the hearts of all creatures, the eldest, and the sovereign even greater than Rudra—
let that mass of splendor, the consumer of oblations, be sought out quickly.
"That god will fulfill the desire that has arisen in your minds.
Having heard these words of the high-souled one, the gods then departed,
their purposes accomplished, searching for Vibhāvasu.
Then the sages, together with the gods, searched the three worlds,
all of them longing for a sight of Agni and having their minds fixed upon him;
they were endowed with supreme ascetic power, illustrious, and renowned throughout the world.

O descendant of Bhrigu, all those perfected beings (siddhas) wandered through the worlds, yet they could not find the sacrificial fire, which had vanished and merged into its own self. Thereupon, filled with alarm and longing for a sight of the fire, they—
With a weary mind, scorched by the heat of the fire,
the water-dwelling frog rose from the depths of the netherworld and spoke to the gods:
"O Lord, Agni dwells in the depths of the netherworld."
"O gods, I have arrived here from the intense heat originating from the Fire-god; that venerable bearer of oblations was sleeping within the water,
and having infused the waters with his splendors, we were scorched by him."
"O gods, if the sight of Vibhāvasu is desired by you,
then go there if you have business with the Fire-god. Depart, O Suras, for we shall accomplish our purpose out of fear of Agni."
Having said this much, the frog quickly entered the water.
But Hutāśana (Agni) then perceived the frog’s treachery;
approaching him, he cursed him, saying, "You shall indeed no longer perceive tastes."
Having joined that frog with a curse,
the powerful Pāvaka departed elsewhere to dwell and did not show himself to the gods.
But the gods, O descendant of Bhṛgu, showed favor toward the frogs.
13,084.029c Listen, O mighty-armed one, as I relate everything to you.
13,084.030 The gods said: 13,084.030a "Though we were tongueless due to Agni’s curse, we were deprived of the knowledge of taste."
"You shall utter the Sarasvatī in its many forms; even when you have entered the dwelling of the cave, devoid of food and unconscious,
the earth shall sustain you, though you are withered and as if lifeless."

"Even during the night when darkness has fallen, you shall wander," having said this to them, the gods then once again traversed this earth for the sake of the blazing fire, yet they did not find the consumer of oblations.
Then, O descendant of Bhrigu, a certain elephant, resembling the elephant of the lord of the gods, said to the deities while standing upon the Aśvattha tree, "This is Agni. Thereupon,
the Fire-god, overcome with rage, cursed all those elephants.
"O descendant of Bhṛgu, your tongue shall become adverse," having said this, Agni, indicated by the elephant, emerged from the *aśvattha* tree;
then the Fire entered the womb of the *śamī* tree, desiring to sleep.
Entering the interior of the *kīcaka* reeds, he was immediately signaled by them;
leaving those bamboo stalks that were heated by his breath, he entered a *śamī* tree.
Now hear, O Lord, what favor the Nāgas bestowed upon him.
"O best of the Bhrigu lineage, the gods, whose prowess is truth, are pleased.
The gods said:
"Even with your tongue turned back, you shall consume all kinds of food."
"You shall utter speech loudly, yet with indistinct syllables.
Having said this, the denizens of heaven once again rushed toward the fire.
Then the fire emerged from the *aśvattha* tree and entered the interior of the *śamī* tree.

O Brahmin, when this was announced by the parrot, the gods rushed toward him. But Agni cursed the parrot, saying, "You shall be deprived of speech," and then the eater of oblations (Agni) even caused the parrot's tongue to curl back.
Seeing the flaming fire, the gods, filled with compassion, said to Śuka:
"O bird, you shall not remain forever one whose speech is lost;
even though your tongue is turned back, your words will become lovely."
"And when your voice is uttered by men upon the earth,
it will be like the wonderful, indistinct, and sweet cry of a child who has grown up;
having spoken thus, the deities beheld the fire within the womb of the Śamī tree."
They made that very place a sacred sanctuary for all ritual acts;
from that time forward, fire was seen within the womb of the *śamī* tree,
and human beings followed that as the means for its production.
O Bhārgava, those waters which were in the netherworld (rasātala) and came into contact with the fire (Citrabhānu), now release heat through mountain springs,
being heated by the splendor of that fire as it lay upon them.
Then Agni, the deity, seeing them, became distressed;
the Purifier asked them, "What is the reason for your coming?
To him all those gods and supreme ṛṣis spoke.
"We shall appoint you to this task; therefore, it behooves you to perform it. And once that is accomplished, there will be a very great benefit for you as well.
Agni said:
"O gods, speak what must be done for you; I shall perform it all. For I am at your command; let there be no hesitation on your part. The gods said:

"O dear one, an asura named Tāraka, arrogant due to a boon from Brahmā, is oppressing us by his prowess; let his slaughter be ordained. [He oppresses] these hosts of gods, O father, as well as the hosts of Prajāpatis."
"O Pāvaka, protect these highly fortunate ṛṣis as well! O Lord,
begetter of oblations, procreate a heroic son endowed with splendor who may destroy the fear we have of that asura."
"Since we have been cursed by the Great Goddess, there is no other refuge for us except your own power; therefore, protect us from that.
Thus addressed, the Blessed One, the consumer of sacrificial offerings (havya) and ancestral oblations (kavya), replied, "So be it."
Then the invincible one went toward the Gaṅgā, the daughter of Bhagiratha;
he united with her, and at that time a fetus was formed within her.
That fetus then grew like a fire in dry grass.
By the splendor of that embryo, Gaṅgā became distracted in mind;
she fell into intense torment and was unable to endure it. Then, when the embryo endowed with fiery energy had been placed there by the Fire-god, [she could not bear it].

13,084.055c A certain asura let out a terrifying roar within the Gaṅgā. 13,084.056a Then, by that vast sound which had fallen upon her unawares, 13,084.056c Gaṅgā, her eyes rolling and agitated with terror, became distraught.
Viśaṃjñā was unable to sustain the embryo within herself.
Then, O Brahmin, Jāhnavī, her limbs overwhelmed by that splendor and trembling,
spoke these words, impelled by the power of the embryo.
"O Blessed One, I am not capable of sustaining this splendor;
I have been rendered utterly bewildered by it, and my well-being has been completely destroyed. O Blessed One, I am overwhelmed, and my strength has perished, O Sinless One."
"O best of those who radiate heat, I am not capable of bearing this fetus.
I shall cast it out from distress, but never from desire;
O divine Vibhāvasu, my mind has no attachment to it."
For even the most subtle connection serves a purpose in times of distress, O one of great splendor.
Whatever is endowed with merit here, or otherwise, O Consumer of Oblations,
I consider that to reside in you alone, as do dharma and adharma themselves.
Then the Fire-god said to her: "Let this embryo be sustained, let it be sustained! Endowed with my splendor, it shall result in the manifestation of great virtues.
For you are indeed capable of bearing and supporting the entire earth."
"Indeed, there is nothing unattainable for you, except for the retention of my seed.
Though she was restrained by Agni and by the gods as well,
that best of rivers then cast off that embryo upon Meru, the most excellent of mountains.

Though capable of bearing [the child], she was overwhelmed by the splendor of Rudra's energy; she was then unable to sustain that embryo by her own strength. Out of distress, she cast it forth—[the child] possessing the brilliance of a blazing fire.
Then, O descendant of Bhrigu, Agni revealed himself to that Gaṅgā;
he questioned the best of rivers: "Is the fetus one whose birth will be auspicious?
O Goddess, what is its color, and of what form does it appear?"
"With what splendor is he endowed? Tell me all this.
Gaṅgā said:
"That embryo is indeed of the nature of gold; in splendor, he is like you, O Fire."
Pure, radiant, and shining like gold, it illuminated the mountain;
its cool fragrance, O best of ascetics, was indeed equal to that of *kadamba* flowers mixed with lotuses and lilies from the lakes.
By the splendor of that embryo, like the rays of the sun,
whatever substance on earth or in the mountains was touched by it,
all of it appeared transformed into gold on every side.
He ran across mountains, rivers, and springs;
with his splendor, he illuminated the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
O Lord, such is your son, the bearer of oblations.
Equal to Sūrya and Vaiśvānara in splendor, like another Moon,
that goddess, having spoken thus, vanished right there. And the radiant Pāvaka, having accomplished the task of the denizens of heaven, [departed].

Then, O descendant of Bhṛgu, he went to his desired destination. Because of these qualities of action in the world, Agni’s name is celebrated by the sages and the gods as "Hiraṇyaretas" (He of the Golden Seed).
And then the goddess Earth became known as Vasumatī. That embryo of great splendor, born of the fire and destined for Gaṅgā,
reached the divine forest of reeds and grew there, wonderful to behold.
The Kṛttikās beheld him, whose splendor was like that of the rising sun;
and having conceived affection for the child, they nourished him with the flow of their breast milk.
Thereupon, that being of supreme luster attained the name Kārttikeya.
Because he had fallen [skanna], he became Skanda; and because he dwelt in a cave (guhā), he became Guha. Thus was gold produced as the offspring of Jātavedas.
Among these, Jāmbūnada is the most excellent, serving as an ornament even for the gods.
From that time forth, this has been called *jātarūpa*;
for that gold is the blessed Agni, the Lord, and Prajāpati.
Indeed, O best of the twice-born, gold is the most sacred of all purifying things.
Jātarūpa is declared to be of the nature of Agni and Soma;
it is the supreme jewel among jewels, and likewise the best among ornaments. It is the most sacred of purifiers and the most auspicious of auspicious things.
Vasiṣṭha said:
Furthermore, O Rāma, I have heard in the past this vision of Brahman,
concerning what occurred to the Grandfather, the Supreme Brahman.
O dear one, when the great god Rudra, the lord and master, assumed the Varuṇa body and exercised his Varuṇa sovereignty, O Rāma,
all the sages and the gods, led by Agni, came to him.
All the components of the sacrifice arrived there, along with the *vaṣaṭkāra* in embodied form; the *Sāman* chants and the *Yajus* formulas came by the thousands in personified forms,
and the *Ṛgveda*, adorned with the *padapāṭha* and *kramapāṭha* recitations, also came to that place.
The *Ṛgveda* arrived there, as did the *Sāmans* and the *Yajus*; likewise, the *lakṣaṇas*, the accents (*svaras*), the *stobhas*, the *nirukta*, and the *svarabhaktis* remained there,
along with the syllable *oṃ*, the *netras*, and the methods of suppression and extension (*nigrahapragrahau*).

The Lord Śiva held the Vedas along with the Upaniṣads, the sciences, and the Sāvitrī; he held the past, the present, and the future. Then, O Lord, he himself offered his own self as an oblation into his own self.
The wielder of the Pināka bow beautified that sacrifice of many forms;
he is the sky, the atmosphere, the earth, and the ether; likewise, this lord of the earth is the master of all sciences, the illustrious one, and he is also the radiant fire.

This Lord, the auspicious one, is celebrated as Brahmā, Śiva, Rudra, Varuṇa, Agni, and Prajāpati; he is the auspicious Lord of all beings. His sacrifice is that of Paśupati, as are his asceticism and his ritual offerings.
The goddess Dīkṣā, whose vows are radiant, the quarters of space together with their presiding lords,
the wives of the gods, the maidens, and the mothers of the gods— seeing that spilled semen, [they were struck with wonder] as he held his trident-weapon.
O descendant of Bhrigu’s lineage, they then arrived there together,
delighted at the sacrifice of the high-souled Paśupati and Varuṇa;
but upon seeing them, the seed of the Self-born One fell to the earth.
From the flow of that semen, Pūṣan gathered the dust from the ground with his two hands and cast it into that very sacrificial fire.
Then, as that sacrifice proceeded with the fire blazing, [the gods departed].
While Brahmā was offering oblations there, an incarnation indeed appeared.
As soon as that semen had been spilled, he caught it with the sacrificial ladle and,
O descendant of Bhṛgu, offered it into the fire like clarified butter, accompanied by sacred mantras.
Then that powerful one brought forth the multitude of beings;
from that splendor (tejas) was born the luminous element (taijasa) in the worlds,
and from darkness (tamas) arose states characterized by darkness (tāmasa), while goodness (sattva) likewise pervaded both.
Light is eternally endowed with qualities, as is space within darkness. Likewise, among all beings, there exist goodness (*sattva*), light, and darkness.
O Lord, when the seed was offered into that fire, these three manifested.
These men were endowed with physical beauty and possessed the qualities born of procreation.
From *bhṛg* (to nourish) came the ancient Bhṛgu; from the charcoal (*aṅgāra*) came Aṅgiras; and from his reliance upon the charcoal, another was born known as Kavi.

Because Bhṛgu arose together with flames, he is known as Bhṛgu. From the rays (marīci) came Marīci, and from Marīci was born Kaśyapa. From the embers (aṅgāra) came Aṅgiras, O dear one, and the Vālakhilyas from the mountain peak.
13,085.017 Even here, O Lord, they say that Atri was born from the very word "atra" (here).
13,085.018 Likewise, from the removal of ashes, there arose the Vaikhānasas, who are equal to the hosts of Brahman-sages and who desire the virtues of austerity and sacred learning.
From his ears were born the two Aśvins, who are highly esteemed for their beauty;
from his other apertures were born the lords of creatures (the Prajāpatis); from the pores of his skin were born the Ṛṣis; and from his sweat was born the Vedic meter, consisting of impurity.

For this reason, the sages, endowed with sacred learning and perceiving the authority of the Vedas, declare that Agni is indeed all the deities. The logs of wood are the months, and the exudations are known as the fortnights.
The days and nights are said to be twelve thousand three hundred and eight muhūrtas; bile (pitta) is the light of Varuṇa.
They say blood belongs to Rudra, and from blood, gold is known to have arisen.
That [gold] should be understood as belonging to Mitra, and from smoke, the Vasus are said to have originated.
Those rays of yours which are the Rudras, as well as the highly effulgent Ādityas,
have been designated as the coals situated in their respective stations in the sky. And the Primordial Lord of the world is that Supreme Brahman, that which is eternal.
"It bestows all desires," they said; there he offered the oblation.
Then Mahādeva Varuṇa, whose nature is the Supreme Self, spoke:
"This is my divine sacrificial session; I am the master of the house here."
"The three former offspring were mine; of this there is no doubt.
Know this, O sky-travelers, for that is indeed the fruit of my sacrifice.
Agni said:
"Those born from my limbs and produced through my support are indeed my own offspring; for Varuṇa is one whose self is not independent.
Then Brahmā, the preceptor of the worlds and the grandfather of the worlds, spoke.
"Those offspring are mine alone, for my seed was offered as the oblation. I am indeed the reciter of the mantra and the priest who offers the seed;
the fruit belongs to him whose seed it is, provided that the seed is considered the cause."
Then all the hosts of gods, having approached the Grandfather, spoke with their palms joined in reverence and having saluted him with their heads bowed:
"O Blessed One, we all, as well as the entire world with its mobile and immobile beings— "
"All these are indeed your offspring; therefore, let Agni Vibhāvasu and the lordly god Varuṇa obtain their desired wish.
By nature, Varuṇa is also the Lord of aquatic creatures, born from Brahmā."

The Grandfather (Brahmā), who knows the truth, first took Bhṛgu as his offspring— he who possessed the splendor of the sun— and he likewise ordained Aṅgiras as the offspring of Agni for the sake of progeny; furthermore,
the Grandfather took Kavi as his own offspring.
Then that Bhr̥gu, known as Vāruṇa, performed the work of procreation;
while the illustrious Aṅgiras was Āgneya, and the highly renowned Kavi was Brāhma. These two, Bhārgava and Āṅgirasa, were the signs of the continuation of the world in the universe.
All these excellent Brahmins are the three lords of progeny; understand that this entire lineage belongs to them. Now, Bhṛgu had seven sons there who were equal to Bhṛgu in their virtues.
Cyavana, Vajraśīrṣa, Śuci, Aurva,
Śukra, Vareṇya, and the powerful Savana— these seven were the Bhārgavas, all descendants of Varuṇa, in whose lineage you also are born.
And eight sons of Aṅgiras are also proclaimed as the Vāruṇas: Bṛhaspati, Utathya, Vayasya, and Śānti; Ghora, Virūpa, Saṃvarta, and Sudhanvan is remembered as the eighth.
These eight, born of Agni, are all established in knowledge and free from affliction;
they are declared to be the sons of the sage Brāhmaṇa and are known as the Vāruṇas. These eight auspicious knowers of Brahman are endowed with the qualities born of their progenitors.
Kavi, Kāvya, Viṣṇu, the wise Uśanas, Bhṛgu, Virajas, Kāśī, and Ugra, the knower of dharma—
these eight are indeed the sons of Kavi, and by them this entire world is pervaded.
For these are indeed the lords of creatures by whom these creatures [are sustained];
thus, O tiger among the Bhrigus, the world is perpetually [sustained] by the lineages and descendants of Aṅgiras, Kavi, and Bhrigu.

O sage, from the beginning the Lord and Master Varuṇa took Kavi and Bhr̥gu; therefore, O dear one, those two are known as the sons of Varuṇa (Vāruṇau). The god Śikhin, the consumer of oblations (Agni), took Aṅgiras from him.
Therefore, all those born of that lineage are to be known as Aṅgirasas.
In former times, Brahmā, the Grandfather, was propitiated by the deities, who said:
"These lords of the world shall carry us across [this difficulty] through their progeny."
All these lords of creatures, all of whom are great ascetics,
shall by your grace deliver this world eternally;
likewise, they shall be the founders of lineages who increase your splendor.
There might be thirteen thousand eight hundred and fifty-four who are all knowers of the Vedas and likewise lords of speech;
gentle great seers belonging to the faction of the gods and to Prajāpati,
who attain both austerity and supreme celibacy.

Infinite Brahman, truth, and supreme austerity on earth—you are all these, O Lord; for you alone are the progenitor of us and of these [others]. Indeed, O Grandfather, you are the creator of both the gods and the brahmins.
"O Grandfather, considering that all the Bhārgavas, beginning with Marīci, are indeed your offspring, we ask for your forgiveness. They shall procreate progeny in this very form."
"And they shall likewise establish themselves at the beginning and the end of the yugas.
Having been addressed thus by them, Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds,
replied with pleasure, "So be it," and they also departed as they had come.
Thus did this occur in the past at the sacrifice of that high-souled one,
the foremost of gods, who at the beginning of the world assumed the form of Varuṇa.
Agni, Brahmā, Paśupati, Śarva, Rudra, and Prajāpati [were present].

"This gold is indeed the offspring of Agni"— this is the traditional doctrine (dhāraṇā). And in the absence of fire, those who know the authoritative measures [of ritual] place gold in the positions of the sacrificial fires,
according to the evidence of Vedic revelation.
One offers oblations into a clump of *kuśa* grass where gold is situated; likewise,
into the mound of an anthill, into the right ear of a horse,
onto the floor of a wagon, into the waters of another, or even into the hand of a Brāhmaṇa.
When an oblation has been offered, the Blessed One considers that it brings about delightful prosperity;
therefore, we have heard that all the deities are devoted to fire.
For Agni was produced from Brahmā, and gold was produced from Agni.
Therefore, those who perceive the Dharma indeed bestow gold; we have heard that all the deities grant their favor to those men who give gold with a pure mind.
As he proceeds toward the supreme goal, his worlds shall be free from darkness;
O Bhārgava, he shall be consecrated with the sovereignty of a king in the heavenly world.
When the rising of the sun has occurred, [he shall perform] the rite preceded by ritual rules and mantras.
He who gives gold indeed wards off bad dreams;
he who gives it at sunrise has his sin shaken off;
for one giving gold at midday, it destroys future evil.
He who, firm in his vows, gives gold at the evening twilight,
attains residence in the same world as Brahmā, Vāyu, Agni, and Soma;
he also obtains a glorious station in the worlds of Indra and the other gods.
Having attained fame in this world, he rejoices with his sins pacified;
thereafter, he always becomes peerless in other worlds,
possessing unobstructed movement and indeed acting according to his will.
He does not fall away from those [worlds], and he eternally attains the Great;
by giving inexhaustible gold, one obtains abundant worlds. But he who, having kindled the fire toward the rising of the sun...
One who gives this gift while dedicated to a vow attains all desires;
they say that this gift is indeed like Agni himself, bringing happiness,
endowed with qualities as one wishes, and is known as the impeller.
"O sinless one, O descendant of Bhṛgu, I have thus described to you the origin of gold, as well as that of Kārttikeya, O Lord; know this, O master.
Then, after a long period of time, Kārttikeya grew up."

O descendant of Bhṛgu, O Brahmin, at the command of the Lord of the Thirty-three and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, he was chosen by the gods, including Indra, as their commander-in-chief; he then slew Tāraka the Daitya and other Asuras as well.
"O Lord, I have described to you the merits of giving gold;
therefore, O best among givers, bestow gold upon the Brahmins.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed by Vasiṣṭha, the powerful son of Jamadagni gave gold to the Brahmins and was liberated from his sin.
All this regarding gold has been told to you, O lord of the earth.
The fruit of giving is indeed such, and the birth from fire is unsurpassed.
Therefore, you too should bestow much gold upon the Brahmins;
by giving gold, O King, you will be liberated from sin.

"Thus, O Great King Yudhiṣṭhira, has this meritorious birth of the noble Suvarṇa been recounted to you, as well as his act of giving. Thus spoke Vasiṣṭha, the preeminent sage of excellent speech, to Rāma.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, perform that greatness which lies in the gift of gold.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The grandfather has here described the rules regarding gold."
Tell me how Tāraka met his end— that very cause for the origin of gold which has been proclaimed here, along with the qualities of its extensive bestowal as characterized in the Vedas.
"O King, it has been said that he is indeed incapable of being slain by the gods;
yet his death here has not been proclaimed by you in detail.
I wish to hear this from you, O upholder of the Kuru lineage."
"In its entirety, tell me of the slaying of Tāraka, for my curiosity is great.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Indra among kings, the gods and the ṛṣis were thus frustrated in their purpose."
The Kṛttikās indeed urged him to take up the offspring;
for among the deities, there was not one who was capable,
nor even a single one who was able by her own power to sustain that embryo.
Then, because they had conceived a fetus, the Fire-god was pleased with those six; by the emission of his own splendor and through his supreme virility,
those six Kṛttikās nurtured the embryo of Jātavedas.
O Lord, the entire splendor of fire is deposited within the six paths;
therefore, as that high-souled prince grew,
those women, their limbs overwhelmed by his brilliance, found no peace anywhere.
Then, O bull among men, when the time had arrived, all those Kṛttikās, their limbs enveloped in radiance, simultaneously gave birth to the embryo. Thereupon,
that embryo, which had been established in six locations, attained oneness.
The Earth received that embryo near the city of Kāntīpura; possessing a divine form, radiant and glowing like fire,
it grew within the divine Śara forest, beautiful to behold.
The Kṛttikās beheld that child, who possessed a splendor equal to fire;
moved by affection and friendship, they nourished him with the flow of their breast milk.
Thus he became known as Kārttikeya throughout the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
Because he had spilled [the seed], he became Skanda; and because of his dwelling in a cave (*guhā*), he became Guha.
Then the thirty-three gods, the quarters along with their presiding deities, Rudra, Dhātṛ, Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pūṣan, Aryaman, and Bhaga [approached].
Aṃśa, Mitra, the Sādhyas, the Vasus, Vāsava, and the two Aśvins;
water, wind, the sky, the moon, the constellations, the planets, and the sun;
and all other distinct beings that are indeed offerings to the gods.
They came there to behold that youth, the son of Agni;
the ṛṣis offered hymns of praise, and the gandharvas likewise sang songs to the six-faced Kumāra, who possesses twelve eyes and is beloved by the twice-born.
Seeing him with broad shoulders and twelve arms, possessing the splendor of fire and the sun,
lying within a thicket of reeds, the gods together with the sages attained supreme joy and considered the Asura already slain.
Then all the gods performed what was pleasing for him;
they gave him toys for his play and flocks of birds.
Suparṇa gave him a peacock with variegated plumage as a vehicle.
The Rākṣasas gave him both a boar and a buffalo;
Varuṇa himself presented a cock as bright as fire;
the Moon gave him a ram, and the Sun gave him a radiant splendor.
The divine mother of cows gave him cows by the hundreds of thousands; Agni gave him a goat endowed with all virtues, and Ilā gave him abundant flowers and fruits.
Sudhanvan gave him a cart and a chariot with immeasurable poles.
Varuṇa gave him auspicious, divine serpents belonging to Varuṇa; Indra, the lord of the gods, gave him lions, tigers, leopards, and other fanged beasts;
and he also gave many terrible wild animals and various kinds of umbrellas.
The hosts of Rākṣasas and Asuras who followed that Lord presented him with the finest vehicles and wealth.
But seeing him growing in power, Tāraka sought to challenge him.

Despite many means, they were unable to slay that omnipresent lord. Having honored Guha, the dweller of the cave, with the office of generalissimo, the gods reported to him the mistreatment caused by Tāraka.
That powerful lord, the commander of the divine army, having grown in strength and possessing great heroism,
struck the Dānava Tāraka with an unerring spear.
When that Asura had been slain by the Kumāra playing in that manner, [the gods rejoiced].
The lord of the gods was re-established in his sovereignty over the deities as their ruler once more;
then the powerful Skanda shone forth as the commander-in-chief,
the protector and lord of the gods, and the one who does what is pleasing to Śaṃkara.
This very Lord, the son of Agni, is Hiraṇyamūrti;
as the eternal Kumāra, he attained the generalship of the gods.
Therefore, gold is auspicious, an inexhaustible and supreme jewel.
The innate splendor of Kārttikeya is considered to be the supreme fire-energy;
thus, O descendant of Kuru, Vasiṣṭha related this to Rāma in the past.
Therefore, O lord of men, strive to give gifts of gold.
Having given gold, Rāma was indeed liberated from all sins and attained a great station in Triviṣṭapa, which is difficult for men to obtain.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sinless one, O virtuous-souled king, you have declared the dharma for the four castes;
likewise, tell me the entire procedure for the *śrāddha*.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed by Yudhiṣṭhira, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu,
then began to explain this entire procedure for the śrāddha.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen attentively, O King, to this auspicious ritual for the *śrāddha*,
which bestows wealth, fame, and sons— a supreme sacrifice to the ancestors, O scorcher of foes—
concerning the gods, asuras, humans, gandharvas, serpents, and rakshasas.
The ancestors are indeed always to be worshipped by the Piśācas and Kinnaras. Having first worshipped the ancestors, they afterwards satisfy the gods.
Therefore, a person should always worship [the ancestors] with every effort.
"O Great King, the *anvāhārya* is said to be the *śrāddha* for the ancestors;
that rite was first ordained by rule with the offering of meat.
On all days, the grandfathers are gratified by the performance of *śrāddhas*."
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having performed the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyajña) on the day of the new moon,
should perform the monthly ancestral rite (śrāddha) consisting of rice-balls (piṇḍas), known by the wise as the *anvāhārya*.
At that time, the first [officiant], pure and with palms joined in reverence, should perform [the rite] with meat offerings.
O sinless one, I shall declare to you all the merits and demerits for each lunar day, and the fruit that is obtained through *śrāddha* rites performed on those days.

I shall proclaim all of that exactly as it is; listen to it from me. By worshipping the ancestors on the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad), one obtains in one’s own home women who give birth to handsome offspring, who are beautiful, and who bear many children.
On the second [day], women are born; on the third, however, bards (vandins);
on the fourth, many small animals appear in the house;
and on the fifth, O King, many sons are born to those who perform [the rite].
Men who perform [śrāddha] on the sixth lunar day become partakers of splendor;
O King, one performing śrāddha on the seventh becomes a partaker of the fruits of agriculture;
and by performing it on the eighth, one shall obtain profit in trade.
For one performing a *śrāddha* on the ninth day, there will be many single-hoofed animals;
for one performing *śrāddhas* on the tenth day, cattle increase in number.
O King, a mortal performing [the rite] on the eleventh day becomes a possessor of base metals.

In his house, sons endowed with spiritual luster (*brahmavarcas*) are born. For one who constantly strives on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*), much silver, various [jewels], and beautiful gold are always seen.
By performing a *śrāddha* on the thirteenth day, one becomes the most excellent among kinsmen;
however, young men in his household will inevitably die. By performing a *śrāddha* on the fourteenth day, a mortal becomes a participant in battle.
A man who performs [the rite] on the fourteenth day shall partake in happiness;
by making offerings on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), however, he shall obtain all his desires.
In the dark fortnight, one should begin from the tenth day onwards, excluding the fourteenth day.

In the performance of the *śrāddha* rite, certain lunar days (*tithis*) are auspicious, while others are not so. Just as the dark fortnight (*apara-pakṣa*) is superior to the bright fortnight (*pūrva-pakṣa*),
so too is the afternoon (*aparāhṇa*) superior to the forenoon (*pūrvāhṇa*) for the *śrāddha*.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Lord, what gift indeed, when offered to the ancestors, becomes inexhaustible?
What oblation lasts for a long time, and what conduces to infinity?"
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to me regarding those sacrificial offerings which those who know the ritual of the Śrāddha prescribe; I shall describe the optional rites and their respective fruits."
O King, by the offering of sesame seeds, rice, barley, beans, water, roots,
and fruits at a śrāddha, the ancestors are gratified for a month. Manu has declared that a śrāddha in which the quantity of sesame seeds increases becomes inexhaustible.
In all offerings of food, sesame seeds are traditionally considered the most important.
Satisfaction for two months indeed comes to the host of ancestors through fish;
they say it lasts for three months through the meat of a sheep, and for four months through that of a hare.
O King, the ancestors are gratified for five months by the meat of a goat;
for six months by that of a boar, and indeed for seven months by that of a bird.
For eight months they are satisfied by the meat of the spotted deer, and for nine months by that of the Ruru deer.
With the meat of a *gavaya*, there shall be satisfaction for ten months;
with the meat of a buffalo, the ancestors find delight for eleven months;
and when a *śrāddha* is offered with beef, it is said here that the satisfaction lasts for a full year.
Just as with beef, so too is milk-rice (pāyasa) prepared with clarified butter (sarpiṣ) appropriate;
with the meat of the vādhrīṇasa, there is satisfaction for twelve years. When offered at the time of the ancestors' passing (pitṛkṣaya), the meat of the rhinoceros (khaḍga) leads to infinity.
"Black pot-herbs and iron are said to grant infinity when offered by a goat.
And here, O Yudhiṣṭhira, they sing these verses sung by the ancestors,
which the blessed Sanatkumāra spoke to me in the past."
"May he who would give us milk-rice mixed with ghee on the thirteenth lunar day under the Maghā asterism during the sun’s southern course (dakṣiṇāyana) be born in our family; or even one who,
restrained in his vows, gives it under the Maghās along with a goat made of iron."
Under the "elephant-shade" (the shadow of an elephant at midday), one should duly be fanned with ear-fans.
One should desire many sons, so that even if only one among them goes to Gayā,
or performs a horse sacrifice, or releases a dark-colored bull.
There stands that banyan tree, renowned throughout the worlds as the "Maker of the Imperishable. Whatever—
be it water, roots, fruit, meat, or even food— is offered at the Pitṛkṣaya (the ancestors' festival) beneath it,
if mixed with honey, it conduces to infinity.
Bhīṣma said:
Listen to me as I describe those optional *śrāddha* rites which Yama proclaimed to Śaśabindu, categorized individually according to the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*).

The man who constantly performs a *śrāddha* during the conjunction with Kṛttikā, having established the sacred fires, shall sacrifice as one free from anxiety and accompanied by offspring. One desiring offspring should perform it under Rohiṇī; one desiring vigor, under Mṛgaśiras.
A man performing a *śrāddha* under the asterism Ārdrā becomes a doer of cruel deeds;
a mortal performing a *śrāddha* under Punarvasu becomes a sharer in the fruits of agriculture;
furthermore, a man desiring prosperity should endeavor to perform a *śrāddha* under Puṣya.
One who offers a *śrāddha* under Āśleṣā gives birth to heroic sons;
by performing a *śrāddha* under Maghā, one becomes the most distinguished among kinsmen. One who offers a *śrāddha* under the Phalgunīs becomes fortunate as a giver of *śrāddhas*.
Under the *uttarās*, one becomes a sharer of offspring; under *hasta*, one becomes a sharer of fruits.
By offering a *śrāddha* under *citrā*, one obtains handsome sons. By offering a *śrāddha* under the *phalgunīs*, one obtains handsome sons.
By offering a śrāddha under the Uttarās, one is reborn handsome; by offering a śrāddha under Hasta, one enjoys ultimate happiness;
and by offering a śrāddha under Citrā, one obtains various fruits.
By worshipping the ancestors under the conjunction of Svāti, one lives by trade;
under Viśākhā, a man becomes the father of many sons through his ancestral efforts; and by performing rites under Anurādhā, one shall set in motion the circle of kings.
O best of the Kuru clan, a mortal man who offers oblations in the constellation Jyeṣṭhā, preceded by faith and self-restraint, shall attain sovereignty. Furthermore,
one may obtain health under Mūla, and unsurpassed fame under the Aṣāḍhās.
Under the *Uttarā-Aṣāḍhās*, one may wander the earth free from sorrow;
performing a *śrāddha* under *Abhijit*, one shall obtain the most excellent knowledge.
By giving a *śrāddha* under *Śravaṇa*, one goes to the supreme goal after death.
Under Dhaniṣṭhā, a man who shares in royal power shall meet no misfortune;
performing [medical] acts under the Vāruṇa asterism, a physician shall attain success.
Under Śravaṇa there is perfection of learning; under Dhaniṣṭhā, there shall be wealth.
Likewise, under the conjunction of Śatabhiṣaj, there is liberation from disease as well as strength.
By performing [rites] under Pūrva-proṣṭhapadā, one will obtain many goats and sheep;
furthermore, by performing them under Uttarā-proṣṭhapadā, one obtains cattle by the thousands.
Resorting to Revatī, one obtains wealth made of much silver;
under Aśvinī, one acquires horses; and under Bharaṇī, one attains the highest lifespan.
Having heard this rule for the Śrāddha, Śaśabindu acted accordingly.
He conquered the earth without any affliction and indeed ruled over it.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, to what kind of persons should a śrāddha offering be given?"
"O tiger among the Kurus, you ought to explain to me that [which concerns] the twice-born.
Bhīṣma said:
"A Kṣatriya who understands the duty of giving should not examine Brāhmaṇas."
In rites for the gods and in those for the ancestors, they say that examination is proper.
Here, the deities are worshipped by means of divine splendor alone;
therefore, having approached them, a man should cause gifts to be given to all the gods.
Furthermore, O great king, at a *śrāddha* ceremony, a wise man should examine the Brahmins according to their lineage, conduct, age, physical form, learning, and noble birth.
Among these, some are defilers of the row (*paṅktidūṣaka*), while others are purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*).
"O King, listen as I enumerate those who are unworthy of the company at a meal (apāṅkteya):
a gambler, a killer of an embryo, one afflicted with chronic disease, a cattle-herder, an outcaste, a village servant, a usurer, a singer, and a seller of all kinds of goods."
An arsonist, a poisoner, one who eats the food of a harlot, a seller of Soma,
a sea-faring merchant, a royal servant, an oil-presser, a forger,
one who quarrels with his father, and he in whose house lives a paramour— [these are those who must not be invited].
One who is falsely accused, a thief, one who lives by his craft, a maker of arrows, a spy, a betrayer of friends, an adulterer,
a teacher of those who do not observe vows, and likewise a *kāṇḍapṛṣṭha*.
He who walks with dogs, he who has been bitten by a dog, the younger brother whose elder brother is unmarried, the leper, the violator of his teacher’s bed, the actor,
the temple-priest, and he who lives by the stars.
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, when an offering is eaten by such Brahmins who are unworthy of the row,
those who discourse on the Veda say that the sacrificial oblation goes to the Rākṣasas.
Furthermore, he who has eaten at a Śrāddha should not study the Vedas, nor should one who has approached the bed of a low-caste woman."
His ancestors lie for that month in his excrement;
what is given to a seller of Soma becomes ordure, and to a physician, pus and blood. What is given to a temple-priest (devalaka) is lost, and what is given to a usurer finds no firm foundation.
Whatever is given to a trader brings no fruit either in this world or the next;

it is like an oblation poured into ashes. Likewise, [what is given] to a twice-born man who is the son of a remarried woman, or to those who have fallen away from dharma and whose conduct has degenerated, is of no avail.
If those of small intelligence offer *havya* (oblations to the gods) and *kavya* (oblations to the ancestors) to them [the unworthy] with knowledge [of their status],
it is certain that after death their ancestors will consume excrement.
One should recognize these as the lowest of the twice-born, unworthy of the company at a meal (apāṅkteya):
those of small intellect who provide instruction to Śūdras. A one-eyed man destroys the merit of sixty, a eunuch a hundred, and a leper as many as he gazes upon.
O King, when those seated in a row are thus defiled—
whatever one eats with the head wrapped, whatever one eats facing south,
and whatever one eats while wearing shoes, know all that to be asuric.
Whatever is given with malice and whatever is devoid of faith—
all that Brahmā assigned as the portion for the lord of the Asuras.
Dogs and those who defile the row of diners should not look [at such offerings] under any circumstances.

Therefore, one should give [the offerings] while surrounded and scatter sesame seeds [around them]. For when sesame seeds are not given, and when the Śrāddha is performed by one under the sway of anger, those who are flesh-eaters and the hosts belonging to the Krodhavaśa class [are present].

Yātudhānas and Piśācas plunder that sacrificial offering as long as one perceives those unworthy of the row (*apaṅktya*) eating within the row. For that duration, they cause the foolish giver to fall away from the fruit [of his gift].
"O best of the Bharatas, these indeed should be known as those who sanctify the company (paṅktipāvana).
I shall now describe those who are other than these; examine here those twice-born ones. For all Brāhmaṇas are indeed purified by the study of the Vedas and by their vows."
Those who are ever devoted to right conduct should be known as purifiers of all;
those whom I shall describe as worthy of the company at a meal (pāṅkteya) should be known as purifiers of the assembly (paṅktipāvana).
One who has mastered the three Nāciketa fires, one who maintains the five sacred fires, one who knows the Triṣuparṇa hymns, and one who is learned in the six Vedāṅgas.

One who maintains the lineage of a gift to a Brahmin, a singer of the *Chandas* (Veda), a chanter of the *Jyeṣṭhasāman*, one who is obedient to his mother and father, a *Śrotriya* whose ten generations [of ancestors] are pure,
and one who always approaches his lawful wives only during their fertile seasons.
A Brahmin who has completed his vow of Vedic study and ritual bathing purifies the entire row [of diners];
likewise one who studies the *Atharvaśiras*, who is a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) restrained by his vows,
who speaks the truth, whose character is rooted in dharma, and who is devoted to his own duties.
And those who have exerted themselves in ablutions at sacred fords (tīrtha), and who have performed the final purificatory baths (avabhṛtha) at sacrifices accompanied by mantras—
those who are free from anger, not fickle, patient, self-controlled, and masters of their senses.

And those who are intent on the welfare of all beings—one should invite these to the *śrāddha* rites. What is given to these is inexhaustible; indeed, they are the purifiers of the row (*paṅktipāvana*).
O Great King, these others also should be known as purifiers of the row.

13,090.025c The *yatis*, who know the dharma of liberation, the *yogins* who have well-performed their vows, 13,090.025d the foremost knowers of the *Pañcarātra*, as well as other *bhāgavatas*, 13,090.025d the *vaikhānasas*, the best of families, who follow the conduct prescribed by the Vedas.
Those who, being self-restrained, cause the best of the twice-born to hear the *itihāsas*;
those who are experts in the commentaries (*bhāṣya*), those who are devoted to grammar (*vyākaraṇa*),
and those who study the *purāṇas* as well as the treatises on dharma (*dharmaśāstra*).
Having studied according to the rule and in accordance with the prescribed rites, he who acts accordingly, established in the teacher’s household, truthful in speech, and a giver of thousands,
becomes foremost among all the Vedas and all the sacred expositions.
As far as these can see while standing in a row, so far indeed do they purify;
therefore, because of this purification of the row, one is called a *paṅktipāvana* (a purifier of the row).
Indeed, even a single such person may purify [the assembly] from within a distance of two and a half *krośas*.
Those who know Brahman understand that the lineage of a gift to a Brahmin is an uninterrupted succession. If one who is neither an officiating priest nor a teacher should take the seat of honor,
being unpermitted by the officiating priests, he takes upon himself the misdeeds of the entire row.
But if one who knows the Vedas is free from all defects that defile the company (*paṅktidoṣa*),
and if he is a knower of the Atharvaveda, he shall dispel every defect of the company. [One should honor] a Brahmin who knows the Vedic scriptures and is free from all faults.
O King, he would not be fallen; rather, he would be one who purifies the company at a meal.
Therefore, with every effort, one should examine and then invite Brahmins who are devoted to their own duties, self-controlled, born of noble lineage, and deeply learned in the scriptures.
He whose *śrāddha* rites and sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are centered primarily on friends does not gratify the ancestors or the gods, nor does he go to heaven.
Furthermore, he who forms social alliances during a *śrāddha*—
He does not travel by the path of the gods; indeed,
though released from his bond like a fruit from its stalk,
he falls from the heavenly world, for his friendship was based on ritual offerings.
Therefore, one who performs ancestral rites (*śrāddha*) should not show favoritism toward a friend;
he should bestow wealth upon friends for the sake of maintaining them.
He toward whom one considers oneself neither an enemy nor a friend— [to him one should give].
One should feed such a neutral person at rites for the gods and ancestors;
just as seed sown in saline soil does not sprout,
so too the sower shall not obtain a share of the seed.
Thus, a śrāddha meal eaten by those who are unworthy yields no fruit either in this world or in the next;
for a Brāhmaṇa who has not studied the Vedas is extinguished like a fire of straw.
To such a person, a *śrāddha* must not be given; for indeed, no oblation is poured into ashes.
That which is called the "feasting gift" (*saṃbhojanī*) is a sacrificial fee for the *piśācas*;
it reaches neither the gods nor the ancestors.
Right here she wanders, her merit exhausted,
like a cow that has lost its calf wandering within a stall;
just as one pours clarified butter into a fire that has been extinguished.
That which is given for dancing and singing reaches neither the gods nor the ancestors; likewise,
the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) that one bestows upon one who is unlearned in the Ṛgveda.
That sacrificial fee which is given to one ignorant of the Ṛgveda destroys both [the giver and the receiver] and does not benefit them;
it is censured as a slaughterhouse, for it falls [upon them].

O Yudhiṣṭhira, those who constantly observe the covenant of the seers— resolute and knowers of all dharma— the gods recognize them as true Brāhmaṇas; they would cause such preta-spirits to fall from the path of the gods.

O Bhārata, you should understand that there are sages devoted to the study of the Vedas (*svādhyāya*), as well as those devoted to knowledge (*jñāna*), those devoted to austerity (*tapas*), and those devoted to ritual action (*karman*).
O Bhārata, offerings to the ancestors (*kavya*) should be established for those devoted to knowledge.
Among them, those few Brāhmaṇas who do not find fault are indeed excellent;
however, those who do find fault in their talk, one should not feed at Śrāddha ceremonies. O King, Brāhmaṇas who are reviled destroy the family for three generations.
"O King, the words of the Vaikhānasa sages are heard:
'One should examine from afar those Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas;
whether they be dear or even hateful, one should offer that Śrāddha to them.'"
O Bhārata, a man who might feed a thousand times a thousand people ignorant of the *Ṛgveda* is surpassed by a single person who knows the mantras and is pleased; such a one is worthy of all of them.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

By whom was the *śrāddha* conceived, at what time, and of what nature? During the era of Bhṛgu and Aṅgiras, by which sage was it established? Furthermore, which roots and fruits are to be avoided in *śrāddha* ceremonies?
"Tell me, O Grandfather, which types of grain should be avoided?
Bhīṣma said:
Listen to how the Śrāddha was first instituted, at what time, and of what nature it is."
"O lord of men, hear from me that which was resolved by him:
O descendant of Kuru, there was the great seer Atri, the son of Svayambhū, endowed with supreme power;
in his lineage, O great king, was born the one known as Dattātreya."
Dattātreya had a son named Nimi, whose wealth was his asceticism. And Nimi’s son was the illustrious Śrīmat, who was endowed with splendor.
At the completion of a full thousand years, having performed difficult penance, he—
His soul enveloped by the law of time, he met his end. But Nimi, having performed the purificatory rites according to the prescribed ritual,
fell into intense anguish, being wholly devoted to grief for his son.
Then, having prepared offerings on the fourteenth day, the high-minded one,
brooding over that very same grief, woke up at the end of the night.
As he awoke, his soul was shrouded by sorrow.
Withdrawing his mind from sense objects, his intellect— which had been wandering at large— became concentrated;
then, with a composed mind, he reflected upon the ritual procedures for the *śrāddha*,
considering those very foods, roots, and fruits that were suitable for him to eat.
Having mentally deliberated upon all those other things that had been spoken and those that were dear to him, the one whose wealth is asceticism,
O highly wise one, summoned and honored the brahmins on the new moon day.
Then he himself prepared seven mats, all of which were wound to the right.
Thereafter, the lord simultaneously served seven brahmins at their meal;
he gave them food consisting of śyāmāka grain, with the exception of salt.
Then, darbha grass with its tips pointing southward was placed upon the seats;
likewise for the feet of the Brahmins who partake of the food.
Having arranged the darbha grass with its tips pointing southward, one should remain self-restrained and pure.

He offered a funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) to Śrīmat, pronouncing his name and lineage. Having performed that act, which he perceived in his mind as a confusion of his own dharma, that best of sages, with a concentrated mind, meditated upon the Blessed One.
Tormented by great remorse, he reflected:
"What is this that I have performed, which was never done before by the sages?
How is it that the brahmins do not consume me with their curse?"
Then he reflected upon the founder of his own lineage;
and as soon as he was thought of, Atri, whose wealth is asceticism, arrived there.
Then Atri, seeing him thus emaciated by grief for his son, [spoke].
The Imperishable One consoled him greatly with pleasing words:
"O Nimi, this ancestral sacrifice has been prepared by you, O ascetic;
let there be no fear in you, for this dharma was seen of old by Brahmā himself."
This very dharma ordained by the Self-Existent One has been envisioned by you;
for who else but the Self-Existent One could have proclaimed such a venerable rite? And I shall further explain to you this supreme ritual for the *śrāddha*.
"O son, understand this which has been ordained by the Self-Existent One; perform it according to my instruction.
O one whose wealth is asceticism, having first performed the fire-offering with the appropriate mantras, you must then constantly offer oblations to Aryaman, Soma, and Varuṇa."

The Viśvedevas, who are eternally associated with the Pitṛs, have had their portions assigned by the Self-born One himself. Here, the Earth, the sustainer of the funeral offering (nivāpa), must be praised.
"O sinless one, Vaiṣṇavī, Kāśyapī, and likewise Akṣayā—
while fetching water, the all-pervading Varuṇa should be praised;
thereafter, both Agni and Soma should be gratified here."
The gods known as the Pitṛs were indeed created by the Self-Existent One;
those highly fortunate ones who drink the steam (ūṣmapāḥ) have their portions assigned. Likewise, there are the Somapas, the Haviṣmants, and also the Barhiṣads.
When they are honored with a *śrāddha*, they are indeed liberated from sin.
The sevenfold lineage of the ancestors was envisioned of old by the Self-Existent One (*Svayambhū*);
and those Viśvedevas, headed by Agni, were enumerated even previously.
I shall declare the names of those high-souled ones who are entitled to their shares:
Saha, Kṛti, Vipāpman, Puṇyakṛt, Pāvana,
Grāmi, Kṣema, Samūha, and likewise Divyasānu.
Vivasvān, Vīryavān, Hrīmān, Kīrtimān, and Kṛta;
likewise Vipūrva, Somapūrva, and Sūryaśrī by name;
as well as Somapa, Sūryasāvitra, Dattātmā, and Puṣkarīyaka.
Uṣṇīnābha, Nabhodaśa, Viśvāyu, and Dīpti;
Camūhara, Suveṣa, Vyomāri, Śaṅkara, and Bhava;
Īśa, Kartṛ, Kṛti, Dakṣa, Bhuvana, and Divyakarmakṛt.
Gaṇita, Pañcavīrya, Āditya, and likewise Raśmimant;
Saptakṛt, Somavarcas, Viśvakṛt, and Kavir; Anugoptṛ, Sugoptṛ, Naptṛ, and Īśvara.
Aja, Marīci, and likewise the eternal Viśvedevas; Jitātmā, Munivīrya, Dīptaloma, Bhayaṅkara,
Atikarman, Pratīta, Pradātṛ, and Aṃśumān.
Śailābha, Paramakrodhin, Dhīra, Uṣṇī, Bhūpati,
Sraji, Vajrin, and Varin— these are the eternal Viśvedevas.
These highly fortunate ones have been proclaimed as those whose sphere of activity is the course of Time.
Grains such as *kodrava* and *pulaka* are unfit for the ancestral rites (*aśrāddheya*).
Among substances, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) is forbidden; among vegetables, onions (*palāṇḍu*) and garlic (*laśuna*) likewise.
So too are the *saubhañjanaka*, the *gṛñjanaka*, and other such plants.
The *kūṣmāṇḍa* gourd, the *alābu* gourd, black salt,
village-pig meat, and whatever has not been consecrated by sprinkling (*aprokṣita*);
likewise, black cumin (*kṛṣṇājājī*), *viḍa* salt, and *śītapākī*.
Likewise, sprouts and the like, as well as *śṛṅgāṭaka* fruits, should be avoided here;
one should avoid all types of salt, as well as *jambū* fruits;
and at *śrāddha* rites, one should avoid food that has been sneezed upon or over which someone has wept.

Whether at a funeral offering (*nivāpa*) or at an oblation to the gods or ancestors (*havya-kavya*), the sight of a dog is censured; neither the ancestors nor the gods take pleasure in such an oblation.
When the funeral offering has arrived, both the *caṇḍāla* and the *śvapaca* should be excluded.
One wearing saffron robes, one afflicted with leprosy, one who has fallen from his caste, or even a slayer of a Brahmin; a Brahmin of mixed birth, and one whose kinsman has fallen—
all these must be avoided by the wise when the time for the funeral offering (nivāpa) has arrived.
Having spoken thus to the seer born of his own lineage in former times, the Blessed One, Atri, whose wealth is asceticism, departed for the divine assembly hall of the Grandfather. Bhīṣma said:

When the rite had thus commenced, all the great seers performed the ancestral sacrifices (pitṛyajña) according to the ritual procedures prescribed by rule. Having performed the offerings of the funeral cakes, the seers, ever devoted to dharma, [proceeded].
Those of firm vows also performed libations with the waters of the sacred fords. O Bhārata, being satiated by the offerings of food given by the four castes,
the ancestors and the gods indeed did not digest that food.
Afflicted by indigestion, those gods, together with the ancestors, were overcome; oppressed by the food offered as oblations, they sought refuge in Soma.
Having approached Soma, the ancestors, tormented by indigestion, spoke.
"We are being oppressed by the food offered as oblations; let what is for our welfare be ordained here.
To them Soma replied, "O gods, if you desire your own welfare, go to the abode of the Self-Existent (Svayambhū); he will ordain your welfare."
At the word of Soma, O Bhārata, those gods together with the Pitṛs approached the Grandfather (Brahmā), who was seated upon a peak of Mount Meru. The Pitṛs said:
"O Blessed One, we are greatly distressed by the food offered as a funeral oblation. O God, show us favor; let that which is for our welfare be ordained.
Having heard these words of theirs, the Self-Existent One spoke this.
"This fire at my side will provide for your welfare.
Agni said:
"O dear one, we shall eat together when the funeral offering (nivāpa) has been presented."
"You shall also consume food together with me; of this there is no doubt.
Having heard this, O King, those ancestors then became free from their feverish distress;
for this reason, the offering is first made to Agni.
O bull among men, when the offering is poured out, beginning with the fire,
the Brahma-rākṣasas do not dare to violate that offering; moreover,
the Rākṣasas turn back while the god Vibhāvasu stands present.
One should first offer a rice-ball (piṇḍa) to the father, then offer one to the grandfather, and then to the great-grandfather; this is remembered as the rule for the śrāddha.
And being composed, one should recite the Sāvitrī at each rice-ball during the śrāddha.
One should say, "To Soma," and likewise, "To those who have fathers.
A woman who is menstruating, as well as one who is deformed in her ears, should not stand at the offering of the funeral cakes; nor should women born of other lineages be accepted there.
While crossing the water, one should invoke the ancestors;
having reached a river, one should perform the offering of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and libations (*tarpaṇa*) for the ancestors,
first performing the libation with water for those born of one's own lineage.

Then he should offer handfuls of water to his circle of friends and kinsmen. Furthermore, the ancestors truly desire [offerings] from one crossing the water with a pair of brindled oxen, or from one boarding a boat.
Those who know this, being composed in mind, always offer water in a boat.
Indeed, one should perform the funeral offerings (*nivapana*) during the fortnight of the dark half of the month;
for those who serve the ancestors, there is nourishment, long life, vigor, and prosperity.
Pitāmaha, Pulastya, Vasiṣṭha, as well as Pulaha,
Aṅgiras, Kratu, and the great seer Kaśyapa—
these, O best of the Kuru lineage, are remembered as the great lords of yoga.
"O King, these are the ancestors, and this is the supreme rule for the *śrāddha*. By that ritual act, the deceased (*preta*) are liberated from their connection to the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*).
Thus, O best of men, is the origin of the *śrāddha* according to the sacred tradition."
The previously mentioned [topics] have been declared; hereafter, I shall speak of giving.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"If twice-born men who are observant of vows eat your sacrificial oblation (havis)..."
"O Grandfather, how is it that food is [offered] for one who desires the status of a Brāhmaṇa?
Bhīṣma said:
"Those who perform their duties while eating, even though they do not observe the vows prescribed in the Vedas..."
"But those who eat while the Vedas are being recited, O Yudhiṣṭhira, have violated their vow.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Ordinary people say that this fasting is what constitutes austerity."
"Is this indeed austerity, or might there be another kind of austerity here?
Bhīṣma said:
"Fasting for a month or half a month—this is what people consider to be austerity."
One who harms his own body is neither an ascetic nor a knower of dharma. The perfection of renunciation is taught as the highest austerity;
likewise, one should always observe fasts and remain a celibate student.

A Brahmin should always be a sage and should always worship the gods; O Bhārata, he who desires dharma should always support his family and never sleep. He should always subsist on nectar and should always remain pure.
One should always be a speaker of truth and always remain self-restrained; one should always subsist on *vighasa* and always be fond of guests;
one should always abstain from meat and always remain pure.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, how may one always be a fast-observer and a celibate student? How may one be an eater of *vighasa*, and how indeed may one be fond of guests?"
Bhīṣma said:
He who does not eat again in the interval between the evening meal and the morning meal is always one who observes a fast.
He who does not eat becomes one who always observes the fast, O twice-born;
even when approaching his wife, he remains ever a celibate student (brahmacārī). Furthermore, that man should always be a speaker of truth and one whose nature is generosity.
By not eating meat that has been prepared in vain, one indeed becomes a non-eater of meat;

by giving a gift, one becomes purified; and by sleeping during the day, one becomes sleepless at night. That man who always eats only after his dependents and guests have eaten, [attains these merits].
"Know this, O Yudhiṣṭhira: he who does not eat while the Brāhmaṇas have not yet eaten, eats nothing but immortality (amṛta) alone;
by that very abstention from food, heaven is conquered by him."
"He who eats what remains after [offering] to the gods, the ancestors, his dependents, and guests— him they call a *vighasāśin*. For them,
it is recorded that there are infinite worlds in the abode of Brahmā."
For they are attended by Apsarases and Gandharvas, O lord of men;
together with deities, guests, and ancestors, they enjoy [their rewards]. They rejoice with their sons and grandsons, and their destination is unsurpassed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, regarding those who bestow various kinds of gifts upon Brāhmaṇas,
what is the distinction between the giver and the recipient?"
Bhīṣma said:
A twice-born man who accepts gifts from a virtuous person likewise [accepts them] from an unvirtuous one; in the case of the virtuous, his fault is slight, but in the case of the meritless, he sinks.
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, the conversation between Vṛṣādarbhi and the Seven Sages:
Kaśyapa, Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Bharadvāja, and Gautama.
Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, and the virtuous Arundhatī; Kāśyapa, Atri, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, Gautama,
Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, and the virtuous Arundhatī.
Now, among all of them, there was a woman named Gaṇḍā who performed manual labor;
her husband was indeed a Śūdra named Paśusakha.
In former times, they all wandered this earth while practicing austerities.
Training themselves through meditative absorption for the eternal world of Brahmā,
O joy of the Kurus, there then occurred a great drought,
during which this world was indeed filled with hunger and life became a struggle.

Long ago, at a certain sacrifice, it is said that the son of Śibi gave his own son as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests. At that time, O Lord, he met his end due to his short lifespan.
Afflicted by hunger, they stood surrounding him; then,
O Bhārata, seeing that the son of their patron had lost his life, those best of sages, tormented by hunger, cooked him in a cauldron.
In this wretched world of mortals, those ascetics, desiring to preserve their very selves, had fallen into a miserable state of livelihood for the sake of food.
Then the lord of the earth, while wandering along the road, saw them cooking [their meal].
King Śaibya Vṛṣādarbhi beheld those who were being tormented on account of receiving gifts;
that monarch then addressed them.
Vṛṣādarbhi said:
"Acceptance [of gifts] saves; indeed, prosperity belongs to those who accept.
Therefore, I give you wealth; take it, O you whose wealth is asceticism! Hear, O you whose wealth is asceticism, what wealth exists within me."
"A Brahmin who comes as a petitioner is indeed dear to me;
I shall give you a thousand mules,
and I give ten thousand cows in their entirety."
Each one was born with a bull,
all swift-moving and white-haired;
I give them away by the millions, as fast as thought.
I shall give hundreds upon hundreds of excellent draft-oxen capable of bearing the yoke and supporting the family, as well as an equal number of stout oxen fit for drawing the earth.
Excellent first-calving cows that are well-behaved,
choice villages, rice, barley, and juices;
and what other rare jewel shall I give?
"Do not entertain such an intention toward what is unfit for consumption;
indeed, for the sake of your nourishment, what shall I provide for you?
The sages said:
"O King, the acceptance of gifts from a king is like honey in taste but like poison in effect. Knowing this, why do you attempt to seduce us?
A butcher with ten slaughter-houses is equal to one who possesses a cart; one who possesses a cart is equal to one who bears a banner."
A prostitute is equal to ten gamblers; a king is equal to ten prostitutes. A soldier who maintains ten thousand slaughterhouses is equal to a king; dreadful is the acceptance of gifts from him.
For the Kṣatriya power rests upon the Brāhmaṇa as if upon a deity;
indeed, this stainless one, gratified by asceticism, gratifies the gods.
For even in a single day here, ascetic merit arises for a Brāhmaṇa.
That supreme ascetic merit accumulated over many days may be consumed like a forest fire upon receiving a gift from a king;
O King, may you always possess prosperity along with the virtue of giving.
"Let everything be given to those who seek it," they said, and then they departed. That meat remained uncooked for those wise men;
then, abandoning it, they all went to the forest seeking food.
Then, urged by the king, his ministers went to the forest and began to collect *udumbara* fruits in order to give them as a gift;
they then brought other *udumbara* fruits containing gold within them.
Then their servants ran forward to seize those fruits; but seeing them, the sages ran toward them to take them. Then Atri, realizing they were heavy, said, "They must not be taken."
"O, we were not of deluded understanding; O, we were not of dull intellect! Now we know these things to be made of gold; we have awakened and we are awake.
For that which is acquired here may result in bitter consequences after death."
"13,094.025c This must certainly not be accepted by one who desires happiness both in this world and after death.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"13,094.026 A gold coin (niṣka) is reckoned as a hundred, and measured against a thousand."
"For by accepting too much, one indeed attains the most sinful state.
Kaśyapa said:
"Whatever rice, barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth—"
All that is not enough for even one person; therefore, the wise man should seek tranquility.
Bharadvāja said:
"The horn of a deer grows as it is born and continues to grow as it matures."
Like the desire of a man, there is no measure to it.
Gautama said:
"There is no substance in this world that could fill the world."
A man who is like the ocean is never filled.
Viśvāmitra said:
"When the desire of one longing for his wish is fulfilled..."
Then another desire, craving, pierces him like an arrow. Atri said:
Desire is never extinguished by the enjoyment of the objects of desire.
Like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more.
Jamadagni said:
"Restraint in receiving gifts certainly sustains asceticism."
13,094.031c That wealth of a Brahmin who is greedy in this world shall leak away.
13,094.032 Arundhatī said:
13,094.032a The accumulation of goods for the sake of dharma is indeed approved by both sides.
"In this world, the accumulation of austerity alone is superior to the accumulation of material wealth.
Gaṇḍovā said:
"Because these lords of mine are afraid of this terrible danger,"
"Though they are stronger, I fear them as if they were weak; beyond this, [I am terrified].
Paśusakha said:
"The wise act in such a way that they are devoted to righteousness."
Therefore, that alone should be performed by the wise man who desires his own welfare;
for there is nothing higher than dharma—Brahmins know that to be true wealth. For the sake of discipline, one should attend upon a truly learned man in accordance with the truth.
The sages said:
He who possesses a longing for wealth and whose thirst is excessive should diligently attend upon those who have attained great prosperity through disciplined conduct.

Blessings upon him who gives these subjects of yours for the sake of charity; wretched indeed are those base subjects who strive only for the lowest form of giving— such as you, who bestow upon us fruits tainted by deceit.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, all those sages of firm vows abandoned those fruits containing gold within and departed for another place.
Then all those ministers spoke thus to the king.
The ministers said:
"Suspecting a deception, they indeed abandoned these fruits."
"Then they depart by another way; let this be known to you, O King.
When he was thus addressed by those servants, Vṛṣādarbhi became enraged and went home to take retaliatory action against them all.
Having gone to the *āhavanīya* fire and undertaken a rigorous vow,
the king offered each consecrated oblation with sacred mantras. From that fire there arose a *kṛtyā*, terrifying to the world.

Vṛṣādarbhi then gave her the name Yātudhānī. Like a malevolent spell (kṛtyā) or the Night of Doom (Kālarātrī), she stood before King Vṛṣādarbhi with palms joined in reverence and said, "What shall I do?"
Vṛṣādarbhi said:
"Go to the minds of the seven ṛṣis, as well as that of Arundhatī, and of the husband of the slave-girl and the slave-girl herself; hold their names in your mind."
"Having learned their names, destroy them all.
Once they have been destroyed, go wherever you desire as you please. Having promised "So be it," that female demon (yātudhānī) assumed her own form.
13,094.044c He went to that forest where those great ṛṣis were wandering.
13,095.001 Bhīṣma said:
13,095.001a Then, O King, those great ṛṣis, headed by Atri, in that forest—
13,095.001c They wandered about, indeed devouring roots and fruits.
13,095.002a Then they saw a wandering mendicant with thick shoulders, hands, feet, face, and belly, a man of stout limbs, Śunaḥsakha.
But the auspicious Arundhatī, seeing him with all his limbs fully developed, said to the ṛṣis, "You shall indeed not become like this. Vasiṣṭha said:
"His *agnihotra* here is not unoffered as ours is;
it must be offered by him both evening and morning, and for that reason Śunaḥsakha is fat.
Atri said:
"His vigor has not been struck down here by hunger as ours has been; his learning, though acquired with great hardship, has not perished. That is why Śunaḥsakha is fat.
Viśvāmitra said:
"Unlike us here, this man does not have a scripture that is as old as a worn-out ox;
he is lazy, devoted to hunger, and foolish, and for that reason his friend Śunaḥsakha is fat.
Jamadagni said:
"Unlike us here, he does not have to provide food and fuel for the rainy season; having reflected on this, Śunaḥsakha is fat.
Kaśyapa said:
"Unlike us here, he has four uterine brothers;
they beg him, saying 'Give! Give!', and for that reason Śunaḥsakha is fat.
Bharadvāja said:
"Unlike that of us here, this mindless wretch of a Brahmin feels no grief over the accusation against his wife; for that reason, Śunaḥsakha remains fat.
Gautama said:
"His [garment] here is not like ours made of triple-layered silk or of deer-skin; indeed, each one of his has been worn for three years, and by that means Śunaḥsakha has become stout.
Bhīṣma said:

Then, having seen those great seers, the wandering mendicant Śunaḥsakha approached them according to custom and performed the ritual touch of their hands. He then offered them service in the forest that would ward off hunger.
Having thus informed one another, they set out together; with a single resolve regarding their task, they wandered through the forests,
gathering and uprooting roots and fruits.
Once, while wandering through a place covered with dense trees,
they beheld a beautiful lotus pond of pure, clear, and abundant water,
adorned with lotuses that shone like the orb of the rising sun.
It was covered with lotus petals resembling the color of lapis lazuli,
frequented by various kinds of water-dwelling birds,
having a single entrance, impassable [to others], possessing excellent landing-stairs, and free from mud.

But the *kṛtyā* (magical spell) dispatched by Vṛṣādarbhi, hideous in appearance and known as the *yātudhānī*, guarded that lotus pond. However, those great ṛṣis, accompanied by Śunaḥsakha, went there for the sake of lotus stalks.
13,095.018c They all approached the lotus-lake, which was guarded by a *kṛtyā*.
13,095.019a Then, seeing that *yātudhānī* of hideous appearance,
the great seers spoke to the *kṛtyā* as she stood on the bank of the lotus-lake.
"Who are you that stand alone? For whose sake and for what purpose are you here?
Having taken refuge on the bank of the lotus pond, tell me, what do you intend to do?
Yātudhānī replied:
"Whoever I am, I must not be questioned in any way.
Know me, all you whose wealth is asceticism, to be the guardian of this lotus-pond.
The seers said:
"13,095.022 All of us are afflicted by hunger, and we have nothing else at all. With your permission, let us all gather lotus stalks.
13,095.023 The Yātudhānī said:
"By this agreement, you may take as many lotus stalks as you desire; each of you, having announced your name to me, may then take them without delay.
Bhīṣma said:
Having recognized that she was a Yātudhānī— a magical spell (*kṛtyā*) seeking the destruction of the sages—
Atri, his soul overcome by hunger, then spoke these words:
"For Atri, this night is no night, since he has not recited [the Vedas] three times today."
"Know this, O beautiful one, that my name is indeed Arātri Atri.
Yātudhānī said:
"O great sage, this name of yours has been uttered by me exactly as it was told."
"This is difficult for the mind to grasp; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"I am Vasiṣṭha, I am the most excellent; I dwell even in houses."
"Know me as Vasiṣṭha because of my being the most excellent (*variṣṭha*) and because of my dwelling (*vāsa*).
Yātudhānī said:
"This etymological explanation of your name consists of syllables that are difficult to pronounce."
"This cannot be sustained; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Kaśyapa said:
"Kula, Kula, Kupapa, Kupaya, Kaśyapa the twice-born!"
"13,095.029c Because I shine like Kāśa grass, O Kāśya, remember this name of mine.
13,095.030 The Yātudhānī said:
13,095.030a 'O great sage, this name has been uttered by me for you.'"
"This is difficult for the mind to grasp; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Bharadvāja said:
"I support my sons, I support my disciples, I support the gods, and I support the twice-born."
"O beautiful one, I am Bharadvāja, free from deceit; I shall bear you as my wife. Yātudhānī said:
"This etymological explanation of your name consists of syllables spoken with difficulty."
"This cannot be sustained; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Gautama said:
"O Godama, you are the tamer of the self, free from smoke, self-controlled, and difficult to behold."
"The darkness was destroyed by the rays of light as soon as I was born from my body. Know me to be Gautama; O Yātudhānī, understand my purpose.
The Yātudhānī said:
"O great sage, this name of mine which you have thus proclaimed is impossible for me to bear; go, descend into the lotus pond. Viśvāmitra said:
"O Yātudhānī, understand from me that I am known as Viśvāmitra because all the gods (*viśvedevāḥ*) are my friends (*mitram*), and likewise, I am the friend (*mitram*) of cattle. Yātudhānī said:
"13,095.036a This etymological explanation of your name consists of syllables that are difficult to pronounce.
13,095.036c It is not possible to maintain this; go, descend into the lotus pond.
13,095.037 Jamadagni said:
"Jājamadyajajā by name, I am called Mṛjā; I desire to give birth. Therefore, know me as Jamadagni, O beautiful one.
Yātudhānī said:
"O great sage, this name of mine which you have thus proclaimed cannot be borne; go, descend into the lotus pond. Arundhatī said:
"I abide immediately after my husband—the earth, the supporter, the bearer of wealth—following his mind; know me, therefore, as Arundhatī. Thus spoke the Yātudhānī.
"13,095.040 This etymological explanation of your name consists of syllables that express suffering.
13,095.040c It is not possible to maintain this; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Gaṇḍā said:
She went from cheek to cheek and was thus designated "Gaṇḍagaṇḍā.
Know me, O daughter of Mānasa, as "Gaṇḍā," just like Gaṇḍagaṇḍā;
they declare this root *gaṇḍa* to mean a single part of the face.
"Know me as 'She with High Cheeks' (Unnatagaṇḍā), O you born of pride.
Yātudhānī said:
"This etymology of your name consists of syllables that are difficult to pronounce."
"This cannot be sustained; go, descend into the lotus pond.
Paśusakha said:
"O friend, you who are my friend worthy of friendship, and always the friend of all creatures!"
"Know me, O you who are born from fire, as 'Paśusakha' (Friend of Beasts) by this secondary name.
Yātudhānī said:
"This etymological explanation of your name consists of syllables spoken with difficulty."
13,095.044c "It is not possible for me to maintain this; go, descend into the lotus pond.
13,095.045 Śunaḥsakha said:
13,095.045a "As it has been spoken by these [others], so indeed I do not venture to speak here myself."
"O female sorceress (*yātudhānī*), recognize me as the friend of Śunaḥsakha.
The female sorceress said:
"The name you have spoken is indeed indistinct, uttered with a voice full of doubt."
"Therefore, O twice-born one, tell me now once more what your name is.
Śunaḥsakha said:
"I have spoken my name only once, yet it was not grasped by you."
"Therefore, struck by my triple staff, go to ashes without delay!
Bhīṣma said:
"Then she was struck on the head by that [staff], which was equal to the staff of Brahmā."
The magical spell fell upon the earth and was reduced to ashes. And Śunaḥsakha, having slain that mighty Yātudhānī, planted his triple staff in the ground and sat down upon a grassy spot.
Then all those sages, having taken as many lotuses and lotus stalks as they desired, rose up filled with joy; yet,
though they were joined by great exhaustion, they carried the stalks in bundles.
Having set them down on the bank of the lotus pond, they performed the libation with water.
Then, rising from that water, they all gathered together;
yet, O bull among men, they did not see those lotus stalks.
The sages said:
"By what sinful and cruel person have the lotus stalks been carried away from us, who are overcome by hunger and desiring food?"
Suspecting one another, those best of the twice-born questioned each other.
They all said, "O crusher of enemies, let us all take an oath. Having said this, they all replied to Śunaḥsakha, "So be it."
Afflicted by hunger and utterly exhausted, they proceeded to take an oath.
Atri said:
"May he touch a cow with his foot and void his urine toward the sun."
