"He who steals lotus stalks shall study during times when study is forbidden.
Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this world, may he be intent on forbidden study and be dragged along by dogs."
Let him who steals the lotus stalks be a wandering mendicant who acts according to his lust;
let him kill one who has sought refuge, let him live off his own daughter,
and let him seek wealth from a miser— he who steals the lotus stalks.
Kaśyapa said:
"May he who steals lotus stalks be one who stakes everything everywhere, who misappropriates a deposit, and who becomes a false witness."
"Let him who steals the lotus stalks eat meat that has not been offered in sacrifice, let him make gifts for no sacred purpose, and let him approach a woman during the day. Bharadvāja said:
Cruel and having abandoned righteousness toward women, kinsmen, and cattle,
he who steals lotus stalks while conquering even a Brāhmaṇa must study the *Ṛg* verses and the *Yajus* formulas after placing his teacher beneath him.
"Let him who steals the lotus stalks offer them as a libation into a fire of dry grass.
Jamadagni said:
"Let him discharge excrement into the waters, and let him kill a milch cow."
May he who steals the lotus stalks engage in sexual intercourse outside the proper season;
may he become hateful, dependent on his wife for livelihood, estranged from his kin, and full of enmity; and may he who steals the lotus stalks be a guest to another [in this state].
Gautama said:
"Let him who steals lotus stalks study the Vedas and then abandon them; let him cast away the three sacred fires; let him likewise sell the Soma juice."
"May that Brāhmaṇa who steals the lotus stalks attain the same world as the husband of a Vṛṣalī in a village where the only water is from a well.
May the husband of a Vṛṣalī discharge phlegm and urine into that well."
"May he who steals the lotus stalks go to the world of the wicked.
Viśvāmitra said:
"May other people support his elders and dependents while he himself remains alive."
May he who steals the lotus stalks be childless; may he who steals the lotus stalks be one who finds no refuge; may he be one with many sons yet lacking a path [to liberation].
May he who steals the lotus stalks be impure, a hypocrite in his devotion to the Veda, and arrogant because of his prosperity;
may he be a miserly farmer. May he who steals the lotus stalks become thus.
"May he serve as a hired servant for thirteen thousand and ninety-five years and six months, and may he become the domestic priest of a king.
May he be the officiating priest for one who should not be sacrificed for, he who commits the theft of lotus stalks.
Arundhatī said:
May she who steals the lotus stalks constantly revile her mother-in-law and remain ill-disposed toward her husband;
may she quarrel with her mother-in-law and live deprived of her husband;
and may she eat sweet food all alone.
"Let her who steals the lotus stalks dwell in the midst of her kinsmen's house and eat barley meal at the end of the day;
let her be unfortunate and bear no heroic sons. Gaṇḍovā said:
May she always speak untruths, may she oppose the virtuous;
may she give away her daughter for a bride-price, and may she commit the theft of lotus stalks.
May she eat what she has prepared herself, and may she live as a slave.
She who commits theft of lotus stalks shall perish through her own misdeed.
Paśusakha said:
"She shall be born as a slave, childless and destitute."
"He who commits theft of lotus stalks shows no reverence toward the deities.
Śunasakha said:
"Let him give his daughter to the Adhvaryu priest."
Or a Sāmavedin who has observed the vow of celibacy; having studied the Atharvaveda, a Brahmin should perform the ritual bath— provided he does not steal lotus stalks.
The sages said:
"O Śunaḥsakha, this oath which you have taken is pleasing to the twice-born; you have committed the theft of the lotus stalks for the sake of us all."
Śunaḥsakha said:

"What was said by those who had completed their task because they did not see the first [lotus] that had been set aside—that is true; it is not false. This theft of the lotus-stalks was committed by me."
"Behold these lotus stalks here, which have been made invisible by me; O sinless ones,
this was done by me for the sake of testing you all,
and I have come for the purpose of protecting you."

"O you whose wealth is asceticism, this is indeed a most enraged Yātudhānī, a magical spell (kṛtyā) seeking your destruction. Sent forth by Vṛṣādarbhi, she has been slain by me. For if she had reached you, this wicked and evil creature, born of fire, would have harmed you."
"Therefore, O Brahmins, know me to be Vāsava who has come here.
Because of your lack of greed, these imperishable worlds that fulfill all desires have been attained by you.
Arise quickly from here, O twice-born ones, and indeed attain them!"
13,095.082 Bhīṣma said: Then the great ṛṣis, being pleased, said "So be it" to Purandara,
and together with the lord of the thirty gods, they all went to Triviṣṭapa.
Thus, although these great-souled ones were afflicted by supreme hunger and offered various kinds of enjoyments by other great-souled beings,
they did not yield to greed at that time; consequently, they attained heaven.
Therefore, in all circumstances, a man should abandon greed;
for this is known as the supreme dharma, O King—namely, freedom from greed. A man should proclaim this righteous conduct in assemblies.
He becomes a partaker of happiness and does not encounter difficulties;
his ancestors, as well as the sages and the deities, are pleased with him;
and after death, that man becomes a partaker of fame, righteousness, and wealth.
Bhīṣma said:
In this very connection, they cite this ancient history concerning what occurred during a pilgrimage regarding an oath; listen to that.

O best of the Bharatas, O great king, in former times theft was committed for the sake of the lotus by royal sages as well as by brahminical sages. The sages assembled together at Prabhāsa in the west;
Having assembled, they consulted one another:
"Let us all wander the earth with its sacred fords;
this is our task—come, let us all go."
Śukra, Aṅgiras, and the learned Kavi; likewise Agastya, Nārada, and Parvata; Bhṛgu, Vasiṣṭha, Kaśyapa, and Gautama.
O King, Viśvāmitra, Jamadagni, the sage Gālava, as well as Aṣṭaka, Bharadvāja, Arundhatī, and the Vālakhilyas;
Śibi, Dilīpa, Nahuṣa, Ambarīṣa,
King Yayāti, Dhundhumāra, and Pūru followed,
placing that high-souled one at their head.
O lord of men, while circumambulating all the sacred fords, they went on the full moon day of Māgha to the Kauśikī, a ford of great merit, [to reach] Śatakratu, the slayer of Vṛtra.
Then, having shaken off their sins at all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), they went to the most meritorious *Brahmasaras*; at the ford of the God, those who were like fire entered the water.
Having plunged in and eaten the lotus flowers,
O King, some of those brahmins there dug up the lotus roots, while others dug up the lotus stalks.
Then they saw the lotus being carried away,
having been pulled up from the lake by Agastya.
Agastya said to all those foremost of sages:
"By whom has my well-grown lotus been taken?
I suspect you; let my lotus be returned, for you ought not to steal this flower."
"I hear that Time indeed destroys the power of dharma; thus has this oppression of dharma arrived and it increases. Before unrighteousness grows here further—"
I shall go to the other world for a long time.
Formerly, in the midst of the village, the Brahmins used to proclaim the Vedas with loud voices, making even the Śūdras hear them.
"Before long, I shall go to the next world, while still seeing kings who engage in unrighteous legal proceedings—
those who are superior, inferior, or even more venerable."
As long as all men do not hold me in contempt,
and as long as this darkness does not prevail,
so long shall I depart for the next world for a long time.
In the past, I beheld mortals being devoured by a superior power, the weak by the strong; therefore,
I shall go to the other world for all time.
"Indeed, I cannot bear to look upon such a sight in the world of men.
To him, the distressed great seers said: "O great seer, we did not steal your lotus."
"You must not harbor a false accusation against us;
O Great Seer, we swear by sharp oaths.
Those Great Seers there have reached a firm conclusion in this matter."
O lord of men, while thus deliberating upon what was right,
they then took oaths in turn,
together with their sons and grandsons, O king.
Bhṛgu said:
"In this world, one who is reviled should revile in return; one who is struck should strike back;
and one should eat the flesh from his own back—whoever steals his lotus."
Vasiṣṭha said:
"In this world, let him who steals your Puṣkara be devoted to no sacred study and let him drag a dog about; and let him become a mendicant in the city."
Kaśyapa said:
"Let him who steals your lotus be one who betrays everything in every situation, let him harbor greed regarding deposits, and let him become a false witness."
Gautama said:
"May he who steals your lotus live possessed of egoism, may he trade with his intellect as if it were base coin, and may he be a miserly farmer."
Aṅgiras said:
"May he who steals your lotus be impure, a falsifier of the Veda, and a dragger of dogs; may he be a perpetrator of the sin of killing a Brahmin."
Dhundhumāra said:
"May he be ungrateful toward his friends, may he be born of a Śūdra woman,
and may he eat alone the fine food that you take away as your lotus."
Pūru said:
"Let him practice medicine and live supported by his wife;
his livelihood shall come from his father-in-law—he who steals your lotus."
Dilīpa said:
"In the village of Udapānaplava, there was a Brāhmaṇa who was the husband of a Śūdra woman;
may he go to those worlds of yours who steals your lotus."
Śukra said:
"Let him who steals your lotus eat the flesh of the back, engage in sexual intercourse during the day, and become a servant to the king."
Jamadagni said:
One might study during times unfit for study, and one might feed a friend at a *śrāddha* feast;
one might even eat at the *śrāddha* of a *śūdra*, but he who steals your lotus (*puṣkara*) commits a grave offense.
Śibi said:
"May he who steals your lotus be one who dies without having established the sacred fires, may he cause obstacles to sacrifices, and may he come into conflict with ascetics."
Yayāti said:
"May he who steals your lotus be born out of season from a wife who wears matted hair and observes vows, and may he be one who rejects the Vedas."
Nahuṣa said:
"Let a householder repel a guest; let one who has been initiated act according to his own desires;
and let one who is paid for teaching impart knowledge—just as you have taken my lotus."
Ambarīṣa said:
"May he who steals your lotus be cruel, may he abandon dharma toward women, kinsmen, and cows, and may he even forsake a Brāhmaṇa."
13,096.030 Nārada said:
He who, being ignorant and secretive, reads the scriptures aloud with discordant syllables while disregarding his elders—
he steals the lotus from you.
Nābhāga said:
"May he who steals your lotus always speak untruth and be at odds with the virtuous; may he give away his daughter for a bride-price."
The poet said:
"May he who steals your lotus strike the earth with his foot, urinate facing the sun, and abandon one who has come to him for refuge."
Viśvāmitra said:
"Let this hired servant remain without rain [in his own land], and let him be the domestic priest of the king;
let him be the officiating priest for one who should not be sacrificed for, he who steals your lotus."
Parvata said:
"Let him be appointed as the overseer of the village; let him travel by means of a donkey-cart;
and for the sake of his livelihood, let him plow with dogs—he who steals your lotus."
Bharadvāja said:
"May that sin which consists of the accumulation of all evils in cruelty and falsehood always belong to him who steals your lotus."
Aṣṭaka said:
"That king is of unrefined intellect, driven by desire, and a doer of evil;
he rules the earth unrighteously and seizes your lotus."
If a twice-born man should intentionally discharge his semen in a womb of the Śūdra caste,
or if a renunciant should engage in sexual intercourse— he who steals the lotus (the merit of his vows).
Yama said:
But he who has abandoned the *aupāsana* fire, who reviles the gods and Brahmins,
and who steals the lotus from one authorized to perform a sacrifice for the gods— [he goes to hell].
Gālava said:
"May that man who, having given a gift, boasts while seizing your lotus, be more worthy of the price of the most wicked among sinners for his own evil deed."
Arundhatī said:
"Let her speak ill of her mother-in-law; let her be ill-disposed toward her husband;
let her eat sweet food all alone—she who steals your lotus."
Śunaka:
"May he abandon Vāsudeva and worship another deity.
"Let the renunciant always dwell, whether in a village or even in a city;
let him live together with his kinsmen, for he who takes away your lotus is your relative.
The Vālakhilyas said:
"Let him who steals your lotus root stand at the village gate on one foot for the sake of his livelihood; let that knower of dharma become one who has abandoned dharma.
Paśusakha said:
"Let that twice-born man who steals your lotus disregard the *agnihotra* sacrifice and sleep in comfort; let him be a wandering mendicant who acts according to his own whims.
Surabhi said:
"Let there be a milking vessel of bronze with a handle made of *bālvaja* grass;
let her who steals your lotus be milked by means of another's calf.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, O lord of the Kauravas, as they were being sworn with those many various oaths,
the thousand-eyed king of the gods was greatly delighted.
Having observed that foremost of Brahmins who was so prone to anger,
Maghavan then addressed that rishi, whose wrath had been aroused, and spoke these words of reassurance.
"O King, learn from me today that which occurred in the midst of the Brahman-sages, celestial-sages, and royal-sages.
Śakra said:
Let him give his daughter to an *adhvaryu* priest,
or to a *chandoga* who has observed the vow of celibacy, after the learned Brahmin has studied the *Atharvaveda*.
He who takes your lotus stalk shall bathe;
let him study all the Vedas, be virtuous in conduct, and be righteous.
Let him go to the abode of Brahmā—he who steals your lotus stalk.
"May he who steals your lotus go to Vāsudeva— the source of the world, the support of all, the nameless, and the supreme beyond the supreme.
Agastya said:
"O slayer of Bala, you have uttered a blessing; let it instead be a curse!
Let Puṣkara be given to me; this is the eternal law.
Indra said:
"O Blessed One, it was not out of greed that I took this lotus today;
rather, I took it desiring to hear the Dharma. You ought not to be angry.
The Dharma is the excellence arising from sacred revelation, the bridge of righteousness, and the state of well-being."
"This Vedic hymn, eternal, constant, and imperishable, has been heard by me.
Therefore, O learned one, O best of sages, please accept this lotus.
O Blessed One, O blameless one, you ought to forgive my transgression."

O best of the twice-born, for the sake of the welfare of the world, you indeed drank the salt ocean; by you the Vindhya mountains were restrained and Vātāpi was destroyed; and it was you who reduced Nahuṣa to the state of a serpent.

"Since I acted while desiring to know [the truth], you ought to forgive me. Addressed thus by Mahendra, that ascetic, though exceedingly prone to anger, took up his lotus-stalk; the wise sage became serene.
Then those forest-dwellers proceeded further to various sacred fords; they bathed their limbs at holy bathing places,
and they quickly immersed their bodies in those sacred waters.
He who, being disciplined, recites this narrative on every auspicious lunar day (parvan),
shall not beget a foolish son, nor shall he be one of low birth;
no calamity whatsoever shall touch him, nor fever, nor diseases.
13,096.053c Free from passion and endowed with excellence, he shall attain heaven after death.
13,096.054a And he who would meditate upon the scripture protected by the seers, 13,096.054c that best of men shall go to the imperishable world of Brahmā.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, by whom was this practice established— this giving of an umbrella and a pair of sandals among the duties of the śrāddha?"
13,097.001e How did this come about, and for what purpose is it given?
13,097.002a It is given not only according to the rules of the *śrāddha*, but also during meritorious acts;
13,097.002b even on many other occasions, it is given by relying upon merit.
"O King, I wish to hear this in detail and according to its true essence.
Bhīṣma said:
"Listen attentively, O King, to the detailed account of the umbrella and the sandals."

O lord of men, I shall explain all of this in its entirety: how it became celebrated in the world, by whom it was set in motion, how it attained inexhaustibility, and how it came to possess the nature of merit.
O lord of men, listen to this history of events from the past,
the dialogue between Jamadagni and the high-souled Sūrya.
Formerly, O Lord, that blessed one sported visibly with his bow.
The descendant of Bhṛgu, it is said, discharged arrow after arrow;
but Renukā, having brought back all those shafts of his blazing splendor as they were thrown,
repeatedly gave them back to him, O Acyuta.
Then, delighted by that sound of the bowstring and the arrow, he discharged them, and she brought them back again. Then,
when the sun had reached midday under the constellation Jyeṣṭhāmūla.
Having pierced [the targets] with his arrows, the twice-born said this to Reṇukā:
"Go, O large-eyed one, and fetch these arrows discharged from the bow,
O fair-browed lady, so that I may shoot them again," O lord of men.
That beautiful woman went and took refuge in the shade of a tree;
for her head and likewise her feet were scorched by the heat.
That auspicious lady remained there for a moment indeed, out of fear of her husband’s curse.
The dark-eyed and illustrious lady went forth again to fetch more arrows, and she returned carrying them;
perspiring and with her beautiful limbs, she endured the pain with her feet.
Trembling with fear of her husband, she approached her lord.
Then that seer, enraged, spoke these words to the fair-faced woman:
"Reṇukā, why have you taken so long? Why have you come back so late? he asked again and again.
Reṇukā said:
"O one whose wealth is asceticism, my head and my feet are burning;
obstructed by the sun's radiance, I have taken refuge in the shade of this tree."
"For this reason, O Brahmin, I have acted thus for a long time.
Knowing this, O Lord, O one whose wealth is asceticism, do not be angry with me.
Jamadagni said:
"O Reṇukā, today with my arrows, possessing the fiery brilliance of celestial weapons, I shall strike down this sun of blazing rays that brings you such sorrow. Bhīṣma said:
Having drawn his divine bow and taken up many arrows, he stood facing the sun, turning whichever way the sun moved. Then,
as he was about to strike him, Sūrya approached and spoke these words:
"O son of Kuntī, what offense has the Sun committed against you in the guise of a twice-born?
The wise Sun draws up moisture from here and there with his rays in the sky; it is that very essence which the Maker of Day pours down as rain during the rainy season."
From that, O Brahmin, food is produced, which brings happiness to human beings;
for it is recited in the Vedas that "food is life.
Then, hidden within the clouds and enveloped by rays of light, [it remains].
O Brahman, he rains down upon these seven continents with a shower of 13,097.022c.
Then, O Lord, all food produced from the leaves and flowers of herbs and creepers comes into being through that rain. 13,097.023a-c.
All birth-rites, as well as vows and initiations, the rites of tonsure,
marriages, and the prosperities of sacrifice; likewise, sacrificial sessions, gifts, unions, and the accumulation of wealth.
O Bhārgava, as you know, all things proceed from food—
from whatever is delightful and from whatever constitutes the means of undertaking action;
everything originates from food, which is well known, and I shall declare it to you.
"O Brahmin, you indeed know everything that has been recounted by me. I seek to propitiate you, O brahmin-sage; why is the sun being cast down?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
When Bhāskara had thus entreated him, what did Jamadagni, the best of sages and possessed of great splendor, resolve to do? Bhīṣma said:
O descendant of Kuru, although Jamadagni, whose splendor was like fire, was thus being entreated by him, the sage did not at all attain peace. Then Sūrya spoke these words to him in a sweet voice:
O lord of the people, having bowed with palms joined together in the form of a brahmin, he said this:
"O brahmin-sage, the movement of the sun as it constantly travels is its sign;
how will you perceive the movement of the sun as it perpetually goes?"
Jamadagni said:
"Whether you are stationary or moving, I know you by the eye of knowledge;
today, I must certainly instill discipline in you."
"O Divākara, you remain for half a moment in the afternoon;
there, O Sūrya, I shall know you—of this I have no doubt.
Sūrya said:
"O Brahmin-sage, best among archers, you will undoubtedly know me;
know me, O Blessed One, as one who has done you wrong yet has come to you for refuge.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, laughing, the blessed Jamadagni said to him:
"O Sūrya, you need have no fear, for you have come to me in prostration. The uprightness found in brahmins and the steadfastness found upon the surface of the earth—"
He who would indeed transgress the gentleness of Soma, the profundity of Varuṇa,
the brilliance of Agni, the splendor of Meru, and the heat of the Sun—
he would be one who slays one who has come for refuge.
He would become one who has violated the preceptor’s bed and likewise a slayer of a Brahmin;
he who kills one who has come for refuge would commit the drinking of liquor.
O dear one, consider a remedy for this man once he has been removed.
"May the path become easy to traverse, scorched by your rays.
Bhīṣma said:
Having spoken thus, that descendant of Bhrigu then became silent.
Then Sūrya quickly gave him an umbrella and sandals.
Sūrya said:
"O great seer, this umbrella is a protection for your head, warding off my rays."
"Accept these leather sandals for the protection of your feet;
from this day forward, they shall circulate throughout the world as the supreme and inexhaustible gift among all meritorious donations."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Bhārata, this pair of sandals and this umbrella were indeed introduced here by the Sun; they are celebrated as meritorious throughout the three worlds."

Therefore, bestow upon the brahmins excellent umbrellas and sandals; great merit shall accrue to you, of this I have no doubt. For, O best of the Bharatas, he who gives an umbrella to a twice-born man—
Having given a bright umbrella with a hundred ribs, he indeed prospers in happiness after death;
O bull of the Bharatas, he dwells in the world of Śakra, constantly honored by the twice-born, by the Apsarases, and by the gods.

O mighty-armed one, he who gives a pair of sandals to a Brahmin whose feet are being scorched, or who gives a pair of smooth sandals imbued with oil to a Snātaka of the twice-born who is firm in his vows— [attains great merit].
He too attains worlds honored by the gods;
O Bhārata, after death he dwells in Goloka, filled with joy.
This has been recounted to you in its entirety, O best of the Bharatas.
O best of the Bharatas, such is the fruit of giving umbrellas and sandals;
Yudhiṣṭhira,
service to Śūdras is here described as their constant duty.
By what causes and of how many kinds is service said to be?
And what worlds are ordained for those who serve, O bull among the Bharatas?
O best of the Bharatas, tell me the defining characteristics of the dharma of Śūdras.
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history concerning what was spoken by the knower of Brahman out of compassion for the Śūdras.
The aged Parāśara spoke of the pure and wholesome Dharma,
endowed with purity and right conduct for the sake of favoring the social classes—
the entire instruction on Dharma, exactly as it is and in its proper sequence.
Knowing the meaning, he taught the meaningful scripture to his disciples— he who was patient in his senses, possessed of dignity, pure, free from fickleness,
neither weak nor wavering, and who spoke with progressive depth.
By one who is free from greed, compassionate, upright, a speaker of the Veda,
devoted to virtuous conduct, and whose very self is dedicated to the welfare of all beings— by such a person must the six enemies, which constantly reside within one's own body, be conquered.

Having established firm resolve through the prescribed method, free from egoism and desiring to serve, one who is approved by the three castes should act according to their capacity and strength, overcoming desire, anger, greed, pride, delusion, and arrogance.
Adopting a fourfold discipline through action, mind, speech, and sight, the wise one— tranquil, self-controlled, with senses conquered,
hating *rakṣas* and *yakṣa* beings, and eating only the remnants of food— [should practice].
Just as a bee takes honey from the three colors [of flowers], so should one practice dharma. If a Śūdra should perform ascetic penance through rites prescribed in the Vedas,
he will suffer affliction in this world and an inauspicious destiny after death.
Austerity that is unrighteous and brings ill repute is established among the Śūdras. Having practiced austerity by an improper path, one reaps the fruit among the Mlecchas;
for a Śūdra who conducts himself otherwise does not deserve the Dharma.
For those who have proceeded by an improper path, it is perceived through direct observation that they have abandoned the fourfold caste system and assumed various births and physical forms;
such as the Śakas, Cīnas, Kāmbojas, and Pāradas.
The Śabaras, the Paplavas, and likewise the Tuṣāra-Yavanas; the Dārvas, the Daradas, and others such as the Ujjihānas; the Veṇas, the Kaṅkaṇas, the Siṃhalas, and the Madrakas.
The Kiṣkindhakas, Pulindas, Kahvas, Āndhras, and Sanīragas; the Gandhikas, Dramiḍas, Barbaras, and Cūcukas;
as well as the Kirātas, Pārvateyas, Kolas, Colas, and Khāṣakas.
The Ārukās, the Dohas, and other Mleccha tribes—
deformed, of deformed conduct, and cruel-minded— are seen; having resorted to the Dharma by an improper path, they have consequently gone to other species of birth.
This is the known fruit of austerity acquired by unrighteous means. An action performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, does not perish.
Even here, these [beings] have obtained wealth acquired through the austerity of improper labor.

Those who desire righteousness, yet exert themselves in vain, will worship heretics. O King, as the four castes and the four stages of life thus proceed in a contrary manner, the unintelligent will become Mlecchas.
For Brahmins, wealth consists of Vedic study; for Kṣatriyas, strength is their wealth;
for Vaiśyas, trade and agriculture; and for Śūdras, service. By the abandonment of that duty, one falls into hell.
Then these Mlecchas will become pitiless and devoid of dharma;
for them there shall again be hell and an eternal existence in the wombs of animals.
But those who, having previously established themselves on the true path according to the system of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), [remain steadfast]...
Having abandoned all wrong paths and taken refuge in the way of their own dharma,
they were compassionate toward all beings, worshippers of the gods and the twice-born, and,
with subdued anger, followed the rites prescribed in the scriptures with faith.
I shall explain their procedure correctly and in due order: the entire ritual for taking up [the Veda], as well as the acquisition through service,
the initiation by the learned, and the various mantras.
Likewise, having demonstrated the authority of the treatise, I shall explain the examination of disciples according to reality, as it truly is, and in proper sequence; specifically,
all matters concerning the practice of purity for the sake of purification.
13,098.022d@010_0061 Those who perceive the true nature of reality have observed [the rules] beginning with the *mahāśauca* (great purification).
13,098.022d@010_0062 Even in that regard, a Śūdra should prepare this and the remaining portions for the monks.
13,098.022d@010_0063 [This is to be done by] monks who are wise in well-performed deeds and who rely solely upon the Dharma.

This pure space, free from the creepers of desire, was created by those seeking the welfare of others who were endowed with right vision and had traversed the path; having recognized it as secluded and enclosed, one whose self is restrained and senses conquered [should enter].
Having placed a vessel containing water and examined clay,
and having inspected the ground, one who desires to urinate should then sit with speech restrained;
facing north during the day, or facing south if it is at night.
When the ground has been covered over, and likewise when his head is concealed,
he should not utter any speech until his purification is complete. Having performed his duties and sipped water (ācamana), he should not speak while walking away.
Seated for the purpose of purification, with the vessel of earth placed before him,
he should take his water-pot and place it between his side and thigh;
then the hero, acting with deliberate awareness, should perform the purification slowly and without confusion.
Having taken pure water with his hand according to the prescribed rule,
he should do so in such a way that no drops fall and his thighs are not touched;
three applications of clay should then be made to the anus in successive order.
A Brahmin should likewise touch hand with hand;
nine applications of earth should be given to the anus—this is the instruction of the elders. For the earth being applied will indeed purify the area immediately.
Therefore, earth should be applied again and again to the palms of the hands with deliberate effort, so that it does not touch the buttocks; for in this way,
no moisture-born affliction shall arise from the undergarment.
In that manner, one should wipe the anus repeatedly for the sake of purification;
then, having discarded [the earth] from each foot, one should stand up and perform the purification.
Twelve applications should be made on the left hand, and three each time again and again.
They should be applied repeatedly to the elbows, the hands, and the back-bands;
likewise, one should apply four to the mirror on both [sides],
and seven each to both hands.

Then, taking another portion of clay, they should again perform the purification of those two hands; for in this way, this great purification is ordained. One should not act otherwise than this, for this is the eternal rule.
The purification of urine in the lap is prescribed from this point forward;
however, he who should act otherwise must perform an expiation. For one whose garment is defiled by impurity, double the [prescribed] purification is ordained.
13,098.022d@010_0097 Along with the feet and the thighs, there is no doubt regarding the cleansing of the hands. 13,098.022d@010_0098 For one who disregards this, a doubt arises.
13,098.022d@010_0099 To whatever extent it is purified, in that same manner one should proceed.
Having entered a cramped house that is muddy during the rainy season,
one should apply three applications of clay to the hands and six to the feet; having applied as much as desired to the anus, one should likewise apply three to each foot.
The cleansing of the hands must be performed after the rite for cleansing from urine;
likewise, during the cleansing from urine, the hands and the feet are to be cleansed in successive order.
However, in the case of the perpetual student (*naiṣṭhika*), the purification of the standing place is prescribed as a great purification (*mahāśauca*).
One should perform the cleansing of a cloth with alkaline substances, saline earth, and clay;
the removal of stains and odors from an impure object is thus prescribed. For a bathing garment, three applications of clay should be made to both hands in successive order.

Having performed purification with great care, one should extract [the tooth] while trembling. Four, three, two, or even one [tooth] should be given away, depending on the time, the place, and the relative gravity or lightness of the purification required in times of distress.
By this rule, one should always perform purification without sloth;
having washed his feet with focused attention, without looking around and without agitation,
he should then wash his hands up to the wrist.
Then he should touch his hands from below and above;
with the mind focused and remaining silent, he should silently drink water three times.
The wise man should then wipe his mouth twice and touch the cavities of the head.
He who drinks the water first gratifies the *Ṛgveda* with it;
the second time he gratifies the *Yajurveda*, and the third time, the *Sāmaveda*. By this, the *Atharvaveda* is purified first and attains satisfaction.
Through the second [eye], he offers the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Smṛtis, and the deities;
by that which he concentrates upon the eye, he indeed gratifies Āditya.
He gratifies Vāyu and the sense of smell, as well as the quarters of space through the two ears.
By concluding [the ritual] at the head, one pleases Brahmā;
by raising the bow upward toward the sky, one pleases him;
and by placing water at the feet, one indeed pleases Viṣṇu.
Facing either the east or the north, with his hands between his knees, he should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśet*).
This rule applies everywhere, constantly, in matters such as eating.
When food particles remain stuck between the teeth, one becomes impure; in that case, one should sip water again.
This rule has been prescribed; for purification, sprinkling with water is ordained.
This rule is seen as applicable to a Śūdra when he is departing from his home. However, one who has disciplined his self must always conduct himself with unimpaired purity.
Parāśara said: 13,098.022d@010_0133 A Śūdra, desiring fame and seeking his own welfare, [should give] to the monks.
13,098.022d@010_0134 Sacrifices involving physical exertion are prescribed for Kṣatriyas, while sacrifices involving valor are prescribed for Vaiśyas.
Śūdras live by service and are without sacrifice; Brāhmaṇas, however, perform the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña).
Śūdras live by servitude; Vaiśyas live by trade. Kṣatriyas restrain those who do wrong; Brāhmaṇas live by the study of the Vedas.
A Brahmin shines through austerity, a Kṣatriya through protection and other such duties,
a Vaiśya through hospitality, and a Śūdra shines through service. Furthermore,
a Śūdra who has restrained his self must always perform service.
This should generally be practiced by those in the three social orders who dwell in the stages of life; indeed,
those dwelling in the stages of life should be served by one who is incapable [of fulfilling the three goals] himself,
according to his ability, according to his wisdom, according to dharma, and according to what he has heard.

Service must be performed with particular care in the stage of life of the mendicant (bhikṣuka). Among all four stages of life, the wise, in their determination according to the scriptures, describe the stage of the mendicant as the most preeminent.

Whatever is taught by the learned according to the injunctions of the Śruti and Smṛti, in that manner one who is incapable [of more] should remain; that is determined to be Dharma. A human being who acts otherwise than this does not attain the highest good.
Therefore, a Śūdra should always perform what is beneficial for his own self among the monks;
whatever good he does here, that he enjoys after death.
And that must be done without envy, for it is that which one considers to be his duty.
One who is envious reaps the fruit of their actions here in the form of suffering.
One who speaks kindly, has conquered anger, is free from sloth, is without envy,
is patient, endowed with virtuous conduct, and is devoted to truth and righteousness— [attains happiness].
Indeed, one should perform service in the mendicant’s stage of life through a state of renunciation;
"This is my supreme duty, and by means of this, which is so difficult to practice,
I shall cross the terrible ocean of saṃsāra— of this there is no doubt."
"Abandoning this body, I shall go to the supreme goal;
there is no other eternal dharma for me beyond this.
Having thus reflected in his mind with focused intelligence, the Śūdra—
One should always perform the supreme duty of service with an undistracted mind;
one should always abide by the discipline of service here, eating only what is left over,
being endowed with tranquility, self-controlled, and always knowing what ought and ought not to be done.
In all matters, one should show that tasks have indeed been accomplished;
one should carry out affairs in such a way that the monk becomes beloved.
Whatever may be improper for a monk, he should not perform that task.
Whatever is not inconsistent with the stage of life (*āśrama*) and is intended solely for the sake of Dharma,
that should always be performed without hesitation by one who desires what is auspicious.
One should always seek to propitiate [the deities] through mind, action, and speech.
One should stand when [the teacher] is standing, follow after him when he is walking,
and always sit when he is sitting; one should constantly attend upon him with affection acquired through dharma, and should press his feet [in service].
He should likewise perform the anointing and other such services even without being prompted.
Having performed his nightly duties and always remaining unbidden,
he should touch water according to the prescribed rule and set down the water vessel.
Having gone to the dwelling of the monks and having prostrated according to the prescribed rite, he,
with his senses restrained, should likewise perform salutations there to the elders beginning with the Brahmins,
and pay homage to those headed by the teachers.
Having inquired after the welfare and offered salutations to those who practice their own dharma,
one should always pay homage to whoever has been previously perfected and is equal in dharma, but never to others.
Having spoken to them and always rising with his vows restrained,
he should then perform the sweeping and the smearing [of the floor],
and thereafter, taking flowers, he should offer a flower-oblation according to the Dharma.

Having quickly departed from the dwelling, one should perform other duties in such a way that no harm comes to the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) of those belonging to the [four] stages of life (*āśramin*). However,
one who causes such harm becomes joined with sin.
One should direct one's self in such a way that they may obtain satisfaction;
for I am traditionally remembered as a servant of the three castes according to dharma,
how much more so of those who are elders of the stages of life and who subsist on whatever they happen to receive?
I must especially serve with a self-restrained mind those monks who are free from passion and possess exclusive knowledge and vision;
through their grace and my ascetic penance, I shall attain the desired and auspicious state.
Having thus determined this, if one should serve mendicants according to the method taught by oneself, one attains the supreme goal—
Parāśara.
Neither by giving gifts nor by fasting and other such practices does one attain a desired state as one does through the act of service;
for with whatever kind of water a man effects purification, [so is his merit].
Just as water becomes like that which it has washed by its very nature,
so too even a Śūdra, by this path, becomes like the person he serves through association;
of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, with self-restraint, one should diligently serve the monks by providing water for their use, as well as baths,
ointments, and care for those exhausted by travel or afflicted by illness.
One should constantly and diligently perform service for them in times of distress;
one should look after the *darbha* grass, the deerskin, and the alms-bowl,
and accomplish all their tasks according to their wishes.
One should perform all actions in such a way that no expiation (prāyaścitta) becomes necessary.
For those who are ill, however, one should diligently attend to them by washing their clothes and performing other services,
as well as providing medical treatments and bringing medicines.

One should not provide for others' service grinding, ointments, powders, decoctions, or medicinal preparations for the sake of pleasure; rather, one who wanders for alms should approach wise physicians.

Then, one should acquire goods for the purpose of ransoming [the life]; and whatever man should give with a joyful mind, one may take that medicine. For those things given without faith are not to be consumed by monks.
Whatever is received with faith and whatever is offered with faith— by the enjoyment of that, merit is gained and one is freed from diseases.
Thus, until the fall of the body, [one should serve] with unwearied devotion for the sake of service.
One should never, however, abandon righteousness (dharma) to retaliate against them;
for by their very nature, pairs of opposites come and go,
and by their very nature, all things come into being and pass away.
The wise man who knows this— knowing reality and seeing reality as it is— is like one who understands that the qualities (guṇas) are like the waves of the ocean;
thus says Parāśara.
He would not be stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Thus, one should strive with unwearied diligence for the sake of service,
so that ascetics may be satisfied by all such ministrations.

One should not offend a monk, nor should one treat him with contempt; one should not offer a retort, but rather appease him even when he is angry. One should speak only what is beneficial and act with a joyful disposition.
By remaining silent, one should not speak to an angry person there;
one should not take the property of others, nor should one accept what is not requested. One should live on whatever is obtained or not obtained, and likewise remain contented.
One should not, out of hatred for knowledge, beg for a loincloth;
one should show compassion toward stationary things and toward moving living beings,
and one should cast an equal gaze upon others as one does upon oneself.

Perceiving the Self in all beings and all beings in the Self, one who moves about in this manner is fit for becoming Brahman. One should not commit violence or non-violence for the sake of one's own self.
Where another person would always incur a fault, one should not cause that fault to be committed there;
in this way, by acting while relying on others, he is freed from the fault.
For it is the man of small intelligence who becomes tainted by a fault through his own reliance.
Those born from a womb, those born from an egg, those born from a sprout, and those born from sweat—
all these are declared by the wise to be incapable of being slain;
however, for the sake of the certainty of the enlightened, an expiation is prescribed.
Just as violence is ordained in other cases, so too should it bring about its corresponding fault;
for when a disciple follows the prescribed rule taught by the teacher,
neither greed nor violence inherent in that [greed] prevails.
For this vision of the scriptures has indeed been ordained by the Source of the Universe.
If one should think thus: "Even a Śūdra may be wise;
he who performs [the rites] shall attain the state of those who have performed them—how much more so he who practices [this teaching]!"

No Śūdra whatsoever falls [from his status], nor does he deserve the purificatory rites (saṃskāra). He has no entitlement to dharma, yet there is no prohibition against dharma for him. This was described by Manu for the sake of favoring all the social classes.
If a scandal should arise concerning a servant caused by a woman,
his punishment is prescribed as sleeping in the open air for one year;
through this, his peace shall be restored, and thereafter he may return again.
This [penance] shall apply to one who has approached a woman of equal caste; however, for one who has approached a woman of lower caste, he deserves half.
For approaching a Vaiśya woman, it is three years; for a Kṣatriya woman, six years;
and for a Brāhmaṇa woman, twelve years are prescribed for one who has united with her.
Or he should be burned by a fire of straw at that very moment;
or else, by having his penis cut off, he may attain purification,
provided he deprives only a single boneless limb of life.
Having fasted for one day, one should perform twelve breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*);
by bathing three times in water, one is liberated from that sin. For injuries to the joints of the bones, double the penance is prescribed.
By this method, there is no doubt that one is liberated from offenses committed against stationary beings with the body, the feet, or the hands. Furthermore,
he who causes [this text] to be recited among all castes shall pass his time free from fault.

One should know that for him as well, the penance is eightfold; however, that same penance is fourfold when committed through action and twofold when corrupted by speech. But having committed a mental sin, it is likewise remembered as being single-fold.
Therefore, having understood all these things, one should not practice them;
rather, for the sake of the welfare of all beings, one should practice wholesome deeds.
If, with a mind thus composed, one serves the most excellent ones...
Following his way, practicing his conduct, with his mind fixed on him and making him his supreme goal,
one should neither rejoice in death nor rejoice in life;
one should simply await the time, just as a laborer awaits his wages.
Proceeding in this manner, disciplined and self-controlled,
Parāśara quickly arrives at the certain conclusion regarding merit and sin.
Constantly devoted to service, one should observe the omens of misfortune (*ariṣṭa*),
whether they arise every three years, every two years, or annually;
or every six months, every month, or even every seven nights.
One should know all those objects and observe their characteristic marks. If one observes a golden man standing facing south, death will occur within three years.
For one who perceives the sun as a pure orb devoid of rays,
one should predict his death within exactly two years.
Furthermore, he who perceives his own shadow in the moonlight as having a hole [in it]— [his life is likewise numbered].
The wise man should know that death will come within a year;
when a person sees his own shadow without a head,
the intelligent one should know that his own death is here in six months.
If, covering his ears with both hands, a man does not hear sound,
the wise man should know that his own death will occur within exactly one month. Or if a man smells the odor of a corpse, or any other foul smell instead of a fragrant one;

One who stays in a temple of the deities shall indeed meet death within seven nights. The removal of the ears and nose, the discoloration of the teeth and eyes, and the loss of consciousness— these symptoms of the senses indicate immediate death.
If one should perceive any one of these omens of death,
one should not examine that time as it was calculated according to the omen; rather,
one should go quickly to a pure sandy bank.
There, one should release the vital breaths while recollecting that Lord Īśāna;
then, having attained another body, one shall reach the state of a Gandharva. Abiding there, that one of great splendor dwells for twenty padmas.

Honored by the Gandharvas, headed by Citrasena, he was likewise accompanied by them; illuminating the expanse of the sky with a celestial chariot the color of blue lapis lazuli, he, undaunted in spirit, moved together with hosts of Apsarases.
Following his desires and inclinations, he is honored here and there;
with a self equal to the immortals, he always rejoices together with the hosts of gods.
And when the time for his decline arrives, he of stainless radiance falls in an instant.

Having obtained birth there in a preeminent family of a wealthy Vaiśya possessing much cattle and wealth, he was purified by divine rites; then, through the Jāgata meter, he received the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*).
Having attained the status of the twice-born and the requisite equipment of linen garments,
he becomes a student of the Vedas, devoted to the service of his teacher;
thereafter, he is born as a celibate student (brahmacārī), one who has conquered anger and is dedicated to austerity.
Having studied the Vedas and given the teacher’s fee according to the prescribed rules,
he takes a wife and enters upon the excellent vow of a householder;
he gives gifts and performs sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees.

Performing the *agnihotra* sacrifice and maintaining it according to the prescribed rules, he who moves with gentleness and has conquered his senses constantly accumulates merit (*dharma*). However, through the transformation of time, he eventually encounters death.
Refined by the Agnihotra sacrifice and having prepared the sacrificial vessels,
one who is thus consecrated casts off the body and attains union with the Maruts;
accompanied by the Maruts, possessing equal splendor and great radiance.
Resplendent in a celestial chariot with the color of the rising sun,
he moves about happily there, surrounded by hosts of *gandharvas* and *apsarases*,
clothed in stainless garments and adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
Following his desires and passions, he shall dwell for double that time;
having fallen from that state, he shall return after a period of time,
still unsatisfied in his dwelling, yet having abandoned divine enjoyments.
He is born into a royal family crowded with elephants, horses, and chariots;
having attained earthly sovereignty, he is glorious like a lord of Dharma.
From birth, he undergoes the purificatory rites, including the tonsure and the initiation ceremony.
Having reached that royal court there in the prescribed manner according to the rules,
one is initiated into the state of the twice-born by means of the *traiṣṭubha* meter;
having studied the entire Veda and the science of archery (*dhanurveda*) preeminently.
Having returned from his studies, he was then consecrated as the crown prince by his father;
having performed the rites of marriage, the illustrious one, having obtained the kingdom according to dharma,
protected his subjects properly, having established the agreement of taking a sixth share [of their produce].
Having performed many sacrifices with properly bestowed sacrificial fees,
that illustrious king, whose splendor was equal to Indra’s, ruled the earth,
ever devoted to his own duty and supported by his sons and grandsons.
Falling under the power of time, he gave up his life in battle;
he attained the world of Indra, the abode of the king of the gods,
and wandered at ease, being honored by the thirty deities.
Like the Lord of the Gods, he is praised by royal sages who have performed meritorious deeds; he is awakened by those bards with various musical instruments,
while [the throne] made of divine Jāmbūnada gold shines brilliantly on all sides.
Having ascended a celestial vehicle filled with excellent *apsarases* and frequented by gods and *gandharvas*, he shall roam about like Śakra, the lord of Śacī;
there he dwells for sixty *padmas* of years, filled with joy.
Wandering through all the worlds and illuminating them with his great supernatural power,
he was then established on earth due to the exhaustion of his merit, O Bhārata—
Parāśara.
And he is born into a family of the twice-born who have mastered the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences; thereafter, having acquired sacred learning and been consecrated according to the rules,
the tonsure and initiation ceremonies are duly performed for him by the twice-born.

Then, in his eighth year, through rites such as the initiation for vows (*vratopanayana*) performed according to the prescribed rules, he is led toward the state of Brahmanhood; having been consecrated by the *gāyatrī* meter, he has completed his observances.
The wise man, pure in soul and firm in his vows, while studying,
shall master the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences in a very short time; he is then a righteous soul who has completed his studies and fulfilled his duties.
Devoted to officiating at sacrifices and teaching, established in wholesome action,
constantly intent on the *agnihotra* fire-sacrifice, and a worshiper of the deities and guests,
he performs various sacrifices as well as the sacrifice of silent recitation (*japayajña*).
Seeking wealth acquired through righteous means, virtuous in conduct, rich in asceticism,
devoted to the welfare of all beings, and proficient in all the scriptures;
content with his own wife, approaching her only during her season, he is one who has conquered his senses.

Abstaining from slandering others and always devoted to the vow of truth, he was eventually joined with the law of time through the transformation of time; and he had been consecrated by the Agnihotra sacrifice according to the rules and in due order.
Upon casting off the body, one attains the world of Soma; of this there is no doubt.
There, one dwells with the radiant gods who partake of Soma, the Agniṣvātta deities, as well as the Barhiṣad gods and the divine Aṅgirasas.
Together with all the gods, as well as the Brahman-sages,
the incomparable celestial rishis, and likewise the hosts of Apsarases,
and constantly honored by the Sādhyas and Siddhas, he rejoices there.
He ascends a divine celestial chariot made of gold, brilliant as the sun and swift as thought, crowded with gods and gandharvas;
[there he finds] women of gentle form, pleasing to the mind, adorned with ornaments of refined gold.
The daughters of Soma, filled with joy, delight him as he sits within his celestial chariot;
there he rejoices, pleased, together with the gods and the ṛṣis,
wandering through all the worlds with blazing splendor and the speed of thought.
He constantly goes to the assembly hall that moves at will,
having paid homage to the Grandfather, the seer who is the lord of all worlds,
the Supreme Lord of infinite glory, the source and dissolution of the worlds.
From which all the transformations of creation and dissolution proceed,
there that illustrious best of the twice-born dwells for two hundred [years]. Then,
due to the exhaustion of time, he returns again from that place.
Having reflected upon and realized that all these things— the nature of birth, as well as all creations and cycles of return— are entirely impermanent,
one attains that which is eternal, divine, immovable, undepressed, and free from rebirth.
He shall eternally abide in that state of fearlessness where there is no returning;
having gone there, one does not die, nor is there any further birth. By me have been experienced the sufferings of the womb and being born again and again.
Various bodily afflictions and diverse dualities—
cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as those born of envy and hatred—
have been experienced here and there; nowhere is there a state of permanence.
Having thus made this resolve and liberated himself from the bonds of worldly attachment,
having severed the snare consisting of his wife as well as that arising from offspring,
he took refuge in the dharma of an ascetic and devoted himself to the service of his teacher.
In no long time at all, he attains the highest good,
having understood the Yoga-śāstra and Sāṃkhya according to the reality of their meaning,
and being authorized by his teacher, he abides in accordance with the scriptures.
Frequenting sacred fords and taking refuge on the sandy banks of rivers, making his home in empty dwellings and dwelling in forest trees and caves,
he constantly roams the great forests, having the celestial groves as his abode.

For one night or two nights, the twice-born man does not cling to anything anywhere. Even in a vessel made of withered leaves, the mendicant wanders during the day; he does not pursue enjoyment, but partakes of food only for the sake of sustenance.
He consumes what is obtained through Dharma and does not eat anything out of desire;
looking only a yoke’s length ahead on the road, he does not travel more than a *krośa*.
He is equal toward honor and dishonor, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
He who grants fearlessness to all beings and likewise bestows the gift of security; who is free from dualities, free from prostrations, and free from joy and possessions;
who is without "mine-ness," without egoism, and has no dependence on any being.

Then, one who knows the truth of enumeration and is always devoted to reality should desire nothing— neither above, nor below, nor across. Thus indeed, delighting in this manner, he follows the duty of an ascetic according to the rule.
Just as a ripe fruit [falls] due to the measure of time, so too he,
having cast off his own body, shall enter the eternal Brahman—
free from disease, without beginning or end, gentle in its qualities, and beyond consciousness.
It is without syllables and without seed, devoid of senses, and likewise unborn;
it is invincible, imperishable, indivisible, and indeed subtle;
it is without qualities, beyond primordial nature, and entirely changeless.
Parāśara [attains] the Supreme Lord of the past, present, and future time; he takes refuge in the unmanifest Puruṣa, the Field (kṣetra), for the sake of infinity.
Thus, that monk, having burnt away his defilements, shall attain Nirvana;
remaining here, he casts off the body just as a bird leaves its nest. By relying solely upon the true path, even a Śūdra attains a happy destination.
From one station, one may attain another— the immovable station of Brahmā. Just as one digging with a spade finds water in an arid land, so too, through perseverance, one attains the desired state.
This very goal, which is without beginning or end, has been realized by all;
therefore, Śūdras should always conduct themselves with perseverance and faith according to their ability, as prescribed by the wise.
Whatever one does, that one experiences—whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
An unperformed action is not experienced, nor does the fruit of a performed action perish.
Thus, one who practices auspicious conduct obtains only an auspicious result.
For one who practices unwholesome conduct indeed attains what is unwholesome;
likewise, one who practices wholesome conduct indeed avoids what is unwholesome.
One who desires his own welfare should undertake only what is wholesome.
Prosperity cannot be attained by Śūdras from any other source; this is the settled conclusion.
The virtuous have determined that it is possible only through service to ascetics. Therefore, one should be endowed with the sacred scriptures and possess well-restrained senses.
For indeed, it is possible to attain the state free from suffering solely through scripture—
the supreme goal of these [beings] which the virtuous seek,
wherein one attains immortality after casting off endless suffering.
For by relying on this Dharma, even those who are of low birth—
women, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— may attain the supreme goal;
how much more so, then, a learned Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya of great erudition?
Furthermore, knowledge does not arise for an embodied being whose sins have not been exhausted. The attainment of knowledge occurs when one has fulfilled all duties;
having attained such discernment or wisdom, one remains free from envy.
In that very same way, one should behave toward teachers with even greater composure;
yet, if one should treat a teacher with contempt, one behaves toward them accordingly. His learning becomes fruitless, and his knowledge turns into ignorance.
He would surely go to an evil destiny and fall into hell, without a doubt;
his merit would perish and his knowledge would be obstructed,
like a man who, having never before seen what is auspicious, sees it for the first time through a ritual injunction.
Having fallen into delusion through arrogance, he attained the knowledge of reality. Indeed, one should never act with such arrogance regarding the arising of knowledge;
for the fruit of knowledge is tranquility, and one should always strive for that tranquility.
One who is tranquil, self-controlled, always endowed with forbearance,
and ever free from malice should constantly practice service.
One should guard the genitals and the stomach through fortitude, and the hands and feet through the eyes.
One should withdraw the sense objects with the mind and fix the mind upon the intellect. Then, having gone to a pure and well-secluded place, one should sit with fortitude;
having obtained a seat as prescribed, one should practice according to the rule.
Thus, endowed with knowledge, one should perceive the Lord dwelling within the heart,
blazing with his own form like a smokeless fire,
like the radiant sun, or like a flash of lightning in the sky.
One should behold the Lord, eternal and immutable, established within the heart;
yet the Great Lord cannot be seen by one who is undisciplined,
whereas the disciplined man, having fixed the mind in the heart, beholds Him through the intellect.

Now, if one is indeed unable to perform this holding of the heart, one should practice according to Sāṃkhya and abide properly in Yoga. Here, there are five organs of perception and also five organs of action.
The five specific elements and the mind make sixteen;
likewise, there are the five subtle elements (tanmātras), the mind, and ego (ahaṃkāra). Including the unmanifest (avyakta) as the eighth, these are designated as the "primordial natures" (prakṛtis).
These eight are the primary constituents (*prakṛti*), and the sixteen are the transformations (*vikāra*).
Thus, one established here should understand this with a mind directed toward reality (*tattva-buddhi*).
Having thus crossed over the rain [of worldly existence], one has truly crossed; it is not otherwise.
This should be understood as a definitive enumeration by one possessed of wisdom and intelligence.
Day after day, with a tranquil soul, it leads to purification and well-being.
Having thus reflected upon this, one whose intellect perceives reality is liberated.

One who knows the reality of the pure principle becomes partless and absolute; the wise Śūdra, established in the stage of a mendicant and devoted to service, is liberated through the very contact with that pure being, and not otherwise.
One should associate with the virtuous;
one should also serve those who are superior in knowledge;
through such association, one attains the same character as they.
"Like a blue bird taking refuge on Mount Meru," said Bhīṣma;
having spoken thus, the great sage then—
Having understood the injunctions regarding the fourth caste,
and having mastered the course of conduct through service and meditative concentration,
he, endowed with *samādhi*, departed for his own hermitage.
Yudhiṣṭhira:
To which high-souled ones do the illustrious gods bow down?
Bhīṣma: [Answer follows].

"O best of beings, I desire to hear about all those sages in this world. O Yudhiṣṭhira, listen to that which the wise Brahmins, knowers of antiquity, recite as this ancient history (itihāsa) regarding this matter."
Having returned from the slaying of Vṛtra, he was honored by the thirty gods;
he had arrived before Mahendra, being praised by the great seers,
endowed with supreme splendor, seated upon his chariot, borne by tawny steeds.
Mātali, with palms joined in reverence, spoke to the god Indra:
"O Blessed One, you are the foremost of all those who are honored;
you are Bhīṣma."
"Tell me, who are those in the world to whom one should pay homage?
Having heard those words of his, Indra, the king of the gods and husband of Śacī,
replied to that charioteer who was questioning him.

O Mātali, I pay homage to those whose minds, when contemplating dharma, artha, and kāma, never constantly dwell upon what is unrighteous— those who are endowed with beauty and virtue, and who are captivating to the hearts of women.

O Mātali, I pay homage to those who have turned away from the enjoyment of sensual pleasures; those who are content with their own possessions, who are well-spoken, patient in speech, free from pride, and worthy of honor— I pay homage to them, O Mātali.
I always honor those whose minds are not shaken by wealth, knowledge, or power; who restrain their wavering thoughts;
and who, being pure and endowed with beloved wives, maintain the sacred fire.
O Mātali, I bow down to those who possess four-legged cattle;
they have attained great ascetic merit as well as abundant wealth. One should certainly not practice renunciation of that which one does not truly understand to be one's own.
O Mātali, I pay homage to those for whom wealth and desire are increased by the root of dharma, and for whom both dharma and wealth are constant;
and likewise to Brahmins and cows, whose wealth and desires have dharma as their root.
I offer my salutations to those women who are devoted to their husbands. O Mātali, I constantly honor those men who, having enjoyed human pleasures in their youth, attain heaven through asceticism.

I honor in my mind those who do not enjoy worldly pleasures and are free from attachment, who are constant in the Dharma and have conquered their senses; who have renounced all things and are as immovable as mountains,
and who desire the firmly established Dharma of those whose knowledge is purified by wisdom.
"O Mātali, I bow down to those whose purity has been proclaimed by others.
"O tiger among the Bharatas, what more do you wish to hear from me?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O joy of the Kurus, O bull of the Bharatas, I wish to hear from you today what fruit is obtained from groves and ponds.
Bhīṣma said:
"Beautiful to behold, abounding in forests, adorned with various minerals,
and endowed with all kinds of seeds— this is called the most excellent soil here. Furthermore, one should consider its specific field characteristics and the location of ponds."
I shall describe all matters concerning water in their proper sequence; I shall also declare the merits of constructed reservoirs,
for the owner of a reservoir is honored everywhere throughout the three worlds.

Alternatively, the construction of a reservoir is the abode of Mitra, friendly, and a promoter of friends; it generates fame and is the most excellent among works. The wise say that it is the fruit of virtue, wealth, and pleasure.
A well-constructed reservoir in a suitable location is indeed a great refuge for living beings;
one should regard a reservoir as the support for the four classes of beings.
Furthermore, all such reservoirs bestow supreme prosperity.
Gods, humans, Gandharvas, ancestors, serpents, and Rākṣasas,
as well as immobile beings, all take refuge in a reservoir of water.
Therefore, I shall describe to you those merits which are traditionally attributed to a tank.

Whatever fruit for the attainment of rewards has been proclaimed there by the sages regarding a pond that holds water for even a single year, the wise declare that its fruit is equal to the merit of the Agnihotra sacrifice.
He in whose pond water remains during the autumn season obtains, after death, the supreme fruit of giving a thousand cows. He in whose pond water remains during the winter season...
He indeed obtains the fruit of a sacrifice in which much gold is bestowed;
for those wise men say that he who possesses water in his pond during the winter season obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who has constructed a well-made pond that serves as a great refuge in the springtime— indeed,
he who has water remaining in his pond during the spring season—
attains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
The sages know that for him in whose pond water remains during the summer season, the fruit is indeed equal to that of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
he saves his entire lineage who possesses a dug-out reservoir of water.
Thirteen thousand and ninety-nine cows, as well as virtuous men,
always drink water from the pond of that person whose thirsty cows, deer, birds, and humans drink its water; he shall obtain the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Whatever water people drink there, whatever they bathe in, and whatever they rest by— that all conduces to the infinite welfare of the maker of the pond after death,
O dear one, for water is indeed difficult to obtain, especially in the world beyond.

By the gift of water, eternal joy is attained. Give sesame seeds, give water, give lamps, and remain vigilant; rejoice together with your kinsmen, for this is difficult to find after one has passed away.
Heavier than all gifts and distinguished above all gifts, O tiger among men, is water; therefore, it must indeed be given. Thus has this supreme fruit regarding reservoirs been proclaimed.
"O Kaunteya, by providing water for even a single day to one who stands upon the earth,
one rescues seven times seven times seven generations of one's lineage.
Hereafter, I shall speak concerning the planting of trees as well."
Six classes of immobile beings are proclaimed:
trees, shrubs, creepers, climbing plants, those with bark-fiber, and species of grass.
These are the classes of trees; now, these are the merits gained from planting them.
The *panasa*, mango, and other trees; the shrubs beginning with the *mandāra*; the *nāgikā* and *marica* vines; the creepers such as the *mālatī*;
the bamboos, *kramuka*, and *tvaksāra*; and the grains and various kinds of grasses.
From the planting of these crops, there arises eternal satisfaction;
one gains renown in the world of men and, after death, an auspicious fruit. One acquires a name in the world and is honored by the ancestors.
Even for one who has gone to the world of the gods, his name does not perish— neither in the past nor in the future, O Bhārata— nor does it fail for his paternal lineage,
extending to a hundred ancestors and a hundred descendants, including his parents and grandfathers.
The planter of trees shall deliver [beings] from [suffering]; therefore, one should plant trees.
For he who, having planted trees, tends to those forest-dwellers at the proper time, these very trees become his sons; of this there is no doubt.

Having gone to the other world, he attains heaven and imperishable realms. O dear one, trees worship the hosts of gods with their flowers, the ancestors with their fruits, and guests with their shade.
Trees always honor guests with their shade; likewise,
Kinnaras, Uragas, Rakshasas, gods, Gandharvas, humans,
and hosts of sages take refuge in trees.
Bearing flowers and fruits, they gratify human beings here in this world;
moreover, those who have planted trees rescue the planter like sons in the next world.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should always plant trees by a pond.
And they are to be protected like sons; according to the Dharma, they are considered your sons.
The twice-born who constructs tanks, plants trees, and performs sacrifices—these, as well as others who speak the truth, are glorified in heaven.
"Therefore, one should construct a pond, plant groves,
perform various sacrifices, and always speak the truth.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, explain in its entirety the dharma of the householder.
O King, what must a man do here in this world to attain prosperity?
Bhīṣma said:
13,100.002a Here, O lord of men, I shall relate to you an ancient account,
13,100.002c a conversation between Vāsudeva and the Earth, O Bhārata.
13,100.003a Having praised the goddess Earth, the powerful Vāsudeva—
13,100.003c O best of the Bharatas, he asked that which you now ask me today.
13,100.004 Vāsudeva said:
13,100.004a "Having resorted to the dharma of the householder, either by me or by one like me,"
"O Earth, what must necessarily be done, or by doing what would one become happy? Pṛthivī replied:
"O Mādhava, the sages, the ancestors, the gods, and human beings—"
Learn from me how those who are to be sacrificed for and those who are to be honored [should be treated]:
one should always worship the gods with sacrifice, men with hospitality, and worthy guests constantly and according to one's inclination, as is the eternal rule.
For by this, O Madhusūdana, the hosts of ṛṣis are delighted.
One should constantly attend to the sacred fire and perform the bali-offering even before eating;
in this way, O Madhusūdana, the gods are indeed pleased.
Day after day, he should perform the *śrāddha* for the ancestors with food and water, or even with milk, roots, and fruits, bringing them satisfaction; furthermore,
from the prepared food, he should perform the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice in the fire according to the prescribed rule.
One should offer oblations to Agni and Soma, then to the Viśvedevas, and immediately after to Dhānvantari (13,100.009c). Furthermore, a separate oblation is prescribed for Prajāpati (13,100.010a);
in that same sequence, one should perform the ritual of offerings (balikarma) (13,100.010c).
To Yama here in the south, and to Varuṇa in the west;
to Soma indeed in the north, and to the twice-born in the center of the site;
to Dhanvantari in the northeast, and to Śakra in the east, O Mādhava.
They say that one should indeed offer a bali-oblation at the door of the house with the words "To Manu"; and one should carry the bali-oblation for the Maruts and the deities within the house;
likewise, one should offer the bali-oblation to the Viśvedevas from the open space.
One should likewise offer an oblation at night to the nocturnal beings and the spirits.
Having thus properly performed the oblation, one should give alms to a twice-born man.
If a Brāhmaṇa is not available, one should cast the first portion into the fire.
When a man wishes to offer a *śrāddha* to the ancestors,
he should perform [the offering to the spirits] afterwards, once the *śrāddha* rite has been concluded.
Having satisfied the ancestors, he should then present the *bali* offering according to the prescribed rule.

Then one should perform the Vaiśvadeva rite, followed by the recitation for the Brahmins. Thereafter, O Great King, one should feed even the guests with the remaining food, honoring them first; thus one gratifies human beings.
Since he dwells for only a short time, he is called a guest (*atithi*).
One should always announce to the teacher, the father, a friend, and a trusted guest: "This is what is available in my house."
Whatever they may say, that one should do; such is the dharma ordained.

O Kṛṣṇa, a householder should always be one who eats only what remains after others have been fed. [One should honor] the king, the officiating priest, the *snātaka*, the teacher, and likewise the father-in-law.
One should honor those who have stayed for more than a year with the honey-mixture (madhuparka). One should scatter food on the ground for dogs, for outcastes (śvapacas), and for birds;
for this is called the Vaiśvadeva rite, which is prescribed for both morning and evening.
But he who, free from malice, performs these duties pertaining to the householder’s life, attains supreme prosperity in this world and, after death, is glorified in heaven.
Bhīṣma said:
Having heard these words of the Earth, the powerful Vāsudeva acted accordingly;
you too should always conduct yourself in this same manner. O lord of men, by thus keeping the duties of a householder in mind, you shall succeed.
"Having attained fame in this world, you shall obtain heaven after death.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, what is this so-called gift of light like?"
"How did this come about? Tell me also of the fruit in this matter.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O Bhārata, there was a discourse between Manu Prajāpati and Suvarṇa.
There was once an ascetic known by the name Suvarṇa;
because his complexion was like the color of gold, he became renowned as "Suvarṇa."
Endowed with noble lineage, virtuous conduct, and excellent qualities, and having reached the highest proficiency in sacred study,
he surpassed many born of his own lineage by means of his own merits. Once, that brahmin saw Manu and approached him.
There, the two of them exchanged inquiries regarding each other's welfare. Then,
their purposes accomplished, they sat down together upon a delightful rocky surface on Mount Meru, the mountain of gold.
There, the two of them conversed on various subjects concerning the ancient, high-souled Brahman-sages, gods, and Daityas. Then Suvarṇa spoke these words to the lord Svāyambhuva Manu:
For the benefit of all beings, you ought to answer my question: O Lord of Creatures,
why are the deities worshipped with flowers,
and why are the deities worshipped with perfumes, incense, and other offerings?
"What is this, and how did it arise? Tell me of its connection with the fruit.
Manu said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
The dialogue between Śukra and Bali at their meeting— Śukra, the scion of Bhrigu’s lineage, quickly approached Bali, the son of Virocana, as he was ruling over the three worlds here.
Having honored that descendant of Bhṛgu with the guest-offering and other rites, that lord of the asuras,
who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, sat down upon a seat according to the prescribed rules.
Then this conversation took place there, which has been related by you.
Regarding the fruit of offering flowers, incense, and lamps,
the lord of the Daityas then asked the lord of poets this supreme question:
"O best among the knowers of Brahman, what is the fruit of flowers, incense, and lamps?"
"O best of the twice-born, you ought to explain that regarding the act of giving.
Śukra said:
"In the creation of Agni, Soma, and the others, [there is the power] of Viṣṇu, the Lord who is the Self of all."
Austerity arose first, and from that, Dharma followed immediately after.
In this very interval, as well, the creepers and medicinal herbs appeared;
and the self of Soma was likewise manifested in many forms upon the surface of the earth.
Ambrosia, poison, and whatever other substances are of similar nature—
ambrosia immediately bestows joy upon the mind and nourishment,
whereas poison intensely withers the mind from every side by its very scent.
Know that nectar (*amṛta*) is auspiciousness and great poison is inauspiciousness.
For all medicinal herbs are nectar, while poison is a fiery energy born from fire. Since it gladdens the mind and bestows prosperity as well, [it is called *amṛta*].
Nectar gladdens the mind and indeed bestows prosperity; therefore, they are called *sumanasaḥ* (wreaths) by men of virtuous deeds. The pure man who offers these *sumanasaḥ* to the deities—

Therefore they are called *sumanasaḥ*, because by them the deities are satisfied. When he is satisfied, the gods indeed become satisfied; being satisfied, they even bestow prosperity. Because the gods [are pleased] with him through these *sumanasaḥ*, they are therefore known as *sumanasaḥ*.
O Lord, O Daitya-king, whichever deity the flowers are offered to for the sake of auspiciousness, that deity becomes pleased with him by means of them. Furthermore,
those [flowers] should be known individually as fierce, gentle, or radiant.
