There are medicinal herbs of many potencies and likewise of many forms. Now learn from me concerning the trees fit for sacrifice and those unfit for sacrifice,
as well as the garlands belonging to the Asuras and those beneficial to the deities.
They are likewise beloved by the Rākṣasas, the gods, and the Yakṣas;

they are the favorites of the ancestors and of human beings, respectively. Here, there are wild plants, those grown in villages, as well as those sown in cultivated fields, and those that take refuge in the mountains.
13.101.025c Thorny plants that are thornless, endowed with fragrance, form, and flavor;

13.101.026a For the fragrance arising from flowers is traditionally held to be of two kinds: pleasant and unpleasant. 13.101.026c One should understand that for the gods, flowers are those possessing pleasant fragrance.
O Lord, the flowers of thornless trees that are predominantly white in color are always desired by the gods;
likewise, the lotus and the *tulasī* plant are honored among all of them.
A wise person should offer water-born garlands and lotuses and other such flowers to the Gandharvas, Nāgas, and Yakṣas. Likewise,
one should offer medicinal herbs that have red blossoms, as well as those that are pungent and thorny.
These [plants] taught in the Atharvavedas for the purpose of sorcery against enemies are of sharp potency, difficult to grasp,
thorny, and should be offered as oblations when they are predominantly red in color or black.
O Lord, those flowers which delight the mind and heart, which are sweet during the crushing [of the body],
and which possess beautiful forms, are known as "human" (mānuṣa); however,
those produced in cremation grounds or arising from temples are not.
One should offer them at sacrifices for prosperity, at marriages, and in private rites. One should present gentle plants grown on mountain peaks to the gods—
plants that are auspicious, consecrated by sprinkling and washing, according to the requirements and according to the traditional law.
The gods are satisfied by fragrance; the yakṣas and rākṣasas, by sight;
the nāgas, by enjoyment; and humans, by all three of these. Indeed, one satisfies the gods immediately, and when they are pleased, they in turn bring prosperity.

The gods, whose wills are accomplished through the desired objects of mortals' hearts, constantly gratify those who honor them and likewise honor them in return; yet when they are treated with contempt or cast aside, they utterly consume those base men.
13.101.037a Hereafter, I shall proclaim the fruit resulting from the ritual offering of incense.
13.101.037c Learn from me the various types of incense—both those that are excellent and those that are not. 13.101.038a Resin, *sarala* resin, and artificial incense: these are the three.
Whether a fragrance be desirable or undesirable, hear that from me in detail: Resins, with the exception of sallakī, are dear to the gods;
among all of them, guggulu is the most excellent—this is the settled conclusion.
Aguru is the best among resinous substances for Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, and serpents;
likewise, sallakī-juice is desired by Daityas and those of similar nature. Furthermore, there are the fragrances of sarjarasa and others, as well as those derived from earth and wood.
Combined with molasses-based spirits (phāṇitāsava), it is prescribed for human beings;
it is traditionally held to provide immediate satisfaction to gods, dānavas, and bhūtas. As for those other types used for recreation, they are traditionally considered for humans alone.
Those very qualities and causes that were mentioned regarding the gift of flowers should also be understood to apply to incense, as they likewise increase joy.
Now I shall declare the unsurpassed connection of fruits resulting from the gift of lamps.
In what manner, by whom, at what time, and of what nature those [gifts] are to be given;
and how light, brilliance, and radiance are described as moving upward— therefore, the giving of such splendors increases the luster of men.
Blinding darkness, deep gloom, and the southern course of the sun—
because the northern course is the opposite of these and is the remedy for darkness, the gift of light is highly praised.
Therefore, it is certain that one should be a giver for the sake of ascending to higher realms.
Since the gods are radiant, powerful, and illuminating,
while the *rākṣasas* are characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*), for this reason a lamp is offered.
By the gift of light, a person becomes possessed of vision and endowed with radiance;
having given those [lights], one should not harm them, nor take them away, nor destroy them.
A stealer of lamps will become blind, moving in darkness, devoid of splendor.
The giver of lamps shines resplendent in the world of heaven, adorned with garlands of light.
The first method [for an oblation] is with clarified butter (*havis*); the second is with the juices of medicinal herbs.
One who desires prosperity should not perform [the rite] with fat, marrow, or the extracts of bone.
On a mountain precipice, in a dense forest, at a shrine, at a crossroads,
in a temple, in an assembly hall, on a mountain, at a sacred tree, at a crossroads,
in the abode of cows or Brahmins, and in a fortress— a pure lamp bestows prosperity.
One who desires prosperity for oneself should always be a giver of lamps. Such a person becomes the illuminator of their lineage, pure in soul, and attains radiance;
indeed, the man who gives lamps always attains the same world as the luminaries.
I shall now describe the merits arising from the fruits of actions performed in the rites of *bali* offerings for gods, yakṣas, serpents, humans, spirits, and rākṣasas—
those for whom Brahmins, deities, guests, and children do not eat first.
Know those [beings] to be nothing but Rākṣasas, devoid of the *vaṣaṭ* call and all auspicious rites.
Therefore, one should offer the first portion to the gods with due honor;
bowing one’s head, one should present the oblation (*bali*) without sloth.

For the household deities always desire [offerings] from the home; likewise, the external guests and others—yakṣas, rākṣasas, and pannagas—who are not [household deities], live upon what is given from here.
So too do the deities and the ancestors.
Being pleased, they in turn please these [beings] with long life, fame, and wealth. One should offer oblations (*bali*) together with flowers to the gods—
oblations that are auspicious, fragrant, pleasant to behold, and mixed with drops of curd.
Offerings rich in blood and flesh should be prepared for the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas; they should be preceded by wine and spirits, adorned with parched grain and ointments.
For the Nāgas, offerings mixed with lotuses and water-lilies are always beloved.
One should offer sesame seeds well-prepared with molasses as an oblation to the spirits;
by being the first to give, one shall become the first to enjoy [the fruits], endowed with strength and a fine complexion.
Therefore, one should present the first portion to the gods after it has been duly honored.
"The house blazes day after day for those household deities (*gṛhadevatā*) of his;
they should be worshipped by one who desires prosperity and offers them food with the tips of the fingers extended.
Thus did Kāvya Bhārgava speak this to the lord of the Asuras.
Manu spoke this to Suvarṇa, and Suvarṇa spoke it to Nārada;
Nārada, in turn, spoke these qualities to me, O one of great luster.
Having understood all of this here, you too should practice it, my son.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the Bharatas, I have heard from you the fruit for those who offer flowers and incense, as well as for the performance of bali-offerings; you should speak of that further."
You ought to speak further regarding the fruit of making offerings;
likewise, [explain] the fruit of offering incense and lamps. And for what purpose are bali-offerings cast by householders?
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
a dialogue concerning Nahuṣa between Agastya and Bhṛgu.

O great king, Nahuṣa was indeed a royal sage of immense ascetic power who attained the sovereignty of the gods through his well-performed deeds in this world. Even while dwelling there in the third heaven, O King, Nahuṣa remained self-restrained.
Performing various activities, both human and divine,
all his human deeds there, O King, as well as his eternal divine ones, proceeded for that high-souled one in the third heaven.
The fire-rituals, sacrificial fuel, *kuśa* grass, and likewise flowers; the offerings (*bali*) consisting of food and parched grain, as well as the incense and the lighting of lamps—
all these proceeded in the palace of that high-souled king.
He performed sacrifices of recitation and sacrifices of the mind even in heaven; and that lord of the gods, O subduer of enemies, worshipped all the deities according to rule,
in due order, and as was done before.
Then, because of his impending status as Indra, egoism entered him;
and all his ritual activities fell into neglect, O King.
Possessed by the intoxication of the boon he had received, he compelled the sages to carry out his tasks.
Having fallen away from his religious duties and having reached a state of weakness,
a great deal of time passed for him as he, overcome by egoism, drove those foremost sages whose wealth was their asceticism.
Then he proceeded to appoint the sages to the task of carrying him in turn;
and in due course, O Bhārata, it became Agastya’s turn.
Then the highly effulgent Bhṛgu, the best among the knowers of Brahman, arrived.
Approaching Agastya, who was staying in his hermitage, he spoke these words:
"O great sage, for what reason do we tolerate such ill-treatment from this evil-minded Nahuṣa, the lord of the gods?"
Agastya said:
"O great sage, how can this man be cursed by me, since he has been granted a boon by the Giver of Boons, and that boon is known to you?"
"Whoever comes within the range of my sight shall become subject to my will"—this was the boon requested from the god by him as he was departing for heaven.
For this reason, he was not burnt by me, nor by you; of this there is no doubt.
He has never been cursed nor cast down by any other chief of sages;
furthermore, O Lord, the nectar of immortality was given to him for his drink in the past. For that reason, we do not strike down this high-souled one.
The god granted a boon that causes suffering to living beings:
"That lowest of men shall commit unrighteous acts against the twice-born.
O best of speakers, tell us what is appropriate for us to do in this matter.
"And whatever you may say, we shall do accordingly.
Bhṛgu said:
"By the command of the Grandfather, I have come to you."

To counteract the pride of the powerful Nahuṣa as he stands arrogant, the evil-minded king of the gods shall yoke you to his chariot this very day. Today, by my power, I shall deprive this overweening one of his sovereignty.
"Today, while you look on, I shall establish Indra, the performer of a hundred sacrifices,
having displaced that evil-doer of wicked mind from his station as Indra.
And today this false king of gods shall insult you with his foot."
Because his mind was struck by fate, that dull-witted man acted for his own destruction;
transgressing the dharma, I, being deeply provoked by his insolence, shall curse that wicked hater of brahmins in my wrath, saying: "Become a serpent!"

Then, while you look on, O great sage, I shall cast this evil-minded Nahuṣa— whose splendor is struck down by the cry of "Fie! and who is deluded by the power of his sovereignty— upon the earth for his sinful deeds.
"And whatever pleases you, O sage, that I shall do.
Thus addressed by Bhṛgu, the imperishable Agastya, son of Mitrāvaruṇa,
became exceedingly pleased and was freed from his distress.
He performed all that [rite] in such a way that Nahuṣa fell down.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"How indeed did he perish, and how was he cast down to the earth?"
"And how did he come to lose his status as Indra? You ought to tell me that. Bhīṣma said:
"While the two of them were thus conversing, the deeds of that high-souled one [proceeded]."
All [the goddesses], both those who were divine and those who were human, turned toward him;
likewise, there were offerings of lamps, all kinds of requisites, ritual oblations (*balikarma*),
and various other types of libations.
All those practices of good conduct remembered by the wise, which exist in both the world of the gods and the world of men, arose from that high-souled king of the gods;
and if these are observed, O Indra among kings, householders attain success.
Through the offering of incense, lamps, and likewise through prostrations—
just as the first portion of prepared food is given to a twice-born man,
and offerings (bali) are made within the house— the deities are thereby pleased.
Just as the satisfaction of householders arises from the performance of the *balikarman* offering,
so too does the joy of the deities arise a hundredfold.
In this same way, virtuous people perform the offering of incense and the offering of lamps.
They praise that which brings about one's own virtues when joined with prostrations. Whatever rite is performed by a wise man through bathing and with water,
when it is employed with prostration, by that the deities are pleased.
"The highly fortunate ancestors, the seers whose wealth is asceticism,
and all the domestic deities are pleased when honored according to the prescribed rites.
Having adopted this understanding, that lord of men, Nahuṣa, [acted accordingly].
Having attained the great sovereignty of the lord of the gods, he performed this wonderful deed. Then, after some time had passed and his fortune began to decline,
disregarding all of this, he no longer performed such acts.
Then that lord of the gods was deprived of his power by the ritual of Bali;
he did not perform the rites of incense, lamps, and water according to the rules.
Consequently, his sacrificial domain was harassed by the Rākṣasas.
Then, as if smiling, the one of great strength summoned Agastya, the best of sages, from the bank of the Sarasvatī to serve as his vehicle. Thereupon,
Bhrigu, endowed with great splendor, spoke to the son of Mitra and Varuṇa.
"Close your eyes while I enter your matted locks.
For the sake of toppling the lord of the gods, he closed his eyes;
then Acyuta entered the matted locks of him who had become as motionless as a pillar.
Then Bhrigu, possessed of great splendor, [prepared] for the downfall of the king.
Thereupon the king of the gods approached that rishi to serve as his vehicle.
Then Agastya spoke these words to the lord of the gods, O ruler of the people:
"O Indra, harness me quickly; to what place shall I carry you?
O Lord of the Gods, wherever you tell me, there I shall lead you.
Having been addressed thus by him, Nahuṣa harnessed that sage.
Bhrigu, dwelling within his matted locks, became exceedingly joyful;
yet Bhrigu did not reveal himself to him at that time,
for he was aware of the power of the boon granted to the high-souled Nahuṣa.
O Bhārata, although Agastya was indeed being driven by Nahuṣa, he did not become angry; however, that king of the gods urged him on with a goad,
arguing whether the Śruti and Smṛti were authoritative or not.
That righteous-souled king of the gods did not become angry;
instead, being enraged, he then struck Agastya on the head with his left foot.
When that head was struck, Bhṛgu, who was dwelling within the matted locks, [was provoked].
Greatly incensed, he cursed the evil-minded Nahuṣa.
Bhṛgu said:
"Since you have struck this great sage on the head with your foot out of anger..."
"Therefore, O evil-minded one, quickly go to the earth and become a serpent!
Thus addressed by him, he then became a serpent and fell to the surface of the earth,
unseen by Bhrigu, O bull of the Bharatas.
For if that Nahuṣa had seen Bhṛgu, O lord of the earth, he would not have been capable of casting him down by his own splendor. He,
however, [attained this] through various gifts, ascetic penances, and likewise through religious observances.
Even though he had fallen to the earth, O Great King, he remained mindful;
he sought to propitiate Bhṛgu, saying, "May there be an end to my curse.
Then Agastya, filled with compassion, interceded on his behalf with Bhṛgu.
O great king, filled with compassion, he granted that end to the curse.
Bhṛgu said:
"There shall be a king named Yudhiṣṭhira, a sustainer of the Kurus."
"He shall release you from the curse," having said this, he vanished.
Then Agastya, of great splendor, having accomplished the task of Indra,
returned to his own hermitage while being honored by the twice-born.
"O King, Nahuṣa too has been delivered from that curse by you;
O lord of men, he went to the abode of Brahmā while you were looking on.
Then, having cast that Nahuṣa down to the earth, Bhṛgu—"
He went to the abode of Brahmā and informed Brahmā [of what had occurred].
Then, having summoned Śakra and the gods, the Grandfather said:
"O gods, by virtue of a boon granted by me, Nahuṣa has obtained the kingdom."
He was cast down to the surface of the earth by the enraged Agastya.
Moreover, it is not possible for the gods to subsist anywhere without a king;
therefore, let this Śakra be consecrated once again in the sovereignty of the gods.
While the Grandfather was thus speaking, O Pārtha, the gods,
filled with joy, replied to the Grandfather, "So be it.
Then Vāsava was consecrated by the Blessed One in the sovereignty over the gods.
O tiger among kings, by means of the *brahman*, he shone as he did before. Thus occurred this ancient event due to the transgression of Nahuṣa;
yet that Nahuṣa was once again perfected through those very same deeds.
Therefore, lamps should indeed be offered in the evening by householders;
the giver of a lamp attains divine vision after death,
and those who give lamps become as radiant as the full moon.
For as many years as there are twinklings of an eye while the lamp burns,
for that long does the giver of the lamp become possessed of beauty and wealth.
Furthermore, O best of the twice-born, whoever hears this or recites it—
He attains the world of Brahmā; of this there is no doubt at all.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, those dull-witted men who seize the property of Brāhmaṇas—"
"Where do those foolish men who commit cruel deeds go?
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, they cite this ancient history."
O Bhārata, listen to the conversation between a Caṇḍāla and a base kṣatriya.
Indeed, this—forcibly seizing the property of a Brāhmaṇa—is the supreme among all sins;
those Caṇḍālas, along with their lineages, perish both in this world and after death.
The Kṣatriya said:
"O Caṇḍāla, you have the appearance of an old man, yet you behave like a child. Why do you tremble at the dust raised by dogs and donkeys, while serving the cattle?"
"A deed censured by the virtuous is prescribed for a Caṇḍāla. Why do you sprinkle water from a pool upon that which has been defiled by the dust of a cow?
The Caṇḍāla said:
O King, in former times, the dust raised by the cows of a Brahmin as they were being led away defiled the Soma;
and those twice-born who drank that Soma had their sacrifice likewise defiled by the dust of kings who were but servants.
And by drinking that, all those twice-born men quickly entered hell;
and that consecrated king also quickly entered hell along with all those officiating priests, having lived off the property of a Brahmin.
Those men there— Brahmins along with Kṣatriyas— who drank the milk, ghee, and curds, all entered hell; for those [cows],
while shaking themselves, had killed their sons and grandsons with that milk.
And as the couple looked upon the cattle with virtuous conduct,
O King, I dwelt there as a celibate student with my senses subdued.
O lord of men, my alms-food became covered with their dust.
"O King, having eaten that [food], I then became a Caṇḍāla after death;
and that king, who had stolen the property of a Brahmin, went to a state of no standing. Therefore, one should never take even the slightest bit of a Brahmin's property."
One should not look upon it, nor approve of it, nor act to take anything away. Having consumed me, who am destroyed by the dust of the Brahman-sound, see what I have become.
Therefore, even the *soma* must not be sold by a wise man.
For this is indeed the most excellent wealth for the twice-born without distinction;
for the wise in this world condemn the sale of soma.
O King, those people who buy it and those who sell it [are likewise censured].
Having reached the realm of Vaivasvata, they go entirely to the Raurava hell. But a Śrotriya who intentionally sells Soma defiled by dust, having become a usurer, perishes for a long time.
Having fallen into thirty hells, he subsists on the excrement of dogs.
After experiencing the torments of hell for having stolen the property of a Brahmin, he becomes a worm among filth and subsists on the excrement of dogs.
Dharma weighed in the balance between dog-life and excessive pride, as well as the transgression committed against a friend’s wife; indeed, excessive pride outweighed [the other].
Behold this sinful dog, discolored, pale, and emaciated.

Through excessive pride, I have come to this state among living beings. O Lord, in another birth I was born into a vast family endowed with wealth, having reached the further shore of both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and practical wisdom (*vijñāna*).
At that time, being intoxicated, I was unaware of these faults;
thus, in a state of agitation, I devoured the back-flesh of living beings. Now, I am known by all as one who has gone far into the forest, defiled.

Desiring to humiliate the virtuous and arrogant toward Brahmins because of his wealth, I have indeed reached this present state through that very conduct and that same food; behold the reversal of time!
Like one whose garment-edges are set ablaze, or as if tormented by bees,
see me running in great agitation, covered in dust.
But householders cross over even great sin through the study of the Vedas.
And just as the wise have declared regarding various kinds of gifts,
O lord of the earth, so indeed do the Vedic hymns rescue even a Brahmin who has committed evil, provided he dwells in a hermitage and is liberated from all attachments.
"But I, O bull among Kṣatriyas, have indeed been born from a sinful womb; I cannot find a certain way as to how I might be liberated. However, my memory of past lives is due to some previous karma."

"O King, by what auspicious means do I desire to attain liberation? O best of beings, tell this doubt to me who has approached you for refuge and asks: how may I be released from my status as a *caṇḍāla*?"
The Kṣatriya said:
"O Caṇḍāla, promise me that by which you shall attain liberation;
by giving up your life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa, you shall attain the desired goal."

"Having offered your body to the flesh-eaters in the fire of battle for the sake of the twice-born, and having sacrificed your life-breaths, you shall attain liberation; you do not deserve liberation in any other way.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed at that time, O King, O scorcher of foes, he offered up his life-breaths at the front of the battle for the sake of a Brahmin’s property and attained his desired goal.
Therefore, O son, O bull of the Bharatas, the property of a Brahmin must be protected by you.

"If you desire, O mighty-armed one, the eternal and supreme goal," Yudhiṣṭhira said: "O Grandfather, is there only one world for those who have performed meritorious deeds, or are there all [of them]?"
"Moreover, O Grandfather, tell me of that diversity which exists even there.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Pārtha, it is by their actions that human beings attain diversity among the worlds."
The doers of merit go to meritorious realms, and the doers of evil, O people, go to evil ones.
In this regard, my dear, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between the sage Gautama and Vāsava.
A certain Brāhmaṇa named Gautama— gentle, self-controlled, and with senses subdued—
saw a young elephant in the great forest, distressed and motherless;
seeing it, he, compassionate and firm in his vows, brought it back to life.

After a long time, he became exceedingly powerful and great. Śakra, in the form of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, seized that great elephant when it was in rut, with its temples split open and ichor flowing from all sides.
Seeing him being carried away, Gautama, of rigid vows and great asceticism, addressed King Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
"Do not take this elephant, my son!"
O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, you who are ungrateful, they say that a friend is strengthened by suffering and that friendship among the virtuous is formed in seven steps;
O King, may treachery toward a friend never touch you.
One who provides fuel and water in the hermitage, protects the empty dwellings,
is disciplined in the family of the teacher, is well-engaged in the service of the guru, and is refined, self-controlled, grateful, and always dear to me.
"O King, you ought not to take away the elephant while I am crying out to you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"I shall give you a thousand cows."
A hundred female slaves, five hundred gold coins,
and various other riches, O great seer;
what need has a brahmin here for an elephant?
Gautama said:
"O King, may the cows, along with female slaves adorned with golden coins and various kinds of jewels, attend upon you alone."
"O lord of men, there is also various other wealth;
what need has a Brāhmaṇa here for riches?
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Brahmin, there is no need for elephants for Brāhmaṇas;
for Kṣatriyas, O sage, there are lineages of Nāgas.
There is no unrighteousness in one leading away his own vehicle."
"O Gautama, turn us back from this best of nāgas!
Gautama said:
"Where the deceased who has performed meritorious deeds rejoices;"
Where the evil-doing ghost grieves in the abode of the great-souled son of Vivasvat,
there I shall cause you to drive an elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those who are inactive, atheistic, lacking in faith,
evil-minded, and intent upon the objects of the senses;
"They undergo the torments of Yama;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall go elsewhere, not there.
Gautama said:
The city of Vaivasvata is the gatherer of people;
there falsehood is not spoken, and there truth prevails; there the weak bring the strong to account.
"In that case, I shall cause the elephant to be sent for you.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"My elder sister, my father, and my mother—"
O Great Seer, this world belongs to those who conduct themselves by honoring their guru as they should;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra will go to a realm beyond that.
Gautama said:
"The Mandākinī belongs indeed to King Vaiśravaṇa;
it is of great enjoyment and accessible to those who possess enjoyments."
"13,105.018c It is frequented by Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Apsarases;
there I shall cause you to drive the elephant.
13,105.019 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Those people who are devoted to guests and firm in their vows, who provide shelter to Brahmins,
who eat only what remains after sharing with their dependents;
They also adorn the Mandākinī.
Gautama said:
"The forest that shines beautifully on the summit of Meru;"
Where the vast Jambu tree, beautifully blossomed and graced by the songs of kinnaras,
stands— there I shall cause you to drive the elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those Brahmins who are gentle, devoted to truth, deeply learned, and pleasing to all beings—
Those who study the Purāṇa together with the Itihāsas,
and who offer honeyed oblations to the twice-born—
to such as these belongs this world, O Great Seer.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra will go to that supreme place which exists as a known destination;
tell me that, for I am departing in haste.
Gautama said:
"The Nandana forest, beautifully blossomed and frequented by the king of the kinnaras, is dear to Nārada."
"13,105.023c It is the abode of the Gandharvas and Apsarases;
there I shall cause you to drive the elephant.
13,105.024 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"O Great Seer, this world belongs to those people who are always skilled in dance and song, and who move about together without ever begging."
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra will go to that supreme place where the delightful Northern Kurus shine," Gautama said.
O lord of men, rejoicing together with the gods,
there dwell those brahmins who are born of fire,
those who are not born from a womb, and those whose source is the mountain.
Where Śakra rains down all desires; where women move about according to their own will; where there is no jealousy among men and women;
"There I shall cause you to ride an elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Those who have turned away from desire for all beings..."
Those who do not eat meat, who have laid aside the rod of punishment, and who move about without harming anything stationary or moving—
they are those for whom all beings have become their own self.
Free from expectations, free from possessiveness, devoid of passion,
equal toward gain and loss, and the same toward blame and praise—
for such as these, O Great Seer, this world belongs.
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra will go to that which is beyond.
Gautama said:
"Beyond that shine eternal worlds;"
Possessing the fragrance of great merit, stainless, and free from sorrow,
in the abode of the high-souled King Soma;
there I shall cause your elephant to go.
13,105.030 Dhṛtarāṣṭra said: Those who are always disposed toward giving and never accept gifts,
nor do they take wealth from others.
Those for whom there is nothing that should not be given to one who is worthy, who are hospitable to all and of gentle disposition,
and who are patient and do not speak ill of others;
"O Great Seer, having been constantly capable and virtuous in conduct, such people go to that world;
Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall not go there."
Gautama said:
Beyond that shine eternal worlds,
free from passion, free from darkness, and free from sorrow.
"Those wheels of the sun are very large and well-rounded;
there I shall cause your elephant to go.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Devoted to the practice of private Vedic study, intent on serving their gurus,
ascetic, firm in their vows, true to their word,
and speaking without contradiction to their teachers.
Ever diligent in heavy tasks and requiring no prompting—
such is the world for those like you, O Great Seer,
who are pure and have cultivated both speech and mind.
"Among those great-souled ones who stand firm in truth and are knowers of the Vedas, Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall go to the highest state; he is not there [in the lower realms].
Gautama said:
Beyond that shine eternal worlds,
fragrant with pure merit, free from dust and devoid of sorrow,
in the abode of the high-souled King Varuṇa.
"In that regard, I shall cause you to become an elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Those people who always perform the Cāturmāsya sacrifices..."
Likewise, those brahmins who, full of faith, offer the agnihotra sacrifice according to the rule for three years, obtain the merit of a thousand iṣṭi sacrifices. (13.105.36c)
For those great-souled ones who bear the yoke of dharma regarding their own wives,
who are well-established on the path appropriate to them, and who uphold that way of life of the righteous-souled;
"Dhṛtarāṣṭra is going to the supreme state, not there.
Gautama said:
"The worlds of Indra are free from passion and free from sorrow."
"Difficult to follow and desired by men (13.105.38c),
O King, I shall cause this elephant to go to the abode of that one of great splendor."
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"A man who lives for a hundred years, who is brave,
who studies the Vedas, and who performs sacrifices with vigilance;"
"All these go to the world of Śakra; Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall go to a higher place, not there.
Gautama said:
On the back of the firmament, there exist great worlds belonging to Prajāpati— abundant and free from sorrow—
which are desired by all those born in the world.
"In that regard, I shall cause you to ride an elephant.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
"Those kings who have been consecrated by the Rājasūya sacrifice..."
Those who are righteous-souled protectors of their subjects,
and those whose limbs have been bathed in the final purificatory ablution of the horse sacrifice— their worlds exist, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, but you are not there.
Gautama said:
Beyond that shine eternal worlds,
fragrant with great merit, free from passion, and devoid of sorrow.
"In that world of cattle, which is difficult to attain and invincible, I shall cause your elephant to wander.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
He who gives a thousand cows every year, he who gives a hundred cows according to his ability, and likewise he who gives even a single cow here to ten [recipients];
Or from five [qualities], namely generosity and morality; likewise,
those Brahmins who age within the holy life and who fully preserve the speech of Brahmā.
Those wise ones, devoted to pilgrimages,
rejoice there in the celestial vehicle of cows at Prabhāsa, the holy Mānasa, and the great lake of Puṣkara.
The meritorious Naimiṣa ford, the Bāhudā, and the Karatoyinī; Gayā and Gayaśiras, as well as the Vipāśā and Sthūlavālukā;
the Tūṣṇīṃgaṅgā, the Daśagaṅgā, and also the Mahāhrada.
The high-souled ones, firm in their vows, go to the Gautamī, the Kauśikī, the Pākā, the Sarasvatī, the Dṛṣadvatī, and the Yamunā;
there they abide in celestial forms, wearing divine garlands, and are auspicious.
They depart, rich with holy fragrances; Dhṛtarāṣṭra is certainly not there.
Gautama said:
"Where there is no fear of cold, nor even the slightest fear of heat."
There is neither hunger nor thirst, neither exhaustion, nor likewise pain or pleasure;
there is no one who is hateful and no one who is dear, neither kinsman nor enemy;
and there is neither old age nor death, neither merit nor sin.
"In that dustless, expansive, and holy abode of the Self-Existent One, which is established in wisdom and goodness, he will strive for my elephant. Dhṛtarāṣṭra said:
Freed from all attachments, self-realized, and firm in their vows,
those established in the practice of internal yoga have attained the path to heaven;
as beings of pure essence (*sāttvika*), they reach the holy abode of Brahmā in this world.
"O great sage, Dhṛtarāṣṭra cannot be seen there by you.
Gautama said:
"Where the *Rathantara* and the *Bṛhat* are sung..."
Where the altar is strewn with lotuses,
and where the drinker of Soma arrives with his bay horses—
there I shall cause you, O elephant, to go.
I recognize you as the slayer of Vṛtra, the Lord of a hundred powers,
who traverse all the worlds. Have you ever committed any wrong through speech?
"I have done this out of an attachment of my mind.
Śakra said:
"Since [you have obstructed] this path of the world for living beings;"
I have followed in the footsteps of the elephant as it was being spoken of; therefore, may you instruct me, who am bowed before you,
for I shall do everything that you command.
Gautama said:
"The white elephant calf, my son,
whom you have carried away from me while he was but ten years old."
"O Lord of the Gods, give me that very same nāga who was my companion while I dwelt in the forest.
Śakra said:
"O foremost of the twice-born, this elephant, your son,
smells you while gazing intently at you;
he even sniffs your feet with his trunk."
"May it be well with me; meditate upon me, and let there be salutation to you.
Gautama said:
"O Lord of the Gods, may it always be auspicious for you here."
I meditate and always perform worship.
O Śakra, grant me also your auspiciousness;
I accept the elephant given by you.
Śakra said:
"Those wise, virtuous, and high-souled ones in whose secret cave the Vedas are indeed deposited..."
"By you alone, O Great-Souled One, have I been awakened among them;
therefore, I am filled with joy toward you today.
Come quickly, O Brahmin, together with your son Hastin."
"May you attain auspicious worlds, both for a brief moment and for a long time.
Bhīṣma said:
"Placing Gautama at his head, together with his son Hastin,"
The wielder of the thunderbolt ascended to heaven, difficult for even the virtuous to reach, together with those who were righteous.
He who would constantly hear this, or he who, having conquered his senses, would recite it,
goes to the world of Brahmā, just like the Brahmin Gautama.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"You have described various forms of giving, as well as tranquility, truthfulness, non-violence,
contentment with one's own wife, and the very fruit of giving."
"O Grandfather, what is known to you other than the power of asceticism? You ought to explain to me that which is superior even to asceticism today.
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, as far as they speak of austerity, so far extend the worlds;
but in my opinion, O son of Kuntī, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history."

The tradition records that Bhagīratha, having passed beyond the world of the gods and the world of the cows, O Bhārata, went to the world of the ṛṣis, where he held a conversation with the high-souled Brahmā.
Seeing him, O King, Brahmā spoke these words to Bhagīratha:
"Bhagīratha, how have you come to this inaccessible region?
For neither gods, nor Gandharvas, nor humans, O Bhagīratha, [can reach it]."
"Those who have not performed austerities do not come here; how indeed have you come here?
Bhagīratha said:
"I gave food to the Brahmins without hesitation."
Know that I have always bestowed hundreds of thousands of gifts while constantly adhering to the Vedic vow;
yet it was not from the fruit of that that I have come here.
Ten sacrifices of eleven nights each, ten of five nights each,
and eleven sacrifices of eleven [verses] each;
and that hundredfold Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice which was performed;
And it was not because of that fruit that I have come here,
nor because I dwelt constantly on the banks of the Jahnavi for a hundred years, performing ascetic penance.
And there I gave away a thousand mares;
yet I did not come because of that city of women. And [I gave] one million horses and twenty thousand more.
At Puṣkara, I gave thousands of cows to the twice-born,
as well as excellent maidens adorned with garlands who bore the radiance of golden moons.
I gave sixty thousand [beings] adorned with ornaments of Jāmbūnada gold; by that [merit], I did not give ten arbudas [of cows] in the Gosava sacrifices.
O Lord of the World, ten cows each,
with their calves of equal age, full of milk,
and yielding milk into vessels of gold and bronze— were not worth even a fraction of that [gift].
In the Aptoryāma sacrifices, ten thousand cows were given at each stage;
they were first-calving, milk-yielding, ruddy, and indeed capable of giving much milk. By that [act], he did not [satisfy his debt]. There were truly ten million such milch-cows.
O Brahmin, I gave ten times that amount, yet I did not return because of it. I gave away one hundred thousand horses born in Bāhlīka,
white as cranes and adorned with golden garlands, yet I did not return because of them.
O Brahman, O Grandfather, at each individual sacrifice I gave away eight crores and then ten crores of green horses with black ears; yet, despite that fruit, I have not returned.
O Brahmin, I gave away seventeen crores of elephants adorned with golden garlands—
elephants with tusks like plowshafts, massive in body, and decorated with golden chains— and I bestowed upon him seventeen thousand wives.
O Lord of Gods, I gave ten thousand chariots with golden frames, adorned with divine golden ornaments,
as well as seven other thousands yoked with well-decorated horses.
Even those certain sacrificial components that are proclaimed by the Vedas,
which I bestowed during ten Vājapeya sacrifices— by that merit alone, nor yet by my sacrifice or my prowess, have I attained a power equal to Śakra’s.

"O Grandfather, having conquered all kings and performed eight *rājasūya* sacrifices, I gave as a sacrificial fee a thousand men with golden neck-ornaments; yet I have not attained [the goal] by that."
O Lord of the World, the entire course of the Gaṅgā was covered by the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) distributed by me for that purpose;
likewise, two thousand horses adorned with hundreds of pieces of gold were given.
I gave a choice of a hundred villages to each one, three times over;
then, as an ascetic with restricted food, established in tranquility and restrained in speech,
I dwelt for a long time on the Himavat and by the Ganges, which is difficult to endure.
"O Grandfather, it was not by that fruit alone— the stream which Mahādeva bore upon his head— that I came here;
nor by the sacrifices I performed for the gods with the throwing of *śamyā* sticks."
O Lord, even by means of tens of thousands of Sadyaska sacrifices,
as well as those consisting of thirteen and twelve-day rites along with the Pauṇḍarīka, you have not attained their fruit.
I gave eight thousand humped,
white bulls to the Brahmins,
each indeed having horns made of gold.
I gave them wives with golden neck-ornaments; I gave mountains of jewels heaped with gold and gems,
and villages abundant in wealth and grain by the hundreds of thousands.
Without weariness, I gave away hundreds upon hundreds of young cows;
yet, despite having performed many great sacrifices for the Brahmins, it was not by that alone that I sacrificed with the eleven-day rites accompanied by ritual fees.
O Lord, O Brahmin, by means of twelve double sets of horse sacrifices and sixteen Ārkiyaṇa sacrifices,
I have not come here because of their fruit.
I gave him a necklace of a single *niṣka* jewel, extending for a *yojana*;
it was a vast grove of golden mango trees, adorned with jewels.
And it was not for the sake of their fruit that I came; for I have performed the Turāyaṇa vow for thirty years, invincible and free from anger.
Day after day, I gave to the Brahmins one hundred and eight hundred cows— indeed,
milch-cows of the Rohiṇī breed.
In that same way, O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Gods, I constantly gave oxen to the brahmins;
yet, because of that fruit, I have not come here.

O Brahmin, I have circumambulated the earth three times by the distance of a *śamyā*-throw while performing sacrifice; I have constantly worshipped Agni thirty times with eight *sarvamedhas* and seven *naramedhas*.
"O Lord of the Gods, I have not come here for the sake of the fruit of ten thousand and eighteen hundred Viśvajit sacrifices performed at the Sarayū,
the Bāhudā, the Gaṅgā, and at Naimiṣa."
I gave away ten thousand times a hundred cows, yet by that alone I did not find what Indra had hidden in a secret place—
that which the descendant of Bhṛgu discovered here through austerity.
It blazed here with the splendor of Uśanas;
he accomplished that great and excellent task.
Whatever deeds and whatever battles I perform, they are for the sake of the Brahmins.
Then, when that rite had been accomplished, the brahmins were satisfied with me;
having been constantly honored by those brahmins, I departed according to their word. And there were a thousand sages who had indeed assembled there.
"O Lord, I was told by them, 'Go to the world of Brahmā.
But when I was addressed with affection by a thousand Brāhmaṇas, O Lord, I have returned to this world; let there be no doubt in you regarding this."
Granted that this has been ordained by the Creator as it is,
yet being questioned, I must speak the truth: for in my view, there is no austerity other than fasting.
"Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious!
Bhīṣma said:
To King Bhagīratha, who had spoken thus, Brahmā [replied].
He honored the one worthy of worship with rites prescribed by rule. Therefore, being disciplined through fasting, honor the Brahmins constantly;
by the word of the Brahmins, everything is accomplished both in this world and in the next.
The twice-born should indeed be gratified by you with garments, food, cattle, auspicious wedding gifts,
and excellent protections; practice this supreme secret with freedom from greed.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, it is stated in the Veda that a man has a lifespan of a hundred years and possesses a hundredfold virility;
why then do men die even as children?"
By what does a man become long-lived, or by what does he become short-lived? By what does he obtain fame, and by what does he obtain prosperity?
[It is obtained] through austerity, celibacy, recitations, burnt offerings, and likewise medicinal herbs.
"Whether it be by birth or by conduct, tell me that, O Grandfather.
Bhīṣma said:
"In this regard, I shall relate to you that which you ask of me."
By what a human being becomes short-lived or long-lived;
by what one obtains fame or by what one obtains prosperity;
and how a person conducts himself so as to be joined with the highest good.
For through right conduct one obtains long life; through right conduct one obtains prosperity;
through right conduct one obtains inexhaustible wealth; and right conduct destroys sin.
Through right conduct a person attains fame both in this world and after death.
For a man of evil conduct does not attain a long life in this world;
from him all beings tremble and likewise seek to humiliate him.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should practice right conduct in this world.

Even for one of sinful body, right conduct destroys inauspicious marks. Dharma is characterized by right conduct, and the virtuous are characterized by right conduct; such is the characteristic of right conduct, namely, the behavior of the good.
Whether seen or even merely heard of, people hold dear that man who practices righteousness and performs acts for prosperity;
whereas those who are atheists, inactive, and transgressors of their teachers and scriptures [are not so regarded].
Those who are ignorant of dharma, of evil conduct, and whose life-span has come to an end, become devoid of virtue,
transgressors of the bounds of propriety, and constantly engaged in promiscuous sexual intercourse;
such men, short-lived in this world, go to hell.
Even a man devoid of all auspicious marks, if he is possessed of good conduct,
full of faith, and free from malice, lives for a hundred years. One who is free from anger, truthful in speech, and non-violent toward living beings [attains the same].
One who is free from envy and straightforward lives for a hundred years.
But that man who crushes clods of earth, cuts grass, bites his nails,
is a cook, or is impure, quickly goes to destruction.
One who is constantly impure and fickle does not attain a long life in this world.

One should wake during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and reflect upon dharma and artha. Having risen and sipped water for purification, one should stand with palms joined in reverence during the morning twilight (*pūrvā saṃdhyā*).
In this very manner, one should perform the evening twilight worship while restraining one's speech;
having risen, attended to the necessities of nature, performed purification, and composed the mind,
one should never look at the sun as it rises nor when it sets.
Neither obscured by clouds, nor situated in the water, nor having reached the middle of the sky—
by virtue of their long *saṃdhyā*, the sages attained long life. With darbha grass in hand, performing that rite, restrained in speech, focused in mind, and pure.

Therefore, one should always remain restrained in speech during both the morning and the evening twilight. A righteous king should compel those twice-born men who worship only the morning twilight and not the evening to perform the duties of Śūdras.
One must never, under any circumstances, go to another man’s wife among any of the social orders;
for there is nothing in this world so detrimental to longevity as a man’s pursuit of another's wife in this world.
As many as are the pores created upon the bodies of women,
for so many thousands of years do they dwell in hell. There exists nothing in this world that is so detrimental to the lifespan of men.

Such things as the grooming of the hair, the application of collyrium, the cleaning of the teeth, and the worship of the deities— one should perform these in the forenoon alone, for they take away the wealth and lifespan of men in this world.
One should never look at feces or urine, nor should one ever stand upon them.
One should never engage in conversation with a woman in her courses. One should not void excrement in a field or in the vicinity of a village.
One should never void either urine or feces in water.
When desiring to eat food, one should touch water three times with the mouth;
having eaten the food, one should likewise rinse the mouth three times and wipe it twice again.
In a temple, among a herd of cows, at a shrine, or while resting among crops;
after eating or while about to eat; upon sneezing; after traveling on a road; or after voiding urine or excrement—one should rinse twice according to the rule, drinking water that reaches the heart.
One should always eat facing the east, restrained in speech and not disparaging the food;
one should mentally offer the remnants of the meal into the fire, and after eating, touch the fire. Having sipped water there, one should touch the fire and then proceed with a gentle gait.
One who eats facing east gains long life; one facing south gains fame;
one facing west gains wealth; and one facing north eats according to the cosmic order (*ṛta*).
Having touched fire, one should touch all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) with water.
With the palms of his hands, he should touch all his limbs and his navel. Seated at the foremost place, having conquered anger, and adorned as before,
one who has offered oblations into the fire should consume food purified by offerings of clarified butter without casting it away.
One should never step upon husks, hair, ashes, or potsherds;
one should also avoid from afar attending upon another's [funeral] rites. One should perform propitiatory fire-offerings (*śāntihoma*) and have the *Sāvitrī* verses recited.
One should eat while seated, but never while walking. One should not void urine while standing, nor on ashes, nor in a cow-pen.
One should eat with wet feet, but one should not go to bed with wet feet.
One who eats with wet feet lives for a hundred years.
One who is still impure from eating must never touch three radiant things:
fire, a cow, and a Brahmin; by doing so, his life will not be harmed.
One who is impure from eating should never look upon these three splendors:
the sun and the moon, and all the stars.
For when an elder approaches, the vital breaths of a youth rise upward.

Through rising to meet them and saluting them, one regains those [merits]. One should salute the elders and offer them a seat. With palms joined in reverence, one should attend upon them; when they depart, one should follow behind them.
One should not sit on a broken seat, and one should avoid broken bronze vessels. One must not eat wearing only a single garment, nor should one bathe naked.
One should never sleep naked, nor should one go to bed while still impure from food.
One who is impure from eating should not touch the head, for all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) are dependent upon it. One should avoid seizing the hair or striking the head;
nor should one ever scratch the head with both hands.

One should not wash the head too frequently; in this way, one's lifespan is not impaired. After washing the head, one should not touch any part of the body with oil, nor should one eat sesame paste; thus one attains a long life.
One should not teach while impure from eating, nor should one ever study [while so impure]. When there is wind or a foul odor, one should not even contemplate [the texts] in one's mind.
Regarding this, those who know the past recite the verses sung by Yama:

"I cut short his lifespan and seize his progeny: that twice-born man who speaks while impure from food remains, or who undertakes the private recitation of the Veda; and he who, out of delusion, practices his studies even at times when study is forbidden."

His Veda would perish and his lifespan would diminish if he studies in the presence of a Śūdra or an outcast, or upon hearing the sound of a Caṇḍāla. Therefore, even when prepared for study, one should never recite during these times of suspension.
Those who urinate facing the sun, facing the wind, facing a cow, or facing twice-born brahmins,
as well as those who urinate on a path, become short-lived.
During the day, one should void both urine and feces while facing the north.
Facing south at night, his life will likewise not be harmed.
One who desires to live a long life should not despise three things that are weak:
a Brahmin, a Kshatriya, and a snake; for all three are venomous serpents.
An enraged venomous serpent burns as far as it can see with its eye;
a kṣatriya, when angry, may burn as far as he can touch with his fiery energy;
but a brāhmaṇa may destroy an entire lineage through his meditation and even by a mere glance.
Therefore, a wise man should diligently cultivate these three:
one should never persist in enmity toward a teacher;
rather, O Yudhiṣṭhira, when a teacher is angry, he should be honored and propitiated.
In this world, one must behave properly toward a teacher even if he acts wrongly;
there is no doubt that reviling a teacher consumes the lifespan of men.
One should urinate far from one's dwelling, and far from it should one dispose of the water used for washing the feet.
One who desires his own welfare should dispose of food remnants far away;
he should not go out too early, nor too late in the evening, nor when it is midday;
he should not travel with unknown persons, nor alone, nor with *vṛṣalas*.
One should yield the path to a Brāhmaṇa, to cows, and to kings; likewise to the elderly, to those afflicted by heat, to a pregnant woman, and to the weak.
And one should circumambulate to the right well-known large trees.
One should make all crossroads circumambulate to the right;
one should never frequent crossroads at midday, at night, or at midnight, nor likewise during both twilights.

One should not wear shoes or garments that have been worn by others; one should always remain a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārī) and should not place one foot upon the other. On the new moon day, the full moon day, and on the fourteenth day [of the lunar fortnight], in every respect—
On the eighth day of every fortnight, one should always remain celibate;
one should not eat meat in vain, nor likewise the flesh from the back [of an animal]. One should avoid abuse, slander, and calumny.
One should not be a wounder of others' vitals, nor a speaker of cruel words;
one should not take from another what belongs to an inferior person.
One should speak that speech by which another would be agitated.
One should not utter that harsh speech which leads to worlds of evil;
for word-arrows fly forth from the mouth,
and by them struck, one grieves day and night.
They fall upon the vital spots of another;
a wise person should not discharge them at others.
A forest pierced by arrows or struck down by an axe grows back again.
A wound caused by speech— revolting and ill-spoken— does not heal; whereas barbed arrows, reed-shafted arrows, and iron shafts can be extracted from the body,
the arrow of speech cannot be removed, for it lies deep within the heart.

One should not look down upon those who are deficient in limbs, those with redundant limbs, those lacking in learning, those advanced in age, those lacking in beauty or wealth, or those lacking in strength of character. One should avoid atheism, reviling the Vedas, and disparaging the deities.
One should completely avoid hatred, arrogance, pride, and harshness.
One should not raise a staff against another, nor, when angry, should one strike him down;
however, beating for the sake of instruction is prescribed for a son or a pupil.
One should not revile Brāhmaṇas, nor should one point out the constellations;
one should not speak of the lunar day of the fortnight, for in this way one's lifespan is not diminished.
Except on the new moon day, one should always practice the cleaning of the teeth.
One should constantly study the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, the Dharmaśāstras, and the Vedas;

one should always perform the Gāyatrī meditation and the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) with a concentrated mind. Furthermore, having voided urine or feces, or having stepped upon a road, [one should likewise perform purification].
One should perform the washing of the feet before Vedic study as well as before eating.
The gods ordained three purifiers for Brahmins:
that which is unseen [by the eye], that which is cleansed with water, and that which is commended by speech.

One should not prepare *saṃyāva*, *kṛsara*, meat, *śaṣkulī*, or *pāyasa* for one's own sake; rather, one should prepare them for the sake of the gods. One should constantly tend the sacred fire and always give alms.
Restraining his speech, he should always use a tooth-stick;
one should maintain silence while using the tooth-stick, during the twilight prayers, when voiding excrement,
and when attending to the recitation of mantras to be chanted— silence is praised at these times as well as during bathing.
One should not sleep while the sun is rising, for in that case one becomes liable to penance.
One should never sleep during the twilight hours; one should always bathe and remain pure.
Having risen, one should first of all salute one's mother and father.
Or likewise, by serving this teacher, one attains a long life.
Upon seeing his elders, he should rise from his seat on the ground with one hand.
One should always avoid those tooth-sticks that are forbidden;
one should chew those prescribed by the scriptures, and one should also avoid them on the sacred festival days (parvan).
Furthermore, facing north and remaining composed, one should constantly perform the rite of purification.
Without having performed worship of the gods, one should not practice the cleaning of the teeth. Without having performed worship of the deities, one should never go elsewhere—
except to a teacher, an elder, a righteous person, or a wise man.
A mirror that is soiled should not be looked upon by those who are highly intelligent;
nor should one ever approach a woman who is unknown or one who is pregnant. Before taking a wife, a wise man should not engage in sexual intercourse.
Otherwise, he would be a transgressor and should perform an expiation.
He must not look at another man’s wife, nor should he sit alone in private with her. He should always restrain his senses and remain pure-minded even in dreams.
One should not sleep with the head toward the north, nor with the head toward the west; a wise man should sleep with his head toward the east or toward the south.
Furthermore, one should not sleep on a broken or dilapidated bed.
One should never [approach] when [the teacher] is out of sight, nor when he is occupied with others, nor when he is turned away;
nor should one go [to him] on business, nor even from a commitment, if he is an atheist.
Furthermore, a man should not draw a seat toward himself with his foot, nor should he sit down in such a manner.
One should never bathe naked, nor ever at night;
having bathed, a wise man should not rub his limbs dry. He should never sleep on his side, nor remain constantly covered by a screen.
One should not bathe again at night, except in an emergency or in the presence of fire or twice-born men.

During bathing, one should avoid using discarded flower-garlands (*nirmālyaka*); having bathed, one should not wipe the limbs with them. One should not apply ointments without having bathed, nor should one wring out one's garment after bathing.
A man should always wear his garments while they are still damp;
he should not pull at his garlands, nor should he wear them outside [the body]. Red garlands should not be worn; rather, white ones should be worn by the wise.

O Lord, with the exception of the *kamala* and the *kuvalaya*, a red flower should be worn on the head; likewise, even one grown in the wild (*vāneya*) is acceptable. Furthermore, a garland made of gold is never considered defiled.

O Lord of the people, one who has bathed should always apply unguents while the body is still moist; a wise man should not wear his garments in reverse order, nor should he wear those already worn by another, nor even those that are frayed at the edges.
"O best of men, the garment on the bed should be one thing;
another indeed for the roads of the gods; and yet another for the worship of the deities.
[It should be scented] with priyaṅgu, sandalwood, bilva, and tagara."
The wise man should apply [the ointment] separately with the filaments as well;
having bathed, being pure and adorned, he should observe a fast.
One should not observe a fast in vain, nor should one take away another's wealth in this world.
On all festival days, one should always remain celibate (*brahmacārī*).
One should never eat food that has been licked by a dog,
nor should one eat what has been licked, despised, or smelled.
Likewise, one should not look upon things from which the essence has been extracted, nor upon those that have not been offered;

a wise man should not sit too close to others, nor be impure, nor stand behind those who are virtuous; and he should not consume forbidden foods, even when they are presented in accordance with dharma.
One who seeks his own welfare, O best of men, should not eat the fruit of the *pippala*, nor the *vaṭa*, nor likewise the *śaṇa* vegetable, nor the *udumbara*.
He should also avoid the meat of goats, cows, and peacocks.
One should avoid dried meat as well as anything that has been kept overnight;
one should not eat dry food and should avoid the food of a Śūdra. A wise man should not eat salt from his hand, nor should he do so at night.

One should not eat curd-mixed barley meal (*dadhi-saktu*), and one should avoid meat not intended for sacrifice (*vṛthā-māṃsa*). One may drink curd-mixed barley meal at night, and one may always drink honey.
However, one should not eat from a single hair-bowl, nor likewise partake in a funeral feast (*śrāddha*) offered by another.
One should eat in the evening and in the morning, with a concentrated mind, and not in between.
Restrained in speech, wearing more than one garment, and never while lying down; one should always eat on the ground, neither while seated on a seat nor making noise.
O Lord of the People, having first given food to guests with water,
a wise man should eat afterwards, and not with a distracted mind. O Ruler of Men, however, food served in a single row must be eaten by all equally.
One should eat in silence; one should eat with a friend, not with an enemy.
He who eats together with the elderly without first giving to guests and children, and he who eats without giving to his circle of friends, consumes the *hālāhala* poison.
Having discarded water, milk-rice, clarified butter, curd, barley-meal, and honey,
the remainder of these must not be given to anyone;
while eating, O tiger among men, one should not entertain any doubt.
One who desires prosperity should certainly not take curd as a post-drink.
Having sipped water and likewise rinsed the hands,
one should then sprinkle water upon the big toe of the right foot.
Placing his hand upon his head and touching fire with a concentrated mind,
a man skilled in ritual practice attains preeminence among his kinsmen. Having touched the vital breaths with water and the navel with the palm of his hand, he achieves success.
One should stand touching [the water], but not with a wet hand.
The space between the thumb and the forefinger is declared to be the *brāhma* tīrtha; that which is behind the little finger is here called the *deva* tīrtha.
O Bhārata, one should perform the ancestral rites (pitrya) by touching the space between the thumb and the forefinger, after likewise touching water according to the rule; furthermore,
one should never utter slander against others nor anything unpleasant.
No anger whatsoever should be provoked by a man who seeks existence;
he should not desire conversation with those who have fallen from their status, nor should he even look upon them, and he should avoid association with them— thus one attains a long life.
One should not engage in sexual intercourse during the day, nor with a maiden, nor with a prostitute;
one should not approach a woman who has not bathed; in this way, one attains a long life. Having sipped water at their respective *tīrthas* when a ritual act is to be performed, [one should proceed].
Having drunk water three times and wiped his mouth twice, a man becomes purified;
having touched his sense organs once and sprinkled himself with water three times,
a person should perform rites for the ancestors and the gods according to the rituals prescribed in the Veda.
O Kaurava, hear from me that purification which pertains to the sake of a Brāhmaṇa:
having spoken what is beneficial and relevant at the beginning and end of a meal,
one should touch water for purification in all instances using the *brāhma* tīrtha.
Having spat or sneezed, one should indeed touch water and become pure. After spitting, after sexual intercourse, after sneezing, after loosening the girdle,
upon seeing a woman in her courses, and likewise upon seeing a naked person, sipping water (ācamana) is prescribed.
One should touch the ear while reciting the *praṇava* (Oṃ) and then always gaze at the sun.
An elderly kinsman, a friend, or even one who is poor— whether he be of noble birth or a scholar— those who are destitute must be protected by one according to one's own ability.
They should be kept in the house; it is indeed auspicious and conducive to long life.
Pigeons in the house are auspicious, as are parrots together with mainas. Also auspicious are images of deities, mirrors, sandalwood, and flowering creepers.
Pure water, gold, silver, and auspicious household items—
these do not lead to sin when found in houses; likewise, oil-drinking insects,
flamingos, vultures, pigeons, and bees [do not cause harm].
When they settle there, one should practice only tranquility.
These are inauspicious omens, as is the reviling of great-souled ones;
and the secrets of great-souled ones must never be spoken.
One should not approach those who are forbidden, such as the wives of kings, friends,
physicians, children, the elderly, and servants, O Yudhiṣṭhira;
likewise, one should avoid the wives of kinsmen, Brahmins, and those seeking refuge.

O Indra among kings, one likewise attains a long life through one's kinsmen. O lord of men, a wise person seeking prosperity should always dwell in a residence constructed by a Brāhmaṇa and an architect (sthapati).
O King, one should not sleep during the twilight, nor should one practice sacred learning;
a wise man should also not eat then, for in this way he attains a long life.
One should not perform ancestral rites at night, nor should one engage in personal adornment after eating.
One who desires prosperity should not perform the act of drinking at night;
furthermore, O Bhārata, roasted barley flour (saktu) must always be avoided at night. At a meal, only pure remnants and water [are permitted].
One should not eat to full satiety, nor should one engage in sexual intercourse at night;
after eating, one should not have sex, run about, or laugh excessively. One should not cut the nails of the twice-born, nor should one do so after a meal.
O man of great wisdom, he ought to marry a maiden born of a noble family, endowed with auspicious marks,
and of marriageable age; having thus produced offspring and established his lineage.
O Bhārata, sons should be given [in marriage] to those possessed of knowledge and established in the family traditions;
and having produced a daughter, she should be given to a wise son of noble family.
Sons should be settled in their stations, and servants should be obtained from the family, O Bhārata.

Having bathed his head, he may then perform rites for the gods and for the ancestors. However, one should not apply oil as an ointment on the eighth day, the fourteenth day, on the days of the lunar nodes (parvan),
nor under the lunar mansion in which a man was born.
O Bhārata, one should not perform [the rite] under the two Proṣṭhapadas nor under the Āgneya constellation;
one should avoid it daily during all the harsh [asterisms],
and one should avoid all those [times] which are declared in the science of astrology (jyotiṣa).

Facing the east, or facing the north, O Indra among kings, one should have the work of shaving performed with a concentrated mind; in this way, one obtains a long life. Bathing in seawater, shaving, and eating at *śrāddha* ceremonies [are likewise forbidden].
A husband who treats his pregnant wife with contempt does not enjoy the fruit of having a son.
One should never utter slander against the virtuous, one's teachers, the elderly, or especially noble women, nor should one speak ill of others or oneself.
Slander is not said to be for the sake of dharma, O bull of the Bharatas. One should avoid a woman with a physical deformity, as well as a maiden, O best of men;
likewise, one should avoid a woman who shares the same *ṛṣi* lineage, one who is deformed, and one born of one's own mother’s family.

One should avoid an elderly woman, as well as one who has renounced the world, and likewise one devoted to her husband; similarly, one should avoid a woman of extremely dark complexion and one of superior caste.
A wise man should not approach a woman of non-human origin or one of inferior origin.

"You ought not to marry a woman who is tawny-eyed or afflicted with leprosy; O lord of men, one should avoid a girl born into a family of epileptics, one who is low-born, or one born into a family of those afflicted with vitiligo— these three."

One should avoid a woman who is excessively wicked, as well as one afflicted by disease or who is deformed; one should avoid a girl who is hairy, too corpulent, or dependent upon her mother and father;
and one should avoid a shameless girl born of a brother, a corrupt woman, or one with blood-red hair.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, you ought to marry one who is endowed with auspicious marks, praised for her characteristics, pleasing to the mind, and beautiful to behold; you should marry into a great family or one that is your own equal."
One who desires prosperity should not accept a woman who is of lower caste or one who has fallen from her status.
Having diligently established the sacred fires and performed those rites well-ordained which have been proclaimed by the Brahmins in the Vedas, he should practice them all.

One should not practice jealousy toward women, and one's wife must be protected in every way. Jealousy shortens one's lifespan; therefore, one should avoid jealousy. Sleeping during the day and sleeping while the sun is rising are likewise detrimental to longevity.
Those who sleep while still impure from food at dawn or at night, as well as those who commit adultery, shorten their lifespan; likewise, being left impure by a barber— these,
O Bhārata, should certainly not be practiced, nor should they be repeated with effort.
One should indeed exercise restraint in eating and avoid overeating.
One should not eat during the twilight hours, nor bathe, nor void excrement. One should consider oneself pure and should not touch Brāhmaṇas.
One should speak against that slayer of a Brahmin, and his life-span shall perish.
For a man desiring prosperity must always honor Brahmins;
he should remain self-restrained during that [observance] and should not perform any improper act whatsoever.
O lord of men, having bathed in this manner, one should also honor the Brāhmaṇas;
having returned from his studies, he should bow to pure Brahmins, the gods, and his gurus.
He should perform the *vyāhṛti-homa* and other rites, and he should always be worthy of receiving the *arghya* offering.
Having bathed, one should bow to the gods and also offer salutations to one's teachers. One should not go to a sacrifice unless invited; however, one may go as a spectator.
For going there uninvited, O Bhārata, is detrimental to one’s lifespan.
One should not wander as a mendicant alone, nor should one travel thus at night. One should not take food from another when in distress unless specifically invited.
One should not eat at a *ekoddiṣṭa* rite, especially on the first occasion.

The *sapiṇḍīkaraṇa* rite and the monthly (*māsika*) ceremonies, along with their prescribed procedures, must be avoided [at that time]. Before the evening twilight has arrived, he should remain at home.
He must certainly carry out the instructions of his mother, father, and teachers.
Whether it be beneficial or even harmful, O bull among men, it need not be deliberated upon;
however, a Kṣatriya especially should practice the science of archery (Dhanurveda).
O lord of men, one should apply effort toward both the Dhanurveda and the Veda.
On the backs of elephants, on the backs of horses, and indeed in the maneuvers of chariots, O Indra among kings, be diligent; for he who is diligent prospers in happiness.
He shall be invincible to his enemies, to his servants, and to his own kin.
Engaged in the protection of his subjects, he shall suffer no harm anywhere.
O Bhārata, you must master the science of logic (*yukti-śāstra*) and the science of grammar (*śabda-śāstra*);
O lord of men, you must also fully understand the science of the Gandharvas and the fine arts (*kalā*).
You should constantly listen to the Purāṇas, the Itihāsas, as well as those various Ākhyānas, and the life-stories of the great-souled ones. Furthermore,
you should show honor to those worthy of honor, and likewise censure those deserving of censure.
One should fight for the sake of cows and Brahmins, even at the cost of sacrificing one's own life;
one should not be attached to women, but should look upon them with the eye of discernment and take delight in giving gifts.
One should not treat Brahmins with contempt, nor should one adopt the wretchedness that characterizes some Brahmins.
One should not speak to those who have fallen from their status, nor should one call out to a woman in her courses. One should not approach a wife who is in her courses, nor should one call her.
A wise man should approach her on the night of the fourth day after she has bathed.
On the fifth day it is a female, and on the sixth day it becomes a male.
According to this rule, a wise man should approach his wife;
the period of fertility (*ṛtu*) is declared to be the primary time for the birth of a son until the sixteenth day.

Relatives, kinsmen, and friends should always be honored; one should also perform sacrifices according to one's ability with various ritual fees. Beyond this, O lord of men, the forest should be resorted to.
This brief enumeration of the characteristics of longevity has been proclaimed to you;
the remainder, O Yudhiṣṭhira, is to be learned from those aged in the three Vedas. Right conduct generates prosperity; right conduct increases fame.
For through right conduct life is increased, and right conduct destroys inauspicious marks.
Indeed, among all the scriptures, right conduct is said to be the most excellent;
dharma originates from right conduct, and from dharma, life is further increased.
This [account], which brings fame, longevity, and heaven, and is a great means of securing well-being,
was proclaimed by Brahmā out of compassion for all social classes.
Whoever should hear this constantly, and whoever should recite it aloud—
O King, one who is devoted to right conduct shall attain auspicious worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
O bull of the Bharatas, how does an elder brother behave toward his younger brothers?
"Tell me how the younger brothers should conduct themselves toward the eldest.
Bhīṣma said:
"O dear one, behave toward him as you would toward an elder, for you are always the eldest."
O Bhārata, if a disciple’s conduct toward his teacher is more weighty [than that of the teacher],
it is impossible for him to behave properly toward a teacher who lacks wisdom;
for whatever constitutes the long-sightedness of a teacher, O Bhārata, that belongs to the disciple as well.

One should be blind at the time for blindness, or even a fool though wise; one should speak with such avoidance that there may be no transgression against them. Men with divided hearts might openly cause a breach in what has been settled.
O son of Kuntī, enemies who are tormented by prosperity likewise desire to create dissension;
being tormented by that prosperity, they may become divided, yet if they remain composed, they will not be split.
Furthermore, the eldest son either causes the lineage to flourish or, conversely, brings it to ruin.

The eldest son destroys even the entire family in which he is born [if he acts wrongly]. Now, if the eldest brother should treat his younger brothers with injustice, he shall lose his status as the eldest, be deprived of his share, and be restrained by the kings.
For a deceitful man undoubtedly goes to the worlds of the wicked;
like the flower of the *vidula* reed, he is considered a fruitless birth for his progenitor.
Wherever a sinful man is born, there arises every kind of misfortune for the family.
It surely produces infamy and obscures one's reputation.
Furthermore, all those who persist in improper occupations do not deserve a share of the inheritance, even if they are uterine brothers—
especially so if the eldest is ill-behaved, let alone the younger ones.
An elder brother shall not make a separate property for himself without first giving to the younger brothers;
for the inheritance from the father is like the fruit of a traveler’s weary journey on his legs.
However, what he has acquired by his own effort, he is not obliged to give away unless he so desires.
Even if brothers who have not divided their inheritance live together,
the father must under no circumstances give unequal shares to his sons. He should not show contempt for his eldest son, whether he has acted wickedly or virtuously.
Indeed, an offense against one’s gurus must certainly be forgiven;
whether it be a woman or a junior, one should act in such a way if one perceives it to be for one’s own welfare.
For those who know the Dharma understand that they declare the Dharma alone to be the highest good.

But they are always equal in their dependence on the eldest, even if he is slightly inferior; ten teachers are equal to one sub-teacher (upādhyāya), ten sub-teachers are equal to one father, ten fathers are equal to one mother, or [the mother is equal to] the entire earth.
One is overcome by reverence; there is no teacher equal to a mother. Because the mother is most venerable, people regard her as such.
O Bhārata, when the father has died, the eldest brother is equal to a father.
For he would be the provider of their livelihood and he should protect them;
all the younger ones should pay him homage and follow his will,
and they should depend upon him alone, just as they would upon a father.
"O Bhārata, the father and the mother create this physical body;
but that birth which is under the instruction of the teacher is the true one, which is undecaying and immortal.
Furthermore, O bull among the Bharatas, an elder sister is equal to a mother."
And likewise, the wife of one’s brother is she from whose breast one drank milk in childhood.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, [this applies] to all the social orders as well as to the Mlecchas."
"We do not understand this intention regarding fasting, nor its underlying cause.
We have heard that observances are to be practiced by the Brahmins and Kṣatriyas;
O Grandfather, what purpose does fasting serve for them?"
O King, tell me the rule for all fasts:
what destination does one who is devoted to fasting attain?
Fasting is supreme merit; fasting is the ultimate refuge.
"O best of men, what fruit does one obtain by fasting here?
By what means is one released from unrighteousness, and how indeed does one attain righteousness?
