And how, O best of the Bharatas, does one obtain the merit of heaven?"
"O lord of men, having observed the fast, what should be given by him?
Tell me that by which one may obtain through righteousness both happiness and wealth.
Vaiśampāyana said:
To the son of Kuntī, the knower of dharma, who was speaking thus, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu and knower of the true nature of dharma, addressed these words to the son of Dharma:
"O Great King, this ancient account was indeed heard by me in the past."
O bull of the Bharatas, those qualities which are supreme in the rite of fasting—
O descendant of Bharata, I indeed questioned Aṅgiras, the son of Prajāpati,
just as you have questioned me, that ascetic rich in penance.
"O bull of the Bharatas, when asked this very question by me, the Blessed One born from fire explained the meritorious rule for fasting. Aṅgiras said:"
O joy of the Kurus, for a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya, a three-night fast is prescribed;
furthermore, O bull among men, two such three-night periods are likewise indicated here.
However, if a Vaiśya or a Śūdra should perform a fast out of delusion, [the following applies].
For those two [castes], nourishment is not found for three nights or twice three nights;
rather, the practice of skipping the fourth meal is prescribed for the Vaiśya and the Śūdra.
However, a fast of three nights has not been ordained by the knowers of dharma who proclaim the Veda.
On the fifth, the sixth, and the full moon day, O Bhārata,
having fasted by eating but a single meal, with self-restraint and conquered senses,
one is born endowed with forgiveness, beauty, and sacred learning.
A wise man shall never be childless or poor,
provided he performs sacrifices and fasts on the fifth and sixth lunar days, feeding the twice-born;
and likewise, O son of Kuntī, on the eighth and the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight.

Having fasted, one who is free from disease becomes endowed with vigor. He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa by taking only a single meal per day and feeds the twice-born with devotion shall be liberated from diseases and sins.
Filled with every auspiciousness and endowed with all medicinal herbs,
he is born as one who shares in the fruits of agriculture, possessing great wealth and many sons.
O son of Kuntī, he who passes the month of Pauṣa by eating but a single meal [attains these rewards].
He becomes fortunate, handsome, and a partaker of glory. He who, devoted to his father, passes the month of Māgha eating but one meal a day,
attains greatness among his kinsmen within a prosperous family.
He who passes the month of Bhādrapada eating but one meal a day becomes beloved by women, and they come under his control. He who,
being self-restrained, passes the month of Caitra eating but one meal a day—
He who, with his senses subdued, passes the month of Vaiśākha by eating but one meal a day, is born into a great family enriched with gold, jewels,
and pearls; whether he be a man or a woman, he shall attain preeminence among his kinsmen.
He who passes the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla subsisting on a single meal a day—
whether man or woman— is born into incomparable and supreme sovereignty.
Having remained diligent throughout the month of Āṣāḍha, subsisting on a single meal a day...
He who passes the month of Śrāvaṇa with a fixed practice of eating only one meal a day will be born with abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many sons;
endowed with beauty and riches, he shall be happy forever.

In whatever [month] one performs the consecration, he becomes a prosperer of his kin; wealthy and renowned, he is born into a great family. Furthermore, the man who eats but a single meal during the month of Prauṣṭhapada—

One attains abundant wealth, a prosperous and stable sovereignty. Likewise, he who passes the month of Āśvayuja eating but a single meal a day is born possessed of progeny, rich in vehicles, and blessed with many sons.
The man who observes the practice of eating only once a day during the month of Kārttika becomes brave, possesses many wives, and is endowed with great fame.
Thus, O tiger among men, have the months for those practicing fasting been fully described.

O King, listen now also to those rules regarding the lunar days (*tithis*). O Bhārata, he who eats only once when each fortnight has passed becomes wealthy in cattle, blessed with many sons, and long-lived.
By observing three-night fasts month after month for twelve years,
one attains the leadership of a *gaṇa* that is unrivaled and free from impurity.
All these observances (*niyamas*), however, must be performed for ten autumns.
And two others, O best of the Bharatas, follow this practice:
he who eats in the morning and likewise in the evening, drinking nothing in between,
who is constantly devoted to non-violence and offers oblations into the sacred fire.
O King, by six years he attains perfection; of this there is no doubt. That man obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, dwelling among the Apsarases amidst the sounds of dance and song.
The virtuous man, free from passion, rejoices amidst a multitude of thousands of women;
he ascends a celestial chariot with the luster of molten gold and is honored in the world of Brahmā for a full thousand years.
Upon the exhaustion of that [merit], he returns here and attains greatness. But the man who, for a full year, eats only once a day,
enjoys the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice.
He is honored in heaven for ten thousand years;
upon the exhaustion of that merit, he returns here and attains greatness. But he who eats only every fourth meal for a full year—
One who is constantly devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and has his senses restrained,
indeed attains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
for thirty thousand years, he is glorified in heaven.
O son of Kuntī, by fasting for a year at the sixth mealtime,
a man obtains the fruit of the Aśvamedha sacrifice;
he travels in a celestial chariot drawn by ruddy geese.
For forty thousand years he rejoices in heaven. Furthermore, O King, a man who lives for a year eating only every eighth meal attains the fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice.
He travels in a celestial chariot yoked with swans and cranes;
for fifty thousand years, he rejoices in heaven. O King, he who eats only once every fortnight for an entire year [attains this].
The Blessed Aṅgiras declared that for him there shall be a fast of six months;
he shall dwell in heaven for sixty thousand years,
O lord of the people, [hearing] the sounds of lutes, harps, and flutes.
He is awakened from sleep by sweet and resonant sounds. O King, that man who drinks milk here month after month for one full year attains, my dear, the fruit of the Viśvajit sacrifice.
He travels in a celestial chariot drawn by lions and tigers,
and he rejoices in heaven for seventy thousand years. O tiger among men, beyond one month, no further fast is prescribed.
13.109.050c O Pārtha, those who know the Dharma have declared this to be the rule for fasting.
13.109.051a He who, being neither afflicted nor diseased, undertakes a fast, 13.109.051c obtains the fruit of a sacrifice at every step; of this there is no doubt.
He goes to heaven by means of a celestial chariot yoked with swans;
and a hundred maidens who are Apsarases also delight that man. Furthermore, whether one is distressed or afflicted by disease, he who undergoes fasting shall likewise go there.
O Lord, he rejoices in heaven for a hundred thousand years;
even while asleep, he is awakened by the sound of waist-bands and anklets,
riding in a moon-bright celestial chariot yoked with a thousand swans.
Having gone there, O bull of the Bharatas, he sports among a multitude of hundreds of women.
For one who is wasted away, nourishment is seen; for one who is wounded, the healing of the wound;
for one who is diseased, a collection of medicines; and for one who is angry, appeasement.

The bestowing of goods upon those who are suffering for the sake of wealth and honor does not please those who desire heaven and thrive in happiness; nor does this practice appeal to those who prosper in happiness through riches.

Therefore, filled with desire, that man— adorned, healthy, successful in his resolves, happy, and free from stain— delights in a beautiful celestial chariot resembling gold, crowded with hundreds of women.
By casting off the body while fasting, a human being attains the fruit [of his merit]:
he dwells in a celestial chariot shining like the rising sun, possessing the luster of gold,
inlaid with lapis lazuli and pearls, and resounding with the music of lutes and drums.
Amidst a place strewn with banners and lamps, resounding with the ringing of divine bells,
and frequented by thousands of women, that man prospers in happiness;
as many as are the pores on his limbs, O Pāṇḍava—
For exactly that many thousands of years, he rejoices in heaven.
There is no scripture superior to the Veda; there is no teacher equal to a mother. There is no gain higher than dharma; there is no austerity greater than fasting.

There is nothing more purifying than the Brahmins, both in heaven and here on earth; likewise, no ascetic practice is found equal to fasting. By fasting according to the prescribed rules, the gods attained the third heaven.
And by means of fasts, the seers attained supreme perfection.
Indeed, for a thousand divine years, the wise Viśvāmitra endured on a single meal; by that [austerity], he attained the status of a brahmin.
Cyavana, Jamadagni, Vasiṣṭha, Gautama, and Bhṛgu—
all these great ṛṣis, possessed of forgiveness, have attained heaven.
This was previously demonstrated by Aṅgiras to the great ṛṣis.
He who constantly demonstrates this [practice] does not encounter suffering.
O Kaunteya, this is indeed the sequence of rites set forth by the great seer Aṅgiras.
Whoever should indeed recite this or hear it constantly, no sin exists for that man;
he is also liberated from all impurities.
His mind is not overcome by defects,
he understands the cries of those born from non-womb sources,
and that best of men attains enduring fame.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The high-souled grandfather has duly described the sacrifices,
as well as their qualities in their true nature, both in this world and after death, in every respect."
"O Grandfather, those sacrifices cannot be attained by a poor man;
for sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
O Grandfather, they can only be performed by kings or princes."

"O Grandfather, tell me of that rite which can always be accomplished even by the poor— using means that are not deficient in purpose, free from defects, requiring only a single person, and needing no collective effort— and which is equal in merit to the fruits of Vedic sacrifices."
Bhīṣma said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, learn this procedure, proclaimed by Aṅgiras, which consists of the fruits of fasting and is equal to the fruits of sacrifices."
But he who eats only in the morning and likewise in the evening, and does not drink in between;
who is constantly devoted to non-violence and offers oblations into the sacred fire—he attains perfection in exactly six years; of this there is no doubt.
A man obtains a celestial chariot with the color of molten gold;
he shall dwell for a lotus-number of years in the abode of the divine women, resounding with the sounds of dance and song, in the realm of Prajāpati which blazes like fire.
He who, devoted always to his lawful wife, eats only one meal per day continuously for three years, shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. He,
however, who eats only one meal on every second day, [obtains the same fruit].
Constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months,
one should perform a sacrifice involving much gold, which is dear to Vāsava; such a person should be truthful in speech, charitable by nature, devoted to Brahman, and free from malice.
Patient, self-controlled, and having conquered anger, he goes to the supreme goal.
In a celestial chariot resembling a white cloud and marked with swans,
and in two perfect lotuses, he shall dwell together with Apsarases.
A person who is constantly devoted to the fire-ritual (*agnikārya*) and always wakes at dawn attains the fruit of the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice;
such a man obtains a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) yoked with swans and cranes.
He dwells in the world of Indra, surrounded by excellent women. He who eats but a single meal on every third day,
constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire for twelve months—
A man obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice;
he gains a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) yoked with peacocks and swans,
and shall dwell forever in the world of the Seven Sages together with Apsarases.
They know that his retreat there lasts for three padmas;
he who eats but a single meal on the fourth day,
constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months.
A man obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice;
he gains a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) mounted by the daughters of Indra,
and he shall dwell in the world of Vāsava at the very edge of the ocean.
And he constantly beholds the play of the King of the Gods. He who eats but a single meal on every fifth day,
while constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months—
Free from greed, truthful in speech, devoted to Brahman, and non-violent;
free from envy and established in righteousness—one shall obtain the fruit of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).
[One shall ascend] a divine celestial chariot made of Jāmbūnada gold, marked with the sign of a swan.
Having obtained the fruit of the *atirātra* sacrifice, he rejoices with celestial nymphs (*apsarases*).
Possessing a radiance equal to a garland of suns, he ascends to a white palace.
There are four whirlpools as well as twelve lotuses.
For a period measured by eleven thousand, one hundred and ten years and two days, he dwells there in happiness. Furthermore, that sage who eats food only on every sixth day,
constantly offering oblations to the sacred fire for twelve months— [he too attains that same state].
Always bathing at the three daily sessions, practicing celibacy, and free from malice,
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of the Gavamaya sacrifice—
a realm possessing a radiance like the flame of fire and frequented by swans and peacocks.
One should prepare an excellent vehicle made of gold, equipped with all its parts;
likewise, he awakens while still sleeping on the lap of an apsaras,
to the sound of anklets and the tinkling of waist-bands.
One thousand ten million years, three hundred million,
eighteen padmas, two patākās,
and fifty ayutas of a hundred bear skins.

One who eats a single meal on every seventh day for twelve full months, while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire, is glorified in the world of Brahmā for as many years as there are hairs on his body.
Protecting the Sarasvatī and practicing celibacy (*brahmacarya*),
he should avoid flowers, cosmetics, honey, and meat.
Such a man goes to the world of the Maruts and the world of Indra.
In each of those places, having attained his goal, the man is carried away by celestial maidens;
he obtains the fruit of a sacrifice involving much gold and rejoices in those worlds for a number of times exceeding all measure.
But that man who, remaining patient for a year, eats only on every eighth day,
constantly devoted to the service of the gods and offering oblations into the sacred fire,
attains the unsurpassed fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
He ascends a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) that resembles the color of a lotus;
he obtains women who are dark, golden-fair, and others who are dusky, all endowed with youth, beauty, and charm— of this there is no doubt.
But that man who eats only on every ninth day for a full year,
constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire for twelve months,
attains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha).
That man obtains a celestial chariot (vimāna) as radiant as a white lotus;
and by means of the splendors of the blazing sun and fire, as well as divine garlands,
he is led by the maidens of Rudra into the eternal firmament.
He rejoices in those worlds for eighteen thousand years, a full kalpa, and a hundred thousand times ten million years— [the merit of] him who eats [only] once every ten days for an entire year.
Constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months,
in the abode of the daughters of Brahmā— which is enchanting to all beings—
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices.
And beautiful maidens always delight that man,
with complexions like blue lotuses as well as red lotuses.
His celestial chariot, Maṇḍalāvarta, is enveloped in a dense whirlpool of eddies.
One should accomplish that supreme vehicle, which resembles the waves of the ocean,
resounding with various garlands of jewels and the blare of conchs and drums,
and featuring well-constructed altars supported by pillars of crystal and diamond-hard stone.

On the eleventh day, he who has been consuming sacrificial oblations for twelve full months and has been constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire ascends a great vehicle drawn by swans and cranes.
One should not desire another’s wife, either by word or even in thought;
nor should one speak untruth, even for the sake of one’s mother or father. One should approach Mahādeva, the one of great power, as he resides within his celestial chariot.
He beholds the Self-Existent One (Svayambhū) and sees a celestial chariot standing before him.
Beautiful maidens with the luster of gold lead him away to that divine,
heart-stealing abode of the Rudras in heaven.
One may dwell even until the end of the age for immeasurable years—
ten million, a hundred thousand millions, and ten billion—
constantly bowing before Rudra, who is honored by gods and dānavas alike.
He who obtains a vision of him day after day shall,
on reaching the twelfth day, partake of the sacrificial oblation (*havis*); indeed,
by doing so for twelve months, he shall obtain the fruit of the *Sarvamedha* sacrifice.
Offering oblations into Jātavedas while joined with self-restraint,
a celestial chariot is prepared for him by the twelve Ādityas.
It was adorned with highly precious gems, pearls, and corals;
it was encircled by rows of swans and crowded with avenues of elephants;
and it was graced by the warbling of peacocks and ruddy geese.

"O King, it is joined with great palaces and established in the world of Brahmā; there the highly fortunate seer Aṅgiras, the knower of dharma, said that he dwells eternally, surrounded by men and women."
Having swiftly ascended a celestial chariot (*vimāna*), he is glorified in the world of Brahmā. Furthermore,
he who, when the thirteenth day arrives, eats only sacrificial oblation (*havis*) for twelve full months, shall indeed obtain the fruit of a divine sacrificial session (*devasatra*).
A man shall accomplish the celestial palace named Raktapadmodaya; having gone there, he shall arise surrounded by divine maidens,
[the palace] fashioned from gold and adorned with a collection of jewels.
It was crowded with celestial maidens, adorned with divine ornaments,
filled with the rising of holy fragrances, and graced by divine breezes.
Therein were the Śaṅku and Patāka mountains, as well as the Yugānta and Kalpa peaks.
He shall dwell for an ayuta, an ayuta, a padma, and likewise a samudra [of years].
Always delighted by the songs and melodies of the gandharvas, and by the sounds of kettledrums and tabors, he is praised by those celestial maidens.
He who eats sacrificial oblation (havis) on the fourteenth day when it is full,
for twelve months continuously, shall indeed obtain the fruit of a great sacrifice (mahāmedha). [He shall see] celestial maidens, well-adorned, whose age and form are indescribable.
Wearing polished and heated armlets, they follow him in celestial chariots;
they are awakened here and there by the cries of kalahamsas, the tinkling of anklets, and the jingling of waist-bands.
A man who dwells for a full year in that abode of celestial maidens, strewn with the sands of the Ganges,
and who, having conquered his senses, eats but a single meal once every fortnight, [attains this state].
Constantly offering oblations to Jātavedas for twelve months,
one obtains the unsurpassed fruit of a thousand Rājasūya sacrifices;
one constantly ascends a celestial vehicle frequented by swans and peacocks.
Variegated with circles of jewels, covered in gold,
adorned by excellent women radiant with divine ornaments,
it had a single pillar, four doors, seven stories, and was most auspicious.
Adorned with thousands of victory banners and resounding with the sounds of song,
he ascends a divine celestial chariot endowed with divine qualities,
decorated with jewels, pearls, and corals, and radiant as lightning.
He shall dwell for a thousand yugas, mounted upon a sword and an elephant; he who,
when the sixteenth day arrives,
consumes the sacrificial oblation (havis) for twelve full months, shall indeed obtain the fruit of the Soma sacrifice.
He dwells eternally in the abodes of the daughters of Soma;
anointed with gentle fragrances, he moves according to his will,
accompanied by women who are both beautiful to behold and sweet of speech.
Seated upon a celestial chariot (vimāna), he is indeed honored and served with the enjoyments of his desires;
for more than ten great kalpas, he enjoys a fruit resembling a hundred lotuses,
and that man remains there until the four cycles of the ocean have passed.
He who, for twelve months, eats the sacrificial oblation only when the seventeenth day arrives, while constantly offering oblations into the fire,
attains the realms of Varuṇa, Indra, and Rudra.
He goes to the world of the Maruts, to that of Uśanas, and to the world of Brahmā;
there he is served with a seat by the daughters of the gods,
and he beholds the divine seer Viśvarūpa, who pervades the earth and the atmosphere.
There, thirty-two maidens of the God of Gods— possessing beautiful forms, sweet, and well-adorned— delight him.
O Lord, as long as both the moon and the sun move in the sky, [they remain there].
For that long, that hero moves about, subsisting on the essence of nectar and ambrosia;
on the eighteenth day, however, he should take a single meal.
Indeed, for twelve months, he constantly beholds the seven worlds.
He was followed from behind by chariots with joyful sounds,
mounted by celestial maidens who were radiant and well-adorned;
[he also saw] a vehicle yoked with tigers and lions, resounding with a roar like the clouds.
He indeed ascends that supreme, divine celestial chariot and experiences great happiness;
there, for a thousand kalpas, he rejoices with beautiful women and partakes of the finest nectar-like essence of ambrosia.
He who eats but one meal on the nineteenth day,
for twelve full months, beholds the seven worlds and attains the supreme station frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
And there, in a celestial chariot radiant as the sun and celebrated by the songs of Gandharvas,
he rejoices, freed from all distress, wearing divine garments, glorious, for a hundred times ten thousand years, in the company of the foremost women of the immortals.
Now, he who eats but a single meal on every twentieth day,
for twelve full months— speaking the truth, firm in his vows,
abstaining from meat, practicing celibacy, and devoted to the welfare of all beings— [attains the merit of a sacrifice].
He attains vast, divine worlds belonging to the Ādityas;
followed from behind by Gandharvas and Apsarases adorned with celestial garlands and unguents, he travels in divine golden celestial chariots.
He who eats but one meal on the twenty-first day,
doing so for twelve full months while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire (jātavedas),
goes to the divine world of Uśanas and the world of Śakra.
Always delighting in the pleasures of the Aśvins and the Maruts,
and being unacquainted with sufferings, that lord,
seated upon his excellent celestial chariot and attended by beautiful women, sports like an immortal.
When the twenty-second day arrives, he who eats but a single meal,
doing so for twelve full months while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire—
being steadfast, devoted to non-violence, truthful in speech, and free from malice— [attains the highest goal].
Possessing a splendor equal to the sun, he attains eleven thousand worlds of the Vasus;
moving at will and subsisting on nectar, he dwells in an excellent celestial chariot,
sporting with divine maidens and adorned with celestial ornaments.
He who eats a single meal on the twenty-third day,
always for twelve months, eating moderately and with his senses subdued,
goes to the worlds of Vāyu, Uśanas, and Rudra.
Moving at will and going wherever he desires, honored by hosts of apsarases,
he dwells in a supreme celestial chariot of manifold virtues;
adorned with divine ornaments, he delights in the company of celestial maidens.
He who eats a single meal on the twenty-fourth day,
constantly for twelve months while offering oblations to Jātavedas,
shall dwell for a long time rejoicing in the abode of the Ādityas.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, and anointed with divine perfumes and unguents, he rejoices in a divine golden celestial chariot yoked with swans and full of delight,
together with thousands and tens of thousands of celestial maidens.
He who eats but a single meal on the twenty-fifth day for twelve full months shall mount a magnificent vehicle drawn by lions and tigers, resounding with the roar of thunderclouds.
He was followed from behind by chariots with joyful sounds,
and by celestial maidens mounted upon bright, stainless, and auspicious silver chariots; he had ascended a supreme, divine, and most enchanting celestial vehicle (vimāna).
There, surrounded by a hundred women, he dwells for a thousand kalpas,
subsisting on the finest essence of nectar that is like ambrosia. Furthermore,
he who eats but a single meal on every twenty-sixth day [attains this].

Constantly for twelve months, self-restrained and restricted in diet, having conquered his senses and freed from passion, he who offers oblations into the sacred fire— that highly fortunate man attains [the celestial realm], being honored by hosts of apsarases.
He enjoys the worlds of the seven Maruts and the Vasus as well;
in a divine crystal celestial chariot adorned with every kind of gem,
he rejoices while being honored by Gandharvas and Apsarases.
For two thousand divine *yugas*, by means of divine splendor,
he who eats but a single meal on the twenty-seventh day,
while constantly offering oblations into the sacred fire (*jātavedas*) for twelve months—

He obtains vast fruit and is honored in the world of the gods; dwelling there as an eater of nectar, he remains satisfied and rejoices. O King, this is the conduct of the celestial ṛṣis, presided over by the royal ṛṣis.
Seated upon an excellent celestial chariot, that divine-souled one dwells there,
sporting with women who delight the mind, intoxicated with joy; indeed,
he lives happily for three thousand yugas and kalpas.
He who, for twelve months, always eats but one meal on every twenty-eighth day, being self-controlled and having conquered his senses,
attains the vast fruit practiced by the divine sages.
Possessing great enjoyments, he shines with splendor like the stainless thousand-rayed sun.
And women of exquisite beauty and radiant luster take delight in him—
women with full breasts, thighs, and hips, adorned with celestial ornaments.
Beloved women delight his mind in a celestial chariot resembling the sun,
which moves at will and is divine, for a full hundred thousand aeons.
He who eats but a single meal on the twenty-ninth day [attains this].
For twelve months he remains constantly devoted to the vow of truth;
his worlds are auspicious and divine, honored by the kings of gods and the ṛṣis,
and he attains a celestial chariot with the brilliant luster of the moon.
It was made of gold, equipped with all kinds of jewel ornaments,
filled with throngs of *apsarases*, and made resonant by *gandharvas*. There, auspicious women adorned with divine ornaments [waited upon him].
Delightful to the mind, sweet, and intoxicated with passion, they bring pleasure;
he is possessed of enjoyments, endowed with splendor, and possesses a radiance equal to Vaiśvānara.
Divine, with a divine body, he shines like an immortal god.
He goes to the worlds of the Vasus, the Maruts, the Sādhyas, and the Aśvins, as well as the worlds of the Rudras and the world of Brahmā. Furthermore,
he who, having passed a month, eats but one meal with a tranquil mind, [attains these realms].
For twelve months, indeed, he shall always attain the world of Brahmā;
subsisting on the essence of nectar, glorious and captivating to all,
he shines with splendor, form, and beauty like the sun.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
the yogin delights in pleasures and remains unaware of sufferings;
seated in his celestial chariot, he is honored by women who possess their own radiance.
He is constantly worshipped by the daughters of Rudra, the gods, and the ṛṣis—
daughters who possess various beautiful forms, various passions,
various sweet modes of speech, and various pleasures.
With various fragrances and diverse garments,
[they were seated] in a celestial chariot (*vimāna*) shaped like a city, resembling the sun and glowing like the sun;
behind it was one resembling the moon, and above it was one resembling a cloud.

In the southern direction, upon a red-hued [region] below a blue mandala and above one resembling a variegated appearance, he dwells alone, honored [by all]. As long as a thousand years, he causes rain to fall upon Jambūdvīpa.
As many drops as fall from the surface of the sky, so many years are said to constitute the lifespan of the wise Brahmā in the world of Brahmā, measured by the duration of those showers of rain.
During the rainy season, he who possesses the splendor of an immortal dwells there for that duration as it rains.
By fasting for one month for ten years, he attains the highest heaven;
then, having achieved the status of a great seer (*maharṣi*), he shall attain the state of moving with his physical body.
The sage who is self-controlled, who has conquered anger, and who always has his genitals and belly subdued; who,

being disciplined, offers oblations into the fires and practices the worship of the twilights— such a man who eats in this manner for months according to many restrictive observances, [attains the goal].
And his dwelling is said to be in the open air under the clouds;
having gone to heaven in his own body, O King, like an immortal,
he enjoys the meritorious celestial realm at will according to the prescribed rule.
13.110.134 This, O best of the Bharatas, is the supreme procedure for sacrifices,
explained by you in due order as consisting of the fruits of fasting.
13.110.135 O Pārtha, it is the means by which even poor men may obtain the fruit of sacrifice.
Having performed this fast, one shall go to the supreme goal—
whether it be the state of Viṣṇu or that of Rudra. For those practicing celibacy, having observed the vow for a year on the fifth lunar day, they ascend to the highest world.
O best of the Bharatas, he who delights in the worship of the gods and the twice-born—
this rule for fasting has been proclaimed in detail for those who are self-controlled, vigilant, pure, and high-souled.
O Bhārata, let there be no doubt in you regarding those who have turned away from deceit and malice, whose intellects are firmly established, and who are immovable and unshakable—
Yudhiṣṭhira.
The discourses concerning the dharma of giving, as told by the Grandfather (Brahmā),
were heard by me in the presence of the sages and Keśava; yet,
once again, curiosity arose regarding that very same spiritual [discourse].
"O Indra among kings, tell the story; who else but you could recount it?
This descendant of Yadu is worthy to grant permission. For when he is known, O Bhārata, that which is to be known becomes known."
"O Grandfather, we shall hear later the duties worthy of being heard from kings;
however, you ought now to dispel the curiosity of the sages.
Bhīṣma said:

13,110.137d@011_0010 Hereafter, O Great King, we shall explain the dialogue between two teachers who are endowed with the vision of reality as it truly is, attained through the study of both the Sāṃkhya and Yoga scriptures. It was as follows: the venerable Sanatkumāra was seated upon a great and excellent celestial couch, which was a thousand *yojanas* in circumference and radiant like the rising sun; he was sitting in the bound posture (*baddhāsana*), meditating on [the Self] while being no larger than the size of a thumb-joint.
Then the Blessed One approached the venerable teacher, who had taught that which is immortal, non-returning, formless, and born of the inexhaustible;
the venerable teacher Rudra said to him: "Welcome, Maheśvara, son of Brahmā!
Let the Blessed One be seated upon this seat."
When this was said, the Lord Rudra, who possesses infinite forms, sat down and spoke to him: "The Blessed One also practices meditation.
When this was said, the Blessed Sanatkumāra replied, "So be it."
Having been addressed with "So be it," the Blessed Lord Śaṅkara then spoke to that great sage, who knew the higher and the lower and was the knower of all the three worlds:
"What is there to be seen through meditation, which you perceive?"
And that which, having meditated upon, the ascetics who perceive reality do not grieve—
O best of ascetics, tell me of this God among embodied beings;
and that which is called the "Pure Puruṣa" in the systems of Yoga and Sāṃkhya.
What is the internal (*adhyātma*), what is the elemental (*adhibhūta*), and likewise what is the divine (*adhidaivata*)?
O God, what is the calculation of time (*kālasaṃkhyā*) that should be seen in relation to that Brahman—
the calculation of the reckoning itself as proclaimed by the supreme seers?
O best of ascetics, according to the path seen in the scriptures and as it truly is,
that which is the Puruṣa— pure, awakened, undecaying, and eternal—
is likewise to be known through knowledge by both the awakened and the unawakened.
O best among those who know liberation, tell me of the threefold liberation;
tell me also the enumeration of the Sāṃkhyas, meditation that is meaningful within the yogas,
as well as the vision of unity and likewise the vision of diversity.
O best of ascetics, you have truly described the omens of death as well as the processes of departure from the body,
and all the deities in their entirety and in due order,
who reside within the bodies of embodied beings.
O best of sages, explain all of this according to its true nature; for you,
O blameless one, are the most excellent among all who know Brahman,
being the fourth among those three who have attained the supreme goal.
By means of primordial knowledge (*prākṛta-jñāna*), one is liberated from the bonds of death;
we, however, have always resorted to the modified path (*vaikṛta-mārga*), which is perishable,
having abandoned the supreme path that is immortal and imperishable.

But having sunk into a diminished path, we nevertheless move about at our pleasure, having grasped this greatness consisting of the eightfold sovereign power (*aṣṭaguṇaiśvarya*). Yet this happiness is not absolute; it is inferior to that which follows.
O best of beings, this very state may indeed be supreme in its embodied form;
yet, the repeated falling [into rebirth] is taught as being embodied,
whereas for those liberated from embodiment, there is no further death.
Indeed, O great sage, endless faults of death arise for those who have perfected themselves, among mortals, on the heights of heaven, and in the hells; there men sink,
driven by pleasure and pain.
And that which they call the immortal state, free from pleasure and pain—
that I desire to hear exactly as it is seen in the sacred revelation (Śruti).
Sanatkumāra.
Regarding that statement which was made by you, that "the notion of reality belongs to embodied beings," some wise ones here say there are exactly twenty-four [principles],
while others say there are twenty-three, according to the indications of the revealed scriptures (*śruti*).
We, however, consider that twenty-fifth principle, known as the Adhiṣṭhāna, to be the true reality (tattva), because it is the ultimate discourse of all the Tantras. Furthermore,
both the Imperishable (Avyakta) and the Manifest (Vyakta) are indeed the wielder of the Pināka bow (Śiva).
Together and yet apart, those two are established in relation to one another.
O best among embodied beings, having entered his golden form,
O dear one, that Puruṣa created both the Puruṣa and the Vikāra-puruṣa.
From the unmanifest, this single Great Self alone is produced;
having pervaded the worlds through egoism and indeed through that which is characterized by ego,
know all that [world] to be from the unmanifest, O Bearer of the Trident.
Know that the third creation of beings proceeds in sequence from the ego (ahaṃkāra).
Know that the fourth, the modified (vaikṛta) creation among beings, also arises from the ego.
And these were born simultaneously from the ego, O Lord of the Gods.
The wise declare that the five elements possess specific qualities.
Indeed, the twenty-fifth principle presides over those proclaimed as the twenty-four. Thus, these four types of creation, which are here considered primordial (prākṛta), have been described by me.
And from the *ahaṃkāra*, O Lord of the Gods, [the elements] were born simultaneously;
and from the *ahaṃkāra* among the beings, the manifold objects of sense arose.
By means of all the senses simultaneously, that [object] is perceived as impermanent.

Marut-tva, the creation of the *sattva*, contentment (*tuṣṭi*), and likewise perfection (*siddhi*)—I shall declare these modifications; listen to them, O high-minded one. This is the twenty-fourfold principle (*tattva*) according to my teaching and inference.
O Lord of Gods, this [nature] consisting of twenty-five principles has been described to you;

likewise, the fifth is grace (*anugraha*). These nine, together with the [eight] primordial elements (*prākṛta*), reside within me, as does that radiant one in the realm of Indra and elsewhere within my own self.
Whatever consists of a body that exists within the three worlds,
O Destroyer of Tripura, all of that must be regarded by you as yourself;
for those who see otherwise do not see the Brahman-born.
This [Prakṛti], which has the unmanifest as its object and is endowed with the twenty-fifth [principle],
is for this very reason called "tattva" by the wise;
yet they declare that this [Prakṛti] is merely a modification (vikāra), while the supreme is the "tattva."
O Lord of Gods, this man is devoid of reality (nistattva) and does not understand that which is to be understood.
O bull among gods, if he were to understand the supreme Buddha while in the process of understanding,
he would become Sanatkumāra.
O Lord, he who has awakened would indeed think, "I am not this [body].
O best among the knowers of Brahman, you have heard this enumeration of the principles (tattvas),
and I have declared to you the enumeration of the nine creations in their proper order.
I shall, however, declare to you the inner self (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata).
This is not [attained] by those householders who, though disciplined and learned in the Vedas, are honored for their asceticism or have attained [merit] through penance.
The reality of the supreme self has been perceived with effort; this very reality,
as it has been described, is to be attained in its true essence—
the supreme reality of immortality that transcends all other things.

O best of great asuras, having attained the state of absolute liberation (kaivalya), I declare this to you, O lord of sages, according to its true nature: that the Lord, though established in the reality of his own being, is himself without a master.
Having obtained another divine secret, purified by that which sanctifies, you [will cut] the snare of death,
even if this earth were filled with jewels.
One should give [this] to one who is worthy, but it should not be given to one who has not been examined,
nor to one who lacks faith, nor to one whose mind is set on something else, nor to one possessed by ignorance, nor to one who is arrogant.
This should be given to one who is devoted to sacred study, endowed with virtues, and has his senses restrained;
and furthermore, O Bull-bannered One, here is a summary of these principles.
I shall declare that internal [self], along with its elemental and divine counterparts, for those born in the natural order and those born in the inverse order; indeed,
they say it is just like the web of rays of the sun.
When the day of Brahmā has been exhausted, the world enters the ocean;
the earth dissolves into water, and water dissolves into fire;
likewise, fire dissolves into wind, and wind dissolves into space alone.
Space dissolves into the mind, and the mind as well as the ego dissolve into that very [ego]. Likewise, the ego dissolves into the Great One (mahat);
they call the Great One the Unmanifest (avyakta), and they describe that as unity.
O Mahādeva, know that the dissolution of the unmanifest occurs within Brahman.
Thus, those who know reality say that this is his repeated play;
likewise, they speak of the self-referential (adhyātma), the elemental (adhibhūta), and the divine (adhidaivata).
Just as this scripture was duly proclaimed for yoga by the great-souled ones,

so too has it been set forth here in the Sāṃkhya system by those great-souled ones who contemplate the self through enumeration; thus far, O Mahādeva, has its meaning been elaborated by these high-minded ones.
One should know that Brahman is the Adhyātma (the inner self) and the Puruṣa is the Adhidaivata (the divine principle).
It is the source of all beings, and its function therein is protection. They say that Prāṇa is the Adhyātma and Kratu is the Adhidaivata.
The chariot here is the sacrifice, and its driver is action as well as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

One should know that the mind is the internal self (*adhyātma*), while the moon is the presiding deity (*adhidaivata*). Likewise, the divine power, the source of manifestation, action, and the sacred utterances (*vyāhṛti*) are likewise [the constituents].
One should know that the ear is the *adhyātma* (the internal self), and space (*ākāśa*) is the *adhidaivata* (the presiding deity).
Sound is always remembered as the action for the purpose of denoting all states of being.
Furthermore, one should know that the skin is the *adhyātma*, and wind (*vāyu*) is the *adhidaivata* therein.
13,110.137d Gather consciousness and all action there indeed.
13,110.137d@011_0128 They say that the eye is the internal [organ], and the sun is the presiding deity (adhidaivata) here.
13,110.137d@011_0129 The making known of all colors is traditionally held to be the function (karma) of form (rūpa).
One should know that the tongue is the *adhyātma* (the internal), and the waters are the *adhidaivata* (the divine) here.
The best of ascetics say that the anus is the *adhyātma*,
while emission is the *adhibhūta* (the elemental), and Mitra is the *adhidaivata*.
"O God of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow, the wise say that the generative organ is the *adhyātma*;
its *adhibhūta* is experience, and its presiding deity (*daivata*) is Prajāpati.
O you marked with the trident, the wise say that the feet are the *adhyātma*."
The object of speech is the *adhibhūta*, while Viṣṇu is the *adhidaivata* therein;
likewise, those who perceive reality say that speech itself is the *adhyātma*, and Pinākin is the deity there.
Furthermore, the object to be spoken is the *adhibhūta*, and Agni is the *adhidaivata* therein.
This incomparable inner self, together with the elements and the presiding deities,
has been fully described by me for embodied beings, O bull among the immortals;
it exists even in worms and insects, in outcastes, in dogs, and in elephants.
In a daughter, a gadfly, a mosquito, a Brahmin, a cow, and a king—indeed, all these must be viewed as equal; do not think otherwise. Those who view things differently do not possess right vision.
The gods, dānavas, gandharvas, yakṣas, rākṣasas,
and kiṃnaras do not know who this Blessed One is or from where he comes;
[they do not know] that single-syllable Brahman, "Om," which is beyond both being and non-being.
Without beginning, middle, or end, immutable, immovable, and eternal;
the Lord of Yoga, Padmanābha, Viṣṇu, the Victorious One, the Lord of the World;
the God without beginning or death, the God of gods, the Primeval One.
Having become pure and composed, with palms joined in reverence, one should bow down and worship Hari, the Lord Nārāyaṇa, who is immeasurable and unknowable.
Neither the gods nor the seers know that supreme Brahman, which is without beginning or end.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, is the one who knows this; he is the protector.
From Nārāyaṇa came the hosts of ṛṣis, as well as the Siddhas and the great serpents (mahoragas), and the gods and divine seers (devarṣis) who know him as the medicine for suffering.
They call him the one who has conquered the afflictions, in whom all creatures are established,
and in whom these worlds tremble like birds in a net. The seven seers are the seven minds, according to the vision of the Sāṃkhya sages.
The seven seers are the [seven] senses, namely the five organs of perception;
they say that the quarters of space reside in the two ears, and the moon resides in the mind.
With the mind as the sixth and intellect as the seventh, these are established within the self.
Not in the bodies, but in the self (13.110.137d). For its causes exist;
they employ all [causes] in all actions or regarding all objects, just as one's own actions proceed within the self.
These [subtle elements] pervade all seven objects of the senses.

When the collection of beings sleeps, these very subtle elements enter the unborn Self—which is comparable to the station of the world of the gods, which migrates to another body, and which is the seeker of liberation—and they dissolve;
at the time of liberation, no one perceives that solitary one, whether as self or as other.
When all beings have thus entered [into sleep], it is asked: "Who remains awake?

Here, while others are fast asleep in slumber, he who is awake is the one whose nature is dreaming; here in this abode, it is the Lord Devadyotana, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), or else the Intellect (*buddhi*).
For he perceives the visions of dreams even for one who is asleep.
While the worlds remain unawakened, he alone is awakened;
he is Sanatkumāra,
he is this wise one.
Now, there is the fiery bodily fire;
for it either belongs to the self of one who is asleep,
or it digests the food of an ignorant person who does not wake up, and thus it persists until the end.
"This has been authorized with reference to the Self.
"O dear one, the origin and the dissolution have been described by you in due order;
likewise the internal, the elemental, and similarly the divine [aspects] herein."
I shall, however, describe in its entirety the deities residing here within embodied beings—
those which abide in the bodies about which you ask, O Śaṅkara. Fire is to be known as being in the tongue, while Soma is in the speech and Māruta is in the vital breath.
In his form is the constellation, and in his tongue is indeed water;
in his navel is the pervasive ocean, as well as his nails and body hair.
The lords of the forest, the medicinal herbs, and likewise the Maruts reside within his limbs.
The years, the lunar nodes (*parvan*), and the celestial and human realms were in the ether (*ākāśa*); lightning arose in the *udāna* breath, and Parjanya likewise in the *vyāna*;
the sky was in the two breasts, and Indra was established in strength (*bala*).
Moreover, Īśāna is in the *māna* [vital breath], while Rudra is indeed in the *apāna*;
the Gandharvas and Apsarases are in the *vyāna*, as are Satya and Mitra, O Śaṅkara;
Varuṇa is in *prajñā*, and Āditya is in the eye.
In the body, the earth itself resides, and Viṣṇu is in the feet; Mitra is in the anus, and Prajāpati, O subduer of enemies, is in the generative organ.
They say that the quarters of space are in the head, and Brahmā is established in the intellect.
O Śaṅkara, the one who is awakening should be established in the Self as the presiding controller;
therefore, he is awakened, and there is no doubt that he is distinct from those who are not yet awakened.
O Śaṅkara, in the declarations of the Vedas, there is another, supreme Awakened One beyond these two.
When the various deities residing separately within bodies [are understood],
he who constantly sacrifices to Agni is a self-sacrificer (*ātmayājī*) who is fully concentrated;
he who, being composed, perceives the deities in this manner.
He who perceives in this way truly becomes a yogin here;
for he who sacrifices to the Self surpasses all those who perform external sacrifices.
He who constantly offers this entire universe as an oblation into his own mouth—[is a true sacrificer].
O Mahādeva, he who sacrifices to the Self is called a knower of the Self by the great-souled ones who know that truth.
For one who sacrifices to the Self, there is indeed a destination higher than all the highest deities; desiring the supreme, he should contemplate only the Supreme.

O Śaṅkara, O Destroyer of Tripura, just as the embodied soul transmigrates from one body to another, so shall I describe its various stations here individually. Through the application [of mantras], one attains the station of Viṣṇu by means of the two feet.
Through the anus one attains Mitra; through the generative organ, Prajāpati. Through the navel one attains the station of Varuṇa, and through the breasts, one obtains the world of Bhūḥ.
Through the two arms one attains the station of Vāsava, and through the two ears, one shall obtain the quarters.

One should place the sun in the eye and the station of Brahmā in the head. Then, he who, being composed, should hold the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) within his heads, attains through his intellect the state of the substance; of this there is no doubt.
Higher than the unmanifest is that which is supremely pure, immeasurable, and free from affliction;
they call that the supreme eternal, which the wise man attains. Because he is awakened through both the awakening and the non-awakening, he is recited as "the Awakened One" (Buddha).
One constantly perceives both the awakened and the unawakened;
this "transforming person" (vikārapuruṣa) is traditionally known as the "awakening one. That which consists of the twenty-five principles is proclaimed therein—regarding this, there is doubt.

Because he abides in his own nature, he is taught to be "stationed. The Great Self, Mahādeva, presides over this great [universe]. On account of this presiding, he is called the "Presider" (adhiṣṭhātā), according to the vision of the scriptures.

This unintelligent god perceives the web of delusion; the wise say that this is indeed the similarity between [the self] and the unmanifest. Thinking "I am he, I am he" because of this eternal ignorance, [he is bound].
If this radiant one were to perceive [it], I would think [he is awake];
yet, being unawakened, he would not move about like a small fish in water.
O Lord of the Three Worlds, all these deities have thus been described in their entirety.
Now, learn from me in due order the practice of yoga:
having stayed in empty houses, in forests, on the seashore, or in caves,
and having steadied the three staffs, one indeed becomes non-dual.
Facing either the east, the north, the west, or even the south, having assumed the seat according to the prescribed rule and seated himself in the *svastika* posture,
he should raise his radiant body.

One should hold fast to that Brahman exactly as it has been taught by the Guru. Restrained and moderate in diet, one should avoid [sexual intercourse] during the three periods; one should be fully composed regarding the voiding of urine and feces and regarding food.
During the remaining time, however, one should apply oneself with a well-composed mind; one should withdraw the senses from their objects by means of the mind,
and likewise restrain the mind by means of the intellect, O best among the wise.
Restraining that which runs about and quivers here and there with its lack of fortitude,
and having suppressed all mental constructions (*saṃkalpa*), one should then attain steadiness. One should know that state of one-pointedness to be the supreme, most secret of all secrets.
Like a lamp standing in a windless place that shines intensely without flickering,
so too the mind is made to revolve only upwards and not sideways,
when that [Self] which dwells in the heart stands facing it directly.
O Lord of Gods, the mind becomes as motionless as a stone. Whether dwelling in a solitary, noiseless place or among people where there is clamor,
the disciplined yogi who does not waver has heard the method of yoga.
Then one beholds that Brahman, blazing and established within oneself;
like lightning in a cloud, it is singular and without support.
It stands in profound darkness, yet is free from darkness and devoid of consciousness.
Whether conscious or unconscious, blazing with its own splendor,
that which is the size of a thumb’s joint is the blameless state of supreme beatitude—
the Great Being, infinite, independent, and free from all feverish distress.
The light of lights, the god Viṣṇu, who is utterly stainless; Nārāyaṇa, subtler than the subtle, the supreme lord of lords;
the eternal one who is beyond the universe, the Lord Nārāyaṇa who is the universe itself.
Without understanding this, O dear one, people sink into the ocean of saṃsāra;
but having seen it, the ascetics, freed from fever and liberated from the fear of birth and death, have crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra and no longer grieve.
Aṇimā, laghimā, bhūmā, prāpti, and prākāmya,
as well as īśitva, vaśitva, and yatrakāmāvasāyitā—
this eightfold yoga is traditionally taught as the culmination of all yogas.
Having perceived themselves as selfless, immeasurable, and eternal, they—
being the most powerful by virtue of their strength among Daityas, gods, and humans— enter radiant bodies through this yoga.
This reality, which you inquire about, is without beginning or end;
we constantly worship this eternal dharma of yoga. O best of gods, there is no dharma more weighty than the dharma of yoga.
For some wise men say that among all dharmas, this dharma— which is unconditioned and free from rebirth— is in truth supreme;
others, who rely upon the fruit of knowledge, say that there is nothing beyond it.
This person established in knowledge has been described by me as being subject to transformation;
yet some call that very person the God Maheśvara, whom those devoted to yoga constantly perceive through meditation.
Some always declare that knowledge is considered the supreme [means];
the Sāṃkhyas, being liberated through knowledge alone, attain the absolute. The Yogas of supreme intelligence, however, apply their contemplation both to the inner self and elsewhere.
Thus far has this supreme vision of yoga been declared to you. Sanatkumāra said:
"I shall now proclaim the knowledge of Sāṃkhya, which is the demonstration of thorough enumeration."
Prior to the senses is the mind; after that, the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Beyond the ego-sense is the intellect (buddhi); higher than the intellect is the Great One (mahat).
Beyond the Great One is the Unmanifest (avyakta); higher than the Unmanifest is the Puruṣa.
This much, O best of gods, is the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas:
the unmanifest, intellect, ego, and the five great elements;
likewise the mind, the specific objects, and the ten sense organs.

This is the twenty-fourfold reality, commensurate with the Great Puruṣa; O Lord of Gods, those who possess awakened consciousness and are high-souled speak of the eternal union between these two— the Unmanifest and the Puruṣa.

O Wielder of the Trident, they declare that this which is designated as *tamas* consists of both unity and multiplicity throughout millions of creations and dissolutions; for it is from the Unmanifest that individual souls are repeatedly uprooted and go forth again and again.

"O Lord, this Great Self (mahān ātmā) is the source of the qualities (guṇas); yet, because it abides within the qualities, they call this one—which is characterized by the unmanifest (avyakta)—a quality itself. Occupied by this [Self], the manifest (vyakta) then perceives the three qualities."
This [self] is of the nature of insentience and does not perceive another;
for the ego-maker (ahaṃkāra), though conscious, is perpetually unawakened due to its conceit. [It belongs to] the stainless, pure, healthy, and great Self.
One should possess stainless and noble conduct toward both the awakened and the unawakened.
He becomes a witness and a non-enjoyer, the embodiment of pure being, and devoid of qualities.
Indeed, he who is devoid of qualities is entirely distinct from both the awakened and the unawakened.
Equanimous and pure, he is likewise inseparable from both of those;
though perceiving, he does not perceive, for the eternal is thus awakened.
He alone is insentient because the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*) is unmanifest.
I am that very self; there is no other than me who conceives such an egoistic notion (*abhimanyate*).
No one else thinks "there is another me" by which the mind would become insentient.
Even though he is conscious, one who lacks self-knowledge (*anātmavān*) would conceive of himself in this very way.
I alone exist; there is no other for me who follows the power of the awakened. Abiding in the unmanifest, this [unawakened self] constantly identifies with the qualities (guṇas).
Therefore, it is described by the great ones who know reality as being presided over by that [Puruṣa].

Joined with egoism, he then conceives of that [field] as "I"; having entered the field, the one of poor intellect, lacking self-mastery, perceives it thus: "I alone create another, a second, the charioteer of the world."
The third creation, known as the *sarga*, consists of all states of being (*bhāva*) and ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).
From that, the elements (*bhūta*) arose; from ego-sense, the mind (*manas*) was produced.
Then the wise one turned toward all the streams [of sensory perception].

In the same way, O one marked by the trident, the Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati), seeking sense objects among living beings at the sacrifice again and again, does not know the mind, nor the self, nor the ego through the five senses and their five corresponding objects.
"O best among the wise, even the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) does not know the intellect (*buddhi*).
Thus it is, O illustrious one; others do not speak of this principle. United with the ego-sense, [the self] is always directed toward the stream [of rebirth]."
Thus, this principle whose nature is transformation, designated as the Great Puruṣa,
repeatedly expands the entire universe and withdraws it again;
because of its attachment, the entire universe remains situated within the heart of the Unmanifest.
He remains lying through the entire night, and at the end of the night, with the arrival of day,
he awakens again; likewise, many who are devoid of qualities are overcome by ignorance, which is unmanifest and of the nature of darkness.
For if he were to think, "I have another [self] beyond this one," then he would repeatedly create and dissolve himself. A wise person should consider this subtle subject as being unmanifest.

O Mahādeva, the twenty-fifth principle is the transformation of the Great Puruṣa. Having awakened, he perceives this; yet, while creating, he did not perceive it. Furthermore, he deposits those very *guṇas* within himself by means of himself.
He has come under the sway of the unmanifest, which is ignorance and of the nature of darkness.
For while he is conscious, he experiences that which is unconscious; though awakened, he remains as if unawakened.
He is indifferent, pure, detached, signless, unblemished, and stainless.
The twenty-sixth Lord exists as the Buddha, pure and free from affliction.
Physicians indeed declare that this [universe] extends from the unmanifest (avyakta) up to the particularized (viśeṣa). However, some wise men say it is devoid of these very [categories].

But some, O Great-minded One, perceiving it as devoid of reality (nistattva), speak thus; others, those of great soul, declare it to be indeed designated as reality (tattva). Because of hearing about reality, they truly call this very thing reality itself.
And because of his taking recourse in the *tattva*, O Maheśvara, he becomes possessed of *sattva*.
Thus, O mighty-armed one, this self of transformation, while becoming conscious, exists as the unmanifest within the manifest; such is *sattva* and such are the two qualities (*guṇa*).

Knowledge becomes ignorance, and that which is designated as "grasping" arises; those who understand this in truth through Yoga and Sāṃkhya, possessing the wisdom of the scriptures, are released from the dense darkness of the Unmanifest (avyakta).
While those who perceive with subtle insight were thus discussing the meaning of the scriptures,
their understanding expanded in every direction like a drop of oil upon water. Indeed,
among all branches of knowledge, true wisdom is traditionally known as awakening.
By means of which the best of ascetics perceive both knowledge (*vidyā*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), this is that supreme triple science (*trayī*); the fourth is remembered as *ānvīkṣikī*.
Understanding this, one who has attained equanimity within the Self should awaken through awakening.
That which is unawakened and unmanifest is known by the name of ignorance (avidyā).
It is a delusion joined with nothing but sorrow.
Having understood this, one becomes awakened; what other characteristic of an awakened one could there be?
But those who do not understand this follow the power of the awakened; being of unawakened nature, they will be born again and again from the unmanifest,
and remaining under the sway of the unawakened, they will continue to weigh themselves against that very same [unawakened state].
And those others as well who have their minds fixed on that, they too shall partake in this fruit.
Having known this, those who perceive the goal endowed with yoga do not grieve;
they shall attain sovereignty and radiant isolation.
Released from the bonds of ignorance, they have crossed over the fetters of *saṃsāra*. They have crossed the terrible, bottomless, and nameless ocean of ignorance,
O subduer of enemies, wherein all beings sink again and again.
This knowledge and likewise ignorance have been explained by me to you according to their true meaning;
as well as that which is to be given and not received, the Sāṃkhya system and its followers,
as well as unity and diversity, and the imperishable and the perishable.

O Lord of Gods, I shall explain to you the threefold liberation: the elaboration concerning the awakened, the unawakened, and the one who is not yet awakened. Listen further, O best of gods, regarding the gods.
Whatever has not been heard and nothing whatsoever that has not been seen—
Sanatkumāra,
I shall explain all that to you; listen with one-pointed mind and devoted attention.
I shall declare the omens of death according to their true nature; listen to them, sir.

If a man should see a person standing in the middle, toward the north, facing the south, with the appearance of lightning— 13,110.137d@011_0371 13,110.137d@011_0372—if a human being should behold such a person situated there.
Within three years, one should know that the departure of the body is imminent;
the wise Śaṅkara has declared this to be the fruit of such an ill omen (ariṣṭa). Furthermore, for one who sees the solar disc as pure and devoid of rays—

One should know that the casting off of the body is imminent after six months if one perceives a hole in the shadow of the moon, or even if one perceives one's own feet [reflected] therein. One should know that the casting off of the body is imminent after one year.
If one sees a headless person within the pupil of the eye,
one should know that the casting off of the body is imminent within six months.
If, having covered the ears with both hands, one does not hear any sound, [the same should be known].
One should know that within a month, the casting off of the body will have arrived; one smells a putrid odor even upon encountering something fragrant and radiant;
and even while staying in a temple of the gods, one becomes subject to death within seven nights.
One who is composed should maintain the state of holding [the breath] in all the limbs;
in this way, O Maheśvara, he conquers death and not otherwise,
if he wishes to live for a long time, O great sage.
If he does not desire [to remain] for a long time, he should abandon the self by means of the self,
contemplating solely that which is partless and free from affliction;
then, being pure, he [contemplates] that which is changeless and beyond primordial nature (*prakṛti*).
Through that, one attains a state of similarity with the Puruṣa upon the casting off of the body.
For I have truly described to you these omens of death for one who is awake;
and by means of concentration (*dhāraṇā*) upon all the limbs, O bull among gods, one may conquer death.
Furthermore, learn from me the vision of unity and multiplicity,
as well as the imperishable and the perishable, according to the fourfold arrangement;
for all principles, O one of great luster, have the unmanifest as their beginning.
They say that the twenty-fourth transformation is endowed with the Puruṣa; moreover, the vision of oneness is considered inferior to [the vision of] diversity.
The group of twenty-five constitutes liberation, which is free from old age and death.
That Puruṣa is taught as being without modification by his very nature;
yet that same Puruṣa is traditionally known as the twenty-fifth when he is subject to modification.
If he were entirely without modification, he would not be the principle (tattva), but rather mere existence (bhava).
But when modifications exist, that which is designated as "reality" (tattva) is spoken of;
if this [reality] does not attain unmanifestness, there is no doubt because of its distinction.
Thus it becomes devoid of reality, thus it is existence, and thus it is a quality.

Through the abandonment of the qualities of transformation and by becoming distinct from primordial nature (*prakṛti*), one becomes pure. Then, free from the process of creation, one attains manifoldness as a partaker of liberation (*apavarga*).
Being awakened, the wise one awakens and becomes equanimous.
And this [Self] becomes imperishable (*akṣara*), or it may, in an instant, become fallen [from its state];
the manifestation of that which is unmanifest, which is devoid of qualities yet the source of all qualities, has been described.
This is both unity and diversity, being both the imperishable (*akṣara*) and the perishable (*kṣara*).
O you who are marked by the trident, I have thus explained to you the omens of death as well as the signs of liberation; I shall now speak here of that which remains,
knowing which ascetics have attained the state of absolute, stainless freedom.
The followers of Sāṃkhya and the followers of Yoga, having burned away their impurities and being freed from the fever of passion,
have attained formlessness; they are devoid of qualities and free from fear— O Mahādeva, they are sinless and liberated from the ocean of saṃsāra.
In the process of procreation, the primordial nature (prakṛti) is always the source of all qualities;
though she is perpetually distracted, she is the cause of this much activity. She repeatedly brings forth both the non-existent and the existent.
By means of primordial consciousness,
he who is beyond both the conscious and the unconscious perceives the mind through the intellect as a single unity;
he is remembered as neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent.

It is distinct, pure, other, and likewise not of the nature of primordial matter (*aprakṛti*); it is remembered as the Puruṣa who is indifferent toward primordial matter. United with this Puruṣa of transformation, she creates the world.

And again, he assumes various qualities within himself in a different manner; like a fish known to exist within water, he arises from the very activity of primordial nature (prakṛti). In that same way, he alone will bring forth thousands of fields (kṣetra).
But he who knows the dissolution of the field is called the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña). Those people who perceive reality declare that their union is eternal.
Thus, this Person of Transformation is traditionally held to be both the unreal and the real.

But when it undergoes modification, they call that "transformation" (*vikṛti*). However, when one considers this [Self] to be the original cause (*prakṛti*) of transformation, then it attains the state of being a transformation and proceeds to a state distinct from transformation.
When it is distinct from both primordial nature (*prakṛti*) and its transformations (*vikāra*),
it is pure, supreme, stainless, awakened, and eternal;
it is unjoined, partless, clean, imperishable, ageless, and without wound.
Having united with that pure [element], becoming conscious, and radiant,
he attains liberation from the manifest, the unawakened, and the insentient—
just as a gnat emerges from a fig tree after its destruction.
Likewise, through the renunciation of the unmanifest, the twenty-fifth principle becomes free from the sense of "mine. Just as a drop of water resting on a lotus leaf does not adhere to it,
even so the twenty-fifth principle is not tainted by the sphere of the unmanifest.
Like space, he is unattached; thus unattached, he is the supreme one. The twenty-fifth is the Buddha, who has attained equality with the Buddha.
For this is the primordial gnosis that has arisen from reality itself.
O sinless one, O mighty-armed one, from those who were born before and from those born of Brahmā, there arose the primordial creation, which was supreme yet enveloped in darkness;
it entered the Lord, whose limbs are indivisible, who is unbreakable, undecaying, and immortal.
Sanaka, Sanandana, and the third, Sanātana—
they know the supreme, imperishable Dharma, which transcends all decay,
[arising] from the Unmanifest, the subtle, the woundless, and that which is designated as Form.
The Lord Kṣetrajña dwells there, devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
To us, who were born together with him, this supreme knowledge has arisen.
Indeed, we wander through the worlds in embodied forms.

Being born again and again in various places, the wielder of the Pināka bow attained supreme knowledge as he became dispassionate toward the pairs of opposites; from Kapila, his root teacher, he gained the definitive realization of the principles of reality.
I have acquired Yoga and Sāṃkhya in their entirety from that best of sages.
By him many disciples were awakened as seers of reality;
having understood that, many disciples have been instructed by me as well.
The truth that removes birth and death, the eternal knowledge and the object of knowledge—
having known which, those who possess the knowledge of reality do not grieve, being free from the senses,
pure of the seeds of impurity, truly free from mud, and beyond the syllables.

They are independent, equal to the Independent One, and remembered as partless; they are eternal, immutable, graspable by darkness, and luminous; likewise, they are all free from sin, established in purity (*sattva*), and without blemish.
They are liberated and solitary, likewise free from delusion and fear; O illustrious one, they are all formless and devoid of the fever of passion.
[So too are] Hiraṇyanābha, Triśiras, as well as Prahrāda and Bhāskara.
Vasu and Viśvāvasu, as well as Pañcaśikha; Gārgya, Āsuri, Āvantya, Gautama, and Avrata;
Kātyāyana, Namuci, Hari, and Damana.
These and many others have been shown to be the very reality:
some are liberated and remain so, some abide [in their state], and others die according to their own will;
thus has the threefold bondage and likewise the threefold liberation been demonstrated.
Ignorance, passion, and likewise primordial union—from these, bondage is said to arise; now hear from me also about liberation.
To that extent, one is completely bound by whatever connection has been formed.

"Through the abandonment of the complete destruction [of all taints], liberation occurs; such is our sacred tradition," said Bhīṣma. "The person who has desisted from all attachments is solitary and stainless."
Having spoken thus to the high-souled Īśvara,
the Blessed One Sanatkumāra departed, taking his place in the sky.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, tell me that which is the best of all sacred fords (tīrthas);
you ought to explain to me that wherein supreme purity indeed resides.
Bhīṣma said:
Indeed, all sacred fords (*tīrtha*) are virtuous for the wise;
however, listen with a concentrated mind to what constitutes that which is both a sacred ford and purity. It is a deep, stainless, and pure lake whose waters are truth and whose depths are fortitude.
One should bathe in the mental ford (mānasa-tīrtha), taking hold of eternal being (sattva).
The purification of the ford consists of freedom from desire, gentleness, truth, straightforwardness,
non-violence toward all beings, kindness, self-restraint, and tranquility.
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from dualities, and free from possessions—
those who subsist on alms are pure and have become sacred fords (*tīrtha*). However, one who knows reality and is free from the notion of "I" is said to be the supreme ford.

Devotion to either Nārāyaṇa or Rudra is considered the supreme sacred ford (tīrtha). This is the characteristic of purity for you: the constant observation of all things. For those whose passion (rajas), darkness (tamas), and even goodness (sattva) have been washed away from the self—
They are not attached to purity or impurity; they seek only their own task. Delighting in the renunciation of everything, they are all-knowing and all-seeing.
Through purity, they have purity of conduct as their goal; they are the true bathing-places and they themselves are pure.
One whose limbs are merely wet with water is not called "bathed.
He is truly bathed who is bathed in self-restraint, being pure both outwardly and inwardly. Those who have no longing for things past and are free from the sense of "mine" regarding things acquired—
Purity alone is supreme for those in whom no desire arises;
in this world, wisdom is indeed the purity of the body in particular,
as well as the state of possessing nothing and the clarity of the mind.
Purity of conduct, purity of mind, and purity at sacred fords are highly beneficial;
however, that purity which arises from knowledge is considered the supreme purity.
Furthermore, by means of the mind as a lamp and through the power of the knowledge of Brahman—

Those who have bathed in the mental sacred ford (*mānasa-tīrtha*), who possess knowledge of that [ford] and perceive the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), are truly pure. A man who has established internal purity, who is constantly endowed with right disposition (*bhāva*),
and who is perfected solely in virtue, is always pure indeed.
O Bhārata, these sacred fords (*tīrtha*) situated within the body have been declared;
now hear also of those meritorious sacred fords that exist upon the earth,
just as certain regions of the body are fashioned as pure.
Likewise, through the regions of the earth, the sacred waters,
the longing for a holy ford, bathing therein, and the libations offered to the ancestors,
they shake off their sin at these tīrthas; purified, they go happily to heaven.
Through their support of the virtuous and by the power of the earth itself,
those regions became exceedingly meritorious; likewise, other holy fords (tīrthas) became so through the power of the waters and of the mind, as well as the earth.
He who has bathed in both [the fire and the water] shall quickly attain success.
Just as strength devoid of action, or action bereft of strength,
does not accomplish any task in this world, so too one who is endowed with both succeeds.
Thus, endowed with both physical purity and purity through sacred bathing-places, one then attains success; this is the twofold, supreme purity.
Yudhiṣṭhira.
"Whatever great fruit is the most excellent among all fasts—
Bhīṣma,
you ought to tell me that which is also undoubtedly present in the world."
Listen, O King, to that which was sung by the Self-born One himself;
having performed this, a person shall become liberated—of this there is no doubt.
On the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one should [worship] Keśava for a full day and night.

One obtains the merit of an Arcya-Aśvamedha sacrifice, and one’s evil deeds are destroyed. Likewise, in the month of Pauṣa, by worshipping [the Lord] with the name "Nārāyaṇa," one attains the Vājapeya sacrifice and shall reach supreme perfection.
On the twelfth day of the month of Māgha, by means of a single day and night,
one obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and uplifts one's entire lineage;
likewise, in the month of Phālguna, one should worship [the Lord] as Govinda.
He obtains the Atirātra sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma;
by remembering "Viṣṇu" on the twelfth day of Caitra at dawn and dusk,
he obtains the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice and goes to the world of the gods.
On the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha, by worshipping Madhusūdana,
one obtains the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the world of Soma. On the twelfth day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, by [worshipping] Trivikrama for a full day and night...
One attains the Gavāmaya sacrifice and rejoices with the Apsarases.
On the twelfth day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship [the deity] as Vāmana;
one thereby attains the Naramedha sacrifice and gains great merit.
On the twelfth day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, by worshipping Śrīdhara for a full day and night,
one obtains the merit of the five great sacrifices and rejoices seated upon a celestial chariot.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, by worshipping him as Hṛṣīkeśa—
One obtains the merit of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice and indeed becomes purified in soul.
By worshipping [the Lord] as Padmanābha on the twelfth day of the month of Āśvina, one shall obtain the meritorious fruit of a thousand cows; of this there is no doubt.
On the twelfth day of the month of Kārttika, by worshipping [the Lord] as Dāmodara, a man or a woman attains the merit of the Gavya sacrifice; of this there is no doubt.
Thus, he who worships the Lotus-eyed One for an entire year...
One attains the recollection of past births and shall find much gold. He who daily attains that state of Upendra should,
at the conclusion [of the rite], feed the Brahmins or cause clarified butter to be given as a gift.
"From this point forward, there shall be no further fasting; this is the settled conclusion," said the Lord Viṣṇu himself in ancient times. Vaiśampāyana related this.
Having approached Bhīṣma, the aged grandfather of the Kurus, who was lying upon a bed of arrows, the highly wise Yudhiṣṭhira questioned him. Yudhiṣṭhira.
"How may one possess knowledge, beauty, good fortune, and popularity?
Bhīṣma:
