How may one become a partaker of happiness, joined with virtue, wealth, and pleasure?"
In the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon was conjoined with the Mūla asterism,
O Indra among kings, he placed his feet under Mūla, then Rohiṇī upon his shanks,
Aśvinī upon his thighs, and likewise the two Āṣāḍhās upon his upper legs.

One should know that Phālgunī is the secret place, and likewise Kṛttikā is the hips; one should know Bhādrapadā is the navel, and Revatī is the circle of the eyes; Dhaniṣṭhā, Anurādhā, and Uttarā are the back.
One should indicate the two arms during the Viśākhā constellation, and the hands during the Hasta;
O King, the fingers during the Punarvasu, and likewise the nails during the Āśleṣā;
the neck during the Jyeṣṭhā, O Indra among kings, and the ears during the Śravaṇa.

O Indra among kings, the face is [ruled] by Puṣya; the teeth and lips are said to be Svāti. One should know that Hasta, Śatabhiṣaj, and Maghā constitute the nose, while Mṛgaśiras is the eyes and Anurādhā (Mitra) is the forehead.
One should know that the head is under Bharaṇī, and the hair under Ārdrā, O lord of men. When [the rite] is completed, one should give ghee to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
[the donor] is born fortunate, handsome, wise, and an enjoyer of pleasures.
He is born with all his limbs complete, like the lord of the stars on the night of the full moon.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O mighty-armed one, you who are learned in all the scriptures!"

I wish to hear the supreme rule regarding the cycle of existence for mortals. O Indra among kings, by what conduct do men living in this world attain the highest heaven, and how, O King, do they fall into hell?
"Having abandoned the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, people depart from this world to that other world; who indeed follows them?
Bhīṣma said:
"The venerable Bṛhaspati of noble intellect is approaching. Ask this highly fortunate one about this eternal secret;
for indeed, it cannot be explained by anyone else today."
"There is no other speaker equal to Bṛhaspati to be found anywhere.
Vaiśampāyana said:
"While Pārtha and Gāṅgeya were thus conversing at that time,"
The blessed Bṛhaspati, whose soul was purified, arrived there.
Then the king, preceded by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, rose up,
and all those members of the assembly offered him incomparable worship.
Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, firm in his vows, approached the blessed Bṛhaspati and, having approached him according to the proper custom, asked a question.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, expert in all treatises:
who is the true companion of a mortal—is it the father, the mother, the son, or the teacher?
For when people have cast off the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth,"
"When one goes to the other world, who indeed follows him?
Bṛhaspati said:
"O Indra among kings, a creature is born alone, and alone it perishes."
Alone one crosses over difficulties, and alone one goes to a miserable rebirth;
for there is no companion— neither father, mother, brother, son, nor teacher,
nor the circle of kinsmen and relations, nor likewise the circle of friends.
Having abandoned the dead body, which is like a piece of wood or a clod of earth, people attend to it for a mere moment and then depart with their faces turned away;
once that body has been left behind by them, Dharma alone follows it.
Therefore, men should always cultivate Dharma for the sake of companionship;
a living being endowed with Dharma goes to the supreme heavenly realm,
while likewise one joined with Adharma is reborn in hell.
Therefore, a wise person should practice dharma with wealth acquired through righteous means;
for dharma alone is the companion of human beings in the world beyond.
Even one who is not deeply learned [might act wrongly] out of greed, delusion, compassion, or fear.
Deluded by greed for the sake of another, a man commits improper deeds.
Dharma, artha, and kāma—this triad is the fruit of life.
This triad should be attained while strictly avoiding unrighteousness (adharma).
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"I have heard the words of the Blessed One, which are consistent with dharma and supremely beneficial;
yet, a desire arises in my mind to understand the investigation of the body."
"When one has died, being devoid of a body, subtle, and having reached a state of unmanifestness— having entered a realm beyond the reach of the eye— how does dharma follow him? Bṛhaspati said:
Earth, wind, space, water, and light as the fifth,
together with the intellect and the self, constantly behold the *dharma* of all living beings here, serving as their perpetual witnesses.
And along with these, Dharma also follows that living being. O Great-Minded One, skin, bone, flesh, semen, and blood—
these abandon the body once it is bereft of life.
Then that living being, endowed with dharma, prospers in happiness;
for the living being itself indeed attains [the fruit],
and thereafter they behold its karma, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious.
"The deities reside within the five elements; what more do you wish to hear?
Concerning this world and the next, what further shall I tell you?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The Blessed One has shown how the dharma follows;
however, I wish to know this: how does semen come forth?
Bṛhaspati said:
"O lord of men, those deities residing within the body who consume food—
namely earth, wind, space, water, light, and likewise the mind—
when these five elements are thus satisfied, O king of kings,"
When the self is purified through the mind as the sixth [sense], the great semen is produced.
From that, O Pārtha, the embryo arises from the union of a woman and a man.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
You have explained how the embryo is formed;
now let it be told how a person, once born, proceeds through life.
Bṛhaspati said:
"As soon as he is near them, he is constantly overwhelmed by those elements;
and when released from those elements, he again goes to another state."
But that very *jīva*, joined with the elements, indeed attains [its state].
Then the deities residing within the five elements behold its karma, whether it be auspicious or inauspicious. What more do you wish to hear?
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Blessed One, having cast off skin, bone, and flesh, and being divested of those elements, where does that living soul abide when it experiences pleasure and pain?"
Bṛhaspati said: Having encountered these three— subjection to enjoyment, subjection to karma, and subjection to torment— he experiences their fruit according to his actions.
The individual soul (jīva), joined with merit, quickly attains the state of semen;
having reached the menses of women, O Bhārata, it gives birth in due time.
[It experiences] the suffering of Yama’s messengers and the slaughter by Yama’s messengers.
A person experiences suffering, the wheel of saṃsāra, and affliction;
O King, from birth onwards in this world,
that living being indeed reaps the fruit of his own actions, depending upon the result of dharma.

If, from birth onwards, one practices dharma according to one's ability, then that person, having become [a god], enjoys happiness eternally. But if, in the interim, one practices adharma instead of dharma...
Immediately after happiness, that living being encounters suffering;
immediately after suffering, happiness.
Bound by these two, this pair is constant.

One who is joined with unrighteousness, having gone to the realm of Yama and encountered great suffering, is born in the womb of an animal. By whichever specific action one performs here, one is born into that particular womb.

Listen as I declare how the living being, joined with delusion, enters the terrible realm of Yama, as it is described in the scripture along with the histories and the Vedic hymns. 13.112.039–039c. Mortal man enters the dreadful domain of Yama.
It is said that the person who always fails to perform this [rite] constantly falls many times into the womb of a worm; likewise,
there are here on earth holy places equal to the abodes of the gods.
Excluding those born of animal wombs, all other sentient beings throughout the realm of Yama— though that realm is meritorious and equal in its qualities to the world of Brahmā—
a living being, bound by their fixed karma, undergoes sufferings.
I shall hereafter describe to you by which specific sinful action a man goes to a terrible hell.
Having studied the four Vedas, a twice-born man who is possessed by delusion—
Having accepted [a gift] from one who has fallen [from his caste], one is then born in the womb of a donkey.
O Bhārata, as a donkey he lives for fifteen years;
having died as a donkey, he lives for seven years as a bull.
Even a bull that has died is born as a Brahmarākṣasa;
after being a Brahmarākṣasa for three months, he is then born as a Brāhmaṇa.
But having officiated at a sacrifice for one who is fallen (patita), one is born in the womb of a worm.
There he lives for fifteen years, O Bhārata;
then, released from the state of a worm, he is born as a donkey. He remains a donkey for five years, and for five years he is a pig.

For five years he becomes a cock, for five years a jackal, and for one year a dog; thereafter he is born as a human being. This applies to the foolish disciple who commits an evil act against his preceptor.
That living being undoubtedly undergoes three transmigrations in this world:
first, O king of kings, he becomes a dog; then a carnivorous beast; then a donkey;
thereafter, as an afflicted ghost (preta), he is finally born as a Brāhmaṇa.
That sinful disciple who, even in his mind, approaches the wife of his guru,
goes to the lowest states of transmigratory existence because of his unrighteous mind;
having been born in the womb of a dog, he lives there for three years.
Even there, having met his end, he is born in the womb of a worm;
having attained the state of a worm, he lives for one year. Then, meeting his death, he is born in the womb of a Brahmin.
If a teacher should strike a disciple who is like a son without cause, acting out of his own self-will, he too is born as a *haṃsa*. Furthermore,
that son who disregards his father or mother [is likewise reborn].
O King, that creature, having died, is first born as a donkey;
having attained the state of a donkey, it lives for ten years. Then, after one year, that human is born as a crocodile.
If both the mother and father of a son are angry with him, he too,
due to his ill-will toward his elders, is born as a donkey after death;
the donkey lives for ten months, and the dog for fourteen.
After seven months as a cat, he is then born as a human being;
by reviling his mother and father, he is born as a sarika bird,
but by striking them, O King, he is born as a tortoise.
For ten years he becomes a tortoise, for three years a porcupine,
and having been a predatory beast for six months, he is then born as a human being—
[this is the fate] of one who, while subsisting on his master’s food, serves those who are hostile to the king.
Having fallen into delusion, he dies and is born as a monkey;
for ten years he is a monkey and for three years a mouse.
Then, having become a dog for six months, he is thereafter born as a human being.
Having died, he may be born in the womb of a monkey, and from there he becomes a pig;
then he becomes a dog, and after that he becomes a human. But a man who misappropriates a deposit, having gone to the realm of Yama, [suffers there].
Having passed through a hundred transmigrations, he is born in the womb of a worm;
there he lives for fifteen years, O Bhārata, until,
having exhausted his evil deeds, he is thereafter born as a human being.
Furthermore, a man who is envious is born after death as a *śārṅgaka* bird;
one who is envious, contemptuous, and a *caṇḍāla* experiences suffering.
But a wicked-minded man who betrays trust is born as a fish.
Having been a fish for eight years, O Bhārata, he is born as a deer;
after four months as a deer, he is then born as a goat. Having reached his end as a goat, he does so when the year is complete.
That creature is born as an insect, and from there it becomes a human being.
[One may eat] grains, barley, sesame, mung beans, horse gram, mustard seeds, chickpeas, peas,
lentils, mung beans, wheat, and linseed.
And that insentient creature who, out of delusion, steals other crops,
O Great King, is born as a shameless rat.
After being born as a rat, he is then born as a pig.
Then, O great king, after passing away, he is born again as a pig;
as soon as he is born as a pig, O ruler of men, he dies of disease.
Thereafter, O monarch, that deluded one is born as a dog because of that very karma.
Having become a dog for five years, he is thereafter born as a human. But having committed the violation of another's wife, he is indeed born as a wolf;
then as a dog, a jackal, a vulture, a snake, a heron, and likewise a crane.
But that evil-minded man who, deluded, violates his brother’s wife,
O King, becomes a male cuckoo for one year.
The same applies to one who violates the wife of a friend, the wife of a teacher, or likewise the wife of a king.
Having committed an assault out of lust, one who dies is born as a pig;
he may also be born as a dog, a cat, a cock, or even an ant.
As a pig for five years, and for five years as a porcupine.
For five years he is a *vilāḷa*, for five years a cock;
for six months he is an ant, and for one month he is a worm. Having undergone these transmigrations, he is born from a womb of worms.
There he lives for thirteen months in the womb of a worm;
then, having exhausted his demerit, he is born again as a human being.
O Lord, this occurs when a marriage, a gift, or even a sacrifice is about to take place.

He who, out of delusion, creates an obstacle [to the offering], is born as a worm after death; indeed, he who consumes that substance shall hold the position of a temple guardian. Having been a dog for seven births, he is thereafter born as a human.
Having held the lordship over a village of twice-born Brahmins and having consumed the property of a Brahmin,
Puṣkala then entered a hundred births as a dog and subsequently became a Caṇḍāla; fifteen years ago, he gradually became a human being once more.
O Bhārata, such a worm lives for fifteen years;
having exhausted the results of his unrighteousness, he is thereafter born as a human being.
Furthermore, he who, having previously given away a maiden, bestows her upon a second man...
O King, that creature too, having died, is born in the womb of a worm;
there it lives for thirteen years, O Yudhiṣṭhira, until,
through the exhaustion of its unrighteousness, it is joined with merit and is thereafter born as a human being.
Then, having met his end, he attains human status. But if, after performing rites for the gods and likewise rites for the ancestors,
he eats without having first offered them, he is indeed born as a crow.
For ten years he is born as a crow, and from there he becomes a cock;
he is also born as a quail for a month, and after that, he becomes human again.
This applies to one who treats with contempt an elder brother who is equal to a father.
Having met his death, he is born into the womb of a crane;
as a crane, he lives for twenty-four months— ten, two, seven, and five—
and then, having met his end, he attains human status.
A *vṛṣala* who has approached a Brāhmaṇī woman is born in the womb of a worm;
having produced offspring there, he is thereafter born as a mouse.
But an ungrateful man, O King, having died and gone to the realm of Yama, [suffers there].
In the realm of Yama, one meets with terrible slaughter at the hands of the enraged;
[one encounters] the *paṭṭisa* spear, the mallet, the trident, and the dreadful pot of fire;
the horrific forest of sword-leaves, the sands, and the thorny *śālmalī* tree.
Having gone to the realm of Yama, he undergoes these and many other torments; having experienced further agonies, he is born from a womb of worms.
Then, O bull of the Bharatas, that ungrateful man is struck there by fierce [beings].
Having undergone fierce torments there, O Bhārata, he is then slain;
having entered the wheel of saṃsāra, he is born in the womb of a worm. He remains a worm for fifteen years, O Bhārata.
Then, having entered the womb, the infant dies right there;
thereafter, the creature is born again through many hundreds of wombs.
Having passed through many cycles of transmigration, he is then born as an animal.
Having experienced suffering for many groups of years here after dying,
and being joined with the state of no-return [to higher states], he is then born as a tortoise. That lowest of men, having killed an unarmed man while himself armed, [is reborn thus].
If one who seeks wealth, or even an enemy, dies, he is born as a donkey.
That donkey lives for two years and is then killed by a weapon.
Having died, he is born in the womb of a deer, constantly filled with anxiety.
When a year has passed, that deer is slain by a weapon;
having become a deer, he is then slaughtered most cruelly with weapons.
Once the deer is killed, he becomes a fish, and he too is caught in a net.
When the fourth month has arrived, he is born as a beast of prey;
he remains a beast of prey for ten years and a leopard for five years.
Then, impelled by the turn of time, he meets his death.

Having brought about the destruction of unrighteousness, one is thereafter born as a human being. But the evil-minded man who has killed a woman, having gone to the realm of Yama and encountered many afflictions, undergoes twenty cycles of rebirth.
Thereafter, O great king, he is born into the womb of a worm;
having been a worm for twenty years, he is born as a human being. Furthermore, a man who steals food is born as a fly.
Subject to the power of a swarm of flies, he remains so for many months;
then, having exhausted his evil karma, he attains human status.
But by stealing musical instruments, a man is born as a mosquito.
Likewise, that man who steals food mixed with oil-cake is born as a fierce mouse resembling a mongoose,
O lord of the people; that evil-souled one constantly bites human beings.
Having stolen clarified butter, the evil-minded person is born as a *kākamadgu* water-bird;
having stolen fish or meat, the wicked-minded one is born as a crow;
and having stolen salt, one is born as a cricket.
Having stolen curd, one becomes a crane; having stolen unprepared fish, one becomes a water-fowl (*plava*). Having stolen milk, one is born as a heron (*balākā*);
and he who steals oil is born as an oil-drinking insect.
O King, that man who is possessed by delusion—
even such a creature,
having died after stealing honey, is reborn as a gadfly because of his evil intent.
A man of evil intellect who steals iron is born as a crow; by stealing milk-rice (*pāyasa*), one attains the state of a partridge (*tittiri*);
and having stolen a cake made of flour, one is born as a screech-owl (*kumbholūka*).
Having stolen fruit or a radish, or a cake, one becomes an ant;
having stolen fruits, one becomes a monkey, and having stolen a cake, an ant.
But having stolen beans, one is born as a *halagolaka* worm.
Having stolen bell-metal, a man of evil intellect is born as a green pigeon;
having stolen a silver vessel, he is born as a dove;
and having stolen a golden vessel, he is born from the womb of a worm.
Having stolen *patrorṇa* silk, one becomes a chameleon;
having stolen *kauśika* silk, a man is born as a quail;
and having stolen fine *aṃśuka* cloth, a person is born as a parrot.
Having stolen *dukūla* cloth, one dies and is born as a swan;
having stolen cotton cloth, a man dies and is born as a crane. Having stolen cotton cloth, one becomes a snake; having stolen linen cloth, one becomes a hare.
Having stolen a goat or a sheep, one becomes a tortoise; and having stolen leather, one becomes a tortoise as well. O Bhārata, a man who steals silk or wool, or takes linen cloth, is born as a hare.
Having stolen pigments, a man is born as a peacock after death;
having stolen dyed garments, he is born as a jīvajīvaka bird. Furthermore, a human who steals cosmetic ointments and perfumes [is likewise reborn].
O King, one who is devoted to greed attains the state of a muskrat;
there he lives for fifteen years. Having reached the exhaustion of his unrighteousness, he is thereafter born as a human being.

But that man who denies a deposit entrusted to him out of trust is a person whose life-force has departed; he is born in the womb of a fish. Having entered the womb of a fish, upon death he is born as a human.
Having attained human status, one is reborn with a diminished lifespan;
but having committed evil deeds, O Bhārata, a man is born as an animal,
for they do not know anything of the law that serves as their own measure.
Those men who, having committed sins, always seek to cast them off through vows,
become afflicted by disease and joined with both pleasure and pain; moreover, they are born as outcasts (mlecchas) unfit for social intercourse— of this there is no doubt.
Men who are of sinful conduct and possessed by greed and delusion [are different from those]—
those men who, from birth onwards, avoid sinful deeds;
and those men who, from birth onwards, refrain from sins.
They become healthy, handsome, and wealthy as well. Even women, by committing sin according to this same method,
shall attain the status of wives to these very creatures.
All the evils inherent in seizing the property of others have been proclaimed;
O sinless one, this has indeed been told to you by me in mere outline. You shall hear more, O Bhārata, in connection with another discourse.

"O Great King, this which was spoken by Brahmā in the past, I heard in the midst of the celestial rishis; and when questioned, he explained it to me exactly as it is. I have now described it to you in its entirety and according to the truth."
"Having heard this, O great king, always set your mind upon dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O sinless Brahmin, you have described to me the course of unrighteousness."
"O best of speakers, I wish to hear about the course of dharma:
having committed sinful deeds, how do they go to a fortunate rebirth?
And by what action performed here in this world do they attain a fortunate rebirth?"
Bṛhaspati said:
Having performed sinful deeds and fallen under the sway of unrighteousness,
one who possesses a perverted mind goes to hell.
He who, having committed an unrighteous act out of delusion, later feels remorse and is endowed with mental composure, shall not practice evil again;
for as his mind increasingly reviles that wicked deed, so shall he be purified.
In that very manner, O King, the body is liberated from that unrighteousness if one speaks with those brahmins who proclaim the Dharma;
thus, one is swiftly freed from the censure resulting from the commission of unrighteousness.
To the extent that a person correctly reflects upon unrighteousness with a concentrated mind, to that same extent he is liberated,
just as a snake is freed from its old, worn-out skin.
Even without giving various gifts,
one who is composed and endowed with mental concentration attains a happy rebirth.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, I shall now describe those gifts which, when given, lead to such a result.
Even after committing forbidden acts, a man is then joined with righteousness.
Of all gifts, food is declared to be the best;
one who desires righteousness should first give food with an upright mind.
For food is indeed the life-breath of human beings; from it a creature is born.
All worlds are established upon food; therefore, food is made manifest.
Gods, sages, ancestors, and humans alike praise food alone.
"Indeed, by the gift of food, Kauśika attains heaven.
One should give the finest food, acquired through righteous means, to the twice-born who are devoted to the study of the Vedas, with a joyful inner self."
For he whose food a thousand Brahmins eat, given with a joyful heart— ten hundred times that number— he shall not go to a state of birth as an animal,
O bull among men. Having fed ten thousand Brahmins, O best of men...
A man who has always delighted in sinful acts shall be liberated from unrighteousness. Having gathered food by means of alms, a Brahmin who is devoted to the Vedas—
by the gift of gold, even very many sins are destroyed.
By granting land that provides a livelihood, one is released even from mortal sin;
by reciting the Vedas in their entirety (*pārāyaṇa*), a twice-born man is released from sins;
and by a hundred thousand recitations of the *Gāyatrī*, as well as by the satiation of a thousand cows.

Having made the pure Brahmins understand the meaning of the Vedas according to their true significance, the twice-born is liberated from sins through such acts as universal renunciation. Indeed, hospitality toward all is supreme for them; therefore, food is considered their highest [duty].

By giving here to a Brahmin devoted to the study of the Vedas, one prospers in happiness; likewise, the Kṣatriya who, while never harming a Brahmin and always protecting him according to justice, bestows food obtained through his own prowess, [attains great merit].

13,113.015a Being self-restrained and well-composed, [he should give] to the twice-born who are advanced in Vedic knowledge; 13,113.015c by that means, O son of Pāṇḍu, the righteous-souled one wipes away his evil deeds.
13,113.016a And [he should give] the portion acquired from agriculture, purified by the taking of a sixth part.
A Vaiśya who gives to the twice-born is liberated from sins; a Śūdra,
having obtained food through hardship at the risk of his life,
is freed from sin by giving that food to the twice-born.

He who, having acquired food by his own strength without causing injury, bestows it upon the Brahmins, does not encounter difficulties. Furthermore, a man who is free from greed and has obtained food through righteous means [attains the same].
By giving to the twice-born who are advanced in Vedic knowledge, one is liberated from sin.
By giving strengthening food in this world, a man becomes strong himself.
Brahmins devoted to dharma must never consume the food of a Śūdra.
In times of distress, one may eat what has been prepared by one's own servants;
by following the path of the virtuous, one is liberated from all evil.
This is the path established by those who practice generosity, along which the wise travel.

They are indeed the givers of life; toward them, the eternal dharma is owed. Food acquired by a man through righteous means in every circumstance must always be directed toward a worthy recipient, for food is the supreme goal.
For by the giving of food, a man does not encounter misfortune;
therefore, food should be given while avoiding all that is unjust.
A householder should always strive to eat his food only after first serving the Brāhmaṇas.
A man should make his day fruitful by the gift of food,
O King, by feeding a thousand men who are knowers of the Vedas,
as well as those who are learned in logic, experts in dharma, and likewise conversant with the Itihāsas.

He does not go to a terrible hell, nor does he undergo the cycles of rebirth; endowed with all desires, he enjoys the fruit even after death. Thus, joined with happiness and free from feverish distress, he rejoices.
One is reborn endowed with beauty, fame, and wealth.
All this has been told to you regarding the great fruit of giving food;
for this, O Bhārata, is the very root of all virtues and of all gifts.
Yudhiṣṭhira said: Non-violence, Vedic ritual action, meditation, restraint of the senses,
austerity, and service to the teacher— among these, which is the highest good for a person?
Bṛhaspati said:
"O bull of the Bharatas, all these are the various doors of dharma in every respect; listen as they are being enumerated, for there are exactly six."
"Come now, I shall declare the unsurpassed highest good for living beings:
the dharma based upon non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). That man who indeed accomplishes this dharma, always setting aside the three faults toward all creatures,"
Having restrained both desire and anger, one then attains perfection. He who, seeking his own happiness, strikes harmless beings with a rod shall not be happy after death.
That man who indeed treats all beings as himself,
who has laid aside the rod of punishment and conquered his anger, prospers in happiness after death.
For one who has become the self of all beings and perceives all beings as himself—
Even the gods are bewildered on the path as they seek the footprints of the trackless one.
One should not do to another that which is disagreeable to oneself;
this is the Dharma in brief, while anything else proceeds from desire.
In rejection and in giving, in pleasure and pain, and in the pleasant and the unpleasant,
a person attains equanimity by treating others as oneself;
just as one proceeds toward others.
Likewise, another person proceeds toward the beyond;
let this very thing be your analogy in the world of the living:
just as the Dharma has been taught with skillful precision.
13,114.011 Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to the Dharmarāja Yudhiṣṭhira,
the wise preceptor of the gods then ascended to heaven even as we were looking on.
13,115.001 Vaiśampāyana said: Then King Yudhiṣṭhira, possessed of great splendor, once again questioned his grandfather, the best of speakers, as he lay upon the bed of arrows.

"O Great-minded One, the seers, the brahmins, and the gods praise the Dharma characterized by non-violence (ahiṃsā), because they recognize the authority of the Vedas. For a human being who performs violence through action, O best of kings..."
"By what means—both through speech and through the mind—is one liberated from suffering?
Bhīṣma said:
"This non-violence has been declared by the exponents of Brahman to be fourfold."
O destroyer of enemies, even if it falters in one respect, this [dharma] does not fail; for just as a four-legged creature cannot stand on only three legs,
so too, O protector of the earth, is this said to be supported by three causes.
Just as the footprints of all other creatures that walk are encompassed within the footprint of an elephant,
so too is non-violence declared by the Dharma to be supreme among all things in the worlds.
A living being is stained by action, by speech, and indeed by the mind.
But he who, having first renounced it through the mind, and likewise through speech and then through action,
does not eat meat— he is liberated in a threefold way.
The three causes have been pointed out and are heard from those who discourse on Brahman: namely, mind, speech, and taste; for faults are established in these.
One should not employ violence, for violence is fourfold.
These faults have indeed been proclaimed regarding the body, the mind, and speech;
therefore, wise men endowed with austerity do not eat meat.
O King, learn from me now the faults that arise here from the consumption of meat.

Knowing it to be like the flesh of his own son, the man who, devoid of sense and possessed by delusion, eats meat is considered the lowest of men. Just as the state of being a son arises from the union of mother and father...
Just as one who has committed violence helplessly becomes predominantly sinful,
so too does cognition of taste arise for the tongue;
likewise, according to the treatises, passion certainly arises from that which has been tasted.
Just as conditioned and unconditioned things, as well as those that are salty and those that are not salty,
are perceived, so too does the mind cease.
[One perceives] the sounds of kettledrums, conchs, clay drums, and the like, as well as the abundant sounds of stringed instruments.

How indeed will those dull-witted men, who eat meat, continue to practice [this way of life]? They are destroyers of the wealth and grain of others, yet they praise and extol meat; such people are eternally excluded from heaven.
Those who are overcome by greed for flavor and seek only the fruits [of their actions] praise meat that has not been thought of, not intended, and not even mentally resolved upon;
yet such praise of meat is indeed fraught with the consequences of its sinful karma.
Since the certain end of this body is such— that it becomes ashes, excrement, or even worms— how can a wise person maintain it by inflicting suffering upon others?
For many virtuous people have indeed sacrificed their very lives.

Having protected the flesh of others with their own flesh, they have gone to heaven. Thus, O Great King, this non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), which is endowed with the purpose of all dharmas, has been described to you by means of these four reasons.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Non-violence is the supreme dharma; this has been stated by you many times. Yet, regarding the śrāddha rites, you have also said that the ancestors desire meat."
"In the past, you described the ritual for ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) as involving many kinds of meat;
yet how can there be meat without killing? Thus, a doubt has arisen in us regarding the dharma of abstaining from meat."
What fault would there be for one who eats it, and what merit for one who does not eat it—
whether one eats it after killing it oneself, or if it is offered by another;
whether a man kills it for the sake of another, or buys it and then eats it?
"O sinless one, I desire this to be told by you in its true essence;
I wish to practice this eternal dharma with certainty.
How does one attain long life? How does one become possessed of the quality of goodness (sattva)?"
"How does one attain freedom from physical defects? How is one born with auspicious marks?
Bhīṣma said:
"O King, O bull among the Kurus, regarding the unrighteousness that exists in the eating of meat—"

Listen to me regarding that according to its true nature, as well as the supreme rule for it: indeed, by men who have disciplined their souls and who desire to obtain beauty, freedom from physical defects, long life, intelligence, goodness, strength, and memory, non-violence must be practiced.

O bull among the Kurus, O Yudhiṣṭhira, hear now that which was the opinion of those sages regarding the discourse they held there many times: "He who, restrained in his vows, should perform the horse sacrifice month after month; [he would thereby attain the highest state]."
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, one should avoid honey and meat; these two are equal.
O King, the Seven Sages, the Vālakhilyas, and likewise the Marīcipas—these wise ones praise the abstention from eating meat."
He who does not eat meat, nor kills, nor causes others to kill,
him Svāyambhuva Manu has declared to be a friend to all beings—
unassailable by all creatures and trusted by all living things.

One who constantly abstains from meat will always be esteemed by the virtuous. The righteous-souled Nārada said that he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another will surely perish.
"He would perish as one who cannot be trusted," so said Nārada.
"He gives gifts, performs sacrifices, and even practices asceticism—
by abstaining from honey and meat," Bṛhaspati declared thus.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every month for a hundred years, and he who does not eat meat—these two, in my opinion, are equal.
He always sacrifices with the *sattra* rite; he always bestows gifts.
One who always abstains from honey and meat becomes an ascetic; O Bhārata, all the Vedas and all sacrifices do not achieve what is accomplished by one who,
having eaten meat, later desists from it.
Even after having eaten [meat], he performs difficult asceticism for the sake of a religious sign;
indeed, it is difficult for one who knows the taste to renounce meat. To practice this supreme vow, which grants fearlessness to all living beings, is truly hard to do.
The wise man who bestows the gift of fearlessness upon all beings becomes, in this world, a giver of life; of this there is no doubt. Thus indeed do the sages praise the supreme dharma.
As one's own life-breaths are dear to oneself, so are they to all living beings.
Wise and high-souled persons should proceed by treating others as themselves;
even when strewn with sharp thorns, there is fear at the mere rustling of a blade of grass.
For the wise who desire prosperity, there is fear of death;
how much more so for those being violently slaughtered while seeking life—
those who are healthy and sinless, yet being harmed by sinful meat-eaters?
Therefore, O Great King, know that the total avoidance of meat is the supreme foundation for dharma, for heaven, and for happiness;
for when there is the apprehension that "there is fear of death," suffering is the consequence.
Therefore, the source of Dharma is the total avoidance of meat.
Non-violence is the supreme Dharma, and likewise, non-violence is the highest austerity. Non-violence is the supreme truth; from it, Dharma proceeds.

For meat does not arise from grass, wood, or even stone; rather, meat comes from having killed a living being. Therefore, there is fault in its consumption. The gods, who delight in truth and uprightness, are consumers of *svāhā*, *svadhā*, and nectar.
Know that the flesh-eating Rākṣasas are crooked and devoted to falsehood;
yet, freed from the fear of the lord of Rākṣasas, they have become devoted to all living beings in dreadful wildernesses,
difficult passes, and dense forests.

O King, for one who abstains from eating meat, no fear arises in the end—whether at night, by day, or during the twilights; in crossroads or in assemblies; when weapons are raised; or in the face of danger from wild beasts and serpents.
A refuge for all beings, trustworthy among all creatures,
he causes no agitation in the world and is himself never agitated.
If there were no eater, then there would be no killer.

A man kills that [animal] for the sake of the eater; indeed, the thought "this is not to be eaten" causes violence to cease. Therefore, violence toward deer and other creatures proceeds for the sake of the eater.
O one of great splendor, because it consumes the very life of those who do harm,
one who desires their own welfare should avoid meat.
Those fierce ones who injure living beings find no protector.
Like predatory beasts, they are terrifying to all living beings.
Whether through greed, or through delusion of the intellect, or for the sake of power and prowess,
or through association with the wicked, men come to delight in unrighteousness.
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another dwells in a state of agitation, being born here and there wherever he may be.
[This practice] is auspicious, conducive to fame, long life, and heaven; it is a great means of securing well-being.
"13,116.035c Restrained supreme ṛṣis have declared the non-eating of meat [to be the highest].
13,116.036a But this, O son of Kuntī, was indeed heard by me in the past,
as Mārkaṇḍeya was speaking, regarding the faults in eating meat."
Bhīṣma said:
O Yudhiṣṭhira, mighty-armed one, hear from me these supreme words spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya regarding the faults that exist in the eating of meat.
For he who eats the flesh of living beings who desire life—
whether they have been killed by him or have died naturally— is just like the killer himself.
The buyer kills with his wealth, and the eater kills through consumption.

The executioner [is responsible] for killing and binding; thus, this is the threefold nature of slaughter. A person who, through a defect of disposition, neither eats [the meat] nor approves of it, yet consents to one who should be killed, is also tainted by that fault.
By not eating meat here, one who is compassionate toward living beings becomes invincible to all creatures, long-lived, free from disease,
and happy; [this is superior] to gifts of gold, gifts of cows, and gifts of land in every respect.
13.116.041c There is a sacred revelation (śruti) stating that the merit (dharma) gained by not eating meat is preeminent.

13.116.042a One should not eat meat that has not been consecrated (aprokṣita), meat prepared for no sacred purpose (vṛthāmāṃsa), or meat offered without following the prescribed rules (vidhihīna). 13.116.042c By eating such meat, a man goes to hell; there is no doubt about this.

Meat that has been sprinkled with water or consecrated for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa’s desire should be known as involving little fault in this world; however, one is tainted by sin in the opposite case. That lowest of men who would kill a living creature for the sake of a consumer [of meat] [is likewise stained].
In that regard, the consumer causes great demerit, but not the killer.
That ignorant person who, through paths consisting of sacrifices, rituals, and the study of the Vedas,
kills a living being out of greed for meat— that man indeed partakes in hell.
But even he who, having eaten meat, later desists from it, possesses very great merit, for he has turned away from sin. [Furthermore, there are these:
the one who procures it, the one who consents to it, the one who slaughters it, and the buyer and the seller.
The preparer, the eater, and the killers—all of them are indeed [guilty].
Furthermore, I shall state another authority established by the sacred law (vidhi):
the ancient [tradition] cherished by the seers (ṛṣi) and firmly settled within the Vedas.

O tiger among kings, when the Dharma characterized by worldly activity is pursued by those seeking rewards, it is as has been described; however, that is not for those who desire liberation. Just as an oblation, when consecrated with mantras, sprinkled, and washed, becomes pure—
According to the authority declared in the Vedas regarding the rites for the ancestors,
Manu has stated that meat other than this is useless and unfit to be eaten;
it does not lead to heaven, brings ill repute, and is like that of a Rakshasa, O bull of the Bharatas.

"O King, in former times men did indeed eat meat according to the prescribed rule; the conclusion here among the self-controlled is that it was even by means of a non-Vedic rule. A man who desires his own self to be entirely free from affliction [should abstain]."
One should avoid the flesh of living beings here in every respect.
For it is heard that in a former age, there was a sacrificial animal for men made of rice,
with which the sacrificers, intent upon the worlds of merit, performed their sacrifices.
In ancient times, O Lord, when questioned by the sages regarding a doubt, Vasu, the lord of Cedi, declared that meat was inedible, yet he later declared it edible. Consequently,
that lord of the earth fell from the sky to the earth.
Having spoken this very same thing once more, the high-souled Agastya, desiring the welfare of all creatures, entered the depths of the earth; meanwhile,
the wild animals, consecrated by his ascetic power, became deities for all.
For when a sacrifice is performed with the mind, the gods are indeed satisfied;
thus, the rites dedicated to the ancestors and the deities are not neglected,
and the ancestors are truly gratified when they are offered meat according to the rule.

But hear this, O Indra among kings, as it is being proclaimed by me, O sinless one: the total happiness found in the non-eating of meat, O lord of men. For he who might perform most severe penance for a full hundred years—

And he who would abstain from meat for even one [day], this is considered by me to be equal [in merit]. O lord of men, one should especially avoid all meats during the bright fortnight of the month of Kārttika; for dharma is ordained therein.
He who avoids meat for the four months of the rainy season obtains four auspicious things: renown, longevity, fame, and strength.
Or, indeed, by abstaining from all meats for even a single month, he gains these same rewards.
Having transcended all sufferings, those who live happily and free from disease—
those who avoid meat whether month by month or even fortnight by fortnight—
for them, who have desisted from violence, the world of Brahmā is ordained.
O Pārtha, meat during the fortnight of the month of Kārttika was avoided by kings who had become the self of all beings and who understood the higher and lower truths—
by Nābhāga, Ambarīṣa, and the high-souled Gaya.
[He was endowed] with the longevity of Anaraṇya, Dilīpa, Raghu, and Pūru;
of Kārtavīrya and Aniruddha; of Nahuṣa and Yayāti; of Nṛga, Viṣvagaśva, and likewise of Śaśabindu.
And likewise by Yuvanāśva, and by Śibi the son of Uśīnara,
by Mucukunda, by Māndhātṛ, and by Hariścandra, O Lord—
speak the truth, not untruth; truth is the eternal dharma.
Hariścandra indeed wanders in heaven by means of his truth, like the moon, O Indra among kings, together with Śyenacitra, Somaka, Vṛka,
Raivata, Rantideva, Vasu, and Sṛñjaya.
By these and others, O Indra among kings— by Kṛpa and Bharata, by Duḥṣanta, Karūṣa, Rāma, Alarka,
and Nala, as well as by Duḥṣanta, O Indra among kings, and by Kuśa and Lava.
By Virūpākṣa, by Kurūṣa, and likewise by Nṛga, Ālarka, and Nara;
by Virūpāśva, by Nimi, and by the wise Janaka;
by Śila, by Pṛthu, and indeed by Vīrasena.
By Ikṣvāku, Śambhu, Śveta, and Sagara;
by Aja, Dhundhu, and likewise Subāhu;
and by Haryaśva, O Indra among kings, as well as by Kṣupa and Bharata.
O Indra among kings, because they and others did not eat meat during the month of Kārttika in the autumn season in former times, they attained heaven;
and they remain in the world of Brahmā, blazing and endowed with splendor.
Being waited upon by Gandharvas and accompanied by thousands of women,
those high-souled ones who practice this supreme, auspicious dharma characterized by non-violence (ahiṃsā) dwell upon the vault of heaven.
Those righteous ones who always avoid honey, meat,
and liquor from birth onwards are remembered here as sages;
they attain distinction among their kinsmen, of this there is no doubt.
Whoever should practice or cause others to hear this Dharma of non-meat-eating—
even if they are of very wicked conduct— shall never go to hell.
O King, whoever should recite this or listen to it repeatedly, [shall likewise attain such merit].

The pure rule for abstaining from meat, honored by the seers: one who is liberated from all sins is glorified by the fulfillment of all desires. He is non-violent, devoted to charity, and avoids honey and meat.
One who has fallen into calamity shall be released from calamity; one who is bound shall be released from bondage.
Likewise, the sick shall be freed from disease, and the suffering shall be freed from suffering.
Such a man shall not go to a womb of an animal, but shall be endowed with beauty.
O best of the Kurus, the wise man shall indeed attain great fame.
This has been told to you, O King, regarding the avoidance of meat—
the ordinance established by the sages concerning both its consumption and its renunciation.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Indeed, these men in the world are excessively greedy for meat;
having abandoned various other foods, they behave just like hosts of Rākṣasas."
They desire various kinds of cakes and diverse vegetables, as well as *ṣāḍava* preparations and flavorful condiments, just as they do meat;
my mind is utterly bewildered regarding the disposal of these very things.
"I do not consider there to be anything here superior in flavor to meat, nor is there anything else like it in its substance. Therefore,
O bull among men, I wish to hear of the virtues even in the non-eating of meat, as well as the faults that lie in eating it."
O Knower of Dharma, tell me all this according to its true nature and in accordance with the principles of dharma here:
what is edible and what is inedible? Tell me all of this—what it is, of what kind it is, and what the merits are in its avoidance.
"Tell me, O Grandfather, what are the faults of one who eats it?
Bhīṣma said:
"O mighty-armed descendant of Bharata, it is exactly as you say."
There is nothing else on earth superior to meat in terms of flavor;
for those who are wounded, emaciated, or afflicted by heat, for those devoted to sexual pleasure,
and for those exhausted by travel, there is nothing better than meat.
It immediately increases the vital breaths and bestows supreme nourishment;
it is considered by the virtuous to be the very destruction of the fault of eating [forbidden things],
and the life-sustenance for all hungry twice-born ones.
Having given with faith and free from greed, one becomes pure in soul;
they instruct rather than beg, demonstrating their own forms, [saying]:
"This is the state of one who does not give; may you not become like this."
Having become pure through acts such as giving, he should never again eat meat.
O scorcher of the foe, there is no food whatsoever superior to meat;
yet, O delighter of the Kurus, there are many virtues in its avoidance.
Listen as I declare those things that belong to human beings:
there is no man more base than he who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of others, nor is there any man more cruel.
For there is nothing in this world found to be dearer than one's own life;
therefore, a person should show compassion toward others just as they do toward themselves. And from semen, my dear, the birth of flesh occurs here—of this there is no doubt.
But in eating [forbidden food], there is great fault; it is reckoned as equivalent to killing. Those who know the Veda understand that dharma is characterized by non-violence (*ahiṃsā*).
A self-possessed man should perform only that action which is non-violent.
In sacrifices to the ancestors and the gods, the oblation is said to be consecrated by sprinkling;
having consumed that according to the rite seen in the Vedas, one does not incur sin in this world.
It is also heard in the sacred revelation (Śruti) that "animals were created for the sake of sacrifice."
For those who act otherwise than this, the Rākṣasa rule is prescribed. Now hear from me also that rule which has been seen for Kṣatriyas,
by which one does not incur sin when eating meat acquired through valor.

O King, in ancient times Agastya consecrated all wild animals as belonging to all the gods; therefore, hunting is honored by him. Furthermore, for the sake of protecting living beings, one may kill predatory animals.

"O King, there is no such thing as hunting without abandoning one's self; having attained equanimity, one may either kill or not kill a creature. Therefore, O Bhārata, all royal sages go out on hunts."

They are not stained by fault, for they know this to be no sin. Indeed, there is nothing else in this world or the next that is so supreme as compassion toward all beings in this world, O delighter of the Kurus.
Fear never exists for a compassionate man in this world; these worlds belong to those who are compassionate, as do the worlds beyond, for those who practice austerity.
He who, devoted to compassion, grants freedom from fear to all beings—
"We have heard that all beings grant him fearlessness:
they protect him from wounds, stumbles, falls, afflictions, and blows, whether on even ground or uneven."

Neither predatory beasts, nor *piśācas*, nor *rākṣasas* slay him; they are liberated from times of fear, as are those who liberate others. There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of life.
For it is certain that there is nothing dearer than oneself;
O Bhārata, death is indeed undesirable to all living beings,
for at the time of death, trembling arises instantly in creatures.

In the ocean of saṃsāra, sentient beings constantly revolve amidst the sufferings of birth, old age, and death, and they tremble at the prospect of dying. Within the dwellings of the womb, they are cooked by alkaline, sour, and pungent fluids.
By the extremely agonizing contacts with urine, phlegm,
and excrement, they are born there helpless; being torn apart again and again, those greedy for flesh are seen, powerless, as they are being split open.
They are cooked in the Kumbhīpāka hell, having entered various wombs;
being attacked and slaughtered, they indeed wander there again and again. For, having searched throughout the earth, one finds no one dearer than oneself.

Therefore, one who possesses self-control should be compassionate toward all living beings. O King, he who does not eat any kind of meat for as long as he lives shall attain a vast place in heaven; of this there is no doubt.
Those who eat the flesh of living beings who desire to live, they too shall be eaten by those very beings; of this I have no doubt. Since he eats me, I too shall eat him.
13,117.034c This is the "meat-ness" of meat; understand this, O Bhārata.
13,117.035a The slayer is always slain, and likewise the binder shall be bound.
13,117.035c The abuser is abused, O King, and the hater incurs hatred.

By whatever body one performs whatever action, by that very same body one experiences the corresponding fruit. Non-violence is the supreme dharma; likewise, non-violence is the supreme self-restraint.
Non-violence is the supreme gift; non-violence is the supreme austerity. Non-violence is the supreme sacrifice; likewise, non-violence is the supreme strength.
Non-violence is the supreme friend; non-violence is the supreme happiness.
Non-violence is the supreme truth; non-violence is the supreme sacred teaching.
Whether it be giving in all sacrifices, bathing in all sacred fords, or even the fruit of all acts of charity—none of these are equal to non-violence.
The asceticism of one who practices non-violence is inexhaustible; such a person always performs sacrifice through non-violence.
One who is non-violent toward all beings is like a mother and like a father.
O King, in ancient times, Agastya [prohibited] the eating of meat even in the *jāṅgala* region.
"This is the fruit of non-violence (*ahiṃsā*), and even more so, O bull among the Kurus;
for its qualities cannot be fully described here even in hundreds of years.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O Grandfather, tell me this: what wombs did those slain in this great battle enter—those who were without desire and those who were full of desire? For men to give up their lives in a great conflict is a source of suffering."
"I know the truth, O knower of dharma, that the abandonment of life is extremely difficult.
Whether in prosperity or adversity, whether in good fortune or misfortune—
tell me the reason for this, for you are considered by me to be all-knowing."
Bhīṣma said:
O lord of the earth, whether in prosperity or adversity, whether in auspiciousness or inauspiciousness, all living beings born into this cycle of existence are subject to these conditions.
Listen to the reason why I am devoted to that state.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, this question you have asked is indeed appropriate;
in this regard, O King, I shall relate to you this ancient history.
13,118.006c O Yudhiṣṭhira, this is the conversation between Dvaipāyana and a worm.
13,118.007a In ancient times, the Brahmin Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, while wandering as one who has become Brahman,
13,118.007c saw a worm running swiftly along the path of a cart.
Knowing the destinies of all beings and understanding the cries of all creatures,
the omniscient one, having observed everything from every side, spoke these words to the insect:
"O insect, you appear terrified and you seem to be in great haste."
"Where are you running? Tell me that; from where has this fear come upon you?
The insect said:
"Hearing the roar of this great cart, fear has come upon me."
"O one of great intelligence, this terrible sound is indeed heard coming from here;
thinking 'it might kill me,' I therefore retreated. And I hear the sound of the cowherd boys as they are being urged on."
O Lord, as they carry this immense burden,
the various sounds of men carrying it are heard in close proximity;
these cannot be endured by one such as I, born from the womb of an insect.
Therefore, I shall depart from this most dreadful fear;
for death is indeed painful for living beings, and life is very difficult to obtain.
Thus, being afraid, I flee; may I go from happiness to unhappiness.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, he replied to him: "O worm, from where could there be happiness for you?
I consider death to be your happiness, for you exist in the womb of an animal."
"You do not recognize sound, touch, taste, smell, or many various kinds of enjoyments; O worm, for you, death alone is better.
The worm said:

"O one of great wisdom, since I perceive that the living soul (jīva) is present everywhere, I find happiness even here; therefore, I desire to live. Moreover, all objects of the senses here function according to the body."
Human beings and animals alike have distinct enjoyments, especially so.
In former times, I was indeed a human being, a Śūdra of great wealth; I was hostile to Brahmins, cruel, miserly, and lived by lending at interest.
Sharp in speech, clever in deceit, and a plunderer of everything from all sides; one who acts treacherously toward others, devoid of compassion, and devoted to seizing the property of others;
even my own servants and guests have been made to dwell in my house in a state of exhaustion by me.
Out of stinginess, desiring delicious food for myself, cruel and wishing to prosper,
I did not give the food prepared with faith by me for the sake of the gods and the ancestral sacrifice; yet food, when given by one who desires the welfare of others, purifies.
Having sought refuge in a protected shelter when in fear, those who had come to us for protection were suddenly abandoned by us out of dread; we did not rescue those seeking safety,
and having abandoned them suddenly in the night, I did not grant them freedom from fear.
Seeing the wealth, grain, beloved wives, vehicles, wonderful garments,
and the prosperity of men, I feel a useless sense of envy. Envious upon seeing the happiness of others, I am a malevolent person who desires to do them harm.
A destroyer of the three goals of life for others, following only my own desires,
I performed deeds in the past that were preponderant in cruelty;
by that, this state of being a worm has been attained, which is a constant source of fear.
13,118.025c Recalling that, I am filled with remorse, as if I had abandoned a beloved son.
13,118.026a I recognize the fruit of even auspicious deeds performed;
13,118.026c for my aged mother was honored by me, and the Brahmin was worshipped.

"O Brahmin, because a guest endowed with noble birth and virtue once came to my house by chance and was honored by me, my memory has not deserted me. By that very deed, I perceive here a hope for happiness."
"I desire to hear that from you, O ascetic, for it is conducive to my welfare.
Vyāsa said:
"Indeed, it is by virtue of your auspicious deeds that you do not lose your composure even while born in an animal womb."
13,119.001c "O worm, that very deed is mine by which you are not deluded.
13,119.002a For by my power of asceticism, I deliver [beings] by the mere sight of me;
13,119.002c indeed, no other power is found to be more powerful than the power of asceticism."
"I know, O worm, that through your own evil deeds you have fallen into this state of being a worm. You shall attain the supreme Dharma, provided you consider yourself established in Dharma.
Both gods and those who are animals experience the results of actions performed upon this earth."
Even among men, desire and wealth arise from dharma according to one's qualities;
for what is lacking for a wise man— even if he be dull-witted— provided he lives endowed with speech, intellect, hands, and feet?
For while living, that foremost of Brahmins performs worship of the moon and the sun;
even as he speaks holy stories, you, O worm, shall attain that state.
There, you shall experience the elements as their constituent qualities.
"13,119.007c There, I shall instruct you in that state of Brahmanhood which you desire.
13,119.008a Having promised "So be it," the worm stood across the path.
13,119.008b And by chance, a very great multitude of carts arrived.
Pierced by the movement of a wheel, the insect gave up its life-breaths;
through the grace of that one of immeasurable power, it was reborn in a kṣatriya family.
Having passed through all other wombs, it went to see that ṛṣi.
And he saw, O Great King, that he had attained the status of a prince among the species of badgers,
iguanas, and boars, as well as among deer and birds,
and within the wombs of outcaste dog-cookers, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and Kṣatriyas.
In these very wombs, he dwelt in due succession by virtue of his own karma.
Then, having been addressed as "O worm" by the truth-speaking Ṛṣi,
he regained his mindfulness and, with palms joined, grasped the sage’s feet with his head.
Having attained, by means of this method, that unsurpassed station of a kṣatriya,
the worm said:
"This is that incomparable station, desired for its ten qualities."
13,119.011c Since I attained the state of an insect, I have now reached the status of a prince.
13,119.012a Extremely powerful elephants adorned with golden garlands carry me, And Kamboja steeds, the finest of horses, are yoked to my chariots.
Vehicles yoked with camels and mules carry me;
together with my kinsmen and ministers, I eat rice mixed with meat. I dwell in well-housed mansions upon comfortable couches.
O highly fortunate one, well-honored here among these most excellent [beings],
I sleep during all the latter parts of the night while sweet-spoken bards, chroniclers, and panegyrists praise me like the god Mahendra.

"By the grace of you, whose promises are true and whose splendor is immeasurable, I, having attained the state of a worm, have now reached the status of a prince. Homage be to you, O one of great wisdom; command me, what shall I do?"
"For this has been attained by me as it was ordained by the power of your asceticism.
Vyāsa said:
"O King, I have been honored by you today with these words, which have come to you spontaneously."
"Today, having attained the state of a worm, a loathsome memory has arisen in you;
yet there is no destruction of the evil that was accumulated by you in the past— by you,
a Śūdra devoted to wealth, cruel, and an assailant."
"You have obtained a vision of me, and that is indeed due to merit performed in the past; likewise, because you were born in an animal womb yet offered worship to me,
you shall attain the status of a Brahmin from this state of being a prince."
Having offered up your own life-breaths on the field of battle for the sake of cows and Brahmins,
and having attained the happiness of a prince as well as sacrifices with abundant sacrificial fees,
you shall then rejoice in heaven, become one with Brahman, immutable and blissful.
One from the animal womb attains the state of a Śūdra;
a Śūdra [attains] the state of a Vaiśya, and a Vaiśya [attains] the state of a Kṣatriya;
and a Kṣatriya who praises his own conduct [attains] the state of a Brāhmaṇa.
"A virtuous Brahmin attains the meritorious heaven.
Bhīṣma said:
"Remembering this, that heroic one adhered to the duty of a Kṣatriya."

13,120.001c Having cast off his state as a worm, O King, he performed extensive austerities. 13,120.002a Seeing that vast austerity of him who was learned in dharma and artha, the best of the twice-born, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, then arrived there.
Vyāsa said:
"O worm, the vow of the kṣatriya is the protection of all beings;
by meditating upon this very vow of the kṣatriya, you shall thereafter attain the state of a brahmin."
Protect all subjects properly, you who are self-possessed and discerning between the auspicious and the inauspicious;
do so by distributing among them auspicious desires and purifying means for those that are inauspicious.
Be self-possessed, well-pleased, and devoted to the practice of your own duty.
"Having cast off this kṣatriya body, you shall thereafter attain the state of a brahmin.
Bhīṣma said:
"Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, he went once again to the forest."
Having heard the words of the great seer and having protected his subjects with righteousness,
Kīṭa, O best of kings, attained the state of a Brahmin after death in a very short time through the merit of protecting his subjects.
Then, having seen that brahmin, the highly illustrious and immensely wise Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana returned once more. Vyāsa said:
"O illustrious bull among brahmins, do not be distressed in any way.
Because of his protection of the distinguished, his death in fair combat, and his service to the virtuous, he has attained the supreme goal."
Then, O dear one, when his subjects were oppressed by a foreign kingdom and their wealth was seized, he came forth for battle; having slain that king,
he himself was killed in the fight, and from that he attained the state of a Brahmin.
Then the wise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana arrived;
the son of Parāśara, possessed of great wisdom, supreme in compassion,
with a perpetually serene countenance, and radiant like a cloud in the sky.
"I bow eternally to Vyāsa, the sun that dispels the darkness of ignorance.
Having said this, he fell at [his] feet, and the Great Sage spoke with affection:
"Devoted to recitation and truth, honor the Brahmins here."

"By meditating on Viṣṇu, you will gradually attain the stainless Brahman. O knower of dharma, the doer of good is reborn in auspicious wombs, while the doer of evil is reborn in sinful wombs, according to their respective actions and according to the scriptures."
"Therefore, O worm, do not be distressed in any way by the fear of death;
rather, you should have fear of the loss of dharma. Therefore, practice the highest dharma.
The worm said:
"O Blessed One, it is because of you that I have attained a happiness even greater than happiness.
Having spoken thus, the best of the twice-born, being duly permitted, acted accordingly;
and having obtained prosperity rooted in dharma, my evil has today been destroyed here.
Bhīṣma said: O King,
having attained the status of a Brāhmaṇa— which is difficult to obtain— by the word of the Blessed One,
the worm marked the earth with hundreds of sacrificial posts.

Then, O best among the knowers of Brahman, that worm attained the same world as Brahmā (sālokya). And by the word of Vyāsa, O Pārtha, he then reached the supreme, eternal Brahman, which is brought about by the fruits of one's own actions.

"O tiger among kings, having heard this, be devoted to virtuous deeds. Since even those bulls among Kṣatriyas were slain by their own nature and have attained a meritorious state, do not grieve for them, my son."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best of the virtuous, O grandfather, I ask you: among knowledge, austerity, and generosity—which of these is distinguished as superior? Tell me that."
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, they cite this ancient history,
the conversation between Maitreya and Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.

O King, Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, wandering in disguise, arrived at Vārāṇasī in the household of Maitreya, who lived with a wanton woman. Knowing that the best of sages had arrived and was seated there, [he approached him].
Having honored him, Maitreya fed him with the finest food.
Having eaten that excellent food, which was endowed with all qualities and provided every desire,
the high-minded Kṛṣṇa smiled with joy as he prepared to depart.
Seeing him smiling, Maitreya said to Kṛṣṇa: "O righteous-souled one, tell me the reason why you smiled; from what cause has this joy come upon you, a man of asceticism and fortitude?"
Having saluted and prostrated before you, O wise one, I ask this of you:
[tell me] of my own fortune in asceticism (*tapas*) and likewise my great good fortune (*mahābhāgya*), O illustrious one, as well as my fortune in asceticism and my fortune in happiness.
"O dear one, for those who act separately, both with respect to external objects and within their own selves,
I consider there to be little difference, even if one is superior to you.
Vyāsa said:
Through excessive cutting and excessive speech, this pride has arisen:
"The word of the Veda is untrue; why would the Veda speak a falsehood? Yet they say that there are only three steps which constitute the supreme vow for a man.
One should not bear malice, one should give, and one should speak only the highest truth;
what must be done by us now has been ordained as supreme for the future. Thus was it declared in the Vedas and envisioned of old by the seers.
Even a small gift such as this becomes one of great fruit when it is given with a heart free from malice to one who is thirsty;
for you, being thirsty yourself, have given this food to me, who am thirsty.
"O Lord, you have conquered great worlds as if by means of great sacrifices;
therefore, I am pleased both by the purity of your gifts and by your asceticism. For your scent is indeed holy, and your appearance is likewise holy."
And this meritorious fragrance wafts forth; I believe it is due to the performance of ritual acts.
O dear one, it is superior even to sweeping and likewise to anointing.
Of all purifying things, the gift of charity alone is supreme.
"O twice-born one, charity alone is supreme;
it is superior even to all those purifying rites which you praise here as the highest and are declared in the Vedas."
Of these, the gift of life is the most excellent; of this I have no doubt.
It is the path created by those who practice giving, along which the wise travel.
For they are the givers of life, and in them righteousness is firmly established.
Just as the Vedas when well-studied, and just as the restraint of the senses,
and just as total renunciation here, so too is giving unsurpassed. For you, my dear, shall proceed from happiness to auspicious happiness.
The wise man attains a state of happiness even more blissful than happiness itself.
This has been perceived by us directly and is beyond doubt:
that wealth, gifts, sacrifice, and likewise happiness, accrue to one who possesses prosperity.
From happiness alone comes supreme suffering, and from suffering comes supreme happiness;
for this is seen, O one of great wisdom, as being fixed by its very nature. Wise men say that there are three kinds of conduct here for a human being.

Merit is one thing, and evil another; there is neither merit nor evil. One does not consider the conduct of another, nor does one consider the evil of another. Likewise, that which is produced by one's own karma is neither merit nor evil.
Those men who are devoted to sacrifice, charity, austerity, and virtuous conduct are indeed performers of meritorious deeds;
but those people who harbor malice toward living beings are indeed evildoers.
They seize the possessions of others, they go to suffering, and they fall [into lower realms].
Furthermore, whatever other action there may be that is neither meritorious nor sinful,
he always eats without meanness when requested by his own kin; yet,
through the exhaustion of his fortune, his stores diminish, not through consumption.
"Rejoice, prosper, be glad, give gifts, and perform sacrifices;
neither the learned nor the ascetics shall overcome you.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, Maitreya, who honored ritual action, replied:
"Born into an exceedingly illustrious family, wise and deeply learned,
O one of great intelligence, there is no doubt that it is exactly as you have said."
"Permitted by you, O Lord, I would like to say something.
Vyāsa said:
"O Maitreya, whatever you wish, to whatever extent, and in whatever manner."
"Speak first, O one of great wisdom; I wish to hear your words.
Maitreya said:
"These words concerning the practice of giving are indeed faultless and pure."
"Without a doubt, you have cultivated your soul through both knowledge and asceticism.
Because your soul has been so cultivated, this inheritance is exceedingly great for me;
I perceive it even more clearly with my intellect, as if it were already fully realized through your penance."
"Merely by the sight of you, a great prosperity has come to me;
I consider this to be your grace, for that is the nature of action. Asceticism, sacred learning, and noble birth—these are the causes of Brahminhood."
Endowed with these three qualities, he indeed becomes a twice-born man. When he is satisfied, the ancestors and the deities are satisfied as well;
for among those who possess sacred learning, there is nothing superior to the Brāhmaṇa.
This world would be blind darkness; nothing at all would be discerned. The four social orders would not exist, nor would dharma and adharma, truth and falsehood.
Without the *saṃskāras*, the Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas would perish, being without a Brāhmaṇa.
A Śūdra who fails to serve the stages of life (āśramas) as they deserve perishes. Just as a man obtains fruit from a well-tilled field,
so does a donor reap the fruit by giving to one who is learned in the Vedas.

If there were no Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and good conduct to receive the gift, the wealth of the wealthy would be in vain. For the ignorant man who eats destroys the food, and the food being eaten destroys him.
And he destroys him whose food he eats; having destroyed that [person], the ignorant man is himself destroyed. For the wise lord, while eating the food, generates it again.
And he is born from that food; therefore, the transgression is indeed subtle.
For the master would undoubtedly be one who enjoys nothing if he did not give food;
indeed, the wise man who delivers his honored ancestors and gods,
the merit gained by the giver is exactly the same as that gained by the recipient.
"For a single wheel does not turn," so the seers have known.
Wherever there are Brahmins endowed with learning and virtuous conduct,
there one enjoys the merit and fruit of giving, both in this world and in the next.
Those who are always pure in their conduct, intensely devoted to austerity,
and perfected in charity and study— they are indeed always most worthy of honor.
For one who follows the path established by those virtuous ones does not become deluded.
"For they are the leaders to heaven, the eternal bearers of the sacrifice.
Bhīṣma said:
"Thus addressed, that Blessed One replied to Maitreya."
"By good fortune you understand this; by good fortune you possess such wisdom.
For this world, without a doubt, praises primarily the measure of beauty, the measure of age, and the measure of prosperity."
"By good fortune they do not overcome you; this is a divine favor bestowed upon you. Listen as I shall relate to you that which is far superior to mere giving.
Whatever scriptures there are here for the attainment [of goals], and whatever worldly activities there may be..."
These [scriptures] have proceeded in their proper order, placing the Veda at their forefront.
I praise generosity, while you praise austerity and sacred learning;
yet that very generosity becomes manifold in its merit through faith and one's own virtues.
Austerity is the purifier of the Veda; austerity is the means to attain heaven.
We have heard that through austerity one attains greatness, and likewise through knowledge. And by austerity alone, one may dispel whatever other evil deeds remain.
Whatever austerity a person performs with a specific aim in mind,
all that a Brahmin who has mastered the Vedas attains—
be it difficult to follow, difficult to assail, difficult to reach, or difficult to overcome.
One attains everything indeed through austerity, for austerity is most powerful.
Even a drinker of spirits, a thief of what is not given, a killer of an embryo, or one who violates the teacher’s bed—
through austerity he overcomes all this and is liberated from sin.
But one who possesses all knowledge is truly sighted, regardless of his outward appearance;
they say that those two are ascetics, and one should always pay homage to them. All those whose wealth is sacred learning are worthy of worship, as are those who practice austerities.
Those who give gifts obtain happiness after death and prosperity in this world;
through gifts of food, virtuous people attain this world of Brahmā and even more powerful worlds.
Those who have been honored honor these [in return], and those who have been respected show them respect;
but where an ungenerous man goes, he is repelled from every side.
Both the non-doer and the doer receive exactly what corresponds to their own actions.
Whether you go upward or downward to the world,
you shall obtain whatever food and drink you may give. You are wise, born of noble lineage, learned, and free from cruelty.
"O Maitreya, be devoted to the vow of a wife faithful to her youth;
accept this first of all, which is praised for householders.
He who is satisfied with his wife, and whose wife is satisfied with her husband—"
In whatever family all this auspiciousness exists,
there darkness is removed like dirt from the limbs by water, or as darkness is dispelled by the light of fire; likewise,
every evil is cast off through charity and austerity.
And by the worship of Viṣṇu,
O highly fortunate one, that Brahmin shall cross over the ocean of saṃsāra—
[he who belongs] to those whose being is purified by their own actions and whose souls are stainless through ascetic penances.

Hari is remembered for the sake of delivering those whose delusion has been dispelled by knowledge; always intent on his worship, a devotee of him, bow down to him. Indeed, those devoted to him do not perish, for they are dedicated to the eight-syllable mantra.
Those here who are devoted to the worship of the *praṇava* and intent upon the supreme truth—purify yourself with them, Maitreya; may you attain well-being. Farewell, I shall now depart for my home.
"This must be kept in mind; thus will there be welfare.
Then Maitreya, having bowed to him and performed a circumambulation, [departed].
Bhīṣma.
"O King, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana, with palms joined in reverence, said to Maitreya, the best of the twice-born: 'May the Blessed One attain well-being.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O best among all upholders of dharma, I wish to hear from you about the proper conduct of virtuous women; tell that to me, O Grandfather. Bhīṣma said:
In the world of the gods, Kaikeyī— whose mind was well-disposed— questioned the high-minded Śāṇḍilī, who was omniscient and possessed knowledge of all dharmas:
"O blessed lady, by what conduct or by what practice [have you attained this]?"
Having shaken off all evils, you have come to the world of the gods;
blazing with your own splendor like the crest of a flame,
you have reached heaven with a radiance like that of the daughter of the Lord of Stars.
Wearing stainless garments and free from fatigue,
you shine with a thousandfold splendor while stationed in your celestial chariot.
This is not due to meager austerity, nor by giving, nor by religious observances alone.

"Having reached this world, tell me the truth. Thus questioned by Sumanā, the sweet-smiling Śāṇḍilī spoke these words privately to Sumanā: 13,124.006c Having reached this world, tell me the truth. 13,124.007a Thus questioned by Sumanā, the sweet-smiling Śāṇḍilī 13,124.007c spoke these words privately to Sumanā.
I have not attained divinity by wearing saffron robes, nor by wearing bark garments; neither by shaving my head nor by wearing matted hair have I reached this state.
[Rather, it was through] all those words that were harmful and harsh.

And being ever vigilant, I never spoke ill of my husband; I was always attentive and devoted in the worship of the gods, the ancestors, and the brahmins, remaining ever obedient to my mother-in-law and father-in-law.

I do not engage in slander, nor does such a thought ever arise in my mind; I do not linger at places other than the gate, nor do I speak for long. Nor do I laugh improperly, nor perform any action that is harmful.
Whether it be a secret or not a secret, I do not disclose anything under any circumstances. Even when my husband has returned home from having gone out for the sake of business,
I honor him with a seat, being composed in mind.
