Whatever I do not recognize, whatever food I do not take pleasure in— whether it be solid food, or that which is to be licked— I renounce all of that.
Furthermore, whatever task has been brought forth for the sake of the household, I renounce it as well.
Rising early in the morning, I perform and carry out all of that: devoted to the protection of the sacred fire, I have the house cleaned,
as well as the vessels, the wealth and grain, and the items for sleeping and sitting.
I shall always protect the boys and thoroughly instruct the girls;
even at the cost of forsaking my own dear pleasures, I am devoted to protecting the fetus.
I shall always avoid inflicting curses, anger, or torment upon children.
Grains should not be scattered about, nor should there be a scattering of food in the house.
Like jewels, I desire cows with fodder and water in my home. Having risen, being pure, I shall give alms to the twice-born.
If my husband goes abroad on account of some business,
I shall always remain self-restrained and endowed with many auspicious rites—
using collyrium, yellow pigment, bathing, garlands, and ointments.

I do not take pleasure in my husband’s adornment when he has gone out; I never rouse my husband from his pleasant sleep. Indeed, I do not wake him while he sleeps comfortably, for I protect my husband even when he is ill.
Even when there are urgent matters to be done, my mind is satisfied by that [conduct]. I never weary my husband for the sake of the household;
I always keep secrets concealed and maintain the house well-swept.
I strictly avoid an unchaste woman, as well as deceit and the practice of sorcery.
A woman who, with a concentrated mind, maintains this path of dharma,
is honored in the heavenly world like Arundhatī among women.

that illustrious and ascetic goddess, devoted to the dharma of her husband, then vanished from sight.
Whoever recites this narrative of the Pāṇḍavas on every festival day,

Yudhiṣṭhira.
"That which is to be known, the supreme duty to be performed by the great-souled ones—
O Bhīṣma,
out of favor toward me, you ought to tell me the essence of all the scriptures."
Listen to this which is extremely profound and brings liberation from saṃsāra;
it should be heard by you correctly and understood thoroughly, O lord of the people.
Formerly, there was a brahmin named Puṇḍarīka who, at a sacred ford, was engaged in silent recitation.
He questioned Nārada, the sage devoted to yoga, regarding the highest good.
Nārada then spoke to him that which had been told by the high-souled Brahmā:
"Listen attentively, my son, to this unsurpassed yoga of knowledge."
Though small in extent, it contains abundant meaning and the essence of the purpose of the Vedas and Shastras.
That Supreme Person, declared to be beyond primordial nature (prakṛti) as the twenty-fifth principle (pañcaviṃśaka),
is the self of all beings and is designated as Nara.
The principles born from Nara are known as "Nārāḥ"; since they are his place of resort (*ayana*), he is therefore remembered as Nārāyaṇa.
From Nārāyaṇa, the entire world is produced at the time of creation.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution, that very [universe] is completely absorbed back into him.
Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality. He is even higher than the highest; therefore, there is nothing higher than the Supreme.

They know him as Vāsudeva, as Viṣṇu, and likewise as the Self; he alone is the one [reality], refined by all the scriptures through various designations. Having churned all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, [one should know this].
This one thing is perfectly established: Nārāyaṇa is always to be meditated upon.
Therefore, having abandoned all those profound and extensive elaborations of scriptural meaning, meditate with undivided mind on the unborn, all-pervading Nārāyaṇa.

He who meditates upon Nārāyaṇa for even a moment without weariness attains that same goal; how much more so one who is devoted to Him as his supreme refuge! He who knows the eternal Brahman through the mantra "Obeisance to Nārāyaṇa" [attains the same].
At the time of death, by chanting this, one attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.
A person desiring their own welfare should always worship Brahman through hearing, reflecting, and through singing, praising, and worshipping.
He who is devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa is not stained by sin;
like the risen thousand-rayed sun, he purifies the entire world.
Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—
Abandoning the worship of Keśava, one never attains the supreme goal. The inclination toward Him is difficult to obtain even in thousands of future births.
Therefore, O observer of noble vows, propitiate that God who is affectionate toward His devotees.
Thus addressed by Nārada, that brahmin worshipped Hari—
the lotus-eyed one who bears the conch,
discus, and mace, who wears a crown and earrings, and upon whom the radiant Śrīvatsa and Kaustubha gems shine.
Having seen that Lord of the gods of gods, he breathed with intense agitation. Then, after a long time, he appeared before him in person,
being praised with Vedic hymns by gods, gandharvas, and kiṃnaras.
Then,
having been worshipped by all, the Blessed One, Hari, the indweller of yogis and the one who transcends the senses, departed for his own realm;
therefore, O Indra among kings, you too should be devoted to him and take refuge in him.
Having worshipped Him according to the proper method, devote yourself to the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama)—
the one who is undecaying, immortal, the sole object of meditation, devoid of beginning or end,
possessed of attributes yet free from qualities, primordial, both gross and exceedingly subtle.
"Take refuge in Viṣṇu, the peerless one who is beyond all comparison, who is accessible through the wisdom of yogis, the Lord and teacher of the three worlds.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Between conciliation or even the giving of gifts, which do you consider superior? Speak, O best of the Bharatas, as to which excels the other.
Bhīṣma said:
One person is appeased by conciliation, and another likewise by gifts;
having understood the nature of men, one should employ one or the other of these two. Hear from me, O King, bull of the Bharatas, the virtues of conciliation.
Just as one should win over even the most cruel beings through conciliation,
in this regard they cite this ancient history:
how a twice-born man, having been seized by a *rākṣasa* in the forest, was released.
But a certain Brahmin, endowed with wisdom, having been seized in a lonely forest by a Rakshasa intent on devouring him and fallen into great distress—
endowed as he was with intelligence and sacred learning— beheld that exceedingly terrifying creature.
He employed the *sāman* itself toward him; he did not become deluded, nor did he tremble. But the *rākṣasa*, having honored him with his speech, asked that twice-born man a question:
"You shall be released; answer my question: by what means have I been made pale and emaciated?"
Then, having reflected for a moment, the brahmin, remaining composed, answered the question of that rākṣasa with these verses:
"Surely you are staying in a foreign land, dwelling in a desolate place, and deprived of your kinsmen."
"You enjoy incomparable objects of sense; for that reason you are pale and thin.
Surely, O Rākṣasa, even though your friends have treated you with kindness, they have become alienated because of your own fault; for that reason you are pale and thin."
Those who are superior in wealth and power, yet inferior to you in your virtues, are arrogant;
they surely despise you, and for that reason you are pale and emaciated. Being virtuous yourself, you surely see others who lack virtue being honored.
"O wise one, you who have disciplined your self, you are pale and emaciated because of those who lack wisdom. Though tormented by the lack of means of subsistence, you despise such means;
surely it is from your own greatness that you suffer, and thus you are pale and emaciated."
"By tormenting yourself out of a sense of nobility, you have been adorned by some [virtue]; O virtuous one, thinking 'I have conquered,' you are thus pale and emaciated.
[Those] who are afflicted on wrong paths, their souls shrouded by desire and anger—"
I think you must be brooding over people; that is why you are pale and thin.
Surely you are esteemed by the wise but not associated with the unwise;
modest, yet intolerant of the wicked—that is why you are pale and thin.

Surely some enemy with the face of a friend, acting like a noble man, has deceived you and departed; it is because of him that you are pale and emaciated. He is surely one whose conduct is directed toward open goals, yet who is skilled in secrets and accomplished.
Surely you are not honored by those who know [the truth], and for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Surely you perceive that undertakings, though initiated with great effort and destined for magnificent results, have failed in their purpose; and for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Surely you have been humiliated by one who is intent upon a single object, whose wealth consists of the mere sound of words of equal meaning; it is for that reason that you are pale and emaciated,
speaking with certainty while those who are attached to what is unreal listen.
Your virtues do not shine forth; therefore you are pale and thin.
Deprived of wealth, intelligence, and sacred learning, yet endowed with spiritual luster alone, you surely aspire to something great; for that reason you are pale and thin.
I consider you to be one whose soul is dedicated to austerity and who longs for the forest; because your circle of kinsmen does not accept you, you are emaciated like a deer.
Surely, while you are devoted to your beloved wife, there is a wealthy neighbor living nearby.
You are young, graceful, and full of desire; therefore you are pale and emaciated.
Whether it be a very ill-behaved son or a son-in-law who is a source of trouble, or a wife who is antagonistic toward you; therefore you are pale and emaciated.
Your brothers were exceedingly hostile, or perhaps your father died tormented by hunger;
or your mother, your elder brother, or even your preceptor [was harmed]—for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Or perhaps a Brahmin was killed, or a cow, or sacred property (*brahmasva*) was seized in the past.
Perhaps you have lost your divine wealth or more at the wrong time; for that reason, you are pale and emaciated.
Or perhaps you have been robbed of your wife, or you are old, or hated by men in this world;
or perhaps you are an unknown elder—for that reason, you are pale and emaciated.

Seeing wealth intended for your old age, or even your own prosperity seized by others, or finding your livelihood dependent on the wicked— for these reasons you have become pale and emaciated; yet, my dear son, your virtue has not diminished even in times of adversity, despite those who merely call themselves your friends.
Because you did not renounce [your wealth] there at that time, for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Surely, among those who possess wealth, your speech—though unsurpassed—is not shining forth when spoken at the proper time; for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Because you are unable to appease one who is stubborn despite his former learning, foolish, yet angry and dear to your heart, you have become pale and emaciated.
Surely, having failed to bring someone to agreement regarding some desired task of yours...
Someone desires you excessively, and for that reason you are pale and thin;
false faults have been attributed to you by those who speak behind your back. Surely a friend, considering your own virtues, must certainly honor you.
"You know that this is for my sake; therefore you are pale and thin.
Surely you do not wish to speak out your inner intention out of shame, because of the difficulty of attaining [your goal]; therefore you are pale and thin."
"Surely you desire to win over all the people in this world with their various intellects and tastes by means of your own virtues; for that reason, O deer, you have become thin.
"One who is ignorant, timid, and of little purpose [cannot obtain] that which arises from learning, valor, and generosity."
13,125.028b You have sought out those who are base; for that reason you are pale and emaciated. 13,125.028c You surely seek after fame; for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
13,125.029a Some fruit longed for by you has not yet been obtained.
"Your wealth was seized by others; for that reason you are pale and emaciated.
Surely, seeing no fault of your own committed by yourself, you have been falsely accused without cause; for that reason you are pale and emaciated."

Because you have failed to secure the welfare of your vigilant friends, you suffer the pain born of the loss of your purpose—a pain devoid of the merits that wealth usually brings; for this reason, O deer, you are emaciated.
Furthermore, having seen virtuous householders as well as unvirtuous forest-dwellers, [you are likewise distressed].
Because pearls were released and yet remained stuck in your dwelling, you have become pale and emaciated.
Since words spoken at the right time and place, which are consistent with dharma and purpose,
do not find a firm footing in you, you have surely become pale and emaciated.
"O wise one, desiring to live, you surely subsist on wealth given by the unvirtuous; for that reason, you are pale and emaciated. Having seen the wicked prospering and the virtuous perishing,"
13,125.035c Surely you are seeking a worthy [consort], and for that reason you are pale and thin.
13,125.036a You surely desire to do what is pleasing to those who are mutually opposed, 13,125.036c without causing discord among your friends; for that reason you are pale and thin.

"I think you are reflecting upon those who, though learned in the Vedas, are engaged in improper acts, and those who, though wise, have not conquered their senses; for that reason you are pale and thin.
Thus honored, the Rākṣasa in turn paid homage to that Brahmin.

By whatever [offering] a god is pleased, by that same [offering] the ancestors are likewise pleased.
The sages, the Pramathas, Śrī, Citragupta, and the elephants of the quarters;
where the dharma of the sages is remembered along with its secret mysteries and great fruit,
as well as the fruit of great gifts and the fruit of all sacrifices.
O sinless one, whoever should know this thus, or having known it, acts accordingly,
he becomes a transgressor and is joined here with those very faults along with their qualities. A cartwheel is equal to ten slaughterhouses, and a banner is equal to ten cartwheels.
A courtesan is equal to ten banners; a king is equal to ten courtesans. It is said that a king is superior by half [the value] of all these combined.
This scripture, which encompasses the three aims of life (*trivarga*), is pure and possesses the characteristics of merit.
The merit of the prophecy of the Dharma and the great secret of its hearing is vast;
that which is joined with the Dharma should be heard, for it was ordained by the Thirty-three Gods themselves.
In this [teaching], the secrets of the ancestors are proclaimed during the rite of the *śrāddha*.
The secret of all the deities is told in its entirety;
therein is recorded the dharma of the sages along with its secret, which yields great fruit,
as well as the fruit of the great sacrifices and likewise the fruit of all gifts.
The Lord Nārāyaṇa himself declares the fruit for those mortals who always recite this, for whomsoever it remains present, and for those who, having heard it,
proclaim its fruit: the fruit of [giving] cows, the fruit of sacred fords, and whatever fruit belongs to sacrifices.
That man who honors his guests obtains this fruit. For those listeners who possess faith and whose minds are pure, the worlds have clearly been won by that faithful and virtuous person.
He is indeed released from sin and is not tainted by evil; that man, having gone to the world hereafter, constantly attains merit. Then, after some time, by chance, a messenger of the gods [arrived].
Remaining there, having become invisible, he addressed Vāsava:
"By the command of those two Aśvins, the best of physicians, who are endowed with all objects of desire,
I have arrived here along with the humans, ancestors, and gods."
Why indeed is sexual intercourse forbidden for both the giver and the eater at a *śrāddha*?

"Whose son is Uttara said to be? This I wish to know.

O ancestors!"
All the former gods and the ancestors, having honored the sky-walker, said:

If a man, having given a *śrāddha* and having eaten at it, should approach a woman,
his ancestors lie within that semen for that entire month.
Now, I shall explain the distribution of the funeral cakes (*piṇḍa*) in their proper order.
For the *piṇḍa* descending from below, having entered the water, one should contemplate it;
as for the middle *piṇḍa*, there alone does a single wife partake of it. The third *piṇḍa* among those, one should offer into the fire (*jātavedas*).
This procedure for the *śrāddha* has been declared so that dharma is not lost;
his ancestors are always satisfied and delighted in mind.

His progeny increases, and it remains inexhaustible;
you have explained the sequential distribution of the funeral cakes (piṇḍas) individually for all three classes of ancestors.

Even they do not thus understand the determination regarding the rites for the ancestors,
with the exception of that high-souled, supreme Cirajīvin;

listen attentively to me as I explain the destiny of those three balls of rice.

And the progeny of one who bestows [a daughter] in this manner increases.

And the highly fortunate ancestors honored that sage. Having meditated in his mind upon Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Gaṅgā, Prabhāsa, and the Puṣkara lakes, he should then plunge into the water.

which I heard being spoken by Bṛhaspati at the abode of Sthāṇu.

having ascended a mountain, one should gaze at the fire with one foot raised, abstaining from food, with arms upraised and palms joined in reverence.
Endowed with great austerity, one obtains the fruit of fasting;
scorched by the rays of the sun, one casts off all evil.
Whether in the summer season or in the cold, in this way one casts off evil.
Then, for one who is liberated from that evil, there arises eternal splendor;
blazing with brilliance like the sun, he shines again like the moon,
as the king of the gods, Śatakratu, in the midst of the host of the thirty.
Bṛhaspati spoke these most excellent and sweet words to the Blessed One regarding the secret of Dharma that brings happiness to human beings.
And declare accurately those faults along with their secret causes:
those who urinate facing the sun, those who hate the wind,
and those who do not offer fuel into the kindled sacrificial fire.
And those who milk a cow that has a young calf for the sake of its milk—I shall declare their faults; listen to them, O Lord of Śacī. Bhānumat, Anila, and Havyavāha, O Vāsava...
Cows were created by the Self-Existent One as the very mothers of the worlds;
they are deities among these mortals, capable of delivering the worlds.
May you all listen to each of these determinations of dharma.
For eighty-six thousand years, those of evil conduct who bring disgrace upon their families,
as well as all women of evil conduct who urinate facing the sun,
O Śakra, shall have offspring that perish while still in the womb due to their hatred of the wind.

Those men who do not offer fuel into the blazing carrier of oblations during their fire-rites— the Purifier does not consume their offerings. Furthermore, those humans here who drink the milk of cows with young calves...
Among them, none are born as milk-drinkers who increase the lineage;
they are joined with the destruction of progeny and the decay of the family line.
Thus was this observed of old by the twice-born who had grown old in their clans.

Therefore, those things that should be avoided must always be avoided, and those things that should be performed must always be performed by a mortal who desires prosperity; this I tell you as the truth.
Then all the highly blessed deities, together with the hosts of Maruts, [spoke].
Then the highly fortunate ṛṣis questioned the ancestors:
"By what means are the ancestors satisfied by mortals of limited intellect?
And how may a gift for the sake of the deceased become inexhaustible?"
"How may mortals attain freedom from debt, and by what action?
O ancestors,
we desire to hear this, for our curiosity is great."
O highly fortunate ones, this doubt has indeed been raised according to the principles of logic.
Listen to that by which we may be satisfied regarding mortals who perform virtuous deeds:
through the release of blue cattle and with water mixed with sesame seeds on the new moon day.

By offering lamps during the rainy season, one becomes free from debt to the ancestors. This gift is inexhaustible, sincere, and yields great fruit; it is proclaimed that our satisfaction thereby shall be eternal.
"And those mortals who, full of faith, shall maintain this lineage,
they will deliver their great-grandfathers from the difficult path of hell.
Hearing these words of the ancestors, the ascetic, his hair standing on end with joy, [spoke].
The highly resplendent Vṛddhagārgya spoke these words to them:

"O you whose wealth is asceticism, what are the merits of one who releases a dark-colored bull (*nīlaṣaṇḍa*) during the rainy season, as well as those of giving lamps and offerings of sesame seeds with water?"
O ancestors,
if one were to draw up water from the tail of Nīlaṣaṇḍa,
by that act the ancestors would be satiated for sixty thousand years.
But he who, having removed the mud from the bank that has reached the peak, remains there,
by that act his ancestors undoubtedly go to the world of Soma.
By the gift of a lamp during the rainy season, a man shines like the moon.
There is no form of darkness for him who offers a lamp;
and those mortals who, on the new moon day (amāvāsyā), offer water mixed with sesame seeds,
O ascetic, having taken a vessel made of udumbara wood and mixed it with honey.
By them, the *śrāddha* is performed according to the truth, together with its secret mysteries.
Their progeny shall always be joyful and well-nourished;
indeed, the increase of the family lineage shall be the fruit for the giver of the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*).
But he who performs [the rite] with faith shall become free from debt to the ancestors.
Thus has this sequence of times for the *śrāddha* been fully described.
Bhīṣma.
The ritual procedure, the recipient, and the fruit have been duly proclaimed. "By what means do you become pleased, and how do you attain satisfaction?
Thus questioned by the Lord of the Gods, the imperishable Hari spoke.
Censuring the Brāhmaṇas is a source of great enmity for me.

When the Brāhmaṇas are constantly honored, I am honored as well; of this there is no doubt. The lords of the Brāhmaṇas must always be saluted, and likewise, after eating, one’s own feet should be touched.
I am pleased with those mortals who offer an oblation,
who behold Vāmana the Brāhmaṇa and Varāha risen from the waters,
and who bears upon his head the earth that has been uplifted.
No inauspiciousness or defilement whatsoever shall befall those men who always worship the Aśvattha tree, the Rocanā, and the cow;
by them the entire world, including gods, asuras, and humans, is worshipped.
In that form, I truly accept their worship;
this is my worship, and there is no other as long as the worlds endure. Otherwise, mortals of small intelligence worship in vain.
"O Indra, I do not accept that; it brings me no satisfaction.
[I see] the discus, the feet, the boar, and also the dwarf Brāhmaṇa."
"Why do you praise the earth when it has been uplifted?
You create all beings; you withdraw all creatures.
Bhīṣma.
The eternal nature of all beings, including mortals, [is thus].
Then Viṣṇu, smiling, spoke these words:
"The Daityas have been slain by my discus, and the earth has been traversed by my feet."
Assuming the form of a boar, the earth was lifted up;
assuming the form of a dwarf, King Bali was conquered by me.
In this way, I am well-pleased with these high-souled men.
Those who shall honor me— there is no defeat for them.
Moreover, having seen a Brahmin who has arrived as a religious student (brahmacārin),
and having offered an oblation to that Brahmin, his food is nectar.
Having performed the twilight devotions dedicated to Indra and standing facing the sun,
he is as one who has bathed in all sacred fords and is liberated from all sins. O you whose wealth is austerity, this secret has been told to you in its entirety.
Baladeva said:
"To you who ask with doubt, what more shall I tell?
Listen to this supreme secret that brings happiness to human beings."
Unaware and ignorant, those who suffer, oppressed by malevolent spirits,
are liberated from their taints if that mortal rises at dawn and touches a cow, ghee, curds, mustard seeds, and *priyaṅgu* grains.
All beings, whether in front or behind,
as well as the gods, avoid the remnants of food and the vulnerable points of those whose wealth is their austerity.
Holding an udumbara vessel filled with water and facing north,
one should undertake a fast or resolve upon a vow;
thus the deities are pleased with him and his desired goal is accomplished.
Otherwise, mortals of small intellect act in vain;
for both in fasting and in the *bali* offering, a copper vessel is superior.
The *bali*, alms, the *arghya* offering, and the water with sesame seeds for the ancestors [should likewise be offered in such vessels].
It should be given with a copper vessel; otherwise, the fruit will be small.
This secret has been declared so that the deities may be pleased. This is the Dharma.
A Brahmin who serves a king, one who rings a bell, a personal attendant,
a cowherd, a merchant, as well as an artisan or an actor, one who betrays a friend, one who does not study the Vedas, and he who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* (a woman of low caste).
In these cases, one must never, under any circumstances, offer oblations to the gods or the ancestors;
for his ancestors are deprived of their funeral cakes (piṇḍas) and he certainly does not gratify them. This is so when a guest turns away from someone’s house with his hopes frustrated.
The ancestors, the gods, and likewise the sacred fires depart in despair from that man who does not offer hospitality to a guest.
[They depart] along with those who have killed women, those who have killed cows, those who are ungrateful, those who have slain Brahmins, and those who have violated the teacher’s bed.
Agni becomes equal in fault to those by whom a guest is not honored. That evil-minded mortal who, having raised his foot, should touch cows, incurs the same sin.

Whether it be a highly fortunate Brāhmaṇa or likewise a blazing fire, I shall declare the faults regarding him; listen to that with concentrated minds. His soundless [flame] touches heaven, and the ancestors indeed tremble.
Great dejection is produced among the gods,
and the fire of great splendor does not accept the sacrificial offering; moreover,
he is cooked in hell for a hundred lifetimes.
They never permit even an expiation for such an act;
therefore, cows must never be touched with the foot. A Brāhmaṇa possesses great splendor, just as fire blazes forth.
By a mortal who is faithful and desires his own welfare— Viśvāmitra says:
these faults have been declared by me for one who would abandon even a single quarter-verse among these three.
Listen to this supreme secret, a mystery consistent with the Dharma:
he who should offer an oblation to the ancestors with *paramānna* during the "elephant's shadow" (*gajacchāyā*) at the Kutupa moment, facing southward toward the east.
When the month of Bhādrapada arrives and the constellation Maghā is in its dark fortnight,
hear what the extent of the merit of that gift is like:
by him, a great *śrāddha* has been performed here for thirteen years.
There are many cows, well-proportioned, with symmetrical limbs, free from fear from any quarter,
secure, and indeed as numerous as a vast multitude.
Just as formerly in the City of Brahmā she was with her calf, and at the sacrifice of Śatakratu, the wielder of the thunderbolt;
and furthermore, she who is established in the station of Viṣṇu.
And those who stand upon the path of the sun,
as do all the gods together with Nārada,
bestow upon him the name "Sarvasaha" (All-enduring).
Whoever indeed pays homage with this mantra is liberated from the karma of evil deeds and attains the worlds of Purandara.
The fruit of cows and the splendor of the moon— indeed,
whoever recites this mantra, which is favored by the thirty gods, in the midst of a cow-pen on the sacred festival days (parvan), [attains these].
For him there is no sin, no fear, and no sorrow;
Bhīṣma said that he goes to the world of the Thousand-eyed One.
Then seven highly fortunate sages,
world-renowned and headed by Vasiṣṭha, all approached Brahmā, who was born from the lotus;
having circumambulated him, they all stood with palms joined in reverence.

Vasiṣṭha, the foremost among those who know Brahman, spoke these words to them regarding a question beneficial to all living beings, especially concerning the field of Brahman: "How do mortals who are destitute of wealth, poor, yet of virtuous conduct [attain their goal]?"
"By what action in this world do people here obtain the fruit of sacrifice?
Having heard these words of theirs, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O highly fortunate ones, what a profound question! Its meaning is hidden, supreme, and auspicious."
That which has been described by you as subtle and superior for mortals—
listen, O you whose wealth is asceticism; I shall relate it all in its entirety,
so that a mortal may obtain the fruit of sacrifice, of this there is no doubt.
When Rohiṇī coincides with the bright fortnight of the month of Pauṣa,
one should lie down upon the open sky during that conjunction of the lunar mansion.
Wearing a single garment, pure, bathed, full of faith, and composed in mind, one should observe this vow.
Having drunk the rays of the Soma, one obtains the fruit of a great sacrifice.
O best of the twice-born, this supreme secret has been told to you by Vibhāvasu.
13,125.038d@014_0276 You, who perceive the subtle meaning of reality, ask me about this:
13,125.038d@014_0277 Regarding the full handful of water and the unbroken grains topped with ghee 13,125.038d@014_0278 offered as the moon is rising—
what becomes of that water and those unbroken grains?
For a mortal who stands facing [the deity] on the full moon day should offer an oblation;
by him the fire-ritual is performed, and his three fires have been sacrificed into. And as for the foolish man who would kill a tree on the new moon day—
For even by a single leaf one is tainted by the sin of killing a Brahmin; indeed,
that foolish man who chews a tooth-stick on the new moon day has harmed the Moon, and the ancestors tremble with fear because of him.
The gods do not accept his sacrificial offerings on the festival days;
his prosperity declines, his ancestors become angry with him, and his lineage perishes.
Where vessels are scattered about, as are drinking cups and seats;
where women are struck down in a house overcome by dejection;
and where the gods and ancestors are neglected during festivals or sacred occasions.
Dejected, they depart from that house which is afflicted by dejection.
Aṅgiras said:
"But he who should give a lamp at a Karañjaka tree for a full year,"
Gārgya says:
One who holds the root of *suvarcalā* in his hand finds his progeny increasing.
He should constantly practice hospitality and provide a lamp in a shelter.

Avoiding sleep during the day, one should not eat meat; one should not harm cows or Brahmins, and one should recite the *puṣkara* verses. This is the most excellent dharma, accompanied by its secret, and it yields great fruit.
Even after performing hundreds of sacrifices, that oblation goes to destruction;
but those dharmas performed by the faithful never perish. And understand this supreme secret, along with its esoteric mystery.
In the Śrāddha-rite, in rites for the gods, at sacred fords, and on festival days,
the deities do not consume the sacrificial offering (havis) that has been seen with the eyes of a woman in her menses, or one who has white leprosy, or one who has only daughters.
And his ancestors will not be satisfied for thirteen years.
Having become pure and dressed in white garments, he should cause the Brahmins to pronounce a blessing.
— Dhaumya.
One should likewise recite the *Bhārata*, for thus the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) becomes inexhaustible.
A broken vessel, a bedstead, a cock, and likewise a dog—
all these are inauspicious, as is any tree growing within a house.
They say that when a vessel is broken, there is strife; on a bedstead, there is loss of wealth.
The deities do not consume the sacrificial offering when there is a cock or a dog present.
At the root of a tree, a being is surely established; therefore, one should not plant a tree [there].
Jamadagni said:

Whether one should perform a horse sacrifice or a hundred Vājapeya sacrifices, or hang head-downward, or undertake a prosperous sacrificial session (sattra)— [all these do not equal the merit of this].
If his heart is not pure, he will certainly go to hell;
sacrifice, truth, and purity of heart are all equal. Having given a *prastha* of barley-meal with a pure mind to a twice-born man, [one attains great merit].
Vāyu has reached the world of Brahmā; that illustration is sufficient. I shall now proclaim a certain Dharma that brings happiness to human beings.
Listen with concentrated minds to those faults along with their secret aspects. The fire-ritual must be performed, and one should eat the finest food;
a lamp must also be lit, and an offering of water mixed with sesame seeds must be made for the ancestors.
By this method, a mortal who is faithful and composed,
who offers water with sesame seeds for the four months of the rainy season,
and who provides food according to his ability to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas—
In this world, one obtains the full fruit of a hundred animal sacrifices.
Furthermore, learn this other secret and censurable matter:
that a *vṛṣala* (outcaste) is the leader of the fire, and foolish women are the sacrificial offerings.
He thinks, "This is indeed dharma," yet he is tainted by adharma;
his sacred fires become angry with him, and he goes to a birth as a Śūdra. Furthermore, the ancestors, together with the gods, are not pleased with him.
Now listen to me as I describe the expiation for that [offense],
by performing which a man properly becomes happy and free from distress:
with the urine and dung of cows, and with milk and ghee.
For three days, one should perform the fire-ritual (agnikārya), abstaining from food and remaining composed.
Then, when a full year has passed, the deities accept [the offering],
and his ancestors rejoice when the time for the śrāddha ceremony arrives.
For this has been proclaimed as both unrighteousness and righteousness, a secret doctrine that brings the happiness of heaven after death for mortals who desire heaven. — Lomaśa.
Those who are attached to the wives of others without having taken a wife for themselves—
their ancestors truly become hopeless at the time of the *śrāddha* offering. So too it is for him who delights in another’s wife and he who serves a barren woman.
He who seizes the property of a Brahmin incurs the same fault as those [who commit other sins];
they become unworthy of conversation with the ancestors—of this there is no doubt. Neither the deities nor the ancestors accept their sacrificial offering.
Therefore, one should avoid the wife of another and a woman who is barren;
for he who desires his own welfare must not seize the property of a Brahmin.
Listen now to another secret, a mystery conjoined with dharma.
One who possesses faith should always carry out the instructions of their gurus.
On the twelfth lunar day and on the full moon day, month after month, one should offer clarified butter and unbroken grains to the Brahmins; learn now the merit of that act.
By that [gift], Soma increases as does the great ocean;
Vāsava bestows a fruit equal to one-fourth of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Through this gift, a man becomes radiant and heroic.
And the blessed Lord Soma, being pleased, grants desired boons.
Listen now to another duty, along with its secret, which yields great fruit and brings happiness to human beings upon reaching this Kali Yuga.
That mortal who, having risen at dawn and bathed, wearing white garments,
with a concentrated mind offers a vessel of sesame seeds to the Brāhmaṇas,
and he who offers water with sesame seeds along with honey to the ancestors— [he attains great merit].
Listen now to the fruit of that which consists of lamps and *kṛsara*;

regarding this, the Lord Pākaśāsana has declared the fruit for a vessel of sesame seeds. Furthermore, he who should perform the gift of a cow and the eternal gift of land—[the fruit of these is as follows].

The deities consider a vessel of sesame seeds to be equal to one who performs the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice with abundant sacrificial fees. The ancestors consider water mixed with sesame seeds at a Śrāddha ceremony to be inexhaustible.
His ancestors are satisfied by offerings of lamps and *kṛsara*.
This is honored in heaven and in the world of the ancestors, as well as by the gods.
Thus has this ancient teaching, seen by the seers, been declared by me.
Then all the hosts of ṛṣis, along with the ancestors and the gods,
being composed in mind, questioned Arundhatī, who was advanced in ascetic merit.
Equal in character and vigor to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha,
we wish to hear from you the secrets of dharma,
O Arundhatī.
"O auspicious lady, you ought to speak that which is most secret to you.
Indeed, through the mere remembrance of you, an increase in my ascetic merit has been attained;
and by your grace, I shall proclaim the eternal dharmas."
Listen now in their entirety to those [teachings] along with their secrets and esoteric doctrines.
They should be imparted to one who possesses faith and whose mind is likewise pure.
To one who lacks faith, to the arrogant, to a slayer of a Brahmin, or to one who has violated the teacher’s bed, they must not be given.
Indeed, there are four with whom one should not converse; one should not reveal the Dharma to them.
Even if a man were to give away tawny cows day after day for twelve years, or were to perform a sacrificial session month after month forever—
Even if one were to give a hundred thousand cows at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara,
that fruit of merit would not equal [the merit of him] with whom a guest is satisfied. Listen now to another duty that brings happiness to human beings.
One who possesses faith should perform this rite, which includes its secret mysteries and yields great fruit.
Having risen at dawn and taken darbha grass along with water into the midst of the cows,
he should sprinkle that water upon the horns and the heads of the cows.
Listen to the fruit of his merit if he should receive [the gift] while fasting:
whatever sacred fords (tīrtha) are heard of in the three worlds, frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas, and served by great Ṛṣis— [he obtains the merit of all of them].
The sprinkling of them with the water from the horns of cows was equal [to other rites], and "Excellent! Excellent! was proclaimed by the gods as well as the ancestors;
so said the Grandfather (Brahmā).
And Arundhatī was also honored by the spirits who were greatly rejoicing:
"O highly blessed lady, oh, the Dharma has been proclaimed along with its secret!—
Yama."
"I grant you a boon, O blessed one; may your ascetic merit increase forever. The divine and delightful discourse that I have heard from you is wonderful.
Now listen to the words of Citragupta, which are pleasing to me."
This secret, joined with the Dharma, can be heard by the great seers,
and by a mortal who possesses faith and desires his own welfare. For indeed, no merit or evil deed that has been performed ever perishes.
Whatever a person offers to the Sun during a festival day,
when that mortal has departed for the world of the departed, the virtuous-souled Vibhāvasu acknowledges all of it, and it is utilized there accordingly.
I shall proclaim a certain auspicious Dharma, the teaching of Citragupta:
water and likewise lamps should always be given,
as well as sandals, an umbrella, and a Kapila cow, each according to the prescribed rule.
At Puṣkara, a tawny cow should be given to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas;
one should also diligently maintain the *agnihotra* sacrifice in every respect.
And this other duty was likewise proclaimed by Citragupta.
The most excellent beings ought to hear separately the fruit of this;
for all living beings must undergo dissolution through the passage of time. Having reached that difficult place, they are tormented by hunger and thirst.
Being burned, they are tormented; there is no escape from that place.
Those of small intelligence enter into blinding and terrible darkness. Therein I shall proclaim the Dharma, by which one may cross over difficult passages.
It involves little expense but yields great benefit, and brings about the arising of happiness after death. The divine qualities of water are especially prominent in the world of the *preta*s.
There, a river named Puṇyodakā (Meritorious Water) is ordained for them.
There, the water is inexhaustible, cool, and indeed like nectar.
He who gives a gift of drink drinks that very water there.
Now hear the detailed account of the virtues resulting from the gift of a lamp.
The giver of light certainly does not see the darkness of gloom;
the moon, the sun, and fire bestow their radiance upon him,
and the pure deities regard him from every direction.
And just as the sun shines, so does a man who has gone to the world of the departed shine;
therefore, a lamp should be offered, and especially water. Those who give a tawny cow (*kapilā*) to a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas—
Listen now to the specific fruit that accrues from [visiting] Puṣkara:
by him, a hundred cows along with a bull have been given eternally;
and whatever sinful deed there may be, even if it be equal to the murder of a Brahmin.
Indeed, a single tawny cow (kapilā) purifies [the donor] just as a hundred cows given away would;
therefore, a tawny cow should be given during the Kaumudī festival at Jyeṣṭha-puṣkara.
For them, there is nothing uneven, no suffering, and no thorns.
And he who gives a pair of sandals to an excellent twice-born man who is a worthy recipient,
obtains a pleasant shade when gone to the next world through the gift of an umbrella;
for there is never any destruction of a gift once given in this world.
Having heard the opinion of Citragupta, the immensely radiant Vibhāvasu, his hair standing on end with joy, spoke to all the deities and the ancestors: "Indeed,
I have heard the secret of Dharma from the high-souled Citragupta."
Those mortals who, full of faith, bestow this gift upon high-souled Brahmins— no fear exists for them. However,
there are these five defects of dharma for which no atonement exists here.
Those who are unfit for conversation, lacking in proper conduct, and base among men should be avoided;
namely, the killer of a Brahmin, the killer of a cow, he who is addicted to another's wife,
the man who lacks faith, and he who lives off a woman.
For these evildoers have gone to the realm of pretas and are cooked in hell like fish, feeding upon pus and blood;
they are five kinds of beings who cannot even converse with the ancestors or the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"The *snātaka* Brahmins, those others whose wealth is their asceticism,
and all the highly fortunate gods and ancestors [were there]."
And the highly fortunate ṛṣis spoke these words to the Pramathas:
"O highly fortunate ones, you who are indeed direct perceivers of night-stalkers, why do you harm men who are impure, unholy, and base?"
And what are remembered as obstacles by which you do not harm mortals? What are the demon-slaying [rites] by which you would perish in the houses,
O Pramathas?

"O night-stalkers, we wish to hear all this from you: why are you always impure after sexual intercourse, and why do you invert the order of high and low? Why, out of delusion, do you eat meat and sleep at the foot of a tree?"
He upon whose head is the food offering, and he who lies at his feet— all such men are defiled by leftovers and full of many flaws;
they discharge impurities and phlegm even into the water.

13,125.038d@014_0461 These humans are both to be eaten and to be slain; there is no doubt in this matter. 13,125.038d@014_0462 For we overpower those men who possess such character and conduct. 13,125.038d@014_0463 But listen to the countermeasures by which we are unable to cause harm.
Those who apply yellow orpiment [to their bodies], those whose hands hold *vacā* root,
and those who, being devoted to that [practice], offer clarified butter and unbroken rice-grains upon the head— we are indeed unable to harm them, nor those who do not eat meat.
In whose house fire burns constantly by day and by night—
the hide and fangs of a hyena, as well as a mountain tortoise,
the smoke of clarified butter, a cat, a goat, and a tawny-brown dog— [in that house, O King, there is no fear of Yama].
In the houses of those householders where these [images] remain,
their dwellings shall be unassailable by the most dreadful flesh-eaters,
as well as by those like us who roam through the worlds at will.
Therefore, O lord of the people, these [mantras] are destroyers of Rākṣasas within houses.
Bhīṣma said:
All this has been told to you, regarding which you had great doubt.
Then the Grandfather, who resembles a lotus and was born from a lotus,
spoke these words to the gods and to Vāsava, the lord of Śacī:
"This mighty Nāga is powerful and dwells in the subterranean realm."
There is one named Reṇuka, radiant and possessed of great being and prowess;
all these great elephants are exceedingly brilliant, of great heroism,
and they support the entire earth with its mountains, forests, and groves.

"Permitted by you all, let Reṇuka go there and inquire about all those secret teachings of Dharma from those great elephants. Having heard the words of the Grandfather, those gods then [addressed] Reṇuka.
13,125.038d@014_0484 The calm Reṇuka dispatched [messengers] to where those upholders of the earth were.
13,125.038d@014_0485 "O you of great strength, I have been authorized by both the gods and the ancestors."
I wish to hear from you, in accordance with reality, the secrets of the Dharma. O illustrious elephants of the quarters, tell me that which is your intended truth.

In the month of Kārttika, on the auspicious eighth day of the dark fortnight under the asterism Āśleṣā, he who gives rice mixed with molasses while reciting this mantra at a śrāddha ceremony— being restrained in diet and free from anger— [attains great merit].
Baladeva and the other Nāgas who are exceedingly powerful,
as well as Ananta, Akṣaya, and the eternally coiled ones of great strength—
those great beings and serpents who are born from their lineage.
"May they offer tribute to me for the increase of my strength and splendor.
When the glorious Nārāyaṇa lifted up the earth,
such was the power of that god as he raised the world."
Having spoken thus, one should offer the *bali* there at the anthill;
strewn with the flowers of the lordly elephant and adorned with blue garments and unguents,
one should present it at the anthill when the sun has set.
Thus, all of us below, oppressed by the burden, are content;
we do not perceive that fatigue while supporting the earth. Thus, though afflicted by the weight, we consider it our duty, remaining indifferent to our own exhaustion.
Whether he be a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, if he has fasted and performs this for a year, he shall obtain great fruit from his gift.
By offering an oblation upon an anthill, we consider that to be of great fruit for us.
And all those nāgas of great prowess throughout the three worlds,
having been offered hospitality for a hundred years in accordance with reality—
having heard that, the world-elephants, as well as the deities and the ancestors, [were filled with joy].
Maheśvara and the highly fortunate ṛṣis honored Reṇuka, saying:
"Having extracted the essence, you have rightly proclaimed the Dharma."
Listen all of you to this secret of the Dharma from me—
those men whose intellects are grounded in the Dharma and who are full of faith;
to them should this [teaching], together with its secret, be imparted, for it yields great fruit.
But he who, free from anxiety, gives daily fodder for a cow for one month and likewise eats but a single meal— listen now to the fruit of his merit:
these cows are highly blessed and are remembered as the supreme purifier.
They sustain the three worlds, including the gods, asuras, and humans.
In them indeed lies great merit, and service toward them yields great fruit;
day by day, one is joined with righteousness through the daily provision for cows.
For these were indeed authorized by me previously in the Kṛta Yuga;
thereafter, I was entreated by Brahmā, who is born from the lotus.
Therefore, the bull stands above me, stationed in Vraja.
I rejoice together with the cows; therefore, they should always be honored. Possessing great power and granting boons, they bestow desired gifts when they are worshipped.
Those cows approve of whatever fruit results from all one's actions.
Skanda said:
"Of that merit, one-fourth belongs to him who gives daily fodder to cows;
listen with concentrated minds to that dharma which is also approved by me."
Listen now to the merit of one who, having taken earth from the two horns of a blue bull, performs an ablution for three days:
he shall purify all his inauspiciousness and attain sovereignty in the hereafter.
As long as a mortal is born, so long shall he be a hero.
Furthermore, learn this other secret along with its esoteric mystery:
having taken up a vessel of udumbara wood filled with cooked food together with honey.
On the full moon day, when the moon is rising, one should offer an oblation to Soma.
Listen with faith to the eternal fruit of that merit:
the Sādhyas, the Rudras, the Ādityas, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the two Aśvins.
The Maruts and the Vasus indeed accept that offering;
by it Soma increases, as does the ocean, the great reservoir of waters.
Viṣṇu...

This dharma, together with its secret teachings, which brings happiness, has been taught by me. Whoever should always recite daily all the secrets of dharma belonging to the high-souled deities and the secrets of the sages, [attains the highest goal].
Whoever hears this without malice, with faith and a concentrated mind,
for him no obstacle arises and no fear exists; and whatever auspicious, meritorious dharmas have been proclaimed along with their secret teachings, [he shall attain them].
The fruit of the Dharma belongs to those who, having conquered their senses, should recite this;
for such a person, evil does not prevail, nor is he defiled by evil. Whether one recites it, causes it to be heard, or merely hears it, one obtains the fruit.
The ancestors and the gods partake of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, which become inexhaustible.
Furthermore, on the festival days (*parvan*), a self-restrained man should cause the foremost of Brahmins to recite [the sacred texts] constantly for the sake of the seers,
the deities, and the ancestors.
He becomes beloved and illustrious, always diligent in his duties; even having committed a sinful deed, provided it is one that excludes the great mortal sins—
thus said Bhīṣma.
Having heard this secret Dharma, one is liberated from all sins. O lord of men, this is indeed the secret of the Dharma of the deities;
it has been proclaimed by me as taught by Vyāsa, and it is honored by all the gods.
Even if the earth were filled with jewels, this unsurpassed knowledge is superior to that;
therefore, one who knows the Dharma should consider this alone as what ought to be heard,
and not by one who lacks faith or is an atheist.
This should not be disclosed to one who has lost their dharma, nor to one devoid of virtue, nor to one whose reasoning is corrupted, nor to a hater of the guru,
nor to one who has not realized the Self.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who, indeed, are those whose food may be eaten by a Brāhmaṇa here, and who are those whose food may be eaten by a Kṣatriya?
Bhīṣma replied:
13,125.038d@014A_0002 Likewise, O Bhārata, who are those whose food may be eaten by a Vaiśya, and who are those for a Śūdra?
13,125.038d@014A_0003 In this world, Brāhmaṇas are to be fed by a Brāhmaṇa, as well as Kṣatriyas;
13,125.038d@014A_0004 likewise, Vaiśyas are also to be fed, but Śūdras are to be avoided.
Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas are indeed those whose food may be eaten by a Kṣatriya;
however, Śūdras must be avoided, for they eat all things and are devoid of ritual action.
Likewise, Vaiśyas are those whose food may be eaten by Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas as well.

Those who maintain the perpetual sacred fires, those who dwell in solitude, and those who are devoted to the four-monthly rites— if one eats the food of such people, he eats the impurity of the earth;
he drinks the filth of men and consumes the impurity of the people.
He who eats in such a manner from the hands of Śūdras eats the impurity of the earth.
Those twice-born men who eat the food of Śūdras consume the impurity of the earth;
even one established in his own duty is cooked in hell if he partakes of the labor of a Śūdra.

A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and a Vaiśya who stands in his improper occupation are all cooked [in hell]. On the other hand, Brāhmaṇas devoted to the private study of the Veda are for the well-being of men;
they say that the Kṣatriya exists for protection, and the Vaiśya for nourishment.
Whatever work a Vaiśya performs, he indeed lives by that after having entered it;
agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the blameless occupations of a Vaiśya.
But he who, having abandoned his own duty, should perform the work of a Śūdra—

He should be known as a Śūdra and must never be fed. A physician, a professional soldier, a city magistrate, a domestic chaplain, an astrologer, and one who studies for no purpose— all these are equal to Śūdras.
Now, he who shamelessly eats among these occupations of Śūdras,
having consumed food that should not be eaten, encounters terrible fear; [he loses] his lineage, his vigor, and his splendor, and is reborn as an animal.
He goes forth like a dog—indeed, inactive and devoid of dharma.
He eats the food of a physician, and that food is like excrement;
the food of an unchaste woman is like urine, and the food of an artisan is like blood.
Even if one who is esteemed by the virtuous eats the food of those who live by their learning, that food is like that of a Śūdra; the virtuous man should avoid it.
They say that he who eats the food of one who is censurable is eating from a pool of blood.
They know that eating food given by a slanderer is equal to the sin of killing a Brahmin. One should never eat food that is offered disrespectfully or with contempt;
for a Brahmin who does so quickly encounters disease and the ruin of his lineage.

One who eats the food of those who guard cities becomes inclined toward the status of a dog-cooker (outcaste). Having eaten the food of a killer of cows, a killer of Brahmins, a drinker of liquor, or one who violates the teacher’s bed, a Brahmin is born as one who increases the lineage of Rākṣasas.
Having enjoyed the wealth of one who misappropriates a deposit, or of an ungrateful person, or of one who behaves like a eunuch,
one is born in the dwelling of a Śabara, outside the Middle Country.
Thus have I declared, according to the rule, those whose food should not be eaten and those whose food may be eaten.
"O son of Kuntī, what else do you wish to hear from me today?
Yudhiṣṭhira replied:
"You have indeed spoken of all those things that may be eaten and those that must not be eaten."
13,125.038d@014A_0043 Herein lies a doubt regarding my question; tell me that, O Grandfather.
13,125.038d@014A_0044 Specifically concerning the acceptance of offerings to the gods and ancestors (havya-kavya) by Brāhmaṇas.

"Tell me the expiations for various kinds of food. Very well, O King, I shall declare to you those [expiations] by which one is released from sin regarding the acceptance of gifts and the eating of food belonging to high-souled Brāhmaṇas."
In the acceptance of clarified butter, O Yudhiṣṭhira, the *sāvitrī* mantra and an oblation of fuel-sticks (*samid-āhuti*) are required;
this is the same for the acceptance of sesame seeds,
as well as for the acceptance of meat, honey, and salt.
Standing at sunrise, a Brāhmaṇa becomes purified. Furthermore,
by receiving gold while reciting the Veda heard from his teacher,
and by wearing a three-stranded cord of black iron, the twice-born is liberated.
Thus it is when wealth, clothing, or women are accepted;
likewise, O best of men, it is the same regarding the acceptance of gold,
as well as food, milk-rice, and sugarcane juice.
At the three junctions of the day, one should immerse oneself in water [after consuming] sugarcane,
oil, and sacrificial strainers; likewise, [one should recite the Sāvitrī] a hundred times while eating rice, flowers, fruit, water, food made of flour, barley-gruel, curd, and milk.

Having accepted shoes and clothing as funeral gifts, one should recite [the sacred syllable] a hundred times with focused concentration; by that, one is released from the evil. This also applies to the acceptance of land, as well as during eclipses and periods of birth-impurity.

Having fasted for three nights, one is thereby freed from evil. When a twice-born man partakes of the *śrāddha* food offered to the ancestors during the dark fortnight, that Brāhmaṇa becomes purified after a day and a night.
One should not perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyā*), nor should one engage in the recitation of prayers (*japya*);
one should not mix that food, for in this way the Brāhmaṇa is purified.
For this purpose, the *śrāddha* for the ancestors is prescribed in the afternoon.
If those Brahmins who were previously invited should eat as prescribed,
a Brahmin who eats the food on the third day after a death is purified by bathing three times a day for twelve days.
When twelve days have passed, having especially performed the purification rites and offered sacrificial oblations (*havis*) to the Brahmins, one is liberated from that sin;
for one who has died, one should cause the penances to be administered after ten nights.

If one partakes of food at a funeral rite designated for the third night after death, that Brāhmaṇa becomes purified by bathing three times a day for seven days while reciting the Sāvitrī, the Raivatī sacrifice, the Kūṣmāṇḍa hymns, and the Aghamarṣaṇa.
He attains vast success and shall never encounter calamity. However, if even a Brāhmaṇa should eat in a single meal together with Śūdras,
the prescribed impurity for him is ordained as merely the act of purification itself.
If a Brāhmaṇa should eat even a single meal together with Vaiśyas,
he must undergo initiation for three nights to be purified from that act. If a Brāhmaṇa should eat even a single meal together with Kṣatriyas...
Having bathed together with his clothes, he shall be released from that evil.
It destroys the family of a Śūdra, the cattle and kinsmen of a Vaiśya,
the prosperity of a Kṣatriya, and the spiritual luster of a Brāhmaṇa.

One should perform an expiation and a propitiatory rite (*śānti*); by that, one is liberated. One should recite the *Sāvitrī*, perform the *Raivatī* sacrifice, the *Kūṣmāṇḍa* rites, and the *Aghamarṣaṇa*.
Then, there is no doubt that they may consume the leftovers and each other’s portions.
Rocanā, Virajā, Rātri, and auspicious objects for touching;
Yudhiṣṭhira said,
"O Bhārata, one should conduct oneself with both generosity and austerity."
"O Grandfather, dispel this mental anguish of mine.
What indeed is it on earth that you ought to explain to me?
Bhīṣma said:
Listen to how those kings, devoted to the Dharma, who had cultivated their souls through austerity and were dedicated to the merit of giving, undoubtedly attained the higher worlds;
and likewise, how Atri’s son [Vasiṣṭha] honored the quality-less Brahman for his disciples.

O King, having always taught [the dharma], Śibi Auśīnara departed for the unsurpassed worlds; having offered up his own life and his beloved son for the sake of a brahmin, he went from here to the vault of heaven.

Pratardana, the lord of Kāśī, by bestowing his own son upon a brahmin, enjoys incomparable fame both in this world and the next. And Rantideva, the son of Saṃkṛti, [bestowed his son] upon the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.

Having offered the *arghya* according to the prescribed rite, he attained unsurpassed worlds. And having given a divine, auspicious golden umbrella with a hundred ribs for the sake of sacrifice to a Brāhmaṇa, Devāvṛdha ascended to heaven.
The Blessed One and Ambarīṣa, having bestowed their entire kingdom upon a Brāhmaṇa of immeasurable splendor, attained the world of the gods;
likewise, Janamejaya obtained a divine earring and a celestial vehicle from the son of Savitṛ.
Having given cows to a brahmin, he went to the unsurpassed worlds. And the royal seer Vṛṣādarbhi, having given various jewels and delightful dwellings to the twice-born, ascended to heaven.

Nimi, the king of Vidarbha, having given his daughter to the high-souled Agastya, went to heaven along with his sons, cattle, and kinsmen; and the highly illustrious son of Jamadagni, having given land to a brahmin, [went to heaven].

Thus Rāma went to imperishable worlds that exceed even the mind's reach. And when the rain-god Parjanya failed to send rain, the King of the Gods, Vasiṣṭha, brought all living beings back to life, by which he attained the imperishable state.

Rāma, the son of Daśaratha, having indeed offered wealth in sacrifices, went to the imperishable worlds— he whose great fame is established in this world. And the royal seer Kakṣasena [offered it] to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.
Having performed the ritual consigning of his body (*nyāsa*) according to the rules, the highly illustrious one departed.
Marutta, the grandson of Karaṃdhama and son of Avikṣita,
having given his daughter to Aṅgiras, quickly ascended to heaven.
And Brahmadatta, the king of the Pañcālas and the best among the upholders of dharma,
having offered the treasure Śaṅkha, attained the supreme goal.
And King Mitrasaha likewise [offered it] to the high-souled Vasiṣṭha.

Having given his beloved, intoxicating wife as a gift, he departed for the third heaven. And Manu’s son, Sudyumna, having raised up the rod of punishment according to righteousness for the sake of the high-souled Likhita, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
The royal sage Sahasracitti, of great renown, having renounced his beloved life for the sake of a brahmin, went to the unsurpassed worlds;
he did so after giving away a golden mansion filled with all objects of desire.
O Maudgalyāyana, King Śatadyumna went to heaven after giving heaps of food and edibles, like unto mountains,
to Śāṇḍilya in former times; he ascended to the celestial realm while filled with joy.
The king of Śālva, named Dyutimat and possessed of great splendor,
having given his kingdom to Ṛcīka, went to the unsurpassed worlds. And the royal sage Madirāśva, having given away his slender-waisted daughter, [went to the highest realms].
Hiraṇyahasta went to the worlds presided over by the gods; and the royal seer Lomapāda, the lord, having given his daughter Śāntā to Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, was united with all abundant objects of desire.
Having given the illustrious maiden named Haṃsī to Kautsa,
the royal seer Bhagīratha went from there to the imperishable worlds. Indeed,
King Bhagīratha gave away a hundred thousand cows.
Kohala, by giving away cows along with their calves, went to the unsurpassed worlds.
These and many others, O Yudhiṣṭhira, have gone to heaven through charity and austerity; yet they return again and again.
The fame of those who, as householders, have conquered the worlds through charity and austerity shall endure as long as the earth remains. For this,
O Yudhiṣṭhira, is the conduct of the virtuous that has been proclaimed by me.
For it is by means of gifts, sacrifices, and the procreation of offspring that these have ascended to heaven. Therefore,
O leader of the Kauravas, may your mind be constantly intent upon the performance of giving and sacrifice, for such a disposition increases righteousness.
"O tiger among kings, regarding that in which you shall have doubt,
Yudhiṣṭhira,
tomorrow at dawn I shall speak, for the twilight has now arrived."
"I have heard from you, dear father, whose prowess lies in the vow of truth,
how those kings attained the third heaven through the great merit of the duty of giving.
But now, O best among the upholders of dharma, I wish to hear about these duties."
How many kinds of gifts are there to be given, and what fruit does one obtain from them? How and to whom is it desired that a righteous gift be bestowed? Bhīṣma: [replies].
"By what causes and of how many kinds is it? I wish to hear this according to the truth.
Listen, O sinless son of Kuntī, to the truth regarding giving from me, O Bhārata—how a gift should be bestowed upon all the social classes."

O Bhārata, one should know that giving is fivefold—arising from righteousness, from wealth, from fear, from desire, and from compassion; learn now the reasons for these. By such means, one attains fame in this world and unsurpassed happiness after death.
Thus, one should give gifts to Brahmins without malice.
Whether [thinking], "He gives," or "He will give," or "He has given to me"—
having heard such things from supplicants, everything should be given to the seeker.
"He is not mine, nor am I his; if insulted, he might commit evil"—thinking thus, the wise man should give even out of fear to the fool.
"He is dear to me, and I am dear to him"—perceiving this, the intelligent man [should act].
One should thus give a gift without weariness to a friend;
for this person is destitute, he begs, and he is satisfied even with very little. Therefore, one should always give to the poor out of compassion.
"Thus, these five kinds of gifts increase merit and fame;
they should be given according to one's ability—so said Prajāpati.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:

"O Grandfather, O one of great wisdom, you who are learned in all the scriptures; you are renowned in our lineage as one enriched by many traditional teachings. From you, [we shall hear that which is] joined with dharma and artha, and which results in happiness for the future."
"O subduer of enemies, I wish to hear that which is a marvel to the world.
This time has arrived when kinsmen and relatives are difficult to find;
for there is no teacher for us other than you, O bull among the Bharatas."
"O sinless one, if I, together with my brothers, am worthy of your favor,
you ought to answer the question that I ask you, O King. This glorious Nārāyaṇa is honored by all the kings."
Out of great respect and humility, he serves you; therefore,
for my sake and out of affection, you ought to speak before him and all these kings, as well as before my brothers, for the purpose of what is pleasing to me.
13,126.007 Vaiśampāyana said: Having heard those words of his, Bhīṣma, the son of Bhāgīrathī, overcome with agitation out of affection, spoke these words.
"Come, I shall relate to you a most enchanting tale;
O King, this power of Viṣṇu was heard by me in the past,
and hear from me also that power which belongs to the one whose banner is the bull."
Listen to me regarding the doubt concerning Rudrāṇī, as well as that which concerns the couple. The righteous-souled Kṛṣṇa performed a twelve-year vow;
while he was consecrated for it, both Nārada and Parvata came to see him.
Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana and Dhaumya, the best among those who recite prayers; Devala, Kāśyapa, and Hastikāśyapa;
and other virtuous sages endowed with consecration and self-restraint.
Accompanied by all their disciples, who were like unto gods and rich in asceticism,
the son of Devakī, being pleased, joyfully provided them with guest-hospitality that was worthy of worship, appropriate to their lineage, and godlike.
The great seers, filled with joy, sat down upon seats made of fresh, golden-colored, and green *barhis* grass. Then they engaged in sweet conversations concerning the dharma.

From the mouth of Kṛṣṇa, whose deeds are miraculous, there issued forth the splendor of Nārāyaṇa, kindled by the fuel of his observance of vows— a fire that dwells within the royal sages and the gods who are rich in asceticism.
That fire consumed the mountain together with its trees, creepers, and shrubs;
along with its multitudes of birds and deer, and its beasts of prey and reptiles.
With its various kinds of animals, it became a scene of "Alas! Alas!"—senseless and desolate.
The peak of that mountain, blazing in appearance, was shattered. That fire, with its great flames, having consumed everything without exception,
approached Viṣṇu and touched his feet like a disciple.

Then Viṣṇu, the crusher of enemies, seeing the forest consumed by fire, restored it to its natural state with his gentle glances. Thus that mountain once again became covered with trees and creepers in full bloom.
Resounding with flocks of birds and filled with beasts and reptiles,
the assembly of sages, having then beheld that wonderful and inconceivable sight, became struck with amazement; their hair stood on end and their eyes grew dim with tears.

Then Nārāyaṇa, the best among speakers, seeing those sages filled with wonder, questioned them in a humble, sweet, and affectionate manner: "What is this [state] of this assembly of sages who have eternally abandoned all attachment?"

"O blameless ones, a sense of wonder has come upon me, who am free from possessiveness and learned in the scriptures. O sages, whose wealth is asceticism, you ought to explain this entire doubt of mine to me exactly as it is, with its definitive meaning."
The sages said:
"You create the worlds, and you again withdraw them;
you are the cold, you are the heat, and you alone cause the rain to fall."
"Of all beings on earth, whether stationary or moving, you are their father, their mother, their lord, and their very source. This is a cause for wonder to us; please explain it, O Madhusūdana."
"O auspicious one, you alone are worthy to speak of the emergence from the fire.
Therefore, O crusher of enemies, being free from fear,
we too shall relate to you, O Hari, all that has been heard and seen by us."
Vāsudeva said:
"This is that Vaiṣṇava splendor which has issued forth from my mouth;
it is the fire with blackened tracks, resembling the end of an eon, by which this mountain was churned."
The sages, who had conquered anger and mastered their senses, were overcome with distress; those god-like ones, whose wealth was their asceticism,
were deeply troubled by his adherence to vows and his devotion to the practices of an ascetic.
"Fire has arisen from me; you should not be distressed.
I have come here to this auspicious mountain to observe a vow, having arrived to create through asceticism a son equal to myself in valor."
Then that self of mine which was in my body emerged as fire;
it went to behold the Giver of Boons, the Grandfather of all the worlds. And by him, O best of sages, my self was instructed to become his son.
"By half of his splendor, your son shall be born," said the bull-bannered god.
That very fire, having approached the base of my feet in my presence,
served me like a disciple and, becoming tranquil, returned to his natural state.

This secret of the wise Padmanābha has been recounted by me to you out of affection; O you whose wealth is asceticism, no fear should be felt. O far-sighted ones, your movement shall be unhindered everywhere.
"Blazing with the vows of ascetics and adorned with knowledge and realization,
tell me of whatever supreme wonder you have heard or seen, whether in heaven or on earth."
I have a longing for that honey-like speech of yours, which resembles nectar,
as it was spoken here by you who dwell in the forest of asceticism;
even if it concerns something unseen, divine, or of wondrous appearance.
O you of pure vision, whether in heaven or on earth,
I see nothing that my supreme nature does not penetrate;
nor does the sovereignty residing within myself appear to me as anything marvelous.
For a matter that is trustworthy, when recounted and heard by virtuous people,
remains for a long time upon the earth like an inscription carved upon a rock; therefore,
I shall [recount] what has issued from the mouths of the virtuous in this assembly.
"I shall relate day by day [this account] which illuminates the intellect of men.
Then all the hosts of sages, humble in the presence of Kṛṣṇa,
gazed upon Janārdana with eyes resembling lotus petals.
Some were increasing [his glory], while others were honoring him;
they praised Madhusūdana with words whose meanings were adorned by the *ṛg* verses.
Then all the hosts of sages addressed Nārada, who had the vision of the gods.
Then they urged that master of speech to speak of whatever wonders and inconceivable things, O Lord, were experienced by the hosts of sages devoted to pilgrimage on Mount Himavat.
"Therefore, impelled by all for the sake of the welfare of the assembly of seers,
you ought to relate everything exactly as it was seen regarding Hṛṣīkeśa.
Thus addressed by the sages, the venerable seer Nārada—
The celestial sage related that auspicious tale of former events.
Bhīṣma said:
Then the venerable sage Nārada, a friend of Nārāyaṇa, [spoke].
He related the dialogue of Śaṃkara together with Umā:
"The righteous-souled lord of the gods, whose emblem is the bull,
performed austerities on the holy mountain Himavat, which is frequented by Siddhas and Cāraṇas."
In that delightful place, filled with various medicinal herbs and crowded with diverse flowers, thronged by hosts of Apsarases and frequented by multitudes of spirits,
the Lord dwelt there, filled with joy and surrounded by hundreds of spirit-hosts.
With various forms, both deformed and divine, of wondrous appearance—
resembling lions, tigers, and elephants, and possessing every kind of species—
with faces like jackals and leopards, and likewise with faces like bears and bulls.
With terrifying owl-faced beings, as well as those with faces like hawks and vultures; resembling various species of animals and possessing the characteristics of every kind;
[there were] kinnaras, divine gandharvas, and hosts of yakṣas and bhūtas.
That assembly hall of the bull-bannered Lord was strewn with celestial flowers, adorned with divine garlands, anointed with divine sandalwood paste, perfumed with divine incense,
and resounded with the music of celestial instruments.
Resounding with the sounds of *mṛdaṅga* and *paṇava* drums and the blare of conchs and kettledrums,
it was filled on all sides by throngs of dancing spirits and peacocks;
it was a divine place where the *apsarases* danced and were attended by hosts of celestial women.
Delightful to behold, indescribable, divine, and wonderful to see,
that mountain shone because of the asceticism of that Lord of Beings,
resounding with the Vedic chants of Brahmins devoted to sacred study.
O Janārdana, that mountain, which was peerless in its springtime beauty and resounded with the songs of bees,
appeared once more like a great festival; yet, seeing it again bearing such a terrifying form,
the host of sages was filled with supreme joy.
The highly fortunate sages and the perfected ones (siddhas) who have sublimated their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas),
the Maruts, the Vasus, the Sādhyas, and the eternal Viśvedevas;
the Yakṣas, Nāgas, Piśācas, the world-protectors (lokapālas), and the fire-gods (hutāśanas).
All beings, having become humble, were gathered together right there. The seasons scattered all manner of most wonderful flowers,
and the blazing medicinal herbs illuminated that forest.
And birds, filled with joy, danced and sang aloud on the delightful mountain ridges, uttering cries dear to people. There,
upon the mountain slope adorned with divine minerals, the god [dwelt].
Seated upon a couch, the high-minded one shone resplendently;
he was clad in a tiger-skin garment with a lion-skin as his upper covering,
wearing a serpent as a sacred thread and adorned with red armlets.
With a tawny beard and matted hair, formidable and the instiller of fear in the enemies of the gods,
he who bears the bull upon his banner grants fearlessness to all beings who are devoted to him.
Upon seeing him, all the seers prostrated themselves, touching the earth with their heads.
Liberated from all sins, patient, and free from defilement,
the abode of that Lord of Beings shone forth, assuming a terrifying form,
exceedingly invincible, and teeming with great serpents.
In an instant, O Madhusūdana, everything became wondrous;
that assembly hall of the bull-bannered Lord shone, assuming a terrifying form.
Then the daughter of the mountain, surrounded by a host of female spirits, approached him.
Wearing garments equal in beauty to those of Hari, observing the same vows,
she carried a golden pitcher filled with water from all the sacred fords;
she bore a supreme form that captivated the hearts of all living beings.
Following all along the auspicious and holy mountain streams, the beautiful [goddess],
showering down rains of flowers and various fragrances,
attended upon the side of the Himalayas and approached the side of Hara.

Then, smiling and for the sake of sport, that goddess of lovely appearance suddenly covered the two auspicious eyes of Hara with her hands. When his eyes were thus covered, everything became shrouded in darkness and devoid of consciousness.
Devoid of oblations and devoid of the *vaṣaṭ* call, that assembly hall suddenly became desolate;
and all the people were dejected, filled with fear and trembling,
as if the sun had vanished when the Lord of Beings closed his eyes.
Then, in an instant, the world became free from darkness;
and a great, blazing flame issued forth from his forehead,
and a third eye, resembling the sun, appeared upon him.
Blazing like the fire at the end of an eon, by which that mountain was churned;
then, seeing Hara whose eyes resembled blazing fire, the daughter of the mountain,
the large-eyed one, bowed her head in salutation and gazed upon him.
While that forest— filled with *śāla* and *sarala* trees,
beautiful groves of sandalwood, and illuminated by divine medicinal herbs— was being consumed by fire,
herds of deer, fleeing in terror, approached the side of Hara.
And as they found no refuge, that assembly appeared crowded and tumultuous.
Then there arose a blazing fire, touching the heavens, with flickering flames like lightning,
resembling twelve suns and like another fire at the end of an eon.
In that moment, the mountain Himavat was consumed;
its expanse of peaks and minerals, along with its forests and medicinal herbs, became withered and burnt.
Then, seeing the mountain thus ravaged, the daughter of the king of mountains [spoke].
Having sought refuge in the Blessed One, she stood with her hands joined in reverence.
Then Śarva, seeing Umā— her softness having been brought about by her female nature—
