and seeing that she did not wish for her father’s distress, looked upon the Mountain with affection.
Then everything became once again beautiful in its natural state;
the birds were filled with joy, and the forest trees were in full bloom. Seeing the mountain restored to its natural condition, the Goddess was delighted with Maheśvara.
The blameless lady spoke to the Lord, the master of all beings:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, wielder of the trident, observer of great vows!
A great doubt has arisen within me; you ought to explain it to me."
For what purpose has a third eye indeed arisen on your forehead?
And for what purpose was the mountain, along with its flocks of birds and forests, consumed by fire?
Furthermore, O Lord, why were they restored to their natural state in an instant?
"In this very way, O Maheśvara, this [place] has been made by you covered with trees.
Maheśvara said:
"O blameless Goddess, my two eyes were covered by you out of childishness."
Then, in an instant, the world became deprived of light.
When the sun had vanished and the world was thus enveloped in darkness, O daughter of the mountain,
you created a third blazing eye to protect all creatures.
"O Goddess, by the great splendor of that eye, this mountain was churned;
yet for the sake of your pleasure, it has been restored to its natural state in an instant.
Umā said:

"Blessed One, by what means is your eastern face so pleasing to behold like the moon? And likewise, why are your northern, western, and southern faces so beautiful with splendor? Why is your southern face so fierce, and why are your matted locks tawny and turned upward?"
By whom was your throat made blue, resembling the plumage of a peacock? And by whom does this Pināka bow always remain in your hand?
For what purpose are you perpetually matted-haired and a celibate student?
"O sinless Lord of Beings, tell me all of this doubt of mine;
for I am your fellow-practitioner of dharma and your devotee, O Bull-bannered One.
Thus addressed by the daughter of the mountain, the Blessed One, the wielder of the Pināka bow, [replied].
The Lord was pleased with her conduct and her intellect;
then the God said to her, "O blessed one, O lady of lovely countenance, hear the reasons why these forms belong to me."
Maheśvara said:
"In ancient times, a most excellent woman named Tilottamā was created by Brahmā;
she was fashioned auspiciously by taking minute particles from every jewel."
O Goddess, she who was peerless on earth in beauty approached me; O auspicious one, that lady of radiant countenance and beautiful teeth circumambulated me,
seeking to entice me from close at hand.
Then, O Goddess, my beautiful face emerged from each of those [apertures].
Desiring to see her, I assumed a fourfold form through yoga; thus I became four-faced, demonstrating my own yogic power.
"By my eastern face, I indeed exercise sovereignty as Indra;
by my northern face, O blameless one, I take delight together with you. My western face is gentle and brings happiness to all living beings."
The fierce one, of terrifying appearance, withdraws all creatures with his right hand;
matted-haired and a celibate student, desiring the welfare of the worlds and for the sake of accomplishing the purpose of the gods' work, the Pināka bow remains in my hand.
In ancient times, Indra, desiring glory, hurled his thunderbolt at me;
having scorched my throat, it passed through, and by that I acquired the name Śrīkaṇṭha.
Umā said:
"O Lord, since you possess many other magnificent vehicles, how did you come to have a bull as your mount? Maheśvara said:
Brahmā created Surabhi, the cow of nectar who pours forth milk. Once created, she manifested in many forms, flowing with the milk of immortality.
The froth released from the mouth of her calf fell upon my body.
Then the cows were burned by me and attained various colors.
Thereupon, I was brought to a state of peace by the Teacher of the World, who understands all matters;
he gave me this bull for the sake of my banner and as my very vehicle.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, you have many dwellings endowed with universal forms and qualities; why is it that, having abandoned them, you take delight in the cremation ground?"
In that terrifying place, thick with hair and bones, crowded with skulls and jars,
teeming with vultures and jackals, filled with hundreds of funeral pyres,
impure, mired in flesh, and bogged down in fat and blood;
Amidst heaps of scattered flesh, resounding with the howls of jackals,
Maheśvara said:
"Seeking what is pure, I wander over the entire earth during the nights."
"And nothing more pure than the cremation ground is found here;
therefore, among all dwellings, my mind delights in the cremation ground—
covered by the branches of the banyan tree and adorned with discarded garlands."
"And there, O fair-faced one, my hosts of beings take delight;
nor do I, O Goddess, wish to dwell without these throngs of beings. For this dwelling of mine is considered pure and conducive to heaven."
He is meritorious and supreme, and is worshipped by those desiring purity.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, best among the upholders of all dharmas!"
O wielder of the Pināka bow, O granter of boons, I have this great doubt:
O Lord, this entire host of sages wanders through the world in various forms, seeking penance and exclaiming, "Perform austerity, perform austerity!"
Out of a desire to do what is pleasing to this assembly of sages and to me,
O subduer of enemies, you ought to explain this doubt of mine here:
what are the characteristics of dharma as they have been declared, and how is it to be practiced by men?
"O Knower of Dharma, O Lord, tell me how it is possible for those who have not found the Dharma [to attain it].
Nārada said:
"Then the entire assembly of sages honored that goddess in return."
With words whose meanings were adorned by the *ṛg*-verses, and with hymns, O best among those who know the meaning,
Maheśvara said:
"Non-violence, truthful speech, and compassion toward all beings."
Peace and giving according to one's ability constitute the supreme dharma of the householder; refraining from desire for another’s wife, protecting the wives of others,
abstaining from taking what is not given, and the avoidance of honey and meat.
This fivefold dharma, with its many branches, brings about happiness;
embodied beings who are devoted to dharma should perform this accumulation of merit.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, you have been asked about a doubt; you ought to explain it to me:
what is the dharma of the four castes that brings merit to each respective caste? What kind of dharma is there for a Brāhmaṇa, and what kind would there be for a Kṣatriya?"
"What are the characteristics of dharma for a Vaiśya, and what would they be for a Śūdra?
Maheśvara said:
"O highly fortunate lady, you have raised this doubt in accordance with reason."
The highly fortunate twice-born ones are always the gods upon earth in this world.
For a Brāhmaṇa, fasting is always his duty; of this there is no doubt.
For he was born for the sake of dharma and is fit for becoming one with Brahman.
O Goddess, his performance of dharma and the observance of vows according to the rule, as well as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*), are appropriate only for a twice-born;
it consists of the study of the sacred texts for the sake of worshipping the guru and the deities.
Those embodied beings who are devoted to dharma should practice that which gives rise to dharma.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, I have a doubt in this matter; you should explain it to me."
"Proclaim with skill the dharma of the four castes.
Maheśvara said:
"Listening to the secret [teachings] is dharma, as is the practice of Vedic vows."
Devotion to the practice of vows is dharma; pleasing the feet of the guru is dharma.
Devotion to the practice of begging for alms is dharma; constant fasting is dharma. Constant study of the Vedas is dharma, as is the stage of life of the religious student (brahmacarya-āśrama).

Once permitted by his teacher, the twice-born man should indeed perform the *samāvartana* ceremony; immediately thereafter, he should take a suitable wife according to the prescribed rule. His duty consists of avoiding the food of *śūdras* as well as following the path of the righteous.
Dharma consists in constant fasting as well as celibacy; likewise,

a householder who has maintained the sacred fires, who studies and offers oblations, whose senses are restrained, who eats only the remains of the sacrificial meal, who is moderate in diet, truthful in speech, and pure.

Devotion to guests is dharma; dharma consists in maintaining the three sacred fires. One should perform the *iṣṭi* sacrifices and the animal sacrifices according to the prescribed rules. Sacrifice is the supreme dharma, as is non-violence toward living beings.
Eating food that has not been tasted before is a duty, as is eating only the remnants of the meal;
it is said to be the duty of a Brāhmaṇa householder, especially one learned in the Vedas, to eat only after his dependents have eaten.
The shared character of husband and wife, the duty of householders,
the constant offering of flowers and oblations to the domestic deities,
the daily smearing [of the house with cow-dung], and likewise the regular observance of fasts— these constitute their dharma.
In a house that is well-swept, plastered, and filled with the rising smoke of clarified butter,
this is the dharma of the twice-born pertaining to the householder’s life, which sustains the world;
it is always and eternally practiced by those who are true members of the twice-born.

"O Goddess, as for the duty pertaining to the Kṣatriya that you have mentioned, I shall explain it to you; listen to it from me with a concentrated mind. From the very beginning, the duty of a Kṣatriya is recorded as the protection of the subjects."
For the king who enjoys the fruits as they have been ordained is joined with dharma; indeed,
that lord of men who protects his subjects according to dharma attains worlds acquired through dharma, accumulated by the protection of his subjects.
In that regard, the supreme duty of the king is self-restraint, as well as the private recitation of the Vedas; the performance of the *agnihotra* sacrifice, giving, and study;
the wearing of the sacred thread, the performance of sacrifices, and likewise the practice of righteous deeds.
The maintenance of dependents is dharma; the non-futility of actions performed is dharma;
standing firm in just punishment is dharma; the performance of Vedic sacrifices is dharma; standing firm in legal procedure is dharma; and likewise, delighting in truthful speech is dharma.
A king who extends a helping hand to those in distress is honored both in this world and after death.
Having displayed valor for the sake of cows and Brahmins and met his end in battle,
he attains the worlds won by the horse sacrifice in the abode of the third heaven.
The constant duty of a Vaiśya is the tending of cattle as well as agriculture;
also the maintenance of the *agnihotra* fire, the giving of gifts, and the study of the Vedas; furthermore, trade, abiding in the path of the righteous, hospitality, tranquility, and self-restraint.
Welcome to the Brahmins! Renunciation is indeed the eternal duty of the Vaiśya.
He should never sell sesame seeds, perfumes, or liquids;
though he may follow the path of trade, the Vaiśya remains established on the path of the righteous.
Hospitality toward all, the pursuit of the three goals of life according to one's ability and as is appropriate,
and constant service toward the twice-born— this is the supreme duty of a Śūdra.
Such a Śūdra, firm in his asceticism, true to his word, and having conquered his senses, [attains the highest state].
By serving a guest who has arrived, he accumulates great ascetic merit.
Free from violence, pure in conduct, and a worshiper of the gods and the twice-born,
the wise Śūdra shall be endowed with the desired fruits of dharma.
"O beautiful one, all this regarding the four castes has been told to you.
O fortunate lady, what else do you wish to hear concerning each of them here?
Umā said:
13,129.001 “The auspicious duties beneficial to the four castes have been described by you separately.
O Blessed One, tell me now that dharma which is all-pervasive.
13,129.002 Maheśvara said:
The Brahmins were created by the Creator, who seeks excellence, as the essence of the world;
they are the gods upon earth among mortals, created to deliver all the worlds.
Of them, I shall now declare this arising of the fruits of righteous deeds.
For that which is the duty among the Brahmins is considered the supreme duty.
However, these three were created by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the world's purpose;
they were created eternally at the time of the earth’s creation—listen to them from me as well.

The supreme dharma is that declared in the Vedas; another is that contained in the Smṛti scriptures; and the third is said to be the conduct practiced by the virtuous (*śiṣṭa*). These are the three eternal dharmas.
A learned Brāhmaṇa who possesses the threefold knowledge (*traividya*) should not make his living through the study [of the Vedas].
One who performs the three duties, who has transcended the three [qualities], and who is friendly— such a twice-born man is remembered as a true Brahmin.
Now listen with a concentrated mind to those six duties which the Lord of the World proclaimed for the livelihood of Brahmins.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, as well as giving and receiving gifts, teaching, and studying— these six duties constitute the twice-born man’s share of dharma;
constant study of the Vedas is dharma, and sacrifice is the eternal dharma.
Generosity is praised for him according to his capacity and according to the prescribed rule; yet this is the supreme dharma, which is constantly practiced by the virtuous:
the state of a householder among the pure is a great accumulation of dharma.
One whose self is purified by the five sacrifices, truthful in speech, free from malice, a giver, a hospitable host to Brahmins, one whose dwelling is well-swept,
free from pride, always straightforward, and likewise one who speaks with affectionate words— [such a person is worthy].
He who finds delight in guests and visitors, who eats only the food remaining after others have been fed,
and who provides water for the feet, the respectful offering (arghya), a seat, a bed, as well as a lamp and shelter according to the rules— he is a righteous man.
Having risen at dawn, sipped water for purification, and invited [guests] with food, one should honor them and follow them as they depart; this is his eternal duty.
He should practice hospitality toward all according to his ability, day and night, for the sake of the three goals of life.

The duty of the Śūdra is declared to be the service of the three [higher] castes. The dharma characterized by active engagement is ordained for householders; I shall proclaim that auspicious path which is beneficial to all beings.
One should give repeatedly according to one's ability, and likewise, one should sacrifice repeatedly;

and the performance of rites for prosperity should be carried out by one who desires well-being. Wealth should be acquired through righteousness, and wealth obtained through righteousness is of three kinds.
A man should strive with diligence to make dharma his supreme goal.
One who desires prosperity should pursue the aims of dharma and artha with one portion [of his time],
pursue the aim of kāma with another portion, and increase the remaining portion [for spiritual welfare].
But another dharma, characterized by cessation, is known as liberation.
O Goddess, I shall declare its practice to you; listen to me according to the truth.
Compassion for all beings is that dharma, not residing in a single village.
The liberation from the bonds of hope is praised for those who long for liberation.
He has no attachment to his water-pot, nor to water, nor to his garment, nor to his seat;
neither to his triple staff, nor to his bed, nor to fire, nor to a sheltered dwelling.
One whose mind is turned inward, whose thoughts are fixed thereon and who has that as his ultimate goal, who is always disciplined in yoga and in analytical discernment,
constantly lying at the foot of trees and dwelling in empty dwellings—
Sleeping on the sandy banks of rivers and finding delight on river shores,
that twice-born man, liberated from all attachments and bonds of affection,
wanders about having fixed his being solely within the Self.
For one who wanders as a mendicant, disciplined, motionless like a pillar, abstaining from food through actions directed toward liberation, his is the eternal Dharma;
he should not be attached to any single place for long, nor should he frequent only a single village.
For he wanders about disciplined and liberated, and does not lie down alone on a riverbank.
This is the dharma of those who know liberation, the path of truth declared in the Vedas for the virtuous;
for one who follows this path, no [further] state of existence is found.
O monks, there are four kinds of mendicants: the *kuṭīcara*, the *kṛtodaka*, the *haṃsa*, and the *paramahaṃsa*. Whichever comes later among these is superior.
Beyond that, there is nothing higher, nothing lower, nothing behind, and nothing before.
[It is] free from suffering and pleasure, gentle, ageless, immortal, and imperishable.
Umā said:
"The dharma of liberation pertaining to the householder's life has been practiced by you, just as it is practiced by the virtuous."
13,129.031c You have spoken of the great path leading to the highest good for the world of mortals.
13,129.032a But, O knower of dharma, I wish to hear about the unsurpassed dharma of the rishis; 13,129.032c for I always feel a longing for those who dwell in the forests of asceticism.
The fragrance arising from the smoke of clarified butter seems to envelop the penance grove;
seeing this, O Maheśvara, my mind is always filled with joy. O Lord, O All-pervading One, resolve this doubt of mine concerning the dharma of the sages.
"O Knower of the true essence of the meaning of all dharmas, O God of gods, speak to me;
O Mahādeva, explain everything exactly as it is, just as I have asked.
Maheśvara said:
"Come now, I shall declare to you the unsurpassed dharma of the sages,
by practicing which, O auspicious lady, the sages attain perfection through their own asceticism—
the dharma that is eternally observed by the foam-drinking rishis who are knowers of dharma."
Listen to me from the beginning, O highly fortunate lady who knows the dharma, regarding that dharma:
in that [place], they constantly gather the auspicious foam of the Brahman,
the sweet nectar drunk by Brahmā as it spread through the heavens.

O you whose wealth is asceticism, hear now of the path created by the practice of dharma belonging to those pure Phenapas, within the host of the Vālakhilyas. The Vālakhilyas are sages perfected through austerity who dwell in the solar orb.
13,129.039c Those who know the Dharma, following the way of life of birds, gather grain by gleaning. 13,129.040a Clad in the sloughs of deer, or wearing rags and bark garments,
free from the pairs of opposites and having attained the path of the righteous, are the Vālakhilyas, whose wealth is their austerity.
Measuring only the size of a thumb-joint, they are established within their own limbs;
they strive in the practice of austerity, and the fruit of their dharma is great.
They attain equality with the gods for the sake of accomplishing the purposes of the gods.
13,129.042c Illuminating all directions, their sins burnt away by asceticism (tapas),
13,129.043a those others who are pure-minded and devoted to the dharma of compassion, who are virtuous, wandering the earth, meritorious, and those who frequent the world of Soma—
Dwelling near the world of the ancestors, they subsist according to rule by gleaning;
likewise, there are those who wash their food, those who grind with stones, and those who use their teeth as a mortar.
And there are the Soma-drinkers among the gods, as well as those who drink the steam.

For those who live nearby, gathering gleanings and whose senses are naturally restrained, the following is declared to be their duty: the maintenance of the sacred fire, the worship of ancestors and gods,
and likewise the performance of the five sacrifices.

O Goddess, this dharma of the sages has always been practiced by the twice-born who move in circles and roam the world of the gods; now hear from me that other [dharma] as well. In all the dharmas of the sages, the self must be conquered by one whose senses are subdued.
"Thereafter, desire and anger must be conquered; this is my conviction.
The performance of the *agnihotra*, the observance of the *dharmarātri* fast, the authorization for the *soma* sacrifice, and the fifth, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."
The constant performance of sacrificial rites is their duty, as is devotion to the worship of the ancestors and the gods;
they must practice hospitality toward all guests with food gathered by gleaning,
and they should take delight in abstaining from the consumption of dairy products.
Sleeping on the bare ground, the practice of yoga, subsisting on vegetables and leaves,
eating fruits and roots, consuming air, water, or moss—
these are indeed the observances of the seers by which they conquer the unconquerable state.
When the smoke has ceased, the pestle is laid aside, the embers are extinguished, the people have finished their meal,
the movement of dishes has ended, and the time for begging alms has passed, he,
desiring a guest, eats only the remaining food.

Delighting in the dharma of truth, patient, and disciplined according to the way of the sages— he who is neither arrogant nor conceited, who is neither heedless nor deluded, who is equal toward friend and foe, and who is friendly— he is the supreme knower of the Dharma.
"In delightful regions, at mountain cascades, in the thickets of rivers,
and in mountain groves."
In various regions that yield fruit and possess roots, those of fixed vows dwell with concentrated minds. O Śaṅkara, I wish to hear the meritorious rule concerning them as well.
"O Lord of Gods, among those forest-dwellers who subsist on their own bodies—
among the forest-dwellers who live by gleaning and whose minds are expanded through austerity"—
Maheśvara said:
"Listen with a concentrated mind to that dharma which pertains to forest-dwellers (vānaprastha). Having heard it, O Goddess, become single-minded and devoted to the understanding of dharma.
[This is the dharma] for the perfected, self-restrained, and virtuous ones who have entered the life of forest-dwelling."
Listen now to the kind of duties that must be performed by forest-dwellers (*vānaprastha*):
the ritual bathing at the three times of day, the worship of the ancestors and the gods, the maintenance of the sacred fire (*agnihotra*), and likewise the performance of sacrifices and oblations.
The gathering of wild rice (*nīvāra*), the consumption of fruits and roots,
the use of *iṅguda* and castor oils for the purpose of lubrication,
and the avoidance of desire and anger through the perfections achieved by the practice of yoga.

By those who attend upon the hero’s bed, those who frequent the hero’s station, by the virtuous who are disciplined and carry out their yoga, likewise by those who practice the "five-fire" penance in summer,
and by those restrained in the "frog-posture" who follow the prescribed rules.
Those whose minds are fixed on dharma must constantly remain in the *vīrāsana* posture and likewise sleep upon the bare ground; they must practice the discipline of cold and the discipline of fire.
They should subsist on water, feed on air, or take only moss as their final meal.
13,130.011c By those who grind with stones, by those who are self-controlled, and by others who wash themselves clean;
13,130.012a Clad in rags and bark, and dwelling in deer skins— their journey must be conducted at the proper time, according to dharma, and according to the prescribed rule.
13.130.013 Those who dwell in the forest, roam the forest, protect the forest, and range through the forest—
those who live by the forest must dwell having approached the forest as if it were their teacher.
13.130.014 For them, the performance of fire-offerings (*homa*) and the practice of the five sacrifices (*pañcayajña*) constitute their duty.
The observance of the sacrifice in which the serpent is the fifth, as prescribed in the Vedas; devotion to the eighth-day sacrifice and the practice of the Cāturmāsya rites;
and likewise the sacrifice on the full moon day, which is the perpetual sacrifice.
Freed from the bonds of wife and family, freed from all impurities,
and freed from all sins, the sages wander in the forest. Always devoted to the sacrificial ladle and vessels, they constantly take refuge in the three sacred fires.
13.130.017 Those who are peaceful and ever-devoted to the path of the righteous attain the supreme goal.
13.130.018 They go to the highly meritorious world of Brahmā and the eternal world of Soma; for by relying on the dharma of the seers, perfected sages proceed [there].
"O Goddess, this auspicious dharma pertaining to the forest-dweller has been described by me in detail, endowed with its full meaning, according to its general outlines.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, honored by all beings,

please declare that Dharma of the assembly of sages which exists within the teachings on spiritual accomplishment (*siddhivāda*). Those who dwell in the forest are fully perfected in those teachings on spiritual accomplishment."
13,130.021c "How is the dharma of those who are self-willed yet united with wives traditionally remembered?
13,130.022 Maheśvara said:
13,130.022a "O Goddess, all those self-willed ascetics sport with their wives."
For them, the causes are the shaving of the head, the wearing of saffron robes, and the observance of the day and night;
as well as bathing at the three times of day, the great sacrifice performed by the sages, meditative concentration, abiding on the path of truth, and practicing according to what has been taught.
And those duties previously described for forest-dwellers—
if they practice those duties, they obtain the fruit of austerity. And those who observe the duties of a married couple, with their senses restrained toward their own wives, [attain the same].

13,130.025c They act according to what is prescribed by rule, approaching their wives during the proper season. 13,130.026a For those virtuous ones, the dharma established by the seers is appropriate; no other desire should be pursued at will by those who perceive the true nature of dharma.
He who properly bestows the gift of fearlessness upon all beings,
his soul liberated from violence and anger, is indeed united with dharma. He who is compassionate toward all beings and whose vow is uprightness toward all beings [is likewise united with dharma].
And he who has become the self of all beings is indeed united with dharma. Between bathing in all the Vedas and straightforwardness toward all beings,
these two may be equal, or rather, straightforwardness is superior.
13.130.030a They say that uprightness is dharma; crookedness is called adharma.
13.130.030c A man endowed with uprightness here is united with dharma. 13.130.031a One who is ever upright dwells in the world in the presence of the immortals.
Therefore, one who desires his own dharma should be constant in uprightness. Patient, self-controlled, having conquered anger, become dharma itself, and non-violent—
a man whose mind is always delighted in dharma is united with dharma.
Free from weariness, righteous in soul, capable, and established on the path of truth— such a one who is supreme in conduct and awakened is fit for becoming Brahman.
Umā said:

O Lord, by what conduct do those ascetics who delight in hermitages and whose wealth is their austerity become radiant? And how is it that kings and princes, or those who are poor or very wealthy, [attain such states]?
"By what action, O Blessed One, do they attain the great fruit,
reaching the eternal station and being anointed with divine sandalwood? Or by what action, O Lord, do they become forest-dwellers?"
"O God, O Three-eyed One, O Destroyer of Tripura, explain to me in its entirety this auspicious doubt concerning my practice of asceticism.
Maheśvara said:
Self-restrained by fasts and vows, non-violent, and speakers of truth,
they attain perfection and, after death, rejoice without affliction together with the Gandharvas—
just as one who lies upon the "frog-posture" (maṇḍūkayoga) remains in its proper place according to the rule.

The righteous-souled one who undergoes the initiation (*dīkṣā*) rejoices together with the *nāgas*. He who, having been initiated, joyfully partakes of the young grass (*śaṣpa*) dropped from the mouths of deer while dwelling among the deer, goes to Amarāvatī.
He who observes that vow by subsisting on *śaivāla* or withered leaves,
and who constantly endures the rigors of cold, shall go to the supreme goal.
Whether subsisting on air, or drinking water, or even eating fruits and roots—
Having established sovereignty over the yakṣas, he rejoices with hosts of apsarases.
By carrying fire on his shoulder during the summer according to the prescribed ritual,
and having performed this for twelve years, he becomes a sovereign king of the earth.

Having observed a restriction on food for twelve years, the sage who has diligently mastered the desert becomes an earthly king. Having encompassed the pure sky upon the bare ground on all sides, he remains there.
Having entered with joy, he undertook the twelve-year initiation. O beautiful lady, they say that the fruits of the sacrificial ground are vehicles, couches,
and highly precious houses as bright as the moon.
He who lives for the sake of the Self, being self-restrained and restricted in his diet,
or who casts off the body through fasting, attains heaven. He who, living for the sake of the Self, undergoes the twelve-year initiation—
Having cast off his body in the great ocean, he attains the world of Varuṇa.
He who lives by means of his own self and undergoes a twelve-year initiation,
having pierced his feet with a stone, rejoices among the Guhyakas.
Having perfected himself by means of the self, free from dualities and without possessions,
and having observed for twelve years that single initiation directed toward the mind,
he attains the heavenly world and rejoices together with the gods.
He who lives by his own self and undergoes the twelve-year initiation,
casting off the body after offering oblations into the fire, is glorified in the world of Agni. But that twice-born man, O Goddess, who is initiated according to the rule and remains self-restrained—
Having established the self within the Self, free from dualities and without possessions,
and having observed for twelve years a single initiation directed toward the mind,
he goes forth unencumbered, with the fire-drills bound upon his shoulder.
Always having his mind fixed on the path of heroes, likewise devoted to the hero’s posture (*vīrāsana*),
and constantly remaining in the state of a hero, he shall attain the destination of heroes. He will eternally go to the world of Śakra, honored with all objects of desire.
Strewn with celestial flowers and adorned with divine sandalwood,
that righteous-souled one dwells happily in heaven together with hosts of gods;
having reached the world of heroes, the hero always practices the yoga of heroes.
Established in *sattva*, having renounced everything, initiated, self-restrained, and pure— he who embarks upon the hero’s path attains eternal worlds. Indeed,
he travels at will by means of a celestial chariot that moves according to his desire.
Having gone to the world of Śakra, the glorious one rejoices, free from all affliction.
Umā said:
O Blessed One, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, you who caused the teeth of Pūṣan to fall!
O Three-eyed One, destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, I have this great doubt:
by what ripening of karma does a Vaiśya, who was previously created by the Self-born Lord as part of the fourfold varṇa system, descend to the state of a Śūdra?
"By what means does a Vaiśya or a Kṣatriya become a twice-born [Brāhmaṇa], or how does a Brāhmaṇa become a Kṣatriya?
O Lord, how can one practice the dharma that goes against the natural order (*pratiloma*)?
Or by what action is a Brāhmaṇa born from a Śūdra womb?"
"O Lord, by what action does a Kṣatriya fall to the state of a Śūdra? O sinless God, Lord of Beings, resolve this doubt of mine:
how may the three castes here attain the status of Brāhmaṇas by their very nature?"
Maheśvara said:
"O auspicious goddess, the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain;
it is by nature that one is a Brāhmaṇa, as are the Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—this is my conviction."

Through evil action in this world, a twice-born man indeed falls from his station; therefore, having attained the highest caste, a twice-born man should truly protect it. Abiding by the duty of a Brāhmaṇa, he lives by means of that Brāhmaṇahood.
Whether he be a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, he attains the state of Brahman. But he who, having abandoned the status of a Brāhmaṇa, devotes himself to the duty of a Kṣatriya,
falls away from his Brāhmaṇahood and is reborn in a Kṣatriya womb.
That Brahmin of small intellect who, relying on greed and delusion, always performs the work of a Vaiśya after having attained the difficult-to-attain status of a Brāhmaṇa— he,
that twice-born man, falls to the state of a Vaiśya; or a Vaiśya may likewise fall to the state of a Śūdra.

A Brahmin who has fallen away from his own duty then attains the state of a Śūdra. Having fallen from his caste and been cast out, he reaches hell there; fallen from the world of Brahmā, he is reborn as a Śūdra.
O highly fortunate lady who practices dharma, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya who abandons his own duties and serves the duties of a Śūdra falls from his own station and becomes one of mixed caste.
A Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, or a Vaiśya who acts in such a manner falls to the state of a Śūdra;
however, he who is pure through his own duty, possessed of knowledge and realization, clean,
knowing the Dharma, and devoted to the Dharma, enjoys the fruit of that Dharma.
And this other [teaching], O Goddess, was proclaimed by Brahmā:
the ultimate spiritual knowledge (adhyātma) which is practiced by the virtuous who desire dharma.
Food from fierce men is censured, O Goddess, as is food from a group, food from a funeral rite, or food from one in a state of birth-impurity.
One must never eat food that has been publicly proclaimed for sale, nor ever the food of a Śūdra.
O Goddess, the food of a Śūdra is censured by the high-souled gods of gods;
it is my conviction that this is the authoritative teaching issued from the mouth of the Grandfather (Brahmā).
If one who has maintained the sacred fires and performed sacrifices should die with the remains of a Śūdra’s food still in his belly, he shall attain the destination of a Śūdra;
for by those remnants of a Śūdra’s food, he is cast down from the station of Brahman.

A Brahmin becomes a Śūdra; there is no doubt about this. Whatever womb a Brahmin enters by subsisting on another's food, he shall go to that very womb if he should die with the remnants of that person's food still in his stomach.

Having attained the auspicious state of a Brahmin, which is so difficult to obtain, he who treats it with contempt and eats food that should not be eaten shall indeed fall from his status as a twice-born. [So too shall] the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brahmin, the base man, the thief, the breaker of vows, and the impure.

A Brahmin who is devoid of Vedic study, sinful, greedy, dishonest, and deceitful; one who neglects his vows, who is the husband of a Śūdra woman, who eats from a *kuṇḍa* vessel, who sells Soma, and who serves those of low birth— such a man indeed falls from his Brahmanic origin.
One who violates the bed of his guru, one who hates his guru, one who delights in reviling his guru, and also one who hates the Veda—
such a Brahmin falls from his Brahmanic birth. But by performing these auspicious deeds, O Goddess, as well as others, [one attains the highest state].
A Śūdra may attain the status of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Vaiśya may reach the state of a Kṣatriya,
provided he performs all the duties of a Śūdra according to the rule and according to the ordinance— namely,
service and attendance toward the higher caste with great effort.
A Śūdra, remaining constantly on the path of the righteous, should act with an undistracted mind; he should honor the gods and the twice-born, observe the vow of hospitality toward all guests,
approach his wife only during her season, and be self-restrained in his eating.
Clean, seeking out clean people, eating only the remnants of food,
and refraining from eating meat not prepared for sacrifice, a Śūdra indeed attains the status of a Vaiśya.
Speaking truthfully, free from egoism, beyond the pairs of opposites, and skilled in tranquility—
Devoted to the study of the Vedas and pure, he performs the regular sacrifices;
self-controlled, honoring Brahmins, and desiring the welfare of all social orders, he observes the vows of a householder, eating his meals only twice a day.
Eating only what remained, having conquered his appetite, free from desire and devoid of the sense of "I," he attended to the *agnihotra* fire, offering oblations according to the rules,
while practicing hospitality toward all guests and consuming only the food that was left over.
If a Vaiśya is indeed ordained by the mantras of the three sacred fires,
that Vaiśya is born into a pure and great Kṣatriya family.
Having been born as a Kṣatriya, that Vaiśya is consecrated with the sacraments from birth onwards.
Once initiated and devoted to his vows, the twice-born becomes honored;
he gives gifts and performs sacrifices with consecrated rites accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees. Seeking heaven, he studies while always taking refuge in the three sacred fires.

Always extending a helping hand to those in distress while protecting his subjects according to dharma, he who is pleasant to behold always acts with truth; possessing the rod of justice rather than being without it, he is the instructor of righteous deeds.

Restrained in the performance of his duties and characterized by the practice of giving a sixth part [of his income], he who is skilled in matters of wealth should not indulge in vulgar pleasures according to his own will;
rather, being righteous in soul, he should always approach his wife during her fertile season.
Constantly fasting, self-restrained, devoted to sacred study, and pure, he always slept upon a bed of *barhis* grass within the fire-chamber;
ever cheerful, he performed hospitality toward all and attended to the three goals of life.
Always saying to Śūdras who desire food,
"It is ready," he should not notice anything for his own sake or out of desire;
and he who prepares the means of sustenance for the sake of the ancestors, the gods, and guests.
He lived in his own home according to the prescribed rule, subsisting solely on alms; he offered the Agnihotra sacrifice three times a day according to the injunctions,
and was slain facing the enemy in battle for the sake of the welfare of cows and Brahmins.
Or, having entered a body purified by the mantras of the three sacred fires, he becomes a twice-born;
endowed with knowledge and realization, consecrated, and a master of the Vedas,
the Kṣatriya becomes a righteous-souled Brahmin through his own action.
O Goddess, by these fruits of action, even a Śūdra born of a low caste and family becomes a twice-born man, refined and endowed with the sacred scriptures;
whereas a Brāhmaṇa of evil conduct, who eats all kinds of impure food, [falls from his status].
Having abandoned the merit of Brahminhood, one becomes such a Śūdra;
yet, O Goddess, through pure deeds, one whose soul is purified and whose senses are conquered—
even if a Śūdra— is to be served like a twice-born, so Brahmā himself has declared.

"Wherever pure conduct and virtuous action reside—even in a Śūdra—he should indeed be known as a pure twice-born man; this is my conviction. Neither birth, nor sacramental rites, nor sacred learning, nor noble lineage [determine one's status]."
There are many causes for the status of being twice-born, but conduct alone is the true cause.
Everyone in this world is designated as a Brāhmaṇa by virtue of their conduct; and one who stands firm in conduct, O lady of beautiful hips, attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa.
"O auspicious lady, my mind holds that the Brahmanic nature is equal toward all things.

That twice-born man in whom the stainless Brahman, devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), abides is truly such. O Goddess, these [distinctions] are merely the fruits of the womb, indicating one's place and portion."
And she was herself told by Brahmā, the giver of boons, while he was creating living beings:
"A Brāhmaṇa is indeed a great field that moves about in the world like a footed creature;
whatever seed one sows therein, that is the agriculture for the next world."
One who desires prosperity should always eat moderately and always adhere to the path of the righteous; having transcended the path of Brahmā,
he should conduct himself as a householder within his home, devoted to the study of the *saṃhitā*.
By one who is constantly devoted to the private study of the Veda, who lives by means of giving and studying;
for that Brahmin who is thus constituted and always established on the path of the righteous, maintaining the sacred fires and engaged in study, is fit for becoming Brahman.
"O lady of pure smiles, having attained the status of a Brahmin, it must be protected by those who have restrained their selves through [careful] conception, marriage,
and ritual acts. All this has been told to you regarding how a Śūdra may become a twice-born."
13.131.058 Just as a Brāhmaṇa, fallen from his dharma, attains the status of a Śūdra.
13.132.001 Umā said: O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, you who are saluted by gods and asuras!
"O Lord, O All-pervading One, tell me, who am in doubt, about the dharma and adharma of men.
For by means of action, mind, and speech, a person is always bound by threefold fetters and bonds, or else is liberated from them."
"By what conduct, O God, or by what kind of action, by what behaviors, virtues, or words do human beings here go to heaven?
Maheśvara said:

O Goddess, who knows the truth of dharma and its purpose, who is constant in truth and devoted to self-restraint— listen to this question, which is for the welfare of all living beings and increases the intellect.
The virtuous are devoted to truth and dharma, and are entirely free from the desire for gain.
Those whose doubts have been severed are bound neither by unrighteousness nor by righteousness;
knowing the truth of dissolution and origination, omniscient and seeing with equanimity,
those persons free from passion are liberated from all bonds.

Those who do not harm anything by deed, mind, or speech; those who do not cling to anything—they are not bound by their actions. Abstaining from taking life, they are virtuous and endowed with compassion.

Those who treat enemies and loved ones equally, who are self-controlled, and who possess compassion for all beings, are liberated from the bonds of karma. Those men who have abandoned the practice of violence and are trusted by all creatures go to heaven.
Those men who are always free from possessiveness regarding the property of others, who avoid the wives of others,
and who enjoy wealth acquired through righteous means, go to heaven.
Those who always regard [other women] as a mother, a sister, or a daughter...
Those men who do not pursue the wives of others go to heaven; those who constantly refrain from theft and are content with their own wealth,
living instead upon their own fortunes— those men go to heaven.
Those men who are devoted to their own wives, who approach them only during the proper season,
and who enjoy pleasures that are not vulgar, go to heaven. Those who always keep their eyes shielded by virtuous conduct regarding the wives of others [go to heaven].
Those men who have restrained their senses and are devoted to moral conduct go to heaven.
This path created by the gods should always be followed by men;
likewise, the path free from passion should always be pursued by the wise.

Endowed with the virtues of generosity, righteousness, and austerity, and characterized by moral conduct, purity, and compassion, this [path] should always be practiced by men— whether for the sake of livelihood or for the sake of dharma—
by those desiring residence in heaven; however, one should not practice anything superior to this.
Umā said:
"O God, O sinless Lord of Beings, tell me those actions by which one is bound by speech, or by which one is likewise liberated."
Maheśvara said: Those men who do not speak falsehoods here— whether for their own sake, for the sake of others, or even out of jest and laughter— are destined for heaven.

Those men who do not speak falsehoods— whether for the sake of livelihood, for the sake of dharma, out of desire, or likewise for any other reason— they go to heaven. They speak words that are gentle, harmless, sweet, and free from evil.
Those men who address others with a welcome,
who do not speak bitter, harsh, or cruel words, and who are devoted to refraining from slander— those virtuous men go to heaven.

Those men who do not speak slanderous words that cause the breach of friendship, but instead utter truthful and friendly speech, go to heaven. Those men always avoid backbiting and malice toward others.
Those men who are impartial toward all beings, self-controlled, abstaining from deceitful speech, avoiding what is contrary [to the Dharma],
and always speaking with gentleness— they are destined for heaven.

Those men who do not utter words that tear the heart out of anger, but speak with gentleness even when provoked to wrath, go to heaven. O Goddess, this is the duty established by speech which must always be practiced by men.
13,132.026c A pure person who always possesses the quality of truthfulness—falsehood must always be avoided by the wise.
13,132.027 Umā said: 13,132.027a By what action is a person constantly bound by the mind?
"Tell me that, O highly fortunate one, O God of gods, wielder of the Pināka bow.
Maheśvara said:
"Men here who are always endowed with mental dharma..."

O auspicious lady, they go to heaven; listen as I proclaim this to you. By a mind that is ill-directed, a person of even more ill-directed form is bound by which—listen to another thing, O fair-faced one.
Those men who, upon seeing another's property left in a lonely forest,
do not harm it even in their minds, go to heaven.
Whatever object belongs to another, whether in a village or a house, if it remains in a secluded place—
Those men who never take delight in [worldly pleasures] are destined for heaven;
likewise, those men who do not even in their minds harm the wives of others when they are alone and acting out of desire are destined for heaven.

Those men who always regard enemy and friend with an equal mind, who are friendly and associate with others— they are destined for heaven. They are learned in the scriptures, compassionate, pure, and true to their promises.
Those men who are content with their own possessions go to heaven; those who are free from enmity, effortless, always devoted to a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*),
and compassionate toward all beings— those men go to heaven.
Those men who possess faith, who are compassionate, who are pure, who are dear to the pure,
and who always know what is dharma and what is adharma, go to heaven.
[They do so] regarding the accumulation of the fruits of both auspicious and inauspicious deeds.
O Goddess, those men who understand the ripening of karma,
who are endowed with justice and virtue, and who are always devoted to the gods and the twice-born— having attained equanimity, those men go to heaven.
"O Goddess, these [paths] leading to the way of heaven, resulting from the fruits of auspicious deeds, have been proclaimed by me to you. What else do you wish to hear?
Umā said:
"O Maheśvara, I have a certain great doubt regarding mortals; therefore, you ought to explain it to me today with precision. By what action, O Lord, does a person obtain a long lifespan?"
"O Lord of Gods, by what austerity does one obtain a long life?
By what action on earth does a human being become short-lived?
O irreproachable God, you ought to explain the ripening of these karmas."
Some possess great wealth while others have meager means; some are of low birth while others are of noble lineage. Some men appear unpleasant to behold, like mere pieces of wood.
Likewise, other men are pleasant to behold merely by their appearance;
some appear to be of poor intellect, while others appear to be wise. Similarly, there are those of great wisdom who perceive through knowledge and discernment.
"O God, some men are seen to have few afflictions, while others have great afflictions; you ought to explain that to me. Maheśvara said:
"Come now, O Goddess, I shall explain to you the arising of the fruits of karma,
by which all men in the world of mortals experience their own respective results. He who takes life, who is fierce, and likewise has a raised staff in his hand— "
A man who constantly wields the rod of punishment slays the hosts of living beings;
merciless toward all creatures, he is a constant source of agitation, utterly devoid of compassion and offering no refuge even to insects and ants.

O Goddess, a man who is such as this falls into hell; but one who is the opposite, whose soul is righteous, is born handsome. Indeed, the violent-souled man goes to hell, while the non-violent man goes to heaven.
That man undergoes fierce and agonizing torment in hell. Then, if he should ever emerge from that hell,
he may attain human birth, but he is born there with a short lifespan.
O Goddess, a man who delights in violence is bound by his evil deeds;
he becomes disliked by all beings and is born with a short lifespan. But he who belongs to the pure class and refrains from killing living beings—
Having laid aside the rod of punishment, being free from violence, he never harms anyone at any time;
he does not cause others to kill, nor does he kill himself, nor does he approve of one who kills. He is full of affection for all beings, regarding others just as he regards himself.
O Goddess, such a preeminent person attains divinity;
endowed with joy, he enjoys the pleasures and delights that have come to him. Then, if he is ever reborn in the world of humans, [he remains distinguished].

There, that man born with a long life prospers in happiness. Thus has the path to long life been proclaimed by Brahmā for those of good conduct and virtuous deeds, through their liberation from harming living beings.
Umā said:
"What is their character, what is their conduct, and by what actions or by what kind of gift do men attain heaven?"
Maheśvara said:
He is a donor, one who honors brahmins, and one who shows compassion toward the poor, the blind, the wretched, and others;
he is a giver of foods to be chewed and swallowed, of meals, of drinks, and of garments.
He provided shelters, assembly halls, wells, water-stations, and lotus-pools;
likewise, all regular offerings and whatever else was desired in abundance.
He also provided seats, beds, vehicles, wealth, jewels, and houses.
O Goddess, that man who, with a mind always full of joy, bestows all kinds of grain, cattle, fields,
and women, is born in the world of the gods after death.
Having dwelt there for a very long time and enjoyed unsurpassed pleasures, rejoicing and sporting with the apsarases in the Nandana groves and other such places,
he falls from that heavenly realm and is reborn among the world of human beings.
O Goddess, in a family of great wealth, endowed with riches and grain,
that man becomes possessed of all the qualities of desire, filled with joy, possessing great enjoyments, a vast treasury, and great riches.

"O Goddess, these beings who possess great enjoyments and are inclined toward giving were indeed declared of old by Brahmā to be of pleasing appearance to all. Other men, O Goddess, are stingy in their giving toward the twice-born."
Those of little intelligence, though possessing wealth, do not give when asked,
even upon seeing the wretched, the blind, the miserable, mendicants, or guests;
possessed by greed of the tongue, they turn away when entreated.
They never bestow wealth, nor garments, nor enjoyments, nor gold; nor cows, nor preparations of food—
those who are inactive, greedy, atheistic, and devoid of charity.
O Goddess, such ignorant men go to hell.
When, by the turning of time, they eventually attain human status,
those of meager intellect take birth in families destitute of wealth.
Overcome by hunger and thirst, excluded from all enjoyments, and hopeless regarding every pleasure, they live a wretched life; born into families of meager means, these men delight in meager things.
By this karma, O Goddess, men become destitute;
others are constantly arrogant, conceited, and devoted to evil. These senseless ones do not offer a seat to one who deserves a seat.
Those of small intelligence who do not grant the path to one who deserves the path;
those of small intelligence who do not offer water for the feet to one who is worthy of water for the feet;
and those who do not honor with due rites those worthy of the guest-offering (argha) according to the rule.
Those of small intelligence do not offer the guest-offering (*arghya*) or water for sipping (*ācamanīya*);
nor do they, out of pride, desire to honor with love a teacher who has arrived as one would a teacher. They remain settled in greed that is driven by arrogance.
They honor those who should be honored, yet they insult them; they treat the elderly with contempt.
O Goddess, men of such character all go to hell. Indeed, even if those men should eventually emerge from that hell, [they remain fallen].
After many groups of years, they then take birth in a contemptible family—
among those such as Śvapākas and Pulkasas, who are despised and devoid of intelligence.
Born into those families, they become respectful toward their teachers and elders.
He who is neither arrogant nor conceited, who honors the deities and the twice-born,
who is worthy of worship by the world, who offers salutations, who is humble and speaks sweetly,
who acts for the pleasure of all classes and is always devoted to the welfare of all beings— [he attains this].
Free from malice, pleasant-faced, gentle, and always bestowing kind words; he is non-violent toward all beings and attends upon them,
honoring each according to their merit with a welcoming greeting.
Giving way to one who deserves the way, honoring his teacher as a teacher, and being devoted to receiving guests and likewise worshipping those who have arrived—
a man who is thus disposed, O Goddess, attains the heavenly state.
Then, having attained human status, he shall be born into a distinguished family. There, endowed with abundant enjoyments and possessed of all kinds of jewels,
he shall be a giver of what is appropriate to those who are worthy, and remain devoted to the practice of Dharma.
Esteemed by all beings and honored by the whole world,
a man always experiences the fruit of his own actions by himself;
he is born into a noble family and possesses a noble lineage for all time.
13,133.031c This dharma has been proclaimed by me, as uttered by the Creator himself.
13,133.032a But as for one of fierce conduct who causes fear to all beings,
[whether] with his hands or his feet, or again with a rope or a staff—
O beautiful one, he who is of deceitful intellect torments living beings with clods of earth, pillars, or various other means; for the sake of violence,
he causes them agitation and always assails creatures, generating distress in them.
One who possesses such character and conduct falls into hell.
If, however, by the turning of time, he should attain human status,
he is born into a low family, afflicted by many ailments.
"O Goddess, this lowest of men, who is hated by the world due to the fruits of his own actions, should be recognized among men as one who is alienated from his kinsmen and relatives;
whereas another looks upon all beings with compassion."

Possessing a friendly vision, equal toward all as a father, free from enmity, and with senses restrained, he does not cause agitation among beings nor does he harm them; with hands and feet well-controlled, he is trusted by all creatures.
Neither with a rope, nor with a staff, nor with clods of earth, nor with weapons does he cause distress to living beings; gentle in his actions and devoted to compassion,
one whose character and conduct are thus is reborn in heaven.
There, in that divine abode, he dwells with joy like a god.
If, upon the exhaustion of his karma, that mortal is born among human beings,
he is born free from affliction and calamity, and he prospers in happiness.
"O Goddess, this man who shares in happiness, free from exertion and always free from anxiety— this is the path of the virtuous, wherein no affliction is found.
Umā said:
"These humans are seen, O Lord, as being skilled in reasoning and refutation;
they are endowed with knowledge and discernment, possessed of wisdom, and proficient in meaning.
Yet others, O Lord, are of poor wisdom, deprived of both knowledge and discernment."
By what ripening of karma does a person become possessed of wisdom?
O Virūpākṣa, how does a human being become one of little wisdom?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O best among those who know all dharmas.
"O God, other men are seen who are born blind, others likewise afflicted by disease, and others who are impotent; tell me truly what the cause of that is. Maheśvara said:
Day after day they inquire of Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas, perfected beings, and likewise knowers of dharma, concerning what is auspicious and inauspicious;
thus practicing the auspicious, they avoid inauspicious action.
They constantly attain a heavenly rebirth and likewise find happiness in this world.
If such a person returns to the human state, he is born there as one endowed with intelligence;
his learning follows after wisdom, and auspiciousness arises for him.
Those fools who cast a wicked eye upon the wives of others become blind from birth because of that corrupt disposition. Furthermore,
those who, with a corrupted mind, look upon a naked woman [suffer the same fate].
Those men who have performed evil deeds become afflicted by diseases in this world.
But those fools of wicked conduct who take pleasure in sexual intercourse with those of inferior birth— those of very poor intelligence— attain the state of impotence among men.
Those men who bind animals, those who violate the bed of their preceptor,
and those who engage in promiscuous sexual conduct, are born as eunuchs.
Umā said:
"What indeed is blameworthy action, and likewise what is blameless?
O best of gods, what does a human being obtain by performing that which leads to welfare?
Maheśvara said:
He who always abides by the superior path, who constantly consults the twice-born,
who seeks dharma and longs for virtue— he attains heaven. O Goddess, even if he should ever descend again to the state of humanity, [he remains distinguished].
One who is intelligent, endowed with retentive memory, and wise is born therein. O Goddess, this dharma of the virtuous, which brings about prosperity,
has been fully declared by me to you for the benefit of human beings.
13,133.057 Umovāca: Other men, possessing very little wisdom and being haters of dharma,
do not wish to approach Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas.

Some men were observant of vows, devoted to faith and self-restraint; others were without vows, fallen from their rules, and like Rākṣasas. Likewise, some were performers of sacrifices, while others were devoid of oblations.
"By what ripening of karma do these things come to be here? Tell me.
Maheśvara said:
"The boundaries of worldly dharmas were established of old according to the scriptures."
For those of firm vows are seen to follow [the scriptures] with authority;
however, those who have fallen under the sway of delusion and declare unrighteousness to be righteousness,
being devoid of vows and having lost all moral boundaries, are called *brahmarākṣasas*.
If those humans are born here through the exertion of Time,
they become the lowest of men, devoid of *homa* offerings and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ*.
O Goddess, all this has been told by me for the sake of cutting away your doubt.
"The ocean of Dharma for men, both wholesome and unwholesome, has been explained.
Nārada said:
"Having spoken thus, the Lord Mahādeva himself desired to hear [more]."
He spoke to his devoted and beloved wife who was standing by his side.
Maheśvara said:
"O knower of the higher and the lower, O knower of dharma, O dweller in the penance grove!"

"O virtuous one, O fair-browed one, O you with beautiful hair-ends, daughter of the Himavat mountain! O skillful one, endowed with tranquility and self-restraint, O faultless one who walks the path of dharma!
I ask you, O lady of excellent hips; being questioned, tell me what I desire."
Sāvitrī is the virtuous wife of Brahmā; Śacī is the faithful wife of Kauśika; Dhūmorṇā is the wife of Mārtaṇḍaja; and Ṛddhi is the wife of Vaiśravaṇa.
Then Gaurī is the wife of Varuṇa, and Suvarcalā is the wife of Sūrya.
Rohiṇī is the virtuous wife of the Moon, and Svāhā is the wife of Agni;
Aditi is the wife of Kaśyapa, and all of them hold their husbands as their deities. O Goddess, you have constantly questioned and served them.
Therefore, I question you, O knower of dharma, O speaker of dharma;
I wish to hear from you, as it was first proclaimed, the duty of women.
You are my partner in the practice of dharma, equal in character and equal in vows.
She is equal to you in essence and vigor, and she has performed intense asceticism. For when addressed by you, she will attain authority and shall become possessed of excellent qualities.
And so it is in the world, O Goddess;
indeed, women especially are always the refuge for womankind.
O lady of beautiful hips, a cow goes toward a cow; such is the constant order of things in the worlds.
"Half of my body is yours, and you have emerged from half of me. You are the one who fulfills the work of the gods and the one who ensures the continuity of the world.
O auspicious lady, the eternal dharma of women is entirely well known to you."
"Therefore, explain to me in detail the duties of women without omission.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, source of the past, the future, and the present!"
"O Lord, by your power this speech manifests within me.
O Lord of Gods, these rivers, filled with the waters of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
wait upon you in your presence for the purpose of ritual ablution."
Having consulted with these [goddesses], I shall speak in due order:
he who, though possessing power, is free from the notion of "I," is indeed called a true man.
But a woman, O Lord of Beings, always pursues only women.
These best of rivers shall indeed be honored by me.
This is the holy Sarasvatī, the most excellent of rivers;
she is the first among all streams, a river that flows to the ocean.
The Vipāśā, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Irāvatī, the Śatadrū, the Devikā, the Sindhu, the Kauśikī, and likewise the Gomatī;
and also this divine river here, encompassed by all sacred fords (tīrthas).
"O Goddess Gaṅgā, the best of all rivers, you have descended from the sky to the earth.
Having spoken thus to the wife of the God of gods, that foremost of the upholders of dharma then addressed all those rivers with a slight smile.

The queen of the gods, who was devoted to righteousness, questioned those foremost of rivers, Gaṅgā and the others, who were skilled in the duties of women, regarding the duties of women. "This question concerning the duties of women has been posed by the Blessed One."
Having consulted with you on this matter, I wish to speak to Śaṅkara;
for I do not see anyone on earth or in heaven, O river that flows to the ocean, whose specialized knowledge could accomplish this alone. Therefore, I honor you.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus were all those most meritorious and auspicious rivers, the best of streams, questioned. Then the celestial river Gaṅgā, having honored her in return, was appointed [to answer].
Abounding in many insights, knowledgeable in the duties of women, and possessed of a pure smile,

she was endowed with wisdom and humility, and was proficient in all branches of knowledge; [she praised] the goddess, the daughter of the King of Mountains, who is holy, auspicious, and the destroyer of sins.
Rich in great wisdom, Gaṅgā spoke these words with a smile:
"O Goddess devoted to dharma, we are blessed and favored that you,
who are honored by the entire world, O sinless one, show such respect to us rivers."
For he who, being powerful, questions others or shows them respect— surely that man of pure soul attains the reputation of a wise man,
provided he is endowed with knowledge and discernment and is skilled in reasoning and refutation.
He who asks other speakers about [the truth] indeed does not fall from his station.
Otherwise, though rich in great intelligence, he speaks words in the assembly that are contrary [to the truth];
for one possessed of ego-conceit speaks weak words quite differently.
"O Goddess, you who possess divine knowledge, who are supreme in heaven, who are ever-arisen through divine merit—
you alone are worthy to instruct us in the duties of women.
Bhīṣma said:
Then, having been propitiated by Gaṅgā with many virtues, that celestial beauty spoke in its entirety regarding the entire dharma of women—
how the dharma of women appears to me, according to the rule.
I shall proclaim that [account], so that it may likewise become renowned:
this duty of women was established by their kinsmen at the time of marriage;
in the presence of the fire, she becomes the partner in dharma with her husband.

Of excellent character, pleasant in speech, virtuous in conduct, and delightful to behold; with a mind focused on no other and a gracious countenance, she is a wife who practices the Dharma with her husband.
This indeed is the auspicious duty of a couple, performed together in accordance with the Dharma.
She who constantly regards her husband as a god and performs service and attendance toward him as if toward a deity, she shall be supreme in dharma and she shall be a partaker of dharma.
For she who is not of another mind, who is steadfast in her vows, pleasant to behold,
and who gazes constantly upon her husband’s face as if it were the face of her own son— she is a virtuous woman, self-restrained in conduct, and a follower of dharma.
Having heard the auspicious duties of a husband and wife, which are to be performed together, that virtuous wife,
with a cheerful countenance and an undistracted mind toward her husband,
remains steadfast even when addressed with harsh words or looked upon with a cruel eye.
That woman whose face is ever bright with joy toward her husband is a devoted wife (*pativratā*).
That woman of noble form who does not look upon the moon, the sun, or a tree bearing a masculine name— save for her husband— is a practitioner of dharma.
She who waits upon her husband— whether he be poor, diseased, distressed, or worn out by travel— as if he were her own son, that woman partakes in the merit of dharma.
That woman who is self-restrained and skillful, and who possesses sons, [is likewise blessed].
That woman who is dear to her husband and whose life is her husband, she shares in the dharma;
she always performs service and attendance with an undistracted mind, being well-pleased and humble— she, that woman, shares in the dharma.
That woman who has no longing for sensual pleasures, nor for wealth, nor for sovereignty, nor for happiness, but rather for her husband alone, is a partaker of dharma.
She is always delighted in rising at dawn and devoted to the service of her elders.
Her dwelling was well-swept and smeared with cow-dung;
she was constantly devoted to the fire-ritual and always offered flowers and oblations.
Having first presented offerings to the deities, guests, and servants together with her husband, [she would then attend to herself].
Constantly consuming the remaining food according to rule and according to ordinance,
with her people always contented and well-nourished, a woman endowed with virtues pleases the feet of her mother-in-law and father-in-law through her righteous conduct.
That woman who is always devoted to her mother and father possesses the wealth of asceticism.
That woman who supports with food the Brahmins, the weak, the helpless, the wretched, the blind, and the miserable, shares in the merit of devotion to her husband.

She who constantly observes a vow difficult for one of weak character to perform, whose mind is fixed on her husband and who is devoted to her husband, shares in the merit of a wife devoted to her husband.
This is merit, this is austerity, and this is eternal heaven.
That woman who is devoted to her husband, faithful to her husband’s vows, and auspicious—[for] the husband indeed is the god of women; the husband is their kinsman, the husband is their refuge.
There is no goal equal to the husband, nor any deity like the husband.
Whether it be the restoration of favor or heaven itself, these may or may not be equal to a noble woman;
yet, O Maheśvara, I would not desire heaven if you were displeased. Even if it were an improper act, or unrighteousness, or even the destruction of my life.
Whether he be poor or diseased, or in any way distressed, or situated among enemies, or even afflicted by a Brahmin’s curse— the husband should,
having considered the duties for times of distress, perform that task without hesitation.
"O Lord, this duty of women has been declared by me according to your word;
that woman who conducts herself in this manner shall be a partaker of dharma.
Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, the Lord of the Gods, having honored the daughter of the Mountain,
dismissed the worlds along with all their attendants.
Then the hosts of beings and the rivers departed as they had come.
And the Gandharvas and Apsarases, having bowed their heads to Bhava, [departed].
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having exhorted the high-minded one with auspicious words, Bhīṣma then spoke.
Janamejaya said:
O brahmin-sage, out of affection for Yudhiṣṭhira, my grandfather again desired to hear those words regarding Bhīṣma, who had come under the power of time.
13,134.057d@015_0004 What did the king then ask, that which is beneficial for all in brief?
13,134.057d@015_0005 That which is appropriate for both worlds, the unsurpassed goal of human endeavor?
13,134.057d@015_0006 Vaiśampāyana said:
"Tell me that, O one of great wisdom, for I have a great curiosity to hear it. Furthermore, O Great King, listen again to this compendium of Dharma,
which King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, asked at that time."
13,134.057d@015_0009 To Bhīṣma, who was lying upon a bed of arrows in the presence of all the kings, 13,134.057d@015_0010 Yudhiṣṭhira,
the one whose enemies are unborn, with a joyful heart, spoke once again.

O Grandfather, of great wisdom and learned in all the scriptures, please listen to my words; I speak them out of necessity. You are the knower of the high and the low among beings, compassionate toward all creatures.

Abounding in many scriptures, you are the supreme one in our lineage; such a person as you, possessed of knowledge and vision, is difficult to find in the world at present. O Lord, we are indeed blessed by having you as our teacher.
This time has now arrived, which is difficult for kinsmen and relatives to encounter.
O bull among men, there is indeed no teacher for us other than you.
Therefore, [speak] that which is joined with the Dharma and its purpose, and which results in welfare for the future.
"O Bhārata, I wish to hear this most wonderful speech:
how this glorious Nārāyaṇa, in the presence of all the kings,
attends upon you out of great respect and affection."
"In the very presence of us kings,
and likewise for the sake of the listeners, [you should relate] this ancient history which is supremely beneficial;
if I, along with my brothers, am worthy of your favor, O sinless one."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O descendant of Kuru, for the sake of my pleasure, you ought to speak out of affection.
Having heard those words of his, he was overcome with agitation born of love.
Seeing him as if drinking that [speech], Bhīṣma spoke these words:
"Listen, O King, to this ancient history of what occurred in the past.
Having said this much, the son of Gaṅgā bowed his head to Hari.
Having beheld the King of Dharma, he began to speak again:
"This glorious Nārāyaṇa, the mighty-armed one, formerly undertook initiation for twelve years out of a desire for a vow for the sake of a son."
The great seers approached to behold Keśava, who had been initiated for sacrifice; those high-souled ones came with affection to serve Janārdana—
Nārada, Parvata, and likewise Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana.
Devala and Kāśyapa, as well as Hastikāśyapa;
Jamadagni, O king of kings, and Dhaumya and Vālmīki;
and others who were perfected through austerity and devoted to the vow of truth.
Accompanied by all their disciples— knowers of Brahman who were free from stain—
Keśava received them with affection as they approached,
performing for them the hospitality due to guests and the worship appropriate to his lineage.
The son of Devakī, being delighted, provided [seats] equal to those of the gods.
O sinless one, when they had all sat down upon their mats,
they were full of trust and satisfied once again by the worship of Keśava.
Divine and delightful conversations proceeded between them.
By the grace of Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa himself, I shall relate those [conversations]. Formerly, I was filled with wonder by the sages regarding his very practice of vows.
And as for the power that belonged to the high-souled one who bears the bull as his emblem—
wherein, in former times, the Goddess questioned Mahādeva regarding her doubts, and Śarva explained them to her, desiring to do what was pleasing to her.
And listen, dear son, to the delightful dialogue between Umā and her Lord; therein, dear son, the duties of the castes and stages of life are fully set forth,
as well as the entire duty of sages and the abundant duty of kings.
The auspicious duties of the householder, the fruits resulting from the ripening of karma, the various secrets of the gods, the rules for the practice of the dharma of giving,
and the ordinances regarding *yama* and *niyama* were then fully proclaimed here.

The ordinance concerning the world of Yama, as well as the procedure for the heavenly realm; the ritual for the liberation of the vital breath, and the full account of pilgrimage to sacred sites; and the ordinance on the dharma of liberation, endowed with Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
And the duties of women were personally expounded by the Goddess to the God of gods;
all such auspicious matters as these, O dear one, are contained therein. It is there, O dear one, that the inquiry regarding the doubts of Rudrāṇī proceeds.
Listen as I relate this divine method for nourishment, which brings prosperity, fame, long life, and is righteous and supremely beneficial; it is a divine history, pure and most auspicious.
One who desires prosperity should always listen to this properly, both morning and evening.
Then the god Nārāyaṇa, distressed by his observance of the vow,
emitted from his mouth a fire of wondrous appearance belonging to Kṛṣṇa.
As that great fire issued forth from the mouth of the Lord,
even as everyone looked on, the best of mountains was utterly consumed—
crowded with beasts and birds, and teeming with wild predators.
Covered with trees, shrubs, and creepers, the mountain had been ravaged and appeared wretched;
yet, as soon as it was beheld by the gentle-minded Hari,
that mountain quickly became filled with forests of blossoming trees.
Adorned by throngs of joyful Siddhas and Cāraṇas,
joined with rutting elephants and flocks of various birds,
that [palace] became truly wonderful and inconceivable to everyone.
Seeing him, all the hosts of sages then had their hair stand on end;
they were struck with wonder, overcome with great anxiety, and their eyes were agitated with trepidation.
They said nothing there, whether auspicious or otherwise.
Then the lotus-eyed god Nārāyaṇa, beholding that assembly of sages filled with great wonder, spoke sweetly to them: "For what reason has this unsurpassed wonder arisen among the assembly of sages?"
"O blameless ones, you ṛṣis who are experts in the meaning of things, ought to explain this doubt of mine to me exactly as it is, with certainty.
Having heard the words of Keśava, the bulls among sages offered him praise.
You indeed create the worlds; you withdraw all creatures.
You are the cold, you are the heat; you are truth, you are the sacrifice. You are the beginning, you are the end; nothing else exists apart from you.
O Supreme Person, you alone are all that is stationary and moving;
O Father, this entire wheel of the world proceeds from you.
It is fitting for you alone to explain how fire issued forth from your mouth.
"O Madhusūdana, this has become a source of wonder for us;
O Puruṣottama, we were thereafter overcome with terror,
O Blessed One."
Whatever you wish to say on that matter, why should we speak out of compulsion? You perform austerities for the constant welfare of the worlds;
therefore, listen as I tell you a secret for the benefit of the world.
At present, there is a certain Asura who is harmful and a destroyer of the worlds;
skilled in the use of illusory weapons and endowed with strength and pride,
he must be slain by me out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
"O bulls among sages, my death at the hands of my own son was foreseen;
for that reason, I have come to the forest desiring to procreate a son who would be equal to myself through ascetic observances."
Thus, for me who was thus enveloped by vows through the intensity of my asceticism,
that Self residing within my body then became fire and issued forth. Having issued forth, it went in an instant to behold the Grandfather (Brahmā).
By Brahmā, Manmatha was designated as my son under the name Anaṅga;
having been granted permission by him, he returned once more to my presence.
This is indeed my Vaiṣṇava splendor that has issued forth from my mouth.
By that splendor, this mountain standing before me was ground down;
yet, seeing the destruction of that mountain, because of my gentle nature,
as soon as he looked upon it again, the mountain became as it was before.
This secret has been truly told by me to you in brief,
O ascetics rich in austerity, by which you have been both distressed and amazed.
The Blessed One.
Having spoken thus to the sages, he addressed them once more:
"By the mere sight of you, my joy has become even greater;
for you are perfected through asceticism, and you possess the vision of the gods."
They possess movement everywhere, being cultivated by knowledge and discernment;
they know the coming and going of all worlds, and all are cleansed of impurity.
Therefore, whatever has been seen or heard by you—
