"Tell me, sirs, that which is a marvel among the worlds—whatever has been spoken by you whose souls are purified by austerity. That would be like nectar; there is a longing to hear the honey of your speech."

The speech of the virtuous, who are forever free from passion and hatred and always speak the truth, is indeed worthy of trust and worthy of being heard. Therefore, let there be for me union with them; you ought not to act in vain.
Therefore, let my meeting with you be fruitful indeed. Thus,
day after day, I shall recount before the assembly of people what has issued from the mouths of the virtuous— a teaching that serves as a lamp for the intellect of men.
Others will cause it to increase, while others will honor it;
still others, free from the thorns of speech, will praise that which is ancient.
— Bhīṣma.
While Govinda was speaking thus, the great ṛṣis, for the sake of hearing [his words],
addressed Janārdana with these words, their hands joined in salutation:
"O Giver of Boons, it is improper for you to speak to us in such a manner."
All have their mouths directed toward your teaching, and all have their efforts dependent upon you. O Keśava, it does not behove you to honor us in such a way;
for we see no other thing in this world that is not already known to you.
"Whether in heaven or on earth, whatever exists—all that is indeed pervaded by you.
O God, we do not understand what is being told in your presence.
Thus addressed, Hṛṣīkeśa spoke these words with a smile.
"O bulls among sages, I am currently situated in a human womb;
therefore, O you of excellent vows, know my prowess to be like that of a human."—
Bhīṣma.
And what is being told by you would be as if it were unprecedented.
Thus urged by the high-souled Keśava,
all the ṛṣis followed the command of Vāsudeva.
Then all the hosts of sages considered Nārada, who has the vision of the gods, to be wise and capable of understanding that matter through his intellect;
for this sage of fierce austerities was exceedingly dear to Keśava.
Knowing the Purāṇas and eloquent in speech, they all considered him worthy for that purpose; having offered him due honor, they addressed these words to Nārada:
"While you were wandering on the Himavat mountain for the sake of a pilgrimage to sacred sites..."

Bhīṣma said: "That which was seen as a marvel is indeed most dear to the listeners; you [should relate] that truth in its entirety, without omission, from the beginning, for the sake of their welfare."
"You ought to speak for the sake of this Keśava’s welfare. Thus urged by all the ṛṣis, Nārada then bowed his head to Viṣṇu, who is devoted to the welfare of all the worlds.
Having gazed upon Hṛṣīkeśa, he began to speak. Then Nārada, the friend of Nārāyaṇa and the best among speakers—
Nārada.
He related the conversation between Śaṃkara and Umā:
"O Blessed One, while I was wandering for the sake of a pilgrimage to sacred sites,
I beheld the divine forest of the Himalayas, which appeared truly wondrous."
It was endowed with various trees and creepers, frequented by flocks of various birds;
it was strewn with various jewels and possessed of various states of being;
it was infused with divine sandalwood and perfumed with divine incense.
It was strewn with celestial flowers, suffused with divine fragrance, a dwelling for *siddhas* and *cāraṇas*, frequented by hosts of spirits,
crowded with the most excellent *apsarases*, and teeming with various *gandharvas*.
Resounding with the sounds of mṛdaṅga and muraja drums and echoing with conchs and lutes,
it was adorned on all sides by throngs of spirits dancing—
beings of various forms, some misshapen, some of terrifying form, and others fearsome.
With faces like tigers, lions, and serpents, and likewise with faces like cats;
with faces like donkeys, camels, and leopards, and likewise with faces like elephants;
with faces like owls and hawks, and likewise with faces like crows and vultures.
Thus, it was intensely crowded with hosts of beings of many kinds;
it resounded in many ways with the loud cries of Hara’s attendants;
it was terrible in form, difficult to behold, and surrounded by hundreds of throngs of Rākṣasas.
Long ago, O Lord of Beings, I beheld that divine assembly in the forest,
where Apsarases were dancing and it resounded with the songs of gods and Gandharvas; it was celebrated by bees during the first month, Mādhava.
It was filled with the cries of crying cranes, curlews, cranes, and jīvajīvaka birds,
and crowded with intoxicated cuckoos warbling;
it resembled a great festival, yet was even more terrifying in appearance.
It is for all those who partake in the Dharma to behold it,
as well as for the perfected ones (siddhas) who have restrained their vital energy (ūrdhvaretas) and have gathered there from various places,
and likewise for the hosts of the Viśvedevas who move with the rays of the sun.
Likewise, the Nāgas, the Ādityas, the World-Protectors, and the Fires,
as well as all the Winds, blew forth, filled with celestial flowers;
scattering every kind of blossom, they appeared wondrous to behold.
The medicinal herbs blazed forth, illuminating the ten directions;
and the birds, filled with joy, danced and sang. There, exceedingly sweet and divine voices were heard, beloved by celestial beings.
There, on a mountain slope adorned with gold ore, the god of great splendor sat resplendent like one upon a couch;
he was clothed in a tiger skin, with an elephant hide as his upper garment.
Wearing a serpent as his sacred thread and adorned with red entrails,
with tawny beard and matted locks, he is formidable and the instiller of fear in the enemies of the gods;
yet he is the destroyer of the fear of all beings and the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees.
Being praised on all sides by *kiṃnaras* and divine *gandharvas*,
and graced everywhere by *ṛṣis* and *apsarases*,
there stands the abode of the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*), crowded with gods and *dānavas*.
Consisting entirely of splendor by its abundance, it was frequented by the world-protectors;
it was crowded with great serpents and caused the hair of all to stand on end.
O Lord, it was of terrifying form, indescribable, and most invincible.
There, having bowed their heads to Hara, the Lord of Beings, who was seated upon the highest peak, the sages and hosts of spirits praised Maheśvara with words of supreme purity.
They were liberated from all evils and became free from feverish distress—
the Vālakhilya ṛṣis, as well as those brahmin-ṛṣis,
the great seers born both from wombs and not from wombs, who had attained perfection through austerity.
There they worship the Blessed One, the Lord of the Gods, who resides therein. Then, at that very moment, the Goddess, attended by hosts of female spirits,
wearing garments equal to those of Hara, and observing identical vows, [appeared].
Taking a golden pitcher filled with the waters of all sacred fords,
raining down a shower of flowers imbued with divine fragrance,
that excellent woman was followed from behind by all the best of rivers.
With a pure smile, she came to the side of the Blessed One to serve him;
having arrived in the presence of the God of gods, the daughter of the mountain desired to do what was pleasing to his heart for the sake of sport in the vicinity of Śaṅkara.
Having covered the eyes of Hara with her two captivating hands,
she looked back at her own attendants with a smile; while the Goddess stood behind him, the God, rendered blind, fell into a state of dejection.
When the Lord of Beings had closed his eyes, the world became shrouded in darkness; the moon, sun, and stars vanished, the recitation of the Vedas and the utterance of *vaṣaṭ* ceased,
and all beings were dejected, terrified, and overwhelmed by fear.

Then there arose a cry of "Alas! Alas! from the sages and the worlds, as the world was overwhelmed by darkness, bewildered, and filled with fear for its life. And a third long eye appeared upon his forehead.
Resembling the twelve Ādityas, he illuminated the worlds with his radiance. There, by that fire from his eye, which was like the fire at the end of an eon,
the entire Himavat mountain standing before him was consumed.
While that mountain, teeming with beasts and birds,
along with its Vidyādharas and Gandharvas and endowed with divine medicinal herbs, was being consumed by fire,
the daughter of the Mountain, her eyes wide with wonder, [beheld it].
And the entire world became filled with wonder as all the gods, dānavas, and rākṣasas looked on;
by that fire born from his eyes, the best of mountains was indeed consumed.
Seeing that mountain crushed, the daughter of the mountain,
overcome with distress and desiring her father’s pacification, fell to the ground at his feet.
Seeing that, the Lord of the Gods of gods beheld the unsurpassed suffering of the Goddess.
And for the sake of pleasing Haimavatī, he looked again toward the mountain.
As soon as it was beheld by the Blessed One with a mind endowed with gentleness,
the Himavat mountain was restored to its natural state in an instant.
With its birds joyful and well-fed, its forests of trees in full bloom,
and crowded with throngs of Siddhas and Cāraṇas filled with delight,
Haimavatī beheld her father restored to his natural state and was deeply moved.
Filled with joy and delighted,
the Goddess, overcome with wonder and desiring to question Maheśvara for the benefit of all the worlds and out of a wish for the welfare of all creatures, addressed the wielder of the Pināka bow.
The Great Goddess spoke these meaningful words to the God of gods:
“O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, wielder of the trident, of great splendor!
Great wonder has arisen in me regarding that [being] who was overwhelmed by the fire from his eye.”

"O Lord of the gods of gods, for what purpose does this third, elongated eye shine upon your forehead, resembling the sun and fire more intensely than even they? By the great fire of that eye, indeed, was that Himavat consumed."
"O God, as soon as my father was seen again, he returned to his natural state;
this doubt now dwells within my heart. O God of gods, salutations to you; you ought to explain that to me."
Thus addressed by the goddess, Bhava, being pleased, spoke:
"O Goddess, knower of dharma, sweet-spoken one, it is only fitting that you should have such doubts."
"O beloved, indeed no one else is able to question me except you;
whether it be public or secret, I shall speak for your sake.
Listen, O beautiful lady, to all of this in its entirety within this assembly."
"Know me, O beloved, to be the immutable foundation of all the worlds. The three worlds are dependent upon me, just as they are dependent upon Viṣṇu.
Know this, O beautiful lady: Viṣṇu is the creator and I am the protector."
Therefore, O auspicious one, whenever anything touches me, whether it be pleasant or otherwise,
this entire world likewise becomes that very thing. This secret was not known by you out of childishness, O blameless lady.
"O Goddess of firm vows, my eyes have been covered by you for the sake of sport;
because of you, the world has become utterly distressed, with the moon and sun lost.
O beloved daughter of the mountain, when the sun has vanished and the world is shrouded in darkness,"
A third eye was created by me to protect the worlds. By the splendor of this very eye of mine, O auspicious one, this mountain—
thick with trees, shrubs, and creepers, and its caves inhabited by predatory beasts— has been churned.
"O Goddess, for the sake of what was dear to you, Nārada has been restored by me to his natural state. O beloved, I have explained this point of doubt; be free from anxiety."
Desirous of hearing what was pleasing and beneficial from the God of gods, the goddess Umā, who knows the moments, questioned Mahādeva once again:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are saluted by all the gods!"

By what cause did the Blessed One indeed become four-faced? O Blessed One, by what means did the eastern face become so wondrous to behold, and likewise, O Blessed One, the northern and the western faces of auspicious appearance?
Why is the southern face fierce, and why is the upper face matted? O Mahādeva, I wish to hear the reason for each according to its direction.
Maheśvara said:
"O Lord, this is my doubt; you ought to explain it to me.
"I shall tell you that which you ask, O beautiful lady.
"In the past, there were two most terrible Asuras who caused great agitation to the worlds."
There were two [demons] named Sunda and Upasunda who were exceedingly proud,
incapable of being slain by weapons, powerful, and intent on each other's welfare;
they were created by Viśvakarman specifically for their own destruction.
Having extracted the essence from all sides— from the multitudes of beasts and birds, and likewise from the stationary beings— the one honored by the world was divided into pieces like sesame seeds;
thus she became the celebrated Apsaras known as Tilottamā.

Intending to perform the work of the gods, she was endowed with alluring gestures and expressions. Having approached the edge [of the mountain], she who was peerless in beauty on earth and highly esteemed by me will accomplish the task of the gods.
Thinking thus, O beloved, as she was then circumambulating me, I likewise became four-faced, desiring to behold her;
this eastern face of mine is that of Indra, which is ever devoted to the practice of austerity.
My southern face is divine and fierce; it destroys all creatures.
My western face, O beloved, is eternally intent upon the affairs of the world. My northern face is wondrous; it constantly studies the Vedas.
"O Umā, all this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
O Blessed One, wielder of the trident, granter of boons, I wish to hear more."
Maheśvara said:
"For what reason does this blue color, resembling a peacock's plumage, shine upon your throat?
Ah, I shall tell you; listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind."
Formerly, in another age, the great ocean was churned for a long time with effort by the powerful gods and asuras for the sake of the nectar of immortality;
while the great ocean was being churned with the serpent-king as its rope.
Therein arose a poison capable of destroying all the worlds.
Seeing that, all the gods then became despondent.
"O Goddess, I have indeed swallowed it for the sake of the welfare of the worlds."
By that act, O auspicious one, a blue hue like that of a peacock’s plumage appeared upon my throat;
from that time forth, I have been known as Nīlakaṇṭha.
— Umā.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
O Blue-throated One, salutations to you, the bringer of happiness to all the worlds!
Among many weapons, you desire to wield the Pināka.
"O Maheśvara, O Lord of the gods, for what purpose [did this occur]? You ought to explain that to me.
O lady of pure smiles, I shall tell you the origin of the weapons; listen to this righteous account."
In another age, O Great Goddess, there was a great sage named Kaṇva;
he indeed began to perform divine ascetic practices.
As he was thus engaged in severe penance, with the passage of time—
O beloved, an anthill arose once again upon his very head;
due to its connection with the anthill, a bamboo stalk grew upon his crown,
and while bearing all of that, he continued his practice of austerity.
13,134.057d@015_0328 Brahmā, honored by his asceticism, went to grant him a boon.
13,134.057d@015_0329 Having granted him the boon, the god, seeing the bamboo, thought:
13,134.057d@015_0330 "O beautiful lady, with this bamboo, for the sake of the world's affairs..."
Having reflected on this and taking it, he employed it for the purpose of the bow;
and having recognized the power of both Viṣṇu and myself, the Grandfather of the worlds then bestowed two bows, one upon Viṣṇu and one upon me.
My bow is named Pināka, and the bow of Hari is named Śārṅga;
the third became the bow Gāṇḍīva by virtue of what remained. Having entrusted that [Śārṅga] to Soma, he returned once more to the world of Brahmā.
"O Umā,
O blameless one, I have thus explained to you this entire tradition of weapons.
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, you who are fond of the Pināka bow and the axe!"
O Lord of Beings, while you possess other such vehicles,
why has this bull alone attained the status of your vehicle,
O Maheśvara?
"O Lord, this is my doubt; you ought to explain it to me.
I shall tell you how that vehicle came to be. O lady of radiant smiles, in the primordial creation, cows were once white in color."
Endowed with strength and firmness, they roam about filled with pride;
but at that time, O lady of auspicious countenance, I performed austerities on the Himavat mountain for the sake of the world, standing on one foot with my arms raised upward.

"O Goddess, my cows, intoxicated with pride, have entered upon my flanks from all sides; they have thus repeatedly caused me to lose my footing. And because of this misconduct on their part, there has arisen a disturbance in my mind."
Therefore, with my mind possessed by rage, I burned the cows. While that terrible calamity regarding the cattle was occurring, I was pacified by this bull through his means of propitiation.
From that time forward, they became peaceful and attained the state of distinct castes.
O Goddess, this white bull, endowed with his former impressions (*pūrvasaṃskāra*),
has from that time been appointed as my vehicle and as my banner.
Therefore, my status as the Lord of Cows was ordained by the gods and the cows themselves. O Goddess Umā, having become gracious at that time, I attained the state of being the Lord of Cows.
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, wielder of the trident, whose banner is the bull:
how is it that you take delight in cremation grounds, rather than in various dwellings that are beautiful, auspicious, and other excellent places?

In that terrifying place, thick with hair and bones, crowded with hundreds of skulls, filled with jackals and vultures, pervaded by the smoke of corpses, uneven with funeral pyres, dreadful, dense, and fearsome—
"How is it that you take delight in this field of the body, so difficult to behold?
O Maheśvara, O God, this is my doubt; you ought to explain it to me."

"Come, O Goddess, I shall tell you; listen with a concentrated mind. Long ago, O Goddess of pure smiles, while seeking a pure place for the purpose of dwelling, I could not find a most holy region for a long time, O auspicious one."
At that time, this was my obsession regarding the creatures:
a vast and terrible agitation arose on all sides,
and a horrific creation of beings came into existence, bringing fear to the world.
Of various colors and hideous forms, with sharp fangs and striking blows, having the faces of *piśācas* and *rakṣasas*, they were snatchers of the life-breath of living beings;
they roamed here and there, violently slaughtering creatures.
When the world had thus come to destruction and was bereft of living beings, the Grandfather (Pitāmaha),
reflecting upon the remedy for that and knowing me to be capable of its suppression,
then employed me in that task.
"And that was approved by me as well, O beloved, for the sake of compassion toward living beings.
Therefore, O Goddess, you have protected creatures from fear of other beings;
yet, O blameless one, there is nothing here in this cremation ground that is pure."
Because it is free from the passage of humans, it is remembered as the most pure place. I established that creation of beings within the cremation ground;
stationed there, O beloved, I destroy the fear of all the worlds.
I cannot endure to dwell apart from my host of spirits;
therefore, my mind delights in dwelling in the cremation ground. It is always declared by the twice-born who desire purity that this place is pure.
"O beloved, by those who practice the fierce vow (raudravratam) and desire liberation, my station is frequented there; it is ordained as the 'Station of Heroes' (vīrasthāna),
filled with hundreds of skulls, of terrifying form, and fearsome."
At midday, at the two twilights, or under a lunar mansion presided over by Rudra, those desiring long life or those who are impure must not go there; such is the established rule.
Indeed, it is impossible for anyone other than me to destroy the fear born of these beings.

Abiding there, I protect all creatures day after day; by my command, the hosts of beings do not harm anything here. Therefore, for the sake of the welfare of the world, I take delight in the cremation ground.
"O Umā, all this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear? O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Three-eyed One, whose banner is the bull!"
Your form appears tawny, deformed, and most terrifying;
it is smeared with ashes, three-eyed, with sharp fangs, and matted with locks of hair.
It is clothed in tiger and serpent skins and covered with tawny facial hair.
Fierce, terrifying, and formidable, equipped with a trident and a sword—
O Maheśvara,
you ought to explain to me for what purpose you have assumed such a form.
I shall speak of that; listen with a concentrated mind to the truth.
O beloved, worldly existence is twofold: cold and heat.
This entire world, composed of both the lunar and the fiery elements, is bound together by these two.
The quality of gentleness is eternally established in Viṣṇu, while the fiery nature resides in me. With this form, I constantly sustain all the worlds.
[I am] of fierce appearance, three-eyed, and equipped with a trident and a sword.
"O Goddess, this form of mine, which is devoted to the welfare of the world, is called 'Agni-like.
O lady of beautiful countenance, if I were to become perverted by abandoning this [form],
then at that very moment, everything for all the worlds would turn perverse."
Therefore, this form is maintained by me, desiring the welfare of the world. Thus, O Goddess Umā, I have told you; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, whose banner is the bull:
for what purpose does the crescent moon shine upon your head,
O Maheśvara?"
"I wish to hear it, O God; you ought to explain it to me.
"I shall tell that to you; listen, O auspicious one, to the reason.
"Formerly, O Goddess, O lady of pure smiles, I was filled with anger for a certain cause."
Surrounded by a multitude of beings for the purpose of destroying Dakṣa’s sacrifice,
when that terrible slaughter of the ritual occurred on account of the sacrificial portions,
those gods whose shares had been assigned in the rite were indeed cast down.
O Goddess, there Soma was severely tormented by me in my wrath;
though he was innocent, he was gazed upon and then pressed with the big toe of my foot. When I had thus been treated with such humiliation, I was propitiated by him through conciliatory words.
As I reflected upon this, O beloved, remorse arose within me once again.
From that time forward, I indeed carry the moon upon my head;
such was my thought, that in this way my sin might be destroyed.
"From that time forth, Soma has indeed always been visible upon the head," said Nārada. When the Lord of Gods had spoken thus, the supreme ṛṣis were filled with wonder.
With words and with garlands of folded hands, they praised the Lord from all sides:
"Obeisance to Śaṅkara, O Lord of Gods; obeisance to the Teacher of the entire world!
Obeisance to the God of gods; obeisance to the wearer of the crescent moon!"
Homage to you, more terrible than the most terrible; homage, O Rudra, the inspirer of fear!
Homage to you, more peaceful than the most peaceful; homage to the protector of the moon! Homage to the divine Soma; homage to you, O four-faced one!
Homage to you, Lord of Beings, Śambhu, whose crest-jewel is the water of the daughter of Jahnu! Homage to the one who holds the trident in hand and who is adorned with serpents!
Homage be to the odd-eyed one, the burner of Dakṣa’s sacrifice!
Homage be to the one with many eyes, who is intent upon protecting the world!
Oh, how great is the majesty of the God, and indeed the compassion of Mahādeva!
Thus, he truly deserves the status of the God of gods and his devotion to the Dharma.
While the sages were speaking thus, the Goddess addressed Dharma with words that were supremely beneficial and appropriate for the occasion, for the sake of pleasing the sages:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are worshipped by all the worlds!"

Out of a desire to do what is pleasing to this assembly of sages and to me, you ought to explain, in its entirety, the dharma pertaining to the social classes and stages of life. O Lord of Gods, there is no satiety for us, for your words are indeed worthy of being heard.
"O Lord, O Ruler of the Gods, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds, you ought to declare: 'She is a fellow-practitioner of the Dharma,' and 'She is devoted.
Thus [spoke] Maheśvara.

"O Śaṅkara, you ought to tell all of that exactly as it is. Ah, O Goddess, I shall indeed tell you that which is dear to your heart. Listen to all of that in its entirety—the Dharma pertaining to the castes and stages of life."
The fourfold classes— Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras—
were created of old by Brahmā, who desired to establish the governance of the world; and indeed,
duties appropriate to each were ordained for them in the scriptures.

If the entire world were to consist of only one caste, it would perish along with the gods; therefore, the four castes were indeed ordained. The Brāhmaṇas were created from the mouth; for that reason, they are masters of speech.
The Kṣatriyas were created from his two arms; therefore, they are endowed with the strength of the arm. The Vaiśyas emerged from his belly; therefore, they subsist by means of trade and agriculture.
And the Śūdras were created from his feet; therefore, they are the servants.
Listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, to their duties and their actions:
the Brahmins have been made the gods of the earth and established for the support of the worlds;
those Brāhmaṇas must not be treated with contempt by those who desire the welfare [of all].

O Goddess, if those Brāhmaṇas did not always exist as the carriers of the practice of giving, there would be no stability in either of the two worlds in brief. Yet, it is traditionally held that the status of a Brāhmaṇa is difficult to attain in the worlds.
Whether he be ignorant or poor, such a person is always worthy of honor.
That lowest of men who would despise, revile, or cause a Brahmin to be censured; or who would strike him or even seize his wealth—[he is the most base].
Driven by the delusion of desire and greed, he would have me perform menial tasks;
he would despise me, revile me, and condemn me.
That fool, a thief of my wealth, would even strike me.
Having gazed upon me alone, the one of deluded mind rejoices.
His established duty consists of Vedic recitation, sacrifice, and giving.
His specific duties are teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and the acceptance of gifts.
Truth, tranquility, austerity, and purity are his eternal duty.
The sale of liquids and grains is censured for a Brāhmaṇa;
likewise is the eating of food from a Śūdra and the keeping of a Śūdra woman [as a wife] when there is no distress.

Austerity alone is always the duty of a Brāhmaṇa; of this there is no doubt. He was created by the Creator in the beginning for the sake of dharma through the power of austerity. His initiation is his duty, as is the constant carrying of water.
Listening to the secret [teachings] is a duty; the observance of Vedic vows is a duty;
the fire-ritual is the supreme duty; and the constant wearing of the sacred thread is a duty. Avoiding the food of a Śūdra is a duty; following the path of the righteous is a duty.

Dharma consists in constant fasting and likewise the supreme practice of celibacy; dharma consists in eating only ambrosia and likewise offerings of household flowers; dharma consists in the sweeping of the house and likewise the rite of anointing it with unguents.
Devotion to guests is dharma; dharma consists in maintaining the three sacred fires, performing *iṣṭi* sacrifices and animal sacrifices according to the rules as the highest austerity,
and the shared virtue of husband and wife— this indeed is the dharma of householders.

This is the duty of the twice-born in the householder stage, the upholding of dharma. But as for the duty pertaining to the kṣatriya which you have requested, O Goddess, I shall declare it to you; listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind.
Likewise, O Goddess, the Kṣatriyas are ordained for the protection of the subjects.
If there were no Kṣatriya in the world, the universe would fall into disorder;
it is through the protection provided by the Kṣatriyas alone that the world remains eternal.
For him also, study, giving, and sacrifice according to dharma are prescribed;
as well as the protection of those who are afraid, the punishment of the wicked,
the nurturing of the virtuous, and living by taking a sixth part of the produce as tax.

Enthusiasm and mastery of weapons are his eternal duties; supporting his dependents is his duty, and ensuring that actions performed are not in vain is his duty. Standing firm in battle is his duty, as is acting for the welfare of the citizens.
The constant maintenance of legal proceedings is a virtue of the lord of the earth; a king who extends a helping hand to the distressed attains unsurpassed merit.
Thus have these duties been ordained by the ancients according to the rules of action.
In the same way, O Goddess, Vaiśyas are traditionally held to be the ones who ensure the welfare of the world's course;
others depend upon them, for they indeed bestow visible fruits.
If there were no Vaiśyas, then others likewise would not exist.

For them, study, giving, and sacrificing are held to be their duty (*dharma*). For the Vaiśya, the constant duties are cattle-rearing and agriculture. The three castes who maintain the *agnihotra* fire are the twice-born (*dvija*).

Trade, abiding in the path of the righteous, and constant hospitality toward guests— welcoming Brahmins and acting with justice is the eternal duty of a Vaiśya. Furthermore, sesame seeds, perfumes, and liquids must never be sold under any circumstances.
By Vaiśyas following the path of trade, established on the merchant's way,

hospitality toward all guests of the three classes should be extended according to their ability, day and night. Thus, O Goddess, has the course of worldly life been ordained for you by the Self-existent One.
In the same way, Śūdras are ordained as the accomplishers of all duties;

for if there were no Śūdras, there would be no one to perform the work. The three former [classes] have their foundation in the Śūdra; therefore, they are traditionally known as those who provide labor.
Service toward Brāhmaṇas and others is recorded in the Smṛti as the duty of a slave.
Likewise, agriculture, the crafts of artisans, and the arts of dance and drama [are his duties].
He should be non-violent, of virtuous conduct, and a worshiper of the deities and the twice-born.
The Śūdra is engaged through his own duty with the desired fruits of dharma;
such and other [acts] are likewise remembered as the duties of a Śūdra. These auspicious applications of action have been thus ordained in the world, O fair-faced one.
Thus, for the four castes, meritorious worlds in the hereafter have been ordained and likewise observed for those who practice the Dharma according to their station.
This is the Dharma based on caste, and action is its dedication.
13,134.057d@015_0531 Umā said: "I have told you what was requested by me who desired to hear; what more do you wish to hear?
13,134.057d@015_0532 Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, salutations to you, O Bull-bannered One!"
"O Maheśvara, O Lord, O All-pervading One, I desire to hear the dharma of those belonging to the stages of life (āśrama). Now,
O Goddess, listen with a concentrated mind to the dharma pertaining to the stages of life."
Regarding the duty that is performed by the exponents of the Veda for the various stages of life (*āśrama*),
the householder is the most excellent among them, having taken up the vow of domestic life.
His duties consist of the performance of the five sacrifices, purity, and tireless contentment with his wife.

Approaching one's wife during her fertile period, practicing charity, sacrifice, and austerity; not living abroad, as well as Vedic study and the worship of the sacred fires—these are desired for him.
Furthermore, being attentive toward guests and offering invitations according to one's ability are required.
He should show favor to all through the actions of mind, speech, and body;
a householder who follows such conduct should perform other virtuous deeds as well. For one who conducts himself in this manner, there is no doubt that he will attain the worlds of merit.
In that very same way, the eternal duties (*dharma*) of the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) have been proclaimed:
having abandoned life in the household, he should, with a resolute and one-pointed mind, subsist always on auspicious forest-grown foods; such is the established rule.
Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, a beard, animal skins, and bark garments;
honoring deities and guests, and performing great acts of austerity— these, along with the *agnihotra* sacrifice and the three daily ablutions, are prescribed for him constantly.
Celibacy, forbearance, and purity are his eternal duties.
Thus, when his life has departed, he is glorified in the world of the gods. Likewise, O Goddess, the duties of an ascetic consist in abandoning attachments from every side.

Possessionlessness, non-undertaking, purity in all respects, and straightforwardness; wandering for alms everywhere and dwelling nowhere at all; constant devotion to meditation, purification from defects, forbearance, and compassion.
The rule for his dharma is that his intellect should follow the truth. O Goddess, he who has been initiated as a celibate student (*brahmacārī*) from birth,
having become devoted to celibacy, should take refuge with a teacher of his own self.
At all times and in all places, one should perform worship of the guru;
the practice of begging for alms, the fire-ritual, constant attendance upon water,
and the perpetual study of the scriptures, O Goddess, constitute his eternal dharma.
It is the established rule that his service for the sake of the guru shall continue until the end of his life.
In the absence of the guru, one should behave toward his son as one would toward the guru.
In this way, that Brahmin attains the stainless worlds.
13,134.057d@015_0565 This duty of those dwelling in the stages of life has been told to you, O Goddess.
13,134.057d@015_0566 The world is known to exist as joined with the four castes and the stages of life. 13,134.057d@015_0567 Umā.
13,134.057d@015_0567 This has been told to you in brief; what more do you wish to hear?
13,134.057d@015_0568 O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Destroyer of Tripura, Śaṅkara!
13,134.057d@015_0569 O God, O Lord, this host of sages is performing penance.
Constantly emaciated by austerity and devoted to the practice of penance, [they ask]:
"What are the characteristics of his dharma, and what is his scripture like? I wish to hear this; tell it to me, O bestower of boons."
While Rudrāṇī was speaking thus, all the ṛṣis, their minds fixed upon her and their hearts filled with joy, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent! (Nārada).
As she listened to the duties of the sages, the sages honored her, saying:
"O Goddess, through your grace we shall hear what is supremely beneficial;
indeed, we are all blessed, having taken refuge at your feet."
"O Maheśvarī!"—
thus did they all then honor the Goddess with their speech:
"O illustrious one, O wise lady, you have a desire to hear [this] according to the proper method."

Come, O lady of pure smiles, I shall describe to you the dharma of the sages. Having resorted to the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vānaprastha*), it is practiced by men in many ways; the eternal dharma of the seers is multibranched and manifold.
For the most part, the seers perform asceticism for the sake of enjoying the heavenly realm;
O Goddess, hear now the rule of dharma for those who move about in that state. Having first been a householder and having attained freedom from debt toward one's sons, [one may depart].
Having settled the affairs of his family for a specific reason, he should abandon his home;
having steadied his mind through fortitude and preceded by resolute effort,
whether free from dualities or accompanied by his wife, he should depart for life in the forest.
Those regions which are supremely meritorious, endowed with rivers and forests, generally free from afflictions, and possessed of sacred fords and shrines—
one should go there, understand the prescribed ritual, and undergo initiation in the proper sequence.
Having been initiated and becoming single-minded, one should perform the service:
rising at dawn, purification, prostrating before all the gods,
smearing the body with cow-dung, and remaining free from faults and negligence.
Morning and evening, one should perform the ritual ablution and the *agnihotra* sacrifice according to the rules;
one must also attend to bodily purification, wear matted hair and bark garments,
and constantly dwell in the forest for the sake of gathering sacrificial fuel and flowers.

Gathering wild rice (*nīvāra*) at the proper time, the collection of vegetables and roots, constant purity of the dwelling place, and being intent upon guests in every respect— this is prescribed for his dharma.
Worship with water for the feet and a seat, as well as an invitation to eat; cooking non-vulgar food at the proper time, likewise the worship of the ancestors and the gods;
and afterwards, the honoring of guests—these are his eternal duties.
The learned should engage in conversations concerning dharma and artha while seated upon the Dharma-throne; they should provide shelter and dwellings, or sleep upon the ground or on stones;
they should practice vows and fasts, and cultivate patience and restraint of the senses.

Day and night, as appropriate, there should be purification and reflection upon dharma and purpose. Thus were the duties of forest-dwellers observed in ancient times; indeed, for one striving in this manner, when the law of time (death) should occur—

At that very moment, O lady of pure smiles, he would be born in the heavenly world; there, O blameless one, enjoyments provided by celestial women await him. When he eventually falls from heaven, he shall become a distinguished king.
"O Goddess Umā, such is always the law for all forest-dwellers.
I have told you all this; what more do you wish to hear?"
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, I desire to hear the auspicious life-story of the sages and their specific dharmas, for my curiosity is great.
"O Maheśvara, I desire to hear the specific dharmas; indeed, my curiosity is great."

I shall declare that to you; listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind. It is the settled conclusion that one must dwell in the forest, relying upon it as if upon a guru, by great seers who are constant in the forest, devoted to the forest, and established in the forest-dwelling stage (vānaprastha).
By those who attended upon the hero’s bed, who dwelt in the place of heroes, who observed many vows and fasts, who practiced the "five-heat" penance in the summer,
who were constantly devoted to the five great sacrifices, and who were dedicated to the full-moon festivals.
In the winter, some lay like frogs, subsisting on sprouts of *śaivala* moss;
others were clothed in rags and bark, wearing deer skins,
while some were devoted to the four-month fasts and dedicated to the dharma of the gods.
In this manner, those who have gone to the forest perform very great asceticism;
having performed such auspicious deeds, they subsequently go to the third heaven.
Having dwelt there for a very long time according to their pleasure, they remain.
He is born in the world of men endowed with the capacity for giving and enjoyment. O Umā of pure smiles, those who are joined with specific forms of austerity have been described by you.
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, among those who are joined with wives, O Maheśvara, what is their conduct like? You should explain that to me.
Those who observe the dharma of having only one wife and practice extensive austerity—

whosoever they may be on the foothills of the Vindhya mountains, those who dwell in Naimiṣa, those at Puṣkara, and others who have taken refuge in rivers and forests— [all these attain the highest state].
They all perform extensive austerities according to the prescribed rules;
free from violence and malice, they are compassionate toward all living beings. Peaceful, self-controlled, and having conquered anger, they are devoted to the hospitality of all guests.
Always regarding all living beings as themselves, approaching their wives only during the proper season,
and remaining devoted to their own spouses, O Goddess, they practice this supreme vow. Endowed with sons and wives, they dwell in happiness, free from anxiety.
Their clothing, ornaments, and the implements for their duties are provided according to their requirements and in due measure, just like those of householders;
this is for the sake of maintaining their wives and for the performance of the fire-rituals.
Cattle and agriculture—all this is ordained for them. O Goddess, those who have gone to the forest must act thus while joined with their wives.
Firm in their vows, they go together with their own wives to the meritorious worlds.
Those wives who perform extensive asceticism together with their husbands, because of their undistracted state and their single-minded devotion, indeed go to heaven.
This has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, O All-pervading One, Maheśvara, what is the fruit of their karma?

"O God, granter of boons, through your grace I desire to hear all that pertains to the forest-dweller (*vānaprastha*) regarding the ripening of fruits; O beloved, listen. A man practicing the yoga of fire during the summer for twelve years [attains this]."
By performing the rite prescribed by the rules, one shall indeed be born in the world of Rudra;
a man of firm vows who performs the *udavāsa* vow during the rainy season shall be born in the world of Soma for twelve years.
Having maintained silence like a log of wood for twelve years, a man,
having attained the world of the Maruts, is endowed with enjoyments there. The sage should lie down upon a bare ground strewn with thorns and gravel.
He shall be born in the world of the yakṣas for fourteen thousand years, endowed with enjoyments for twelve years. Furthermore,
he who remains in the vīrāsana posture, supported by thorns and a wooden plank, [attains this].
A man who stands for twelve years as a hero,
with his arms raised aloft, shall be born among the Gandharvas for twelve years;
he shall be born in the world of the gods, endowed with divine enjoyments.
Standing on his big toe with arms raised upward, having conquered his senses,
he shall be born in the world of Indra for fourteen thousand years,
provided that the sage observes a restriction on food for twelve years.
O Goddess, those of firm vows and forest-dwellers likewise abide in those places, endowed with enjoyments according to their deeds, for many groups of years in the world of the Nāgas.

Falling from those [states], O Goddess, they are born again among humans as enjoyers of pleasures, in families of the highest caste, endowed with wealth and grain. This has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
O bestower of honor,
Maheśvara, I desire to hear the dharma of these Yāyāvaras.
"Overcome by supreme compassion, tell me that, O Maheśvara! Listen, O beautiful lady, intent upon it, to the dharma of the Yāyāvaras:
those whose limbs are purified by vows and fasts, and who are devoted to bathing at sacred fords."

Possessing fortitude and endowed with forbearance, they were devoted to the vow of truth; emaciated by fortnightly and monthly fasts, these seers of dharma performed supreme austerity through enduring rain, cold, and heat.
By the power of time, O lady of pure smiles, they go to the world of Śakra;
there, endowed with enjoyments and possessed of divine fragrances,
adorned with celestial ornaments, they dwell in excellent celestial palaces.
Accompanied by hosts of divine women, they roam about as they please.
O Umā, goddess, this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Maheśvara, O Lord, I truly desire to hear the dharma of those who move upon wheels. Well then, I shall tell it to you; listen, O auspicious Śākaṭikā."
Constantly bearing the yoke of their wives like cart-drivers,
they seek their livelihood through begging with carts, just as those living in villages do; yet,
devoted to the practice of austerity and having their impurities destroyed by that very austerity, they remain independent of others.
Wandering through all directions, free from desire and anger,
they constantly long for death by their own will alone;
likewise, stores of enjoyments have been prepared for them in the world of Indra.
O blameless one, endowed with enjoyments like the gods, they go together with the immortals; joined by excellent apsarases for a long time,
O beautiful one, they go to the third heaven through that very course of time.
There, O Umā, they roam at their pleasure, delighted by enjoyments.
This has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Maheśvara, O Lord, I wish to hear the dharma of the Vaikhānasas. Among them,
O lady of auspicious gaze, are those forest-dwellers known as the Vaikhānasas."
Endowed with intense austerity, they were radiant with their own splendor;
devoted to the vow of truth, their penance was stainless. Some were stone-grinders, and others likewise used their teeth as mortars.
Some subsist on withered leaves, while others gather grain by gleaning; some follow the vow of the pigeon, adhering to the "pigeon-like" mode of life,
and others are devoted to tending cattle or subsist on drinking foam.
Others wander like deer in the practice of the deer, while others subsist on water, subsist on air, or likewise remain without food;
they perform severe austerities, free from disease and death.
By their own will alone, they constantly desire death;
likewise, in the world of Indra, stores of enjoyments have been prepared for them.
Endowed with such enjoyments, they go there together with the immortals like gods.
O blameless Umā, joined by excellent apsarases, you shall remain there for a long time. This has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
Maheśvara said:
"O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the Vālakhilyas, whose wealth is their asceticism.
O Goddess, likewise hear of the practice of dharma as it pertains to the Vālakhilyas."
Clad in the sloughed skins of deer, free from dualities, those whose wealth is asceticism are the size of a thumb, O lady of beautiful hips, absorbed within their own limbs.
Having transcended the realm of death, they have attained perfection through austerity and possess the power of asceticism.
Having conquered their hunger and subdued their anger, they were free from desire for all enjoyments; desiring to practice asceticism for the sake of the world, they were supremely diligent,
constantly praising the rising sun with various hymns.
Those who know the Dharma and speak the truth always travel together with the rays of the sun; they illuminate all directions,
for it is in them alone that stainless truth is established for the sake of the world.
"O Goddess, this world is sustained by the power of the asceticism of those very ones; O lady of pure smiles, it is through the asceticism, truthfulness,
and forgiveness of those great-souled ones, O highly fortunate one, that the stability of all beings is known."
Great men perform asceticism for the sake of their subjects and for the sake of the world;
by means of asceticism everything is attained, and by means of asceticism every fruit is obtained—
even that which is difficult to attain in this world is indeed attained through asceticism.
The stability of the five elements and the expansion of the creation of the world—
all this was fashioned through the power of austerity (tapas).
Therefore, O beloved, this host of sages performs austerity.
"O beloved, one who seeks the Dharma should constantly strive to perform austerities;
through austerity, one should always pray for immortality and mastery.
All this has been told to you, O beloved, as you were listening; it has now been heard by you."
"For the sake of the host of sages and out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds," said Nārada.
As the Lord of the Gods was speaking thus, the sages also offered him praise.
From that time forward, they exerted themselves with even greater supreme effort.
You have described the most auspicious and supreme dharma of the three goals of life.
Maheśvara said:
"O Blessed One, tell me that Dharma which is all-pervading. The Brāhmaṇas were created in this worldly cycle by the Creator who seeks [the fulfillment of] qualities."
The gods upon earth among mortals are destined to deliver the worlds;
to them, therefore, I shall proclaim the Dharma that arises with auspicious fruit.
Among the Brahmins, the supreme Dharma is characterized by fearlessness and auspiciousness.
For these dharmas were created in the past by the Self-Existent One for the sake of the world.
Understand from me that which is always being proclaimed on earth by virtuous men:
devotion to one’s own wife is dharma, as is constant recitation.

Day and night, according to his ability, he should provide hospitality to all; a Śūdra devoted to dharma should always be intent on service. A Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the three Vedas and is advanced in age, provided he does not live by the study [of the Vedas], [is worthy of honor].
But for one who has transgressed the three aims of life (trivarga), his eternal dharma is lost.
Six duties were proclaimed and created by Brahmā in ancient times; O best of women, hear now those which are most righteous and most excellent.
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, receiving gifts from worthy recipients,
teaching, and studying— these six duties constitute the upright man who shares in the Dharma. Through constant study of the Vedas, one fulfills the eternal duty of the perpetual sacrifice.

Giving is always praised among the Brahmins who perform the three duties; this is the supreme dharma that exists among the virtuous. For those pure in the womb [of their lineage], the great ordinance of dharma prevails.
One whose self is purified by the five sacrifices, who is constant in ritual performance, free from malice, self-controlled, a hospitable host to Brahmins, who keeps his dwelling well-swept,
and who always bestows sight, mind, and pleasant speech and complexion upon others.

One who delights in guests and visitors, eating only what remains after others have been fed; one who gives water for the feet, the respectful offering (*arghya*), a seat, and likewise a bed, as well as a lamp and shelter according to the rules— he is a righteous person.

Having risen early in the morning, one should subsequently invite [guests] for a meal; one who honors them and follows them as they depart practices the eternal dharma. This dharma, characterized by active engagement (*pravṛtti*), is prescribed for householders.
I shall proclaim that, and how it relates to the three aims of life (trivarga).
One who desires his own welfare should accomplish dharma and artha with one part,
and he should increase the aim of kāma with the other single part.
The meritorious dharma characterized by cessation (*nivṛtti*) is prescribed for liberation. I shall explain its practice; listen to it with a concentrated mind.
Compassion toward all beings is the dharma that is always supreme in cessation.
O lady of excellent limbs, those who honor a guest who has arrived weary, hungry, and afflicted by thirst, obtain great fruit; indeed,
those who desire merit should give to everyone simply because they are a worthy recipient.
Whatever vessel shall come here, that vessel he will deliver.
When a guest arrives at the proper time, desiring food and standing before him, one should honor the mind there; this Vyāsa has now arrived.
With a gentle mind, one should perform worship toward him according to one's ability.
Dharma has its root in the mind; fame has its root in dharma. Therefore, O Goddess, one should always give with a gentle mind.
But he who gives with a gentle mind— that indeed is the unsurpassed gift. Just as by fine drops of water falling upon the surface of the earth,
irrigation channels, ponds, lakes, and likewise rivers [are filled].
O beautiful one, they are seen full of water, beyond all calculation;
for even when given away little by little, this increases further.
Even at the expense of distressing one's servants, giving alone is superior.
Sons, wives, wealth, and grain do not follow those who have died.
O illustrious lady, having acquired wealth, both giving it away and enjoying it are superior;
for by means of giving, O highly blessed one, men become lords of men.
There is no gift equal to land; there is no treasure equal to a gift. There is no dharma higher than truth; there is no sin greater than falsehood.
He who, in a hermitage, performs austerities while subsisting on roots and fruits—
Facing the sun, covered with matted hair and bark garments, one should sleep like a frog during the winter and practice the "five-fire" austerity during the summer,
performing penance properly here in the forest hermitage with faith.
"O Goddess Umā, the practices of the householder's stage of life, as well as its vows and observances, do not equal even a sixteenth part of yours."

And how the deities are to be constantly worshipped by the householder; and whatever is to be avoided by the householder on lunar days and festival occasions—[Maheśvara said: *Note: The provided text consists of fragmented lines from a verse (likely from the Mahābhārata, Anuśāsana Parvan). The translation reflects the available fragments.* ...and how the deities are to be constantly worshipped by the householder; and whatever is to be avoided by the householder on lunar days and festival occasions—Maheśvara [spoke].
O Lord, I wish to hear all of that as it is being told by you:
what is the root of the householder’s stage of life, and what is this supreme dharma;
wherein dharma is perpetually established upon four feet.

O lady of beautiful hips, that which is the essence, extracted like clarified butter from curds, I shall declare to you; listen, O practitioner of dharma. He who serves his father and mother while in the householder stage of life—
The gods, led by Indra, are pleased with those women who honor their husbands and with those twice-born men who maintain the *agnihotra* fire. —
Umā.

The ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers rejoice according to their own dharma. What is the conduct of householders who are separated from their mothers and fathers, and of widowed women? May you tell this to me.
Maheśvara;
service to deities and guests, salutation of teachers and elders,
non-violence toward all beings, freedom from greed, and steadfastness in truth.
Celibacy, being a refuge for others, purity, being the first to speak, gratitude, absence of backbiting, constant adherence to righteousness,
bathing twice a day, and the worship of ancestors and deities.
One should provide daily fodder for cows, share food with guests,
and likewise offer lamps, shelter, water for the feet, and seats;
on the fifth, sixth, twelfth, or eighth day.
During the fourteenth and fifteenth [lunar days], one should always remain a celibate student (*brahmacārī*).
On these days, one should not perform grooming of the beard, oiling of the head, application of collyrium, or cleaning the teeth; for misfortune (*alakṣmī*) is established upon them.
Vows, fasting, and observances; austerity and giving according to one's ability; the maintenance of the circle of dependents; compassion for the wretched;
abstention from the wives of others; and constant delight in one’s own wife.
A single body for a husband and wife was fashioned by the Creator from the beginning;
therefore, one who is devoted to his own wife is ordained as a celibate (*brahmacārī*). This applies to one who is disciplined in conduct and character, and whose senses are restrained.
For one who abides in straightforwardness, who seeks the welfare of all beings,
who is hospitable to guests, patient, and whose wealth is earned through righteousness— while remaining in the state of the householder’s life, what need is there for other stages of life?

Just as all living beings live by depending upon their mother, so too do all the other stages of life (āśramas) exist by depending upon the householder stage (gṛhāśrama). So it is with kings, all heretics, and all those who subsist on the stage [of performance].
Snake-catchers, impostors, thieves, and likewise royal officers;
those possessing various sciences, those skilled in all crafts, and all physicians;
and men who have set out on long journeys with their provisions for the road exhausted.
These and many others— cats, mice, dogs, pigs, parrots, as well as pigeons, crows, sparrows, and those that frequent crawling reptiles— reflect upon the life of the householder’s stage.

And there are other hosts of forest-dwellers among the beasts and birds; thus, O Goddess, are the various kinds of beings, both moving and stationary, in this world— by the hundreds and thousands— in houses, fields, and caves.
Whatever action is performed by a householder is enjoyed by all of them; and regarding that which has been consumed by them, the wise man does not grieve.
Listen now to the fruit of that which he performs, having resolved it as "this is dharma."

O Goddess, in the twelfth year, one is endowed with the fruit of a horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) performed with every possible effort; know that the liberation from the bonds of hope is the unsurpassed dharma.
Always dwelling at the foot of trees and making his home in empty dwellings,
sleeping on river sandbanks while following along the riverbanks,
that twice-born man was indeed liberated from all attachments and the bonds of affection.
Having fully concentrated the state of the self within the self here in this forest, you—
become one with the self, restrained in diet, and purified by action seen through the vision of liberation— possess that eternal dharma which is ever-pure and disciplined.
He does not delight in staying in one place, nor does he remain confined to a single village;
though disciplined, he wanders as if undisciplined, and he does not lie down on a single riverbank.
Umā.

This is the dharma of those who know liberation, as declared in the Vedas and established upon the path of the righteous. O God of gods, obeisance to you, the three-eyed one whose banner bears the bull!
O Blessed One, Maheśvara, by your grace I have heard all this.
I have grasped those unsurpassed words of yours;
yet now there remains some doubt regarding humans alone:
this man appears to be a king with hands, head, and body identical [to others].
By what ripening of karma does one deserve preeminence over all?
And how does he, even while punishing mortals, rebuking them, and even destroying them,
attain the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds after death?
"O Maheśvara,
O giver of honor, I wish to hear from you the conduct of kings; therefore,
O lady of auspicious countenance, I shall proclaim that dharma of kings to you."
For all that occurs in the world, whether auspicious or inauspicious, depends upon the king. O Queen, sovereignty is traditionally held to be the fruit of great asceticism;
a kingdom consisting of austerity and charity is ordained as the supreme station.

Therefore, mortals always bow down to the king from every side. O illustrious and beautiful lady, since you desire to hear this according to the principles of justice, listen, my dear, to his very life-story, which is beneficial for the world.
In former times, when there was no king, there was great chaos among the subjects. Having witnessed that chaos, Brahmā established Manu in the kingship.
From that time forward, the auspicious and inauspicious conduct of kings has been observed.
Listen to that from me, O lady of excellent limbs, which is beneficial for him and for the welfare of the world—
how one may obtain heaven after death, as well as heroism and fame,
whether inherited from one's ancestors, acquired by those who came before, or produced once again by oneself.
Having duly performed the duties of a king, he deserves to enjoy [the fruits];
first, he should establish himself in self-discipline,
and afterwards his servants and subjects— this is the sequence of discipline.
O lady of auspicious gaze, by taking their lord as their model and desiring to emulate his conduct, subjects themselves become endowed with discipline;
therefore, a king should first of all lead himself into discipline.
A king who is himself disciplined indeed disciplines his subjects;

yet such a one may become an object of ridicule if he fails to examine his own faults. Therefore, through the study of knowledge and association with the aged, he should lead himself toward discipline.
Knowledge that bears fruit in the form of dharma and artha is designated as "mature" by those who know it. O Goddess, the conquest of the senses is taught to follow this;
in its lack of conquest, there is a very great fault that may bring ruin upon the king.
Having brought the five [senses] under his own control, he should dry up those other five objects;
having abandoned the six [defilements] as appropriate through knowledge and discipline,
and becoming one who relies on policy with the eye of the treatises, he should gather his servants.

He should appoint as ministers those who are endowed with good conduct, learning, and noble birth, who have been tested by secret trials (*upadhā*), who have proven themselves through those trials, who employ spies, and who have conquered their senses;
he should assign them to their respective duties according to their fitness and merit.
Ministers endowed with wisdom, a kingdom beloved by the people,
an invincible and preeminent city, a treasury known to endure hardships, an army that is loyal and essential, and likewise a friend who is free from duplicity.
These six constituent elements and the lord who knows the principles of policy—
all this has been created for the sake of protecting the subjects.
By means of these, acting as instruments, the king should accomplish the welfare of the world.
The protection of the lord of men is desired for the sake of protecting his subjects;
therefore, he should always protect himself with vigilance,
even regarding food, clothing, bathing, and going outside.
A self-possessed man should always protect himself from association with groups of women,
both from his own people and from others, even from weapons and even from poison;
a self-possessed man should constantly protect himself from his sons and wives.
A self-possessed man should protect himself from all situations;
for the sake of protecting his subjects, he should act for the welfare of the people.
For the work of the subjects is his work, and the happiness of the subjects is his happiness.
What is dear to the subjects is dear to him; for his own welfare is indeed the welfare of the subjects.
For the sake of the subjects, he dedicates his entire being; nothing is ordained for his own sake.
And having cast aside passion and hatred, he acts for the purpose of resolving the disputes of the constituent elements of the state.
Having heard the arguments of both sides exactly as they were,
he should himself reflect upon that matter with his intellect until he perceives the truth,
sitting together with many aged and eminent men who are experts in that field.

Having correctly ascertained, in accordance with the scriptures, the offender, the offense, the place and time, and what is right and wrong, the king should then administer punishment among men. By acting in this way, he attains merit through his avoidance of partiality.

A king should constantly ascertain, through direct perception, authoritative instruction, or inference, the auspicious and inauspicious conduct of the country; having understood it through spies and by observing the course of affairs, he should deliberate upon it.
One should immediately cast off what is inauspicious for oneself and cultivate what is auspicious;

one should indeed censure those who deserve censure and likewise honor those who are worthy of honor; and one should punish those deserving of punishment, O Goddess—there is no need for deliberation in this matter.
One should always perform the mantra with men endowed with intelligence who possess the five dependencies;
one should be constantly devoted to the mantra with those who are possessed of noble lineage, conduct, and learning.
One should never be intent on the mantra with fools who are driven by sensual passion.
The king, looking toward the welfare of the realm, should cause the principles of truth and righteousness to be practiced.
The monarch himself should always exert all effort regarding fortresses and other such matters. He should, with vigilance, employ those servants who bring about the prosperity of the country.
One should avoid all those who cause the ruin of the country, even if they are beloved.
Day after day, he himself should inspect his circle of dependents;
being pleasant-faced and well-disposed, he should correctly instruct them regarding their conduct.

One ought not to speak words that are unrighteous, harsh, or sharp; one ought to properly discern the virtues and faults in every individual; out of fortitude, one should conceal one's own internal state and should not engage in base conversation.
Having become one who understands the gestures of others and knows the ways of the world, he should cultivate social associations;
and whether from himself, from others, or even out of mutual fear,
as well as from fears of non-human beings, the king should protect his own subjects.

Superintendents who are greedy, harsh, and of a predatory nature toward men must certainly be restrained by the king wherever they are found. From birth onwards, one should apply the princes themselves to disciplines of training.
One should appoint from among them, one endowed with personal virtues, to the position of crown prince,
so that the subjects may not experience fear arising from the loss of the kingdom;
reflecting constantly upon this, he ought to arrange it accordingly.
O beautiful one, a kingdom should not remain without a ruler for even a moment; therefore,
the position of crown prince is desired for the sake of following one's own [the king's] example,
as well as for the sake of those of noble birth, the learned, the Vedic scholars, and the ascetics.
He ought to establish a distinction for others who are endowed with virtuous conduct.
For his own sake and for the sake of the administration of the kingdom, he should undertake the accumulation of a treasury from forts,
the countryside, the sea, merchants, and from the proceeds of men’s labor.
One should provide for the maintenance of servants based on the excellence of both their own and others' qualities; having ensured the nourishment of mounts at the outset for military operations,
one should always remain respectful and observe the vow of consideration.

A king who understands statecraft should divide his treasury into four parts for the sake of dharma, his servants, and himself, as well as for the purpose of meeting emergencies according to the requirements of place and time. The king should support those in his own country who are helpless, the sick, and the elderly.
Having carefully deliberated upon peace and war, as well as their various other distinctions, he should act with deliberate intelligence.
Having become beloved by all, he should constantly conduct himself within the circle of states (*maṇḍala*).
Even in auspicious undertakings, one should not act alone;
rather, having reflected upon calamities both from oneself and from others,
one should not transgress the righteous principles of others out of hatred or greed.
The duty of subjects is indeed to be protected, while the duty of the Kṣatriya is protection.
Therefore, one should protect the subjects everywhere when they are oppressed by wicked kings;
having observed the proper time for an expedition, one may thereafter direct anger toward the fruit of the enemy's rise.

One should consider that misfortunes associated with those [allies] may arise even before the departure [for battle]. One should protect the army from calamities, whether through prudent conduct or by avoiding expenditure;
generally, one should avoid battle for the sake of preserving life.
One should fight for a specific cause alone, and not out of self-interest or because of another's fault.
In a well-fought battle, even the sacrifice of one’s life is considered meritorious for the sake of dharma.
When assailed by a powerful foe, a king should adopt measures appropriate for times of calamity.

Having thus conciliated all those who act for the welfare of their subjects, he ought not to employ those kings who are joined with other natures, who deliberate on improper conduct, or others who have fallen into calamity.
O Goddess, when both auspicious and inauspicious conduct are remembered as occurring from both [internal and external sources],
one should perform that which is auspicious oneself and direct the inauspicious toward others. Thus has it been declared in brief, so that there may be freedom from defilement.
Thus, in this manner, the duty of kings has been proclaimed in brief. Acting in this way— punishing and rebuking his subjects—
he incurs no sin, just as a lotus leaf remains untainted by water.

When the time for the law of death (kāladharma) comes for one who has conducted himself in this manner, then that king shall be gratified in the heavenly world by the thirty gods. And the conduct of a king is twofold, endowed with both justice and prosperity.
Thus, O fair-eyed one, conduct that follows the path of justice has been described to you. A kingdom that follows justice is said to follow the wisdom of the scriptures;
it shall be righteous, beneficial, conducive to fame, and likewise lead to heaven.
When the king sides with the divine, the kingdom shall follow the path of justice;
for when actions are performed there after duly reflecting upon the logic of the scriptures,
and the doer is free from hatred, then the state shall follow the path of justice.
That which is called a kingdom following after enjoyments is seen to be improper; for that,
being devoid of the sacred scriptures, would cause the anger of the virtuous and would certainly be unrighteous, disgraceful, and of evil end.
Where all actions are performed by kings according to their own whims; where servants receive no special rewards due to the power of fate;
and where the lowest of men, who ought to be punished, are not punished but are instead honored.

Where the virtuous are frustrated, there fortune must prevail. When auspicious and inauspicious signs appear in reverse, whether regarding a king or one on the side of the asuras, there fortune must prevail.
But kings who act contrary to their destiny,
O fair-eyed one, incur ill repute and misfortune in this world,
and in the next world they fall into a most terrible darkness that is difficult to escape.

"O Goddess, it is the established rule that they remain in hell until the end of the dissolution; however, for evildoers, liberation occurs through the passage of time. But for kings who have committed evil deeds, O Goddess, there is no liberation at all."
"O Umā, O highly fortunate one, all this conduct of kings, both auspicious and inauspicious, has been told to you in brief. What more do you wish to hear?"
O God of gods, Mahādeva, you who are saluted by all the gods, O Maheśvara! I desire to hear those secrets of the Dharma; may I hear them.
"O Goddess, listen to this secret that brings happiness to human beings:
on this earth, those who desire to follow dharma must not discharge their semen into eunuchs, barren women, or those born of improper unions."
O beloved, seed sown upon these [places] does not indeed sprout. A man seeking merit should never cast seed anywhere at all;
by the destruction of the seed, a man is tainted by the sin of foeticide.
Non-violence is the supreme dharma; non-violence is the supreme happiness. Non-violence is the highest state in all the treatises on dharma.
Constant service to the gods and guests, and a constant nature of righteousness—these are the marks of the virtuous.

O lady of excellent hips, the study of the Vedas, sacrifices, austerity, charity, self-restraint, service to teachers and gurus, and pilgrimage to sacred fords do not equal even a sixteenth part of non-violence.

13,134.057d@015_1032 Umā: This supreme secret, most highly honored, has been declared to you. 13,134.057d@015_1033 If non-violence is indeed dharma, O best of the immortals, for what purpose [is this]?

In sacrifices and animal-offerings, animals are slain by the twice-born. O Blessed One, O slayer of enemies, how is it that kings, who are constantly committing such violence, go to heaven, which is so difficult to attain?
King Rantideva, that lord of men, gave food along with meat, even though twenty thousand cows and more were slaughtered day after day for the sake of the flesh of the twice-born.
"How did he attain heaven? For my curiosity is indeed great.
Do those kings not hear the Dharma, or do they lack faith in what they have heard, that having gone out for the hunt, they kill deer?"
O Bull-bannered One, I wish to hear all this in detail and with its specific distinctions; O Blessed One, let this truth be told to me by Maheśvara.
"O Queen, this is highly esteemed: there is no one who is entirely non-violent.
Listen to the reason for this, how it may be of many kinds;
indeed, in this world, not a single person is seen who is completely free from violence."
While walking with his feet, he kills numerous living beings— whether minute, medium-sized, or dwelling upon the earth;
and those beings who are on his bed or seat, whether through ignorance or even knowingly.
Whether sitting or lying down, they kill living beings many times over. Those creatures born from the sweat of men that dwell upon their heads and garments—
they constantly harm them, as do gadflies and mosquitoes.
In the water there are living beings, and likewise in the air; the earth is garlanded with life.
Since the world is thus crowded with living beings—whether gross, medium, or subtle, including those born from sweat, from moisture, or as plants—who indeed could be non-violent?
O beautiful lady, this entire space as well as the earth is pervaded by living beings— both visible and invisible, and of many forms— who,
being stronger, indeed injure one another who are weaker.
In this world, fish devour fish, and birds likewise devour birds;
pigeons and other winged creatures subsist on reptiles;
and others that move upon the earth or through the sky are flesh-eaters, greedy for meat.
Those who eat the supreme meats of others, and by whom living beings subsist upon other beings by the hundreds and thousands— even they,
O beautiful one, do not live without having oppressed another living being.
With the flesh, milk, or blood of a single living being— a large-bodied creature such as a donkey or a buffalo—
many living beings, namely carnivorous flesh-eaters, are satisfied.
A single human being always devours thousands of living beings through the consumption of even a small amount of food; therefore, one should avoid meals containing meat, grain, or seeds.

He who does not harm grains for three nights, five nights, or even seven nights is proclaimed as non-violent (*ahiṃsaka*). As many living beings as he does not eat, with that much merit he is endowed.
Through the lack of food, the body suffers;
when the body suffers, O fair-hipped one, both the body and the senses remain under control, just as servants remain under the command of kings.
He who restrains his very senses is happy and wise;
through the restraint of the senses, as well as through generosity and self-control,
a man obtains everything that he desires in his mind.
This root of non-violence is proclaimed to be fasting. O Goddess, those who consume food and those who tread upon the earth are all indeed harmful beings, as is seen in the sacred laws (dharmas).
"O Goddess, just as a man who practices non-violence is known here as a knower of reality, so shall I explain it to you; listen, O practitioner of dharma!
Even he who might consume only fruits, withered leaves, or ashes..."
I consider him to be non-violent who is as motionless as a painting;
for undertakings joined with violence are like fire enveloped by smoke. Therefore, I consider him to be non-violent who abstains from food.
But that man who, having renounced everything, is initiated, self-controlled, and pure,
and having established the boundaries of his sacred circle, makes a solemn resolve (*saṃkalpa*)—
fasting for as long as he lives, awaiting his time with firm vows— [attains the highest goal].
"Endowed with meditation and austerity, I consider him to be non-violent;
for otherwise, I do not see any man who could be truly non-violent. This is a matter of much reflection, O Goddess: there is no one who is entirely non-violent."
O illustrious lady, wherever there might be great violence, by abstaining from honey and meat, that violence becomes much less. Abstention is the supreme dharma; abstention is the supreme happiness.
For those whose minds are turned away [from unwholesome things], there is a great accumulation of merit;
virtues and non-virtues are preceded by the mind, of this there is no doubt.
By the mind alone, a human being is both bound and liberated.
If [the victim] is restrained, heaven shall be attained; if released, hell is certain.
If a killer, having raised his weapon, should think in his mind:
"Since their lifespan has now come to an end, I shall strike them once they are dead," [he incurs no fault].
"13,134.057d@015_1105 Thus, if a slayer should kill [one], he is not tainted by sin.

13,134.057d@015_1106 He who was previously slain by destiny—that slayer is merely the instrument. 13,134.057d@015_1107 For destiny, O Goddess, is powerful; indeed, that which was done in the past is difficult to avoid."
Living beings, bound by their own past actions, are born as animals and reptiles in various wombs, enveloped by their own karma;
they possess various and diverse bodies, and various powers and prowess.
In various regions and lands, living beings have diverse kinds of food;
for a living being who is being born, death is already produced beforehand,
whether it be happiness or suffering, exactly as was previously performed.
When, where, and by what means men meet their death,
it is impossible to transcend the decree of past karma;
the Law remains vigilant among living beings, even while they are heedless.
For to him there is no one dear, no one hateful, and none who is indifferent;
he is equal toward all beings. Time watches over time;
indeed, it seizes away the life-force of every embodied being whose lifespan has run its course.
