In whatever manner and by whatever means one must die, one is joined with death in that very way; one is led there helplessly, wherever and by whatever means one must die—
whether in the forest or in one's own home, by night or by day, it is the same.

For by whatever means one is destined to die, one does not die otherwise; nor is anyone seen in this world, whether past or future, who has escaped death through higher knowledge, heroic prowess, or various mantras and medicines.
For Maheśvara alone is capable of deceiving the fixed course ordained by Fate;
O Goddess, this procedure for the ritual slaughter of living beings has thus been explained to you.
"Listen, O Goddess, to the reason why destiny is indeed so difficult to overcome when death has arrived for all beings;
struck down by the exhaustion of their lifespan, O fair-faced one, they have come together."
Many insects, moths— large, small, and medium-sized—
all fall of their own accord into the blazing lamps. [Likewise,
there are] many herds of deer frequenting various forests.

But he among them who is struck down by Time is indeed slain by Time. O Goddess, he whose lifespan is exhausted and who is bound for the sake of a sacrifice reaches the hand of the slayer on that very day, powerless.

Just as flocks of birds traveling swiftly through the vast sky are bound when their life-span is exhausted, even though they are capable of fleeing; or as many aquatic fish of various species [are caught].
By the power of destiny itself, they climb onto a net; and,
O beautiful one, having climbed upon the tip of a porcupine’s tongue by themselves,
those reptiles, struck down by the exhaustion of their lifespan, fall down.
Even among farmers who are plowing, there is no intention to cause injury;
yet, by the tips of their plows and other tools, inexhaustible numbers of living beings are killed. Furthermore, the injury that a man inflicts with even a single step—
Even a cruel elephant would not do such a thing even in a hundred lifetimes;
for the farmer does not kill those [crops] that must die when he plows,
for his mind is set on "I am farming," and he has no thought of causing harm.
Therefore, even after killing thousands of living beings, one is not defiled; for a creature ordained by destiny in the past perishes later. Thus, among all beings, destiny is indeed insurmountable.
Once one's life-span has passed, it is impossible to live even for a moment longer. While one ought to live, one must not die; this has never been the case, nor will it ever be.
It is impossible to escape the fruit of one’s actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
In that same way, they must die and likewise enjoy those [cows];
for the cows of Rantideva have indeed come under the power of destiny,
O beautiful one, where the cows come of their own accord and are then slaughtered.
From the blood of cows being slaughtered, a river arises;
it is renowned as the Carmaṇvatī, difficult to traverse due to its hooves, horns, and bones.
O beautiful one, when blood reaches that river, it becomes water.

Sacrificial, meritorious, and pure, endowed with excellent fragrance, color, and taste— there the twice-born, the hosts of gods, the world-protectors, and the great lords perform their ablutions, having completed their silent prayers and daily rites.
O beautiful one, having come in person to that king’s perpetual sacrificial session,
they accept his flesh according to the prescribed rule, with mantras, in accordance with the law and the ritual procedure as previously seen.
While the twice-born were eating food with meat in abundance, by the hundreds and thousands, the sun set;
even as cows were being slaughtered there for that king’s supreme sacrifice.
While the mantras were being recited according to the rule and according to the ritual,
those cows went to heaven and King Rantideva,
that lord of men, attained perfection through the constant performance of the sacrificial session.
Now, as for the man who may have been mentioned by kings for the sake of assistance—
through a sharing of enjoyments, with garments, ornaments,
and decorations, and through various honors such as shared meals and social bonds.
When the time for assistance has arrived, one should raise a weapon in battle;
just as weapons are raised when the armies are arrayed in formation, so too in both opposing forces filled with elephants, horses, and chariots, and crowded with the strength of infantry.
Variegated with yak-tail whisks and umbrellas, blazing with banners, shields, and weapons; [the field was filled] by those bearing spears, javelins, lances, swords, tridents, and pattisas,
and by those employing mallets, clubs, bows, arrows, and *bhuśuṇḍī* missiles, as well as clenched fists.

In both armies, there were warriors skilled in combat, shouting like bulls against bulls, who carried *bhindipāla* slings, maces, discuses, darts, and javelins, and were armed with various other weapons.
With the sound of conchs and kettledrums, and the noise of various musical instruments; with the neighing of horses and the trumpeting of elephants;
with the lion-like roars of warriors and the tinkling sounds of bells.
The cardinal and intermediate directions were deafened on all sides,
like clouds thundering in the sky at the end of summer,
by the reddish dust of battle raised by the rims of chariot wheels and hooves.
When the sky was being covered on all sides as if by tawny clouds,
and when the clash of weapons had begun among the warriors of those two armies,
their blood from wounds inflicted by blows shone with the luster of red sandalwood.
Flowing blood from their own limbs, they crossed over the front of the battle like moving heaps of *palāśa* and *aśoka* flowers,
as they advanced together in the fray with weapons raised in their hands.
Shining heroes challenged one another in battle;
while the brave were being struck down and striking back in the thick of the fray,
those lowest of men who then turned their backs upon the leader there—
Even if the leader desires it,
those who turn back uninvited incur all the misdeeds of the leader;
however, the leader is joined with whatever merit they possess.
Even those men who know that non-violence is the supreme dharma,
yet do not fight in battles when properly engaged as mercenaries,
go to a terrible hell, for they have betrayed the food provided by their masters.
But he who, casting aside his life, enters the battle— which is like a blazing fire— fearlessly like moths with weapons raised,
enters into a state of heroic being (*sattva*) there, having recognized the warrior’s resolve.
Possessed by *sattva*, a man becomes pitiless; O Goddess, he who is presided over by *sattva* indeed rejoices in blows. Even when pained by blows, he does not fall into despondency.
But he who, protecting his own leader on the most terrifying battlefield,
scorched the enemy armies like a lion among herds of deer,
was as difficult to look upon on the field of battle as the sun at midday.
But he who strikes mercilessly in battle with uplifted weapons—having purified his soul through that combat—he performs a great sacrifice.
His armor is the black antelope skin; his wooden staff is known as the bow.
The chariot is the altar, the banner is the sacrificial post, and the chariot-reins are the *kuśa* grass. Pride, arrogance, and egoism are known as the three sacred fires of the *tretā*.
The whip is the *sruva*-ladle, and his preceptor is the charioteer.
The sacrificial ladle, the vessels, and whatever other implements for sacrifice there were— all these are known as his weapons; the fuel is said to be his arrows,
and the sweat flowing from the limbs of that illustrious one is his honey.

The sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*) are the human heads, and blood is known as the oblation (*āhuti*). The quiver (*tūṇa*) is to be understood as the cooked rice offering (*caru*), and the stream of wealth (*vasor dhārā*) is known as the fat (*vasā*).
In that sacrifice, the twice-born ones were the flesh-eating beings and the hosts of spirits.

Their food, drink, and provisions were seized; their slain men, elephants, and horses they consumed at will, just as one might enjoy the offerings at a sacrifice performed according to one's desire. And the garments, ornaments, and decorations of the fallen warriors [were likewise taken].
Gold and fine gold that indeed constitute the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)—
O Goddess, whatever man is slain there while mounted on the shoulder of an elephant,
he attains the world of Brahmā when struck down facing the enemy in battle.
Whether situated in the middle of a chariot or even mounted on the back of a horse,
he who is slain in battle is honored in the world of Śakra;
in heaven, the slayer is honored by them, and the one slain is honored in that very same place.
Both of these prosper in happiness: the slayer and he who is slain.
Therefore, having entered into battle, one should strike fearlessly. He who, free from fear, strikes in battle with uplifted weapon—
A family attains favor with the king and prospers when it serves him,
just as thousands of rivers enter the great ocean; even so, O best of those who uphold dharma, all [virtues] converge in you— of this there is no doubt.
The duties of kings, as well as the discipline of teachers, have been entered [into this work];
likewise, those duties declared in the Vedas and those proclaimed among the heretics, as well as the laws of Manu and other various laws.
The customs of regions, castes, and families, as well as the local laws of villages;

whatever laws exist among those dwelling in the mountains and whatever laws exist in cities and other such places— it is the duty [of the king] to protect these practices that have been established from of old.

Dharma, when violated, destroys; Dharma, when preserved, protects. Therefore, Dharma must especially not be violated by a ruler, wherein the lord of the earth protects his subjects through righteousness.
When the king is devoted to his own duty, the Brahmins are intent upon the six rites, and the ancestors and deities are honored;
in that land there is no drought, nor diseases, nor calamities,
for all the subjects are virtuous in character.
O Goddess, a king must always be sought out as one who follows disciplined conduct,
who knows the vulnerabilities of his enemies, who is vigilant, and who possesses great majesty; for there are many Śūdras on this earth who bring about the destruction of kings.

Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, a wise king should not be negligent regarding those friends, nor toward mortals, nor even toward elephants; he must never place his trust in them while they are bathing or drinking.

One who, for the sake of the welfare of the kingdom, for the sake of cows and Brahmins, and likewise for the sake of a captive or a friend, gives up his life which is so difficult to abandon— such a person attains the favor of the king and causes his own lineage to flourish.

O Goddess, O lady of excellent hips, one should give to the twice-born the earth, which is filled with wealth, which yields all desires like a cow, which sustains the world, and which extends to the edge of the oceans along with its mountains, groves, and forests.

O lady of beautiful hips, nothing is equal to that; one who renounces his life is distinguished above all, even if he were to perform a thousand sacrifices with great prosperity. What wonder is there in his performing sacrifices? The renunciation of life is exceedingly difficult to accomplish.
Therefore, among all sacrifices, the sacrifice of weapons is distinguished as the greatest;
thus have those sacrifices of battle been described to you according to their true nature.
I shall now describe the practice of hunting; listen to it, O practitioner of dharma. Hear how a protector of the earth, having slain deer, is not tainted by sins.
All these deer desire this earth to be devoid of humans.
And those who devour the crops must be punished by the king; for the punishment of the wicked and the protection of the virtuous are the duty of the protector of the earth,
who must always act with integrity in all his affairs.
Deer go to heaven when they are slain by the king himself;
for just as cows without a cowherd [perish], so does a kingdom without a leader.
Therefore, [the king] is indeed a portion of the gods, Gandharvas, serpents, and Rākṣasas.

Appointed to sovereignty over kingdoms for the purpose of protecting the subjects— both in the punishment of the ill-behaved and in the protection of the disciplined— I shall declare their conduct; let it be heard in due order.
O illustrious lady, as those kings conducted themselves in this manner,
their kingdom, righteousness, wealth, glory, and fame all increased;
for this was the ancient duty of kings, O best among the upholders of dharma.

Assembly halls, water-stations, tanks, and temples, as well as dwellings for Brahmins, should be constructed by the best of kings. Brahmins must not be treated with contempt, for they are like fires covered by ashes.
Those twice-born ones, possessed by anger, might destroy the entire lineage; for just as a fire being fanned consumes all fuel,
so too might the Brahmins burn this earth with the fire of their wrath.

For when the Brahmins are enraged, the protectors of the earth do not enjoy their kingdom; Vātāpi, Nahuṣa, and others, out of delusion, treated the twice-born with contempt and perished along with their kinsmen and friends, consumed by the wrath of the Brahmins.
And even the body of Śakra was made devoid of its private parts.
Then all the hosts of gods, for the sake of Indra, caused the high-minded one to show favor through prostrations, hymns of praise, and salutations.
O lady of beautiful hips, when the high-souled Gautama was pleased,
he instantly covered that body of Śakra— marked with a thousand sexual organs—
with a thousand eyes, making it seamless in an instant.
Having cut off the testicles of a ram and consecrated them with mantras, Gautama [offered them];
having become the testicles of Indra, they quickly indeed became joined.
Thus, when the Brahmins were enraged, Śatakratu, the king of the gods, [acted].
If even he is unable to govern a kingdom, how much less so a mere human on earth? A Brahmin possessed by anger would burn [everything] like fire consumes dry fuel;
having reduced the entire world to ashes, he could create another world once again.
He could turn non-gods into gods, and gods into non-gods;
therefore, the twice-born should not give rise to anger, for the twice-born have anger as their weapon. Even for great offenses, a twice-born man does not deserve corporal punishment.
O blameless one, neither the falling of weapons nor the deprivation of life is seen among Brahmins in the three worlds; yet they possess both vast and terrible wrath, as well as unsurpassed grace.
Therefore, one should never give rise to anger; the twice-born are always to be honored.
No such person is seen in this world, nor has there ever been, nor will there ever be, a lord of men who enjoys his kingdom while the Brahmins are enraged.
One should never mock the Brahmins, nor should one reproach them.
Having waited for the right time, one may show anger; at the right time, one should bestow favor. And kings must not engage in excessive joking with their servants.
He incurs insignificance, and his authoritative command ceases;
through the derision of his servants, the king is humiliated.
They beg for what should not be asked for, and they speak what should not be spoken.
Even with appropriate gains, they do not reach satisfaction;
therefore, a king should avoid excessive indulgence toward his servants.
He should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should he place full trust even in the trustworthy.

One should not trust, by any means whatsoever, especially those of the same lineage; danger arising from misplaced trust destroys one just as a thunderbolt fells a tree. A king is destroyed through negligence and when he is brought under the sway of greed.
Therefore, one should neither be negligent nor greedy, nor should one place undue trust [in others]. One should be a protector of those afflicted by fear and a benefactor to the distressed;
thus, being knowledgeable in specific duties, one should always be devoted to the welfare of the kingdom.

True to his promise, he remained established in the kingdom, intent upon protecting his subjects; free from greed and speaking with justice, he lived off a sixth part [of their produce]. Discerning the distinction between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, he viewed everything through the lens of dharma.
He should show compassion toward his own kingdom so that no improper act occurs;
he should regard those men who praise him and those who revile him as equal,
and look upon an enemy who is free from offense as if he were a friend.
One should punish the wicked with a penalty proportionate to their offense. Where the king delights in the application of punishment, there righteousness prevails;
where the king is endowed with forgiveness, there unrighteousness does not exist.
The duty of the unrefined is to punish, while the duty of the refined is to protect.
He who causes those deserving of death to be executed and protects those who should not be killed performs his duty;
for Brahmins, cows, a messenger, and likewise a father, are not to be slain.
One who imparts knowledge, those who have previously rendered assistance,
women, and a man who is hospitable to all guests— these must not be killed. [Likewise, one should not take] land, a cow, gold, prepared food, sesame seeds, or clarified butter.
By constantly giving [gifts] to the twice-born, one is liberated from royal sin. Thus,
for that king who always conducts himself in this way, devoted to the welfare of his kingdom,
his realm, wealth, righteousness, glory, and fame increase.

That lord of men who enjoys a sixth part [of the produce] yet does not protect his subjects from evils or calamities— whether by means of his own army or that of another, or through wealth or valor— is joined with neither merit nor prosperity.
That king who is devoid of effort in striking down the enemy kingdom—
his own realm is destroyed by the hostile army of one lacking prowess.
Whatever sin lies in the destruction of an enemy army, [that same sin falls upon him].

The king whose kingdom has been destroyed incurs all that sin. One may kill an approaching assassin, even if it be one's maternal uncle, a sister’s son, a mother, a father-in-law, a teacher, or one's own father— provided he is the sole offender.

Listen now to the destination of him who, fighting for the protection of his own kingdom, is slain in battle by an enemy force— O lady of beautiful hips, he shall dwell in a celestial chariot frequented by hosts of Apsarases.
O beautiful one, a king slain in battle goes from here to the world of Śakra;
for as many hair-pores as there are upon his body,
for that many thousands of years he is honored in the world of Śakra.

If one is ever reborn in the world of humans, one becomes either a king or a high-ranking official, endowed with great prowess; therefore, effort must be exerted in the protection of one's own kingdom.
Constant judicial administration and espionage, constant fidelity to truth,
vigilance, joy, lack of harshness even in the face of exertion,
the maintenance of servants, and the nourishment of mounts.
The honoring of warriors and the infallibility of their performed deeds— this is the great lordship,
the very welfare of kings both in this world and in the next.
Those animals that are slain in animal sacrifices and in ritual offerings,
when bound to the sacrificial post with mantras according to the rule and according to the prescribed rite, go to heaven, O illustrious lady, purified by those mantras and oblations.
O fair-faced one, when the sacrificial fires, the thirty gods, and the world-protectors together with their lords have been gratified by their portions of the sacrifice and by their flesh,
whatever fruit belongs to that sacrifice shall arise once they are satisfied.
O Goddess, the sacrificer is united with that [state] without a doubt,
together with his wife, his sons, and along with his fathers and brothers;
O Goddess, all those who have been initiated there go to heaven.
"13,134.057d@015_1381 Umā: All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
13,134.057d@015_1382 Blessed One, Lord of all beings, wielder of the trident, of great splendor!"

I wish to hear the conduct of all householders; O Lord, what is their way of life that is consistent with the three aims of existence? And how is their means of livelihood described for the sake of sustaining life?
How do all those who exist attain the highest goal?
O Maheśvara,
O giver of honor, you ought to explain all of this to me in brief.
"O highly fortunate and beautiful lady, you wish to hear this according to the principles of logic.
For the most part, the virtuous conduct of the world is desired for those living as householders; it is for their protection that kings are ordained upon the earth."
Now listen to the general mode of livelihood for all mortals: learning, commerce, service, craftsmanship, and likewise acting— these, O beloved, have been ordained for the sustenance of mortals.

Even for human beings, especially so, the fruit of birth is ordained by one's own conduct; listen as I describe that to you. For the human state is the field of action, whereas other states are joined with the suffering of worldly enjoyment.
Therefore, for all living beings, conduct is desired within the human state. However, knowledge and yoga are prescribed for all [beings] even previously.
O Goddess, one discerns what ought to be done and what ought not to be done through knowledge, and not otherwise.
Through learning, knowledge expands; from knowledge comes the vision of reality.
One who has seen reality and whose self is disciplined becomes a vessel for all goals. For one disciplined by learning, a happy life in this world is possible.
Therefore, having first made oneself a vessel through knowledge,
and having become one whose senses are subdued and whose anger is conquered, one should meditate upon the Self;
having thus meditated upon the Self, one becomes worthy of worship even by the virtuous.
One should adopt a conduct that has been followed by one's family or one already established from before;
for living as a householder, the taking of a wife is desired as it was in the past. If, however, one should desire a livelihood for oneself through learning, then [one may do so].
Whether it be the science of kings (*rājavidyā*) in debate, or even the worldly sciences (*lokavidyā*),
one should acquire them from a teacher (*tīrtha*), endowed with qualities such as service;
and one should diligently consolidate them both in terms of the text and its meaning.

O Goddess, in this way a man shall obtain the fruit of knowledge, and not otherwise. If he desires to reap the fruit of knowledge through right means, he should avoid unrighteousness therein. If he should desire a livelihood through his professional occupation, he should do so according to the prescribed rules.
In a field endowed with water, one should practice agriculture suited to it; or one should engage in trade at the proper time, according to the requirements of that region,
after carefully considering the cost, the profit, the effort, and the resulting yield.

And Paśusaṃjīvaka shall certainly raise cattle in that region; many various kinds of animals serve as his means of accomplishment. Any wise man who desires a livelihood through service [should do so].
One who has restrained the self should indeed become an employer of those whose words are worthy of being heard;
whether by means of intelligence, or through the application of action, or by means of battle, one should take recourse [to them].
Having thus taken recourse according to the path, one shall then become dear to them.

In whatever way he may be pleased, one should satisfy him in that way. Endowed with the virtues of a dependent and devoted to his own welfare, one who has taken refuge [in him] should not act against his interests; this, in brief, is service.
Previously, due to separation from him, one would not perceive any other state; craftsmanship and drama generally belong to low-born castes,
and for those two as well, the wages for the work should be determined according to what is appropriate and just.
One should receive wages from all types of laborers with honesty; taking them through dishonesty leads to sin. One should first consider all undertakings with foresight and according to policy.
Having reflected upon one's own power, the means, the place and time according to one's capacity,
the causes, the journey, the investment, and the emergence of the fruit—
having considered such matters as these and observed the favorability of destiny;
From this point forward, one should undertake that in which one's own welfare is established. Having thus attained this mode of conduct, one should always maintain it,
so that one does not fall away again from it due to divine or human obstacles.

Protecting, increasing, and enjoying it, one should not destroy that [wealth] once it has been obtained; for even something as vast as a mountain wastes away if consumed without regard [for others]. Having acquired wealth from his means of livelihood, a wise man should divide it into four parts.
O beautiful one, listen to the rule regarding all four divisions: for the sake of Dharma, for the sake of Artha, for the sake of Kāma, and for the alleviation of calamities—
for the purpose of sacrifice, for the purpose of giving food, and for the sake of showing favor to the wretched.
For the sake of honoring gods and Brahmins, for the sake of honoring ancestors,
for the sake of the family, for the sake of communal residence, and for the sake of those who perform constant religious rites—
on account of these and other such matters, one should relinquish wealth for the purpose of dharma.
One should give wealth for the sake of religious duty (*dharmakārya*) without regard for the arising of results;
nor for the sake of attaining power or status, nor as a cause for gaining the king’s favor, nor when undertaking a livelihood, nor in the acquisition of servants and friends.

At the time of bringing a bride home or giving her away in marriage, for the sake of providing a livelihood for sons, upon the attainment of an increase in wealth, or for the prevention of misfortune— and in other such circumstances— one should divide the property for the sake of the common interest.

Having observed the consequence, the fruit, and the cause, one should renounce wealth; for wealth indeed brings about misfortune, as do its fruits. Men who are destitute do not attain wealth even by hundreds of efforts.
Therefore, wealth must be protected and given away according to the prescribed rules; for the sake of nourishing the body, one may indulge in specific types of food,
as well as in the company of actors and musicians, and in amorous processions and diversions.
In the company of those dear to the mind, as well as in the giving of gifts that bring joy,
and in other such matters, one may spend wealth for the sake of pleasure; yet,
having weighed the merits and defects, one should renounce even that with moderation.
O lady of pure smiles, one should set aside a fourth portion for times of distress; O beautiful one, for the sake of preventing the loss of the kingdom, for the sake of famine,
for liberation from great diseases, and indeed for the sake of old age.
For the sake of retaliating against enemies, out of indignation at their audacious acts,
for the purpose of setting out toward another land, or for the purpose of escaping calamities—
one should set aside one's own wealth for such purposes as these.
In this world, there is happiness for those who possess wealth, as it provides liberation from hardships.
For one who has no wealth at all, there is neither [happiness] nor the two worlds. Just as the senses function through food, everything proceeds from wealth.
One should make a storehouse according to measure; otherwise, it will go to ruin.
Thus, O Goddess, regarding the livelihood of human beings in this world, listen again to the worldly conduct of such a person who is thus engaged.

This supreme speech brings merit, fame, long life, and leads to heaven; it is joined with the three aims of life (trivarga) and is ordained for all. By conducting themselves accordingly, people shall attain the welfare of both worlds.
Rising at dawn, maintaining purity, devotion to the gods and Brahmins,
service to one's gurus, saluting Brahmins,
rising to greet elders, and bowing in the places of the gods.

Placing hospitality before him, he provides food for his guests; he follows the instructions of the elders and listens to what is beneficial and wholesome; and he sustains his circle of dependents through kind words, gifts, and protection.
Performing one's duties according to justice, avoiding what is produced by injustice,
conducting oneself properly with one's own wife, and the prevention of faults; one should provide discipline for one's sons and employ them in their respective tasks.
The avoidance of unwholesome matters and likewise the cultivation of wholesome ones; the proper preservation of duties appropriate to one’s lineage;
the avoidance of quarrels and the like, and their pacification through devotion.
Providing assistance to the virtuous when they encounter calamity according to one's own power; gathering in those who are distressed out of a regard for compassion;
and the avoidance of speech that is unbound, false, or terrible.
The upholding of the lineage through manly effort in every respect—
all such auspicious conduct as this is recorded as his way of life. He should always serve the elders for their own welfare and out of a desire for knowledge.
One should never take another's property for the sake of others without first having asked for permission.
A wise man should not beg from others; he should rely on the strength of his own arms.
He should always protect his own body, even in matters of food and conduct.
One should eat wholesome and beneficial food that has been properly digested in the proper measure;
having performed the honoring of deities and guests according to all prescribed rules,
one should eat the remainder while remaining pure and should not speak anything unpleasant.
A householder should provide shelter, water, offerings, and alms in every way; he should offer [these] and nourish cows and calves.
He may go outside during the day only for a specific purpose.
One should never favor traveling at midday or at midnight;
one should not plunge into difficulties, but should act according to one's own capacity. In this world, the state of balancing income and expenditure is highly praised among householders.
One should never, whether out of fear or greed, perform an action that brings ill repute, destroys wealth, or causes suffering to others;
having first reflected with discernment upon its merits and defects from afar.
Then one may undertake an action, whether it be auspicious or otherwise; for the self is the eternal witness of one's own good and evil deeds. — Umā.
In thought, deed, or word, one should not desire to commit a sin.
O Blessed One, destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, slayer of Kāla, Śaṃkara!
Are these four castes indeed established by their own inherent nature?
"Or rather, O Maheśvara, do the castes arise through action?
This is my question born of doubt; you ought to sever it for me."
The four [castes], beginning with the Brāhmaṇas, exist by their very nature;
those of a single birth have attained the state of another caste, which is extremely difficult to reach,
and that arises again in a future birth through the power of specific karma.

Therefore, I shall explain all that to you according to the ripening of karma: having become a man who is a Brāhmaṇa, one should preserve one’s own caste and firmly perform the duties of a Brāhmaṇa as declared in the Vedas.

Becoming devoted to truth and uprightness, as well as to charity and sacrifice, one born into that caste should not neglect the duties of that caste. Thus conducting oneself, when one eventually meets the law of time [death], one is reborn again.
O beautiful woman, one may be born in the heavenly world for the enjoyment of heaven;
when that merit is exhausted, having become a Brāhmaṇa, one is likewise born among men.
Thus, by his own karma, a mortal obtains his own caste again.
But another person, likewise born from the womb of Brahman,
being shrouded by the darkness of ignorance, disregards that very birth;
acting otherwise, he abandons the duties pertaining to his caste.
He should move about in the world like a *śūdra*, desiring the duties of a *śūdra*;
constantly associating with *śūdras*, he is devoid of purity and auspiciousness. And when he meets his end, he is punished in the worlds of Yama.
If one were to be born among mortals, one is born as a *śūdra* alone;
O Goddess, even a *brāhmaṇa* becomes a *śūdra* by his own action.
Likewise, another *śūdra*, by avoiding the duties of a *śūdra*, [attains a higher state].
Having become devoted to truth and uprightness, as well as devoted to the duty of giving; honoring the *mantras* and the *Brāhmaṇas*, and being dear to the *Brāhmaṇas* in his mind—
even a Śūdra who has passed away while possessing such conduct [attains the highest state].

He would be born in the heavenly world, and upon its exhaustion, he is born among men in a preeminent family of Brahmins, endowed with the study of the Vedas; in this very way, a Śūdra may always attain the status of a Brahmin in this world.

In this way, Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, joined with their respective caste-dharmas, are born through their own actions among both superior and inferior [conditions]. Thus, there may be a reversal of caste for men in the state after death.

Otherwise, however, they cannot [be maintained] for the sake of the stability of the world. Therefore, having somehow attained a distinguished birth, a wise person should protect it in every way so that it does not fall away again.
"Thus, O Goddess, has this been told to you; what more do you wish to hear? By what means, from birth onwards, does a man become pure and obtain the fruit of his birth?"
Maheśvara himself,
performing all actions— whether beautiful or ugly— under the influence of his sovereign authority, is not defiled, provided he acts with straightforwardness.
One should perform that very same auspicious action oneself and never engage in what is inauspicious.

One should act with deceit toward the deceitful and behave with straightforwardness toward the noble. One should not despond in times of adversity and should cause one's enemies to suffer through terrible hardships.
One should first endeavor to accomplish all tasks through conciliation alone,
so that one does not personally incur misfortune, unrighteousness, or grief;
this is the conduct in brief.
Having attained this state and taking refuge in the home, human beings—
free from affliction and free from anxiety— attain the supreme goal. This is the eternal fruit of birth for all those who dwell in a household.
"This is the established rule: one who has entered the householder's life must always conduct himself in this manner.
I have declared all of this; what more do you wish to hear?"—Umā.
O Lord of gods and asuras, granter of boons, increaser of joy! Among human beings, those who are wealthy and free from affliction,
enjoying various pleasures, are seen to be without calamity.
Others are joined with afflictions, impoverished, and deprived of enjoyments;
for what reason have they not been established as equal in the world of humans?
Maheśvara.

"O Mahādeva, I have a great curiosity to hear this. O illustrious one, O beautiful lady, you wish to hear it according to the proper method; listen then to all of those words in their entirety, which are for the benefit of human beings."
In the beginning, at the first creation, Brahmā created all beings with impartiality.
For this Lord of Creatures (Prajāpati) is eternally free from both attachment and aversion;
therefore, at that time, all men were equal in every respect.
Thus, as the Yuga was undergoing dissolution due to the reversal of time,
some there, their intellects deluded, fell into misfortune; and seeing the decline of those who were once equal, O beautiful lady—
They approached Brahmā to inform him of the cause;
"O Lord of Gods, you ought not to show such partiality. O God, since our status as sons is equal, why should there be strife among us?"
Thus rebuked by them, Brahmā spoke these words:
"O progeny, do not be angry with me; remember your own actions. For it is by yourselves alone that your good and evil have been woven together."
Whatever kind of action one performs, such is the fruit one experiences.
One enjoys the fruit of what one has done oneself; no other is entitled to enjoy it. Thus were they enlightened by him, the self-existent creator of the world.

Having returned once more, they undertook only auspicious deeds. Thus, having realized the truth and being devoted to the dharma of giving, they performed virtuous acts according to the rules and subsequently passed away according to the law of time.
Those who enjoy happiness consume only the fruits of their own giving;
therefore, a person experiences for themselves what they have done. But others, O fair-eyed one, have turned away from righteous deeds.
13,134.057d@015_1595 Miserly and pitiless, they are generally devoted only to themselves.
13,134.057d@015_1596 Having met such a death, O auspicious Umā, they are reborn again. 13,134.057d@015_1597 Umā.
Those among human beings who,
despite being endowed with wealth and grain,
are seen to be devoid of enjoyments even though all enjoyments are present, become poor and afflicted by suffering; of this there is no doubt.
"O Maheśvara, why do they not eat? You should explain that to me. Urged by others, they practice dharma, but not out of their own desire."
Having cast aside their own faith, they both laugh and weep;
having met such a death, O beautiful one,
they never enjoy those fruits in a future birth.
O Maheśvara, some remain guarding and increasing [their wealth] like guardians of a treasure, while others are devoid of wealth yet possessed of enjoyments.
Maheśvara,
human beings are seen [in various states]; you should explain that to me—
those who are devoted to compassion, who desire righteousness, yet have fallen into misfortune.

They perform acts of assistance for others out of a desire to favor the distressed; they would restore another's lost property or wealth taken by others; these men are always intent on giving, even when their own riches are non-existent.

Those men who have fallen under the power of the law of time undergo rebirth; some of them become deprived of wealth, while others become endowed with enjoyments. It is certain that one must provide instruction on the gift of Dharma.
"Thus has it been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear? O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Three-eyed One, whose banner is the bull!"
O Lord, O God, three kinds of human beings are constantly seen, O All-pervading One:
some enjoy themselves while remaining seated, possessing their stations and sovereign powers;
others, however, obtain the accumulation of enjoyments only through prior effort.
"But others, though striving diligently, do not obtain anything at all. By what ripening of karma does Maheśvara [attain his state]? You should explain that to me."
"O highly fortunate one, O beautiful lady, it is by right that you, desiring to hear,

[inquire] regarding those humans in the world, O Goddess, who are devoted to the duty of giving; for they recognize worthy recipients from afar indeed by means of inference according to the prescribed rule."
Having approached there in person and having propitiated them,
they cause gifts to be accepted through mere gestures, or even without it being known;
O Goddess of the Gods, such beautiful men [are born] again in a future birth.
Moreover, they obtain those very fruits without effort;
sitting still, those who enjoy the fruits of their good deeds partake of pleasures.
And there are others who give gifts even when solicited.
O Goddess, in whatever manner those men, out of wretchedness, give again when entreated, for that long a time shall they remain in rebirth; moreover,
through effort joined with toil, they obtain those very things once more.
Even when entreated, there are certain mortals whose minds are struck by greed who do not give anything at all; intent on malice,
those men strive in many ways for a fortunate rebirth.
Even though men search for it, they do not obtain even a little;
just as grain does not grow unless it has been sown, so too do they know the fruit of giving.
Whatever a person gives, that alone they receive in return.
"Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear? Umā said:
"O Blessed One, destroyer of Bhaga's eyes, some are joined with old age."
But at the time when they are fit for enjoyment, having become aged, they obtain enjoyments and wealth, as well as power and sovereignty from here and there;
you should explain to me by what ripening of karma that occurs.
Maheśvara said:
"Come now, I shall tell you; listen to that with a concentrated mind. Having forgotten the practice of Dharma for a long time, you have become intent only on the accumulation of wealth."
When the time of the end of life has arrived and they are oppressed by diseases, men again begin to practice the Dharma or give gifts;
yet, having been reborn in an auspicious state, they are once more overwhelmed by suffering.
When the time of youth has passed and one has reached old age,
O lady of auspicious marks, one reaps the fruits of deeds performed in the past.
Thus, O Queen, the fruit of karma arises through the conjunction of time.
O Mahādeva, some who are endowed with enjoyments are overwhelmed by disease; [so too are] the Maheśvaras,
O Maheśvara.

And they become incapable of enjoying them; what then is the reason? O lady of auspicious marks, those who are afflicted by the onset of disease and have lost all hope for their own lives then begin to perform acts of giving.
Furthermore, having obtained those fruits in a future auspicious birth,
they are unable to enjoy them; indeed, they become afflicted by disease.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, among human beings themselves, some are seen to be endowed with beauty, possessing auspicious limbs and pleasing appearance—
O Maheśvara."
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
"Indeed, I shall tell you; listen with a concentrated mind. O Goddess, those men of old who were possessed of modesty and spoke kindly,"
Always being naturally very sweet-tempered and capable,
they never eat meat and are always endowed with compassion for living beings;
they also provide services and gifts of clothing for the sake of dharma.
Those who purify the earth or worship fire for a specific purpose,
and whose conduct is thus disciplined— those men, O Umā, [attain a higher state] in their next birth.
They certainly become objects of desire for their beauty, there is no doubt;
yet some among humans are seen to be even deformed.
Maheśvara [is the cause].
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You ought to explain that to me.
"I shall tell you that; listen, O auspicious lady, to the cause.
"In former times, mortals were possessed of beauty and joined with pride and egoism."

Those who laugh at the deformed, those who excessively employ praise and blame, those who cause suffering to others, those who eat meat, as well as those intent on envy and those who are impure— [all these go to hell].
Those whose conduct is thus disciplined by severe punishment in the world of Yama,
having somehow attained human birth, are there devoid of beauty; they are born indeed as deformed, of this there is no doubt.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, some women are seen to be endowed with great fortune, yet they are devoid of beauty and enjoyments, even though they are beloved by men."
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
Maheśvara replied:
"O Goddess, those men of old who were gentle in character and spoke kindly,"
Contented with their own wives alone, they maintain an even disposition toward them; through courtesy, they behave kindly even toward women who are unpleasant,
yet they never point out the faults of women that reside in secret.

Those who give food and drink at the proper time, and those who provide sweet things to men; those who remain faithful to their own wives, who are steadfast and free from harm— those whose conduct is thus disciplined will experience a beautiful rebirth.
O Goddess Umā, those humans indeed become perpetually and exceedingly fortunate; even without wealth, O Goddess, they become beloved by women.
Unfortunate people are seen even when they are wealthy and possessed of enjoyments;
by what ripening of karma does this occur, O Maheśvara? You should explain that to me.

I shall declare that to you; listen to it all with a concentrated mind. O Goddess, those men of old who, without regard for their own wives, lived according to their whims, shameless and free from restraint—[for them, this was the rule].
Those men who cause displeasure to others through the actions of speech, mind, and body; who are without support, deprived of food, and who provoke the hearts of women—
men whose conduct is thus characterized will [suffer] in their future birth.
Unfortunate indeed are those who are disliked by the hearts of women;
O Umā,
they derive not even the slightest pleasure from sexual union with their own wives.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, among human beings themselves there are some who are endowed with knowledge and realization, wise and discerning;
yet others are seen to be in a miserable state, despite striving according to the prescribed rules."
"By what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
"I shall tell you that; listen, O auspicious lady, to the cause."
O Goddess, those men of old who, though possessed of learning alone,
were without refuge, lacking food, and utterly dependent upon themselves—
even they, when born again in an auspicious state, become endowed with knowledge and wisdom.
Those who possess nothing indeed become so; for what has not been sown does not sprout. Fools are seen in the world—firmly deluded and devoid of discernment.
Devoid of both wisdom (*jñāna*) and discernment (*vijñāna*), yet prosperous on all sides—
by what ripening of karma is this so? You, Maheśvara, ought to explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who, even if they were ignorant in every respect,
practiced acts of giving for the sake of showing favor to the wretched—
even if they spoke without prior reflection, they gave gifts here and there.
Furthermore, in a future auspicious birth, they indeed obtain that very same result;
whether he be wise or unwise, a man enjoys the fruit of his giving. — Umā.
A gift given without regard for intellectual calculation bears fruit in every way. O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, among human beings there are some who are wise,
possessors of sacred learning, and articulate in speech.
13,134.057d@015_1722 By what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
13,134.057d@015_1723 O Goddess, those men of old who were exceedingly devoted to serving their gurus—
Having gathered [the water] from the sacred ford according to the prescribed rule for the sake of knowledge,
they cause others to receive it by that very same rule and not otherwise;
being unboastful in their knowledge, they are tranquil and restrained in speech.
O Umā, those who diligently establish the branches of knowledge in this world have likewise met with death and attained rebirth in a beautiful state.
O Lord, some humans become wise, possessing retentive memory and clear articulation; yet others are seen to be excluded from learning, wisdom, and intelligence, despite their efforts in every way.
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
Maheśvara said:
"O Goddess, those men of old who were possessed by the pride of knowledge..."
Having attained that [state], they boast, deluded by the egoism of knowledge;
puffed up with their superior knowledge, they constantly torment others. Out of pride in their knowledge, they harbor malice toward others and cannot endure them at all.
O Umā, having met such a death, they obtain a human birth again in a beautiful future life; having attained that state for a very long time, they remain there devoid of awakening.
O Goddess, those of inferior intelligence constantly strive [in vain].
O Blessed One, are there any humans who are endowed with every auspiciousness—
possessing sons and wives endowed with virtues, as well as female and male servants and attendants?
Endowed with mutual supernatural powers through their stations, lordships, and possessions;
free from disease and unafflicted, they were possessed of beauty, health, and strength; and they were abundant in wealth, grain, palaces, vehicles, and mounts.
Endowed with all objects of enjoyment and various charming wonders,
they rejoice together with their kinsmen day after day without hindrance—
thus says Maheśvara.
"By what ripening of karma is this so? You should explain that to me.
"I shall tell you that; listen with a concentrated mind to everything.
O Goddess, those men of old, whether they were wealthy or otherwise,"
Endowed with learning and virtuous conduct, they were desirous of giving and fond of sacred knowledge; always attentive to the gestures of others, they were resolved that "it must be given";
they were true to their word, patient by nature, and free from greed and delusion.
The givers give gifts from their own hands, endowed with vows and restraints;
remembering the suffering of others as if it were their own,
those high-souled ones are gentle in character, pure in conduct, and worshippers of the gods and Brahmins.
O Goddess, those whose conduct is thus disciplined are born again in a beautiful state,
whether in heaven or on earth, as experiencers of the fruits of their karma;
even among humans, those who are so born become such as these.
Just as all these things you have described are endowed with auspiciousness— beauty, wealth, strength, longevity, enjoyments, sovereignty, noble lineage, and learning—
all such excellence arises from giving and not otherwise.
"Know, O fair-faced one, that all this consists of the gift of asceticism (tapodāna).
Then, some humans are seen among other humans."
They are in miserable states, abounding in afflictions, and deprived of both giving and enjoyment; they are constantly beset by the three fears, tormented by the fear of disease and hunger,
overcome by wicked wives, and perpetually beholding obstacles.
"O Goddess, by what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain his state]? You should explain that to me. Those men of old, O Goddess, who resorted to an asuric disposition—"
Constantly devoted to anger and greed, lacking food and devoid of ritual action,
they were atheists, rogues, and fools who relied solely upon themselves; O Goddess, they generally tormented others and were merciless toward living beings.

Those whose conduct has been thus disciplined, having somehow attained human birth again in a fortunate future existence, will nevertheless be afflicted by suffering there in every respect, due to their former self-negligence.
Just as you have previously described, so indeed do they arise; the deeds performed, whether auspicious or inauspicious, result in the emergence of the fruits of happiness and suffering.
— Umā.
"Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, you who increase my joy!
People are seen who are blind from birth, or who have lost their sight after being born."
“By what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
“Indeed, I shall tell you; listen, O auspicious lady, to the cause.”

Those who, formerly greedy for the houses of others due to passion for sensual desire, gazed upon the wives of others with their own wicked eyes; those mortals, possessed by anger and greed, who blindfolded [the vision of] others.
Those who know the characteristics of forms yet demonstrate them incorrectly,
and whose conduct is thus characterized— even when they have passed away according to the law of time, O beloved— they are punished by the rod of Yama and remain in hell for a long time.
If such men were to obtain a human birth,
they would either be blind by nature or born blind; or else, they would be afflicted with eye disease— of this there is no doubt.
Some men, afflicted with diseases of the mouth, suffer constantly;
they are greatly tormented by ailments located in the teeth, ears, and cheeks.
Whether they were mortals from the very beginning or born later due to some cause,
by what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain his state]? You ought to explain that to me.
"Come now, O Goddess, I shall tell you; listen with a concentrated mind.
Those who are evil speakers, O Goddess, who with their tongues utter what is exceedingly bitter, untruthful, harsh, and terrible toward their gurus and toward others—"
Likewise, others cause affliction to the tongue out of anger;
generally, men who are full of falsehood, whether by their own nature or due to some purpose,
develop diseases located in the region of the tongue.
But those who are malicious listeners and destroyers of the ears of others,
they in turn obtain various diseases of the ear in their future rebirths,
as well as diseases of the teeth, diseases of the head, and diseases of the ears.
O Lord, among human beings alone, some who are afflicted by all the various defects residing in their mouths are constantly tormented; yet all this is the fruit of one's own actions.
Afflicted by humors (doṣas) residing in the abdomen and flanks, and by diseases localized in the belly, men are tormented by sharp pains and overwhelmed by suffering—
thus says Maheśvara.
By what ripening of karma [is this]? You should explain that to me.

O Goddess, those men of old who were intensely possessed by desire and anger, and who ate food solely for their own sake, being devoid of concern for others—[by what karma do they come to such a state]?
Those who give food that is unfit to be eaten, those who administer poison to the trusting,
those who give both forbidden and permitted foods, and those devoid of purity and auspicious rites—
those whose conduct is thus characterized will, O beautiful one, [suffer] in their next birth.
Having somehow attained human birth, they there are afflicted by diseases;
Umā, they are tormented by the suffering of those various and manifold kinds of illnesses.
O Goddess, it is exactly so; as was done by each in the past, so do they come to be. O Lord, mortals are constantly seen being afflicted by urinary diseases, such as gravel and urinary calculi.
"O Maheśvarī, by what ripening of karma do those men who in former times violated the wives of others [attain such a state]? You should explain this to me."
Indeed, those rogues who,
driven by the fault of lust and possessed by pride in their beauty and wealth, approach maidens and widows by force, wander through the wombs of animals.
Having met such a death, O beautiful Umā, if those of such a kind should obtain a human birth again in a future life, [they would be of that same nature].
There, O beloved, humans are afflicted by terrible diseases born of the male organ.
O Maheśvara, some humans are seen who are emaciated and suffering from consumption.
"By what ripening of karma, O Goddess, does this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
Those men of old who were greedy for flesh, intensely covetous, seeking their own pleasure out of a craving for savory tastes, and who caused pain to others for the sake of their own enjoyment—"
Furthermore, those men who are intent on finding fault with the enjoyments of others,
and whose conduct is characterized by such traits, will in their next birth, O auspicious one,
be afflicted with wasting diseases and have their bodies covered in a network of veins.
"O Goddess, there are indeed men who experience the fruits of their evil deeds.
Blessed One, some humans suffer as those afflicted with leprosy."
"O Maheśvarī, by what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were destroyers of the beauty of others—"
Those who, deluded by greed and ignorance, inflict injury, slaughter, or imprisonment, or impose unjust punishment;
those men who cause the loss of what is desired by providing unwholesome food;
or those who are corrupt physicians, possessed by greed and delusion.

Cruel in the harming of living beings, defiled, and destroyers of the mind— those whose conduct is thus constituted, even if they should obtain a human birth in a fortunate future life, will be exceedingly miserable.
13,134.057d@015_1844 Here, they are joined with afflictions, possessed of the disease of leprosy;
13,134.057d@015_1845 some are afflicted with skin disorders and joined with ulcerous leprosy;
13,134.057d@015_1846 or even possessed of vitiligo and leprosy, joined with many kinds of leprosy.
"O Goddess, men indeed become exactly as they have made their own fruit.
O Blessed One, some humans are deprived of limbs and are lame."
"By what ripening of karma is this [brought about]? You should explain that to me.
Maheśvara said:
"O Goddess, those men of old who were completely enveloped by greed and delusion..."

O Goddess, those who, for the sake of harming the lives of living beings, deprive them of their limbs by cutting them off with weapons, thus destroying the vital movements of creatures— those whose conduct is joined with such practices, O beautiful one, [reap the consequences] in their future birth.
They will indeed be deprived of their limbs after death; of this there is no doubt. Whether by their very nature or by birth, they become those who are lame.
"Bhagavat, some humans are seen to be afflicted by knots (*granthi*) and pustules (*piṭaka*);
O Maheśvara,
you should explain that to me."
O Goddess, those men of old who were breakers of the knots of others,
harsh in their use of the fist, cruel, and evildoers— those who were revilers, tormentors, and likewise those pierced by spears.
O Umā, those whose conduct is thus disciplined may yet suffer intensely in a future birth, tormented by knots and tumors.
“O Blessed One, some humans are seen to be constantly afflicted with diseases of the feet, O Maheśvara, O God; you ought to explain that to me.”
O Goddess, those men of old who were possessed by anger and greed caused even the abodes of the gods to fall by their own feet;
they committed violence against living beings with their knees and their heels.
O Umā, those whose conduct is thus disciplined may, in a future birth,
be afflicted by various diseases of the feet, such as elephantiasis and the like.
"O Blessed One, many humans are seen on earth who,
afflicted by various kinds of diseases— those born of wind, those born of bile, and those arising from the combination of all three— are tormented and deeply distressed, O Lord."
"By what ripening of karma are beings thus enriched or likewise fallen into misfortune, both by those who are ununited and those who are united? You, Maheśvara, ought to explain that to me."

I shall explain that to you; listen, O auspicious lady, to the reason. O Goddess, those men of old who resorted to an asuric disposition were self-willed, prone to anger, and likewise hostile toward their gurus.
Those who, through the actions of mind, speech, and body, produce suffering for others— merciless toward living beings, constantly cutting, piercing, and tormenting them—
possessing such conduct as this, will [reappear] in a beautiful future birth.
If those of such a kind were to obtain a human birth,
they would there, O beloved, be tormented by many terrible diseases; some would be afflicted with elephantiasis, and others would be possessed of chronic cough.
Others were afflicted by fever, diarrhea, and thirst; likewise,
others were possessed of many wind-tumors (vātagulma), as well as swellings and abdominal enlargements (śophodara),
and various diseases of the feet, ulcers, leprosy, and fistula-in-ano.
Whether they are wealthy or even destitute, they are seen afflicted by disease;
thus, indeed, they experience their own self-performed karma in various places.
Truly, it is impossible for anyone to conceal the fruit of what they have done themselves.
"Thus, O Goddess, has this been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, Protector of Beings, homage be to you!"
O God, other humans are seen who have short limbs, crooked limbs, or who are hunchbacked and dwarfish; others have arms like those of a withered tree.
Maheśvara.
By what ripening of karma does this come about? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were possessed by greed and delusion used to manipulate the measures of grain for the sake of buying and selling.
O Goddess, likewise, the defect of the scales when weights are constantly used,
the reduction of value in all buying and selling,
and those who cause defects in the limbs of others for the sake of provoking anger— [all these are sins].
And those fools who are meat-eaters, always acting improperly and in vain— O Umā, for such people whose conduct is thus characterized, there is rebirth in this auspicious world.
Some among humans are seen indeed among men, O Blessed One, who have short limbs, are dwarfs, and are even hunchbacks;
they are like madmen and Piśācas wandering here and there.
"By what ripening of karma, O Maheśvara, did you become so? You ought to explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were possessed by pride and ego..."
They prattle on in many ways and laugh excessively at others;
for the sake of greed, they delude others with sensual pleasures and intoxicants.
Those fools even mock their elders and teachers in vain.
Those who are intoxicated by [worldly] pleasures, clever in the scriptures, and likewise speakers of falsehood—
those whose conduct is thus characterized, O beautiful lady, become insane and like *piśāca* demons in their next birth; of this there is no doubt.
"O Blessed One, there are certain humans who are childless and deeply distressed;
though they strive by every means, they do not obtain offspring at all."
"By what ripening of karma [did this happen]? You should explain that to me.
Maheśvara said:
"O Goddess, those men of old who were merciless toward all living beings..."
They kill children and eat [the flesh] of deer and even birds;
they harbor hatred toward their gurus and envy the sons of others;
they do not perform the worship of the ancestors as prescribed in the Aṣṭaka and other rites.
O Umā, those whose conduct is thus disciplined, after obtaining a human birth once again in a beautiful future life after a very long time, remain childless.

Even those filled with grief for their sons do not exist there; of this there is no doubt. Blessed One, some humans are seen who are deeply afflicted, devoted to agitation, and full of anxiety here and there.
Constantly overcome by grief and likewise fallen into misfortune— by what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [become so]? You should explain this to me.
Those men of old who were constantly devoted to bribery,
who perpetually terrified others and likewise acted with malice,
and who, having imposed interest on loans, extorted as they pleased from the poor— [they have fallen into this state].
Those who lend money for interest constantly pursue their debtors;
indeed, the borrowers tremble upon seeing them for that reason. According to the law, one must not charge excessive interest from the poor.

Those who play with dogs and terrify the deer in the forest, and likewise, O Goddess, commit violence against living beings here and there; and those in whose houses dogs pointlessly frighten men— [they go to hell].

O beloved, those who have conducted themselves in such a manner, having passed away according to the law of time, are again tormented by the rod of Yama and remain in hell for a long duration. Even if they somehow attain human birth, they are there joined with suffering.
In an evil land, abounding in suffering and crowded with hundreds of obstacles,
O Umā,
people are born there grieving and agitated, wandering here and there.

“Blessed One, why are certain humans seen in the lands of the Mlecchas, endowed with positions of sovereignty and possessed of the power of the Mlecchas? By what ripening of karma does this occur? You should explain that to me.”
O Goddess, those men of old who, though endowed with wealth and grain, gave away [their possessions] improperly or indeed without faith— Maheśvara [knows them].
Those who give gifts to unworthy recipients, those devoid of purity and auspiciousness,
and those fools who give either out of self-praise or even with contempt—
those whose conduct is thus characterized will, in a future birth, be born in a beautiful state.
In a bad country abounding in barbarians, difficult to traverse, and crowded with forests,
having attained sovereignty over the barbarians, they are indeed born here and there under the name of Umā.
"O Blessed One, destroyer of the eyes of the Bhagas, among humans themselves some are seen who are impotent, eunuchs, and likewise pandakas; they are base,
devoted to lowly deeds, and experience only base pleasures on this earth."
“By what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
“I shall tell you that; listen, O auspicious lady, to the cause.”

Those who were formerly human beings, yet were devoted to terrible deeds, and who lived and took pleasure in the destruction of the virility of animals, as well as those who destroyed the virility of men for the sake of provoking their anger— [they all fell into this state].
Those rogues who approach women improperly and according to their own whims,
and those who create obstacles to desire for reasons of hatred or malice—
those of such conduct will, in a future birth, [be born] in a beautiful [state].
O beloved, having been punished by the rod of Yama, they shall dwell in hell for a long time;
even if such individuals as those were to obtain a human birth,
they would become eunuchs, hunchbacks, and impotent men.

In this world, those who delight in base actions, being shameless and devoid of decorum, place the censuring of others at the forefront; yet through their own deeds, they come to be as they are. If, however, they were to reflect deeply, they would indeed be liberated from their transgressions.
Even there they might become negligent and fall into the abode of hell;
O Goddess Umā, for women as well, [the experience] born of karma is just as it is for men.

"Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear? O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, wielder of the trident, whose banner is the bull! Regarding those women among women who are known as 'unchaste' and devoted to base conduct—"
"O Goddess, by what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
Those women who formerly, O Goddess, were possessed by delusion of intellect—"

Possessed by sensual passion, they indeed act improperly toward their husbands; those women who are hostile toward their husbands in every way, having forgotten purity and modesty, behave according to their own whims.
Those whose conduct is thus disciplined by severe punishment in the world of Yama,
if they should obtain a human birth, become such women as these—
whores common to many men.
O Goddess Umā, that conduct of women known as unchastity is considered the most grievous; from that moment on, they surely fall, there is no doubt.

If they grieve for that past conduct, they might attain what is beneficial for their minds. O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, widowed women are seen in the world of men to be utterly deprived of all auspiciousness.
"O Maheśvara, by what ripening of karma did she [become so]? You ought to explain that to me.
O Goddess, those women who were formerly possessed by delusion of intellect—"
In that state, they indeed ruin their husband's household in vain;
they are givers of poison and kindlers of fire against their husbands, utterly merciless.
For, out of hatred for their own husbands, they go to the husbands of others.
Those whose conduct was thus disciplined by severe punishment in the world of Yama,
remaining for a long time in hell, somehow attained human birth once more.
(Umā)
In that regard, those women indeed become widows, deprived of enjoyments;
yet, O Blessed One, other women are seen even while their husbands and kinsmen are still living,
wearing the marks of ascetics and having resorted to heretical doctrines.
"By what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain this]? You should explain that to me.
Those women who formerly, due to the fault of their disposition, were possessed by greed and delusion—"
Those who, out of greed, are intent on the property of others and are stealers of others' wealth;
those who are devoted to malice and are detractors of their co-wives;
and those who are full of envy, prone to anger, and always detrimental to their kinsmen.
O Umā, those women who, even when possessed of such conduct, are endowed with inauspicious marks and have resorted to heretical doctrines, will [suffer] in their next birth, O Beloved.
Women and those with the character of renunciants certainly exist [in that way], there is no doubt.
Blessed One, among humans some are seen who have resorted to the livelihood of artisans; among humans, there are people devoted to lowly occupations.
"O Maheśvarī, by what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were arrogant and excessively conceited..."
O Goddess, O beautiful one, such men— endowed with pride and egoism, devoted solely to themselves— are born again in their next life as artisans, actors,
and musicians, according to their deeds.
O beloved, barbers, bards, and likewise panegyrists—
men such as these live by depending on a lowly livelihood;
they act to please others and receive their wages from them.
They experience the fruit of their previous life’s contempt.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, there are some among humans alone—
They are seen to have become slaves, performing all kinds of labor with great intensity;
they endure beatings and threats, being oppressed from every side—
thus [it is said] by Maheśvara.
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You ought to explain that to me.
"I shall tell you that; listen, O auspicious lady, to the cause.
O Goddess, those men of old who were stealers of others' wealth..."
One should make [the debtor] pay interest on the debt, and likewise for what was given as a deposit;
[one should recover] what was given by reason of a pledge from those who misappropriate property,
and what was lost through negligence or forgotten by those who seize the wealth of others.
Those who, while in a state of servitude, cause others to suffer through execution, imprisonment,
and affliction— such people, having met their death, were punished by the decrees of Yama.
Having somehow attained human birth once again, O Goddess, they are in every way [subject to that same fate] there.
From birth onwards, human beings are indeed born as slaves;
they perform the labors of those from whom they take their wealth,
and it is certain that they continue to do so until their own sins are exhausted.
Likewise, others become cattle or plunderers of wealth;
in that manner, their karma born of prior transgressions is exhausted. Otherwise, that karma cannot be cast off even by the gods or the asuras.
However, the method for their liberation is, in every respect, the propitiation of Him;
for one who desires liberation but acts otherwise is intended [to remain] in rebirth. One who desires liberation, performing actions in every way according to the rule, [attains it].
One should desire the favor of the master and always endure hardships;
he who is released by the master out of affection is truly released from his own sin. The husband should always support such laborers in this manner.
One should cause the work to be done according to what is appropriate and inflict punishment based on the underlying cause. By protecting the elderly, the young, and the infirm, one attains dharma.
— Umā.
"Thus has it been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
Blessed One, among human beings themselves, there are humans who possess equal vision, yet they appear like Caṇḍālas, defiling others by the mere act of touch."
O Lord, those who perform lowly tasks are the removers of the filth of all;
they are wretched, full of affliction, deformed, and evil-minded—
[so says] Maheśvara.
"By what ripening of karma did this come to pass? You ought to explain that to me.
I shall tell it to you; listen with a one-pointed mind. Those men of old were terrible and exceedingly full of pride."

Filled with self-conceit, stubborn, and possessed by pride, those evildoers do not offer salutation even to their gurus; out of excessive arrogance, they do not perform the duty of dedicating themselves to their own dharma.
Those who, by force of their own will, compel others to obey their commands; those men who, through the power of their supernatural success (*ṛddhi*), constantly treat others with contempt;
those who are drinkers, eaters of all things, and men who are harsh and bitter.
Those whose conduct was thus disciplined by the punishments of Yama’s decrees,
having somehow attained human birth, are born as Caṇḍālas;
they delight in lowly deeds and are the scavengers of all.

Devoted to bowing before others, they become humiliated; deformed and dwelling in evil wombs, they are even deprived of touch. Having become washermen and the like, they subsist upon a wicked livelihood.
Due to the fault of excessive pride in the past, they now experience the fruit of their own actions.

Even toward those who are wretched in their condition— even toward outcasts— a wise person should neither revile nor be excessively angry, for they too are experiencing the fruit of their own actions.
Even Caṇḍālas, by grieving for that birth, may attain purity.
O Blessed One, some humans are ensnared by hundreds of bonds of hope.
They stand at the doors of others, barred from entry; they do not obtain permission to see or to inform, despite their efforts—
such is Maheśvara.
By what ripening of karma is this? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were endowed with positions of sovereignty, yet—deluded by their power—did not enter into consultation with others.
Enveloped by hatred, greed,
and other such passions, joined with delusion regarding their state of being, and devoted solely to their own self-interest,
whether they are greedy or possessed of enjoyments, they are utterly fruitless for everyone.
Even those who, though capable, would not act for the sake of benefiting others,
being merciless and devoid of any outlet toward the attainment of enjoyments and sovereignty—
those whose conduct is thus constituted will, O beautiful one, [suffer] in their future birth.
If those of such a kind should obtain a human birth,
being wretched, in a miserable state, and beset by the distractions of karma,
they all run toward him, seeking to inform him of their needs.
O Umā, kings or royal officials stand at the gate, barred from entry; they do not obtain permission by any means whatsoever to report their business,
O blessed lady.
Even at your gate, they stand outside in longing to enter,
O Blessed One; though there are many humans in the world of men,
they have suddenly lost all their possessions and been stripped of their treasury and retinue.
Some humans are seen [to suffer] from kings, thieves, water, and so forth;
by what ripening of karma does this occur, O Maheśvara? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who resorted to an asuric nature, who,
out of hatred and greed, brought about the ruin of others' livelihoods, and who were intent on bribery and slander— such were they.
Those who seize the property of others through theft or by other means are terrible;
merciless and devoid of compassion, they destroy the livelihoods of others.
Abounding in atheism and falsehood, they are stealers of the wealth of others.
Those who have behaved in such a manner, punished by the ordinances of Yama,
shall dwell in hell for a long time, filled with suffering. If those of such a kind should obtain a human birth, [they will be born as such].
Those situated there certainly experience the sudden loss of wealth;
they certainly encounter suffering, whether caused by a specific reason or even without cause.
Umā.
O Blessed One, some humans suffer the destruction and ruin of their possessions in every way, and through the agency of relatives, they are suddenly separated from them;
and for reasons both with and without cause, they undergo the sudden loss of life.
By what ripening of karma do men meet their death by the sword or otherwise? O Maheśvara, you should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who were devoted to terrible deeds—
mostly asuras, foolish, and exceedingly fond of harming living beings,
merciless in their injury to life, and destroyers of living beings— [attained this state].
Those who kill the trusting, as well as those who strike while one sleeps;
who for the most part consist mostly of falsehood, are nihilists, and are meat-eaters— those whose conduct is thus constituted are, moreover, followers of the dharma of living beings.
O beloved, having been punished by the rod of Yama, they shall remain in hell for a long time;
then, having again entered the womb of an animal, and after the exhaustion of suffering there,
if such beings as those should obtain a human birth, [they will be born] in such a state.
There they surely encounter slaughter and bondage in whatever manner;
whether wealthy or even destitute, they experience the fruit of their own actions.
Even while asleep, intoxicated, or trusting, they likewise undergo those consequences.
The suffering caused by a threat to life, suddenly separated from one's kinsmen;
O Umā,
or the destruction of sons and wife, or death by weapon or by other means.
"O Blessed One, in this human world on earth, certain humans are constantly punished by kings who are experts in statecraft,
O Maheśvara."
By what ripening of karma is this? You should explain that to me.
O Goddess, those men of old who, being merciless toward living beings, killed humans or others by means of cruel slaughter; [what is their fate]?
O auspicious lady, those Asuras of terrible deeds who delight in cruel punishment and slaughter—
kings who, deluded by anger, punish those who do not deserve punishment;
men who take pleasure in violence, eaters of flesh, and nihilists— are born there.
O beloved, some who have killed women and men, as well as those who have killed their gurus,
being thus engaged in such conduct and having fallen away from the dharma of living beings,
are punished with the rod of Yama and remain in hell for a long time, O beloved.
