In this world, living beings experience the karma performed in their previous bodies;
likewise, the karma performed right here bears fruit in the life beyond.
O Goddess, this established order is seen among human beings alone.
Neither for the sages nor for the gods, due to their immortality or the power of their asceticism,
is the fruit of karma experienced by them with only a single body.
Umā.
It would not be so for humans; for that [punishment] would exist only by disappearing from view.
For what purpose are humans in the world punished by the lords of the earth? It is on account of their committed offense, thinking, "This one is a killer" or "This one is a thief."
One who desires a son obtains sons in this very world through the Putrakāmeṣṭi sacrifice;
for they are seen in the world of men enjoying the fruits of their actions with that very same body— this is what you yourself acknowledge.
"Maheśvara—this is a point of doubt for me; you ought to explain it to me. O Goddess, what you have questioned is appropriate; listen to that with a concentrated mind."
Action and the fruit of action are not held to exist simultaneously on earth. O Goddess, as for what you have said— that "this one is a killer" or "this one is a thief"—
it is their prior action that is punished by kings in such cases.

In the teaching [of the Buddha], their physical misdeeds become the cause; under the pretext of an offense, the king punishes the subjects. Punishment by kings is traditionally held to be for the sake of maintaining order in this world.
Pointing out that offense to cause alarm in the rest,
that punishment for the one being punished is certainly the fruit of their own past deeds—
thus spoke Umā.

I have already declared this before; be free from doubt regarding it. Blessed One, for mortals on earth who have been punished by kings, does the destruction of their sin occur through that very punishment here, or not?
"Maheśvara, this which has been doubted by me, you ought to dispel.
O Goddess, what has been doubted is indeed appropriate; listen to it with a concentrated mind."
Those who have been punished on earth by kings under the pretext of some offense are not punished there in the world of Yama by the punishments of Yama;
nor are those who were unjustly punished on earth, or those who were falsely punished as mortals.
Yama indeed punishes them, for he knows what has been done and what has not been done. No human being here, having performed an action, can escape Yama;
O beautiful one, both the king and Yama merely inflict punishment.
Whether punished or unpunished by both Yama and the King of Justice,
one later experiences the fruit of one's karma in hell or among human beings;
for there is no one in all the three worlds who can cut off the fruit of karma.
"O Umā, thus everything has been told to you; be free from doubt, my dear.
For what purpose do humans on earth constantly commit evil deeds?"
Furthermore, they perform expiations (*prāyaścitta*) for the destruction of those actions;
they say that the horse sacrifice (*hayamedha*) removes all sins,
and they perform other expiations as well for the destruction of evil.
"Maheśvara is [the cause];
therefore, a doubt has arisen within me, which you ought to dispel here. O Goddess, it is appropriate that I have this doubt; listen to it with a concentrated mind."
Indeed, this is a great point of doubt even for the wise men of old:
evil is performed in two ways, both by the virtuous and by the wicked—
either with deliberate intent or otherwise, by chance.
Whatever action one performs solely out of malice or through violent impulse,
there is no destruction whatsoever of that karma;
for in this world, there is never any destruction of an action performed with intentional purpose.
Whether by a thousand horse-sacrifices or even by hundreds of expiatory rites,
whatever sin has been committed otherwise— whether through negligence or by chance—
is utterly destroyed through purification by means of expiation and the horse-sacrifice.
"Expiation and the like are prescribed for the sake of worldly convention;
know this regarding sinful deeds, O beloved, and be free from doubt."—
Umā.
"Thus has it been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, humans and others as well die in many ways in this world, whether by cause or without cause."
"O Goddess, by what ripening of karma did Maheśvara [attain his state]? You should explain that to me. Those men of old, O Goddess, even for the sake of a cause or without a cause..."
Just as living beings are deprived of their lives by those who are merciless toward living beings,
so too do they receive exactly the fruit of their own actions.
One who administers poison is slain by poison itself, and the murderer by weapons.
In this very way, O Goddess, just as humans in the world kill other humans by means of various causes, so too do they meet with the destruction of their own lives;
there is no doubt about this.
"Thus, O beloved, I have told you all regarding the fruit of evil deeds.
Furthermore, I shall speak to you again in brief; listen to that. [It is] the making of truth one's authority, which is eternal and unerring."

O Goddess, by whomsoever among men this was performed in former times, at whatever time, and in whatever manner; and for whatever reason, whatever action— whether auspicious or inauspicious— it was done, O Goddess, at that very time, in that same manner, and by that very means, those [results] occurred for them.
After death, men undoubtedly experience the results of their good and evil deeds;
know this to be the truth regarding the laws of worldly existence.
Having performed an action, a man is its experiencer; there is no one else in heaven or on earth who is so.
It is not possible for anyone—including gods, asuras, and humans—to escape the experience of karma;
bound by karma, the world has existed thus from the very beginning.
My dear, this fruit of the ripening of karma has been declared to you in brief.
And whatever else I have not spoken regarding this compendium of karma, you should understand all of that exactly as it is through the reasoning of your own intelligence.
Umā.
13,134.057d@015_2206 This has been told to you who desired to hear it; what more do you wish to hear?
13,134.057d@015_2207 Blessed One, Lord of all worlds, honored by the world-protectors!
13,134.057d@015_2208 Through your grace, O Great God, I have heard the course of karmic actions.
All that is gathered together is in truth like nectar; I know that all, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is bound by karma—
just as a calf seeks its mother, or as water flows toward a low place.
The action performed by oneself always follows its doer;
it is certain that there is no destruction of an action performed here in this world, whether it be unwholesome or wholesome— this too has been understood by me.
"O Mahādeva, granter of boons, increaser of joy, you ought once again, by resorting to the course of actions, to dispel my doubts,
O Maheśvara."
"O Goddess with dark eyes, whatever you wish to say, even if it be a secret,
O Umā of auspicious marks, ask me all of that without hesitation."
Such being the state of the world, O Bull-bannered One, after a person has performed an action— whether auspicious or otherwise—
when does he again experience the fruit of that deed committed by himself in this world?
"O Lord, whether in this world or after death, you ought to explain that to me, O God. It is fitting, O Goddess, that I have this doubt; for it is indeed a most profound secret—listen."
O lady of auspicious countenance, for the sake of what is dear to you, I shall proclaim this secret of the gods:
beings here experience the karma performed in their previous bodies;
whatever is done by men in this very world will bear fruit in the next.
13,134.057d@015_2227 This established rule, O Goddess, is seen only among humans;
13,134.057d@015_2228 for gods and asuras, due to their immortality and the power of their asceticism,
13,134.057d@015_2229 experience the fruit of their actions with a single body alone.
"O Goddess Umā,
such a distinction is not desired by humans;
O Blessed One, O Destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes, [consider] the conduct of mortals."
"I have heard, O Blessed One, that it is your teaching that everything is self-caused; yet,
perceiving all auspicious and inauspicious action in the world as being caused by the planets, people constantly devote themselves for the most part to the planets and the lunar mansions."
"O Maheśvara, O God, you ought to sever this doubt of mine regarding that matter. O Goddess, it is right that you have doubted; hear now the definitive determination of the truth."

O highly fortunate one, the constellations and the planets indeed announce the auspicious and inauspicious for human beings; however, they do not themselves perform actions. Rather, regarding the ordinances of good and evil, they exist for the sake of the welfare of all creatures.
The future and the past are made known by the wheel of luminaries;
however, therein, auspicious karma is revealed by the favorable planets,
while there may be a conjunction with evil deeds through the unfavorable ones alone.

For it is because of the inequality of the planets that a person experiences misfortune; when the planets are in harmony, they bring about auspiciousness according to what was performed in each respective birth. Planets and constellations alone do not produce good or evil fortune.
"All action is performed by the self; the worldly saying that 'the planets [are the cause]' is false.
The planets are distinct and the agent is distinct; by the agent, one's own fruit is experienced."—Umā.

"Thus everything has been told to you; cast away your doubt, O beautiful one. Blessed One, having performed various kinds of auspicious and inauspicious karma, which of those two does a living being experience first in another birth?"
"O Maheśvara, O God, this is my doubt; you ought to dispel it for me here. It is fitting that you explain that which is doubted by you, O Goddess, according to its true nature."
Some say that the unwholesome comes first, while others say the wholesome does;
both of those statements are declared to be false. I shall tell you the absolute truth:
in the human state, karma is always experienced simultaneously.
Both [the results of] what has been done according to its nature and according to its application are experienced in succession; and indeed, human beings on earth are seen experiencing, in due order,
prosperity and decline, happiness and suffering, as well as fearlessness and fear.

The wealthy experience sufferings, and the poor experience pleasures; they are seen enjoying both simultaneously, witnessed by the world. But such a state of affairs does not exist, my dear, in hell or in the heavenly realm.
For suffering is indeed constant in hell, and likewise, happiness is constant in heaven;
because of the predominance of wholesome and unwholesome karmas, one experiences them there. In heaven and in hell, happiness and suffering would be uninterrupted.
Even there, O auspicious Umā, having first performed a very great [rite], one should perform a small one again.
All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Blessed One, for what reason do living beings in the world die? Having been born again and again, they do not remain; you ought to explain that to me, O Maheśvara."
I shall explain that to you; listen with a concentrated mind to the truth.
Listen to how they abandon the body through the exhaustion of their own karma. A living being is designated as the combination of the body and the self.

In that regard, they say the self (*ātman*) is eternal, while the field (*kṣetra*) is said to be impermanent. But that [field], O beautiful one, becomes worn out in the world through the power of time;
and time cuts away lifespans by means of days, months, seasons, and years.
Time ripens all beings; by Time the world is agitated. Indeed, neither gods, nor asuras, nor humans can transcend Time.
Just as no insentient substance could remain suspended in space, [so nothing remains outside of Time].
In this way, time flows on; it does not pause for even a single moment.
Thus, by time, the body is transmigrated and worn out. Having abandoned that shattered body, which is no longer fit for action, the embodied soul then departs.
Because of the eternal abandonment of the impermanent in this world, they know that to be death;
yet, O auspicious one, no destruction exists for the eternal soul,
which is born again elsewhere, entering a new body.

13,134.057d@015_2284 Thus, O Umā, the course of the world has proceeded eternally from the very beginning. 13,134.057d@015_2285 Blessed One, it is observed that among living beings, the young also meet their death.
Even those who are extremely old are seen living on as long-lived ones;
O Maheśvara, death at a fixed time alone is not the sole measure of life,
O Maheśvara.
"Therefore, tell me my doubt regarding the cause of the life of living beings.
Listen, O Goddess, to that cause; the conclusion is indeed one and the same:
Time brings about only the state of decay; it does not cast down the body."
When the karma is exhausted, the aggregate dissolves of its own accord. Life or death occurs according to the measure of prior karma;
as long as the previously performed karma remains, so long does the human being live.
In the same way, children die due to the power of time through the exhaustion of their merit;
likewise, those who have lived long and grown old continue to live according to the measure of their karma. — Umā.
"Thus has it been told to you, O Goddess; be free from doubt, my beloved.
"Bhagavān, by what conduct do people become long-lived? [Maheśvara: "O Goddess..."
"By what means do men become short-lived? You ought to explain that to me.
Listen to all of that in its entirety—the secret which is most beneficial for men—and how those men who are endowed with right conduct become long-lived."
Non-violence, truthful speech, freedom from anger, forbearance, and straightforwardness;
constant service to one’s gurus, honoring the elderly,
purity, the renunciation of improper acts, and always eating what is wholesome.
Such auspicious conduct as this belongs to men who live long lives; through austerity, celibacy, and the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*),
those of exalted spirit become strong and long-lived.
The righteous abide for a long time either in heaven or among humans;
others, however, are generally evildoers, speakers of falsehood,
fond of violence, haters of their gurus, inactive, and devoid of purity.
Nihilists of terrible deeds, who constantly consume meat and drink intoxicants,
who are of sinful conduct, hostile toward their gurus, wrathful, and fond of quarreling—
those of such unwholesome behavior remain in hell for a long time.

Likewise, they remain for an extremely short time in the animal realm and even shorter in the human realm; therefore, those mortals who are born with such short lifespans do so because of traveling to forbidden places and consuming unwholesome food.
The lifespan of men would come to an end, for those [factors] cause the exhaustion of life;
by various such [conditions], they become short-lived, whereas otherwise they live long—
thus said Umā.
13,134.057d@015_2318 All this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
13,134.057d@015_2319 O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, I have heard that which is supremely beneficial for me.
13,134.057d@015_2320 Tell me of the connection between my own births within the transition from woman to man.
Is the life-force of a woman and the life-force of a man one and the same, or are they distinct? O God, this is my doubt; you ought to sever it for me.
I shall explain that to you; listen to it all with a concentrated mind. O lady of auspicious eyes, the states of masculinity and femininity do not exist within the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
The Self is eternally changeless; neither femininity nor masculinity resides in the Self.
Through the various modes of action, one is thus born again and again in birth after birth.
The *puruṣa* is traditionally held to be neither an agent nor subject to transformation, and is eternal. Action performed in a female body is experienced through a female state of being.
The action performed by a person is experienced by that very person;
thus it follows repeatedly in the world through the oneness of the self.
Yet, due to the diversity of karma, the body appears as something contrary [to the true nature of the self].
Having performed manly deeds, even a woman is born as a man;
O Umā,
a man endowed with a feminine nature becomes a woman through his actions.
"O Blessed One, Lord of All Worlds, if Maheśvara is not the agent of action,
who else is the performer of action in that body? You should explain this."
Listen, O beautiful lady: the self is indeed the agent, yet it is not the performer of action.
Action is performed constantly by means of *prakṛti* endowed with the *guṇas*, just as the bodies of living beings in this world [are sustained] by bile, phlegm, and wind.
It is pervaded by the three defects, and likewise it is pervaded by the three qualities (*guṇas*).
These qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—belong to the embodied being. Among these, sattva is always held to be of the nature of illumination.
Rajas is of the nature of suffering, and therein tamas is known to be of the nature of delusion.
By means of these three qualities, all action proceeds in the world.
Truthfulness, compassion for living beings, purity, spiritual welfare, affection, forbearance, and self-restraint—[these are the marks of sattva].
Such as this and other actions of a similar kind are considered *sāttvika*. Diligence, devotion to duty, greed for the means of enjoyment,
attachment to wife, sweetness of disposition, and constant longing for power— these are also [characterized by *sattva*].
And this is the manifestation of passion (*rajas*): various kinds of actions at all times,
falsehood, harshness, intense hatred for what has been heard [in scripture],
devotion to violence, atheism, sleep, laziness, and fear.
And this origin of darkness is always associated with sinful action;
therefore, every undertaking of action, whether auspicious or inauspicious, consists of the qualities [of nature].
Therefore, know the Self to be undistracted, the non-agent, and immutable.
Those characterized by *sattva* dwell in the worlds of merit; those characterized by *rajas* in the human state;
and men characterized by *tamas* shall abide among the animal species and in hell—thus spoke Umā.
"For what purpose should one's own self be pierced by a weapon when in doubt, or why does the Great Lord himself perish when the embodied being is slain? You ought to explain this to me."

I shall explain that to you; listen, O auspicious one, to the reason. Even those logicians of subtle intellect are bewildered by this, when the exhaustion of karma has been reached for living beings who bear bodies.
Whatever affliction may arise in the body due to any cause whatsoever, for that reason the embodied soul— having reached the dissolution of the body—
departs from it, abandoning it, and proceeds thereafter under the power of karma.
Even when the body is wounded, the self is not moved by the sensations;
it remains as long as the fruit of karma persists, and departs again upon the exhaustion of that karma. From the very beginning, such has always been the course of the self in this world.
"O Goddess, this has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear? O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, [it is said that] good and evil arise through action alone."
It is certain that a living being obtains a fruit according to its application. How could one who does what is disagreeable to others obtain auspiciousness?
[Only] Maheśvara [could do so].
"O Lord, if this is so, you ought to explain it to me.
Even that exists, O highly blessed one: for men, there is the fruit of their intentions;
having acted for the benefit of others, one may instead incur misfortune."
By punishing and rebuking his subjects, a king obtains merit;
by threatening his disciples, a teacher, and his own servants, a master; and by restraining those who have entered upon wrong paths, a ruler shall obtain the fruit of dharma.

Even a physician may incur suffering while bringing about what is beneficial; and even one who performs the slaughter of animals for the sake of sacrifice is not a perpetrator of violence. In this way, others of virtuous mind who [seemingly] commit acts of violence shall attain heaven.
"O wicked woman, if one person is slain, many may attain happiness;
if he is killed, merit (*dharma*) will arise—how indeed could there be sin? Because his intention was not crooked, and because of the weight of the merit that is pure."
Having performed this, one shall never incur the most sinful faults. O Blessed One, among all mortals, the man of knowledge is the most excellent.
"Having perceived what did that knowledge arise, and what is its fruit? Is it artificial or is it innate? You ought to explain this to me. Nārada: [replies]...
Having heard this, Maheśvara, the Great God, sang of the origin of knowledge:
"The world is said to be twofold, consisting of the immobile and the mobile."
Therein, the four classes of living beings arise in succession as follows:
among them, trees, creepers, climbing plants, and shrubs are born from sprouts;
while gadflies, lice, and other such species, as well as various kinds of worms, are born from sweat.
Birds and creatures with perforated ears are known as those born from eggs;
know that deer, beasts of prey, and humans are among those born from a womb.
Thus the self remains, having resorted to these four kinds of birth.
In beings born from sprouts, the self indeed exists with touch as its single sense-faculty;
in those born from moisture, it likewise exists with body-sense, touch, and form;
and those born from eggs or from a womb live by means of the five doors of the sense-faculties.
Likewise, O beloved, those born from sprouts arise from the conjunction of earth and water;
those born from moisture arise from the conjunction of cold and heat, O beloved;
and even those born from eggs arise from the conjunction of the field and the seed.
From the union of semen and blood, those born from a womb (jarāyuja) come into being.
Among all those born from a womb, the human state is the highest. Mortals are endowed with all the sense faculties and likewise possess the capacity for speech.
Fear and pleasure exist in that mind even among beasts and birds; however, dharma and adharma, as well as consciousness (*vijñāna*), do not exist at all in birds, beasts, and the like.
Intellect (*buddhi*), being (*sattva*), fortitude (*dhṛti*), modesty (*lajjā*), knowledge (*jñāna*), and discernment (*vijñāna*) [are likewise absent].
Among mortals, reasoning and deliberation, as well as various kinds of virtues, are traditionally taught;
therefore, the human state is perceived here as distinguished. Indeed, a human birth is attained through great religious merit.
Henceforth, O Goddess, listen with a concentrated mind to the origin of that darkness:
for in this world, darkness is of two kinds—namely, that of night and that born of the body.
Of these, the nocturnal darkness is destroyed in the world by lights and by fire.

But that terrible darkness born of the body was not extinguished by all those [means] combined. To destroy that darkness, the Grandfather, the creator of the worlds, did not find any other means; he performed extensive austerities.
The four Vedas, together with their auxiliary limbs and the subsequent [Upaniṣads], emerged;
having obtained them, Brahmā rejoiced for the sake of the welfare of the worlds. That terrible darkness born of his body was destroyed by that very [light].

If there were no teacher of conduct in this world to declare, "This is what should be done and this is what should not be done," or "This is what should be said and this is what should not be said," then human beings would act no differently from beasts.
The undertaking of sacrifices and other rites is prescribed by the Śruti alone;
through the connection with the fruits of sacrifice, the world of the gods is made prosperous.
Furthermore, the gods, being filled with affection, bestow rewards upon human beings.
In this way, heaven and earth perpetually increase one another;

therefore, understand that what has been heard regarding the sustenance of the world is established. Furthermore, there is nothing superior to knowledge for living beings, even within the three worlds.
That which is innate is primary, while that which is acquired through hearing is secondary;
however, where both are perfected, there it is truly excellent.
Indeed, by fully grasping all that has been heard, people become fulfilled.
And like a god above mortals, he shines forth;
desire, anger, fear, pride, and even ignorance born of the intellect—
he quickly drives these away through what has been heard, just as the wind disperses the clouds.

Even a very small amount of dharma performed by those possessed of knowledge becomes great; indeed, even a great amount of dharma performed through ignorance becomes fruitless. One who knows the higher and the lower regarding all beings is truly wise and a knower of reality.
"O lady of auspicious eyes, thus has the entire fruit of hearing [this] been told to you.
Blessed One, are there some humans who are endowed with the recollection of their past lives?"
"For what purpose are they born, knowing their former existence?
O Maheśvara,
O God, tell me this in its true essence regarding human beings."
I shall explain that to you; listen, O beautiful one, to the reason.
Those mortals who die suddenly are born again suddenly;
their ancient habit remains with them for some time.
Therefore, those who possess the memory of their past lives are born in this world endowed with awakening;
as they grow, that consciousness perishes like a dream.
— Umā.
And that is the reason why the ignorant are deluded regarding the existence of the next world.
O Blessed One, there are indeed some humans who, having died,
are now seen returning once more into bodies as men.
Maheśvara said:

"O beautiful one, I shall explain that cause to you; listen. Because of the great number of living beings being deprived of their lives at the time of destruction, [the world is filled with suffering]."
In the same way, on earth, the messengers of Yama carry away other men due to some delusion regarding the commonality of names;
yet Yama knows all that has been done and left undone, for it remains entirely free from error.
Therefore, having reached Saṃyaminī and being released by Yama,
they return once again to experience the remainder of their own karma. —
Umā.
Indeed, human beings do not die until their own karma is exhausted. O Blessed One, Maheśvara [is the one who grants] the vision of dreams to mortals as soon as they have fallen asleep.
Is that its own nature or something else? You should explain this to me.
Furthermore, the movement of those who are asleep is designated as "dreaming. Wandering through the mind, one perceives what is yet to come and what has already passed.
And for that reason, Umā, the seeing of dreams by living beings occurs as a sign.
Thus everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, regarding the path of ritual action in the world,
some maintain that everything proceeds from fate;
others maintain it proceeds from effort, having observed action through direct perception."
"Since this [matter] is divided into two sides, my mind remains in doubt. O Mahādeva, tell me the truth, for I have a great curiosity to hear it.
Thus spoke Maheśvara.
I shall declare that to you; listen to it with a concentrated mind. O Goddess, in this world, destiny does not perform actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious.
O fair-faced one, the two kinds of action belonging to human beings are observed.
Of those two, one is performed previously and the other is performed in this life;
that prior, unseen action is characterized as *daiva* (fate),
while that which has visible causes in this life is remembered as *mānuṣa* (human).
Human action is merely a means, while the fruit arises from destiny;
thus, all that is twofold exists among men in its human form. I shall now explain that worldly [order] which is fashioned by both destiny and human effort.
In agriculture, however, the following actions are observed: plowing, sowing, planting, reaping, and whatever else is considered human effort;
as well as rain at the proper time, good seed, germination, and ripening.
Whatever else there is of this kind is traditionally known as *daiva* (fate).
Sowing is human action (*pauruṣa*), while success is traditionally known as *daiva*. Furthermore, failure may arise from fate, yet there is also the possibility of failure in human effort.
Through great effort one attains fame, and likewise through lack of effort one incurs infamy;
O Umā,
such is the course of the world, O Goddess, which has existed from the very beginning.
O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, worshipped by gods and asuras,
how does the Self always enter the womb due to the cause of karma?
O Maheśvara!
"Tell me that, O Mahādeva, for it is the supreme secret to me.
"Listen, O beautiful lady, my dear one; that secret is the highest among secrets.
"It is remembered as the secret of the Self, even higher than the secret of the gods."
The gods and asuras do not know that coming and going of his own,
for he is invisible to the gods due to his swiftness, subtlety, and lack of support;
the self-illusion of those who possess supreme illusion is regarded as his own illusion.
This very one enters the fourfold birth through his own *māyā*. Sexual union, blood, seed, and destiny (*daiva*) are also the causes therein.
When the conjunction of seed and blood occurs, O auspicious lady...
Then that self enters the embryo in the case of those born from eggs or from a womb; it remains in moisture-born beings through the conjunction of cold and heat,
and in sprout-born beings through the union of seed, earth, and water.

Thus, at the time of union, the self enters the state of being an embryo; from the *kalala* it becomes a *piṇḍa*, from the *piṇḍa* it becomes a *peśī*, and from the *peśī* it becomes an *arbuda*. Once it has attained a manifest form, action (karma) takes hold of it in due order.
"O beautiful lady, know that the union of man and woman is human effort;
that which results in the acquisition of offspring and other such matters is traditionally remembered as destiny (*daiva*).
Thus, as he grows, the self consisting of action (*karmātmā*) proceeds together with him."
"Thus, O lady of excellent vows, know the course of the self about which you ask me;
as well as the stability of the five elements and the movement of the luminaries—
that which is inaccessible to the intellect of mortals and cannot be known through logical reasons."

Such a cause is destiny, whether it be auspicious or otherwise; that which can be accomplished by oneself is known as human effort (*pauruṣa*). However, the complete production of a result cannot be achieved by one factor alone.
O beloved, human effort and destiny are entwined simultaneously;
likewise, the actions of those two are unified like cold and heat occurring at once.
However, one who possesses discernment should first initiate human effort between the two.
For it is indeed not possible by one's own self alone, nor would one attain such fame;
just as in this world water and fire are obtained through digging and churning,
so too is the perfection of destiny brought together through human effort.
For a man who does not perform action, success achieved through destiny is not obtained;
therefore, every undertaking is produced by both destiny and human effort.
Thus do the leaders of the world consider it, as well as the Asuras and Rākṣasas.
Those wicked ones who subsist solely on meat do not perceive this;
for all that is concealed, as the deities are fond of secrets. Therefore, I shall declare to you that ancient secret of the gods.
In the beginning, all creatures, having performed good and evil deeds,
experienced them while observing the events of both worlds,
just as people who have traveled to another land know what they themselves have done.
Just as lightning [flashes], so too at the time of death does one's own past deeds from previous lives manifest.
When the world was thus established, all were devoted to dharma;
in a very short time, heaven was then filled to capacity.
Seeing even the gods crowded together, Brahmā also reflected:
"How do the gods move about? Indeed, how do humans enter? Having reflected thus, he deluded the humans completely.
From that time forward, those mortals no longer knew their ancient [nature]. At that time, he cast desire and anger upon human beings;
struck by these two, mortals did not attain the heavenly world.
Due to ignorance of their past deeds and being oppressed by desire and anger,
thinking "this [world] does not exist," they again produced transformations;
out of their own nature, they undertook great evils such as improper actions.
Having forgotten their religious duties as well as the fear of the next world,
when the world had come to such a state, O beloved, a profound corruption arose for the destruction of both the people and the Vedas.
The hells were filled with living beings who had committed evil deeds.
Seeing this once again, the Grandfather, the creator of the world,
reflected upon that very matter for the sake of the welfare of the worlds.
O Umā, dear one, Brahmā then reflected again and again with wisdom and austerity as to how the world might proceed in a state of equilibrium.
One perceives the next world through the vision of knowledge, not with the physical eye.
O Blessed One, this one who is remembered as "born" immediately upon dying is likewise seen as born; how, then, could there be a self (ātman) therein?
"O Blessed One, it is your teaching that the Self is already situated within the womb at the very beginning;
O Lord, this is my doubt, and you ought to sever it for me,
O Maheśvara."
I shall explain that to you; listen to it with a concentrated mind.
One [being], having entered the womb, meets its end right there;
then, entering yet another body, it is born upon the earth.
That occurs in some places but not everywhere; rather, it arises through the conjunction of destiny.
For the sake of the welfare of the woman in childbirth and for the purpose of deluding embodied beings, know, O beautiful one, that this is the ordinance of Yama’s work.
Having experienced a hell the size of a pit for the duration of a moment, some indeed depart;
that which exists between birth and death is called the watchman of Māyā.
Thus it has been told to you, O Goddess; what more do you wish to hear?
“O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Protector of the world, whose banner is the bull!
There is no self that experiences the fruits of karma; once a living being has died, it is not born again.”
Everything arises from its own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), just like the fruit of a tree;
just as waves arise, so too does the form of the world.
Whatever action there is—such as austerity or charity—the self (*ātman*) therein is seen to be in vain.
Some maintain that there is no rebirth,
having heard the word of one who is beyond perception rather than from the direct observation of what is manifest;
others likewise remain in doubt as to whether all that exists does not exist.
"Furthermore, regarding this other division of the side [of the argument], you ought to tell me the truth.
Nārada replied:
"That which has been spoken by the Blessed One is indeed the established order of the world."
While Rudrāṇī was thus asking this question, the assembly,
filled with curiosity to hear [the answer], then became focused in mind upon Maheśvara.
"O highly fortunate lady, that which the atheists here proclaim does not exist;
this is merely the opinion of those who are accursed and hostile toward the Vedas.
Everything that was previously stated by me to you has been heard and seen as the ultimate truth."
From that time forward, relying upon what has been heard, the wise among mortals—
having severed the barriers of desire with the supreme sword of fortitude—
truly advance toward heaven, beholding the fruit of their actions.
Thus, the fruit of faith in this world is a very great fruit hereafter.
Intelligence, faith, and a desire to serve are the causes for those who seek one's welfare;
therefore, there have been some men who have gone to heaven.

Others, due to their lack of the means [of knowledge], have resorted to the state of nihilism; these fools, haters of the sacred revelation, are atheists of firm conviction. Devoid of ritual action and lacking food, they surely fall into the lowest state.
"Rebirth does not exist"—even the wise are deluded in this regard;
they do not comprehend that eternal truth even through hundreds of logical arguments.
This is the illusion created by Brahmā, difficult to discern even for gods and asuras."
How much more so for humans in this world who desire knowledge through their own actions?
O Goddess, those who possess only faith established upon mere hearing should think,
"That indeed exists," for in this way they shall attain it.
O Goddess, in the secrets of the Vedas and other [teachings], logic is useless.
One who desires their own welfare should conduct themselves here like one who is deaf and blind.
All this, the secret of the gods for the benefit of living beings, has been told to you.
For the sake of pleasing you, this secret, though it should not have been spoken, has been told.
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Destroyer of Tripura, Śaṅkara!"
What are those rods of Yama like, and what are his attendants like?
How do living beings, once dead, go to the abode of Yama?
What is his palace like, and how does he punish his subjects?
"O Maheśvara, O Mahādeva, O Lord, I wish to hear all of this. Listen, O auspicious one, O Goddess; hear all that which is dear to your heart."
In the auspicious southern direction lies the great abode of Yama,
variegated, delightful, and endowed with various states;
it is constantly filled with the ancestors, hosts of departed spirits, and the messengers of Yama.
Filled with vast multitudes of living beings subject to their own karma,
Yama dwells there, constantly inflicting punishment while remaining devoted to the welfare of the world;
through his power of illusion, he perpetually knows whatever is auspicious or inauspicious regarding those beings.
There, withdrawing the multitudes of living beings from here and there by means of his illusory power (*māyā*),
his snares composed of illusion are not perceived even by gods or asuras;
for who, being merely human, could know that great conduct?
For while Yama rules in this manner, his attendants seize living beings whose karma is exhausted and lead them away;
by whatever pretext it may be, that pretext arises from him.
In this world, living beings are classified as superior, inferior, or middling according to their karma.
Having gathered them as is appropriate, [the messengers] lead them to the abode of Yama. Know that those who are righteous are superior; they belong to heaven, just like the immortals.
Those who obtain birth among human beings by their karma are known as middling;
those who go to the animal realm or to hell are indeed the lowest, the most base of men.
Thus, three kinds of paths are seen for all living beings according to their destinies.
It was delightful, free from affliction, and known by the name Durdarśa.
Indeed, that beautiful main road was crowded with banners and flags;
it was perfumed, sprinkled, swept clean, and adorned with garlands of flowers.

It would be captivating and pleasant to the touch for those who travel upon it; it would be free from affliction and as highly praised in the world as possible. But the third is difficult to behold, foul-smelling, and shrouded in darkness.
Rough, strewn with gravel, and abounding greatly in thorny shrubs, it is extremely difficult to traverse for those who walk upon it, being swarming with worms and insects.
By these three paths, the superior, the inferior, and the middling [beings] constantly travel.
Listen to me, O lady of pure smiles, as I describe how they are led at the proper time. At the time of death, the well-restrained messengers of Yama lead away those who are most excellent.
(Umā)
They lead him away comfortably by a delightful path,
O Blessed One; and there, Maheśvara [leads] the self that has cast off the body and is without support.
"How do they take that which is invisible and lead it into the presence of Yama?
"Listen, O beautiful lady, to all of that: the maintenance of the body is of three kinds—under the power of karma, under the power of experience, and under the power of suffering, my dear."
The human body is subject to karma; the celestial body is a means for enjoyment; and the third body, created by *māyā*, is subject to torment—it is seen in the world of Yama and nowhere else.
O beautiful lady, having bound the living soul with bodies destined for torment,
the wardens lead the creatures there by means of their illusory power as if they were dead; likewise, they carry those being crushed by means of a middle-sized body along the middle path.

Assuming the guise of Caṇḍālas, they seize those lowest of men, rebuke them with threats, and dragging them with nooses, they lead them away through the Path of Hardship (Durdarśa). Having thus taken these three classes of beings, they lead them to the abode of Yama.

O highly fortunate lady, having informed them, the guards showed those [beings] to you as they were seated upon the Dharma-throne, skillful, radiant with their own splendor, acting as guardians of the world and presiding over the assembly, likewise situated within the council.
Honoring some and punishing others, while listening to their good and evil deeds,
Yama remains there constantly engaged with many thousands [of attendants].
But for those who have gone to him, Yama honors the most excellent among them.
Having approached them according to the prescribed rite and inquired after their welfare,
Yama initiates a virtuous conversation with them and instructs them regarding the world [they have attained].
Permitted by Yama in this manner, they subsequently proceed to the third heaven (Triviṣṭapa).
Having heard the deeds of those who are of middling conduct exactly as they were,
Yama instructs them, saying, "Be born among human beings. However, Yama does not look upon those who are base and joined with evil when they have arrived.
The terrible messengers of Yama, who appear like outcasts,
inflict these torments upon them by the command of the World-Guardian;
cutting, pushing, and dragging them here and there.
While they are crying out, these [beings] cause them to fall headlong into pits;
moreover, O beloved, masses of stones fall upon their heads,
and most dreadful crows with iron beaks devour them.
In the terrible Asipatravana hell, they cause others to wander;
there, dogs with sharp fangs indeed bite some of them. There flows the river named Vaitaraṇī, teeming with crocodiles.
Difficult to enter, terrible, and carrying urine and blood— into that [river] they plunge these [beings], and when they are thirsty, they make them drink it; indeed,
they cause some among them to climb the thorny śalmali tree there.
In the mechanical wheels there, some are crushed like sesame seeds;
likewise, those who have committed evil deeds are burned upon glowing coals.
They are cooked in boiling pots and indeed fried in ghee.
They are cut with weapons like trees, and their eyes and other organs are tormented;
they are split limb by limb with spikes and pierced with fine needles. This punishment is for the very fault committed by you.
Thus they cried out with their very voices as they were being punished on all sides; having thus undergone those torments with bodies subjected to torture,
they endured that suffering while remembering the transgressions from which it arose.
Crying out and weeping, they are not released by any means;
remembering there, they suffer for the fruit of the evil they themselves have committed.
In this way, various kinds of punishments are experienced by those who have done evil.
Having experienced such torments, they are cooked again in hell;
others, having experienced the torments, are released there from their transgression.
For humans, these torments are traditionally held to bring about the exhaustion of the faults of sin.
Just as iron that has been thoroughly heated becomes stainless, so it shall be.
O Blessed One, how indeed are they punished there in the hells?
"Maheśvara, how many are your terrible hells, and what are they like, O Maheśvara?
Listen, O beautiful lady, to all of that: these five are called hells."
Beneath the earth are established the terrible realms for those who have performed evil deeds.
The first is named Raurava, extending for a hundred yojanas;
it is of the same measure in width, shrouded in darkness, and tormented by sin.

Exceedingly foul-smelling, harsh, and infested with dreadful worms— most terrifying, indescribable, and disagreeable in every direction— they remain there for a long time; there is neither bed nor seat for them there.
Devoured by worms and permeated by a putrid stench,
they remain there in such a state, agitated; the suffering in hell is held to be ten times greater than these torments.
Know, O fair-eyed one, that there is absolute suffering there;
crying out and weeping, they experience agonizing sensations. They wander for the sake of liberation from suffering, yet no protector is to be found.
But neither an end to suffering nor even an opening is found;
O beloved, know that the second hell, named Mahāraurava,
is twice as great in extent and in suffering as Raurava.
The third hell there is known as Kaṇṭakāvana (the Forest of Thorns).
It is twice the size of the previous two, and its suffering is likewise doubled. Indeed, those joined with great sins enter that terrible place.

O Dear One, the fourth hell is known as Agnikuṇḍa; it is twice as large as that [previous one], and its suffering is likewise according to the degree of one's evil intent. Indeed, the suffering there is exceedingly great and non-human in nature; so it is remembered.
In those very places, those who have committed evil deeds experience suffering.
O beloved, the fifth hell is known as Pañcakaṣṭa;
the suffering there is indescribable and most terrible, exactly as it is.
Because it cannot be endured by the five sense-faculties, it is known as the "fivefold agony.
There, the doers of evil deeds experience suffering right where they are;
that suffering, which is beyond human endurance, is experienced by the great elements themselves.
Having endured that most terrible state for a long time, the great elements go toward darkness;
indeed, there is no suffering equal to the fivefold agony.
O beloved, they say that the end of suffering is reached through this fivefold agony forever.
In this way, those living beings who partake in suffering remain within them;
and there are other hells as well, my dear, foremost among them Avīci,
where they cry out and weep, afflicted by pain and exceedingly distressed.
Some wander about, some writhe, and some run about in distress;
they are driven hither and thither by those with spears in their hands and are restrained. Afflicted by pain and overcome by thirst are the living beings who have committed evil deeds.
Crying out and wailing, they are not released in any way; being devoured by worms, afflicted by pain, and possessed by thirst,
they remember their own past actions born of their own transgressions.
They remain there lamenting, O beloved, until the exhaustion of their sins;
having thus experienced hell, they are released through the complete destruction of their evil deeds.
— Umā.
"Blessed One, for how long indeed will they remain in the hells?
O Maheśvara, I wish to know this; tell it to me, O Maheśvara."
Starting from a hundred thousand years,
living beings remain in the abodes of hell for as long as the dissolution of the world; such is the established rule.
Maheśvara said:
"O Blessed One, O Lord, tell me where they dwell among those [hells].
The established rule is that the duration in Raurava is one hundred thousand years.
Those who kill humans, those who are ungrateful, and likewise those who speak falsehoods; adulterers, thieves, and women who behave improperly in every way;
bribe-takers, slanderers, and those who cause the confusion of social classes.
Such men are tormented in the Raurava hell:
those who destroy the land, those who kill kings, those who slay their fathers or mothers,
and kings who rule unjustly or speak falsely as witnesses.
Those who kill many, those who destroy families, those who kill the unborn, those who slay their gurus,
those who betray the trusting, and likewise those who kill themselves out of anger; women who, through delusion, kill their husbands, and those who create obstacles to sacrifices— [all these fall].

Such men are cooked for twice that duration in the second [hell]; those possessed of great sins (mahāpātaka) shall experience suffering in the third. This much is the maximum human lifespan observed in other [realms].
Yakṣas, Vidyādharas, Kādraveyas, Kiṃnaras,
Gandharvas, and hosts of Bhūtas— those who are intensely joined with sin—
are fully cooked in the fourth [hell] until the reversal of the Yuga.
Enduring such terrible torment as that found in the Fivefold Hell,
know that human beings are unfit for such suffering. Having thus experienced those hells, their defilements are there exhausted.
Released from the hells, they are born among the species of worms; some are born among those produced by sprouting, there too their defilements being exhausted;
and once again, O beautiful one, they are born among beasts and birds.
Having eaten that among beasts and birds, they obtain a human state;
by what means are evildoers born into various species?
O Maheśvara,
I shall explain that to you which you desire, O beautiful lady;
in every way, the self is seen in various births through the power of karma.
He who is constantly fond of meat will be touched by the state of being a heron or a vulture;
a mortal who constantly drinks liquor will certainly go to the state of a pig;
and a mortal who eats what is unfit to be eaten will be reborn among the species of crows.
One who constantly causes distress to others is born among the species of predatory beasts; the man who, out of anger, takes his own life remains among the species of *preta* ghosts;
and through backbiting and slander, one attains the state of a cock.
The fool who is an atheist goes to the state of a deer; the man who delights in violence is born among worms and insects;
and one who is always full of pride here goes to the state of a donkey after death.
He who speaks untruthful or harsh words shall go to the state of a fish;
and from approaching those who should not be approached, as well as from violating the wives of others,
a mortal shall become a mouse— of this there is no doubt.
The ungrateful person and the betrayer of friends are born among the species of jackals and wolves;
the killer of a teacher and the murderer of a father remain among stationary beings (plants).
Through vocal sins one attains the state of birds and wild animals, and through mental sins, the state of other [lower] species.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a man goes to the state of an immobile being;
having performed such and other unwholesome deeds, men resort to hell and undergo various states of existence solely because of their own past actions.
Thus, living beings who have committed evil deeds and been scorched through successive births somehow manage to be reborn and attain the human state,
just as iron that has been heated many times becomes exceedingly pure.
Just as one who is tormented by many sufferings purifies the self from impurity,
O Umā,
know therefore that a birth as a true human being is very difficult to obtain.
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods, wielder of the trident, whose banner is the bull!
By your grace, O granter of boons, I have heard this supreme secret;
now, for the sake of the welfare of all creatures, I desire to hear more.
In brief, it is said that all action (karman) is either auspicious or inauspicious.
Tell me in detail regarding the procedure for what is auspicious and what is inauspicious;
what kind of inauspicious action causes living beings to fall downward?
"O Lord, how does auspicious karma lead living beings upward?
Tell me this, O Lord of Gods; I am desirous of hearing it—please proclaim it.
Maheśvara [replied]:
I shall declare that to you; listen to all of it, O beautiful one.
Good action and evil action—such is the twofold expansion of karma. Of these two, that which is evil action arises in three ways.
Through mind, action, and speech, that which arises from the delusion of the intellect occurs;
for the action of speech is preceded by the mind, and from that, the activity consisting of speech is produced. Thus, O beloved, the sequence of effort arises through the application of action.
Malice, envy, and longing for the wealth of others with one's own eyes; the conduct of mortals toward both the auspicious and the inauspicious in a perverted manner;
lack of faith in religious duties, and taking delight in sinful actions.
Such and other unwholesome actions performed by the mind are called mental evil. Furthermore,
that which is false, harsh, incoherent, or bitter speech, as well as untruth and slander— this is the evil consisting of speech.
Sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached, consorting with the wives of others,
causing pain to the lives of others through killing, imprisonment, and affliction,
as well as theft— the seizing and likewise the destruction of the property of others.
Eating what is unfit to be eaten, being addicted to vices, causing distress to others out of pride, stubbornness, and arrogance, performing improper acts, impurity, and the drinking [of intoxicants].
Immorality, association with the base, assistance in evil deeds, and the pursuit of unrighteous and disreputable activities— these and other such inauspicious things are called bodily evil.
It will be stated that verbal sin is more significant than mental sin;
yet bodily sin is considered even greater than verbal sin.
Thus, action joined with such sin causes a person to fall in three ways.
Causing pain to others is considered an extreme evil.
That twofold committed sin leads the doer to hell;
even that sinful act which is performed intentionally through the exercise of the intellect.
Whatever was done under some pretext, thinking "it must certainly be done," even if it was performed in such a manner, the doer is not tainted by it. —
Umā.
The cause would be obstructed by the necessity of its own existence.
O Blessed One, how is it that Maheśvara, having committed evil karma, is not defiled by it?
"You ought to explain to me that which is untruth yet joined with dharma:
when a man, being innocent, for the sake of protecting his own life,
[encounters] an enemy with raised weapon, or one who has previously been killed by him."

If a man, having returned [to his home], should kill those who are terrified by thieves or forest-dwellers, he does not become tainted by sin, provided it is for the sake of countering that threat; killing them in such a manner,
the man does not become tainted by sin.
A man who kills for the sake of his livelihood is not tainted by sin.
By acting for the sake of the village, for the sake of his master’s maintenance, or out of compassion for the distressed,
he is released from the evil of inflicting slaughter, imprisonment, or torment.

During a famine, one who has entered a state of solitary wandering for the sake of his own livelihood is not defiled by sins, even if he commits what is improper or consumes what is forbidden. Likewise,
one who is afflicted by disease is not defiled by consuming what is forbidden for the sake of being freed from that illness.

An untruth spoken out of courtesy toward women, even if it is contrary to dharma; that which is spoken out of fear for one's own life; that spoken by an unrighteous person for the sake of liberation; and likewise, speaking an untruth during the performance of a marriage according to worldly custom—[these are not considered mortal sins].
One is not tainted by falsehood when it is spoken for the purpose of stabilizing those who are terrified;
this is the rule generally taught for householders,
even regarding that which is unspeakable or improper, depending on the exigencies of place and time.
When a person acts intentionally, he may be tainted by sins according to the measure of that purpose, or he may not be tainted at all. —
Umā.
"Thus, O Goddess, you should know; there is no room for doubt in this matter.
Blessed One, Maheśvara [has explained] the faults of drinking liquor and the reasons for what may or may not be drunk."
"I desire to hear this; tell it to me, O Maheśvara.
Very well, I shall tell you of the origin of liquor, O lady of pure smiles.
In ancient times, all mortals were wise and followed the path of right conduct."

O beloved, all people were pure, of auspicious conduct, and well-disposed toward one another. When the world had become thus, there was no longer any state of servitude among them; and due to the absence of servants, the undertaking of labor for others indeed perished.

Seeing the destruction of both worlds due to the exhaustion of *karma*, the Lord Pitāmaha [Brahmā] commanded the gods, "O Goddess, delude human beings so that the ritual of sacrifice may continue in the world."

O beloved, having extracted the essence of darkness— a drink that destroys the intellect and brings about the fault of sin— they poured it among human beings. From that time forward, having drunk it, human beings on earth became deluded.
Not knowing what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, what should be spoken and what should not be spoken, or what is virtuous and what is not,
some laugh after drinking that [liquor], while others likewise weep;
some dance with joy, and others sing both the auspicious and the inauspicious.
They constantly engage in quarrels and strike one another;
some run about suddenly, stumble, and fall. They speak much that is improper and lie down wherever they please.
Naked, with their limbs flung about, they lose consciousness and lie like the dead.
Thus do those men, possessed by evil, perform various sinful acts when their minds are stolen away by drinking that which leads to great delusion.
Drinking liquor destroys fortitude, modesty, and intelligence;
therefore, men become shameless, devoid of decorum,
their intellects and vital essences exhausted, lacking luster, and filled with impurity.
Having drunk again and again, those lowest of men, possessed by thirst, are reborn as drinkers;
desiring drink, speaking of drink, and longing for the acquisition of drink,
those wretched ones are reborn under the power of their karma for the sake of drinking.
Driven by thirst and the exhaustion of their mental faculties (*buddhi-sattva*), those who desired drink became known as *pānapa* (drinkers);
they became the servants of the *pānapas* and were excessively addicted to drink. From that time forth, indeed, in the world, men of low status fell under the power of drink.
The wise ones, however, being drinkers of *apāna*, performed their various tasks; whereas the drinkers of *pāna* fell into the state of artisans, slaves,
and servants, becoming performers of all kinds of labor, bound with ropes like cattle.
But those addicted to drink, due to being blinded by intoxication, the consequent destruction of their intellect,
ignorance of what ought and ought not to be done, acting according to their own whims,
and being beyond the control of the wise, fall into sin alone.
The drinker of intoxicants and the sower of discord among friends shall be despised in the world;
he shall be perpetually impure and a consumer of all things,
hated by his distinguished kinsmen, and ever given to strife.
He speaks everywhere words that are bitter, harsh, and terrible;
intoxicated, he speaks excessively against his elders and violates the wives of others.
He consorts with drunkards and never listens to what is beneficial.
Thus, O beautiful one, there are many such faults in drinking;
they go only to hell—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, the virtuous who desire their own welfare avoid that drink.
If the virtuous did not refrain from drinking for the sake of their conduct,
this entire world would surely become lawless and devoid of moral action;
therefore, for the protection of the intellect, the wise have avoided drinking.
"Thus, O beloved, all three kinds of misdeeds have been described to you.
O lady of pure smiles, listen further to the procedure for meritorious deeds as well," said Maheśvara.

O Goddess, that well-performed action (*sukṛta*) is briefly said to be threefold: that which is conducive to cessation (*auparamika*), which is free from affliction (*nirupadrava*), and likewise that which is accompanied by its means (*sopakaraṇa*); by these much is well-performed action known.
"O beloved, abstention from evil deeds is that which arises from cessation;

hear from me how the defects born of mind, speech, and body become auspicious through their abandonment. That which results from the cessation of the threefold defects is [attained] by disregarding those very defects."

But he attains everything by avoiding all that is evil; like one observing a vow, he should avoid faults either simultaneously or individually. In this way he attains Dharma, for the abandonment of faults is indeed difficult to achieve.
By completely abandoning all faults, a human being becomes a sage. Even without the undertaking of formal duties, the ease of following another’s dharma is attained;
through the mere act of establishing it within oneself, the highest merit is obtained.
Alas, cruel and small-minded humans are being cooked [in hell], for they do not realize that such a state— which is independent of others and free from decay—
is attained simply by abandoning evil deeds. Indeed, the higher realm is obtained through the mere renunciation of wrongdoing.

"O Goddess, by merely fearing evil and thereby avoiding faults, one becomes most excellent; how much more so when there is regard for the Dharma? Thus, O Goddess, has the merit pertaining to the final stage been described to you."
Through learning, association with the elderly, restraint of the senses,
contentment, and fortitude, the abandonment of faults is possible;
that very thing, O beloved, they call *yama*, the restraint of faults.
By the dharma of Yama, there exists no other dharma more auspicious than this, O auspicious one;
by the dharma of Yama, ascetics attain the supreme goal—
whether they be lords, powerful men, or indeed poor people.
The abandonment of faults is fruitful even more than giving or even auspicious merit.
O Great Goddess, austerity and giving may burn away only a small fault;
however, that which is called "the watchman's good deed" is wholesome and requires no further means.
Kindness toward the worlds, truthfulness, purity, and straightforwardness;
vows, fasting, affection, celibacy, self-restraint, and tranquility—
such auspicious actions are well-performed when based on discipline.
Listen, O beautiful lady, and I shall proclaim their specific distinctions to you:
truth is the staircase to heaven, like a boat for crossing the ocean;
there is no gift superior to truth, and no austerity superior to truth.
Whatever has been heard, whatever has been seen, and whatever has been done by oneself in such a manner—
that speech which accords with that without deviation is the characteristic of truth. That which is joined with deceit, even if it has the appearance of truth, is indeed falsehood.
One who understands the distinction between the higher and the lower must always speak the truth;
through truth one becomes long-lived, a protector of the lineage,
and a guardian of the world’s stability.
"How may a mortal, while maintaining the auspicious vow, attain [its fruit]?"
Whatever sin was previously mentioned as committed through the actions of mind, speech, and body,
the renunciation of that— just like a vow— is the vow of cessation (*auparamika-vrata*). By observing it thoroughly, one attains merit just like one who observes a formal vow.

One should perform auspicious rites and virtuous deeds through vows alone; by observing a vow that is pleasing to the self and associated with purity through constant actions of mind, speech, and body, a person attains dharma.

The renunciation of one who possesses vows is established as the vow of austerity (*tapovrata*). Whether something is to be abandoned or to be enjoyed, he who acts in vain without a vow does not obtain the fruit; therefore, one should practice dharma through a vow.
Having become a man of pure body and having bathed at a sacred ford according to the prescribed rule,
he should offer himself to the five elements, the moon and the sun, the two twilights, Dharma, Yama, and the ancestors;
thus, as if by his own self, he should perform his vow.
One should observe the vow either until death or for a limited period of time;
one should perform the vow with vegetables and the like, as well as with flowers, fruits, and so forth; one should observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) and likewise the vow of fasting.
Thus, one who desires their own welfare should perform the vow in many other ways as well;
the wise should protect it so that there may be no violation of the vow. Know, O fair-eyed one, that a violation of the vow is a great sin.
If, for the sake of medicine, out of ignorance, or even at the word of one's elders,
or for the sake of favoring one's kinsmen, a violation of a vow occurs, it is not considered blameworthy. At the times of concluding a vow, one should perform worship of the gods and the Brahmins.
A man, however, should perform [this] according to his ability; thus he shall attain success. Maheśvara said: [13,134.057d@015_2954]
"You ought to explain to me how the rule for purification is applied there.
Purification is held to be twofold: external and internal.
That which consists of mental good deeds is remembered as internal purification."
The constant purity of food, as well as the washing of the body,
constitutes external purification; likewise, it includes the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth,
as well as earth from a pure location, cow dung, and cow urine.
With fragrant substances that promote nourishment,
one should repeatedly cleanse the body with these and with water—
whether it be the Akṣobhya, the scattered, or the ever-flowing water.
One should generally immerse oneself in such [water], or otherwise avoid it;
thrice sipping water with foamless and pure water is best.
Likewise, purification from feces and urine shall be accomplished with water and abundant clay.
At that very time, purification by water is required when one touches something already purified;
the purification of the ground is by means of excrement, and for metals it is traditionally held to be by ashes;
while for wooden objects, purification consists of planing and scrubbing.

The purification of earthen vessels is by burning, and for mortals it is through the endurance of difficult penance; O Goddess, for all the remaining things, purification shall always be by means of sunlight, water, and the word of Brahmins.
What is not defiled, washed with water, and praised by word—such is purification in times of distress; such is the rule for purity.
Thus spoke Umā.
Maheśvara said:
"O Great Lord, tell me how the purity of food is achieved;
it should be meatless, free from intoxicants, not moist, and indeed not stale."
Free from excessively bitter, sour, or salty flavors, and possessing a pleasant fragrance; free from worms,
insects, and impurities, and prepared in a clean vessel— such food,
honored by gods and brahmins, [should always be offered].
It should be understood as pure; otherwise, it would be impure.
Know that what is prepared by forest-dwellers from village-grown [grains] is pure. However, if taken in excessive measure, even that which is given in small quantity would become impure.
The remnants of the sacrifice, the remnants of the oblation, and the remnants of the ancestors are stainless; O Goddess Umā, this has been told to you. What more do you wish to hear?
Some on this earth eat meat, while others abstain from it;
O Maheśvara,
O Mahādeva, tell me the reason for what is fit to be eaten and what is unfit to be eaten.
The fault in eating meat and the merit in its abstention—I shall proclaim that; listen to it exactly as it is.
Sacrifices performed, gifts given, study undertaken, and rituals accompanied by sacrificial fees—[all these are surpassed by the merit of abstaining from meat].

These do not equal even a sixteenth part of the merit of abstaining from meat. He who, for his own sake and out of a desire for delicious food, would harm the lives of others, is equal to a serpent, a vulture, a jackal, and a *rākṣasa*.
That man who constantly eats meat in vain becomes the lowest of men;
there is nothing more grievous than eating meat that one has procured for oneself. He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another [is truly base].
Wherever one is born, one finds a dwelling full of anxiety;
just as the cutting of one's own flesh would cause pain,
so too should it be understood by the wise regarding the flesh of another.
But he who does not eat any meat for as long as he lives attains a vast place in heaven; of this there is no doubt. He who performs supreme austerity for a full hundred years—
Whether one avoids meat or not, these two are equal;
for there is nothing in this world dearer than one's own life. Therefore, compassion for living beings should be practiced toward others just as toward oneself.
O beautiful lady, all sacrifices and all the Vedas together could not accomplish that which one achieves by tasting the essence of meat and then renouncing meat once more—
a practice that is righteous, conducive to fame, life-prolonging, leading to heaven, and a great source of well-being.

13,134.057d@015_3007 Thus the sages have spoken of the virtues of abstaining from meat. 13,134.057d@015_3008 O Goddess, the avoidance of meat possesses such manifold benefits for men. 13,134.057d@015_3009 Yet, when one is unable to abandon meat by any means while remaining alive—
Or specifically, one should avoid [certain actions] for at least three months of merit; likewise,
one should not be able to do so even during the month of Kaumudī,
nor on the lunar days of one's birth-star, nor always on festival nights.
Meat should likewise be avoided by one who desires what is beneficial in the next world. If a mortal, due to incapacity, should wish to eat it for some reason, hear the rule:
by eating according to this procedure, one is not tainted by sin.

O beautiful lady, one who desires his own welfare may, according to the law, purchase an animal that has already lost its life at a slaughterhouse and eat it for the sake of honoring Brahmins and guests;
when eating for the purpose of medicine during illness, one is not tainted by sins.
Eating meat that remains over from offerings to the ancestors (*pitṛ*), one likewise incurs no evil.
Umā and Maheśvara.
"O Lord, how is the worship of the guru performed by those who desire the Dharma?
O beautiful one, I shall explain the worship of the guru to you exactly as it is;
for the teaching of the Vedas is that the highest duty belongs to those who are grateful."
Therefore, one's own gurus are to be honored, for they have been benefactors in the past;
among all gurus, three are especially revered in the worlds:
the teacher, the father, and the mother—they are to be honored above all.
Those who are paternal uncles, elder brothers, and likewise those who are his younger brothers,
as well as the father of one's father— all these are to be honored just like one's own father. So too are the mother’s elder sister and her younger sister.
The maternal grandmother and the nurse— these are all remembered as mothers. The son of one's preceptor, whoever may be his teacher,
the officiating priest, and the father are proclaimed to be gurus.
An elder brother, a king, a maternal uncle, and likewise a father-in-law,
as well as one who protects from fear and a husband— these are proclaimed to be gurus. Thus has been declared this complete compendium of those who lead to heaven.
Learn from me also their conduct and the manner of honoring them:
both mother and father are inviolable, and likewise the preceptor;
they must never be disregarded by a man who desires his own welfare.
By that which pleases the father, Prajāpati is pleased;
by that which pleases the mother, the divine mothers are pleased;
by that which pleases the preceptor, Brahmā is thereby honored.
If they, however, remain displeased, a person indeed goes to hell.
One should never, under any circumstances, persist in enmity toward one's teachers; through such devotion to the teacher, one does not go to hell even by thought alone.
One should not speak what is unpleasant to them, nor should one engage in what is undesirable for them. One should never speak to them in their presence with a contentious spirit or out of rivalry.
Whatever they wish to do, one should perform that without asserting one's own independence.
The instruction of a teacher is held to be equal to the teaching of the Vedas. One should avoid quarrels and disputes with teachers,
as well as deceit, jesting, and conversations based on anger and desire.

He who, free from egoism, carries out the commands of his gurus without weariness— among all mortals, there is no one more meritorious than he. One should completely avoid malice and slander toward one's gurus.
Seeking what is pleasing and beneficial for them, one should always attend upon them;
neither the fruit of sacrifice nor great austerity performed would produce such a result as the constant worship of one's guru performed here by a man.
There is no dharma without following [the teacher], even among all the stages of life (āśramas). Therefore, at the proper time, one should respectfully practice the conduct toward the guru.
A wise man should sacrifice his own interests and even his own body for the sake of the guru.

One should not engage in disputes with them, whether for the sake of wealth or out of delusion. For one who has been forbidden by his teachers, celibacy, non-violence, and various kinds of gifts— all these are rendered fruitless.
Those who would betray their preceptor, father, or mother, whether by thought or by deed,
their sin is no different from that of killing an embryo.
There is no other doer of evil in the world besides them; Umā is Maheśvara.
Therefore, you ought to explain to me the procedure for fasting.
For the sake of reducing the impurities of the body and for the drying up of the senses,
men maintain their vows through eating once a day and by means of fasts.
They obtain abundant merit through such an exhaustion of food;
however, one should not cause obstruction to many for the sake of oneself. Likewise, the destruction of living beings is avoided, for grain is considered the very life-sustenance of all.
Therefore, a mortal may personally obtain merit through the emaciation of his own diet;
it is certain that this should be performed by householders according to their capacity.
When the body is afflicted by fasting, milk or water is for the sake of emergency.
Having obtained permission from the Brāhmaṇas, one who eats does not become a violator of his vow. O Lord,
how should a wise man protect his celibacy?
Maheśvara said:
"I shall declare that to you; listen, O Goddess, with a concentrated mind. Celibacy is the supreme purity; celibacy is the supreme austerity."

The supreme state is attained solely through celibacy (brahmacarya). It is protected in five ways: from intention, from sight, from conversation with one who is attached [to sensual things], from touch, and from union.
Just like a vow, stainless celibacy is maintained;
for lifelong students (*naiṣṭhika*), its constant protection is prescribed,
whereas for householders, it is required for a specific period based on a particular cause.
On the conjunctions of one’s birth-star, on auspicious days, and on festival days;
during rites for the deities and for Dharma, one should observe the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya*). One who observes the vow regarding his wife shall always obtain the fruit of the vow of celibacy.

Purity, long life, and likewise health are obtained by those practicing celibacy (brahmacārins). Umā said: "O Lord, how is the practice of visiting sacred fords (tīrthacaryā) performed by those desiring dharma?"
"O Maheśvara, O Lord of the World, which are the sacred fords (tīrthas) in this world? You should explain them to me.
"Very well, my dear, I shall describe to you the ritual for bathing at the sacred fords."
In ancient times, they were created by Brahmā for the sake of purification and ritual cleansing. All those great rivers that exist in the world are designated as *tīrthas*.
Among them, those whose currents flow eastward are the most excellent, as is their confluence with one another.

The confluence of those rivers with the ocean is known to be most excellent; O Goddess, wherever their banks are frequented on both sides by great seers or by gods, that sacred ford is remembered as supreme.
And the ocean is a great sacred ford (*tīrtha*), supremely purifying and auspicious; the sacred fords situated upon its shores have been bathed in by the great ones,
as well as the streams, the mountains, and the places frequented by the great seers (*maharṣi*).
O beloved, even a well or a pond frequented by sages should be known as a *tīrtha* because of the power of those ascetics; indeed,
from that time forward, it attained the status of a *tīrtha* for the benefit of the world.

In this way, know that which arises from the sacred ford (*tīrtha*); now hear the procedure for bathing there. With the mind fixed on that, abounding in vows, and having gone with a longing for the sacred ford, one should perform three fasts, or even one, while remaining observant of the rules.
At a time joined with an auspicious month, on the full moon day according to the prescribed rite,
having become pure, one should enter that sacred ford (tīrtha) outside, with the mind fixed upon it;
having bathed three times near the water and given sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas.
Having worshipped the temple of the deity, he then departed as he had come.
O beloved, this is the procedure for every sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*);
however, a distant *tīrtha* is more highly honored than bathing at a nearby one.

For one who has been pure from the very beginning, bathing at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) shall be auspicious. Immersing oneself in a sacred ford for the sake of austerity, for the destruction of sin, and for the sake of purification—
thus, bathing at a sacred ford during the meritorious months shall be auspicious.
Maheśvara said:
"All this, which has been well-spoken, has been declared to you as the obligatory rule:
