namely, gifts, the worship of the gods, and likewise the worship of the ancestors."
Other religious duties, well-performed along with their means of accomplishment—
all that, O auspicious lady, listen to out of a desire for the welfare of all creatures;
as well as whatever wealth exists in the world, consisting of both sentient and insentient things.
O lady of beautiful eyes, after death a man obtains this very purpose;
for that substance which is established in the world is common to all.
If that [wealth] were common to all, how could a man obtain merit by giving it?
Maheśvara said:
"In this way, when a substance is common to all, whose ownership would it be, and how could it come to be?"
In this world, material substance composed of the elements is common to all;
hear now how a mortal becomes meritorious by giving it away—
[namely,] the donor, the recipient, the gift, and likewise the manner of its presentation.

Furthermore, this gift is said to possess six qualities when it is endowed with the proper place and time; learn from me as I describe the specific excellence of these factors. He who has been pure from the very beginning through the actions of mind, speech, and body—
One who speaks the truth, has conquered anger, is free from greed, and is not envious;
one who possesses faith and is a believer—such a giver is praised. Pure, self-controlled, having conquered anger, and likewise born of a noble lineage.
One who is endowed with learning and conduct, likewise possesses many wives,
is constantly devoted to the five sacrifices, and has a body free from disease—
know these to be the qualities of a worthy recipient; such a recipient is highly praised.

Whatever is given by him in rites for the ancestors, the gods, and the sacred fires yields great fruit; whoever in this world is worthy of a gift, he becomes a fit recipient for that person. Furthermore, he by whom one fallen into misfortune is liberated is indeed his true recipient.
For one who is hungry, food is indeed the worthy recipient; for one who is thirsty, water is the worthy recipient.
Thus, a diversity of recipients is recognized with respect to each individual person.
[Such unworthy recipients include] a paramour, a thief, a eunuch, a violent man, and one who breaks his agreements.
And others who create obstacles for the world have been entirely avoided, O Beloved.
Whatever property is obtained by men through harming others, or through theft, or likewise whatever is obtained through reproach or through deceit;

O Goddess, know that any wealth obtained through unrighteousness, delusion, or by obstructing many people— or even if it were otherwise taken— is stolen; O beautiful lady, know that any dharma performed with such means is fruitless.

Therefore, one who desires merit should give only what has been acquired through righteous means. It is the established rule that whatever is always dear to oneself should be given; know this to be the foremost benefit for donors.

But having approached and propitiated a worthy recipient who is far away, a donor should give a gift in such a way that he is satisfied by it. This is the best method of giving; however, inviting [the recipient] is the middling method.

O beloved, having first ascertained their worthiness, having summoned them, and having informed them [of the gift], one should— with faith and accompanied by purity and worship— bestow [the gift] upon supplicants,
treating them with the highest degree of hospitality.

Having first received [the recipient] with honor, one who desires prosperity should give at the appropriate place and time; indeed, even to others who are not worthy vessels, one should give after having carefully examined both the recipient and the gift.

The supreme gift is that which exceeds one's power; the middling gift is according to one's capacity; and the third gift is that which does not seem appropriate for oneself. That which was previously promised should be given in exactly that same manner.
Whatever is given in sacred fields or likewise at auspicious times— know that, O Umā, to be far more excellent due to the gravity of the place and the time.
And tell me, O Maheśvara, what is the most meritorious place and likewise the time— Kurukṣetra, the great rivers, and that which is frequented by the celestial rishis.
Excellent mountains, sacred fords (tīrthas), and regions are honored according to their respective parts;
whatever is given there to one who desires [the gift] yields great fruit. Likewise, the seasons of autumn and spring, as well as the meritorious months, [are likewise honored].

Know that the bright fortnight among the fortnights, the full moon among the lunar nodes, the asterisms presided over by the ancestors and the gods, the stainless days, and likewise the eclipses of the moon and sun, are most auspicious.
The time that is mentally intended for the recipient during an auspicious moment—
on such occasions as these, a gift given becomes great.
The donor, the object to be given, and the recipient, along with the ritual action performed with proper application [constitute the excellence].
Place and time—the perfection of these is proclaimed as purity. Wherever there is a simultaneous perfection of all these, there the purification shall be great.
Even a very small gift, when endowed with these six qualities, [becomes vast].
Having become infinite, it leads the donor—freed from all faults—to heaven;
for even a very great gift, if it is devoid of these qualities, [is of no avail].
Umā.
Indeed, that [gift] would result in very little fruit or be fruitless;
thus, even a gift endowed with such qualities, if given [to an unworthy recipient], would reach a state of fruitlessness—
so says Maheśvara.
"If that exists, O Mahādeva, you ought to explain it to me.
"That too exists, O highly fortunate one, for men due to the defects of worldly existence,
if after performing dharma according to the rules, they feel remorse."
Or if one should speak with self-praise regarding what was done in the assembly,
he should mentally assign that fruit to the afterlife; likewise,
whatever righteous deed has been performed constantly with a desire for its fruit [should be assigned there].
Thus, what is done or given in this manner may become fruitless in the next world;
these faults should be avoided by givers who desire merit. This is the eternal conduct practiced by the virtuous.
"Indeed, favoring others who are householders is a debt;
having fixed their minds thus, the wise should constantly give. When done in this very way always, that becomes a great merit."
Having thus given away common property, one obtains a great fruit.
O Blessed One, what things should be given by men with reference to the Dharma?
O Maheśvara,
I desire to hear about those; you should explain them to me—
both the constant duties of dharma and likewise the occasional ones, O beloved.
Food, shelter, a lamp, water, grass, and fuel; oil, fragrance, medicine, sesame seeds, and likewise salt—
such things and others like them are called constant gifts.
Because it is given incessantly, it is determined to be "ajasra" (constant). Listen with a concentrated mind to the common gift shared by all social classes:
food is the life-breath of human beings; thus, the giver of food becomes a giver of life.
Therefore, human beings especially desire to give food;
he who gives desired food to a worthy Brāhmaṇa lays up for himself an excellent treasure that is infinite in the world beyond.

One should honor with great effort a guest who has arrived at one's home, weary and exhausted from the road; for he is remembered as the most excellent sacrifice. Furthermore, even after having committed a sinful deed, he who gives food to those in need [is purified].
Especially for the sake of the Brahmins, he destroys his own darkness;
his ancestors rejoice like farmers at a timely rain, thinking,
"Whether it be my son or my grandson who will feed the learned Vedic scholars."
Moreover, one is not censured for giving food even to Caṇḍālas and Śūdras;
therefore, with every effort and without stinginess, one should give food. Even by causing hardship to his own wife, he should always nourish his guests.
Even birth in the world of humans is ordained for that purpose alone.
O blameless one, I shall now describe those worlds attained through the gift of food;
the palaces of those great-souled ones shine resplendently in heaven.
They have many hundreds of stories and contain internal waters and groves;
they shine with the radiance of lapis lazuli, resemble gold and silver,
possess various shapes and forms, and are composed of various jewels.
White as the lunar disc and adorned with networks of tinkling bells,
possessing the hue of the rising sun, both stationary and moving,
they provide food and drink according to one’s desire, along with beds and seats.
And here, trees situated within the dwellings bear the fruit of all desires;
there are many ponds, wells, and thousands of oblong lakes—
various, free from disease, free from sorrow, and eternal.
Those who bestow food and water in this world constantly enter the secluded abodes of the life-givers in the third heaven— those of Vivasvat, Soma, Brahmā, and Prajāpati.
Having sported there for a very long time with hosts of apsarases,
they are born in the world of humans endowed with every excellence— possessed of strength and firmness, free from disease, and long-lived.
Men who give food become noble and wise;
therefore, one who desires prosperity should especially give food at all times, to everyone, everywhere, and always.
The gift of gold is supreme for attaining heaven and is a great means of securing well-being;
therefore, I shall describe it correctly and in due order.
Even a cruel evil deed committed is destroyed by the giving of gold.
Those of pure mind who bestow gold upon those learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) satisfy all the deities; such is the Vedic teaching. For Agni is all the deities, and gold is said to be Agni.
Therefore, by the gift of gold, all the deities are effectively given.
In the absence of fire, however, they place gold in the positions where the fires belong.
Consequently, the givers of gold shall obtain all their desires.
Having quickly bestowed gold, they enter the various auspicious worlds of Āditya and Hutāśa; of this there is no doubt.
Moreover, that which is fashioned as an ornament shall excel even that which is merely [unadorned].
Having adorned the Brahmins at the proper time with those golden ornaments, one should feed them.
Having given this supreme gift, he will certainly obtain an extraordinary complexion,
radiance, intelligence, physical beauty, and fame upon being born again.
Therefore, men on earth should give gold according to their own capacity;
for it is said that there is nothing else in the worlds more purifying than this.
Hereafter, O blameless one, I shall proclaim the gift of cows.
O beloved, there is no gift in this world superior to cows.
In the beginning, when he desired to create the worlds, the Self-born One first created cows;
they were created for the sustenance of all beings, and therefore they are remembered as mothers.
The elders of the world, engaged in the conduct of the world,
are dependent upon me; they are as the flowing of the moon,
gentle, meritorious, bestowers of desires, and givers of life.
Therefore, those who desire merit should honor such cows; for by giving a cow that is well-behaved, healthy, accompanied by a fine calf, and full of milk, one gains great reward.
As many hairs as there are on that cow,
for so many years does he who gives away a tawny cow along with its garment enjoy the fruits of heaven.
A cow with bronze milking vessels and golden tips on her horns saves one's sons,
grandsons, and the entire family up to the seventh generation in the hereafter.
Those born in the house, those purchased, those obtained through gambling,
those bought with living beings, those acquired by force or water,
those released from hardship, and those who have come for the sake of being nourished.
Deceived by these means,
one should give them away to a man who is emaciated, who has many sons, who is learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*), and who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*).
By giving a healthy cow, one attains unsurpassed worlds.
One should never, under any circumstances, give cows to one who is cruel, ungrateful, greedy, a speaker of falsehood, or who has abandoned the offerings to the gods and ancestors. However,
one should give a milch cow with a calf of the same color to a Brahmin.
He who gives a black cow that is well-behaved, provides milk, has a calf of the same color, is adorned with fine garments, and is bound with cloth, is honored in the world of Soma;
he attains the worlds of the Lord of Waters.
He who gives away a tawny cow with a calf of the same color,
one that is well-behaved, milk-yielding, bound with cloth, and golden-hued with reddish-brown eyes, along with a bronze milking vessel, is glorified in the world of Agni.
Having given a cow bound with cloth, he goes to the abode of Kubera. But having given a cow the color of wind-blown dust, together with its calf and a bronze milking vessel,
and bound with cloth, one is glorified in the world of Vāyu.

Those who bestow upon high-souled Vedic scholars a bull that is young, strong, dark-hued, the leader of a herd of a hundred, a lord of cattle with massive horns, and well-adorned; (they attain the highest world).
Being born again and again, they are reborn into states of sovereignty.
One should never be repelled by the urine or dung of cows;
one should not eat their flesh, but should always remain devoted to cows.
For one year, being pure, he should give a handful of fodder to another’s cow;
having not prepared his own food, that vow fulfills all desires. He should always recite prayers for the welfare of cows at both times of day.
Those who know the Dharma understand that one should not think ill of them;
cows are the supreme purifier, and the worlds are established upon cows.
Cows, the mothers of the world, must never be treated with contempt under any circumstances.
Therefore, the gift of cows is said to be preeminent;
worship and devotion toward cows bring longevity to a person.
Hereafter, I shall describe the gift of land, which yields great fruit.
It is certain that there is no gift equal to the gift of land. Whether it be a house, a field, or even a portion of land,
it should be given after first providing a dwelling site that is pleasant to enjoy and free from reproach.
Having adorned the recipient with garments, flowers, and ointments,
and having fed him along with his servants and retinue to his heart's content,
one who gives at the time of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should say three times, "Let it be accepted with water."

When land has been thus bestowed with faith by those free from envy, they know that his reward lasts as long as that land endures. Having ascended to heaven, the giver of land rejoices for eternal years.
For the immovable and inexhaustible earth yields all desires. Whatever sin a man emaciated by his livelihood may commit,
he is liberated from it even by a gift of land the size of a cow’s ear.
Gold, silver, clothing, jewels, pearls, and wealth—
all these, O highly wise lady, are established within the gift of land. Those who, intent on the supreme welfare of their master, have cast away their lives and been slain in battle [attain them].

Those perfected beings destined for the world of Brahmā do not surpass the giver of land. He who gives land ploughed by the furrow, provided with seeds and fruit, or even a well and a shelter, shall have that gift fulfill all desires.
He who gives land with its crops fully ripened to the twice-born,
being liberated from all impurities, goes to the world of Śakra;
just as a mother nourishes her own son with her milk.
In this way, the earth, through all its fruits, causes the donor to prosper—
provided he causes a Brāhmaṇa who is endowed with good conduct, who has maintained the sacred fires, and who is pure in his vows,
to accept his own land; such a man does not go to the abode of Yama.
Just as the increase of the moon is seen day by day, so a gift bestowed upon land increases with every harvest. Just as seeds, when scattered upon the surface of the earth, sprout and grow.

In this way, desires acquired through the merit of the gift of land sprout forth. The ancestors dwelling in the world of the fathers and the deities stationed in heaven satisfy with enjoyments that person who gives the earth.
A mortal who bestows the earth obtains long life, freedom from disease, and supreme, abundant prosperity in the hereafter;
all this is the fruit of the gift of land that has been declared by me.
This eternal [teaching] should always be heard by faithful men.
Hereafter, I shall explain the gift of a daughter according to the prescribed rule;
thus, O Goddess, a daughter should be given away, whether she belongs to others or even to oneself.

Having first deliberated upon a maiden who is pure in her vows and conduct, endowed with noble lineage and beauty, and highly desired by the recipient for whom he intends to give her, and having reached a firm decision together with his kinsmen;
Having first constructed a house provided with female and male servants and attendants,
as well as household utensils and pure grain,
he gave that daughter, fully adorned, to a suitor who was worthy of her.

He should give her away according to the rule, with due ceremony and in the presence of the sacred fire; having thus provided for her livelihood and future prospects, he should establish them both in a virtuous household.
By giving his daughter in this manner, he gains the full merit of that gift.
After passing away, one shall be magnified in the heavenly world according to one's pleasure;

furthermore, upon rebirth, one shall obtain good fortune and the prosperity of one’s lineage. Likewise, O Goddess, by giving the gift of knowledge to one who is a worthy recipient, one attains these same rewards.
After death, a mortal shall obtain wisdom, growth, fortitude, and memory.
For him who imparts his own knowledge to a worthy disciple,
the fruit of that gift is said to be infinite, as previously described.
Furthermore, O lady of auspicious countenance, know that the imparting of sciences to the poor for a monetary fee is equal to a gift given by oneself;
thus have these great gifts been described to you, O beautiful one.
"O Great Goddess, for the sake of what you desire, what more do you wish to hear?
Umā said:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, how should [the gift] be given together with sesame seeds?"
O Maheśvarī,
tell me the fruit of each gift given and each deed performed.
O Goddess, listen with a concentrated mind as I describe to you the ritual procedure for the *tila-kalpa*.
Whether they be abundant or not, sesame seeds should especially be given. Sesame seeds are remembered as being pure, destroyers of sin, and highly meritorious.
Having thus collected pure sesame seeds according to one's own capacity and in accordance with justice, [one should proceed].
One should further prepare a heap of sesame seeds resembling a mountain, adorned with jewels—
whether large or small— and endowed with various substances,
including gold, silver, gems, pearls, and coral.
Having decorated it appropriately with banners, altars,
ornaments, and cloths, and equipped it with beds and seats—
especially on the full moon day of the month of Kārttika.
Having fed many worthy Brahmins according to the prescribed rules,
and having himself observed a fast while endowed with proper conduct and purity, he should circumambulate the heap of sesame seeds and give it away along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
Whether for one person or for many, he who desires prosperity should give;
O Goddess, the fruit of that gift is equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Or, having fashioned the shape of a cow on the ground using only sesame seeds—
Along with jewels and garments, it should be given by a man desiring the merit of the gift of a cow to one who is worthy; he obtains the fruit equivalent to that of gifting a cow.
[One should give] bowls filled with sesame seeds, together with gold and campaka flowers.
By giving water to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes a partaker of meritorious fruit.
In this same way, one who desires his own welfare should give gifts consisting of sesame seeds.
Listen further with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, to the manifold fruits of various kinds of giving.
By the gift of food, a man shall obtain strength, long life, and health; by the gift of water, a man shall obtain good fortune and the knowledge of flavors;
by the gift of clothing, a man shall obtain physical beauty and ornaments.
By giving a lamp, one obtains clarity of intellect, as well as luster and beauty;
furthermore, by giving an umbrella, one obtains the fruit of liberation from oppression by kings.
By the gift of male and female slaves, a man becomes a master of his laborers.

A man who gives various male and female slaves endowed with good qualities to one worthy of them shall obtain such servants after death; furthermore, by giving vehicles and mounts to one who deserves them,
he shall be freed from the affliction of diseases of the feet and become full of vigor.
He obtains a diverse and delightful vehicle and mount;
and by providing shelter to one who is worthy and desires it,
he shall obtain auspicious strength of wings during the rainy season and at night.
A man who constructs bridges, wells,
and tanks obtains long life, good fortune, and likewise auspicious prosperity after death. Furthermore, he who plants rows of trees provides shade, flowers, and fruit.
In the afterlife,
a man who builds a bridge for those crossing rivers in this world shall obtain merit and, having reached that state, be liberated from calamities.
A mortal who constantly practices the path shall again possess a continuous lineage;
being liberated from the defects of the body, he shall always be a founder of a spiritual tradition,
and filled with compassion, he shall always be a giver of medicines.
He shall be free from disease and especially long-lived. Furthermore, he who nourishes those who are protectorless— the wretched, the blind, and the lame—
obtains the fruit of merit after death and liberation from hardship.
The man who builds cow-pens for the gods, assembly halls, pavilions, and lodgings for monks,
always obtains auspicious fruit after death;
such a man shall attain various palatial dwellings and the splendor of celestial wings.
The man who constructs a beautiful cow-pen that is always provided with various kinds of food and drink of diverse forms and excellent qualities,
obtains a virtuous birth after death, as well as liberation from disease.
Thus, the donor and the performer shall obtain the fruit corresponding to the various kinds of substances given and the manner in which they were offered;
whatever fruit he obtains is exactly as it was performed and bestowed.
O Maheśvara,
O Lord of Gods, tell me this, for my curiosity regarding it is great. Listen now to the fruit of what is given and what is performed after death.
Or a gift endowed with the six qualities, according to rule, for one who is worthy;
a gift should be given by men according to their means,
[yielding] intelligence, longevity, health, noble lineage, fortune, and likewise spiritual attainment.

Divided sevenfold by means of its form, it certainly bears fruit as a human being. That which is given with the desire for a reward, thinking "this has been given; may this be mine," will result in that very thing, but nothing else whatsoever is obtained.
"O Goddess, the fruit is certain in the highest gift, while in the middling and lowest it is likewise;
O Umā,
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods, sacrifice is said to be the most distinguished."
O Maheśvara,
you ought to explain to me that which is both worldly and Vedic;
for the worship of the deities is indeed centered upon sacrifices.
Sacrifices are dependent upon the Vedas, and the Vedas are joined with the Brāhmaṇas. Know,
O beloved, that all this wealth— whether in heaven or on earth—
was created for the sake of sacrifice, out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.

Having understood this, O twice-born one, the performer of that rite together with his wife shall, through constant concentration on the Brahman-act, attain the worlds hereafter. That Brahman, O Goddess, is eternally established even within the Brāhmaṇas.

Therefore, when the entire sacrificial rite is performed by Brahmins according to the scriptures and through action prescribed by rule, it shall satisfy all the deities. Generally, both Brahmins and Kṣatriyas are remembered as being worthy of sacrifice.
It is the settled conclusion that sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma, as prescribed in the Vedas,
should be performed according to the rules by means of pure sacrificial materials and implements, by a sacrificer and officiating priests who are thoroughly purified.
When sacrifices are performed in this manner, there shall be satisfaction for the gods;
when the hosts of gods are satisfied, the sacrificer shall obtain the fruit of the sacrifice.
Furthermore, the gods, being gratified by sacrifices, cause the worlds to flourish.
O Goddess, the prosperity of both worlds is seen to be attained through sacrifices;
therefore, the sacrificer, having gone to heaven, rejoices together with the immortals. There is no gift equal to sacrifice, and there is no treasure equal to sacrifice.
O Goddess, the exposition of all dharmas was delivered with focused concentration at the sacrifice.
This is the worship performed by the sacrificer; now hear about another, worldly [form of] worship. Worldly festivals are performed for the purpose of honoring the gods.
O Goddess, he who, having purified the cow-pens, performs a festival, and being pure, duly offers sacrifices and oblations to the gods,
shall satisfy the deities and thereby attain dharma.
With various perfumes, garlands, excellent food, and incenses,
and with many hymns of praise, the disciplined men offered worship; likewise, with dances, instrumental music, songs, and other means that captivate the sight.
O Goddess, those men on earth who perform acts of veneration directed toward the worship of the gods—
they, being honored by that very act of devotion,
attain satisfaction just as the gods do in the triple heaven.

O Goddess, whether by humans or others who are pure, devoted to that goal, and intent on the practice of celibacy (*brahmacarya*), this fruit of dharma is produced; it is not achieved by mere praises accompanied by perfumes and garlands alone.
When they are well-honored in a pure place by those who are self-restrained and whose bodies are purified,
the gods indeed attain satisfaction when thus worshipped with devotion. —
Umā.
O Goddess, only by satisfying the gods does one attain dharma.
Indeed, the gods reside in Triviṣṭapa, yet they observe human conduct upon the earth.
Maheśvara—
"How shall they know the various [states]? You ought to explain that to me.
"I shall declare that to you, O beloved, as it is known by them:
the inner self (antarātman) is established within the bodies of living beings."
"Know yourself to be the supreme deity, O lady of auspicious gaze;
through the stability of the mind, the self perceives all that is auspicious and inauspicious. The gods are indeed the self; let them, with undistracted minds, know what has been done."
Through the mental composure of the virtuous, men indeed attain auspiciousness;
therefore, O beautiful one, there is the worship of the gods, likewise the worship of the ancestors,
sacrifices, religious duties, and the worship of gurus.

With pure bodies, endowed with virtuous conduct, absorbed in that [practice], and devoted to it—this is the certainty: that one must always remain thus established. By acting in this way, one who desires what is auspicious rejoices both in this world and in the next.
"Otherwise, O beloved, an action performed with the mind directed elsewhere does not bear fruit.
Umā said:
"But even without [directed] intent, O Goddess, an inauspicious act certainly bears fruit."
"O Lord, you ought to explain to me how the Pitṛmedha [sacrifice] is performed;
for all ancestors are worthy of worship and are the bestowers of all prosperity.
Thus spoke Maheśvara.

I shall now proclaim the Pitṛmedha (the rites for the ancestors) as it truly is; listen with a focused mind. I shall explain the proper place and time, the ritual procedure, and the auspicious and inauspicious results of that performance.
In all the worlds, the ancestors are worthy of worship, and they are the deities even of the gods.
Pure, stainless, and meritorious, they have taken refuge in the southern direction;
just as all creatures dwelling upon the earth await the rain,
so too, O lady of auspicious gaze, do the ancestors in this world await the Pitṛmedha sacrifice.
His sacred regions are Kurukṣetra, Gayā, the Gaṅgā, the Sarasvatī, Prabhāsa, and Puṣkara; what is given in these places yields great fruit.
So too do sacred fords, holy rivers, and secluded forests.
River sandbanks are praised as places for the *śrāddha* rite;
the months of Māgha and Prauṣṭhapada are honored for the performance of the *śrāddha*; and between the two fortnights, the dark fortnight is more highly esteemed than the bright fortnight.
On the new moon day, the thirteenth, the ninth,
and the first lunar days— on these dates, the ancestors are satisfied by what is given here. Also on the forenoon of the bright fortnight, at night, or on one's birthdays.
A wise man should not perform a *śrāddha* on even-numbered days. This honored time for the ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛmedha*) has been declared by me;
however, that time is also traditionally prescribed when one perceives a worthy Brahmin recipient.

Those twice-born who are excluded from the company at a meal (*apāṅkteya*) should be avoided; however, those who purify the company (*paṅktipāvana*) should be accepted. If one honors the most wicked at *śrāddha* rites, he shall go to hell.
[One should instead honor] those endowed with good conduct, Vedic learning, and noble lineage, who are accompanied by their wives and possessed of virtues.

Know, O auspicious lady, that those Brāhmaṇas who are learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) and of unpaired (odd) number are worthy for this purpose. A wise man should invite them either on the previous day or early in the morning;
thereafter, he should commence the performance of the *śrāddha* according to the prescribed rules.
Three things are purifying at a *śrāddha*: a daughter’s son, a *kutapa* blanket, and sesame seeds. Furthermore, three qualities are praised here: purity, freedom from anger, and lack of haste.
The wool of a *kutapa* blanket, *kuśa* grass, *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and honey [are also purifying].
Blue vegetables and the "elephant-shadow" (gajacchāyā) are pure for the performance of *śrāddha* rites. One should scatter sesame seeds of various colors all around there;
O beautiful one, that which is impure in the ancestral sacrifices (*pitṛyajña*) is purified by sesame seeds.
One should avoid from afar one wearing blue or saffron-colored garments, one with a pierced ear or a fresh wound, one with missing limbs, or one who is impure; likewise,
one should avoid cocks, pigs, a naked person, a eunuch, and a woman in her menses.
One should avoid iron, tin, and lead at the performance of *śrāddha* rites.
Here, the ancestors are gratified by meats, as well as by mung beans, black gram, and barley.
It is held that satisfaction lasts for six months with the meat of the hare and the common deer.
For one year, [the ancestors remain satisfied] by means of an oblation of cow's milk and milk-rice (*pāyasa*);

by the meat of the *vārdhrāṇasa* (a type of boar), their satisfaction lasts for twelve years; and when offered on the anniversary of the death of a father, the meat of the rhinoceros (*khaḍga*) leads to infinite satisfaction.
Milk-rice mixed with sesame and honey, equal in merit to the meat of a rhinoceros;
large *śapharī* fish, or a goat entirely red;
and *kālaśāka*—these are proclaimed as leading to infinity [of reward].
One should prepare food that is accompanied by cakes, contains meat, and is rich with fats;
having prepared that food, one should then honor the Brahmins,
who have had their beards groomed and bathed their heads, by seating them on seats in due order.
One should adorn these [ancestors] with fragrant perfumes, garlands, ornaments, and wreaths. When they have been adorned and are seated, one should present the offering of the rice-balls (*piṇḍa*).
Then, having spread out a layer of *darbha* grass, one should face the south.
Then, near that [fire], he should offer oblations to Agnibhīt and Svadhā;
likewise, near that, he should offer to Agni and Soma, and to the Pitṛs.
Then, facing south, he should place three rice-balls (piṇḍas) upon Darbha grass.
Keeping the sacred thread over the right shoulder and excluding the thumb, one should offer [the water] while pronouncing the names [of the ancestors].
By this procedure, what is given becomes inexhaustible for the ancestors. Thereafter, being self-controlled and pure, one should honor the Brahmins according to one's desire.

One should perform all that ritual action directed toward the Brahmins for the ancestors, accompanied by sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and the necessary materials, in such a way that those twice-born ones are satisfied; and one should perform it entirely preceded by the *vaiśvadeva* offering.
One should not shed tears there, nor chatter, nor whisper in private; having restrained both speech and body, one should commence the *śrāddha* rite.
Then, when the offering of the oblations has been performed, immediately thereafter those *piṇḍas* [should be disposed of].
A Brahmin, a fire, a goat, or a cow may eat [the middle piṇḍa], or he may throw it into the water.
Or, if he desires a son, he should have his wife eat the middle piṇḍa, saying:
"O ancestors, bestow a fetus—a boy adorned with a lotus-wreath."
Having raised those brahmins who have been satisfied, he should offer the remnants of the food to them.
Afterward, that man, together with his servants, should eat the remainder of it.
This eternal sacrifice to the ancestors has thus been declared in brief.
By this, the ancestors are satisfied and the performer obtains the fruit.
One should perform it day by day, or again month by month,
or twice a year, or four times, according to one's ability.
By means of the *pitṛmedha* rite, a human being becomes long-lived, healthy,
possessed of sons, endowed with many servants, and rich in abundant wealth and grain;
the giver of the *śrāddha* attains a stainless heaven of manifold wonders.
Resounding with throngs of *apsarases*, free from dust, and infinite—
those wise ones who, desiring prosperity, perform ancestral rites (*śrāddha*),
to them the ancestors will always grant prosperity and progeny.
The wise declare that the *śrāddha* is auspicious, conducive to fame, longevity, and heaven, destructive of enemies, and the sustainer of one's lineage; thus it is called *Umā*.
"O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, those creatures who have died on earth are born again quickly among various species by the power of their karma;
how is it, then, that they remain there like gods, being called 'fathers'?"
What is the location of the ancestors? How do they consume the funeral cakes (*piṇḍas*)?
When food is given, how does nourishment come about for those who have died?
Nārada:
"O Blessed One, you ought to sever this doubt that has arisen within me;
for while Rudrāṇī was asking this, which is contradictory [to what she previously said], the assembly was greatly agitated,
O Maheśvara."
Everyone became joyful, for they were eager to hear that supreme [teaching]. "O Goddess, it is fitting that you have had this doubt; listen, O auspicious one, to the truth.
It is the most secret of secrets, the most essential of all essentials."
O Goddess, O beloved, as it is with the hosts of gods, so it is with the hosts of ancestors;
O auspicious one, all the hosts of ancestors reside in the southern direction. Whatever worship is performed here by humans on behalf of the *pretas*, [it reaches them].
By that, the ancestors are satisfied, for they are remembered as *pitṛ*s, not as *preta*s; just as the gods rejoice in the northern region through sacrificial rites,
so too do they find satisfaction in various sacrifices in the southern region.

Action is performed in two ways, based upon *havya* (offerings to the gods) and *kavya* (offerings to the ancestors). Of these two, the performance of *havya* nourishes the gods, while *kavya* nourishes the ancestors.
The rite of *havya* is prescribed to be performed counter-clockwise with auspicious materials.
The *kavya* offerings are also prescribed to be made counter-clockwise (*apasavya*) along with inauspicious items;
together with the gods, asuras, and gandharvas, they worship the ancestors,
and being nourished by the *śrāddha* rites, they in turn nourish them.
If one performs a ritual action without first having offered oblations to the ancestors, the *rakṣasas* and *piśācas* will consume its fruit. Therefore,
the performance of offerings to the gods (*havya*) and the ancestors (*kavya*) must be carried out by men on this earth.

Human birth is indeed the field for action; it is not found elsewhere. Through *kavya* (offerings to ancestors), progeny is seen; through *havya* (offerings to gods), various kinds of prosperity arise.
Umā.
"Thus, O Goddess, I have told you this eternal secret of the gods. O Lord Maheśvara, I now wish to hear about the dharma of one who has thus acted."
"You ought to explain to me the measure of the measures of fruits. O Goddess, O beautiful lady, hear now the calculation of the measure of giving:
whatever is the essence of a person in this world, that is considered the highest form of giving."
They say that the method for all gifts is the same on this beautiful earth:
a *prastha* is the essence for a poor man, while a hundred crores is the essence for one possessing a hundred million. By giving even that *prastha*-essence, one obtains a great reward.
One who gives ten million *koṭis* of *sāra* coins shall obtain a great reward;
both of these are considered equal in their great fruit. However, that which is possible within the enjoyment of virtue, wealth, and desire is considered middling.
But that gift which is far inferior to one's own wealth is considered the lowest.
Listen, O Goddess, to the fivefold determination of the fruit of what has been given:
it is infinite, great, equal, inferior, and sinful.
I shall describe their distinctions; listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess.
The giving of that which is difficult to relinquish to a worthy recipient is said to be infinite.
A gift endowed with six qualities is designated as "great."
A gift given according to one's faith and according to what is appropriate is said to be equal. However, a gift that is deficient in its qualities is remembered as being inferior.
They say that a gift becomes a transgression when there is a reversal of the six qualities.
They know that the fruit of an infinite gift is a long time in the world of the gods;
likewise, a great gift is honored in the heavenly world,
while a gift from one who is equal brings about human enjoyment.
"O Umā, they say that a gift devoid of ritual action is fruitless in this auspicious world; or else, it may attain its fruition in the lands of the Mlecchas."
After death, due to an unwholesome gift, one may go to hell or among the animals. [Objection: Maheśvara, how could there even be a wholesome fruit from an unwholesome gift?
With a mind that is pure in its true essence and preceded by compassion,
one shall obtain the fruit of all gifts by giving them with love.
Know this, O fair-eyed one, to be the secret of all gifts.
Listen also to other deeds performed by the virtuous:
pleasure groves, temples for the gods, bridges, wells,
cow-pens, tanks, assembly halls, and halls of all kinds.

He should provide dwellings for mendicants, as well as water, fodder, and grass; he should provide medicine for the sick and food for the destitute; he should perform the funeral rites for the helpless dead and keep the sacred fords and roads clean.
Providing relief from calamities for all according to one's own capacity—
all this, in brief, is recorded in tradition as the duty of dharma.
That should be performed by a person according to their ability and with faith, O auspicious lady.
After death, one shall obtain merit; there is no doubt in this matter. A man shall obtain beauty, good fortune, health, strength, and happiness—Umā.
Whether in heaven or even among humans, he is indeed nourished by those various [virtues].
O Blessed One, Lord of the World-Protectors, how many divisions does Dharma have? It is seen being practiced by the virtuous; you should explain that to me.
Maheśvara said:
"Listen, O Goddess, to the summaries regarding the diversity amidst the complexities of dharma. Many kinds of dharmas have been heard in the world, originating from the mouth of the Vedas."

The dharma of memory and the dharma of conduct are desired by the virtuous in many ways; likewise, regional dharmas, family dharmas, caste dharmas, and the dharmas of guilds are seen, O beautiful one.
Due to differences in body and time, the duty of distress (āpaddharma) is observed;
this diversity of dharma is established by those dwelling in the world. In each particular case, the fruit of dharma is intended accordingly.
When there is a conjunction of its causes, a person performing [the action] shall obtain the fruit;
otherwise, one who is unworthy and merely instructs [others] shall not obtain merit.
Thus, by performing [the action], a person obtains the various fruits of dharma.
The *śrauta* and *smārta* [rites] are called the primary (*prākṛta*) dharma among all dharmas. Thus, O Umā, everything has been told to you; what more do you wish to hear?
"O Blessed One, Lord of all beings, Destroyer of Tripura, Śaṅkara, O Bestower of boons! I have heard of the suffering of evildoers in the world of Yama;
O God, I now wish to hear about the fate of men who have performed virtuous deeds."
O Maheśvara, how do they enjoy the worlds in the heavenly realm?
What kind of worlds have been described for those men who perform virtuous deeds?
O Maheśvara!
"Tell me this, O Lord of Gods, for I have a great curiosity to hear it.
"Listen, O auspicious one, O beautiful lady, to all that you desire to know. There are various worlds of merit that have become inaccessible due to the failure to perform [prescribed] actions."
Indeed, surrounding Meru, which is composed of gold, on every side in all directions—
namely Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, the Northern Kurus,
and the regions such as Jambūvana— these are like heavens, free from [the fruits of] karma.
In those [abodes], enjoyments appear spontaneously from every direction;
each measures one thousand yojanas in extent,
and there, on all sides, trees are laden with flowers and fruits at all times.
With their garments and ornaments clinging to them, all were like gold; there, the bees and the birds, resembling coral and jewels,
adorned those [trees] with their various and charming warblings.
The delightful lotus ponds there are covered with groves of water-lilies,
and breezes of divine fragrance, bringing happiness, blow there constantly.
All [the beings] there wear unfading garlands and are clothed in stainless garments.
Thus, O Goddess, there are many kinds of delightful enjoyments in heaven;
both women and men, all of whom have performed meritorious deeds,
take pleasure there together, filled with the passion of desire.
Adorned with divine ornaments and endowed with celestial fragrances,
they were charming, highly fortunate, and all wore elegant earrings;
such were the mortal women who had gone there, lovely to behold.
Always endowed with various states of being and established in youth,
they were lovely, full of desire, skilled in the arts of love, and graceful; agreeable to the mind and sweet, they were prepared for the enjoyment of those who seek pleasure.
Just as women arise in the heavenly world,
so too do such women and men here take delight in one another with their senses composed and their bodies refined by enjoyment.
"O beloved, let there be only the two qualities of desire and joy, and no others such as anger;
O beautiful one, there shall be neither hunger nor thirst, nor any bodily afflictions here. It is delightful on all sides and endowed with the flowers of every season."

For as long as the fruit of their merit lasts, they remain there together; endowed with uninterrupted enjoyments, the inhabitants of heaven take their delight. Having enjoyed pleasures there according to their fitness, [they fall] again upon the exhaustion of their merit.
O beloved, as they are being born, they suddenly perish along with their bodies;
fallen from the heavenly world, they are born again among humans,
and by the remainder of their former merit, they are born into distinguished circumstances.
13,134.057d@015_3683 This path to heaven has been described to you, O beautiful lady, as you asked.
13,134.057d@015_3684 Hereafter, O beloved, hear of the eight stages that result from action, 13,134.057d@015_3685 which are endowed with enjoyment, meritorious, and increasingly exalted.
Vidyādharas, Kiṃpuruṣas, Yakṣas, Gandharvas, and Kiṃnaras;
Apsarases, Dānavas, and Devas are mentioned in their respective order.
In those places, living beings who have performed meritorious deeds are born.
Furthermore, those worlds of theirs are remembered as being comparable to the heavenly realm;
there they enjoy pleasures and take delight just like those in heaven,
endowed with beauty, vitality, and strength, and likewise possessed of long lifespans.
The undertaking of all their activities is seen among humans alone;
yet there is a superhuman wonder wrought by the power of weapons and illusions,
for aging, birth, and death are seen within those very realms.
O beautiful lady, both virtues and faults exist here; likewise, traveling through the sky,
invisibility, all types of strength, and long life—
these qualities arise for them from the excellence of their ascetic penance.
The progression to the world of the gods is ordained for them alone;
for the world of the gods is not like that, as the gods are remembered as being superior to it. Therein exists enjoyment beyond description and immortality.
The constant journeying in celestial chariots, attended by throngs of Apsarases—
such other deeds as these distinguish him from the gods;
all this activity within the world of the gods is directly perceptible to you.
Therefore, O auspicious Goddess Umā, I shall not describe it further, for you already know it; indeed,
that entire supreme state is attained solely through one's own meritorious deeds.
While humans themselves are alive, it is not known whether their destiny is [good] or not;
one cannot say, "This person, while living, has a fortunate destiny," or "That person, while living, shares in an unfortunate one.
Thus says Maheśvara.
"I wish to hear this; you ought to explain it to me.
"I shall declare that to you, as it exists for those who live.
"In this world, living beings are of two kinds, depending on whether they resort to the divine or the demonic."
Know those who are hostile in thought, deed, or speech to be such asuras; they are mortals whose abode is hell.
Those who are possessed by passion and hatred, shameless and devoid of modesty—[know them to be asuras].
Men who are possessed of pride and egoism go to hell; likewise, those who are nihilists, deceitful, terrible, and who cause suffering to others,
as well as those whose conduct follows their own whims, go to hell.

But he who is of ill-disposed mind, fickle-hearted, and devoid of form; the fool who delights only in his genitals and belly—he, the lowest of men, goes to hell. Those who are constantly fond of meat and drink, harsh, and of base conduct—
Know such beings to be asuras; they all have their abode in hell— those who constantly delight in violence, who are merciless in the destruction of living beings,
who are averse to their own duty, and who covet the property of others.
Know that those men who are possessed by strife and envy, who are devoted to vulgar pleasures,
who are filled with arrogance and conceit, and who are fools excluded from the truth— such are the asuras destined for hell.
Those men who constantly harbor hatred toward the Vedas are destined for the abode of hell;
those who, out of delusion, always speak falsehoods and harsh words,
being ungrateful, treacherous, and terrible, become inhabitants of hell.
For they are violent, thieves, rogues, and violators of others' wives;
they perform base deeds, are devoid of purity and auspicious rites, hate the sacred scriptures, are sinful, and corrupt the conduct of the world.
Those who behave in such a manner while living as inhabitants of hell,
who cause terror to the world, and others such as beasts, reptiles,
and thorny, harsh trees— know them to be asuras.
But listen with a concentrated mind, O Goddess, to those who belong to the faction of the gods:
know that those men who are always favorable through their thoughts, words, and deeds— such immortals are they who go to heaven.
Those men who, devoted to purity and straightforwardness, do not seize the property of others for their own sake;
who are equal toward all beings; and who do not speak untruth out of fear or for the sake of livelihood—they go to heaven.
Those men who always speak the truth go to heaven;
they are righteous, endowed with purity, bright, and sweet-spoken. Those men do not even mentally desire what ought not to be done; they go to heaven.
Even those who are poor, when asked with affection, give whatever little they have; such men go to heaven. They are believers, devoted to auspiciousness, and always serve their elders.
Those men who are constantly devoted to meritorious deeds go to heaven;
they regard the suffering of others as their own suffering,
and those men go to heaven because they assist others according to their ability.
Those men who observe vows and are charitable by nature, who are pleasant in their conduct, upright, and ever gentle, go to heaven;
they are devoted to the service of their teachers and are worshippers of the gods and Brahmins.
Those men who are grateful and accomplished in learning go to heaven;
those who have conquered their senses, conquered their anger, and conquered pride, intoxication, and greed;
and those who are free from avarice and envy—those men go to heaven.
Free from possessiveness and free from egoism, compassionate toward their own kin, and always sympathetic toward the wretched— those men go to heaven.
One's state in the world beyond is inferred from one's conduct in this life.
Men of such a kind who live in this world go to heaven; furthermore,
whatever else in the world brings benefit to living beings— be it cattle or trees— that acts for the welfare of all creatures.
"Know them, O fair-faced one, to be such as stand on the side of the gods;
for in this world, everything— both stationary and moving— is composed of the auspicious and the inauspicious," said Umā.
"O beloved, they say that the divine is auspicious, while the demonic is indeed inauspicious.
O Blessed One, when certain humans have arrived at the time of death,
by what means of relinquishing life may they attain their welfare in the hereafter?"
Maheśvara said:
"Come now, O Goddess, I shall tell you; listen with a concentrated mind.
Death in this world is of two kinds: that which occurs through natural causes and that which results from effort."

Neither their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor that which arises from effort (*yatnaja*), nor that which originates from causes (*kāraṇodbhava*) [is the cause]. O Goddess, O beautiful one, hear the procedure for both of these.
For a body that is either healthy or unhealthy, that which arises from effort is traditionally held to be of two kinds.
Death resulting from effort (*yatnaja*) consists of self-surrender through the desire to die;
in that case, the causes are a diseased body, old age, or illness,
as well as setting out on the Great Journey (*mahāprasthāna*) or fasting unto death (*prāyopaveśana*).
Plunging into water, entering fire, and entering a consecrated fire-altar—
thus, O beautiful one, the fourfold abandonment of the self by those desiring death has been declared. Listen now to the procedure for these, according to their proper sequence.
Having lived for a long time in the householder stage, engaged in his own duty according to the prescribed rules,
and having attained freedom from debt therein, he may, when old or even afflicted by disease,
demonstrate his own infirmity and, having obtained the permission of all [his dependents].
Having made arrangements for his kinsmen and the maintenance of their duties,
and having duly performed acts of charity for the sake of his own religious merit,
he took leave of all the people, speaking to them with sweet words.
Having covered himself with a new, unwashed garment and bound it with a rope of *kuśa* grass,
and having touched water and made a formal vow preceded by firm resolve,
he should then leave the village and thereafter act as he desires.
If one should desire the Great Departure, one should set out toward the northern direction; having become abstinent from food until the release of the vital breath,
one should lie down when movement ceases and, with the mind fixed on that alone, relinquish the life-force.

In this way, he attains the stainless worlds of those who have performed meritorious deeds. If a man should desire to fast unto death (*prāyopaveśana*), he should do so according to that very same rule; he should lie down without food in a most excellent and most holy place.
Remaining pure until the end of life, performing acts of charity according to one's ability,
and remembering Hari while giving up the vital breaths— this is the eternal dharma. Having thus abandoned the body, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
O auspicious lady, if one should desire to enter the fire, one should do so according to that very same rite:
having constructed a funeral pyre made of wood either in a sacred field or by rivers,
and having paid homage to the deities and circumambulated the fire.
Having become pure and resolute, he should enter the bed of fire;
he too shall attain, according to the rule, the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds. O auspicious lady, if he should desire immersion in water, he should do so by that very same rite.

Remembering his own deeds, he should immerse himself in that most meritorious and renowned sacred ford; by that very act, he attains the worlds of the merit-makers through the power of nature. Next, hear in truth about the renunciation of one whose body is healthy.
It is ordained for the sake of protection, because of the duty to guard the subjects of a Kṣatriya;
for the sake of the warriors' master's sustenance; for the sake of the preceptor and for celibate students;
for the sake of cows and Brāhmaṇas; for the sake of the village; and for the sake of all people.

Or, if his subjects are oppressed by wicked kings, one who desires to liberate them for the sake of protecting his own kingdom should sacrifice his life on the path of battle according to the prescribed rule; well-armored, resolute, and never turning his back, he should enter the fray.
Thus, a king who has died is immediately honored in the heavenly world;
indeed, no such happy destiny exists for a kṣatriya more particularly than this.
Or, when the master’s work has presented itself, a servant may [die] for the sake of his master’s sustenance.
Providing assistance there without regard for his own life,
he who would sacrifice his life for the sake of his master goes to the meritorious worlds;
he is envied by the hosts of gods— of this there is no doubt.

In this way, one may sacrifice the body for the sake of cows and Brahmins, or for the sake of the distressed; such a person also attains merit through his regard for compassion. Thus have these paths regarding the renunciation of life been fully described.
If one should abandon the body out of desire, anger, fear, or delusion,
he goes to an eternal hell because of the act of killing his own self;
for death occurs through its own nature, and not by the will of the self.

Listen to me regarding the rites for the deceased according to the prescribed rule: even there, the abandonment of delusion is superior to the abandonment of consciousness. One should lay the body of a dying man upon the earth.
One should immediately cover the lifeless body with a cloth,
O beautiful lady; having adorned it with garlands, perfumes, and gold,
one should burn the deceased in the funeral fire upon a pyre in the southern part of the cremation ground.
Alternatively, one may cast the lifeless body upon the ground during the daytime,
during the bright fortnight, and specifically during the northern course of the sun;
these are recommended for those about to die, while the opposite is censured.
The *audaka* and *aṣṭakā* śrāddhas have been performed many times by many people;
that shall become a source of nourishment for the deceased and a blessing in the next world.
All this has been declared by me for the benefit of human beings.
O Umā,
O God of gods, salutations be unto you, O Śaṅkara, destroyer of Time! By your grace, I have heard the various dharmas throughout the worlds.

I wish to hear that Dharma which is distinguished above all dharmas— eternal, constant, and imperishable— for my mind is bewildered in this regard. Some twice-born ones praise liberation, while others praise the fruit of sacrifice.
Some [praise] the forest-dweller’s stage, some the householder’s stage of life;
some rely upon the duties of kingship, and some upon the study of the Vedas; some praise the stage of celibacy, and some rely upon the restraint of speech.
Some, by serving their mother and father, have gone to heaven;
another is glorified in the celestial realm through non-violence and truth. Some, slain while facing the enemy in battle, have gone to the third heaven.
Some, perfected through the vow of gleaning, have taken their stand on the path to heaven; others, endowed with uprightness, though slain by dishonest people,
remain upright and, being pure in soul, are established upon the back of the firmament.

Thus, by these many various well-guarded gateways to the Dharma in the world, my mind too has been stirred, like a streak of cloud by the wind. Regarding this point of doubt, that which cuts through doubt—
"O Lord of Gods, speak these words characterized by definitive knowledge," thus was Mahādeva,
the wielder of the Pināka bow, questioned by the Goddess herself.
Maheśvara spoke these sweet words, subtle and concerning the inner self:
"O highly fortunate lady, you desire to hear the definitive conclusion according to right reasoning."
This very thing is distinguished for you, O beloved, that you ask me this:
Dharma is ordained everywhere as having the heavenly world as its fruit;
for Dharma, which has many doors, there is no action here that is fruitless.
Whichever object a person reaches a definitive conclusion regarding,
that alone they recognize, and no other phenomenon, O lady of pure smiles. Listen, O Goddess, in brief, to this unsurpassed knowledge of liberation.
For this is the most distinguished, secret, and imperishable [truth] among all dharmas. O Goddess, there is nothing higher than liberation; liberation alone is the supreme goal.
The wise know that it is absolute happiness, most excellent, and irreversible.
O Goddess, here there is neither old age nor death, nor grief, nor even suffering;
O Goddess, that is the supreme bliss, unsurpassed and inconceivable.
The wise know the knowledge of liberation to be the highest among all forms of knowledge.
The sages and the hosts of gods proclaim that supreme state,
which is eternal, imperishable, unshakeable, ageless, constant, and auspicious.
Wise men desire that state, which is coveted by both gods and asuras.

The three aims of life— though they involve suffering and the like, are difficult to master, are subject to destruction, and are mutually contradictory— are said to be happiness when they are constantly pursued together. Therefore, liberation is indeed superior to the three aims of life.
O lady of auspicious marks, hear now this path to that liberation.
This cycle of existence, from Brahmā down to the stationary beings,
proceeds, joined with the defects of grief, disease, and old age, as well as death.
Just as clusters of celestial lights repeatedly appear and disappear in the sky,
so too do all living beings repeatedly return within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*). In that regard, liberation from the wheel of *saṃsāra* is seen through knowledge.

The knowledge of the reality of the inner self is designated as "gnosis" (*jñāna*). I shall duly explain the means of acquiring that gnosis, as well as the conduct of the knower; listen with a single-minded focus to this truth.
Whether he was previously a Brāhmaṇa or a Kṣatriya living at home,
once he has attained freedom from all debts, he should then renounce those domestic ties;
having thus abandoned the householder's state, he should resolutely take refuge in the forest.
Commanded by his guru, he should undergo initiation in the forest according to the prescribed rules.
Having received initiation in accordance with the law, he should maintain his own conduct. Diligent, he should also receive from his teachers the knowledge of liberation.
Furthermore, liberation is traditionally said to be twofold: Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
The knowledge of the twenty-five principles is designated as Sāṃkhya;
according to the determination of the Yoga scripture, [liberation consists of] sovereignty and union with the divine.

One who has become a disciple should hear one of these two types of knowledge; it should not be taught by a teacher out of affection to anyone who is not shaven-headed, nor one who does not wear ochre robes, nor one who has not resided [as a student] for a year.
Furthermore, Sāṃkhya and Yoga should not be taught by a teacher out of mere affection.

The sage should always endure cold, heat, joy, and other such opposites with equanimity; through knowledge and meditative concentration, he should become invincible to hunger and thirst. He should not undertake any other activity without having informed his own teacher.
He should always remain like a shadow, never abandoning his guru;
he should withdraw his senses from their appropriate objects,
abandon the knots born of mental constructions, and always be intent on meditation.
A water-pot, a skin, a cushion, an umbrella, a staff, sandals,
and a garment— one should not establish ownership over these things for oneself.
One should rise before the teacher and lie down after him.
One should not go even for a necessary purpose without having obtained permission from her husband.
Twice a day, at the two twilights, he should perform ablutions with a bathing cloth;
eating only once a day was ordained for him by the ascetics of old.
One should accept alms from everywhere and constantly reflect upon them at night;
even when a cause for anger arises, one should never become angry. Celibacy, dwelling in the forest, purity, and restraint of the senses [are required].
Compassion toward all beings is his eternal duty;
freed from all sins, moderate in diet, and having conquered his senses,
he becomes disciplined in the self and attains supreme wisdom that destroys evil.
When one does not commit any harmful act toward any living being by deed, thought, or word, then one attains Brahman—
free from envy, free from egoism, and liberated from all bonds.
One attains the state of Brahman, reaching which one does not return;
having abandoned both truth and untruth, grief and joy, fear and fearlessness,
and having relinquished the pleasant and the unpleasant, one becomes fit for becoming Brahman.
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, free from the pairs of opposites, and devoid of envy;
with sorrow, fear, and affliction gone, he attains the unsurpassed state.
Equal toward blame and praise, observing silence, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same.
He who is impartial toward both enemy and friend attains Nirvāṇa.
One whose conduct is thus disciplined, who is devoted to that [practice], and who contemplates the inner self,
is a Great Lord (Maheśvara).
By that very practice of knowledge, one attains the supreme goal. For a person whose mind is undisturbed within this circle of saṃsāra,
there is no attainment of nirvāṇa amidst the sufferings of grief, disease, and old age.

Therefore, I shall fully declare to you that knowledge which produces detachment and establishes the mind, for it is indeed the root of immortality. There are thousands of occasions for sorrow and hundreds of occasions for fear.
Day after day, these afflictions enter the fool, but not the wise man.
When wealth is lost, or when a wife, a son, or a father has died, one who broods, "Oh, what misery! enters the domain of grief.
One should not dwell upon those qualities belonging to things that have already passed away;
for one who disregards them, the bond of grief perishes,
arising from the encounter with the undesirable and the separation from the beloved.
Those of small intelligence are joined with mental sufferings. He who grieves over what is dead, or lost, or past,
is joined with torment, yet that [past] does not return to him.

But once human birth has arisen here, from the moment of conception, a person encounters various kinds of both sufferings and pleasures. If one of these two paths should incline toward him, [he follows it].

Having attained happiness, one should not exult; having encountered suffering, one should not be distressed. One should perceive the defects in that wherein affection arises, so that one may quickly become dispassionate toward what is undesirable.
Just as two logs might come together in the great ocean and,
having met, drift apart, so too is the meeting with kinsmen;
having appeared from the unseen, they have once again gone back to the unseen.
One should not feel attachment there, for separation from them is certain.
Family, wife, children, the body, and the accumulation of wealth—all these belong to others and are impermanent; what is one's own? Only one’s good and evil deeds.
Beings who are attached to children, wives, and family members sink down,
like aged great elephants submerged in the mud-ocean of a lake.
[One has had] thousands of mothers and fathers, and hundreds of sons and wives.

The incalculable [aeons] that have passed, and likewise those yet to come— there is no need for me to act toward them, nor do they have any need to act toward me. Seeing that which is past as not past, one is not deluded.
When physical or mental suffering has arisen,
one should not dwell upon that which cannot be remedied even with effort; for whatever causes grief, fear, or indeed suffering, [one should abandon it].
One should abandon even a single limb from which effort originates.
Youth, beauty, life, a collection of jewels, sovereignty, and health are impermanent; a wise person should not be deluded by them.
There is no absolute happiness even for Śakra in the triple heaven (triviṣṭapa);
even there, suffering is very great and happiness is but slight.
One does not experience suffering eternally, nor does one experience happiness eternally.
After happiness comes suffering; after suffering comes happiness.
All accumulations end in depletion; all elevations end in a fall. Unions end in separation, and life ends in death.
Having personally witnessed through direct experience both rises and falls,
one should resolve that everything is indeed impermanent and unsatisfactory;
there is suffering in the acquisition of wealth, and suffering in the protection of what has been acquired.
There is suffering in its loss, suffering in its expenditure; fie on wealth, that vessel of misery! Five enemies constantly strike down a man who possesses wealth:
kings, thieves, heirs, living beings, and even the decay [of the things themselves].
Know for certain that wealth alone is the root of misfortune.
For misfortunes do not afflict a man who is devoid of wealth. The acquisition of wealth is great suffering; poverty is the supreme happiness.
For in the misfortunes of wealth, suffering is indeed inevitable; by the acquisition of riches, no satisfaction of craving is found. Having gained more, it increases further, like a fire with fuel.

Even after conquering the entire earth, girdled by the four oceans, he undoubtedly desires to conquer the further shore of those very oceans. Enough with worldly acquisition here; for acquisition is fraught with defects.
O Goddess, even a silkworm is bound by its own grasping; likewise,
a king who rules the entire earth under a single umbrella must nevertheless dwell within but one kingdom.

In that kingdom, he presides over only a single city; in that city, there shall be only one house as his residence. There shall be only one foundation, and even within that house, it is his dwelling alone.

In a dwelling where one lies down at night and dissolves into sleep, only half of that bed belongs to the man; half is ordained for the woman. Therefore, by this very circumstance, he is joined with her only in a very small measure.
The foolish person, utterly deluded, perceives everything as "mine. Yet, among all these enjoyments, his actual need is but slight;
the sustenance of all embodied beings could be maintained with a mere *prastha* of rice.
Then there is an even greater portion leading to suffering and downfall.
There is no suffering equal to craving; there is no happiness equal to renunciation. Having abandoned all desires, one is fit for becoming Brahman.

That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, which does not decay even as one decays, that disease which ends only with life— happiness belongs to him who renounces that craving. Desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of the objects of desire.
Like a fire fed by oblations, it increases all the more;
through the failure to obtain desires here, the wise man abandons them.
The fire of desire is fierce, its fuel being toil and its kindling-wood thirst.

Through delusion regarding the objects of the senses, people cook up unwholesome states. Seeing that the rice and barley on earth, gold, cattle, and women are not enough for even one person, one does not become deluded.
Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine happiness there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the happiness that comes from the exhaustion of craving. A wise person should never engage the senses in the objects of the senses.
Having restrained the senses, with the mind as the sixth, one should constantly yoke them to the Self. By the outward discharge of the senses, one undoubtedly incurs fault;
but by fully restraining them, one shall thereafter attain perfection.
The wise man who attains mastery over the six [senses] when they are joined with the self shall not be joined with sins nor with misfortunes. The wise man, ever vigilant, should guard his senses.
When these [faculties] are not guarded, a man quickly goes to hell;
for within the heart there is a variegated desire, born from an accumulation of delusion,
with ignorance as its deep-rooted foundation and the urge to act as its irrigation.
With anger and greed as its great trunk, possessing the essence of past misdeeds,
with intense exertion as its branches, sorrow as its flowers, and fear as its sprouts,
it is rich with the leaves of various volitions and nourished by negligence.

Fanned on all sides by great thirsts, that tree born of desire grows ever higher for one of unrefined wisdom; it does not grow at all in one who knows reality, or if it has grown, it is cut down once more.

What delight can there be in the enjoyments of desire, which involve arduous means, are impermanent, devoid of essence, and unstable; which are suffering from the start and end in misery? For by him who has seen through a single year, desire has been experienced but once.
By him this entire world, which is subject to recurrence, has been seen;
the enjoyments experienced by that man become like dreams.
What delight can there be in sensual pleasures, which are equal to the enjoyment of a dream?
When the sense faculties are decaying and life itself is being cut short,
and while death stands before one, what happiness can there be for one who perceives these evils,
as they are constantly tormented by physical and mental diseases?

O beloved, what happiness can there be for a man who has not accomplished his purpose— he who is merely amassing wealth while remaining unsatiated in his desires? Death seizes him and departs, just as a tiger in the forest seizes its prey.
Constantly assailed by the sufferings of birth, death, and old age,
and being cooked within the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), O Umā, people do not tremble at their sins.
"By what means, O Blessed One, can old age and death be turned away for mortals? If this exists, tell it to me without delay—
whether by very great austerity, or by ritual action, or by sacred learning."
"O Maheśvara,
by what means, even through the application of elixirs (*rasāyana*), can one transcend old age and death?
O highly fortunate one, there is no such thing as the reversal of old age and death."
O beautiful lady, know that in all the worlds, there is nothing other than liberation;
embodied beings do not transcend death through wealth, nor through sovereignty, nor even through fierce asceticism, except by means of liberation.
Even with a thousand horse-sacrifices and a hundred *vājapeya* sacrifices,
people do not transcend old age and death without the attainment of *nirvāṇa*. Likewise, sovereignty, wealth, grain, learning, gain, and asceticism [do not avail].
Even those who employ elixirs of rejuvenation do not cross over old age and death;
nor do those devoted to charity, sacrifice, austerity, and virtuous conduct, nor even those who know the elixirs,
nor those intent on the private recitation of the Vedas— none of them cross over old age and death.

Time brings gods, dānavas, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, uragas, and rākṣasas under its own control; there is nothing that is beyond the reach of Time. For days do not turn back, nor months, nor again nights.
He enters this path that is eternal, constant, and imperishable;
it flows on like the currents of rivers, never turning back,
continuously taking away the life of mortals through days and nights.
Exhausting the inexhaustible life of all living beings,
this sun indeed sets and rises again and again;
when that night has passed, one's lifespan becomes even more diminished.
Like a fish in shallow water, what indeed is his state of childhood? For death is certain and inevitable for the body;
even while standing still for a moment, everyone again falls under the power of Time.
If all embodied beings were neither to die nor to decay,
and if no misfortune or sorrow ever befell living creatures anywhere,
Time would remain vigilant among heedless beings.
One who has reached the end of time while being heedless is not liberated.
One should do today what is to be done tomorrow, and in the forenoon what belongs to the afternoon.
For who knows when death will not look upon him?
"I shall do this during the rains; I shall do that during the summer and spring"—thus the fool thinks, not perceiving the obstacle.
"May this be mine, may that be mine"—such is the mind of men.
While their desires remain unfulfilled, beings are carried toward death; bound by the noose of time and decaying day after day,
what confidence can living beings have in a path upon which they are constantly wandering?
One should be devoted to righteousness while still young, for life is indeed without cause;
for just as ripe fruits are always in danger of falling,
what use has a mortal for those wives, sons, enjoyments, and even dear things?
Having abandoned everything in a single day, one indeed falls under the power of death. Observing those being born and likewise those dying,
if a man feels no sense of urgency, he is indeed equal to a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
For one who is subject to destruction and whose life is unstable,
what is the use of kinsmen or the company of friends, since he must depart, leaving everything behind?
Having gone in an instant, it does not return;
for one who thus constantly contemplates the impermanence of all things,
a perpetual sense of renunciation arises, which precedes the attainment of Nirvāṇa.
Through that agitation, a further reflection arises within him;
through reflection, detachment toward everything then arises in him. Through detachment, O auspicious one, human beings attain supreme peace.
"O Goddess, dispassion (*vairāgya*) is proclaimed to be the secret doctrine (*upaniṣad*) of liberation. O Goddess, this speech which generates dispassion has been told to you by Maheśvara."
Having reflected upon all this, those who seek liberation are indeed released.
O lady of pure smiles, I shall proclaim to you the knowledge of Sāṃkhya exactly as it is—
that knowledge by knowing which a mortal no longer enters into cycles of rebirth.
Those Sāṃkhyas, who are experts in renunciation, are liberated by knowledge alone. The Sāṃkhyas declare that severe bodily austerity is useless;
their knowledge is traditionally defined as the knowledge of the twenty-five principles.

The root-nature is the unmanifest; from the unmanifest, the Great One (mahat) is born. From the Great One arose the ego (ahaṃkāra), and from that, the five subtle elements (tanmātra). Furthermore, the eleven sense organs arise from the subtle elements.

From these, the five elements arise; such is the compendium of the field (*kṣetra*). This field is held to be a compendium of twenty-four [principles], while they say it consists of twenty-five by including the *puruṣa* here.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities arise from Prakṛti. By means of these qualities born of her own self, Prakṛti creates the entire world.
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate [of the body], consciousness, and fortitude—[these are her forms].
These modifications of primordial nature (prakṛti) are to be understood by the wise;
I shall explain in detail their characteristics and their individual distinctions from the very beginning— listen to this exposition of mine.

Eternal, one, atomic, pervasive, devoid of action, and causeless; ungraspable by all the senses—this is the characteristic of the Unmanifest (avyakta). The Unmanifest is Nature (prakṛti), the Root, the Primal Matter (pradhāna), the Womb, and the Imperishable.

The names of the Unmanifest itself are expressed by synonymous words; because of its subtlety, it is indefinable, and it is designated as "Being" (sat). It is the root of the entire world, and creation is held to have that as its source.

I shall now declare those qualities born of *prakṛti*, beginning with *sattva*: pleasure, contentment, and illumination—these three are the qualities of *sattva*. Attachment, aversion, pleasure, pain, and rigidity are the qualities of *rajas*.
Lack of illumination, fear, delusion, and drowsiness are the qualities of *tamas*.
