Faith, joy, discernment, freedom from delusion, compassion, and fortitude increase when *sattva* prevails; when it is the opposite, the reverse occurs.
Desire, anger, mental anguish, malice, greed, and likewise thirst—
these always increase perpetually when rajas has grown strong.
Despair, doubt, delusion, lassitude, sleep, and likewise fear [increase when tamas prevails].
When darkness has increased through causes and non-causes, these qualities flourish;
thus they increase one after another again and again,
and likewise they constantly diminish when overwhelmed by the many.
In that regard, whatever state associated with joy may arise in the body or the mind,
one should regard it as a sattvic state and remain equanimous toward it; likewise,
when it becomes associated with distress and causes agitation of the mind, one should remain equanimous.

When that which is joined with delusion and causes despondency occurs—being inconceivable and unknowable—one should then understand that to be *tamas*. At such times, one should reflect thus: "It is *rajas* that prevails.
One should discern that as *tamas*, which is beyond ratiocination and difficult to comprehend.
In brief, dharma is characterized by sattva; in brief, wealth is characterized by rajas;
and in brief, desire is characterized by tamas—such is the sequence of the three qualities within the three aims of life (trivarga).
That creation which begins with Brahmā and the gods is proclaimed as being of the nature of sattva.

The creation consisting of passion belongs to human beings, while that consisting of darkness belongs to the animal realm. Those established in goodness go upward; those characterized by passion remain in the middle;
and those established in the activity of the lowest quality, characterized by darkness, go downward.
Whatever exists among gods, humans, and animals— including all beings,
both moving and stationary— has from the very beginning been joined with and pervaded by these three qualities (*guṇas*).
Hereafter, I shall explain the principles beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) according to their characteristics.
Consciousness (*vijñāna*) and discernment (*viveka*) are the characteristics of the Great One (*mahat*).
The wise know that *mahat*, *buddhi*, *mati*, and *prajñā* are synonyms for the Great One.
Through its connection with the activities of the Great One and the rest, "greatness" (*mahattva*) arises.
Furthermore, from that great transformation, self-conceit (abhimāna) arises;
that is to be known briefly by its characteristic as the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra).
Through the ego-sense, there is the origin and dissolution of all beings.
For the cessation of egoism leads to nirvāṇa.
Space, wind, fire, water, and earth as the fifth—
these are the great elements (mahābhūta), the source and the dissolution of all beings.
Sound, the sense of hearing, and the bodily cavities—these three originate from space (ākāśa). Touch, the skin, and the movement of living beings are recorded as the qualities of wind (pavana).
Form, digestion, the eyes, and light—these four are the qualities of fire (tejas).
Taste, moisture, as well as the tongue and coldness—these are the qualities born of water. Odor, the sense of smell, and the body—these three are the qualities of earth.
Thus, O Goddess, all the qualities derived from the five elements have been explained.
Each subsequent element acquires the qualities of each preceding one;
therefore, the creations of the elements are not seen here to possess only a single quality. If some unskilled persons should perceive a smell in water and speak [of it], [they are mistaken].

O lotus-eyed one, the wise do not admit that smell is a quality of water; therefore, water possesses no smell, for that is a quality of earth alone. Smell belongs to the earth, moisture to taste, and light resides in the eye.
The wind is the support for the out-breath and in-breath of embodied beings within the cavities, while space is [the support] in the voids.
Hair, bones, nails, teeth, skin, hands, feet,
and the head, as well as the back, belly, hips, and neck— all this is traditionally held to be of the nature of earth.

Whatever in this body is dependent upon the humors, defects, and impurities—know all that to be composed of the primary elements; there is nothing in the body that is not elemental. The sense organs are the ear, the skin, the eye, the tongue, and the nose.
The organs of action are speech, the hands, the feet, the generative organ, and likewise the anus.
One should know that sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as the fifth are the objects of the sense organs,
which have emerged from the primary elements.

Speech, action, movement, pleasure, and excretion—these five one should know as the objects of the organs of action; they are considered to have arisen from the elements. Furthermore, the mind is said to be the lord of all the sense organs.
That which is characterized by longing is known as the faculty of the mind (*manas*). The self of the elements (*bhūtātman*) always directs those [senses] together with the mind;
the Lord is the cause for both the restraint and the release of the mind.
The sense organs, the objects of the senses, innate nature, consciousness, fortitude,
and the transformations of the existent and non-existent— these are designated as the "body. And the embodied one is distinct from the body, yet he is dependent upon the body.
The sage who indeed knows the difference between the embodied soul and the body— [he sees that soul] as devoid of taste, touch, and smell, and free from form and sound;
bodiless among bodies, he should seek to behold it as devoid of sense organs.
The Unmanifest, which resides within all mortal bodies as the immortal,
he who perceives that Supreme Self is liberated from all bonds.
This [Self] cannot be grasped by the eye, nor even by the other senses.
By means of the lamp of the mind, this Great Self is clearly perceived.
For He alone, of great prowess and endowed with manifold states of being, dwells within all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
Neither above, nor across, nor below, nor from any direction whatsoever,
is it ever seen here by the senses or by the intellect; yet,
having entered the city of nine gates, that *haṃsa* is brought under control.
The Lord dwells within all beings, both the stationary and the moving.
They call Him subtler than the subtle and greater than the great.
Pervading all beings in manifold ways, He abides as the eternal.
Placing the Knower of the Field on one side and the entire field on the other,
the wise man, ever self-controlled, should thus reflect in his heart:
"For the Puruṣa, abiding in Prakṛti, experiences the qualities born of Prakṛti."
The Self is the non-doer, untainted, eternal, and indifferent toward all actions. Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause in the agency of cause and effect;
the Person (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain.

Some know this embodied being to be ageless, inconceivable, unmanifest, and eternal; they know that the embodied one dwells within the body as composed of fire. Knowledge, heat, and vital breath—these, designated as the "living soul" (jīva), reside in the body.
Thus some who contemplate with their intellect are certain in that regard; others say that the Lord stands pervading all worlds,
situated right here like oil within a sesame seed.
Other fools, being nihilists, because they lack the subtle characteristics [of discernment],
have determined that "the self does not exist," and thus, destined for the abode of hell, they speak so.
In this way, through various means, they deliberate upon Maheśvara.
The wise Brahmin perceives in this world that there exists within all bodies an eternal, immutable, and imperishable Self; the cause [of its manifestation] therein is extremely difficult to discern,
yet it is clearly perceived even by the seers and the gods.
Having seen that Great-Souled One, one does not return to that [cycle] again;
therefore, by the very sight of Him, one attains the supreme goal. Thus, O Goddess, has this eternal Sāṃkhya doctrine been declared to you.
Maheśvara,
who is served by the great seers such as Kapila and other teachers—
this [truth] has been proclaimed by me for those endowed with the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
Furthermore, I shall proclaim the entire yoga-dharma; listen to me.
That yoga is divided into two kinds, practiced by the Brahmanical and celestial sages. In both cases, the conduct prescribed by the scriptures is the same.
And that is ordained with reference to the eightfold sovereignty;
union (*sāyujya*) with all the gods is considered the supreme yoga-dharma.
Understand that knowledge is the root of all yoga.
One should nourish that [oneness] through various vows, fasts, and restraints;
this is the knowledge of yogins: the complete unification of the intellect, the mind, and the senses within the imperishable, wise Self.
One should honor the Brahmins, the sacred fires, and the temples of the deities;
one should avoid inauspicious speech and remain established in goodness (*sattva*). Likewise, one should practice charity, study, faith, vows, and observances.
Proper purity of food, cleanliness, and restraint of the senses—
by these one's vital energy (*tejas*) increases and evil is shaken off. Having shaken off evil, being radiant, moderate in diet, and having conquered the senses, [one attains success].
Free from sorrow, pure, and self-controlled, one should subsequently practice yoga. First, one should fix the mind as a fisherman fixes his attention on the bait.
In a solitary, secluded place, entirely enclosed and clean—

One should prepare a seat there, well-spread with soft *kuśa* grass; having sat upon that seat with the body and neck held straight, undistracted and sitting comfortably, one should not cause one's limbs to tremble.
Gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking about in any direction,
having fixed the mind between the eyebrows and contemplated the embodied self—
he from whomsoever the restless and unsteady mind wanders away.
Restraining it from here and there, one should bring it under control within the self alone; O Goddess, the stabilization of the mind is the secret essence (*upaniṣad*) of yoga.
Therefore, with every effort, one should always stabilize the mind.
Then the wise one should withdraw the skin, the ear, the tongue, the nose, and the eye; having concentrated the five sense organs within the mind,
he should cast away all volitional thought and establish the mind in the Self.
When these [senses], with the mind as the sixth, abide within the self,
then both the prāṇa and apāna remain simultaneously under his control.
For when the prāṇa has come under control, the perfection of yoga becomes certain.

One should contemplate the entire body by dissecting it closely; one should also thoroughly contemplate the movement of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) within the body. Then, protecting the physical fire located in the head, [one should proceed].
The vital breath (*prāṇa*), abiding in the head and in fire, performs its functions;
it is that living being, the self of all elements, the eternal Person (*puruṣa*).
He is the mind, the intellect, the ego, the elements, and the objects of the senses.
Residing in the base of the bladder, the anus, and the digestive fire,
the *apāna* wind moves about, carrying both urine and feces;
its function in the bodies is considered to be downward movement.
Arising and setting all the elements in motion, it proceeds from there upward;
those who are skilled in the internal [teachings] should know that as *udāna*.
Situated at every joint, it is the initiator of all movements.
In the bodies of human beings, it is taught that this is called *vyāna*.
Pervading the bodily constituents (*dhātus*) and the digestive fire (*agni*), it is the *samāna* wind;
it is that very same wind which, at the time of death, brings all activities to a halt.

That heat which arises from the conjunction and contact of the vital breaths (prāṇas) should be known as fire; it digests the food of embodied beings. Situated between the apāna and prāṇa, it is established within both the prāṇa and apāna.
Endowed with the *samāna* breath, the purifying fire (*pāvaka*) digests [the food] properly;
however, the fire below is protected by the *apāna* and the *prāṇa*,
while from behind it is supported by the *samāna*, each relying upon its own respective course.
In the middle of the body is the navel; in the navel, fire is established. The vital breaths (prāṇas) are joined with fire, and the self (ātman) is situated within the vital breaths.
The receptacle of digested food (pakvāśaya) is below the navel, while the receptacle of undigested food (āmāśaya) is known to be above it.

The navel is in the center of the body; all the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) depend upon it. All the breaths, beginning with *prāṇa*, remain there, moving sideways, upwards, and downwards. Ten channels (*nāḍīs*), impelled by *prāṇa*, carry the essences of food.
This is the path of yogins; it abides within these five [elements].
Having overcome fatigue and sitting composedly, one should place the self in the crown of the head.
Having placed the self in the crown of the head, one should likewise fix the mind between the eyebrows.

Then, having completely restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), one should contemplate the Supreme Self. One should join the downward breath (*apāna*) with the upward breath (*prāṇa*), and the upward breaths with the function of the downward breath. Having blocked the movements of both the *prāṇa* and *apāna*, one should be devoted to the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).
In this manner, one should apply the five vital breaths (*prāṇas*) to one another within;
in a solitary place, with measured food, the sage should remain silent and without exhaling,
contemplating yoga without weariness, rising again and again.
Whether standing, walking, or even sleeping, one should thus apply oneself with vigilance.
For the yogin who applies himself in this way, whose mind is disciplined, the mind quickly becomes serene; and when the mind is serene, the Supreme is perceived.
Like a smokeless, blazing fire, like the radiant sun,
or like the fire of lightning in the sky, the imperishable Puruṣa is seen. Having beheld that light of the Self, endowed with the eightfold qualities of sovereignty—
One attains the supreme state, which is desirable even to the gods. These ten defects of yoga are fully described;
O lady of excellent hips, obstacles for yogins are traditionally held by the wise to arise from these defects.
Lust, anger, fear, sleep, affection, overeating,
as well as mental confusion, disease, laziness, and greed is considered the tenth;
by these ten obstacles caused by the gods, their [practice] may be hindered.
Therefore, having first cast aside these [obstacles], one should employ the flickering mind.
These eight qualities of yoga are also proclaimed;
through these eight qualities, the substance of sovereignty is attained.
Minuteness, magnitude, attainment, lightness and luminosity,
mastery, sovereignty, and the power to dwell wherever one desires—
having somehow attained these eight qualities, the best among yogins [proceed].
The lords of the entire world even surpass the gods. Yoga exists neither for one who eats too much nor for one who does not eat at all;
likewise, it does not exist for one whose habit is excessive sleep nor for one who stays awake too long.
For one who is disciplined in diet and recreation, disciplined in performing actions,
and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.
By this very method, union [with the Divine] is also attained.
Having dedicated oneself to union with the God through devotion to the Self,
O Goddess, one should practice with a mind focused on nothing else, always having the consciousness fixed upon Him;
for union is attained by the gods only after a long time and through great effort.
Having worshipped their own deity according to their capacity with oblations, adorations, burnt offerings, prostrations, and constant meditation, they enter [the divine state].
Among the various forms of union (*sāyujya*), two are distinguished: mine and that of Viṣṇu.
"Having reached me, O fair-eyed one, they do not return, nor do they return to Viṣṇu. Thus,
O Goddess Umā, has this eternal dharma of yoga been declared to you.
This dharma of yoga cannot be explained even by others without you—
O Three-eyed One, Best of the Thirty-three, Three-eyed Lord, Sovereign of the Gods,
Destroyer of Tripura, Remover of the Body of Kāma, Upholder of the River that Flows Through the Three Paths.
O destroyer of Dakṣa’s sacrifice, O wielder of the trident, O slayer of enemies!
Salutations to you, O Lord of the world-protectors, O protector of the worlds, O bestower of boons!
[You have taught] the supreme knowledge of the inner self, which has many branches and is limitless.
Inconceivable and indescribable, endowed with Sāṃkhya and Yoga— O Lord, now that you are well-pleased, I wish to hear from you as I listen to your speech about attaining union (*sāyujya*) with you.
How do these devotees serve you, O Supreme Lord?
What is their conduct, and by what means are you, Maheśvara, pleased?
Being described by you in person, this indeed gladdens me exceedingly. Come, I shall tell you of my wondrous *sāyujya*,
by which the disciplined, supreme yogis return [to their source].

I am unmanifest and inconceivable even to the great seers of old; by me were created both Sāṃkhya and Yoga, as well as all that is moving and unmoving. I am to be worshipped, I am the Lord, I am the imperishable and eternal.
I am well-pleased with my devotees; I grant even immortality to them.
Neither the hosts of gods nor the sages whose wealth is austerity know me. For your sake, O Goddess, I shall describe my own manifestations to you.
O auspicious goddess, having summoned from the four hermitages four Brāhmaṇas who were my devotees— pure, meritorious, and ascetic— I then expounded to them the great Pāśupata Yoga.
All of that was received by them from my own mouth;
and having heard it, they established it throughout the three worlds. Now, O blameless one, you have asked me for your own pleasure.
I shall tell you all of that; listen to it with a one-pointed mind.
I am named Paśupati, and those men who are my devotees—all of them should be known as Pāśupatas, their hair and bodies smeared with ashes.

O beautiful lady, in the past, I gave sacred ash (bhasma) for the sake of protection, for the sake of auspiciousness, for the sake of purification, and indeed for the sake of the *liṅga* of my devotees; by that,
the celibate students have all their limbs marked with ash.
Some had matted hair, some were shaven-headed, and others wore various crests; they were deformed, tawny-hued, naked, and wielded diverse weapons.
Wandering everywhere for alms, they were free from desire and possessed no belongings.
With skull in hand, my devotees— whose intellects are fixed upon me—
wander throughout the entire world, increasing my joy;
[they follow] my divine and unsurpassed *Yogaśāstra* of Pāśupata.
Investigating the subtle within all the worlds, they move about. For those ascetics, my devotees, who are thus constantly engaged,
I quickly devise a means by which they may come to me.
O beloved, I have established this Śiva-liṅga throughout the three worlds;
by bowing down to it, one is liberated from all sins. Whatever has been sacrificed, given, or studied, as well as sacrifices accompanied by ritual fees, [are all fulfilled].
They do not equal even a sixteenth part of the prostration made to the Śiva-liṅga.
O beloved, I am well-pleased by the worship of the Śiva-liṅga;
now hear from me the procedure for the worship of the Śiva-liṅga as well.
Whoever worships my Śiva with cow’s milk and fresh butter shall obtain that same fruit which belongs to the desired horse sacrifice (Aśvamedha). Indeed,
whoever constantly worships my Śiva with the scum of clarified butter (ghṛtamaṇḍa) [shall likewise attain that fruit].
That mortal shall obtain the fruit of one who maintains the *agnihotra* fire for a Brāhmaṇa;
and he who bathes my Śiva with even mere water alone obtains merit and becomes dear to me.
Whoever properly burns guggulu resin mixed with clarified butter in the presence of Śiva shall obtain the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice. Furthermore,
whoever should burn even a mere lump of pure guggulu resin [shall likewise attain that fruit].
Whatever fruit belongs to that gift of gold,
that shall be his who worships my *liṅga* with various kinds of flowers;
for he indeed obtains the fruit of having given away a thousand cows.

But whoever, having gone to another land, should worship the Śiva-liṅga— among all human beings, there is none who does what is more pleasing to me than he. Thus, one should worship the Śiva-liṅga with various kinds of materials.
By my grace, a man is not born again among human beings.
With acts of worship, prostrations, offerings, and even hymns of praise,
a devotee should constantly worship me with vigilance in the forms of the Śiva-liṅgas.
The leaves of the *palāśa* and *bilva*, as well as garlands of *rājavṛkṣa*,
the flowers of the *arka*— these are pure and especially dear to me.
Whether it be fruit, or a vegetable, or a flower, or even water [offered with devotion].
O Goddess, that which is given by devotees whose minds are absorbed in me brings complete satisfaction;
for when I am thoroughly pleased, there is nothing in the world that is difficult to obtain.
Therefore, those who are constantly devoted worship me alone.
My devotees do not perish; my devotees are freed from all impurity.
My devotees are especially worthy of worship in all the worlds. And those mortals who hate me, as well as those who hate my devotees—
Even those who have performed hundreds of sacrifices go quickly to hell.
All this, my Pāśupata yoga, has been told to you;
O Goddess, this should be heard day after day by men devoted to me.
Whoever should hear or even recite this determination of Dharma by me,
that best of men, O Nārada, shall obtain heaven, fame, wealth, and grain.
Having spoken thus, the Lord Mahādeva himself, the Great Lord (Maheśvara), desiring to hear,
addressed his beloved and compliant wife who was standing by his side.

O lady of beautiful hips, I ask you— who knows the higher and lower truths of the dharmas of those dwelling in the penance groves, who is endowed with initiation, self-restraint, and tranquility, and who constantly observes her vows— answer what I desire when questioned.
Sāvitrī is the wife of Brahmā; Śacī, the auspicious, is the wife of Kauśika; Lakṣmī is the beloved of Viṣṇu; Dhṛti is the wife of Yama;
Dhūmorṇā is the wife of Mārkaṇḍeya; and Ṛddhi is indeed the wife of Vaiśravaṇa.
Likewise, Gaurī was the wife of Varuṇa, and Suvarcalā was the wife of Savitṛ;
Rohiṇī was the wife of the Moon, and the blameless Svāhā was the wife of Agni;
Aditi was the wife of Kaśyapa, and Arundhatī was the wife of Vasiṣṭha.
These and other goddesses, all of whom have their husbands as their deities, are renowned throughout the world; they were heard of by you and lived together with you.
And you, O honored lady, were worshipped by them through your devoted service and your attentive speech.
Therefore, I question you, O knower of dharma, esteemed by the world;
I wish to hear the duty of women as expounded by you alone. You are my partner in dharma, a fellow practitioner of the same vows.
"O fair-faced one, you are equal to me in essence through your vigor;
O auspicious lady, you were fashioned from half of my own body in the past. You perform the work of the gods and likewise sustain the worlds."
For this host of women follows you and does not leave you;
O lady of auspicious marks, through your favor they wish to hear what is beneficial regarding the conduct of women.
Indeed, that which has been spoken by you remains especially weighty.
"O beloved, in this world women are always the refuge for a group of women;
just as a cow always goes among cows and her mind finds no pleasure elsewhere,
so too, O Goddess, has the course of the world proceeded from the very beginning."
Whatever is spoken by women is highly esteemed among women; O blameless one, what is spoken by men is not so regarded among them. For you yourself know this eternal law (dharma) of women.
"Therefore, I question you; being asked, speak what I desire. Nārada:
Thus addressed then by Mahādeva, the beautiful goddess—
Agitated and ashamed, she said nothing there at all.
Then the god spoke again and again to the goddess, asking, "Why [do you not speak]?
Being thus urged many times, the goddess, full of modesty, spoke this.
O Blessed One, Lord of the Gods of gods, saluted by gods and asuras,
Maheśvara!
"In your presence, how could I speak of the duty of women?
Yet, at my command, O beloved Umā, it must certainly be told."
"O Mahādeva, these rivers, endowed with the waters of all sacred fords (*tīrtha*),
do not leave your presence for the sake of performing ritual ablutions (*upasparśana*).
Having consulted with them, I shall declare what you desire."
"It is improper to speak thus, bypassing those who are virtuous and knowledgeable;
Nārada,
these best of rivers shall indeed be honored by me."
Thinking thus, the Great Goddess summoned the divine rivers: the Vipāśā, the Vitastā, the Candrabhāgā, the Sarasvatī,
the Śatadru, the Devikā, the Sindhu, the Gomatī, and likewise the Kauśikī.
[He saw] the Yamunā, the Narmadā, and the river Kāverī,
as well as the auspicious celestial river Gaṅgā, which flows through the three paths and carries the waters of all sacred fords, destroying all sins.
Having summoned these rivers and gazed upon them, he spoke this:
"O you holy ones, best of rivers, who dispel all sins!"
"O you who are perfected in knowledge and discernment, listen to my words!
This question concerning the nature of women has been posed by the Blessed One;
it cannot be resolved by me alone, therefore I shall bring you [to him]."
"O auspicious ones, I wish to speak only after you have deliberated upon this.
Nārada said:
How, then, should the supreme duty of women be spoken to the God of gods?"
"13,134.057d@015_4458 Thus questioned by that queen, the celestial rivers trembled.
13,134.057d@015_4459 Among them, Gaṅgā, the most excellent, spoke these words:
13,134.057d@015_4460 'We are blessed and favored by these words of yours.'"
O sinless one, you who are honored by gods and asuras alike, and who in turn honor the rivers—
you alone, O auspicious lady, deserve such conciliation and pacification. For those fools who, filled with self-conceit, [speak thus] even though it is impossible.

In assemblies, they speak words of their own accord as they please; yet one who is both capable and free from egoism is considered most rare. For you, O Goddess, being truly capable, are able to answer this question in its entirety.
Because you are a woman, you do not wish to speak, and thus you honor us in such a manner; for you, O Goddess, are equal to the gods, skilled in reasoning and refutation,
endowed with divine knowledge, and kindled by the fuel of divine wisdom.

"You alone are worthy to speak of that dharma of women, both auspicious and inauspicious. We beg you to hear the nectar issuing from your mouth. O Goddess, do what is pleasing; O Goddess, speak the supreme dharma of women."
Nārada said:
Thus was the goddess Umā, who is honored by the worlds, propitiated by Gaṅgā.
The beautiful goddess of the gods spoke all the duties of women in their entirety:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Sovereign of the gods, Great Lord;
O Best of Suras, by your grace and out of a desire to do what is pleasing to you."
Nārada said:
"I shall proclaim that to you; you ought to hear it as it truly is.
While the goddess was thus speaking on the duties of women by the command of the God, [the assembly gathered].
The wives of the ṛṣis, gandharvas, and yakṣas, as well as hosts of apsarases, the women of the nāgas and bhūtas, and even the rivers,
all assembled together and stood around, desiring to hear his supreme words.
The goddess Umā, filled with joy and being honored by throngs of women,
was ever devoted to compassion toward the multitude of women, acting for their welfare and desiring to do what was pleasing to Bhava.
Umā began to speak words that were beneficial and based on the dharma of women:
"O Blessed One, knower of all dharmas, please hear my words."
A girl who has reached puberty and is perfectly pure is designated as such.
Regarding that girl, these five— her father, mother, brother, maternal uncle, and paternal uncle— possess the authority to give her away in marriage.
Furthermore, for the sake of dharma and artha, there are five types of marriage for them;
however, mutual giving out of passion, fear, or by force—
whichever among these may be the case— is how a wife becomes given to a man.

Givers ought to give only after careful deliberation, and not otherwise. For the highest castes, the taking of the hand accompanied by mantras is said to be the performance of marriage; for Śūdras, it is said to be through cohabitation.
When the maiden has been given by her own [kinsmen] to that suitor seeking a wife,
from that time forward, having avoided [him] for ten nights,
she should be well-disposed toward him in thought, deed, and speech.
"Thus, a virtuous woman should observe the vow of devotion to her husband with her husband in mind;
from that time forward, she should do whatever is pleasing to her husband, for whatever he desires on account of dharma, pleasure, or wealth."
At that very time, becoming devotedly affectionate, she should serve her husband in that same manner;
for this, in brief, is the essence of a woman’s devotion to her husband (*pativratātva*). She should always be exactly as her husband is.
This is the conduct, in brief, regarding the practice of what is auspicious and inauspicious:
that virtuous woman who constantly regards her husband as a divinity— of her,
it is understood that her husband is indeed her deity.
For this reason, O Lord, an ancient sacred tradition is heard;
by your grace I shall relate it—listen, O Lord, with a concentrated mind.
Now, a certain Brahmin had two wives.
Of those two, one, desiring merit, out of devotion directed toward the gods,
disregarded her husband and remained focused on the deities;
she performed extensive religious duty accompanied by worship and adoration.

Another beautiful woman, desiring dharma, for the sake of her husband— making her husband her deity— indeed performed what was pleasing to him. While they were thus proceeding on the path toward simultaneous death, [the end of the age arrived].
When Mahādeva had indeed departed, a certain devoted wife remained there;
while Devapriyā stayed behind, she went to the world of merit. And Devapriyā, remaining there, lamented in great distress.
Then Yama, the guardian of the world, spoke these abundant words to her:
"Do not grieve; turn back, for there are no worlds for you, O auspicious lady.
You have turned your face away from your own duty; therefore, those worlds do not exist for you."
For the husband is established as the deity of a woman by all the gods;
O auspicious one, disregarding him, how will you go to the worlds?
O lady of lovely hips, through delusion you do not recognize your own deity.
"A woman who has a husband must practice that dharma which is dedicated to her husband;
therefore, you indeed should turn back and perform what is beneficial for your husband. Then you shall go to those worlds which women devoted to their husbands attain."
"In no other way can the supreme world of wives be attained. Having spoken thus, Yama turned back once more;
she, devoted solely to her husband's pleasure, took hold of her husband and remained there.
"Thus it is, O Mahādeva; for the husband is indeed the deity of women. Therefore, O Umā, having become devoted to her husband, she should serve her husband."
Listen to the auspicious account of a married woman’s conduct day and night: having risen before her husband in the morning, she should direct him toward his morning duties;
and having ascertained her husband’s state of mind, she should thereafter attend to him.
Then she herself should perform the morning duties according to the prescribed rule;
having offered food with the thought,
"May it be prepared," she should do all that in such a way that it becomes pleasing to her husband.
She conducts herself toward her husband just as she does toward her elders;
in the performance of service and nourishment, she acts with the desire to please her husband.
When her husband departs on a journey, she should mindfully remember his duties.
Upon seeing her husband arrived, she should herself, with great affection, promptly perform the supreme service that relieves his physical fatigue,
using water for washing the feet, seats, beds, and words that are dear to his heart.

She should always be full of joy at the arrival of guests; she should always satisfy the guests through both her actions and her speech. She should maintain auspiciousness, cleanliness of the house, and all necessary household implements.

At all times, whether she is having [work] done or doing it herself, she should look after [the household]; and when a religious duty has arisen, she should likewise be devoted to that duty. Furthermore, regarding her husband’s worldly affairs, she should be free from negligence and laziness.
She should exert the greatest effort to provide him with assistance;
as a virtuous wife, she should always be like a *yugaṃdhara* (a companion in yoke) to her husband in matters of dharma and worldly affairs.
Indeed, at the time of recreation, having understood the state of mind residing in her husband's heart—
Having adorned herself appropriately and endowed with graceful gestures and amorous expressions,
she should please her husband with words joined with sweetness while smiling;
in whatever way he may be pleased, she should please her husband in that manner.
One should not speak harsh words to another woman even at other times;
one should act so as to bring pleasure to her with whom her husband is in love.
Placing heedfulness foremost, she should please her husband with her mind.
Immediately thereafter, he should oversee the feeding of others:
female and male slaves, oxen, as well as *caṇḍālas*, dogs,
and likewise those who are destitute, miserable, and beggars.
She should honor her husband with offerings and alms for the increase of his merit;
she should attend to her husband when he is angry, impoverished, or exhausted,
so that he may become satisfied and at ease, and thus she should please her husband.
Likewise, when summoned for the sake of assistance during family affairs, disputes, or matters involving doubt regarding wealth, she should then speak what is pleasing and beneficial;
or she may speak what is unpleasant but beneficial, out of a desire for his welfare and prosperity.
One should speak of practicing in solitude and avoid quarreling with others; one should also avoid looking outward, delusion, shamelessness, backbiting,
overeating, and sleeping during the day— one should avoid such things as these.
A virtuous wife should not share a single seat even with her own sons in private.
Whatever her husband may give her, she should set it aside and preserve it as a trust;
or, if the husband’s property has been forgotten, she should restore it from her own savings.
Having received whatever has been given by her husband, she should be cheerful;
she should avoid excessive begging and jealousy from afar.
To a woman, her husband is always like a child, like an elder, and always like one who is ill.
"O Lord, she must always be supported by her husband with the thought, 'This is my wife’s vow.
O God, this conduct of a devoted wife has been described in brief;
yet she does not [depend] on enjoyments, nor on sovereignty, nor on wealth, nor likewise on pleasure."
That woman who possesses such longing for her husband as this is the devoted wife among women;
for the husband is indeed the deity of women, the husband is their kinsman, and the husband is their refuge. I see no other refuge for women like the husband.
Furthermore, it is my conviction that even among the various births, the female state is indeed distinguished;
for while a man may attain the fruit [of his practice] through great physical austerity,
a woman attains all of that while still indulging in the objects of the senses.
"Acting in accordance with her husband's will, she may do everything as she pleases. O women, behold such ease in the practice of dharma regarding wives;
yet, forgetting this, wicked women act under the delusion of sin."
Her ascetic practice and her charity were both dedicated to her husband;
her beauty, lineage, fame, and heaven—everything was established in him.
Thus, she was radiant through her own conduct, possessing such virtuous behavior.
She shall go together with her husband to the worlds of merit through her own deeds—
whether he be old, deformed, loathsome, wealthy, or even destitute— for such a husband is indeed the supreme ornament of women.
Whether he be wealthy or endowed with beauty, or deformed and destitute of wealth—
the virtuous woman who pleases her husband is the one among women who is devoted to her husband. [She remains so] even if he is poor, deformed, foolish, or afflicted with leprosy.

Having thus gratified such husbands, O King, a woman devoted to her husband goes higher and higher through those worlds together with her husband alone. If, while she is conducting herself in this manner, her husband should die first—
Then she should either follow him in death or practice the Dharma once more.
O Umā,
this very thing has been declared by me as the beneficial path for women based upon Dharma.

Thus have I declared this; women are indeed remembered as being of many kinds—divine, nāga, gandharva, and human, in manifold ways. Yet all of them, O gentle one, can indeed arise with a mild disposition and virtuous conduct.
Now, O Maheśvara, I shall declare the inauspicious conduct of women—
those who belong to the Asuras, the Piśācas, and the Rākṣasas.
Listen to their conduct in its entirety for the sake of the world.
Whether spoken according to reason or otherwise, they are possessed of defects of disposition;
driven by the force of passion and hatred, they indeed act treacherously toward their husbands.
Having turned away from their own duty, they become corrupt in every way.

Constantly obsessed with sense objects, they speak in opposition [to what is right]; they utterly destroy their wealth and never accept what is beneficial. Remaining devoted to their own [limited] intellects, they live on merely as they happen to.
Having at times been virtuous and seemingly devoted to the duty toward their husbands,
they again become most wicked, resorting to erratic conduct;
lacking established boundaries, assuming many disguises, and being fond of wasteful expenditure.

They are discontented and greedy, intensely possessed by envy and anger; they are fond of luxury, hostile toward what is beneficial, and devoted solely to sensual pleasure. Being intent on opposition, they even treat their husbands with contempt.
For the most part, they are full of falsehood, acting in opposition to their elders;
with such conduct as this, they have resorted to an asuric nature. Others are evildoers, always fond of quarreling.
Harsh, speaking with rough words, pitiless, and shameless; devoid of affection and prone to anger toward their husbands, sons, and kinsmen;
terrible, always fond of meat, they both laugh and weep.
In whatever way they thus stray from the right path by being unfaithful to their husbands,
they become rebuked by their kinsmen and perform domestic chores;
or else, O Lord, those of base conduct are rebuked by their own relatives.
In that very way, they would undoubtedly resolve upon a terrible self-destruction; merciless and pitiless, plundering their own households for the sake of wealth,
these fierce men constantly perform deeds devoid of both dharma and artha.
Those women who are unskilled in seeking what is beneficial, sinful, merciless toward the lives of others, and whose conduct is thus characterized, have resorted to the state of Piśācas.
Others, possessed by delusion, shameless, and fond of weeping, [are likewise].
Impure, their limbs smeared with filth, they are intensely addicted to drink and meat; they speak words of falsehood, they laugh and they lament;
difficult to appease and full of great wrath, they are constantly given over to sleep.
Those of the nature of darkness (tāmasa), who have lost sight of the true meaning of reality, being dull in character and pot-bellied,
eat various kinds of prepared food with great haste; they seek an excellent, lustful husband endowed with virtue, beauty, and youth.
Abandoning others, those exceedingly wicked women go their own way;
they are shameless, suspicious of dharma, and hostile in every respect. Women who behave in such a manner have taken on the nature of rākṣasīs.
For all such women as these, there is no happiness either in this world or in the next; O Maheśvara, when these wicked women die,
they are undoubtedly destined to dwell in hell for a long time.
For those who have somehow been liberated from hell after the lapse of time,
a human birth is desired; yet even there they experience suffering,
due to the persistence of their evil deeds, which follows them even into other births.
The poor, those overwhelmed by afflictions, the deformed, and those despised by others—
whether widows or unfortunate women— experience such suffering. An unfaithful woman [endures this] until the end of a hundred thousand years.
She would lead her paramour to hell and unite her husband with sin;
yet, if they were to recognize this and again act for their own welfare by relying upon their husband, they would thereby attain righteousness.
Those women who previously treated their husbands with contempt due to a wicked mind, yet now constantly behave in opposition to their husbands, go to worlds that are meritorious and most beautiful.
Those women who, at the proper time, follow their husband in death out of such motives—
whether out of lust, anger, fear, or delusion— become objects of ridicule.
For from the very beginning, the posthumous following of wicked women is thus in vain.
From the very beginning, the virtuous woman who was devoted to her husband’s welfare ascends upward there, having followed her husband in death;
thus, I behold with my own eye the worlds of her who has died in this manner.
Those devoted wives who go to realms desirable even to the hosts of gods,
or else, upon the death of their husband, having resorted to the dharma of widowhood,
perform such ascetic penance directed toward their deceased husband.
In this way, that woman goes to the supreme world of her husbands—
a delightful and indescribable realm, difficult for gods and humans alike to attain.
Only she who is devoted to her husband shall reach such a world.
"Thus, O God, I have declared to you this unsurpassed dharma of women—
what I have spoken in your presence out of a desire to please you alone."—
Nārada.
"O Lord of Gods, you ought to forgive that fickleness of mine. To Rudrāṇī, who was speaking thus and filled with a sense of shame,
the Lord of Gods, honoring his beloved, gratified her with his words.
The ṛṣis, the gods, the gandharvas, along with the asuras and the hosts of apsarases, as well as the celestial maidens and the divine rivers, having gathered together,
bowed their heads to the goddess and praised her with hymns of praise.

Others, filled with joy, worshipped the God of gods; others, overcome with wonder, reflected upon that matter and spoke of it. Śarva, his mind greatly delighted, repeatedly contemplated their conversation.
At that very moment, the Lord spoke these words to the Goddess:
"Listen, O auspicious one, to my words regarding this conversation which has been conducted by you and me; it shall reach the three worlds."

This narrative shall be meritorious and purifying; of this there is no doubt. O beloved, that wise man who, having become pure, recites this dialogue between us to disciplined men, shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice.

But those who would constantly hear this righteous [account], with their minds fixed upon it, shall obtain a great fruit of merit simply from hearing it. Whoever— be they anyone— should always recite or listen to it as part of their daily ritual, [shall likewise attain that fruit].
"O Goddess, he shall be dear to me; I remember him day after day who constantly recites this auspicious dialogue of ours. He attains fame, long life, and health both in this world and in the next."
"Having heard this, how could the practitioner not become great?
Having said this, Mahādeva vanished right there.

"O slayer of Keśin, in the past, while wandering for the sake of visiting sacred fords in the Himavat forest, we did not perceive the Goddess or the God there by their power; such was the wonder seen by me long ago."
"O Keśava, all of that has now been told to you as you listen.
Having said this much, the divine seer Nārada fell silent."
Vaiśampāyana said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, all of that has now been told to you in its entirety.
Having heard this, Dharmarāja was filled with joy along with his brothers.
All of that has been told to you here in its entirety, O Janamejaya. O Ṛṣis! O wielder of the Pināka bow! O destroyer of Bhaga’s eyes! O you who are honored by all the worlds!
O Maheśvara,
O Śaṅkara, we wish to hear of the majesty of Vāsudeva;
Hari is the eternal Person, superior even to the Grandfather (Brahmā).
Kṛṣṇa, shining with the luster of Jāmbūnada gold like the sun risen in a cloudless sky, ten-armed, of great splendor, the destroyer of the enemies of the gods,
bearing the Śrīvatsa mark on his chest, Hṛṣīkeśa, worshipped by all the deities.

Brahmā lay within his belly, and I likewise was born from his head; the celestial luminaries arose from the hair of his head, and the gods and demons from the hairs of his body; the sages were produced from his frame, as were the eternal worlds.
He is the grandfather’s own abode and the manifest dwelling place of all the gods;
he is the creator of this entire earth and the lord of the three worlds,
as well as the destroyer of all beings, both stationary and moving.
He is the conqueror of the enemies of the gods, the manifest lord of the gods, the scorcher of foes;
he is omniscient, connected with all, omnipresent, and facing in every direction;
he is the supreme self, the lord of the senses, the all-pervading Great Lord.

There is no being whatsoever in the three worlds superior to him; having manifested for the sake of the gods' mission, he has assumed a human form. Indeed, the hosts of deities are not capable [of accomplishing this] when deprived of Trivikrama.
In this world, those devoid of a leader are unable to perform the tasks of the gods.
This leader of all the gods is honored by all beings;
he is the lord of the deities and is solely devoted to the work of the gods.
For one who has become Brahman and constantly takes refuge in the Brahman-sages,
Brahmā dwells within the womb of the body, established in bliss;
and all the deities likewise abide in bliss within that person's body.
That god, the lotus-eyed one, whose womb is Śrī and who dwells with Śrī,
who bears the Śārṅga bow, the discus, and the sword as his weapons, and whose banner has all enemies of the Nagas [as its emblem],
is endowed with supreme purity, virtuous conduct, and self-restraint.
He was endowed with prowess, heroism, physical form, and appearance; with height, proportion, fortitude, and the perfection of uprightness; and with kindness, beauty, and strength.
Endowed with all divine weapons of wondrous appearance,
he is possessed of yogic power, thousand-eyed, irreproachable, and high-minded;
steadfast, praised by his circle of friends, and beloved by his kinsmen and relatives.
Forgiving, free from egoism, devoted to Brahman, and a leader of Brahmins; a remover of fear for those afflicted by fear, increasing the joy of his friends;
a refuge for all beings, and intent upon protecting the distressed.
Learned, endowed with wealth, and honored by all beings;
a benefactor to those who depend on him and even to his enemies, a knower of dharma;
wise, perfected in statesmanship, a celibate student, and one who has conquered his senses.

Endowed with supreme intelligence for the sake of the gods in this world, Govinda shall arise here in the auspicious path of Prajāpati, which is consistent with the dharma of Manu, within the lineage of the high-souled Manu.
Aṅga shall be the son of Manu, and after him Antardhāman;
from Antardhāman shall come the blameless Prajāpati Havirdhāman,
and the great Prācīnabarhis shall be the son of Havirdhāman.
He shall have ten sons, headed by Pracetas;
thus Dakṣa shall become the Prajāpati known as Prācetasa here on earth. From Dākṣāyaṇī shall come Āditya, and from Āditya, Manu.
Iḍā and Sudyumna will be born in the lineage of Manu; from Budha, Purūravas will arise, and from him, Āyu will be born. From him, Nahuṣa will come into being, and Yayāti shall be his son.
From him shall come Yadu, that great being; from him Kroṣṭā shall arise. And the great son of Kroṣṭā shall be Vṛjinīvān.
From Vṛjinīvān indeed shall come Uṣadgu, the unconquered.
Uṣadgu will have a son named Śūra Citraratha;
his younger son shall be named Śūra.
Of those [sons], whose prowess is renowned and who are distinguished by their virtuous conduct—
In a lineage honored by Brahmins, belonging to those who have performed sacrifices and are perfectly pure,
that hero— the best of Kṣatriyas, possessed of great valor and great fame,
and a bestower of honor— will procreate a son who will cause his own lineage to expand.
He will have a son known as Ānakadundubhi, celebrated as Vasudeva; his son will be the four-armed Vāsudeva,
a giver, a worshiper of Brahmins, one who has become Brahman, and a lover of the twice-born.
That giver of honor will liberate all the kings who have been imprisoned;
having conquered King Jarāsaṃdha in his mountain cave,
that heroic one shall become enriched with the jewels of all the earth’s rulers.
He shall be unopposed on earth by virtue of his prowess,
endowed with valor, and the sovereign of all kings.
Born among the Śūrasenas, that lord shall dwell in Dvārakā.
Having conquered [the earth], that god-like king will always protect the goddess Earth with statesmanship;
having approached him, you all should honor him according to the rules with words, garlands, and excellent offerings, as if he were the eternal Brahmā.
For whoever should desire to see me, or Brahmā the Grandfather,
by him the blessed and majestic Vāsudeva must be seen;
when he is seen, I am seen— of this I have no doubt.
"O you whose wealth is asceticism, know that he is the Grandfather, the Lord of the Gods. Whosoever the lotus-eyed one shall favor with affection,
for him the host of gods, led by Brahmā, shall likewise be pleased."
And whatever man in this world shall take refuge in Keśava,
for him there shall be fame, victory, and even heaven;
he shall become a direct teacher of the dharmas and a partaker of righteousness.
That Lord of Gods should be constantly saluted by those who know the Dharma and are ever-striving;
for when that All-pervading One is worshipped, the Dharma itself becomes supreme.
Indeed, that God of great splendor acts out of a desire to promote the welfare of all creatures.
O tiger among men, for the sake of dharma, he indeed created ten million rishis;
those created by that powerful lord abide on Mount Gandhamādana,
endowed with ascetic power, headed by Sanatkumāra.
Therefore, O best of the twice-born, that eloquent knower of dharma is worthy of salutation;
for he who is saluted should salute in return, he who is honored should honor in return,
he who is worshipped should always worship in return, and he who is revered should revere in return.

O best of the twice-born, that deity, when seen, should be beheld day after day; when approached, he should be resorted to; and when honored, he should always be honored in return. This indeed is the supreme vow of that faultless Viṣṇu.
The conduct of the great primordial god is always practiced by the virtuous;
he, the eternal one, is eternally worshipped in the world even by the gods. Those devoted to him worship him with both kinds of appropriate offerings.

He is always to be saluted by the twice-born through action, mind, and speech; having approached with diligence, the son of Devakī is to be beheld. This path has indeed been declared to you by me, O best of sages.
O best of sages, having seen that Great Boar, the God who is the grandfather of all the worlds, the gods would have been truly seen in every respect;
and I too always pay homage to him, the Lord of the universe.
There, a triad will undoubtedly be seen;
for all of us gods dwell within his body. And his elder brother has the luster of a mass of white clouds.
The upholder of the earth shall be known as Halī Bala. For that god, there will be a tree made of gold as his triple-headed banner, which,
as the lord of grasses, shall be mounted upon his chariot.
The head of that great-souled one, the mighty-armed lord of all the worlds, will be covered by serpents with massive coils; indeed,
all weapons and missiles shall appear as soon as they are thought of.
And he alone is called the infinite Lord Hari, the imperishable;
O Lord, he was thus commanded by the gods as he revealed himself:
"He by whose power Suparṇa, the mighty son of Kaśyapa, [was enabled to fly]."
He was unable to see the end of that divine Supreme Self;
and he wandered upon Śeṣa, filled with supreme joy,
dwelling within by embracing the earth with his body.
He is this Viṣṇu, he is Ananta, the Blessed One, the upholder of the earth;
he who is Rāma is Hṛṣīkeśa, and he who is Acyuta is the upholder of the earth. Both of them are tigers among men, divine, and possessors of divine forms.
Those who bear the discus and the plow are to be seen and honored.
O ascetics rich in penance, this is the meritorious favor that has been proclaimed by me,
Nārada.
"O best of the twice-born, you should worship him with great effort.
Then, a great sound arose in the sky, accompanied by lightning and thunder,
and the firmament became shrouded by dense, dark clouds.
Like a rain-cloud in the monsoon, he rained down pure water;
the sky became terrible, and the quarters of the horizon did not shine. Then, on that delightful, holy, and eternal mountain of the gods...
At that time, the sages did not see the entire host of beings;
and instantly, in a moment, the sky became free of clouds.
Then the brahmins went on their pilgrimage, while others returned as they had come.
Having witnessed that wonder and the inconceivable, they were filled with amazement at the dialogue between Śaṅkara and Umā concerning that narrative—
the Lord, that tiger among men, who is eternal and of the nature of Brahman.

"O Kṛṣṇa, that for which we were instructed on the mountain ridge by the Great-Souled One— this second marvel has indeed been wrought by your splendor today; seeing it, we are utterly amazed, and that memory has returned to us."

"O Janārdana, O mighty-armed one, this majesty of the god of gods, the lord of the mountains with matted hair, has been told to you, O Lord. Thus was Kṛṣṇa addressed at that time by those dwelling in the forest of asceticism.
The son of Devakī honored all those sages. Then the sages, filled with great joy, spoke again to Kṛṣṇa:
"O Madhusūdana, show yourself to us at all times."
"O Lord, that delight we find in beholding you is not found even in heaven;
O mighty-armed one, it is exactly as the Blessed Lord Bhava has said.
Thus, O crusher of enemies, I have told you this entire secret."
For you alone are the knower of the true nature of reality; though we have always questioned you, you now question us in turn.
Therefore, for the sake of your pleasure, we have declared this secret to you. Indeed, there is nothing in the three worlds that remains unknown to you.
Birth, procreation, and whatever other cause exists on earth— we, however,
due to the fickleness of our youth and our inability to maintain secrecy, prattle on out of levity while you, O Lord, remain present.
Indeed, there is nothing here, whether in heaven or on earth, O Lord, that you do not know; for everything is known to you. May we succeed, O Lord; may you attain prosperity and growth.
"O dear one, your son shall be your equal or even superior;
O Lord, he will be endowed with great power and will bring forth splendor and fame."— Bhīṣma.
Then, having bowed down to the Lord of Gods, the Yādava Puruṣottama,
and having performed a circumambulation, those great ṛṣis departed. This is that glorious Nārāyaṇa, endowed with supreme radiance.
Having duly performed that vow, he returned again to Dvārakā.
And when the tenth month was complete, O Lord, a most wonderful son was born to him by Rukmiṇī— a beloved hero who would uphold the lineage.

O King, that Kāma, who belongs to all beings and to all the Bhāgavatas, always moves within, dwelling among both the gods and the asuras. He is this very one, a tiger among men, cloud-colored and four-armed.

Out of love, he has taken refuge with the Pāṇḍavas, and you likewise have taken refuge in him. Wherever he is established, there dwells the Lord Viṣṇu, the Trivikrama— the very embodiment of fame, prosperity, fortitude, and the path to heaven.

The thirty-three gods, together with Indra, abide here; of this there is no doubt. He is the primordial god, the great god, the refuge of all beings—the beginningless and endless, unmanifest, high-souled Madhusūdana.

Self-born and possessed of great splendor, Mādhava has appeared for the accomplishment of the purpose of the gods; he is both the speaker and the doer of the most difficult-to-traverse truth of reality.
O Pārtha, yours is the entire victory, and likewise yours is incomparable fame.
This entire earth belongs to you because of your reliance on Nārāyaṇa;
this inconceivable Lord, in whose heart Nārāyaṇa dwells, is yours. As a protector of the earth, you have been the *adhvaryu* priest who offered kings as oblations into the fire of battle.
With his great *sruva* ladle, which was like the fire at the end of an eon, Kṛṣṇa [consumed him].
Duryodhana, along with his sons, brothers, and kinsmen, is indeed to be pitied— he who,
out of ignorance and anger, provoked this conflict between Hari and Gāṇḍīvin.
The sons of Diti and the lords of the Dānavas, possessed of massive bodies and great strength,
met their destruction in the fire of the discus like moths in a forest fire;
for he cannot indeed be fought by humans in battle.
O tiger among men, although inferior in terms of courage, power, strength, and other qualities,
this Savyasācin, standing at the forefront of battle, has— like the fire at the end of an eon—
overcome with his splendor the entire army of Suyodhana, O King.
Now, listen as I recount that Purāṇa which was proclaimed by the Bull-bannered Lord to the sages on the slopes of the Himavat— concerning its origin,
its satisfaction, its splendor, its heroism, and its prowess.
O Lord, these three—his power, his humility, and his birth—belong to Kṛṣṇa;
they cannot be made otherwise, even if they were to become as small as an atom.
For wherever the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa is, there is unsurpassed satisfaction.
For we are of childish intellect, dependent on others, and utterly distressed;
yet, with full knowledge, we have entered upon the supreme path toward death. And you, too, being devoted to uprightness, have provided us with a complete refuge.

O King, you do not deviate from the conduct of kings, being devoted to the fulfillment of your promise; indeed, O subduer of enemies, you would consider even your own death in this world to be more significant than to abandon that which was given by your word.
All these people have been slain at the front of the battle by Time;
we too have been struck down by Time, for Time is indeed the Supreme Lord. O knower of Time, one who is touched by Time ought not to grieve.
Time is black, with eyes red as blood, eternal, and bearing a staff.
Therefore, O son of Kuntī, you ought not to grieve here for your kinsmen. Be forever free from anger, O delighter of the Kurus.
The majesty of Mādhava that has been heard by me as it was told— that alone is sufficient for you as an illustration of a virtuous person. Having heard the words of Vyāsa and of the wise Nārada...
O Great King, I myself have related the exceedingly great power of the most venerable Kṛṣṇa and of the host of sages,
as well as the dialogue between Maheśvara and the daughter of the mountain, O Bhārata.
Whoever shall uphold this [sūtra] concerning the origin of the Great Being,
or whoever shall hear it or speak of it, will indeed obtain the supreme good;
moreover, all his desires shall then be fulfilled exactly as he wishes.
After departing this life, one attains the world of Maheśvara; of this there is no doubt.
O King, Janārdana should not be approached by one who desires his own welfare;
for he is remembered by the Brahmins as the inexhaustible one, O Janārdana.

O King of the Kurus, those qualities of dharma which are remembered as having been emitted from the mouth of Maheśvara should be held by you in your mind day and night. As you conduct yourself in this manner, acting as a wielder of just punishment, [you shall attain success].
For one who is skilled in protecting his subjects, the heavenly world shall be attained.
Indeed, it is by means of righteousness that a king ought always to protect his subjects;
that which is his extensive power of punishment is rightly proclaimed as righteousness.
O King, this dialogue between Śaṅkara and Umā, which is consistent with dharma, has been recounted by me in the presence of virtuous people.
Whether one has heard it or desires to hear it, one should worship the Bull-bannered Lord.
"For he who desires his own prosperity must act with a pure disposition. This is the message from that faultless and high-souled Nārada regarding the worship of the gods; act accordingly, O Pāṇḍava."
O son of Kuntī, this most wonderful and meritorious account of Vāsudeva and Sthāṇu, born of their own nature on the Himavat mountain,
has been told; for ten thousand years, this Sātvata dwelt in Badarī.
Together with the wielder of the Gāṇḍīva bow, he performed extensive austerities—
those two lotus-eyed ones, Vāsudeva and Dhanañjaya, who appear in the three ages.
O King, these two are known to me through Nārada and Vyāsa.

Even as a mere child, the mighty-armed, lotus-eyed one wrought great slaughter against Kaṃsa for the sake of protecting his kinsmen; O son of Kuntī, I am not able to reach the end of enumerating his deeds.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for you who have this Janārdana as your companion— this tiger among men— there will surely come, my dear, the highest and most excellent, eternal, and ancient welfare.
I grieve for Duryodhana, who was exceedingly wicked-minded in the world beyond,
because of whom the entire earth, along with its horses and elephants, has been destroyed; through the transgression of Duryodhana, as well as that of Karṇa and Śakuni.
13,134.057d@016_0245 Vaiśampāyana said:
13,134.057d@016_0245 With Duḥśāsana as the fourth, the Kurus have met their destruction.
13,134.057d@016_0246 While that bull among men, the son of Gaṅgā, was speaking thus—
The Kuru prince remained silent in the midst of those great-souled ones.
Hearing that, King Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the other monarchs were filled with wonder;
honoring Kṛṣṇa in their minds, they all stood with palms joined in reverence.
And all those sages, headed by Nārada, likewise accepted and honored those words, and rejoiced in them. Thus,
the Pāṇḍava, together with his brothers, [related] all of this in its entirety.
Having heard that most great, wonderful, and meritorious instruction of Bhīṣma,
Yudhiṣṭhira, the lord of the earth, possessed of great intelligence, questioned the son of Gaṅgā once again after he had rested and received many sacrificial gifts.
Yudhiṣṭhira:
What is the means for all those who have committed sinful deeds to obtain the boon?
Bhīṣma: [Answer follows].
And tell me, O Grandfather, about that supreme knowledge here; this method for obtaining the boon has been proclaimed as the highest:
meditation upon Nārāyaṇa, worship, sacrifice, and praise.
Listening to those stories and likewise protecting the wise,
delighting in serving the learned, and following their instructions—
one who is even an ordinary person is swiftly liberated through such meditation and recitation.

Recitation (*japa*) is declared by the wise to be of four kinds: Vedic, Tantric, Puranic, and likewise Smārta. Knowledge [is attained] either through service to the twice-born or by the protection of the learned.

Nothing is impossible for those possessed of knowledge; therefore, you must protect the twice-born. Formerly, a woman of excellent vows who was alone and without kin in the forest was consoled by Yama himself, owing to the fruit of protecting the learned.
"The cause of the Brahmin's death was his wife, who brought grief to her father;
you, however, were a Vaiśya woman, yet now you desire to be the daughter of a Brahmin.
Having been addressed thus, she was comforted and asked: "By whom have you been joined with such sin?"
Yama said:
"Born properly into a brahmin family, tell me what is for your ultimate welfare;
[for you were] a learned man in another birth who was tormented by blows."

Having been liberated by Yama through the release from the fear of thieves, she was addressed as "Sujanmikā"; and by means of the welfare consisting of the meditation on and recitation of the eight-syllable mantra, she was graced by Yama and became an inhabitant of the world of merit.
Therefore, O King, be ever intent on protecting those who possess knowledge;
by protecting them, one is gratified and liberated from all sins.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having heard the teachings in their entirety and all the means of purification in every respect,
Yudhiṣṭhira spoke once more to the son of Śāntanu:
"What is the one deity in the world, or what is the one supreme refuge?"
By praising whom and worshipping whom can human beings attain auspiciousness? What dharma among all dharmas is considered by you to be supreme?
By reciting what is a living being released from the bondage of birth and saṃsāra?
Bhīṣma said:
A person who is constantly diligent, praising with the Thousand Names the Lord of the World, the God of Gods, the Infinite, the Supreme Person—
Constantly honoring that very same imperishable Person with devotion,
meditating upon Him, praising Him, bowing down to Him, and sacrificing to Him alone—
Viṣṇu, who is without beginning or end, the Great Lord of all the worlds.
By constantly praising the Overseer of the World, one shall transcend all suffering—
he who is devoted to the Brahman, the knower of all dharmas, the increaser of the worlds' fame,
the Lord of the World, the Great Being, and the source of the existence of all beings.
This, I consider, is the most excellent of all dharmas:
that a man should always worship the Lotus-eyed One with devotion through hymns of praise—
he who is the supreme great splendor, he who is the supreme great austerity.
He who is the supreme, great Brahman; he who is the supreme ultimate refuge;
he who is the purifier of purifiers and the auspiciousness of all that is auspicious;
he who is the deity of deities and the imperishable Father of all beings.
O King, from whom all beings arise at the arrival of the first age,
and into whom they again enter at the dissolution of the age—
that foremost of the worlds, the Lord of the Universe— [of him...]

Listen to my thousand names of Viṣṇu, which remove the fear of sin. I shall proclaim those names of the Great Soul that are derivative, well-known, and celebrated by the seers, for the sake of your welfare.
For the *Viṣṇusahasranāma*, the great seer Vedavyāsa is the *ṛṣi*; the meter is *anuṣṭubh*, and the deity is the Blessed Lord who assumes the universal form (*viśvarūpadhṛk*).
For this thousand names, the great sage Vedavyāsa is the *ṛṣi*.
The meter is Anuṣṭubh; likewise, the deity is the Blessed One, the son of Devakī.
His seed-syllable (bīja) is Amṛtāṃśūdbhava, and his power (śakti) is Devakīnandana. The Trisāman is his heart-mantra, employed for the purpose of pacification.
I bow to Viṣṇu, the Victorious, the Great Viṣṇu, the All-powerful, the Great Lord, the Supreme Person who possesses manifold forms and is the destroyer of the Daityas;
he is the universe itself, the sacred syllable *vaṣaṭ*, and the Lord of the past, the future, and the present.
The creator of beings, the sustainer of beings, existence itself, the self of beings, and the source of beings;
the purified self, the supreme self, and the ultimate goal of the liberated; the imperishable Puruṣa, the witness, the knower of the field, and indeed the immutable.
Yoga, the leader of those who know yoga, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa;
the glorious Keśava, the Supreme Person, whose form is that of the Man-Lion;
Sarva, Śarva, Śiva, Sthāṇu, the source of all beings, the inexhaustible treasure-house.
The source of existence, the creator, the sustainer, the origin, the lord, the sovereign;
the self-existent, the auspicious one, the sun, the lotus-eyed, the one of great sound;
without beginning or end, the supporter, the ordainer, the supreme creator.
He is the immeasurable Hṛṣīkeśa, the lotus-navelled Lord of the immortals;
he is Viśvakarman, Manu, Tvaṣṭṛ, the most massive, the ancient, and the eternal;
he is the ungraspable, the everlasting Kṛṣṇa, the red-eyed crusher of foes.

The abundant abode of the three peaks, the purifier, the supreme auspiciousness; the Lord, the giver of life, the vital breath, the eldest, the most excellent, the Lord of Creatures; the Golden Womb, the Womb of Beings, Mādhava, the slayer of Madhu.
The Lord, the valiant, the archer, the wise, the one of prowess, the stride; the unsurpassed, the unassailable, the grateful, the creative, the self-possessed;
the Lord of gods, the refuge, the bliss, the seed of the universe, the source of all creatures.
The day, the year, the serpent, the means of cognition, the all-seeing;
the unborn, the Lord of All, the perfected one, perfection itself, the origin of all, the infallible;
Vṛṣākapi, the immeasurable self, who has emerged from all yoga.
Vasu, Vasumān, Satya, Samātmā, Saṃmita, Sama; Amogha, Puṇḍarīkākṣa, Vṛṣakarmā, Vṛṣākṛti;
Rudra, Bahuśiras, Babhru, Viśvayoni, Śuciśravas.
The immortal, the eternal, the immovable, the one of noble gait,
the great ascetic Yudhiṣṭhira— O Grandfather, O highly wise one, you who are proficient in all the scriptures!
What should be constantly recited by one performing *japa* so that there may be the great fruit of Dharma?

Whether at the time of departure or entry, or when an action has commenced; whether during a rite for the gods (*daiva*) or at the time of a *śrāddha*, what is the *japa* that accomplishes the ritual act?
It brings peace, nourishment, protection, the destruction of enemies, and the removal of fear.
Bhīṣma said:
You ought to speak that which is to be recited, which is equal to the Veda.
O King, listen with a one-pointed mind to this mantra proclaimed by Vyāsa—
divine, ordained by Sāvitrī, and providing immediate liberation from sin.
O sinless one, hear the entire procedure for the mantra as it is being declared by me.

O best of the Pāṇḍavas, having heard which one is liberated from all sins; O knower of dharma, that by which one is not stained by sins during the night or the day—that I shall fully declare to you; listen with a single-minded focus, O King.
O Prince, having heard this, a person becomes long-lived; indeed, having accomplished his purpose, he rejoices both in this world and after death.
O King, it has been constantly practiced since ancient times by the best of royal sages.

O tiger among the Bharatas, by kings who are ever devoted to the duty of the Kṣatriya, dedicated to the vow of truth, and who always perform this daily ritual with self-control and composure, unsurpassed prosperity is attained.
Homage to Vasiṣṭha of the great vows; having bowed to Parāśara, the treasury of the Vedas;
homage be to Ananta, the great serpent.
Homage be to the Siddhas who are imperishable here;
homage be to the Ṛṣis, supreme among the supreme;
to the God among gods, the bestower of boons upon those who seek them.
Salutations to Śiva, who has a thousand heads; salutations to Janārdana, who possesses a thousand names; [salutations] to Ajaikapād, Ahirbudhnya, Pinākin, and the unconquered Aparājita.
Ṛta, Pitṛrūpa, Tryambaka, Maheśvara,
Vṛṣākapi, Śambhu, Havaṇa, and likewise Īśvara—
these are the eleven renowned Rudras, the lords of the three worlds.
This is declared to be the hundred [names] of the great-souled ones in the Śatarudra:
Aṃśa, Bhaga, Mitra, Varuṇa the lord of waters,
as well as Dhātṛ, Aryaman, Jayanta, and likewise Bhāskara.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Pūṣan, as well as Indra, and Viṣṇu is said to be the twelfth.
Thus, according to the Śruti, these are the twelve Ādityas who are the sons of Kaśyapa:
Dhara, Dhruva, Soma, Sāvitra, Anila, and Anala;
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. Nāsatya and Dasra are remembered as the two Aśvins;
these two are the sons of Mārtaṇḍa, born from the nostrils of Saṃjñā.
Henceforth, I shall declare those who are witnesses to the deeds of the worlds—
those who know even of sacrifice, of what is given, and of meritorious action;
invisible among all beings, these lords of the thirty gods behold all.
Auspicious and inauspicious deeds, death, and time in its entirety;
the Viśvedevas, the hosts of ancestors, embodied ones whose wealth is asceticism;
and the sages as well as the Siddhas who are devoted to austerity and liberation.

Those of pure smiles bestow auspiciousness upon men who recite [their names]. By means of divine splendor, they dwell in these worlds created by Prajāpati; being disciplined in all their actions, they abide in all the worlds.
A man who, being self-restrained, recites these names of the lords of the vital breaths,
is indeed constantly endowed with abundant virtue,
wealth, and pleasure; and he attains the auspicious, meritorious worlds created by the Lord of All.
These are the thirty-three gods, the lords of all hosts of beings:
Nandīśvara, Mahākāya, Grāmaṇī, and Vṛṣabhadhvaja;
they are the lords of all worlds, the Gaṇeśvaras and Vināyakas.
The gentle ones and the fierce hosts, as well as the assemblies of *yoga*-beings; the luminaries, the rivers, the sky, and Suparṇa, the lord of birds;
and those perfected on earth through austerity, both the stationary and the moving.
Himavat, the mountains, and the four great oceans—
all these are the attendants of Bhava, possessing prowess equal to that of Hara.
So too are the god Viṣṇu, Jiṣṇu, and Skanda, together with Ambikā.
Reciting all these names with self-restraint, one is liberated from all sins.
Hereafter, I shall proclaim the best of sages among men:
Yavakrīta, Raibhya, Arvāvasu, and Parāvasu.
Auśija Kakṣīvān, Bala the son of Aṅgiras,
the Ṛṣi Kaṇva the son of Medhātithi, and likewise Barhiṣad—
all these, composed of the splendor of Brahman, have been proclaimed as the creators of the worlds.
Indeed, all those who possess the splendor of Rudra, Agni, and Vasu obtain auspiciousness;
having performed virtuous deeds on earth, they rejoice in heaven with the gods.
The seven preceptors of Mahendra reside in the eastern direction.
One who, being self-restrained, recites these [names], is honored in the world of Śakra.
Unmucu, Pramucu, and the valiant Svastyātreya;
Dṛḍhavya, Ūrdhvabāhu, and likewise Tṛṇasoma and Aṅgiras.
The son of Mitra and Varuṇa was the powerful Agastya.
These seven, the priests of Dharmarāja, took refuge in the southern direction:
Dṛḍheyu, Ṛteyu, and the illustrious Parivyādha.
Ekata, Dvita, and Trita, who were resplendent like the sun,
as well as the righteous-souled sage Sārasvata, the son of Atri—
these seven priests of Varuṇa took their place in the western quarter.
Atri, the venerable Vasiṣṭha, and Kaśyapa the great ṛṣi;
Gautama, Bharadvāja, Viśvāmitra, and Kauśika;
and the fierce Jamadagni, the son of Ṛcīka, who is possessed of great majesty.
These seven preceptors of Dhaneśvara reside in the northern direction;
other seven sages are established in all directions,
celebrated as the creators of the worlds who bring fame and auspiciousness to human beings.
Dharma, Kāma, Kāla, Vasu, Vāsuki,
Ananta, and Kapila— these seven are the upholders of the earth.
Rāma, Vyāsa, as well as Drauṇi Aśvatthāman, and Lomaśa.
These divine sages, each one consisting of sevenfold groups,
are proclaimed as the guardians of the directions who bring peace and well-being to the world; indeed, in whichever direction these reside, one should seek refuge facing that very direction.
The creators of all beings, the purifiers of the world, have been proclaimed:
Saṃvarta, Merusāvarṇa, and the righteous Mārkaṇḍeya; Sāṃkhya and Yoga, Nārada, and the great seer Durvāsas.

Those who have practiced extreme austerities, self-controlled, and renowned throughout the three worlds—others, resembling Rudra, are celebrated as belonging to the world of Brahmā. A sonless man obtains a son; a poor man obtains wealth.

In this way, a man attains success in virtue, wealth, and pleasure. One should praise Pṛthu Vainya, the best of kings, whose daughter was the Earth, the sovereign lord of all lands, and the master of the world.

One should praise the lord of the earth, the beloved son of Budha, who was born of the lineage of the Ādityas, whose prowess was equal to that of Mahendra, and who was known throughout the three worlds as Purūravas Aila.
One should proclaim the hero Bharata, renowned throughout the three worlds,
by whom the Gavamaya sacrifice was indeed performed in the Kṛta age;
one should also proclaim Rantideva, the great god of supreme splendor.
One should likewise proclaim Viśvajit, who was endowed with ascetic power, possessed of auspicious marks and the characteristics of desire; and the royal sage Śveta of supreme splendor,
by whom Sthāṇu was propitiated and for whose sake Andhaka was slain.
By the grace of Mahādeva, he by whom the Gaṅgā was brought down;
one should praise Bhagīratha, who is invincible and possesses supreme splendor,
for it was by him that the sons of Sagara were both bathed and delivered.
One should praise these gods, who are like fire, possessed of great forms and great power, fierce in anger yet of noble being, and who increase one's fame—
both the hosts of ṛṣis and the kings who are lords of the world.
Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and likewise the supreme offerings to the gods and the ancestors—
this has been proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate refuge of all the Vedas,
auspicious for all beings, and a purifier celebrated in many ways.
This is the supreme pacifier of diseases and the nourisher for all rites. O Bhārata, one who is self-restrained should recite these at dawn and at dusk.
Indeed, these [deities] move, rain, shine, blow, and create.
These eminent Vināyakas— skillful, patient, and masters of their senses—
are proclaimed to dispel all the inauspiciousness of men; these high-souled ones stand as witnesses to both evil and good deeds.
By reciting these [names] upon rising at dawn, one indeed attains auspiciousness;
there is no fear of fire or thieves there, nor any obstruction on the road.
