For men who constantly recite these, bad dreams are destroyed.

He is released from all sins and shall go home in safety. That twice-born man who, being self-restrained, righteous, devoted to the Self, patient, self-controlled, and free from malice, recites this at all times of initiation—
Whether afflicted by disease or beset by calamity, one who recites this is liberated from evil. For one who recites it in the center of a dwelling, there shall be prosperity for the family.
For one who recites it in the middle of a field, all the crops will flourish.
One who has traveled to another village and is reciting this [text] shall find a safe journey;
one should employ this protection for oneself, for one's sons, for one's wives, for one's wealth, for one's seeds, and for one's medicinal herbs.
When a Kṣatriya recites these at the time of battle,
his enemies go to destruction and security returns. Indeed, for a man who recites these during rites for the gods or the ancestors, [the same result follows].
The ancestors partake of the *havya* offerings, and the dwellers of the triple heaven partake of the *kavya* offerings.
There is no fear of disease or wild beasts, nor from elephants or thieves;
one’s mental distress diminishes and one is liberated from evil.
On a ship, in a vehicle, on a journey, or in a royal palace,
one who recites the supreme *Sāvitrī* attains the highest success.
For them, there is no fear of kings, nor of *piśācas*, nor of *rākṣasas*.
No fear arises for him from fire, water, wind, or predatory beasts;
nor does he face danger from any of the four castes, especially those in the various stages of life (āśramas),
as he constantly recites this supreme Sāvitrī mantra which brings perpetual peace.
Where the Sāvitrī is recited, fire does not burn the wood;
there no child dies, nor do serpents remain.
For them, no suffering exists, and they go to the supreme goal.

Those who hear this great Brahman, the glorification of the qualities of the Sāvitrī, [attain merit]. For one reciting it in the midst of cows, the cows become exceedingly affectionate toward him. Whether at the time of departure or upon entering, one should recite it in every situation.

O lord of men, this ancient history, having been related exactly as it is, is the supreme secret to be recited by the ṛṣis who are constantly self-restrained, engaged in silent prayer (*japa*), and performing oblations (*homa*).

In ancient times, the divine doctrine of Parāśara was told to Śakra; that very same truth, the eternal Brahman, has now been fully declared to you. This is the ancient Vedic revelation, the heart of all living beings.
All the Rāghavas, as well as the Kurus— descendants of Soma and Āditya—
constantly recite the *Sāvitrī*, the refuge of all living beings;
they dwell perpetually in the presence of the gods, the Seven Seers, and Dhruva.
It is the liberation from all hardships; it always releases one from the unwholesome.
It has been practiced by the elder Brahman-sages, such as Kaśyapa and Gautama, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, and Atri, as well as Śukra, Agastya, Bṛhaspati, and others.
The doctrine of Bhāradvāja was received from Vasiṣṭha by the sons of Ṛcīka;
having mastered the Sāvitrī, Śakra and the Vasus completely conquered the Dānavas.
He who gives a hundred cows with horns adorned with gold—
To a brahmin who is learned in the Vedas and possesses great erudition,
one should constantly recount the divine narrative of the *Bhārata*;
the fruit for both of them is indeed equal.
Dharma increases by the recitation of Bhṛgu; valor increases by bowing to Vasiṣṭha;
and one becomes a victor in battle by paying homage to Raghu.
For one who recites the names of the Aśvins, there shall be no disease.
This eternal Brahman, Sāvitrī, has been declared to you, O King. Whatever else you wish to speak of, that I shall tell you, O Bhārata.
The all-pervading, the all-knowing, the Sun, Viṣvaksena, Janārdana;
the Veda, the knower of the Veda, the unimpaired, the one whose limbs are the Vedas, the knower of the Vedas, the Seer;
the overseer of the world, the overseer of the gods, the overseer of dharma, the doer of what has been done and what is yet to be done.
He who has four natures, four manifestations, four tusks, and four arms;
he who is radiant, the food, the eater, the patient one, and the source of the world;
he who is sinless, the victorious, the conqueror, the womb of the universe, and the treasure of renewal.
Upendra, Vāmana, Prāṃśu, Amogha, Śuci, Ūrjita;
Atīndra, Saṃgraha, Sarga, Dhṛtātman, Niyama, Yama;
Vedya, Vaidya, Sadāyogin, Vīrahā, Mādhava, Madhu.
Transcending the senses, a great master of illusion, possessing great energy and great strength;
endowed with great intelligence, great heroism, great power, and great splendor;
his form is indescribable, he is glorious, immeasurable in soul, and the upholder of the great mountain.
The great archer, the sustainer of the earth, the abode of prosperity, the refuge of the virtuous;
Aniruddha, the delight of the gods, Govinda, the lord of the knowers of the Veda; Marīci, the subduer, the swan, the well-winged one, the best of serpents.
Hiraṇyanābha, Sutapā, Padmanābha, Prajāpati;
Immortal, All-seeing, Lion, the Uniter, the One who possesses union, the Steadfast; Unborn, Irresistible, Teacher, the Renowned Soul, the Slayer of the Enemies of the Gods.
The teacher, the most venerable, the abode, the truthful one whose prowess is truth;
the blinking and the unblinking, the garlanded one, the lord of speech, the noble-minded; the leader, the guide of the multitude, the glorious, the principle of justice, the leader, and the wind.

He has a thousand heads, is the soul of the universe, has a thousand eyes, and a thousand feet; he is the one who causes the world to revolve, whose nature is withdrawn, who is concealed, and who crushes all things;
he is the day, the fire of destruction, the wind, and the upholder of the earth.
He who is most gracious, whose self is serene, the sustainer of the universe, the enjoyer of the universe, the all-pervading Lord;

the one who honors the worthy, the one honored by the virtuous, the holy one, Jahnu, Nārāyaṇa, and Nara; he who is incalculable, whose self is immeasurable, the preeminent one, the benefactor of the disciplined, and the pure.
Siddhārtha, Siddhasaṃkalpa, Siddhida, Siddhisādhana;
Vṛṣāhī, Vṛṣabha, Viṣṇu, Vṛṣaparvan, Vṛṣodara; Vardhana, Vardhamāna, Vivikta, Śrutisāgara.
Subhuja, Durdhara, Vāgmin, Mahendra, Vasuda, Vasu;
Naikarūpa, Bṛhadrūpa, Śipiviṣṭa, Prakāśana;
Ojas, Tejas, Dyutidhara, Prakāśātman, Pratāpana.
He is the prosperous one, the mantra of distinct syllables, the moonbeam, and the radiance of the sun; he is the light born from the moon, the sun, the moon-marked one, and the lord of the gods;
he is the medicine for the world, the bridge, and the one whose prowess is truth and dharma.
The Lord of the past, the future, and the present; the purifying wind, the breath of life;

the destroyer of desire, the creator of desire, the beloved, desire itself, the bestower of desires, and the Sovereign; the maker of the ages, the one who causes the ages to revolve, the master of manifold illusions, and the great consumer.
Invisible yet manifest in form, the conqueror of thousands, the conqueror of the infinite; the beloved, the most distinguished, the one desired by the disciplined; the crested one, Nahuṣa, the bull;
the destroyer of wrath, the creator of wrath, the agent, the one with universal arms, the upholder of the earth.
The infallible one, the celebrated life-force, the giver of life, the younger brother of Vāsava; the reservoir of waters, the foundation, the vigilant, the firmly established;
Skanda, the bearer of Skanda, the leader, the granter of boons, whose vehicle is the wind.
Vāsudeva, Bṛhadbhānu, Ādideva, Puraṃdara; Aśoka, Tāraṇa, Tāra, Śūra, Śauri, Janēśvara; Anukūla, Śatāvarta, Padmī, and Padmanibhekṣaṇa.
Padmanābha, Aravindākṣa, Padmagarbha, Śarīrabhṛt;
Maharddhi, Ṛddha, Vṛddhātmā, Mahākṣa, Garuḍadhvaja; Atula, Śarabha, Bhīma, Samayajña, Havis, Hari.
Marked by all auspicious characteristics, endowed with fortune, and victorious in assembly;
Vikṣara, Rohita, Mārga, Hetu, Dāmodara, and Saha; Mahīdhara, Mahābhāga, Vegavān, and Amitāśana.
The god who is the source of manifestation and the agitator, the glorious womb, the Supreme Lord;
the instrument, the cause, the agent, the transformer, the impenetrable, the secret one; the resolve, the foundation, the structure, the giver of stability, the eternal.
He is supreme prosperity, the highest clarity, contentment, nourishment, and auspicious vision;
he is Rāma, the cessation, the dispassionate one, the path, the leader, the policy, and the one beyond policy;
he is the hero, the best among the powerful, righteousness itself, and the supreme knower of dharma.
Vaikuṇṭha, Puruṣa, Prāṇa, Prāṇada, Praṇava, Pṛthu;
Hiraṇyagarbha, Śatrughna, Vyāpta, Vāyu, Adhokṣaja; Ṛtu, Sudarśana, Kāla, Parameṣṭhin, and Parigraha.
The fierce one, the year, the skillful, the rest, the all-bestowing; the expansion, the immovable, the pillar, the measure, the imperishable seed;
the purpose, the non-purpose, the great treasury, the great enjoyment, the great wealth.

He is undaunted, the most steadfast, the earth, the sacrificial pillar, and the great sacrifice; he has the stars as his rim, he is the lord of the stars, the patient one, the one who withers, and the one who exerts himself;
he is the sacrifice, the object of worship, the great object of worship, the ritual, the session, and the refuge of the virtuous.
The all-seeing one whose self is liberated, the omniscient one of supreme knowledge;
he of noble vows, the fair-faced one, the subtle one, the sweet-sounding one, the giver of happiness, the friend; the heart-stealing one who has conquered anger, the hero-armed one, the rending one.
The one who induces sleep, the self-controlled, the all-pervading, the one who is not of a single nature, the performer of manifold deeds;
the year, the affectionate, the protector of creatures, the one whose womb is jewels, the lord of wealth;
the guardian of dharma, the creator of dharma, the possessor of dharma; existence and non-existence, the perishable and the imperishable.
The Unperceived One, the Thousand-rayed One, the Ordainer, the One marked with auspicious signs; He whose rim is His rays, He who abides in Being, the Lion, the Great Lord of Beings;
the Primordial God, the Great God, the Lord of Gods, the Sustainer of Gods, the Preceptor.

The Supreme Lord, the Protector, attainable through knowledge, the Ancient One; the Sustainer of the body and of all beings, the Enjoyer, the Lord of Monkeys, the Bestower of Abundant Sacrificial Gifts;
the Drinker of Soma, the Drinker of Nectar, the Moon, the Conqueror of Many, the Best of Men.
He is discipline, victory, true to his promise, the descendant of Daśārha, and the lord of the Sātvatas;
he is the life-force, the subduer, the witness, Mukunda, and one of immeasurable prowess; he is the ocean, the infinite self, the one who reclines upon the great sea, and the end-maker.
The Unborn, the Most Worthy, the Self-Existent, the Conqueror of Enemies, the Delighter;
Ānanda, Nandana, Nanda, the One Whose Dharma is Truth, Trivikrama; the Great Sage, the Teacher Kapila, the Grateful One, and the Lord of the Earth.
The lord of the thirty-three gods who consists of three steps, the one with the great horn, the executor of destiny;
the Great Boar, Govinda, Suṣeṇa, and he who wears golden armlets;
the secret one, the profound, the impenetrable, the hidden one, the wielder of the discus and the mace.
Vedhas, Svāṅga, Ajita, Kṛṣṇa, Dṛḍha, Saṃkarṣaṇa, Acyuta, Varuṇa, Vāruṇa, Vṛkṣa, Puṣkarākṣa, Mahāmanas,
Bhagavān, Bhagahā, Nandī, Vanamālī, and Halāyudha.
Āditya, the light, Āditya, the patient one, the best of goals; Sudhanvan, Khaṇḍaparaśu, the formidable, the giver of wealth;
Divaspr̥k, the all-seeing Vyāsa, Vācaspati, the one not born from a womb.
He who possesses the three *sāmans*, the singer of *sāman*, the *sāman* itself, Nirvāṇa, the medicine, and the physician;
he who performs renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*), tranquility (*chama*), peace (*śānta*), the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhā*), and the supreme refuge (*parāyaṇa*);
he whose limbs are auspicious, the giver of peace, the creator, the white water-lily, and he who reclines upon the white water-lily.
The benefactor of cattle, the lord of cattle, the protector, the bull-eyed one, the lover of bulls;

he who does not turn back, whose self is withdrawn, the gatherer, the maker of security, the auspicious one; he whose chest bears the *śrīvatsa*, the abode of prosperity, the lord of prosperity, the best among the prosperous.
The giver of prosperity, the Lord of Śrī, the abode of Śrī, the treasure-trove of Śrī, the creator of Śrī;
the bearer of Śrī, the maker of prosperity, the supreme good, the possessor of glory, and the refuge of the three worlds;
the one with beautiful eyes, the one with beautiful limbs, the hundredfold bliss, the source of joy, the light, and the Lord of the hosts.
He who has conquered his self, whose self is disciplined, whose fame is true, and whose doubts are severed; who is exalted, whose eye is everywhere, who is without a superior, eternal, and firm;
who lies upon the earth, who is the ornament, who is prosperity, who is free from sorrow, and the destroyer of grief.
Arciṣmān, Arcita, Kumbha, Viśuddhātman, Viśodhana,
Aniruddha, Apratiratha, Pradyumna, Amitavikrama,
the slayer of Kālanemi, Vīra, Śūra, Śauri, and Janēśvara.
The soul of the three worlds, the lord of the three worlds, Keśava, the slayer of Keśin, Hari;
the god of desire, the protector of desire, the desirous one, the beloved, the author of the sacred scriptures; Viṣṇu of indefinable form, the hero, the infinite, Dhanañjaya.
The friend of Brahman, the creator of Brahman, the Supreme Spirit (Brahmā), the Absolute (Brahman), the augmenter of Brahman;
the knower of Brahman, the Brāhmaṇa, the one endowed with Brahman, the knower of Brahman, and the beloved of the Brāhmaṇas;
he of the great stride, of great deeds, of great splendor, and the great serpent.
The great sacrifice, the great sacrificer, the great offering, the great oblation; he who is to be praised, who loves praise, the hymn, the eulogy, the praiser, and who delights in battle;
the full, the fulfiller, the meritorious, the one of holy fame, and the one free from ailment.
He who is as swift as thought, the founder of a school, whose seed is wealth, the bestower of wealth;
the bestower of wealth, Vāsudeva, the Vasu, the one of vast mind, the oblation; the true goal, the act of honoring, existence, true prosperity, and the supreme refuge.
Śūrasena, the best of the Yadus, Sannivāsa, Suyāmuna, Bhūtāvāsa, Vāsudeva, the abode of all life-breaths, Anala,
the destroyer of pride, the giver of pride, the proud one, the unassailable, and the unconquered.
He is the universal form, the great form, the radiant form, and the one who is formless;
he is the manifold form, the unmanifest, the hundredfold form, and the hundred-faced. He is the one, the non-one, the existent, the interrogative "who," and that which is the unsurpassed state.
The kinsman of the world, the lord of the world, Mādhava, who is affectionate toward his devotees;

he who is gold-colored, whose limbs are of gold, the one with excellent limbs, who wears sandalwood armlets; the slayer of heroes, the Uneven One, the Void, the consumer of ghee, the Immovable, and the Moving.
Free from pride, yet the giver of honor and worthy of worship, he is the Lord of the world and the sustainer of the three worlds.
He is of excellent intellect, born of wisdom, blessed, possessed of true intelligence, and the upholder of the earth.
He is splendor itself, the bull of radiance, the bearer of light, and the foremost among all wielders of weapons.
The one who seizes and subdues, the undistracted, the one without a single horn, the elder brother of Gada;
he of four forms, four arms, four manifestations, and four goals;
the fourfold self, the fourfold being, the knower of the four Vedas, the one-footed.
He who is the return to the Self, whose mind is withdrawn, who is difficult to conquer and difficult to transcend;
who is hard to attain, hard to traverse, difficult of access, difficult to dwell in, and the slayer of formidable enemies;
he of auspicious limbs, the essence of the world, the excellent thread, and the increaser of the thread.
Indrakarman, Mahākarmā, Kṛtakarman, Kṛtāgama;
Udbhava, Sundara, Sunda, Ratnanābha, Sulocana;
Arka, Vājasana, Śṛṅgin, Jayanta, Sarvavin, and Jayin.
Suvarṇabindu, Akṣobhya, Sarvavāgīśvareśvara;
Mahāhrada, Mahāgarta, Mahābhūta, Mahānidhi;
Kumuda, Kundara, Kunda, Parjanya, Pavana, Anila.
The moon-rayed one, whose body is nectar, the omniscient one, whose face is turned in every direction;
he who is easily attained, who is firm in his vows, the perfected one, the conqueror of enemies, and the scorcher of foes;
he who is the banyan tree, the udumbara tree, and the holy fig tree, and the slayer of Cāṇūra and Andhra.
He who possesses a thousand rays, seven tongues, seven fuels, and seven vehicles;
he who is formless, sinless, inconceivable, the creator of fear, and the destroyer of fear;
he who is minute, vast, thin, and thick; he who bears qualities and yet is devoid of qualities, the Great One.
Unconquered, self-supported, fair-faced, the fore-chamber, the increaser of the lineage;
the bearer of the burden, the one proclaimed as the Yogi, the Lord of Yogis, the granter of all desires;
the hermitage, the ascetic, the emaciated, the fair-winged one whose vehicle is the wind.
He is the wielder of the bow, the science of archery, the staff, the subduer, and self-restraint;
he is unconquered, the endurer of all, the restrainer, the rule, and the controller;
he is possessed of being, characterized by goodness, truth, and devoted to the dharma of truth.
He whose intention is worthy of love, who is himself worthy of love, who performs what is pleasing, and who increases joy;

he who moves through the sky, who is light, who is radiant, who consumes the oblation, and who is all-pervading; he who is the sun, the illuminator, the maker of day, the progenitor, and whose eyes are like the sun.
Ananta, Hutabhuj, Bhoktṛ, Sukhada, Anaikada, Agravaja;
Anirviṇṇa, Sadāmarṣin, Lokādhiṣṭhāna, and Adbhuta;
Sanāt, Sanātanatama, Kapila, Kapi, and Avyaya.
Bestower of well-being, creator of well-being, well-being itself, enjoyer of well-being, and the one whose sacrificial fee is well-being;
free from cruelty, wearing earrings, bearing the discus, having stepped forth with valor, and possessing exalted command;
transcending sound, enduring sound, cool, and the maker of night.
Akrūra is charming, skillful, dexterous, and the best among the forgiving;
he is the most learned, free from fear, and one whose hearing and chanting of his name are meritorious. He is a deliverer, a destroyer of evil deeds, holy, and the dispeller of bad dreams.
The slayer of heroes, the protector, the virtuous, the life-giver, the one who stands firm; he of infinite forms and infinite glory, the conqueror of anger, the remover of fear;
the four-cornered, the profound-souled, the intermediate directions, the specific directions, and the cardinal directions.
He is without beginning; he is Bhūḥ, Bhuvaḥ, and Lakṣmī; he is the heroic Suvīra and the one with beautiful armlets (Rucirāṅgada).
He is the progenitor and the origin of the birth of all beings; he is Bhīma and possesses terrible prowess.
He is the foundation and the abode, the Sustainer (Dhātṛ), the one whose smile is like a flower, and the ever-wakeful Prajāgara.
Moving upward, following the conduct of the true path, the giver of life, the sacred syllable *praṇava*, the stake (*paṇa*);

the standard of measure, the abode of the vital breaths, the creator of the vital breaths, the life of the vital breaths; the ultimate reality, the knower of reality, the single self, transcending birth, death, and old age.
Bhūr, Bhuvaḥ, Svaḥ; the Tree, the Savior, Savitṛ, the Great-Grandfather; the Sacrifice, the Lord of Sacrifice, the Performer of Sacrifice, the Limb of Sacrifice, the Conveyance of Sacrifice;
the Sustainer of Sacrifice, the Maker of Sacrifice, the Possessor of Sacrifice, the Enjoyer of Sacrifice, and the Means of Accomplishing Sacrifice.
The end-maker of sacrifice, the secret of sacrifice, food, and the eater of food;
self-born, born of himself, the forest-dweller, the singer of Sāman hymns; the delighter of Devakī, the creator, the lord of the earth, and the destroyer of sins.
Bearing the conch, the Nandaka sword, and the discus; armed with the Śārṅga bow, the mace,
the chariot-wheel in hand, the unshakeable one who possesses all weapons and missiles—
this is the praise of the high-souled Keśava, who is worthy of being celebrated.
This thousand divine names has been proclaimed in its entirety.
Whatever man should hear this constantly, or should recite it, shall encounter no inauspiciousness whatsoever, both in the hereafter and in this world.
A Brāhmaṇa shall become a master of the Vedānta; a Kṣatriya shall be victorious;
a Vaiśya shall be enriched with wealth; and a Śūdra shall obtain happiness. One who seeks righteousness shall attain righteousness, and one who seeks wealth shall attain wealth.

One who desires objects of desire shall obtain them; one who seeks progeny shall obtain progeny. That devoted person who, rising daily and remaining pure with a mind fixed upon Him, should recite these thousand names of Vāsudeva.
He obtains vast fame and preeminence among his kinsmen;
he attains unshakable prosperity and achieves the highest good. He encounters no fear anywhere and finds valor and splendor.
One becomes free from disease, radiant, and endowed with strength, beauty, and virtue;

one afflicted by illness is liberated from illness, and one who is bound is released from bondage. One who is afraid is freed from fear, and one who has fallen into calamity is delivered from that calamity.
A person who constantly praises Puruṣottama with the Thousand Names, endowed with devotion, quickly overcomes all difficulties;
such a mortal takes refuge in Vāsudeva and has Vāsudeva as his supreme goal.
With his soul purified of all sins, he goes to the eternal Brahman. For those who are devotees of Vāsudeva, no inauspiciousness exists anywhere,
nor does the fear of birth, death, old age, or disease ever arise.
One who studies this hymn, endowed with faith and devotion,
shall be joined with self-bliss, patience, splendor, fortitude, mindfulness, and fame;
[in such a person] there shall be neither anger, nor envy, nor greed, nor an unwholesome mind.
These things belong to those who have performed meritorious deeds and are devoted to Puruṣottama:
the heavens with the moon, sun, and stars; the sky, the quarters, the earth, and the great ocean—all are sustained by the power of the high-souled Vāsudeva.
This entire world, including the mobile and the immobile, along with the gods, asuras, gandharvas, yakṣas, serpents, and rākṣasas, remains under the control of Kṛṣṇa.
The senses, mind, intellect, being, energy, strength, and fortitude— [all these are his].
They say that both the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) have Vāsudeva as their essence.
Right conduct (*ācāra*) is established as the foremost among all the scriptures; dharma originates from right conduct, and Acyuta is the lord of dharma.
The sages, the ancestors, the gods, the great elements, and the constituent principles;
this entire world, both moving and unmoving, has its origin in Nārāyaṇa.
Likewise, yoga, knowledge, Sāṃkhya, the sciences, the arts, and action [all proceed from him].
The Vedas, the scriptures, and specialized knowledge—all this comes from Janārdana.
Viṣṇu alone is the Great Being; as the Self of all beings, he pervades the three worlds and, as the imperishable consumer of the universe, enjoys manifold individual entities.
13,135.141a Whoever desires to attain the highest good and happiness should recite this hymn to the Blessed Viṣṇu proclaimed by Vyāsa.
13,135.141d This hymn was fully proclaimed by the Blessed Vyāsa.

Whoever reads or even hears this attains unsurpassed welfare. Those who worship the lotus-eyed one— the unborn Lord, the Sovereign of All, the source and dissolution of the universe— never suffer defeat.
Arjuna said:
"O lotus-petal-eyed one, O lotus-navelled one, O best of gods!
The Blessed Lord said:
O Janārdana, be the protector of those devotees who are devoted to you.
O Pāṇḍava, he who wishes to praise me with a thousand names has already praised me with a single verse; of this there is no doubt.
Homage be to the Infinite One, who possesses a thousand forms,
whose feet, eyes, heads, thighs, and arms are a thousandfold,
the eternal Puruṣa known by a thousand names.
Homage to the one who maintains thousands of millions of ages!
Arjuna said:
"By the dwelling of Vāsudeva, the three worlds have been perfumed by you."
You are the abode of all beings; O Vāsudeva, homage be to you! Homage be to you, Vyāsa of vast intellect, whose eyes are like the broad petals of a full-blown lotus.
By you, this lamp consisting of knowledge, filled with the oil of the *Bhārata*, has been ignited;
this is the path free of thorns, wherein Hari is worshipped.
One should know that path to be a wrong path which is a teaching devoid of Govinda.
Rudra said:
"Rāma, Rāma, Rāma! I delight in Rāma, the one who brings joy to the mind."
"O fair-faced one, the name of Rāma is equal to the glorious *Sahasranāma*.
Having thus praised Hṛṣīkeśa, Pārtha then remained silent. "Salutations to the God who is the friend of Brahman, and who acts for the welfare of cows and Brahmins."
Salutations again and again to Kṛṣṇa, to Govinda, who acts for the welfare of the world. Just as water falling from the sky flows toward the ocean,
so do all salutations to the gods go toward Keśava.

Whatever merit is found in all the Vedas, whatever fruit is found in all the Vedas—that fruit a person attains by praising the god Janārdana. Victory to you, O lotus-eyed one; salutations to you, O creator of the universe!
"Salutations be unto you, O Hṛṣīkeśa, the primordial source of the Great Puruṣa.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Who are worthy of worship? Who are to be saluted? How should one conduct oneself, and toward whom?"
"O Grandfather, what kind of conduct and toward what sort of people does one not come to harm?
Bhīṣma said:
"The humiliation of Brahmins would bring even the gods to ruin."
O Yudhiṣṭhira, one who pays homage to the Brāhmaṇas does not come to harm.
They are to be honored and they are to be saluted; you should behave toward them as toward a son. For those wise ones sustain all these worlds.
The Brāhmaṇas are the great bridges of dharma for all the worlds;
they delight in the renunciation of wealth, take pleasure in the restraint of speech, are pleasing to all beings, are repositories [of virtue], and are firm in their vows.
They are the illustrious leaders of the worlds and of the scriptures,
whose wealth is eternal austerity and whose abundant speech is their great strength; for those high-souled ones who possess knowledge, austerity alone is the supreme wealth.
They are the source of all dharmas, knowers of dharma, and perceivers of the subtle; desiring dharma, they are established in dharma as bridges of dharma through their well-performed deeds,
relying upon whom all four classes of beings live.
These paths are the leaders of all, the eternal bearers of sacrifice;
they always carry the heavy burden inherited from their fathers and grandfathers.
Like excellent oxen, they do not falter at the yoke, even on difficult ground.
They are the mouths of the ancestors, the gods, and guests; they consume the first portions of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings.
By their very feeding, they protect the worlds from great fear;
they are the lamps of the entire world and the eyes even for those who possess sight.
They were masters of all arts and sciences, skillful and possessed of subtle insight;
they knew the courses of all living beings and were contemplators of the inner path of the self;
they were knowers of the beginning, middle, and end, with all doubts severed.
Those who know the distinction between the higher and the lower go to the supreme goal;
liberated, cleansed of evil, free from the pairs of opposites, and without possessions,
they are always worthy of honor and are honored by high-souled ones who possess knowledge.
They are the same toward sandalwood and foul mud, and toward food and fasting;
for them, fine silk, hempen cloth, linen, and deerskins are all equal.
They may even remain for many days without eating at all.
With their senses restrained, they might wither their own limbs through the practice of Vedic study;
they could turn a non-divine being into a deity, and a deity into a non-divine being;
and when provoked to anger, they could even create other worlds and world-protectors.
The ocean became undrinkable due to the curses of those great-souled ones,
whose fire of anger even today has not been extinguished in Daṇḍaka;
they who are gods even to the gods, and the cause of the very cause.
Who among the wise could overcome those for whom both the authority and the means of knowledge are such that everyone—
whether old or young— deserves equal respect? Among them,
both the elders and the youth all behold the true path.
However, on account of their specific asceticism and learning, they honor one another.
An unlearned Brāhmaṇa is a god and indeed a great vessel for purification;
a learned one is an even greater god, resembling the full ocean.

Whether ignorant or learned, a Brāhmaṇa is a great deity; whether consecrated or unconsecrated, he is a great deity just as fire is. For even in a cremation ground, the radiant purifier (fire) is not defiled.
Carrying the oblation in sacrifices, he shines all the more brightly.
Thus, even if he is engaged in all kinds of undesirable actions, a Brahmin is in every way worthy of honor; know him to be the supreme deity.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O lord of men, having seen what fruit from the worship of Brahmins,
or considering what result of action, do you, O high-minded one, honor them?"
Bhīṣma said:
In this regard, O Bhārata, they cite this ancient history, a conversation between Pavana and Arjuna.

The glorious and mighty lord Kārtavīrya, possessing a thousand arms, became the ruler of this entire world from his capital at Māhiṣmatī. He [ruled] over the earth, which is filled with mines of jewels, together with its islands and clothed by the ocean.

The Haihaya king, whose valor was true, ruled over the entire earth. Out of devotion to the duty of a Kṣatriya, as well as discipline and sacred learning, he gave his own wealth to Dattātreya for a specific purpose.
And the son of Kṛtavīrya gratified that sage;
delighted, the twice-born one invited him with three boons. Entreated by him with those boons, the king spoke these words:
"Indeed, may I possess a thousand arms in the midst of the army, but otherwise in my home. Let the soldiers behold my thousand arms in battle;
O you of vast vows, may I conquer the entire earth through my prowess."
"Having obtained that kingdom through righteousness, I shall protect it without weariness.
But, O best of the twice-born, I ask you for a fourth boon;
O blameless one, you ought to grant it to me as a favor."
"May the virtuous instruct me, who have followed a false course and taken refuge in that [evil].
When he had spoken thus, the twice-born one said to the lord of men, "So be it.
In this manner, those boons were obtained by him of radiant splendor.
Then, mounting his chariot, he who possessed a splendor like that of fire or the sun spoke out of the intoxication of his own prowess: "Who indeed is equal to me in heroism,
fortitude, fame, purity, valor, or even in vital energy?"
At the conclusion of those words, an incorporeal voice spoke from the sky:
"O fool, you do not understand that a Brāhmaṇa is superior to a Kṣatriya;
it is together with a Brāhmaṇa that a Kṣatriya here protects the subjects."
Arjuna said:
"When pleased, I can create all beings; likewise, when enraged, I can bring about their destruction. In deed, thought, and speech, there is no twice-born one superior to me."
The first discourse was that which holds the Brahmins superior, while the second was that which holds the Kṣatriyas superior;
yet these two reasons you have stated show a distinction here:
the Brahmins depend upon the Kṣatriyas, but the Kṣatriyas do not depend upon the Brahmins.
13,137.015c Relying on the pretext of sacred knowledge (*brahmopadhā*), Brahmins devour Kṣatriyas on this earth.
13,137.016a Dharma, which consists in the protection of subjects, rests upon the Kṣatriyas.
13,137.016c The livelihood of Brahmins comes from the Kṣatriyas; how then can the Brahmin be superior to them?

Those brahmins, who are the foremost among all beings, who subsist on alms, and who are self-conceited— I always keep them under my own control. For this truth was spoken by this maiden Gāyatrī in heaven.
"I shall conquer all those helpless Brahmins who are clothed in skins;
nor shall anyone in the three worlds—whether god or man—be able to displace me from my kingdom. Therefore, I am superior to the twice-born."
"Today I shall make this world one where Brahmans are supreme, yet Kṣatriyas are supreme;
for no one is able to withstand my strength in combat.
Having heard Arjuna's words, the night-stalker woman became terrified.
Then, as he was situated in the intermediate space, Vāyu spoke to him:
"Abandon this defiled state of mind; pay homage to the Brahmins. For if you commit a sin against them, there will surely be a disturbance in your kingdom."
"Or else, O protector of the earth, the twice-born, being of great strength, will surely pacify you or expel you from the kingdom once your energy is destroyed.
To him, the king said, "Who are you? and then Māruta replied to him.
"I am indeed Vāyu, the messenger of the gods; I speak for your benefit.
Arjuna said:
"Oh, today you have displayed devotion and affection toward the Brahmins!"
"Tell me of a twice-born man who is exactly like the earth;
or tell me of one who is in some way similar to the wind;
or indeed tell me of one who is like water, or like the sun, or even like the sky."
Vāyu said:
"Listen, O fool, to some of the qualities of the high-souled Brāhmaṇas, O King, which have been mentioned by you; indeed, the Brāhmaṇa is superior to them."
Having abandoned her status as the great earth, the Earth herself, out of rivalry with the king of Aṅga, was on the verge of perishing; however, the Brahmin Kaśyapa propped her up.
O King, Brahmins are eternally indestructible, both in heaven and here on earth.
For in ancient times, Aṅgiras himself drank up the waters by his own splendor. Drinking them like milk, that one of great asceticism was not satiated;
O King, he filled the entire earth with a mighty flood.

When he was indeed enraged, I abandoned the world and departed from there; out of fear of Aṅgiras, I remained for a long time at the Agnihotra sacrifice. And the blessed Purandara was cursed by Gautama.
"Indeed, while desiring Ahalyā, he was not harmed for the sake of dharma.
Likewise, O King, the ocean, though full of pure water,
was cursed by the Brahmins, O Lord, and made to have salt water."
Golden-hued, smokeless, with its flames gathered and rising upward—such is the Fire, the Seer (Kavi).
Cursed by the enraged Aṅgiras, he was deprived of these qualities.
Behold the Maruts, who mocked the great ocean, now reduced to powder.
"Constantly cursed by the twice-born Suvarṇadhārin:
'O lord of men, you are not equal to the twice-born; know that the Brāhmaṇa is the most excellent. Indeed, the Lord bows properly even to Brāhmaṇas staying in the womb.'"
The great kingdom of the Daṇḍakas was destroyed by a single Brāhmaṇa; the vast Kṣatriya host of the Tālajaṅghas was destroyed by the single Aurva.
And by you, likewise, a vast kingdom, as well as strength, righteousness, and sacred learning, have been attained.
"By the grace of Dattātreya, that which is most difficult to attain has been obtained.
O Arjuna, why do you constantly worship fire instead of a Brāhmaṇa? For he is the carrier of oblations for the entire world; do you not know him?"
Or rather, O best of Brahmins, why are you bewildered, knowing him who is the protector of all beings, the creator of the world of living creatures,
the Prajāpati Brahmā, the unmanifest source of both origin and dissolution?
By whom this entire universe, both the stationary and the moving, was generated.
Yet some unwise ones maintain that Brahmā was born from an egg;
from the split egg emerged the mountains, the quarters, the waters, the earth, and the sky.
"This is not to be viewed in that way, for how could he be the most superior?
It is remembered that the Egg was space; from that the Grandfather (Pitāmaha) was born.
Tell me, how could he have remained [there], for at that time nothing else existed?"
"He who is called Ahaṃkāra is the lord pervading all splendor. There is no cosmic egg, O King, but there is Brahmā, the creator of the worlds.
When he had spoken thus, [Brahmā] remained silent, and Vāyu said to him:
Vāyu said:
O King, in former times, a king named Aṅga desired to give this earth as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to the Brahmins; thereafter, the earth became filled with anxiety.

"Having obtained this *dhāraṇī* of all beings, how can this excellent king wish to give me, the daughter of Brahmā, to the twice-born? Abandoning this state of being on earth, I shall go to the station of Brahmā."
"May this king, along with his kingdom, not exist"— thinking thus, she departed.
Then, seeing the Earth departing at that time, Kaśyapa,
being composed, immediately released himself and entered the earth.

O King, that earth was then known to be enclosed on all sides and endowed with grasses and medicinal herbs; it was preeminent in righteousness and free from fear. Thus did he of extensive vows remain for thousands of divine years.
O King, for thirty [years], Kaśyapa remained unwearied as the earth.
Then, O great king, having approached and paid homage to Kaśyapa,
the Earth became known as Kāśyapī, the daughter of that high-souled one.
"O King, such indeed was this Brāhmaṇa Kaśyapa. Name another Kṣatriya who is superior even to Kaśyapa. The king remained silent, but Pavana spoke again:
Listen, O King, to the story of Utathya, who was born in the lineage of Aṅgiras.
Bhadrā, the daughter of Soma, was considered supreme in beauty. Soma beheld Utathya as a husband equal to her.
And that illustrious and highly fortunate lady performed intense ascetic penance;
for his sake, she then chose the highly fortunate Utathya as her husband. For the sake of Utathya, the lovely-limbed woman undertook the highest vow of self-restraint.
Then, having summoned Sotathya, he gave the illustrious woman to him as a wife; and he, who bestows abundant sacrificial fees, accepted her according to the prescribed rites.
However, the glorious Varuṇa had already desired her previously.
Having arrived at the forest retreat, he carried her away to the Yamunā;
but the Lord of the Waters, having seized her, led her toward his own city,
which was most wonderful to behold and possessed six hundred thousand lakes.
Indeed, there is nothing more delightful than that supreme city,
which is adorned with palaces, celestial nymphs, and divine objects of desire.
There, O King, the god who is the lord of the waters took his pleasure together with her.
Then, after [the matter] had been told to Utathya regarding the violation of his wife,
Utathya, having heard everything from Nārada, then spoke to Nārada:
"Go and speak harsh words to Varuṇa."
"Release my wife at my word! Why have you abducted her? You are a guardian of the worlds, not a destroyer of the world.
My wife was given to me by Soma, yet she has been taken away by you today."
Having been addressed thus by Nārada, the Lord of Waters replied to him: "Release the wife of Utathya. Varuṇa then said to him:
"Why have you killed her?"
"Having heard these words of his, [Nārada said:
'This is my very dear wife; I cannot bear to abandon her.
Thus addressed by Varuṇa, Nārada then approached that sage."
13,139.020c Utathya spoke these words, as if his mind were not at all joyful:
13,139.021a "O great sage, having been seized by the throat, I have been cast out by Varuṇa;
13,139.021c he will not give back your wife; do whatever you must do."

Having heard the words of Nārada, Aṅgiras blazed up in anger; that great ascetic, having restrained the waters with his splendor, drank them all. And as the entire water was being drunk, the Lord of Waters—
Though being urged by his friends, he did not let go of her at that time.
Then the enraged Utathya, the best of brahmins, said to the Earth:
"O blessed one, show me dry land where there are six hundred thousand lakes!"
Then that region became a barren wasteland and the ocean receded;
from that place, that best of the twice-born spoke to the river:
"O timid Sarasvatī, go unseen toward the desert."

"O auspicious one, let this region become devoid of merit since it has been abandoned by you. When that land had been thus devastated, the lord of the waters, taking Bhadrā with him, sought refuge and gave his wife to the son of Aṅgiras.
Having accepted her as his wife, Utathya became joyful in mind;
he released the world from suffering and Varuṇa as well, O Haihaya.
Then, having regained his wife, that knower of dharma spoke to Varuṇa.
"You shall soon become untouchable and unfit for the use of water.
Listen, O lord of men, to what Utathya of great splendor has said:
'You have been released because a remnant of your lifespan remains; do not fear, O Lord of Waters, go [your way].'"
"Do not despise me again out of delusion; let not Yama’s abode lead you away.
"O Lord of Waters, this [goddess] was obtained by me through ascetic power while you were crying out.
Having said this, he took her and went to his own abode.
"O King, such indeed was Utathya, that bull among Brahmins. I speak thus; you may speak of a Kshatriya who is superior to Utathya.
Bhishma said:
Thus addressed, he then became silent; Vāyu then spoke:
"Listen, O King, to the majesty of the Brahmin Agastya.
The gods were defeated by the Asuras and rendered devoid of energy."
O bull among the Haihayas, all their sacrifices were seized by the Dānavas, as was the *svadhā* offering for the ancestors, and likewise the ritual worship of men; consequently,
having been deprived of their sovereignty, the gods wandered the earth— so it is heard.
Then once, O King, they beheld Agastya, who was endowed with great ascetic power and possessed the radiant splendor of the sun; having seen him, illustrious and firm in his vows,
the gods saluted him.
O lord of men, at that time they spoke these words to the high-souled one:
"We have been defeated in battle by the Dānavas and likewise fallen from our sovereignty.
Therefore, O bull among sages, protect us from this intense fear."
Thus addressed by the gods, Agastya then became enraged;
the radiant one blazed forth like the fire of time at the end of an eon. By that mass of blazing rays, the Dānavas were then consumed.
O Great King, by the thousands they fell from the intermediate space;
being consumed by the fiery splendor of that Agastya, those Daityas abandoned both worlds and fled toward the southern quarter.
But Bali, having gone to the earth, performed the horse sacrifice (*aśvamedha*).
Those other great Asuras who were healthy and remained on the earth were not consumed by fire. Then the worlds were regained by the gods, and that dust was pacified.
Then the gods said to him, "Slay the Asuras who stand upon the earth.
Thus addressed, he said to the gods, "I am not able to burn those who have taken refuge in the great earth; for my ascetic power would be exhausted. Yet, O King, I shall consume them."
Thus were the Dānavas consumed by the Blessed One with his own splendor,
O King, by Agastya, whose soul was purified through asceticism.
And such indeed is Agastya as he has been described to you by me, O sinless one.
"I shall speak; or you yourself tell me of a Kṣatriya superior to Agastya.
Thus addressed, he remained silent; then Vāyu spoke:
"Listen, O King, to the preeminent deed of the illustrious Vasiṣṭha."
Resorting to the banks of the Gaṅgā according to the rules of the Vaikhānasas,
the Ādityas performed a sacrificial session (*sattra*) near Lake Mānasa,
having mentally approached Vasiṣṭha and heard of his presence there.
Seeing those sacrificers agitated and emaciated by their initiatory rites,
the Dānavas named Khalins, who resembled mountains, desired to slay them.
Not far from them was a lake that had received a boon from Brahmā.
Those Dānavas, though slain again and again, indeed lived on by plunging into the water;
seizing most terrible mountains, iron clubs, and trees,
they rose up, agitating the waters for a hundred yojanas.
Ten thousand of them indeed rushed toward the gods.
Then, afflicted by them, the gods went to Vāsava for refuge.
And Śakra, distressed by them, went to Vasiṣṭha for refuge.
Then the venerable seer Vasiṣṭha granted them freedom from fear;
for the sage, devoted to compassion, knowing them to be so distressed,
consumed all those Khalins effortlessly by his own splendor.
The one of great asceticism brought the river Gaṅgā, which was flowing toward Kailāsa,
to that divine lake; and because that lake was pierced by her,
it became the river Sarayū from that point onward.
And because the *khalinas* were slain there, that region became known as Khalina.
Thus, the inhabitants of heaven, including Indra, were protected by Vasiṣṭha;
and the Daityas, having received boons from Brahmā, were likewise slain by that high-souled one.
"O sinless one, this deed of Vasiṣṭha has been told to you by me. Shall I speak further, or will you tell me of a Kṣatriya superior to Vasiṣṭha? Bhīṣma said:
Thus addressed, Arjuna remained silent; Vāyu then spoke to him:
"Listen to me, O best of the Haihayas, concerning the deeds of the high-souled Atri.
In a terrible darkness, the gods and the Dānavas fought together."
There, Svarbhānu pierced both the Moon and the Sun with arrows;
then, O tiger among kings, those gods were seized by darkness and struck down by the powerful Dānavas.

Being slaughtered by the Asuras and their vital strength exhausted, those denizens of heaven beheld the brahmin Atri performing austerities in the great forest. Then the gods spoke to him, who was free from anger and had conquered his senses.
"Both these, the moon and the sun, have been pierced by the arrows of the Asuras;
we too are being slain by our enemies while shrouded in darkness.
We find no peace; protect us from this fear, O Lord!"
"How shall I protect you? they asked him; he replied, "Become the moon.
"And become the sun, the destroyer of darkness, and the slayer of our enemies.
Thus addressed, Atri then became the moon, the dispeller of gloom.
He beheld the gentle nature of the sun’s reflection;
having seen that Soma was not very radiant and likewise the sun, O King,
Atri produced light there through his own ascetic power in that encounter.
Then he made the world free from darkness and set it ablaze;
by his own splendor, he conquered the hosts of the gods' enemies.
Seeing those great Asuras being consumed by Atri, the gods...

Then, even those who were unprotected struck back with their prowess; the sun was made to shine, the gods were saved, and the Asuras were slain. Then, by Atri of supreme splendor, the state of Soma was established.
O royal sage, behold the deed performed by the peerless sage Atri, who subsisted on fruits, wore skins, and was devoted to silent recitation.
The deed of that high-souled Atri has also been told in detail.
"I shall speak; or you yourself may speak, O Atri, regarding the best of Kṣatriyas.
Thus, O Great King, was this wonderful deed of Atri recounted.
Having been addressed in this way, Arjuna remained silent, and Vāyu spoke to him.
"Listen, O King, to the great deed of the high-souled Cyavana.
Having made a promise to the Aśvins, Cyavana spoke to the subduer of Pāka (Indra), who was accompanied by the gods: 'Make the Aśvins drinkers of the Soma.'"

O Great King, hear now the supreme majesty of Cyavana. Having performed a sacrifice, O illustrious one, Cyavana of great ascetic power made the two Nāsatyas strong and indeed partakers of the Soma juice, O King.
Indra said:
"How can these two become drinkers of Soma when they have been excluded by us? They are not equal to the gods; therefore, do not speak thus to us."
"O observer of great vows, we do not wish to drink the *soma* together with the Aśvins.
Cyavana said:
"O Brahmin, whatever else you shall say, we will carry out those words of yours."
"O Aśvins, drink the Soma together with these two;
both of them are gods, O Lord of Gods, sons of the Sun. O deities, let my word be carried out exactly as it has been spoken."
Indra said:
"O best of the twice-born, by performing this for you, your welfare will be secured; it will not be so by failing to do so. Indeed, I shall not drink the Soma together with the two Aśvins."
"Let others drink as they please; I do not venture to drink here.
Cyavana said:
"O slayer of Bala, if you will not do as I have spoken,"
"Having been crushed by me this very moment, you shall indeed drink the Soma at the sacrifice.
Thereupon, Cyavana swiftly commenced a ritual for the benefit of the Aśvins;
consequently, the gods were overwhelmed by his mantras.
But seeing that ritual commenced, Indra, overwhelmed with rage,
raised a massive mountain and rushed toward Cyavana;
likewise, the Lord, his eyes agitated by indignation, [advanced] with the thunderbolt.
As soon as he saw him rushing toward him, Cyavana, endowed with the power of asceticism,
sprinkled him with water and paralyzed him along with his thunderbolt and the mountain.
Then he unleashed a most terrible enemy against Indra himself.
The great sage [beheld] Mada, who consisted of mantra-offerings and had his mouth wide open;
he possessed a thousand teeth extending for a hundred yojanas,
and his most terrible fangs were two hundred yojanas long.
One of his jaws rested upon the earth, while the other touched the heavens.
All the gods, including Indra, remained at the root of his tongue,
like fish that have entered the mouth of a timingila in the great ocean.
Then, having deliberated together, those gods, with Mada entering their mouths,
spoke in unison to Śakra: "Bowing down before this twice-born one,
let us drink the Soma together with the Aśvins, freed from our fever."
Then Śakra, having bowed down, performed that service for Cyavana;
saying "So be it," O King, Śakra then made his prostration to him.
Cyavana then made those two Aśvins drinkers of the Soma.
Then the powerful sage withdrew his action and distributed his intoxication among dice, hunting, drinking, and women.
O King, by these vices a man goes to ruin; of this there is no doubt.
Therefore, a man should always avoid these from afar.
O King, this deed of Cyavana has been proclaimed to you. Shall I speak further, or will you tell me of any Kṣatriya superior to Cyavana?
Bhīṣma said:
Arjuna remained silent, but the Wind-god spoke again:
"Listen to me, O lord of men, regarding the foremost duty toward brahmins."
When the dwellers of heaven, including Indra himself, had come before this Madhu,
then Cyavana seized this earth from them.
Thinking that both worlds had been taken away, those gods became distressed.
Afflicted with grief, they sought refuge with the high-souled Brahmā.
The gods said:
"O one honored by the worlds, [we are those] whose mouths have been joined together."
"O Lord, the earth was taken away by Cyavana, and heaven as well by the Kapas.
Brahmā said:
"O dwellers of heaven, including Indra, go quickly for refuge to the Brahmins."
"By propitiating them, you shall regain both worlds as before.
They went for refuge to the brahmins and asked, "Whom shall we conquer?
Being thus addressed, those brahmins said to them, "Conquer the Kapas here."
"O King, we shall surely conquer those who have descended to the earth. Having said this, the Brāhmaṇas then commenced the rite that destroys the Kapas.
Hearing of this, the Kapas dispatched a wealthy messenger to the Brāhmaṇas.
And he spoke to those brahmins in words like those of a monkey:
"All of you are like monkeys; what is it that is happening here?
You are all knowers of the Vedas, wise, and all performers of sacrifices."

All of them are devoted to the vow of truth, and all are equal to the great seers. Prosperity delights in them, and they uphold prosperity themselves. They do not approach their wives in vain, nor do they eat meat in vain.

They offer oblations into the blazing fire and abide by the words of their elders; all are self-controlled and share their food with children. They travel by means of carts when necessary and do not consort with women in their courses.
Those who perform virtuous deeds likewise go to a happy rebirth;
they do not eat while others have not yet eaten, nor do they sleep during the day,
out of consideration for those who are pregnant or nursing infants.
They do not gamble in the forenoons;
endowed with these and many other virtues, how will you defeat the Kapas? Turn back! For there is good fortune for you who have desisted.
The Brāhmaṇas said:
"We shall conquer the Kapas; we are known as those who are the gods.
Therefore, O wealthy one, the Kapas are to be slain by us; go back the way you came."
Dhanī went to the Kapas and said, "The Brahmins are not acting for your benefit.
Then, taking up their weapons, all the Kapas rushed toward the Brahmins. Seeing the Kapas with their banners raised high, all the twice-born ones [prepared for battle].
They discharged blazing fires that destroyed the lives of the Kapas;
having consumed the Kapas, those eternal devourers of oblations, created by Brahmā,
shone like clouds in the sky, O lord of men.

Having slain the Dānavas in battle by uniting together, all the gods did not realize at that time that the Kapas had been killed by the Brāhmaṇas. Then, O Lord, the highly effulgent Nārada arrived and spoke.
Just as the Kapas were struck down by the power of the illustrious Brahmins, so too,
having heard the words of Nārada, all the inhabitants of heaven were delighted;
they praised the twice-born and the glorious Brahmā.
Then the splendor and prowess of those gods increased,
and they attained immortality, which is honored throughout the three worlds.
Having spoken these words, Arjuna replied to Vāyu.
"O mighty-armed lord of men, listen to that which I have honored:
O Lord, I live for the sake of Brahmins in every way and at all times;
I bow down perpetually to Brahmā and to the Brahmins."

"Through the grace of Dattātreya, I have attained this fame; I have achieved supreme renown in the world and practiced great righteousness. Oh, Māruta, such indeed are the true effects of the deeds of a Brāhmaṇa!"
"13,142.022c These have been proclaimed by you and heard by me in their entirety with great diligence.
13,142.023 Vāyu said:
13,142.023a Protect the Brāhmaṇas according to the duty of a Kṣatriya, and protect your own senses."
"From the Bhṛgus you shall have a terrible fear, but that will come about in due time.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O King, you always honor the Brāhmaṇas who are firm in their vows."
"O lord of men, seeing what rise of merit do you worship them?
Or, O observer of great vows, seeing what reward in the honoring of Brahmins do you worship them, O mighty-armed one? Tell me all of this."
Bhīṣma said:
"This Keśava, the high-minded one who has witnessed the results of his own great vows, will explain to you all the prosperity that comes from honoring a Brāhmaṇa."
My strength, hearing, speech, mind, and eyes,
as well as my knowledge, are not pure today;
I believe that the casting off of this body will occur before long.
The sun does not travel too swiftly today;
those great duties of the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas have been declared as they appear in the Purāṇa.
And those who follow the ancient rod of punishment—
learn the rest from Kṛṣṇa, O Pārtha,
for I know this Kṛṣṇa in his true essence.
For he who is Keśava of immeasurable soul, O lord of the Kauravas, who possesses that ancient power,
will speak of dharma in matters of doubt.
Kṛṣṇa created the earth, the atmosphere, and the heavens;
he is this ancient boar of terrible strength.
From the body of Kṛṣṇa, the Medinī came into being.
This entire world, both stationary and moving, he indeed released— the mountains, the quarters of space,
and below this, the intermediate region and the heavens.
The four cardinal directions and the four intermediate directions—
just so was this creation produced in succession;
he fashioned this ancient universe.
From his navel a lotus was produced,
where he himself of immeasurable luster was born;
by him, O Pārtha, that terrible darkness was severed.
That which stands threatening the ocean—
in the Kṛta age, Dharma was complete;
in the Tretā period, it attained the state of knowledge.
In the Dvāpara age, O Pārtha, Kṛṣṇa was strength;
in the Kali age, unrighteousness came to the earth.
That ancient god slew the Daityas.
He became the sovereign emperor of the ancient gods; he is the creator of beings, the source of what has been and what is to be,
and the protector of this entire world.
Whenever the dharma of the gods indeed declines,
then Kṛṣṇa is born among human beings; established in dharma, he is one whose self is purified.
He goes to both higher and lower worlds,
having abandoned those things to be abandoned for the sake of slaying the asuras; O Pārtha, he is the cause of what should and should not be done.
Know that the God who has done, will do, and is doing, is repeatedly Soma and this very Śakra;
he is Viśvakarman and he is Viśvarūpa.
He is the sustainer of all, the creator of all, and the conqueror of all; having conquered Śatakratu, he is Viśvakarman,
O Pārtha, he is the creator of all, and he is the one whose form is the universe.
He is the consumer of all, the sustainer of all, and the conqueror of all; he is the wielder of the trident, the bearer of blood, and the formidable one—
they praise him who is indeed known through his deeds.
Hundreds of Gandharvas and Apsarases constantly attend upon him, as do hundreds of deities; and the Rākṣasas carry him about on all sides.
He alone is the one who desires to conquer and possesses the increase of wealth (rāyaspoṣa);
at the sacrifice, the reciters praise him,
and the chanters of the Sāmaveda praise him with the Rathantara.
The Brahmins praise him with Vedic mantras;
the Adhvaryu priests prepare the sacrificial oblation for him. He has entered the ancient secret cave of Brahman.
He beheld the Mahī-sacrifice, O foremost of the Bharatas (13.143.16c);
and he of preeminent deeds rescued the Earth,
having agitated the Daityas, Uragas, and Dānavas.
13,143.016d*0659_01 Indra praises him with songs for the sake of his voice; 13,143.016d*0659_02 and he alone, O Bhārata, is the lord of cattle. 13,143.017a They offer various kinds of food to him;
They declare him alone to be the vehicle in battle;
for that eternal one, the intermediate space, the earth, and the heavens— all remain under his control.
He, Kumbharetas, emitted the ancient [seed],
from which they say the seer Vasiṣṭha was born; he is Mātariśvan, the pervasive one, possessing the vigor of a horse.
He is the radiant Savitṛ, the primordial god;
by him all the Asuras were utterly defeated,
and by his strides the three worlds here were conquered.
He belongs to the gods, to humans, and to the ancestors;
him alone they call the expansion of those who know sacrifice.
He alone rises, dividing time.
Its two solstices, northern and southern, measure 13,143.020 [yojanas]; its rays move upwards, sideways, and downwards,
heating the earth.
The Brahmins who know the Vedas take pleasure in him;
having employed his radiance, the sun shines.
Month after month, he, the performer of the sacrifice, ordains it.
Those who know the Vedas recite this at the sacrifice:
"He, the one with a single yoke, carries this three-naved wheel; joined by seven horses, he indeed bears it, possessing three abodes."
Possessing great splendor, all-pervading, and the lion among all,
Kṛṣṇa alone sustains the worlds;
he is golden, hidden in the seven, and endowed with consciousness.
Four-armed, lotus-dwelling, lotus-navelled,
the wise one who both eats and does not eat—
O Pārtha, always approach Kṛṣṇa as the creator.
Once,
that high-souled and all-pervading one, having consumed the Khāṇḍava forest and being like smoke-bannered fire, was satiated; he had conquered the Rākṣasas and the serpents.
Sarvatraga offered everything into the fire. He alone gave a white horse to Aśva; he alone then made all [beings] horses.
His chariot had three seats, three wheels,
a triple-layered pole, and was four-cornered;
it possessed five hubs and traversed the sky.
He fashioned the earth, the heavens, and the intermediate space; thus did Hṛṣīkeśa, whose splendor was like a fire of immeasurable brilliance, create the beautiful mountains.
Leaping over the rivers and desiring to slay him,
he warded off that thunderbolt as it was being hurled;
that Mahendra is indeed praised at the great sacrifice.
In the beginning, with thousands of ancient *ṛc*-verses,
the sages praise that Puruṣa, the Ancient One, as Suparṇa through the sacrificial piling (*cayana*).
"O King, that Durvāsas of great power can indeed be housed in one's home by no one other than him;
they call him the one ancient ṛṣi."
He, the creator of all, ordains his own manifestations—
he who makes the Vedas known as the supreme deity,
and who resorts to the ancient ordinances.
Know that whatever fruit exists in desire, in the Vedas, and in worldly affairs— all this resides in Viṣvaksena;
as do all the bright lights in the entire world.
The three worlds and the three guardians of the world,
the three fires and the three *vyāhṛtis*—
all the gods are indeed the son of Devakī.
He is the year, he is the season, he is the half-month;
he is the day and night, he is indeed the *kalā*, he is the *kāṣṭhā*; he is the *mātrā*s, the *muhūrta*s, the *lava*s, and the *kṣaṇa*s.
Understand all this as being within Viṣvaksena:
the moon and the sun, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the stars; all the new-moon days and the full-moon days.
The conjunctions of the constellations and the seasons, O Pārtha—
all this has been produced from Viṣvaksena;
as well as the Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and the two Aśvins.
The Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, and the six hosts of Maruts; Prajāpati, Aditi the mother of the gods, and all seven Ṛṣis from Kṛṣṇa.
Becoming the wind, he scatters the universe;
becoming fire, he burns with his universal form; becoming water, he submerges everything.
Having become Brahmā, he creates the multitudes of the universe; he is that which is to be known and that which causes one to know the Vedas;
he is the prescriptive rule and that which relies upon what is to be performed.
Know that Keśava is everything— in dharma, in the Veda, and in power— both the moving and the unmoving;
he stands under the control of him who is the source of all.
Having become light, that supreme one was in the beginning;
manifesting by his radiance, he is of universal form.
Having created the waters, he is indeed self-born and self-sprung.
Then he created the entire universe:
the seasons, various portents, diverse wonders,
the clouds, lightning, and all of Airāvata.
The seasons, the months, the various multitude of duties, the clouds descending with masses of lightning—
all that is stationary and all that is moving proceed from Kṛṣṇa.
Know this Viṣṇu as the one celebrated as Viśva;
they call Vāsudeva the abode of the universe and devoid of qualities, and Saṃkarṣaṇa the one who has become the individual soul (jīva).
Then the high-souled Self-born One commanded Pradyumna and Aniruddha as the fourth;
he [the Self-born] [created] that which consists of five parts and is endowed with the five elements.
Desiring to emit this entire universe,
O Pārtha, he then brought forth earth and wind, as well as space, light, and water.
Having thus created this fourfold world— both the stationary and the moving—
and having brought forth the universe, the Great-Souled One, the source of all, [remained].
There Viśvarūpa indeed remained through yoga;
from there he established the earth with its five seeds,
for the sky shall pour down abundant water upon the earth.
By him, O King, this entire universe was indeed created;
he, whose source is the Self, sustains it by means of his own self.
From him [proceed] the gods, the asuras, and human beings.
Desiring always to create all the worlds, the sages, the ancestors, and progeny— in short, the various worlds of living beings— the Lord of Beings [remained] intent on creation.
Know that all this— the auspicious and the inauspicious, the stationary and the moving—
that exists here and that which will come to be, all proceeds from Viṣvaksena.
Know all this to be Keśava:
he is death itself for living beings at the time of their end; Kṛṣṇa is manifest as the eternal upholder of dharma.
Whatever has been and whatever we do not know here—
know that all this proceeds from Viṣvaksena;
whatever is praised in the worlds, whatever is meritorious, and whatever is auspicious or inauspicious.
All that [which you have said] regarding Keśava would be the reverse, for he is inconceivable.
Such is this Keśava: he is the Self-Existent One, Nārāyaṇa, supreme and imperishable.
He is the center of this world, both moving and stationary;
he is the origin and the dissolution of all beings.
Such is the divine Keśava, who is further Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme.
Hari is the beginning, the end, and the middle of all things in terms of space and time; he is the source and the dissolution of all beings, both those that move and those that are stationary.
— Vaiśampāyana.
Having heard the words of his grandfather, O King, your great-grandfather bowed to the lotus-eyed one and spoke these words. Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Tell me, O Madhusūdana, the fruit of honoring a brāhmaṇa;
for you are the knower of this matter, since even the Grandfather knows you.
Vāsudeva said:

Listen attentively, O King, bull among the Bharatas, as I speak of the virtues of the twice-born according to their true nature, O best of the Kurus. Long ago, O joy of the Kurus, while I was seated in Dvāravatī—
13,144.003a Provoked by the brahmins, Pradyumna questioned him:
13,144.003c "O Madhusūdana, what is the fruit of honoring brahmins,
both for one who is a lord in this world and in the next?"
"O giver of honor, what is the fruit of always honoring the twice-born?
O father, tell me all of this, for I have a very great doubt in this matter. When these words were spoken by Pradyumna, I [then]—
"O Great King, listen with a concentrated mind to what I replied;
O son of Rukmiṇī, learn from me the prosperity resulting from the worship of Brahmins—
[the fruit] regarding the three aims of life, liberation, fame, fortune, and the pacification of diseases."

"O son of Rukmiṇī, O dear son, in this world and likewise in the next, these twice-born ones— these lords who have Soma as their king— are indeed to be gratified by us during the worship of deities and ancestors; for they are the masters of happiness and suffering."
There is no doubt in my mind that happiness has the Brahmin as its foremost;
likewise, vigor, longevity, renown, fame, and strength have the Brahmin as their foremost.
All the worlds and the lords of the worlds themselves have the Brahmin as their precursor.
"How then, my son, could I not show respect, thinking 'I am the lord'? Let there be no anger in you, O mighty-armed one, toward these twice-born ones;
for a Brāhmaṇa is a great being, both in this world and in the next."
If, when enraged, these seers who perceive the truth directly could reduce this entire world to ashes,
and could likewise create other worlds as well as lords of those worlds, how could I not behave with perfect propriety toward them, given my knowledge of their great splendor?
"O dear one, a brahmin lived in my house— he was tawny like a monkey,
dressed in bark garments, carrying a *bilva* staff, and possessing long hair, beard, and nails;
in stature on this earth, he was taller than even the tallest men."
He wandered through the worlds, both divine and human,
singing these verses in crossroads and assembly halls:
"Who would provide lodging in their home for the honored Brahmin Durvāsas?"
Angry with all beings even when only a slight offense has been committed, who indeed would grant me shelter after hearing my reproaches? Whoever might let me dwell here should not provoke my anger.
No one paid him any heed; therefore, I took him in as my guest. At times he would eat the food of many thousands, and at other times he would eat very little, or he would not go home again.
He laughs without cause and likewise weeps without cause;
at that time, there was no one on earth equal to him in age.
Having gone to our dwelling, he [inspected] the beds and the coverlets.
Having burned the decorated maidens, he himself then departed.
That one of great splendor then set fire to [the city] himself and rushed forward.
Then that sage of rigid vows spoke to me again.
"I wish to eat milk-rice with black sesamum," he said, being in great haste.
Since I was always aware of his mind, I had all kinds of food and drink, as well as various high- and low-quality delicacies, prepared for him in my house.
"May they be honored," he had previously urged me; therefore, I presented him with the glowing milk-rice (*pāyasa*). Having eaten it, he quickly spoke these words:
"Quickly anoint your limbs with this milk-rice," he said; and without reflection, I did exactly as he said. With that remnant, I smeared my limbs and my head.
Then he saw his mother, of beautiful countenance, nearby;
smiling,
the sage smeared her as well with the milk-rice and quickly yoked her to the chariot.
Having mounted that chariot, he departed from my house;
blazing with the color of fire, that wise brahmin acted like a driver of a chariot,
goading the young Rukmiṇī with his whip even as I looked on.
"And at that time, not even the slightest suffering born of envy arose within me.
Then he went out by way of the great royal highway.
Seeing that great marvel, the members of the Daśārha clan were filled with indignation.
There, some whispered among themselves, having conversed with one another:
"Only Brāhmaṇas should be born, and no other caste by any means;
for what other man here could live after mounting this chariot?"
The venom of a poisonous snake is fierce, but the poison [of this] is even fiercer than that;
for one consumed by the Brahma-poisonous snake, there is no physician whatsoever.
As that invincible one was proceeding, Rukmiṇī stumbled on the path.
The illustrious one could not endure that; he then quickly urged [his chariot] forward.
Then, extremely enraged, that twice-born man leaped down from his chariot and, on foot, ran along a bypath toward the south.
As that best of the twice-born was running along the wrong path, I ran after him, smeared with milk-rice, saying, "Be gracious, O Blessed One! Then,
looking at me, the radiant brahmin spoke to me.
"O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, anger has been conquered by you by your very nature. O observer of noble vows, I have seen no transgression in you here.
I am pleased with you, Govinda; choose whatever boons you desire."

"O dear one, behold the kind of prosperity that has come to me through my devotion. As long as there shall be a desire for food among human beings, so too shall their devotion toward you be equal to their devotion toward food."
As long as your merit shall endure in the worlds,
so long will you attain preeminence throughout the three worlds;
O Janārdana, you shall be beloved by all the world.
"Whatever of yours was broken, burnt, or otherwise destroyed,
O Janārdana, you shall see it all exactly as it was, or even more excellent than before— provided,
O Madhusūdana, that this remains smeared upon your limbs."
"Therefore, O Acyuta, there is no fear of death for you as long as you desire [to live]. But why, my son, is your sole foot now smeared?
This is not pleasing to me. Thus he spoke to me with affection at that time.
Having been addressed thus, I beheld my own body endowed with splendor. Delighted, I spoke to Rukmiṇī, who possesses the highest fame among all women:
"O beautiful one, you shall attain unsurpassed renown and glory in the world."
"O beautiful lady, neither old age, nor disease, nor even discoloration shall touch you;
endowed with a holy fragrance, you shall worship Kṛṣṇa,
who has sixteen thousand wives."
"You shall become most excellent and share the same world as Keśava.
Having spoken thus to your mother,
Durvāsas, blazing like fire, possessed of great splendor, then addressed me as he was about to depart.
"O Keśava, let this very same disposition of yours be maintained toward the Brāhmaṇas.
Having spoken thus, O son, he vanished on the spot. When he had disappeared, I prescribed the *upāṃśu* vow.
"O Lord, whatever a Brāhmaṇa might say, I shall do it all"—
having made this vow with your mother, O son,
I then entered the house with a most joyful heart.

As soon as I had entered the house, O dear son, I saw that everything was new— everything that had been broken and everything that had been burnt by that brahmin. Then, seeing it all restored, firm, and new, I was filled with amazement.
"And at that time, O son of Rukmiṇī, I honored that twice-born one with my mind.
Thus, O bull of the Bharatas, when questioned by the son of Rukmiṇī,
I then related all of this regarding the majesty of that foremost of the twice-born.

In the same way, O Kaunteya, O Lord, you too must always worship the highly fortunate Brahmins with words and gifts at all times. It was by this means that I attained such prosperity, born from the grace of the Brahmins.
"And that which Bhīṣma said to me, O bull of the Bharatas, is true.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Madhusūdana, that which occurred then through the grace of Durvāsas was yours."
"O best among the wise, you ought to explain to me that wisdom which has been attained here; I wish to know in truth his great majesty, as well as the names of that high-souled one."
Vāsudeva said:
"Behold, O great king, having paid homage to Kapardin, I shall tell you what spiritual welfare was attained and what fame was acquired."
O Lord of the People, listen as I recite that *Śatarudrīya* which I study every morning after rising purified and with palms joined in reverence.
Listen to me concerning that Śiva, the omnipresent Rudra, who is the creator.
At the end of his ascetic penance, the great ascetic Prajāpati created that [world];
but Śaṃkara, O dear one, created all beings, both stationary and moving.
There is no being superior to Mahādeva, O lord of the people.
For he is indeed the source of all beings in these three worlds;
no one at all dares to stand before that Great-Souled One,
for there exists no being equal to him in the three worlds.
For even by the scent of him when he is enraged in battle, his enemies become unconscious, mostly struck down, trembling,
and falling; and his terrible roar is like the sound of rain clouds.
Upon hearing this, even the hearts of the gods would shatter in battle;
and those whom the wielder of the Pināka, enraged, might behold with his terrible form,
he would reduce to ashes in that very instant, just as a crest of fire consumes its fuel.
Neither the gods, nor the asuras in the world, nor the gandharvas,
nor the pannagas find happiness when he is enraged— even those who have retreated into caves.
This was so even while Prajāpati Dakṣa was sacrificing at his extensive ritual.
Then Bhava, free from fear, became enraged and pierced the sacrifice;
releasing an arrow from his bow with a roar, he let out a great shout.
The gods found no comfort, much less peace, and were overcome by despair.
When the sacrifice was suddenly dispersed and Maheśvara became enraged,
all the worlds were thrown into turmoil by the sound of his bowstring striking his palm;
O Pārtha, the gods and asuras became helpless and fell into despair.
The waters were agitated and the earth trembled;
even the mountains flowed away and the sky split asunder on all sides. Enveloped by blinding darkness, the worlds did not shine.
O Bhārata, the light of the luminaries, together with the sun, was utterly extinguished. Then,
being greatly terrified, the ṛṣis— desiring the welfare of all beings as well as their own— performed rites for peace and auspiciousness.
Then, filled with rage and possessing fierce prowess, he rushed toward the gods;
in his fury, he struck out and destroyed the eyes of Bhaga.
Endowed with a supreme form, he then charged at Pūṣan.
As he was consuming the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), Rudra caused his teeth to fall out.
Then those gods, trembling, bowed down before Śaṅkara;
yet Rudra again took up his blazing, well-sharpened arrow.

Having witnessed the prowess of Rudra, the gods, together with the ṛṣis, were terrified; then those foremost of the wise sought to propitiate Śarva. Thereupon, the gods, having joined their palms in reverence, recited the Śatarudrīya.
Being praised by the thirty gods, Maheśvara was appeased;
they assigned a distinguished portion of the sacrifice to Rudra,
and out of fear, O King, the thirty gods sought his protection.
By that very great anger, that sacrifice was restored;
whatever had been destroyed there was offered back exactly as it was.
Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O mighty-armed one, that Maheśvara conquered the three cities;
[who was] Vāsudeva? O omniscient Madhusūdana, tell me this according to the truth."
Listen to me, my son, as I tell you how the three cities were burnt. In ancient times, there were three cities belonging to the powerful Asuras in the sky:
one made of iron, one of silver, and another of gold.
Maghavan was unable to shatter them even with all his weapons;
then all the immortals, being oppressed, went to Rudra for refuge.
Thereupon, all the high-souled gods assembled and spoke.
O Rudra, the creatures will become fierce in all their undertakings.
Slay that Rudra—the Lord skilled in all weapons—who performs terrible deeds;
destroy the Daityas along with their cities and protect the worlds, O giver of honor!
Thus addressed, he said "So be it," and made Viṣṇu the tip of his arrow;
likewise, he made Śalya the shaft and Vaivasvata Yama the nock;
he made all the Vedas the bow and the supreme Sāvitrī the bowstring.
Having made the gods his chariot and having employed them in every way,
he pierced those [demons] with that three-jointed, three-pointed arrow—
[an arrow] radiant as the sun and possessing a splendor equal to the fire of cosmic destruction.
O Bhārata, those Asuras, along with their cities, were burnt there by Rudra;
struck down, they suddenly fell into the vast waters of the ocean.
And he saw again that boy with five tufts of hair resting upon his lap.
Then Umā, desiring to know who he was, spoke thus;
and as Śakra, being envious, was about to strike with his thunderbolt,
she paralyzed that arm, which resembled an iron club, along with the thunderbolt itself.

Neither did all the gods, together with the Prajāpatis, perceive that Lord of the World; they were utterly bewildered by that Sovereign. Then, having meditated, the Blessed Brahmā [beheld] him of immeasurable splendor.
Realizing, "This is the most excellent one," he paid homage to that Lord of Umā.
Then those gods propitiated Umā and Rudra;
