and that arm of the slayer of Bala became as it was before.
And he, having become a powerful brahmin named Durvāsas,
dwelt for a long time in my house at Dvāravatī;
he employed many acts of hostility within my abode.
And because of their nobility, I could not endure that unbearable [power] of his.
He is indeed Rudra, he is Śiva, he is Agni, he is Śarva, he is the All-conqueror;
he is the Lord of the Gods, he is Vāyu, he is the two Aśvins, and he is the lightning.
He is the moon and he is Īśāna; he is the sun and he is Varuṇa.
He is time, he is the end-maker, death; he is darkness, night, and days.
He is the months, the fortnights, the seasons, the twilights, and the year.
He is the Ordainer and the Disposer; he is Viśvakarman, the omniscient one. He is the stars, the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, and likewise the planets.
The Blessed One is the universal form, the immeasurable self, of unfathomable splendor.
He is indeed one-fold, two-fold, and many-fold;
he is hundred-fold, thousand-fold, and likewise hundred-thousand-fold.
Such is that Mahādeva, and the Blessed One is even more than this.
"Indeed, his virtues cannot be fully described even in hundreds of years.
Vāsudeva said:
"O Yudhiṣṭhira, O mighty-armed one, [listen to] the great fortune of that high-souled one."
Learn from me concerning Rudra, who possesses many forms and many names.
They call him Agni, Mahādeva, as well as Sthāṇu, Maheśvara,
Ekākṣa, Tryambaka, Viśvarūpa, and Śiva.
The Brahmins who know the Vedas understand two bodies of that god:
one is terrible, the other is auspicious; yet those two bodies are further divided in many ways. That body of his which is fierce and terrible is Agni, it is lightning, and it is the sun.
That which is auspicious and gentle in him is his dharma, as well as the waters and the moon;
O bull of the Bharatas, half of his self is said to be fire. He practices celibacy, and that which is his auspicious body is likewise so.
By that most terrible form of his which destroys the world,

he is remembered as Maheśvara because of his lordship (*īśvaratva*) and his greatness (*mahattva*). That he burns [the world], that he is sharp, that he is fierce, and that he is majestic— [for these reasons he is so called].
Because he consumes flesh, blood, and marrow, he is therefore called Rudra.
Because he is the most eminent among the gods, because his domain is vast,
and because he protects the great universe, he is remembered as Mahādeva.
Because he constantly promotes all goals through all his actions,

desiring the welfare of human beings, he is therefore remembered as Śiva. Furthermore, because he stands above and burns away [impurities], and because he is the origin and the sustenance of the vital breaths (prāṇa).
Because his linga is eternally fixed, he is therefore remembered as Sthāṇu.
Since his form is manifold— consisting of the past, the future,
and the present, as well as all that is stationary and all that moves— he is therefore remembered as Bahurūpa.
Because his form is smoke-colored (*dhūmra*), he is therefore called Dhūrjaṭi; and because all the gods (*viśve devāḥ*) reside within him, he is remembered as Viśvarūpa.
He is the thousand-eyed, the ten-thousand-eyed, or even one whose eyes are on every side.
His origin is from the eye, and there is no end to his eyes;
because he protects the animals in every way and rejoices with them,
and because he is their sovereign, he is therefore known as Paśupati.
When his *liṅga* remains established through perpetual celibacy (*brahmacarya*), the worlds honor him; thus he is remembered as Maheśvara.
Furthermore, those worlds who worship him are dear to that Great-Souled One.
For the sake of bestowing grace upon his devotees, he is therefore remembered as having a concealed *liṅga*.
Indeed, whoever worships the body or the *liṅga* of the Great-Souled One,
that person who constantly worships the *liṅga* attains great prosperity.
The sages, the gods, as well as the gandharvas and apsarases,
likewise worshiped only that linga which stands upright;
when it was thus being worshiped, Maheśvara rejoiced.
With a joyful heart, Śaṅkara, who is affectionate toward his devotees, bestows happiness upon his devotees; indeed,
he is delighted and grants supreme happiness and wealth in this world.

This very god dwells eternally in cremation grounds; people there worship him who frequents the abodes of heroes. He is Death here in this world, situated unequally within the bodies of living beings.
And that wind is the *prāṇa* and *apāna* within the bodies of embodied beings.
Its many forms are both terrible and radiant;
the wise Brahmins know those which are worshipped in the world.

Many names of his are etymologically explained in the Vedas according to their true meaning, on account of his greatness, his omnipresence, and likewise his deeds. And in the Veda, the learned brahmins know his supreme Śatarudrīya hymn.
Following Vyāsa, there was also the attendance upon that high-souled one.
He is called the giver of all worlds and the great universe itself;
other brahmins and sages declare him to be the eldest-born.
For this Agni was born first from the mouth of the gods;
he releases even the vital breaths that have been obstructed by various kinds of seizing spirits.
That virtuous soul, the protector, liberates those who have come to him for refuge.

He bestows upon human beings long life, health, sovereignty, wealth, and abundant objects of desire; he alone withdraws them again. And it is said that his sovereignty extends even over the gods, beginning with Śakra.
He alone is eternally superior in both the auspicious and inauspicious matters of the three worlds;
moreover, because of his sovereignty over all desires, he is called Īśvara. And he is Maheśvara, for he is the Lord of the great worlds.
This entire world is pervaded by that deity through many diverse forms;
his mouth is the submarine fire in the ocean.
Vaiśampāyana said:
When Kṛṣṇa, the son of Devakī, had spoken these words,
Yudhiṣṭhira questioned Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu, once more:
"O man of great intelligence, O best among all upholders of dharma, [please speak further] regarding the final determination."
"Is it direct perception or scripture? What could be the cause of these two?
Bhīṣma said:
"There is no doubt whatsoever in this matter; such is my conviction."
"Listen, O wise one; I shall speak to you, for you ask correctly. O King, while the doubt is easy to understand, its resolution here is difficult;
for where there is the perception of doubt, what is seen and heard is indeed infinite."
Those who consider themselves wise logicians perceive only direct perception as the cause;
they conclude that truth, doubt, and even the non-existent do not exist.
Thus, those fools who imagine themselves learned reach an improper conclusion.
Now, if you think that there might be a single cause for this,
O Bhārata, it is possible— through a long period of time, by one who is disciplined and unwearied, and by providing various means for the maintenance of life— to discover it.
This cause can indeed be realized by that alone and not by anything else;
for having reached the end of causes, one attains vast and supreme knowledge. Whether addressed through reasoning or through the supreme scripture of Dharma, this is the highest truth.
One attains the vast light of the entire world;
O King, this is the arrival through reality, as well as the departure by means of another cause—
the relinquishing of speech that is ungraspable and unbound.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Perception is established through the world, and the worlds are preceded by the scriptures;
there are many kinds of conduct of the cultured (śiṣṭas). Tell me about that, O Grandfather."
Bhīṣma said:
When dharma is being carried away by powerful and evil-minded men, its established order,
even if maintained with great effort, is shattered by the force of time.
Unrighteousness, disguised in the form of righteousness, is like wells covered over with grass;
by means of these, the established conduct (*vṛtta*) is destroyed—listen to this, Yudhiṣṭhira.
And those who, being destitute of livelihood, destroy it while being devoted to the abandonment of sacred learning (*śruta*), [are likewise to be known].
Regarding those dull-witted ones who hate the Dharma, there is doubt concerning them. But as for those who are never satiated with the virtuous, whose intellects are rooted in the scriptures,
and who find contentment in the Supreme alone— worship them and question them.
Having cast behind them the pursuit of desire and wealth, which follow greed and delusion, those who are perfectly awakened perceive only the Dharma; attend upon them and question them.
Their conduct does not deviate from the performance of sacrifices and the study of the Vedas.
The *Mūlācāra*, however, [is established] for the virtuous (*sādhūnām*) through sacrifice, Vedic study, and conduct. Furthermore, conduct, its cause, and dharma—these three [are the foundation].
Those who find fault with dharma attend upon dharma.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
Once again, my intellect is utterly bewildered here by doubt,
as I search for the further shore in this boundless sea without seeing it.

"If the Vedas, direct perception, and traditional conduct are each a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), and if these three are established as distinct, how can *dharma* be one while the three are separate? Bhīṣma said:
When Dharma is being carried away by powerful and evil-minded men,
O King, if you consider it thus, know that the investigation of Dharma is indeed one, though its manifestation is threefold.
My understanding of the distinctness of these three is likewise;
the path for all three has been declared—practice it exactly as such. One should not, however, engage in speculative inquiry regarding dharma.
"O best of the Bharatas, let there never be any doubt in you regarding this.
Like one who is blind or dull-witted, act without hesitation upon what I say.
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, and charity—this is the fourfold path."
O Ajātaśatru, practice this eternal dharma:
follow that conduct toward the Brahmins which was practiced by your fathers and grandfathers, O mighty-armed one; for they are the guides to heaven.
If an ignorant man were to treat what is authoritative as non-authoritative,
he would not deserve to be considered authoritative himself, for he is merely a source of dispute.
Therefore, serve the Brāhmaṇas alone, honoring them and holding them in high esteem.
"Understand that all these worlds are contained within these very [beings].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"Those who revile dharma and those who devotedly worship it—"
"May the Blessed One explain this: where do those such as they go? Bhīṣma said:
"Their minds are completely shrouded by passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas)."
Men who hate righteousness fall into hell;
but those men, O Great King, who constantly attend to righteousness and are devoted to truth and uprightness, they indeed enjoy the heavenly realm.
For them, delight in Dharma alone shall arise from the service of their teacher. Those who worship Dharma thoroughly attain the world of the gods,
whether they be humans or indeed gods, having truly disciplined their bodies.
Those who possess righteousness and are free from greed and hatred prosper happily.
The wise say that Dharma is the first son of Brahmā; those who possess righteousness wait upon him, just as one waits expectantly for ripe fruit.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
What is the appearance of the wicked, and what do the virtuous do?
May your lordship tell me this: what are the characteristics of the good and the bad?
Bhīṣma said:
Those who are of evil conduct, difficult to restrain, foul-mouthed, and wicked,
as well as those virtuous ones endowed with good character— these are the characteristics of refined behavior.
Devoted to truth and uprightness, these virtuous ones, whose conduct is in accordance with Dharma,
[walk] upon the royal highway, amidst cows, and within the cow-pens.
O Indra among kings, they do not discharge urine or feces while standing.
Having given food to the five, the virtuous eat what remains. They do not chatter while eating, nor do they sleep with wet hands.
They circumambulate the fire, the ox, a deity, a cow-pen, a crossroads, a righteous Brāhmaṇa,
a sacred tree, the elderly, those afflicted by heat, women, children, and the sick.
They yield the right of way to Brahmins, cows, and kings,
as well as to all guests, servants, and their own kin.
One should provide food in common and not personally consume the finest portion.

There is nothing else equal to the dharma of truth and uprightness; it is said that by this, a cow named Bahulā attained the highest state. Through the curse of a sage, a certain brahmin was transformed into a tiger.
Having tasted her abundant fondness for eating through a solemn oath, and having released that cow whose calf had been weaned, she beheld it and, remembering her former state,
departed once more to her own kingdom and the stainless worlds.

Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, a king who delights in truth and uprightness, having protected his kingdom impartially, shall go happily to heaven after crossing over [this world]. Likewise, he should be a protector of those seeking refuge and one who offers a warm welcome.
Morning and evening is the meal ordained for human beings by the gods;
eating in between is not seen as permissible, for that is the rule of fasting.
Just as the sacrificial fire awaits its specific time at the hour of the oblation, so too does the body await its appointed time for food.

Likewise, when a woman is in her season, she awaits that very season and does not go to another man; this indeed is remembered as *brahmacarya*. "The nectar of the gods (*amṛta*), the Brahmins, and cows—these three are one."
Therefore, one should always honor cows and Brahmins according to the prescribed rule. One does not incur sin by consuming meat that has been consecrated with sacrificial formulas (*yajus*).
However, meat from the back, meat not prepared for sacrifice (*vṛthāmāṃsa*), and the flesh of one's own son are equal [in their forbidden nature].

Whether in one's own country or in a foreign land, one should never let a guest go hungry; having made one's work truly fruitful, one should present it to one's teachers. After saluting and honoring them, a seat should be offered to the teachers.
By honoring their gurus, they increase in longevity, fame, and prosperity.
One should never speak over those who are aged, nor should one ever command them; likewise, one should not sit while they are standing. In this way, one’s lifespan remains unimpaired.
A wise man should not look upon a naked woman, nor even men;
he should always engage in sexual intercourse and take food in private.
Among all sacred sites, the teacher is the highest sacred site; among all pure things, the heart is the purest.
Knowledge is the highest of all visions; contentment is the supreme happiness.
Morning and evening, one should listen to the abundant words of the elders;
for by constantly serving the elders, a man attains sacred learning.
In a gift-hall, in the presence of cows and Brahmins,
during Vedic recitation, and while eating, one should always raise the right hand;
one should constantly restrain speech and mind, as well as the wandering of the senses.
Refined milk-rice, constant offerings of gruel, rice-and-pulse porridge, and oblations;
the Aṣṭakā rites dedicated to the ancestors, the honoring of elders,
auspicious acts during the shaving of the beard, and the welcoming of those who have sneezed.
One should offer congratulations on the recovery from illness for all people;
even when in great distress, one should never say "you" to another who is superior.
Among the wise, the address "thou" and actual killing are not distinguished in their gravity.
One should behave toward inferiors, equals, and disciples in this same manner.
The hearts of evildoers constantly proclaim their sin;
those who conceal it while knowing its nature perish before the great assembly.
For the wicked conceal the karma they have performed with deliberate intent: "Men do not see me, nor do the deities see me.
Stricken by evil, the sinner is reborn indeed as evil.
Just as a moneylender awaits his interest when his body perishes,
so too, evil covered by righteousness causes that very righteousness to increase.
Just as salt submerged in water dissolves away, [so do sins vanish when covered by dharma].

Sin destroyed by expiation perishes instantly; therefore, one should not conceal a sin, for it increases when concealed. Having committed it, however, it should be confessed to the virtuous, and they will indeed pacify it.
Wealth accumulated with expectation that is not enjoyed in due time passes to others upon the departure of that embodied being; therefore,
one should always acquire wealth through the resolve to practice Dharma.
The wise declare that the mind is the dharma of all beings;
therefore, all beings abide in dharma alone. One should practice dharma alone and not be one who makes a banner of dharma.
For those who consume the Dharma are indeed merchants of Dharma. One should worship the gods without hypocrisy and serve one's teachers without deceit.
For the sake of one’s journey to the next world, one should deposit a treasure known as "giving."
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"The great seers praise the mental tīrthas in this world.
Bhīṣma [replied].

O tiger among the Kurus, you ought to tell me those things as they truly are. Listen, O giver of honor, as I speak of the mental *tīrthas* here, by bathing properly in which a man attains the supreme goal.
Truth is a sacred ford; forgiveness is a sacred ford; truth is the restraint of the senses;
compassion toward all beings is a sacred ford, as is straightforwardness.
Generosity is a sacred ford; self-control is a sacred ford; contentment is the supreme sacred ford.
Celibacy is the supreme ford, and kind speech is a ford;
knowledge is a ford, austerity is a ford, and fortitude is declared to be a ford. Yet that which is the ford even among fords is the supreme purity of mind.
One whose limbs are merely moistened with water is not truly called "bathed.
He is truly bathed who is bathed in self-restraint, whose mental impurities are thoroughly purified. He who is greedy, malicious, cruel, hypocritical, and devoted to sensual objects is not bathed.
Even if he has bathed in all the sacred fords (*tīrtha*), the sinner remains truly defiled;
those whose mental impurities have not been purified do not go to heaven. Even passion for sense objects is called a mental impurity.
And detachment toward those very things is declared to be his purity. A mind that is corrupted within is not purified by bathing at sacred fords;
even if washed in water a hundred times, it remains as impure as a vessel that once held liquor.
Wherever a man may dwell, having restrained the collection of his senses,
there for him is Kurukṣetra, Naimiṣa, Puṣkara, and Gayā—
in that lake of knowledge whose waters are truth, which removes the impurities of passion and hatred.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"He who has bathed in the Mānasa-tīrtha attains the supreme goal.
O Bhārata, what is the basis of evil, and what is its origin?"
Bhīṣma said:
"O Grandfather, tell me what is declared to be the cause of this;
greed is the foundation of evil, and greed alone is its source."
Let there be no doubt in you regarding this: greed is the cause of evil.
From greed arises anger; from greed proceeds malice. From greed come delusion and deceit, as well as pride and envy.
Lust cannot be filled by objects, even by those of many kinds,
just as the ocean cannot be filled by rivers with eternally deep waters.
One should have no trust in any living beings and be merciless toward all living beings.
O Bhārata, even those who are straightforward toward all beings become crooked through greed;
and even those of great learning who retain vast scriptures and are capable of cutting through doubts, fall downward when seized by greed.

When greed is destroyed, all the sins of embodied beings go to destruction; and when greed increases, O King, they increase as well—of this there is no doubt. Therefore, O Yudhiṣṭhira, abandon greed with every effort.
"If you desire, O Great King, an eternal state for yourself," Yudhiṣṭhira said: "Even one who is very powerful does not obtain wealth if he is devoid of good fortune."
13,149.001c One who is endowed with fortune obtains wealth even when he is weak and young;
13,149.001d how does he obtain that, and by what means? You ought to tell me this. 13,149.002a At a time when there is no gain, one does not obtain it even when effort has been exerted.
At the time of gain, one obtains abundant wealth without effort;
yet hundreds of men are seen whose efforts are fruitless,
for a man is often seen to remain poor despite always exerting himself.
Many people are seen prospering without effort; O best of the Bharatas, if mortals could obtain results through effort alone, nothing unattainable would remain unobtained by men.
When a man is seen to have exerted effort yet remains fruitless,

while another who does not seek wealth through hundreds of methods is happy; and when men are seen to remain poor despite having repeatedly committed improper acts— [then one understands the nature of destiny].
Yet other people are seen who, though possessed of wealth, abide in unrighteousness. Furthermore,
for what reason is it that one who has studied the science of polity is not seen to be endowed with policy,
while one ignorant of it is raised to the position of a minister?
For one who possesses learning may be destitute, while one lacking learning may be wealthy; likewise,
if a man were to obtain happiness by relying solely on his learning,
then a learned man would not resort to one devoid of learning for the sake of a livelihood.

Just as a man overcomes thirst upon obtaining water, so too does a person abandon ignorance once the truth has been perceived through knowledge. One whose time has not yet come does not die, even if pierced by hundreds of arrows.
Even if touched by the tip of a blade of grass, one whose time has come does not live.
Bhīṣma said:
"If, despite striving and undertaking endeavors, one does not obtain wealth..."
One should undertake fierce austerity, for what is not sown does not sprout.
By giving, one becomes an enjoyer; by serving the elders, one becomes wise;
and by non-violence, one attains long life—so say the wise.
Therefore, one should give and not beg; one should also honor those who are righteous.
One should be gentle in speech, a doer of what is pleasing, pure, and non-violent toward all sentient beings.
When [the world] arises from valid cognition, and when its intrinsic nature consists of pleasure and pain...
"Be as firm as gnats, insects, and ants, O Yudhiṣṭhira.
Bhīṣma said:
"Whatever is caused to be done and whatever is done—whether it be good or evil—is thus performed."

13.150.001c One should take heart there by honoring [others], but one should not place trust in them by failing to honor them. 13.150.002a Time alone here, bestowing restraint and favor through its own course,
enters the intellect of beings and impels them toward their duties and purposes.
But when his intellect becomes righteous and reveals what is beneficial, then that virtuous-souled one should take heart; though firm in resolve, he should not be overconfident.
For this much alone is the characteristic of a wise person among living beings.
Even one who is endowed with the right time and understands both [sides] should carry out the remaining purpose.
For just as men who have attained sovereignty honor other men,
even so do the righteous here honor themselves by means of their own selves.
The purification of one's being comes through austerity, through the worship of the deities,
through eternal purity, and also through sacred learning, giving, and the recitation of prayers; for Time never bestows righteousness through unrighteousness in any way whatsoever.
Therefore, one should know that the self which practices the Dharma is pure;
for unrighteousness is unable even to touch it, just as one cannot touch a blazing fire,
since the Dharma is constantly protected by Time.
For these two must be accomplished by Time; indeed, Dharma brings victory and shall become the light-maker for all three worlds.
In this matter, some wise man might lead another person by taking him by the hand.
Carried by Dharma through the Dharma, which abounds in fears and deceptions,
he shall attain the supreme, imperishable state; indeed,
trust alone must be placed [in it].
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"O Grandfather, O mighty-armed one, best among all upholders of dharma,
please tell me of that gentle dharma which is endowed with the qualities of truth and straightforwardness."
"I wish to hear from you the unsurpassed word of truth;
you ought to tell me that which was previously spoken by Bahulā.
Bhīṣma.
O gentle one, I shall proclaim the Dharma endowed with truth and straightforwardness—
the supreme dialogue between a tiger capable of assuming any form at will and a cow—
taking place in the delightful region of Mathurā, which was filled with wealth and grain.
13,150.009d@020_0008 Crowded with people from various lands and adorned with sacrificial enclosures,
13,150.009d@020_0009 there lies that delightful city situated on the bank of the Yamunā;
13,150.009d@020_0010 resembling a half-moon in shape, it is graced by learned men.
It was strewn with Indra-poles and banners, graced by cowherdesses,
crowded with many twice-born brahmins, adorned with various market goods, perfectly proportioned, most delightful, and fashioned under the constellation Svāti.
It was difficult to conquer due to its walls, watchtowers, and gateways, as well as its moats and other defenses;
it was adorned with *āmrātaka*, *kapittha*, and royal *vṛkṣa* trees,
and beautified by divine temples and groves of plantain trees.
It shines with white houses resembling rows of swans;
it is filled with *panasa*, *bakula*, *tāla*, *priyāla*, and *nāgakesara* trees,
as well as *karavīra*, *karṇikāra*, *pāṭala*, *aśoka*, and *campaka*.

It was adorned with gardens featuring *mallikā*, *kundaja*, and *jātī* jasmine; *kubjaka*, *hlādaka*, and *kuraṇṭaka* flowers; golden and white *yūthī*; *kiṃkirāta*, blue lotuses (*utpala*), and others; as well as *puṃnāga* trees and *bakula* shrubs.
It was completely filled with wealth and grain, adorned with herds of cattle;
its auspiciousness was purified by the sounds of Vedic recitation,
and it was beautified by delightful sacrificial altars, crossroads, triple-junctions, and market squares.
And there is the great city of Laṅkā, rich in jewels, like that of Rāvaṇa;
there dwells King Indrasena, endowed with the duties of royalty,
who is constantly devoted to dharma and a worshiper of the gods and guests.
Devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, glorious, and equal to Prajāpati on earth,
that lion among kings protected that beautiful city,
which was ever-joyful with constant festivals and resounded with the music of conchs and instruments.
It was filled with performances by those skilled in fine singing and worthy of being beheld; it was graced by well-arranged market-streets, crossroads,
and long ponds, wells, pools, and lakes.

"O Yudhiṣṭhira, have you seen or heard of the city named Candravatī, which was filled with assembly halls and water-stations, and crowded with weddings and sacrifices? Listen to the truth concerning what occurred in that city in the past."
A certain eminent brahmin possessed an excellent, auspicious cow,
well-nourished, very contented, and famous by the name Bahulā. She was the chief of his herd of cattle, white as a swan, and yielded a jarful of milk.
With a long nose, well-proportioned limbs, excellent hair, and delicate skin;
with broad hips, divine, and full buttocks and breasts;
she was endowed with all auspicious marks and beautiful in every limb.
Blue-throated, with a beautiful neck, wearing a bell and possessing a sweet voice,
she moved fearlessly at the head of the entire herd. Having gone alone, she would graze at her pleasure upon the hidden village grain.
There he grazes upon grass that is thick, well-flowered, fragrant, and uncut.
On the bank of the Yamunā, there is another mountain there named Rohita,
adorned with many caves, grottoes, and waterfalls.
In its north-eastern quarter, in a place that was terrible, thick with grass, narrow, uneven, impassable, fearsome, hair-raising,
filled with deer and lions, and inhabited by many beasts of prey—
In this fortress, dense with creepers, trees, and the like, and resounding with the howls of hundreds of jackals, dwells a fierce, terrifying being who can assume any form at will— a leopard,
a consumer of blood and flesh, possessing great fangs and immense strength.
Resembling a great mountain, with a voice like the roar of clouds,
having the mouths of great caves and ravines, with sharp fangs and claws as his weapons— he was the righteous-souled one named Nandin, devoted to the welfare of the cowherds.
With long grasses whose tips were uncut, he protected his wealth of cattle. A cow from that herd, strayed and wandering out of thirst for grass, arrived right before the tiger.
Rushing toward her, the tiger cried out, "Stay! Stay!
"Today you have been ordained as my prey; you have come to the forest of your own accord.
Hearing these cruel words of the tiger, which caused his hair to stand on end, she [remained there].
Afflicted with affection, her voice faltering, that cow— Bahulā, who is deeply devoted to her calf— remembers her young son, endowed with beauty and radiant as the moon,
while she herself burns with grief for her offspring.
Weeping piteously and despairing of seeing her son, she was seen by the tiger Bahula as she cried out in extreme distress;
he spoke these terrible words: "Bahula, why do you weep?"
"By fate you have come to me as food, appearing here by chance. Your life cannot be sustained whether you weep or laugh;
O cow, you have arrived here of your own accord, and what is ordained must be consumed in this world."
"Your death has been ordained this very day; why do you grieve in vain?
And the tiger asked again, "For what reason were you weeping?
Curiosity has arisen within me today; tell us everything."
Having heard the tiger’s words, Bahulā spoke these words: "O Lord, you who can assume any form at will, you ought to forgive me; homage be to you!
Upon beholding you, no protection remains for the world."
I do not grieve for the sake of life, for death must be encountered by me;
for indeed, death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died.
Therefore, you ought not to grieve over a matter that cannot be avoided.
Even by all the gods, it is certain that one must inevitably die;
therefore, O tiger, I do not grieve for my life alone.
Rather, O tiger, I wept out of sorrow due to the power of affection.
"I have a deep anguish in my heart, and you ought to hear it from me.
O lord of beasts, while still in the prime of my youth, I gave birth;
and my son, my firstborn, was a beloved infant."
My calf drinks milk; even now it has not yet smelled the grass. Bound in the cowherd's family, it gazes at me in hunger. I mourn for that son; how will my son survive?
Driven by the power of maternal affection, I desire to give him my breast; having let that child drink and having licked his head,
I shall entrust him to his friends and instruct them on what is beneficial and what is harmful.
"I shall return again; you may eat as much as you desire. I will come back quickly to your side, O great tiger.
Having heard the words of Bahulā, the king of beasts spoke once more.
"What is to be done by you with your son? Do you not see death?
All living beings tremble upon beholding me and die;
yet you, overcome by compassion, cry out, 'O son! O son!'"
Neither mantras, nor asceticism, nor charity, nor mother, nor father,
nor son are able to protect one who has come into my presence.
How then, having gone to that cowherd settlement crowded with the community of gopīs?
Resounding with the bellowing of bulls, delightful, and adorned with young calves,
it is the ornament of the world of the gods; of this there is no doubt, for it is equal to heaven itself—
eternally joyful, beautiful, and worshipped by all the deities.

It is the purifier of purifiers and the most auspicious of all auspicious things; it is the sacred ford among all sacred fords, the most beautiful of beauties, and the supreme. It is a great abode of the Lord, filled with every excellence.
That place of all the Siddhas, the unsurpassed ground of heaven,
where Lakṣmī is not struck down by the sound of the *gargarī* vessel,
and where the calves utter piteous lowing out of longing for their mother—
It was protected by heroic cowherds skilled in hand-to-hand combat;
it resounded with singing, dancing, and conversation, and with the sounds of leaping and slapping;
and it was surrounded on all sides by calves standing here and there, bleating.
The cow-pen shines like a lake with glorious lotuses; having seen that beautiful abode of fortune, as well as your mother, brother, son,
and circle of friends, how will you return again?
"O blessed lady, let the five elements drink your blood!
O Bahulā,
I do not leave the elements in despair by mere words."

O King of Beasts, listen to my words: first, I saw the calf; then, having seen my circle of friends, the young boys, and the cowherd attendants, I approached the cowherd women and especially my mother.
"O tiger,
if you think that I will come by means of oaths, then release me. What kind of oaths are these, O blessed lady, that have been urged upon me by you?"
"O Bahulā,
convey this message to Bahulā with great care:
'O Queen of Beasts, if you have no confidence in me...'"
By these oaths I shall return; I shall speak the truth, there is no doubt.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again—to him who says "do not give" regarding a teacher, the sacred fire, or a Brahmin.
Whatever sin there is in [eating] honey and meat, and likewise in the sale of lac—
may I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again.
And whatever brahmin is a seller of the Vedas, or he who recites them in a public square;
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by the sin of that brahmin who is discontented and constantly becomes a beggar;
and of him who is envious by nature and a destroyer of the virtues of living beings.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by the sin of those twice-born who perform sacrifices using the wealth of others, and by that woman who does not honor her husband from his youth.
Those who, having abandoned their own cooking, take delight in the food of others;
those men who are attached to the wives of their gurus or the wives of their masters; and a Brāhmaṇa who has gone to a Śūdra woman and does not resort to sacred fords (tīrthas).

May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again; may I be tainted by that sin if I, a Brahmin who has undergone the purificatory rites, act as a spectator for a Śūdra. May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again.
Those who give false testimony regarding matters connected with wealth—
may I be tainted by that same sin as the murder of a Brahmin or the killing of one’s mother or father, if I do not return again.
Whatever sin belongs to hunters, to barbarians, and to those who administer poison— by that sin may I be tainted if I do not return again;
[and likewise for those] who touch cows with their feet and do not bow their heads.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again;
may I be tainted by that sin if they treat cows with contempt, curse them, and beat them.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that sin who, having once given his daughter in marriage, bestows her upon a second [man],
or who creates an obstacle while a story is being told.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again;
may I be tainted by that sin if a Brahmin who has come to my house departs disappointed, because I have not returned again.
If I do not return again, may I be tainted by that same sin as a man who has two wives but looks upon only one with affection;
or as that lowest of men who eats delicacies all alone.
May I be tainted by that sin if I do not return again;
may I be tainted by the sin of one who would yoke three oxen unevenly to the plough, if I do not come into your presence.
"Through these terrible transgressions, I shall return once more.
Having gained confidence, that tiger spoke these words again:
"We have developed full confidence in you through your many oaths."
Sometimes you think, "Having gone there, that fool has been deceived by me.
In this world, there are some atheists who, though fools, consider themselves wise;
they cause one's intellect to whirl like an eye fixed upon a spinning wheel.
Even though they are untrue, those who are skillful display them as true;
like depressions and elevations on level ground, people who understand karma perceive this as a marvel.
Generally, this world does not acknowledge one who has rendered it a service once its own purpose has been achieved.
Seeing the exhaustion of the milk, the calf abandons its mother.
I do not see anyone in this world who returns a favor for what has been done;
for when everyone has achieved their purpose, their minds turn toward something else.

In the past, oaths were mutually sworn by the hosts of ṛṣis, gods, and asuras for the sake of accomplishing their purposes; how can we not respect that? One should swear an oath by truth in the presence of the gods, fire, and one's guru.
King Vaivasvata cuts away half of one's dharma.
Let your mind not be thus constrained by oaths alone;
since he has previously shown you this, do now as you wish.
"O Bahulā, go and see your son, you who are so devoted to your child! Having let that calf drink and having licked its head,
look upon your mother, your brother, your friends, and your kinsmen."
"O Bhīṣma,
placing truth alone at the forefront, make your return quickly. Having thus gained confidence, that truthful Bahulā [prepared to depart].
Permitted by the lord of beasts, she who was so devoted to her son departed;
with a face filled with tears, miserable, trembling, and deeply distressed,
she fell as if into an ocean of grief, sighing like a female osprey.
Like a female elephant seized by a male in a pool of water,
she was unable to protect herself and lamented again and again;
having gone to the cowherd settlement, Bahulā had her strength of will stolen away.
Hearing her calf crying out as if for its own sake, she ran toward it; with eyes clouded by tears, she approached that calf. When his mother had arrived, the calf questioned her anxiously.
I do not perceive your usual gentleness; you appear as if troubled in mind. Your gaze is restless and agitated, and it seems utterly terrified.
"Drink from my breast, my son, if you ask for the reason;
I have come out of affection for you, so satisfy yourself as much as you desire. This is the last time, my child, that it will be difficult to behold your mother."
"Having drunk me for a single day, whom will you drink at dawn?
My son, I must depart; indeed, I have come here bound by oaths.
I must give my life to the tiger Kāmarūpa."
Having heard the words of Bahulā, Vatsa spoke these words:
"I shall go wherever you wish to go;
for me too, death together with you is praiseworthy, of this there is no doubt."
Even alone, I must inevitably die without you;
O Mother, if a tiger should kill me while I am with you in the forest,
that destiny which belongs to those devoted to their mothers will surely be mine.
Therefore, I shall certainly go with you; of this there is no doubt. O mother, stay here, and let my oaths be your guarantee:
what purpose is there in life for one who is separated from his mother?
13,150.009d@020_0216 For one who is constantly without a protector in the forest, who will be my protector?
13,150.009d@020_0217 There is no kinsman equal to a mother for children who drink milk; 13,150.009d@020_0218 There is no protector equal to a mother; there is no refuge equal to a mother.
There is no affection equal to that of a mother; there is no happiness equal to that of a mother.
There is no deity equal to a mother, both in this world and in the next.
This is our supreme duty, ordained by Prajāpati.
But those true sons who remain shall go to the supreme goal. My death alone was ordained; you, my son, shall not go [with me].
Nor can this death of mine be the cause of death for other living beings.
"My son, carry out this final and supreme instruction from your mother; follow my word, for there service is paramount. Whether wandering in the forest or in the water, do not fall into negligence."
Through negligence all living beings perish; of this there is no doubt. One should never act out of greed, even for a blade of grass situated in a precarious place.
Through greed comes the destruction of all, both in this world and in the next.

Deluded by greed, they enter the ocean, the forest, and battle; out of greed, even a wise man may commit an extremely terrible misdeed. A man is indeed bound by three things: greed, negligence, and misplaced trust.
Therefore, one should not harbor greed, nor negligence, nor should one place trust [in others].
O son, one must always protect oneself with great effort from serpents,
wild beasts, and the perils posed by barbarians, thieves, and the like.
"O son, even among animals of evil nature who dwell together in one place, their contrary minds are not known;
this is true of rivers, clawed beasts, horned creatures, and those with weapons in hand."

One should never place trust in women or in courtesans. One should not trust the untrustworthy, nor should one even trust the trustworthy. The danger arising from misplaced trust cuts away even the very roots.

One should not place trust even in one's own body, for the living consciousness is ever-fickle; one should constantly contemplate that [body] which is utterly deluded regarding its manifestation and perpetually asleep. One must always diligently perceive the fragrance [of the Self] everywhere.
Cows see by means of their sense of smell; Brāhmaṇas see by means of the Vedas;
kings see by means of spies; and other people see with their eyes. One should not dwell alone in a fearsome forest, nor should one contemplate the Dharma alone.
You should not feel agitation; death is certain for everyone.
For just as a certain traveler might rest by taking refuge in the shade, and having rested, would depart once more, such is the meeting of living beings.
Since the entire world is impermanent, why is this one person alone lamented? O child, casting aside your inner grief, follow my words.
Having smelled the crown of his head and licked his forehead, [he spoke].
Overwhelmed by great sorrow, her eyes clouded with tears,
she sighed like a doe fallen into the power of tigers;
deprived of her son, she beheld the entire world as if she were blind.
Sunk deep in a great mire, she remained there, sinking; lamenting profusely, she spoke these words again to her son:
"There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no happiness equal to that for a son."
There is no affection equal to that for a son; there is no refuge equal to a son.
For one without a son, the world is empty; for one without a son, what is home?
Through a son, one conquers the worlds; through a son, one may conquer hell.
The world speaks untruth, saying that sandalwood is indeed cool;
yet the embrace of a son’s body is cooler even than sandalwood. [He sees him] naked, devoid of shame, with matted hair and grey with dust.
Without merits, they do not behold their own son, just as one cannot see the Lord of the Gaṅgā. What is the use of sandalwood, what use a drop of nectar,
and what use the moon, if one’s body were to become a vessel for the embrace of a son’s limbs?
Having thus described the virtues of her son and looking at him again and again,
she questioned her mother, her friends, and the cowherds in succession:
"The king of beasts fell upon me as I was grazing at the head of the herd."
"I was released by him with oaths, saying, 'Having seen your family, you shall return. Therefore,
having come here to see you, my mother, my own family, and my son,
I shall return there once again by virtue of that word of truth."
"O Mother, forgive all that was done by me in my childhood. This grandson of yours is your trust; what else can I say to you?
O Vipulā, Campakā, Dāmā, Bhadrā, Surabhi, and Mālinī!"
O Vasudhārā, Śrī, Nandā, Mahānandā, and Ghaṭasravā:
whatever unpleasant thing has been spoken by me anywhere, whether out of ignorance or intentionally, O highly fortunate ones, please forgive that, as well as whatever was done by me afterwards.
All of you, endowed with every virtue, the mothers of all the world— All of you, who are ever-givers, protect my young son, Who is helpless, weak, miserable, and sinking down.

"O sisters, you shall protect him who is tormented by grief for his mother; for he is now, and especially so at this moment, the son of you sisters. This child must be nourished and protected like a son by all of you women."
"O friends, you must restrain him when he wanders in difficult places, goes to the cow-pens of others, or engages in improper acts—
those whose hearts are equal toward their own sons and the sons of others."
They are blessed, they have fulfilled their purpose, they are true women, and they are true mothers;
those cows and those women rejoice in the worlds of the gods who protect the helpless children of others as if they were their own sons.
"Therefore, you shall protect my sonless son like a son of your own. O highly fortunate ones, guard him; I shall depart, relying upon truth, for death stands before every living being."
"And you must not feel any resentment toward our departure, my friends, under any circumstances.
Having heard these words of Bahula, her mother and her friends were overwhelmed;
they fell into a state of extreme despondency and, filled with great astonishment, spoke as follows.
Oh, what a truly great marvel it is, that these many women, out of a commitment to truthful speech, are prepared to enter the terrifying mouth of a tiger—
having thereby warded off danger through their oaths and truthful words!
That which has been destroyed must be restored with effort; how can it be reached again?
One should certainly not go to Bahula. What kind of dharma is this of yours, that you abandon your own family, who are like children, out of greed for truth?
13,150.009d@020_0306 Here are verses sung of old by the seers who perceive the truth:
13,150.009d@020_0307 When the loss of life is imminent, there is no sin in taking oaths; 13,150.009d@020_0308 Whereby, by speaking a falsehood, the lives of living beings may be preserved.
In those cases, falsehood indeed becomes truth, and truth becomes falsehood:
in matters concerning women, in marriages, and likewise in business involving cattle.
In these instances, [falsehood] is manifold.
In assisting a Brahmin, there is no sin in swearing oaths;
for the sake of protecting the lives of others, I shall indeed speak a false word. But I do not venture to speak even the slightest falsehood anywhere for my own sake.
Alone one is joined in the womb; alone one is born; and alone one dies.
Alone one experiences pleasure and pain, O Mother—I speak the truth. The world is established in truth; Dharma is established in truth.
By virtue of his truthful speech, the ocean does not overstep its boundaries;
having given the earth to Viṣṇu, Bali took refuge in the netherworld (pātāla);
and though Bali was bound through deception, he remains steadfast by means of his truthful speech.
The lord of mountains, though increasing to a height of a hundred *yojanas*,
the Vindhya remains established by truth and does not grow further now. Heaven, liberation, and hell— all are established in speech.

Whoever suppresses that speech has suppressed it entirely. What sin has not been committed by that thief who steals his own self, who represents himself to the virtuous as something other than what he truly is?

Therefore, I shall not destroy myself with untruth; having destroyed myself by my own hand, I would go to a terrible hell. [I shall enter] the deep, vast, and pure ford of truth, the lake of forbearance.
Having bathed there, one is liberated from sin and attains the supreme goal.
If a thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale,
truth would indeed outweigh a thousand horse-sacrifices.

Truth is excellent; it is supreme austerity and learning, free from afflictions and the like. It is self-dependent, exceedingly difficult to attain, a universal ornament for the world, the touchstone of the virtuous, the family wealth of the noble, and the strength of all stages of life.
Since even a barbarian, having performed this, goes to heaven, how could one abandon it and remain? O friends,
you are to be honored by all the gods and asuras alike.
"Do not, by means of the supreme truth, abandon your life-breaths, which are so difficult to give up.
What can we say here, O auspicious lady, you who bear the yoke of Dharma? For what is to be attained through this renunciation, who in the three worlds is equal to you?"
"And we perceive that through this renunciation of your son, there will be supreme spiritual attainment (adhiyoga);
for indeed, no calamities exist anywhere for those whose minds are virtuous.
Having seen all the cowherds and having circumambulated the cow-pen..."
Having set out for the gods, she took leave of those trees once more—
the earth, water, fire, wind, the sun, the moon,
the deities of the ten directions, the mountains, as well as the lunar mansions and the planets.
Today, bowing down again and again, I inform you all:
protect my helpless child with your respective powers,
for to those whose minds are imbued with compassion, there can be no such thing as a stranger.

Therefore, out of compassion, you shall protect my young son who is without a protector— those perfected ones (*siddhas*) who have taken refuge in the forest, and all the forest deities; may they guard my child as he wanders in the woods.
O *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, *sarala*, *arjuna*, and *kiṃśuka* trees—
let all you plants hear my distressed message concerning the young,
solitary, and wretched one wandering in the treacherous forest.
Protect this young calf with affection, as if it were your own biological son— this helpless, wretched, and afflicted creature, abandoned by its mother and father,
wandering this earth, crying out in extreme distress.
As my son cries out here in the great forest, overcome by grief for his mother, afflicted by hunger and thirst,
abandoned and alone, beholding the entire world as empty—
"Protection must be afforded with compassion to one who wanders [the world].
Having thus instructed Bahula, she fell under the power of affection for her son;
utterly consumed by the fire of grief, her hope for seeing her son was severed.
Like a female cakravāka bird separated from her mate, like a creeper fallen from a tree,
like a blind woman without a staff stumbling at every step—
having gone back once more to where that flesh-eater was.
He sat there, terrifying with his gaping jaws and sharp fangs.
Upon seeing the tiger, the cow spoke these words:
"O illustrious one, I have come here established in the law of truth."
“O tiger, satisfy yourself now with my flesh according to your desire; gratify your five senses with my blood.”

"Welcome to you, O auspicious Bahulā, speaker of truth! Indeed, nothing inauspicious ever befalls those who possess truthfulness. You spoke previously, O Bahulā, and have now returned once more because of your truth."
"Because of that, curiosity has arisen in us: how might she come back again?
Otherwise, having encountered me, how could you depart alive?
And that curiosity of ours has been fulfilled; I have seen the truth regarding the cows."
Therefore, by this truth, you are now released by me. The worlds are established in truth; the Dharma is established in truth;
knowledge is established in truth; everything is established in truth.
The gods are pleased by truth, and likewise the ancestors;
by truth the seers attained perfection, for everything is established upon truth. Blessed are cows, blessed is the earth, and you too, O cow, are blessed!
"Blessed is that king in whose realm you dwell, O speaker of truth! Blessed is his kingdom, along with its grass, its living beings, and its trees,
wherein you have wandered at will, O destroyer of sin."
They are blessed and they have fulfilled their purpose; by them alone has a virtuous deed been performed. They have attained the very essence of birth who drink the milk of cows.
Having gained confidence, the king of beasts was filled with the utmost wonder.
"This is the instruction shown to us by all the gods:
I shall perform that deed by which I will be freed from my transgression. By me, thousands of living beings have been eaten and slain."
"Having seen such a true nature of cattle, what destiny indeed shall I go?
I am a sinner, of evil conduct, cruel, and a slayer of living beings;
having performed such a most terrible deed, to which worlds shall I go?"

I shall go to sacred fords and perform the purification of my body; having reached a mountain, I shall cast myself down, or else enter the fire. For I must perform extensive austerities for the sake of purifying my sins.
13,150.009d@020_0399 O Bahula, explain that in brief; there is no time for me to hear it at length.
13,150.009d@020_0400 They praise the practice of austerity in the Kṛta age, and sacrificial rites in the Tretā age.
In the Dvāpara age, meditation and yoga [are supreme], and in the Kali age, charity alone is so. Among all forms of giving, this one alone is the most excellent:
the gift of fearlessness to all living beings; there is no gift superior to this.

He who grants fearlessness to all beings, both moving and unmoving, is liberated from all fears and attains the Supreme Brahman. There is no gift higher than non-violence; there is no self-restraint higher than non-violence.
Just as every other footprint is subsumed within the footprint of an elephant,
O tiger, so too are all dharmas established through non-violence (*ahiṃsā*). It is the shadow of the tree of yoga that destroys the threefold suffering.

Having attained the supreme nirvāṇa, he who has taken refuge in the shade of the tree of yoga— whose beautiful flowers are the knowledge of the Dharma and whose fruit is heaven and liberation— is no longer bound by sufferings, even though scorched by the sun of the threefold suffering.
13,150.009d@020_0413 Thus, this supreme good has been proclaimed to you in brief.
13,150.009d@020_0414 O Vyāghra, all of this is already known to you; you ask me only for the sake of formality.
In former times, I was cast down by all the gods in the form of a tiger. In that place of terrible slaughter of living beings, everything was forgotten by me;
however, through the instruction resulting from contact with you, memory has arisen once again.
"O cow, by your grace, the curse has been lifted;
O Bahulā, go forth, for I am pleased. Remain together with your calf, and by this truth, you too shall attain the supreme goal."
Then, having resorted to yoga with his mind fixed upon it, the tiger abandoned his own body through breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) and went to heaven,
his soul purified of all sins and endowed with the sovereign powers of yoga.
In a celestial chariot yoked with swans and surrounded by a great multitude of Apsarases,
she beheld [him] seated within that chariot and was filled with supreme wonder; then,
her limbs bristling with joy and contentment, she returned once more to Gokula.

Having arrived, she related to her friends the excellent account of the encounter with the tiger exactly as it had occurred, and especially that of her son; Bahulā, reunited with her son, was exceedingly joyful and free from all anxiety.
Surrounded by herds of cattle, bulls, calves, and the community of cowherds and cowherdesses,
she wandered through the entire forest, free from all fear;
by her power, that settlement of cowherds (Gokula) was able to act according to its own will.

Seeing the king together with his kingdom, his servants, and his ministers, along with the women of the inner apartments and their retinue, and seeing all those cowherds as well as the circles of cowherd girls,
Bahulā took them all and set out for heaven.
Surrounded on all sides by countless, magnificent great celestial palaces (mahāvimānas),
they reached heaven; then, having ascended higher and higher through all the worlds in succession, they together established themselves in Goloka.
There, in that realm crowded with enjoyments, Bhīṣma sports together with all [the gods] in innumerable supreme cities until the dissolution of all beings.
Thus has been declared the greatness of truthful speech;
whoever recites or even hears this shall go to the heavenly world.
The twice-born who constantly recites this dialogue between Bahula and the tiger [attains the same].
And he who listens with a single-minded focus shall not be overcome by tigers. A woman or even a man who is separated from their children should always recite this;
they too, being liberated from sins, will be reunited with their children.

Whoever, having risen at dawn, recites this on the fourteenth and eighth lunar days, goes to the worlds of the virtuous and meritorious; of this there is no doubt. And for those who recite it in a cow-pen, there is an increase in cattle; of this there is no doubt.
For those reciting this in the midst of a field, an increase in the harvest arises;
for children reciting it within the home, there is an increase in peace. And whoever recites this protection for those overcome by malevolent spirits, [they shall be freed].
For those who constantly recite this in difficult places, in forests, and in sacred groves,
no fear exists anywhere, whether by day or by night.
Upon hearing this, bad dreams, portents of death, and evil friends are utterly destroyed.
Even the sonless shall have a son, and he who is not esteemed shall become a lord;
and a maiden, always listening [to this], shall obtain a heroic husband. Whether woman or man, even one who is unfortunate shall become fortunate.
On the festival days of the cows, one should recite this greatness with devotion before [the image];
he attains prosperity in cattle and goes indeed to Goloka.
"I am a Śūdra; I have no authority to practice the four stages of life."
Thus, others do not attribute consciousness to the self;
moreover, I shall speak specifically regarding the characteristics of the four castes,
concerning all bodies composed of the five elements whose selves are alike.
13,150.009d*0692_05 A distinction has been made between worldly phenomena (*lokadharma*) and the Dharma;
13,150.009d*0692_06 therein, living beings again attain oneness—of that there is an extensive explanation.
13,150.009d*0692_07 For how is the world considered unstable, and how is the Dharma considered stable?
Where time is constant, my dear, there the eternal Dharma resides. For all beings of equal bodies and all beings of similar natures,
time joined with Dharma is indeed the perfect means of preservation.

This being so, there is no fault in living beings practicing the Dharma; even for those existing in the animal realm, the world itself is considered their teacher. Therefore, with a peaceful mind and being well-instructed, you must protect all your subjects.
"Let this Dvaipāyana be your eye, O Kṛṣṇa; let him be your ultimate refuge.
Having said this, the high-minded one ceased speaking for the sake of his worship.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Then Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Pāṇḍu and best of the Kurus, desiring his welfare and seeking to remove his own taints, questioned Bhīṣma as he lay upon his bed of arrows— Bhīṣma, who destroys all sins.
Yudhiṣṭhira said:
"What is the highest good for a person in this world? By doing what does one increase in happiness? By what may one become free from sin, and what is the destroyer of impurity?
To him, who was thus desirous of hearing, Śāṃtanava then spoke again.
The bull among men duly recounted the lineage of the gods.
Bhīṣma said:
"This is indeed the lineage of the deities, accompanied by the lineage of the ṛṣis."
"O son, when recited at the two twilights, this is the supreme remover of impurities.
Yudhiṣṭhira,
it is a mantra to be chanted that brings peace to all, for those afflicted by poverty and suffering."
"O Grandfather, tell me that which eternally bestows contentment and prosperity.
Bhīṣma said:
"This great recitation (*mahājapya*), joined by the kings and ṛṣis of the gods, is praised."

By serving [the senses], a person is not deluded by suffering or fear. Whatever evil a man commits during the day while acting through his senses—whether intentionally or unintentionally—and whatever he does at night or during the two twilights; [all that is washed away by bathing at dawn].
By reciting this always with purity, one is indeed liberated from all sins;
one is never blind nor deaf, and remains forever well-being at the appointed time.
Furthermore, such a person shall not go to a womb of animals, nor to hell, nor to the mixed castes.
He has no fear of suffering, nor does he lose consciousness at the time of death. He is the god who is the teacher of gods and asuras, honored by all beings;
he is inconceivable, indescribable, the life-force of all, and indeed not born from a womb.
The Grandfather is the Lord of the World; Sāvitrī is the virtuous wife of Brahmā.
Then there is Viṣṇu Nārāyaṇa, the Lord, the source of the Vedas and the Creator.
From the lotus-navel of Viṣṇu was born Brahmā, the purifier of the worlds.
Umāpati, Virūpākṣa, and Skanda the commander-in-chief; Viśākha, Hutabhuj, Vāyu, and the two light-makers, Candra and Āditya; Śakra the lord of Śacī, and the god Yama together with Dhūmorṇā.
Varuṇa with Gaurī, the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) with Ṛddhi,
the gentle cow Surabhi the goddess, the great seer Viśravas,
the six seasons, the ocean, the Gaṅgā, the flowing rivers, and the hosts of Maruts.
The Vālakhilyas perfected in asceticism, as well as Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, Nārada, Parvata, Viśvāvasu, Hāhā and Hūhū,
Tumburu, Citrasena, and the renowned messenger of the gods.
The highly fortunate daughters of the gods and divine throngs of Apsarases—
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Miśrakeśī, Alambuṣā,
Viśvācī, Ghṛtācī, Pañcacūḍā, and Tilottamā.

The Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, along with the Aśvins and the Pitṛs; Dharma, Truth, Penance, Consecration, Resolve, and the Grandfather (Brahmā); the nights and the days; and likewise Kaśyapa, the son of Marīci.
Śukra, Bṛhaspati, Bhauma, Budha, Rāhu, and Śanaiścara; the lunar mansions, the seasons, the months, the twilights, and the years;
the sons of Vinatā, the oceans, and likewise the serpents born of Kadru.
The serpent king Ananta, Vāsuki, and likewise Takṣaka;
the renowned Mahāpadma, Karkoṭaka, and Dhanañjaya; as well as the Śatadrū, Vipāśā, Candrabhāgā, and Sarasvatī.
The Sindhu and the Devikā, as well as the sacred site of Puṣkara;
the great river Gaṅgā, and likewise the Kapilā and the Narmadā; the Kampunā and the Viśalyā, and the Karatoyā which carries its waters.
The Sarayū, the Gaṇḍakī, and the great river Lohitya;
the Tāmrāruṇā, the Vetravatī, the Parṇāśā, and likewise the Gautamī; the Godāvarī, the Veṇṇā, and the Kṛṣṇaveṇā born from the mountain.
The Dṛṣadvatī, the Kāverī, the Vaṅkṣu, and likewise the Mandākinī;
Prayāga, Prabhāsa, and the holy Naimiṣa;
and that abode of Viśveśvara where that stainless lake is located.
Kurukṣetra is celebrated as being filled with sacred fords (puṇyatīrtha). Furthermore, there are Sindhūttama, Tapodāna, and Jambūmārga;
likewise, the Hiraṇvatī, the Vitastā, and the river Ikṣumatī.
The Vedasmṛti, the Vaidasinī, and the Malavāsā rivers;
likewise the sacred regions of the earth, Gaṅgādvāra,
the Ṛṣikulyās, and the pure river Citrapathā.
The Kauśikī, the Yamunā, the Sītā, and likewise the river Carmaṇvatī;
the holy river Carmaṇvatī, the Kauśikī, and the Yamunā;
as well as the river Bhīmarathī and the great river Bāhudā.
Mahendravāṇī, Tridivā, Nīlikā, and Sarasvatī; Nandā and Aparanandā, as well as the sacred site of Mahāhrada;
and Gayā, Phalgutīrtha, and Dharmāraṇya, which is frequented by the gods.
Likewise, there is the holy celestial river and the lake created by Brahmā— meritorious,
renowned throughout the three worlds, auspicious, and the remover of all sins. All these celestial rivers are proclaimed to be destroyers of sin.
Himavat, the mountain endowed with divine herbs;
Vindhya, whose limbs are variegated with minerals, possessing sacred fords and medicinal plants; Meru, Mahendra, Malaya, and Śveta, which is strewn with silver.
Śṛṅgavān, Mandara, Nīla, Niṣadha, and likewise Dardura;
Citrakūṭa, Añjanābha, and the mountain Gandhamādana; the holy Somagiri, and other such mountain ranges as well.
May the quarters and the intermediate directions, the earth and all the trees,
the Viśvedevas, the sky, the lunar mansions, and likewise the planets—
may these gods, whether named by me or unnamed, protect you constantly.

For a man who recites these [names] is indeed liberated from all sins; by praising them and rejoicing in them, he who delights in the praise of the deities is released from all fear and from all the evils of impurity.

Immediately after the deities, I shall proclaim the names of the brahmins who have attained perfection through austerity and are preeminent in asceticism— those whose praises have been sung and which liberate one from all sins:
Yavakrīta, Raibhya, Kakṣīvān, and Auśija.
Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Kaṇva, Medhātithi the lord, and Barhi,
endowed with all virtues, took refuge in the eastern direction;
likewise, the highly fortunate Ulmucu and Pramucu occupied the auspicious quarter.
The highly fortunate Svastyātreya and the valiant Agastya,
the son of Mitra and Varuṇa,
as well as the renowned Dṛḍhāyu and Ūrdhvabāhu— those two most excellent sages— also released [their weapons].
Learn now of those who prosper by resorting to the western quarter:
Uṣadgu together with his uterine brothers, the heroic Parivyādha,
the seer Dīrghatamas, Gautama, and likewise Kaśyapa.
The great seers Ekata, Dvita, and Trita;
the righteous son of Atri; and the lord Sarasvata—learn now of those who dwell, taking refuge in the northern quarter.
Atri, Vasiṣṭha, Śakti, and the powerful Pārāśarya;
Viśvāmitra, Bharadvāja, and likewise Jamadagni;
Rāma, the grandson of Ṛcīka, and the seer Auddālaki as well.
Śvetaketu, Kohala, Vipula, and likewise Devala;
Devaśarman, Dhaumya, and Hastikāśyapa; Lomaśa, Nāciketa, and Lomaharṣaṇa.
The seer Ugraśravas, as well as Cyavana of the Bhṛgu lineage— this assembly, O King,
accompanied by seers and gods,
has been proclaimed as the primordial one that liberates from all sins.
Nṛga, Yayāti, Nahuṣa, Yadu, and the heroic Pūru; Dhundhumāra, Dilīpa, and the majestic Sagara;
Kṛśāśva, Yauvanāśva, Citrāśva, and likewise Satyavat.
Duḥṣanta and Bharata, the highly illustrious universal monarch; Yavana and Janaka, as well as King Dṛḍharatha;
Raghu, the best among men, and likewise King Daśaratha.
King Rathantara, Bhārgava Cyavana,
the heroic Rāma, slayer of the Rākṣasas, Śaśabindu, Bhagīratha,
Hariścandra, Marutta, and Jahnu, who was served by the Gaṅgā.
Mahodaya, Alarka, and Aila the lord of men;
Udarka, Māndhātṛ, and likewise Uḍa Mahodaya;
Karaṃdhama, the best of men, and Kadhmora the lord of men.
Dakṣa, Ambarīṣa, Kukura, and the highly illustrious Ravata; Kuru, Saṃvaraṇa, Māndhātṛ of true prowess,
the royal sage Mucukunda, Mitrabhānu, and Priyaṃkara.
Jahnu, who was served by the Jahnavī;
Pṛthu Vainya, the first king;
Trasadasyu, as well as King Śveta, the best of royal sages.
The renowned Mahābhiṣa, King Nimi, and likewise Aṣṭaka; the royal seer Āyu, Kṣupa, and Kakṣeyu the lord of men; Śibi the son of Uśīnara, and Gaya the lord of men.
Pṛthu, as well as Uparicara, and the highly illustrious Kekaya; Pratardana, Divodāsa, Saudāsa the lord of Kosala;
the royal sage Aila, Nala, and Manu the progenitor of beings.
Haviṣmān, Pṛṣadhra, Pratīpa, and likewise Śaṃtanu;
O King,
Haviṣmān, Aja, Rantideva, and Purūravas.
Aja, Prācīnabarhis, and likewise the highly illustrious Ikṣvāku; the lord of men Anaraṇya, and likewise Jānujaṅgha;
Suhotra, Sṛñjaya, and likewise Rantideva.
The royal sage Rambhodbhava, Māndhātā the best of kings,
the royal sage Kakṣasena, and others who have not been mentioned—
whosoever, rising at dawn, constantly performs the two *saṃdhyās* at sunset and sunrise...
If one recites this while pure and unencumbered, he shall partake in the fruit of dharma.
The gods, the celestial sages, and likewise the royal sages have been praised;
these lords shall bestow upon me prosperity, long life, fame, and heaven.
May there be no obstacle for me, may there be no evil for me, and may there be no adversaries for me. May victory be certain for me always, and in the hereafter, the supreme goal.
Homage to them, homage to them; and may there be no adversaries for me.
One should recite: "May there be a goal even higher than the highest. To Viṣṇu, the sovereign Lord, who is changeless, pure, eternal, the Supreme Self, whose form is always of one nature.
13,152.001 Vaiśampāyana said: 13,152.001*0714_00 Janamejaya said:
13,152.001*0714_01 When Bhīṣma, the bearer of the burden of the Kauravas, had fallen upon the bed of arrows—
While he lay upon the hero’s bed attended by the Pāṇḍavas,
my great wise grandfather Yudhiṣṭhira,
having heard the traditional teachings on dharma and understood his doubts regarding dharma, [spoke].
"Having heard the rules for various kinds of gifts, his doubts regarding the meaning of the Dharma were severed.
O Brahmin, you should tell me what else he did.
Vaiśampāyana said:
For a moment, that entire circle of kings became motionless,
as silent as a painting fixed upon a canvas when Bhīṣma had fallen mute. Then,
having meditated for a moment, Vyāsa, the son of Satyavatī, spoke.
Then he spoke these words to the king, the son of Gaṅgā, as he lay there:
"O King, Yudhiṣṭhira, the Kuru monarch, has returned to his natural state,
accompanied by all his brothers and the kings who follow him."
"O tiger among men, he waits upon you along with the wise Kṛṣṇa;
you ought to grant him permission to enter the city.
Thus addressed by the blessed Vyāsa, the lord of the earth—
The son of the River gave leave to Yudhiṣṭhira along with his ministers;
then King Śāntanava spoke sweetly to him:
"Enter the city, O King; let the fever of your mind depart."

Perform various sacrifices with abundant food and excellent sacrificial fees, O Indra among kings, like Yayāti, preceded by faith and self-restraint. Devoted to the duty of a Kṣatriya, O Pārtha, gratify the ancestors and the gods.
"You shall indeed be united with what is most excellent; let the fever of your mind depart.
Delight all your subjects and console the constituent elements of the state. Honor your friends with rewards and hospitality according to their merit."
"O dear one, may your friends and well-wishers live following you,
just as birds follow a fruit-bearing tree standing at a sacred shrine.
And you, O King, must return to me when the appointed time has come."
When the sun had turned back and the northern solstice had begun,
the son of Kuntī, having said "So be it" and having paid homage to his grandfather,
set out for the city named after the elephant (Hastināpura) along with his retinue.
Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra and the devoted Gāndhārī at the forefront,
the king, together with all those sages, his brothers, Keśava, the citizens and country-folk, and the elder ministers, [proceeded].
13,152.013c He entered the city named Vāraṇasāhvaya, O best of the Kurus.
13,153.001 Vaiśampāyana said:
13,153.001a Then the king, the son of Kuntī, [addressed] the people of the city and the countryside.

Having honored them according to custom, he gave them leave to return to their homes. Then the king, the son of Pāṇḍu, consoled the women whose heroes had been slain and whose lords had been killed with abundant gifts of wealth.

Having been consecrated and having obtained the kingdom, O Yudhiṣṭhira, that highly wise one, the best of men, then established all his subjects— the twice-born, the leaders of the army, and the merchants— in their respective positions throughout the entire realm.
Having accepted the principal blessings, that best of the upholders of dharma,
the illustrious bull among men, dwelt for fifty nights in that excellent city and then remembered the appointed time of the foremost of the Kauravas.
Then the best of the upholders of dharma spoke to the lotus-eyed one:
"O Blessed One, you are engaged in yoga; O slayer of enemies, you meditate in silence. Speak to me, O foremost of men, for I am to be commanded by you."
"O lotus-eyed one, meditate for my supreme welfare and highest good.
The Blessed Lord:
Bhīṣma, lying upon his bed of arrows, was like a fire about to be extinguished.

"That tiger among men meditates upon me; therefore, my mind is fixed on him. Having seen that the sun had turned back and that the northern solstice (uttarāyaṇa) had begun, he departed from Gajapura, surrounded by his sacrificial priests.

Having first dispatched clarified butter, garlands, perfumes, silken garments, and the finest sandalwood and aloe-woods, as well as black aloe-woods, Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, set out for the funeral rites of Bhīṣma.
Placing Dhṛtarāṣṭra at the forefront, along with the illustrious Gāndhārī, his mother Pṛthā, and his brothers, that wise bull among men [offered] costly garlands and various kinds of jewels.
Placing his brothers and his mother Pṛthā at the forefront,
the Kaurava king, O Lord, was followed by Janārdana, the wise Vidura, Yuyutsu, and Yuyudhāna.
Surrounded by a vast array of royal regalia and being praised, O Great King, he followed Bhīṣma’s sacred fires and departed from that city like the Lord of the Gods himself.
Then, at Kurukṣetra, he approached King Śāṃtanava,
who was being attended by the wise Vyāsa Pārāśarya,
as well as by the royal sage Nārada, Devala, and Asita.
Then the king beheld that high-souled one lying upon the hero’s bed, surrounded on all sides by other surviving kings gathered from various lands and by guards who were protecting him.
[He was] meditating upon the Supreme Self, the eternal Kṛṣṇa-dharma.
Then the King of Dharma (Yudhiṣṭhira), together with his brothers, descended from the chariot.
Having saluted his grandfather, the subduer of enemies, the son of Kuntī [proceeded].

13,153.016c–d: And having been greeted in return by the Brahmins headed by Dvaipāyana, Acyuta was welcomed by the sages beginning with Dvaipāyana. 13,153.017a: Together with his brothers, who were like Brahmā himself, he was honored by the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*).
Having approached the great king, who was lying on a bed of arrows surrounded by sages, Mādhava Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds spoke to Yudhiṣṭhira, the King of Dharma and best of the Bharatas.
O descendant of Kuru, Yudhiṣṭhira addressed the son of the River as he lay there with his brothers:
"O King, O son of Jahnavī, I am Yudhiṣṭhira; salutations to you. If you hear me, O mighty-armed one, tell me what I may do for you."
"O King, O Lord, at this very moment I have arrived bringing the sacred fires with me,
as well as the teachers, the Brahmins, the officiating priests, and my brothers;
and also your son, the highly resplendent Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the lord of men."
Vāsudeva, the heroic, has arrived along with his ministers;
so too have all the kings who survived the slaughter and all those from Kurujāṅgala. Behold them, O tiger among the Kurus; open your eyes.
"Whatever was to be done here, all that has been accomplished by me;
everything exactly as you instructed at the proper time has been performed.
Thus addressed by the wise son of Kuntī, Gāṅgeya—
He saw all the Bharatas standing there, surrounding him on every side. Then Bhīṣma, his eyebrows moving, raised his massive arm and,
eloquent as he was, spoke these words at the proper time with a voice like the roar of a torrential cloud.
"By good fortune you have arrived, O Kaunteya Yudhiṣṭhira, together with your ministers!
For the blessed thousand-rayed sun has indeed turned back.
Fifty-eight nights have passed while I have been lying here."
Just as a hundred years pass for one lying upon sharpened-pointed arrows,
so too has this month of Māgha arrived, O Yudhiṣṭhira, a month that is meritorious;
of this fortnight, only a third part remains, and it must be the bright fortnight.
Having thus spoken to Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, the son of Gaṅgā then addressed Dhṛtarāṣṭra and at that time spoke these words:
"O King, you are one who knows dharma, and whose doubts regarding the meaning of things have been thoroughly resolved."
For you have served many learned Brahmins,
O lord of men, and you have understood all the Vedic scriptures and the codes of dharma,
as well as the four Vedas with their auxiliary branches, in their entirety.
"O descendant of Kuru, you should not grieve, for it was destined to be so. You have heard from Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana himself the secret of the gods:
O King, the sons of Pāṇḍu are yours by right of dharma."
Protect them, who are established in dharma and devoted to serving their elders;
for the pure-souled Dharmarāja will abide by your command. Indeed, I know him to be supremely compassionate and affectionate toward his teachers.
"Your sons were evil-minded, devoted to anger and greed, overcome by envy, and of wicked conduct; you ought not to grieve for them.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken these words to the wise Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
the Kaurava addressed the mighty-armed Vāsudeva:
"O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, you who are saluted by both gods and asuras!"
O Trivikrama, homage be unto you, the bearer of the conch, the discus, and the mace! You are Vāsudeva, the golden-souled Puruṣa, the progenitor, the Virāj;
you are the living soul, the conforming one, the eternal Supreme Self.

O lotus-eyed one, O Supreme Person, protect me forever— I who am your devotee, whose heart is fixed on you, who am without wife and without possessions. Grant me leave, O Kṛṣṇa, O Vaikuṇṭha, O Supreme Person.
The sons of Pāṇḍu must be protected by you, for you are their ultimate refuge. Long ago, I spoke to the evil-minded and dull-witted Duryodhana—
to that man of wicked conduct, Duryodhana, who brought about the end of the Kṣatriyas in battle.
"Where there is Kṛṣṇa, there is Dharma; where there is Dharma, there is victory. O son, through Vāsudeva as your mediator, make peace with the Pāṇḍavas.
Together with your friends, O King, enjoy the kingdom free from thorns."
"‘This is the last opportunity for peace,’ he said again and again;
yet that fool, possessed of very dull intellect, did not heed my words. Having caused the destruction of the earth here, he has now met his end."
"And I know you, O hero, as the ancient and most excellent of sages,
the god who dwelt for a very long time at Badarī together with Nara.
Thus did Nārada and Vyāsa, of great ascetic merit, tell me."
"These two, Nara and Nārāyaṇa, have been born among men.
O Kṛṣṇa, grant me your permission; I shall cast off this body. Permitted by you, I shall go to the supreme goal.
Vāsudeva said:
"I grant you leave, Bhīṣma; attain the status of the Vasus, O king.
No fault whatsoever has been seen in you by me, O one of great splendor."
"O royal sage, you are devoted to your ancestors like another Mārkaṇḍeya;
