therefore, Death stands under your control, bowed down like a servant.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Thus addressed, the son of Gaṅgā spoke these words to the Pāṇḍavas, as well as to all those headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra, along with their friends:
"I wish to cast off my life-breaths; you ought to grant me your permission for that."

"You must strive for truth, for truth is the supreme strength. You should always be compassionate, self-restrained, devoted to the Brahmanas, virtuous in character, and disciplined in austerity, O Bhārata."
Having spoken thus and embraced all his friends,
O King, and having given various kinds of wealth to the twice-born,
the wise one addressed these words once more to Yudhiṣṭhira.
"O lord of men, Brāhmaṇas must always be honored, especially those who are wise, as well as teachers and officiating priests.
Vaiśampāyana said:
Having spoken thus to all the Kurus, Bhīṣma, the son of Śāntanu and subduer of enemies,
remained silent for a moment, O Kauravya;
he then sustained his self through the meditative concentrations (*dhāraṇā*) in their proper sequence.
The vital breaths of that great-souled one ascended upward, completely restrained.
And this was a marvel among those high-souled men:
whatever part of his body the son of Śaṃtanu then released, [it remained intact].
For him who was thus engaged in yoga, those arrows indeed became free from their shafts;
while they were looking on, he then became arrowless in an instant.
Seeing this, everyone, led by Vāsudeva, were struck with amazement.
Then, O King, together with all those sages headed by Vyāsa,
his self was indeed restrained within all the vital centers;
having burst through the crown of his head, it ascended to heaven.
The sound of celestial drums arose along with showers of flowers;
and the Siddhas and Brahman-sages, filled with joy, exclaimed, "Excellent! Excellent!
O lord of men, [a light] like a great meteor appeared from the region of Bhīṣma’s head.
Having emerged and entered the sky, he vanished in an instant.
Thus, O tiger among kings, that king Śāṃtanava,
the upholder of the Bharata lineage, was then united with his own worlds.
Then, taking wood and many various kinds of perfumes,
as well as many precious pieces of sandalwood,
the high-souled Pāṇḍavas and Vidura constructed the funeral pyre.
Yuyutsu, the descendant of Kuru, also remained there, while the others became mere spectators.
Yudhiṣṭhira and the high-minded Vidura both covered the Kaurava, the son of Gaṅgā, with silken cloths and garlands.
Then Yuyutsu held an excellent parasol over him;
both Bhīmasena and Arjuna held two bright yak-tail fans;
and at that time, both sons of Mādrī held two turbans.
Accompanied by Yudhiṣṭhira, Dhṛtarāṣṭra followed behind on foot;
the women of the Kuru lord, taking up palm-leaf fans, fanned Bhīṣma, the scion of the Kuru lineage, from all sides.
Then the officiating priests performed the funeral rites for that high-souled one according to the prescribed rules;
they offered oblations into the fire and the chanters of the Sāmans sang the hymns. Then, with sandalwood logs as well as Kālīyaka wood, they proceeded.
Having covered the son of Gaṅgā with various kinds of fragrances, such as black aloe-wood and others, and having ignited the sacrificial fire,
the kings headed by Dhṛtarāṣṭra performed the ritual circumambulation from right to left (apasavya).
Having performed the funeral rites for the son of Gaṅgā, the best of the Kurus,
those foremost of the Kurus went to the bank of the Bhāgīrathī, a place frequented by sages,
followed by Vyāsa, Nārada, and Asita.
Accompanied by Kṛṣṇa, the women of the Bharatas, and the citizens who had assembled there,
those best of Kṣatriyas and all the people then performed the water-libation for the high-souled son of Gaṅgā according to the prescribed rites.
Then, when the water-rites for her son had been performed, the goddess Bhāgīrathī rose from those waters, weeping and overwhelmed with grief; lamenting there,
she addressed the Kauravas.
"Listen, O sinless ones, as I relate what happened according to the facts:
he was endowed with the conduct of a king, possessed of wisdom and noble lineage,
a respectful honorer of the elders of the Kurus, devoted to his father, and firm in his vows."
"He who was not defeated in the past by Rāma, the son of Jamadagni,
that one of great heroism has today been slain by Śikhaṇḍin with celestial weapons. O kings, my heart must surely be made of adamant."
Since I cannot see my beloved son today, my heart truly tears asunder. He who,
having conquered the assembled host of kings at the svayaṃvara in the city of Kāśī,
carried off those maidens in battle on a single chariot.
Hearing that he— whom no one on earth could equal in strength—
has been slain by Śikhaṇḍin, my heart does not shatter;
for it was by that high-souled one that the son of Jamadagni was defeated in battle at Kurukṣetra.
"Afflicted and not slain with great effort by Śikhaṇḍin"—
to the great river lamenting thus in many ways at that time,
the all-pervading Lord Dāmodara then consoled her with gentle words.
"Take heart, O blessed lady; do not grieve, O lady of auspicious appearance.
Your son has attained the supreme perfection; of this there is no doubt.
He was a Vasu of great splendor, O beautiful one, who was brought here by the fault of a curse."
Having attained human form, you ought not to grieve for him. Fighting on the field of battle according to the duty of a kṣatriya, he was slain by Dhanañjaya; he was not struck down by Śikhaṇḍin.
For even Śatakratu himself would not have been able to slay Bhīṣma, that tiger among the Kurus, with his arrows raised in the great battle; yet,
O lady of auspicious countenance, your son has gone to heaven by his own will.
"Indeed, all the gods together would not be able to slay him in battle.
Therefore, O best of rivers, do not grieve for the joy of the Kurus;
O goddess, he has gone to the Vasus—be free from your fever."
Thus addressed by Kṛṣṇa and Vyāsa, O great king, that best of rivers cast off her grief and resumed her own flow. Then those kings, headed by Kṛṣṇa, paid their respects to that river.
Permitted by her, all those lords of men returned;
with heavy hearts and grieving again and again,
they all reached Hastināpura by means of elephants, horses, chariots, and other vehicles.
Thus ends this extensive and auspicious Ānuśāsana Parvan,
the thirteenth book, in which all the Dharmas have been declared,
hearing which Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Dharma, attained a state of well-being.
From Bhīṣma, the son of Bhāgīrathī, who removes all doubts—
this is the thirteenth book, which establishes the determination of dharma.
It contains exactly one hundred and forty-six chapters.
Ninety-eight thousand and one hundred and fifty-four verses were seen by the high-souled Vyāsa of noble intellect;
having heard this Ānuśāsana Parva, one should be filled with devotion.
One is liberated from all sins and shall obtain the fruit of all dharmas,
after having worshipped Nārāyaṇa with supreme devotion; thereafter,
a libation for the Brahmins must be performed on behalf of Bhīṣma.
One should proclaim: "Hari himself, in the form of Vyāsa, is present before those who behold him.
One should especially give cows, gold, and other gifts to the reciter;
thus one attains all desires and finds long life.
By the grace of Dvaipāyana, one shall always be possessed of festivals.
